Unpacking policy layering: a micro-level analysis of China’s new energy vehicle policy mix evolution
abstract: While academic interest in policy layering in policy mix evolution is increasing, its modes and underlying drivers remain underexplored. Drawing on a longitudinal analysis of China’s new energy vehicle policy mix, this study examines how policy layering unfolds at the micro level by focusing on the configuration and functional positioning of policy mix elements. The findings reveal multiple modes of layering, including goal layering, instrument type layering, and instrument design feature layering, which develop in interconnected ways over time. These modes are shaped by changing external conditions and feedback from target groups. Moreover, policy layering exhibits a integrated logic that can enhance the internal consistency of the policy mix. By clarifying how different forms of layering emerge and interact, this study contributes to a more nuanced understanding of policy layering in policy mix evolution, helps reconcile debates on its effects, and provides insights for the design and adaptive governance of policies in emerging industries.

title: Symbolic and Substantive Governance in County-Level Digital Governance: A Configuration Analysis Using the TOB Framework
abstract: This study examines whether digital governance in Chinese counties produces symbolic or substantive performance. Using the TOB (Technology–Organization–Behavior) framework and applying Necessary Condition Analysis (NCA) and Qualitative Comparative Analysis (QCA) to Top 100 Digital Rural Counties, the analysis identifies multiple institutional configurations leading to high symbolic and substantive outcomes. Digital utilization capability emerges as a core enabling factor, while low-performance patterns reflect insufficient capability and weak infrastructure. The findings clarify how symbolic and substantive digital governance are configurationally related and offer comparative insights into local governance capacities and digital transformation strategies.

title: Identical Platform, Divergent Publics: Sweden and Finland During the 2022 NATO Crisis
abstract: ABSTRACT Digital platforms are often theorized as universal drivers of political polarization, yet empirical patterns remain inconsistent across countries. Leveraging the natural‐experiment logic of Sweden's and Finland's simultaneous 2022 NATO applications and the NATO–Turkey diplomatic crisis, this study examines how national political cultures condition the enactment of identical Twitter/X affordances. Using a most‐similar systems design, it analyzes geolocated posts from the Nordic Tweet Stream (January 2022–May 2023). Communicative structure is measured through participation inequality (Gini; top‐share‐of‐voice), and communicative behavior through @mention and #hashtag densities, complemented by qualitative profiling and a supplementary stance and framing analysis. Sweden exhibits a more concentrated, broadcast‐leaning configuration (Gini = 0.59; top 1% produce 34.1%; lower mention/hashtag densities), whereas Finland shows a more distributed structure with higher interaction/coordination proxies (Gini = 0.46; top 1% produce 20.4%; higher densities). A stance analysis reveals that both publics support NATO accession, with anti‐accession sentiment absent; the divergence lies not in substantive political position but in communicative repertoire, with Swedish discourse dominated by adversarial‐blame framing and Finnish discourse by analytical‐informational framing ( χ 2 = 117.40, p < 0.001). The findings support a “cultural filter” operating as a framing selector, linking political culture to divergent configurations of platformed publics.

title: Can Online Participation Match In‐Person Democratic Engagement? Evidence From a Cross‐National Experiment
abstract: ABSTRACT Democratic innovations increasingly take place online, yet little is known about how online citizen participation affects perceived legitimacy compared to in‐person formats. This study presents findings from a preregistered vignette experiment conducted in Spain and Switzerland. With over 6000 respondents, it compares online participation, offline participation, and no participation across two selection mechanisms, self‐selection and sortition, and examining how effects differ between decision winners and losers. The results show that online citizen participation follows the same general logic as offline participation: both can improve fairness perceptions relative to non‐participatory decision‐making, though offline participation produces somewhat stronger effects. Critically, these benefits are concentrated among decision losers, for whom participation meaningfully improves perceived fairness, while winners' evaluations remain largely unchanged. The selection mechanism proves more consequential than the participatory format: self‐selection consistently improves legitimacy perceptions across both online and offline settings, while sortition reduces both perceived fairness and acceptance likelihood, particularly among decision winners. These findings suggest that the predominant design of existing digital platforms, open and self‐selected, is also the design citizens perceive as most legitimate, though online participation has not yet fully realized the legitimacy‐enhancing potential of in‐person formats.

title: Digital Governance Enhancement: Quantifying Smart City Policy Effectiveness in China's Urban Transformation
Rebel Victory and Authoritarian (Dis)Order
abstract: Many authoritarian regimes originating in violent rebellion are exceptionally durable. Yet others collapse quickly after their birth. We argue that the structure of the founding rebellion explains these divergent trajectories by shaping power-sharing dynamics in the new regime and the nature of conflict recurrence. Regimes founded by unified rebellions (single armed group) usually become highly durable autocracies because their members can credibly share power within the same armed organization. By contrast, regimes founded by fractured rebellions (multiple armed groups) often fail quickly because armed rivals must attempt to share power across their organizations, prompting defections and recurrent rebellions. Empirically, we support these arguments by analyzing originally compiled data on every regime founded by successful rebellion worldwide from 1900 to 2020. Neither alternative rebellion characteristics, like social revolution or leftist ideology, nor country-level factors can explain why rebel regimes follow divergent trajectories.

title: Collective Deterrence
abstract: Abstract We analyze a model of collective deterrence in which (1) one state may challenge a status quo defended by a great power and an arbitrary number of partners and (2) defender war costs are private information. We show first that the great power’s intra-coalition dominance shapes which cooperative failure, free riding, or uncertainty over others’ willingness to fight may weaken deterrence. Second, increasing the great power’s war payoffs increases both deterrence and partner free riding. Third, the extent of great power dominance determines whether a larger or more capable coalition enhances or weakens deterrence and ensures that size and capabilities work in opposite directions. Finally, increasing uncertainty over a great power’s war costs can decrease or increase deterrence, depending on the prior strength of its commitment. We also use the model to illuminate differing responses of American allies in Europe and East Asia to the 2016 election of Donald Trump.

title: No fear needed when trust runs deep: The interplay of risk perception and institutional integrity shapes vaccination
abstract: Abstract Understanding the psychological determinants of vaccination behavior remains a key challenge for public health. In two studies conducted in Belgium during the COVID‐19 pandemic, we examined how risk perception and trust in the government interact to predict vaccination intention (Study 1) and vaccine uptake (Study 2). People's trust rests on their evaluation of the target's trustworthiness. In the present studies, we considered three components of trustworthiness: integrity, benevolence, and ability. We found that integrity was the component most strongly associated with vaccination. In addition, our results show that risk perception does not only add up to trust, and specifically its integrity component, but that these two factors interact in predicting vaccination. Specifically, either high risk perception or high integrity was sufficient to motivate vaccination, while individuals low on both were the most likely to be hesitant (consistent with a distrustful complacency hypothesis). Taken together, our findings provide a deeper understanding of the psychological mechanisms underlying vaccination. In addition, they highlight the value of adopting a multidimensional approach about trustworthiness as this points to the key role of integrity.

title: Limits to Tolerance: The Politicization of Liberal Values
abstract: The defense of gay rights and other liberal values by some right-wing populists is often perceived as an opportunistic strategy to justify anti-Muslim policies. But this explanation for co-optation of liberal values by parties that are considered to be in conflict with liberalism circumvents a proper analysis of the phenomenon. I will therefore investigate this element within populist politics as a problem of liberalism, rather than of populism. Doing so, this paper holds that co-optation of liberal values by right-wing populists follows from a distinctly liberal dialectic and, genealogically, represents a distinct strand of liberalism. Firstly, I will discuss the origins of populism in the Netherlands and present them as an exemplary case of what Adam Tebble calls “identity liberalism.” Secondly, I will analyze two foundational texts of the Dutch Party for Freedom to demonstrate its indebtedness to liberalism, and the correspondence of its argumentation to the philosophical problem known as the Böckenförde dilemma. Finally, I will show how identity liberalism is a conceivable, although not necessary, response to this dilemma. The politicization of liberal values by right-wing populists proves to be an attempt to solve the Böckenförde dilemma by turning these values into a marker of identity. This results in a type of liberalism that turns the initially inclusive liberalism into a politically exclusive doctrine.

title: Compromised Labor Rights and Regime Legitimacy Under Authoritarianism
abstract: Abstract How do citizens in authoritarian regimes respond when state promises go unfulfilled? In many such regimes, leaders enact prolabor legislation to signal responsiveness, yet enforcement often falls short in practice. This research note provides the first experimental evidence regarding how enforcement gaps in prolabor legislation shape mass political attitudes under authoritarian rule. Drawing on a preregistered survey experiment in China, I show that the absence of enforcement significantly erodes political support: Unmet expectations surrounding labor rights produce a measurable decline in trust in government. Partial enforcement, in contrast, generates markedly less negative public reactions—an effect that seems to be driven by the perceived material benefits associated with this enforcement. A follow-up study incorporating a list experiment to detect preference falsification replicates the core findings. By examining mass reactions to varying levels of labor rights enforcement in authoritarian contexts, this study advances our understanding of authoritarian legitimation strategies and clarifies the conditions under which cooptation can sustain public support.

title: Strategic Legislation under Weakened Judicial Review

On Preference for Simplicity and Probability Weighting
Reflections on Editing Social Forces, 2010-2026
abstract: As Volume 105 (1) of Social Forces begins under the editorship of Neal Caren, I conclude my 16 years as editor, a role I formally completed on June 30, 2026. While I am no longer editor, the papers I accepted during my tenure will continue to appear in the journal at least through Volume 106 (2). It has been a privilege to steward the journal, and I am grateful for the opportunity to have worked with so many terrific authors and reviewers in advancing its mission. As editor, I joined a distinguished group of sociologists at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill who edited Social Forces since its founding in 1922 by Howard W. Odum (see Kalleberg and Newell 2022). My successor, Neal Caren, continues this long-standing tradition of scholarly leadership. Editing Social Forces has been a rewarding experience. Being an editor provides, in some respects, a front-row seat to the evolution of a discipline, a person who is, as long-time editor Dick Simpson noted, “… close enough to hear the many voices of scholars/researchers, close enough to watch the birth and maturation of new projects and approaches, and even close enough to take the pulse of the field from time to time” (Simpson 2004). Editing Social Forces has been especially valuable in this regard, as it is a generalist journal of broad interest to sociologists and social scientists. Its mission to foster high-quality, theoretically engaged, and empirically rigorous research—especially comparative, international scholarship—has exposed me to the breadth of good work being done around the world by first-rate scholars doing smart and important work. The diversity of topics and authors—geographically, methodologically, and theoretically—has kept Social Forces vibrant and relevant. During my editorship, which began in July 2010 (Kalleberg 2011), Social Forces celebrated its 90th (Kalleberg 2012) and 100th anniversaries (Kalleberg 2022). These events have highlighted the long history of the journal and its impact on the social sciences.

title: Power Dimensions in Journalism: A Framework for Intersectional Journalism Studies
abstract: We offer “Power Dimensions in Journalism” as a framework to systematically and holistically expose understudied intersections in journalism studies. This framework emphasizes two under-researched axes of identity in gender media studies: migration and intra-national identities. We adapt Patricia Hill Collins and Sirma Bilge’s four domains of power of intersectionality to examine how intersecting axes of identity are researched in journalism scholarship, in media production, content, and reception. Applying this framework as a heuristic tool in the German context demonstrates its utility in diverse national contexts to reveal connections between macro, meso, and micro levels.

title: Institutional environment, government hierarchy, and industrial land expansion in China
Making the elephant dance: five dimensions for government digital transformation
abstract: Digital transformation has emerged as a major force in reshaping bureaucratic governance, yet whether it can render entrenched administrative systems more agile remains contested. This study develops a five-dimensional analytical framework, covering public service delivery, organizational structure, operating logic and processes, departmental responsibilities and administrative authority, and leadership, by drawing on the literature on bureaucracy and organizational change and a thematic synthesis of digital government transformation. The framework is applied to an in-depth qualitative case study of the One-Second Approval reform in Shenzhen City, China’s pioneering Special Economic Zone. The findings show that digital transformation reduces information silos, enables parallel processing, standardizes approval rules, and embeds them in unified platforms. Rather than dismantling bureaucracy, it produces a neo-bureaucratic form in which frontline discretion is compressed, authority shifts toward data governance, rule-setting, and platform operation, and hierarchical arrangements persist in hybrid forms. These effects emerge through the interaction of data integration, process redesign, and power reallocation, with sustained leadership serving as a key enabling condition. By showing that digital transformation can enhance agility through bureaucratic recomposition rather than de-bureaucratization, this study refines technology enactment theory and offers a transferable framework for future administrative reform.

title: Anti-Corruption Efforts and Citizen-Initiated Accountability: Evidence from Administrative Litigation
abstract: Abstract Despite widespread recognition that institutional environment shapes citizen behavior, we have limited understanding of how anti-corruption efforts influence citizens’ willingness to challenge government actions through formal accountability mechanisms. This study examines how provincial leaders’ corruption convictions affect citizen-initiated administrative litigation in China, exploring the mediating role of judicial remedies and the moderating effect of local corruption environments. Drawing on comprehensive data including over 1.25 million judicial documents and corruption prosecutions, we find that provincial leaders’ corruption convictions significantly increase citizen accountability actions, with this effect mediated by enhanced judicial remedies. However, this direct relationship is substantially weakened when local corruption levels are higher. These findings reveal that anti-corruption efforts can catalyze citizen engagement with accountability institutions, but their effectiveness depends critically on the broader institutional context. This research advances public administration literature by revealing how anti-corruption efforts and judicial review function as institutional mechanisms that activate citizen-initiated legal accountability, reshaping incentive structures for citizen participation in government accountability.
journal_name: Journal of Public Administration Research and Theory

title: Whose responsibility is it anyway? Unpacking prevention during service delivery to support value co-creation
abstract: Preventive reforms typically emphasize individual responsibility or the mobilization of community assets, but an enduring implementation gap exists. The ongoing stalemate calls for a fundamental shift in the way public services are understood and delivered. Central to this shift is understanding the complex interplay between roles, responsbility and multi-layered contexts shaping service delivery and outcomes. Drawing on qualitative research on health and social care, we explore how roles, responsibilities and service delivery approaches are framed. Through our analysis, we propose three broad approaches to service delivery, contributing to the nascent literature on value co-creation in complex public service settings.

title: My workgroup or my desire to serve the society? The influence of workgroup identification and public service motivation on whistleblowing intentions
abstract: Socio-psychological processes are important when it comes to whistleblowing. While prior research has explored the direct relationship between workgroup identification and whistleblowing, it has overlooked individuals’ multiple identities. This article examines whether public service motivation (PSM) moderates this association and whether a public service identity salience prime amplifies this dynamic. Using a survey experiment with 582 Chinese public employees, we find that the relationship between workgroup identification on whistleblowing depends on PSM and that a salience prime marginally boosts this interaction. The discussion addresses the findings and provides directions for future research.

title: The cognitive fabric of collaborative governance: paradox mindset in transformation-oriented collaborations
abstract: This theoretical article develops a micro-foundational perspective on how and under what conditions collaborative governance groups generate transformative outcomes. It integrates literature on collaboration, transformation, and paradox to advance three core propositions. First, collaborating for transformative outcomes constitutes a distinctive paradoxical context, in which the tensions of collaboration and the tensions of transformation are nested, reinforcing, and constitutive of the process itself. Second, diversity in collaborators’ cognitive-emotional capacity to perceive and navigate tensions (i.e. paradox mindset) shapes collaborative outcomes, with diversity in paradox mindset enhancing the likelihood of transformative outcomes. Third, the paradoxical leadership behaviours of designated leaders further increase the likelihood of transformative outcomes. By highlighting the dual challenge of transformation-oriented collaborations of eliciting tensions to stimulate change while containing them to sustain collaboration, the article links individual-level cognitive-emotional predisposition to group dynamics and system-level outcomes, offering a broader theorizing of collaborations in public administration.

title: The paradox of co-production: how austerity and structural scarcity reshape street-level discretion and public value in Scotland’s disability support system
abstract: Co-production promises empowerment , yet masks austerity's realities. Drawing on qualitative data from across Scotland's disability support services, we apply the Gioia methodology to model links between street-level discretion, public value co-contamination, and citizen adaptation. A ‘public service gap’ forces State Street Level Bureaucrats (SLBs) to ration support, locking vulnerable citizens and third-sector SLBs into forced substitution to compensate for institutional retreat. We conceptualize this as peripheral co-production:necessity-driven participation sustaining service continuity while masking systemic fragility. Extending Street-Level Bureaucracy and Public Value theories, we reframe co-production as a technical compulsion where unpaid, adaptive labour systematically co-contaminates public value.

title: When Markets and Democracy Coincide: Perceived Sector Differences in Participation in Government-Funded Programs
abstract: This article investigates the effects of participation on performance assessment in government, for-profit, and nonprofit organizations that deliver public services. In addition to examining the impact of participation on public assessments of performance, we also test the perceived tradeoff between efficiency and participation, as well as the sectoral differences in the participation-performance relationship. We conducted a preregistered vignette experiment using the context of US nursing homes where various organizational information, including participation opportunities, and sector of operation (public, for-profit, and nonprofit sectors) serve as key treatment manipulations. We find that participation plays a critical role in enhancing perceptions of organizations regardless of sectors, but government organizations may obtain greater benefits by pursuing participation, especially in improving public perception of bureaucratic effectiveness and efficiency. These findings suggest that participation is not only normatively desirable, but also practically beneficial for organizations. The findings from this study contribute to advancing our knowledge on public participation, sector differences, performance management, and public values. Clinical Trial Registration This research was pre-registered at the American Economic Association's registry for randomized controlled trials (RCT ID: AEARCTR-0011918 and URL hidden for peer review).
journal_name: The American Review of Public Administration

title: Policy uncertainty and public sentiment in the digital era: evidence from Thailand’s Digital Wallet policy
abstract: Policy uncertainty in government digital initiatives frequently fuels backlash and erodes public trust, yet real-time empirical studies remain scarce. This research investigates how policy uncertainty influenced public sentiment and perceived trust regarding Thailand’s Digital Wallet policy, a flagship welfare initiative marked by ambiguity. Applying a five-dimensional uncertainty typology (fiscal, temporal, technical, procedural, and distributive), the study uses supervised machine learning to analyze 14,448 YouTube comments from June 2023 to September 2024. Results reveal a highly volatile landscape overwhelmingly dominated by negative sentiment (79%), which fluctuated sharply in response to 104 identified uncertainty events rather than following a linear trend. Crucially, distributive and procedural ambiguities, specifically regarding eligibility and project conditions, elicited the strongest hostility, as citizens interpreted these shifts as breaches of fairness. Conversely, technical implementation issues generated comparatively lower antagonism. These findings demonstrate that persistent uncertainty transforms specific policy dissatisfaction into broader political cynicism. Ultimately, in emerging economies, technical infrastructure cannot compensate for communicative ambiguity; governments must adopt affective literacy through transparency and anticipatory communication to sustain digital-era legitimacy.

title: How inclusive welfare reforms shape political trust: understanding the feedback effects in China’s urban-rural health insurance integration
abstract: An emerging paradigm of inclusive welfare developmentalism is reshaping the social policy system in China and beyond. However, the specific causal mechanisms through which such reforms influence residents’ political trust in local governments remain underexplored. This study theorizes the connection between inclusive welfare reforms and political trust by employing a policy feedback framework. Empirical tests focus on China’s health insurance integration, a major policy initiative designed to reduce urban-rural disparities and promote social equity. Using a difference-in-differences design, this study demonstrates that the health insurance integration reform significantly enhanced political trust among rural residents, while yielding no significant effect among their urban counterparts during the study period. Further analysis reveals that the increase in rural political trust was driven simultaneously by the material benefits of expanded insurance coverage and by positive reassessments of government performance in social security provision. These results extend the attitudinal feedback framework to the context of developmental welfare states, and offer insights into how equity-oriented social policies cultivate political support.

title: Artificial intelligence in government: why people feel they lose control
abstract: The use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in public administration is expanding rapidly. While AI promises greater efficiency and responsiveness, its integration into government and administration raises concerns about fairness, transparency, and accountability. Relying on principal-agent theory and related frameworks, we conceptualize AI adoption as a case of algorithmic delegation involving power and information asymmetries. This perspective highlights three core tensions: assessability (can the delegate’s decisions be understood?), dependency (can the delegation be reversed?), and contestability (can the delegate’s decisions be challenged?). These structural challenges may lead to a ‘failure-by-success’ dynamic, where early functional gains obscure long-term risks to democratic legitimacy. We conducted a pre-registered factorial survey experiment across tax, welfare, and law enforcement domains. Our findings show that although providing information about efficiency gains initially bolsters trust, it simultaneously reduces citizens’ perceived control. When the structural risks come to the foreground institutional trust and perceived control both drop sharply, suggesting that hidden costs of AI adoption significantly shape public attitudes. The study demonstrates that delegation theory offers a powerful lens for understanding the institutional and political implications of AI in government, emphasizing the need for policymakers to address delegation risks transparently to maintain public trust.

title: Researching Regulatory Innovation: The UK Digital Regulation Cooperation Forum
abstract: As digital technologies and AI develop at unnerving speed, can regulation keep pace? By inventing a notable innovatory model, the UK's Digital Regulation Cooperation Forum (DRCF) has shown that statutory agencies can cross boundaries and pool their knowledge. Other states have adopted the forum's prototype at a time of far‐reaching geopolitical and geoeconomic powerplays and profound domestic crises. Drawing on our in-depth interviews and engagement with the DRCF's staff, we reflect both on its neo‐regulatory practice and doing fieldwork on regulation.

title: Regulating Reality: Exploring Synthetic Media Through Multistakeholder AI Governance
abstract: ABSTRACT Artificial intelligence's integration into daily life has brought with it a reckoning on the role such technology plays in society and the varied stakeholders who should shape its governance. This is particularly relevant for AI‐generated, or synthetic, media, an emergent visual technology impacting perceptions of media as records of reality. Studying the stakeholders governing synthetic media is vital to assessing safeguards that help audiences make sense of content in the AI age; yet little qualitative research examines how actors from civil society, industry, media, and policy conceptualize, develop, and implement such practices. This paper addresses this gap by analyzing 23 semi‐structured interviews with stakeholders governing synthetic media alongside real‐world cases of multistakeholder synthetic media governance. Inductive coding reveals how temporal perspectives—spanning past, present, and future—mediate multistakeholder governance of synthetic media. Analysis also illustrates the critical role of trust, both among stakeholders and between audiences and interventions, as well as the limitations of technical transparency measures like AI labels for supporting effective synthetic media governance. These findings inform literature on multistakeholder AI governance through rare insight into such processes, while also supporting the practical design of synthetic media policy that serves audiences.

title: A Comprehensive Taxonomy of Rules for Nuanced Analysis of Governance Systems
abstract: ABSTRACT Understanding how institutions shape collective action requires analytical tools that capture the complexity of governance arrangements. Ostrom's typology of rules provides a foundational framework for examining institutional configurations, yet limited specificity in rule types reduces its effectiveness in comparative analysis. To address this, we present a detailed classification of the seven rule types into subtypes, enhancing the study of institutional diversity and structure. Based on the initial description of the seven rule types, a systematic review of scientific articles, an analysis of written regulations, and an internal mutual exclusivity check, we propose a taxonomy that expands the seven types into subtypes. Utilizing these detailed subtypes enables a more comprehensive characterization of institutional configurations, thereby strengthening comparisons of governance systems.

title: NGOs As Regulatory Intermediaries: Risks of Capture in Policy Implementation
Inclusive representation and perceived democratic performance under democratic backsliding. Evidence from a full-factorial experiment in Hungary
abstract: This study investigates how perceived political representation shapes evaluations of democratic performance in a polarized, backsliding context. Using a survey experiment in Hungary (n=1,005), the research moves beyond the traditional winner–loser framework to analyze how the representational status of both government and opposition voters jointly influences perceived democratic quality. The findings reveal that evaluations depend heavily on representational balance: respondents rate democracy highest when both blocs feel represented and lowest when neither does. Perceptions of opposition representation emerge as a primary driver of quality ratings, highlighting the salience of partisan inclusion for democratic assessments. While evaluations are filtered through in-group interests – with opposition supporters particularly sensitive to their own exclusion – pluralist benchmarks remain detectable across the partisan divide. These results indicate that even in a backsliding regime, citizens anchor evaluations of democracy in pluralistic criteria.

title: Blueprints and Blind Spots: Sixty Years of Mediation Scholarship and the Design of Peace Processes
abstract: This article reviews 60 years of academic research on peace mediation. Drawing on 395 academic articles published between 1966 and 2025, we assess the field through six core mediation process design questions: why, when, who, how, what, and where . We show that scholarship has generated important insights but has often addressed design questions in isolation, with limited attention to how they interact in practice. The literature on peace mediation is therefore marked by blind spots and conceptual fragmentation, not fully capturing the integrated nature of mediation processes. Organizing existing research through a process design framework allows us to identify key gaps and connections across strands of scholarship. We argue that research should more explicitly address the interdependence of design factors. This perspective clarifies priorities for future mediation research by identifying analytically promising questions and highlighting opportunities for more systematic and comparative inquiry.

title: Does Unequal Representation Bias Policymaking? Quasi‐Experimental Evidence From the Italian Senate
abstract: ABSTRACT How does unequal representation affect policymaking? Existing research shows that overrepresented districts exert disproportionate influence over public policy, yet our understanding of the underlying sources of this advantage remains limited. I argue that increased representation can independently bias policymaking via two channels: a mechanical effect, whereby additional representatives increase a district's likelihood of shaping the legislative agenda, and a behavioral effect, whereby legislators intensify constituency‐oriented effort due to intra‐district competition. To test this, I leverage the quasi‐experimental setting created by the electoral rule of the Italian Senate (1994–2006), which allowed districts with similar population sizes to elect either one or two senators. Using a regression discontinuity design and comprehensive data on bill (co‐)sponsorship, I find evidence consistent with both channels. Examining policy outcomes, I do not find that unequal representation yields distributive benefits, but I do find suggestive evidence of a broader legislative advantage.

title: European strategic antinomy
abstract: Over the last decade, “strategic autonomy” has emerged as a key geonarrative in debates on EUrope's relation to the world. Initially focused more narrowly on matters of security and defence, it is now being applied to a much wider set of issues. Confronted with the rise of non-Western powers, uncertainties about the future of transatlantic relations, and a wide-spread sense that one-sided dependencies must be reduced, the concept of strategic autonomy is the lens through which EUrope tries to address a broad array of geopolitical and geoeconomic challenges. Yet, Europe struggles to come to terms with the “geo” in geopolitics and geoeconomic. The article advances the argument that these difficulties are an effect of EUrope's self-description and self-observation in universal terms: Obviously, EUrope recognizes the presence of other players on the international scene. But to the extent that European modernity is seen as universal rather than merely European the organization of political space in terms of difference (e.g. geopolitical or geoeconomic competition) runs into contradictions. EUrope envisions itself both as a province among provinces (competing with China and increasingly also the US) and it retains the ambition to singularly represent the world. In a nutshell, casting itself in universal terms, EUrope struggles to process and acknowledge difference, and faced with difference tends to talk to itself about itself. The article demonstrates that this is not due to a lack of strategic resolve but rather the effect of antinomies at the core of EUropean geonarrative production.

title: A land between solid and fluid: Situating permafrost within more-than-human geopolitics
abstract: This article aims to situate permafrost, a type of soil characterized by temperature and relationality rather than pure composition, within debates around the role of materiality in geopolitics. While permafrost's materiality is quite like ice, it differs in terms of having a more complex and non-linear relationship to temperature and a higher level of local variability. Because permafrost has only very rarely been considered in debates around territory and geopolitics, we first review the broader literature on permafrost and how it is discussed and understood in engineering and the natural sciences, identifying its crucial relational dimensions and its ontology of tipping points. We then deploy these insights to analyse the Qinghai-Tibet Railway in China to illustrate how permafrost is more than inert matter and poses geopolitical risks to the state even when it is successfully stabilized. We argue that permafrost becomes geopolitical through its unpredictability, which results from its highly local composition and thresholds for melting.

title: Complicated Loyalties: Latino Attitudes About Immigration in an Era of Changing Identities and Demographics
abstract: As evidenced by its prominence in the 2024 presidential election, and subsequent Trump administration policies, immigration remains a polarizing and controversial topic in U.S. politics. While Latinos have historically been perceived as largely supportive of liberal immigration policy, recent events and the shifting identities and demographics of the Latino population call this perception into question. Given changes among the Latino electorate, we investigate immigration attitudes within this increasingly diverse community. Using the largest public opinion dataset in the United States, we analyze attitudes toward restrictive immigration policy of over 30,000 Latinos. We evaluate the effects of identity through predictors such as nativity, immigration status, group perceptions, partisanship, and ideology to understand the correlates of Latino public opinion toward immigration. Our findings highlight the role of conservative ideology, which is increasingly becoming an important component of Latino identity, in driving support for restrictionist policies and the minimal influence of nativity or language use. We also find that other components related to identity, such as beliefs about discrimination, correlate strongly with immigration attitudes. Our results underscore the complexity of Latino public opinion and the countervailing factors that result from various identities among Latinos regarding immigration policy.

title: A principal–agent theory and network analysis of high-end cooperation among militant groups
abstract: Abstract This study develops a principal–agent theory of why armed groups engage in high-end cooperation involving training or intelligence. While such cooperation enhances capacity, it generates downstream risks. Principals mitigate these risks by selecting agents who are skill-wise complementary but politically non-substitutable. Agents accept high-end support when doing so does not leave them politically overshadowed by a dominant actor. Using original network data on 53 groups in Northeast India (1981–2021) and temporal exponential random graph models, I show that high-end cooperation is more likely in dyads characterized by organizational capacity differentials, complementary attack portfolios, and distinct constituencies. The findings recast militant alliances as products of competitive threat perception and carry broader implications for the study of multiparty conflicts.

Behavioral responses to inheritance taxes: Evidence from Brazil
abstract: I examine behavioral responses to inheritance and gift taxes in a setting where individuals knew the tax would increase three months before the new tax code took effect. Using tax microdata from Brazil, I employ bunching and difference-in-differences (DD) methods and find that individuals significantly retime their wealth transfers to avoid taxes. Retimed gifts resulted in smaller inheritances for nearly three years. Moreover, I find that responses are sensitive to changes in top gift marginal tax rates and tax design (flat rates vs progressive brackets). Finally, evasion increased in the medium run in reform states, particularly among small inheritances.

title: The youth dividend: Political impacts of demographic transitions
Party Organizations and Complementary Political Control,
abstract: Abstract We study how political parties engage in political targeting of resources by coordinating politicians across multiple levels of government. We combine thousands of election outcomes from the Indian state of West Bengal with 300 million payments from a welfare scheme jointly controlled by state and local governments. We show that the state government gives disproportionate funding to co-partisan local councils, which target payments to raise votes for national candidates. Welfare payments are diverted to reward local councilors who successfully deliver votes, and to recruit opposition councilors. The ruling party recruits candidates only where it lacks a majority, systematically expanding its control.

Exploring the Psychological Mechanism of Passengers Adhering to Emergency Evacuation Signs During Subway Fire Emergencies: An Application of the Protective Action Decision Model and the Heuristic–Systematic Model
abstract: ABSTRACT In emergency evacuation scenarios, ensuring the safe and prompt evacuation of passengers is of utmost importance. Although emergency evacuation signs hold significant meaning, passengers often hesitate to comply with them during emergencies. Therefore, it is crucial to understand the psychological decision‐making process that passengers undergo in these critical situations. This study focuses on subway fire emergencies and examines the psychological decision‐making mechanisms influencing passengers’ evacuation sign compliance (ESC) intention. To achieve this, a psychological mechanism framework model based on the protection action decision model (PADM) and the heuristic–systematic model (HSM) is constructed. The study adopts a questionnaire survey to establish a structural equation model for passengers’ ESC intention, followed by mediation and moderation analyses of the predictive factors. The research findings reveal that passengers’ ESC intention is positively correlated with risk perception (RP), hazard‐related attributes, information seeking (IS), and systematic information processing (SIP), while being negatively associated with resource‐related attribute (RRA) perception. The mediation analysis indicates that both IS and SIP act as mediators in the relationship between RP and ESC intention. Furthermore, SIP serves as a mediator between IS and ESC intention. The moderation analysis demonstrates that the importance of RRAs intensifies the negative association between RRAs and ESC intention. This research enhances our understanding of the psychological mechanisms underlying passengers’ ESC intention and provides practical suggestions for subway engineering design and emergency management.

title: Media capture, academia capture? Rising authoritarianism and public knowledge capture
Cultivated Memories and Selective Nationalism in China: Evidence on the United States and Russia
abstract: Despite China’s similarly complex modern relationships with both the United States and Russia, contemporary Chinese public opinion is far more favorable toward Russia than toward the United States. Why? Combining observational analysis, survey experiments, and conventional regression, we argue that state regulation of collective memory about the two countries plays a key role in producing this selective nationalism. Using original data from two survey experiments in China, we show that exposure to more balanced historical information, rather than the one-sided narratives promoted by the state, reduces both anti-Americanism and pro-Russian sentiment. We also find that educational attainment, as a vehicle for political indoctrination, is associated with stronger anti-American and pro-Russian views. Our study highlights memory engineering as a powerful instrument of political misinformation.

title: Who is Deserving of What? A Qualitative Analysis on German Street-Level Bureaucrats’ Attitudes Toward Deservingness and Need
abstract: This article examines how German street-level bureaucrats exercise administrative discretion in welfare provision, focusing on perceptions of deservingness and need. Based on 37 interviews in job agencies, we identify four types of SLBs (hardliners, administrators, pragmatic social workers, and altruists), – each guided by distinct normative dispositions. These dispositions strongly influence decision-making and, ultimately, client outcomes and policy implementation. Findings show decisions are often value-based, shaping welfare practices. Our study contributes to public administration theory by linking discretion to justice principles and offers practical insights for fostering fairness and consistency in welfare services, particularly regarding need.

title: Subnational Resilience During Crisis: How Brazilian Municipalities Responded to COVID‐19 and Public Health Budget Cuts
Organizational Policy Complexity in Hybrid Organizations: Evidence from Scandinavian State-Owned Enterprises
abstract: The state and its organizations have grown more complex in recent decades. Because this may pose substantial challenges to public governance, it is essential to advance our understanding of the conditions influencing the complexities in modern organizations. Therefore, we study organizational policy complexity in relation to dimensions of publicness in hybrid organizations. Specifically, we focus on one type of hybrid organization, namely state-owned enterprises (SOEs), and one type of policy, namely privacy policies. Our general expectation is that organizations with a lower degree of publicness will tend to have more complex policies. However, our analysis reveals a complicated picture: both business-like SOEs and larger state ownership shares are linked to higher levels of policy complexity. These organizations embed a range of policy elements to align with diverse normative expectations and navigate complex institutional environments with both state and market norms.

title: Performance system design factors that encourage information use: a survey experiment of decision-making by school principals
abstract: Performance management scholarship has mostly neglected the behavioural mechanisms through which performance-system design factors – reflecting macro-level institutional and organizational arrangements – shape public managers’ individual-level use of information. We examined such mechanisms by employing a nationwide survey experiment with 394 school principals in Chile that tested how policy-relevant features of the country’s education monitoring system influence their intention to use performance data for decision-making. Our findings show that use intentions increase when managers obtain timely performance information, experience high stakeholder involvement, and have access to training and knowledge-sharing opportunities. However, reporting formats did not affect use intentions. These results provide insights into how targeted adjustments to real-world performance-system design can function as behavioural levers for encouraging evidence-based decision-making by public managers.

title: Transnational Nonprofit Action: Diaspora Giving, Collective and Social Remittances, and the Provision of Public Goods and Services
abstract: This article explores transnational nonprofit action through diaspora-led nonprofit organizations in the United States (U.S.) and their funding and support of public goods and services in the home country. Diaspora communities around the world make contributions to their homelands in various ways that have impact on public governance. Specifically, diaspora members engage in philanthropic giving behaviors towards their countries of origin, including via collective and social remittances. How does this diaspora giving contribute to the provision of public goods and services in the country of origin? This research uses a multi-sited, comparative case study design that included extensive fieldwork in the U.S. and Colombia, and the transnational space between these settings. Building on theory about public governance and nonprofit organizations, the research generates and further explores empirically a framework of three sets of resources that condition transnational nonprofit action—material, relational, and institutional. Material resources illuminate how diaspora-funded projects directly support public service delivery. Relational resources capture how trust, credibility, and embedded community ties via diaspora-led organizations provide access to both networks and funding sources. Institutional resources, namely norm-setting, explain how collective and social remittances have the potential to shape expectations, standards, and practices about the nonprofit sector, philanthropic giving, and public governance more broadly.
journal_name: The American Review of Public Administration

title: Exploring How Demand and Supply Knowledge Can Improve Centralized Public Health Procurement
abstract: Despite the growing shift towards procurement centralization among governments around the world, questions remain as to how to increase purchasing within centralized frameworks. While centralized purchasing offers many benefits related to efficiency and quality control, users often prefer more flexible options for purchasing. An unanswered question is how knowledge of user requirements and market trends leads to framework agreements that reduce the inclination for users to purchase goods and services on their own. This study employs healthcare purchasing data from 21 regions in Italy from 2013–2023 to explore how different sources of knowledge about demand and supply affect centralization rates—both in respect to asset-specific and non-asset-specific products. Fixed effects regression results indicate that knowledge of supply gleaned from integrating technical experts into procurement teams enhances centralization for a range of offerings. The influence of demand-related knowledge on centralized purchasing varies by product type, however, with interpersonal exchanges proving more effective for non-asset-specific categories and logistical support mechanisms proving more critical for asset-specific product categories. The results provide longitudinal insights into conditions that are typically studied through cross-sectional data. They also offer important implications for the many countries operating publicly provided health programs, as well as those pursuing broader reforms tied to procurement centralization.
journal_name: The American Review of Public Administration

title: Collaborating across academia and local government: augmenting the use of academically produced evidence
abstract: In the UK, increasing attention is being given to strengthening the use of academically produced evidence within local government. Recent investment from the National Institute for Health and Care Research has supported various initiatives designed to foster closer collaboration between universities and local authorities. This includes the Health Determinants Research Collaborations (HDRCs) and a separate researcher-in-residence programme focused on social care. While existing literatures explore research–practice partnerships, embedded research, knowledge mobilisation and evidence use, there remains considerable value in sharing reflections emerging from these recently funded forms of collaboration. Drawing on experiences within one HDRC and from a researcher-in-residence, this reflective article examines efforts to strengthen engagement with academically produced evidence within the public health and social care functions of local government. In reflecting on these experiences, we draw on a conceptual framework which emphasises the importance of capacity, motivation and opportunity in shaping engagement with research evidence. We organise our reflections around three themes: (1) developing engagement with academically produced evidence; (2) negotiating time, pace and policy pressures; and (3) communication, language and professional cultures. Across these areas, we identify recurring tensions and challenges that emerge when academia and local government work together, while also highlighting practical strategies that may strengthen engagement with research evidence. Our experiences suggest that effective collaboration depends not only on producing robust research findings, but also on sustained engagement with research processes, shared expectations around time and policy relevance, and accessible forms of communication.

title: Fertility intention and household consumption patterns among public rental housing residents: evidence from Seoul
abstract: Persistently low fertility across East Asia has heightened policy attention to the role of housing security and broader socioeconomic conditions in shaping family formation. Prior work has documented associations between housing conditions and fertility intentions and the burden of childrearing on household budgets, but the consumption patterns of households that express fertility intentions within publicly supported rental settings remain little examined. This study examines how fertility intentions relate to household consumption patterns among residents of public rental housing in Seoul, South Korea. Drawing on the 2016 Seoul Public Rental Housing Panel Survey, we estimate a generalized structural equation model that captures direct and mediated associations between demographic, housing, and income characteristics and household expenditure shares. Households whose anchoring woman expresses fertility intentions report a lower total expenditure on average but allocate a larger share of education spending to public education and a larger share of total spending to cultural and leisure activities. Fertility intention also is associated with mediated pathways linking age, education, and housing quality to expenditure allocation. Findings highlight the value of integrating housing, education, and childcare policy in Asia’s high-cost urban contexts.

title: Who benefits from stakeholder consultations? Fire alarms or procedural politicking?
Measuring stakeholder influence: a comparison of automated and manual approaches
abstract: Democratic governments routinely consult with those in society who would be affected by policy changes before they go into effect. The extent to which stakeholders’ preferences influence government policies, however, can vary considerably. Measuring interest organisations’ influence in consultations is therefore an important research endeavour. We generate a dataset encompassing more than 1,000 submissions from stakeholders in response to consultations carried out with respect to Danish bills in the parliamentary year 2021/22. By comparing these submissions against official government statements, we measure influence in three distinct but comparable ways: 1) manual coding of influence, 2) a text reuse approach, and 3) AI chatbot-assisted coding of influence. In applying each of these to the same data, we draw three key conclusions. First, each method has advantages (and disadvantages). Second, text reuse methods can find compelling evidence of stakeholder influence, even if it does not identify all influence. Third, and most innovatively, we demonstrate that AI-assisted influence measurement shows considerable promise by reducing the time and effort required to identify influence while achieving similar, and possibly more objective, results relative to manual coding. This study helps move the discipline toward better understanding of outside influence in government decision-making.

title: Democracy, security and European Union enlargement: rhetorical articulation in Albania’s accession negotiations
abstract: The EU enlargement policy’s ‘geopolitical turn’ has prompted reappraisal of established concepts, including rhetorical action. Originally defined as the strategic use of norm-based arguments to pressure political actors into upholding the EU's liberal-democratic order, this article argues that rhetorical action can also be deployed to pressure them into aligning with the EU's response to external security threats. In turn, the co-existence of two rhetorical action modes – liberal-democratic and geostrategic – opens up the possibility of rhetorical entrapment through articulation, i.e., entrapping political actors into conceding outcomes they would otherwise oppose by holding them to the inconsistencies between their commitments to two potentially conflicting normative sets. Empirically, we draw on thirty-seven interviews with government officials involved in EU-Albania accession negotiations to provide actor-level evidence of two instances of successful entrapment. Our findings show that EU negotiators deployed rhetorical articulation to secure Albania’s geostrategic alignment beyond what accession criteria require, while Albanian negotiators deployed it to secure new rewards in negotiations beyond what merit-based conditionality would warrant. In doing so, this article advances rhetorical action theory, explains Albania's recent rise as accession frontrunner and contributes to relational approaches to enlargement highlighting the agency of candidate member states.

title: When Legislators Do Not Differentiate: A Field Experiment on British MPs’ Responses to Constituent Policy Queries
The Sirens of Revolution: Revolutionary Legacies and State Building in Early Communist China
Hydraulic State: Hydropower Construction and Extension of State Capacity in Contemporary China
Political power and the global expansion of the value-added tax
abstract: Abstract How does political power shape tax collection? This article addresses this question by focusing on the most prominent fiscal phenomenon of the recent decades – the rise of the value-added tax (VAT). Drawing on insights from the political economy literature, I test the argument that governments with strong legislative support raise more revenues from the VAT as an effective tool to improve public finances in the short term. Results from a global sample of democracies between 1990 and 2020 provide support for this argument. The effect is particularly pronounced among developing countries, where the VAT is often the tax type that accounts for the largest share of public revenues. These findings illustrate the role of domestic political dynamics in shaping the rise of the VAT to its status as a primary revenue source for the modern tax state.

title: Occupational labor markets, skills, and immigration concerns: Panel data evidence for Germany
abstract: Abstract Economic crises, technological change, and labor market transformations have long shaped political attitudes, particularly toward immigration. While existing research links occupational risks to anti-immigration preferences, which specific occupations drive this relationship remains underexplored. This research note addresses this gap by examining how occupation-specific skills (OSS) – defined as the amount of skills required to work in a given occupation – moderate the relationship between occupational labor market conditions and immigration attitudes. Drawing on sociological and comparative political economy perspectives, the paper argues that individuals with high levels of OSS are especially sensitive to deterioration in their occupation’s labor market conditions. The central theoretical implication is that adverse changes in occupational labor markets generate stronger political anti-immigration reactions among high-OSS workers, including Managers and (Associate) Professionals. Importantly, OSS are conceptually distinct from other occupational dimensions used in the literature, such as task specificity, and from other skill dimensions, such as general skill. The empirical analysis draws on over 20 years of longitudinal data from the German Socio-Economic Panel (GSOEP), finding evidence consistent with the argument. The findings contribute to ongoing debates about the political behavior of high-skilled workers, a group whose attitudes toward immigration remain contested.

title: Norm Making from the Margins: Armed Groups, the Algerian War, and South–South Legal Politics
abstract: Abstract How do armed groups waging asymmetrical wars assert political and legal subjectivity in an international order that historically excluded them? This article recovers the FLN’s groundbreaking legal activism during the Algerian War of Independence, arguing that it staged the most far-reaching challenge of its kind to international humanitarian law’s (IHL) imperial order from below through South–South legal politics. Acting as norm entrepreneurs, FLN jurists contested the existing limits on IHL’s scope and applicability while developing new institutional practices of insurgent normativity that established a disseminable model for other armed groups. In doing so, they put forward a set of legal arguments and practices that helped structure how later armed groups would invoke and substantially develop IHL under conditions of asymmetry. Based on previously inaccessible Algerian, Southern African, and state socialist archival materials, this article deepens existing accounts of normative change by reconstructing the concrete legal practices, institutional strategies, and legal-political thought through which Southern actors challenged IHL and international organizations from the margins of the international order.

title: Do Voters Understand the Benefits of Taxes?
abstract: We use economic experiments to study a fundamental question in political economy: Do voters understand the benefits of taxes? Participants play an economic game as members of a virtual society composed of computer players. In each round, the players earn low or high income, see the distribution of income, and then vote for low or high taxes. We test whether participants vote rationally for high taxes when poor and low taxes when rich, following a classic model in political economy, or whether they focus on the burden of taxes more than the benefits. Across three experiments, poor players voted against high taxes 30% to 50% of the time, and they were more opposed when the same policy was labeled “taxes” than when it was labeled “sharing.” In Experiment 2, Singaporean participants opposed taxes at about the same rate as those of Americans in Experiment 1. In Experiment 3, participants’ opposition to taxes persisted when they received low income every round. These results support the burden hypothesis: voters focus more on the burden of paying taxes than on the benefits they provide. We reflect on what the results imply for the politics of taxes.

title: Silencing Dissent: Academic Freedom and Transnational Suppression of Palestinian Solidarity
abstract: Israel’s war on Gaza has prompted a wave of protests against human rights violations that has spread across most European countries. As universities have become arenas of contestation, there has been an increase in forms of repression of academic freedom and of political rights within academia. Our systematic, case-oriented analysis of an original database enables us to identify specific repertoires of repression employed by different institutions, as well as the characteristics of the targeted academics. By comparing Germany and the United States as case studies of high and increasing levels of repression—albeit characterized by differing systems of higher education and conceptions of academic freedom—we analyze the strategies used by these actors and how they interact. In this article, we focus on the mechanisms through which repression has been promoted, anchored in a resignification of antisemitism that treats it as distinct from racism and accords it a special status in the defense of Western civilization. We use the concept of moral panic to analyze the construction of a narrative that portrays a specific challenge to society’s fundamental values, which has resulted in the scapegoating of the Left and migrants. We also identify the main moral panic entrepreneurs responsible for the creation of this environment both within and outside universities.

title: Descriptive and Substantive Representation in Single-Party Legislatures: Evidence from China
Electoral Alliances and Spatial Patterns of Vote: Evidence from Brazilian Local Elections
The gaps on our maps
Reevaluating News and Opinion Dynamics in the Iraq War: New Evidence for Social Identification Effects
abstract: Abstract What causes changes in popular support for American wars? Competing theories posit that either the tone and content of wartime news or social identity cues conveyed through mass media should play the larger role. We offer new evidence in this debate by analyzing a novel set of rolling cross-sectional opinion data collected continuously over 13 months during an early phase of the Iraq War and pairing it with data on news intensity and the evaluative tone of news coverage during that same period. Contrary to conventional information updating explanations of war support but consistent with a social identification process, we find that greater intensity of wartime news coverage is associated with increases in aggregate support even after controlling for the evaluative tone of that news coverage.

title: The incidence of rent subsidies: Evidence on rents, housing choices and supply
abstract: This paper asks whether, and under which circumstances, rent subsidies to low-income households increase rents. We study a reform of the Finnish housing allowance system that caused large quasi-random variation in housing allowances. Using register data spanning five years before and after the reform, we find that large increases in allowances for affected housing units had little or no effect on their rents relative to other units. The effect of a one-euro increase in housing allowance on rent is roughly 0.036 euros with a standard error of 0.028. We provide novel evidence on the underlying demand- and supply-side responses that drive the rent effects. The reform led to only small changes in recipients’ housing choices, and at most modest changes in rental supply. Our interpretation is that rent subsidies can be effective in helping recipient households even in supply-constrained contexts, if recipients’ housing choices are unresponsive to the subsidy.

title: Departmentalized instruction and elementary school effectiveness
The Green Revolution and individualism: Evidence from Indonesia
abstract: This paper studies the effects of the Green Revolution, one of the largest development projects in the late 20th-Century, on individualism. We use a difference-in-differences approach to investigate how rapid technological and organizational changes in traditional agriculture reshaped cultural norms in Indonesia, where Green Revolution rollout was largely driven by centralized government interventions. Regions with greater exposure to Green Revolution policies experienced significant and persistent increases in individualism (as measured by a higher prevalence of infrequent names) decades after the end of the program. Results are not driven by pre-trends and hold across a battery of robustness checks. We further document suggestive, correlational evidence of a persistent fall in community funding for public goods, a key measure of collective action. Our findings suggest that technical change can lead to rapid and persistent changes in culture.

title: Suing the Leviathan: The Effect of Trans-Regional Jurisdiction Reform on Corporate Investment
Monitoring and delivering: Evidence from dropout rates in Brazil
The economic footprint of short-term rentals on local businesses: evidence from Portugal
abstract: Abstract We analyze how the proliferation of short-term rentals (STRs) affects firm survival, performance, and entry in two European cities with high STR density. Using administrative firm-level accounting data, a shift-share instrument, and an event-study design, we find that STR growth increases exit rates among underperforming firms, while surviving firms experience relative gains in sales and profits, with no effects on employment or investment. Corporate tax revenues accruing to the central government also rise, pointing to broader fiscal spillovers. STR expansion stimulates entrepreneurship, though new entrants face higher costs and lower initial profitability. These findings underscore the nuanced impacts of tourism-driven demand shocks on urban economic ecosystems.

title: Are mass layoffs individually costly but socially beneficial?
The Wells–Riley Model Revisited II: Parameter Uncertainty and Population Heterogeneity
abstract: ABSTRACT In this work, we revisit the Wells–Riley model, which has been widely used to estimate airborne infection risk in indoor settings. In particular, we consider a probabilistic (i.e., “stochastic”) framework of the Wells–Riley model which allows one to quantify infection risk in terms of the per‐capita probability of infection for each susceptible individual, as well as the probability distribution of the number of infections (here referred to as “exposures”) during the indoor interaction. Directly extending the work by Edwards, King, Noakes et al. (2024), we consider here the situation where the main parameters in the Wells–Riley model (namely, the quanta generation rate , the ventilation rate , the number of infectors , or the duration of the indoor interaction ) may be random or uncertain. We show how, in this case, the per‐capita infection risk becomes a random variable between 0 and 1, and compute its density function under some parametric assumptions. This allows for a comprehensive analytical quantification of uncertainty when dealing with heterogeneous populations, uncertain environmental conditions, or stochastic human behavior. Our results reveal that infection risk can vary significantly depending on the distribution and variability of model parameters. In particular, using mean parameter values in the classical Wells–Riley model can lead to systematic inaccuracies: Uncertainty in , , or leads to infection risk overestimation, while environmental stochasticity (i.e., uncertainty in ventilation or removal rates) can lead to infection risk underestimation. We also investigate which parameter mainly drives the uncertainty in infection risk when two model parameters are simultaneously random.

title: China’s UN Diplomacy on the Russo-Ukrainian War
abstract: This article examines how China conducts its diplomacy on Ukraine within the United Nations framework and assesses whether its stated principles align with its actual behavior. Using corpus linguistics, discourse analysis, and UN voting data from 2014 to 2025 across the United Nation Security Council (UNSC), General Assembly (UNGA), and selected UN technical bodies, it analyzes the relationship between China’s words and its deeds. A comparison with the Palestine/Gaza corpus shows that China applies more attribution and selective framing, challenging the notion of a uniform ‘principled neutrality’. The findings show that China’s abstention doctrine is conditional, and that its UN behavior reflects strategic differentiation across political and technical arenas of global governance.

title: Does Public Transit Serve People Experiencing Homelessness? A National Assessment of Homeless Shelter Accessibility in the US
abstract: Public transit offers critical access to opportunities and services, especially for people experiencing homelessness who often face significant mobility challenges. Despite evidence on vulnerable populations’ dependence on public transit, there is no systematic assessment of transit access around homeless service providers nationwide. This study integrates Homeless Inventory Count Raw data with the National Transit Map, General Transit Feed Specification (GTFS), and OpenStreetMap (OSM), to examine the spatial disparity of transit accessibility of homeless services across the U.S., as well as the patterns from 2015 to 2022. Geocoding each homeless service project in relation to its local public transit network, the analysis finds substantial disparities between urban and non-urban communities despite increased accessibility over time. Being located in a service area with a higher Black or Hispanic population and unemployment rate related with better transit access. However, transit access was worse for emergency shelters, the frontline of homeless services, indicating transit inequity for service providers or emergency shelters serving relatively remote locations where people may not have access to other services. Beyond identifying the transit access for homeless services, this study contributes to the social equity literature by extending the intersections of multiple inequities, specifically, homelessness, transit, urbanicity, and socio-economic and demographic characteristics.

title: Citizens' perspectives on administrative burden in digital government services
Do Culturally Varying Expert Narratives and Social Group Cues on COVID ‐19 Influence Chinese Support for Policy Change?
Election salience revisited: How elections (do not) boost affective polarization
Midstream geopolitics: Processing power in critical mineral supply chains
abstract: The emerging geopolitics of critical minerals hinges not only on their extraction but also on their transformation. Smelters, refiners, magnet factories, and other processing facilities are new sites of geopolitical competition and dependencies, linking countries that increasingly see one another as strategic rivals. This article introduces the concept of midstream geopolitics to move beyond notions of resource geopolitics often focused on extraction sites and supply routes to account for the diverse narratives, regulations, commercial relations, and technologies that shape and enable the transformation of ‘critical’ raw materials, including cobalt, lithium, rare earth elements, and other minerals, into industrially useable forms. These midstream capacities are now central to competition among great powers such as the US, EU, and China, as well as regional actors (e.g., Japan, South Korea, Malaysia), each seeking to secure, control, or bypass processing chokepoints in supply chains. China's longstanding investment in processing, enabled in part by Western divestment from industries deemed too polluting, shaped the contemporary strategic landscape. Our framework identifies multidirectional influences—between the downstream, midstream, and upstream—structuring midstream geopolitics and details nine policies through which states exert geopolitical and geoeconomic power over industrial and technological advances. Our analysis underscores the need for attention to the midstream and highlights its growing (geo)political significance, particularly in relation to strategies of onshoring, reshoring, and friendshoring.

title: Mapping ocean worlds through the data revolution
Media, Electoral Accountability, and Partisan Polarization
Open-Ended Survey Responses and Political Conceptualizations in a Polarized Era
The Long Shadow of Housing Discrimination: Evidence from Racial Covenants
Money and gender: Proxy respondents and the mismeasurement of income in surveys
The endogenous nature of war and its economic consequences
Real effects of credit supply shocks: Evidence from Danish banks, firms, and workers
Government Trading and Efficiency in Imperfectly Competitive Financial Markets
Agency within structure: Strategic behavior and network position in explaining premium buyer access in global buyer–seller networks
Overconfident youth, underconfident elders: Age differences in algorithmic knowledge confidence and information perceptions
abstract: Age-related differences in algorithmic knowledge are typically interpreted as competence gaps that render younger “digital natives” better equipped and older users more vulnerable in algorithmically curated environments. This study challenges these assumptions by examining (a) algorithmic knowledge confidence—whether users’ subjective algorithmic knowledge exceeds or falls short of their algorithmic awareness and knowledge—and (b) what consequences such misalignment has for information environment perceptions. Using US survey data ( N = 1205), this study found systematic misalignment between subjective and awareness-based algorithmic knowledge: younger users overestimate their understanding, whereas older users underestimate theirs. Social media use partially mediated the age–knowledge confidence relationship. Knowledge confidence, in turn, predicted perceived information reliability and diversity. These findings reveal that critical assessment of information environment is determined not by knowledge level alone but by alignment between subjective and awareness-based knowledge, highlighting the need for age-tailored interventions addressing knowledge overconfidence and underconfidence.

title: Advancing public policy to expose it: A preliminary framework for guerrilla coproduction
abstract: The expression of collaborative governance—specifically, coproduction—that emerged in response to Donald Trump’s election as president of the United States in 2024 challenges public administration scholars to expand our thinking around these concepts under the current administration. While existing research points to coproduction as a means to advance public policies and programs that citizens support, our article explores the current political landscape to show how coproduction can serve as a mechanism for citizens to advance policies that they find objectionable. We integrate theories of guerrilla government and coproduction to introduce the concept of guerrilla coproduction, which we define as the actions of citizens who work with the government to further public policies they oppose, with the primary objective of exposing the policies’ harmful effects. Our article’s central aims are to introduce a preliminary framework for guerrilla coproduction, discuss its implications, and lay a foundation for future research on this topic.

title: Investigating the Dynamics of European University Alliances as Multi‐Level Governance Spaces
Democratic Control and Legitimacy of Finnish European Union Policy Process in Crisis Test: Trust, Openness, and the NextGenerationEU
Land matters, gender, and de facto authority in (un)expected places
