title: Do elite cues affect public opinion? Evidence from Switzerland's EU negotiation breakdown
abstract: On 26 May 2021, the Swiss Federal Council announced the unilateral termination of negotiations with the European Union on the institutional framework agreement, effectively abandoning a years-long effort to formalize bilateral relations. We study if this decision functioned as an elite cue about Switzerland's future relationship with the European Union, influencing public attitudes toward European integration. Using survey data from May to June 2021, we employ a regression discontinuity design leveraging interview timing around the announcement. Our findings suggest the announcement prompted a modest shift in public opinion, with some evidence from ordinary least squares models indicating a stronger response among French-speaking respondents. We discuss the implications for studying elite cues in direct-democratic contexts, suggesting that salient political events may generate limited change even when signals are ambiguous and the political context makes such effects rather unlikely.

title: Conceptualizing Democratic Embodiment: Feminist Movements Advancing Democracy Amid Backsliding
abstract: Abstract Feminist movements in times of democratic backsliding are primarily framed as defensive, resilient, or resistant. However, such an approach overlooks the agency underpinning the enactment of democratic practices. In this article, we introduce the concept of democratic embodiment to shift the focus from what democracy achieves to how democratic agency is materially, affectively, and relationally constituted in contexts of vulnerability. Drawing on feminist and democratic theory, we conceptualize democratic embodiment as a constitutive mode of political agency through which feminist actors defend, enact, and expand democracy by centering embodied presence, affective solidarities, and infrastructures of care. Rethinking the relationship between democratic resilience and democratic innovation, we argue, helps better highlight how feminist actors enhance democracy, simultaneously resisting the erosion of gender equality while also embodying alternative visions of democracy.

title: Allocating faculty compute budgets
The long decline of trust in democratic institutions
abstract: Abstract I document declining trust in the Executive and Legislative branches of the US federal government from 1972 onwards. Data are from General Social Survey questions asking whether respondents “have a great deal”, “only some,” or “hardly any” confidence “in those running these institutions”. Net confidence (percentage difference between “great deal” and “hardly any”) in the two branches has declined continually from nearly zero in the early 1970s, accelerating substantially from the 1990s on. Different processes drive this decline for each branch. Partisan and ideological opponents of the President increasingly distrust the incumbent while supporters are roughly neutral. Trust in the US Congress has been eroding more uniformly across all parties and ideologies. In recent years net confidence has been around -30 for the Executive and -45 for Congress. This profound distrust (10 times as many have hardly any v a great deal of confidence in Congress) is widely shared across main socio-demographics, such as age, gender, income, etc., though the decline is steeper for older and white respondents. The decline is also greater than for other institutions, including until recently the third branch (Supreme Court). I close by discussing implications for research in public choice.

title: Beyond free riding or free racing: a framework for understanding subnational tax policy interdependence
abstract: Abstract Subnational governments operating under the same federal fiscal arrangements often make markedly different tax policy choices. Research explains this variation through vertical relationships between subnational and national governments, horizontal relationships among subnational governments, or both, and along either economic or political logics. This study offers a unifying analytical framework integrating these dimensions and logics to help scholars locate their research within the wider literature, identify adjacent processes that may interact with or confound their focal mechanisms, and specify appropriate empirical strategies. I illustrate the framework’s value through analysis of Mexico’s state vehicle ownership tax (2008–2024). Situating the analysis within the framework yields three competing arguments about how horizontal economic and political logics interact. Spatio-temporal analysis shows that partisan competition, not geographic proximity, is the primary channel of horizontal tax policy interdependence. This partisan effect is conditional on neighbors’ tax activity, but in an unexpected way: it is strongest where neighboring states hold their taxes steady and weakest where they are cutting most heavily. The case demonstrates the framework’s usefulness in revealing new substantive findings and prompting new theoretical questions.

title: Climate-related hazards and issue attention to climate policy in the European Parliament
abstract: The European Parliament is often portrayed as an environmental champion, but we still know little about what drives individual legislators’ attention to climate policy. This article examines whether MEPs are responsive to climate-related hazards in their constituency by matching climatological data from the subnational electoral districts of MEPs from five Member States with their issue attention to climate change during the 2004–2024 terms. It is shown that extreme heat episodes, wet spells and temperature anomalies in the constituency are associated with increased MEP issue attention to climate change. However, further analyses suggest that these findings are driven primarily by cross-country differences rather than within-country temporal variation. Contrary to expectations in previous party politics scholarship, this study does not find evidence that the effect of climate hazards is conditioned by MEPs’ party positions on the environment.

title: The political benefits of the monoculture: Estimating the electoral effect of the market facilitation program
abstract: Does the distribution of government transfers affect elections? We analyze a natural experiment in the 2019 wave of the US Department of Agriculture's Market Facilitation Program (MFP). The 2019 MFP allocated $14.5 billion via a formula combining historical production data and commodity-specific trade damages. We show how a methodological quirk resulted in arbitrary variation in these damages that propagated through the formula into excessive county-level compensation rates. We estimate the effects of this payment shock using a novel, design-based, randomization inference approach to account for complex dependencies across US counties. We find that counties receiving greater compensation rates, on average, have higher two-party Republican presidential vote shares in the 2020 election. Instrumenting for actual 2019 MFP disbursements, we find an additional $1 million in payments to a county increased that county's 2020 two-party Trump vote share by about .18 percentage points on average. Had the 2019 MFP maintained the spending levels of the 2018 wave, we estimate that Candidate Trump's two-party vote share would have been .117 percentage points lower nationally, with particularly pronounced effects in swing states like Arizona (.41 percentage points) and Georgia (.159 percentage points).

title: When is Separate Sales Optimal?
abstract: Abstract This paper studies a multi-product monopolist facing a privately informed consumer with additive and type-increasing valuations. Separate monopoly pricing is robustly optimal with respect to the type distribution if and only if the marginal rate of substitution between each pair of goods is monotone. This result is obtained by extending the conventional Myersonian approach.

title: The Value of Communication for Mental Health
abstract: Abstract Mental health disorders account for a significant share of the overall global disease burden. The economic losses from such disorders are staggeringly large, particularly in low-income countries, where people are faced with several unexpected shocks. We test whether improved communication can mitigate such mental health disorders. Partnering with a major telecommunications company, we implement low-cost communication interventions that provide mobile calling credits to a nationally representative set of low-income adults in Ghana during the COVID-19 pandemic. Individuals’ inability to make unexpected calls, need to borrow SOS airtime, and to seek digital loans decreased significantly relative to a control group. As a result, the programs led to a significant decrease in mental distress (-9.7%), the likelihood of severe mental distress by -2.3 percentage points (a quarter of the mean prevalence), and domestic violence, with null impact on overall consumption expenditure. The effects are stronger for monthly mobile credits than a lump-sum. We present evidence that improvements in both business-related services and social inclusion and/or protection are relevant explanations. Simple cost-benefit analysis shows that providing communication credit to low-income adults is a cost-effective policy for improving mental health. Communication – the ability to stay connected – meaningfully improves mental well-being and interventions about communication are particularly valuable when implemented as many installments.

title: Editorial Board
A folk theorem for finitely repeated games with public monitoring
Predicting member churn in dynamic groups: A multi-dimensional analysis
abstract: Predicting churn in dynamic groups remains a challenge in the field of social network analysis and group behavior modeling. While previous research has focused predominantly on static networks or individual-level predictors, the complex interplay of group dynamics over time is still underexplored. This work proposes a multidimensional framework for analyzing and predicting member churn in dynamic groups by integrating structural and temporal dimensions. Drawing on theories from social networks, group cohesion, and organizational behavior, we examine how fluctuations in individual behavior, group stability and performance, as well as network characteristics relate to member retention and change. We apply key concepts such as individual engagement, group stability, and performance using a comprehensive set of features derived from a dataset of the massively multiplayer online game (MMOG) Travian, which covers over 4700 groups (alliances) and 18,000 players, providing a rich setting to observe dynamic group processes. By applying machine learning models, we demonstrate the predictive value of these multidimensional features, achieving robust performance across various classifiers. This study contributes to the theoretical understanding of churn as an emergent group-level phenomenon and offers practical insights for designing interventions in online communities and team-based environments.

title: Networked Counterpublics and Contentious Publicity: A Cross-Platform Analysis of QAnon on Parler and Twitter
abstract: Extremist online movements often leverage social media affordances to shape in-group identity and influence broader publics through agenda-setting practices. This study uses QAnon as a case of a networked counterpublic to examine how these processes unfolded between 2018 and 2021. Drawing on affordance theory, we analyze how QAnon discourse activated the affordances of visibility, association, and persistence on Parler and Twitter – two platforms similar in technical features but distinct in their cultures of use. We identify differentiated affordance-activation practices that support different counterpublic functions: for example, hashtag stacking on Parler can be interpreted as contributing to identity-oriented meaning-making, whereas calls to “do your own research” on Twitter may function as epistemic invitations aimed at drawing mainstream users into conspiratorial interpretation. We further show that QAnon’s contentious publicness – the contestation of pro- and anti-QAnon claims – shifted dynamically across the movement’s developmental stages, and that identical informational resources (shared URLs) generated divergent discursive trajectories across platforms. By tracing these temporal and cross-platform dynamics, we illuminate how extremist counterpublics navigate visibility, identity work, and public contestation, offering insights for the study of political communication in an era of networked extremism.

title: Place-Based Policies Diffusion: Development Zones and Labor Distribution in China
Food insecurity and federal nutrition policy: Administrative change and safety net strain
abstract: Food insecurity in the United States has intensified as rising food prices, the end of COVID-19–era supports, and new federal policies have tightened SNAP eligibility. We explore the mechanisms underpinning the shift of administrative and financial burdens from federal to state and local governments. Particular attention is given to groups disproportionately affected, including the working poor, college students, single mothers, people with disabilities, and rural households. By decentralizing responsibility, these structural changes risk exacerbating regional disparities and straining the community resources tasked with supporting a fraying safety net.

title: Human Capital for the Knowledge Economy: Upskill Journeys in Advanced Capitalist Democracies. By NiccolòDurazzi, Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2026 £84.00 (hardback); £58.99 (ebook)
abstract: Data sharing not applicable to this article as no datasets were generated or analyzed during the current study.

title: When officials disagree with AI: public perceptions of bureaucratic discretion in algorithmic governance
abstract: While existing research has examined how officials interact with AI systems, less is known about how citizens evaluate the legitimacy of bureaucratic discretion in relation to AI recommendations. This study develops a theoretical framework that contrasts two competing sources of authority, bureaucratic professionalism and algorithmic rationality, and examines the moderating role of AI explainability. Using a vignette-based survey experiment in China within a public recruitment setting (N = 1,150), we find a pronounced asymmetry in public evaluations. Divergence from AI recommendations significantly reduces perceived legitimacy, whereas adherence has no significant effect. AI explainability modestly enhances legitimacy when officials follow AI recommendations. Exploratory analysis further suggests that greater familiarity with AI may strengthen the tendency to privilege algorithmic outputs. The findings suggest that AI establishes a new benchmark for legitimacy judgements, creating new challenges for the professional authority of public officials in the context of algorithmic governance.

title: Institutional context and performance-based procurement: Evidence from welfare services in three countries
abstract: This study explores why similar performance-based procurement designs produce different outcomes across welfare service settings. Drawing on ten case studies from the United Kingdom, United States, and the Netherlands we develop a three-mechanism framework linking institutional context to procurement outcomes. We propose that outcomes are associated with three interacting factors: institutional distance (the structural gap between what a procurement model requires and what the existing environment provides), institutional logic alignment (the fit between market-based mechanisms and prevailing normative expectations), and organizational learning capacity (the ability of implementing organizations to adapt over time). We apply this framework to two procurement instruments: Most Economically Advantageous Tender (MEAT) and Payment by Results (PbR). Our case analysis suggests that procurement models building on existing institutional infrastructure and aligning with prevailing normative logics tend to produce more stable outcomes, while those requiring departures from established norms are more frequently associated with cream-skimming, market concentration, and implementation drift. While exploratory, these findings suggest that procurement effectiveness may depend less on the choice between MEAT and PbR than on how carefully either instrument is calibrated to its institutional environment.

title: Public service motivation and performance: a meta-analysis of the relationship and its organizational and cultural moderators
abstract: Despite a substantial body of empirical work on the relationship between public service motivation (PSM) and performance, there has been considerable variation in the findings. This study identifies and codes 69 relevant studies, representing 237,058 respondents from 20 countries, and conducts a three-level meta-analysis to measure the average relationship between PSM and performance. The findings reveal that PSM positively affects performance (r = 0.203, 95% CI [0.164, 0.241]), but that the relationship between PSM and performance is moderated by the types of public organizations and the cultural context. Theoretical and policy implications are discussed, including the robust capacity of PSM to predict both individual and organizational outcomes. Furthermore, we highlight the necessity of accounting for cultural variations (e.g., individualism vs. collectivism) and advise public managers to create opportunities for employees to see their societal contributions.

title: Digital transformation and internal control: When and how it works for local government in Japan
abstract: This study examines the determinants of digitalisation and internal control in the public sector, with a particular focus on Japanese local governments. Although research on digitalisation and digital transformation (DT) in local governments has expanded in recent years, the adoption of DT and its effects on internal control remain underexplored. In this context, we address the following research question: What factors enhance DT and internal control in local governments? Based on an integrated framework of legitimacy theory and stakeholder theory, this study highlights the role of human errors in information systems and the pressures exerted by key stakeholders on local governments that implement DT for internal control purposes. Using survey data, we find that local governments with experience in human errors and those facing stronger stakeholder pressures, including lawsuits from residents, are more likely to establish internal control systems through DT. The results indicate that local governments develop and adopt internal control systems through DT primarily to defend their legitimacy and respond to the oversight of citizens as key stakeholders. These findings demonstrate that the integrated framework effectively explains the development of DT for internal control, where the goals and expectations often present a paradox.

title: Institutionalized Enforcement of Administrative Compliance: State Regulator Use of Noncompliance Burdens
abstract: Abstract Administrative burden scholarship typically examines rules and regulations affecting access to public benefits during initial citizen-state interactions. Scholars agree that individual burdens function as “hidden politics” because policy changes during implementation through bureaucratic discretion. Less is known about bureaucratic behavior or hidden politics enforced on third-party service providers maintaining compliance. In this article we address this by examining noncompliance burdens imposed on abortion providers to understand if regulators emulate peers’ behavior. Using an institutional theoretical framework and administrative records from the Florida Agency for Health Care Administration (FAHCA) on abortion provider oversight, we construct a directed dyadic event history model using 1540 dyad-year observations to predict isomorphism or divergence of sanction activities across regulatory field offices. We find that regulatory field offices emulate behavior of others based on peer’s previous sanction behavior and oversight workload. We also find that regulators diverge from peers based on the regulatory conditions of their own jurisdiction.
journal_name: Journal of Public Administration Research and Theory

title: American Administrative Capacity: Decline, Decay, and Resilience By M.Ernita Joaquin and Thomas J.Greitens, Cham, Switzerland: Springer, 2021. 213 pp. $97 (hardcover). ISBN : 978‐3‐030‐80563‐0
Rethinking plural policing and network governance: internal and external mechanisms in the governance of security
abstract: The governance of security has been studied in both criminology and public administration research, but mainly within their separate disciplines. This integrative literature review argues that governance of security research would benefit from integrating insights from both disciplines, specifically the literatures on plural policing and network governance. This results in a reconceptualization of the governance of security that distinguishes between internal and external governance mechanisms. This distinction allows for a more precise positioning of researchers in the study of governance processes and enables more specific operationalization of the governance of security to support further empirical research.

title: Strategy and urban reinvention: Universities as catalysts of city transformation in Cluj-Napoca, Romania
abstract: IMPACTThis article provides practical insights for local and regional policy-makers, municipal strategists, urban development practitioners, and university leaders involved in shaping knowledge-based urban development. Drawing on the long-term experience of Cluj-Napoca’s post-industrial transformation, the authors show how structured strategic planning and sustained collaboration between universities, local governments, and the private sector can support economic restructuring and urban innovation. The article is particularly relevant for city-level decision-makers, strategic planning units within municipalities, regional development agencies, and university leadership teams seeking to position higher education institutions as active partners in territorial development. It highlights how institutionalized collaboration mechanisms, trust-building, and leadership continuity can enable universities to move beyond advisory roles toward becoming strategic co-creators of urban development agendas. Rather than presenting a rigid model, the authors offer transferable governance lessons that can help practitioners design more resilient university–city partnerships capable of supporting long-term urban transformation in post-industrial and emerging knowledge economies.

title: Beyond GDP: how performance evaluation reform unlocks the public service promise of digital policy
abstract: Digital policies hold considerable promise for improving public service delivery, yet their effectiveness varies markedly across jurisdictions. This study argues that performance evaluation systems serve as a critical institutional catalyst conditioning how digital policies translate into service outcomes. Exploiting a natural experiment derived from China’s de-GDP evaluation reforms and the establishment of big data management institutions, our difference-in-differences estimates indicate that performance evaluation reform enhances digital policy effectiveness in improving public service delivery by 2.35%. Mechanism analysis identifies two pathways: reallocation of administrative attention and redirection of fiscal resources. Heterogeneity analysis further reveals that evaluation frameworks oriented towards agricultural development and ecological protection outperform poverty-alleviation-focused frameworks in amplifying service gains. These findings suggest that policymakers seeking to maximize returns on digital investment should treat performance evaluation redesign as a co-equal institutional priority – ensuring that incentive structures align explicitly with service quality objectives rather than legacy economic metrics.

title: Administrative coordination, integrated plans, and policy capacities for local climate policy implementation
abstract: Abstract The literature has gone to great lengths to describe how administrative coordination can support climate policy implementation. Yet few studies have adopted both a configurational and an actor-oriented perspective to understand which combination of policy capacities and policy design features bureaucrats perceive as necessary or sufficient to effectively engage in administrative coordination for climate policy implementation. Analyzing eighteen local departments implementing climate plans in four cities (Bologna, Lausanne, Padua, Zurich) and across various policy sectors, a configurational approach based on mixed methods allows testing two hypotheses: the first (H1) is that a combination of multiple, high-level organizational capabilities is sufficient for effective coordination. The second one (H2) is that both integrated planning and high organizational policy capacities together are sufficient for effective coordination. Finding evidence for H2, this paper contributes to the ongoing debate regarding the integrative policy capacities needed to foster the ecological transition at the local level. It makes a distinctive contribution by systematically clarifying how the interplay between policy capacities and policy design features shapes administrative coordination outputs.

title: All opinions are equal, but some opinions are more equal than others. How politicians discount low-income citizens’ preferences
Beyond technocracy: a systematic review of individual policy capacity in the Westminster tradition
abstract: Research on policy advisory capacity has expanded rapidly but has tended to focus on the system rather than the individual. This systematic review investigates what knowledge, skills, experience, and dispositions individual policy advisers in the Westminster tradition require. Peer-reviewed studies of Westminster jurisdictions published between January 2000 and December 2024 were searched in Scopus, combining the paired term “Civil Service” and “Skills” with “Policy Capacity”, “Civil Service Skills”, and “Policy Advisory Skills” (n = 75). These were thematically analysed, guided by Collins and Evans's (Collins, H., and R. Evans. 2007. Rethinking Expertise. London: The University of Chicago Press) categorization of expertise, to produce an integrated typology: three types of knowledge (specialized policy, general policy, and system); four skill domains (policy-making, relational, communication, and integrative balancing); two experiential dimensions (lived experience of users and occupational culture); and seven dispositions (political astuteness, creativity, judgement, leadership, adaptive capacity, risk-taking, and resilience). A significant limitation is the absence of the ministerial perspective from the literature, despite ministers being the pre-eminent consumers of policy advice. The article concludes that individual policy capacity is socially constructed, institutionally conditioned, and politically situated; that competency-based models cannot capture its relational character; and that it emerges from the interaction of technical expertise, political judgement, relational capacity, and organizational context.

title: Combining democratic, regulatory and coordination hybridity for achieving robustness in turbulent times
abstract: In recent years, crisis has become the norm for governments. Rather than alternating between stable conditions and moments of crises, political and administrative institutions now experience consistent crisis-induced turbulence. This has affected the legitimacy of established institutions, as the overlap of short and long-term shocks puts pressure on existing structures, actors, processes and procedures. Governments have increasingly looked to foster both change and stability through robustness by means of reevaluating the decision-making venues (the ‘who’), the regulatory tools (the ‘what’) and modes of coordination (the ‘how’). This article aims to capture the complex dynamics in fostering robustness of policies through the lens of hybridity. To achieve this, the paper reconceptualizes hybridity in crisis response from the interconnected perspectives of democratic decision-making (representative; direct; deliberative), regulatory tools (substantive; framework; reflexive) and coordination (hierarchical; market; network). It does so through empirical examples drawn from 108 interviews across 19 case studies in nine European countries, focusing on responses to COVID-19 vaccination promotion and school closures. By understanding the interactions within the dimensions of governance in democratic decision-making, regulatory tools and coordination, we can better comprehend the enablers and limitations for robust crisis responses. The paper argues that hybridity is linked to robustness through the ability of actors to foster complementary effects by repurposing different ideal types (mixing) and substituting the conflicts that develop over time (matching).

title: One problem, two ontologies: How administrative coordination impacts policy coherence
abstract: This paper studies the impact of different coordination instruments used by local public administrations in Switzerland on policy coherence. It contributes to the special issue by demonstrating how insights from public management and public policy literatures, often working within distinct ontological frameworks, can effectively be combined to address shared challenges at the intersection of organisational structures and policy outcomes. Empirically, the paper focuses on a mutually relevant topic of state action: the role of administrative coordination in fostering coherent policy implementation. Using data from two recent surveys of local governments in Switzerland, we examine which coordination instruments are employed within a municipality and assess their impact on policy coherence using regression analysis. We find that the more coordination instruments used in a municipality, the higher the policy coherence. Further, while hierarchical, network- and market-based coordination instruments all display a significant positive effect on coherence, network-based instruments are most effective. By integrating theoretical insights and empirical evidence from two distinct and often disconnected debates, our study not only advances the understanding of various intra-organisational coordination instruments and their effects on policy coherence but also contributes to the broader discourse of the special issue. It demonstrates how insights from different academic disciplines can be combined to address shared challenges at the intersection of public management and policy implementation research.

title: Mind the gap: connecting AI innovation to widespread public value
Why do Open Science policies fall short? Institutional logics and ethical framings in policy implementation in Finland
abstract: Abstract This article explores the ethical and institutional dimensions of Open Science (OS) policy implementation in hybrid research organizations in Finland by mapping ethical framings across five institutional logics. It uncovers reinforcing ethical framings across institutional logics that support OS implementation; however, it also reveals tensions, especially where market and corporate logics conflict with professional and disciplinary values and norms. Drawing on both survey and interview data and by combining the institutional logics framework with the concept of openness as a performative process, the study offers a novel analytical lens to understand how researchers interpret and negotiate OS policies in practice. It contributes to ongoing scholarly discussions on science policy implementation and dynamics that shape OS practices and by proposing a typology of researcher responses ranging from advocacy to policy alienation. These responses span a continuum from proactive engagement to ethical resistance and disconnection.

title: Contested Governance and Civilian Prosocial Behavior: Evidence from Lab-in-the-Field Experiments in India
abstract: How does contested governance by states and competing armed actors affect the behavior of the governed? During civil conflicts, rebel organizations frequently provide public goods, judicial arbitration, and security, but these forms of governance often operate alongside local state institutions. Beyond avoiding violence, therefore, noncombatants must navigate the daily uncertainty of local governance by states and armed groups vying for territorial control. This, we argue, shapes their quotidian interactions with one another. Using a series of lab-in-the-field experiments and surveys from Naxal-affected Bihar, India, we find that individuals living under such contested governance exhibit greater interpersonal trust and trustworthiness and less opportunistic behavior. We propose two mechanisms to explain these patterns—fearing intra-community retaliation or substituting for the state with interpersonal reliance. Most evidence is only consistent with the latter. By connecting governance, rebellion, and social capital, this work makes important contributions toward understanding the micro-politics of local order during longstanding armed conflicts.

title: Is Blood Thicker Than Water(-and-Earth)? Partisanship Geography in Imperial China and the Limits of Quantitative History
Disproportionality in Geographic Representation
The Equality Positions and Policies of Governments, 1970–2020: How Egalitarian Parties Evoke Equality While Evading Real Redistribution
The Information Paradox: Aid, Social Protection, and the Social Contract in Areas of Conflict and State Fragility
Exodus and vote: Mass emigration and voter turnout in Honduras
abstract: Does emigration motivate or discourage political participation in migrant sending countries? While emigration can reduce participation by removing opposition voters and weakening political efficacy, it may also signal widespread grievances and encourage participation among those who remain. This paper examines the immediate political effects of large-scale emigration and argues that emigration alone is insufficient to mobilize participation. Instead, when emigration is visible and perceived as a collective act, it sends a political signal that updates citizens’ beliefs about the status quo. Drawing on a pre-registered survey experiment conducted in Honduras ahead of the 2021 presidential election, I test how framing emigration as either a private decision or a collective act in the form of migrant caravans shapes intentions to vote. Respondents exposed to the caravan framing were five percentage points more likely to report intentions to vote than those in the control group and four percentage points more likely than those exposed to the private decision framing. Using causal mediation analysis, I examine whether these effects operate through nationalized perceptions of migration and politics but find no clear evidence of mediation, which may reflect ceiling and floor effects. These findings highlight the importance of framing in shaping how emigration influences political participation among those who remain.

title: Learning in Committee? How Racial Diversity Shapes Speech, Evidence Use, and Substantive Representation in Congress
abstract: ABSTRACT Research on descriptive representation has primarily examined whether and how descriptive representatives themselves advance group interests. In the context of race, this work shows that nonwhite lawmakers advance nonwhite interests, but less is known about whether nonwhite representation also shapes white lawmakers' behavior. I argue that repeated contact with nonwhite lawmakers in racially diverse committees may shape how white Democrats engage race‐related issues, making them more likely to support race‐related hearing statements with evidence. To test this expectation, I combine large‐scale text classification with a detailed content analysis of more than 11,000 race‐related committee hearing statements and 87,000 full bill texts from the 105th–117th Congresses. Using a within‐legislator design, I find that white Democrats serving on racially diverse committees are more likely to cite evidence when discussing race and to cite the same sources as their nonwhite colleagues. I also show that race‐based expertise is associated with substantive representation: legislators who more frequently cite evidence when discussing race are more effective at advancing race‐related legislation. Together, these findings suggest that descriptive representation may foster substantive representation, in part, by shaping how white Democrats engage race‐related issues in racially diverse legislative committees.

title: How to Upend America in 100 Days: Unilateral Power at the Outset of Trump’s Second Term
abstract: ABSTRACT President Trump used the unilateral power of the presidency in extraordinary ways during the first 100 days of his second term. This article examines his use of executive action using a dataset of every action issued in the first 100 days of Trump’s second term, along with a similar dataset for his first term and other recent administrations. At the outset of his second term, Trump issued substantially more executive actions than his own first administration and his recent predecessors; however, this also came with historically low legislative productivity. His unilateral policy making is notable for the many revocations of previous executive actions and startling uses of the pardon power. The areas that Trump acted within most were government operations, tariff policies, and policies related to law and crime. These findings reveal important details of Trump’s unilateral presidency and demonstrate that his executive actions are likely to erode the traditional boundaries of presidency power if not held in check by other institutional actors.

title: Predatory Journals: Do They Publish Undergraduate and AI-Generated Papers?
abstract: ABSTRACT Predatory journals are criticized widely for weak peer-review and profit-driven editorial practices, but little empirical evidence assesses their capacity to publish low-quality or AI-generated research. This study examines the level to which these journals publish undergraduate essays and AI-generated manuscripts. We submitted papers to 144 predatory journals identified through spam solicitations, Beall’s list ( https://beallslist.net ), and the Predatory Journals database ( www.predatoryjournals.org/news/predatory-journals-list-2025 ). This included 19 undergraduate political science and human rights essays and 10 AI-generated engineering case reports to test the degree to which these essays are published. We find that most undergraduate essays and AI-generated manuscripts are accepted, which confirms the low quality of these outlets and the risk emanating from them.

title: Beyond the Greenback: Currency Power in a Greener, More Fragmented World
abstract: ABSTRACT Structural shifts in the global economy are reshaping the foundations of international currency power. This article explores how the green transition, geopolitical realignment, and sustained US protectionism could interact to transform the global currency hierarchy, with a particular focus on the US dollar and the Chinese renminbi (RMB). We highlight two key drivers of currency usage: (1) the liquidity and availability of a currency for cross-border transactions; and (2) the strategic economic and political alignment between currency issuers and their partners. Considering developments in green value chains, evolving alliances, and trade policies, the article outlines how China’s growing role in critical minerals, infrastructure finance, and alternative financial systems can enhance the internationalization of the RMB. Concurrently, US protectionism and withdrawal from multilateralism may open up space for regional currency diversification. These trends point to an increasingly fragmented and multipolar international monetary system, in which currency power will have a central role in shaping the future global order.

title: Repression as Aesthetic Ordering: How UK Universities Make Palestine Solidarity Illegible in a Time of Genocide
abstract: This paper analyzes the repression of Palestine solidarity activism on UK university campuses following October 7, 2023. To explain why institutions whose mission centers on critical inquiry and open debate have enacted far-reaching restrictions on Palestine solidarity, we compile an original dataset of 114 incidents across 70 universities (October 2023–March 2025). Drawing on Jacques Rancière’s concept of the “distribution of the sensible,” we conceptualize repression not simply as deterrence or punishment but as a mode of aesthetic ordering through which universities govern political visibility and legitimacy. Repression is multilayered, operating through coercive enforcement and legal actions, procedural and bureaucratic controls, punitive disciplinary processes, and the symbolic erasure of visual and affective expressions of dissent. These practices are enabled by—and in turn reinforce—neoliberal managerialism, racialized securitization, and imperial governance logics that produce racialized hierarchies of threat and safety and recode solidarity as risk and disruption. By rendering Palestine solidarity illegible and illegitimate as politics, UK universities contribute to conditions through which genocidal violence becomes tolerable.

title: Populism and territoriality
Locating critical AI geopolitics
Infelicitous Political Talk: Disparaging Institutions and Support for Democracy
abstract: Infelicitous political talk is now a routine feature of American politics, with scholars debating the extent to which it meaningfully shapes citizens’ democratic attitudes. We seek to contribute to this body of work by showing that the degree of inappropriateness of a criticism is continuous and subjective; that rhetorical denigration of democratic institutions is more likely to influence evaluations of the speaker than to erode broader commitments to democracy; and that criticisms that “cross the line” of appropriateness can create backlashes that actually wind up increasing support for democratic institutions and values. Using an experiment embedded in a national survey, we evaluate the effects of inappropriate attacks on the U.S. judiciary. Perceived rhetorical denigration does not weaken democratic values; instead, it produces a small but consistent backlash that slightly increases support for democratic institutions. Our various findings strongly challenge the assumption that rising infelicitous talk poses a serious threat to democratic stability in the U.S.

title: Social identification and equilibrium law enforcement
abstract: Abstract This paper studies how social identification reshapes the political economy of law enforcement. In a two-class economy with property crime, individuals choose whether to offend, vote over the detection probability under majority rule, and choose whether to identify with their class or with the encompassing nation. In the absence of identity concerns, class-specific material preferences over enforcement depend on victimization exposure, tax incidence, and the option value of offending. With class identification, voters place greater weight on the relative payoff of their own group, so social identity amplifies the underlying distributive conflict. With national identification, voters place greater weight on aggregate payoffs, compressing preferred enforcement levels across groups. Endogenous identity choice produces distinct political regimes and can generate multiple equilibria: societies in which class differences are more salient in identity space are more likely to sustain class identification and more extreme enforcement outcomes, whereas higher national prestige favors national identification and policies closer to the aggregate benchmark. An extension in which offending carries an action-based social deviance cost preserves the main mechanism and shows how compliance norms can reinforce class-based identity.

title: The costs of environmental land use regulation
Agency incentives and disparate revenue collection: Evidence from Chicago parking tickets
Capital Services in Global Value Chains
abstract: Abstract This paper constructs the first global dataset on inter-sectoral capital service expenditures. I use this data to disaggregate capital services and intermediate inputs in a dynamic multi-sector trade model. Steady state allocations and responses to shocks are determined by a capital-augmented global input-output matrix. Two properties of the measured network deliver larger long-run consumption gains from globalization than existing estimates, as well as larger gains in more capital-intensive countries. First, more trade-exposed sectors supply capital to more consumption-influential producers. Second, heterogeneity in the network reallocates sectoral expenditures towards producers with larger declines in capital rental prices. These reallocations raise capital incomes and lower consumption price indices.

title: Macro Shocks and Firm Dynamics with Oligopolistic Financial Intermediaries
abstract: Abstract Motivated by a secular increase in the concentration of the U.S. banking industry, I develop a new macroeconomic model with oligopolistic financial intermediaries and heterogeneous firms. Market power allows banks to price discriminate and charge firm-specific markups, exerting greater market power over productive and more financially constrained firms. This dampens capital accumulation and amplifies the effects of macroeconomic shocks. During a crisis, banks exploit the higher share of financially constrained firms to extract higher markups, inducing a larger decline in real activity. When a large bank fails, the remaining banks use their increased market power to restrict credit supply, worsening and prolonging the downturn.

title: An Evaluation of Protected Area Policies in the European Union
Managerial Coordination in Decentralized Markets
abstract: Abstract Why do some buyers contract directly with producers, while others contract via an intermediary that coordinates assignments and monitors performance? We develop a repeated-game model in which intermediaries aggregate fluctuating demand, lengthening productive relationships and making cooperation easier to sustain. This benefit comes at the cost of double marginalization: an added layer of rents is needed to motivate the intermediary. The trade-off determines which buyers rely on an intermediary and which contract directly. In equilibrium, producers working through intermediaries earn lower, less variable pay but greater job security. Intermediaries expand trade, yet shift its gains from producers to buyers. Managerial coordination also promotes specialization. The framework sheds new light on professional service firms, global sourcing intermediaries, and digital matching platforms.

title: The making of sustainability standards in the Global South: power, contestation, and global value chain governance
The effect of transaction partners’ location on firms’ relocation choice: a natural experiment using a massive earthquake in Japan
INFERENCE ON COMMON TRENDS IN FUNCTIONAL TIME SERIES
abstract: We study statistical inference on unit roots and cointegration for time series in a Hilbert space. We develop statistical inference on the number of common stochastic trends embedded in the time series, that is, the dimension of the nonstationary subspace. We also consider tests of hypotheses on the nonstationary and stationary subspaces themselves. The Hilbert space can be of an arbitrarily large dimension, and our methods remain asymptotically valid even when the time series of interest takes values in a subspace of possibly unknown dimension. This has wide applicability in practice; for example, to cointegrated vector time series that are either high-dimensional or of finite dimension, to high-dimensional factor models that include a finite number of nonstationary factors, to cointegrated curve-valued (or function-valued) time series, and to nonstationary dynamic functional factor models. To illustrate our methods, we include two empirical examples.

title: Towards Operationalizing Ecological Resilience for Infrastructure Decision‐Making
abstract: While definitions of resilience from ecology recognize the potential for systems to shift between multiple stable states and adapt to a changing environment, traditional engineering assessments of infrastructure resilience overemphasize stability and recovery. These engineering approaches may be limiting society's ability to effectively adapt and manage change. We propose to incorporate ecological resilience ideas into engineering projects by leveraging mathematical models, originally developed to describe ecological systems, to identify and describe equilibria in socio-technical systems. We present a conceptual case study of coastal communities facing competing pressures of urban growth and managed retreat to exemplify the use of these tools. We discuss how metrics of ecological resilience relate to existing definitions of resilience in engineering and their implications for infrastructure decision-making.

title: A parsimonious probability weighting function
A Viral War: Threat Perceptions in Light of Social Media News Consumption on the Russo-Ukrainian War
abstract: This article explores how social media news on the Russo-Ukrainian War shapes people’s perceptions of security through the lens of cultivation theory. Drawing on focus groups ( N = 31), Study 1 shows that Austrian citizens experienced war coverage as immediate but overwhelming, with graphic visuals often triggering anxiety. Study 2, a quota-representative survey ( N = 1,000), finds that frequent exposure to such content heightens Austrians’ perceptions of becoming a victim of this war and makes news appear more emotionally unsettling. Together, we demonstrate that cultivation processes persist in today’s fragmented media environment, with important psychological and societal consequences.

title: Constructing the Journalistic Self: Habitus, Subjectivation, and the Politics of Inequality
abstract: How do journalists make sense of themselves and their work in postcolonial societies marked by enduring race and class inequalities? This article examines how journalists discursively represent newsroom dynamics, paying particular attention to how their subjectivities are formed. Drawing on 27 semi-structured in-depth interviews with current and former journalists in Jamaica, this study aims to understand how subjectivation and habitus, shape the ways in which journalists reproduce or contest inequalities. It also examines the professional subjectivities and ideologies that are revealed in the discourse of Jamaican journalists and how they relate to race and class inequalities. Existing work on journalism and inequality has largely focused on questions of voice, whose perspectives are included or excluded, and on how media institutions perpetuate structural inequalities. The findings reveal that journalists’ own subjectivities, social backgrounds, and internalised dispositions shape the way they see themselves and the work that they do. The study identifies a typology of journalistic subjectivities that emerge within postcolonial contexts: the class-conscious journalist, the racially conscious journalist, and the racially neutral journalist.

title: Learning the Limits of Belonging: Classroom-Newsroom Gender Paradox in Nigerian Journalism
abstract: We examine women’s dominance in Nigerian journalism classrooms despite their lack of commensurate representation in newsrooms. Drawing on 27 in-depth interviews with female students, we find that journalism is often pursued as a fallback option, limiting initial motivation. Within training institutions, perceptions of poor teaching, lack of practical training, and toxic learning environments appear to contribute to disengagement from the practice. Patriarchal norms, including assumptions about men’s provider role and privileging men’s authority, shape their perception of these discouraging lessons. The findings compound existing pipeline explanations for this disparity, with implications for scholarship on gender equity, journalism pedagogy, and practice.

title: Monitoring Boosts Alignment: Evidence from China’s Top-down Central Inspections
In the Global Vanguard: Agrarian Development and the Making of Modern Taiwan James Lin. Oakland: University of California Press, 2025. 290 pp. $34.00; £30.00. ISBN 9780520398665
Collaborative Governance Capacity as the Mechanism Linking Metagovernance and Strategic CSR to Public Service Performance: Evidence from Local Governments in Indonesia
abstract: Contemporary public service delivery increasingly relies on multi-actor governance arrangements, in which public agencies, private firms, and civil society organizations jointly contribute to public value creation. However, in decentralized governance systems, persistent coordination problems and weak alignment between government steering and corporate social responsibility (CSR) initiatives often limit performance outcomes. This study examines collaborative governance capacity (CGC) as a causal mechanism linking governance, strategic CSR, and public service performance in local Indonesian governments. Drawing on survey data from 200 respondents representing local government officials, CSR managers, and civil society actors, this study employs multiple regression and mediation analysis using Hayes’ PROCESS macro. The findings show that metagovernance and strategic CSR significantly strengthen collaborative governance capacity, which in turn robustly predicts public service performance. The mediation results confirm that CGC fully transmits the effects of metagovernance and strategic CSR on service outcomes, indicating that governance steering and corporate engagement improve performance primarily through enhanced relational and operational collaboration rather than direct intervention. By conceptualizing collaborative governance capacity as a mechanism rather than a contextual condition, this study advances governance and CSR theory. It provides actionable insights for improving public service performance in decentralized multi-actor governance settings.

title: Guerrillas in the library? Public libraries as sites of ethical resistance
abstract: Public libraries in the United States have faced increasing political pressures in recent years. These pressures have impacted libraries in a variety of ways including censorship, funding cuts, and threats to the personal and professional wellbeing of library personnel. While these issues were occurring prior to the 2024 Presidential election, President Trump’s second term amplified the pressures and took direct aim at libraries. At the same time, working to stay true to professional values and ethics, libraries are actively resisting such political pressures at the individual, organizational, and networked levels. This article draws from bureaucratic resistance, dissent, and guerrilla government research to explore how ethical resistance arises in the public library context. We examine publicly documented actions by public libraries and librarians to demonstrate this resistance at various levels. We conclude by discussing the implications of ethical resistance during times of democratic backsliding and offer a series of hypotheses for future research.

title: Distinguishing and integrating universalism and context in the common good: A normative conceptual framework for evaluating public goods
abstract: Despite its long history in public policy and administration, the common good remains a subject of debate and ambiguity. Debates over whether it is universal or contextual have complicated its application and the evaluation of public goods’ contributions. Drawing on common good, public administration, and policy research, this paper develops a normative conceptual framework that distinguishes and integrates these perspectives while enabling the evaluation of public goods. The analysis focuses on three linked features of the common good: sharing, community, and goodness—understood as collective benefit, participation, and well-being. The paper concludes by summarizing the results, discussing implications for governance, policy, and research, acknowledging limitations, and suggesting directions for application and future empirical study.

title: 40 Years of Corruption Research in China: Theory, Evidence, and Future Directions
abstract: Corruption is often referred to as the “cancer of politics” and it poses a severe challenge to a government’s foundation of governance and the legitimacy of its power. Since the launch of China’s reform and opening-up policy in 1978, alongside the institutional transition toward a market economy, corruption continues to proliferate in China and attracts increasing scholarly attention. This article systematically reviews the corruption research conducted by Chinese scholars during the past 40 years, and synthesizes the definitions, types, causes, and consequences of corruption, as well as the strategies and measures for combating and preventing corruption in China. Through a comprehensive literature search in the seven most influential Chinese journals, we identified a total 497 articles of corruption or anti-corruption studies, and found that Chinese scholars, while borrowing much existing knowledge from Western corruption literature, have already made significant progress in developing their own theoretical framework by incorporating cultural dimensions and also by adapting to the centralized political environment to address the unique challenges posed by corruption in contemporary China. This article concludes by summarizing the particular contributions of Chinese scholars and the limitations of current corruption research in China, and suggesting useful ways to improve the quality of corruption research and explore new research directions in the future.

title: Legislative Pork‐Barrel Funding and Public Policy Outcomes: The Role of Local‐Level Factors
abstract: ABSTRACT The growing legislative influence over budget allocations through pork‐barrel funding raises concerns that this type of distributive policy may undermine effectiveness. We examine Brazil's mandatory pork‐barrel system to assess whether funding availability affects health outcomes and how local conditions shape these effects. We focus on municipalities' abilities to attract resources (“funding concentration”) and their autonomy over investment decisions (“funding flexibility”), with expectations conditioned by administrative capacity. Using panel data on 4114 Brazilian municipalities (2015–2021) and controlling for endogeneity and selection bias, we find that pork‐barrel funding is associated with higher short‐term rates of preventable hospitalizations. These effects dissipate over time but reveal how political‐electoral dynamics shape implementation. Such dynamics undermine the expected benefits of administrative capacity, suggesting that political oversight patterns condition policy outcomes. Evidence on funding concentration indicates that, in contexts of politically allocated funding, administrative capacity may facilitate the rapid execution of concentrated, electoral‐driven allocations, which can amplify inefficiencies. These findings highlight the importance of aligning legislative budget governance with local administrative capacity to mitigate the risks of funding fragmentation and ensure more effective governance of distributive policies.

title: Bureaucracy Remade, Citizens Reconfigured: Accountability, Digitalization, and the Transformation of Public Administration
abstract: Something quietly consequential has been unfolding within democratic institutions over the past 40 years, though it rarely announces itself in obvious ways.Two recent books, emerging from different corners of public administration scholarship, circle this transformation from distinct vantage points.Karl Löfgren and Patrik Hall's The New Public Bureaucracy, alongside the edited volume Digital Co-Production of Public Services: Citizens, Challenges and Cases, led by Taco Brandsen, Ina Radtke, A. Paula Rodriguez Müller, and Trui Steen, were not conceived as companions.They speak in different voices and address partially overlapping audiences.Yet, when read side by side, something sparks between them.The tension is not accidental.It is revealing.

title: The Matthew Effect in American Generosity? Philanthropic Disparities and the Role of Government Support
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines how economic, racial, and ecological dimensions of community disadvantage shape philanthropic donations to local human services nonprofit sectors, and whether government support mitigates these place‐based disparities. Using a novel county‐level panel dataset spanning 2000–2019, we combine descriptive analyses with mixed‐effects regression models to estimate both direct and moderating relationships. We find that per capita private donations are significantly lower in economically deprived communities and significantly higher in rural communities, while minority prominence shows no statistically significant association with private giving. While government funding crowds in private donations overall, its moderating role is context specific. Government support does not attenuate philanthropic disparities linked to economic deprivation or minority prominence, but it crowds in private donations more strongly in rural counties than in urban counties. These findings highlight the contingent role of government support and underscore the need for targeted policy strategies to address philanthropic disparities across communities.

title: Social enterprises in the shadow of the State
abstract: Despite growing interest in social enterprises and public value creation, little attention has been paid to how social enterprises create public value in contexts of state retrenchment and institutional voids. This paper examines FOQUS (FOndazione QUartieri Spagnoli) in Naples through a longitudinal qualitative case study. We identify three mechanisms underpinning public value creation—strategic flexibility, multi-stakeholder ecosystem governance, and storytelling—and four related challenges. Findings show that social enterprises create public value not only through collaboration with public actors but also through autonomous action in the shadow of the State, revealing tensions that characterise public value creation in institutional weak contexts.

title: Understanding red tape perceptions of street-level bureaucrats: a multilevel cross-country analysis
abstract: Despite extensive research on red tape’s negative consequences, its antecedents remain underexplored. Building on the psychological process model, this article investigates antecedents of street-level bureaucrats’ red tape perceptions across the micro, meso, and macro levels. Using a dataset of 90,480 teachers across 44 countries, results show that antecedents across all levels relate to teachers’ red tape perceptions. Specifically, red tape perceptions are weaker among teachers having a growth mindset, working in schools with a wide span of control, and living in low uncertainty avoidance and individualism cultures. Across these antecedents, the cultural contexts are particularly important.

title: Governance in action: the role of pediatricians in childhood immunization
abstract: Pediatric vaccination consultations are central to how childhood vaccination is organized and sustained in practice, particularly in contexts where vaccination is voluntary, delivery is physician-led, and formal provider oversight is limited. Drawing on street-level bureaucracy literature and a biopolitical perspective on health governance, we conceptualize pediatric vaccination consultations as sites of governance-in-action and explore how pediatricians interpret and shape childhood vaccination governance. Our analysis builds on qualitative data collected in Austria between 2023 and 2025, including ethnographic observations of 243 pediatric consultations and 43 interviews with parents and pediatricians. We identify four roles pediatricians assume: guidance through expertise; facilitating education; advocacy for individual health; and safeguarding public health. Building on this, we propose conceptualizing vaccination consultations as public encounters in which pediatricians and parents negotiate responsibilities, values, and health-related concerns through relationships of care while simultaneously advancing population-level health goals. This study sheds light on the often informalized work through which pediatricians sustain vaccination governance and calls for greater scholarly and policy attention to clinical encounters through which public health is realized.

title: Shared keywords and methods do not make for common ground
Governing aging through learning: later-life education policy in China, 1982–2025
abstract: As population aging accelerates, later-life education has become an increasingly visible policy response across aging societies. However, it is still more often understood as a welfare service or participatory good than as a political technology through which aging is governed. Drawing on Foucauldian discourse analysis, this article examines how national later-life education policy in China from 1982 to 2025 renders later life governable through learning. The analysis shows, first, that later-life education has developed from a selective arrangement for retired veteran cadres into a dispersed governance technology embedded in aging strategy, community infrastructures and society-wide aging education. Second, education is justified through the problematization of aging as a developmental pressure, a burden on elderly care systems and a risk to social stability. Third, these governing technologies are translated into five educational tracks: health, vocational, digital, volunteer and ideological education, through which policy promotes a desirable older subject who is independent, responsible, adaptable and politically aligned. While policy expands learning participation, it simultaneously recodes structural inequalities as individual deficits, rendering some older adults less visible and less supportable within the policy field.

title: Exploring citizen participation and network collaboration: the observation action of air pollution policy
abstract: This study investigates a voluntary citizen observation action embedded in air pollution policy implementation in Taiwan to examine how collaborative network roles structure participation across heterogeneous urban and rural contexts. By integrating social network analysis with mediation modelling, the findings reveal three core insights: (1) While actors with professional knowledge serve as essential brokers, collaborative structures vary from decentralized, multi-core patterns in urban areas of Taichung City to more locally anchored networks in rural Yunlin shaped by strong place attachment among long-term residents; (2) Participants’ socio-demographic backgrounds – particularly female, older, and mid-educated residents – are empirically associated with critical network roles, highlighting the importance of non-elite actors in collaborative participation; (3) Brokerage positions rather than centrality alone appear to function as key relational mechanisms linking local attachment and age with sustained participation outcomes. These results suggest that institutionalizing support for non-elite brokers through community-based organizations and NGOs may enhance the sustainability of participatory air pollution policy implementation.

title: Promoting Citizens' Policy Compliance Willingness Through Adjusting the Psychological Distance Toward Policy Tools
Contesting boundaries: understanding industrial–health policy integration across time and contexts
A Democratic Theory of Labor Unions
abstract: Recently, political theorists have been increasingly concerned with the implications of democratic values for work. This article contributes to these debates by examining the main vehicle through which workers, historically, have sought democracy at work: the labor union. The article defends a vision of economic democracy that arises from the practice of labor unions. It then emphasizes the distinctive features of labor unions that make them potential vehicles for democracy in other domains. Labor unions are particularly important means of advancing democratic values for three reasons: (1) their ability to appeal to the short- and mid-term self-interest of their members; (2) their anchor in the material reproduction of society; and (3) that they rely on attitudes of cooperation and solidarity among their members. Yet these three features also point to potential limitations of labor unions as laboratories of democracy.

title: Redistricting Reforms Reduce Gerrymandering by Constraining Partisan Actors
abstract: Political actors often manipulate redistricting plans to gain electoral advantages, a process known as gerrymandering. Several states have implemented institutional reforms to address this problem, such as establishing map-drawing commissions. Estimating the impact of these reforms is challenging because each state structures its processes and rules differently. We model redistricting as a sequential game whose equilibrium solution summarizes multistep institutional interactions as a univariate score. We argue that this score measures the leeway political actors have over the partisan lean of the final plan. Our differences-in-differences analysis demonstrates that reforms reduce partisan bias and increase competitiveness by constraining partisan actors. We perform a counterfactual policy analysis to estimate the effects of enacting recent reforms nationwide. Though commissions are likely to reduce bias, reforms that restrict partisan actors in multiple ways, such as removing veto points (Michigan), are more effective than commissions where parties retain some control (Ohio).

title: Democratic Satisfaction and the Public Sphere
Constructing representation: Political actors’ representative style on Facebook during European and national election campaigns
abstract: Abstract This study investigates contemporary forms of political representation by analyzing the Facebook communication of 110 political leaders from eight European countries during both national and 2024 European Parliament (EP) election campaigns. Based on constructivist theories of representation, we introduce the concept of ‘representational style’, defined as the specific combination of six communicative elements: policy focus, personalized communication, direct voter connection, appeals to social groups, references to a homogeneous people, and antagonism toward opponents. Using manual content analysis of 7,854 posts, the study identifies three distinct representational styles through inductive cluster analysis: People’s Policy Warriors, Technocratic-Pluralist Heroes, and (Wo)man of the People. The findings reveal substantial variation across political and national contexts. A clear East–West divide emerges with Western European leaders tending to adopt a Technocratic-Pluralist approach, while Central and Eastern European politicians more often represent themselves as responsive figures closely connected to the people.

title: Threat perception and partisan animosity: Evidence from Argentina and Brazil
abstract: Abstract This study examines antagonism between opposing political camps in Argentina and Brazil, two Latin American countries that have experienced heightened polarization and growing support for contentious right-wing populist leaders. Using original survey data, we analyze how specific perceived threats relate to social distance toward supporters of rival presidential candidates, which we use as a proxy for outgroup animosity. We examine multiple threat domains, including perceived threats from rival political camps, other social groups (racists and immigrants) and threats to symbolic values (equality and the nation). Our findings show that threat perception is a significant correlate of outgroup distance in both countries, but the forms of perceived threat linked to outgroup distancing differ across political camps. We also find partial support for the hypothesis that threat perception is more strongly associated with outgroup distance among supporters of the populist right, particularly once potential confounders are taken into account. While this pattern is evident in Brazil, in Argentina, the left and right camps do not differ significantly in how strongly threat perception predicts outgroup distance.

title: Beyond Single-Shot Designs: Repeated Treatments, Affective Polarization, and Democratic Norms
abstract: Abstract Although theory and observational work suggest that affective polarization should shape citizens’ support for democratic norms, experimental tests of this causal claim largely find null effects. Most studies assume any impact would be immediate and rely on one-shot manipulations. Yet democratic norms are sticky; brief shifts in partisan feelings may be too weak or fleeting to move them. I therefore test whether repeated treatments over several waves of a survey shift affective polarization and, in turn, support for democratic norms. I find no significant first-stage effects: the treatments do not change respondents’ affective polarization, so repeated exposures do not cumulatively move it and downstream effects on norms cannot be identified. I conclude by considering why my findings differ from studies that report significant effects for similar treatments. Many experiments measure affective polarization as hostility toward the outparty, whereas this study and observational work conceptualize it as the gap between inparty and outparty evaluations.

title: When Does Term Length Matter? Party Status, Polarization, and Legislative Productivity
abstract: ABSTRACT Longer terms should increase legislative productivity by extending time horizons, yet the empirical evidence for this outcome is inconsistent. This manuscript argues that the effects of term length depend on both party status and polarization. Using data from across U.S. state legislatures, the results demonstrate that the productivity advantages of longer terms depend on the political context. As polarization increases within states over time, the relative benefit of longer terms shifts from minority to majority party members. At low polarization levels, minorities would benefit more from term extensions than majorities. At high polarization, this pattern reverses. These findings reconcile prior research and reveal how the political context can shape institutional effects.

title: Editorial Board
A characterization of Black’s voting rule
Proportional representation primer
abstract: Abstract This primer provides a systematic introduction to proportional representation (PR) electoral systems for scholars and students unfamiliar with their mechanics and political consequences. PR is now used for legislative elections in approximately 118 countries, making it the world’s most common family of electoral systems. However, its formal structure and political effects are often poorly understood outside specialist communities. The primer covers the main families of apportionment algorithms (quota, divisor, and ranked-choice methods), the principal types of PR electoral systems (list PR, STV, mixed, and semi-proportional), and their key structural components, including district magnitude, thresholds, measures of disproportionality, volatility, and the effective number of parties. It surveys major empirical regularities, including Duverger’s Law, the impact of district magnitude on party fragmentation, women’s and minority representation, voter turnout, and coalition formation, before turning to paradoxes and problems, including apportionment paradoxes and the Balinski–Young impossibility theorem, STV Non-Monotonicity and the No-Show paradox, spoilers and ballot-position primacy effects in list PR, and overhang seats and decoy parties in mixed compensatory systems. The primer concludes that every apportionment method is formally flawed, that institutional parameters interact with strategic behavior in ways that frequently produce unexpected outcomes, and that the empirical regularities anchoring the field rest on identification strategies that are vulnerable to the endogeneity of electoral institutions. A Glossary of key concepts is included as an Appendix.

title: Office-seeking under demographic change: immigration, coalition government, and municipal budget reallocation in Sweden
abstract: Abstract This paper examines how local governments adjust public budgets following immigration-induced demographic change. It argues that office-seeking incumbents reallocate fiscal resources towards newcomers if these are expected to become voters within a short time horizon. Such adjustments are constrained by uncertainty within governing coalitions over who will capture any resulting electoral gains. The argument is evaluated using data from 290 Swedish municipalities between 2014 and 2023. Empirically, the analysis relates annual changes in budget shares across 11 expenditure categories to annual changes in the local non-EU foreign-born population share. The findings show that larger increases in the non-EU population share are associated with budgetary reallocation towards spending areas that are particularly relevant to these groups. Ideological differences between left- and right-leaning governing coalitions do little to condition these reallocations, whereas broader coalitions exhibit weaker fiscal adjustment. The paper contributes to public choice and political economy research by showing that fiscal responses to demographic change take the form less of uniform expansion than of strategic budget recomposition, and that such adjustment is weaker where coalition partners are uncertain about the distribution of electoral gains.

title: Nonpolitical Identity Signals as Information Shortcuts: Evidence from Three Experiments
Information manipulation and repression: Theory and evidence from the COVID-19 response in Russia
Effects of climate activism on firm productivity and uncertainty: Evidence from global oil extraction
