An equilibrium theory of nominal exchange rates
abstract: This paper proposes an equilibrium theory of nominal exchange rates, which offers a new perspective on various issues in open economy macroeconomics. The nominal exchange rate and portfolio choices are jointly determined in equilibrium, thus providing a new approach to overcoming the indeterminacy results in Kareken and Wallace (1981). The distinctive features of this theory are that the nominal exchange rate is determined in international financial markets, that the risk premium and UIP deviations are fully endogenous equilibrium objects and that the real exchange rate inherits its properties from the nominal exchange rate. In terms of policy, this novel theory implies that a country with an exchange rate peg and free asset mobility faces a tetralemma and not a trilemma, because it loses not only monetary policy independence but also fiscal policy independence.

title: Progressing towards efficiency: The role for labor tax progression in reforming social security
Human-capital formation: The importance of endogenous longevity
HIGHER-ORDER DEBIASED ESTIMATORS FOR GENERAL TREATMENT MODELS
abstract: We have witnessed tremendous progress in developing the foundation for econometrics and causal inference in the past decades. The most popular paradigm is the classical (first-order) semiparametric theory, in which a key building block is the (first-order) influence function. However, it is well known that estimators based on influence functions can be sub-optimal in various settings. To address this issue, higher-order influence functions (HOIF) are developed. However, most existing results in this regard focus on treatment effect parameters defined in explicit forms, such as average treatment effects (ATE). Economists are often confronted with tasks of inferring more complex parameters, such as quantile treatment effects (QTE) or effects of complicated treatment regimes/policy. These more complex parameters can often only be implicitly defined as the solution to nonlinear estimating equations, or M/Z-estimation problems. Given the foundational role of HOIF for estimating explicit parameters such as ATE, a modest step toward enriching the foundation of econometrics and causal inference is to develop higher-order estimators of those more complex parameters. Here, we consider parameters of a class of non-separable structural models in the econometrics literature. Statistical properties of the corresponding higher-order estimators are derived using recent advances in U-processes. Our proposed higher-order estimators relax complexity-reducing assumptions, quantified by Hölder smoothness, imposed on the nuisance parameters compared to existing estimators for many important examples, including QTE and quantile dose-response functions, among others.

title: Correction to: Environment and the racialization of space in US cities
Mathematical Modeling of Viral RNA Copies in Indoor Environments: Pre‐Processor for Risk Assessment and Decision‐Making Support Tool for Public Health
abstract: Quantifying human exposure to airborne respiratory viruses is essential for infection risk assessment modeling and evidence-based infection control policies. However, accurate size and time resolved estimates of airborne viral RNA copies in indoor spaces are often hindered by existing models that compress complex droplet physics into too simplified processes. Therefore, we present a size-resolved framework that couples saliva-specific evaporation and residue formation with gravitational settling to compute airborne viral RNA covering 1-2000 µm under varied temperature, relative humidity, and ambient pressure (101.325 and 75.3 kPa). Our framework also combines particle volume contribution considering saliva mass uncertainty, viral load, viral half-life, exhalation mechanisms (talking, coughing, sneezing), and ventilation effects. Under literature-based half-life inputs and volume-proportional RNA allocation, viral load and size-resolved airborne lifetime dominated the simulated RNA-copy trends, although the role of viral half-life may vary if RNA decay differs from infectivity decay or if viral RNA concentrates in long-suspended fine aerosols. Talking dominates persistence of airborne RNA copies since coughing and sneezing produce larger droplets that settle quickly. Also, model predictions are compared with hospital air-sampling datasets. The 50-percentile of saliva mass provides the closest match, with most samples falling within roughly one order of magnitude and central tendency close to unbiased. Our model is designed to serve as (1) pre-processor that supplies inputs for infection-risk assessment modeling studies and (2) decision-making support tool, facilitating public-health intervention. Therefore, we also provide an online web tool that allows users to directly adjust inputs and immediately analyze scenario-specific outcomes.

title: Presumed media influence and support for social media bans: The roles of social and elite-based validation
abstract: The study examines how presumed influences of social media on young people, as well as perceptions of how widely such beliefs are shared, shape support for social media bans. Extending the Influence of Presumed Influence (IPI) model, we introduce second-order presumed influences, defined as perceptions about how widely others presume media influences, and propose a mechanism of social validation. We additionally examine elite-based validation, referring to perceived beliefs of influential actors (i.e. scientists, politicians, and the media), as well as perceived social norms. Using survey data ( N = 1270) collected in the context of debates about a social media ban for minors under 16 in Switzerland, we find that stronger presumed influences predict support for a ban. While we find no support for social validation, the results point to the relevance of elite-related perceptions, particularly presumed scientific consensus. Perceived social norms of ban support emerge as an additional predictor of regulatory preferences.

title: Happiness in Political Communication by Men and Women Members of the US Congress
Shortcuts and scholarship: A cross-generational reflection on AI and academic formation
abstract: Generative AI is changing not just how academic work gets done, but whether the processes that build genuine understanding are happening at all. This essay, written collaboratively by an early career researcher and a senior scholar in communication and media studies, argues that the real risk is not that AI will replace researchers, but that it will quietly erode the conditions under which researchers are formed, and indeed, what counts as research process. When doctoral students can produce coherent, polished outputs without sustained reading, critical thinking, or sitting with difficulty and uncertainty, something important is lost: the slow, often uncomfortable process through which understanding develops. Drawing on communication theory, critical pedagogy, and political economy, we examine the distinction between AI as a thinking tool and AI as a substitute for thought. We also argue that meaningful change requires institutional reform, not just better pedagogy. The machines are doing exactly what they are designed to do. The question is what we are designing our universities to do.

title: Navigating Precarity: Gendered Labor Inequalities and Economic Vulnerability Among Women Journalists in Ghana
abstract: Women journalists in Ghana navigate a precarious professional environment marked by job insecurity, prolonged unpaid labor, and systemic gender discrimination within a patriarchal society. This study, based on in-depth qualitative interviews with 27 journalists, explores how precarious employment conditions shape their careers and personal lives. Ghanaian women face increased workplace exploitation, harassment, and career stagnation under weak labor protections. This study contributes to broader discussions on journalism precarity in the Global South, highlighting the need for locally grounded perspectives that reflect the unique sociopolitical and economic realities shaping women’s experiences in media.

title: A Changing Legal World: Christianity and Extraterritoriality in a Sichuan Courtroom (1810–1911)
abstract: This article examines the juridical interactions between Christian congregations and local communities in late Qing Sichuan by tracing how extraterritoriality operated in everyday judicial practice. Moving beyond accounts centered on anti-Christian violence, it analyzes how Chinese converts, non-Christian litigants, Western missionaries, and Qing officials navigated the uncertainties that imperial encroachment brought to local adjudication. Drawing on county-level judicial cases, imperial documents, local gazetteers, and missionary accounts, the study shows how Chinese Christians learned to mobilize missionary-backed extraterritorial leverage to circumvent routine barriers to legal access, while non-Christians and local elites developed strategic countermeasures to cope with foreign interference. Rather than treating extraterritoriality solely as a colonial imposition, the article argues that it became embedded as an additional, treaty-produced dimension of judicial operation in local society. By foregrounding the agency of multiple social actors, this study offers a nuanced account of how extraterritoriality reshaped late Qing local justice.

title: The Rise of Midocracy: How NPM and Post‐ NPM Reform Ideas Recombine in Contemporary Public Organizations
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper introduces and conceptualizes midocracy as an emergent organizational form in the public sector, characterized by the growth and dominance of a professionalized administrative middle layer. The study argues that midocracy draws on elements associated with both New Public Management (NPM) and post‐NPM reform agendas. While administration is essential for coordination, we show how its unchecked expansion can lead to self‐reinforcing dynamics that distance governance from core operations. Midocracy, we contend, reflects a shift from service delivery to symbolic value signaling, strategic abstraction, and polycentric goal‐setting. Our contribution is both conceptual and diagnostic, offering midocracy as a framework for understanding contemporary administrative expansion and its implications for public sector legitimacy and performance. Finally, we relate and critically examine different explanatory accounts of administrative expansion, highlighting how they interact within the dynamics of midocracy.

title: State‐Owned Enterprises as Semi‐State Actors: Explaining Regulatory Diversity in Developmental Contexts
abstract: ABSTRACT Regulatory intensity varies substantially across jurisdictions, with important implications for market development, fiscal sustainability, and state capacity. Yet existing scholarship has devoted greater attention to the consequences of regulation than to the institutional sources of its subnational diversity. This question is particularly important in developmental contexts, where governments must balance financial risk control with growth‐oriented policy objectives. This study highlights the role of state‐owned enterprises (SOEs) as semi‐state actors positioned between governmental authority and market coordination. We argue that these organizations reshape local regulatory outcomes by mediating between state authority and market activity. Using subnational evidence from China, where centralized regulatory authority coexists with pronounced local variation in implementation, we show that regions with a stronger SOE presence tend to adopt less stringent penalizing regulation. By theorizing SOEs as organizational intermediaries, this study contributes to comparative debates on regulatory governance and uneven policy implementation. More broadly, it offers a transferable framework for understanding how semi‐state actors generate regulatory diversity.

title: The balancing act of public service spaces: understanding service ecosystems and advancing the public service logic
abstract: This article advances Public Service Logic (PSL) by examining how spaces are constructed and navigated within service ecosystems. In this study, ‘space’ is understood as the relational configurations through which actors coordinate, negotiate, and enable action. Based on a study of three citizen-led cross-sector support centres for cancer patients in Sweden, the findings show that the centres address unmet needs, facilitate collaboration, and navigate boundary issues with traditional patient associations. By integrating a spatial perspective into PSL, the study introduces the concept of Public Service Space to explain how cross-sector collaborations sustain service ecosystems through relational arrangements, enabling welfare provision.

title: SDG-reporting in different regulatory contexts: A comparative study of Austrian and New Zealand state-owned enterprises
abstract: IMPACTThis study examines Sustainable Development Goal (SDG)-reporting practices by state-owned enterprises (SOEs) in Austria and New Zealand (NZ). While SDG-reporting is improving in both countries, the improvement is more pronounced in Austria. The quality of disclosures in both countries remains low; however, Austria continues to outperform NZ. The findings suggest that Austria’s integrated SDG governance framework, characterized by greater co-ordination and stakeholder engagement, is associated with more comprehensive disclosures in contrast to NZ’s decentralized SDG-reporting approach. This highlights the importance of cross-government alignment and institutional support. Larger, more profitable SOEs disclose more while high government ownership does not lead to better disclosures. This suggests that national governments are hesitant to instrumentalize their SOEs in implementing the UN Agenda 2030. The findings demonstrate how governance arrangements and organizational capabilities influence SDG-reporting in the public sector and are of interest to policy-makers in countries with the same or similar regulatory contexts.

title: From markets to missions: Where should public services meet the ‘third’ sector on this forcefield spectrum, how should they relate there, and why?
abstract: IMPACTThe article illustrates how, by defaulting to competition to handle the size and profit-motive of the private sector, guidance around public spending (on both procurement and grant) is designed expressly for managing transactional ‘market economy’ logic. The article contrasts this against logic needed for working with the ‘voluntary economy’ as a significant natural ally of the ‘public service’ economy. It highlights how the voluntary and community sector’s (VCS’s) relational leverage of voluntary resources from communities is a unique economic role played alongside governmental missions. Better differentiated understanding of all three economies, and tools for understanding who (including social enterprises) works out of which economy’s logic, will equip commissioners to make better use of existing provisions for working with the VCS. It highlights direct grant as essential for VCS ecosystem-resilience, identifying how guidance and research can equitably help such tools become business-as-usual practice under the UK government’s recent Civil Society Covenant.

title: What We Know and Don’t Know About Public Management Practices and Financial Performance: A Systematic Literature Review
abstract: Over recent decades, significant attention has been given to understanding the ways to improve performance in the public sector. However, persistent challenges in defining and measuring public sector financial performance have made it difficult to assess the effects of diverse management practices on financial outcomes. This study addresses this critical issue through a systematic literature review of studies examining the relationship between public management practices and financial performance. To guide this synthesis, we propose a conceptual framework that categorizes financial performance into capacities, constraints, and net financial condition, along with solvency classification. We also use two approaches, including Waldo (1948)’s conceptual framework and causal theories, to classify management practices used in public organizations. Our findings reveal that while many management practices are associated with improvements in certain financial dimensions, the results are often mixed and context dependent. We urge more attention to dynamic interactions between administrative efficiency and democratic governance to improve financial performance, as well as more consistent and explicit use of financial performance measures, to advance both research and practice in public management.

title: More Than Stress: How Supervisor Support Shapes the Effects of Workplace Harassment on Employee Satisfaction
abstract: This study examines the effect of workplace sexual harassment on job satisfaction by investigating the mediating role of job stress and the moderating role of supervisory support. Using data from the Sixth Korean Working Conditions Survey, the study employs the PROCESS macro to estimate mediation, moderation, and conditional process models. The results indicate that workplace sexual harassment increases job stress and decreases job satisfaction. Contrary to expectations, however, job stress does not mediate the relationship between workplace sexual harassment and job satisfaction. Instead, in the full model controlling for organizational and demographic characteristics, job stress exhibits a small but statistically significant positive association with job satisfaction, suggesting that employees’ responses to workplace sexual harassment involve more complex psychological and organizational processes than previously assumed. Supervisory support significantly influences both relationships. Although greater supervisory support reduces job stress, its positive effect on job satisfaction diminishes as the frequency of workplace sexual harassment increases. In addition, private-sector employees reported higher levels of job stress and lower levels of job satisfaction overall, whereas public-sector employees reported a slightly higher frequency of workplace sexual harassment. These findings suggest that preventing workplace sexual harassment and promoting employee well-being require managerial approaches that simultaneously consider supervisory practices, sectoral organizational characteristics, and demographic differences.

title: Why Improvements Fail in Public Service Ecosystems: Meso-Level Value Co-destruction
abstract: Why do improvement initiatives in public service ecosystems fail, even when individual actors are competent and well-intentioned? This article argues that such failures are not merely the product of isolated organizational deficiencies but are influenced by a configurational dynamic.our meso-level mechanisms—lack of direction, lack of management support, lack of autonomy, mandate, and ownership, and insufficient knowledge management—interact in a self-reinforcing cycle that converts localized value failure into systemic value decline. Drawing on a four-year longitudinal study of an improvement program in Sweden’s sick leave system, we identify a lack of management support as the primary mechanism for escalation, and the withdrawal of organizational legitimacy and resources prevent corrective responses to other failures. We further demonstrate that this cycle is reproduced by a structural ownership gap at the macro-level: because no single actor holds both the mandate and the incentive to claim stewardship of cross-boundary public services, the meso-level conditions necessary for sustained improvement are never stabilized. The implication is that meso-level value co-destruction in public service ecosystems cannot be addressed by improving individual mechanisms in isolation; it requires resolving the governance architecture that makes the self-reinforcing cycle inevitable.

title: Process as power: the legitimacy of Indigenous consultation in British Columbia environmental assessments
abstract: As the highest levels of executive government authority, power and decision-making in my home province of British Columbia deliberate over the implementation of the UN Declaration on the Rights of ...

title: Explaining divergent sustainable finance taxonomies: comparing Taiwan and South Korea
abstract: Sustainable finance taxonomies are increasingly used by governments as policy instruments to define environmentally sustainable activities and guide economic transition. How these frameworks are translated into domestic governance arrangements outside Europe remains underspecified. This article compares Taiwan and South Korea, two export-oriented East Asian developmental states that initially referenced the EU Taxonomy but produced divergent frameworks. The empirical basis comprises 2 focus groups and 10 semi-structured interviews involving 23 participants, together with 31 policy and media documents covering 2017 to 2025, analysed through within-case process tracing and cross-case comparison. The analysis traces divergence to three institutional filters: the pre-existing legal-administrative pathway through which taxonomy authority was organized, the locus of coordination authority over taxonomy design, and the configuration of organized interests around energy and industrial transition. Each filter operates as either a critical antecedent or a juncture-period causal force, channelling shared external signals into contrasting frameworks: a statutorily anchored, environment-led, transition-oriented framework in South Korea, and an administratively anchored, finance-led, disclosure-oriented framework in Taiwan. The findings indicate that policy instruments travelling across Asia acquire different governance functions when filtered through nationally embedded institutional arrangements.

title: Framing Extremist Narratives: A Multi‐Stage Computational Analysis of Discourse Structures, Emotional Mobilization, and Cross‐Platform Migration
abstract: ABSTRACT Online extremism poses a particularly difficult governance challenge when radical actors adapt and spread grievance, authority, enemy, and recruitment narratives across heterogeneous platforms. This study develops a multi‐stage computational framework for analyzing extremist narratives across platforms. Using a corpus of 22,347 English‐language documents from Twitter/X, Telegram, Gab, public web archives, and extremist‐adjacent forums posted between 2020 and 2023, the study integrates topic modeling, frame classification, psycholinguistic and emotion scoring, semantic cross‐platform matching, qualitative validation, and negative‐control checks. The findings identify eight topic clusters, six recurring narrative frames, and a platform‐migration pattern associated with semantic drift and stronger enemy‐focused framing in less‐moderated destination spaces. The results are consistent with a displacement‐and‐intensification mechanism, although they do not establish causal effects of deplatforming or individual radicalization. The study contributes to computational discourse analysis, coordinated platform governance, and frame‐aware counter‐narrative design.

title: From Perceived Reform Delivery to Vietnamese Citizens' Political Culture: Mixed‐Methods Evidence on Policy Feedback
abstract: ABSTRACT This article examines how Vietnamese citizens' perceived reform delivery is associated with political trust and modes of citizen engagement. Using a convergent mixed‐methods design, it combines a 2024–2025 cross‐sectional survey of 1594 respondents with qualitative analysis of policy documents, implementation materials, and governance assessments. The findings show a strong association between perceived reform delivery and political trust, but trust translates more clearly into low‐cost voice than into repeated participation or monitoring. Higher‐cost engagement depends more on usable information, actionable channels, and visible feedback loops. Qualitative evidence indicates that reforms generate durable policy feedback only when official commitments become verifiable everyday experiences, including predictable procedures, usable digital services, integrity enforcement, intelligible information, and responses to citizen input. The article contributes by distinguishing policy commitments, implementation signals, and perceived delivery in the study of political culture and policy feedback. Related Articles Thayer, C. A. 2010. “Political Legitimacy in Vietnam: Challenge and Response.” Politics & Policy 38, no. 3: 423–444. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1747‐1346.2010.00242.x . Duong, T. L. and Muhammad, N. S. 2026. “Illusions of Control: Authoritarian Learning and the Geopolitics of Technocratic Tyranny.” Politics & Policy 54, no. 1: e70099. https://doi.org/10.1111/polp.70099 . Béland, D., Gregory, P. M., Anahely, M., and Philip, R. 2024. “Policy Feedback, Varieties of Federalism, and the Politics of Health‐care Funding in the United States, Mexico, and Canada.” Politics & Policy 52, no. 1: 41–69. https://doi.org/10.1111/polp.12575 .

title: Follow the technology or follow the leader? Radical innovation and strategic leadership at a crossroads
abstract: Radical innovation and strategic leadership research share a foundational challenge of theorizing how firms make choices about an uncertain future that shape their competitiveness, survival, and long-term performance. Yet, each field has developed a distinct explanatory signature. Radical innovation research has followed the technology, tracing how the architecture and trajectories of technological discontinuities determine organizational fates. Strategic leadership research has followed the leader(s), tracing how the cognition, composition, and interactions of those at the organizational apex shape organizational choices. We argue that this productive division of labor is being jointly frustrated by four shifts in contemporary organizing: structurally , innovation is migrating from firms to ecosystems; technologically , AI is transforming both the creative process and the cognitive conditions of leadership; relationally , permeable boundaries are redistributing influence across actors; and culturally , evaluative criteria are expanding from performance to purpose. We identify the foundational assumptions these shifts unsettle and propose four research frontiers organized around where, how, with whom, and why radical innovation happens. We conclude with key reflections from three foundational scholars on the future of the field.

title: Education for Mobilization: The Effects of Knowledge about Labor History on Union Support
Diplomats in Camouflage: A Dataset of China’s Military-Diplomatic Engagements
abstract: Face-to-face diplomacy is central to international politics, yet existing research focuses largely on civilian leaders and diplomats. We introduce an original meeting-level dataset of China’s public military-diplomatic engagements from 2000 to 2023. Drawing on four authoritative Chinese-language party, state, and military outlets, the dataset records over 2,500 engagements involving senior Chinese military leaders and foreign counterparts. It classifies engagements as receptions in China, outbound visits, multilateral organization meetings, and defense and security fora, while preserving information on participants, timing, location, sources, and reported content. Official reporting frames these engagements primarily around cooperation and exchange. An illustrative analysis of outbound visits finds little evidence that China concentrates senior-level military outreach on U.S. allies. Outbound visits are instead positively associated with pre-existing security-specific and economic relationships with China. This dataset enables future research on how military diplomacy complements civilian diplomacy, signals strategic priorities, and shapes security cooperation, crisis management, and political influence.

title: The Power of Prognosis: Improving Covariate Balance Tests with Outcome Information
abstract: Abstract Scholars frequently use covariate balance tests to test the validity of natural experiments and related designs. Unfortunately, when measured covariates are unrelated to potential outcomes, balance is uninformative about key identification conditions. We show that balance tests can then lead to erroneous conclusions. To build stronger tests, researchers should identify covariates that are jointly predictive of potential outcomes; formally measure and report covariate prognosis; and prioritize the most individually informative variables in tests. Building on prior research on “prognostic scores,” we develop bootstrap balance tests that upweight covariates associated with the outcome. We adapt this approach for regression-discontinuity designs and use simulations to compare weighting methods based on linear regression and more flexible methods, including machine learning. The results show how prognosis weighting can avoid both false negatives and false positives. To illustrate key points, we study empirical examples from a sample of published studies, including an important debate over close elections.

title: Enjoying contradictions: The spectacular fantasy of tourism authenticity in southern Africa
abstract: This article uses Debord's ‘spectacle’ and Lacanian psychoanalysis to theorize tourism authenticity as a fantasy (i.e. a story we tell ourselves to make sense of the world). Some tourism types sell ‘authenticity’ by offering experiences of ‘pristine’ nature and ‘exotic’ people. Often, such tourist destinations are ‘spectacularized’, referring to the triumph of representations in modern capitalism that creates an ‘authentic’ reality through repetition. However, such representations are selective and conceal uncomfortable elements. They are crucial for creating and perpetuating fantasies, which sustain their appeal through desires yet remain practically unattainable. We analyze the institutionalized promotional tourism discourse surrounding the Kavango Zambezi Transfrontier Conservation Area (KAZA), in particular representations regarding nature, local cultures, adventures, and attempts to ‘do good’. Covering parts of Angola, Botswana, Namibia, Zambia, and Zimbabwe, KAZA was created for conservation, peace-building, and socio-economic development purposes, largely relying on tourism. We examine the narratives of diverse national and international stakeholders involved in KAZA and how these create and maintain an authentic fantasy in their publicity efforts. This way, we contribute to tourism studies and psychoanalytic political ecology by combining Lacanian fantasy and the specific role of spectacularization, developing a synthesis that helps to analyze and understand the appeal and implications of selling authenticity. We argue that spectacularized fantasies stimulate jouissance : a particular type of ambivalent enjoyment/pleasure that includes ‘painful’ (dark and horrific) elements that generate and sustain desire by promising illusory fulfillment while ensuring its persistent suspension by concealing underlying hierarchies and contradictions in society and nature.

title: The green territorialization of high Asia: national security, transboundary power, and the politics of climate legitimacy
Belief and Betrayal: Institutional Trust in the Shadow of Religious Violence
abstract: Religious violence erodes the moral and social fabric that binds communities, striking at the very heart of societal cohesion. As fear and intolerance spread, the foundations of institutional trust weaken, leaving nations vulnerable to deep-seated divisions and governance challenges. Present investigation analyzes the asymmetric impact of religious violence on institutional trust in 10 selected emerging countries (India, Indonesia, Pakistan, Nigeria, Egypt, Brazil, Turkey, South Africa, Mexico, and the Philippines). Departing from conventional analyses that rely on standard econometric techniques and often overlook regional heterogeneity, the present investigation uses the cutting-edge Quantile-on-Quantile method. This approach facilitates a nuanced examination of cross-country variation, enhances analytical precision, and reveals intricate, nation-specific behavioral dynamics. The results exhibit a strong negative association between religious violence and institutional trust in most sample countries. In contrast, South Africa and Mexico exhibit a mixed association. These findings underscore notable variations across quantiles, highlighting the asymmetric nature of the relationship between the variables. They emphasize that policymakers must undertake thorough assessments and formulate strategies tailored to each country’s specific social and regional contexts, ensuring that the multifaceted and sensitive link between religious violence and institutional trust is addressed effectively and in a locally responsive manner.

title: From the courtroom to the public: Judicial influence on People’s attitudes toward same-sex marriage in Japan

Talent Hoarding in Organizations
abstract: Most organizations rely on managers to identify talented workers. However, managers who are evaluated on team performance have an incentive to hoard workers. This study provides the first empirical evidence of talent hoarding using personnel records and survey evidence from a large firm. Talent hoarding is self-reported by three-fourths of managers, is detectable in manager ratings of worker talent, and occurs more frequently under stronger hoarding incentives, proxied by performance-related pay, team size, and talent visibility. Using quasi-random exposure to talent hoarding, I show that hoarding deters internal job applications, inhibiting career progression and altering talent allocation in the firm. (JEL D22, J23, L60, M12, M51, M54)

title: Merger Effects and Antitrust Enforcement: Evidence from US Consumer Packaged Goods
Community Engagement and Public Safety: Evidence from Crime Enforcement Targeting Immigrants
abstract: We study the role of victim reporting in the production of public safety. We examine the Secure Communities program, a crime-reduction policy that involved police in detecting unauthorized immigrants and increased deportation fears in immigrant communities. We find that the policy reduced the likelihood that Hispanic victims report crimes to police and increased offending against Hispanics. The number of reported crimes is unchanged, masking these opposing effects. We show that reduced reporting drives the offending increase and provide the first elasticity of offending to victim reporting in the literature, calculating that a 10 percent decline in reporting increases offending by 7.9 percent. (JEL J15, K37, K42)

title: Uncertainty and Change: Survey Evidence of Firms' Subjective Beliefs
Additionality and Asymmetric Information in Environmental Markets: Evidence from Conservation Auctions
abstract: Mechanisms that aim to reduce environmental degradation at low cost can be undermined when participants' conservation actions are not marginal to the incentive—or “additional”—as the lowest-cost participants may not be the highest social value. We investigate this challenge in the Conservation Reserve Program's auction mechanism for ecosystem services, linking bids to satellite-derived land use. Three-quarters of marginal auction winners are not additional. The heterogeneity in counterfactual land use introduces adverse selection. We develop a model of bidding and additionality to quantify welfare implications. Alternative auctions increase efficiency by using scoring rules that incorporate expected land use impacts. (JEL D44, D82, Q24, Q57, R14)

title: Professional Motivations in the Public Sector: Evidence from Police Officers
Random Utility with Unobservable Alternatives
abstract: The random utility model (RUM), a cornerstone in economics, is typically studied under the assumption that choice frequencies of all alternatives are observable. In practice, however, some alternatives have unobservable choice frequencies and are commonly aggregated into a single category called an outside option. We study RUM in such environments and derive a finite, nonredundant system of inequality constraints on observed choice frequencies that characterizes RU-rationalizability. We show that the conventional practice of aggregating unobserved alternatives can miss key information leading to incorrect conclusions such as that observed choices are rationalizable, even when no RUM is consistent with them. (JEL D11, D44, D83)

title: Remote Work and City Structure
Impacts of childhood disability on family: Labor, marriage, fertility, and depression
Green spills: Peer effects in pro-environmental behaviors
Long-run effects of technological change: the impact of automation on intergenerational mobility
abstract: Abstract We examine how automation affects intergenerational income mobility. Using Swedish register data for parents and children from 1985–2019, we study how parental exposure to robots during the 1990s shaped children’s outcomes up to thirty years later. Combining occupational exposure measures with industry- and firm-level robot adoption, we find that automation reduced children’s income and upward mobility and worsened long-run labour market and educational outcomes. These effects are concentrated among low-income families and appear driven primarily by adverse parental labour market shocks and financial strain. Our findings suggest that technological change can reduce intergenerational mobility and increase long-run inequality.

title: Understanding Cost Pass-Through when Prices are Dispersed
abstract: Abstract We study cost pass-through in a model of price dispersion where consumers differ in the number of firms they consider. By analysing how cost changes affect each quantile of the price distribution, we demonstrate how the effects on price dispersion and consumers’ expected purchase prices depend upon whether demand is log-concave or log-convex. We further show that consumers who consider fewer firms tend to experience a relatively smaller change to their surplus. This provides new insights into the distributional consequences of cost changes. Additionally, we examine the relation to demand shocks and the roles of competition and endogenous consideration sets.

title: Risk Assessment Models for Heated Tobacco Products
abstract: Heated tobacco products (HTPs) are marketed as alternatives to conventional cigarettes with a potential reduced risk profile. Yet, their actual impact on cancer and noncancer disease risk remains uncertain and requires rigorous quantitative assessment. In this study, we develop a unified and transparent computational framework for toxicological risk assessment of HTPs, integrating chemical emissions data with compound-specific toxicological thresholds derived from regulatory agencies. Our work (i) systematically reviews and harmonizes existing risk models used in the literature, (ii) formulates generalizable mathematical models for estimating lifetime cancer risk, hazard quotients, and margins of exposure that account for population demographics, smoking habits, and compound characteristics, and (iii) validates these models by reproducing published results and exploring the sensitivity of risk estimates to model parameters and emission sources. Using emissions data from conventional cigarettes and HTPs, we quantify per-compound and aggregated cancer and noncancer risks, and evaluate the relative risk reduction associated with switching from cigarettes to HTPs. The proposed risk analysis models provide a reproducible, extensible, and transparent approach for computational toxicology assessment, and can be readily applied to emerging nicotine and tobacco products within harm-reduction evaluation paradigms.

title: A Multidimensional Model of Entrepreneurial Career Success: A Literature Review and Research Agenda
abstract: People are choosing to pursue entrepreneurship as a career at increasing rates; yet, we lack an overarching conceptualization of entrepreneurial career success. Instead, scholars rely on a fragmented set of measures and outcomes, limiting cumulative knowledge about the factors that shape persistence and long-term success in entrepreneurial careers. To address this gap, we integrate career success and entrepreneurship research to develop a multidimensional model of entrepreneurial career success. Drawing on an empirically validated multidimensional framework from career literature, we organize the variety of individual success measures that have been used in the entrepreneurship literature, distinguishing entrepreneurial career success from related constructs such as venture performance and well-being. We further identify entrepreneurship-specific dimensions, including legacy and venture satisfaction, that reflect the heterogeneity of entrepreneurial careers and extend existing career success models. Using the ability-motivation-opportunity (AMO) framework, we review antecedents of entrepreneurial career success and suggest patterns of relationships with different objective and subjective success dimensions. We conclude by presenting an integrative model of antecedents, mechanisms, and boundary conditions to guide future research on entrepreneurial career success.

title: Do WhatsApp news channels help users navigate the information environment? A field experiment on information-related attitudes
abstract: Messaging applications have become central sources of news, especially in the Global South, raising concerns about the quality of information circulating in these spaces. This study examines how receiving news through WhatsApp channels shapes key information-related attitudes in Brazil, including misinformation belief, news fatigue, and media trust. In a pre‑registered experiment conducted in November/December 2024, 601 participants from multiple Brazilian states were asked to subscribe to either a regional news channel or a fact‑checking channel operated by Globo, the largest media group in Latin America. The results show that accessing news via WhatsApp does not alter more stable attitudes, such as belief in misinformation or trust. However, it does reduce news fatigue and increases engagement with news on WhatsApp. As news consumption shifts toward private messaging platforms, these findings suggest their value lies less in reshaping political attitudes and more in maintaining routine connections between audiences and journalism.

title: The politics of blame avoidance in China: A review of the field
abstract: Blame avoidance by governments and officials is common across various political systems. An increasing body of literature analyses the methods of blame avoidance utilized by both central and local governments, as well as local officials in China. This article reviews existing studies on blame avoidance in China, detailing the motivations, strategies, and limitations of these approaches. It highlights the commonalities and differences between government blame avoidance in China and in other contexts. The article also identifies gaps in the current literature, particularly the limited research on the effectiveness of blame-avoidance strategies and their implications for governance in China.

title: Poverty in Urban China 2012–2020: Applying an Income-Asset Joint Framework
abstract: Despite China’s remarkable poverty reduction, policy debates and empirical research have focused largely on rural areas, leaving urban poverty comparatively understudied. Using five waves of the China Family Panel Studies (2012–2020), this study applies an income-asset joint poverty framework to examine trends, correlates, and public subsidy coverage across protected poverty (income poor only), vulnerable poverty (asset poor only), and twice poverty (both income and asset poor). Absolute protected and twice poverty declined markedly, whereas absolute vulnerable poverty and all three forms of relative poverty remained substantial. The vulnerable poor were less likely than the protected or twice poor to receive public subsidies. These findings call for differentiated, inclusive interventions across poverty categories, especially for the vulnerable poor underserved by current support systems.

title: The Death and Life of Chinese Civil Society Mujun Zhou. Ann Arbor: University of Michigan Pess, 2026. 286 pp. $35.00 (pbk). ISBN 9780472057856
Senior Bureaucrats, Coalitions and the Quality of Government: Accounting for Effective Governance in Fragmented Settings
abstract: ABSTRACT Debates over the consequences of party and cabinet fragmentation for government performance remain unsettled. While some scholars argue that coalition governments foster instability and rent‐seeking, others contend that they enhance accountability and inclusion. This article argues that the effects of cabinet fragmentation depend on the rules of recruitment and promotion of the senior civil service. Using data from the Quality of Government Expert Survey covering 89 democracies, we examine how fragmentation interacts with both bureaucratic politicization and bureaucratic career systems. The results show that fragmentation amplifies the negative effects of politicized senior appointments, although we find limited evidence that fragmentation itself reduces the quality of government under high politicization. By contrast, fragmented cabinets are associated with more effective governance in the presence of career‐based structures characterized by internal recruitment of senior bureaucrats and long‐term careers. The findings highlight the importance of bureaucratic career structures for effective governance in multiparty systems.

title: From independence to interdependence: Mapping good governance pathways in OECD and EU economies
abstract: This study examines the interdependencies among good governance components using data from the Sustainable Governance Indicators project. Employing expectation-maximization clustering, Bayesian network-tree augmented naive Bayes classification and Bayesian structural equation modeling, the analysis reveals key governance drivers, including parties and interest associations, adaptability, and interministerial coordination. Additionally, evidence-based instruments and societal consultation amplify systemic interactions, reinforcing governance effectiveness. The findings challenge the assumption of independent governance components, highlighting synergistic and cascading effects. This study extends the application of governance theory and resource dependence theory, demonstrating the necessity of integrated governance strategies. By offering a nuanced understanding of governance dynamics, this research provides policymakers with actionable insights to enhance resilience, inclusivity, and adaptability in OECD and EU governance frameworks. Points to practitioners: Policymakers should strengthen interministerial coordination, adaptability, and societal consultation to leverage governance synergies and enhance policy coherence and implementation. Investing in data-driven policymaking—through impact assessments and policy evaluations—improves transparency, accountability, and public trust. Fostering institutional adaptability, political participation, and citizen engagement is essential for inclusive and sustainable governance in dynamic policy environments.

title: Community identity, empowerment, and willingness to co-produce: experimental evidence from urban China
abstract: Co-production is vital for effective urban governance, yet its drivers remain underexplored in China’s collectivist, state-led governance context, where prior studies overlook how individual and community factors jointly shape participation across co-production levels. This study investigates how residents’ community identity and community empowerment jointly influence three types of co-production (individual, group, and collective) using vignette-based experiments. Drawing on data from a tier-one city in China, we find that fostering community identity significantly enhances individual co-production but is insufficient to drive group and collective forms. In contrast, community empowerment emerges as a pivotal factor in promoting co-production at the group and collective levels. Notably, the motivation for group and collective co-production show no substantial differences. Situated in China’s urban grassroots governance context, these findings refine co-production theory by articulating a multi-level, level-contingent motivational framework. By demonstrating how different forms of co-production are underpinned by distinct motivational foundations, this study contributes to a more nuanced understanding of citizen engagement in state-led governance systems and offers policy-relevant insights for designing targeted strategies to mobilize diverse forms of co-production.

title: Consolidating Liberal Democracy From Within A Theory of Public Institutional Leadership
abstract: ABSTRACT Recent developments in also established democracies have made clear that public administration and management research alike have neglected giving scholarly attention to public organizations as institutions. Drawing upon research on leadership of institutions and leadership in public organizations we suggest a theory of public institutional leadership . Public institutional leadership reconnects public management with democracy by suggesting three central dimensions of leadership behaviors that instill and sustain liberal democratic values in public organizations. These behaviors include articulating and reaffirming democratic values through top‐down vision‐setting; building “character” bottom‐up through role modeling and fostering psychological safety to enable dialogue and deliberation around these values as well as demonstrating constrained responsiveness to political principals relative to those values enabled by the cultivation of bureaucratic autonomy. Although the necessity of such behaviors is made salient by rising populism and democratic backsliding, their relevance extends to public management situated in liberal democracies in general.

title: Social Capital and Policy Compliance in a Polarized Democracy: A Necessary Condition Analysis of COVID Vaccination Rates Across US Counties
abstract: ABSTRACT Policy compliance, the extent to which citizens adhere to government policies, remains a central test of democratic governance, especially during the COVID‐19 pandemic in the United States. This study examines how distinct forms of social capital—relational, structural (bonding versus bridging), cognitive, and vertical linking—serve as critical preconditions for COVID‐19 vaccination uptake in 2021. Using necessary condition analysis (NCA), we uncover nuanced and context‐specific impacts of distinct social capital on policy compliance. NCA also identifies threshold levels of various social capital required to achieve specific vaccination outcomes, yielding actionable diagnostics for policymakers and administrators. Strategies to raise compliance must align with local social capital configurations, prioritizing bridging in Republican‐leaning counties and relational support and careful use of bridging in Democratic‐leaning counties. The study advances civil society research by pinpointing the civic preconditions under which democratic institutions can function effectively in a polarized environment.

title: Accountability systems and coping in the bureaucratic environment
abstract: Advocates for strengthening accountability in government assume stronger consequences will change bureaucratic behavior. This study considers whether more strict accountability regimes change bureaucrats’ discretionary efforts. We consider this puzzle using a conjoint experiment with teachers in New York State. Our results show street-level bureaucrats in high accountability settings prioritize low-performing clients, while street-level bureaucrats in moderate accountability settings prioritize clients exhibiting high levels of effort. Overall, teachers demonstrate a weak preference to provide extra assistance to students who are hardworking and low-performing.

title: The European Universities Initiative and National Higher Education Governance in Interaction: The Case of the Arqus European University Alliance
Promising security, delivering dependency: the material constraints of EU semiconductor collective securitisation
abstract: This article argues that the European Union’s collective securitisation of semiconductors reveals an overlooked constraint in securitisation theory: the structural mismatch between the ‘urgency’ logic of securitisation, and the multi-year timescales required to develop material capacity in infrastructure-intensive technological domains. While the EU successfully constructed access to semiconductors as an existential threat and key strategic vulnerability to realising its ambitions of digital sovereignty, Europe lacks the fabrication infrastructure, workforce, and raw material access necessary to translate this discursive success into operational security. While the EU Chips Act serves as an example of a successful securitisation move in terms of policy, it does not necessarily translate into effective action. In this article, we develop the concept of material security constraints, with an emphasis on their temporal dimension, to explore how capital intensity, technical complexity, and supply chain dependencies systematically obstruct rapid implementation despite successful discursive securitisation moves. This produces a significant performance-capacity gap, whereby securitisation succeeds politically and institutionally but fails materially. The EU semiconductor case thus challenges core assumptions in (collective) securitisation scholarship and reveals the limits of digital sovereignty strategies in domains where regulatory and discursive power cannot compensate for entrenched material dependencies.

title: Cross‐Jurisdictional Collaboration, Social–Ecological Fit, and Water Quality Improvement: Evidence From the Yellow River Basin
abstract: ABSTRACT The inherent contradiction between the spatial diffusion of water pollution and administratively‐demarcated jurisdictions necessitates transboundary collaboration. A consensus has been reached that effective collaboration crucially depends on the delicate alignment of institutional arrangements with underlying social and ecological interdependencies, a concept referred to as “social–ecological fit (SEF)”. However, less is known about whether and how SEF could help collaborating local policy actors effectively solve their own water problems. Taking the Yellow River Basin of China as a case study, an auto‐logistic actor attribute model was developed to empirically examine the statistical correlations between social–ecological fit and water quality outcomes among prefecture‐level cities. Results reveal substantial heterogeneity in the effects of social network structures and SEF on water quality outcomes. Social activity is positively correlated with improvements in prefectural water quality, while social contagion and network transitivity are negatively associated with such improvement. In terms of SEF, collaborative management within the same sub–watershed improves the water quality of engaged jurisdictions, whereas collaborative management of two or more ecologically interconnected sub–watersheds shows no significant relationship with local water quality. These findings suggest that the effectiveness of collaborative governance depends on the specific forms of collaboration and SEF involved, rather than collaboration per se. This study contributes to the SEF literature by providing empirical evidence that different social and social–ecological configurations relate to governance outcomes and helps inform institutional design for collaborative responses to cross‐jurisdictional watershed governance challenges characterized by complexity and interdependency.

title: Concessions and Protest Demobilization
abstract: How and why do concessions, or promises to implement reform in the future, affect protest mobilization in autocracies? Concessions are a routine response to protest and generate a puzzling empirical regularity: Although autocrats often renege once protest abates, concessions can produce demobilization. We develop a model showing that concessions demobilize by exploiting heterogeneity among protesters. A subgroup of moderates, who derive symbolic value from the autocrat’s promise to reform, and a subgroup of radicals, who value only implemented reforms, must coordinate to sustain protest after a concession. Concessions undermine the between-group coordination necessary for protests large enough to prevent reneging. Some moderates demobilize in response to promised concessions, and in turn, declining turnout demobilizes radicals. Even autocrats in highly repressive regimes may concede because concessions and repression demobilize through distinct mechanisms. However, concessions lose efficacy as moderates lose trust in the autocrat. Morocco’s Feb20 movement illustrates the theory.
