title: How snap election calls shape vote intention uncertainty
abstract: While prior research has examined attitudinal and behavioural responses to snap elections, we know little about how the institutional act of calling a snap election shapes voters’ immediate uncertainty about their vote choice. Measuring this uncertainty through “don’t know” (DK) responses in large public opinion surveys, we show that snap election calls produce a discontinuous reduction in vote intention uncertainty that is distinct from the gradual uncertainty decline associated with regular pre-election campaigns. We demonstrate this through two cases: the 2025 German Federal Election and the 2024 UK General Election. Leveraging a quasi-experimental unexpected event design in Germany and individual-level panel data in the UK, we show that these sudden announcements accelerate the timing of vote preference formation in a way that ordinary elections do not. Yet, the distribution of effects differs across contexts: in Germany, reductions are concentrated among non-partisans, whereas in the UK they are more broadly distributed. We also demonstrate that snap election calls operate as a distinct institutional mechanism that alters the baseline of voting uncertainty before the campaign begins. In doing so, we advance our understanding of how disruptions to the electoral calendar shape the formation and expression of voters’ preferences.

title: The winner–loser gap in democratic attitudes among politicians: Individual and collective outcomes
abstract: Abstract Rooted in concerns about losers’ consent to electoral outcomes, a vast literature documents a winner–loser gap in democratic attitudes among voters, with winners displaying systematically more positive attitudes than losers across a range of indicators. Surprisingly, we know much less about whether this gap extends to politicians. This paper addresses this question both theoretically and empirically. Theoretically, we distinguish between politicians’ reactions to electoral outcomes at the individual level – whether candidates secure a seat in parliament – and the party level – whether their party enters government, and theorise about their interaction. Empirically, we present comprehensive observational evidence from 27 elections showing that losers systematically report lower satisfaction with democracy, weaker support for representative institutions, and lower perceptions of citizens’ trust. The gap is present at both levels, but the individual-level gap is conditioned by party outcomes: it is most pronounced within winning parties and disappears within losing parties. A complementary analysis leveraging close races and administrative data from Iceland provides plausibility that these associations are, at least in part, causal. Taken together, the findings reveal that democratic attitudes among rank-and-file politicians are, like those of voters, highly malleable and responsive to electoral outcomes. While politicians maintain overall positive attitudes towards democracy, this malleability raises questions about when and how such contingency might translate into anti-democratic behaviour.

title: Success and failure in complex collective decision making: The Random Exchange Decide model
abstract: We present the Random Exchange model, an extension of the bilateral exchange model of collective decision-making of Stokman and Van Oosten. Compared to more elementary models, the Random Exchange model generates predictions of the process leading to the outcome and enhances understanding of deadlock or difficulties in the negotiation process. After explaining its logic, the Random Exchange model is applied to collective decision-making in the international setting of two climate agreements, chaired by the European Union; the 2009 Climate Conference of Parties (COP) in Copenhagen, and the 2015 COP in Paris. The applications show how Random Exchange model not only may be used to predict collective decision-making outcomes but also deadlock when powerful actors attach high relative saliences to at least two issues on which they have opposite positions.

title: Elite Interactions and Social Bonds: How Partisan Cooperation Shapes Perceptions of Cross-Party Friendships
At the limits of property: Tent encampments and political life
Welfare reform and migrants’ long-term labor market integration
abstract: We study the effect of reducing welfare assistance on migrants# long-term integration in Australia. The policy postponed a migrant&apos;s eligibility for benefits during their first two years in the country. It mainly affected mothers and was announced after their arrival. Using a regression discontinuity design and 21 years of administrative welfare data, we find significant reductions in welfare receipt, where the gap widened over time, and stabilized in the long run. Benefit receipt amounts reduced by 28%, and time-on-benefits by 19%, particularly in the unemployment and disability categories. We observe larger treatment effects for mothers from disadvantaged backgrounds.

title: ESTIMATION OF RANDOM CYCLES IN PERSISTENT TIME SERIES
abstract: A number of economic, financial, and climatic time series exhibit persistent cycles which are characterized by time-dependence patterns and peaks in the spectrum. In this article, we introduce a class of semiparametric cyclical–memory processes which enable the modeling of random cyclical patterns in stationary and non-stationary time series. We develop a theoretical background and asymptotic estimation theory for the frequency of a cycle represented by the location of a peak in the spectrum. The estimation procedure is easy to implement and allows for the construction of narrow confidence intervals around the location point. Monte Carlo simulations confirm the good finite sample performance of our estimator. We illustrate our method with three empirical applications. We uncover (quasi-)periodic cycles in macroeconomic series, both nominal and real (U.S. nominal GDP and real industrial production), and <mml:math xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xmlns:mnf="http://cambridge.org/core/manifest" xmlns:cup="http://contentservices.cambridge.org" xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:m="http://cambridge.org/core/metadata" xmlns:core="http://cambridge.org/core" xmlns:c="http://cambridge.org/core/content" display="inline"> <mml:msub> <mml:mrow> <mml:mi>CO</mml:mi> </mml:mrow> <mml:mrow> <mml:mn>2</mml:mn> </mml:mrow> </mml:msub> </mml:math> $\mathrm {CO}_{2}$ upper C upper O 2 concentration levels.

title: ON ASYMPTOTIC OPTIMALITY OF LEAST SQUARES MODEL AVERAGING WHEN TRUE MODEL IS INCLUDED
abstract: Asymptotic optimality is a key theoretical property in model averaging. Due to technical difficulties, existing studies rely on restricted weight sets or on the assumption that there is no true model with fixed dimensions in the candidate set. The focus of this article is to overcome these difficulties by studying a class of least squares model averaging methods with nested candidate models, which includes Mallows model averaging (MMA) of Hansen (2007, Econometrica 75, 1175–1189) and parsimonious model averaging (PMA) of Zhang et al. (2020, Journal of the American Statistical Association 115, 972–984) as special cases. The main results are as follows. First, MMA with fixed model dimensions is neither asymptotically loss optimal nor asymptotically risk optimal. Second, when the true model dimension diverges, MMA is asymptotically both loss and risk optimal. Third, when the true model dimension is fixed, PMA is asymptotically risk optimal but not asymptotically loss optimal, which differs from the corresponding result in Fang, Yuan, and Tian (2023, Econometric Theory 39, 412–441). This finding also reveals that the discrete weight set of Hansen (2007) and the usual weight set can lead to different asymptotic properties: asymptotic loss optimality holds under the former but fails under the latter. Finally, when the true model dimension diverges, PMA is asymptotically both loss and risk optimal. Simulation studies illustrate the theoretical findings in a variety of settings.

title: Review of “Trading Beyond Understanding: Machine Learning, Risk, and Markets”
Seismic Risk of Critical Transport Systems: Sensitivity Analysis of the Campania Railway Network to Bradyseism's Features
abstract: This study examines the impact of epistemic uncertainties on the seismic risk of a critical transport system, the Campania railway network, during the ongoing bradyseismic unrest at Campi Flegrei, south of Italy. Seismic risk is quantified as the length of the railway requiring post-event inspection, an operational proxy for service disruption. A scenario-based risk formulation is adopted, integrating fragility functions for tunnels and masonry arch bridges with a ground-motion model tailored explicitly to volcanic areas. Peak ground acceleration serves as the intensity measure, whereas the annual acceptable probability of failure from the Eurocode informs safety decisions. Epistemic inputs comprise epicenter-location error and azimuth, duration-magnitude error, central-value variability in the ground-motion model, a soil term, and median fragility parameters. A regional sensitivity analysis (SA) using Latin hypercube sampling reveals that uncertainties in epicenter location have a negligible impact on the length of the inspected network. In contrast, hazard- and vulnerability-related variables, including magnitude, ground-motion median, soil class, and fragility medians, exert a strong influence. Increases in magnitude or ground-motion median, or softer soils, markedly expand the network to be inspected, whereas lower component vulnerability, such as bridges and tunnels, reduces it. A variance-based global SA extends the assessment to capture first-order and interaction effects, supporting the prioritization of data collection and model refinement to achieve the greatest reductions in disruption. The methodology provides actionable guidance for infrastructure managers to target and enhance monitoring and mitigation strategies under bradyseismic crises.

title: Patriotic Criminals: China’s Covert Netherworld in Southeast Asia and the Pacific
abstract: Existing literature on Chinese-origin transnational criminals in Southeast Asia and the Pacific Islands tends to portray the problem as a pathology afflicting China equally, or as being beyond China’s control. In contrast, this paper presents cases where there is evidence of a crime-state nexus in forms ranging from deliberate to opportunistic. It applies McCoy’s concept of the ‘covert netherworld’ to a Sinic domain where business, criminal and United Front-affiliated actors interact. In this ambiguous milieu, ethnically-Chinese criminals brush shoulders with PRC state actors, occasionally swapping favours, whilst extolling patriotism in order to legitimise their exploits to home audiences. This paper argues for a mutual benefit relationship of periodic cooperation, in contradistinction to one in which Beijing firmly directs all ethnically-Chinese criminal activities.

title: Getting the Priorities Straight: Public Values in AI Adoption
abstract: ABSTRACT Artificial Intelligence (AI) is adopted in public organizations as a transformative innovation, yet how value prioritizations unfold in AI adoption processes remains underexplored. Therefore, we ask: How do public values unfold in AI adoption processes in public organizations? We conducted a qualitative case study of an AI adoption process at the radiology department of a Dutch academic hospital after the decision to adopt is made and before implementation, using ethnographic fieldwork, interviews, and document analysis. Our findings highlight how public values and the AI adoption process are balanced in the transition from the initiation to the implementation stage. We find a recursive relationship between public values and the AI adoption process. We show an interplay of instrumental and intrinsic values. We highlight the importance of top‐down adoption decisions for how public values are perceived, and we show the importance of public organizations ensuring public values are safeguarded in public‐private partnerships.

title: Improving Cooperation in Government Purchasing Through Formal‐Relational Contracting
abstract: ABSTRACT A central challenge in government contracting is fostering cooperation between buyers and sellers where contract terms are incomplete. This article introduces a framework for formal‐relational contracting (FRC) in public sector contexts, where rigid regulations, competing values, and market imperfections make cooperation both difficult and valuable. FRC promotes cooperation through contract terms defining shared goals, guiding principles, and governance mechanisms. We present the theoretical foundations of FRC and examine its potential through 320 government contract management decision simulations where public contract managers acted as government buyers and business sellers facing sequential choices under both FRC contracts and the more conventional formal contracting approach. The results show that FRC increased managers' cooperative behavior by around 30 percentage points compared to formal contracting. Qualitative evidence further suggests that FRC shifted managers' mindsets from adversarial to cooperative. We discuss theoretical and practical implications for how FRC can enhance cooperation and mutual value in government contracting.

title: Reference points, negativity bias and citizens’ performance evaluations: a replication and extension
abstract: Experiments on how cognitive biases, such as social and historical reference points and negativity bias, shape citizens’ evaluations of government performance have produced mixed findings, which typically come from Western contexts and focus on single reference points. To address these gaps, we replicated (N = 3710) and extended (N = 2356) Olsen’s ‘Compared to what?’ to interactions between multiple social and historical reference points in Hong Kong. Very low baselines are found in the replication alongside trivial evidence for the importance of reference points in citizens’ performance evaluations and negativity bias. In the extension, we found that (1) when both social and historical reference points are presented to participants, they have stronger effects when negative information is provided and (2) the effects of combinations of historical and social reference points differ across policy domains. Though survey experiments can be noisy, the study demonstrates the value of replication to question the generalization of cognitive biases.

title: A grandparenthood gap in political attitudes? Family ties and attitudes on intertemporal redistribution
abstract: Many policy issues concern not only how we allocate societal resources today, but also how we distribute between present and future. Relations with younger family members could expand the time horizon through which societal challenges are perceived, giving more weight to future welfare. Still, whether and how family relations with younger generations matter for opinion on intertemporal redistribution issues has rarely been studied. This paper examines the relationship between family ties to children and grandchildren and willingness to bear short-term costs to ad-dress long-term issues, focusing on two policy areas: climate action and the longevity of welfare policies. Using novel survey data, including an exploratory survey experiment, collected among individuals aged 55 or older in Denmark (N = 2518), the study ﬁnds that ties to younger family members are related to a higher willingness to sacriﬁce for long-term solutions. While this relationship is observed in both policy areas in the observational study, the exploratory experimental analysis only ﬁnds this for climate policies. The paper contributes to the understanding of the relationship between family ties and political attitudes, providing insights into how emphasising familial roles can enhance the willingness to prioritise long-term societal issues.

title: Designing under uncertainty: cybersecurity policy architectures in Brazil and Chile
Co-constructing the ERC proposal: grant writing support professionals, domains of expertise and value conflicts
Getting to know her: Information and gender bias in preferential voting systems
abstract: <div> <div> <div> <p></p> <div> <div> <div> <p><span>Low voter information can disadvantage female candidates, especially in commonly used preferential voting systems where intraparty choice reduces the heuristic value of party labels. We argue that such disadvantages can be overcome by (1) providing voters with candidates’ biographical information, and (2) making preference voting compulsory. The former can reduce bias or gender-based informational asymmetries, while the latter can counteract inequalities in the use of preference voting by men and women. We test our expectations with two survey experiments conducted during open-list proportional representation elections in Japan, where women’s representation has notoriously lagged. The results confirm that each experimental treatment (information and compulsory preference voting) increases support for women candidates, both among the actual candidates running and in a post-treatment conjoint experiment featuring hypothetical candidates. These findings underscore how simple rule changes can potentially reduce barriers to women’s electoral success in preferential voting systems.&nbsp;</span></p> </div> </div> </div> </div> </div> </div>

title: The Legislative Effectiveness of Congressional Oversight Reports
abstract: ABSTRACT This article assesses the linkage between the House and Senate oversight committees' reports and subsequent legislative efforts in those policy areas from the 106th to the 116th Congresses (1999–2020). The analysis finds support for the three proffered hypotheses. First, the policy topics covered in the reports spur the referral of bills on those topics to the oversight committees. Second, the oversight reports on topics that the majority staff releases are more reflected in downstream legislative activity than the topics covered in the minority staff reports. Finally, the majority's advantage in pushing legislation related to its oversight reports' topics is greater in the House than it is in the Senate. These initial findings substantiate the importance of gathering and coding congressional oversight reports for not only how Congress conducts oversight, but also how it legislates.

title: Urban refugee children's integration through a spatial lens: Everyday emotional geographies in two cities
abstract: With over 60% of refugees living in urban areas, understanding refugee children's urban citizenship and integration is critical yet remains underexplored. This article frames analyses of refugee children's urban integration by treating it as a fundamentally spatial problem, rather than primarily a legal or policy one. Situated within political geography, it argues that the urban neighborhood—through its infrastructures, institutions, and everyday encounters—operates as a key site where governance is enacted and where citizenship and (non)citizenship are practically negotiated. By foregrounding spatial relations, it makes visible dimensions of legal liminality that are often flattened in policy-centric accounts. Ambiguous legal status is experienced through access to schools, mobility constraints, and contested claims to public space, producing distinct everyday emotional geographies of belonging, fear, or uncertainty. Methodologically, the article proposes a mixed, child-centred spatial approach and provides two different examples of how it was used to understand urban refugee integration. In Kampala, teachers' perceptions and geospatial analyses of school and residential patterns show how location and school-level opportunity structures mediate educational access amid uncertainty. In Tel Aviv, residents' perceptions, children's accounts, and municipal and traffic data show how everyday encounters in contested spaces shape safety, recognition, and exclusion. Read in juxtaposition, the cases generate broader conceptual insights into how spatial politics, refugee policy, and urban inequality co-produce refugee children's integration, underscoring spatial analysis as essential for understanding children's urban non-citizenship.

title: Consistency, not waste aversion, explains apparent sunk‐cost effects in politics
abstract: Abstract Do sunk costs shape how voters judge political leaders, or do reputational signals carried by current choices dominate? Across three preregistered experiments (total N = 1462) using vignettes about a national rail project, we orthogonally manipulated sunk costs (high vs. absent), leaders' decisions (continue vs. abandon), campaign commitments (pro, anti, none), and reminders of prior voting behavior. In Experiment 1 ( N = 346), Bayesian ANOVA showed that evaluations (vote likelihood, perceived honesty, competence) were reliably higher when leaders continued rather than abandoned a project, with no main effect of sunk costs and no interaction. Experiment 2 ( N = 719) replicated the null sunk‐cost effect and further found no effect of campaign commitments once the leader's current decision was known. Experiment 3 ( N = 397) used a structural equation model to test mediation: perceived commitment—but not perceived sunk costs—robustly predicted evaluations, and abandonment sharply reduced perceived commitment; prior‐vote cues were weak and did not mediate effects. Together, the studies indicate that people take continuation to signal commitment and view it positively, whereas abandonment stopping signals a breach of commitment and is penalized. Apparent sunk‐cost sensitivity in politics may often reflect a premium on consistency rather than waste aversion. We discuss implications for designing “face‐saving” off‐ramps and reframing evidence‐based reversals as fidelity to higher order commitments.

title: AAPOR Presidential Address AAPOR Presidential Address 2026: Bearing Witness to This Moment
abstract: When I first became AAPOR’s vice president/president-elect in 2024, I thought I might focus my presidential address on something like “the business of research,” reflecting my perspective as chief business officer of a research company and considering how the association might think about its financial stability and growth. Then in 2025, a little something happened… A new administration arrived and took a chainsaw to the statistical and scientific institutions of this country. A national leader sued and threatened some of the most public faces of our industry. And the economic fallout of these and other actions shook our industry to the core. Once I got out of the fetal position, I had to grapple with new priorities for my AAPOR presidency. So today, what I want to do is bear witness to this time we are living through and provide hope for the future. There are four things I will reflect on: the moment we are in; the work we do; the community that makes that work possible; and how we respond to these times. I want to present not just my own voice, but those across our community. To do so, I have talked to members from a wide variety of fields, experiences, and circumstances. I share their views, along with my own, and I thank them for the honesty, vulnerability, and inspiration they gave me. We are living through a period of profound instability in the systems that produce and protect evidence. The federal statistical system—one of the pillars of how we understand this country—has faced extraordinary pressure. Programs have been halted. Funding has been threatened or withdrawn. Statistical leaders have been dismissed. Institutions designed to operate independently have faced increasing political pressure. Many of us have lost our jobs or found our work threatened. The American Statistical Association reported that all 13 federal statistical agencies lost staff in 2025, with some, like the National Center for Education Statistics (NCES)—at least temporarily—almost totally demolished (American Statistical Association 2025). The shuttering of USAID halted critical research projects and is projected to lead to a staggering number of avoidable deaths (Cavalcanti et al. 2025). These systems were built over decades. The people who have dedicated their lives to these objectives have created a body of knowledge that is essential to understanding the way we live and how that changes—the statisticians and survey methodologists, analysts and researchers, project managers and directors, contractors and subcontractors. There has been messaging through DOGE actions and other high-level communications that the work of these individuals is biased, wasteful, unneeded, or worse. Many of those people are members of this community. And this rhetoric and these actions are having a profound effect. One experienced federal researcher told me she was considering getting out of the field altogether. She couldn’t see a path forward for herself. We are losing some of our greatest assets and future leaders. For those that remain, we bear witness to their integrity, persistence, and quiet professionalism as they continue to produce evidence when the environment around them is uncertain and unsupportive. We see and empathize with the “survivors’ guilt” many experience. We also recognize the disruption in the lives of many who have lost their positions and now face remaking their careers. They must do so at a time when uncertainty and trepidation have affected the entire industry, making it a less-than-hospitable place for job seekers and career changers. A displaced federal worker I spoke to said she feels a sense of grief and loss. Grieving not only for her own personal losses, but for the bigger picture of what is happening to federal government data collection, to public health research, and to the scientific community. I spoke to a small business owner who saw critical work that she and her colleagues had done shelved, to possibly never see the light of day. A graduate student shared with me the challenges she has experienced—having her research funding terminated, seeing fewer placements for her fellow students at universities, and being forced to grapple with new worries about her international student status. She said, “When I was coming to the US, I didn’t think that I would have to worry that scientific research could be compromised in a country like this.” Others shared: “The last 18 months have felt like a ticking countdown clock”; “The institutional knowledge we have lost will take years to recover”; and “The foundation is shakier than I thought.” I want to acknowledge the extreme stress that has characterized our field and so many of our members in 2025 and 2026 and bear witness to the professional and personal toll this has taken. Next, I want to talk about the importance of our work. At its core, what we do is deceptively simple. We ask people about their lives—how they live, think, work, and experience the world. We do so carefully, systematically, and with the goal of understanding more than just the loudest voices. The importance of that work becomes clearer in moments like this, when increasingly, we are living in a world where the idea of shared evidence itself is contested. Where data can be dismissed because it is inconvenient. Where research can be labeled fraudulent if it challenges power. Some specific examples of this are the lawsuits against Ann Selzer (Doyle 2024); the litigation threats to the New York Times (Svirnovskiy 2026), CNN (Grynbaum and Haberman 2020), and their research partners; the demand for cancellation of programs deemed focused on DEI (Exec. Order No. 14151 2025; Hsu 2025); and the removal of nonbinary gender categories from federal research (Exec. Order No. 14168 2025), to name just a few. This runs counter to everything our field stands for. We may never measure perfectly. But through rigorous methods and transparency, we highlight the experiences, hopes, and fears of everyday Americans. In a democracy, that matters. Because governing without understanding the public is governing in the dark. What we produce is not just data. It is a record. A record of what people think, what they experience, and how society is changing. We must protect that, celebrate it, and feel pride in the importance of the work that we do. A researcher at the Census told me that she was most proud to be part of a system where, despite current narratives, the goal is to “measure truth, to the best of our ability, across time, across administrations, and across events.” Through all of this, the work continues. A statistician at a large research company spoke of his pride in what we do. He said, “Linking what people are thinking and saying to policy has never been more important.” I now want to reflect on the community, because this work does not happen in isolation. It depends on a diverse and interdependent community. The work we do is the product of government, academia, nonprofit organizations, and the private sector. Each plays a distinct role. Government statisticians establish benchmarks. Academics develop and test new ideas and train future researchers. Nonprofit and election researchers help us understand civic life. And commercial researchers innovate—finding ways to make data collection more scalable and accessible. We often approach problems differently. We use different methods. We operate under different constraints. We do not always agree (looking at you, AAPORnet). We debate probability and nonprobability sampling (boy, do we debate probability and nonprobability sampling!). We debate qualitative and quantitative approaches. We debate new tools, new data sources, and, more recently, artificial intelligence. These debates can be intense. They can feel divisive. But they exist because we are all trying to answer the same questions: How do we understand people accurately? How do we do this work responsibly? And how do we do it within real-world budgetary and time constraints? Our disagreements are a sign of a healthy scientific community—a community that makes our work possible, improves it, and, at times, helps us bear it. Multiple people I spoke to talked about the importance of having people to turn to that believe in the work that we do, to bounce ideas off of, to call when we need questions answered. A sympathetic human to talk to, not an obsequious chatbot. The government employees I spoke to remarked on how important this community has been in making it possible to keep going when they felt disparaged, and in helping make connections in the search for a new opportunity. A private-sector researcher reflected on how we share expertise to improve the work for us all, even when there could be commercial reasons for not doing so. A multicultural researcher noted that perhaps our recent struggles have brought us together. She said, “I have co-pollinated with so many others that I wouldn’t have before, because we’re working through the same struggles.” A methodologist at a start-up company noted that through all this craziness, he is seeing more acceptance and creativity in our community; more openness to the wide variety of practices and innovations. I can see frustration among our ranks as we debate how to respond to today’s challenges, how to move forward, how to value and publicize what we do. Some have called for the community to have a stronger voice. Some have expressed that doing so would put their membership at risk. Some have suggested our separating ourselves based on method. Some have felt marginalized, seeing the work that they do categorized as lesser. I urge our community to recognize that what unites us is more important than our differences. Remember that your fellow researchers are seeking to do just what you are doing—increase our understanding of a given population or issue. They may be doing it with different methods, budgets, and styles, but we are united in seeking clarity, and we are family in this enterprise. Be kind to each other. Seek to understand and empathize. Show respect for your fellow researcher, even if the work that they do seems only marginally connected in our big Venn diagram of the research industry (see figure 1). Humorous Venn diagram depicting our shared commitment to research. Now, what do we do with all of this? How will we respond to this moment—not just endure it, but build a more resilient, innovative, and inclusive future for our field? This is why AAPOR is so important. Through AAPOR we can support the work and strengthen the community that makes it possible. AAPOR facilitates the critical work of public opinion research by creating task forces, providing forums for debate and discussion, educating on best practices, and evolving standards for the industry. Our work on cell phone samples and text messaging has paved the way for the wide use of new methodological tools. Our pre-election polling task forces have changed the way we conduct and talk about election research. Our reports on opt-in and probability panels have given us frameworks for transparency and a shared language for these sample sources, to name just a few examples. Our response to these times should be to keep driving forward. We must continue what AAPOR has done for 81 years—help the industry understand itself, improve what we do, and identify new challenges and opportunities. In the past 18 months, through these challenging times, AAPOR has released major resources on pre-election polling (American Association for Public Opinion Research 2025a), establishment surveys (American Association for Public Opinion Research 2025b), texting for research (American Association for Public Opinion Research 2025c), linking survey and nonsurvey data (American Association for Public Opinion Research 2025d), and, most recently, on responsible AI integration (American Association for Public Opinion Research 2026). We have updated our code of professional ethics and practices, hosted webinars and short courses, organized new workshops, and put together two major conferences. Table 1 highlights a small selection of these achievements. Selected AAPOR resources and activities produced during 2025–2026. All of this is carried out by volunteers, supported by a small staff, who work collaboratively, from their different vantage points and experiences, to express the latest information about our field. Keeping this collaborative enterprise going is what will keep our industry vibrant and resilient through these times, and it is what AAPOR does best. AAPOR’s response is also to foster the community doing this important work. We are A Meeting Place (American Association for Public Opinion Research 2020). Every year, through our conference, we provide an opportunity to come together to share ideas and network. If lately the conference has felt like a therapy session (as in figure 2), it is needed for us to support each other during these times. Cartoon highlighting AAPOR’s annual conference as a place for mutual support around the emergence of AI. Created by author using ChatGPT. We also need to ensure that our industry is expanding and inclusive. AAPOR’s commitment to diversity has helped reshape the field and made this organization stronger and better able to respond to today’s challenges. We must continue to prioritize this. The AAPOR Affinity Groups give us more ways to connect and share our challenges. As shown in table 2, today we have 11 Affinity Groups, including ConsultPOR, formed in early 2026 in part as a reaction to the movement of practitioners out of traditional employee settings into business for themselves, and the Global Research Affinity Group, inaugurated at our May 2026 Conference. List of AAPOR Affinity Groups as of May 2026. We need to provide tangible, practical support to our community as well. Last year, when so many faced layoffs, travel restrictions, and financial hardships, we rallied as a community and raised a record amount of donations to support conference travel grants. We also provide upskilling sessions, professional development, job coaching, and networking opportunities, all led by volunteers in this room and beyond. In terms of our individual responses, the people I spoke with offered a clear message: steady on, stay curious, and do this together. One academic said, “We need to keep doing what we have always been doing—learning, innovating, and using evidence-based approaches.” A business owner urged us to “lean into the unknown.” And a student reminded me that when we multiply our efforts with others, “it’s way stronger than we can imagine.” My call to action today reflects these sentiments. Stay the course, seek help when you need it, and provide a hand up to another when you can. And don’t give up. Because what we do is important. The industry has faced challenges before: shifts in methodology, new technologies, declining response rates, new forms of data, and now a double whammy of a federal administration hostile to research and the rapid proliferation of artificial intelligence. What do we do? We engage with these challenges. We communicate our values. We set standards. We adapt our practices. And we continue the work. Get involved. AAPOR needs each of you. Join a committee. Say “yes” if I ask you to run for council! Ask me, or any of us on council, how to participate. Be a deeper part of this organization that provides a voice, a space, and a framework for what we do. Get involved outside of AAPOR, too. Write local op-eds, contact your representatives, reach out to colleagues in need, and support causes that support the industry, including AAPOR. Join us in this moment, in this community, and in being the way forward. As I close, I want to return to where I began. How do we bear witness to the moment we are living through? And how do we ensure that this work and this community can thrive in the years to come? AAPOR has existed for more than eight decades. Through profound change, the purpose of this work has remained remarkably consistent: to create valid and transparent data about behaviors, attitudes, and characteristics that enable informed societal decision-making. That work is not always easy. But it remains essential. Because no society can understand itself without evidence about the people who live within it. When we do this work well—carefully, ethically, and openly—we create something larger than a dataset, report, or publication. We create a record of the public’s voice. In that sense, this field helps our society bear witness to itself. One of the people I talked to said, “We are writing history right now.” How we respond to this moment is something future researchers will examine. They will seek to understand the foundations of our systems that produce evidence. They will ask how those systems were challenged. And they will ask what we did in response. Our responsibility is to strengthen what we do, improve our tools, defend our standards, and support one another. We continue by doing what this field has always done: help the public be heard, help society understand itself, and strengthen the democracy that depends on both.

title: Clause and Effect: Theory and Field Experimental Evidence on Noncompete Clauses
College, Cognitive Ability, and Socioeconomic Disadvantage: Policy Lessons from the U.K. in 1960–2004
abstract: Abstract University access has significantly expanded in OECD countries, and further growth figures prominently in political agendas. We study possible consequences of historical and future expansions in a stochastic, general equilibrium Roy model where tertiary educational attainment is determined by cognitive ability and socioeconomic disadvantage. In our analysis, individual productivity depends not only on education but also directly on cognitive ability. The expansion of university access in the U.K. that started in the 1960s provides an ideal case study to draw lessons for the future. We find that this expansion led to the selection into college of progressively less talented students from advantaged backgrounds. Appropriate counterfactual policies existed that would have achieved the dual goal of increasing college graduates’ cognitive ability while improving tertiary education opportunities for the disadvantaged.

title: Household consumption and savings over the life cycle: The roles of demographics and durables
Migration Incentives and Elderly Health: Evidence from the Hukou Reforms in China

Career guidance and investments in education: Experimental evidence from Cambodia
The Returns to Viral Media: The Case of US Campaign Contributions,
abstract: Abstract Social media has created new, highly competitive markets for attention. But to what extent does attention on social media generate tangible economic returns and how are these returns characterized? Using a daily dataset of Twitter activity and campaign contributions for US Members of Congress (2019-2020), we show that attention on Twitter, as measured by likes, increases small donations. However, the effect is highly skewed: only a few members benefit substantially, consistent with a winner-takes-all market. These results are confirmed using a geography-based causal design tracking donation patterns across counties, showing that the increase in donations from attention on Twitter comes disproportionately from high Twitter usage areas.
journal_name: Journal of the European Economic Association

title: Coupling Labor Supply Decisions: An Experiment in India,
abstract: Abstract Joint household decision-making becomes more common as economies develop. Can external intervention advance this transition? We study this question in the context of female employment in India. We randomized which spouse was given a ticket enabling enrollment in a women’s weaving job, and cross-randomized the other to receive no information about the ticket, information, or information and discussion with their spouse. Academic and local experts predict information and discussion should raise enrollment. Instead, information had no effect, and discussion reduced enrollment by 50%. We do not find an effect of giving the wife the job ticket rather than the husband. Our results show that interventions toward joint decision-making about an opportunity can lower take-up.
journal_name: Journal of the European Economic Association

title: Monetary Policy, Bank Fragility, and the Modern Financial Intermediation
abstract: This article reviews recent research on monetary policy transmission through banks and the broader financial intermediation sector, and its implications for financial stability. Traditional banks remain fragile due to high leverage and maturity transformation, making them vulnerable to interest rate, credit, and liquidity shocks. Meanwhile, the rise of nonbank intermediation—now involved in most lending—has reshaped how credit is originated, funded, and distributed, complicating policy transmission and regulation. We examine evidence on six key adjustment margins of monetary policy transmission through banks and the financial intermediation sector: ( a ) balance sheet valuation, ( b ) loan retention, ( c ) securities holdings, ( d ) shadow bank lending substitution, ( e ) deposit substitution, and ( f ) bank-to-nonbank lending. These channels often reallocate credit in response to monetary and capital shocks rather than just altering its aggregate level, highlighting the need for a system-wide perspective that reflects the adaptive, interconnected nature of modern financial intermediation.

title: What Every PhD Student Should Know About Adam Smith
abstract: Widely known as the father of economics, Adam Smith lived in the eighteenth century. Smith was a polymath, and his magnum opus, The Wealth of Nations , is 250 years old this year. In this article, I suggest the nature of Smith's contribution to economics, moral philosophy, and political science. Scholars participating in these fields today tend to see them as separate domains of inquiry. Not so for Smith. I study three main aspects of Smith's political economics. First is his economics; second is his fresh understanding of the political and economic problems confronting the nations of Western Europe when they were developing; and finally (and more briefly) is his moral theory. As I show, the problems facing developing countries of early modern Europe were not unlike those problems facing today's developing countries. Smith approaches these problems from an integrated perspective.

title: The Macroeconomics of Market Power
abstract: This review surveys the literature on the macroeconomics of market power. Since 1980 various aggregate measures of market power, such as markups, profit rates, and market capitalization, have increased in the United States and around the globe. We find that the rise of markups is due in large part to the reallocation of market shares and to the rise of the inverse expenditure share on variable inputs, whereas output elasticities have not risen. We analyze the macroeconomic causes and consequences of this process and use a model to evaluate the potential mechanisms. Key is the underlying heterogeneity in the distribution of parameters, which passes through to heterogeneity in the distribution of outcomes such as output, the labor share, profits, and welfare. Focusing on aggregate measures of market power is misleading, as the same aggregate markups can be associated with different output and welfare. We conclude with a discussion of how competition policy can be a tool not only for restoring economic efficiency but also for redistribution, depending on how the markups and underlying parameters are distributed.

title: Market Power in Artificial Intelligence
Africa as a Success Story: Political Organization in Precolonial Africa
The Bureaucratic Paradox of Citizen Agency: Institutional Crowding‐Out in Government‐Catalyzed Co‐Production in Shanghai, China
abstract: ABSTRACT Public service co‐production is often framed as a means of creating public value, yet its dynamics are complex when citizen‐led participation is catalyzed by strong public institutions. This mixed‐methods study examines government‐catalyzed, citizen‐centric co‐production in Shanghai, China, where the state provides institutional support, policy legitimacy, and infrastructure while citizens undertake much of the work of deliberation, coordination, and implementation. Drawing on 246 interviews and survey data from 1476 residents involved in community new infrastructure projects, we examine how citizen trust, public‐service‐oriented motivation, and perceived co‐production efficacy are associated with process and outcome value creation, and how perceived institutional settings condition these relationships. The findings show that citizen cognitive factors are positively associated with value creation, while stronger perceived institutional settings can negatively moderate these relationships. Recursive qualitative analysis suggests two mechanisms that help interpret this pattern: formal rigidity may crowd out citizen agency in the co‐production process, while informal social density may generate lock‐in effects that weaken the translation of trust into substantive outcomes. The study contributes to co‐production and institutional theory by specifying the boundary conditions under which institutional support becomes over‐institutionalization. Effective co‐production requires not less government, but strong enabling support at the initiation stage combined with greater local discretion, participatory rule revision, and flexible enforcement.

title: Hybrid bureaucracy: The relationship between digital technologies and institutional arrangements in public welfare agencies
abstract: Public agencies are strategically adapting and applying digital technologies to improve their business processes and deliver greater value to society. This development has a profound impact on the agencies' institutional arrangements. While some services that the agencies offer are almost fully automated, others still require a high level of caseworker involvement. The variance in levels of automation and the coexistence of different institutional arrangements within the same agency are interesting and challenging because they contradict predictions made by both scholars and policymakers. Therefore, we present a study of three large Scandinavian public welfare agencies, utilizing document analysis supplemented by interviews with top managers and senior IT and business developers. We apply Bovens and Zouridis' (2002) typology of street-, screen-, and system-level bureaucracies as our main analytical lens, combined with Christensen and Lægreid's (2011) concepts of hybridity and sedimentation, with a socio-technical perspective in the background. We contribute to digital government and public administration research by enhancing theoretical understanding of the relationship between digital technologies, institutional arrangements and organizational trajectories. Specifically, we identify the hybrid bureaucracy as a composite, multifunctional organizational entity that encompasses several institutional arrangements simultaneously and combines aspects of street-, screen-, and system-level bureaucracies while also exhibiting its own distinct characteristics.

title: Editorial Board
From Everywhere to Somewhere: understanding the spatial limits of AI's political power
Care, competence, or control? The evolution of parental supervision tools on social media platforms: A cross-platform comparison
abstract: Interaction with social media constitutes a significant part of children’s online experiences, with the potential for both positive and negative experiences. Social media platforms provide parental “supervision tools” as a mechanism for balancing children’s autonomy with safeguards, promoting this function to parents to ensure safer digital practices for their children. This research adopts a constructivist framework to investigate the evolution and operationalisation of parental supervision across Instagram, Snapchat, and TikTok. Utilising qualitative methodology, this study combines archival data from an ethnographic walkthrough conducted in 2024, simulating a child’s and parent’s account for each platform. The cross-platform comparison reveals how platforms construct parental responsibility through their discursive and interface supervision mechanisms, expressed through macro-narratives, meso-contexts, and micro-practices. In doing so, platforms shift responsibility for regulation to parents as the accountable supervisory actors, while ultimately also controlling the supervision practices of these parents through the affordances and constraints offered through supervision tools.

title: Navigating Ambiguity: Street-Level Managers Discretion in the Implementation of Religious Policy in Divided Societies
abstract: This study explores the intersection of religion and state through a single-case, mixed-methods research design, focusing on Israeli state elementary school principals, who administer religious directives embedded in state legislation. We ask: Under what conditions street-level managers’ discretion in policy implementation increases social satisfaction and cohesion? We argue that such discretion increases social satisfaction and cohesion under the following conditions: (1) When state policies are explicitly or implicitly vague and flexible, (2) When official policy is contested among societal groups, and (3) When street-level managers opt to respond to client preferences. In addition, we suggest that public satisfaction with the resulted public services increases when a manager's personal ideology aligns with client attitudes and expectations. The study demonstrates how principals exercise significant discretion in implementing religious policy and thus contributes to broader public administration literature by highlighting the role of street-level managers in navigating policy ambiguity, while mediating societal tensions.
journal_name: The American Review of Public Administration

title: The politicization of public policy in Indonesia: A Global South perspective
abstract: Abstract This study examines the systemic politicization of public policy in Indonesia, rooted in its historical, political, and sociocultural contexts. Adopting a Global South perspective, it challenges Northern-centric frameworks by showing how political elites strategically set agendas to consolidate power, while bureaucrats respond through adaptive strategies prioritizing visibility over substantive service delivery. Analysis of official documents from Indonesia’s Supreme Audit Agency, Corruption Eradication Commission, Ombudsman (2023–2025), and Ministry of Administrative Reform (LAKIP 2022–2024) reveals systematic decoupling: performance metrics indicate progress, yet independent assessments show persistently medium service quality at 74.64 percent. Donor influence fosters isomorphic mimicry, with 43 percent of foreign-funded e-government platforms inactive. The study develops a five-dimensional framework, elite agenda-setting, bureaucratic adaptation, donor-induced isomorphism, symbolic compliance, and digital governance paradox, capturing their self-reinforcing interaction. This framework offers an analytical tool for understanding governance in Indonesia and comparable Global South contexts.

title: Power Through Visibility: How Policy Narratives Matter in Climate Change Debate on X
Affective, but not ideological, polarization increases tolerance for undemocratic behavior
abstract: Abstract Over the last years, there have been frequent claims that democracy may be endangered by polarization, which has the potential to push voters and elites to embrace undemocratic practices and hence pave the way for democratic backsliding. But what is more decisive to generate tolerance to such practices: ideological or affective proximity? This article examines the effect of ideological vis-à-vis affective polarization on support for undemocratic practices. By using a conjoint experiment fielded in Catalonia in a sample of citizens and politicians, we find that both voters and elites overall reject politicians with undemocratic attitudes in a sizable and consistent way. Among citizens, while ideological proximity does not mitigate punishment of undemocratic attitudes, affective polarization does: individuals with a more intense affection toward their candidate’s party are less prone to punishing him/her for eroding the losers’ consent. The article has important implications for our understanding of the relationship between affective and ideological polarization, and support for democratic undoing.

title: Contemplating Conquest: Public Opinion on the Forcible Seizure of Territory
abstract: ABSTRACT The norm against conquest—a central tenet of the international order—is eroding. This study is among the first to examine public support for this norm, using a real-world case: Israel’s seizure of Syrian territory following the collapse of the Assad regime in December 2024. Our survey experiment in Israel reveals that citizens are sensitive to the prohibition on conquest. They demonstrate greater support for an occupation that involves only military control of the forcibly seized territory and weaker support for civilian settlement in or annexation of the foreign territory: policies that amount to conquest. Our finding—a stronger preference for legally acceptable occupation over illegal settlement or annexation—sends a positive signal for the constraining power of norms.

title: Reconciliation, Decolonization of Relationships, and Egalitarian Bi-nationalism: A Praxis for the Israeli–Palestinian Impasse?
abstract: In this article, I interrogate the theoretical architecture that underpins three increasingly influential normative prescriptions for a just political configuration in Israel–Palestine: reconciliation, decolonization of relationships, and egalitarian bi-nationalism (RDB-N). Although recent scholarship has attempted to integrate them into a shared framework, they remain insufficiently articulated, delaying the emergence of a transformative praxis. Here, I argue that the core impasse lies in the dominant “top-down” conception of reconciliation, which, by presuming that a postconflict political order is a prerequisite for implementation, produces a dependency that obstructs the normative potential of RDB-N as a coherent framework for structural transformation. In response, I advance a “bottom-up” conception of reconciliation that is both theoretically plausible and normatively desirable. This reimagines reconciliation as an implementation-driven and grassroots dynamic capable of initiating decolonial transformation and prefiguring an egalitarian binational future, rather than a postconflict process led by the state and its institutions. In proposing this theoretical rearticulation, I set the groundwork for a new praxis of RDB-N grounded in localized political agency. The analysis culminates in the Palestinian Community of Israel (PCI), whose liminal position and situated political condition potentially make it a particularly fertile site for developing such a praxis. Although largely theoretical, this contribution has practical implications for conflict resolution, settler-colonial critique, and political transformation in asymmetric contexts. It also opens avenues for future empirical and normative research into both justice in non-ideal conditions and collective action.

title: Grounding Hope in Trust: The Case of Climate Activism
abstract: According to the standard definition of hope, for one to be hopeful, the desired outcome must be considered at least possible. The literature on climate activism has incorporated this notion of hope, but we argue that this notion alone cannot fully account for hopeful attitudes in situations where collective action is demanded. For hope to be justified in the case of climate activism, it must be supported by some form of trust. We then outline different forms of trust that can be found in activist practices to ground hopeful attitudes, including procedural and moral trust in institutions and in fellow citizens or activists. We finally argue that mistrust represents a democratic equilibrium between the activists’ duty to exercise vigilance and critique toward institutions and the need for institutions to be perceived as trustworthy by activists and citizens more broadly.

title: Measuring racial attitudes pre-treatment in survey experiments
abstract: Abstract Experimental researchers often need to assess the moderating effect of racial attitudes. However, it is unclear whether the racial attitude battery deployed may bias treatment effects. Less subtle batteries could bias treatment effects toward zero if measuring racial attitudes primes these attitudes for subjects assigned to all conditions, including the control condition. We assess whether bias is introduced across four conditions, pre-treatment: not measuring racial attitudes, using stereotype endorsement measures, using the American National Election Study racial resentment battery, or using the simplified Cooperative Election Study racial resentment battery. We do not uncover widespread instances of treatment bias. However, we do identify bias when the stereotype endorsement measures are used pre-treatment. We conclude with recommendations for researchers.

title: Debriefings in misinformation research should include fact-checks to correct misperceptions and increase perceived learning
abstract: Abstract Debriefings are a cornerstone of ethical research, especially when deception is used. In misinformation experiments, debriefings both disclose the deception and warn participants about misinformation. Unlike other misinformation interventions, they reveal that researchers deliberately introduced the falsehoods, raising concerns about trust and skepticism. In a preregistered U.S. experiment (N = 896), we compare no debriefing, a general debriefing, and a specific debriefing with fact-checks and source links. Only the specific debriefing reduced belief in false claims participants saw, not in novel ones. The general debriefing slightly reduced belief in true news, suggesting warnings may heighten skepticism. Both improved attitudes toward the study and perceived transparency, supporting the use of specific debriefings as an ethical and effective practice in misinformation research.

title: Right-wing terrorism and far-right support: evidence from anti-Roma attacks in Hungary
abstract: Abstract How do ethnically motivated terrorist attacks shape electoral support for the far right? We study a unique case: a coordinated series of anti-Roma murders in Hungary in 2008–2009, the most severe episode of anti-minority violence in the country since World War II. Combining difference-in-differences and synthetic control methods, we compare attacked settlements to multiple counterfactuals, including planned-but-unrealized targets. We find that Jobbik, Hungary’s radical right party, gained 11–14 percentage points more support in attacked villages than in comparable controls in the 2010 election—an increase 53–70% larger than baseline trends. The effect persisted for several years and spilled over to nearby settlements. In contrast to some research from Western Europe suggesting that right-wing terrorism can reduce far-right appeal, our findings highlight how deep-seated prejudice can reverse this pattern. The results underscore the importance of antecedent inter-group relations in conditioning political reactions to ethnic violence.

title: Care and Contemporary Violence: Deconstructing the Monstrous in/as Cavarero’s Horrorism
abstract: This article offers a feminist reworking of Adriana Cavarero’s conceptualization of horrorism as a form of extreme violence that targets and dehumanizes its victims through dismemberment and an ontological assault on human uniqueness. While Cavarero’s intervention is motivated by a commitment to resisting patriarchal logics of war and reorienting political thought toward care, we argue that her framework depends on an overly fixed opposition between the monstrous perpetrator and the defenseless victim, exemplified in her reading of Medusa in contrast with the Christian Madonna. The binary risks reproducing the very logics of exclusion and moral absolutism it seeks to disrupt. Demonstrating the point, we engage in a critical rereading of Medusa across classical and later interpretive traditions that demonstrates how she cannot be reduced to an emblem of absolute monstrosity, but instead appears as a plural figure: victim, goddess, protector, and generative presence—as well as a destructive monster. This reading destabilizes Cavarero’s conceptualization of both horrorism and victimhood, revealing the political and narrative instability of these categories. In reaction, we develop a feminist framework for responding to contemporary violence that shifts analysis away from moralized typologies toward a relational and narratively mediated understanding of violence. This approach retains Cavarero’s commitments to relationality and uniqueness, but rejects the closure produced by the neologism “horrorism,” instead foregrounding the entanglement of care and violence and the contested processes through which both are recognized and named.

title: How You Pay Drives What You Choose: Mental Accounting in Health Insurance Plan Choice
abstract: Abstract We document that the source of funds for paying health insurance premiums has a dramatic impact on plan choices. We focus on the MediSave program in Singapore, a medical savings account that is used to pay out-of-pocket medical spending. Residents can also pay their health insurance premiums with cash or MediSave funds, but are subject to limits that vary by age and over time. By exploiting variations in those limits, we consistently find that when individuals are able to pay their health insurance premiums with MediSave funds, they are less price sensitive and more willing to enroll in more generous plans. We develop and estimate a mental accounting model which explains these patterns. We embed and reject alternative explanations such as hassle costs and liquidity constraints. We then extend this model and show that mental accounting can explain much, but not all, of the misweighting of premiums relative to out-of-pocket expenses in health insurance choice. We also find that allowing MediSave payment for both premiums and out-of-pocket expenses (e.g. putting them in the same mental account) enhances individual welfare and reduces adverse selection.

title: Road to integration? Unraveling the impact of high-speed rail expansion on cross-city government procurement in China
Bidding wars in the housing market: When directed search becomes stock-flow matching
A Systems‐Based Approach for Analyzing Interorganizational Coordination Within Port Risk Control Structures
Identity-based risk and time preference predictions
The disillusionment of mental health network coordinators: A new occupation under pressure
abstract: Following the launch of the Psy107 reform in the Belgian mental health sector in 2010, the ‘network coordinators’ appeared as a new occupation responsible for facilitating its implementation locally. Although they demonstrate strong professional commitment, driven by a desire to make change happen, a sense of unease quickly develops among them. Using qualitative methods, we delve into the coordinators’ experience to examine the emotional dimension of their work. The results show that coordinators face three main tensions in their work: they must reconcile conflicting expectations, manage without authority and align resources and objectives. As a result, coordinators deploy coping strategies that require emotional intelligence and emotional labor to compensate for systemic ambiguities rather than improve mental healthcare. As they struggle to reconcile their professional commitment to stimulate change in the sector with the limited transformative power they actually hold, this situation gradually leads them to experience a form of alienation. Drawing on Graeber’s concept of “bullshit jobs,” we argue that coordinators’ emotions and personal commitment are mobilized to compensate for dysfunctions produced by the policy’s governance arrangement, while their emotional labor ultimately serves to generate visible signs of change rather than address structural issues.

title: Bureaucratic resistance from below: Public administrators and their roles and capacities in advancing environmental justice under the Trump administration
Communicating a historic shift: Policy transparency and public sentiment on Vietnam's 2025 provincial merger and public sector downsizing
abstract: Abstract This study examines the relationship between policy communication transparency and public sentiment during Vietnam's historic 2025 administrative reform, which involved a large‐scale provincial merger and public sector downsizing. It investigates how the communicated transparency of employee downsizing policies influences public perceptions of procedural and distributive injustice versus support for the reform's efficiency goals. A quantitative content analysis was conducted on 2296 public comments from 96 articles published on the major online news platform VnExpress. The results reveal a significant paradoxical effect. While overall transparency regarding the reform was associated with increased public optimism, greater clarity on the specific ‘Process for Redundancy’ and ‘Compensation and Support’ backfired, leading to a significant increase in comments alleging procedural injustice and a marked decrease in support for the reform's efficiency rationale. The findings suggest that transparency acts as a magnifying glass: when a policy's substance is perceived as flawed, transparent communication can fuel public critique rather than build legitimacy. Points for practitioners Designing substantively fair and defensible downsizing procedures should be prioritised before being communicated, as transparency will magnify public criticism of any perceived flaws. The reform's long‐term vision and clear timeline should be emphasised in public communications, as these elements foster optimism, while avoiding a primary focus on compensation details which can undermine broad support. Communication strategies should be segmented by conveying the reform's broad vision to the public while delivering sensitive details on compensation and support directly to affected employees through targeted channels.

title: Transparency and public complaints: the moderating role of information types and NGOs
abstract: This study investigates the effect of transparency on citizens’ complaint behavior, focusing on how this effect is shaped by the types of disclosed information and the involvement of non-governmental organizations (NGOs). Using China’s environmental protection as an empirical setting, we introduced a novel index—incorporating both the quantity and quality of disclosed information—to evaluate local governments’ transparency and examined its impacts on public complaints, a prevalent form of citizen political engagement in the country. Statistical analysis shows: 1) The disclosure of policy content and outcome information tends to aggravate citizen complaints, whereas the disclosure of decision-making information and regulatee information does not. 2) Environmental NGOs (eNGOs) play a buffering role, mitigating the increase in citizen complaints associated with regulatee transparency. To further support these findings, we conducted in-depth interviews with four eNGOs. Qualitative evidence shows that eNGOs reshape how regulatee-level transparency translates into public complaints by monitoring firms proactively, substituting for individual grievance filing, and interpreting technical disclosures to contain unnecessary or risky mobilization.

title: Public Finance Law and Public Administrations: The Shaping Power of Public Finance in the European Union. By ElisaD'Alterio, London: Routledge, 2025. 206 pp. $56.99 (ebk). ISBN : 978‐1‐03‐274124‐6

title: Public Service Delegation and the Mechanisms of Blame Attribution: Evidence From a Survey Experiment on Public Service Failure
abstract: ABSTRACT A growing body of experimental public administration research examines how structural arrangements in public services, such as delegating service delivery to public or private actors, shape citizens' blame attributions for service failures. However, the mechanisms underlying these attributions are less well understood. This article investigates two mechanisms, focusing on the mediating roles of citizens' perceptions of politicians' causal responsibility (perceived control over service delivery) and functional responsibility (perceived duty to ensure service quality). A UK‐based survey experiment on local waste collection failures tests these mechanisms using causal mediation analysis. The results show higher levels of delegation reduce blame primarily by lowering perceptions of politicians' control over service delivery. In contrast, there is no strong evidence of mediation through perceived duty, suggesting that role‐based expectations of functional responsibility are more resistant to change. These findings provide new insight into how different public service delivery methods influence blame attribution for service performance.

title: Putting Democratic Theory and Principles of Justice in the Right Place: Ethical Pluralism in Collaborative and Participatory Governance
abstract: ABSTRACT Participatory and collaborative governance (P&CG) is widely celebrated as an institutional vehicle for democratizing public decision‐making by inviting affected stakeholders into inclusive and deliberative policy processes. This essay argues that underlying appeals to democratic legitimacy in P&CG are tacit commitments to specific (and often ideologically bounded) conceptions of justice. Democracy, far from being normatively univocal, encompasses competing justice principles that yield divergent and sometimes incompatible design imperatives. In response, this essay calls for a shift from vague democratic invocations to a more precise theorization of justice as the operative normative currency in P&CG. To this end, the essay outlines an analytical framework that maps three core dimensions of governance design (input, process, and output) onto corresponding domains of justice: representational, procedural, and distributive. Systematically unpacking the plural and conflicting ethical principles within each domain shows how different principles of justice produce distinct governance dilemmas and trade‐offs.

title: Citizens’ support for behavioural public policy and trust in government: evidence from two online experiments
abstract: We explore citizens’ support for behavioral interventions by distinguishing interventions that exploit citizens’ bounded rationality through choice architecture (Nudge) from those that challenge bounded rationality by promoting reflection through deliberative forums (Think). We also examine the role of trust in government in shaping these preferences. Findings from two experiments involving 3,010 US participants show that citizens are more willing to support Think rather than Nudge. Whereas the adoption of Nudge, as compared to Think, does not seem to influence trust in government, encouraging higher levels of trust in government has a stronger effect on support for Nudge than for Think.

title: A Duty to Care or a Duty to Comply? Gambling Operators' Interpretation of the Legal Concept of Duty of Care and Their Responsibility for Preventing Gambling‐Related Harm
abstract: ABSTRACT From the perspective of negotiated governance, this study examines how companies respond to regulatory measures that combine hard and soft elements, assigning them greater responsibility for addressing social problems. Focusing on the Swedish gambling market, the study analyzes gambling operators' interpretation of the legal concept of duty of care. While this duty obliges operators to protect gamblers from excessive gambling, what it entails in practice and how responsibilities are understood are largely left to operators to define. Guided by the concept of responsibility, the analysis shows that interpretations vary and it is unclear what duty of care aims to prevent. Despite variations, duty of care is often framed in terms of responsible gambling, thereby individualizing responsibility for gambling‐related harm, and the action plans largely describe compliance with other legal requirements. In conclusion, the findings suggest a need for greater regulatory clarity regarding the normative foundations of duty of care regulation.

title: Civic Embeddedness and Public Employment: How Institutional Proximity Structures Civic Participation
abstract: Research on public service motivation consistently finds that public employees volunteer and contribute more than their private sector counterparts, yet less is known about how engagement varies across behavioral domains and institutional contexts. This study examines how civic engagement is structured among public employees compared to other citizens, with particular attention to variation across levels of government. Using the 2023 CPS Volunteering and Civic Life Supplement, the analysis constructs multidimensional measures across four domains: political participation, civic involvement, political expression, and social connectedness. Weighted regressions and propensity score matching show that public employees, especially at the local level, exhibit a distinct civic profile characterized by greater involvement in institutional forms of participation such as voting and volunteering, but lower engagement in informal activities such as political discussion and social interaction. These patterns persist after accounting for observable characteristics and suggest that public employment channels participation into specific forms rather than uniformly increasing overall engagement, with implications for how civil service reforms may alter the civic composition of local communities.
journal_name: The American Review of Public Administration

title: How Front-Line Public Managers Become Institutional Entrepreneurs
abstract: How do front-line public managers become institutional entrepreneurs? This article answers that question through a longitudinal single-case study of a large Norwegian municipality's healthcare services. Drawing on organizational institutionalism and public management scholarship, I first show how front-line public managers initiate divergent change by leveraging a sensing–legitimation nexus. They detect external and internal triggers, frame the need for change, and secure political, administrative, and professional support through direct negotiation and compelling operational narratives. They then act as co-creation catalysts, engaging residents and building cross-sector partnerships to adapt service designs and mobilize scarce resources. Finally, they institutionalize transformative public healthcare delivery by embedding routines in daily operations, formalizing interdisciplinary team structures, clarifying roles, and demonstrating performance gains. Evidence from two innovation projects shows that resource-constrained, non-heroic actors can disrupt entrenched practices and stabilize innovation as the new institutional arrangement. The study contributes to institutional entrepreneurship theory by positioning front-line public managers as credible entrepreneurial agents and by identifying co-creation as a core mechanism of public sector institutional change.
journal_name: The American Review of Public Administration

title: Translating youth participation into policy: a case study of the Seoul Youth Ordinance in South Korea
abstract: This study examines how youth policy in South Korea became institutionalized, using the 2015 enactment of the Seoul Youth Ordinance as a case study. Using Kingdon’s Multiple Streams Approach, it compares central-government approaches with local-level policy innovation. Although youth-related issues expanded beyond unemployment, national policies remained narrowly focused on employment and failed to achieve coupling among the problem, political, and policy streams. In contrast, Seoul’s welfare-centred political environment, reshaped by the 2011 mayoral by-election, activated the political stream and created more favourable conditions for stream alignment. Youth organizations formulated and refined concrete policy proposals, while the mayoral administration provided political sponsorship and institutional brokerage that connected those proposals to formal decision-making processes and facilitated the coupling of the three streams after the policy window opened. The resulting ordinance marked a paradigmatic shift by institutionalizing youth as multidimensional policy subjects and establishing participatory governance mechanisms. By comparing central and local policymaking within the same national context, this study contributes to MSA scholarship by showing how institutional conditions shape stream alignment and coupling, thereby affecting whether youth participation is translated into policy institutionalization.
