title: ‘Unconditionality is a very, very difficult question’ – views on benefit conditionality among Finnish basic income experiment participants
abstract: Abstract A central principle of basic income (BI) is unconditionality, contrasting with the prevailing trend in developed welfare systems that emphasises conditionality based on ‘activation’. While literature exists on attitudes about benefit conditionality and various BI solutions, there is limited understanding of the reasoning by individuals who have experienced a shift from conditionality to unconditionality within a BI framework. This gap highlights the need for more research on individual experiences related to these changing benefit principles. Utilising eighty-one in-depth participant interviews from the Finnish BI experiment targeting the long-term unemployed, we asked: how do experiment participants view benefit (un)conditionality after having received an unconditional basic income? Our results on the views of benefit conditionality among BI recipients proved to be quite varied. Some of the interviewees strongly supported principles of unconditionality, some basing their views on personal experience, while others opposed unconditionality, referring to their political beliefs, associating universal BI with leftist ideas, despite the Finnish experiment having been initiated by a conservative government. Interviews indicate that institutionalised norms and personal ideologies – key factors in welfare state research – significantly influence reasoning on (un)conditionality among participants in BI experiments, reflecting the work ethos of both traditional and current Nordic welfare state models.

title: Different donors, different curves: comparing non-linear governance outcomes of western and Chinese aid
abstract: This article examines the nonlinear effects of development assistance on governance in developing countries, comparing Western (OECD-DAC) and Chinese aid within a comparative policy framework. Challenging linear assumptions about aid, it shows that differences in policy design and delivery generate distinct governance trajectories across recipient states. Using country–year panel data from 2000 to 2023 and quadratic models, the analysis finds that Western aid exhibits diminishing and ultimately negative governance returns as aid intensity increases. Chinese aid, by contrast, follows a U-shaped pattern, with governance effects becoming more positive at higher levels of engagement, especially in countries with greater absorptive capacity. These results are robust across multiple governance indicators and estimation strategies. The findings show that governance outcomes depend not only on aid volume, but also on donor modalities and recipient capacity to absorb and embed external resources.

title: Collaboration of foundations with public administration in cross-border territories
abstract: Place leadership theory explains how collaborative leadership among local actors shapes the development of places and the well-being of local populations. Prior research has concentrated primarily on the role of public authorities in places. However, other stakeholders, such as non-profit organizations, also contribute to fulfilling the needs of local populations. This research examines local foundations, a distinct subgroup within the non-profit sector, which are committed to enhancing the quality of life in their operational areas. We build on the theoretical assumption that non-profit organizations provide services when markets and governments fail. Based on interviews with three foundations in the cross-border region of the Upper Rhine (France, Germany, and Switzerland), we investigate the role of foundations in increasing the quality of life in places. To triangulate our findings, we also interview stakeholders from the public and private sectors, target groups, and civil society organizations. Our findings show that foundations exercise place leadership through informal power, knowledge sharing, and flexible networks that foster dialogue and coordination among local stakeholders, including strong ties to public-sector actors. Their endowment-based resources enable independent project implementation and position foundations as genuine place leaders that create public value by filling those gaps left by market and government failures.

title: Endogenous coalition formation in policy debates
abstract: Abstract Political actors form coalitions around their joint normative beliefs in order to influence the policy process on contentious issues such as climate change or population aging. Policy process theory maintains that learning within and across coalitions is a central predictor of policy change but has yet to explain how policy learning works. This article explains the formation and maintenance of coalitions by focusing on the ways actors adopt policy beliefs from other actors in policy debates. A policy debate is a complex social system in which temporal network dependence guides how actors contribute ideological statements. Belief adoption matters in three complementary ways: bonding , which exploits cues within coalitions; bridging , which explores new beliefs outside one's perimeter; and repulsion , which reinforces polarization between coalitions and cements their belief systems. We formalize this theory of endogenous coalition formation in policy debates and test it on a micro‐level empirical data set.

title: Durable majority gerrymanders: Where partisan gerrymandering can displace democracy
abstract: Abstract We develop the concept of, and estimation tools for, durable majority gerrymanders : electoral district maps drawn to reduce an opposing political party's probability of winning a majority in a legislative chamber. Directly interpretable, forward‐looking, and motivated by the democratic principle that a party in power should have some chance of losing it, this measure provides new insights into the role of redistricting in state legislative elections. We show that, when map drawers are unconstrained, the ability to create durable majorities is so widespread that at least one party in every state can draw a map where a majority of legislative districts withstand almost any likely future electoral swing. Enacted maps are less durable due to a combination of underlying geography, voter partisanship, and state‐level guidelines. This paper provides the theoretical framework and empirical tools to understand which gerrymandered maps enable state‐level majorities to emerge and to endure.

title: Voting for populism? How ‘populist’ labels affect support for candidates
abstract: Abstract Many consider the rise of populism to be a major threat to liberal democracy today. At the same time, voters have given considerable support to such parties and politicians, with their average vote-share quadrupling in the last thirty years. Thus, while research realizes the potential hostility populism poses to the polity at large, it is unclear what connotations of the ideology exist to voters. Do voters recognize they are voting for a politician considered to be averse to democracy? Do they simply not care? I field a randomized survey experiment of 2099 respondents in the United Kingdom to measure (1) the effect labeling a politician ‘populist’ may have on their level of support, and (2) voters’ perception of the link between populism and democracy. Results suggest voters’ perception of ‘populist’ labels are largely dependent on the candidate’s left-right ideology, as well as the level of populist ideology of the voter.

title: Epistocracy and the Commitment Problem
abstract: ABSTRACT The epistocracy debate has turned largely on the character of the electorate—what voters know, whether competence filters can be designed well, and what filtered selection produces. Another strand has focused on the legitimacy of epistocratic justifications. I ask instead about the equilibrium effects of the institution. Epistocracy shifts some political authority from the median voter toward citizens selected on competence grounds, and existing critiques press legitimational, epistemic, abuse‐based, and demographic objections against such proposals. I develop a different objection, focusing on one especially plausible form of epistocracy: Jason Brennan's epistocratic veto , a competence‐selected council empowered to override legislation it judges incompetent. Drawing on Acemoglu and Robinson's account of democratization, I argue that the franchise solves a credible‐commitment problem between elites and the poor under conditions of revolutionary threat: universal suffrage puts redistributive authority in majority hands in a way elites cannot easily reverse, because reversing it requires revoking the franchise itself. The institutionally realistic veto hands some of that authority back to a body whose preferences systematically diverge from the median voter's, reintroducing the commitment problem suffrage solved. I give empirical and theoretical reasons to worry that the magnitude of the problem could potentially be significant, while its actual size (and its comparison with democracy's own commitment problems) remains an open empirical question. A formal appendix maps the veto to Acemoglu and Robinson's imperfect‐democracy parameter and shows that the range of conditions under which democratic institutions avert revolution strictly shrinks.

title: The authoritarian politics of energy infrastructures: Repertoires of contestation, economic relations, and state practices through a multi-scalar perspective
Embracing the Enemy
abstract: Abstract A principal (such as a centrist political party) can partially influence the allocation of power between two competing parties. The principal is closer to one party, the ``Friend'', than to the other, the ``Enemy''. The principal's optimal contract initially seeks to exclude the Enemy. However, once the Enemy gains power, the principal embraces him in exchange for policy moderation. Moderation also disciplines the Friend, inducing him to move closer to the principal's preferred policy. Principals close to the Friend fully embrace the Enemy; more centrist principals divide their support. Commitment benefits the principal only if she is close to the Friend and parties value power little.

title: Designing Flood Insurance to Maximize Public Benefits in High‐Risk Areas
Algorithmic imaginaries: Definition and critical questions
abstract: Algorithmic systems play an increasingly central role across a variety of social domains. Over the last few years, various concepts have been developed in the interdisciplinary field of algorithm studies to understand how people make sense of these systems and interact with them – including mental models of algorithms, folk theories of algorithms, or algorithmic imaginaries. This theoretical article engages with the concept of the algorithmic imaginary in particular. It argues that the concept of the algorithmic imaginary occupies a unique position in literature, foregrounding questions of affect and emotion in human-algorithm interaction, and theorising the dynamics of sense-making about algorithms in such terms. Critically examining work that has explicitly applied and developed the concept, we synthesise the scholarship, offer an updated definition, and pose critical questions for future research, including on emergent artificial intelligence phenomena.

title: Rendering the whole world blank: Precarity, totalising fear and digital scrolling
abstract: This article explores the connection between structurally induced precarity and the material practice of digital scrolling in the global north. It argues in favour of an expanded definition of precarity and that precarity, as a generalised affective condition, results in a state of totalising fear (fear which relates, at once, to discrete objects as well as the world itself). In that context, this article advances the claim that scrolling can be understood as an affective attachment (of the kind outlined by Lauren Berlant), developed in response to totalising fear, and which enables the subject to suspend time and to escape from conscious experience of precarity. In establishing this conclusion, the article also explores how the form of scrolling engenders an absorbing, passive and essentially ‘blank’ experience of the world, and how the attainment of this state is an expression of a limited, precarious mode of agency.

title: Trending Topics, Growing Knowledge? How Curating Actors’ Political Social Media Content Affects Youth’s Political Knowledge
abstract: Whether youth can gain political knowledge through social media is long debated. Existing research has insufficiently accounted for different curating actors of political information, an indirect learning logic, and within-person changes. To fill these gaps, we conducted a large-scale three-wave panel study among 16- to 30-year-olds (NT3 = 2276) to examine how exposure to different social media actors such as politicians, peers, or influencers relates to the acquisition of current affairs knowledge over time. We investigated perceived opinion leadership gratifications as a novel underlying mechanism in this process. While increased exposure to all curating actors’ political content was related to higher opinion leadership gratifications in the same wave, we found little indirect learning effects over time on the within-person level through obtained gratifications. This association emerged only during the national election period, when perceived opinion leadership gratifications from peers’ political content were linked to above-usual gains in objective political knowledge over time.

title: Examining the Influence of Media Coverage on Information-Seeking of Judicial Candidates
“Old Habits Die Hard”: Formal Politicization and the Turnover of Public Hospital CEOs
abstract: This study investigates how formal politicization shapes the turnover of senior public executives. Using a dataset of 138 CEOs across 79 Italian public hospitals between 2017 and 2021, it examines the relative influence of managerial competence and partisan loyalty on the likelihood of CEO exit. Although both factors affect turnover, partisan loyalty emerges as the primary driver. Political stability significantly lowers CEO dismissal risk, even with weak organizational performance or limited managerial human capital, which plays a secondary role. These findings suggest that NPM reforms have been only partially effective, with patronage practices persisting within a formally meritocratic institutional framework.

title: Digital platforms and regulatory coordination patterns in China: Network evidence from Nanjing's “181” integrated emergency management system
AI ambivalence and digital civic engagement: Dual pathways of hindrance and capability development
Strengthening e-government's impact on corruption perception: The moderating role of Financial Management Information Systems (FMIS)
Institutional Amnesia and Public Administration: Does History Repeat?
abstract: Abstract Existing research suggests that a lack of institutional memory causes history to repeat in problematic ways within public administration agencies. However, this claim has not been well supported by theory or data that illuminates the process and effects of history repeating. To remedy this, the nascent concept of institutional amnesia is presented here as a means of theorizing repetitions of public administrative history. A sequential explanatory mixed method research design uses quantitative survey data (n=1608) and qualitative interview data (n=75) generated in the public services of Australia, New Zealand and the United Kingdom to show how institutional amnesia can lead to the recycling of ideas and practices, the inefficient relearning of information seeking processes and the delivery of conducive decision-making environments that can help address historical problems. These findings draw attention to the fact that administrative history does indeed repeat in public agencies because of institutional amnesia, but that it does so in positive as well as negative ways.
journal_name: Journal of Public Administration Research and Theory

title: Public Administration in the 21st Century: A Global South Perspective, 2nd ed. By RumkiBasu, London: Routledge, 2025. 182 pp.
Should we stay or should we go? Implications of trust in the municipality for second-generation migrants’ behavioural intentions towards the municipality
abstract: Public and political debate increasingly problematizes the relationship between second-generation migrants and public authorities, yet little is known about how they evaluate local government. This study examines behavioural intentions towards municipalities – exit, voice, loyalty and neglect – and assesses how trust, local identification and discrimination shape these responses. Using survey data from second-generation migrants in Dutch municipalities, we find loyalty predominates, while trust, local identification and discrimination shape these orientations towards local government. These findings highlight the central role of trust and inclusion in shaping citizen–state relations and demonstrate the value of integrating migrant-centred perspectives into public administration research.

title: Debate: Beyond the Westminster Model: a myth that needs constant refreshing?
abstract: The Westminster model of government rests upon a structural asymmetry: a permanent, professional bureaucracy serving a political class that rotates by design. It is a model that has been widely exp...

title: The realisation of NextGenerationEU: taking stock of the Recovery and Resilience Facility
abstract: This article examines the rich literature on the European Union’s Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF), the central instrument of the NextGenerationEU (NGEU) recovery plan created in response to the Covid-19 pandemic. Worth up to €806.9 bn, NGEU, and the RRF (€577 bn) in particular, represents the most ambitious fiscal intervention in the EU’s history. The article systematises the scholarship on the RRF to clarify its implications for European integration, fiscal governance, and EU policy implementation. It argues that the RRF constitutes a major innovation that combines large-scale common borrowing with significant financial transfers to member states and a novel governance architecture linking EU priorities to national reform and investment plans. Reviewing multiple strands of EU studies and primary documents, the article highlights how the RRF strengthened the European Commission’s executive role, introduced performance-based conditionality, and reshaped interinstitutional relations between Brussels and the member states. The findings suggest that the RRF challenges established EU integration theories: it neither fully aligns with intergovernmentalism nor neofunctionalism, instead reflecting what has been referred to as constrained supranationalism and coordinative Europeanisation. As academic and policy debates on the RRF’s funding and disbursement architecture have matured, attention should now shift towards its longer-term legacy and implications.

title: Climate policy under economic uncertainty: confidence in the welfare state and support for carbon taxation
abstract: Abstract The climate crisis is urgent, yet public support for fossil fuel taxation remains low. Existing research attributes this to material interests, particularly concerns about the regressive nature of consumption taxes. This connects to the literature on the emerging “eco-social divide,” which emphasizes tensions between environmental and equity concerns while leaving potential synergies understudied. Drawing on policy feedback theory, we argue that satisfaction with existing social policies shapes how individuals perceive the risks of carbon taxation. Using original survey data from seven European countries ( n = 10,968), we find that income difficulty and dissatisfaction with social policies reduce support for fossil fuel taxation. Perceived employment risk, contrary to expectations, is positively associated with support, and this relationship is amplified by social policy satisfaction. Confidence in welfare institutions therefore appears to facilitate support for climate policy, pointing to social protection and policy feedback as central to building coalitions for the green transition.

title: A Narrative Walks Into a Forum: Bridging the Narrative Policy and Ecology of Games Frameworks
Correction to “Differentiated Institutionalization: How Is a Policy Innovation Institutionalized Within the Bureaucratic Organization?”
abstract: Cai, C., Z. Zheng, and Q. Shen. 2026. “ Differentiated Institutionalization: How Is a Policy Innovation Institutionalized Within the Bureaucratic Organization?” Review of Policy Research 43, no. 4: e70115. https://doi.org/10.1111/ropr.70115. The author names (given name and family name) were transposed in the submitted manuscript and published article. This has been corrected to Changkun Cai, Ziyu Zheng, and Qiyao Shen. We apologize for this error.

title: Learning without improving: Within-voter changes in political knowledge and vote choice proximity
Does citizen deliberation inside representative institutions enhance legitimacy among non-participating publics?
abstract: Abstract Claims that citizen deliberation can strengthen public confidence in democracy rest on the assumption that it enhances the perceived procedural legitimacy of democratic governance. We test this assumption by examining whether integrating deliberative constituent forums into electoral-representative institutions increases perceived legitimacy among non-participating publics and which specific features of such forums drive these diffuse effects. We extend existing experimental research on democratic innovations by theorising that the deliberative norms of consequentiality and listening shape legitimacy judgements. Drawing on a nationally representative survey vignette experiment in Australia, we show that even minimal, realistic exposure to information about a deliberative citizens’ panel informing a parliamentary committee produces a modest but statistically significant increase in perceived procedural legitimacy. These gains depend on signals that citizens’ input is taken seriously and that participants are sincerely listened to. While legitimacy declines when deliberative input is ignored, the strongest positive effects arise when processes visibly communicate high-quality listening by political representatives. Moreover, legitimacy gains are strongest among respondents with low institutional trust. The findings demonstrate that the legitimacy-enhancing potential of deliberative innovations hinges not only on institutional design but also on the perceived relational quality of engagement between constituents and decision-makers. This contributes to ongoing debates in democratic theory and political behaviour about when and why deliberative innovations can rejuvenate representative democracy.

title: PRRP identity and sense of understanding for citizens who engage in political violence
abstract: Abstract This research note extends existing knowledge on anti-pluralism among identifiers of a populist radical right party (PRRP) by investigating their sense of understanding for citizens who engage in two key forms of political violence: threatening and spreading false information about political opponents. Building on methodological advances in political science research, we estimate a series of Bayesian zero-inflated regression models using original Flemish data ( N = 2,963). Results reveal a positive correlation between PRRP identity and sense of understanding. Results further indicate that this correlation diminishes with higher levels of education in the case of spreading false information, but remains equally strong in the case of threatening. This research note offers new insights into anti-pluralism among PRRP identifiers.

title: Macrodiscontent across countries
abstract: Abstract Public discontent with the political system has become an increasingly salient concern in recent years, with the argument that it undermines democratic stability and effective governance. Nevertheless, the understanding of the nature, trends, and drivers of political discontent remain debated, largely reflecting the constraints from available survey data and items in the construction of measurement. This article takes advantage of state-of-the-art latent-variable modeling to aggregate survey responses and a comprehensive collection of survey data to generate dynamic comparative estimates of public political discontent (PPD) for 136 countries and regions over 56 years (1968–2023). These PPD scores are validated with responses to the individual source-data survey items that were used to generate them as well as the democratic evaluation survey item that was not used in our estimation. Next, a cross-national and longitudinal analysis of PPD in advanced democracies (i.e., OECD countries) highlights that PPD has been on a rising trend, rather than merely trendless fluctuations. Our results reveal that these increased discontents are largely attributable to worsening economic conditions, including low average income, slow growth, and high unemployment rates.

title: Moderation or Amplification? Mapping Speech Distinctiveness Among Green Parties Using a Machine Learning Approach
The Victory Trap: Endogenous Opposition Coalition Weaknesses in Reversing Autocracy
abstract: After opposition parties and alliances defeat dominant autocratic incumbents, what challenges do they encounter in reversing autocracy and what are the consequences? We argue that long-neglected endogenous weaknesses in opposition coalitions undermine re-democratization efforts, easily opening the door to autocratic comebacks. First, coalition intra-elite conflicts post-victory result in fractured and ineffective governance, generating mass disappointment with the new political elites. Second, coalition intra-supporter divergence pressures the new coalition government into implementing pro-democratic reforms at haphazard speeds and fluctuating scopes. Swift actions in reversing autocracy alienate supporters of the ex-autocrat, elicit accusations of partisan revenge, and fuel counter-mobilization against the new government. A most-different case comparison between the recent autocratic reversal experiences of Poland and Malaysia demonstrates our argument. We show in both cases that ideological and distributional conflicts among diverse coalition elites undermined governance after victory, and different supporter bases prioritized different policy agendas. Counter-mobilization by the autocratic ex-incumbents was highly successful in undermining public support for the new government. These findings suggest that profound challenges in reversing autocracy and rebuilding democracy lie within opposition coalitions themselves, in addition to authoritarian legacies.

title: The War on Universities: Illiberal Tactics in Turkey, Hungary, and the United States
abstract: Illiberal governments increasingly target universities as sites of political dissent and ideological opposition. This paper compares three illustrative cases—Boğaziçi University under Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, Central European University under Viktor Orbán, and elite US universities under Donald Trump—to examine how illiberal governments deploy state power against autonomous, high-profile, liberal-aligned institutions of higher education, and how students and faculty respond. Although universities are not always bastions of pluralism, tolerance, and democracy, attacks on universities are often concurrent with illiberal governance. We argue that illiberal governments perceive universities as vanguards of hegemonic liberalism and as partisan opponents in certain contexts, and that state repression operates along a continuum of coercion, legal displacement, and discursive delegitimation. These attacks on academic autonomy trigger varied responses—from mobilization, to fragmentation, to withdrawal—shaped by domestic political opportunity structures, the intensity of state repression, and campus culture. By conceptualizing the university as a contested political institution rather than a neutral educational space, this article contributes to broader debates on democratic backsliding, populism, culture wars, and higher education.

title: Assessing Nonignorable Response: Sensitivity Analysis for Survey Weighting, with Applications to Survey Estimates of COVID-19 Vaccination Uptake
Beyond forbearance? Mapping and assessing the EU’s emergent compliance promotion architecture
abstract: The EU has a highly centralised, potentially powerful instrument for enforcement: the European Commission can instigate infringement procedures against member states that violate EU policies. Yet, recent research has suggested that the Commission curtails enforcement to ensure member states’ political support for new policy decisions. This article argues that this perspective is compelling, but incomplete. Over the past decades, the EU has constructed a variegated compliance promotion architecture in addition to the infringement procedure, spanning the vertical, horizontal, and domestic arenas and comprising managerialist, constructivist and rationalist strategies. The article sketches this emergent architecture, illustrates its sectoral variation, assesses its effectiveness, and provides an agenda for future research on EU compliance promotion. It concludes by discussing the preconditions for the effective functioning of the architecture, arguing that these alternative instruments have an important part to play, but ultimately require a firm shadow of hierarchy in cases of persistent member state opposition to EU law.

title: Capital Unemployment
abstract: Abstract This paper studies the unemployment of physical capital—defined as idle units searching to be traded—and its macroeconomic implications. I provide evidence documenting that capital unemployment is large, volatile, and increases during economic downturns. I construct a capital-accumulation model that explains these patterns, with trading frictions in capital markets, which give rise to equilibrium capital unemployment, and financial shocks, which lead to large fluctuations in trading probabilities and capital unemployment. Using the model, I show that trading frictions and capital unemployment matter for aggregate dynamics. First, unemployed capital affects aggregate investment dynamics: Downturns characterized by large increases in unemployed capital are followed by investment slumps, because the economy tends to recover by absorbing existing unemployed capital rather than by producing new capital goods. Second, capital unemployment constitutes a propagation mechanism from financial shocks to economic activity, which shows up at the aggregate level as measured total factor productivity.

title: Informative Certification: Screening vs. Acquisition
abstract: Abstract We study monopolistic certification in markets where sellers possess partial private information about product quality. A certifier can provide information through two channels: screening sellers’ private information (soft information) and acquiring new quality data (hard information). We prove that any certification menu achieving less than maximal screening is Pareto dominated by one with full screening. Among Pareto-efficient menus, the certifier’s profit-maximising menu provides maximal soft information while restricting hard information provision. The two channels diverge because screening creates value the certifier can fully capture, whereas hard information amplifies costly information rents. Using power value functions, we derive comparative statics showing that information restrictions target low-quality sellers when information value is moderate, but high-quality sellers receive perfect quality revelation when information value is high.

title: Reciprocity and state capacity: Evidence from a national pollution control reform in China
Self-medication under uncertainty: Insights on drug quality and consumer behavior in Burkina Faso
abstract: How does drug quality affect self-medication behavior? We address this question in the context of Burkina Faso, where self-medication with antibiotics is widespread. Using chemical quality tests, we find that one in three antibiotics on the market is substandard or falsified, posing significant health risks. While consumers are broadly aware of the prevalence of poor-quality drugs, they struggle to assess quality based on observable cues such as price or packaging. To identify causal effects, we conduct a novel lab-in-the-field experiment that varies the probability of purchasing effective medicine. We find that self-medication increases as drug quality becomes more certain. These results suggest that market-level interventions to improve drug quality may unintentionally increase inappropriate antibiotic use, with implications for health policy and antimicrobial resistance.

title: local non-bossiness
Co-evolution of cooperation and conflict among organized crime groups: Evidence from the United Kingdom
abstract: This work investigates the co-evolution of cooperation and conflict (violence) among organized crime groups. Using actor-oriented relational event models, we analyze 179 group cooperation and 141 group conflict events from a UK police force (2004–2015). To estimate undirected relational event models for cooperation, we develop a multiple imputation procedure. Cooperation often recurs and follows transitive patterns, likely reducing partner-selection risk. Conflict is characterized by repeated victimization, outdegree activity, and event-level reciprocity. Embeddedness in cooperative triads reduces conflict, as groups avoid losing valuable partners. We find evidence of differential status conflict-wise. Cooperation and conflict tend to be localized.

title: Integrating or segregating? Gentrification, the changing city-suburb divide, and black exceptionalism
Policing the Political Boundary: How the r/BarstoolSports Audience Confronts Politicization
abstract: Recent scholarship attends to politicized popular cultural spaces. Scarcely understood is how audiences of these spaces contend with this scrutiny. In response, I introduce the concept of anti-political space to describe how fans of politicized media spatially distinguish popular cultural spaces from institutional politics. This is conceptualized through a critical discourse analysis of the official Barstool Sports (Barstool) subreddit from 2019 to 2025, where fans share critical news coverage of Barstool. Across 16 analyzed threads, criticism is rendered unfounded or demonstrative of politically obsessed liberal culture. I argue fans’ varied expressions of victimhood and estrangement, while nominally defending against politicization, showcase how reactionary political discourse appears beyond institutional political spaces. Theoretically, this analysis recognizes how symbolic contests over what constitutes politics occur through boundary work. As the political relevance of popular cultural spaces increases in the contemporary media landscape, this analysis underscores how boundary work defends against the felt intrusion of politics into popular culture. Amid broader sociotechnical changes, I suggest anti-political spaces are poised to be a continued feature of the contemporary media environment.

title: The Gendered Path of Least Resistance: First Entry and Exit Behaviors of Public and Nonprofit Employees
abstract: ABSTRACT Public and nonprofit organizations exhibit high rates of female employment often attributed to sector structures and social roles. To better understand how individual behaviors dynamically contribute to these distinctive ratios, we deconstruct public and nonprofit employment into gendered patterns of attraction and attachment. Using duration analysis and following a cohort from the National Longitudinal Survey of Youth 1997, this research finds that women demonstrate a higher attraction to their first public and nonprofit job compared to men, evidenced through a faster rate of entry into this employment. There are no significant gender differences when considering the duration of an individual's first stint in these sectors. Additional investigation finds that these sector‐level patterns, when decomposed to account for gender‐dominant professions, are driven by stronger female attraction to female‐dominated professions while masking higher female turnover from male‐dominated professions. Results inform recruitment and retention strategies for public and nonprofit organizations.

title: Mobilizing the State Without Crushing Local Knowledge: Evidence From China's Poverty‐Alleviation Campaign
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines how the state apparatus can be mobilized by central governments for the purpose of poverty alleviation without undermining local knowledge and initiative, engaging directly with James Scott's critique of top‐down modernization schemes. Using county‐level panel data from 706 nationally designated poor counties (NPCs) in China between 2012 and 2018, we identify the separate and combined effects of two key mobilization tools deployed during China's recent poverty‐alleviation campaign: quantitative poverty‐reduction targets and changes to cadre performance evaluations that prioritized poverty outcomes over GDP growth. A difference‐in‐differences design shows that both policies boosted rural per capita incomes, with effects conditioned by target difficulty, cadre career horizons, and local tenure. From these results, we identify three features that enhanced effectiveness: (1) granular identification systems enabling precise, monitorable goals; (2) incentive realignment toward redistribution; and (3) stability in local leadership to accumulate and apply local knowledge. These findings highlight a governance model that combines central coordination with locally attuned implementation, offering practical lessons for other developing countries seeking to design centrally driven, target‐oriented mobilization strategies while mitigating the risks of overreach.

title: The Cost Savings in Inter-Organizational Cooperation: A Meta-Analytic Review and Extension
abstract: Inter-organizational cooperation is widely promoted as a strategy to improve cost efficiency in public service delivery. However, empirical findings on the efficiency gains remain mixed, and the conditions under which cost savings are realized are not well understood. To further the research field, this meta-analysis synthesizes evidence from 26 studies comprising 152 effect sizes to examine whether cooperation involving public organizations reduces service provision costs and to examine why estimated cost effects vary across studies. Through the analysis, we find a small but statistically significant cost-reducing effect (r = −.05), indicating that cooperation is associated with modestly lower service costs. The meta-regression results further show that the difficulty of achieving cost savings is significantly increased when cooperation spans multiple service areas. The estimated cost effects also vary with the study design and measurement choices: intensity-based operationalizations are associated with larger cost reductions than propensity-based measures, and quasi-experimental designs yield more conservative estimates than simple regressions. In contrast, the type of cooperation, asset specificity, and measurement difficulty do not affect cost outcomes significantly. Based on these findings, we offer cautious implications for policymakers and public managers seeking to design cost-effective cooperative service arrangements and identify priorities for future research.

title: Does Corruption Increase Inequality? Evidence From a European Fact‐Based Assessment
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper examines whether government favoritism in public procurement generates negative social costs, even within redistributive institutional frameworks such as the European Union. Rather than relying on perception‐based corruption indicators, we employ an objective proxy of corruption risk—the share of awarded public contracts which received only one bid. This measure captures non‐competitive allocation and mitigates reverse causality concerns. Using static and dynamic fixed effects panel models, we find that procurement favoritism is systematically associated with adverse social outcomes across EU member states. Specifically, we document robust, statistically significant negative effects on educational attainment, income inequality, and poverty. Our results suggest that governance quality—and not merely the volume of public expenditure—is a critical determinant of social development, and that distortions in procurement processes can undermine the effectiveness of public spending even where formal cohesion commitments exist.

title: Beyond neutrality: QuantCrit as a methodological corrective in quantitative public administration research
journal_name: Perspectives on Public Management and Governance

title: Time's Sentimental Tale: Operationalizing Plot Within the Narrative Policy Framework
How Fear of Domination Affects Public Support for International Organizations: A Conjoint Experiment Approach
Are circular innovations disruptive? An analysis of the role of inventor networks in the European semiconductor industry
abstract: The expansion of advanced technologies is intensifying demand for energy, materials, and efficiency of production systems, with semiconductors exemplifying the tension between rapid technological progress and resource sustainability, and the development of circular innovations. Yet it remains unclear whether circular innovations in this sector tend to be genuinely disruptive. This study examines the disruptiveness of circular (vs. non-circular) innovations and analyses the role of inventor network structures. The empirical analysis relies on the patents of 299 European Semiconductor Equipment Manufacturing (SEM) companies retrieved from the ORBIS IP database for the period 2013-2022. First, we operationalize disruptiveness by adopting a citation-based measure to reveal whether subsequent inventions build upon or bypass a focal patent’s prior art. Then, co-inventor networks are constructed, and inventor centrality and cohesion measures are aggregated to the patent level to link inventor network structure to disruptive outcomes over time. Our findings show that circular patents exhibit, on average, higher disruptiveness than non-circular patents, and that inventor network structures characterized by more peripheral and high local cohesive configurations align with disruptive circular outcomes. The effect of the network antecedents differs systematically between circular and non-circular innovations, indicating distinct pathways to disruption. The study contributes to the innovation literature by integrating a structural disruptiveness measure with inventor network analytics, offering one of the first patent-level comparisons of circular versus non-circular disruptiveness in the semiconductor industry, and by deriving implications for organizing collaboration portfolios and policy instruments that foster circular transitions.

title: Selection at the Frontline: Experimental Evidence on the Effect of Clients' Attributes on Assignment of Active Labour Market Programmes
abstract: ABSTRACT Research on active labour market programmes (ALMPs) suggests the existence of selection and access biases. This article addresses one potential source of such biases: frontline caseworkers' allocation decisions. To investigate how client attributes affect allocation of ALMPs to young clients with reduced work capability, we conducted a pre‐registered factorial survey experiment among Norwegian caseworkers in the public employment service. We test hypotheses derived from the notion of positive and negative selection into ALMPs based on clients' perceived employment prospects and ability to successfully complete programmes. We find that caseworkers' selection of clients into ALMPs occurs primarily based on personal characteristics (i.e., competence, motivation and reliability) and that perceived employability substantially explains these effects. By contrast, clients' immigrant background and health‐related characteristics had limited impact on caseworkers' allocation of ALMPs.

title: Colorism, Descriptive Representation, and the Representation of African Americans in the United States House of Representatives
abstract: Previous research overlooks how certain ascribed characteristics, such as skin tone, correlate with the representation of marginalized groups. Yet research also demonstrates how colorism shapes candidate evaluations and life experiences. We theorize that colorism, the systemic privileging of lighter skin, structures the motivations and electoral incentives of Black lawmakers. We hypothesize that darker-skinned Black members of Congress will better represent Black Americans on racialized issues than lighter-skinned Black members, depending on the form of representation: rhetorical or legislative. We test this hypothesis with a combination of human and computer-assisted content analyses of 204,806 press releases and 18,025 bill introductions from the 114th, 115th, and 116th Congresses and a crowdsourced measure of skin tones. We find that on average, darker-skinned Black members of Congress provide more representation in press releases, but not in legislation. Our findings highlight the need to examine diversity among descriptive representatives.

title: I Read the News Today, but Why? Media Consumption, Socialization, and Autocracy
abstract: Dominant models of news consumption in political science treat citizens as rational individuals, gathering information to make materially or politically consequential choices. This assumption, developed largely in democratic contexts, risks obscuring other incentives that may be equally or more influential—particularly in authoritarian regimes, where the informational value of news is often constrained. This article advances the concept of social rationality: the incentive to consume news to sustain conversations, reinforce social bonds, and participate in communities of shared meaning. Drawing on original survey data from Belarus and Russia—two highly authoritarian states with divergent approaches to media control—the analysis shows that social motivations are powerful predictors of both the intensity and breadth of media consumption, while decision-rational considerations also help to explain breadth. Divergent interactions between social motivations and intrinsic prosocial orientations in the two cases further complicate theories of “informational autocracy.” These findings challenge classical models and underscore the need to place social incentives at the center of explanations of media use.

title: José Carlos Mariátegui’s Archaic Developmentalism: Utopia, the Incan Empire, and Peruvian Reality
abstract: “Developmentalism” refers to the idea that human societies progress through a series of historical stages, along one path or multiple paths, which allows for the comparison and hierarchization of different populations. As numerous works have shown, developmentalism was often called upon to justify Europe’s domination of non-European populations, which were figured as backward or barbaric. To complicate the commonplace equation of developmentalism and empire, I analyze José Carlos Mariátegui’s political thought as a stratigraphic history in which different temporalities—especially archaic temporality, or the remnants of Incan communalism, and developmental temporality—were vertically stacked and in tension, and I elaborate a conception of what I call “archaic developmentalism.” For Mariátegui, while the past temporality, institutions, and practices of the Incan Empire persisted into the present, he did not perceive them as hurdles to be cleared on the upward march of progress. Rather, as I argue, Mariátegui recognized the political potency of Incan communalism’s remnants—particularly, the ayllu , or Incan communal form—and he conjectured that the collision of temporal-historical layers could open an alternative developmental trajectory by which the ayllu would be reactivated as a stage in the process of creating modern communism, skipping over the developmental stage of mature capitalism that was required by Soviet orthodoxy. In other words, Mariátegui thought that the friction generated by the convergence of Peru’s different telluric strata opened a new developmental trajectory in which remnants of Incan archaism could spark socialist struggle and be reconfigured as an arsenal of possibilities in the present.

title: Non-monetary incentives and bureaucratic performance: Evidence from U.S. courts
Fairness perceptions of redistribution and predistribution
An optimal test for strategic interaction in network formation games
abstract: Abstract Consider a setting where N players, partitioned into K observable types, form a directed network. Agents’ preferences over the form of the network consist of an arbitrary network benefit function (e.g., agents may have preferences over their network centrality) and a private, or dyadic, component which is additively separable in own links. This latter component allows for unobserved heterogeneity in the costs of sending and receiving links across agents (respectively out- and in- degree heterogeneity) as well as homophily/heterophily across the K types of agents. In contrast, the network benefit function allows agents’ preferences over links to vary with the presence or absence of links elsewhere in the network (and hence with the link formation behavior of their peers). In the null model, which excludes the network benefit function, links form independently across dyads in the manner described by Charbonneau (2017) among others. Under the alternative, there is interdependence across linking decisions (i.e., strategic interaction). We show how to test the null with power optimized in specific directions. These alternative directions include many common models of strategic network formation (e.g., “connections” models, “structural hole” models etc.). Our random utility specification induces an exponential family structure under the null which we exploit to construct a similar test which exactly controls size (despite the the null being a composite one with many nuisance parameters). We further show how to construct locally best tests for specific alternatives without making any assumptions about equilibrium selection. To make our tests feasible, we introduce a new MCMC algorithm for simulating the null distributions of our test statistics.

title: Correction to: Medium-run local economic effects of a major earthquake
Why Not Tax It? The effects of property taxes on house prices and homeownership
Posting under pressure: Politicians active on social media are more stressed
abstract: While social media has become an indispensable tool for politicians’ communication with citizens and other stakeholders, emerging qualitative evidence suggests that its use may be associated with diminished well-being and reduced performance within the parliamentary arena – potentially undermining democratic processes. Combining insights from a representative survey study of politicians in Denmark ( n = 1233) with data on their observed social media usage (Facebook: 24,625 posts; Instagram: 13,019 posts), this study is the first to test the generalizability of this emerging evidence and advance our theoretical understanding of the conditions under which politicians’ social media usage is connected to stress. The study demonstrates a significant, positive correlation between politicians’ social media usage and self-reported stress symptoms and points to excessive usage as the primary explanation behind the association. Furthermore, exposure to online harassment is a crucial mediating factor in the association.

title: Affective Legitimacy and Digital Populism: Evidence from Romania’s Annulled Presidential Elections
abstract: On 6 December 2024, Romania’s Constitutional Court annulled the first round of presidential elections, triggering an exceptional crisis of democratic legitimacy in post-communist Europe. While procedurally justified, the decision sparked intense public reactions, both emotional and political. The findings confirm that populist interpretations of institutional actions proliferate in fragmented and emotionalized digital media environments, where distrust is personalized and intensified. Drawing on a nationally representative survey (N = 964), conducted by IRES shortly after the annulment, the study examines how Romanian citizens perceived the legitimacy of the Court’s decision and identifies the key socio-political and media-related factors shaping these perceptions. Binary logistic regression and mediation models were used to assess the drivers of perceived illegitimacy. TikTok use, negative emotions (anger, disappointment, resentment), political distrust, and anti-establishment party support significantly increase the likelihood of viewing the decision as illegitimate, whereas trust in journalists reduces it. The study contributes to the literature on populism as a communicative style and emotional register, showing how legitimacy itself becomes a contested symbol in digital environments marked by personalization, fragmentation, and affective intensification. We argue that institutional legitimacy is no longer grounded solely in procedural legality but is increasingly shaped by emotionally resonant narratives circulating through digital platforms. We complement the survey with a headline-level media analysis (N = 3,923; Dec 2024 - Aug 2025), to serve as a contextual counterfactual: instead of escalating antagonism, mainstream media gradually stabilize institutional language. A keyness comparison shows that the Early window (first 14 days) is driven by institutional/legal terms (CCR, decision, annulment), while the Late window becomes actor-centric (Simion, Antonescu, Ponta, Bolojan). Over time, lexical entropy declines markedly, signaling a standardization of vocabulary around procedural frames rather than escalating antagonism. Taken together, the results point to a decoupling between media normalization and individual affect, suggesting that democratic legitimacy in platformized communication environments is increasingly produced through affective legitimacy rather than procedural authority.

title: Entertainment as Trojan Horse: Voluntary Consumption of Propaganda in China
abstract: For authoritarian propaganda to change hearts and minds, it must first reach the masses and capture their attention. In an era of media proliferation, what can an authoritarian regime do to make ordinary citizens consume pro-regime propaganda voluntarily? How can it lower citizens’ resistance to being indoctrinated? In this article, we answer these questions by studying a new generation of propaganda movies in contemporary China. Leveraging observational data and a pre-registered survey experiment, we find that entertainment elements in propaganda movies – both personality-based and narrative-based – play a key role in appealing to viewers and increasing consumption; this effect is especially pronounced among groups that are the least inclined to expose themselves to propaganda in the first place. Also, viewers are more receptive to political indoctrination when it is interwoven with entertainment, even when they recognize such content. Combined, these findings highlight the importance of entertainment in authoritarian propaganda: not only does it serve as a vehicle to disseminate political indoctrination, but it also functions as a source of appeal that renders such indoctrination more palatable to the masses.

title: Kamala is Brat: TikTok and the Affective Politics of Memes
abstract: In this article, we examine TikTok memes about former Vice president Kamala Harris that circulated through the digital registers of the Charli XCX-inspired “Kamala is Brat” trend. By analyzing the form, function, and affective resonance of these memes, we explore how creators interpreted and reframed Harris’s image leading up to the 2024 U.S. presidential election. Using a multimodal analysis, we introduce a three-layer analytic that distinguishes memetic form, communicative function, and affective character. Our findings show how creators mobilized recognizable meme templates, narrative positioning, and affective cues to recast Harris through identity-signaling and aesthetic contrast to her opponent. We also find that TikTok’s features enabled a pop culture intertextuality in which other viral trends – including the appeal of “it girl” Julia Fox, and the symbolic ambiguity of signifiers ranging from Pulp Fiction, The Matrix, and coconuts – become linked to the candidate. We argue that platform-native meme cultures on TikTok operate as mechanisms of vernacular electoral mediation, enabling creators to reinterpret candidate imagery and political narratives through the aesthetic conventions of platform culture. In doing so, this work demonstrates how participatory meme practices contribute to the symbolic construction of electoral candidates in contemporary digital media environments.

title: Governing for positive peace: The role of public administration in addressing violence against children
abstract: This article examines the role of public administration in governing policies addressing violence against children from a positive peace perspective. Drawing on Jane Addams’ normative peace thinking and Johan Galtung’s distinction between negative and positive peace, it develops a peace-based typology of child policies, by forms of violence and policy orientation. This typology distinguishes between negative and positive peace-oriented policies and clarifies why policies addressing structural and cultural conditions that expose children to violence require a different administrative response. The article therefore argues for a child-centered, context-sensitive, and equitable approach to public administration rather than market-driven or purely technical models. It then translates Addams’s notion of lateral progress into four guiding principles that form a normative implementation framework: inclusive accessibility, transformative impact, participation, and social reform through co-production. The article contributes by using positive peace to reframe violence against children as a public administration concern and by advancing a child-centered understanding of administrative theory and practice.

title: Urban growth ‘without vulnerable areas’—intersections between competitiveness, cohesion, and crime prevention in social sustainability policy
abstract: This article explores how social sustainability is discursively constructed and mobilized in urban development policy in the city of Umeå, Sweden. Anchored in the municipality’s strategic goal of reaching 200,000 inhabitants by 2050 in a ‘sustainable manner’ and ‘without developing a vulnerable area,’ the study analyzes how social sustainability is variously articulated through intersecting discourses of competitiveness, safety, and risk. Drawing on a critical policy analysis of municipal documents and political communication, we identify three dominant representations of social sustainability: as a driver of competitiveness, as emotional and cultural cohesion, and as crime prevention. Ultimately, we argue that the emphasis on avoiding ‘vulnerable areas’ – terminology originating in police categorizations – leads to a securitization of sustainable (social) development and residential segregation, directing attention from structural inequalities to community trust and immediate risk management. By treating Umeå as a critical case, the article contributes to debates on post-political governance and the affective dimensions of policy, problematizing how discourses on sustainability, competition, and safety converge to shape and limit the meaning of urban development.

title: Contrasting digital coproductive roles of ‘Alipay’ and ‘Xianghubao’: analysing state’s dual governance approach towards digital platforms in China
abstract: Bridging the hitherto rarely connected scholarship on digital governance studies and that on insurtech, this paper examines how different forms of digital coproduction provided by insurtech platforms and platform-based digital infrastructure shape public service delivery and the state-steered mutuality. It asks why Xianghubao (insurtech) was banned while Alipay continues to support public service delivery. Developing the conceptual framework which integrates digital coproduction and hard/soft policy instruments, this study delves into the dual governance approach towards the state-substituting and state-augmenting forms of digital coproduction. Xianghubao exemplifies a state-substituting form, where insurtech-based risk pooling operated as quasi-insurance outside regulatory oversight, thereby triggering hard regulatory instruments. In contrast, Alipay represents a state-augmenting form of coproduction which enhances public service accessibility and reduces frontline administrative burdens, thereby strengthening state capacity. The paper contributes by theorizing how techno-political configurations of digital platforms shape divergent effects on state capacity and by showing how states selectively deploy policy instruments to manage platform-based coproduction. It offers new insights into public governance in the platform era.

title: (Non)belonging and (un)freedom
abstract: Abstract This article centers on the concept of “belonging” to argue that belonging and freedom are fundamentally related, and that this relationship cannot be easily captured in formal terms alone. I contend that experiences of incomplete belonging among citizens deserve attention from political science because, in addition to their more obvious challenge to equality, they also erode freedom, even in the context of robust formal guarantees. Citizens perceived as not fully belonging are more likely to eschew behaviors or opinions they know can exacerbate the likelihood of being perceived as interlopers. But although this challenge to individual freedom may be by itself worrisome, I focus on the ways in which some citizens’ unequal belonging undermines collective freedom—what Hannah Arendt calls political freedom—by confining some people's sincere expressions to narrow public spaces, limiting pluralism, and depleting the public space of opportunities for deliberation and political action.

title: Global harms, local profits: How the uneven costs of natural disasters affect support for green political platforms
abstract: Abstract Large‐scale fires are becoming increasingly common due to climate change. While conventional wisdom suggests that firsthand experiences with natural disasters foster green coalitions by raising awareness of environmental degradation, we propose an alternative view: Natural disasters can heighten the perceived trade‐off between economic development and environmental policies. This study examines the case of Brazil, where large‐scale fires, by clearing natural vegetation, create new opportunities for land grabbing and the expansion of agriculture and livestock production. Using satellite, administrative, and electoral data, we provide evidence that large‐scale fires increase support for green candidates only in municipalities that are unlikely to reap economic benefits from fires. Survey data further indicate that voters prioritize environmental protection over economic growth only when they stand to receive limited or no benefit from the newly cleared land. Our findings suggest that the potential for natural disasters to foster green coalitions is contingent upon distributive concerns.

title: Covering the Big Tigers in China: Patronage Ties and Political Signaling within Elite Circles
Politics and Justice: Aristotle, Rawls, and the Case for Realism in Political Theory
abstract: ABSTRACT Aristotle's analysis of stasis in Book V of the Politics offers a striking example of “distinctively political thought,” as advocated by Bernard Williams's political realism, and in contrast to the moralist approach exemplified by John Rawls. Aristotle identifies disputes over justice, driven by partial and conflicting conceptions of equality, as a principal cause of civil conflict, advocating institutional measures to manage such disagreements rather than relying on citizens converging on a correct understanding. This focus on stability as the first function of politics, aimed at preventing constitutional breakdown, parallels Williams's “first political question” and emphasizes the pragmatic safeguarding of order to avert catastrophe. By contrast, Rawls treats politics primarily as a means to realizing justice, positing that stability depends on an overlapping consensus. The paper critiques Rawls's neglect of the historical‐institutional foundations of liberalism, his underestimation of the durability of modi vivendi, and his ideal‐theoretic abstraction from the circumstances of politics. Aristotle's realist alternative provides a more plausible framework for understanding the relationship between justice and politics—a necessary corrective to Rawlsian political moralism.

title: Mapping racial voting patterns: Using RPV dispersion plots to measure and visualize voting rights evidence
Rent-seeking and litigation: some underappreciated virtues of reverse contingency fees
Private governance and the limits of state antiquity
Political polarisation of climate-policy-relevant attitudes: longitudinal evidence from Britain
abstract: This article provides a longitudinal study of political polarisation of climate-policy-relevant attitudes in Britain, 2014–2025. It shows that, in a context of increased climate salience, Britons’ climate-policy-relevant attitudes have become much more strongly associated with party support (partisan polarisation) and with other political attitudes (ideological polarisation). Consistent with findings from other West European countries, partisan polarisation is driven particularly by the growing number and increasing attitudinal distinctiveness of right-populist party supporters, while ideological polarisation occurs mainly along the cultural dimension. The article assesses individual-level polarisation mechanisms using cross-lagged panel models. Results suggest that, notwithstanding temporal fluctuation in estimated effects, both party-based attitude change and attitude-based sorting contribute to partisan polarisation. However, additional analysis suggests that ideology-based attitude change – whereby climate-policy-relevant attitudes and right-populist support both align increasingly with voters’ prior cultural attitudes – contributes substantially to both cultural ideological polarisation and partisan polarisation of climate-policy-relevant attitudes.

title: Friends with drugs: The role of social networks in the opioid epidemic
abstract: The current opioid epidemic is the worst drug epidemic the U.S. has ever faced. We examine the role of social connections in its spatial spread. Having many friendship links to counties with high opioid exposure positively correlates with overdose death rates. To address identification concerns, we exploit two quasi-natural experiments that led users to substitute illicit opioids for prescription drugs. Having more friends exposed to counties affected by these shocks leads to more overdose deaths. We also provide suggestive evidence that spillovers affect different stages of addiction, are influenced by both supply- and demand-side conditions, and are attenuated in counties with more cohesive local friendship networks. Our results show how social connections contribute to the spread of the opioid epidemic.

title: Do information and communication technologies empower female workers? Evidence from Vietnam
abstract: We examine the impact of information and communication technology (ICT) adoption on female employment outcomes in Vietnam, using data at both the firm and household levels. Our identification strategy leverages geographic variation in the engineering costs of connecting to Vietnam’s ICT backbone, along with the temporal shock of the 2007 major network capacity expansion. We find that increased ICT adoption raises firms’ female labor share and reduces gender gaps in monthly work days, formal employment, and time spent on housework. We also document a plausible mechanism: ICT adoption shifts labor demand away from routine and manual tasks toward social, customer-facing, and service-oriented tasks—areas in which women are more likely to hold a comparative advantage.

title: The Employment Effects of a Guaranteed Income: Experimental Evidence from Two U.S. States
Refugee immigration and natives’ fertility
The political economy of regional development: Evidence from the Cassa per il Mezzogiorno
Demographic transition and the rise of wealth inequality
abstract: Abstract We analyse the contribution of rising longevity to the increase in wealth inequality in the U.S. over the past seventy years. To do so, we construct an overlapping generations (OLG) model with multiple sources of inequality, carefully calibrated to the data. Our key finding is that improvements in old-age longevity have a substantial impact on wealth inequality, accounting for approximately half the effect of income inequality, which has been the focus of much of the existing literature. In contrast, the impact of tax changes is relatively minor. The contribution of rising longevity is expected to continue driving wealth inequality upward in the coming decades.

title: Political Polarization and Counter-attitudinal Information Consumption and Internalization
abstract: Abstract Political polarization can undermine democratic governance by weakening electoral accountability through biases in voter information consumption and processing. A growing literature, primarily from high-income countries, has identified promising interventions to reduce negative affect toward out-partisans, though evidence regarding their downstream effects remains mixed. We evaluate whether these depolarizing interventions and an open-mindedness nudge that increases awareness of information-processing biases stemming from emotions or partisanship promote counter-attitudinal information consumption and internalization in a survey of nearly 2,500 participants from a nationally representative panel in Mexico, a heavily polarized context. Videos designed to correct misperceptions about out-partisans improved trust in opposition media, while those designed to foster empathy or emphasize shared identities reduced partisan polarization. Although none of the videos affected immediate counter-attitudinal news consumption, exposure to either the corrective video or the open-mindedness nudge led to greater partisan attitudinal updating when participants were exposed to a counter-attitudinal news article. This effect is due to reduced partisan perceptions of the article rather than increased factual retention of its information. These findings provide insights into the potential and limitations of scalable interventions to improve citizens’ ability to consume and process politically relevant information across partisan lines.

title: A Comment on “The Heterogeneous Tax Pass-Through Under Different Vertical Relationships” by Bajo-Buenestado and Borrella-Mas
abstract: Abstract We revisit the heterogeneous tax pass-through analysis in Borrella-Mas (2022a) (B&B). We find that B&B’s estimating equation is misspecified, as it excludes a necessary lower-order interaction between vertical integration and the post-treatment period. Including this term reveals a significant structural price trend for vertically integrated firms in the post-reform period, whose origin is uncertain. A spatial placebo test confirms that this structural shift is present even in never-treated provinces, indicating that it is not a local, province-level pass-through of the regional tax. Without this control, the original specification may conflate this shift with the tax effect. Once the interaction is included, the differential pass-through estimate becomes null for diesel, while for gasoline a significant effect persists—albeit at a reduced magnitude—supporting B&B’s central claim that market structure matters for tax pass-through. These findings highlight the importance of explicitly modelling group-specific time trends when estimating heterogeneous treatment effects in difference-in-differences designs.

title: Blood and Iron: Political Fragmentation in the Ancient Eastern Mediterranean
abstract: <p>The introduction of iron metallurgy around 1200 BCE was a transformative technology shock, marking the end of the Bronze Age. Bronze required a mixture of copper and tin, with the relative scarcity of tin restricting access of the metal to elites and large imperial powers. In contrast, iron was associated with more equal access to weapons and agricultural tools. I put forward the theory that the introduction of iron reduced elite power relative to non-elites, leading to increased political fragmentation. I use newly created shapefiles of ancient polities at the century level to empirically test the hypothesis that more equal access to weapons led to greater inter- and intra-polity competition, leading to higher levels of political fragmentation after 1200 BCE. I find that access to iron metallurgy is associated with a 1.188-1.892 unit increase in polity fragmentation, measured by the number of polities in a given grid-cell.</p>

title: Lockdowns and export growth: the role of domestic production networks
The Isolation index and variations on relative exposure
Birds of a feather at first sight: Decomposing homophily into tie formation and persistence
abstract: Why do some social ties endure while others dissolve? Homophily research typically treats similarity as a single mechanism, conflating processes of tie formation and persistence. I develop a framework based on attribute observability, distinguishing between observable characteristics that guide formation under uncertainty and interaction-revealed attributes that shape tie retention. Using three-wave longitudinal friendship network data and Stochastic Actor-Oriented Models, I decompose homophily into creation and endowment effects across 28 grade networks. Observable attributes (gender, ethnicity) show strong formation effects but little persistence advantage. Interaction-revealed attributes show weaker and less precise patterns. These findings demonstrate that homophily is an information-conditional process and that standard models obscure its underlying mechanisms.

title: Working with semantic machines: The role of semantic reconciliation in public sector data governance
abstract: Local governments are beginning to use artificial intelligence (AI) in internal administrative work, including recruitment. In a decentralized municipality, however, a standardized AI assessment must travel between a technology vendor, central HR specialists, recruiters, and hiring managers responsible for different services. This creates a tension between representational portability and contextual adequacy. Based on a qualitative case study of a large Swedish municipality, we examine an AI interviewing system that translated candidates' open-ended responses into competency indicators and narrative summaries used in early-stage recruitment. We develop a process model of semantic reconciliation comprising five recurrent forms of work: scoping what could be delegated to the system, mapping vendor categories to municipal and occupational vocabularies, refining interpretations when role context was lost, embedding shared interpretations across a distributed organization, and composing AI reports with locally accountable human judgment. The study contributes to research on local-government AI and data governance by showing how semantic machines make evaluative information portable while requiring continuous organizational work to restore context. It also specifies practical arrangements through which municipalities can use common AI tools without allowing standardized outputs to displace role-specific knowledge or human decision authority.

title: Organizational Design for Public Managers By Mary E.Guy, Irvine, CA: Melvin & Leigh, Publishers, 2025. 208 pp. $44.95. ISBN : 979‐8‐99‐293050‐4
Public-Service Motivation and Proactive Administrative Behavior: Organizational Commitment and Servant-Like Supervisory Behavior in the Korean Civil Service
abstract: This study examines how public-service motivation (PSM) is associated with proactive administrative behavior among Korean civil servants and identifies organizational and supervisory conditions that help translate public-service motives into work behavior. Building on a motivation-attitude-behavior framework, organizational commitment is modeled as an attitudinal conversion mechanism, while servant-like supervisory behavior is examined as a contextual condition that may enable committed employees to express their commitment through proactive administrative behavior. Using the 2021 Survey on Civil Servants’ Work and Life ( N = 4,133), the study estimates the proposed model using partial least squares structural equation modeling with bootstrapped tests of mediation and interaction effects. PSM is positively associated with proactive administrative behavior both directly and indirectly through organizational commitment. Servant-like supervisory behavior strengthens the organizational commitment–proactive administrative behavior relationship, whereas its interaction with PSM is not statistically significant. The findings suggest that supervisory context may matter most at the attitude-to-behavior translation stage rather than as a general amplifier of public-service motives. The analysis distinguishes the measured behavioral construct from broader claims about risk-taking and accountability pressure, and treats the single-source cross-sectional design as a substantive limitation rather than as a concern that statistical diagnostics can fully eliminate.

title: Asymmetric policy capacity in hybrid regimes: from structural asymmetry to capacity divergence in Thailand’s political crises
abstract: Hybrid political systems often possess the capacity to impose order during crises without the institutional arrangements needed to legitimate and learn from those responses. This article develops the concept of asymmetric policy capacity to explain the pattern. Building on policy capacity theory, it argues that operational, political, and analytical capacities in hybrid regimes are not necessarily complementary attributes of a unified state but are distributed across rival authority centres with misaligned accountability. The framework distinguishes structural asymmetry as the background distribution, asymmetrization as the crisis-activated use of operational dominance that bypasses institutions carrying electoral legitimacy and plural information, and capacity divergence as the resulting post-crisis configuration.
