title: Democratic backsliding and public administration: lessons for theory and practice
abstract: Democracy and good public administration are often thought to go hand in hand. However, the conceptual and empirical relationship has tended to be understudied and imprecisely defined. This article draws conclusions from the volume on democratic backsliding and public administration. Drawing from the real theory of democracy, high quality public administration was argued to be an essential component of democracy since it provides citizens with the critical services to empower them to live their lives. Drawing on the studies in the volume, the article concludes that there are several ways in which political leaders may undermine public administration quality. These include reducing impartiality, increasing inequalities, creating legal uncertainty, reducing knowledge, and weakening capacity. It also identifies ways in which public administration can be protected. These include constitutional provisions, legal oversight for the police and military, strengthening organizational routines, building a professional civil service culture, and providing international support.

title: Advising governments on ethical issues: exploring the epistemic-democratic tension
Economic Security, Regional Reconfiguration, and Local Governance: The Case of TSMC 's Investment in Kumamoto
Legalised Fiscal Deviation and Data Fragmentation in Social Protection Systems: Evidence From Turkey
abstract: ABSTRACT Fiscal narratives about social protection in middle‐income countries—chronic underfunding and unsustainable institutional deficits—shape reform agendas and constrain policy choices. This article argues that such narratives can be systematically misleading, not because they misread the evidence, but because the evidence itself is produced by fragmented governance structures that prevent coherent fiscal measurement. When institutional fragmentation prevents the integration of administrative data across social protection actors, the indicators used to assess adequacy and sustainability become artefacts of classification choices rather than accurate descriptions of the system. The consequences for policy are direct: reform agendas may be structured around fiscal problems that do not exist in the form presented, while genuine governance failures remain invisible. Drawing on four institutional data sources covering Turkey's social protection system over 2002–2025—TURKSTAT's ESSPROS statistics, central government budget records, Social Security Institution (SGK) financial accounts and disaggregated budget execution data—this article provides the first systematic decomposition of budget transfers to Turkey's SGK. The findings demonstrate that social protection expenditure remained stable at 9%–11% of GDP throughout 2008–2025, that contribution revenues financed 70%–79% of SGK expenditures after 2015, and that the fiscal burden narrative surrounding the institution rests on indicators that conflate actuarial obligations with deliberate policy instruments—a form of legalised fiscal deviation sustained by governance fragmentation. The article contributes to debates on fiscal governance, democratic accountability and evidence‐based welfare state reform, and develops a governance capacity framework applicable to middle‐income countries with fragmented social protection architectures.

title: Demagogues and Despots: Democracies on the Brink
abstract: What if the political vocabulary we used to describe contemporary regimes no longer fits the political world it is meant to explain? This question has long animated John Keane’s work, and it lies a...

title: Violence when flush: commodity windfalls and the autocrat’s repertoire of repression
abstract: The third wave of autocratization is legalistic and gradual: today’s autocrats erode democracy with courts, laws, and spin rather than tanks. What makes a regime abandon the legalistic script and return to violence? We argue that money selects the repertoire. We combine the Democratic Erosion Event Dataset, which records 23,421 dated, classified, and targeted events across 156 countries, with a shift-share design that interacts fixed pre-period export baskets with world commodity prices, a world-price lottery no regime controls, to provide the first causal, event-level test of how income shocks recompose the repressive repertoire. Across 59 commodity-dependent non-liberal regimes (2000–2023), a one-standard-deviation windfall raises state activity against accountability by 5% and tilts its composition towards physical violence by 1.8 percentage points, about 7% of the mean, and away from legalistic-institutional tactics; busts run the substitution in reverse, symmetrically. The effect is contemporaneous and transitory, is driven by state-appropriable non-food commodities, and survives randomization inference; dissent does not respond, and the result replicates in an independently coded subcorpus. Legalism, the evidence suggests, is the constrained autocrat’s substitute, and commodity cycles are an anticipatable early-warning indicator of when erosion turns violent.

title: More mobilisation, same targets: party system institutionalisation and party outreach in Africa
abstract: Do higher levels of party system institutionalization make party mobilization more inclusive, or do they primarily intensify outreach to citizens who are already politically engaged? Prevailing theories of party development assume that organizational consolidation lowers mobilization costs and broadens political inclusion. Yet existing research has focused largely on whether institutionalized party systems mobilize more, rather than on whether institutionalization reshapes who is mobilised. This article advances a capacity-based account of party system institutionalization that distinguishes between the scale and social distribution of mobilization. Using individual-level data on party-initiated campaign contact from Afrobarometer Round 8, combined with system-level measures of institutionalization from the Varieties of Democracy project across 33 African countries, the analysis examines how organisational capacity shapes patterns of party outreach. The results show that higher levels of party system institutionalisation are associated with higher party contact. However, these increases do not translate into more inclusive mobilisation. Politically embedded citizens' partisan identifiers, prior voters, and civically engaged individuals remain significantly more likely to be contacted as mobilization expands with rising organizational capacity. By distinguishing between mobilization volume and mobilization distribution, the article reframes party system institutionalization as a capacity-enhancing rather than redistributive mechanism and highlights the limits of organizational consolidation for inclusive mobilization.

title: Interpersonal political discussion and affective polarization: Comparative evidence from 41 elections and five panel studies
abstract: Using data from 41 democratic elections across 20 countries via the Comparative National Elections Project, this research investigates how political discussion network composition is linked to affective polarization during electoral periods. We differentiate between in-party discussions (with co-partisans) and out-party discussions (with opposing partisans), examining their effects on in-party affinity and out-party animosity. Multilevel analyses reveal asymmetric effects: in-party discussions consistently increase both partisan affinity and out-party animosity, with effects intensifying as homogeneous network size increases. In contrast, out-party discussions reduce out-party animosity only among individuals whose networks consist exclusively of political opponents—a relatively rare configuration. When networks combine both in-party and out-party discussants, the polarizing influence of co-partisan discussion dominates, increasing overall affective polarization. Cross-lagged panel analyses using data from four European democracies—Spain, Germany, the Netherlands, and Portugal— and one Latin American—Chile— provide evidence consistent with reciprocal dynamics: findings suggest that in-party discussions are associated with higher polarization in some contexts, while revealing robust patterns indicating that existing polarization shapes discussion partner selection through affective avoidance. This avoidance mechanism proves remarkably consistent: out-party animosity predicts reduced cross-partisan discussion in four of five countries, suggesting that polarized citizens systematically withdraw from conversations with political opponents. In contrast, the depolarizing potential of cross-partisan contact emerges only in specific electoral contexts. These findings challenge assumptions about the universal benefits of cross-cutting political exposure and highlight the predominant role of homophilous networks in driving democratic societies toward increasing affective polarization.

title: Toft Response: “Getting Religion Even More Right”
Beyond the Average: Revisiting How District Magnitude Shapes Party Systems
abstract: We argue that district magnitude shapes the number of electoral parties through two mechanisms: district permissiveness, which influences incentives for electoral coordination within districts, and variation in district magnitude across districts within a country. When district magnitude varies within countries, larger districts tend to support a greater number of parties. Small parties that succeed in these districts are subsequently incentivized to compete in smaller districts, thereby weakening overall electoral coordination. Using cross-sectional data from 54 democracies and longitudinal evidence from 30 European countries between 1945 and 2019, we find that within-country variation in district magnitude increases the number of electoral parties in permissive electoral systems and erodes electoral coordination over time. We further examine the contamination mechanism from larger to smaller districts using district-level data from legislative elections in Portugal and Spain, both of which employ simple Proportional Representation systems with varying district magnitudes.

title: A hangover like any other: the cost of ruling for populist parties
abstract: Abstract Populist parties have grown rapidly in popularity in many European countries and have increasingly become common in government coalitions. Because these parties often make expansive promises and derive much of their appeal from their outsider status, entering government may become an electoral liability by the next election. Analyzing populist and mainstream parties in 32 European countries from 1980 to 2023, we estimate the average electoral effect of government participation. We find a post-power penalty of about 4.5–5 percentage points on average. This penalty is remarkably similar for populist and mainstream parties, suggesting that populist parties do not suffer an additional electoral cost from governing. Moreover, the size of the post-power penalty does not vary systematically with growth, inequality, social spending, globalization, or unemployment during the governing term. These findings suggest that bringing populist parties into government does not, by itself, impose a distinctive electoral cost on them relative to other incumbent parties.

title: The political economy of exit protection
abstract: Abstract Existing theories explain how exit disciplines governments but generally treat citizens’ ability to relocate as an institutional primitive. This paper instead endogenizes exit protection by modeling jurisdictions that first choose whether to preserve or eliminate mobility before competing through extraction. Although preserving exit uniquely maximizes investment and social welfare, it is not self-enforcing because jurisdictions can profit by creating captive populations. Exit protection is therefore institutionally fragile. The paper then evaluates alternative constitutional architectures capable of addressing this incentive problem and develops one formally. The analysis identifies a benchmark constitutional architecture under which decentralized political orders could, in principle, sustain exit without relying on hierarchical enforcement, repeated interaction, or citizen coercive power.

title: Paying to Match: Decentralized Markets with Information Frictions
abstract: Abstract We experimentally study decentralized one-to-one matching markets with transfers. We vary the information available to participants, complete or incomplete, and the surplus structure, supermodular or submodular. Several insights emerge. First, while markets often culminate in efficient matchings, stability is more elusive, reflecting the difficulty of arranging attendant transfers. Second, incomplete information and submodularity present hurdles to efficiency and especially stability; their combination drastically diminishes stability's likelihood. Third, matchings form ``from the top down'' in complete-information supermodular markets, but exhibit many more and less-obviously ordered offers otherwise. Last, participants' market positions matter far more than their dynamic bargaining styles for outcomes.

title: Why Veil? Religious Headscarves and the Economic Role of Women
abstract: Abstract We show that the emergence of new economic opportunities that draw women away from their traditional domestic roles has significantly influenced the adoption of religious veiling. We measure the prevalence of veiling among young women across Indonesia's districts for more than two decades by hand-coding around a quarter million photographs attached to Indonesia's public high school registers. To establish causality, we exploit exogenous variation generated by international demand for Indonesia's products, interacted with the gender and sectoral composition of local industries. Districts exposed to stronger positive economic shocks---and thus greater economic opportunities for women---exhibit higher rates of veiling adoption. Our findings suggest that veiling facilitates young women's participation in formal labor markets while safeguarding their personal and social image in society.

title: Labor Supply and the Pension Contribution-Benefit Link
abstract: Abstract We estimate the impact of public pension incentives on labor supply far from the normal retirement age by exploiting Poland's switch from a Defined Benefit to a Notional Defined Contribution (NDC) scheme. This reform created a sharp cohort-based discontinuity in the link between current pension contributions and future benefits. Using this discontinuity and the universe of taxpayers, we estimate an employment elasticity with respect to the net return to work of 0.51 for men at ages 51-54. We estimate a lifecycle model to match these responses and discuss the broader implications of the reform. The shift to NDC reallocates work incentives over the lifecycle, strengthening incentives at younger ages, when labor supply is relatively inelastic, and weakening them at older ages, when labor supply is more elastic. This reallocation of work incentives tends to reduce aggregate lifecycle labor supply, which highlights the advantage of targeting pension incentives towards ages at which labor supply is most responsive.

title: Early-Career Discrimination: Spiraling or Self-Correcting?
abstract: Abstract Do workers from social groups with comparable productivity distributions obtain comparable lifetime earnings? We study how a small amount of early-career discrimination propagates over time when workers’ productivity is revealed through employment. In breakdown learning environments that primarily track on-the-job failures, such discrimination spirals into a substantial lifetime earnings gap for groups of comparable productivity, whereas in breakthrough learning environments that track successes, early-career discrimination can be self-corrected, so comparable groups obtain comparable lifetime earnings. This contrast persists in large labor markets and with flexible wages, inconclusive learning, and misspecified employer beliefs.

title: Procedural rationality, endogenous sampling, and the instability of defection
Editorial Board
Temporary exclusion in repeated contests
abstract: Consider a population of agents who repeatedly compete for awards, as in the case of researchers annually applying for grants. Noise in the selection process may encourage entry of low-quality proposals, forcing the principal to commit large resources to reviewing applications and further increasing award misallocation. A temporary exclusion policy prohibits an agent from applying in the current period if they received a low evaluation in the previous. We study the steady-state equilibria under various policies of this type. With exclusion, agents that have low-quality applications self-select to stay out, which reduces the volume of submissions and mitigates award misallocation. At the same time, the volume of high-quality applications is also reduced due to the ineligibility of banned agents. We also show that exclusion has a distributional effect, where higher-ability agents exhibit more self-selection.

title: Labor Associations: The Blue Wall of Silence
abstract: ABSTRACT We present a model showing that when the demand for labor services is inelastic and individual behavior is imperfectly monitored, a firm's employees may prefer to protect its shirkers and conceal information about peers' performance from the firm.

title: Reproduction, rejection, or adoption of indigeneity? Intergenerational patterns of ethnic classification in contemporary Mexico
Sex differences in academic achievement in US adolescents: the role of maturation and impulse control
How to further develop the United Nations’ risk assessment guidance using current risk science knowledge
abstract: The United Nations (UN) uses considerable resources on risk assessments, to enhance the understanding and management of risk, reduce vulnerabilities and strengthen resilience. The UN recommendations and guidance documents have a considerable impact on how risk assessments are conducted and used in different countries. The quality of these recommendations and documents is therefore very important. The present paper performs a review of this quality from a risk science perspective, building on recent documents developed by the Society for Risk Analysis and related scientific work. We conclude that the UN recommendations and documents provide solid guidance on many key features of risk assessments, but there is a potential for improvements in some areas, particularly in relation to the way risk is described. Traditional risk matrices are still promoted, despite their weaknesses in reflecting risk. Potential surprises are not given sufficient attention in the risk assessments.

title: Encoding the nation: Media, compressed modernity, and the global projection of Korean identity
abstract: This article addresses a central puzzle in media studies: how a nation’s turbulent experience of rapid development become a foundational narrative for its global media projection? Focussing on South Korea, the article argues that contemporary national identity and its transnational cultural influence are best understood through a tripartite framework linking ‘the own’ (enduring traditions and ethnic nationalism), ‘the near’ (social ruptures generated by compressed modernity), and ‘the far’ (global repackaging of these experiences through Hallyu ). The study posits that Korea’s global cultural success is not merely a manufactured export but a structural expression of its historical trajectory, aestheticised to transform domestic socio-political tensions into global symbolic capital. Methodologically, the article combines historical scrutiny with illustrative analysis of key cultural texts across cinema, K-drama, and K-pop, alongside a dual-circuit model of cultural diffusion. The findings demonstrate that tensions produced by rapid development are structurally intertwined with international media projection, offering a heuristic framework for analysing similar trajectories of cultural power in the 21st century.

title: Contradicting Epistemic Inequalities: The Case of the Journalist Navina Sundaram
abstract: This contribution asks how social inequalities are perpetuated through colonial silences maintained through practices of knowledge production in journalism. Drawing on postcolonial scholarship, it examines how these silences have historically been challenged between the 1960s and 1980s. Based on documents from the personal files of Navina Sundaram, one of the first non-White journalists on West German television, it traces the practices of contradicting that challenge and uphold journalistic epistemology: contradicting visibility in editorial practices, contradicting through international networks, and denying belonging. Together, these practices show how debates on diversity in German journalism are rooted in historical struggles for epistemic justice.

title: The Trouble With Catching Up: Problematizing the “AI Gap” and its Global Inequities in Journalism
abstract: The “artificial intelligence (AI) gap” in journalism describes a divide between newsrooms equipped to innovate and benefit from AI and those left behind. Rather than an objective condition, this study examines this gap as a discursive construction, drawing on articulation theory. Using the JournalismAI Academy for Small Newsrooms as a case study, we combine ethnographic observation with interviews conducted in 2022 to 2023 and 2025. Findings demonstrate how technological lag is articulated as a problem and AI investment as its solution, a linkage stabilized through assumptions of inevitable, linear technological progress—legitimizing particular ways of thinking about and acting on AI.

title: China’s Soft Power Projection in the Middle East—North Africa
abstract: This paper analyzes China’s expanding soft power strategy in the Middle East and North Africa (MENA). It explores how Beijing shapes regional perceptions through education, language promotion, media cooperation, and cultural initiatives. Using qualitative analysis of policy documents, official speeches, and regional reporting, the study identifies the main tools and audiences of China’s efforts. Findings show that China’s approach is highly state-directed and rooted in official policy. Through language programs, media partnerships, and cultural centers, China seeks to enhance its image and build ties with regional elites. While these initiatives have increased visibility and political alignment, their long-term effectiveness in fostering genuine cultural attraction remains uncertain, underscoring both the potential and limitations of China’s soft power in MENA.

title: South Korea’s Three Kindergarten Laws: A Revision Process Analysis Using a Complex Policy Change Analytical Model
abstract: This study was conducted to assess the usefulness of the complex policy change analysis (CPCA) model and to identify key turning points in the process of revising South Korea’s three kindergarten laws (3KL). Using the CPCA model and its associated analytical methods, the analysis confirmed three main findings: the victory of the pro-revision coalition, which secured both public and presidential support; the failure of the anti-revision coalition due to its reliance on extra-parliamentary struggle; and the limited functional role played by the policy mediators. These findings offer empirical support for the explanatory power of the CPCA model in accounting for policy change.

title: “Real estate compan[ies] with an academic division”: framing anchor institutions as real estate institutions
abstract: Anchor institutions are often critiqued for expanding into and gentrifying areas surrounding their campuses. Simultaneously, institutions frame themselves as beneficial to local communities and use this narrative to justify their property tax exemption status. Cities are sometimes able to recoup a portion of lost property taxes through Payment in Lieu of Taxes (PILOTs), a tool where property tax exempt institutions agree to contribute to the municipality. Existing literature on PILOTs focuses on the mechanics of PILOTs and their agreements. We use counterstories to examine the community movement to get the University of Pennsylvania to commit to PILOTs, which highlights how community members contest the university’s tax status and its role in community development. Through data drawn from interviews with community activists, we find that participants reframe anchor institutions not as philanthropic nonprofits deserving of tax credits but as real estate institutions that ought to be taxed. Where the university views donations to a local school and expansion of its police force as support for community, the movement perceives these as tools to further the university’s real estate interests through boosting land use value. Our finding provides insights into community perceptions of universities and their obligation to public finance.

title: Digital resilience in delivering public services. A conceptual model
Government institutions and data custodianship over personal information: Comparing citizen preferences in Hong Kong and South Korea
abstract: Public administration researchers traditionally approach the use of personal information in public service through the lens of direct user control, but a combination of cognitive constraints and rapid digitization has made privacy-preserving choices exceedingly difficult for citizens to manage independently. Recent research has shifted toward the notion of “data custodianship”, where public institutions serve as custodians of personal information. In a survey experiment conducted in Hong Kong ( n = 1031) and South Korea ( n = 1040), citizens evaluated their trust in various institutions serving as custodians tasked with managing biometric information for facial recognition. The findings suggest that while institutional trust can be influenced by accountability mechanisms, it is also shaped by individuals' experiences with public institutions, as well as their political orientation, social trust, and privacy preferences. Trust in one functional domain of data custodianship—such as data collection—may not carry over to others, like storage or management. Custodianship is only viable as a policy alternative to user control in data-intensive solutions if its design accounts for variation in public trust across societies, individuals, and aspects of data governance.

title: Connected for Survival: How Organizational Networks with Government Strengthen Nonprofit Resilience in Delivering Public Services
abstract: Drawing on pre- and post-COVID-19 surveys of human service and arts-and-culture nonprofits, this study examined how preexisting social connectedness and revenue structure were associated with organizational resilience. Nonprofits with more connections to government reported fewer operational disruptions, particularly in program delivery, contract continuity, and volunteer capacity, than peers whose ties were concentrated within the nonprofit sector. Financial profiles also mattered, although the relationship between revenue diversification and resilience was more complex than expected. Together, the findings identify social connectedness and revenue structure as important correlates of resilience. The study’s central contribution is to specify the conditions under which collaboration and resource diversification translate into organizational capacity during crises and to offer guidance for nonprofit leaders seeking to build more resilient organizations.

title: Implicit-Explicit Incongruence: The Dual Structure of Public Value Preferences in Civil Servants
abstract: Research on public value preferences (PVPs) among civil servants is a key area in public value studies. However, existing research on PVPs has not considered their implicit dimensions, which largely limits the understanding of the concept’s structure and measurement. Drawing on the dual-attitudes model from social psychology, this article proposes an explicit–implicit dual structure of PVPs and empirically tests this structure using a quasi-experimental design. The sample comprised a civil servant group (n = 109) and a non‑civil servant group (n = 116). Findings show that civil servants’ PVPs have a two-dimensional structure of explicit and implicit: Compared with non-civil servants, civil servants have more positive explicit PVPs but relatively negative implicit PVPs. This study systematically examines the existence, direction, and magnitude of the incongruence between civil servants’ implicit and explicit PVPs, offering a more cognitively complex theoretical framework for PVPs.

title: Acts of moral courage among civil servants under democratic backsliding: A comparison of the Trump and Bolsonaro administrations
abstract: Under the administrations of US President Donald J. Trump (2017–2021) and Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro (2019–2022), democratic backsliding intensified through illiberal reforms, institutional erosion, and growing political pressures on public administration. Drawing on in-depth interviews with 82 Brazilian and 66 US career civil servants, this study examines episodes of moral courage, defined as principled actions rooted in higher order democratic and professional standards taken in the face of political pressure and personal risk. We find some distinctive trajectories of morally courageous actions across countries and identify the organizational and individual conditions that enable such acts. Crucially, comparable pressures did not produce comparable responses: Brazilian civil servants mobilized through more collective, open, and confrontational acts, whereas their US counterparts adopted more individualized and cautious strategies. We argue that certain relational and organizational contextual factors explain this divergence. We also identified some key factors in both countries that enabled morally courageous action. At the organizational level, supportive professional cultures and strong internal and external networks emerge as key facilitators. At the individual level, moral courage is associated with commitment to agency missions, a sense of self-efficacy, long-term moral reflection, and civic engagement. Our study contributes a cross-national comparative perspective on bureaucratic responses to democratic erosion and integrates existing insights into a comparative framework to guide future research on defending democratic norms under illiberal rule. Points for practitioners Civil servants are better able to act with moral courage, and are better shielded from political retaliation, where meso-level organizational conditions support such action during periods of democratic backsliding. A professional culture grounded in democratic values and a safe organizational environment for reporting misconduct enable civil servants to uphold their agency's mission and the law under political pressure. Supportive workplaces that encourage collaboration among peers and supervisors help civil servants share strategies and sustain valued work in the face of political threats. Strong ties to professional associations and other external support networks enhance civil servants' capacity to defend democratic norms and, as the Brazilian case shows, can be decisive in enabling collective and open forms of moral courage.

title: Negotiating Presence: The Dynamics of Passive Representation Among Ultra‐Orthodox Women in Public Organizations
abstract: ABSTRACT Studies in representative bureaucracy have focused on whether passive representation translates into active representation. We shift this analytical lens by conceptualizing passive representation not as a static demographic condition or a preliminary stage, but as a dynamic organizational process. Drawing on 15 in‐depth interviews and a focus group with 14 ultra‐Orthodox women serving in mid‐ and senior‐level public positions in Israel, we examine how passive representation is enacted, negotiated, and gradually institutionalized in male‐dominated settings. Findings show how women's underrepresentation structures their entry and advancement through informal expectations and gendered networks, and how women “negotiate presence” by building legitimacy through heightened professionalism, creative networking in the face of gender segregation, and strategic engagement with supportive leaders. Through mentoring and gate‐opening practices, our participants created ripple effects that increased access for others over time. We argue that passive representation is a relational and evolving mechanism shaped by role interpretations and organizational constraints, reshaping access and participation even without formal policy changes.

title: Convergence of Low‐Fertility Policies Beyond Policy Transfer: A Comparative Analysis of Korea and Hungary
abstract: ABSTRACT This study compares policy responses to persistent low fertility in Korea and Hungary, two countries facing similar demographic pressures but embedded in distinct institutional settings. It asks whether the diffusion of pronatalist policies has produced convergence in the design, implementation, and effects of fertility policy in these cases. Drawing on comparative institutional analysis and recent policy and demographic data, the study shows that although both countries have adopted similar instruments—including cash transfers, housing support, and parental leave—their policy frameworks differ substantially in governance, targeting, and political justification. Korea's approach is fragmented, technocratic, and broadly inclusive, whereas Hungary's is centralized, ideologically framed, and more selective in its targeting. The findings suggest that similar policy instruments do not necessarily generate similar demographic or social outcomes: Korea has remained at ultra‐low fertility with limited evidence of behavioral response, while Hungary experienced a modest and temporary increase in fertility alongside heightened political salience. These findings challenge the assumption that benchmarking similar policy instruments ensures substantive convergence in outcomes. This study refines policy convergence theory by distinguishing instrumental similarity from deeper divergence in institutional logic, governance, and implementation intensity.

title: Beyond monolithic state logic: how top-down accountability shapes policy implementation
abstract: How does top-down accountability shape policy implementation? Drawing on institutional logics, this paper distinguishes two state sub-logics: ‘high-stakes context logic’ emphasizing centralized control during crises, and ‘routine governance logic’ allowing discretion during day-to-day administration. These sub-logics condition the perceived legitimacy of accountability demands, felt accountability, and behavioural responses. A survey experiment with over 800 public service respondents shows that, under high-stakes logic, intensified accountability progressively improve compliance, whereas under routine logic, moderate accountability produces optimal compliance, with high-intensity accountability yielding diminishing returns. These findings challenge binary views of accountability and reveal how within-logic variations may alter governance mechanisms.

title: Gender inequality at the street level explained: redoing gender through informal practices
abstract: This study examines whether gendered differences in discretion shape inequality among street-level bureaucrats (SLBs). Focusing on the provision of informal personal resources (IFRs) to clients, we analyzed 59 in-depth interviews with social workers in Israel. While both women and men engage in extensive informal practices, their scope and form differ. Two mechanisms drive the reproduction of inequality: invisibility versus visibility of IFRs, and boundary setting between personal and professional spheres. These findings reveal that discretion in implementation not only is gendered but also reproduces conventional hierarchies, intensifying gender inequality at the street level of public administration.

title: Contingent capacity: navigating organizational dependency in Dutch municipal energy transitions
abstract: Municipalities implementing energy transition mandates rely on contingent workers to fill capacity and expertise gaps, raising concerns about dependency and knowledge loss. Drawing on Resource Dependence Theory and client–consultant literature, this study develops a framework capturing the feedback loop between external reliance and internal capacity development. Fifteen interviews across six Dutch municipalities show that labour shortages and temporary subsidies drive contingent hiring, while short contracts and limited knowledge transfer heighten dependency. Municipalities facing similar constraints diverge through knowledge integration, governance arrangements, and relational dynamics. It advances public administration scholarship by conceptualising dependency as a process rather than structural outcome.

title: Debate: Rearming Europe—divided we fall
abstract: With an aggressive Russia and a deteriorating geopolitical situation, European countries are rushing to rearm. NATO targets 5% of GDP spent on defence in every member country by 2035 (NATO, 2025). ...

title: Household debt relief as financial inclusion policy: Quasi-experimental evidence from Desenrola Brasil
abstract: IMPACTThis article provides evidence-based insights for policy-makers and public finance professionals in debt management and financial inclusion. The authors’ analysis of Brazil's Desenrola program shows that publicly supported household debt relief can effectively reduce over-indebtedness and national credit arrears, even amid economic volatility and low financial literacy. The findings offer actionable guidance for emerging economies designing debt relief programs where digital infrastructure, public guarantees, and income-targeted eligibility are central design features. Beyond Brazil, the evidence contributes to debates on the state's role in credit market stabilization and the conditions under which public intervention reduces financial exclusion without fiscal or behavioural distortions.

title: Legal Corruption in the Government: An Experimental Study on the Role of Civil Servants' Political Ideology
abstract: ABSTRACT Legal corruption, also known as institutional corruption, has become prevalent in the public sector, but empirical research on this subject is still at a nascent stage. Given its potentially detrimental impact on the perceived level of organizational capacity among internal members, understanding civil servants' views of legal corruption is essential. We contribute to this literature a discussion of civil servants' assessment of legal corruption in the government and evidence from a survey experiment with more than 2000 South Korean civil servants. The results of our analysis suggest that civil servants evaluate the degree of legal corruption in the government through their political lens, that is, their political ideology. Specifically, they tend to be more critical when the government is ruled by a chief executive and party that have different political views from their own, compared to when it is governed by those with the same political views. The implications of this study are clear: the central role of political views and policy preferences in understanding perceptions of legal corruption in the public sector.

title: Disparity in Police Disciplinary Outcomes: The Mediating Effect of Complaint Disposition for Organizational Outgroups
abstract: In response to demands for greater police accountability, many departments have adopted policies designed to better regulate the use of force and to make it easier to investigate and punish officers accused of wrongdoing. While not widespread, there is some evidence that these changes have increased disciplinary actions. However, it remains uncertain whether police discipline has been applied equitably across racial and gender groups within departments. Drawing on multiple bodies of scholarship, we develop the expectation that, because of their status as members of organizational outgroups, Black, Hispanic and female officers are likely to be disciplined at higher rates. Importantly, we also argue that racial, ethnic and gender differences in disciplinary outcomes are at least partially mediated by the way in which police departments treat complaints against these officers. We test these hypotheses in data from Chicago's Civilian Office of Police Accountability (COPA) from 1971 through 2018. Analyses of over 249,000 allegations indicate that female and Black officers and officers face a higher likelihood of reprimand and suspension compared to White male officers. Differences across these groups are entirely explained, however, by the greater likelihood that complaints against these officers are deemed sufficiently supported by evidence to warrant disciplinary action. We conclude by discussing the broader implications for understanding employee discipline and the potential impact of recent efforts to enhance police accountability.
journal_name: The American Review of Public Administration

title: Attitudes towards carbon taxation in the EU: messenger effects vs. content effects
abstract: Abstract This paper investigates how European Union institutional sources influence public support for carbon taxes through messenger effects. Our framework predicts that support decreases with higher tax rates, an effect moderated by respondents’ associations with the source, namely trust, euroscepticism, and national identity. We run a pre-registered survey-embedded vignette experiment in Germany and Poland ( N = 3192), in which respondents evaluate carbon tax policies for car, aviation, and heating fuels. Proposals vary in tax rate (10%, 50%, 100%) and supporting source (European Commission, national government, foreign government). We find that higher tax rates decrease support and that source-specific effects are driven by trust, but not by national identity or euroscepticism, which instead structure baseline support across all actors. Moreover, positive messenger cues do not moderate the negative effect of costs. These findings show that institutional attitudes matter for carbon tax support, but that policy costs remain central.

title: Marketization without mitigation? Designing mixed-ownership reform under decarbonization constraints
abstract: This paper asks whether mixed-ownership reform (MOR), the expansion of non-state ownership through reductions in the state share in state-owned enterprises (SOEs), supports or undermines decarbonization goals. MOR is widely adopted to improve efficiency and competitiveness, yet reform designs often understate how stronger profit incentives and market pressures can reshape firms’ emissions behavior. Using matched firm-level production and fuel-use data for Chinese industrial SOEs, we estimate the effect of MOR on carbon intensity. We find that MOR increases carbon intensity by about 1.2%. Mechanism evidence indicates that reform strengthens profit orientation, coincides with weaker environmental management (fewer pollution-control facilities), and shifts energy use toward coal at the margin. Employment also falls following reform, pointing to adjustment costs that can shape political feasibility. The findings imply that ownership diversification is not, by itself, a decarbonization instrument and can generate emissions-intensity backsliding where constraints and monitoring are weak. We recommend designing MOR as a bundled reform: attach enforceable no-backsliding conditions on emissions intensity, embed carbon and energy KPIs in governance and managerial evaluation, apply risk-tier monitoring in high-risk regions and sectors, accelerate coal switching and efficiency upgrades, and pair reforms with just-transition supports.

title: Pushed Out, Not Plugged In: Welfare Disjuncture in Hong Kong‐Guangdong Cross‐Border Ageing
abstract: ABSTRACT Hong Kong's eldercare system faces structural deficits from land scarcity and labour costs. Confronted with care shortages, the government has geographically externalised responsibilities to Guangdong Province, constructing a transborder “welfare hinterland” under “One Country, Two Systems.” Drawing upon fieldwork with 53 Hong Kong older adults enrolled in the Residential Care Services Scheme in Guangdong, this study reveals that spatial displacement generates inter‐jurisdictional institutional misfit: older adults are “pushed out” by the Hong Kong welfare regime yet “not plugged in” to Guangdong's system, acquiring immediate care whilst forfeiting welfare allowances and housing entitlements, becoming “semi‐welfare citizens” suspended between jurisdictions—a condition emblematic of ageing out of place. This article conceptualises this as “welfare disjuncture”—the interruption of eligibility when traversing institutional boundaries. Three dimensions are analysed: healthcare disjuncture exposes non‐transferable and immoveable institutional trust; cash transfer disjuncture reveals incongruity between eligibility thresholds and life trajectories; and housing disjuncture demonstrates how “surrender upon departure” negates cyclical cross‐border realities. These reflect temporal‐biographical disjuncture between institutional and biological time. When bureaucratic rhythms collide with biological exigencies, elders must forfeit entitlements to secure survival. The article argues for moving beyond formalistic “welfare portability” to achieve “disjuncture‐free mobility”.

title: Votes against voting: Recall escalation as behavioural evidence of electoral (mis)confidence in Taiwan’s “Great Recall”
abstract: This article examines public confidence in the results of democratic elections through Taiwan’s “Great Recall” in 2025, during which over half of the legislators were targeted by recall campaigns. Rather than relying on self-reported attitudes, the article conceptualises electoral (mis)confidence as a latent disposition whose behavioural implications can be inferred from institutionalised electoral contestation. The escalation of recall efforts is treated as a behavioural proxy for this latent construct: the further a recall advances, the more clearly it suggests a withdrawal of specific electoral support from an existing representative outcome. Methodologically, the analysis integrates supervised machine learning with Bayesian ordinal estimation. A LASSO regression identifies salient predictors among thirteen variables categorised as structural, behavioural, and discursive, while a Bayesian ordinal model estimates their probabilistic associations with recall advancement. The dependent variable is a four-level ordinal measure of recall progress. Explanatory variables include legislators’ gender, constituency type, party alignment, electoral margins, turnout volatility, and the discursive factors of volume and sentiment in traditional news coverage ( China Times and Liberty Times ) and new-media discussions (PTT and Threads). Results indicate that recall escalation is more likely in urban constituencies and when traditional media coverage is extensive and negative, but less likely for female and ruling-party legislators, and where media sentiment is more positive. The article argues that urban contexts and negative media environments are associated with higher levels of recall escalation, whereas ruling-party affiliation and gendered representational quality are associated with lower levels. The findings suggest how patterned recall escalation can function as a behavioural proxy for analysing electoral confidence under conditions of heightened political contestation.

title: Voter reactions to party policy repositioning: The role of inclusive intra-party decision-making
abstract: Changes in position present opportunities and risks for political parties. Parties reposition themselves hoping that the new stance will prove more popular among voters. Yet, position changes also carry dangers, as they can make parties appear opportunistic or incoherent. This study tests whether intra-party decision-making influences how voters react to party repositioning. We suggest that voters may approve of a position change more if it is based on an inclusive, rather than secretive, decision-making process. Thus, policy repositioning approved by the broader party membership should be appreciated more. We conduct a preregistered conjoint survey experiment in which we present British respondents with hypothetical repositioning on environmental and healthcare policy by Labour and the Greens. We find that more inclusive procedures increase approval of the repositioning and propensity to vote for the party. This study sheds light on how voters evaluate party policy repositioning, with important implications for our understanding of how intra-party dynamics relate to party performance.

title: Populism, radicalism, and protest mobilization by parties in Europe
abstract: Abstract As European democracies struggle with a ‘crisis of representation’, populist parties appear to be instrumental in channeling popular discontent with governments across the continent, including through protests. While contemporary theories propose a strong connection between populism and protest mobilization, this has seldom been tested in a comparative perspective. At the same time, research has found that radical parties are more likely to mobilize for protests, and those parties are often also populist. We empirically disentangle these relationships with a comprehensive dataset of 4.8 million Facebook posts by all active sitting MPs in all EU27 national parliaments plus the UK between 2018 and 2023, using large language models to identify protest-related posts and those that announce protest events. Findings show that it is particularly radical parties mobilizing their followers, with populism itself having little additional explanatory power. This is the first cross-national, longitudinal evaluation of a much-touted theoretical connection between populist parties and protest mobilization, finding that it appears smaller and more conditional than prior research proposed.

title: Whataboutism in International Diplomacy: Shaping Third-Party Public Attitudes Toward U.S. Foreign Policy
abstract: How does whataboutism influence the attitudes of third-party and allied audiences during international diplomatic exchanges? States openly accused of misconduct often employ whataboutism, deflecting criticism by highlighting the accuser’s own transgressions. Although policymakers frequently discuss whataboutism, research on its effects—especially on third-party publics—is limited. This study addresses the gap by examining via survey experiments a “hard case”: the impact of whataboutism targeting the U.S. on Japanese and the British publics, two steadfast U.S. allies. Our findings reveal that whataboutism significantly undermines support for the critic’s actions and diminishes the willingness of these populations to back sanctions led by the critic against states engaging in whataboutism. These results, the first empirical evidence of whataboutism’s effects on third-party allied publics, highlight whataboutism’s potency in shaping international public opinion, even among audiences from nations closely aligned with the critic country, potentially constraining U.S. foreign policy options.

title: Outgroup Empathy and Opposition to Restrictive Voting Laws
abstract: A suite of state-level laws that increase the burden placed on eligible voters has proliferated in the years following the 2013 Shelby County v. Holder decision. Critics have argued that these laws are thinly veiled attempts by Republicans to disenfranchise minority groups who lean toward the Democratic Party. If this is the case, attitudes about these restrictive policies should be powerfully driven by empathy for the groups negatively impacted, so long as individuals recognize the racialized intent behind the laws. This study examines the links between outgroup empathy and opposition to a variety of voting restrictions. Evidence from multiple national surveys conducted from 2018 to 2024 indicates that higher outgroup empathy indeed corresponds to greater opposition to restrictive voting laws. As predicted, however, this relationship is highly conditional on political sophistication: those most likely to be aware that these laws target minorities are also those who bring outgroup empathy to bear on their opposition to voting regulations intended to restrict access to the ballot.

title: Within and beyond the national identity? ‘Post-hill tribe’ Hmong political subjectivities in northern Thailand
abstract: Across mainland Southeast Asia, highland ethnic minority groups were divided by the demarcation of international borders. In Thailand, this coincided with rampant nation-building projects that unfolded throughout the 20th Century. These projects were highly focused on a national Thai identity, and clear demarcations of which subjects were within or beyond this 'imagined community'. The so-called ‘hill tribes’ in the country's north were labelled as outside this national identity, while other ethnic minority groups were seen as better assimilated into ‘Thai-ness’. The Hmong ethnic group has been central to this history, villainized for their ‘disloyalty’ to Thailand, history of opium production, and specific swidden agricultural practices. Demonstrating how feminist nationalism studies can better integrate considerations of history, culture, and ethnicity, I analyze the resultant subjectivities of state-making projects designed to exclude ‘Others within’. A near-century after being rendered an ‘enemy’ of the national interest, or what I call ‘post-hill tribe’ Thailand, I argue that Hmong simultaneously self-identify as non-Thai, while selectively engaging in ‘Thai-ization’. Advancing feminist political geographies of how political subjectivities are experienced in everyday life, I uncover how residents of one Hmong village negotiate their political subjectivities through clans and family names, textiles and cultural beauty, and animist-Buddhist belief systems. I argue that while the government toyed with policies aimed at assimilation and integration, Hmong individuals have chosen to embrace their non-Thai identity as a way of prefacing their strong sociocultural affinity, without forfeiting their right to exist and thrive in Thai-land.

title: Picking Winners: Local Land Allocation and Bottom-Up Industrial Policy in China
Revealed Social Networks
abstract: Abstract The linear-in-means model is the standard empirical model of peer effects and asks that an agent’s choice or outcome is a combination of their ideal point and the mean outcome of their group. Using choice data and exogenous group variation, we develop a revealed preference style test for the linear-in-means model. This test is formulated as a linear program and can be interpreted as a condition about differentiating the behaviour of each agent in a consistent manner. We then study the identification properties of the linear-in-means model. A key takeaway from our analysis is the close relationship between the dimension of the outcome variable and identification. When the outcome variable is one-dimensional, failures of identification are generic. When the outcome variable is multidimensional, we provide natural conditions under which identification is generic.

title: Transport mode and the geography of exchange rate pass-through
Optimal Stopping under Volatility Ambiguity
When Is the Trend the Cycle?
Emotions, political ideology, and socially situated risk perceptions of water-related natural hazards
abstract: Water-related natural hazards such as drought, wildfires, and flooding pose growing risks to water-dependent rural communities, but political polarization complicates adaptation planning and collective responses. Discrete emotional reactions to these hazards can shape how risks are perceived and whether institutional support is viewed as necessary. Drawing on the risk-as-feelings, social amplification of risk, and cultural cognition frameworks, risk perception is conceptualized as a socially situated affective process that is grounded in lived hazard experiences. A representative survey of Wyoming residents (N = 557) was analyzed using moderated mediation models to assess how discrete emotions, organized by arousal (high/low) and valence (positive/negative), predicted perceived risk and institutional support needs, with political ideology as a moderator. High arousal negative emotions (e.g. fear, worry, anger) showed the largest and most consistent effects on risk perceptions across ideological groups, with the strongest effect among conservatives (b = 0.42, p < .001) compared to liberals (b = 0.27, p < .001) and moderates (b = 0.35, p < .001). Higher risk perceptions, in turn, predicted increased need for support to address water-related natural hazards. High arousal positive emotions (e.g. hope, confidence) directly predicted need for support perceptions among liberals only and did not significantly influence risk perceptions. Emotional arousal appears to function as a mechanism of risk amplification. Political ideology influenced the strength of emotional responses on risk perceptions but did not eliminate the associations between emotion, risk appraisal, and governance expectations. These findings clarify how discrete emotions and ideological identity jointly shape perceptions of risk severity and support for institutional responses and offer insights for understanding public expectations about risk governance in politically polarized, hazard-exposed rural communities.

title: The risk of unknown: preventive behavioural intention related to PFAS exposure
abstract: Applying the psychometric paradigm and the extended parallel process model (EPPM), this study examines how highlighting the unknown aspect of the health risks from per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) influences people’s intention to engage in preventive behaviours. U.S. adult participants were recruited from ResearchMatch (N = 533) and took part in a one-way messaging experiment. Results showed that both response efficacy and self-efficacy moderated the relationship between threat appraisal and behavioural intention, which underlines the crucial importance of highlighting actionable strategies in risk communication messaging about PFAS prevention.

title: Silver Spoons in Toxic Soups: Predictors of Protective Action in Affluent Neighborhoods near a Contaminated Research Facility
abstract: The Santa Susana Field Laboratory (SSFL) in Ventura County, California, was among the first sites in the United States to conduct aerospace and nuclear research during the Cold War. Over the nearly 60 years it was in operation, several accidents at SSFL resulted in significant contamination of the surrounding environment. As a result, SSFL was designated as a Superfund eligible site in 1989, although not placed on the National Priorities List, and has since been the subject of numerous lawsuits and health investigations. Prior research near the SSFL has identified hazardous contaminants and possible associations with certain health outcomes, yet uncertainty surrounding the health effects of those exposures has persisted for decades. Despite this uncertainty, one characteristic of the SSFL distinguishes it from many other contaminated sites. The communities surrounding the SSFL are substantially wealthier than those typically studied near Superfund sites. This context allowed us to test protection motivation theory (PMT) as well as other predictors such as health anxiety, morbidity, and distance from the site in a population-type that has been understudied in environmental risk research. Findings indicate that (1) autoimmune and endocrine/metabolic conditions were elevated among those living closest; (2) protective action was most strongly predicted by PMT variables, particularly threat appraisal, and (3) health anxiety partially mediated the relationship between morbidity and protective action.

title: The Reverse Risk Register Approach to Understanding Systemic Factors in Risk Analysis and Management Case Studies
abstract: Although recent developments have improved clarity on the characteristics of high-quality risk science, there is recognition that many of those characteristics relate to specific tasks taken by the risk analyst. However, the effectiveness of risk analysis and management often relies on both internal risk team activities and other external systemic factors. This article leverages reports on past risk events to develop new knowledge on systemic factors that have frequently appeared in connection with major risk events, including whistleblower dynamics, lack of accountability, financial aspects, corruption or fraudulent behavior, scientific disagreement, and political influence and lobbying. Such factors are not typically addressed in existing risk study quality indicators or in training and professional expectations for risk analysts. We explore this issue by introducing the reverse risk register concept to study the role of those factors in past risk events. We utilize the analysis presented in this article to support several areas for risk analyst training and guidance. The findings of this article suggest that although these systemic factors are not typically within the risk analyst's professional responsibilities, awareness and standardized thinking about these areas will improve the risk analyst's perspective within their professional duties. The findings can also help risk analysts, decision-makers, and managers consider whether such factors are present in their organizations and how their presence might influence the risk management process or the risk itself. This article will be of interest to risk analysts, industry professionals, and policymakers.

title: Multiscale Wildfire‐Evacuation Modeling: Assessing Differential Access to Safe Egress in Marin County, CA
abstract: Wildfire evacuation outcomes vary due to interactions among fire progression, human behavior, and traffic dynamics. Most models treat these factors separately, leaving a gap in integrated approaches. This study develops a tri-coupled framework linking fire spread, multichannel communications, and agent-based traffic modeling. The framework integrates a fire model, a communications model capturing varied cognition times, and a spatial-queue traffic model, applied to three Marin County communities. Using a multi-scalar strategic action fields perspective (macro, meso, and micro), the analysis shows how asynchronous communication, background traffic, and localized behaviors interact to shape outcomes. Evacuation efficiency depends on communication timing and coordination, with cognitive delays producing nonlinear congestion. Peak traffic reduces capacity, underscoring the need for governance mechanisms separating emergency from routine flows. At the community level, demographic, infrastructural, and temporal characteristics shape performance, requiring geographically targeted strategies. Micro-level analyses highlight the disproportionate impact of everyday responsibilities, such as child pickup, on congestion, emphasizing behavioral realism in planning. The study offers implications for embedding adaptive communication, dynamic traffic management, and behavioral insights into institutionalized crisis information governance. The findings reveal that evacuation capacity functions as a form of access to safety, unevenly distributed by communications access, mobility constraints, and network characteristics. Linking these to continuous, data-driven evaluation can enhance wildfire preparedness while creating scalable models for other hazard-prone regions, advancing resilience and equity in evacuation systems.

title: #BlackExcellence and #BlackGirlMagic are for all of us: Black influencers’ rejection of neoliberal logics and post-feminist discourses of entrepreneurship
abstract: Situated within feminist media communication studies, this project uses critical technocultural discourse analysis to examine how #BlackExcellence emerges as a form of “digital Black practice” among Black women influencers and users. This study is framed within the context of the George Floyd protests in 2020 and 2021 as mainstream media outlets appropriated Black Excellence rhetoric in columns, listicles, and videos following this watershed moment. Analyses of popular press articles about Black influencers, discourse about race and labor on #BlackTumblr, influencer content on Instagram and YouTube, and interviews with Black influencers comprise the dataset. By leveraging intersectional platform affordances and racialized erotic capital, Black influencers subvert neoliberal and post-feminist logics undergirding digital labor by virtue of the racialized work they are expected to perform, challenging exceptionalist rhetoric. I argue that Black influencers’ uniquely racialized, gendered work contests the assumption that influencer labor is a natural outgrowth of neoliberal conditions.

title: Social Media Savvy? The Use and Effectiveness of Political Parties’ Issue Strategies Across Platforms in the German Federal Election Campaign 2025
abstract: How does the ever-growing relevance of social media shape political campaigning? A vibrant public and academic debate addresses the role of social media in elections and democratic processes. Yet, despite a surge in research, we still know little about the extent to which political parties adjust established issue strategies to the priorities of different social media platforms’ audiences and how effective these are in generating user engagement. Drawing on theories of issue competition – issue ownership, riding-the-wave, and issue yield – we analyze parties’ social media communication during the 2025 German federal election campaign on Facebook, Instagram, and TikTok. Combining manual quantitative content analysis of party and candidate posts with large-scale survey data from the German Longitudinal Election Study (GLES), we assess both strategic use and effectiveness of issue strategies. Our results show that parties strategically prioritize owned issues and those salient on the general public agenda, often combining both dimensions in issue yield strategies. However, these strategies only partly align with what the specific platform audiences value and reward. User engagement is highest for posts that match platform-specific issue preferences, especially when the issues are salient both to a party’s supporters on that platform and to its wider user base. The findings offer new insights into the dynamics of contemporary digital campaigning and cross-platform party competition.

title: ‘This here is a true representation of who I was’: Synthetic media and the authority of the dead
abstract: The dead are increasingly being resurrected through synthetic media. This article draws inspiration from the histories of both manipulated media and mediations of death to examine two contemporary cases in which synthetic representations of dead individuals are deployed in attempts to influence issues of gun violence. The article asks in what ways and to what ends these deceased victims are being exploited. The analytical approach uses qualitative textual analysis. The authors find that these dead are imputed a form of agency within communicative networks and identify communicative strategies of encouraging suspension of disbelief and of invoking deictic references to the here and now in order to leverage the authority of the dead. The article concludes that such exploitation of the authority of the dead raises questions around the rights and responsibilities of publics, of digital platforms, and of the dead themselves.

title: Media visibility and symbolic recognition: Press coverage of Portugal at the 2023 FIFA Women’s World Cup
abstract: The 2023 FIFA Women’s World Cup, co-hosted by Australia and New Zealand, marked a moment of expansion and heightened global visibility for women’s football. In this context, the debut of the Portuguese national team represented a symbolic milestone within the national sporting landscape. This article offers a comparative analysis of media coverage produced by the Portuguese sports press and the general press, examining how distinct journalistic fields discursively framed this event. Drawing on Foucauldian Discourse Analysis applied to a corpus of 24 newspaper articles, the study demonstrates that, despite narrative differences between the two fields, both converged in producing a regime of visibility grounded in the symbolic recognition of female athletes. The centrality of national identity, technical performance and heroic narratives legitimised women’s presence within the sporting sphere, while simultaneously limiting sustained engagement with structural gender inequalities. Media visibility thus operates ambivalently, articulating recognition and discursive containment.

title: Examining our ABC’s: Attention, blindspots and constructions in HIV and AIDS scholarship
abstract: Social constructions are realities created through shared understanding, interactions, and cultural norms that have serious implications in public administration – they influence how public policy is created and implemented. This research takes a reflexive approach to examining the social construction of demographics of HIV and AIDS research scholarship through a combination of attention and framing, as well as related blindspots or negative constructions. Findings demonstrate a broad inclusion of demographics with shifts in framing over time and in combination with intersectional identities. Understanding the social construction of demographics in the past will help illuminate (in)attentions, oversights, and potential unconscious biases as well as more efficient and effective ways to frame policy and implication debates.

title: Cross-Sectoral Collaboration for Work Inclusion and the Governance Perspective: A Systematic Literature Review and Research Directions
abstract: The governance turn in public administration suggests that collaboration with private and third-sector actors can improve services and results. However, evidence remains fragmented at the practice-field level, where such benefits are expected to materialize. To assess the evidence base, we synthesized 71 studies of voluntary cross-sectoral collaborations for work inclusion, that is, initiatives aimed at enhancing employment for vulnerable jobseekers. The literature is predominantly process oriented, emphasizing how these tension-prone collaborations can be organized and sustained. It further suggests that collaboration is often layered onto, rather than challenging, established administrative approaches. While studies report jobseeker empowerment and employment gains, the governance assumption that collaboration improves results remains weakly substantiated. Governance scholarship would benefit from stronger field-based evidence on when, how, and at what cost cross-sectoral collaboration improves results relative to what can be achieved through established approaches.

title: In memory of Professor Akira Nakamura (1940–2026), Meiji University, Tokyo, Japan
Cutting too close to the bone? Fragilizing the democratic resilience of public administration
abstract: This paper develops a conceptual perspective on how a series of major crises, from the “war on terror” (2001) to today's wave of budgetary austerity measures, has created a widespread sense of perpetual emergency among political leaders. Through a habituation effect, prolonged exposure to crisis-driven exceptional measures has gradually normalized illiberal and populist practices, even among mainstream liberal-democratic governments. The paper addresses a notable gap in the existing literature. While democratic backsliding and bureaucratic politicization have received considerable scholarly attention, the long-term cumulative impact of stratified crises on the democratic resilience of public administration remains underexplored. By conceptualizing the habituation effect as a central mechanism, this study identifies four governance trends that undermine the neutrality, autonomy, and democratic character of public administration: the (re)politicization and bullying of civil servants, the erosion of autonomous public agencies, the rapid and often poorly regulated deployment of digital technologies and artificial intelligence, and the increasing bypassing of parliamentary oversight. Ultimately, the study argues that public administration should not be “cut too close to the bone” and therefore instrumentalized to achieve short-term efficiency. Instead, it should be empowered to adopt a public-value-oriented approach that safeguards its democratic resilience and serves as a critical institutional veto point against populist and illiberal encroachments. Points for practitioners Efforts to reduce the size of public administration must never weaken its internal checks and balances or its ability to resist populist pressures and illiberal political interference. Simplifying rules and procedures should always be paired with a stronger focus on the core mission of modern public administration—delivering real value to citizens and society. When using artificial intelligence in the public sector, actively engage AI specialists and relevant stakeholders to prevent problems such as data biases, discrimination, and unfair outcomes. Greater emphasis should be placed on protecting and empowering independent agencies, as they play a vital role in safeguarding the democratic resilience of public administration.

title: Civil Servants and Democratic Backsliding: The Role of Managerial Signals
abstract: Abstract Political efforts to weaken democratic institutions place civil servants in a dilemma between political responsiveness and protecting democratic values. As civil servants are embedded in the political-administrative hierarchy, we argue that signals from their direct hierarchical superiors are critical to understand how civil servants address this dilemma. Using a randomized survey experiment among Norwegian national-level civil servants (N = 1,446) and ordered logistic regression models, we find that democratic backsliding increases opposition to government wishes, internal and external voice, and consideration of exit from the organization. Managerial signals moderate these effects: civil servants are more inclined to voice concerns or consider exit when managers signal responsiveness to government wishes. In a conceptual replication and extension among US federal, state and local civil servants (N = 504) using ordered logistic regression models, we likewise find a greater inclination to exit if the manager signals responsiveness to government wishes, but also that respondents are less inclined to voice concerns to the manager. Overall, our findings imply that managerial signals within the political-administrative hierarchy are shaping civil servants’ immediate reactions to democratic backsliding.
