The Origins of Land Finance: Local Resistance and Top-Down Imposition
abstract: Abstract Land sales have been a significant source of revenue for Chinese local governments since the early 2000s. Contrary to popular belief, local governments did not turn to land finance to make up for lost tax revenues after the 1994 tax sharing reform. Rather, both before and after 1994, corrupt land sales were widespread, as officials sold land far below market prices in return for bribes. Even as the fiscal incentives for local governments to adopt land finance increased in the 1990s, state agents continued acting on their own personal interests rather than the institutional interests of local governments. Local governments only began to sell land at higher, market prices when an anti-corruption campaign launched by the central government made doing so a political imperative in the early 2000s. Local governments were much more responsive to political imperatives than to fiscal incentives.

title: Feminized Revival: Han Chinese Dress, Gender and Cultural Nationalism in Contemporary China
abstract: Abstract Women hold disproportionate authority in China’s contemporary Hanfu revival, where Han-ness operates through implicit cultural codes rather than explicit ethnic claims. Recent scholarship highlights how Han-ness circulates as a moral, etiquette-centred grammar of “proper culture.” Drawing on 18 months of ethnography across six sites in China, this article shows how gender mediates that grammar and shapes the performances of Han-ness. Women, as arbiters of taste and propriety, enact an assertive banal nationalism through aesthetic and organizational labour. Men, marginal within the field, perform defensive overt nationalism through didactic historical narratives and moralized claims to legitimacy. To explain this pattern of identity formation and boundary making, I advance the notion of gendered everyday nationhood. The article contributes to scholarship on nationalism by showing how embodied practices sustain national belonging, and how mundane evaluation and boundary policing reproduce nationhood in everyday life.

title: Autonomy in Prison: Street-Level Bureaucrats Re-Connecting with Their Purpose
abstract: Policy alienation research highlights how public professionals experience powerlessness and meaninglessness when policies misalign with their professional values and work context. While previous research conceptualizes policy alienation as a largely static condition, this article advances a processual understanding by examining how organizational context shapes its development. Drawing on interviews with nurses working in Swedish prisons—a paradigmatic case of misalignment between care and punishment—the study reveals that both expected (tactical powerlessness) and novel (spatial limitation) patterns of alienation coexist with processes that counteract it. Nurses describe how they re-connect with their primary policy domain through considerable work autonomy, trust-based managerial distance, and supportive professional networks. These findings extend policy alienation theory by demonstrating how misaligned organizational environments can generate both alienating and re-connecting processes. The study thus advances understanding of policy alienation as a dynamic, context-mediated phenomenon with important implications for public administration practice.

title: New development: Accountability challenges of today—time for ‘new popular reporting (NPR)’
Fiscal Competition, Intergovernmental Transfer, and Local Debt Management
Managing Through Crisis: Understanding Personnel Stability in the States During Economic Downturns
abstract: The 2008 recession forced U.S. state governments to make rapid personnel and fiscal decisions under austerity. Classic cutback management work catalogues managerial options and personnel stability research links stability to performance, but there is little work to date connecting these fields. This study begins to do so by examining changes in state employment in the wake of the 2008 recession. We conceptualize the components of Kingdon’s Multiple Streams Framework as competing policy influences to assess how state fiscal and organizational conditions shape personnel stability in the following years. Using a state-level panel of by-department employment and a battery of factors that influence the policy process, we estimate two-way fixed-effects models relating Political Competition, Institutional Influence, Policymaking Capacity, and Intragovernmental Conflict indices to two outcomes: year-to-year change in total employment and year-to-year variance in the distribution of jobs across departments. We find significant effects of policymaking capacity on both outcomes. Substantively, the relative strength of policymaking does not prevent recession-era workforce contraction, but it is associated with lower variance in cross-department personnel shifts, suggesting more coordinated adjustments that reduce disruption to routines, coordination, and the distribution of expertise.

title: Artificial Intelligence and the future of policy studies: positivist research and the interpretive pivot
abstract: This essay examines the future of policy studies in the context of artificial intelligence (AI). It critically examines the conventional positivist approach to comprehending public policies, assesses whether AI may carry out traditional policy inquiries more effectively than people, and investigates the potential for interpretive policy analysis to inevitably supersede AI-generated, positivist-oriented knowledge. The interpretive approach is described as a ready-made means to understand programs and activities within the framework of values, narratives, and social constructs. The contention is that human discernment should become the predominant focus of policy studies. AI may supply plenty of empirical information but will intrinsically lack the capacity to grasp the political and cultural judgments that are fundamental to the policy process.

title: Emotions research meets European studies: a systematic literature review and future research agenda
abstract: The importance of emotions is increasingly being recognised in European studies, and a growing number of scholars address emotions to study the EU. However, the literature remains fragmented. In this article, we employ PRISMA – a systematic literature review – to select and analyse 194 articles on emotions in relation to the EU published between January 1998 and January 2025. The objective is (1) to map both main themes and main methods used in this subfield and synthesise main findings; (2) to trace the evolution of this subfield across time; and (3) to identify new avenues of research. Our findings indicate that, with a recent surge in the number of articles, the emotions perspective is becoming increasingly important in European studies. However, we suggest that it may be too early to assess whether this recent interest in emotions in European studies will be sustainable in the years to come, as current research remains in its early stages. Moreover, fully realising the potential of this emerging subfield will require further theoretical innovation, increased engagement between different research clusters, broader empirical application, and sustained engagement with underexplored yet key questions in European integration. In this regard, the article identifies several directions for future research.

title: Public Administration Institutions, Access to Public Services, and Homicide Rates: A Cross‐National Analysis
abstract: ABSTRACT Previous valuable scholarship has examined how numerous political, economic, and social factors affect homicide rates. However, we do not understand how the character of public administration institutions and the equality of access to public services affect homicide rates. Thus, this study examines the relationship between bias in public administration institutions, equality of access to public services, and intentional homicide rates in 142 countries from various levels of development in Africa, Asia, Europe, Latin America, and North America from 1991 to 2021. The results indicate that more biased public administration institutions and less equal access to public services are associated with higher homicide rates. In addition, through conducting a mediation analysis, we find that more biased public administration institutions are associated with greater wealth inequality and higher homicide rates. These results have important implications in considering how the character of public administration institutions and the equality of access to public services affect homicide rates globally. Related Articles Acosta‐González, Nicolás, & Nataly Posso‐Naranjo. 2025. “Crime and Recidivism in Ecuador.” Politics & Policy 53(2): e70030. https://doi.org/10.1111/polp.70030 . Mitchell, Joshua L., & Adam M. Butz. 2019. “Social Control Meets New Public Management: Examining the Diffusion of State Prison Privatization, 1979–2010.” Politics & Policy 47(3): 506–544. https://doi.org/10.1111/polp.12309 . Butz, Adam M., Michael P. Fix, and Joshua L. Mitchell. 2005. “Policy Learning and the Diffusion of Stand‐Your‐Ground Laws.” Politics & Policy 43(3): 347–377. https://doi.org/10.1111/polp.12116 .

title: Minds and machines: Rethinking absorptive capacity in the age of artificial intelligence
abstract: The absorptive capacity construct derives its functions, dimensions, and internal relationships from the implicit assumption that humans are the only learning agents underlying knowledge absorption. I posit that the emergence of artificial intelligence (AI) challenges this assumption and requires a re-examination of the construct. Through a theory-building abductive study combining conceptual mapping with qualitative interviews, this work investigates the complex relationship between AI and knowledge absorption. It theorizes new dimensions of absorptive capacity pertaining to AI-driven processes and analyzes the interactions between these new dimensions and the traditional facets of the construct. Ultimately, the paper seeks to reaffirm the importance of absorptive capacity in the age of AI and develop a nuanced understanding of AI's role in reshaping the construct's antecedents, mechanisms, and implications.

title: Youth movements and opposition parties in times of autocratization: Turkey and Serbia
abstract: Across autocratizing contexts, Generation Z movements have emerged as a prominent force of democratic resistance. Yet their engagement with opposition parties varies considerably. Existing literature explains youth–party engagement through ideological affinity and political trust, but these factors alone cannot account for variation across autocratizing contexts; we instead argue that it is shaped by the combination of opposition parties’ threat capacity and the level of repression they face. When opposition parties possess strong threat capacity and are subject to severe repression, youth movements interpret repression as a signal that these parties represent a credible challenge to the regime and a potentially effective vehicle for democratic change. Under such conditions, engagement becomes strategically attractive. By contrast, when opposition parties have weak threat capacity and face relatively low levels of repression, youth movements perceive them as electorally ineffective and are more likely to pursue autonomous forms of activism. We illustrate this argument by comparing two autocratizing contexts: Turkey, where youth–party engagement is relatively strong, and Serbia, where it is weaker. The analysis triangulates social media evidence from accounts of opposition parties and university solidarity groups with interviews conducted with student activists in Istanbul, Ankara, Belgrade, and Novi Sad.

title: Delegating Away Democracy? Martial Law Support in South Korea
abstract: Why do citizens sometimes accept undemocratic actions by political leaders? Building on growing debates about citizens’ democratic attitudes, we examine whether support for executive power grabs is associated not only with citizens’ partisan alignment but also with their perceptions of government performance and animosity toward political opponents. South Korea’s sudden declaration of martial law in December 2024 offers a unique real-world case for examining this question. Using original survey data collected 1 month after the incident from 1,500 respondents, we find that individuals with positive views of the economy, particularly incumbent supporters, are more likely to endorse the stated justifications for martial law. Hostility toward the opposition is also associated with higher endorsement among incumbent supporters and with a weaker observed relationship between economic evaluations and democratic accountability. Our findings suggest that even in established democracies, public support for democratic norms may be fragile in times of crisis—especially under deep polarization and when citizens view the executive as effective.

title: An overlooked revolution? Party system denationalisation in Western European multilevel election systems
abstract: This article argues that party system denationalisation in Western Europe has been underestimated due to methodological nationalism, which privileges national elections and parties as units of analysis. Regional election data from fourteen multilevel democracies since 1950 is used to uncover growing divergence between regional and national election outcomes, indicating substantial denationalisation despite stability detected by convential indicators. Appropriately revised measures incorporating regions and regional elections reveal that approximately one in five voters supports different parties across electoral arenas. Four types of territorial effects – nationalised, mediated, isolated, and coinciding – are conceptualised to clarify how subnational and national stimuli shape electoral outcomes. An application of this conceptual framework reveals that regional, regionalist, and new parties increasingly drive electoral differentiation and likely contribute to party system renewal at the national level. Moving beyond methodological nationalism improves the understanding of multilevel representative democracy and highlights the importance of territorial agency in shaping electoral competition.

title: Personality, populism and party: support for ‘dark triad’ leaders in the UK
abstract: This article examines whether political party members’ personality traits shape their preferences for political leaders. This is of considerable significance given how many leaders are selected by party members today. Drawing on a post-2024 UK general election survey of over 4,000 members of five British parties, the study investigates the relationship between members’ Dark Triad traits – narcissism, Machiavellianism, and psychopathy – and their preferences for leaders exhibiting similar characteristics. The findings reveal that members of right-conservative parties (Reform UK and the Conservatives) score higher on Dark Triad measures than members of left-liberal parties (Labour, the Liberal Democrats, and the Greens). Moreover, individuals with stronger Dark Triad traits are more likely to favour leaders displaying those qualities. The results highlight the importance of psychological congruence between leaders and followers. The findings also suggest psychological convergence between mainstream and radical-right party memberships, thereby reinforcing an emerging consensus that the UK is characterised by two-bloc, rather than two-party, politics.

title: Broken promises? Voters prefer intraparty democracy, not window dressing
The 2026 Maltese general election: Labour’s staying power
Irreversible investment in divided times: Complementarity and public good provision
Impacts of a partial welfare reform on targeting and political competition
abstract: Over the past decade, India’s BJP-led national government has undertaken various reforms to welfare programs, aiming to reduce the scope for local officials to manipulate beneficiary selection or divert funds. Nevertheless state and local governments retained considerable discretion over beneficiary selection and the local delivery of central government funded welfare benefits, and have maintained exclusive control over state-funded programs. We use longitudinal household survey data from the state of West Bengal to evaluate the effects of these reforms on pro-poor targeting of welfare programs, and political competition between the BJP and the TMC, the incumbent political party in the state. We find that welfare programs were better targeted toward poorer and socially disadvantaged households in the period 2014–2018 than in 2010–2013. However the welfare reforms do not explain why the BJP’s vote share increased, as its electoral gains from the new nationwide programs were outweighed by their losses, stemming from the increased support for the TMC from recipients of new state and pre-existing benefits.

title: Under Pressure: High-Stakes Exams and Media-Reported Student Suicides in India1
Routine-biased technical change, structure of employment, and cross-country income differences
Unlinked: Why alters reported in name generators cannot be used to estimate personal network size
Context disadvantage and residential mobility from early life into adulthood: impacts on socio-economic outcomes
abstract: Abstract Individuals’ socio-economic trajectories are shaped by both persistence and change in their residential environments, making it essential to examine how the socio-spatial dynamics of context disadvantage and residential mobility interact over the life course. While prior research has often studied these factors separately and within specific life stages, less is known about their compound effects and their interrelatedness across childhood and adulthood. This study addresses this gap by investigating how exposure to residential contexts and residential mobility from birth influences socio-economic outcomes in early adulthood. Using Swedish longitudinal register data, we analyze residential trajectories and their association with economic and occupational (dis) advantage among individuals born between 1990 and 1993. Our findings show that mobility magnifies the associations between context exposure and socio-economic outcomes. Prolonged exposure to disadvantaged areas is most harmful when it coincides with moving, consistent with a compound penalty of instability and resource-poor environments. Second, moves in childhood are generally detrimental, while adult moves are opportunity-enhancing unless they occur in disadvantaged contexts, where the mobility premium levels off. Third, exiting disadvantaged contexts is associated with higher attainment than remaining persistently exposed, indicating that later socio-spatial trajectories can attenuate earlier disadvantage. These findings underscore the importance of considering both residential context and mobility across the life course for understanding—and interrupting—the reproduction of socio-economic inequality.

title: Assessing the Sensitivities of Input–Output Methods for Natural Hazard‐Induced Power Outage Macroeconomic Impacts
abstract: Power outages are a substantial global issue across both advanced and developing countries, affecting economic productivity and growth. Consequently, numerous studies have examined the potential macroeconomic impacts of these disruptions, employing a wide variety of modeling methods and data parameterization techniques. A frequent approach is the use of input-output macroeconomic modeling, yet there is a lack of clarity about how ex ante parameterization and other methodological decisions affect output estimates, warranting further investigation. In this paper, we quantify the macroeconomic effects of three significant natural hazard US power outages: Hurricane Ian (2022), the 2021 Texas Blackouts, and Tropical Storm Isaias (2020). Our analysis evaluates the sensitivity of three commonly used data parameterization techniques (household interruptions, kWh lost, and satellite luminosity), along with three static models (Leontief and Ghosh, critical input, and inoperability input-output). We find the mean domestic loss estimates for these three blackout events to be $2.42 Bn, $3.24 Bn, and $2.27 Bn, respectively. However, data parameterization techniques can alter estimated losses by up to 52.8% of the mean. Consistent with the wide range of outputs, we find that risk analysis stemming from gross output estimate severity is highly sensitive to model architecture, data parameterization, and analyst assumptions. Results sensitivity is not uniform across models and arises from important a priori analyst decisions, demonstrated by data parameterization techniques yielding up to 55.9% differences from empircal results within a model. To our knowledge, we contribute to the literature the first systematic comparison of multiple IO models and parameterizations across several natural hazard long-duration power outages, providing guidance and insights for analysts.

title: The disappearance of a Chinese village: How short-video platforms mediatized Clifftop Village’s lifeworld
abstract: This study examines how the secluded Clifftop Village rapidly transitioned from a pre-digital society into a mediatized world via short-video platforms. Drawing on fieldwork and interviews, we find that mediatization in this media-deprived rural community was triggered by an incidental news report and unfolded along leapfrogging trajectories driven by the marginalized group’s short-video practices. This process stemmed from complex negotiations between structural forces—China’s centralized governance, expanding digital infrastructure, and platform capital—and the agency of marginalized subjects. It systematically reconfigured villagers’ spatio-temporal order, social relationships, cultural beliefs, and lifestyles, ultimately precipitating the complete relocation of the entire community. Following the dissolution of the physical community, mediatization extended into the affective realm, as villagers began to rely on short-video platforms to anchor their sense of place and collective identity. Ultimately, the case of Clifftop Village demonstrates that rural mediatization cannot be reduced to either technological empowerment or the reproduction of digital inequality, offering a localized lens on the existential condition of marginalized groups under radical modernization.

title: Counterfactuals: Does bureaucracy produce unfair workplaces?
abstract: Abstract Bureaucracy is often used as a metaphor for organisations that place machine‐like functioning above human needs. In this paper, a mixed‐methods approach is used to investigate the relationship between bureaucracy and fairness in public administration. The research is based on an interview study with 60 employees for the generation of hypotheses and an online survey with 1632 participating employees of the German Federal Criminal Police Office. The qualitative results indicate that aspects of skill underutilisation, bureaucratic organisational structures, and silo mentality are potential predictors of fairness in the public administration context. The relationships of these predictors to fairness are validated using structural equation and mediation models. The results provide insights into the motivational needs of employees who perceive excessive bureaucratic regulations in their organisation. From this, well‐founded measures for improving fairness in public administration can be derived. Furthermore, two preliminary measures for measuring silo mentality and bureaucracy climate are introduced. Points for practitioners A workplace that is perceived as bureaucratic can have negative effects on employee perceptions of fairness. Bureaucracy is often criticised across the board, and it remains unclear which elements of it are perceived as disruptive. Bureaucracy is perceived as unfair, in particular when it hinders transparent and effective communication and personal career development. Unfair bureaucracy can be reduced by dismantling communicative silos and decentralising personnel management.

title: Digital transformation in the global south: Balancing risks and building resilience
abstract: Digital transformation (DT) is increasingly recognized as vital to enhancing the organizational performance of public sector worldwide. Yet many DT projects fail to achieve their intended outcomes. We argue that these failures are partly attributable to the risk environments surrounding projects before and after implementation. Although DT literature emphasizes risk management and resilience, limited attention has been given to integrating both into DT project design. This paper addresses this gap by examining how these considerations are embedded as strategic elements in DT projects in the Global South. Using a convergent-parallel mixed-methods approach, we analyzed 32 World Bank Group DT project proposals from governments in the Global South using BERTopic-based natural language processing, triangulated with thematic analysis of 13 semi-structured interviews with third-party stakeholders. Findings reveal a systematic gap between resilience assumptions embedded in project designs and the contextual realities of implementation. Specifically, limited local capacity, governance fragmentation, remoteness, geopolitical conflict, and dependence on external suppliers can significantly affect project outputs and outcomes. We conclude by proposing project-level mechanisms to strengthen resilience and identify directions for future research on government-led DT projects in developing-country contexts.

title: Debate: Ten reasons why it is difficult to outsource police functions to the private sector (and one reason why it should not be done)
Citizen-oriented popular reporting: Reconciling objective and subjective information needs
abstract: IMPACTThis study offers actionable guidance for public sector accountants, financial managers, and standard setters involved in developing citizen-oriented financial reports. Drawing on IPSAS-based financial statements from a German federal state, it demonstrates how popular reports can reconcile objective transparency requirements with citizens’ subjective information needs. For practitioners at the national and subnational levels, the findings indicate that reports should clearly present revenues, expenditures, debt and personnel costs and link them to major services such as education, infrastructure, and environmental protection. Reports should place less emphasis on presenting technically complex balance-sheet items that citizens find difficult to interpret. Moreover, the results highlight the need for multi-channel dissemination and layered ‘core-plus’ or ‘core and more’ reporting structures to reach diverse citizen groups. Internationally, the results suggest that standard setters (for example IPSASB, national accounting boards) could strengthen comparability and accountability by issuing recommended practice guidelines for popular reporting, fostering consistent approaches to citizen-oriented public sector communication.

title: Public financial management and governance in developing countries: The control-audit chain in PEFA assessments
abstract: IMPACTThis article contributes to both institutional economics and public financial management (PFM) reform by identifying the institutional mechanisms through which PFM improves governance. Rather than treating governance as a uniform country characteristic, it shows that governance gains are driven by the control-audit chain, linking internal expenditure controls, internal audit, external audit, and legislative oversight. This provides a theoretically grounded explanation for why some PFM reforms generate stronger governance outcomes than others. The findings also challenge conventional reform sequencing by demonstrating that strengthening budget execution controls yields greater governance improvements than prioritizing upstream transparency and budgeting reforms. Regional evidence shows that governance returns are particularly strong in Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) and Latin America and the Caribbean (LAC), offering guidance for targeting reform investments. The proposed control-audit chain framework provides finance ministries, supreme audit institutions, and development partners with a practical tool to diagnose accountability weaknesses and prioritize reforms with the greatest governance impact.

title: Culture as Administrative Infrastructure: Crisis Governance and Community Recovery After the Maui Wildfires
abstract: Despite growing attention to culture in public administration responses to crisis events, culture is often treated as background context rather than as part of the administrative infrastructure through which governance occurs. This article extends the theory of administrative capacity by arguing that culture can function as administrative infrastructure in post-disaster public management. Using qualitative interviews with community members, grassroots organizers, and nonprofit leaders in Maui, as well as public forum data collected within 12 months of the 2023 Maui wildfires, we examine how culture shaped legitimacy, coordination, authority, and recovery capacity in the aftermath of disaster. Findings show that culturally grounded relationships to land, water, community, and history shaped how residents interpreted formal recovery efforts, mobilized outside government systems, asserted authority over rebuilding, and defined what recovery should mean. We develop a culture as administrative infrastructure framework that shows how culturally grounded forms of authority, resistance, and place-based knowledge reveal the limits of culturally neutral administrative systems. The article contributes to public administration theory by showing that administrative capacity is not only built through agencies, resources, procedures, and networks, but also through culturally embedded systems of legitimacy, knowledge, authority, and collective care.
journal_name: The American Review of Public Administration

title: Why Government Turns to AI – What Citizens Believe and How it Matters. Survey Evidence from Germany and the Netherlands
abstract: What do citizens believe to be guiding motives behind the increasing adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in government, and how are these beliefs related to AI acceptance? Drawing on moral judgment theory, the present article argues that the presumed intentions behind AI use matter for citizens’ evaluations of this use. It studies how citizens’ beliefs about public values motives are associated with AI acceptance across four types of AI use that involve different citizen-state relationships. The analysis uses survey data from 2072 respondents in Germany and the Netherlands and finds that that acceptance of AI use hinges on whether citizens believe that government AI adoption is guided by performance-related values – efficiency, effectiveness, productivity. Beliefs about procedure-related public values motives – impartiality, equal treatment, transparency – do not matter. The findings have implications for how to engender public support for government AI use and for understanding imbalances in public values driving AI adoption.

title: Internet use and welfare attitudes in East Asia: how Confucian culture matters?
Administrative Burden and the Access–Fraud Trade‐Off
abstract: ABSTRACT Administrative burden represents political choices embedded in policy design that affect how people perceive and experience government. While policymakers frequently invoke fraud prevention to justify imposing burdens in welfare programs, this rhetoric embodies an unacknowledged normative judgment about the relative costs of fraud and abuse versus program exclusion for eligible beneficiaries. This study quantifies this access–fraud trade‐off in means‐tested social welfare programs through a contingent valuation experiment ( N = 2250). We find that respondents were willing to accept approximately 192 ineligible recipients receiving benefits in exchange for 1000 eligible beneficiaries not being excluded due to administrative burdens. While we find no direct evidence that psychological distance (i.e., randomized exposure to “welfare” vs. specific programs) affects this trade‐off across the full sample, political affiliation is a significant moderator in our exploratory analysis. Unlike Democrats/Independents, Republicans demonstrate substantially lower tolerance for potential fraud when evaluating abstract “welfare” compared to specific programs like unemployment insurance. Experience with means‐tested welfare programs, which reduces psychological distance, has a similar moderating effect. These findings extend construal level theory to administrative burden preferences and contribute to the policy implementation literature by quantifying the access–fraud trade‐off—a metric largely absent from academic and policy discussions despite its importance for program legitimacy.
journal_name: Journal of Policy Analysis and Management

title: From Policy Legitimization to Blame Avoidance—Discursive Strategies During Denmark's Mink Culling Crisis
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper examines how governments navigate policy legitimacy during crises through three distinct discursive processes: legitimization, delegitimization, and blame avoidance. Using a sequential mixed‐methods design, the study analyzes Denmark's decision to cull all mink during the COVID‐19 pandemic. The quantitative analysis of 947 newspaper articles indicates that while both periods were characterized by negative coverage, the force and target of delegitimization discourses shifted dramatically from questioning policy outcomes to scrutinizing procedural legitimacy. The qualitative analysis illustrates how, initially, the government successfully legitimized the mink culling through appeals to scientific authority, with broad political and public support. However, following legal and scientific challenges, policy legitimacy collapsed, coinciding with a strategic pivot from policy justification to blame avoidance. The analysis illustrates that legitimization and blame avoidance can be treated as analytically distinct discursive strategies: legitimization proactively affirms policy necessity through evidence and legal appeals, while blame avoidance reactively deflects responsibility through reframing, buck‐passing, and scapegoating. The policy persisted despite sustained delegitimization, initially aided by legitimization efforts and later by blame avoidance strategies. The findings advance policy theory by clarifying how discursive strategies evolve across a policy's lifecycle and offer a framework applicable to other high‐salience domains such as climate emergencies and migration policies.

title: Immigration and firm innovation: Evidence from Finnish manufacturing
Does gender enter the ballot box? Uncovering gender dynamics in Spanish voting patterns
abstract: Gender issues have moved to the centre of electoral politics in many democracies, driven by feminist mobilization on one side and anti-gender backlash on the other. Yet we know relatively little about which specific gender-related attitudes shape vote choice and why some gender policies become electorally consequential while others do not. This paper addresses these questions through an analysis of the July 2023 Spanish general election, combining a post-election survey with systematic analysis of party messaging. We examine both the supply side (how parties positioned themselves on gender-related issues during the campaign) and the demand side (how voters' attitudes toward those issues relate to vote choice). Among a broad range of gender-relevant policies, opposition to trans rights and legal gender self-determination emerges as the only policy attitude significantly associated with vote choice, increasing support for the right-wing PP and the radical right Vox. Sympathy for the feminist movement as a general orientation is positively associated with voting for the left-wing coalition Sumar and negatively associated with right-wing voting. These findings suggest that gender can function as an electoral cleavage, but that its electoral relevance depends on the type of conflict a given policy activates rather than on its salience alone.

title: Divided beyond politics: How perceptions of non-political differentness are linked to affective polarization among citizens
abstract: While affective polarization is commonly attributed to political differences between partisans, recent studies suggest it also relates to perceived non-political differences, such as differences in lifestyle, class, or personality. However, little is known about the relevance of these non-political perceptions beyond political ones, whether different types of non-political traits matter equally, and how these dynamics unfold beyond the U.S. two-party context. This study addresses these gaps by examining the relationship between perceived non-political differentness and two dimensions of affective polarization—partisan dislike and social distance—in Belgium's multi-party context. Using original survey data from Flanders and Wallonia (N = 4823), Belgium's two largest regions with distinct party systems, we show that perceptions of non-political differentness substantially relate to partisan dislike and social distancing, beyond perceptions of political differentness. Moreover, nearly all non-political dimensions studied matter (i.e., personality, values, socio-economic background, and lifestyle), albeit with varying importance across the two contexts and especially for partisan dislike. Altogether, these findings extend research on affective polarization by highlighting the overlooked role of non-political perceptions in our understanding of partisan animosity.

title: Educational contexts and the gender gap in party support – an analysis of young voters in Germany
abstract: In many European countries, the most recent elections featured an unprecedented gender gap in party support among the youngest cohorts: young men disproportionally supported right-wing populist parties, while young women overwhelmingly voted for left-wing and Green parties. This paper explores the new gender vote gap by focusing on the role of education. We propose two mechanisms: placement and context composition. First, placement in lower or higher tracks is a signal of losing or winning in the context of ongoing educational expansion, and young men find themselves more often on the losing side than young women. Second, due to gender differences in occupational choices, lower tracks are more gender segregated than higher tracks, and an unbalanced gender composition often coincides with peers sharing either right-wing or left-wing political attitudes. We argue that this amplifies the new gender gap in party support. We test our arguments with unique data collected shortly after the German federal elections in 2025 among a large-N, register-based sample of 17- to 20-year-olds. Results show that young men on lower tracks are the most likely to support the right-wing populist AfD, and that the political climate in their educational contexts amplifies this association. Young women on both lower and higher tracks are likely to support the Linke, and more strongly so if more than half of their peers in class also are women. The Green party is strong among voters in academic tracks, particularly among women, regardless of the gender or political composition of the educational context.

title: Getting Religion Wrong A Response to Toft’s “Getting Religion Right”
Shared Discrimination’s Effect on Solidarity between People of Color Is Uniform Across Major Racial, Political, and Social Differences
abstract: Abstract Solidarity between people of color (PoC) is key to understanding multiracial coalition-building in the United States. However, limited statistical power has constrained research on whether shared discrimination’s effect on solidarity is reliably moderated by differences in race, political orientation, and social background, which structure the internal diversity of racially stigmatized subgroups within the mega-category, PoC. We report a preregistered meta-analysis of eight published experiments ( N = 5,813), which used a common design to test shared discrimination’s effects among Black Americans, Asian Americans, Latinos, and Middle Eastern and North African individuals. Despite known heterogeneity in these group’s social and political attitudes, we find that shared discrimination’s effect on solidarity is statistically uniform across race/ethnicity, partisanship, ideology, nativity, education, gender, and age. These results indicate that shared discrimination appeals broadly and reliably activate solidarity across diverse PoC subgroups, further affirming this psychological mechanism’s crucial role in fostering robust multiracial coalitions.

title: Women Politicians’ Role Model Effects: The Influence of Shared Identities Beyond Gender
abstract: Abstract Women consistently report lower levels of political interest and political ambition than men. Studies have examined how women politicians as role models can make women more politically engaged, but studies have not typically examined additional shared identities beyond gender. I propose that women politicians with whom women share additional identities will be perceived as more relatable and inspiring and, consequently, have stronger role model effects on women’s political engagement. Through a conjoint experiment (Study 1), I find that having additional shared identities with a woman politician increases perceptions of her as relatable and inspiring. However, a survey experiment with novel video treatments depicting a woman politician’s story (Study 2) did not produce positive role model effects on women’s political interest, internal political efficacy, or nascent political ambition – regardless of additional shared racial and partisan identity with the woman politician. Moreover, the video treatment had remarkably different effects across White and Black women, regardless of additional shared racial and partisan identity. An observational analysis (Study 3) replicates the finding that additional shared racial and partisan identity with women political representatives is not systematically correlated with higher levels of political interest. These findings carry important implications for understanding women politicians’ role model effects and the potential of role models to increase women’s political engagement.

title: Does Listening to Trustworthy News Affect Political Attitudes and Trust?
What does the public know about their State’s abortion laws in the post-Dobbs era?
Smart power limits: Designing shortage mechanisms for extreme events
abstract: As shortages of resources like water and electricity due to extreme weather events become more frequent, high prices alone may fail to curb demand, making shortages more common. We examine a power limit policy for residential electricity households that rations electricity consumption rather than setting it to zero, as in a traditional rolling blackout. We find that power limits can provide equivalent savings to large blackouts, even when generous. Additionally, due to selection, power limits reduce the number of households affected by a shortage event. We conclude by discussing the welfare consequences of power limits and their heterogeneous impact across households. Institutional subscribers to the NBER working paper series, and residents of developing countries may download this paper without additional charge at www.nber.org.

title: Equity Frictions and Firm Ownership
abstract: Abstract In this paper, I document systematic heterogeneity in ownership and financing of firms across Eurozone countries. To rationalize these differences, I build a quantitative general equilibrium model of workers and entrepreneurs who choose debt and equity financing of their firms, subject to rich country-specific financial frictions. The novel data on firm ownership and financing, combined with the structure of the model, allows me to quantify the level of debt and equity frictions in each country. Quantitatively, I find much larger output effects from equity frictions: harmonizing them across countries would lead to nearly four times larger output effects compared to debt frictions, and removing them would increase aggregate output by 73\% more. The larger impact on output is due not only to the estimated levels and dispersion of equity frictions but also to the greater risk sharing provided by equity, which further incentivizes entrepreneurs to expand their firms. Through their effect on risk sharing, equity frictions also rationalize the observed negative relationship between equity financing and wealth inequality. Quantitatively, they are responsible for over 70\% of the explained variation in top wealth shares across countries.

title: FDI Spillovers in History: Interwar Japanese “Zaikabo” investment in China’s cotton spinning industry
abstract: We estimate productivity spillovers from Japanese cotton-spinning firms in China (known as Zaikabo) to local Chinese cotton-spinning mills based on plant-level data for 1925 to 1938. In order to capture the important role of distance in facilitating such spillovers we geo-localised the plants. Our results provide clear evidence for positive spillovers from Zaikabo to local Chinese mills, which go hand-in-hand with an upgrade in production technology towards greater use of capital. Spillovers are very localised, being strongest within a radius of up to 10 km around the Zaikabo and particularly strong for mills in Shanghai. Exploiting information on the workforce composition of the Japanese affiliates, we find suggestive evidence of a skilled-labour channel: spillovers tend to be larger from Zaikabo employing higher shares of skilled labour. We also find some evidence in line with the idea that these gains are larger for Chinese mills with higher initial productivity, consistent with a role for absorptive capacity. Our paper is the first to document FDI productivity spillovers in a historical context and to characterise the channels through which they operate.

title: From LinkedIn to Labor Statistics: Using Revelio Microdata for Labor Market Research in Developing Economies
Allocation of Foreign Aid in Emerging Economies: Investment in New vs Maintenance of Old Infrastructure
Polygyny and the Economic Determinants of Family Formation in Sub-Saharan Africa,
abstract: Abstract Social norms and formal institutions governing marriage markets vary widely across societies. This paper examines how polygyny norms in Sub-Saharan Africa shape marriage market responses to aggregate economic shocks and their resulting welfare implications. Unlike monogamous markets, polygynous markets feature intense competition for brides between young bachelors and older married men seeking a second (junior) wife. I show, both theoretically and empirically, that the latter group is more responsive than the former to aggregate income shocks in areas where the shadow price of marrying a junior wife is low. This difference in sensitivity leads to distinct equilibrium outcomes: adverse shocks increase the incidence of child marriage in monogamous areas but have no detectable effect in polygynous areas. These divergent equilibrium outcomes generate stark differences in the long-term effects of such shocks on female education, literacy, and the utilization of preventive care services.
journal_name: Journal of the European Economic Association

title: A NECESSARY AND SUFFICIENT CONDITION FOR SIZE CONTROLLABILITY OF HETEROSKEDASTICITY ROBUST TEST STATISTICS
abstract: We revisit size controllability results in Pötscher and Preinerstorfer (2025, Econometric Theory 41, 249–301) concerning heteroskedasticity robust test statistics in regression models. For the special, but important, case of testing a single restriction (e.g., a zero restriction on a single coefficient), we provide a necessary and sufficient condition for size controllability, whereas the condition in Pötscher and Preinerstorfer (2025, Econometric Theory 41, 249–301) is, in general, only sufficient (even in the case of testing a single restriction).

title: UNIFIED INFERENCE ON MOMENT RESTRICTIONS WITH NUISANCE PARAMETERS
abstract: This article proposes a simple unified inference approach on moment restrictions in the presence of nuisance parameters. The proposed test is constructed based on a new characterization that avoids the estimation of nuisance parameters and can be broadly applied across diverse settings. Under suitable conditions, the test is shown to be asymptotically size controlled and consistent for both independent and dependent samples. Monte Carlo simulations show that the test performs well in finite samples. Numerical results from the application to conditional moment restriction models with weak instruments demonstrate that the proposed method may improve upon existing approaches in the literature.

title: Hospital Heterogeneous Responses to a Blended Payment Scheme Reform and the Distributional Consequences
abstract: ABSTRACT Hospital payment schemes designed to control expenditure could also influence the medical resource allocation. We study hospital responses to the introduction of a blended payment scheme—a diagnosis‐based payment scheme with a predetermined global budget—and their distributional consequences. Exploiting a quasi‐experimental reform in China, we find hospitals respond by upcoding, shifting admissions toward categories with higher upcoding potential, and increasing total admissions. Hospitals’ heterogeneous responses widen the disparity in their payments, primarily through heterogeneous upcoding. Hospitals with more coding knowledge, greater reform exposure, higher tier, and larger size secure a larger share of the social health insurance fund.

title: One overworking breadwinner or two earners? Family economic standard of living by breadwinner arrangement, 1960 to 2018–2022
Risk Assessment in Peacekeeping: Are Visual Sparse Models Transparent?
abstract: Decision and risk analysis tools must be accurate and transparent. Classification trees, especially sparse ones, and other visual models, such as scorecards or risk tables, have been claimed to strike this balance. There is, however, little empirical evidence for the transparency of such models. We derive relevant hypotheses and test them in a controlled laboratory experiment with an ecologically valid, high-risk, critical task: threat classification in peacekeeping. Three classification models are studied: a complete tree, a sparse (specifically, fast-and-frugal) tree, and a risk table. To focus on transparency, all three models make identical classifications and thus have equal accuracy. We assess and score three aspects of transparency for each model: time required to learn to a strict criterion, accuracy of application under time pressure, and accuracy in a delayed surprise memory recall test. In a between-participants design, the fast-and-frugal tree is learned more quickly, applied more accurately, and recalled more accurately than the complete tree and the risk table; all statistical effect sizes are large. The recall accuracy of the fast-and-frugal tree is, in contrast to the other two models, robust to individual differences in statistical numeracy and risk literacy. In sum, the results of the experiment, together with reflection on limitations and challenges, plus theoretical arguments, suggest that sparse trees might serve as a reasonable benchmark and starting point for designing transparent support for risk assessment.

title: Lost in Projection: Uncertainty is Misrepresented in Climate Risk and Vulnerability Assessments
abstract: In practice, many climate change risk assessments fail to capture the true depth of uncertainty. Despite widespread scientific recognition of deep uncertainty (large ranges of possibility) in climate conditions, this nuance is often lost in translation to policy and planning contexts; instead, conditions are presented as single projections. This means that communities are making large-scale infrastructure investments and long-term policy commitments based on false precision, leaving them unprepared for climate surprises or potentially wasting resources and disrupting communities unnecessarily by overadapting. To examine how climate uncertainties are represented and accounted for in adaptation planning, we conducted a structured review of 39 climate risk and vulnerability assessments from across the world, using sea level rise as a case study. These documents inform policy that guides billions of dollars in infrastructure investments and shape community preparedness strategies. Our analysis reveals that only 54% of these documents correctly represent sea level rise as deeply uncertain. This issue is compounded when making decisions; 71% of decisions were made by misapplying scenarios as individual projections to plan for, rather than as a tool for exploring potential future conditions, directly contradicting their intended use. This demonstrates a gap between scientific understanding of climate uncertainty and planning practice. Addressing this gap requires improved uncertainty communication, moving beyond just quantifying uncertainty to also characterizing uncertainty. This must be done in conjunction with the support of decision makers to incorporate a stronger understanding of uncertainty into planning by using tools designed specifically for decision making in deeply uncertain environments.

title: Including young people in policy development: A youth‐informed adaptation of a Policy Lab method
abstract: Abstract Young people should have a say in policies that affect them. Power imbalances and limiting their involvement to consultative processes in policymaking continue to be barriers to participation. Progress has been made to involve young people directly in policymaking, but barriers to their full participation persist. The aim of this research study was to emulate a Policy Lab to learn from young people how they could be better included in this policy development method. Their reported experience of the workshop and perspectives as young people were analysed using rapid qualitative analysis and used to inform adaptations of the method. Three themes were identified: providing more information, greater accessibility, and facilitating participation. Overall, the collective feedback from young people was focused on being prepared to participate and addressing power imbalances between youth and adult participants. Implications for practice are identified. We present an adaptation of the Policy Lab method to better include young people. Points for practitioners While the importance of involving young people in the development of policy that effects their lives is understood, oftentimes practices continue to limit or restrict this involvement through persistent barriers to their involvement. Young people recognise the barriers they face to being equally involved in workshop activities with adults and have ideas on how to address them to improve their direct involvement in policy development methods. This research presents adaptations to a policy development method through providing more information, greater accessibility, and facilitating participation; that also provides direction for policy practitioners more generally.

title: Editorial Board
Beyond service supply: how trust outweighs performance in shaping public service satisfaction across urban-rural divides
The Practice and Origins of Performance Measurement: Assessing the Sunnyvale Model, 1984–2023
abstract: ABSTRACT Few regulatory reforms are as celebrated or emulated as the performance measurement system of Sunnyvale, California, which inspired the Government Performance and Results Act of 1993 and countless other national and local efforts. This study presents the first longitudinal, cross‐programmatic analysis of a performance measurement system, introducing a digital archival approach to analyze 152 performance indicators across 35,000 pages of documents from 1984 to 2023, supplemented with interviews of key stakeholders. Even if Sunnyvale's system initially functioned as an exemplar of performance‐based decision‐making, it deteriorated with weakened commitment and, more importantly, sustained significant implementation costs while its benefits reduced over time. The findings illustrate three core trade‐offs for performance measurement systems: measuring what matters (the “quantity‐quality” tradeoff); ensuring continuity while allowing for adaptation (the “continuity‐flexibility” tradeoff); and ensuring accountability without having implementation detract from productivity (the “accountability‐productivity” tradeoff).

title: Bureaucratic Reform in Post‐Authoritarian Indonesia: A Bibliometric‐Informed Critical Review (1966–2026)
abstract: ABSTRACT Indonesia's Reformasi of 1998 launched one of the developing world's most ambitious bureaucratic reform programs. Yet 28 years later, a persistent gap between formal institutional design and actual bureaucratic behavior remains. This article presents a bibliometric‐informed critical review of 119 Scopus‐indexed publications on Indonesian administrative and bureaucratic reform (1966–2026), combining VOSviewer keyword co‐occurrence analysis with critical narrative synthesis across five domains: decentralization, anti‐corruption, civil service reform, public service delivery, and digital government. Findings show exponential publication growth since 2018, dominated by NPM and reform theory, while enforcement capacity and sub‐national accountability remain understudied. Drawing primarily on Historical Institutionalism, with Public Management Reform trajectory theory and principal‐agent theory as complementary lenses, the article argues that Indonesia's reform paradox is best explained as institutional layering driven by persistent patronage networks, weak sub‐national enforcement, and reform fatigue. Implications for bureaucratic reform theory and governance practice in post‐authoritarian developing states are discussed.

title: Digitalization as a challenge or opportunity for working mothers? A study of Taiwan
abstract: Digitalization has significantly transformed everyday life and labour markets, attracting growing policy attention worldwide. However, digital transformation may simultaneously expand employment opportunities and reinforce gendered labour market segmentation. Focusing on working mothers in Taiwan, this study examines the extent to which the digital economy shapes employment opportunities for mothers with young children. Based on in-depth interviews with 25 married women employed in the IT sector and digital platforms, the findings indicate that occupational gender segregation has taken on new and more complex forms under the digital economy. On the one hand, more women have gained access to core and higher-quality employment. On the other hand, digital tools enable many mothers to overcome temporal and spatial constraints, allowing them to maintain their attachment to the labour market and engage in both online and offline economic activities through the effective use of interpersonal networks. These opportunities coexist with the continued unequal distribution of care responsibilities. Overall, these developments lend support to the optimistic perspectives of cyberfeminists, suggesting that digitalization can expand women’s employment opportunities rather than primarily reinforcing their marginalization in the digital economy.

title: Exploiting New Public Diplomacy to Sell Racism: Chinese Representation of Africans in China's Social Media Space
abstract: ABSTRACT China's reentry into Africa in the late 1990s and early 2000s coincided with the rise of new public diplomacy, leading to increased African‐related content and accessibility in China's cyberspace. Thus, this study explores the nature of African‐related content in China's cyberspace and social media to explain how the Chinese public perceives Africans and constructs its image of reality about Africa. The study undertook a cybernography (ethnography over the Internet) and a systematic content analysis of 716 African‐related videos purposively selected from two Chinese social media applications—Douyin and Youku. It finds that Chinese non‐state actors in Africa have exploited new public diplomacy to make large volumes of distorted African‐related videos available in China's cyberspace. The analysis finds that this exploitation—sometimes with indirect passive government and state institutions endorsement—has constructed and reinforced stereotypical and discriminatory images of Africans in China. I base the theoretical argument on the new public diplomacy framework. Related Articles Ameyaw‐Brobbey, Thomas. 2024. “The Media in China–Africa Public Relations: Assessing China’s Attractiveness beyond Economic Development Assistance.” Politics & Policy 52(3): 551‐572. https://doi.org/10.1111/polp.12596 . Huang, Xiurong, & Nnamdi C. Nduneseokwu. 2026. “Navigating the U.S.‐China Rivalry: African Leaders’ Perspectives on China’s Non‐Western Economic Engagement in Africa.” Politics & Policy 54(1): e70113. https://doi.org/10.1111/polp.70113 . Otele, Oscar M., & Winnie V. Mitullah. 2025. “The Institutional Dynamics of International Development Cooperation and China’s Aid in Africa.” Politics & Policy 53(1): e70015. https://doi.org/10.1111/polp.70015 .

title: A cord of three strands: Industry-university-research collaboration and corporate ESG performance
Homelessness and Support for Expanded Services: Los Angeles Residents' Perceptions of Public Safety in Their Neighbourhoods
abstract: ABSTRACT Homelessness in U.S. cities is a pressing civic issue, shaping residents' sense of safety and local policy debates. This study examines Los Angeles residents' perceptions of safety, their proximity to encampments, and attitudes towards mental health and substance use services. Using representative survey data from 4408 residents, we assess (1) support for welfare‐oriented services and their relationship to proximity to homelessness, and (2) how encounters with unhoused individuals shape feelings of safety. Findings show that residents closer to homelessness report more urgent support for mental health and substance abuse services, reflecting a shift towards decriminalization and public health approaches. By contrast, support for affordable housing remains polarized, with higher‐income and older residents more resistant. In a political climate favouring criminalization (Grants Pass v. Johnson), these results highlight the urgency of aligning policy with community‐driven, equitable solutions.

title: Calculation and Conscience: Motivations for the Substantive Representation of Ethnic Minorities
Correcting for Nonignorable Nonresponse Bias in Ordinal Observational Survey Data
abstract: Abstract Many political surveys rely on post-stratification, raking or related weighting adjustments to align respondents with the target population. But when respondents differ from nonrespondents on the outcome itself (nonignorable nonresponse), these adjustments can fail, introducing bias even into basic descriptives. We provide a practical method that corrects for nonignorable nonresponse by leveraging response-propensity proxies (e.g., a respondent’s rating of the interview or interviewer-coded cooperativeness) observed among respondents to extrapolate toward nonrespondents, while directly integrating observable covariates and retaining the benefits of post-stratification with known population shares. The method generalizes the variable-response-propensity framework of Peress (2010) from binary to ordinal outcomes, which are widely used to measure trust, satisfaction and policy attitudes. The resulting estimator is computed by maximum likelihood and implemented in a compact R routine that handles both ordinal and binary outcomes. Using the 2024 American National Election Study, we show that accounting for nonignorable nonresponse produces substantively meaningful shifts for life satisfaction (estimated latent correlation ρ ≈ 0.47 $\rho \approx 0.47$ rho almost equals 0.47 ), while yielding only modest changes for retrospective economic evaluations ( ρ ≈ 0.14 $\rho \approx 0.14$ rho almost equals 0.14 ), highlighting when nonignorable nonresponse substantively affects survey estimates.

title: Exclusive Secrets,
abstract: Abstract We investigate the effects of trade secret (TS) protection on supplier exclusivity in vertical industrial relations. We show that manufacturers limit their suppliers’ buyer networks under weak TS protection to safeguard sensitive information while encouraging supplier investment. Using worldwide automotive parts contracts data, we find that weak TS protection constrains suppliers to serve only a few Original Equipment Manufacturers (OEMs), sometimes leading to exclusivity, especially for parts with intermediate relationship-specificity. This association strengthens with greater OEM bargaining power, aligning with theoretical insights. We validate these findings by examining supplier attributes, including size, cartel involvement, and ownership structure. F23, O34, L14, L24, L62
journal_name: Journal of the European Economic Association

title: When There's No November Rain: Developing a Parametric Insurance for Hydroelectric Energy Generators in Brazil
abstract: Hydrological risk is a growing challenge for renewable power systems, as droughts reduce generation, increase costs, and expose gaps in risk-transfer mechanisms. We examine this problem in Brazil, home to the world's sixth-largest electricity system and highly dependent on hydroelectricity, which accounted for 43% of installed generation capacity in 2026. We develop and evaluate a parametric insurance scheme for run-of-river hydroelectric generators indexed to the National System Operator's affluent flow measure. Using monthly energy and climate data from 151 powerplants between 2006 and 2022, we incorporate hydrological network dependence into insurance design. We model generation through a time-varying upstream-downstream spatial network and estimate it using a two-way fixed-effects SAR-IV-GMM-HAC specification. We then use vine copulas to assess the dependence structure among climatic variables, hydrological conditions, and electricity generation, supporting the use of affluent flow as the insurance trigger. Results reveal significant hydrological propagation across connected plants and indicate that parametric insurance can mitigate drought-related losses. However, feasibility depends on plant-specific trigger design, diversification, reinsurance support, and payout magnitude. Water-storage plants exhibit higher basis risk because of their operational flexibility.

title: Systemic Political Capacity and Regulatory Failure: Evidence From Proactive Conservation Under the Endangered Species Act
abstract: Contemporary governance faces mounting environmental challenges, straining governmental capacity to achieve policy objectives. We extend Wu et al.'s policy capacity framework, arguing that systemic political capacity is grounded in political trust, itself conditioned by legitimacy. Applying this framework to proactive conservation under the U.S. Endangered Species Act, we analyze the failure of Colorado’s sage-grouse initiative. Findings suggest contested legitimacy surrounding coercive federal intervention diminished political trust in regulatory authority, constraining systemic political capacity and limiting development of enforceable conservation arrangements satisfying federal requirements. The analysis has broader implications for collaborative governance dependent on credible regulatory authority.

title: Dead Ends and Policy Change in Chinese Experimental Governance
abstract: ABSTRACT Not all policy change is expansive, yet non‐expansive trajectories remain underexamined. This article introduces the concept of dead ends: a stage of the policy process in which initiatives cease to develop or be implemented in their existing form, structuring subsequent policy change such as rollback, redirection, or termination. To examine such trajectories, the article combines large‐scale analysis of 27,103 policy experiments announced in the People's Republic of China between 2013 and 2018 with qualitative case studies. The findings suggest that a substantial majority—up to 90%—of experiments reach dead ends. These dead ends are associated with leadership turnover, policy complexity, and misalignment with bureaucratic incentives and socio‐economic conditions. Altogether, the article provides new frameworks for understanding alternative directions of policy change. In doing so, it also sheds new light on the adaptive capacity and structural constraints of China's governance system.

title: Projectifying urban sustainability transition: the translation of transition initiatives into projects in Northern Sweden
abstract: Recently, a growing scholarship has examined the role of the project in policy implementation, particularly focusing on how it works as a politically charged instrument of governing. This article focuses on the projectification of urban sustainability transition as a policy field. Drawing on a case study of the implementation of transition initiatives in Northern Sweden, I analyze how these initiatives are transformed into transition projects. Mobilizing the concept of translation and drawing on project documentation and interviews with civil servants, I analyze the practices used to make transition initiatives fit the project format. The analysis shows that the transformation of transition initiatives into projects involves evidence-based problem construction, planning based on models and a specific conceptual vocabulary, consensus creation in project partnerships, universalization of common geographical challenges, and the establishment of coherent stories of contribution and learning. The article concludes that translation practices are power-laden and serve to stabilize policy.

title: Judicial conflicts on international law: how disagreements on EU and ECHR law align with broader divisions on the Supreme Court of Norway
abstract: How do supreme court judges’ disagreements about international law (IL) align with broader judicial conflicts? Existing research tends to frame domestic judicial conflicts on international law as a tension between sovereigntism and supranationalism. However, given that judiciaries are often characterised by internal disagreement, this paper investigates how international law aligns with broader judicial conflicts. We expect that IL interacts with domestic judicial politics, such that familiar divisions, e.g., deference to government authority or broader ideological orientations, shape how judges approach IL cases. Taking the Supreme Court of Norway as our case, we analyse the content and structure of judicial dissents in cases citing the European Convention of Human Rights and European Union law from 1990 to 2020 using Optimal Classification. We find that judicial conflicts in IL law cases align with a broader conflict related to deference to public authorities and that the line of conflict shifts depending on the issue at stake. Our results demonstrate that employing general theories of judicial politics and decision making can advance the analysis of how national courts engage with international law, cautioning against modelling judges as torn between national interest and the supranational authority of IL.

title: Correction to “Beyond WEIRD societies: Global social identifications across 45 countries and their socio‐cultural and economic predictors”
abstract: In the interest of full transparency, we report that during the revision of the second manuscript from this project, a minor error was identified in the code used to conduct the multilevel model (MLM) analyses reported in the first manuscript.Thus, all MLMs were recalculated, and the new code has been added to OSF.The resulting changes in the findings are minimal and do not alter the study's main conclusions.We sincerely apologize for this minor error.We report the details of these changes below.To sum up, Humane orientation was previously positively related to identification with citizens of the world (ICW), to identification with all humanity (IWAH) at the level of trend, and not at all to identification with people all over the world (IPOW).Now it is related to both ICW and IWAH, while only at the level of trend to IPOW.This is the only hypothesis that changed-regarding Humane orientation and IWAH (H3b)-previously it was not confirmed, and now it is.The rest of the changes are not connected to any hypotheses, but only to additional analyses: For example, now all three global social identifications are positively predicted by ethnic fractionalization and language fractionalization, but not by religious fractionalization, while previously language fractionalization did not predict ICW.Similarly, now the median age of the population negatively predicts all three types of global social identifications, while previously it did not predict IPOW.On the other hand, identification with people all over the world is no longer predicted by the democracy index or gender structure of societies.

title: Electoral Systems and Electoral Integrity: A Cross-National and Cross-Temporal Analysis With Policy Implications
abstract: This study examines the relationship between electoral systems and electoral integrity across a panel of 1,641 elections held in 141 countries over the period 1832–2024. Employing a correlated random-effects framework, which simultaneously recovers within-country estimates equivalent to fixed effects and between-country estimates capturing stable structural differences, the analysis reveals that proportional representation is associated with short-run reductions in electoral integrity within countries over time, reflecting administrative complexity, diffuse accountability costs, and the institutional turbulence that typically accompanies electoral system transitions. Yet countries with persistently proportional electoral systems exhibit substantially higher electoral integrity in cross-national comparison, reflecting the long-run co-evolution between proportional representation institutions and integrity-sustaining democratic infrastructure. These divergent effects cannot be recovered by cross-sectional or pooled analyses, which conflate two opposing mechanisms. The study shows that while proportional representation ultimately benefits electoral integrity when its full range of benefits is materialized in the process of co-evolution with democracy, the short-term transitional effects should not be overlooked.

title: Do marriage tax penalties cause delayed marriage reporting?
Immigration enforcement and safety net participation in mixed-status households
The accuracy of jobseekers’ wage expectations
abstract: We study the accuracy of wage expectations among unemployed workers by comparing subjective beliefs to benchmark and realized wages using linked survey-administrative data. On average, jobseekers overestimate their reemployment wages, with optimism concentrated among those with low earnings potential. Beliefs are anchored to past wages, and inaccuracies persist over the course of unemployment and in response to stronger search incentives. Moreover, there is an asymmetry in belief formation: individuals who are likely to experience wage losses relative to their previous job are particularly rigid in adjusting their expectations. Finally, wage optimism predicts higher reservation wages, greater search intensity, and delayed reemployment.
