Trust under threat: how AI vs. human mistakes in disaster alerts shape public perception and response
abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly integrated into disaster communication systems, understanding public responses to AI-led alerts is critical for designing trustworthy and effective crisis messaging. In line with an emerging line of inquiry, this study represents early empirical efforts to examine how the public responds to disaster alerts generated and delivered by AI, addressing a critical and timely gap in the disaster communication literature. Across two experiments (N = 599), we investigate how the attribution of disaster alerts (AI vs. human expert) shapes perceptions of message credibility, trust, and disaster coping outcomes. Study 1 finds that AI-led alerts are perceived as significantly less credible than expert-led alerts, although no significant differences emerge in coping outcomes such as self-efficacy, collective efficacy, or behavioral intentions. Study 2 extends these findings by introducing a factual error in the alert, revealing that AI sources suffer greater credibility and trust losses than human sources, despite being blamed less. Across both conditions, participants held human actors, such as experts, developers, and deploying organizations, more responsible than AI, yet consistently rated AI as less credible and trustworthy, even when greater responsibility predicted lower trust. Notably, errors made by human experts also diminished future interest in AI-based alerts, suggesting an interesting and complex shift in cross-source trust. These findings offer new insights into AI as a social actor within the disaster communication ecology and highlight the need for transparent, human-in-the-loop designs when deploying AI in public crisis messaging.

title: Are they virtue-signalling or sincere? The impact of perceived motives on the effectiveness of online collective action
abstract: Social media is an important tool used by supporters of modern social movements to persuade others to participate. However, people who engage in online collective action often face speculation about their motives and may be perceived as acting for self-serving reasons. How do these perceptions impact the effectiveness of collective action? In three experiments ( N = 916), participants viewed posts (Study 1) or an immersive social media feed (Studies 2–3) where a user encouraged them to take action for a political cause. They stated that they acted out of genuine concern (autonomous motivation), to avoid guilt and social disapproval (controlled motivation), or did not specify (baseline). Participants who viewed controlled-motivated posts perceived the user as less autonomously motivated and were therefore less likely to socially identify as supporters or take collective action. Thus, movements will be more effective at mobilising (online) support when they are seen to arise from autonomous motives.

title: Cross-platformization: How U.S. right-leaning media curate their posts on Twitter and Truth Social
abstract: This study examines how seven right-leaning media organizations utilize cross-platformization strategies to reach audiences across multiple platforms; in this case, Twitter and Truth Social. Focusing on both content volume and story packaging, we collect right-leaning media organizations’ social media posts and content from the 2022 U.S. midterm election. Combining computational and qualitative methods, we find that outlets posted only a small share of total stories across the two platforms and were selective in their content, often posting only on Twitter or Truth Social. For content posted on both platforms, the outlets posted content that ideologically aligned with the users of that platform. More specifically, right-leaning outlets on Truth Social tailored their posts to ideologically aligned users.

title: Disappearing Voices, Emerging Resistance: Journalism, Language, and Social Inequality in the U.S.-Mexico Borderlands
abstract: This article examines how linguistic, geographic, and racial inequalities shape journalism in the U.S.-Mexico borderlands. Focusing on Southern Arizona, it analyzes the rise of two community-driven Spanish-language news startups following the closure of the city’s only Spanish-language newspaper. Emerging in connection with a bilingual journalism initiative at a local university, these projects developed through collaborative research, community engagement, and newsroom experimentation aimed at addressing gaps in local news coverage. Drawing on research-action practices, collaborative research, and self-ethnography, the study examines how marginalized communities resist exclusion by producing culturally relevant media. It situates these efforts within broader discussions of news deserts, institutional inequality, and the systemic neglect of linguistic minorities, offering insight into how grassroots journalism—and the institutional spaces that can help incubate it—can challenge dominant media norms and reimagine local news in underserved, multilingual communities.

title: How Does Integrated Ethnic Education Policy Affect Tibetan Students’ National Identity?
Mechanisms of Public Service Motivation Development Through Public Administration Education: A Four‐Year Panel Study in Taiwan
abstract: ABSTRACT Given that public human capital is critical to sustainable development, this study aims to investigate the mechanisms through which public administration education shapes the public service motivation of prospective civil servants, in either positive or negative ways. Data for this study come from a four‐wave panel of 363 Taiwanese undergraduate students majoring in public administration. Our analysis showed that a program curriculum that can successfully enhance students' administrative knowledge, deliver public values, and a learning environment that surrounds peers and faculty members who have the spirit of public service are relevant for the development of PSM. In contrast, curriculum designs that are closely aligned with national civil service examinations, a feature more common in East Asia, may inadvertently undermine the cultivation of PSM.

title: Indonesia's South‐South Triangular Cooperation: Beyond the Great Foreign Aid Debate
abstract: ABSTRACT This article analyzes Indonesia's role as an emerging donor, providing foreign aid through South‐South and Triangular Cooperation (SSTC). To move beyond the typical debate between radical and reformist views on foreign aid, it adopts a “radical reform” approach that blends both perspectives. Employing qualitative methods, including elite interviews, the study investigates how Indonesia, as an emerging donor, embodies a radical reform strategy, showcasing adaptive public administration in shaping international development policies. The article posits that SSTC offers a strategic alternative to traditional aid models, presenting Indonesia's approach as a practical, mutually beneficial framework for international cooperation.

title: Digital Election Platforms, Administrative Performance, and the Accountability Squeeze: Recentralization by Design in Indonesia’s Regional Elections
abstract: Digital election platforms increasingly mediate administrative performance, transparency, and accountability in electoral governance. Examining Indonesia’s regional elections, this study analyzes how such platforms shape administrative performance and redistribute accountability. A qualitative design combining documentary analysis, platform-artifact analysis, and documentary process tracing compares three centrally governed platforms operated by Indonesia’s General Elections Commission: Sidalih for voter registration, Silon for candidate nomination, and Sirekap for results reporting. Findings show that these platforms operate as performance regimes, translating electoral work into visible signals such as synchronization status, validation outcomes, upload completion, dashboard display, correction records, and verification pathways. Platform architecture simultaneously centralizes operational control over data structures, validation rules, user permissions, publication logic, and correction procedures, while subnational offices retain implementation responsibility. Such arrangements create an accountability squeeze: implementing units become increasingly visible as responsible actors without commensurate control over technical conditions shaping performance outcomes. By linking platform-mediated visibility to asymmetries in control, this study shows how digital transparency can strengthen administrative legibility while redistributing responsibility, risk, and authority across organizational levels.

title: Speaking truth to power? Climate activism and the struggle for a digital city twin
Digital eyes, human hands: aI, discretion, and welfare blind spots in South Korea
Algorithmic governance and democratic accountability: rethinking policy design in the age of artificial intelligence
Policy capacity, collaborative governance, and the institutional design of implementation arrangements: food security PPPs in Kenya
abstract: Abstract This article empirically investigates how different institutional designs of implementation arrangements are associated with specific configurations of policy capacity and, in turn, with variation in implementation outputs. Building on the policy capacity framework developed by Wu et al. (2015) and its extension to collaborative settings, the article analyses three irrigation public–private partnership (PPP) projects in Kenya—Galana Kulalu, Perkerra, and Chakama—through a small-N, case-oriented comparative design. The study suggests that variation in implementation outputs is best understood through the interaction between institutional design and the configuration of analytical, managerial, and political capacities activated across individual, organizational, and systemic levels. The findings indicate that political capacity serves as an important enabling condition for more effective collaborative arrangements, while the relative weight of analytical and managerial capacities varies with the coordination logic embedded in each arrangement. More hierarchical and rule-based arrangements are associated with stronger implementation outputs where analytical and managerial capacities are institutionalized, whereas more networked and adaptive arrangements rely more heavily on managerial-political capacities rooted in trust, partner mobilization, and negotiated coordination. By connecting policy capacity research with implementation research on collaborative arrangements, the article contributes to a more relational, institutionally grounded understanding of why similar policy interventions yield different implementation outputs under broadly comparable conditions.

title: Why non-structural flood governance underperforms: brokerage gaps in fragmented bureaucratic systems
Editorial Board
Small time costs matter: Reform-induced polling station congestion reduces turnout in a high-turnout PR system
abstract: Long waiting times at polling stations may reduce voter turnout and potentially undermine democratic legitimacy and, if unevenly distributed, democratic equality. Yet their effects on turnout remain poorly understood and have been studied mainly in majoritarian contexts. We provide the first evidence from a proportional parliamentary democracy by examining Sweden’s 2022 general election, when a reform to strengthen ballot secrecy unexpectedly produced congestion at many polling places. We estimate the turnout effect of congestion, using administrative records on precincts’ closing times together with original assessments from poll workers and local election authorities. Across several independent measures and estimation techniques, precincts experiencing problematic lines exhibit turnout about 1 to 1.5 percentage points lower than comparable precincts without congestion. The fact that congestion was induced by an exogenous legislative change and that Swedish voters were unaccustomed to polling station waiting times facilitates causal inference. Our results align with the few existing studies examining the impact of additional waiting times in majoritarian and presidential systems (the US and Kenya), suggesting that voters in a high-turnout PR system react similarly to voters in other contexts to an increased cost of voting. This underscores the policy importance of preventing congestion. Furthermore, our findings highlight a trade-off in electoral management between efficiency and ballot secrecy that warrants more attention in research as well as in electoral reform.

title: ‘From K2 to Kanyakumari, Bharat is One’: The visual and geopolitical place-making of road signs in Ladakh
abstract: One of the first things travelers to the Indian Himalaya remark upon are the curious, often rhyming and comedic, road signs of the Border Roads Organisation (BRO) dotting the strategic roads of the region. In this article, I ask what role road signs play in physically narrating, constructing and altering the imagination of the contested high-altitude region of Ladakh. I provide a combined discursive and visual analysis of military-origin road signs in Ladakh, drawing on a series of fieldwork trips across 2019-2025. I make two core contributions. First, I add to the literature on the political geography of road signs, by demonstrating their expansive role in re-narrating an entire region. Second, I contribute to our understanding of Ladakh's geopolitics and its place in the Indian state. Specifically, I argue that road signs are an important means of marking contested territory for the Indian Army, and construct specific ideas of nationalism, sacrifice, masculinity, and safety. The crucial narrative of these road signs is India's military prowess and engineering skill, making the region safe for both the nation and for tourism. These ideas are blended with gender, particularly hypermasculinity, and the need to dominate nature for the state.

title: Editorial Board
Matching and Price Competition in Large Markets
The security–efficiency trade-off in ransomware networks
abstract: Ransomware groups pose a threat to both the economy and national security, yet little is known about their structural dynamics. This study analyses the Conti group using leaked Jabber encrypted instant messaging chat data (similar to Messenger) and Relational Event Models to examine how preferential attachment and triadic closure mechanisms shape its communication network. Findings show Conti prioritised efficiency through centralisation but mitigated risks via compartmentalisation, creating a hybrid structure that balances speed and secrecy. This adaptive approach enhances both effectiveness and resilience. The research provides new insights into the evolution of ransomware groups and suggests that disruption strategies should target internal cohesion rather than external infrastructure.

title: Understanding Meritocracy: From an Imagination of ‘Ideal’ to Producing ‘Myth’ and Beyond
abstract: MIchael Young satirizes a global society envisaged for the 21st century, in which all job appointments and rewards are determined solely by merit. Notable advancements in intelligence and ability testing were assumed to enable accurate performance projections and effective educational monitoring. Consequently, the influence of social obstacles such as socioeconomic class, family, race, and religion would be significantly mitigated. The system, however, has shifted to produce winners and losers, a phenomenon Sandel characterizes as hubris . We argue that this hubris stems from meritocracy’s roots in bureaucracy, grounded in a rationalized myth.

title: Silica secrecy: Navigating access to silica dust data under freedom of information legislation
abstract: Abstract Tunnel construction supports vital infrastructure development but can expose workers to serious health risks, including silicosis, from exposure to respirable crystalline silica (RCS). This study examines how Australia's freedom of information (FOI) legislation facilitates or hinders access to information that can support improvements in policy and practice, using RCS exposure of Australian tunnel workers as an example. A review was conducted of FOI requests submitted in 2023–2024 to government agencies. We assessed the availability of information and timeliness of decisions, and reported on facilitators, obstacles, outcomes, and variations concerning information access. Our experience identified operational hindrances including lengthy delays, varying interpretations between government agencies of what was in the public interest, and substantial efforts by third parties to prevent information disclosure. Despite these constraints, FOI use in one jurisdiction generated evidence of government knowledge that challenged prevailing narratives, prompted media and parliamentary scrutiny, and contributed to policy responses addressing RCS exposure in tunnelling. Points for practitioners Freedom of information laws are essential for accessing government-held information, particularly where it has important implications for public health. Public interest tests and disclosure decisions differ significantly across Australian government agencies, creating inconsistency in access to information. Practitioners should be aware of these differences and that obtaining access to information may involve significant delays and require the pursuit of review or appeal processes, reinforcing longstanding concerns about the suppression of data relevant to public health. Withholding information can delay recognition of risks, while greater transparency can support timely intervention and stronger evidence‐informed public health policy.

title: Bridging policy and practice in rural development through village‐owned enterprise
abstract: Abstract Rural poverty worldwide is often associated with multidimensional economic, social, and environmental challenges. Several countries have adopted policy initiatives to support downstream development, one of which is through the development of village‐owned enterprises (BUMDes) in Indonesia. Since 2014, BUMDes represent a systematic approach to institutionalising community‐based economic development through a formal policy framework. However, only one third of the 51,000 BUMDes are actively operating, indicating a critical implementation gap. Key challenges include inadequate communication between BUMDes and communities, limited resources, and cumbersome bureaucratic procedures. Therefore, successful implementation requires a holistic approach that integrates economic development with community empowerment strategies. BUMDes that adopt an integrated model achieve higher levels of sustainability. This model includes a regulatory framework that accommodates local variations while maintaining accountability standards. This BUMDes model offers valuable insights into a participatory governance approach that balances top‐down structural support and bottom‐up community initiatives through a participatory governance framework tailored to the local context. Furthermore, the framework for measuring implementation success must go beyond traditional economic indicators to encompass dimensions of community well‐being, social cohesion, and environmental sustainability. International development practitioners, particularly in developing countries with similar challenges, can adapt these elements of participatory governance while tailoring operational structures to local institutional contexts and cultural preferences. Points for practitioners Implement holistic support systems that combine economic development with community empowerment strategies, as BUMDes adopting integrated models demonstrate 85% higher sustainability rates compared to those focusing solely on economic objectives. Establish flexible regulatory frameworks that accommodate local variations while maintaining accountability standards, since standardised regulations create implementation barriers in 62% of cases due to insufficient consideration of local contexts and community needs. Prioritise sustained technical assistance over one‐time interventions, as BUMDes receiving ongoing support consistently outperform those with limited post‐establishment guidance in operational effectiveness and long‐term viability. Local and village governments can collaborate with higher education institutions to develop a comprehensive success measurement framework that goes beyond traditional economic indicators to encompass community well‐being, social cohesion, and environmental sustainability dimensions, and more accurately assess the impact of rural development. Foster participatory governance mechanisms that balance top‐down structural support with bottom‐up community initiatives, enabling adaptive management responses to local market dynamics and evolving community needs while maintaining program coherence.

title: Karl Löfgren and Patrik Hall, The New Public Bureaucracy: The Expansion of Organisational Professionals in the Public Secto ,
Functionalization Without Instruments: How Local Bureaucrats Make Sense of Unfinished Reform While Managing Public Services
abstract: This study examines how bureaucrats enact functionalization reform under conditions of unfinished reform, conceptualized as instrumental incompleteness in which structural change outpaces the development of operational HR infrastructures. Drawing on a comparative qualitative case study across four Indonesian local government jurisdictions, the study identifies a common mechanism through which an HR-instrument void generates operational ambiguity, prompting collective sensemaking and adaptive coordination. Cross-case comparison shows that these mechanisms follow different reform trajectories according to organizational support conditions, comprising fiscal capacity, administrative support, and reform facilitation. Rather than fiscal capacity alone, the combined configuration of these conditions explains why some jurisdictions move toward partial formalization of functional roles while others continue to rely on hierarchical coordination. The study contributes by conceptualizing unfinished reform as instrumental incompleteness and by integrating structural reform, operational HR infrastructures, and bureaucratic sensemaking into a comparative mechanism-based explanation of reform enactment in decentralized public administration.

title: Muddling together through the fog: Peer trust, exit intention, and innovative work behavior during the pandemic
abstract: What resources enable public employees to remain motivated to engage in innovative behavior at work, even when they consider leaving the organization? In this study, we examine how public employees’ innovative behavior is explained by relational resources, particularly peer trust that fosters psychological safety to take risks and tolerate failure. Using novel survey data from 1861 public employees across 29 central government ministries and agencies in South Korea, collected during the peak of the COVID-19 pandemic, we find significant effects of peer trust on innovative behavior, as well as a moderating effect between exit intention and innovation. These effects are consistent among long-tenured employees, while performance recognition emerges as a stronger determinant of innovative behavior among newcomers. This study's findings contribute to an advanced understanding of the peer trust–innovative work behavior relationship and the importance of psychological safety in the public sector. Points for practitioners Peer trust functions as a critical organizational resource that sustains innovative work behavior even when public employees are considering leaving, making it a priority investment for crisis-period management. Public organizations should not treat exit-intending employees as disengaged; when peer trust is high, these employees continue to contribute to innovation and should remain integrated into collaborative work environments. Formal performance recognition has a limited overall effect on innovation but plays a significant motivational role for newcomers with fewer than three years of tenure, suggesting HRM strategies should be differentiated by career stage. Because crisis conditions deplete the psychological resources that innovation requires, public organizations must proactively cultivate peer relationships.

title: Policy Entrepreneurs and Policy Change When Politicians Are Absent: The Inclusion of Autistic Individuals in Armed Forces
abstract: ABSTRACT How do policy entrepreneurs change policy when politicians are not directly involved in the process? While public policy scholars have examined the conditions under which politicians refrain from direct engagement in policy design, they have paid less attention to the strategies policy entrepreneurs employ in the absence of political actors. Drawing on textual analysis and 30 in‐depth interviews with members of the “Roim Rachok” (“Looking Ahead”) program, which facilitates the inclusion of individuals on the autism spectrum in the Israel Defense Forces as a case study, we addressed this lacuna by exploring how policy entrepreneurs independently advance policy change. The findings suggest that the policy entrepreneurs operated through institutionalized collaborative networks. They also leveraged Israel's security challenges as a structured framework for promoting their new policy. In addition, they created an organizational infrastructure. Finally, they focused on establishing trust with the security organizations with whom they collaborated.

title: Why Politicians Misbehave: A Systematic Review of How Attributes of Political Office Affect Moral Decision‐Making and Behavior
abstract: ABSTRACT The moral decision‐making and behavior of politicians is influenced by the distinctive and characteristic attributes of political office. This literature review analyzes 80 articles from public administration, political science and related disciplines to systematically map these attributes and their underlying mechanisms. This study identifies six categories of attributes of political office that relate to moral decision‐making and behavior: political system design, political role, relations to societal actors, legal and regulatory measures, political cycle, and some general attributes such as the size of the political institution. Interestingly, existing research focuses mostly on unethical behavior, creating white spots in our understanding of how the attributes of political office shape individual and collective processes of moral decision‐making and behavior more generally. We conclude with an agenda for future research that advocates for more targeted research of the sociopsychological aspects that shape the moral decision‐making and behavior of politicians across their different roles.

title: Foreign Aid Governance in China and India: A Comparative Analysis
abstract: ABSTRACT This article uses a structured, focused explanatory paired comparison to examine how China and India translate shared South–South principles into distinct foreign aid governance arrangements. It argues that these principles provide a common legitimacy framework, while differences in strategic priorities and state architecture help explain variation in authority location, fiscal control, and implementation coalitions. Using a policy‐institution‐implementation framework, the analysis shows that China's aid system is more globally ambitious, infrastructure‐centered, and reliant on state and corporate actors, whereas India's is more diplomatically embedded, regionally oriented, and focused on capacity building and state‐to‐state cooperation. By shifting attention from aid volumes and rhetoric to administrative design and delivery, the article highlights institutional variation among major non‐DAC providers.

title: Ministerial Advisers in Personal Patronage Settings: Evidence From Israel
abstract: ABSTRACT The characteristics of ministerial advisers are predicted to correspond to the type of politicization setting in which they operate. The only systematic framework mapping these correspondences was developed predominantly in party‐driven patronage contexts. Whether it holds where personally‐driven rather than party‐mediated logic governs appointments remains an open theoretical question. This study addresses that question through biographical analysis of 196 officials comprising the executive triangle of Israel’s 37th Government, constituting the Israeli case within the COST Action Comparative Research on the Executive Triangle in Europe. Examining adviser visibility, educational profiles, and career trajectories, the study locates Israel within a medium‐high politicization setting and assesses whether its personally‐driven patronage system produces the predicted adviser configurations. Findings confirm the framework’s generalizability while introducing two theoretically significant refinements: personally‐driven systems produce deeper institutional invisibility than party‐mediated ones, and appointments into bureaucracy operate as personalized rather than systematic channels.

title: Performance-measurement systems as actors and boundary objects: a sociomaterial perspective to the provision of prison services
abstract: The paper explores the performance-measurement systems (PMSs) used in the provision of prison services (and their non-human agent role) to reflect on: the role PMSs play in inter-organisational relationships; the boundary objects that connect human and non-human actors across inter-organisational levels; and what affordances such connections generate. The study focuses on the English prison sector, drawing on document analysis and interviews. The findings show that PMSs represent both active non-human agents and boundary objects. The positioning of the actors involved can be seen as a second-order boundary object. Moreover, PMSs can generate affordances that go beyond the initially-intended purposes.
