title: The Negative Impact of Digital Overload on Civil Servants’ Work Outcomes: The Moderating Role of High-Performance Human Resource Management Practices
abstract: As digitalization accelerates, digital overload is placing increasing pressure on civil servants. This study draws on the Job Demands–Resources model and analyzes 3 waves of survey data from 653 civil servants, along with a scenario-based experiment involving 138 participants. Findings reveal that digital overload affects job performance, turnover intention, and burnout through the mediating role of relative deprivation. Furthermore, high-performance human resource management practices moderate this relationship by mitigating the negative effects of digital overload, thus reducing their negative impact. A moderated mediation model is proposed, highlighting strategies to support public employees coping with digitalization.

title: Does the state matter? Institutional trust, structural vulnerability, and the wellbeing of older women in Southeast Asia
Ethnoracial Characteristics and Police Abuse Within Mexico's Criminal Justice System
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines the association between ethnoracial characteristics (ethnoracial self‐identification, speaking an Indigenous language, and skin tone) and police abuse within Mexico's criminal justice system, drawing on street‐level bureaucracy frameworks. Using data from the 2021 National Survey of Persons Deprived of Liberty (ENPOL in Spanish), we analyze whether ethnoracial traits are conditionally associated with reported experiences of police abuse. Logistic regression models suggest that Afro‐Mexican or Afro‐descendant and Indigenous persons have higher odds of reporting abuse, supporting existing literature on discrimination and policing. Unexpectedly, speaking an Indigenous language and having darker skin tones were associated with lower reported abuse, suggesting a complex relationship that merits further examination. These results underscore the need to incorporate ethnoracial variables into the study of police behavior and public administration in Mexico, while informing public policies aimed at preventing and addressing police abuse to strengthen accountability within the criminal justice system.

title: A note on the changing appropriability conditions and technological opportunities for innovation in Japan; 1994–2020
abstract: We report findings obtained by comparing two innovation surveys in Japan conducted in 1994 and 2020. A comparison of statistical means at two points in time, controlling for firm size and industry as covariates, reveals that the following three changes have occurred for appropriabilities and technological opportunities of innovation during the past quarter-century. First, the effectiveness of almost all the mechanisms by which firms' appropriate profits from innovation declined. Second, the imitation lag has lengthened considerably. Third, while universities and government research institutes have become more important sources of technological information, internal sources and competitors have become less important. These results suggest that Japan's innovation system has undergone a fundamental transformation between the two time points.

title: Reshaping the Social Contract? A Systematic Literature Review of Two Decades of Research on the Digital Welfare State in Developing Countries
abstract: ABSTRACT The rapid digitization of welfare states is a global phenomenon, yet its impacts in developing countries, where inequalities and weak infrastructure persist, are poorly understood. This systematic review synthesizes evidence on the implementation of digital welfare systems in developing countries and their effects on social inclusion and exclusion, as well as on the citizen‐state relationship. Following PRISMA guidelines, we conducted a systematic search across four databases: Scopus, Web of Science, PubMed, and ProQuest, for eligible studies. The review spans 25 years (2000–2025) to capture the full genesis and evolution of digital welfare as a distinct policy phenomenon, from early pilot programs to contemporary system‐wide integrations. A thematic synthesis was employed to analyse 26 studies that met the inclusion criteria and methodological quality. The findings identify digital welfare as a double‐edged sword: while capable of enhancing efficiency and transparency, it simultaneously creates new forms of exclusion for vulnerable populations. A critical finding is the indispensable yet often invisible role of human intermediaries who bridge the gap between digital systems and citizens. Furthermore, the integration of digital ID, datafication, and private actors is fundamentally transforming governance, often obscuring accountability and reshaping the social contract. The study highlights that the trajectory of digital welfare in developing countries is not technologically predetermined but contingent on political and design choices. This review concludes that to foster equitable outcomes, policy must prioritize rights‐based, inclusive‐by‐design systems, robust regulation of private actors, and investment in the foundational pillars of digital equity. PROSPERO Registration ID: CRD420251157370

title: Exploring Transitions to Adulthood for Young Disabled People: Personalisation and the Quiet Dismantling of Social Care
abstract: ABSTRACT Across OECD countries, policy frameworks to support disabled young people in their transition to adulthood remain fragmented, under‐resourced and poorly aligned. This article examines how these longstanding weaknesses have been exacerbated by the shift towards personalisation in social care. Drawing on a three‐year qualitative study in England and Scotland, we show that promises of choice, control and autonomy—central to personalisation agendas—have largely failed to materialise for this generation. Instead, the shift to more individualised support in a prolonged period of budget cuts has eroded the social care infrastructure, diminishing both collective provision and the spaces that enable young people to build friendships, identities and meaningful social lives. Our findings highlight how young people encounter reduced support as they move from children to adult services, with families often forced into protracted negotiations within increasingly sparse local care markets. The withdrawal of community‐based provision, alongside inconsistent access to social workers and limited information, contributes to profound isolation and precarious transitions. We argue that personalisation, without adequate investment and collaborative infrastructure, can entrench inequalities and undermine the collective foundations of disabled people's advocacy. Rebuilding social care requires renewed attention to shared spaces, co‐production, and resourcing that enables genuine independence.

title: Designing multi‐site studies for external validity: Site selection via synthetic purposive sampling
abstract: Abstract Multi‐site/context studies have become popular strategies to address the most common and challenging external validity concerns about contexts. Under such studies, scholars conduct causal studies in each site and evaluate whether findings generalize across sites. Despite the potential, there has been little guidance on the fundamental research design question—how should we select sites for external validity? Existing approaches have challenges: random sampling of sites is often infeasible, while the current practice of purposive sampling is suboptimal without statistical guarantees. We propose synthetic purposive sampling (SPS), which optimally selects diverse sites for external validity. SPS combines ideas of purposive sampling and the synthetic control method—it selects diverse sites such that nonselected sites are well approximated by the weighted average of the selected sites. We illustrate its general applicability using both experimental and observational studies. Overall, this paper offers a new statistical foundation to design multisite studies for external validity.

title: The conditionality-corruption nexus: implications for democracy promotion in candidate and neighbourhood countries
Transformative constitutionalism and Kenya: law-making, political process, and the state (2010–2025)
abstract: In Transformative Constitutionalism and Kenya, Bhatia presents a comparative constitutional law project premised on court decisions in constitutional cases. The book addresses the broad question “w...

title: The international and transnational politics of the far right: an emergent research program
abstract: Abstract This article offers a state-of-the-art review of a new and growing research program in International Relations (IR) that analyzes the far right’s inter- and transnational politics. Responding to the rise of far-right leaders, parties, and movements worldwide, this nascent literature sheds light on the inter- and transnational drivers, patterns, connections, and effects of far-right politics. To further consolidate and develop this emerging research program, as this article argues, it is imperative to integrate this literature into a wider framework that delineates different analytical approaches and research agendas. For this purpose, the article identifies and examines five research strands: (1) foreign and security policy, (2) international thought, (3) the global causes of the rise of the far right, (4) trans- and international collaboration, and (5) international norms, institutions, and orders. It appraises their different analytical perspectives and insights, connects each research strand with various IR paradigms, subdisciplines, and literatures, and identifies unexplored lines of inquiry. Thereby, the article aims to broaden and diversify the theoretical, empirical, and methodological scope of this research program and to further facilitate synergies between IR and far-right studies. It then discusses a series of limitations and challenges facing this research program and proposes a level-of-analysis approach to advance it.

title: Elections, Government Turnover, and Citizen Acceptance of Political Violence: Evidence from Election Panel Surveys in Zambia and Kenya
abstract: Elections in unconsolidated democracies are contentious moments with heightened risks of violence. Although elections offer hope to the politically marginalized, ruling parties often enjoy insurmountable advantages, sometimes leading to frustration and concerns for groups and citizens’ exclusion from power. How do elections shape citizens’ acceptance of political violence in unconsolidated democracies? Furthermore, can government turnovers reduce the support for political violence among citizens previously excluded from political power? We argue that citizens respond both to electoral outcomes and their perception of the electoral process when updating their attitudes on political violence. We leverage an original panel survey of the Zambia 2021 election to measure changes in attitudes to political violence before and after an election. Because the 2021 election resulted in a turnover of power, it provides a critical test to evaluate updated perceptions amid political change. We show that election winners reduce their support for political violence and election losers increase their acceptance of violence, even in the case of a turnover. We also show that increased perceptions of election quality reduce the acceptance of violence. Extending our study to an analysis of original panel data from the Kenyan 2017 election (a case without a turnover and low election quality), we find similar patterns.

title: A Few Good Women? Gendered Socialization and Norms of Civilian Protection in United States Military Training
abstract: Many professionalized militaries seek to train combatants in “norms of restraint” (NoR) based on international legal principles of noncombatant immunity. Does training in NoR affect the attitudes of women and men toward the protection of civilians differently? Drawing on unique surveys of United States Army officer cadets at the US Military Academy (USMA), we find that while women and men held similar attitudes at the start of their academy training, women’s attitudes shifted more toward civilian restraint, despite receiving identical formal training in international humanitarian law (IHL), combat ethics, and officership. To explore the causes of this gender divergence, we conduct open-ended, in-depth interviews with former USMA cadets. We find that socialization at USMA is deeply gendered, and that differences in norm socialization are linked to a prevailing “gender order” constructed by formal and informal rules, practices, and norms that attribute distinct roles to women and men in military settings. Despite the seemingly “ungendered” nature of USMA’s intensive training in IHL and combat ethics, this gender order creates different socialization experiences for women and men, resulting in divergent attitudes toward civilian restraint. These findings shed light on how socialization and gender interact to shape combatant attitudes toward NoR, and are especially notable given the USMA’s status as the US Army’s “flagship of ethics education.”

title: Collective action at the margins of the state: Institutional braiding and the micro-politics of development in Solomon Islands
abstract: This article examines how collective action for local public goods is forged, sustained, and sometimes unravels in hybrid governance settings, drawing on four comparative case studies from Solomon Islands. In remote and marginalised communities, infrastructure and services - such as roads, water systems, and agricultural projects - are not always state-delivered but often locally assembled. These efforts unfold within fragmented governance landscapes where authority is claimed simultaneously by state, customary, and religious institutions. Grounded in locally led fieldwork and Indigenous epistemologies, we trace how four village-level initiatives navigate this hybrid landscape to secure tangible, if uneven, improvements in everyday life. Using Ostrom's design principles as adaptable heuristics, we show how participation can be mobilised through shared imaginaries of pride, hardship, worship, and care as much as by material incentive; rule-making can depend less on procedural inclusion than on rendering obligations socially legitimate; monitoring can work through social visibility and accountability rather than formal oversight; and conflict resolution can centre less on adjudication than on preserving cooperation. Collective action is made possible through the active interweaving of socially recognised repertoires of authority, obligation, and meaning across church, kastom, and state domains. We conceptualise this process as institutional braiding: the micropolitical work of translation, role alignment, and relational repair through which plural authority becomes workable and cooperation becomes intelligible, legitimate, and binding. These findings advance political geography by spatialising collective action in marginalised settings and foregrounding the relational labour through which hybridity is mobilised in pursuit of developmental goals.

title: Masking or lexicographic preferences? Using conjoint experiments to distinguish between two fundamental theories of choice
abstract: Abstract Many studies on candidate choice and other political preferences suggest that the effect of one attribute may mask the effect of another attribute, which the respondent has no information about. If, for instance, respondents lack information about party membership, they may infer that female candidates are Democrats, which would lead to biased estimates of the pure effect of candidate gender. We propose an alternative explanation—namely that respondents have lexicographic preferences—and we present an empirical test using conjoint experiments to distinguish between what we call pure masking and lexicographic preferences. We illustrate our method using data on the effect of gender, race, and party in candidate choice and replicate the results in a preregistered conjoint experiment. We offer recommendations for researchers studying candidate and political choices.

title: Violence Against Women Political Activists
abstract: In the last decade, research on violence against women in politics (VAWIP) has increased significantly. First identified by women activists in the Global South, VAWIP refers to behaviors that specifically target women as women by pressuring them to leave politics (Krook and Sanín 2016). Activists in Bolivia and later in other regions of the Global South first called attention to VAWIP in the late 1990s and early 2000s, when countries around the world began adopting gender quotas to increase the presence of women in government (Krook 2019). Most scholarship in this area has focused on violence targeting women candidates and elected officials (Collignon and Rüdig 2020; Dalton 2021; Håkansson 2021; Herrick et al. 2021; Raney and Collier 2024; Schneider and Carroll 2020). Attention to women in formal politics is warranted given their important representational role. Women’s presence in politics is a necessary first step to achieve political change and advance women’s interests (Beckwith 2011).

title: Gendered Political Violence in Transitional Moments: The Cases of Bangladesh and Iran
abstract: Women’s rights advocates and movements play an important role during political transitions, shaping feminist outcomes following these transitions. Women are also often at the forefront of many pro-democratic mobilizations and struggles for political change (Baldez 2002; Goetz 2009; Viterna and Fallon 2008; Waylen 2007; 2011). Yet this participation is not without costs, and one core cost remains undertheorized in the literature: targeted violence against women precisely because of their gender and political engagement.

title: Editorial Board
Review of “Kid Cops: What Communities Gain and Lose from Junior Police in Schools”
A Risk‐Reduction Approach to Roadway Infrastructure Adaptation Prioritization for Improved Public Protection
abstract: Measures to safeguard transportation infrastructure from uncertain hazard events, such as a flooding event, are crucial for public safety, but require significant investment. As it is impractical to try to protect all assets from all possible futures, a risk-based analysis approach for choosing a best protective strategy for adaptation can prove useful. This paper proposes and applies a need-based, risk-reduction methodology to more deeply understand how alternative approaches to mitigating risk via protective infrastructure investments can affect our neighborhoods. A risk measure, based on remaining connectivity to critical facilities, is employed that gives more weight to neighborhoods (represented by census tracts) that have the greatest gap in protection and, therefore, are at greatest risk of being disconnected from critically needed services. The measure is compared against four alternative investment strategies. The analysis is applied to a study area in the Washington, DC metropolitan area under a variety of hazard modeling assumptions. Trade-offs using ten distinct performance metrics are made. The results demonstrate that the choice of risk model in protective investment planning can greatly impact the recommended adaptation plan and which neighborhoods "win" and which "lose." The suggested method provides a balanced distribution of risk and may be a more acceptable approach for setting community protective investment priorities.

title: Acceptance of the COVID‐19 Booster Vaccine Amid the Omicron JN.1 Surge in Southern Bangladesh: A Comparative Analysis of Rural–Urban Disparities
abstract: ABSTRACT Rapid spread of SARS‐CoV‐2 variants, including Omicron JN.1, has revived significant challenges to health systems and regenerates microbial risk to public health security. Although COVID‐19 booster vaccines have ensured enhanced protection against new variants, there remain persistent disparities in vaccine acceptance and uptake between rural and urban populations. This study assesses COVID‐19 booster vaccine acceptance and compares antecedents of acceptance across rural and urban communities in Southern Bangladesh. A cross‐sectional observational study was conducted between December 15, 2023, and March 15, 2024, in accordance with the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) guidelines. By using stratified random sampling, 707 adults comprising 379 rural and 328 urban respondents (refusal rate: 16.7% rural, 23.2% urban) were surveyed. The study employed descriptive statistics and binary logistic regression analysis to identify socio‐psychological predictors of booster acceptance, with statistical significance set at p < 0.05. The acceptance rate of COVID‐19 vaccine booster dose was 69.9% overall, with a significantly lower rate in rural 62.5% (95% CI: 60.6–64.8) compared to urban areas 78.4% (95% CI: 76.2–80.6, χ 2 = 20.87, p < 0.001). Logistic regression estimation revealed that rural and urban participants perceived booster dose as “equally safe” were more likely to accept booster vaccination. Conversely, fear of “side effects” was negatively associated with acceptance in both settings. Among rural respondents, communication with vaccination services, trust in booster vaccine, and social influence, showed strong positive associations with booster vaccine acceptance. In urban settings, “community protection” and “risk–benefit ratio” were revealed as significant predictors of booster acceptance, whereas reliance on non‐pharmaceutical preventative measures following the primary vaccination series was negatively associated with booster uptake in urban areas. The acceptance of booster vaccines was higher among rural and urban populations with higher educational levels. In addition, rural healthcare professionals and urban individuals with comorbidities exhibited greater acceptance of booster vaccines. The study highlighted substantial rural–urban disparities in COVID‐19 booster vaccine acceptance in southern Bangladesh, shaped by differences in risk perception, trust, and communication. Fear of side effects remains a key barrier across both populations and a major reason of booster skepticism. Strengthening health communication, improving vaccine risk‐benefit knowledge, and integrating public health surveillance as a tool for community education to improve booster uptake, particularly in marginalized areas.

title: Risk Calibration: Divergent Interpretations of Risk Assessment in Norway's Early COVID‐19 Response
abstract: During the early phases of novel disease outbreaks, risk management must rely largely on non-pharmaceutical interventions, since consensus-based biomedical solutions are yet to be developed. This paper examines how and why expert organizations arrive at divergent interpretations of the same risk assessments, and what such divergence means for risk management strategies. Using Norway's early COVID-19 response as a qualitative case, the study analyzes the disagreement between national health authorities over suppression versus mitigation strategies. Data consist of interviews with key decision-makers and senior analysts, supplemented by extensive interview material and reports from the Norwegian Corona Commission, and are analyzed using thematic analysis. The findings show that the disagreement did not primarily stem from different estimates of epidemiological risk, but from divergent interpretations of what those estimates implied: where the main consequences of the pandemic would concentrate, and whether existing health-system capacities could control the situation. To explain this, the paper introduces the concepts of (1) risk epicenter, where the risk is interpreted to concentrate and (2) risk controllability, the assessed institutional capacity to control it. Together, these constitute a process termed risk calibration, through which technical risk assessments are socially and institutionally interpreted. The contribution is a two-dimensional framework for analyzing the structure of divergent interpretations during the early phase of novel risk events. The study argues that incorporating both dimensions into early-phase risk analysis is essential for understanding policy disagreement and improving preparedness for future large-scale, novel risks.

title: The Social Amplification of Risk Framework Revisited: Report From an Exst Workshop on Opportunities for Conceptual Advancement
abstract: The Social Amplification of Risk Framework (SARF) is intended to facilitate the integration of studies about risk across natural, biological, physical, and social sciences. Researchers employing SARF have advanced understandings of the complex dynamic responses of social systems to hazards, the ways that risks are experienced and perceived, and the ways that consequences can ripple across social and governance systems, geographies, and economic sectors. In seeking to build on a Special Issue of Risk Analysis on SARF organized and edited by Kasperson, et al. (2022), an international interdisciplinary group of scholars convened an invited expert Workshop on SARF at the Federal Institute of Technology in Zurich during April 2024. Here we report on the outcomes emerging from the workshop. First, we sought to clarify definitions of concepts, such as risk signals, risk amplification, and risk attenuation. Second, we sought to overcome the tendency in studies using SARF to focus on information processing by the public and neglect the ways that other social actors play roles in risk amplification and attenuation. Third, we propose a new metaphor, risk resonance, to focus attention on why certain risk signals gain traction and others do not, which has also been a topic that has to date received minimal attention. Fourth, our discussions led us to highlight the importance of better integration of context and history into analyses employing SARF. We conclude the paper with thoughts about how the framework can achieve its yet unmet potential to inform risk research, policy, and management.

title: The Networks of Others: A Model of Secondhand Brokerage and its Effects on Employee Innovation
abstract: Social network research on creativity and innovation has primarily focused on the focal employee (i.e., ego), implicitly assuming that ego’s own network position determines the resources available for creative work. We advance an alter-centric perspective, arguing that what matters is not merely the availability of diverse information but the capacity of network contacts (i.e., alters) to make it usable. The brokerage characteristics of ego’s alters (i.e., secondhand brokerage) are decisive in that alters who are brokers are likely to have both valuable non-redundant information and the capability to convey it effectively. Prior work treating secondhand brokerage as a monolithic construct has yielded equivocal results; we reconcile these findings by decomposing it into distinct forms and matching each to the demands of a specific phase of the innovation process (i.e., idea generation, idea elaboration, idea championing, and idea implementation). We theorize that external secondhand brokerage facilitates idea generation, internal secondhand brokerage facilitates idea elaboration, internal alters’ network oscillation facilitates idea championing, and external alters’ network oscillation facilitates idea implementation, with ego’s knowledge integration capability, psychological ownership, organizational status, professional status, and tie strength serving as phase-specific and cross-phase boundary conditions. In doing so, we also challenge the prevailing view of brokers as default opportunists, specifying when cooperation, rather than opportunism, is the more rational strategy. By integrating the social network and innovation literatures, our framework clarifies how, when, and why the networks of others shape ego’s success across the innovation process.

title: Balancing Accommodation and Authority: Husbands’ Family Strategies in Transnational Marriages in North-East China
abstract: Abstract This article examines South–South transnational marriages between Vietnamese women and Chinese men in North-East China, focusing on the strategies husbands’ families employ to sustain these unions. Drawing on Bourdieu’s theory of family strategies and in-depth interviews with 26 households, it develops a “departure-restraint” framework to explain how receiving families respond to the persistent possibility of a bride’s marital exit. The findings show that these strategies rest on a balance between limited accommodation and selective authority: Vietnamese brides are granted a degree of autonomy in everyday matters, while husbands’ families retain control over major household decisions. The article further argues that the relatively narrow economic gap between sending and receiving regions in South–South marriages reshapes household dynamics in distinctive ways. Under conditions of limited economic opportunity, husbands’ families maintain marital stability not through outright domination, but through calibrated negotiations over everyday autonomy and household authority.

title: Leading innovation in the public sector: A review of existing quantitative research
abstract: Abstract Existing scholarship widely recognises the importance of leadership as an antecedent of public‐sector innovation. As empirical research on the relationship between public‐sector innovation and leadership grows, it is important to review this scholarship to identify progress, knowledge gaps, and opportunities for future research that will help the field mature. This systematic review focuses on articles that rely on quantitative methods ( N = 62). We examine how public‐sector innovation and leadership are conceptualised and measured, the data sources and research designs used to study the relationship between the two, and the findings that emerge from this growing field of study. We identify the important contributions of this body of work as well as its limitations and conclude by presenting an analytic framework to guide future research in this area. Points for practitioners The relationship between public‐sector innovation and leadership is multifaceted: leaders at various levels in public organisations can shape innovation in different ways. Leaders often shape public‐sector innovation by affecting employee behaviours and actions, but they can also do so by shaping organisational conditions. Leaders need to better understand these nuances to be more effective in advancing public‐sector innovation.

title: Accountability in Public Administration: A Review and Conceptual Integration
abstract: The idea of accountability has shaped public institutions across multiple countries, impacting how institutions are designed and governance is executed. In the public administration domain, it has been studied from a variety of disciplinary perspectives; however, the development of the field remains fragmented across many domains. The fragmentation is not just attributed to the domain of conception and its subsequent development but also the origins and adoption of accountability in practice. To understand this, we explore the intellectual structure of accountability literature. Using the PRISMA framework, we reviewed the literature in public administration and identified 81 peer-reviewed articles influencing the scholarship of the domain. Further, building on this literature, we conducted the citation and co-citation analysis for understanding the intellectual structure of the domain. The findings reveal the way in which managerial reforms, institutional norms, and democratic values have collectively influenced present-day accountability conception and theory.

title: A Model of Agency Behavior in Participatory Budgeting: A Resource Dependence Perspective
abstract: Abstract Based on resource dependence theory, this article theorizes why government agencies adopt citizen proposals in participatory budgeting. Agencies depend on the executive budget office and the legislature for budget approval, which makes them face uncertainty in securing budgets from these political principals. In this context, agencies can adopt citizen proposals to present their requests as reflecting citizen demands, thereby increasing the probability of approval. Building on this logic, this study argues that the greater the uncertainty agencies face in their dependencies on principals, the more likely they are to depend on proposals. This argument is tested using multilevel mixed-effects logistic regression based on citizen proposals (N = 3,609) submitted through Korea’s national participatory budgeting initiative from 2020 through 2023. The results show that agencies with less financial support from the legislature or those with smaller budgets are more likely to adopt proposals, as they face greater uncertainty due to unstable budgetary flows or fewer response options to manage resource instability. Agencies are also more likely to adopt proposals when they previously secured greater funding through proposal adoption, but this effect weakens for larger-budget agencies or those receiving greater legislative support. These findings emphasize the strategic nature of proposal adoption and the role of resource dependence in agency responses to proposals.
journal_name: Journal of Public Administration Research and Theory

title: How Artificial Intelligence Facilitates Collaborative Governance? Research on Mechanisms and Multi‐Dimensional Effects Based on Triple Entities
abstract: ABSTRACT Collaborative governance is becoming a practical imperative. At the same time, resolving complex public affairs could offer opportunities to overcome bottlenecks, while Artificial Intelligence (AI) could help. This study draws on polycentric governance theory and multilayer network theory to explain why collaborative governance could occur and how it could be influenced by AI, respectively. Mathematical deductions from both micro and macro perspectives are employed to reinforce this theoretical viewpoint. Using Chinese cities as a case study, the impact of AI on collaborative governance has been tested in practice, supported by benchmark regression and subsequent tests for endogeneity and robustness. Mechanism tests demonstrate AI's functions by advancing digital government, lifting corporate transparency, and improving public knowledge. Moreover, econometric evidence from difference‐in‐differences, threshold regressions, and spatial econometric models robustly addresses concerns about AI. This study offers a quantifiable multi‐stakeholder governance framework and actionable policy insights for China and the Global South.

title: Strategies for Public Administration Research: Insights From the Scholarship of Christopher Hood
abstract: ABSTRACT In an era of time constraints and publication pressures, scholars risk becoming entrenched in familiar approaches. Christopher Hood's public administration scholarship reminds us that excellence often arises from a broad exploration of ideas. This paper identifies three core elements of Hood's research practice. First, a deep skepticism toward dominant narratives, which often revealed hidden complexities. Second, careful selection of temporal frames: this often meant adopting remarkably long time‐horizons to reveal patterns in administrative and policy reform. Third, genuine interdisciplinarity. While firmly rooted in public administration, Hood drew on concepts, evidence, and methods from a wide range of disciplines. Analyzing how these three elements interacted in Hood's work, the paper reflects on how adopting aspects of his approach can help scholars produce work of lasting value. Hood's legacy is therefore not only a record of past achievement but also a practical guide to navigating the contemporary academic environment.

title: When tasks feel unjustified: effects of illegitimate tasks on public servants’ citizen-oriented boundary-spanning behaviours
So You Want to Build a New Policy Theory? Seven Lessons from the Origins of the Advocacy Coalition Framework
abstract: This paper examines the intellectual history of the Advocacy Coalition Framework (ACF) to draw lessons for building new policy theories. It draws seven lessons: (1) Know your dilemma – know it well; (2) Plot a path forward – be ambitious, even in the midst of uncertainty; (3) Expect obstacles and resistance to your ideas; (4) Think beyond a single article – build a research program; (5) Stay flexible – adapt and adjust to feedback and opportunities; (6) Build your network of supporters and collaborators; and (7) Offer methods. The article argues that the ACF’s origins provide insights into how enduring policy process theories emerge and develop.

title: Situating Policy Entrepreneurship in the Policy Sciences
abstract: This article argues that the policy entrepreneurship (PE) literature exemplifies and contributes to the new policy sciences, a development that seeks to recover Harold Lasswell’s vision of a contextualized, problem-oriented, multi-method discipline bridging basic and applied research. Using tools from the tradition of practical argumentation and formal debate, the article builds a prima facie case, tracing PE scholarship from collective action theory through Kingdon, Capano and colleagues, and Mintrom to show its emphasis on agency and context, and an extended case identifying two connected research practices: an empirical practice generating generalizable knowledge and a translational practice rendering it usable for practitioners.

title: Evolving Contexts and Diverging Strategies: Federalism and the Politics of Immigrant Welfare Exclusion in the US
abstract: ABSTRACT The intersection of immigration and welfare has taken a central stage in the politics of social policy and garnered increasing scholarly attention in welfare politics research. While prior research has examined how immigration affects welfare support and welfare generosity in the US, less is known about the determinants of immigrant‐related welfare policies. This paper investigates how state‐level policymakers shape immigrant welfare policies in response to changing social and economic state contexts across the U.S. states from 2000 to 2020. Using data from the Urban Institute's Welfare Rules Database, we create a policy index of welfare inclusion of immigrants to track policy variations across the American states from 2000 to 2020. We then employ panel data analyses to explore the determinants of state immigrant TANF policies. Our findings reveal diverging strategies of state legislatures: conservative state legislatures tend to be associated with more restrictive immigrant welfare policies than their liberal counterparts; moreover, conservative and liberal state legislatures respond to different types of state contexts in adjusting their immigrant welfare policies. Conservative state legislatures respond to rising poverty by enacting restrictive policies, whereas liberal state legislatures respond to declining levels of anti‐immigration sentiment by adopting more inclusive policies.

title: Do emotions affect political trust judgments?
abstract: Abstract Our study explores the nature of political trust ratings in surveys. We provide novel empirical evidence that, in addition to informed and rational reasoning, emotional states play a role in trust evaluations. Leveraging a U.S. sample, we employ a novel smartphone survey methodology that captures real-time voice responses during the trust evaluation process. We then classify these responses using sentiment analysis and speech emotion recognition techniques. Our findings demonstrate a substantial presence of negative sentiment when respondents evaluate political trust. Moreover, the sentiment conveyed in these responses significantly impacts trust scores, with positive sentiment bolstering trust and negative sentiment leading to its decline. A more granular examination of emotions reveals limited variation with only one notable effect where respondents employing ‘happy’ language and paralinguistics exhibited higher trust scores.

title: Overpromising populists? Why challenger parties make fewer, not more, promises than established parties
abstract: Abstract Many Western democracies have experienced an increase in the prevalence of parties that have never been in government. Since these so-called challenger parties are not held accountable to the same extent as established parties, there is a concern that they will simply churn out promises and fuel a process of rising political distrust. This paper explores the extent to which this image of overpromising populists is accurate. Instead of expecting more promises from challenger parties, the paper argues that we should find the opposite. Using a novel dataset of over one million content-coded quasi-sentences from election manifestos, the paper empirically demonstrates that challenger parties make substantially fewer election promises than established parties and that this is likely due to their lack of governmental experience. These results have important implications for research on the growing phenomenon of challenger parties and their distinct communication in electoral campaigns.

title: Where You Go, What You Do, Who You Are: Predictors of Political Science Job-Market Outcomes, 2023–2024
abstract: ABSTRACT Several studies have found that only graduates of top-ranked PhD programs have a reasonable chance of landing a tenure-track professorship. However, these findings are based on an examination of the backgrounds of current faculty at PhD-granting institutions, which leaves findings vulnerable to several types of bias. I address these limitations by analyzing the placements of political science PhD candidates during the 2023–2024 academic job-market cycle. In my analysis, departmental rank had virtually no impact on whether candidates found tenure-track assistant professorships, but it did predict the types of positions that candidates found. Other factors had stronger associations with placement outcomes. In particular, publishing solo-authored and coauthored articles, having underrepresented minority or female identity, and studying American politics were all associated with significantly higher placement rates.

title: Colonial Legacies and the Dynamics of Opposition: How Factional Power Shapes Cycles of Moderation and Radicalization
abstract: This article explains why opposition movements in the Middle East cycle between radicalization and moderation over long periods. I argue that twentieth-century colonization shaped both exclusionary state institutions and radical opposition groups, structuring how later episodes of inclusion and exclusion influenced movement strategies. The paper explains subsequent oscillations through a single core mechanism: shifting factional balances of power. State inclusion and exclusion redistribute influence between moderates and radicals, generating shifts between confrontation and accommodation. I develop and evaluate the theory through longitudinal process tracing of the Muslim Brothers in Egypt and the Iraqi Communist Party, supplemented by shadow cases illustrating colonial presence (Palestine) and absence (Turkey), using evidence from 96 semistructured interviews, archival materials, and participant observation conducted between 2021 and 2024 in Palestine, Iraq, and Turkey. By foregrounding temporality and factional dynamics, the article reframes debates on Islamist moderation and authoritarian durability as path-dependent and iterative processes rather than linear transformations.

title: Geopolitics in court: judicial epistemology versus hybrid war
Revisiting the SciPop Scale: Measurement alignment, scoring rules, and cross‐context comparability
abstract: Abstract Science‐related populism—populist attitudes toward scientific authority—has attracted growing scholarly attention. Although the SciPop Scale measures this construct, its cross‐national psychometric properties remain underexamined. Using data from the Trust in Science and Science‐Related Populism project ( N = 69,341; 68 countries/regions) and the Swiss Science Barometer ( N = 1124), we evaluate factor structure and reliability, test multigroup invariance, apply alignment for approximate invariance, and compare scoring philosophies (Bollen vs. Goertz approach) on criterion validity. We further employ multidimensional item response theory models to provide complementary item‐level diagnostics, including discrimination, threshold, item information, and differential item functioning. Results show that reliability is high and a four‐factor model fits most broadly. Full measurement invariance holds across sex, age, education, residence, political orientation, and religiosity; partial invariance appears across regions, economic development, cultural values, and regime types. Cross‐national comparability is limited but improves via measurement alignment. Different scoring methods identify different weakest dimensions. For criterion validity, Bollen‐based aligned scores consistently outperform the Goertz approach, yielding higher explanatory power in cross‐national and cross‐group analyses. Finally, we provide guidelines for researchers using the SciPop Scale and future directions for measuring science‐related populism.

title: National security versus human security: Intrastate conflict and states’ rhetoric on conventional arms control in the United Nations general assembly
The Strategic Use of Foreign Events in Parliamentary Debate Issue Competition: Danish and Norwegian Responses to October 7
abstract: ABSTRACT The parliamentary floor represents an important arena for political debate. Recent research shows that politicians use foreign events strategically through parliamentary speeches to achieve electoral success. However, it is not clear how politicians do so to increase attention to their preferred issues. This article argues that by combining key insights from issue competition and legislative debate theory, we can see how issue ownership and the opposition's greater freedom to focus on certain issues interact to shape responses to foreign events. This is demonstrated through a parliamentary speech attention framework tested on Danish and Norwegian responses to the October 7 attacks in Israel. Issue ownership was more strongly associated with attention responses for opposition than government parties, with Denmark driving multiculturalism responses and Norway driving immigration responses. The article shows how foreign events can become assets for issue‐owning opposition parties and thus advances our understanding of issue competition in parliamentary debates.

title: Beliefs and Racial Identity Norms among Black Americans: An Examination of How Black Americans Understand Racism
Electoral results affect beliefs about the past: Evidence from Chile
abstract: Can electoral outcomes shape voters' perceptions of the past? We argue that electoral outcomes provide informational cues that prompt voters to reinterpret prior conditions, shifting the benchmarks on which accountability rests. We focus on perceptions of crime, a valence issue that voters likely take into account when choosing any candidate. We propose that perceptions of crime change immediately after an election, as voters reinterpret prior conditions through the lens of the relevance of crime in the winning candidate's platform. We leverage the timing of opinion surveys in Chile on public security to compare respondents interviewed just before and just after local elections, across municipalities where a right-wing mayor narrowly won versus narrowly lost. We show that shortly after a local right-wing candidate wins by a small margin, respondents report that their neighborhood, state, and country are less safe than those who answered the same survey a few days before the election. Victimization, which is unlikely to be misremembered, does not vary across groups of respondents. The findings show that this shift in perceptions directly affects electoral accountability: When political outcomes shape beliefs about past performance, accountability itself becomes endogenous to electoral results.

title: Fairness Across the World
abstract: Abstract This paper provides the first comprehensive global evidence on people’s fairness and efficiency preferences, beliefs about the sources of inequality and the efficiency cost of redistribution, and policy attitudes toward redistribution. Using a globally harmonized consequential experiment with more than 65,000 individuals across 60 countries, we show that the source of inequality plays a substantially larger role for inequality acceptance than the efficiency cost of redistribution. At the global level, implemented inequality increases by 85 percent when inequality is caused by merit rather than luck, compared to a 14 percent increase when redistribution entails a 50 percent efficiency cost. We document substantial heterogeneity in fairness views and beliefs both within and across societies. The meritocratic fairness view is most prominent in many richer Western societies, while libertarian and egalitarian fairness views are widespread in many other parts of the world. Globally, people are more likely to believe that inequality reflects luck rather than merit, while beliefs in large efficiency costs of redistribution are relatively weak. Fairness preferences and beliefs are strongly associated with redistribution attitudes and actual redistribution through taxes and transfers across countries. Our findings illustrate how the interaction between fairness views and beliefs may shape redistribution across societies, highlighting the importance of jointly understanding preferences and beliefs in the political economy of redistribution.

title: The economics of abduction marriage: Evidence from Ethiopia
The Fall of Constantinople and the Rise of the West,
abstract: Abstract The Renaissance era in Western Europe was marked by a flourishing of economic and cultural life that gave rise to numerous discoveries and inventions. This paper studies the role played by Greek knowledge in this process. Using a newly constructed dataset on Greek migrants in Europe after the fall of Constantinople in 1453, I show that a Greek presence in the second half of the fifteenth century increased city growth in the sixteenth century. In terms of mechanisms, I find that a Greek presence increased the available knowledge stock in astronomy, mathematics, medicine, and humanistic subjects – fields in which ancient Greek and Byzantine knowledge was especially advanced. Finally, I document an increase in upper-tail human capital and inventions in these cities. My findings thus show the important role played by Greek migrants in disseminating knowledge and the positive impact that Greek knowledge exerted on city growth in the early modern period.
journal_name: Journal of the European Economic Association

title: Exercise or Extra Fries? Behavioral Drivers of Obesity Over the Life Cycle,
abstract: Abstract As America faces an obesity epidemic and its economic consequences, the factors driving weight variation across the U.S. population remain unclear, especially since these differences extend well beyond commonly studied channels like income or education. We leverage a unique thirty-year panel of U.S. registered nurses to examine the changes in body mass index (BMI) with age, the impact of lifestyle choices on body weight in adulthood, and the role of inherited metabolic traits and childhood preference formation. Our empirical findings reveal that among individuals who enter adulthood with a healthy body mass, those in the top diet quality or exercise deciles at age thirty are roughly 50% more likely to maintain a healthy BMI and avoid morbidities three decades later, compared to those in the bottom deciles. To better understand the drivers of weight gain, we propose a novel structural framework of endogenous BMI evolution where initial heterogeneity is amplified by behaviors to explain much of the observed divergence in weight. Counterfactual experiments using the model indicate that initial conditions, such as fixed metabolic types, account for at least one-third of the variance in weight at older ages. While course correction through behaviors can only partially compensate for poor initial conditions at the onset of adulthood, we find that promoting healthy behaviors in adults can reduce total health care expenses by at least 8% annually.
journal_name: Journal of the European Economic Association

title: Contingent Trade Agreements: Linking Free Trade and Environmental Conservation
abstract: Abstract There appears to be a tension between trade proponents and environmental activists. This paper shows, however, how Contingent Trade Agreements (CTAs) can motivate conservation. I first analyse a standard trade model where trade-specific investments (e.g., deforestation) cause environmental damage and traditional trade agreements, including free trade, increase deforestation. Next, I define and analyse CTAs, where default tariffs vary with production capacity (e.g., forest cover). In equilibrium, countries conserve to maintain favourable terms of trade. The quantitative model shows that trade liberalisation can dramatically expand Brazil’s agricultural area, but this expansion is avoidable if the EU or US offers a CTA.

title: Helping in the Workplace: The Role of Leadership Relative to Employee Personality and Preferences
abstract: Abstract Helping as an important form of social support is an integral part of a firm’s workplace culture. Using matched employer-employee panel data that are representative of larger, private-sector firms in Germany, we document significant between-firm variation in helping in the workplace. Helping is positively correlated with better organizational outcomes for both employees and firms. Differences in a firm’s quality of leadership together with employees’ level of general trust play a key role in explaining firm-level differences in helping. Our results corroborate the importance of both leadership and workforce characteristics for the manifestation of supportive workplace cultures.

title: Publicly funded R&D networks, knowledge spillovers and innovation performance: Evidence from Norway
abstract: Many countries provide public policy support for R&D networks. In publicly funded R&D consortia, firms collaborate with each other and with public scientific institutions to carry out joint innovation projects. The idea behind these policy schemes is that collaborative innovation enables firms to benefit from knowledge spillovers within R&D networks. Surprisingly, however, there is no empirical research showing that spillover effects actually exist in publicly funded R&D consortia. This paper seeks to investigate the extent and sources of knowledge spillovers in R&D networks and to distinguish them from other drivers of additionality generated by collaborative innovation policy programs. Our empirical analysis focuses on Norway and encompasses the entire population of firms supported by R&D policy programs over the period 2002–2022, comprising approximately 15500 collaborative projects. Based on the information on each project, we construct networks of innovators and new R&D spillover pool variables. We use a spatial autoregressive econometric approach and estimate a network regression estimator that endogenizes peer effects related to knowledge spillovers. The econometric results show that the knowledge spillovers arising from publicly funded R&D networks are positive. We also find that the spillover effects resulting from Research Council programs are much stronger than those of tax incentives, and that the spillover effects are much stronger for collaborations between firms operating in different industries than for within-industry collaborations.

title: Determinants of gender discrimination by teachers: Evidence from an online experiment
abstract: This paper examines whether teachers' gender biases stem from discrimination, and focuses on two of its potential drivers: gender preferences and beliefs. In an online experiment, 1,840 teachers evaluated fictitious transcripts with randomized gender information. Preferences were measured via dictator games, and beliefs through an Implicit Association Test. While teachers showed no gender preferences, they did hold gender beliefs. Analyzing 19,000 transcript evaluations, we find no evidence of gender-based discrimination. Our findings suggest that simply disclosing a student's gender does not trigger discrimination, implying that such behaviours are more likely to emerge during direct student-teacher interactions.

title: Heterogeneous Markups Cyclicality and Monetary Policy
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper studies aggregate markup cyclicality through firm‐level heterogeneity, reallocation, and aggregation. Using the U.S. firm data for 1990–2016, we find that markups are procyclical for young firms and countercyclical for older firms following monetary policy shocks. Economic activity also reallocates modestly toward young firms. As the firm population ages, the aggregate markup response shifts from acyclical or mildly procyclical to countercyclical. These findings help reconcile conflicting evidence on markup cyclicality and imply that firm demographics shape monetary‐policy transmission and the roles of demand and supply shocks in business cycles.

title: Discussion of “The Dynamics of Gender Norms and Fertility Decline”
abstract: ABSTRACT This discussion develops a parsimonious framework for norm dynamics. The interaction between social pressure to conform and older generations attachment to past practices generates intergenerational inertia and a persistent wedge between behavior and the frictionless optimum. I characterize the determinants of this wedge and highlight the role of demographic transition. I illustrate the framework's broader applicability to scientific paradigms and policy reform.

title: Demand Uncertainty, Selection, and Trade
Human rights and populist wrongs: how populist incumbents threaten democracy, 1990–2023
Harmful misinformation as a quantifiable risk in health content: WHO-aligned risk assessment framework for flagging potential harms and informing policy safeguards
abstract: Health misinformation undermines public decision-making, yet prevailing responses lean heavily on binary fact-checking that misses gradations of misleadingness and, crucially, the potential of downstream harms. This article presents the Misinformation Risk Assessment Model (MisRAM), a WHO-aligned framework that conceptualizes misinformation as a quantifiable risk in content and mediating systems, rather than a present/absent defect. Drawing on health-risk research traditions, MisRAM guides the identification and treatment of misinformation risk factors as informational hazards, whose risk contribution varies with intrinsic severity, cumulative load, exposure conditions, and recipient susceptibility. It maps four evaluative dimensions: inaccuracy, incompleteness, deceptiveness, and harm potential, with the latter requiring the highest protection and prioritized as an independent escalation trigger. This facilitates stratification into very-low through to very-high risk of misinforming recipients in ways that may lead to harmful outcomes, and is designed for both domain-led safety evaluation benchmarking and high-throughput automated detection. To inform risk thresholds and calibrated mitigation, the Severity of Potential Harmful Outcomes from Misinformation (SoPHO-M) Scale is introduced as a five-level taxonomy for classifying plausible harm severity (from negligible to fatal). The framework provides a basis for policy-relevant systemic risk assessments, informing governance protocols across digital services and AI systems, as well as regulatory compliance. Tiered safeguards are proposed for different misinformation risk levels in proportion to the likelihood and severity of their effects, ranging from positive incentivization and visibility support of low-risk, well-contextualized content, through friction and conditional visibility for moderate-risk content, to red-line protective controls at very-high risk where life-threatening harms are plausible. By moving beyond truth judgements towards harm-oriented risk estimation, MisRAM provides a roadmap for assessment-tool development and proportionate safeguard operationalization, with potential for extension to other high-stakes domains. The framework offers guidance to decision-makers on preventing serious harm without disproportionately burdening freedom of expression or information access across mediated systems.

title: More Clickbait, But Fewer Shares? Unpacking the Relationship Between Multimodal Sensationalism and Online User Engagement
abstract: This study examined multimodal sensationalism by analyzing how textual and visual sensationalist features embedded in video headlines and thumbnails relate to user engagement. Using a hybrid human-large language model content analysis, we identified 15 sensationalist features across 1,100 trending videos from Douyin. The results show that legacy news outlets used fewer textual sensationalist elements, particularly Internet slang, hashtags, and positive emotions, than non-journalistic producers. Additionally, visual sensationalist features exhibited an inverted U-shaped relationship with user engagement. These findings advance understanding of the nonlinear and modality-specific effects of sensationalism and offer practical insights into the optimal use of multimodal sensationalism on social media.

title: Chinese Intellectual Influencers and the Construction of Algorithmized Nationalism: The Case of Jinri Toutiao
abstract: This study examines how intellectual influencers (wanghong zhishifenzi) contribute to ‘algorithmized nationalism’ on Chinese digital platforms. Through an analysis of 14 high-traffic intellectual accounts and their high-performing videos in Jinri Toutiao (one of China’s largest digital platforms), we argue that these figures actively construct a type of nationalism that is both vocally aggressive and politically conservative, tailored to the platform’s algorithmic recommendation systems. By managing personas, mobilizing emotions, and embellishing facts, they cater to popular sentiment while accruing personal influence and amplifying state-aligned narratives. Their practices signal a new mode of nationalist discourse production, where platform logic, state power, and intellectual performance converge. This dynamic reshapes both Chinese nationalism and the adapted role of intellectuals, who now negotiate influence within algorithmically mediated spaces of discourse.

title: Power distance orientation and the attitudinal mechanisms linking servant leadership to innovative work behaviour among Vietnamese public servants
abstract: Abstract The focus on fostering innovative work behaviour among public servants in Vietnam reflects a strategic effort to enhance public service delivery and citizen satisfaction. However, empirical insights into how to effectively motivate such behaviours remain scarce. This paper adopts a social cognitive theoretical lens to propose a conceptual framework linking supervisors’ servant leadership to employees’ affective commitment and their engagement in innovative work behaviour. The study draws on survey data from 244 public servants across multiple city government agencies in Vietnam to examine power distance orientation as a cultural boundary condition shaping employees’ affective responses to servant leadership and the broader association with innovative work behaviour. Findings indicate that power distance orientation weakens the positive relationship between servant leadership and affective commitment, whereas the direct relationship between servant leadership and innovative work behaviour remains stable across levels of power distance orientation. The study contributes to public administration and leadership research by demonstrating that cultural contingency may operate more strongly for employees’ affective evaluation of leadership behaviours than for behavioural enactment within reform‐oriented public sector settings. Managerial implications are discussed for public sector leaders operating across culturally diverse environments. Points for practitioners Leadership strategies may not be universally effective. Their impact depends on employees’ expectations about authority, particularly power distance orientation, which shapes how supportive leadership behaviours are interpreted. In teams receptive to participatory leadership, managers can stimulate innovation by encouraging staff input, consultation, and shared problem‐solving. In strongly hierarchical settings, combining clear authority with visible concern for staff welfare may build commitment without disrupting organisational norms. Innovation initiatives are more likely to succeed when explicitly linked to organisational priorities and endorsed by senior leaders, reducing perceived risks for employees. Public agencies can use staff surveys to assess leadership climate and employee willingness to propose improvements, enabling targeted interventions.

title: Ethical complexity and service delivery in remote Indigenous communities
abstract: Abstract The scale and scope of disadvantage in remote Indigenous communities mean that ethical dilemmas are day‐to‐day realities for practitioners. Persistent hardship, disadvantage, and discrimination—amid omnipresent policy initiatives aimed at combating them—exacerbate these dilemmas and are a perennial source of workplace tension. Frequently, these tensions escalate to the point of unworkability among those tasked with collaborating in the interests of the community. Under the guise of accountability or advocacy of justice, and backed by the (perceived) power of the state, conflict among practitioners often leads to factionalism and standoffs and can escalate to bullying, harassment, violence, and lawsuits. This article proposes a simple heuristic for ethical deliberation among those working in remote Indigenous community governance. Drawing on deontological and consequentialist ethics, as well as the policy literature, it provides a framework to structure conversations on ethics in decision‐making. Points for practitioners The persistence, scale, and scope of hardship in remote Indigenous communities create ongoing ethical dilemmas for practitioners. Ethical disagreements among staff tasked with alleviating Indigenous disadvantage both in government and government‐funded organisations often escalate to conflict, unworkable relationships among stakeholders, staff turnover, loss of corporate memory, poor policy implementation, and legal battles. This contributes to the ineffective and counterproductive use of public and community resources. Government and non‐government organisations need to acknowledge the ethical complexities and prepare staff for managing them through mechanisms for deliberative, ethical decision‐making as well as avenues for providing feedback on adverse consequences of policy decisions. When ethical disagreements arise, staff should be encouraged to consider whether actions align with existing professional or organisational frameworks (such as Codes of Conduct) and the likely consequences based on corporate memory and the existing evidence base. Where government or corporate directives are likely to breach professional ethics or have harmful consequences, staff should be empowered to provide this feedback.

title: Let the Machine Impose the Fine! Algorithmic Discretion with Negative Outcomes. Experimental Evidence from Germany
Public–private partnership adoption in punctuated policy environments: a dynamic qualitative comparative analysis
abstract: As fiscal and regulatory constraints intensify, governments are reassessing public–private partnerships (PPPs), raising the question of how governments adjust their strategies across changing policy environments. Our study develops a dynamic fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis framework integrating organizational institutionalism and resource dependence theory to examine how configurations underlying PPP adoption evolve over time. Using panel data from 281 Chinese cities, we identify how configurations associated with PPP adoption are reconfigured across two policy environments. Under a supportive policy environment from 2015 to 2017, PPP adoption is associated primarily with legitimacy seeking and resource mobilization. Under a restrictive policy environment from 2018 to 2020, adoption persists through institutional inertia and pressures to sustain economic performance. Policy signals remain involved in several high-adoption configurations across policy environments. In contrast, resource conditions become less consistently involved under the restrictive policy environment: the social participant condition, leader career experience, and government fiscal resources shift from joint presence in the supportive policy environment to differentiated roles in the restrictive policy environment. By demonstrating how institutional pressures and resource conditions are reweighted following a critical juncture, our study refines institutional and resource-based explanations of PPP adoption and offers insights for governments responding to changing policy environments.

title: Unlocking the transformative potential of design: reflections from practice on navigating barriers to designing for societal transformation
abstract: Design is increasingly recognized as a promising approach to foster societal transformation, yet its transformative potential is rarely realized. Empirical guidance on how to unlock this potential remains limited. To address this gap, we first conceptualize design for societal transformation as operating across three levels of design activity – i.e. design within context, designing context, and design of context – in mutually reinforcing ways to enable broad, deep, and lasting change. Using this lens, we then examine three cases from our own design practice to identify (1) key barriers constraining design’s transformative potential, and (2) main strategies that can be employed to navigate them. Our analysis reveals that barriers interrelate across the three levels of design activity, and that design’s inherent transformative qualities can be leveraged to navigate them. Together, these insights suggest that design can function as a mode of transformative governance that operates through a small wins logic.

title: Systemic Imbalances in Integrity Management Systems: A Meso‐Level Framework From Four Corruption Scandals
abstract: ABSTRACT Integrity management systems (IMSs) are increasingly promoted to embed ethical conduct, mitigate corruption risks, and strengthen organizational accountability. Yet empirical evidence on their effectiveness remains sparse and contradictory, offering little insight into how these systems operate in practice and why they often fail in heavily formalized organizational settings. This paper addresses that gap by developing a meso‐level framework for diagnosing systemic imbalances in IMSs. Drawing on systems theory and management control literature, we conceptualize IMSs as an integrity management package structured through four levers: belief, boundary, diagnostic, and interactive systems of control. We deploy this framework through an explanatory, multi‐case design spanning four major corruption scandals in infrastructure, defense, healthcare, and banking in the UK, Italy, Greece, and the Nordic–Baltic region, drawing on a triangulated dataset built through systematic web scraping. The cross‐case analysis shows that integrity failures are not explained simply by the absence of formal controls, but by recurring imbalances among control levers. Organizations tend to privilege boundary and diagnostic systems, such as rules, procedures, monitoring, and performance metrics, while under‐investing in belief and interactive systems that should enable ethical culture, dialogue, challenge, and learning. We theorize this imbalance as a compliance façade: formally robust but weakly embedded in organizational practice. The paper thereby reframes the compliance versus values debate in ethics scholarship, offering the first empirically grounded, cross‐sectoral model of how integrity is embedded, sustained, and undermined in organizations, with implications for redesigning IMSs across public, private, and hybrid settings.

title: Formulating a legislative design philosophy for adaptive governance: marine spatial planning as a case study
Many shades of climate skepticism: Exploring climate change attitudes among local political elites in Germany
abstract: Abstract Climate change – and skepticism toward it – is increasingly present not only among far-right parties but also across the political spectrum in more nuanced forms. This article examines the diverse climate attitudes of local political elites, who play a key role in the implementation of climate policy. We develop an analytical framework to assess varying degrees of climate skepticism, with particular attention to a broader ‘gray zone’ of attitudes that combine acceptance of anthropogenic climate change with doubts about its implications, responsibilities, or policy responses. We empirically examine the views of municipal council members in Saxony and Thuringia – two eastern German states characterized by salient climate and energy policy conflicts and ideologically competitive party systems. Using original web survey data, our findings reveal a wide spectrum of partial climate skepticism extending beyond the Alternative for Germany (AfD) and into parts of the political mainstream. Moreover, we identify substantial variation across different dimensions of climate skepticism as well as significant intra-party heterogeneity. Overall, parties are not monolithic actors on climate-related attitudes but internally diverse organizations in which multiple positions coexist. Understanding these local-level attitudes is crucial for assessing the political feasibility of climate policy implementation. By mapping the ‘gray zone’ of climate skepticism among local political elites, this study contributes to a more fine-grained understanding of climate attitudes within and across party lines.

title: Get Out the Volunteer: Encouraging Diverse Political Party Activism
abstract: Abstract Political parties in advanced democracies face a dual challenge: fewer citizens are willing to volunteer, and those who remain active are disproportionately older and male. This is troubling given the central role that volunteers play in campaigns and party processes. Whether party leaders can recruit a larger and more diverse activist base remains an open question. We partnered with a major party in the Netherlands and conducted two field experiments before the 2021 general and 2022 municipal elections, targeting over 35,000 party members. The party randomized whether members received a personal call, an email or both. Results show that calls—where members could voice their opinions—increased volunteer sign-up rates (83% in Study 1 and 361% in Study 2), especially among younger members. By contrast, emails had no effect. These findings clarify mixed evidence in the literature, suggesting that voice opportunities are key to expanding and diversifying the activist base.
