Teacher Effects on Students’ Socio-Emotional Skills and Young Adult Outcomes
abstract: Abstract Using rich cohort data in the United Kingdom, I estimate teacher value-added on students’ test scores and socio-emotional skills in primary school. I find that teachers play a crucial role in both the development of students’ test scores and socio-emotional skills. Conditional on teacher effects on students’ test scores, the impact of teachers on students’ socio-emotional skills persists over time and extends into early adulthood. These teacher effects predict various economic and social outcomes measured at ages 18-20, including university attendance, labour market outcomes, risky health behaviours, pro-social activities, and overall well-being.

title: Discussion of “Does Digitalization Widen Labor Income Inequality?”
Lessons learned from the COVID-19 pandemic: The role of self-control, risk aversion, and fear of infection in shaping compliance with preventive measures
abstract: Abstract This paper refers to interview data collected in six municipalities in the Lecce province of southern Italy, across three waves: 2020, 2021, and 2022. The principal aim of the research was to determine whether compliance with four government-recommended non-pharmaceutical measures to prevent the spread of COVID-19 — indoor and outdoor mask use, and indoor and outdoor physical distancing — differed over the years and, if so, whether these differences were influenced by personal characteristics. Specifically, we focused on the psychological features of self-control, risk aversion, and fear of contracting COVID-19 and their relationships with these four measures. The results suggest that virus mortality, the regulations in force, and experience of the pandemic affected compliance with certain preventive measures across all waves. With regard to psychological features, the three factors of interest were found to predict preferences for, and substitutions across, the measures, with effects that varied across the waves.

title: Do Emotional Ads Persuade? Evidence from Real-Time Campaign Advertising Experiments
abstract: We evaluate whether campaign advertisements that generate larger emotional reactions also generate larger persuasive effects in contemporary elections. We analyze 29 weeks of experiments conducted during the 2016 U.S. presidential campaign, in which 48 authentic campaign ads were tested in real time, often within days of their debut. The ads and a placebo were randomly assigned to approximately 28,000 subjects. We find that campaign ads reliably move emotions, albeit in largely partisan ways, with comparatively muted reactions among independents. Critically, however, these emotional reactions do not predict the magnitude of an ad’s effect on candidate favorability, vote intention, policy preferences, or turnout intention. Our results cast doubt on emotion-based accounts of advertising persuasion in polarized elections and caution practitioners against using self-reported emotional reactions as a measure of message effectiveness.

title: Looking good, fitting in: co-trajectories of appearance- and friendship-related identity distress and positive online self-presentation in adolescence
Loneliness and the local news environment
Does AI erode street-level discretion? A mixed-methods study on automated decision-making in China's tax authorities
Still Women Help Women? Gender Congruence, Social Stereotypes, and Street-Level Discretionary Decision-Making
abstract: How female street-level bureaucrats navigate decisions involving socially stigmatized female clients lies at the intersection of a theoretical debate between representative bureaucracy and street-level stereotyping research. It also reflects a practical dilemma stemming from regulatory gaps in China’s online-to-offline (O2O) massage apps that compel frontline workers to adjudicate ambiguous disputes involving suspected sexual assault or sex work. Using a within-subject vignette experiment with 679 Chinese bureaucrats, this study examines how gender congruence and social stereotypes interact to shape discretionary decisions in high-discretion contexts. Findings reveal that gender congruence outweighs social stereotypes in shaping female bureaucrats’ decisions regarding stigmatized female massage therapists, suggesting that shared demographic traits foster supportive interactions (representation) even as they are counteracted by stigmatizing stereotypes (discrimination). These results highlight the role of individual-level discretion in protecting vulnerable groups and promoting social equity within regulatory gray areas, underscoring the need for more representative, socioculturally aware street-level bureaucracies.

title: Institutional Conversion and Digital Transformation in Local Governments: A Longitudinal Analysis of Trajectories
abstract: Abstract This article asks a central question in digital government research: why do local governments operating under similar institutional conditions follow sharply different digital transformation trajectories over time? Drawing on theories of gradual institutional change, the study conceptualizes digital transformation not as a discrete adoption outcome, but as a process of institutional conversion through which technological capacity is translated into sustained digital service provision. Information governance is theorized as the key conditioning mechanism linking technological resources to durable organizational outcomes. The analysis combines longitudinal panel models, fixed-effects estimators, and trajectory-based clustering using a panel of all Brazilian municipalities (MUNIC/IBGE; N = 5,569) across seven waves between 2004 and 2024. Results show that increases in technological capacity are associated with subsequent gains in digital services, but these effects are gradual and conditional. Information governance significantly shapes how municipalities mobilize and stabilize technological resources over time, while interaction models reveal non-linear and diminishing returns consistent with institutional coordination limits. Trajectory analyses identify four distinct patterns of digital transformation, ranging from ‘institutionalized pioneers’ to ‘persistent stagnation’, demonstrating that digital development unfolds through path-dependent and institutionally anchored trajectories rather than through simple convergence. The article contributes to public administration research in three ways: provides rare longitudinal evidence on local digital transformation over two decades; integrates institutional change theory into digital government research by conceptualizing governance as a mechanism of institutional conversion; and advances a trajectory-based explanation of digital transformation that shifts attention from episodic technological adoption to cumulative institutional processes shaping long-run administrative performance.
journal_name: Journal of Public Administration Research and Theory

title: How Were Governance Pathways Formed for Public Service Co‐Production? A Contingency Perspective
abstract: ABSTRACT This study addresses the under‐theorized formation of specific co‐production arrangements by exploring governance pathway formation. Using 76 community regeneration projects in Shanghai, we identify a parsimonious two‐level typology: State‐led co‐production (comprising sub‐type A: state as operator and sub‐type B: non‐state as operator ) and Citizen‐led co‐production (comprising sub‐type C: volunteers as operator and sub‐type D: users as operator ). Findings reveal pathway emergence is contingent upon configurations of providers' capabilities, citizen empowerment, political leadership, and public service characteristics, reflecting logics associated with Neo‐Weberian State, New Public Management, and New Public Governance paradigms. The study shifts focus from static lists to dynamic governance pathways by proposing a configurational contingency framework that explains how governance logics are activated by specific contextual conditions.

title: Restoring the Deformed Administrative State? Bureaucratic Repair After Illiberal Rule
abstract: ABSTRACT While scholarship has documented how populist and authoritarian‐leaning executives deform bureaucratic institutions, post‐illiberal reconstruction has only begun to receive attention. This paper develops an exploratory framework distinguishing four repair strategies (neutralizing, rectifying, balancing, and democratic hardening) and two repair modes (formal‐institutional and normative‐capacity repair). Applying the heuristic to Poland, Brazil, and Hungary, we posit that the selection and limits of repair strategies follow the gap between the depth of illiberal entrenchment and the legal‐political capacity of successor governments to overcome veto players and enact rectifying reforms. Within the periods observed, formal‐institutional repair has outpaced the reconstruction of professional norms, expertise, and trust, and repair has produced layered administrative orders in which illiberal‐era instruments partly persist and thus remain available to future governments. Administrative repair is thus structurally asymmetric. Democratic successors can rebuild the administrative state, but they are unlikely to restore it to the status quo ante.

title: The social policy of a shortsighted state: digitalization and informality in Argentina during the pandemic
abstract: Governments worldwide are increasingly adopting digital technologies to address social problems. This emerging ‘dataist state’ relies on administrative and statistical data grounded in law enforcement and compliance. Yet in societies characterized by high levels of informality, these conditions cannot be assumed. This article asks how the ‘dataist state’ is reconfigured when citizens and firms evade records or provide incomplete, scarce, or misrepresented information, and to what extent digitalization modifies or reproduces the limitations of weak states. We address these questions through an analysis of the Argentine government’s response during the COVID-19 crisis, focusing on two major social policies: one targeting registered firms and workers, and another aimed at households dependent on informal labor. Drawing on qualitative fieldwork conducted during and after the pandemic with public officials and policy recipients, the article examines both top-down and bottom-up dynamics. While state actors adhered to an ‘ideology of data solutionism,’ prioritizing technically feasible interventions despite limited data quality, citizens developed practices to adapt to and contest data systems – often circumventing automated decision-making. The findings show that digitalization expanded access to social assistance while simultaneously reproducing and normalizing longstanding patterns of informality and weak regulatory enforcement.

Balancing Particularism and Universalism in Welfare Policy: Insights From China's Hukou Reform
abstract: ABSTRACT Welfare policies often combine particularistic and universalistic elements, yet we know less about how shifts in this balance shape public attitudes toward vulnerable low‐status groups. This article develops a three‐dimensional framework for analyzing welfare policy, distinguishing among welfare scope, welfare benefits, and inclusion criteria. We argue that public attitudes toward lower‐status groups are shaped by the combined signal about the welfare deservingness hierarchy generated by the configuration of particularistic and universalistic elements across these dimensions. Because policy design packages convey a broader normative stance about who belongs and who deserves, they can influence perceptions of groups that are not directly targeted by a policy change, lowering or raising their perceived deservingness. Using difference‐in‐differences and regression discontinuity methods, we analyze Weibo posts during China's two‐round hukou reform. We find that shifts toward more particularistic policy configurations lead to more negative attitudes toward low‐skilled migrant workers, whereas shifts toward more universalistic configurations yield more positive attitudes. Subgroup analyses yield suggestive patterns across local economic contexts and individual characteristics. These findings have broader implications for research on welfare policy systems and for reform efforts regarding social integration.

Narratives as Separating Equilibria: On the Origins of the Ukraine War
abstract: NATO enlargement and Russian occupation of Crimea marked crucial turning points in the process that eventually resulted in the Ukraine war. According to one narrative, that Russian move was part of a plan to re-establish dominion over Eastern Europe. According to a rival view, it was an attempt to counter a U.S. plan to subjugate Russia. This paper scrutinizes the logical requirements of those narratives in a multi-stage game of incomplete information that produces equilibrium play such that first NATO is enlarged and then Russia attacks Ukraine. The two competing narratives correspond to two different separating equilibria. Conditions for their existence inform about the consistency and plausibility of the associated narratives.

Working hard to belong: Meritocratic ideology and deportation sentiments among Latino and Asian Americans
abstract: Abstract Why do some Latino and Asian Americans support conservative policies that may discriminate against them? Elaborating on system justification theory, we argue that ideologies such as meritocracy perpetuate the status quo by placating marginalized groups and assuaging their emotional concerns regarding their unfair treatment. This research examined the extent to which endorsing meritocratic ideology is associated with deportation policy attitudes and the degree of emotional concern about deportation among Latino and Asian Americans. Using data from the 2024 and 2020 Collaborative Multiracial Post‐Election Surveys, we find that higher meritocratic ideology predicted greater support for deportation policies and lower emotional concern about deportation for Latino and Asian Americans. This research demonstrates that Latino and Asian Americans who have ingrained the ethos of meritocracy are more likely to support conservative policies and develop sentiments that work against the interests of their communities.

More on onetary Economics
abstract: Abstract Does the cashless limit of the monetary equilibrium converge to the non-monetary equilibrium? We revisit the question in the context of Menzio and Spinella (2025), a model in which the financial market where households lend savings and firms borrow capital is subject to frictions. The fraction of households that do not meet any firms determines money demand. The fractions of households that meet one or multiple firms determine the extent of competition, and the sensitivity of real rates to inflation. The cashless limit of the monetary equilibrium converges to the non-monetary equilibrium depending on whether the financial market becomes perfectly competitive, which, in turn, depends on the exact specification of frictions.

title: Original sin redux: A model-based evaluation
A new horizon? The effect of a national education reform on student achievement and the academic environment
abstract: This study analyzes the effects of a nationwide school reform in Israel on student achievement and the school learning environment. The New Horizon reform, initiated by the Ministry of Education, was gradually implemented in elementary schools beginning in 2008. It increased the time teachers spend in school, introduced small-group learning, raised teachers’ and principals’ salaries, and established higher requirements and incentives for professional development. Using a staggered difference-in-differences approach, we evaluate the reform’s effects on student achievement and the school learning environment. We find that in the four years following implementation, math and English test scores improved alongside various aspects of the learning environment. We offer suggestive evidence that the math gains are driven by small-group learning targeting lower-achieving students, while English gains are consistent with improved net working conditions for English teachers.

title: School preferences across countries and social groups: a factorial survey experiment in the United States, Germany and Italy
Review of “Life After Epidemics: Ebola Survivors and the Social Dimensions of Recovery”
Where’s the fun in that? On thrill and liability in extreme sports
abstract: Abstract Extreme sports like solo rock climbing and BASE jumping are experiencing a boom in popularity, yet we are only starting to understand why they attract people. Individuals’ decisions to engage in these risky activities has long posed a challenge for utility theory. Contrary to public perception, most adventure sport participants are not reckless or solely motivated by adrenaline rush. They are disciplined, investing years of intensive training to understand the environment in which they operate and to develop the skills necessary to master the risky challenges. In this paper we develop a theory that distinguishes between the endogenous risk inherent to the sport and determined by participants’ own choices, and exogenous or uncontrollable background risk. It is well documented that while inherent risk lures individuals to these extreme sports, participants fear uncontrollable dangers as much as anybody else. This allows us to decompose participants’ utility into the thrill component of the activity and other aspects of the sport such as exercise and time outdoors. The same framework delivers a value of statistical life (VSL) that is risk-type dependent. Because participants weigh safety against the activity’s inherent risk, VSL is identified by their marginal spending on self-protection rather than by the level of risk they accept, so their tolerance for controllable risk does not imply that they value life cheaply. With this decomposition at hand, we study the optimal allocation of risk between participants and providers of these sports. We show that the modern legal doctrine of assumption of risk, in which providers are liable for their own negligence, but not for accidents stemming from the inherent riskiness of the activity, is more efficient than alternative arrangements. We illustrate our results with a calibrated example.

title: An Exploratory Study on the Regional Determinants of Economic Growth: Evidence From Basic Local Governments in Gyeonggi Province, South Korea
abstract: South Korea faces a growing risk of “local extinction,” understood as the declining viability of local communities driven by population decline, aging, and widening regional disparities. In this study, we aimed to identify the factors influencing regional economic development and to propose solutions for balanced growth and a reduction in regional disparities, with a particular focus on enhancing local government capacity. Using panel data from 31 basic local governments in Gyeonggi Province, a policy-relevant setting with substantial internal variation across cities and counties, this study highlights the role of local government capacity and knowledge-based industries in regional economic growth. Our findings showed a strong correlation between per capita budget size, financial independence, and regional growth, which underscores the need for efficient fiscal management. Local governments are thus encouraged to prioritize efforts to attract knowledge-based industries and medical institutions as key strategies to drive future economic growth and differentiate their regions, and the strategic importance of fiscal management, industry attraction, and healthcare infrastructure in regional development is emphasized.

title: Understanding the peacebuilding potential of truth commission recommendations through a public administration lens: The Latin American experience
abstract: This article places truth commission recommendations, the subject of some attention in transitional justice scholarship, at the intersection of peace studies and public administration. Based on data on approximately 1,000 recommendations found in 13 Latin American reports published between 1984 and 2014, we reflect on the role of public administration in implementation. Specifically, we examine challenges surrounding multiple interpretations and negotiations among stakeholders. We find that how recommendations are designed, tracked, and institutionalized is filtered primarily through political will, the capacities and cultures of public agencies, the discretion of public servants, and interagency coordination.

title: Co-laboring for peace: Reimagining the nexus of public administration and peacebuilding praxis
Public value in controversies: A reinterpretation of the strategic triangle through the lens of interorganizational problematization of public action
abstract: As non-governmental partners become increasingly involved in the production and delivery of public goods and services, existing models of public action and management are being challenged. Public value and Moore's “strategic triangle” model are a relevant—and still underutilized—way to analyze such interorganizational relationships. From this perspective, this article applies and adapts the strategic triangle and the concept of public value to the analysis of public–private relationships in order to understand the complex role of public managers involved in the public–private implementation of public action. The originality of this research lies in the analysis of the strategic triangle through the lens of Actor-Network Theory in order to identify links between controversies and the alignment of the triangle's vertices.

title: A Public Values Framework for AI Governance: Evidence From US Federal AI Policymaking
abstract: ABSTRACT Governments at all levels are grappling with AI's implications for public administration. Because federal actions often establish the principles guiding wider governance efforts, this study asks how US federal AI policies reflect—or fail to reflect—core public values. Drawing on a dataset of US federal AI policies from 2020 to 2023, we systematically analyze the risks, harms, and governance strategies employed across government‐issued and enacted policy documents. Specifically, we analyze 120 discrete policy sections or subsections of federal laws and regulations, utilizing the parsing approach of the AI Governance and Regulatory Archive (AGORA), all of which regulate the operation of the government itself rather than private sector behavior. We develop a theoretical and empirical crosswalk linking AI‐related risks and harms to prominent public values. Results indicate that while values such as individual rights, the common good, and accountability are regularly invoked, additional guidance around public values like citizen engagement, workplace standards, and responsiveness may be necessary to prevent public value failure. The study further categorizes governance strategies in AI policy documents into regulatory, service‐based, and informational instruments, and finds that regulatory policies are most likely to engage with public values.

title: Responsible Algorithmization in the Public Sector: A “Natural Perspective” Based on Ethnographic Research in Regulation, Policing, and Healthcare
abstract: ABSTRACT Responsible algorithmization refers to the use of algorithms in the public sector while safeguarding public values. Approaches to responsible algorithmization suggested by the EU, OECD, and others depart from a rational perspective and highlight formal structures and procedures. This paper complements this perspective by adding a “natural perspective,” which emphasizes sense‐making and actual practices. This natural perspective is used for a set of ethnographic studies of algorithmization in three domains in the Netherlands: regulation, policing, and healthcare. Our findings show that algorithmization of government organizations is an emergent, political, open, and fragmented process, rather than, as assumed by rational approaches to responsible algorithmization, pre‐structured, neutral, closed, and simple. This means that rational approaches fall short of providing a comprehensive basis for establishing responsible algorithmization. We conclude that not only passive responsibility but also active responsibility for algorithmization in the public sector needs to be addressed to safeguard public values.

title: Investor Orientation and Commitment in Outcomes‐Based Public Service Contracts
abstract: ABSTRACT Outcomes‐based contracts (OBCs) organize public service delivery around measurable results, yet little is known about how different investors engage with these instruments. This article examines how investor orientation (social, financial, or dual‐purpose) shapes investor commitment in OBCs worldwide. Drawing on a global dataset of 338 contracts, we combine descriptive analyses, regression models, and qualitative interviews to investigate how investor orientation relates to investment scale. We hypothesize that OBCs involving socially oriented investors are associated with higher levels of investment than those involving financially or dual‐purpose investors. Consistent with this prediction, socially oriented investors consistently commit larger amounts, whereas financially oriented and dual‐purpose investors typically participate with smaller contributions. These patterns challenge a central premise of OBCs: that such instruments would mobilize significant mainstream private capital for public services. Interview evidence points to reputational risks, limited familiarity with local conditions, and outcome measurement complexity as key deterrents.

title: Performance Feedback and Strategic Reporting—Evidence from China’s Government Work Report
abstract: Previous research on performance gaming behavior has primarily focused on data manipulation and effort manipulation. This article examines strategic reporting, a broad form of performance gaming in public organizations, by identifying four strategies: text-only reporting, social comparison benchmark shifting, historical comparison benchmark shifting, and absolute level absence. Drawing on theories of bounded rationality and blame avoidance, it investigates how positive and negative performance feedback shape strategic reporting behavior. Using data from Chinese municipal governments (2013–2019), logit model results suggest systematic variation across four strategic reporting strategies. All four strategies are positively associated with negative performance feedback, while all strategies but historical benchmark shifting are negatively associated with positive performance feedback. These findings contribute to the literature on performance gaming and performance feedback, while offering practical implications for strengthening governmental transparency and accountability.

title: Absenteeism and Presenteeism in Times of Change: The Role of Stress and Job Satisfaction
abstract: This study investigates sickness absenteeism and sickness presenteeism in the context of organizational development (OD) changes in the police force, focusing on health-related and motivational pathways. Using panel data from 407 employees from 36 Danish police units (1,021 observations), we analyze attendance patterns before the change, immediately after, and 1 year later. Findings reveal that sickness absenteeism is primarily influenced by the type of OD change rather than by job satisfaction or stress, while sickness presenteeism decreases with higher job satisfaction independent of the change type. Notably, employees experiencing an OD change aimed at supporting a long-term vision exhibit reduced sickness absence in the change period. OD changes focused on distributed leadership and enhancing employee motivation did not have the same effect on sickness absenteeism. These results underscore the importance of considering both motivational and health-related dynamics, as well as the type of change, in understanding attendance during OD change.

title: How can critical actors be incentivised to take a systems approach to pursue preventative public health?
abstract: Introduction In this article we explore how critical actors can be incentivised to take a systems approach to pursue preventative public health. More specifically, we focus on the link between urban environments and their effect on non-communicable diseases (NCDs), such as obesity, cancers, cardiovascular and respiratory disease. Improving urban environments as a route to preventative public health is well known but it is complicated and requires multi-actor decision-making. For example, reducing cardiovascular disease through better urban design will require global investment companies, central government, local planners, public health teams, private house builders and local residents to find ways to develop joint solutions. Methods We draw on 167 qualitative interviews with key actors from across the urban development system in England to explore how an innovative economic valuation tool – the Health Appraisal for Urban Systems (HAUS) tool – could support multi-actor decision-making. Analytic plan We analyse the data using a multi-stage, transdisciplinary thematic analysis. Coding involved a collaborative deductive and inductive process. Results Findings reveal that actors from state, market and civil society could see the value of this tool, which evidences the link between different features of the urban environment, health outcomes and their economic valuation. Indeed, actors confirmed that the tool offered something new to incentivise joint decision-making and there was an appetite for its use. Conclusion We conclude by arguing that the HAUS tool offers an important source of evidence to encourage cross-system collaboration for promoting preventative public health.

title: Closing the EU’s inflation governance gap: the limits of monetary policy and the case for a new policy framework for shockflation
abstract: This article assesses the adequacy of the European Union’s inflation governance framework in the context of frequent inflationary shocks. An inflation governance framework is the set of normative ideas and corresponding practices that govern the interpretation of objectives, the design of instruments, and how decision-making should proceed to prevent inflation. Within the inflation governance framework with which the EU approached the post-pandemic inflation, European policymakers expected that the ECB’s monetary policy would provide a sufficient safeguard for price stability. The framework was geared towards inflation that is demand driven: government spending and wage increases in excess of productivity. The post-pandemic shockflation in contrast, started with specific disruptions in systemically significant sectors and cost shocks which were propagated by firms’ pricing decisions. We argue that the framework’s over-reliance on the ECB and its narrow interpretation of its inflation-fighting role is no longer fit for purpose. Because monetary policy is not an adequate instrument for dealing with these supply-side drivers of inflation, the EU currently lacks adequate governance structures. We also set out the structure of a new inflation governance framework that targets shocks to systemically significant prices directly, before they are propagated through the economy.

title: Carbon pricing, green industrial policy, and the evolution of ideas in EU climate policy
Dynamic platform strategies in an interconnected ecosystem: Navigating standards and complements in the emerging smart home ecosystem
abstract: Whereas prior platform research has mostly assumed standardized interfaces that are platform-specific, we examine how platform strategies based on third-party standards have become prevalent in a nascent ecosystem. Based on a longitudinal analysis of 97 smart home platforms, we analyze the value creation and capture benefits of four platform modes defined by two dimensions: the source of complements (first- or third-party complements) and the standardized interfaces used to connect these complements (first- or third-party standards). Our analysis demonstrates a trend from closed strategies (only first-party complements based on first-party standards) towards strategies that (also) rely on third-party standards. We find that startups and diversifying entrants make different strategic choices at entry and that firms increasingly combine platform modes over time to leverage their distinct value creation and capture benefits. Our findings contribute insights into the ecosystem conditions and pre-entry capabilities of firms under which strategies relying on third-party standards become viable and how this contributes to the proliferation of standards, platforms, and strategies in an ecosystem. We also theorize the time-dependent strategic choices of entrants navigating a nascent ecosystem and the complex complementary and competitive relations that emerge in an ecosystem with interconnected platforms as a result.

title: Enacting Return‐to‐Work Effort: The Employers' Perspective on the Dutch Return‐to‐Work System
abstract: ABSTRACT Activation‐oriented social policy in the Netherlands assigns employers and employees a legally mandated, shared responsibility for facilitating the Return‐To‐Work (RTW) process of sick‐listed workers. This study examines how employers perceive activation‐oriented RTW responsibilities, focusing on the drivers shaping the employer's and employee's RTW efforts and the organisational actors supporting policy implementation. Data was collected through 25 semi‐structured, retrospective interviews with employers, who had experienced a negative evaluation of their RTW efforts at least once. Interview transcripts were analysed using systematic, qualitative template analysis building on policy‐implementation themes. Building on the employers' perspective, results showed several drivers of RTW effort of the employer (i.e., legal, financial and ethical drivers) and the sick‐listed employee (i.e., ability‐, motivation‐ and opportunity‐related drivers). Furthermore, results highlighted how employers perceived the enactment of RTW efforts to be supported by an intraorganisational tripartite of the Human Resource (HR) department, supervisor and occupational health specialists. Concluding, this study sheds light on how employers perceive the drivers and (roles of) actors that play an important role in the policy implementation within the daily RTW practice of organisations. Our findings highlight tensions between the legal mandate of shared responsibility and employers' perceptions of accountability, underscoring the need for mutually reinforcing RTW practices that integrate employer drivers with employees' ability, motivation and opportunity. The Dutch case, with strong employer obligations and sanction mechanisms, offers lessons for other welfare states.

title: Policy as a Bargaining Outcome: Coalition Leverage and Pledge Fulfillment
The Audience of Coalition Bargaining: Voter Reactions to Portfolio Allocation
Drivers of opposition strategic choices against democratic backsliding
Polling and parliamentary representation: Strategic voting in the 2025 German federal election
abstract: How decisive are public opinion polls in influencing the electoral fate of political parties? This article examines this question by focusing on parties at the brink of parliamentary representation. Specifically, Germany's 2025 federal election saw The Left, the FDP, and the BSW hovering around the critical 5% threshold in the polls, with only The Left ultimately succeeding in entering parliament. Drawing on theories of instrumental rationality and information processing, we theorize that polling signals are associated with asymmetric voter responses, with voters disproportionately abandoning parties below the threshold and supporting those above it. Using temporally fine-grained daily survey data together with daily polling scores, we test these expectations. We find that voters have been sensitive to marginal changes in The Left's and the BSW's polling scores, though not the FDP's. Polling at the 5% threshold presented a critical watershed for both parties in attracting strategic voters. This analysis illuminates the relationship between polls and voter decision-making, contributing to broader debates on media influence, voter heuristics, and electoral fairness.

title: From Domestic Contestation to Alpha Male Foreign Policy: Phantasies of Masculinity and the US Self
From Antagonistic Talk to Cooperative Acts: The Effect of Polarization Cues on Newspaper Audiences
abstract: Abstract Do media depictions of a ‘polarized society’ merely describe division or actually deepen it? We report two laboratory experiments in Germany (Study1 $$N=302$$ ; Study2 $$N=295$$ ). After reading authentic newspaper articles in which brief polarization cues were experimentally included versus omitted, participants (i) completed standard affective- and ideological-polarization measures and (ii) played incentivized Dictator, Ultimatum, and Trust Games with ideological out-group partners. Polarization cues increased both affective polarization and ideological extremity. Behavioral responses, however, were mixed. In the Dictator Game, where the recipient cannot respond, treated participants shared less with the out-group. In the Trust Game, characterized by mutual dependence and potential efficiency gains, treated participants sent more to out-group partners. Ultimatum behavior, where interdependence is partial, showed weaker and less consistent shifts. Taken together, polarization cues reliably heighten perceived division but do not uniformly translate into behavioral antagonism: even after cues that increase self-reported polarization, participants can still cooperate with ideological opponents when cooperation is perceived as mutually beneficial.

title: Green hydrogen in the Global South: Politics, spaces, and transformations – An introduction
Capital accumulation and territorial control in West Papua's offshore gas industry
Backlashes to Gender Equality and Authoritarian Populism in the U.S.
abstract: According to recent scholarship, backlash toward gender equality is fueling support for the authoritarian and populist right in many countries and, perhaps, the rise of Trumpism in the U.S. Yet, there are potentially different types of backlash to gender equality. We argue that the rising status of women over the past several decades may result in anti-feminist attitudes, not just among older men who yearn for the traditional gender arrangements of their youth as some scholars argue, but also among younger, single men lacking college degrees, who are less attractive partners for women. We call this “mate-value backlash.” Using ANES data, we find that anti-feminist attitudes have long been associated with support for Republican presidential candidates, but only in recent years have these attitudes become more prominent among unmarried men, without college degrees.

title: Voting for Democracy? Testing Political-Cultural Constraints on Democratic Backsliding
Behavioral Attenuation
Rethinking Reference Dependence: Wage Dynamics and Optimal Taxi Labor Supply
Timing is Everything: Parental Professional Connections and Labor Market Entry
Equilibrium in the Market for Public School Teachers: District Wage Strategies and Teacher Comparative Advantage

Stockups, Stockouts, and the Role for Strategic Reserves
abstract: Abstract We study how supply disruptions interact with monopoly pricing, inventory management, and consumer stockpiling in a continuous-time model. Preemption incentives—consumers prefer to stock up before a price hike while the firm prefers to hike before consumers stock up—lead to an equilibrium with gradual stockpiling and endogenous uncertainty over the timing of a price hike, which can trigger a run at the disruption onset. Consumer storage introduces welfare losses from randomized pricing, but can also strengthen the firm’s incentive to hold buffer stock. Rationing, price controls, and reserve mandates can each improve welfare, but only strategic government reserves can implement the social optimum.

title: The (Hidden) Samaritan Contest*
A time-varying approach to assessing fiscal cyclicality: The role of the European fiscal framework#
The Extreme Points of Mean-Preserving Contractions
Scientific Isolation? The Consequences of Trump's China Initiative on Chinese Research
abstract: ABSTRACT The 2018 China Initiative by the Trump administration complicated procedures and reduced funding for U.S.‐China research collaborations. Using Scopus data, we analyze its impact on Chinese research. We find that it significantly lowered the quality of both publications and co‐authors of Chinese researchers with prior U.S. collaborations compared to those with prior European collaborations, and reduced yearly citations for affected researchers by 6%. The effect was stronger for high‐productivity Chinese researchers in U.S.‐dominated fields. While China is at the forefront of the scientific frontier, it still depends more on the U.S. than the reverse.

title: Discussion of “Local Shocks and Regional Dynamics in an Aging Economy”—The Downward Elasticity of Regional Capital
abstract: ABSTRACT The paper shows that population aging can reduce the welfare cost to individuals of a persistent negative local shock, because slower out‐migration restrains forward‐looking capital disinvestment and the retained capital cushions the wages of those who stay. I consider asymmetric capital adjustment: under irreversibility, disinvestment is less elastic than installation. I extend the paper's capital block to allow for this asymmetry and show that the extension can be tractably incorporated into standard dynamic hat algebra solution algorithms, including the one employed in the paper. I then illustrate the importance of asymmetric capital adjustment through a simple one‐region example.

title: Review of “The Story of a Generation: Life Course Pathways of the Class of ‘73”
The Language of Democratic Resilience and Decline: A Comparative Study of Politicians’ Communication on Facebook in Sweden and Hungary
Public service equity and stakeholder satisfaction: evidence from 56 countries on how parents, teachers, and students respond to gender gaps in education
abstract: This study examines how gender equity in educational achievement relates to the satisfaction of three key stakeholders: students, parents, and teachers. Using cross-national panel data from the Trends in International Mathematics and Science Study (TIMSS), covering 56 countries from 2011 to 2019, we link gender gaps in student math and science performance to student and parent satisfaction with schooling, as well as teacher satisfaction with their jobs. We find that gender inequity is associated with lower satisfaction, but parents with a female student and higher SES respond to the gender inequity the most. These findings extend the citizen satisfaction and public service equity literatures by showing that different stakeholders in the same public service system can respond quite differently to inequities, with implications for how governments communicate about and address performance gaps and equity concerns.

title: When police officers surrender: the effect of citizen incivility on withdrawal and turnover
abstract: Why do seemingly minor acts of citizen disrespect matter for police retention? Drawing on Conservation of Resources (COR) theory and sociometer theory, this study examines how citizen incivility shapes officers’ withdrawal processes over time. Using a three-wave longitudinal survey of 1,397 police officers, we test whether baseline exposure to citizen incivility predicts subsequent trajectories of work disengagement and turnover intention. We argue that citizen incivility functions as a low intensity but psychologically consequential interpersonal cue that subtly threatens officers’ perceived social standing, depleting psychological resources, fostering disengagement, and ultimately increasing turnover intention. We further propose that perceived organizational support (POS), as a valued resource and a signal of institutional recognition, buffers these adverse effects. Results confirm that citizen incivility indirectly predicts turnover intention through disengagement, and that POS attenuates this pathway. These findings advance understanding of resource-loss dynamics in public service contexts and highlight the protective role of organizational support in sustaining frontline engagement and retention.

title: How and When Does Negative Beneficiary Contact Relate to Service Behaviors? Unpacking the Roles of Prosocial Impact and Service-Oriented High-Performance Work Systems in Public Healthcare
Collaborative platforms in digital government: structural and cultural barriers to coordination
abstract: Collaborative platforms are increasingly used to coordinate digital public services across organizational boundaries, yet how they function in practice remains poorly understood. This study examines the coordination challenges such platforms face, drawing on Norway’s “life event” initiatives—programs designed to deliver integrated, user-centered digital services across government sectors. Based on document analysis and semi-structured interviews with 22 government actors and platform coordinators, the study finds that while collaborative platforms are designed to enable cross-sectoral interaction and co-creation, their effectiveness is constrained by structural barriers—including limited resources, unclear roles, and unsupportive regulatory frameworks—and by cultural tensions over norms, expectations, and interpretations of responsibility. These findings clarify the concept of collaborative platforms in public management research, showing how coordination challenges shape their operation and outcomes. The study contributes to digital governance scholarship by identifying the difficulties public managers face in steering and sustaining scalable collaborative arrangements for digital transformation and public service delivery.

title: How context and tensions shape public values assessment: findings from a case study of a Dutch agency
Inspired to Serve: Exposure to Moral Models to Enhance Public Service Motivation
abstract: ABSTRACT Public service motivation (PSM) is widely recognized as a predictor of positive outcomes, yet relatively little is known about how it can be deliberately cultivated. Drawing on conservation of resources (COR) theory, the present research investigates whether and how exposure to moral exemplars embedded in public‐sector training enhances PSM. Employing a multi‐method design that combines a recall experiment with a field survey, we find that exposure to uncommon moral exemplars elicits moral elevation, which functions as a replenishment of psychological resources and, in turn, strengthens public employees' PSM. Moreover, this mediating mechanism is moderated by cognitive load, such that public employees experiencing greater cognitive demands derive stronger motivational benefits from moral elevation. By identifying moral elevation as a psychological resource mechanism and cognitive load as a boundary condition, this research opens the “black box” of PSM development. It highlights how training can serve as an institutional platform for delivering specific moral content that cultivates and sustains public employees' motivation to serve.

title: The “Professional Mortality” Problem in Early City Management: A Study of Organized Denial
abstract: ABSTRACT The early city management profession experienced appalling rates of attrition. This problem of “professional mortality” had been clearly recognized by the end of World War I: causes of attrition included threats and violence against managers, intense political interference in managers' work, and interpersonal missteps. Yet the organized management profession and advocates of the manager plan actively ignored threats and were unwilling to respond collectively or officially to political interference; leading scholars recognized but did not publicly discuss common interpersonal problems faced by managers. This silence on the underlying causes of turnover marked an effort to protect the manager plan's viability in the face of growing electoral opposition during the 1920s, placing the interests of the profession above its practicing members. The optimistic, rationalist discourses of advocates, scholars, and professional leaders rested on self‐conscious denial of uncomfortable realities; a full historical accounting may help avoid repeating these mistakes.

title: Introducing public management and global sporting mega-events: public value, ecosystems, learning and temporality
abstract: We are delighted to introduce this Special Issue which collects authors and studies from around the world; qualitative and quantitative, current, historic, and longitudinal. Each paper contributes ...

title: From academic lab to spinoff: How opportunity beliefs evolve from individual to venture during technology-market matching
abstract: Academic labs are central to the creation of radical-generic technologies. Yet translating these inventions into successful innovations poses a significant challenge as academic scientists often struggle to identify and prioritize viable markets in the early stages of commercialization. This study examines how individual scientists' opportunity beliefs evolve into the shared commercialization strategy of an academic spinoff. Using a longitudinal single-case study of the technology-market matching (TMM) process of a radical-generic technology, we analyze individual and team assessments of eight technology-market combinations over 15 years. We show that opportunity beliefs evolve from an initial emphasis on functional aspects of structural similarity toward an increasing emphasis on commercial viability, eventually integrating balanced similarity considerations. Within TMM, three mechanisms – productive cognitive dissonance, expanded similarity awareness, and team reflexivity – explain how heterogeneous individual beliefs evolve and coalesce into the commercialization strategy of the spinoff. We introduce “simmering-with-the-lab” as an organizational strategy through which latent technology-market options are maintained in the academic lab while the spinoff pursues a narrower set of commercial opportunities. The study advances theory on TMM and organizational learning for deep tech academic spinoffs and has practical implications for science entrepreneurship training, innovation policy, and university IP strategy.

title: Donor Influence at the African Development Bank
Partisans misperceive and are influenced by dynamic norms
abstract: Abstract Perceptions of social norms, and how those norms change over time, play a central role in shaping how people understand and respond to political divides. We developed and iteratively refined dynamic‐norm messages about bipartisan attitude change to reduce divisive outparty perceptions and attitudes in a US context. We first identified real‐world issues that gained support over time among both Democrats and Republicans and were judged as believable. Study 1 documented systematic misperceptions of attitude change across a range of social issues and linked these misperceptions to colder outparty feelings. We then tested intervention messages that adapted standard static‐norm templates with the addition of information about change over time (dynamic norm; Study 2). This intervention increased expectations of future common ground but did not reliably improve downstream outparty attitudes. Next, we tested a refined intervention message that isolated dynamic norm information (Study 3). The refined dynamic norm message increased expected common ground and expected future feelings of belonging among the outparty and was associated with small but reliable increases in outparty warmth and positive outparty impressions relative to control. These results suggest that emphasizing trajectories of public opinion without highlighting current partisan gaps may be a useful strategy for reducing polarization.

title: A theory of conspiracy theories
The health effects of genetically modified crops
On the optimal size of a joint savings association: Part 2 - efficiency
Sabotage as Industrial Policy
abstract: Abstract We characterise sabotage, exemplified by recent US policies concerning China’s semiconductor industry, as trade policy. For some (but not all) goods, completely destroying foreigners’ productivity increases domestic real income by shifting the location of production and improving the terms of trade. The gross benefit of sabotage can be summarised by a few sufficient statistics: trade and demand elasticities and import and production shares. The cost of sabotage is determined by countries’ relative unit labour costs for the sabotaged goods. We find important non-monotonicities: for semiconductors, partially sabotaging foreign production would lower US real income, while comprehensive sabotage would raise it.

title: For the future of our grandchildren: Grandparenthood and climate change concerns
abstract: Concerns about offspring’s life quality are often cited as a motivation for caring about climate change. This paper investigates the hypothesized causal effect of grandparenthood on climate change worries, using panel data surveys among British families. Specifically, we study whether becoming a grandparent increases these worries. We employ two different study designs to deal with endogeneity of grandparenthood. Across designs, the assumptions required to identify causal effects differ and are non-nested but give a remarkably congruent result: We find no empirical support for a relationship between grandparental status and concerns about climate change.

title: “ In a way, I want TikTok to tell me what I want. . . ” Users’ experience of TikTok as a televisual algorithmic flow
abstract: This article revisits Williams’s concept of flow, Firth’s notion of algorithmic flow, and Picone et al.’s concept of Small Acts of Engagement (SAOE) to examine how users experience TikTok’s algorithmic flow. SAOE are understood as low-effort, everyday acts through which users negotiate their identities and shape their digital consumption. While SAOE have been a valuable lens for understanding user agency on earlier social media platforms, we argue that TikTok’s interface design and cultural framing introduce new challenges. The platform’s design, together with users’ perception of TikTok’s algorithmic flow as a televisual experience, reduces their SAOE to a minimal expression: a rhythm of watch, scroll, repeat , discouraging other forms of intentional, identity-driven engagement. Through a mixed-methods study combining interviews and analysis of participants’ donated TikTok data, we show how our participants experience TikTok as a place for effortless entertainment and continuous consumption, closely resembling the experience of traditional television flow.

title: Data-Driven Collaboration in Mandated Networks: US Homelessness Services
Hybridized advisory system: ministerial advisors and donor co-principalship in developing countries
abstract: Ministerial advisors have become increasingly prominent actors in policy advisory systems, yet existing scholarship draws largely from the Global North, leaving significant gaps in understanding their roles in developing countries. Drawing on primary data, this study examines recruitment, positioning, and policy influence of ministerial advisors in the developing country context. The findings reveal that ministerial advisory roles are institutionalized through what this study theorizes as a hybridized advisory system (HAS), a configuration in which donors function as external advisory actors and as co-principals who define advisory mandates, recruit and finance ministerial advisors, and exercise veto-like authority alongside political principals. Once embedded in government, ministerial advisors exert substantial influence over policy design and implementation. Their relationships with bureaucrats are marked by persistent tension: bureaucrats consider them illegitimate intruders, while advisors perceive that bureaucrats lack technical expertise. The paper concludes that HAS offers an alternative analytical framework to existing models developed for advanced democracies. It also argues that strengthening in-house capacity is a necessary condition for building self-sustaining advisory systems.

title: Adoption survival frontiers: Artificial intelligence, financing frictions, and market structure
abstract: Artificial intelligence and other general-purpose digital technologies often diffuse unevenly: large firms adopt early, while smaller firms delay adoption, contract, or abandon the active adoption option. This paper develops a survival-constrained theory of technology adoption in which firms choose when to adopt an irreversible technology while financing operations under uncertain implementation costs. Abandonment/exit is endogenous: firms leave the active adoption race when the value of preserving the adoption option falls below the passive legacy fallback (the value of abandoning the active adoption option, normalized to zero). The key object is an adoption survival frontier , a boundary in financing-cost–implementation-uncertainty space separating environments in which followers survive long enough to adopt from environments in which they abandon the active adoption option first. The Cournot block disciplines the price-pass-through component of follower payoff erosion; additional non-price appropriability losses, captured by a reduced-form term 𝜒 𝐴 (data accumulation, platform lock-in, switching frictions, and reduced access to post-adoption rents), remain reduced-form. Numerical characterization of the corrected nonhomogeneous stopping problem shows that a leader-induced regime shift moves the survival frontier inward and raises the risk that followers abandon the active adoption option before adoption. A welfare decomposition clarifies when this selection is efficient and when it reflects an accounting externality: a leader-induced payoff shift that the follower’s private stopping problem does not represent before the regime shift. We do not solve a dynamic adoption-timing game. Public EU aggregate data show that large-minus-small AI adoption gaps are measurable, but also illustrate that aggregate cross-country regressions are confounded by development gradients and cannot identify the firm-level survival-to-adoption channel; we treat this as a measurement-feasibility map for future linked-microdata tests rather than as a test of the mechanism. The paper contributes a computational theory of adoption survival and a transparent measurement-feasibility map.

title: An (almost) free lunch? Symbolic recognition and knowledge-sharing behavior in online communities
Measuring the production of scientific human capital: New data, methods, and evidence on the U.S. scientific training ecosystem
abstract: We develop a dissertation-based methodology for measuring PhD populations and use it to present new evidence on who funds STEM PhD training in the United States, how many graduates are trained in areas of strategic national importance, and the effects of public investment in PhD training on PhD production. The U.S. government is by far the largest source of financial and in-kind support for STEM PhD training in America. We identify universities and fields where PhD training has high rates of government, industry, or philanthropic support, and the organizations and universities that fund and train the most PhDs in critical technology areas such as AI, quantum science, and biotechnology. Leveraging variation in government support across agencies and over time, we provide evidence suggesting that increasing government-funded PhD trainees increases PhD production additively or with modest crowd-in. To support further research, we provide public data at multiple levels of aggregation. These data and methods complement existing data collection efforts by national statistics agencies, producing information which is otherwise hard to collect or not systematically observed, and can be extended forward in time and to other countries.

title: Disjuncture by default: Arrhythmic life-worlds and intergenerational injustice
The sacred imagination of geographical spaces: The geopolitical spiritualization of the Islamic Republic of Iran
Perceived need and measured well-being: How well do subjective rankings capture relative poverty?
abstract: Subjective well-being rankings are increasingly used to target social protection programs, yet their ability to capture relative welfare and wealth remains debated. This study benchmarks self-, peer-, and elite-based poverty rankings against consumption- and wealth-based measures using Ethiopian household survey data, where about 20 households per village were ranked from neediest to least needy by themselves, peers, and community leaders. We assess concordance between subjective and conventional welfare rankings and explore sources of divergence. Subjective rankings align more with relative wealth than consumption and with total rather than per capita welfare, suggesting they overlook household composition. Elite-based rankings best capture conventional measures, followed by peers’ and self-rankings. Subjective rankings also better reflect relative deprivation among households exposed to covariate shocks. A composite index combining all three improves agreement with standard metrics. Information asymmetries, favoritism, and welfare dynamics partly explain discrepancies, offering insights for enhancing targeting in data-scarce settings.

New development: Patronage police appointments in autocracies—lessons from Serbia
abstract: IMPACTThis article is particularly relevant for senior police leaders, public sector managers, oversight bodies, and international reform practitioners working in contexts of de-democratization and autocratization. It shows how patronage-based appointments of police leadership undermine professional policing by weakening operational independence, distorting internal incentives, and eroding public trust. Practitioners can use these findings to identify early warning signs of politicized appointment processes and to design safeguards that protect merit-based recruitment and leadership selection. The analysis highlights how patronage at the top of the police hierarchy signals to lower ranks that political loyalty outweighs professional standards, thereby reinforcing broader patterns of organizational politicization. More broadly, the article contributes to debates on police professionalism and public sector governance by showing how leadership appointment structures shape institutional autonomy and democratic policing outcomes.

title: Desire for group supremacy: the role of social dominance orientation for social policy attitudes
abstract: Abstract A key concern in the social policy literature is to understand the causes of support for – but also opposition to – egalitarian and inclusive policies and for political parties that champion such policies. While objective socio-economic factors such as class and gender have long had a central role as predictors of those attitudes in the social policy literature, scholars have more recently begun to incorporate psychological variables, notably right-wing authoritarianism (RWA) or implicit attitudes. Curiously, however, one variable that has been central in social psychological research for about three decades has so far been largely absent in the social policy literature: social dominance orientation (SDO). This omission is problematic not only because SDO is a known predictor of regressive and exclusionary attitudes, but also because SDO itself cross-cuts with other predictors of social policy attitudes (notably class) in theoretically relevant ways. Our contribution here is to highlight and demonstrate the relevance of SDO as an explanatory variable in social policy attitudes research. To do so, we draw on data from an original comparative survey covering five European countries (Germany, Switzerland, Sweden, Denmark, the United Kingdom) and the United States.

title: Mapping the uneven impact of education on mental health: a cross-national analysis by income level
abstract: Abstract The relationship between education and mental health is not well understood. Findings are mixed, especially in low- and middle-income countries. We examine the impact of education on mental health using individual-level data from over 120,000 participants across 121 countries, comprising 42 high-income countries and 79 low- and middle-income countries. Results show that better-educated individuals are less likely to experience mental health issues in the overall sample. We observe the same effect in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs); however, the effect is not significant in high-income countries (HICs). The study suggests that mental health policy should be tailored to the socioeconomic environments of LMICs and HICs. In LMICs, education can be leveraged as an important tool for improving mental health by strengthening access to material and social resources. In HICs, where education alone appears insufficient to improve mental health outcomes, the findings point to the need for broader interventions that address social, economic and psychosocial stressors across the population. Coordination between health and education sectors remains essential for developing effective and context-specific policy responses.

title: The Political Economy of Transformative Globalization: Evidence From BRI Participating Countries Using Panel Quantile Regression
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines the effects of transformative globalization on welfare and income distribution using an extensive dataset encompassing 23 Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) participating countries from 2010 to 2020. We conducted a comprehensive data analysis using quantile regression and the Generalized Methods of Moments (GMM), ensuring the robustness and reliability of our findings. The study finds that income and wealth inequality decline as countries integrate into the BRI, highlighting the role of transformative globalization in promoting equity. The impact is more pronounced in the upper percentiles, suggesting a more significant equalizing effect among wealthier segments. Quantile regression analysis reveals that, while globalization positively affects overall welfare, middle‐income groups experience the most significant gains. This underscores the particularly favorable impact of transformative globalization on the well‐being of middle‐income individuals, contributing to a more equitable distribution of resources and improved human welfare across societal strata. These findings will be of interest to policymakers and researchers examining the distributional dimensions of BRI participation. The study provides valuable insights into how transformative globalization, through the BRI, can lead to more equitable income and wealth distribution and enhance human welfare, with a distinctive emphasis on its differential impacts across various income groups. title: Green Hydrogen in Brazilian Media: Dominant Narratives and Missing Dimensions of the Energy Trilemma
abstract: ABSTRACT Media discourses help shape the visibility and legitimacy of energy transition pathways in the public sphere. This study examines how Brazilian mainstream newspapers framed green hydrogen and assesses the alignment of these narratives with the energy trilemma: energy security, environmental sustainability, and social accessibility. We analyzed 286 articles published by G1 and Estadão between January 2020 and June 2023, combining BERTopic‐based topic modeling, supervised LDA, and qualitative contextual interpretation. The findings show that media coverage addressed all dimensions of the energy trilemma but prioritized financing, investment, production costs, regulation, and export opportunities. Social accessibility, environmental impacts, territorial conflicts, and the distributive implications of water and land use remained comparatively marginal. Brazilian media therefore tended to portray green hydrogen as a market‐oriented and export‐driven opportunity rather than as a comprehensive socio‐ecological transition. These findings highlight the limits of mainstream media framing and its insufficient attention to energy and climate justice. Related Articles Kerrouche, N., and C. title: Between expectations and outcomes: Technology adopters' narratives and technology discourse dynamics
abstract: Expectations propel the evolution of emerging technologies, yet existing research generally assumes that expectations are gradually displaced by concrete outcomes as technologies mature and become widely accepted. We revisit this assumption by examining how technology adopters' temporal framings of technology performance, their expressions of concrete outcomes of technology adoption, and the broader technology discourse reflected in trade-press coverage relate to one another over time. We illuminate these patterns by tracing 21 years (2002−2022) of radio-frequency identification (RFID) adoption and analysing adopters' statements in 407 case stories published in The RFID Journal, coupled with a longitudinal corpus of trade-press coverage from the same period. Manual coding of adopters' expressions of concrete realised benefits and challenges in the case stories is combined with a purpose-built dictionary that detects five temporal positions in adopters' framings of RFID performance. We find that associations between concrete outcomes and temporal framings are selective and stage-dependent. Concrete outcomes do not simply replace expectations, instead, they become associated with specific temporal framings over time. We also find that adopters' temporal framings are associated with trade-press coverage in stage-specific ways that change over time, often amplifying but also sometimes tempering broader attention to RFID. We contribute to research on technology framing and expectations dynamics by foregrounding adopters as co-constructors of technology discourse, challenging the displacement assumption with a stage-sensitive explanation of expectation–outcome dynamics, and introducing a replicable, dictionary-based approach for large-scale analysis of temporal framings in technology narratives.

The seniority ceiling: Why some immigrants struggle to rise in political office
abstract: First-generation immigrants face a seniority ceiling that limits their political incorporation as candidates and officeholders. Career ladders that require qualification time in lower positions create structural barriers for this group. We use linked data from Swedish electoral ballots andadministrative records to examine this idea. A novel identification strategy isolates the effect of seniority-based promotion structures from immigrant-specific disadvantages by comparing immigrants’ incorporation patterns to those of internal movers—native-born Swedes whorelocate between municipalities. The seniority ceiling explains about half of the immigrant-native gap in holding political positions and almost the entire gradient of worsening incorporation at higher levels. We find strong selection effects at both the individual and group level. The seniority ceiling restricts incorporation at higher career steps for those with fewer opportunities to accumulate qualification time: those who arrived more recently or at older ages.

The grass is not always greener: The effects of local labor market information on search and employment
abstract: We examine how information about local labor market conditions shapes search and employment outcomes for Indian job seekers. Participants were randomly shown information about either job postings, job applicants, or both from a popular job portal for their preferred city and occupation. Treated respondents are more likely to be employed seven months later. This overall effect varies considerably by baseline employment status. Among the initially employed , treatments reduce search off the portal and increase employment, with suggestive evidence of higher persistence in baseline jobs. In contrast, among the initially unemployed , treatments increase search activity but do not raise employment. Employment gains are concentrated among job seekers with less optimistic beliefs about labor market conditions. These findings suggest that limited information about labor market fundamentals may contribute to job churn in lower-income countries. • An RCT provides real-time local labor market information to urban job seekers. • Information raises employment by 12% after seven months. • Employment gains are concentrated among initially employed job seekers. • Employed workers retain jobs; unemployed search more but don’t find jobs. • Suggestive evidence shows largest gains for workers with lower expectations.

title: Government Recommendations and Health Behaviours: Evidence from Breast Cancer Screening Guidelines
abstract: Abstract We provide novel evidence on how healthcare decision-making responds to government recommendations by examining the 2009 revision to the United States Preventive Services Task Force’s mammography guidelines. Using a difference-in-differences design, we find the revision reduced mammography among women aged 40–49 by 6–10%. We also find spillover effects among women aged 30–39, who became substantially less likely to receive mammogram recommendations or screenings, despite not being the guideline’s target population. Declines were greatest among groups with higher baseline screening rates. We also find evidence of reduced overdiagnosis of early-stage tumors and increased confusion about cancer prevention recommendations.

title: Goal Setting and Feedback: The Power of Joint Use
Do Your Own Research: What Skepticism of Expertise Means for the News Media in the U.S.
abstract: In the U.S. the availability of news information has grown exponentially while trust in traditional sources of news and information has declined. Amid this high-information, low-trust environment, many now advocate for doing your own research (DYOR) to discern accurate claims from false, misleading, or biased information. The perception that it is better to do one’s own research has important implications for information seeking and attitudes toward mainstream news and journalism. In this study, we use a panel survey to investigate DYOR perceptions in the context of the 2020 U.S. election. We find that DYOR perceptions are associated with decreased nonpartisan news use, decreased belief accuracy, and more negative attitudes toward media, highlighting how information skepticism may be contributing to adversarial views toward mainstream media and expertise. Results suggest that such perceptions encourage negative views of news media and may contribute to distrust of public institutions.

title: Religious Change in Post-Mao China: Toward a New Sociology of Religion Yanfei Sun. Chicago, IL: The University of Chicago Press, 2026. 320 pp. $32.50 (pbk). ISBN 9780226845876
Revisiting and Transcending Tradition: The Transformation of Contemporary Chinese Ink Art Language in Global Art Discourse
abstract: Abstract This essay explores the evolution of contemporary Chinese ink painting, focusing on how traditional techniques are integrated with new innovations by modern artists. Deeply rooted in Chinese philosophy and culture, Chinese ink painting has adapted to the 21st century by incorporating digital media, mixed materials, and multimedia techniques, expanding its expressive range and emotional depth. The paper examines the influence of globalization on artistic creation, particularly the integration with global movements like Abstract Expressionism and digital art. Contemporary Chinese ink artists also use their works as platforms for political and social commentary, addressing issues such as social change, urbanization, and environmental transformation. Additionally, the study looks into the role of institutional support and market dynamics in advancing Chinese ink painting globally. The paper highlights the challenges and opportunities that contemporary ink artists face as they adapt to evolving societal and cross-cultural communication trends. Finally, it stresses the importance of balancing the preservation of traditional art forms with the adoption of new innovations to ensure that Chinese ink painting remains relevant in the global art landscape.
