title: Insider or outsider: negative performance feedback and top manager succession in the public sector
abstract: Facing performance pressure, public organizations frequently experience top manager turnover, yet how they select successors is understudied. This study argues negative performance feedback (NPF) critically influences successor origin. Based on 2,045 TM turnovers , we find that NPF reduces the odds of internal succession by 41.7%. Internal promotion history strengthens external successor selection by signalling a break from discredited routines, while exploratory learning emphasis reinforces external selection as strategic identity. This research advances public management by offering a dynamic, antecedent-based explanation for TM selection, challenging monolithic views of organizational history, and highlighting successor origin as a strategic governance tool.

title: Revisiting the political-social dimension of public value
abstract: Public value research increasingly recognizes that societal value is generated by public, private, philanthropic, and hybrid actors. However, empirical tools for identifying public value beyond the state remain underdeveloped, particularly regarding its political-social dimension. This study operationalizes this dimension by identifying and analytically defining eight constituent elements. It draws on a multiple case study of three Brazilian social enterprises, combining document analysis, field visits, and semi-structured interviews. Findings clarify the dimension’s components and demonstrate how they can be identified in organizational practices and relationships. The study advances empirical approaches to public value and extends research to non-state actors in a non-European context.

title: Economic and political drivers of fiscal response to COVID-19: empirical approach
abstract: Abstract What do we know about fiscal response to the COVID-19 pandemic in its early phases? Does the government’s ideology matter for the scope of anti-crisis measures? There is a growing literature and public debate on the economic and social implications of COVID-19. However, we still know little about the drivers of particular reactions of governments to this extraordinary shock. In this paper, we apply econometric tools to analyze the relevance of government ideology regarding economic policies for anti-crisis fiscal packages enacted in 2020. The results imply that right-wing governments provide significantly bigger fiscal packages than those observed in countries ruled by other political parties. Different responses to the crisis are also noted for the wealthy and the Nordic countries.

title: Evaluating the Effectiveness of Open‐Source LLMs for Automated Analysis of Multilingual Consultation Feedback: A Swiss Case Study
abstract: ABSTRACT Public consultations are a cornerstone of democratic policymaking, yet the sheer volume and heterogeneity of submissions often overwhelm traditional analysis. Emerging large language models (LLMs) offer new opportunities for making sense of such data, but their performance in contexts with high linguistic and technical diversity remains underexplored. In this research note, we present a case‐based demonstration rather than a generalizable evaluation, assessing an open‐source LLM (Gemma3:27b) and a proprietary LLM (GPT‐5‐mini) for analyzing stakeholder inputs from three Swiss pre‐parliamentary consultations. The coexistence of multiple languages and varying technical complexity in submissions creates uniquely challenging datasets, providing a rigorous test for automated tools. We benchmark the model against official administrative reports, assessing accuracy and completeness. Results show the open‐source model performs excellently in straightforward consultations, achieving a mean accuracy of 90%, but encounters difficulties in retrieving the substantive content (overall completeness: 70%). Comparatively, the proprietary model obtains better results than the open‐source one in these two settings. Overall, LLMs can streamline analysis and enhance interpretive capacity, complementing (but not replacing) human expertise. The study highlights both the potential and limits of algorithmic support for participatory governance in linguistically and technically diverse environments.

title: Explaining uneven American support for electoral democracy: How partisanship conditions the winner-loser gap
abstract: What explains variation in American support for electoral democracy? We argue that the longstanding winner-loser gap in post-election democracy support is conditioned by partisan identity, reflecting a deeper partisan divide in public commitment to electoral democracy. Using CES panel surveys fielded immediately before and after the 2020 and 2024 U.S. presidential elections, we show that election outcomes cause immediate shifts in individuals’ attitudes about core elements of electoral democracy relative to their pre-election baselines. However, these shifts do not translate into stable differences in overall levels of democracy support. In both victory and defeat, Republicans express weaker overall commitment to electoral democracy than Democrats. This diverges from classic winner–loser gap theory, which expects electoral winners to exhibit greater democracy support than electoral losers, regardless of which party prevails. We further demonstrate that Americans’ near-universal nominal support for democracy masks greater fragility and partisan asymmetry in concrete support for the core institutional practices that sustain democratic governance.

title: Friendship in World Politics: George Padmore, Nancy Cunard, and Dorothy Pizer at the End of Empire
Turning Hazard Models Inside Out
abstract: Abstract Regression Inside Out (RIO) describes a set of related methods based on a decomposition of regression coefficients by individual cases. In this article, we offer three important extensions of RIO: 1) we generalize RIO to any model for which linear predictors are estimated; 2) we introduce an adapted bootstrap approach for determining whether case-level contributions differ from the baseline average contribution for cases; and 3) we describe how RIO is related to model diagnostics, particularly DFBETA. To illustrate the value added of these extensions, we apply RIO to a published example of the Cox proportional hazard model exploring factors associated with democratic durability.

title: Left Behind or Left In? Party Ideology and the Gender Gap in Candidate Persistence
The Limits of Incumbent Blame Games in Times of Crisis: Experimental Evidence from Electoral Autocracy
abstract: Abstract This study investigates how blame-attributing crisis frames influence support for incumbents in an electoral authoritarian context, focusing on Türkiye. It asks how, to what extent, and under what conditions incumbents’ blame frames shape public attitudes toward the government. The study examines four crisis types (i.e., global warming , earthquake , economic collapse , and pandemic ) and compares the effects of religious , conspiratorial , and scientific framing across these contexts. Drawing on original data from seven pre-survey focus groups and a nationwide face-to-face survey experiment with 3,562 respondents, the findings indicate that the independent effects of blame frames are generally limited. However, the effectiveness of religion-based blame framing is highly context dependent. Compared with climate and economic crises, its estimated effects are more favorable in crises characterized by high uncertainty and relatively low perceived governmental responsibility, such as earthquake and pandemic. These findings suggest that the effectiveness of blame attribution is conditioned by the nature of the crisis itself. The study contributes to research on crisis framing, political accountability, and authoritarian durability.

title: Review of Douglas W. Allen and Bryan Leonard. 2025. “Why the rush: an institutional economic analysis of homesteading and the settlement of the west”
Aligning Access and Affectedness in Participatory Governance: Civil Society Organisations in Finnish Preparatory Bodies
abstract: ABSTRACT This article examines whether CSO access to preparatory bodies reflects the logic of participatory governance, according to which those affected by policies should have opportunities engage in their making. Existing research provides limited tools to assess this in a policy‐relevant manner. We propose an exploratory, policy‐specific benchmark based on regulatory impact assessments (RIAs) of policies linked to preparatory bodies. We examine whether access by CSOs aligns with expected affectedness among their constituencies. We test this approach by analysing CSO access to Finnish preparatory bodies over a 3‐year period. We focus on two pairings, citizens and citizen groups, and companies and business groups, and examine preparatory bodies that include at least one such interest organisation ( N = 103). Overall, access patterns align with affectedness. However, this alignment is stronger for business groups than for citizen groups and varies across policy areas for the latter. By introducing a policy‐specific benchmark for evaluating access, this article demonstrates that even when accounting affectedness, inequalities in access persist, resulting in a participatory gap in the involvement of citizen groups.

title: Machine Learning for Dynamic Incentive Problems
abstract: Abstract We present a flexible and scalable computational framework integrating machine learning and optimization theory to solve dynamic adverse selection models with persistent private information and many types. Our approach reformulates the model into a numerically tractable structure that bypasses set-valued dynamic programming; we formally prove that, under verifiable conditions, this relaxation yields the solution to the original problem. The recast problem is solved via a parallelized value function iteration algorithm, where high-dimensional, nonlinear functions are approximated using Gaussian process regression combined with Bayesian active learning. We apply our framework to two previously intractable models: one with persistent hidden information involving up to ten types and another incorporating multiple persistent types and overreporting. Validation against known solutions and rigorous credibility measures confirms accuracy. Allowing overreporting significantly alters long-run contract outcomes, concentrating consumption away from extremes and smoothing utility promises over time.

title: Measuring Markets for Network Goods
abstract: Abstract Market definition is challenging in settings with network effects, where substitution patterns depend on changes in network size. We study these effects in the context of social media. We conduct an incentivized experiment comparing substitution in response to a proposed U.S. TikTok ban, in which all users simultaneously leave the app, with substitution when only a single user deactivates. We find substantially higher valuations of alternative social apps under a collective TikTok ban than under an individual TikTok deactivation. Mechanism evidence shows that both anticipated content-supply shifts and social coordination partly explain the wedge, with the relative importance of each channel varying across platforms. We then show that a collective time limit challenge, where peers jointly reduce TikTok and Instagram use, leads to more time spent on alternative social apps than has been observed in prior individual deactivation experiments. Together, our results suggest that individual-level substitution estimates can be an unreliable guide to market definition for network goods.

title: Returning network findings: An art gallery as a report-back in a rural community
Economic Conditions, Public Sentiment, and News Coverage: A Time-Series Analysis of Economic Agenda Dynamics in South Korea
abstract: Drawing on 23 years of economic news in South Korea, this study investigates how key economic indicators interact with the volume and tone of economic news, which can both shape and reflect public opinion, particularly the public’s economic sentiment. Time-series analyses revealed that unfavorable economic conditions, reflected in lower Stock Market Index and GDP growth rates as well as higher Consumer Price Index (CPI) and unemployment rates, were associated with greater news coverage of these topics in the subsequent month. The tone of news coverage was largely unrelated to economic indicators, suggesting that the overall news sentiment may not closely align with real-world economic conditions. Finally, the relationship between economic news and public sentiment was reciprocal rather than one-directional. Implications for economic journalism are discussed in detail.

title: The unintended consequences of using crisis discourse in school board deliberation to ban Critical Race Theory
abstract: This study examines how a Southern California school board employed crisis rhetoric to justify banning Critical Race Theory despite lacking a clear understanding of CRT’s content or implementation. Through discourse analysis of three board meetings, we found that while crisis framing initially mobilized support for a hardline anti-CRT resolution, it ultimately backfired when board members couldn’t define CRT or address enforcement challenges. Legal counsel’s interventions exposed contradictions in the crisis narrative, forcing the board to abandon their specific CRT definition and pass a watered-down resolution resembling standard nondiscrimination policy. The findings demonstrate how crisis discourse can undermine its own objectives when subjected to institutional scrutiny.

title: Governing sideways: Public-private partnerships and the politics of legitimacy in immigration detention
Relationship: Orientation, politics, ethics, and the idea and practice of self‐determination
abstract: Abstract First Nations people deeply value relational modes of organising politics, governance, and social order that do not feature in European‐derived political ordering or in dominant governance and policy scholarship. While Indigenous peoples have long sought equitable and respectful relationships in the context of forced colonial engagement, the settler state has largely refused relational engagement, accountability, and responsibility. Nonetheless, the configuration and practice of public policy contain possibilities for openness as well as closure. The concept and policy of self‐determination promise a relationship, while its conceptual vagueness and application in complexly ambiguous and unbalanced settler colonial conditions mean that its relational possibilities tend to be gradually and seriously eroded through settler solipsism and dominance. However, self‐determination continues to suggest possibilities for relating that recognise Indigenous political ordering and agency, and thus for ethical and effective forms of Indigenous policy. These and wider possibilities in Indigenous affairs policy can arise through practitioner vulnerability amid relational exchange in policy engagement and practice in response to the conceptual vagueness of self‐determination. Points for practitioners Relations are foundationally important for First Nations people and governance. Dominant public administration retains power by returning to itself rather than entering relationship with First Nations peoples and their systems. Awareness of the history and workings of dominant policy provides a foundation for seeing and engaging difference. Centring relations and relatedness can usefully inform the pursuit of just and effective forms of Indigenous policy. The personal vulnerability of governance practitioners opens possibilities for negotiation and relationship between Indigenous and European‐derived governance systems.

title: Fairness and equity in hybrid work: insights from the Ontario Public Service
abstract: Hybrid work—alternating between office and remote locations—has become the norm across Canadian public services, yet questions remain about whether it is implemented fairly. In 2022, the Ontario Public Service (OPS) mandated three in-office days per week, then announced in August 2025 that all employees must return to the office full-time. Based on qualitative content analysis of OPS subreddit data and semi-structured interviews with Indigenous and Black public servants, this paper explores perspectives on hybrid work, focusing on fairness and equity. It examines access to hybrid arrangements, consistency in implementation and enforcement, and impacts on recruitment and retention. Findings reveal concerns about unequal access, inconsistent enforcement, and disproportionate burdens on racialized public servants, along with implications for recruiting and retaining talent. Fairness and equity should therefore be central considerations in public sector hybrid work and return-to-office policies, given their impacts on recruiting and retaining a diverse government workforce.

title: The promises and pitfalls of AI in public service: a review of AI snake oil,
abstract: In their recent and first coauthored book, computer science scholars, Arvind Narayanan and Sayash Kapoor address promises and pitfalls with the “dawn of AI” (Narayanan and Kapoor 2024:3) amid the e...

title: Preferences for symbolic representation: identity, context, and selection of mental health providers
abstract: Citizens often favor public servants who resemble them demographically, but studies also indicate that this preference for symbolic representation may be unevenly distributed, shaped by individuals’ own lived experiences. Against this backdrop, we ask: in what contexts do citizens express a preference for symbolic representation? Focusing on publicly-supported mental health services as an empirical case, we field a conjoint experiment depicting provider information in a format informed by real-world listings. We find that preferences for symbolic representation are most apparent for social groups that have experienced significant marginalization—women, non-binary respondents, and people of color. Meanwhile, factors describing the organizational context in which services are provided—wait times and modality of service provision—do not appear to consistently moderate the preference for symbolic representation. These results underscore the importance of macro factors, such as systemic racism and sexism, in shaping individual preferences for bureaucratic representation.

title: From Civic Tech to DOGE : The Role of Tech Movements in the American Administrative State
abstract: ABSTRACT The second Trump administration saw the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), a group of outsider technologists given extraordinary power to pursue a massive downsizing of the federal government. They also displaced an alternative approach: the civic tech movement. Civic tech for government applies technology, data, and human‐centered design to improve policy implementation, fueled by prosocial motivation, promising to increase state capacity in a way that centers attention on public service clients. This article explains the origins of civic tech for government in the US setting, its core values, and evolution. The movement grew in prominence and influence from 2014 to 2024, making steady inroads into government but never gaining sufficient power to implement profound change. The conflicting origins, philosophy, and power between civic tech and DOGE offer contrasting visions for how tech can reshape the American administrative state.

title: From co-production to value co-creation: NGOs as catalysts of cyclical public value in rural China
abstract: This study explores how NGOs facilitate the transition from co-production to value co-creation in rural ecological governance through a case study of the Guanba River Basin, China. Drawing on qualitative evidence and social network analysis, it reveals that NGOs’ front-loaded participation in problem framing, planning, and rule formation creates institutional and relational foundations for collaborative governance. Beyond boundary-spanning roles, NGOs function as institutional intermediaries that reshape governance arrangements and enhance local capacity. Value co-creation emerges through institutional embeddedness, actor absorption, and adaptive governance within a recursive ecosystem. This study provides an institutionally grounded explanation of how externally facilitated co-production evolves into locally sustained value co-creation.

title: Welfare State Convergence or Robustness? Comparing Nonprofit Marketization Patterns Across Belgium, Sweden and the United States
abstract: New Public Management (NPM) reforms are argued to have induced welfare state convergence in public sector organizing. However, this argument has been examined mainly at the discourse and decision-making level, leaving the adoption of NPM reforms at the organizational level underexplored. Taking non-profit marketization as a case, this study draws on survey data from non-profits across three welfare states to examine the extent to which (a) different marketization patterns appear and (b) these patterns are explained by contextual differences. Findings suggest that welfare state robustness, not convergence, is the superior frame of reference at the organizational level.

title: Brake or bridge? The dual impact of clientelism on hospital corporatization in Iran
How Citizens Perceive Public Service Performance: Do Reference Points Really Matter?
Institutional complicity under platform economy: welfare misalignment and precarity among platform workers in China
abstract: The expansion of social protection for platform workers has been widely promoted as a response to precarity in the gig economy, yet formal inclusion does not always produce participation or effective protection. This article examines why contributory welfare arrangements remain difficult to use for platform-based food delivery workers in China. Drawing on 20 in-depth interviews with riders and station managers in Chengdu and Shenyang, we identify two intertwined dimensions: welfare misalignment and platform precarity. Volatile earnings make current contribution costs especially salient, while uncertainty about transfer procedures and future entitlements can strengthen workers’ preference for immediate income. Algorithmic management also encourages individualized coping, leaving much of the management of risk with workers themselves. We conceptualize these interactions as institutional complicity, a contingent, non-intentional relation between platform governance and welfare institutions mediated by workers’ adaptive strategies. Within Chengdu, lower out-of-pocket costs were associated with greater willingness to participate, although the qualitative comparison does not isolate subsidy effects from occupational position. The study shows how formal inclusion, affordability, and effective protection can diverge under fragmented employment and highlights contribution costs, transfer uncertainty, and fragmented responsibility as key areas for institutional adaptation.

title: Precarious housing in the aftermath of the financial crisis: protecting owners and selling-out renters
Searching for the social model of health in policy: health in all policies, or wellbeing?
abstract: Abstract International policy efforts to systematise the consideration of health outcomes across social and economic policy – the ‘Health in All Policies’ (HiAP) approach – have faced practical, relational and political difficulties. Meanwhile, new economic policy agendas focused on ‘inclusive growth’ or ‘wellbeing’ may provide an alternative route to improving population health by acting on upstream determinants. This research uses a frame analysis of thirty social, economic and health policy documents, and semi-structured interviews with thirty-four policy actors, to explore conceptualisations of ‘health’ in two devolved policy bodies in the UK – Greater Manchester Combined Authority and the Scottish Government – with declared interests in these economic agendas. Interviews revealed that social and economic policy actors conceptualised ‘health’ narrowly as biomedical, physical illness, and as shorthand for ‘health policy’. Further, some of these participants expressed resentment about health policy, while interviewees across teams expressed scepticism about HiAP. In contrast, ‘wellbeing’ was widely conceptualised similarly to the social model of health, included mental health, and was supported as a plausible common cause. This research suggests that a clearer conceptual distinction between ‘healthcare’ and ‘wellbeing’ – representing the medical and social models of health respectively – may support policy efforts to promote population health.

title: Avoidant rationality and institutional entrenchment in divided societies: evidence from a conjoint experiment in Lebanon
Policy Thresholds for Effective Integration: Does Political Stability Shape the Sustainable Development Gains of Regional Trade Integration in Africa?
abstract: ABSTRACT Africa faces rising political tensions and uneven progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), raising concerns over whether the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) can deliver sustainable development gains. Using data on 42 African countries from 2014 to 2023, this paper examines whether political stability conditioned the impact of regional trade integration on sustainable development in Africa. The study uses dynamic panel threshold regression, supplemented by a two‐way fixed‐effects interaction model. The findings established minimum political stability thresholds of 33.47% for regional trade integration (RTI) and 38.26% for intraregional trade shares (IRTS) to yield sustainable development gains. Additionally, the results revealed strong persistence of sustainable development, especially in politically unstable environments. Thus, maintaining a more politically stable environment mitigates the sustainable development trade‐offs associated with trade integration in Africa. The study adds to the political economy literature by establishing the political stability thresholds for effective integration in Africa. Related Articles Ceesay, Almamo, and Antun Mardiyanta. 2026. “From Policy Reform to Strategic Governance Reconfiguration: Pathways to Sustainable Development in Africa.” Politics & Policy 54(4): e70165. https://doi.org/10.1111/polp.70165 . Adegboye, Alex, Kofo Adegboye, Uwalomwa Uwuigbe, Stephen Ojeka, and Eyitemi Fasanu. 2023. “Taxation, democracy, and inequality in Sub‐Saharan Africa: Relevant linkages for sustainable development goals.” Politics & Policy 51(4): 696‐722. https://doi.org/10.1111/polp.12547 . Villanueva Ulfgard, Rebecka. 2019. “Mexico’s Struggle with Development between Global Compromises and National Development Plans.” Politics & Policy 47, no. 1: 50–78. https://doi.org/10.1111/polp.12288 . JEL Classification: F13, F15, F63, F68, Q01

title: Trump's Revisionism and the Liberal Economic Order: Disruptive Coercion, Roving Banditry, and International Disorder From Within
abstract: ABSTRACT Scholars have paid limited attention to exploring international disorder emanating from the disorderly conduct of the dominant power. The United States, under Donald Trump, is actively undermining the essential elements of the American‐led liberal economic order—commercial openness, a network of institutions and regimes, and nondiscriminatory provision of essential public goods—that the United States created after the Second World War. How can we conceptualize and explain such a situation in which the dominant power actively undermines (from within) the very order that it helped establish in the first place? While employing Olson's conceptual frame of “roving banditry”—also characterized by “coercive leadership” and “international disorder”—this study argues that Trump's international conduct, especially in his second term, should be conceptualized as roving banditry because Trump coercively extracts private profits and contributes little to the system's overall functioning due to his minimal stakes in the long‐term sustenance of the system. This is demonstrated by Trump's practice of rent seeking and private extraction through discriminatory protectionism, economic retaliation, and transactional trade deals that bypass traditional multilateral bodies. While taking Trump's 5 years in office as an empirical reference point, the study further argues that Trump, like a roving bandit who practices coercion, weaponizes interdependence, bypasses systemic rules, and denies any contribution to public goods while coercively undermining and abandoning the system's essential components at will. Related Articles Moynihan, D. 2025. “Trump, Personalism, and US Administrative Capacity.” Politics & Policy 53, no. 4: e70059. https://doi.org/10.1111/polp.70059 . Merry, M. K. 2022. “Trump's Tweets as Policy Narratives: Constructing the Immigration Issue via Social Media.” Politics & Policy 50, no. 4: 752–772. https://doi.org/10.1111/polp.12487 . Garrett, T. M. 2020. “The Security Apparatus, Federal Magistrate Courts, and Detention Centers as Simulacra: The Effects of Trump's Zero Tolerance Policy on Migrants and Refugees in the Rio Grande Valley.” Politics & Policy 48, no. 2: 372–395. https://doi.org/10.1111/polp.12348 .

title: Reverse‐Diffusion of Policy in Multilevel Governance: The Dynamics of South Korea's Lonely Death Ordinances
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines the diffusion of local ordinances addressing lonely deaths in South Korea and introduces the concept of reverse‐diffusion of policy—a process in which local innovations diffuse upward to higher levels of government, become institutionalised and subsequently diffuse downward to late‐adopting jurisdictions. Using Cox Proportional Hazards Models and Kaplan–Meier analysis across 243 local governments (2007–2021), the study finds that ordinance adoption is shaped by a combination of social problems, leadership capacity, communal identity and intergovernmental diffusion mechanisms. Basic local governments adopted earlier and more gradually, whereas metropolitan governments exhibited later but more concentrated adoption patterns, suggesting sequential upward and downward processes following the enactment of the 2020 Lonely Death Act. The findings highlight the dynamic and multidirectional nature of diffusion within multilevel governance systems, offering empirical support for reverse‐diffusion and demonstrating how diffusion dynamics evolve over time during the process of policy institutionalisation.

title: Beyond Beveridge and Bismarck: Revising the Typology of Pension Systems for the 21st Century
abstract: ABSTRACT Pension systems are a major part of welfare states which have been under reform pressures across advanced economies. Established typologies of pension systems stress the difference between Bismarckian social insurance and Beveridgean basic security principles in their historical development. During the last decades, multiple reforms due to population ageing and fiscal challenges have cut back on public pensions, raised retirement ages and promoted pension privatization and financialization, reshaping the pension landscape. Reviewing major dimensions with key indicators of pension systems, our comparative cluster analysis studies the similarities and differences across 31 OECD countries. A typology of at least four clusters describes the main types of today's pension systems: Dominant Public, Hybrid Social Insurance, Mature Multi‐pillar and Residual Public systems. While two common types derive from either the pure Bismarckian model or the Beveridgean basic security with hybrid private tiers, they no longer constitute the majority of cases. The Hybrid Social Insurance model goes beyond Bismarckian principles, whereas the Residual Public is still relatively rudimentary. Overall, past reforms towards multi‐pillarization and financialization have altered pension systems, though these are far from converging, while ongoing reforms could be more impactful for future generations than current retirees.

title: Term limits and corruption: Evidence from a reelection reform in Mexico
The Evolution of Committee Agenda Control in the Antebellum U.S. House of Representatives
abstract: Gatekeeping is viewed as an essential element of committee power in the U.S. Congress, but its emergence is not well understood. The House of Representatives moved to a system of standing committees by 1825. We investigated whether that move gave committees gatekeeping power prior to the Civil War or layered committees atop the earlier Jeffersonian system centering consequential legislative action on the floor. Using original data from the House Journal , we find evidence of institutional layering, with elements of gatekeeping – jurisdictional clarity, positive agenda setting, and negative agenda setting – developing unevenly and largely through changes in the behavior of members rather than formal reform of the House to empower its committees.

title: Attention to the Macroeconomy
abstract: Abstract We measure which economic topics are top of mind using quarterly German household and firm panels from 2020 to 2024, a period that spans the post-pandemic inflation surge and the subsequent disinflation. With these data, we study potential determinants and consequences of having inflation top of mind. In line with goal-directed attention, the likelihood that inflation is top of mind rises with proxies for its true payoff relevance. At the same time, prior experiences predict whether respondents have inflation and energy prices top of mind conditional on a large set of controls for payoff relevance, and this relationship strengthens when the environment becomes more inflationary. Having inflation top of mind predicts stronger increases in information acquisition and inflation expectations over the shock period. At odds with goal-optimality, having inflation top of mind is associated with expectations further away from multiple ex-ante benchmarks. Finally, both key determinants of having inflation top of mind—payoff relevance and prior experiences—are associated with stronger shifts of expectations away from these benchmarks over the shock period.

title: The End of Oil
abstract: Abstract Even as global oil demand has increased in recent years, it is plausible to envision scenarios in which clean energy technologies or climate policies drive demand to essentially zero by the century’s end. This paper asks what such a demand decline, when anticipated, might mean for global oil supply. One possibility is a “green paradox”: producers accelerate extraction. However, because extraction requires durable capital investments, the opposite may occur: producers reduce their investment rate, decreasing extraction. To evaluate the relative strengths of these opposing mechanisms, I develop a model of global oil supply that incorporates both, among other industry features. For model inputs with the strongest empirical support, both effects are modest, with disinvestment typically outweighing the green paradox. In order for the green paradox to substantially increase cumulative global oil extraction, investments must have short time horizons, and producers’ discount rates must be less than 4% real.

title: Demographics, Wealth, and Global Imbalances in the Twenty-First Century
abstract: Abstract We use a sufficient statistic approach to quantify the general equilibrium effects of population aging on the returns to wealth, wealth accumulation, and global imbalances. Combining population forecasts with household survey data from 25 countries, we measure the compositional effect of aging: how a changing age distribution affects wealth-to-GDP, holding the age profiles of wealth and labor income fixed. In a baseline overlapping generations model this statistic, in conjunction with cross-sectional information and two standard macro parameters, pins down general equilibrium outcomes. Since the compositional effect is positive, large, and heterogeneous across countries, our model predicts that population aging will lower returns to wealth, increase wealth-to-GDP ratios, and widen global imbalances through the twenty-first century. These conclusions extend to a richer model in which bequests, individual savings, and the tax-and-transfer system all respond to demographic change.

title: Entry and Profits in an Aging Economy: The Role of Consumer Inertia
abstract: Abstract Over the past four decades, the U.S. economy has seen a decline in the share of young firms alongside a rise in the profit share of GDP. This paper explores how population aging contributes to these twin trends through a demand-side channel. The core hypothesis is that younger households exhibit lower consumer inertia—a tendency to stick with previously chosen products—than older households. As demand shifts toward more inertial consumers, entry becomes harder, incumbents raise markups, and market share tilts toward larger firms. To quantify this mechanism, I develop and calibrate a firm dynamics model with overlapping generations of consumers who differ in their degree of inertia. Using detailed micro data, I show that younger households are significantly less inertial. The model implies that population aging accounts for 20%–30% of the observed decline in young firms and rise in profits. Reduced-form evidence across U.S. states and product categories supports the model’s predictions.

title: Filling in the gaps: Digital platform economies and the agglomeration of urban consumption amenities
Insiders, outsiders, and involuntary unemployment: Sexual harassment exacerbates gender inequality
Policy interventions to mitigate the long-run costs of Brexit
abstract: This paper examines the long-term macroeconomic impacts of Brexit on the UK economy employing a dynamic general equilibrium model that incorporates endogenous firm entry, price markups and market competition. By integrating the trade frictions introduced by Brexit, the model explains how increased trade costs have altered firm behaviour, market structure, and broader economic performance. We assess a range of policy responses, from theoretically optimal but practically difficult tax-subsidy schemes, to more realistic measures aimed at reducing firm entry barriers, encouraging private and public investment, and subsidising labour costs. Our findings underscore the critical role of policies that can most directly influence firm creation, investment, and competition in addressing the structural challenges Brexit has introduced.

title: When Monetary Policy for Financial Stability Backfires: Communication with Strategic Banks
abstract: We develop a model in which the central bank incorporates financial stability concerns into its monetary policy and communication decisions, while systemic banks strategically choose portfolios to influence policy. Because fully responding to economic shocks would generate policy surprises that threaten bank stability, the central bank underreacts to those shocks, consistent with the Federal Reserve’s response during the 2023 banking crisis. Anticipating this accommodation, banks tilt their portfolios to increase the financial-stability costs of rate hikes, pulling monetary policy toward lower rates while giving the central bank an incentive to announce higher future rates than it expects to set. Financial stability concerns can therefore backfire, creating a novel responsiveness–credibility trade-off: the more the central bank accommodates banks’ exposures ex post, the less credible its forward guidance becomes ex ante, making it harder for banks to align their portfolios with future policy and leaving them more exposed to policy surprises. Even when society values financial stability, it benefits from appointing a central banker who places less weight on it. Paradoxically, even banks may prefer such a central banker when the benefits of more credible guidance outweigh the loss of policy influence.

title: Reserve Matching with Thresholds
Discussion of “Human Capital as a Driver of Automation: Theory and Evidence from China's College Expansion”
A Quantile Model of Firm Investment
abstract: ABSTRACT Are firms risk averse? We propose a dynamic model of firm investment under uncertainty that captures firms' risk attitudes through quantile preferences. The firm maximizes its present value, defined as current profits and investment plus the discounted value of the ‐quantile of its value next period. The model implies that the firm's investment policy equates the marginal cost of capital with the ‐quantile of the discounted present value of future marginal profits. Therefore, investment depends directly on the firm's risk attitude. Empirical estimations using the Euler equation derived from the quantile investment model reveal evidence of downside risk aversion.

title: Discussion of “Connectivity and Selective Rural Migration”
Curricular-credential decoupling: how schools respond to college and career readiness policy
Simulation Study of the Decision Logic for 95% Upper Confidence Limit Calculations Applied in ProUCL 5.2
Can Knowledge Counteract Conflict? A Partial Replication Study of PFAS Science Communication
Communicating and Constructing Risk: Government and Public Interactions in Responding to Heat Risks
Propagation Mechanisms of Security Risks in Public Data Circulation via Inter‐Risk Dependencies: A DSM‐Based Network Analysis
Regional Variance‐Based Sensitivity Analysis and a Study of Regional Equifinality
The Influence of Different Types of Trust, Perceived Objectivity, and Perceived Risk on the Preferred Involvement of AI for Subjective and Objective Tasks
Toward AI‐Assisted Methodological Evaluations of Health Risk Analyses Using Diverse Types of Evidence
Optimal Combination of Measures for Flood Risk Mitigation Within Probabilistic and Uncertain Situations
The Democratic Cost of Pursuing Virality: A Study into Parliamentary Communications
abstract: The transformation of parliamentarians into media producers has heightened concerns about emerging forms of political communication. This mixed-methods paper examines the strategies they employ to enhance their digital presence. Based on in-depth interviews, it shows that Brazilian parliamentarians believe that social media penalize them for posting about congressional matters, reporting that content about legislative work and constituency services receives little engagement online. Conversely, they view the production of antagonistic content and alignment with news cycles as essential to maintaining an engaging social media presence. A computational analysis of 4,5 million posts on Facebook, Instagram, and Twitter supports these evaluations: posts about congressional matters are associated with lower engagement metrics, while the use of antagonistic language increases them. The analysis further discusses pathways through which visibility is sustained at the intersection of platform incentives and communicative practices. In sum, this mixed-methods study demonstrates that the mediatization of politics has created perverse incentives for parliamentarians to downplay congressional activity and prioritize confrontations on social media, weakening accountability in ways that may resonate far beyond Brazil.

title: Unmaking inequality in the age of anti-wokeism: Power abuse, sexualised violence and the struggle for safeguarding in media and cultural industries
abstract: This study examines why sexualised discrimination and violence persist in the cultural and media industries despite the momentum of the #MeToo movement. Drawing on 58 expert interviews across five regulatory levels in Germany’s performing arts and music sectors, the study analyses stakeholder assessments of safeguarding measures and priorities for reform. Although policy development has accelerated, findings show that implementation remains fragmented, largely voluntary, and weakly institutionalised. Structural vulnerabilities—project-based employment, informal gatekeeping, and limited independent reporting pathways—continue to undermine accountability and protection. Interviewees emphasise the need for binding standards, independent complaint mechanisms, anti-retaliation safeguards, professional training and funding conditionality. Positioning these findings within an increasingly polarised political climate marked by anti-feminist and anti-‘woke’ backlash, we argue that institutionalising safeguarding in cultural labour is not only an organisational task but a struggle over normative legitimacy and democratic cultural governance.

title: The impact of the bureaucratic environment on public service digitalization
abstract: Research on public-sector digitalization has traditionally focused on macro-level societal, economic and governance conditions, as well as individual-level challenges faced by civil servants in implementing digital public services. Yet it has overlooked the institutional incentives and constraints embedded in bureaucratic environments, and how cross-national variation in these traits shapes digital transformation. Our study addresses this gap by identifying how core traditional Weberian characteristics of bureaucracies comparatively affect public service digitalization. Drawing on cross-national datasets covering 193 countries over 22 years, we examine the effects of bureaucratic professionalization, bureaucratic closedness and the adoption of managerial performance-based practices on the production of digital public services. Our findings show that more professional bureaucracies alone do not necessarily lead to better digitalization, but rather this occurs when such bureaucracies include more ‘open’ elements in their structures, including more open hiring practices and side entries of specialized personnel.

title: The pandemic and the shift in social dynamics: how well do existing theoretical frameworks explain volunteering during COVID-19?
abstract: This study examines how well existing theoretical frameworks explain formal volunteering amid a public health crisis, focusing on dominant status, social networks, role constraints, and risk perceptions. Grounded in these four theoretical frameworks, the study tests whether the relationships between sociodemographic characteristics and volunteering remained stable or changed during and after COVID-19. The findings reveal that socioeconomic polarization during the pandemic restricted the applicability of dominant status theory to only the highest social strata, whereas the role of social networks remained robust. They also suggest that role constraints from paid work during COVID-19 placed an additional burden on volunteering. However, sociodemographic factors associated with higher risk perception showed no significant difference between during and after COVID-19, likely because virtual volunteering offered a safer alternative for participation.

title: The Right Key for the Right Lock: How Government Response Methods and Demand Types Affect Citizen Satisfaction
abstract: ABSTRACT Faced with diverse and complex demands from citizens, the government has consistently sought ways to enhance its ability to respond. Metaphorically, citizens' needs can be viewed as locks, and the government requires keys to unlock them. Artificial intelligence (AI) is an innovative new key offering a fresh paradigm for unlocking the door to high citizen satisfaction. Drawing on government responsiveness theory, this study applies a 2 × 3 between‐subjects survey experiment to explore the impact of government response methods (traditional responses, AI‐enabled responses) and citizen demand types (consultation, complaint/help‐seeking, suggestions) on citizen satisfaction. Findings show that AI‐enabled government responses significantly increase citizen satisfaction compared to traditional approaches. Among demand types, consultation yields the highest satisfaction, while suggestion results in the lowest. Further, the satisfaction level is significantly influenced by the interaction effect between response method and demand type. Perceived fairness mediates the relationship between government responses and citizen satisfaction, with citizen participation experience having a moderating effect. This study offers new insights into increasing citizen satisfaction from the perspective of government responses. It reveals the content‐dependent nature of AI‐enabled government responses, helping the government create unique AI response strategies and enhance digital interaction with citizens.

title: Routledge Handbook on Crisis, Polycrisis, and Public Administration. By KimMoloney, Gloria J.Billingsley, Bok GyoJeong, PabloSanabria‐Pulido, Tonya E.Thornton, and EricZeemering, New York, New York: Routledge, 2025. 390 pp. $280.00 (hardback) ( eBook $58.39). ISBN: 978‐1‐00‐333363‐0
abstract: The only constant in life is change, and for public administrators, responding to crisis and polycrisis has become the norm.Effective crisis management is now an essential skill for public managers, as even a slight delay in response, miscommunication, or insufficient skill can result in the loss of life or property.Recent scholarly discussions at the ASPA Conference highlighted that the last period of relative normalcy was in 2019, prior to the COVID-19 pandemic, and there is skepticism about whether life will ever feel normal again.While there may be different perspectives on this, it is evident that we will never go back, and while types of crises will change, they are here to stay.Therefore, we must plan, prepare, and respond to them better.The Routledge Handbook on Crisis, Polycrisis and Public Administration (Moloney et al. 2025) brings together research, reviews, reflections, and global perspectives on crises from around the world.This review begins with a summary of the book, outlines its main arguments, discusses its limitations, and assesses its contribution to public administration scholarship and practice.Although the conceptual birth of the book may be rooted in the global pandemic, make no mistake: this book is not all about COVID-19.The book starts with a broader-than-expected definition of crisis.Beyond the expected natural disasters, such as hurricanes, storms, earthquakes, and wildfires, the list of crises also includes an aging workforce, cybersecurity, debt, unemployment, rising crime rates, hunger, domestic violence, and so on.This expanded perspective is both refreshing and thoughtprovoking, as many of these persistent and complex issues have traditionally not been classified as crises.In public administration, these problems are called wicked problems (Rittel and Webber 1973), and there is a tendency to accept that they are here to stay and that we have to focus on managing rather than solving them, as they do not have a true or false solution but rather better or worse ones.The book places some of these issues under the umbrella of crisis and polycrisis and suggests analyzing them through the lens of crises.Furthermore, the book provides global perspectives by covering crises from around the world and has a wide and rich representation of the United States, Germany, Ireland, the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, Ghana, South Korea, South Africa, Colombia, El Salvador, Ecuador, Argentina, and Mexico, as well as islands such as Mauritius, Reunion Island, and Madagascar.Methodologically, the book employs qualitative, quantitative, and mixed-methods research, including single-case studies, comparative analyses across several countries, and multistate surveys.

title: Making Water Investible : Development Banking, Regulatory Governance, and the Institutional Production of Sanitation Infrastructure in Brazil
abstract: ABSTRACT Why did long‐horizon private investment in Brazilian water and sanitation expand after 2016 despite fragmented authority and persistent political contestation? This article places the Brazilian Development Bank (BNDES) inside, rather than outside, the credible‐commitment framework. It argues that the bank operated as a credibility intermediary: it assembled service territories at investible scale, financed and coordinated project preparation, translated statutory goals into comparable contracts, and linked concessions to long‐term finance. These functions complemented courts, legislatures, the national standard‐setting role of the National Water and Basic Sanitation Agency (ANA), and post‐award supervision by infranational regulators. Process tracing of laws, concession documents, regulatory instruments, auction records, corporate filings, and attributable investor statements shows how this architecture was repeated across the Temer, Bolsonaro, and Lula administrations, albeit under different political framings. The mechanism is sequence‐sensitive but not universally necessary: Chile demonstrates an alternative route through regional utilities and a central regulator, while Colombia illustrates the continuing constraints of fragmented provision. The article also distinguishes investibility from legitimacy. Financial and contractual discipline can make commitments more legible to investors, but it neither replaces public‐law oversight nor resolves disputes over affordability, participation, and the human right to water.

title: Using gender to choose: voter decision-making in low-information elections
abstract: While a growing body of work suggests that voters no longer penalise women at the ballot box in many institutional contexts, less is known about how gender shapes choice when voters have little else to go on. In this paper, we ask how gender is used as a cue in low-information electoral environments, and whether support for women is driven by gender itself or gender-based expectations about what candidates will do in office. To address this question, we field three novel conjoint experiments in Great Britain that vary whether voters are shown politicians’ descriptive characteristics, their policy priorities, or both. We find a substantial preference for women when gender is the only information available, but this preference disappears once voters are given even minimal information about what candidates care about. Our research contributes to ongoing debates about descriptive and substantive representation, showing how the role of gender in vote choice depends on the information voters have available.

title: Inhibitory Institutions: The Tradeoffs of Public Goods Quantity and Quality
abstract: Governments frequently invest in public goods that citizens don’t want, yet voters hesitate to punish politicians who build useless or corrupt projects. I introduce the concept of inhibitory institutions—rules that allow state or societal actors to review, obstruct, or veto public investments before they are approved—and argue that they improve public goods quality at the cost of reduced quantity. This quantity-quality tradeoff binds most tightly when bureaucrats enjoy career autonomy from politicians and political competition encourages institutional enforcement. I illustrate the tradeoff through case studies of metro projects in Bogotá and Lima, where divergent institutional conditions led to contrasting outcomes for the quantity and quality of construction. Quantitative evidence from local infrastructure projects in Colombia suggests that political alliances to bypass inhibitory rules increase spending but reduce quality. At a time when observers want to cut procedural checks to get things built, this article underscores the risks for what gets built.

title: Do Political Discussion Partners Share Policy Priorities and Policy Frames?
abstract: Abstract To understand politics, people often rely on political discussion. Among the many ways that discussion may shape political perceptions, one possible mechanism is by promoting a shared sense of priorities— which issues are important. A second mechanism is by framing how people think about important issues. We examine these potential mechanisms by answering the descriptive question: Do policy priorities and policy frames tend to co-occur within political discussion networks? We answer this question by reanalyzing the 1996 Indianapolis-St. Louis Study in which participants—and their discussion partners—described the most important problem facing the United States in their own words. We show that the modal outcome is for people to hold both different priorities and different frames than their discussion partners. This finding stands in contrast to network scholarship suggesting that homophily is so often the norm. Yet we also show that people disproportionately share the same policy priorities as their discussion partners, and adopt the same frames in thinking about policy topics, especially when their policy priorities match. This finding suggests that some policy priorities are so embedded in certain frames of thinking that the topic and frame stay linked even as the topic may diffuse through a social network.

title: Credible Prejudice? When and Why Mainstream Party Adoption of Far-Right Rhetoric Weakens Anti-Prejudice Norms
abstract: Abstract This article examines whether mainstream political parties adopt prejudiced rhetoric from the far right and how such shifts shape anti-prejudice norms. Building on existing work, I argue that mainstream parties are particularly influential in weakening anti-prejudice norms because they possess greater normative credibility and legitimacy than far-right parties. Empirically, the article combines cross-national observational evidence with two preregistered survey experiments in Germany and Denmark. Using parliamentary speeches from six European countries between 1994 and 2022, I document rising mainstream party anti-Muslim rhetoric and its association with weaker norms against holding far-right views. The experiments provide causal evidence for the argument. In Germany, exposure to prejudiced rhetoric weakens anti-prejudice norms, but only when voiced by mainstream parties, rather than far right parties, likely due to their normative credibility and legitimacy. In Denmark, comparable effects are absent, consistent with decades of mainstream accommodation having already normalized such rhetoric. The experimental results also show that rhetoric targeting Muslims weakens anti-prejudice norms toward out-groups more broadly, suggesting spillover effects. These findings have important implications for future scholarship: when mainstream parties adopt prejudiced rhetoric from the far right, they affect not only electoral politics, but also the broader social norm environment.

title: Political theology reloaded: Postliberalism and the spectre of Carl Schmitt's eschatology
Neoliberal restructuring, climate de-adaptation, and urban infrastructure failure in Porto Alegre, Brazil
Territorial justice after “green colonialism” in the Quilombo do Cumbe, Brazil
How Bots Threaten Democracy by Misrepresenting Actors and Ideas: The Case of the 2022 Swedish Election
abstract: ABSTRACT Online democratic discourse faces threats from diverse forms of information manipulation, including disinformation campaigns and foreign influence operations. Among these, political bots represent a covert and scalable threat, infiltrating online debates, amplifying select viewpoints, and distorting perceptions of public opinion. This article investigates the scale and nature of political bot activity on Twitter (now X) leading up to the 2022 Swedish general election (August 1–September 11), estimating that over one‐fifth (22%) of election‐related content was generated by likely automated accounts. To assess how such activity impacts democratic deliberation, the article develops and applies “misrepresentation” as an analytical framework for identifying the artificial manipulation of perceived support or opposition toward political parties and candidates, as well as political viewpoints and interests. The “misrepresentation” framework offers a methodology for assessing how bot tactics undermine democratic deliberation. Accounts showing signs of bot‐like behavior disproportionately targeted the Social Democratic‐led “red‐green" coalition with coordinated negative messaging and amplified anti‑immigration viewpoints. These dynamics disrupted principles of democratic deliberation— proportionality , transparency, plurality , and empowerment —within the Swedish online public sphere. The article demonstrates how inauthentic participation challenges high‐trust societies by jeopardizing their democratic foundation, advancing the understanding of digital manipulation tactics in the Nordic context.

title: Voters’ perceptions of ideologically inconsistent parties
abstract: There is a growing consensus in party politics that new fault lines are emerging, and scholars increasingly characterise competition as multidimensional. In a multidimensional space, parties can adopt varied positions, combining left/progressive stances on some issues with right/conservative ones on others. Earlier work found that parties combining such positions – what this article refers to as ideological inconsistency – receive less support than ideologically consistent parties. Yet insights are lacking into why inconsistent parties receive lower support. To address this, this article uses original surveys in ten countries, asking respondents and experts to position parties on economic, social, and cultural issues. Results show that citizens are somewhat less informed about the positions of inconsistent parties. The article also finds that when citizens perceive a party as more inconsistent, they like it less. This effect is not explained by proximity considerations or party type, suggesting a general distaste for ideological inconsistency.

title: Top income taxation: Efficiency, social welfare and the Laffer curve
abstract: This paper develops a structural framework for analyzing top income taxation and applies it to six decades of U.S. tax history and to eight other advanced economies. The paper derives explicit expressions for top-bracket tax revenue and total excess burden across the full range of tax rates, while preserving local consistency with the sufficient-statistics approach of Saez (2001) . Applied to the United States, the analysis implies that the current excess burden of the top federal tax bracket is $101 billion and that raising the top marginal tax rate to its revenue-maximizing level of 72 percent would increase annual revenue by $111 billion, given a taxable income elasticity of 0.25. The current tax rate is lower than what is consistent with a purely utility-based notion of social welfare. By contrast, Nordic countries and the United States in earlier decades appear to have operated at tax rates exceeding revenue-maximizing levels.

title: Prosecutor politics: The impact of election cycles on criminal sentencing in the era of rising incarceration
abstract: I investigate how political incentives affect the behavior of district attorneys (DAs). I develop a theoretical model that predicts DAs will increase sentencing intensity in an election period compared to the period prior. To empirically test this prediction, I compile one of the most comprehensive datasets to date on the political careers of all district attorneys in office during the steepest rise in incarceration in U.S. history (roughly 1986-2006). Using quasi-experimental methods, I find causal evidence that being in a DA election year increases total admissions per capita and total months sentenced per capita. I estimate that the election year effects on admissions are akin to moving 0.85 standard deviations along the distribution of DA behavior within state (e.g., going from the 50th to 80th percentile in sentencing intensity). I find evidence that election effects are larger (1) when DA elections are contested, (2) in Republican counties, and (3) in the southern United States--all these factors are consistent with the perspective that election effects arise from political incentives influencing DAs. Further, I find that district attorney election effects decline over the period 1986-2006, in tandem with U.S. public opinion softening regarding criminal punishment. These findings suggest DA behavior may respond to voter preferences--in particular to public sentiment regarding the harshness of the court system.

title: Fostering institutional trust and organ donation: Evidence from a randomized informational intervention in Tunisia
abstract: Organ transplantation saves lives and improves the quality of life of patients who would otherwise depend on costly and invasive treatments. The technology is becoming available in low- and middle-income countries, but the gap between the demand for and the supply of organ transplants remains large. In a randomized controlled trial at a Tunisian university, we evaluate an expert-led intervention designed to inform about organ donation and strengthen trust in medical institutions. The intervention consists of a short video testimonial from a heart transplant survivor, a presentation led by a medical doctor and a short Q&A session. We find that the intervention significantly increases deceased donor registration, with suggestive evidence of positive spillover effects on the control group. The survey data provides little support for changes in attitudes and social expectations as potential mechanisms. Instead, it reveals large and statistically significant increases in medical and legal knowledge, religious beliefs supportive of donation, and institutional trust among treated students. Finally, we show that treatment effects on organ donor registration are driven by male students and those whose families likely support organ donation. Targeting older segments of the population may further increase the impact and cost-effectiveness of this intervention.

title: Media Slant is Contagious
abstract: Abstract This paper examines the diffusion of media slant. We document the influence of Fox News Channel (FNC) on the partisan slant of local newspapers in the U.S. over the years 1995-2008. We measure the political slant of local newspapers by scaling the news article texts to Republicans’ and Democrats’ speeches in Congress. Using channel positioning as an instrument for viewership, we find that higher FNC viewership causes local newspapers to adopt more right-wing slant. The effect emerges gradually, only several years after FNC’s introduction, mirroring the channel’s growing influence on voting behaviour. A main driver of the shift in newspaper slant appears to be a change in local political preferences.

title: Oil prices and inequality
abstract: This paper provides a unified framework to understand the effect of oil price changes on the dynamics of consumption, income and wealth inequality. Using data on macroeconomic aggregates, oil prices, and inequality metrics, we first employ a structural vector autoregressive model to show that an increase in oil prices leads to a persistent rise in income and wealth inequality. To understand these dynamics, we then solve an incomplete market model with aggregate oil price shocks, and calibrate the model to the US data. We find that when oil serves as both a consumption good and a production input, positive oil price shocks increase inequality. While the initial rise in inequality is driven by oil-induced stagflation, which forces poorer households to deplete more of their wealth to cover basic consumption, the quicker rebound in interest rates compared to the slower recovery in wages explains why inequality remains persistently elevated.

title: Media rituals and cultural authorization: Negotiating representational legitimacy in the Super Bowl halftime show
abstract: National media rituals are key sites where cultural representation and legitimacy are publicly negotiated. This article uses cultural authorization to explain how institutions, media discourse, and mediated representations of audience and community reception define who can legitimately represent the nation within these events. Drawing on symbolic boundary theory and media ritual scholarship, the study analyzes coverage of Bad Bunny’s selection as the Super Bowl LX Halftime Show headliner. Using qualitative media discourse analysis (October 2025 to February 2026), the article identifies four recurring dynamics: institutional authorization through market legitimacy, boundary contestation through authenticity claims, counter-ritual formation, and community recognition. These dynamics show how media rituals transform programming decisions into struggles over national representation. The article contributes by specifying cultural authorization as a mechanism through which symbolic boundaries become publicly consequential in mass-mediated events. It argues that media rituals function as authorization infrastructures where market logics, political discourse, and mediated reception claims shape the terms of legitimate representation.

title: Cross-Source Corroboration and the Dynamics of Local Government Attention: Evidence from an Emerging Policy Field
abstract: Abstract Governments receive simultaneous cues from superior authorities, peer jurisdictions, and societal audiences, yet existing research rarely explains how they decide which cues warrant scarce agenda space. We develop a cross-source corroboration perspective on governmental attention and argue that signals become more consequential when they are corroborated by cues from structurally different sources, because convergence reduces ambiguity and makes an issue appear important, legitimate, and actionable. Using Government Work Reports and the Baidu Index to measure attention to digital government, we estimate two-way fixed-effects models for 283 Chinese cities over 2012–2024. We find that superior, peer, and public attention are each positively associated with local attention. The signals also reinforce one another: superior attention strengthens the associations of both peer and public attention with local attention, while peer attention strengthens the association of public attention with local attention. Temporal patterns also differ: the association of superior attention with local attention becomes stronger in the later period, that of peer attention remains broadly stable, and that of public attention tends to strengthen. These findings advance attention-allocation theory by showing that governmental attention is a relational and configurational outcome of signal interpretation rather than an additive response to isolated institutional pressures.
journal_name: Journal of Public Administration Research and Theory

title: Digital Co‐Production of Public Services: Citizens, Challenges and Cases. By TacoBrandsen, InaRadtke, A.Paula Rodriguez Müller, and TruiSteen (Eds.), Cheltenham: Edward Elgar Publishing, 2026. 204 pp. Open Access (ebook)
abstract: Public administrations have embraced digital tools to engage citizens in shaping the services they receive, yet scholarship has lagged behind practice in explaining when, and for whom, the digital turn strengthens co-production instead of hollowing it out.This edited volume, in Edward Elgar's Policy, Administrative and Institutional Change series, addresses that gap.Drawing on new material from two Horizon 2020 projects, INTERLINK and InGOV, the editors add an introductory chapter to nine substantive chapters in three sections, moving from conceptual foundations through technological trends to lifecycle applications and recommendations.Their central claim is that digital co-production is a distinct socio-technical phenomenon with its own trade-offs, not a simple digital amplification of offline practice.The volume documents, chapter by chapter, that digitalization both expands and narrows the space for citizen engagement.It never says which effect should dominate, or when.

title: Riding the catch-up cycle: how market maturity shapes local provision of ICT contracting in China
abstract: Although governments frequently employ public procurement to advance local economic development, buy-local objectives may conflict with the competition principle that underlies modern procurement systems. This tension may vary with market maturity, which shapes both supplier capability and catch-up incentives. Drawing on the catch-up cycle perspective and analyzing 42,974 Information and Communication Technology (ICT) projects that were launched from 2016 to 2022, we find a stage-dependent, N-shaped relationship between market maturity and local provision. In the low- and high-maturity markets, lower ICT market maturity is associated with lower local provision, suggesting that contract allocations are driven predominantly by supplier capability. A key deviation appears in mid-maturity markets, where less mature regions allocate more ICT contracts locally. This mid-regime bump in local provision is consistent with catch-up urgency, as governments use ICT procurement to support local industrial development once basic supplier capability has emerged. These findings show that contracting behavior changes across the catch-up cycle, and call for stage-sensitive procurement oversight.

title: Shurta Al‐Khamis: A Historical Model of Adaptive Governance Based on Islamic Values for Contemporary Public Administration
abstract: ABSTRACT Islamic governance history contains administrative institutions that remain largely overlooked in contemporary public administration scholarship. This paper explores Shurta al‐Khamis , a relatively overlooked covenant based administrative unit in Islamic governance history, established by Imam Ali and composed of highly trusted members who undertook binding oaths to carry out critical governance and security functions. Drawing on a historical case study, the paper examines how the principles underlying Shurta al‐Khamis align with modern demands for governance structures requiring adaptation, resilience, and ethical commitment. Its decentralized, value driven organizational design fostered loyalty, accountability, and shared purpose, enhancing coordination and responsiveness in complex environments. The analysis compares Shurta al‐Khamis with contemporary models such as adhocracy, showing how value embedded flexibility and covenant based commitment support adaptive governance in rapidly changing contexts. The study highlights the potential and limits of adapting Shurta al‐Khamis to both Islamic and non‐Islamic settings.

title: Unpacking local government responsiveness to social media: evidence from Mexico
abstract: Local governments worldwide increasingly adopt social media to engage citizens. What factors make governments more likely to respond to citizens on social media? We explore how Mexican municipal governments use Facebook to interact with citizens, with a mixed-methods approach analysing data from 635 municipalities. Using a crisp-set qualitative comparative analysis, we distinguish between general responsiveness (channel setup) and interactive responsiveness (substantive engagement). Small municipalities are more likely to engage citizens when adaptive potential and formal participation policies are present. In contrast, larger cities show responsiveness when they have available resources, established participation rules and policies, and a propitious environment.

title: Functional Substitution and Particularized Trust: Governance Mechanisms in Hourglass Socio‐Economic Systems
abstract: ABSTRACT Governance research shows that cooperation can persist despite dysfunctional state institutions, often through trust‐based mechanisms. This paper extends these debates by examining a complex collective action problem: the engagement of small‐ and medium‐sized enterprises (SMEs) in vocational education and training (VET) in post‐communist contexts. Drawing on the concept of “hourglass societies”, where trust concentrates among elites and local actors but is weak at the meso‐level, the paper argues that VET schools act as functional substitutes to meso‐level business associations by leveraging particularized trust and local networks. Evidence from Albania and Slovakia, based on 62 interviews and network analysis, demonstrates how face‐to‐face interaction, reciprocity, and localized knowledge enable SMEs to overcome prisoner's dilemma dynamics. These findings contribute to governance theory by showing how functional substitution and micro‐level trust structures sustain cooperation in fragmented socio‐economic systems, offering insights for designing policies for collective good provision such as education politics beyond Western contexts.

title: Problem-solving ontologies on steroids? The space for critique in policy research on artificial intelligence
abstract: This article critically examines social sciences research on AI and policy as a politics of knowledge production, offering three key contributions. First, it debates the merit of systematic reviews in critical policy research in revealing epistemic hierarchies and biases. Second, it introduces a heuristic to map the disjointed methodologies of AI-policy scholarship across two ontological dimensions: whether AI features as a neutral problem-solving tool or a socio-technical system shaping power relations; and whether technology serves as a governance instrument or a regulatory target. This framework provides a reflexive, yet systematic, tool to expose epistemic hierarchies and the relative space for critical social scientific engagement. Third, I present findings from a systematic review of 229 English-language articles published in social sciences journals through 2025. Results show a pronounced imbalance: three-quarters of studies focus on AI regulation, while empirical research on technology uses in governance remains marginal. Moreover, the majority of the corpus operates within problem-solving ontologies, framing AI either as an optimizer of policymaking or as an objectively manageable risk. In the discussion, the article therefore calls for greater scholarly reflexivity and debate on the role of social sciences knowledge production in examining power asymmetries, techno-solutionist ideologies, and social inequalities in the AI-policy complex.

title: The politics of restricted inclusion: a longitudinal policy analysis of healthcare access for people living as undocumented migrants in Sweden
abstract: This study examines how healthcare access for people living as undocumented migrants has been constituted, contested, and reconfigured in Sweden from the early 1990s to the mid 2020s, challenging institutionalist claims that universalist welfare systems reliably generate solidaristic migration policies. Drawing on a longitudinal policy analysis combined with critical framing analysis, we traced legislative debates and policy outputs across more than three decades, identifying four critical turning points: the 1990s framing of “undocumentedness” as an issue of migration control; the growing influence of human rights and public health arguments in the 2000s; the 2013 reform introducing legally ambiguous restricted inclusion; and the post-2022 recentering of healthcare within an expanded migration control and border enforcement agenda. The findings demonstrate that Sweden’s universal welfare orientation structured, but did not determine, policy outcomes.
