Expanded inclusion emerged when humanitarian, public health, and legal frames aligned across party coalitions, while restriction dominated when deservingness and control arguments converged with fiscal and capacity concerns. Civil society actors and clinicians played a crucial role in sustaining rights-based frames, but without decisively shaping subsequently implemented policies. In conclusion, solidaristic healthcare policies addressing undocumented migration depend less on welfare state design than on shifting political alignments. Policy implications include decoupling healthcare from border enforcement, as a means of maintaining the ethical legitimacy of the welfare state, along with a need to integrate clinical expertise into policymaking.

title: Automation and employment over the technology life cycle: Evidence from European regions
abstract: This paper examines how the labor market effects of automation and digital technologies vary across their technology life cycles. Using data for 158 European regions from 1995 to 2017, we study the phase-specific impacts of robots, information and communication technologies (ICT), and software and databases (SDB) on employment and wages. We identify distinct technology life cycles and their early and mature adoption phases by applying a structural break methodology to investment dynamics. To address endogeneity in regional exposure, we employ a shift-share instrumental-variable strategy that leverages US investment patterns interacted with pre-determined regional industrial structures. We find that labor market effects differ systematically across both technologies and life-cycle phases. Early adoption is skill-biased for intangible digital technologies: exposure to SDB during early diffusion is associated with declining employment and rising wages. In contrast, early ICT adoption is characterized by employment expansion concentrated among lower-paid workers, consistent with productivity-driven demand growth, while robots exhibit largely skill-neutral effects in early diffusion. For tangible technologies, displacement effects emerge in mature adoption phases. Across technologies, labor market adjustment operates mainly through the services sector, even when adoption occurs in manufacturing (robots). Our findings demonstrate that aggregate estimates of ICT and robots often mask opposing life cycle phase- and technology-specific dynamics.

title: Towards a theory of industrial modernity
Monitoring High Court Rulings in New Democracies
The loyal dissent: democratic backsliding and salience-conditional voting by national judges at the European Court of Human Rights
abstract: Can the supranational institutions built to backstop domestic rule of law withstand democratic backsliding? We address this question at the bench of the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR), where Article 26(4) of the Convention seats a judge elected in respect of each respondent state. Using the full retrievable corpus of ECtHR Chamber and Grand Chamber merits judgments with recorded votes against Council of Europe members (1990–2025), merged with V-Dem’s index of judicial constraints on the executive, we test how the elected national judge’s pro-state dissent tracks the erosion of judicial independence at home. The relationship is salience-conditional, consistent with selection, career, and interpretive channels producing selective rather than blanket state alignment: the association is significantly stronger in the Court’s own high-importance cases than on the routine docket, where the estimate is smaller and imprecisely estimated. A within-case design comparing the national judge with the other judges deciding the same operative item returns the same structure, ruling out case composition. The pattern is inconsistent with uniform blanket capture and isolates a conditional permeability of supranational review, concentrated in the Court-designated high-importance docket.

title: Not my democracy: conceptions, discontent, and participation in Europe
abstract: Abstract Citizens differ not only in how strongly they support democracy, but also in what they expect democracy to be. Yet we know less about whether these democratic expectations shape satisfaction with democracy (SwD) and, through it, political participation (PP) in established European democracies. We first develop a mechanism linking citizens’ prioritized understandings of democracy (UoD) to SwD and unconventional political participation (UPP). Satisfaction with democracy is treated as an indicator of perceived congruence between citizens’ democratic ideals and how democracy works in practice. Second, we test this mechanism systematically in Europe using ESS Round 10 data, including almost 60,000 respondents in 31 countries. We find that (a) citizens’ conceptions of democracy affect SwD and (b) that SwD is a mediator for the impact UoD have on UPP.

title: Powerful or Powerless? The Influence of Gender Advocates in Peace Negotiations
abstract: While the Women, Peace and Security sector advocates for the inclusion of gender experts in peace processes to improve outcomes for women, empirical support for their effectiveness remains inconclusive. This paper tests whether individuals designated to advocate for gender-specific issues are influential or ineffective. Leveraging an original dataset capturing the role of 2,300 delegates across 116 comprehensive peace agreements finalized between 1990 and 2020, we find that gender advocates increase the likelihood that agreements contain provisions for women. However, investigating the case of Northern Ireland using interviews and archival analysis, we find that the systemic masculinized structure of peace negotiations hinders advocates’ overall influence. Consequently, this paper explains how these actors are simultaneously powerful and powerless. Findings capture gender advocates’ limitations, caution against individuals bearing sole responsibility for gender considerations in peace processes, and expand the conceptualization of what it is to be an expert.

title: Quantity Commitments in Multiunit Auctions: Evidence from Credit Event Auctions
Feeling rich or looking rich? Self-perceived vs socially-perceived relative income
abstract: Individuals may care about status both because of how they view their own position and because of how others perceive it. We compare these two dimensions using five hypothetical discrete-choice experiments that separately vary absolute outcomes, self-perceived standing, and socially-perceived standing in the domains of income, academic performance, and car safety. The analysis sample includes 4934 U.S. respondents and two elicitation tasks: a non-incentivized own-choice task and an incentivized coordination game in which respondents are rewarded for predicting the modal choice. Across four of the five experimental conditions, socially-perceived standing enters positively, while self-perceived standing is either negative or statistically indistinguishable from zero. The exception is the income own-choice condition, where the pattern reverses—a result that warrants further research.

title: Gender Discrimination in Access to Capital: A Field Experiment in Ethiopia
abstract: Abstract We test whether loan officers discriminate against female business owners in capital decisions affecting real businesses in an Ethiopian business plan competition. Randomizing owner gender across 3,696 evaluations, by 84 loan officers, for 916 businesses, we find no effect on prize scores or consideration for a loan. Incentivized beliefs about future performance did not differ by gender, ruling out statistical and taste-based discrimination. Machine learning predictions of future business performance show that loan officers beliefs were accurate. Gender does not meaningfully improve predictions, implying no trade-off between gender equity and effective capital allocation.

title: Losing Political Representation
abstract: Abstract What are the consequences of losing political representation in a democracy? A reform of Germany’s mixed electoral system left more than 7 million citizens in 23 constituencies without a directly elected representative after the 2025 national election. Which and how many constituencies were affected was unpredictable and quasi-random. We show that losing geographical representation reduces citizens’ satisfaction with democracy. Moreover, discontent is independent of party preferences and spreads through social networks, reducing democratic satisfaction even among individuals who were unaffected or unaware of the reform’s outcome. We conclude that political representation is a cornerstone of democracy.

title: Gender and Electoral Incentives: Evidence from COVID-19 Response
abstract: Abstract This paper provides new evidence on why men and women leaders make different choices. Exploiting Brazilian close elections, we show that female mayors responded differently to the COVID-19 crisis over the year 2020. Female mayors were less likely to close non-essential businesses early in the pandemic and female-led municipalities experienced higher mortality, while the reverse was true later on. We show that these findings can be rationalized by a simple political agency model in which politicians seek re-election and voters are gender biased. Consistent with this interpretation, the gender differences we find are driven exclusively by mayors facing re-election.

title: The Intergenerational Transmission of Employers and the Earnings of Young Workers
abstract: Abstract This paper investigates how parental connections to firms shape early-career earnings. I use employer-employee linked data to study one important type of connection: jobs obtained at a parent’s employer. Twenty-nine percent of individuals work for a parent’s employer at least once by age 30. Exploiting transitory, firm-specific fluctuations in hiring conditions at the parent’s employer, I estimate that working for a parent’s employer increases initial earnings by 24 percent, primarily by providing access to higher-paying firms. Individuals with higher-earning parents are more likely to work for a parent’s employer and experience larger earnings gains when they do. Consequently, the elasticity of initial earnings with respect to parental earnings would be 12 percent lower if no one found a job through these connections. The findings suggest that connections to firms through one’s social network may be an important determinant of intergenerational mobility.

title: Job Loss, Unemployment Insurance, and Health: Evidence from Brazil
abstract: Abstract We study the health impacts of job loss and unemployment insurance (UI) among Brazilian workers, using unique administrative data linking employment, hospitalizations, health insurance, and mortality records over 17 years. Leveraging mass layoffs for identification, we find that job loss raises hospitalization (+33%) and mortality (+23%) risks for men, with no significant effects for women. Impacts are pervasive across age, income, and education levels, with children of male workers also affected. External causes related to risky behavior and violence victimization explain half the effects. Using a regression discontinuity design, we show that UI partially mitigates health risks, suggesting that these are partially explained by income losses.

title: Estimating the Macroeconomic Effects of Oil Supply News
abstract: Abstract We show that structural oil-market shocks identified in prominent SVAR models, as well as high-frequency oil price changes around OPEC announcements, are predictable, indicating informational deficiencies in standard oil-market VARs and contamination of commonly used instrumental variables. We resolve these identification problems for oil supply news shocks by augmenting the econometrician’s information set with financial indicators, yielding markedly different results: the shocks induce a sharper short-run output contraction, are less inflationary, contribute less to oil price variation, exhibit greater stability over time, and account for a substantial share of S&P 500 volatility.

title: Return to Office and the Tenure Distribution
abstract: Abstract Debates over return-to-office mandates have intensified since the COVID-19 pandemic ended, though their economic implications remain poorly understood. Using large-scale resume data, we analyze how these policies affect employee tenure and seniority at three large U.S. tech companies: Microsoft, SpaceX, and Apple. Employing a distributional synthetic controls framework, we estimate a reduction in tenure and seniority at firms returning to the office. We extend the framework with a functional bootstrap procedure and prove its validity for constructing uniform confidence bands. Return-to-office mandates appear to drive senior employees away, posing a risk to firm productivity and innovation.

title: Scientific Talent Leaks Out of Funding Gaps
abstract: Abstract Federal research funding is a key input into scientific work, but funding streams can be disrupted. We study how delays in renewed NIH research grants affect lab personnel’s careers, linking grant records to university payroll, tax, Census, and publication data. Using a difference-in-differences design, we find that interruptions of at least 30 days increase nonemployment among personnel in labs supported by a single NIH R01 grant by 3 percentage points, or 40%. Among those who remain employed in the US, earnings decrease by 20%. The results show that short funding gaps can alter career trajectories, especially for trainees.

title: Social Ties and Fiscal Transfers in a Regional Economy: A Quantitative Spatial Analysis
abstract: Abstract Many governments use fiscal transfers to reduce regional inequality, yet discretionary allocation may also depend on informal communication among officials. We examine this mechanism in a large central-to-provincial transfer system, using policymakers’ shared workplace, alumni, and hometown backgrounds to measure social ties. Exploiting ministerial turnover and controlling for provincial leadership, we find that prior workplace ties significantly increase transfers. We then embed these estimates in a quantitative spatial model with trade, migration, input-output linkages, and fiscal-productivity effects. Social ties redirect resources toward richer provinces with stronger fundamentals, raising welfare and output while weakening redistribution. Under egalitarian weights, however, removing ties improves welfare.

title: Insurance Choice with Non-Monetary Plan Attributes: Limited Consideration in Medicare Part D
abstract: Abstract I propose a model of insurance demand where non-monetary attributes determine which plans an individual considers, and monetary attributes determine an individual's expected utility. This approach reconciles the classic view of insurance as purely financial with the empirical finding that choice is driven by additional attributes. I estimate the model using Medicare Part D data, allowing for unobserved heterogeneity in consideration and preferences. I find the former plays a crucial role: more than 90% of individuals consider 5 or fewer plans, approximately lO°lo of the menu. Additionally, estimates of risk preferences are comparable to existing studies of similar stakes.

title: Transaction Costs and the Gains from Trade in Water Markets
abstract: Abstract Surface water in California is scarce and tightly managed, yet little is traded through a market. This paper studies transaction costs in the existing wholesale water market and estimates the benefits of reducing them. I develop an empirical framework that uses transactions among water districts to analyze welfare, decomposing prices into demand and transaction costs and simulating a market with only physical frictions. Transaction costs are large: median variable costs are 54% of the price, and fixed costs deter many districts from participating. Eliminating them produces gains of several hundred million dollars per year, or 1-3% of statewide water expenditures.

title: From Micro to Macro in an Equilibrium Diffusion Model
abstract: Abstract We quantify the benefits of better firm-to-firm matching in an aggregate diffusion model where individuals acquire profitable knowledge from others. We estimate the model using a small-scale program in Kenya that creates new opportunities for firm managers to interact. Aggregate gains from the program depend on the relative importance of meeting a high-knowledge firm versus learning within that meeting. We show how moments from the intervention identify these parameters, demonstrating how easily estimated moments beyond the average treatment effect inform at-scale gains. We provide sufficient conditions extending the identification procedure to a broader class of experiments and aggregate diffusion models.

title: Cash transfers and social preferences of children
Intergroup Contact, Empathy Education, and Refugee-Native Integration in Lebanon
abstract: Abstract Intergroup contact interventions often yield limited results in deeply divided societies. We test contact and empathy education in Lebanon, where Syrian refugees comprise a quarter of the population. In a fully cross-randomised field experiment with 887 Lebanese and Syrian youth embedded in a psychosocial support programme, we find that contact has little effect on outgroup attitudes and behaviour, while empathy education consistently improves attitudes for Lebanese youth and behavioural engagement for both. The combined treatment achieves little beyond empathy alone, with no evidence of spillovers to parents (n = 595). In polarised settings, empathy education should precede — or replace — contact.

title: History-dependent monetary policy – less is more
Review of “The Religious Left: What It Does and How It Can Do Better”
Review of “Blame the Intern: On (Not) Breaking into the Creative Economy”
Review of “An Elite Education: How Privilege Is Produced in a Private School”
Research on Risk Classification of Online Public Opinion in Emergencies Based on FHCO Algorithm
abstract: Online public opinion concerning emergencies presents challenges to social stability due to its rapid dissemination and complex evolutionary nature. Accurate risk classification is essential for effective early warning. Current risk classification methods, however, face limitations such as difficulty in capturing complex structural features at a single scale, inadequate representation of local risk variations, and imprecision in threshold determination. To address these issues, this article proposes a risk classification method on the basis of the fractal hierarchical clustering optimization (FHCO) algorithm for public risk perception and discursive reflection. First, a comprehensive set of risk indicators for online public opinion is constructed. Next, fractal characteristics-including the correlation function, generalized dimension spectrum, singularity index, and fractal spectrum-are calculated. These fractal features are then clustered using the FHCO algorithm, and the final risk level is determined by integrating the comprehensive risk score. To validate the method's effectiveness, the "7.20" Zhengzhou rainstorm incident was analyzed as a case study, along with 27 other high-risk public opinion events. Results indicate that the proposed method achieves an accuracy of 92.86%, significantly outperforming the traditional K-means (64.29%) and K-medoids (82.14%) algorithms. This demonstrates that the method can effectively improve the accuracy of risk classification, providing new insights and technical support for the early identification of online public opinion risks associated with emergencies.

title: Two Foundational Ideas of Risk—Undesirability and Unexpectedness—With Implications for Risk Science and Its Applications
abstract: This paper contends that the concept of risk is fundamentally shaped by two distinct motivating ideas: (1) that something undesirable may occur (dominant in safety, security, and engineering contexts), and (2) that something unexpected may occur (central to many business, strategic, and decision-making domains). Any framework aspiring to generality across diverse application areas must therefore be sufficiently inclusive to accommodate both perspectives. The paper explores the ramifications of this dual conceptualization for foundational aspects of risk science-including core definitions, the scope and boundaries of the discipline-as well as for risk understanding, communication, and management.

title: Probabilistic Assessment of the Relative Source Contribution Factor While Accounting for Exposure to Other Regulated Media: A Toxicokinetic Proof‐of‐Concept for Volatile Drinking Water Contaminants
abstract: ABSTRACT A relative source contribution factor is applied when deriving noncancer health‐based guidance values for drinking water contaminants. The present work aimed at assessing the adequacy of the 20% default value often attributed to this factor while accounting for concomitant inhalation exposure to the reference concentration (RfC). Steady‐state toxicokinetic equations were applied to calculate constant blood concentration (Cblood ss ) in adults and 1–3‐year‐old children for 12 volatile organic compounds (VOCs). Three exposure scenarios were considered for each compound, namely, (1) ingestion of the reference dose (RfD) alone; (2) inhalation of the RfC alone; and (3) ingestion of 20% of the RfD combined with inhalation of the RfC. Using Monte Carlo simulations, probabilistic ratios of Cblood ss were computed for Scenario 3 over Scenario 1. Ratios >1, demonstrating an exceedance of the RfD‐equivalent Cblood ss by Scenario 3, are obtained at mean and 97.5 th percentile value for eight of the chosen VOCs in adults, with range of 0.3–29 at the mean and of 0.32–52 at the 97.5 th percentile. Nine VOCs exhibited such exceedance in children (ranges: 0.34–36 at the mean; 0.38–57 at the 97.5 th percentile). For eight VOCs, ratios >1 were mainly explained by high RfC‐related intake as compared to RfD‐related intake. Concluding, steady‐state toxicokinetic modeling was successfully used to illustrate the importance of other media's guidance levels‐related exposures, in the present case the RfC, to evaluate the magnitude of the relative source contribution factor required when determining health‐based guidance values for chemicals in drinking water.

title: Does Office Type Determine Gendered Campaign Messages?
abstract: This study examines how candidates’ gender shapes campaign messaging across different branches and levels of political office. Prior research offers mixed evidence on whether women are more likely than men to emphasize communal traits and women-related policies, often because gender effects are examined without fully accounting for institutional context. We address this inconsistency by foregrounding the role of electoral institutions. Building on strategic stereotype theory, we argue that gendered campaign messaging is a strategic response to office-specific incentives and expectations. In particular, we expect gendered appeals to be more prevalent at lower levels of government than at higher levels, and more pronounced in legislative than in executive races. We test these expectations using an original dataset of 46,966 official campaign booklets issued by all candidates competing for district-based executive and legislative offices in seventeen national and local elections in South Korea from 2000 to 2022. These booklets are legally standardized, page-limited documents distributed to voters and provide a rare opportunity to compare campaign messages across offices while holding the communication medium constant. We measure gendered messaging through candidates’ use of relational language and women-related policy terms. The results show that female candidates emphasize relational identities and women’s policy concerns more than male candidates. Crucially, the magnitude of this gender gap varies across institutional contexts. Gender differences are larger in legislative contests than in executive races and increase as elections move from national to subnational levels.

title: Infrastructure nationalism and sovereignty by settlement in Tibet: The case of xiaokang border villages
abstract: This article critically examines China’s Xiaokang Border Village Programme (2017–20) in the Tibet Autonomous Region (TAR), situating it within Xi Jinping’s broader strategy of ‘governing the borders to govern the country’. Ostensibly framed as a poverty alleviation and rural revitalization initiative, the programme mobilized billions in state funding to construct or rebuild more than 600 model villages in Tibet’s border counties. Drawing on a range of new sources, the article argues that these villages are less developmental tools than instruments of territorial consolidation, securitization, and ideological transformation. By reconfiguring spatial relations, relocating border populations, and embedding Han-led Chinese Communist Party (CCP) institutions, these xiaokang villages function as micro-sites of infrastructure nationalism and colonial-style governance, inscribing Han norms into Indigenous landscapes and subjectivities to further CCP control over once autonomous communities in the farthest reaches of the People’s Republic of China.

title: Worldly Engagements: Buddhist Monasticism and Masculinity among the Tai Lue of Southwest China Roger Casas. Honolulu: University of Hawai‘i Press, 2026. 252 pp. $75.00 (hbk). ISBN 9798880700875
Organizational Resilience in Public Workforce Transitions: A Case Study of Continuity and Change under the DOGE Reforms
abstract: This qualitative case study examines how a federal field detachment sustained operational continuity during the initial implementation of the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) workforce reforms. Centered on the loss of a clearance-restricted Security Officer, the study draws on interviews, surveys, and organizational artifacts to examine how responsibilities were redistributed under constrained staffing conditions. Findings indicate that mission-essential operations were maintained through task redistribution, knowledge capture, leadership, and informal coordination; however, these adaptive responses also increased workload concentration, exposed dependence on undocumented institutional knowledge, and heightened reliance on individual effort. The study distinguishes operational continuity from organizational resilience by demonstrating that sustained mission performance can mask underlying degradation in organizational capacity. The findings extend beyond the DOGE reforms and offer practical lessons for workforce restructuring, continuity planning, succession management, and organizational resilience across public and private organizations.

title: Strategic muddling and the quiet hollowing of China’s zero-COVID governance
abstract: This study revisits the concept of ‘muddling through’ in the context of authoritarian crisis governance. Building on the work of Lindblom and Zhou Xueguang and using China’s zero-COVID campaign as a case study, we propose a new crisis-induced variant of muddling through that is characterized by a set of strategic coping behaviours induced by intense political pressure. We call this ‘strategic muddling’. Based on 24 semi-structured interviews with local officials, we identify three mutually reinforcing and embedded forms of local adaptation: symbolic compliance through data manipulation, informal coalition-making, and guanxi-based cautious probing. Although these practices sustained symbolic order in the short term, they ultimately distorted feedback mechanisms, weakened enforcement capacity, and undermined the mobilizational structure of China’s pandemic response. By highlighting a subtle yet highly consequential internal mechanism of institutional hollowing within local crisis governance, this study offers illuminating insights into authoritarian resilience, performative governance, and crisis governance.

title: More than a broker: the commission in trilogues for geoeconomic instruments
abstract: As the EU seeks strategic autonomy, the European Commission is strengthening its supranational role through new trade defence instruments. While the Commission mediated the trilogue negotiations for the anti-coercion instrument (ACI) and the foreign direct investment screening framework (ISF), we lack an understanding of its strategy in these interinstitutional negotiations. This article investigates how the Commission brokers trilogues, exploring how it advances its preferences in new geoeconomic legislation. It theorises a causal mechanism for Commission strategies in trilogues and applies it to the negotiations for the ACI and ISF. Studying the involvement of the Commission in shaping the two instruments’ design (the micro processes) is central to understanding the increased role of the Commission in the macro processes of the EU’s ‘geoeconomic turn’. This article argues that the Commission uses its informational asymmetry strategically to lobby the co-legislators in trilogues. When their preferences diverge from those of the Commission, it invests political capital to reach compromises closer to its preferences. The process-tracing analysis builds on EU policy documents, secondary sources, and interviews with EU officials. This research demonstrates how the Commission is taking an increased role in the EU’s ambition to conduct foreign policy through trade.

title: Different signals, same message? Evidence of mainstream accommodation of the radical right on European integration using parliamentary speeches
abstract: What drives mainstream parties’ reactions to the success of the radical right? Existing research shows that mainstream parties respond by moving closer to the radical right but most studies focus on long-term adjustments based on past election results, overlooking shifts within electoral cycles and not distinguishing between different sources of information on which mainstream parties might rely. We argue that the type of electoral signal (actual vote share versus projected success in opinion polls) as well as its credibility as an indicator of challenger strength (whether the radical right is represented in parliament) is crucial. Drawing on ParlSpeech data, we analyse plenary speeches from seven legislatures over a 20-year period and measure party positions on the EU at the quarter-year level with two fine-tuned multilingual classifiers based on XLM-RoBERTa. We find that mainstream parties adopt more Eurosceptic stances in reaction to increases in support for the radical right, both when measured as share of the vote in the previous elections and as the share of the vote as predicted by opinion polls. This is only the case when the radical right is represented in parliament. However, we find no evidence that mainstream accommodation intensifies as elections draw nearer.

title: Shifting ground to hold firm? EMU rebalancing and the changing politics of euro support
abstract: In a context marked by mounting challenges to international cooperation, public support for the euro has, paradoxically, reached record highs. This article examines whether this reappraisal of the Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) coincided with changes in its macroeconomic policy mix. It specifically explores two plausible pathways: First, partisan accommodation, whereby ‘challenger’ parties moderate their opposition to the EMU as its policy orientation evolves. Second, public receptiveness, with citizens adjusting their attitudes toward the EMU as policy developments align with their ideological preferences. Empirically, this analysis rests on a mixed-methods design combining longitudinal Eurobarometer data (2004-2021), party-level evidence from the EU&I surveys (2019, 2024), and original SOLID survey data (2025). Findings show that partisan accommodation is most pronounced on the radical left but is also visible among some radical-right parties. At the mass-public level, the association between policy awareness and euro support differs across initiatives: for the Minimum Wage Directive, a strong positive association emerges among radical-left respondents, whereas for NextGenerationEU, the pattern extends across ideological groups. Taken together, these findings suggest that supranational policymaking may reshape the political constraints under which it operates, pointing to greater scope for political realignment than post-functionalist accounts typically anticipate.

title: Bridging the gap: A scalable approach to measuring social innovation capacity
abstract: As governments increasingly turn to social innovation to address complex societal and environmental challenges, the lack of robust, scalable measurement frameworks continues to limit the effectiveness of relevant policies. Without such tools, it remains difficult to assess regional capacities, evaluate outcomes, and design targeted interventions that foster societal resilience and adaptability. This paper introduces a novel index of regional social innovation capacity, which is defined as a region's ability to develop, implement, and sustain social innovations. Drawing conceptually from the technological innovation literature, the index integrates multidimensional inputs for social innovation capacity using publicly available data and has been externally validated through an empirical analysis of social innovation activities published on German company websites. By employing regional planning areas as the unit of analysis, our framework enables cross-regional comparison while preserving local specificity. It also advances the measurability, visibility, and accountability of social innovation, offering policymakers an evidence-based tool for strategic resource allocation. From an academic perspective, the index bridges fragmented approaches across disciplines and contributes to a more coherent, comparative, policy-relevant social innovation research agenda.

title: Local implementation of transformative innovation policies: Ambiguities, strategic responses, and intertemporal conflicts
abstract: Transformative Innovation Policy (TIP) offers a compelling framework for addressing societal challenges. However, its implementation requires a deeper understanding of the behavioural and relational dynamics among local actors because these dynamics can enable or hinder sustainable and inclusive policy outcomes. Drawing on an embedded case study of the implementation of residential electric vehicle charging infrastructure in England, we unveil how the interplay between policy ambiguities and emergent conflicts conditions the local pathways of TIP implementation. We show that local actors respond to ambiguities of role, means, and resourcing, and that these responses can shape three conflicts (purpose incongruence, commons contestation, and financial fragility) which evolve over time. Building on these insights, we develop a model of local TIP implementation that explains how implementing actors respond to ambiguities and how these responses shape conflicts. Overall, our analysis contributes to understanding the intertemporal and distributive challenges facing TIP implementation.

title: Peace Under the Influence? The Role of Illicit Drug Economies in Peace Processes and Rebel Splintering
abstract: How do the economic foundations of rebel groups shape civil war dynamics? While prior research has explored how different resource types affect conflict, less is known about how the illicit nature of certain resources—particularly drug economies—affects peace processes. We argue that the inherent illegality of drug-based financing imposes structural barriers to peace, distinguishing it from other forms of rebel revenue. Using cross-national dyadic data from 1990 to 2011, we find that drug-reliant rebel groups have 34 percent lower hazard of initiatiating peace talks and over six times more likely to fragment once peace processes begin. These findings suggest that drug-based financing generates a self-reinforcing cycle that sustains violence. In contrast to accounts emphasizing grievances produced by peace processes, we show that some groups may be structurally predisposed to reject peace altogether. Our findings call for theoretical and policy approaches tailored to the distinct challenges posed by illicit drug economies.

title: Candidate Gender and District Ideological Alignment in U.S. Congressional Elections, 2002–2020
abstract: Candidate ideology impacts a wide range of electoral outcomes, but are there gendered differences in the effects of candidate ideology? Using a unique dataset of U.S. congressional elections between 2002 and 2020, we examine candidate-level factors (gender, ideology, and partisanship) and district-level political factors (district ideology and partisanship), and the interaction between these candidate and district-level factors. We first compare two measurements of candidate ideology for congressional incumbents of both major parties: absolute extremity and ideological distance from the district. Although there are partisan differences, we generally find that women are more ideologically extreme than men. We then examine how ideological distance from the district impacts three dependent variables, likelihood of running unopposed, vote share, and probability of winning election, and test how candidate gender interacts with ideological distance from the district. We find that incumbent women are less likely to run unopposed and have a lower vote share than incumbent men. Overall, it appears that women congressional candidates may be more ideologically extreme and are more likely to be punished for their ideological positions than men.

title: A model of criminal justice discretion
Cross-tier incumbency spillovers: evidence from India
Geopolitical shocks and household financial distress in Europe: The Russia–Ukraine war
Risk-taking by CEOs: Role of exposure to social violence in early childhood
The relational structure of corporate ignorance production
abstract: This study interrogates patterns of interaction through which corporate actors influence environmental knowledge production. I ask 1) How intensive are relationships between corporate actors and knowledge-producing organizations? 2) What types of knowledge-producing organizations are subject to most engagement by corporate actors? and 3) How do these patterns evolve over time? I answer these questions with the landmark case of lead in the United States (1924–2003). I rely on longitudinal network data built from the raw text of Toxic Docs, a database that comprises millions of previously classified corporate documents over eight decades. Using relational event modeling, I find that corporate engagement with scientific organizations is consistently more likely than with other types of actors. In contrast, corporate engagement with regulatory expert organizations is less so. I also find that corporate engagement with scientific organizations is responsive to growing federal interest in the lead problem and anticipates regulatory developments. This suggests that corporate engagement with scientists is best described not simply as reactive but also as preemptive.

title: Colonial continuity and the African film industry: A comparative political economy of structural reproduction
abstract: African cinema produces at scale and commands global cultural prestige, yet captures a fraction of its economic potential. The film sector generates only USD 5 billion from an estimated potential of USD 20 billion; piracy accounts for over half of potential revenues in two-thirds of African countries; Nigeria operates 68 cinemas for a population of over 200 million; and former cinema houses in Burkina Faso, host of the continent’s most celebrated film festival, are now market spaces. This paper argues that these conditions persist because the political-economic arrangements organising African film industries were established under colonialism and reproduced through successive institutional forms, including postcolonial state film companies, structural adjustment and digital streaming platforms, serving global capital at the expense of African producers and audiences. The colonial continuity thesis, developed through Mosco’s framework of commodification, spatialisation and structuration, provides the mechanism-level explanation for this persistence. Applied comparatively across Nigeria, Ghana and Francophone West Africa, three contexts selected for meaningful variation in colonial history, state film policy tradition and industry form, the framework reveals convergence that no country-specific explanation can account for, extending Ngwenya’s challenge to critical political economy by specifying the colonial structural logic that class-based analysis leaves unaccounted.

title: Redefining China’s Approach to AI Governance: Beyond Top-Down, Government-Led, and Command-and-Control
abstract: China’s approach to AI governance has been described as top-down and government-led, relying on command-and-control to pursue state-centered objectives. Drawing on an original corpus of primary sources, this Article challenges this narrative. First, AI governance in China exhibits federalism-like features, with local governments playing important roles and adopting regulatory approaches distinct from those of the central government. Second, market players are active co-regulators and strategic bargainers in the iterative governance process. Third, China’s diverse objectives and methods extend beyond what a command-and-control model can capture. Together, these dynamics reveal a polycentric and layered governance structure. These findings offer a more nuanced and contextual understanding of China’s AI governance, countering simplified geopolitical narratives and helping identify common ground for global cooperation.

title: Administrative fragmentation and AI governance capacity: Institutional interdependence and democratic answerability
Governing through emotion: affective legitimacy, discrimination, and the politics of crisis in India
abstract: This paper examines how emotion functioned as a constitutive force in India’s COVID-19 governance, reshaping administrative practices and legitimizing discriminatory treatment of Muslims. Drawing on Affective Intelligence Theory (AIT) and affect theory, it argues that emotions such as fear, disgust, and suspicion functioned as instruments of governance that displaced scientific reasoning and procedural rationality. The study introduces the concept of affective legitimacy to explain how political authority can be constructed through emotional resonance, particularly fear, moral outrage, and disgust, rather than empirical validation or technocratic expertise. Through a discursive and interpretive analysis of official documents and media narratives, the study shows how preexisting emotional narratives resurfaced and became embedded in institutional practices. The findings demonstrate how state power mobilized collective emotions to justify exclusionary policies and reinforce communal hierarchies. This paper contributes to critical policy debates by conceptualizing emotion as a structured and knowledge-producing element of governance, situating India’s pandemic response within broader discussions on democratic backsliding and the politics of social justice.

title: WFH and productivity: Evidence from the judiciary
abstract: We estimate the productivity effects of eliminating work from home (WFH) in the public sector by evaluating a mandatory return-to-office (RTO) policy in the Catalan judiciary. Leveraging cross-court variation in pre-mandate WFH intensity, difference-in-differences estimates show that terminating WFH reduced recorded procedural output by 5.2 percent, with no detectable changes in document quality or absenteeism. A multi-stakeholder survey shows that these recorded gains from WFH coexisted with coordination costs reported by external users: recorded case-processing tasks are performed on a digital platform, easy to do remotely and to monitor, whereas coordination with lawyers is synchronous, harder to do off-site, and largely unrecorded. Perceived impacts follow a gradient: case managers and supervisors, who observe the bureaucratic-efficiency margin, are positive about WFH, while lawyers, who depend on service coordination, are clearly negative.

title: Review of “Immigration: How the Past Shapes the Present”
Standards Without Substance: A Critical Evaluation of the UK Policy Profession’s Competency Framework
abstract: This article asks whether the UK’s competency framework for policy officials is fit for purpose, and finds that it is not. The quality of policy advice across Westminster systems has been eroding for some time, and reform efforts in several jurisdictions have tried to build the individual policy capacity of officials. In the UK, that effort has produced a succession of frameworks, none with much impact; the most recent, the 2021 Policy Profession Standards , is referenced in only 0.5% of advertised policy roles. The article makes two contributions: the first systematic account of how the earlier frameworks developed into the Standards, and a policy instrument analysis, supported by reflexive thematic analysis, of the Standards themselves. They are functional, specifying tasks to perform rather than the knowledge and capabilities officials need; atomistic, fragmenting the role into hundreds of separate descriptors; loaded with extraneous requirements; and missing fundamentals such as specialised policy knowledge and experience. Because a framework meant to build policy capacity instead carries the power to promote rather than hinder policy failure, these findings offer a design lesson for any jurisdiction that sets out to codify policy capacity.

title: Propaganda, Administrative Deformation, and the Erosion of State Capacity: The Case of the “Censorship Industrial Complex”
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper examines how a propaganda frame alleging the existence of a “Censorship Industrial Complex” was institutionalized and then helped justify the dismantling of US election information resilience infrastructure across multiple federal agencies. Drawing on documentary evidence and process tracing, we show how political entrepreneurs reframed routine, non‐coercive election information coordination and communication practices as a covert censorship regime targeting conservative speech. The article argues that this case is best understood as administrative deformation: weakly evidenced claims were laundered into higher‐status venues, including congressional investigations, litigation, executive action, and budget rationales, where they altered the incentive environment facing public agencies. The result was staff reductions, program cuts, and chilling effects, and weakened state capacity in a core domain of democratic administration. We conclude with recommendations for protecting administrative resilience under conditions of narrative attack.

title: Bricolage in bureaucracies: public leadership and bricolage behaviour in turbulent situations
abstract: Public employees increasingly face turbulent challenges in which principles such as foresight, planning, and consensus-seeking fall short. We examine bricolage as a robust governance strategy and conceptualize turbulence as a contextual moderator of the relationship between public leadership and bricolage behaviour. Based on survey data from 368 German public employees, the findings suggest that bricolage is less practiced under turbulent conditions. While rule-following leadership, contrary to expectations, becomes even more strongly and positively related to bricolage behaviour as conditions grow more turbulent, the positive association between accountability leadership and bricolage behaviour weakens substantially. Surprisingly, network governance leadership does not gain in importance. This study contributes to public administration research by further conceptualizing and exploring bricolage as a micro-level behavioural capacity in response to turbulence, by operationalizing turbulence as a graded situational stressor, and by demonstrating that turbulent contexts constitute a critical boundary condition for the exercise of public leadership.

title: Group heuristics and omnibus policies: how benefits to the “average American” explain public support for the Farm Bill
abstract: Abstract Omnibus bills often emerge from cross-party collaboration, bundling diverse programs to serve different constituencies. How people evaluate these complex policies remains an open question. We argue that individuals rely on an average-person heuristic, a group-based cognitive shortcut that simplifies policy evaluation by assessing broad distributive benefits. Analyzing multiple waves of survey data on the Farm Bill, a hallmark of American omnibus legislation, we find that perceptions of benefits to the “average American” are strongly and consistently associated with support for the policy package. These effects persist over time and when accounting for dominant alternative explanations, including racial resentment and self-interest. This paper is among the first to investigate public support for omnibus policies, presenting the average person as a relevant group-based heuristic that shapes opinion in complex, redistributive contexts.

title: Decentralised welfare services for families with disabled children: a register-based study of local variation and social inequalities
abstract: Abstract The tension between universalism and local autonomy is particularly pronounced in the Nordic welfare states. Decentralisation enables tailoring services to local needs and preferences but can also give rise to local disparities. Using Norway as a case, this study examines local variation and social inequalities in the allocation of decentralised care services to families of disabled children. The study is based on administrative register data on children with disabilities born between 2008 and 2019, identified by selected diagnoses or receipt of the attendance benefit ( n = 21,163). The results show that a non-trivial share of the total variation in service allocation lies between municipalities. Part of this variation was due to differences in care needs, but local conditions such as municipality size also matter, suggesting inequalities in access to services by place of residence. While the municipal variation did not reflect differences in the distribution of families’ socioeconomic status and immigration background, these characteristics were associated with allocation at the individual level.

title: Designing the age-65 boundary: who bears the cost when disability and aged care systems divide by age
abstract: Australia’s National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS) and aged care system are separated by an age-65 eligibility boundary that channels people with similar functional needs into different entitlement regimes, service markets, and assessment pathways. Policy responses have often treated this interface as a coordination problem between adjacent service systems. This article argues that coordination is only part of the issue: the age-65 rule also functions as a boundary-governance device in a layered welfare state. Engaging policy design scholarship on target populations, instruments, policy mixes and institutional constraints, the article develops a theoretical policy analysis and diagnostic heuristic for tracing how an eligibility boundary can translate formal classification into unequal support outcomes. Institutional layering creates nonequivalence between NDIS and aged care; boundary work translates that nonequivalence into administrative categories; street-level discretion handles residual ambiguity case by case; and policy feedback can stabilize the resulting arrangements. The analysis specifies three downstream design pathways: legal-entitlement discontinuity, supply-side market mismatch and discretionary coordination burden. The latter is the article’s main conceptual contribution: it names how the work of making the boundary livable is shifted to frontline actors, families and service users without matching authority, resources or accountability. The analysis explains why referral protocols and information sharing are insufficient on their own unless accompanied by attention to eligibility, bridging support, market alignment and boundary accountability. The Australian case clarifies a broader policy design challenge: how welfare states govern boundary populations when individualized support systems are layered onto older categorical care systems.

title: Public policymaking under uncertain time horizons: cyclicality, synchronization, and temporal delegation
abstract: Abstract What form does public policymaking take when actors cannot tell whether they face a short emergency, a medium-term episode, or a protracted transformation? Theories of cooperation and intertemporal choice assume time horizons that are either fixed or effectively indefinite, yet in many policy domains actors cannot specify how long a problem will last nor whether it will intensify, stabilize, or recede. Under such uncertainty, policymakers rely on short, repeatable policy cycles anchored in established calendars such as budgets and elections, a pattern conceptualized here as cyclicality. Two further mechanisms follow. Where implementation is dispersed across actors whose circumstances the center cannot observe, officials delegate authority over timing; where they delegate, they require synchronizers to keep dispersed cycles aligned, though horizon uncertainty caps how binding that coordination can be. Evidence from legal documents and semi-structured interviews tracks these mechanisms across four episodes of Romania’s implementation of the EU Temporary Protection Directive after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Officials sustained cooperation without resolving the underlying uncertainty, settling into an extended present that remained procedurally stable at the center while producing uneven temporal experiences at the periphery.

title: Epistemic Capabilities of Artificial Intelligence for Public Administration and Policy Research: A Framework for Scholarship in the Age of Intelligent Machines
abstract: ABSTRACT Artificial intelligence (AI) has gained much interest in public administration and public policy fields in recent years. Research on and that uses AI has so far treated it as an object or context within the broader administrative and governance discourse. In this article, we aim to shift the locus of scholarly attention on AI by focusing on its premise as a new epistemic technology that will shape how scholars conduct research. In doing so, it proposes a framework for leveraging AI as a methodological enabler that augments researchers' cognitive and analytical capabilities, thereby overcoming longstanding methodological barriers in the fields. We propose a framework distinguishing AI applications along two epistemological dimensions of research that make use of synthetic data and real‐world data: (1) inductive approaches to discover patterns and build theory to address exploratory questions (“what,” “so what”), and (2) deductive approaches to test hypotheses and establish causal relationships to serve explanatory and predictive purposes (“why,” “how”). We contend that AI has propelled the fields toward a “new normal science” characterized by human‐machine collaboration.

title: From policy drafting to policy capacity: rethinking evaluation of fine-tuned generative AI in public administration
Claiming or Refusing One's Rights: Strategic Appropriation and Non‐Take‐Up of Disability Schemes
abstract: ABSTRACT Drawing on 25 biographical interviews with people living with multiple sclerosis—the qualitative strand of a larger survey on the occupational consequences of the illness—this article analyses the heterogeneous relationship to French disability schemes. Between a right and its use lies a labour of self‐categorisation and moral calculation. We make three arguments. First, non‐take‐up is not reducible to an information deficit: it is the joint product of identity work, moral calculation and the presence or absence of an intercessor, which helps explain why the experimental record finds personal assistance outperforming information provision. Second, the deservingness criteria the literature measures in third parties operate here inside claimants, as a principle of self‐selection out of rights, especially where impairment is invisible and its onset gradual. Third, through their threshold and household‐means effects, the schemes produce the administrative status of disability as much as they compensate for its costs. Beneath the heterogeneity of trajectories lies one tension, between an entitlement defined by diagnosis and threshold and a claim that must pass through an identity; three ideal‐typical logics answer it, patterned by class and by gender.

title: Imperial Aid and Tax Mobilization in Late Colonial Africa
abstract: In 1929, the British Empire launched a four-decade development initiative to modernize colonial economies without self-government. Known as the Colonial Development and Welfare Fund, the program required colonial administrations to raise local taxes to cofinance development projects. This article shows that imperial aid expanded colonial taxation only after organizational reforms in the Colonial Service screened in officials who shared the metropole’s developmental agenda and made tax mobilization incentive-compatible with career advancement. Drawing on original data from 12 African colonies and extensive archival evidence, I show that aid increased tax revenues when patronage-based governors were replaced by career officers and promotion within the Colonial Service became conditional on fiscal performance. These findings highlight how bureaucratic incentives shaped the effectiveness of imperial aid and offer a new explanation for the expansion of fiscal capacity in late colonial Africa.

title: Judging for Democracy: Principles and Strategies in Hybrid Regimes

title: Friends like us? Support for democracy and the perception of great power
abstract: Amid democratic backsliding, the resurgence of authoritarianism in Africa, and the expanding influence of authoritarian great powers, this study examines how pro-democracy citizens perceive the United States, the European Union, China, and Russia. Rather than focusing on how great powers shape democratic trajectories in the Global South, it shifts attention to how pro-democracy publics evaluate these external actors. The findings show that pro-democracy citizens in South Africa view the influence of Russia and China negatively, while viewing the United States and the European Union more positively. Notably, the European Union is perceived more favourably than the United States. In contrast, citizens more receptive to authoritarianism tend to view Russia and China positively, though these patterns are more nuanced. More broadly, pro-democracy citizens appear less receptive to authoritarian external influence than their counterparts who are receptive to authoritarianism and may actively contest such influence through domestic political discourse. When authoritarian powers are viewed negatively by pro-democracy publics, these perceptions shape not only bilateral relations but also the broader resilience of democracy.

title: Foreign Aid and the Performance of Bureaucrats
abstract: Abstract Although much work examines foreign aid’s impact on development outcomes, its effect on bureaucracies—institutions that are key to development and profoundly influenced by aid interventions—remains understudied. I argue that project aid channeled through recipient governments alters financial and social aspects of work over which bureaucrats hold salient preferences, generating trade-offs that drive bureaucrats to redirect effort from routine work toward donor-funded initiatives. Drawing on interviews, surveys, and experiments with more than 600 Ugandan bureaucrats, I find that despite preferring government funding and autonomy, bureaucrats are drawn to better-paid aid projects, thus diverting effort away from regular duties. They also prefer departments with substantial donor funding even if it undermines the equity and teamwork they value. These findings provide micro-level insights into the unintended consequences of external development assistance: the same incentives that boost performance on discrete donor-funded projects divert effort from government programming and erode organizational cohesion.

title: Gender-Role Traditionalism and Opposition to Trade in the United States
abstract: ABSTRACT A recently popular line in American trade politics is that free trade threatens male blue-collar manufacturing employment, thereby undermining “traditional” family gender roles in which men work outside of the home and women work as caregivers within it. This study asks whether American mass politics mirrors these ideas. Does a preference for “traditional” gender roles lead Americans to protectionism? Our analysis of American National Election Studies data suggests that it does. We find a significant and highly robust empirical relationship between gender conservatism and protectionism. That relationship has been evident since 2008 and it decidedly is not a product of Trump-era politics. That relationship holds among men and women and among Republicans and Democrats, and it is robust to the inclusion of controls meant to isolate gender conservatism from other expressions of conservatism. The recent rise of gender-conservative trade skepticism should be understood as elite politics catching up with the public rather than leading it.

title: Survival Before Diplomacy: How Electoral Competition Constrains Leader Diplomacy in Turkey
abstract: ABSTRACT Do election campaigns reduce leaders’ engagement in foreign diplomacy? Whereas existing research argues that elections divert leaders’ time and attention away from international affairs, most evidence comes from the United States and relies on yearly data. This article examines the relationship between electoral cycles and diplomatic travel using the case of Turkey. Drawing on a monthly dataset of official foreign visits by Turkish prime ministers, presidents, and foreign ministers between 1990 and 2025, the analysis reveals that foreign travel declines significantly during election months and the immediately preceding period. The effect is strongest for top leaders, although foreign ministers also reduce travel. By using high-frequency data from a non-US case, the article provides new evidence on how domestic electoral pressures shape foreign-policy activity.

title: Positional Blurring in Context: How Dimensionality and Ideology Constrain Strategy
abstract: Positional blurring is a common and effective party strategy. It enables parties to downplay some issues while highlighting and clarifying their profile on others. However, we know little about how parties use this strategy outside European party systems, in which (right-wing) populist parties are particularly noteworthy for their blurred economic positions and clear cultural positions. Is that strategy inherent to populism or a reflection of context-specific incentives? This article uses data from Europe and Latin America to argue that populists tailor their strategies to the dimensionality of their party system and populism’s host ideology. We find that multidimensional party systems and exclusionary thick ideologies drive populists to blur their economic positions. Extending this research field beyond Europe for the first time, these findings show that populists are heterogeneous actors whose varied thick ideologies embedded in diverse political systems systematically constrain their strategic behavior.

title: The Democracy–Decarbonization Dilemma: Can Climate Assemblies Provide an Escape Route?
abstract: Meeting the goals of the Paris Agreement on climate change demands rapid and systemic economic transformation. Yet, contemporary democracies seem tragically ill-suited to this task. Proposals to insulate climate policy making from democratic control—for instance, through delegation to expert bodies—seem likely to fuel the rise of authoritarian populists, which is already eroding democratic norms and institutions. Deepening democratic engagement with the process of decarbonization may provide an escape route from this apparent “democracy–decarbonization dilemma.” In this vein, there has recently been much enthusiasm for climate assemblies. Such processes can have profound effects on their participants. But can they influence attitudes to democracy and support for ambitious climate policy among the wider public? We conduct a narrative review of the theoretical and empirical literature on democratic mini-publics (DMPs) to answer this question and critically reflect on our findings. We find that DMPs can influence the wider public’s attitudes toward democratic institutions and public policy to some extent. Yet, DMPs alone—even if well publicized—seem unlikely to be sufficient to stimulate the widespread shifts in knowledge, capacities, attitudes and behavior necessary to escape the democracy–decarbonization dilemma. We propose expanding the use, institutionalization, and orientation of DMPs—so that they become a widely recognized and routinized feature of deliberative systems, interacting with both governments and the wider citizenry—while advancing complementary democratic reform initiatives.

title: From referendum to reconciliation: How shared values and identities align with a commitment to long‐term collective action
abstract: Abstract One formal mechanism for effecting change to progress the rights of structurally disadvantaged groups is via citizen referenda. However, referenda are often characterized by divisive public debate. We suggest that sustaining action for long‐term change (beyond a referendum itself) may be associated with identifying with an opinion‐based group and perceiving shared values between advantaged and disadvantaged groups. Among a nationally representative sample of Australians ( N = 2467), we examined collective action intentions for the Reconciliation Movement 1 month before, 1 week before, and 1 week after the 2023 Voice to Parliament referendum. Study 1 used a random intercept cross‐lagged panel model to show that value consensus, opinion‐based identification as a supporter of Reconciliation, and reconciliation action were positively associated at a temporally stable level, but within‐person effects did not vary much from these levels. Study 2 used growth mixture models and revealed five diverging trajectories of reconciliation action, which were explained by differences in value consensus, opinion‐based identification, and support/opposition to the Voice referendum. Our findings offer some of the first evidence showing that value consensus and opinion‐based identification are associated with sustaining action for social change, especially during times of polarization and division.

title: Time dilation: the temporal structure of elite–voter incongruence on redistribution and immigration
abstract: While immigration and redistribution issues have increasingly converged at the elite level in Western Europe, they remain less correlated among voters, leading to significant elite–voter incongruence. This article argues that this incongruence is not static but temporal, rooted in political socialisation. Because earlier cohorts were socialised in an era when the immigration issue was less salient, even among elites, their preferences are less constrained by the current configuration of political competition. An Age–Period–Cohort analysis of data from 16 Western European countries demonstrates that the positive association between pro-redistribution and pro-immigration attitudes is weaker among earlier cohorts. This contrasts with newer cohorts, for whom both stances increasingly form a coherent left–right identity, mirroring the elite shift. The incongruence is therefore driven by earlier cohorts (e.g. ‘Left Authoritarians’) who maintain partisanship towards parties that are not fully aligned with their preferences, and it is expected to narrow through generational replacement.

title: The structural political power of firms – and its boundaries
abstract: This article examines the conditional importance of structural power in determining firms’ political influence. While structural power derived from firms’ economic size has been widely theorised as a key determinant of business influence, it is argued here that its effect is highly conditional, because it may be dampened by organisational, sector-level and institutional factors. Drawing on a unique survey of major firms in Denmark, Finland, and the Netherlands, this article analyses corporate influence across parliamentary and bureaucratic venues. The findings show that structural power is most effective when it is activated by insider lobbying. Moreover, strong variation is found across countries in terms of how important structural power is to gain more influence. These results contribute to debates on corporate political activity by demonstrating that structural power is not automatic but depends on firms’ ability to strategically deploy their political resources through active lobbying. These findings have implications for theories of business power and the study of corporate influence in different institutional and sectoral settings.

title: Revisiting Retirement and Social Security Claiming Decisions
abstract: Abstract The structure of the Social Security program presents a trade-off between benefit duration and size; individuals who claim early receive lower monthly payments. Surprisingly, even wealthy Americans with high life expectancies frequently claim benefits at the earliest eligibility age, a behavior inconsistent with conventional life-cycle theory predictions. In fact, there is a striking similarity in claiming ages across groups with vastly different life expectancies, wealth levels, and incentives to delay. This paper resolves this puzzle by introducing policy details and subjective beliefs about longevity and program rules into a rich, forward-looking life-cycle model. When included in the model, subjective beliefs substantially narrow the claiming-age gaps across education (college vs. non-college) and marital-status (married vs. single) groups. Specifically, differences in program beliefs alone account for 48.6% of the education claiming age gap and 75.1% of the marital status gap. Counterfactual policy simulations demonstrate that failing to account for these claiming mechanisms dramatically overstates individual responses to an increase in the normal retirement age and understates the resulting fiscal savings.

title: Author Requests for Removal from “Raising Health Awareness in Rural Communities: A Randomized Experiment in Bangladesh and India” (Siddique et al., 2024)
A Comment on “Raising Health Awareness in Rural Communities: A Randomized Experiment in Bangladesh and India” by Siddique et al. (2024)
Response to the Comment on “Raising Health Awareness in Rural Communities: A Randomized Experiment in Bangladesh and India” (Siddique et al., 2024)
The security unlock: How rural social pension makes people more entrepreneurial?
abstract: Previous literature on the determinants of entrepreneurship has not explored the role of social pension. Leveraging variation in the roll-out timing of a universal rural pension program across Chinese counties, our analysis, at both the individual and aggregate levels, reveals that pension provision led to an increase in entrepreneurship among the younger generation. We show that this effect operates through two primary channels: an intergenerational transfer channel and a local demand channel. Specifically, the pension program mitigates upward transfers from adult children to elderly parents, while boosting local consumer demand, which exerts a demand-side “pull” effect on enterprise establishment. Our findings may shed new light on the interplay between pension, intergenerational resource allocation, and entrepreneurial activity.

title: Health Shocks, Perceived Mortality Risk, and Financial Preferences: Longitudinal Evidence From Share
abstract: Major health events are salient mortality cues and may reshape financial preferences in later life. However, evidence on the role of subjective mortality risk in shaping financial preferences is scarce. This study uses a longitudinal quasi-experimental design to examine whether incident heart attack, stroke, cancer, diabetes, or high blood pressure are followed by a change in perceived mortality risk and, subsequently, stated willingness to take financial risk and self-reported financial planning horizons. We use longitudinal data from Waves 4-9 of the Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe (SHARE), comprising more than 200,000 observations on individuals aged 50 and older. A propensity score matching difference-in-differences approach estimates the impact of each health shock on changes in subjective 1-year mortality risk. Mediation analysis decomposes total effects of a health shock on financial preferences into components operating through perceived mortality and components acting directly. Major health events, particularly cancer, stroke, and heart attack, produce clear increases in perceived mortality risk. Changes in financial preferences are generally modest: higher perceived mortality is associated with slightly shorter self-reported financial planning horizons and lower stated willingness to take financial risk. Significant direct effects of health shocks on self-reported planning horizons remain after conditioning on perceived mortality, consistent with the influence of the background-risk channel. Overall, perceived mortality risk is an empirically relevant but only partial mediator between health shocks and financial preferences in older age. These findings underscore the importance of distinguishing mortality beliefs from broader consequences of illness when modeling household responses to health shocks and when designing interventions for individuals experiencing health-related uncertainty.

title: How social media produces “Cheap Europe”: Digital Balkanism and the politics of creator mobility
abstract: Digital platforms increasingly mediate how socioeconomic unevenness becomes visible, often recoding structural inequality as consumable value. This article introduces the concept of digital Balkanism to explain how platformed travel content reworks long-standing intra-European hierarchies. Drawing on a critical discourse analysis of 108 English-language YouTube videos about Bulgaria, we identify five recurring frames: cheapness-as-freedom, therapeutic pastoralism, discovery, managed difference, and platformed epistemic authority that are recognizable conventions of platformed travel that often operate across other peripheralized destinations. While these frames are not distinctly Balkanist, we identified two higher-order structuring logics that render their articulation in this corpus specifically Balkanist: conditional Europeanness and off-white Europe, which position Bulgaria as “European” yet persistently deficient, and “white” yet conditionally so. Digital Balkanism therefore operates less through overt denigration than through the conversion of this conditionality into epistemic and platform value. The article extends critical platform and decolonial media scholarship by theorizing othering within Europe rather than across a simple West/non-West divide.

title: The “Netflix Look”: Moving image aesthetics as data under platform logic
abstract: This article examines Netflix’s industrial model through the framework of platform logic, arguing that the data-centric approach it adopts in the production of moving images alters the creative process. The result is a conceptual shift from shooting a film to capturing an image. Bridging platform studies and film theory, I build on David Bordwell’s poetics of cinema, which conceives the production process as a negotiation between institutional constraints and creative intention. Analyzing the Netflix Partner Help Center as a primary document, I argue that it reflects a departure from this traditional dynamic and that Netflix conceptualizes moving image production as a data capture process. I conclude that this transformation reflects a broader data logic that extends beyond Netflix to the production of contemporary moving images.

title: From platform outrage to institutional consequence: Convergent hybrid media accountability in Morocco
abstract: This article develops the concept of convergent hybrid media accountability (CHMA) to explain how informal digital criticism is translated into institutional consequence in Morocco’s hybrid media environment. Moving beyond the view of accountability as an internal professional virtue, the article argues that where formal bodies are fragile or distrusted, citizens use platformed publics to initiate scrutiny from outside media institutions. Drawing on a pragmatist mixed-methods design – combining a survey of 205 social media users, eight semi-structured interviews with journalists and editors, and process tracing of nine accountability episodes (2022–2025) – the study finds that online outrage only matters when it crosses a threshold of convergence . This bridging moment occurs when informal claims gain legitimacy and procedural uptake through two linked mechanisms – amplification and legitimation, then escalation and formalisation. Findings reveal an empowerment paradox : the most active users report high efficacy but also perceive strong institutional resistance. The article concludes that platform acceleration and emerging digital-content regulations have intensified both the speed and selectivity of accountability in Morocco. Ultimately, this study offers CHMA as a de-Westernising, potentially transferable framework for analysing how media accountability operates in hybrid media environments characterised by media pluralism and managed political asymmetry.

title: The Real-World Effects of Constructive Journalism: A Field Experiment on Climate Change News
abstract: To explore the effects of constructive journalism beyond one-shot experiments, this study utilizes a 2-week constructive journalism campaign on climate change in two regional Danish news outlets. Employing a difference-in-differences approach, news users exposed to the campaign were compared to news users from regions not exposed to the campaign. The constructive journalism campaign yielded more positive evaluations of news coverage, but not on core quality aspects like trustworthiness and balance. No effects were found for emotional responses, response efficacy, and behavioural intentions, but a positive effect was found for self-efficacy, indicating the potential of a constructive approach to journalism.
