How Does Participation in the New Rural Pension Program Affect Attitudes Toward Public Services?
abstract: To mitigate and adapt to the challenges posed by population aging, the Chinese government had implemented the New Rural Pension Program (NRPP), a top-down initiative with extensive coverage. As a form of social welfare, it remains unclear whether the implementation of the NRPP improves rural residents’ attitudes toward public services. To identify this causal relationship, this study disaggregates public services attitudes into eight dimensions and employs five waves of CFPS data (2012–2020) to examine the effects of NRPP benefit receipt on public services attitudes. Results show that receiving social welfare significantly improves farmers’ evaluations of public services. Moreover, increased trust in local officials serves as an important mechanism, while household size moderates this effect. This study extends the explanatory scope of theories such as self-interest theory and offers targeted recommendations for the construction and development of China’s social security system.

title: Reform for all? The limits of expertise in producing equitable outcomes
abstract: Administrative reforms often seek to improve performance by changing bureaucratic or professional expertise. Yet technical skills alone may not disrupt the forces that generate unequal outcomes across social groups. We argue that systemic bias shapes professionalization and discretionary judgment, limiting expertise-substitution reforms’ capacity to reduce racial disparities even when they improve average outcomes. We test this using a 2018 Dallas reform that deployed co-response teams pairing police officers with clinicians and social workers on mental health calls. A difference-in-­differences analysis across divisions finds significant reductions in psychiatric holds and arrests, but the gains concentrate among White male citizens; arrests of Black males increase significantly. A complementary incident-level analysis of the conditional probability of a coercive outcome points to a different pattern of heterogeneous effects: White males show a higher post-reform probability of psychiatric holds while Black females and Hispanic males experience lower ones. Both sets of findings shed new light on the scholarship of administrative reform and hold practical implications for both the impact of such programs and the ways in which they are evaluated.

title: Socially oriented contracting and public employees’ job satisfaction: evidence from the federal small disadvantaged business program
abstract: While contracting out is often viewed as having negative consequences for public employees, less attention has been paid to the positive outcomes certain types of contracting may have for them. In particular, recent scholarship proposes that contracting out may improve employees’ work attitudes when it emphasizes pro-social factors in the process. Using the case of the federal Small Disadvantaged Business (SDB) contracting program—which emphasizes diversity and equity in procurement—this study examines whether contracting programs that promote social outcomes are associated with public employees’ job satisfaction. Drawing from research on sector differences, person-organization fit, and representative bureaucracy, we hypothesize a positive association between SDB contracting efforts and job satisfaction, with employees from underrepresented backgrounds experiencing a more pronounced increase. Linking U.S. federal government contracting data to the Federal Employee Viewpoint Survey (FEVS), our analyses provide support for the hypotheses. The implications of these findings for government contracting and public human resource management are discussed.

title: Arrested development: how performance regimes constrain changes to public sector performance measurement
abstract: Public sector organizations increasingly operate within broader performance regimes—the wider systems of rules, actors, and practices that shape how performance is measured and managed—yet little research has examined how these regimes enable or block attempts of public sector organizations to redesign their performance measurement (PM) systems. This study addresses that gap by developing an analytical framework built around the concept of lock-in mechanisms, which provides a structured way to identify regulatory, material, behavioral and discursive barriers to the redesign of public sector PM. This framework is then applied to the performance regime governing Danish employment services, where municipal job centers are actively trying to redesign their PM systems to better reflect client experiences and value creation. Our findings reveal that redesign efforts are constrained by lock-in mechanisms operating at three distinct levels: within the institutional context, mechanisms entrench upward accountability as the dominant purpose of PM; at the level of performance actors, mechanisms preserve rigid boundaries between those who are measured and those who do the measuring; and at the level of performance interventions, mechanisms sustain top-down uses of performance information, limiting more bottom-up approaches.

title: Revisiting the venerable debate on strategy content and public service performance
Differentiating distributed leadership: introducing distributed professional development leadership and its motivational consequences
abstract: Traditional hierarchical approaches to governing and leading public professionals have not always proven successful, and integrative and hybrid perspectives on professionalism are therefore receiving increasing attention. This study integrates professional development leadership (PDL) and distributed leadership (DL) theory and introduces the concept of distributed professional development leadership (D-PDL). D-PDL implies that employees without formal leadership responsibilities are engaged in core PDL activities focused on facilitating and realizing a shared understanding of professionalism within the scope of organizational goals. The study theorizes that professionals’ engagement in D-PDL leads to more autonomous motivation than engagement in generic DL, which covers a broad range of leadership activities that are disconnected from the professional core task. Survey data from approximately 2,400 Danish medical doctors support the theoretical framework and show that doctors’ engagement in D-PDL is associated with more intrinsic motivation and public service motivation, whereas their engagement in generic DL is primarily associated with extrinsic motivation. The study emphasizes the relevance of moving PDL beyond a leader-centric concept and of distinguishing between different types of DL activities.

title: Regulatory Capture, Public Trust and Pro‐Environmental Behaviors
abstract: ABSTRACT Regulatory capture, where special interests steer regulation away from public interest, is widely discussed, but its broader public consequences remain underexplored. We explore the relationship between perceived regulatory capture, public trust and pro‐environmental behaviors using online survey data in China. Findings show that perceived material and information capture (the latter measured with a single scenario‐based proxy) have significant negative associations with public trust in local ( b = −0.154, −0.105) and central government ( b = −0.087, −0.064). Direct associations with non‐activist pro‐environmental behaviors in the public sphere are consistently negative and supported by bootstrapped confidence intervals across specifications (material: β = −0.066 to −0.082; information: β = −0.036 to −0.047), whereas several corresponding private sphere associations are not. Indirect associations are supported only in selected models. These findings highlight the public implications of regulatory capture, distinguishing material and information capture, and extend understanding of public trust and pro‐environmental behaviors.

title: Managing Collaboration Dynamics Under Pressure: Lessons From the COVID ‐19 Medical Supply Shortage
abstract: ABSTRACT In crisis responses such as the COVID‐19 medical supply shortage, senior policy makers often emphasize urgency, a strategy that prioritizes the rapid achievement of intermediate goals. While this approach can drive swift action, it also introduces challenges and trade‐offs that can hinder collaboration toward long‐term success. These challenges often arise from misalignment between organizational norms and priorities of collaborating partners, which can undermine legitimacy and performance. Policymakers should consider how personnel composition, such as large military contingents, shapes task force culture and operational dynamics. Even in fast‐moving crises, clearly aligning roles, goals, and timelines from the start can reduce confusion, while leaders must navigate cultural norms and challenge ingrained practices to support collaboration.

title: The Fragility of Merit: Presidential Power and the Civil Service Under Trump. By J. EdwardKellough, New York: Routledge, 2024. 152 pp. $52.99 (paperback). ISBN: 978‐1‐03‐265634‐2; $190.00 (hardcover). ISBN: 978‐1‐03‐265637‐3
abstract: The author of the book under review, Dr. J. Edward Kellough, served as the chair of the reviewer's doctoral dissertation committee at the University of Georgia.

title: Decarbonizing housing in polarized environments: instrument accumulation and the politics of implementation in German cities
abstract: The growing mismatch between expanding policy portfolios and constrained implementation capacity challenges the problem-solving capacity of modern states. Existing research shows how policy growth drives overload and organizational coping, but neglects how polarization reconfigures the politics of accumulation, creating distinct vulnerabilities for implementers and motivating strategies that decouple implementation from instrument objectives. This paper analyzes Germany’s heat transition, an expansion of the climate policy portfolio aimed at decarbonizing housing by 2045. It compares regulatory instruments created outside channels of vertical policy integration with the heat planning instrument, developed through vertical policy integration, across two polities and four cities. The findings show that rising polarization made it rational for ministerial elites to bypass established policymaking procedures. While this secured enactment, it carried non-decisions about task allocation and burden offsetting into implementation and failed to secure implementer buy-in. Local governments adapted regulatory instruments to polity-specific vulnerabilities and their own political priorities, decoupling implementation from intended objectives. In centralized polities, they used these instruments to expand capacity and mitigate overload; in delegated polities, to rebalance dependence on third parties. By contrast, the heat planning instrument incorporated implementation expertise, offset implementation burdens, and was implemented largely as intended.

title: Townsend’s poverty ‘threshold’ revisited: an analysis that utilises his critics’ insights and all 60 of his deprivation indicators
abstract: Abstract Peter Townsend’s influential 1968/69 poverty study is still lauded. Yet controversy surrounded his claim that it established a meaningful poverty ‘threshold’ at an income level equivalent to 140 per cent of means-tested state benefit rates, below which deprivation increased more rapidly. This article presents findings from the first detailed analysis of the data to offer no support to Townsend’s ‘threshold’ claim. Earlier analyses used his sub-set of twelve deprivation indicators, such as lacking a refrigerator, and Townsend said it was a ‘pity’ more were not used. Using all sixty, the research presented here both replicated Townsend’s methods and utlilised criticisms of them by, for example, employing a ‘mean’ (alongside a ‘mode’) measure of average deprivation. Remarkably, even with only Townsend’s twelve indicators, mean deprivation was lower among those with an income at 120–139 per cent of benefit rates (immediately below Townsend’s 140 per cent ‘threshold’) than at 140–159 per cent. Whether Townsend’s or other methods were applied, deprivation increased significantly as income fell below about 119 per cent of benefit rates, but it plateaued as income fell further. The article highlights the arbitrariness of poverty lines and the advantages of using various lines when evaluating social policies.

title: Managing policy expertise through think tank–state relations in Kazakhstan
abstract: The interconnections among expertise, politics, and policy making remain of persistent scholarly interest, yet they are still insufficiently examined outside consolidated liberal democracies. Addressing this gap, this article analyses think tank–state relations in Kazakhstan, approached here as a case of soft authoritarianism – a political system that imposes systematic restrictions on political rights and civic freedoms while retaining formal democratic institutions and relying more on citizen persuasion, agenda management, and depoliticization than on overt coercion. The study examines how soft authoritarianism shapes the conditions under which think tanks operate and how these conditions evolve during complex crises that heighten the demand for expertise. Empirically, it focuses on Kazakhstan over the period 2010–25. Drawing on original expert interviews, the analysis shows that think tanks in Kazakhstan operate within a selectively pluralistic yet tightly managed policy environment characterized by resource dependence, co-optation, and personalized access to decision-making. Rather than excluding or eliminating independent expertise altogether, the state strategically incorporates and manages it through informal networks, selective funding, and bounded participation in policy consultations. The findings further demonstrate that major crises create temporary openings for expert engagement and role redefinition, but do not fundamentally transform underlying power relations. By examining how expertise is incorporated, constrained, and instrumentalized under soft authoritarianism, while drawing comparisons with both de-democratizing and more restrictive authoritarian contexts, the article contributes to advancing comparative debates on think tanks and policy expertise beyond democratic environments.

title: Public views on the use of AI in scientific research
abstract: Generative AI tools are becoming common in scientific work, yet little is known about how the public – the taxpayers who fund much of this research – view their use. In a preregistered, nationally representative UK survey ( N = 1465), we find that the public attitudes towards AI-assisted research are nuanced: While most respondents support public funding for scientific research in general (77%), support falls sharply when generative AI is involved (42%). This AI funding penalty is strongest among scientifically literate, politically liberal, younger, and female respondents. Moreover, 34–40% say they would trust both the science and the scientists less if generative AI was used during research. At the same time, a majority (83–85%) support scientists' use of generative AI when substantial human input is retained. Results suggest ambivalence about the use of AI as a scientific tool, findings that have direct implications for how AI-assisted research is governed, disclosed, and ultimately judged legitimate.

title: Breadwinner backlash: The gendered effects of industrial decline
abstract: Abstract Low‐skilled men have long been vulnerable to globalization, decarbonization, and other forms of economic disruption. When shocks are realized, women often increase their paid labor to compensate for men's loss of income. We study how layoffs of low‐skilled men and concurrent shifts in workforce composition toward women affect voting. We theorize that this labor market rebalancing produces “nostalgic” coalitions of men and women that seek a return to male‐breadwinner family models. Such attitudes fuel right‐wing movements that pledge to protect conservative gender roles. Evidence from local labor markets and voting in the United States over the last two decades, as well as a longitudinal study tracking individual Americans over several decades, support this theory. These findings contribute a new gender‐based account of the globalization backlash.

title: Selection, Stability, and Shock: Political Attitudes of Chinese Students at Home and Abroad
Candidate deviation and partisan loyalty: Policy divergence, moral failures, and American voter behavior
abstract: Partisanship is the strongest cue in voting behavior in the United States, providing a powerful signal to voters about which candidates to support. This study examines what it takes to dissuade partisans from supporting their party's candidate and what form dissent might take. Using policy and moral deviations, we test the limits of partisan loyalty through two experiments. First, a conjoint study shows that policy deviations and moral failures can reduce the likelihood of a vote for partisan candidates. Then, an online campaign simulation replicates these results and permits a closer examination of how dissent emerges. We find that a combination of policy divergence and moral failures can lead partisans to abandon their party's candidate. We also find that partisans are more likely to abstain from voting in these instances rather than defect to the other party. Only in the most severe cases do deviations convince some subjects to cast a vote for the other party's candidate.

title: Conditional gender gaps in welfare state support: The role of labor market and household inequality
abstract: Abstract Why are women more supportive of the welfare state than men? Existing literature on this attitudinal gender gap focuses mainly on how men and women, on average, experience varied risks in the labor market. Feminist scholarship argues that the welfare state has the potential to equalize within-household bargaining power between men and women, but has not fully explored the political implications of contemporary inequality dynamics within low- vs. high-income households. We theorize that the gender gap in welfare state support is shaped by the interplay between households’ position on the income distribution and women’s relative incomes within households. Using Luxembourg Income Study (LIS) data from 1963 to 2024, we first find that, within households, women’s income relative to male partners falls systematically moving up the income distribution. Next, our analyses of 2016 International Social Survey Programme data show that gender gaps in welfare state support are narrow and statistically uncertain among lower-income households, where need is high. However, in higher-income households, gender gaps emerge and grow moving up the household income distribution. Furthermore, attitudinal gaps in higher-income households are sensitive to inequalities in relative income – large where male incomes predominate and narrow or nonexistent in households where women contribute half or more of income. Gender inequality and its political consequences are thus intertwined with broader structures of income inequality.

title: A risky business: navigating autocratization through ideological legitimation claims
abstract: Abstract Autocratization typically results from measures aiming at seizing, strengthening, and consolidating political power. However, it is not without risks: it may produce adverse reactions from multiple actors and possibly lead to the fall of its perpetrators from power. What makes autocratizing incumbents more capable of surviving during such a perilous process? We argue that the adoption of ideological legitimation strategies makes incumbents more capable of surviving during autocratization in democratic and electoral authoritarian regimes. We test our argument through survival analysis of incumbents in power during processes of autocratization from 1900 to 2024. Though relatively understudied in the context of autocratization, our study highlights ideology as a key factor in the process of transformation of a political regime toward autocracy.

title: Firm Balance Sheet Liquidity, Monetary Policy Shocks, and Investment Dynamics
abstract: I study the role of firms' balance sheet liquidity in the transmission of monetary policy to investment. I develop a heterogeneous firm macroeconomic model with financial constraints, debt issuance costs, and differential returns on firms' cash and borrowing. The model matches key novel moments from U.S. firm-level data on liquid asset holdings, debt issuance activity, and investment responses to identified monetary shocks. Counterfactual analysis shows that the rise in U.S. firms' liquid asset holdings over recent decades has significantly increased the relevance of balance sheet liquidity and the behavior of liquid asset returns in monetary transmission.

title: The importance of school quality ratings for school choices: Evidence from a nationwide system
abstract: Studying a long-running nationwide system of school inspections, we show how school choices and enrollment respond to new information about school quality. We use exogenous variation in the timing of school inspections around the school choice deadline to isolate the effect of information over and above underlying changes in school quality. We find that low- and higher-income parents respond similarly to new information. Conditional on household location, non-targeted information provision therefore does not increase school segregation by household income.

title: Bringing Work Home: Flexible Work Arrangements as Gateway Jobs for Women in West Bengal
abstract: Abstract There is a large latent workforce in developing countries that consists of hundreds of millions of women who prefer to have paid work and yet are out of the labor force. Often, available job opportunities are incompatible with traditional gender roles that encourage women to stay at home. In a randomized experiment with 1,670 households, we partner with a jobs platform to offer short-term data work to women who are out of the labor force. We find three main results. First, flexible work-from-home jobs are highly effective at bringing women into paid work. Job flexibility more than triples take-up from 15% for an office job to 48% for a job that women can do from home while multitasking with childcare. Second, these jobs can act as a stepping stone to less flexible work. Trying paid work from home increases take-up of less flexible jobs two to three months later among women without previous work experience. “Gateway jobs” are especially important for women from more traditional households: their labor supply is more likely to be marginal to flexibility, and in turn, work experience shifts their attitudes to become less traditional. Third, from the labor demand side, remote work comes with trade-offs in worker performance. Working from the office increases accuracy by 3% and speed by 18%. However, these performance drawbacks of work-from-home arrangements may be outweighed by the increase in available workers.

title: Markup Estimation using Production and Demand Data: An Application to the US Brewing Industry
abstract: Abstract We compare and combine two distinct approaches to estimating market power in the US brewing industry—one based on production data, the other on demand. Both methods produce similar estimates of average markups and reveal a recent upward trend. We then combine the two approaches in two ways. First, we replace conventional instruments in demand estimation with a moment involving a production-based markup estimate, yielding similar results. We then evaluate the common (but controversial) assumption that retail markets operate competitively, finding that demand-based markups recovered with the assumption of competitive retail markets align with production-based estimates, as long as downstream costs are accounted for.

title: Knowledge diffusion, rising inequality, and the dynamics of a pulled front
abstract: Abstract A model of economic growth is presented in which workers increase their labour income by learning from higher-paid workers. They also experience individual random income shocks. A calibration of the model to U.S. wage micro data implies that these shocks are Brownian ‘noise’, with drift close to zero. Growth comes from occasional random advances at the frontier, which create novel learning opportunities for others and drive sustained growth. The long-run growth rate is increasing in both the variance of shocks and the knowledge-diffusion rate. The model closely reproduces the evolving shape of the U.S. wage distribution between 1991 and 2023.

title: Threat and Assimilation: Evidence from Refugees in Germany
abstract: Abstract This paper studies how local threat shapes refugees’ cultural assimilation and economic integration, exploiting plausibly exogenous variation in their allocation across German regions between 2013 and 2016. Using representative survey data and administrative records, we measure cultural preferences alongside employment, earnings, and job characteristics, and build a threat index combining contemporaneous and historical local xenophobia. Refugees assigned to more hostile regions converge more rapidly to Germans’ stated preferences, yet do not find jobs faster and experience slower earnings growth. We show that local hostility heightens threat perceptions, prompting quicker cultural adoption, while higher discrimination slows refugees’ successful economic integration.

title: The Content Moderator’s Dilemma: Removal of Toxic Content and Distortions to Online Discourse
abstract: Abstract There is an ongoing debate about how to moderate toxic speech on social media and the impact of content moderation on online discourse. This paper proposes and validates a methodology for measuring the content-moderation-induced distortions in online discourse using text embeddings from computational linguistics. Applying the method to a representative sample of 5 million US political Tweets, we find that removing toxic Tweets significantly alters the semantic composition of content. The magnitudes of the distortions are comparable to removing 4 out of 67 topics from the online discourse at random. This finding is consistent across different embedding models, toxicity metrics, and samples. Importantly, we demonstrate that these effects are not solely driven by toxic language but by the removal of topics often expressed in toxic form. We propose an alternative approach to content moderation that uses generative Large Language Models to rephrase toxic Tweets, preserving their salvageable content rather than removing them entirely. We show that this rephrasing strategy reduces toxicity while mitigating distortions in online content.

title: Ratcheting up Paris
abstract: The Paris Agreement is designed to increase climate ambition gradually through a process of ratcheting up. What is the plausible endpoint of this process? We develop a tractable integrated assessment model in which countries interact through a decentralized general equilibrium and negotiate unanimously over a global carbon budget, with all mitigation implemented via a global carbon price. We prove existence and uniqueness of a unanimous international agreement on global emissions, in which carbon pricing revenues are redistributed across countries in proportion to marginal climate damages. In a quantitative application for 154 countries, the resulting equilibrium limits global mean surface temperature change to 1.51C, at a carbon price of 320 USD/tCO2. The associated international transfers of carbon pricing revenue are progressive toward lower-income countries and amount to about 0.8% of global GDP annually - an order of magnitude larger than the Paris Agreement's climate finance target.

title: Are rich people smarter? A comment
What Explains Growing Gender and Racial Education Gaps?
abstract: ABSTRACT We study why US college graduation gaps by gender and race widened across cohorts. We develop a dynamic life‐cycle model with endogenous education, labor supply, marriage, fertility, and welfare participation. Preferences are fixed across cohorts and race/ethnic groups; changes arise from family background, labor‐market opportunities, and marriage markets. Labor‐market changes account for half of growth in women's graduation from the 1960 to 1980 cohorts. Parental background accounts for one quarter and marriage markets for one fifth. These shares are similar for Whites, Blacks, and Hispanics, but absolute gains were larger for White women, which led to wider racial gaps.

title: Enduring links: mental health effects of ex-partner’s life events among separated parents
Passing on Talent: A Generativity Perspective on the Effects of Perceived Overqualification Among Older Employees
abstract: Drawing on generativity theory, we examine the positive effects of perceived overqualification among older employees. Specifically, we argue that perceptions of overqualification in older employees are positively associated with a core generativity motive—that is, a desire to support and guide the next generation and be needed by them. Further, we argue that generativity motive predicts prosocial attitudes and behaviors in the form of prosocial meaning of work for future generations and helping behavior. Additionally, we identify mature-age practices—that is, human resource practices tailored to address older employees’ needs—as a key contextual factor that strengthens the indirect pathway between perceptions of overqualification in older employees and their prosocial attitudes and behaviors. We test and find support for our hypotheses in two independent field studies—a three-wave field study of older employees (Study 1, N = 261) and a dyadic three-wave field study of employees of various ages and their respective supervisors (Study 2, N = 274 dyads). Theoretical and practical implications of our study are discussed.

title: Political Actors and Their Media Practices: Analyzing the Role of Media Participation in Democratic Backsliding and Resilience
abstract: This paper draws together insights from political science and political communication to advance a new understanding of the role of media in democratic backsliding and resilience. The central argument is that all political actors may also be media actors, although they may do so anonymously or use false identities. Thus, mass participation in media enables mass participation in political change, with better and worse democratic outcomes. As such, when analyzing backsliding and resilience scholars need to move away from focusing solely on particular institutions and actors with presumed democratic functions, as well as assuming that media and expressive freedom will necessarily serve democratic ends. Instead, we advocate analyzing how the participatory media practices of various actors interact with one another via communicative structures within processes of backsliding and resilience. Participatory media practices that prevent democratic breakdown include disseminating early warnings of backsliding, exposing executive errors and corruption, coordinating pro-democratic mobilization, and platforming the opposition, as well as countering disinformation and delegitimizing democratic institutions and processes. We also indicate how participatory media practices may aid democratic bounceback, as well as the challenges involved in reimagining the media infrastructure needed to sustain democratic recovery in the long-term. Thus, we argue that democratic backsliding and resilience should be reconceptualized as profoundly participatory, mediated processes.

title: Rejection of cross-cutting news depends on content, sources, and cultural contexts: evidence from online trace data
The Political Psychology of Citizens in Rising China Yida Zhai. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2026. 397 pp. $150.00 (hbk). ISBN 9781009489713
Policy instability and asymmetric decoupling: A multiple streams analysis of Australia's JobSeeker Payment reform
abstract: Abstract This article asks why the successful coupling of the problem, policy, and political streams during the COVID‐19 reform of Australia's JobSeeker Payment failed to produce durable institutional change. It adopts a longitudinal single‐case design covering 2014–2025 and applies the Multiple Streams Framework to trace the movement of the three streams from pre‐crisis separation to pandemic coupling and post‐crisis divergence. The article develops the concept of asymmetric decoupling, whereby political authorisation is withdrawn before the underlying problem has been resolved or viable policy alternatives have disappeared, causing the problem to recede from the agenda and policy proposals to lose access to authoritative decision‐making. By distinguishing short‐term policy breakthroughs from durable institutionalisation, asymmetric decoupling extends the Multiple Streams Framework from the opening of policy windows to the destabilisation of stream relationships and institutional reversion after those windows begin to close. Points for practitioners Crisis‐driven policy breakthroughs should not be assumed to have secured durable institutional support. Reform durability depends not only on persistent social need or feasible policy design but also on continuing political authorisation and access to authoritative decision‐making. Major temporary welfare reforms should include formal review points, social impact assessment, parliamentary scrutiny, and institutionalised participation by welfare and poverty experts before support is reduced or terminated.

title: The Ratchet Effect of Environmental Policy Combinations
abstract: Governments increasingly pair command-and-control regulation with market-based instruments, but whether the resulting combination produces effects that persist independently of its component instruments remains unclear. We distinguish two claims conflated under “ratchet effect”: that policy effects reinforce over time, and that they resist reversal once intensity is later scaled back. Using 288 Chinese prefecture-level cities (2000–2023) and the staggered rollout of environmental courts and emissions-trading pilots, we estimate two-way fixed-effects, event-study, and asymmetric models. Neither instrument alone reliably lowers PM 2.5 , but their interaction does, with effects strengthening for several years post-adoption. Reductions in policy intensity do not proportionately restore prior pollution levels—a pattern far stronger for command-and-control than market-based instruments. These findings extend policy feedback theory to environmental policy mixes, showing that instrument pairing, not stringency alone, governs the durability of environmental gains.

title: Taming the Careerists: The Politics of Foreign Policy Implementation. By MinjuKim, New York: Cambridge University Press, 2026. 224 pp. $100 (hardback); $33 (ebook). ISBN: 9781009789721
abstract: The author declares no conflicts of interest. Data sharing not applicable to this article as no datasets were generated or analyzed during the current study.

title: Motivated to exhaustion? Public service motivation, curvilinear strain, and the buffer of collaborative culture
abstract: Public service motivation (PSM) is widely treated as a resource that strengthens engagement, yet excessive motivation may yield diminishing returns. Integrating the job demands-resources model, conservation of resources theory, and the too-much-of-a-good-thing logic, this study tests a curvilinear relationship between PSM and job exhaustion, and the moderating role of collaborative culture. Using a two-wave survey of 408 Korean public servants with a one-month lag, hierarchical regressions identify a U-shaped pattern: exhaustion declines at low-to-moderate PSM but rises beyond a threshold. Collaborative culture significantly flattens this curve, indicating that supportive, collective norms mitigate PSM-related strain at very high levels of PSM. The findings challenge the assumption that PSM is uniformly beneficial, recasting PSM as a conditional resource that can operate as a demand at high levels. The study clarifies when PSM is sustainable and positions collaboration as an actionable boundary condition, yielding implications for motivation theory and for the collaborative organization of public service.

title: Executive agencies in developing countries: the case of the parastatal organizations in Suriname
abstract: This article compares agencification in developing and OECD countries, illustrated by the case of Suriname. Findings show that developing countries prefer statutory bodies and SOEs. Motives for establishment are economic development and the provision of collective goods; typical motives from OECD countries are not present. Patronage plays a major role, and governance and accountability relations are generally weak. Based on these findings, existing agencification theory should include motives that are specific to developing countries, such as pressure from international organizations; pay attention to colonial legacies and acknowledge that agencification in developing countries is much less driven by NPM.

title: Design anthropology for transforming power relations in societal transitions
abstract: This article makes the argument that design can serve the purpose of transforming power relations in societal transitions. The article discusses diverse theories of power and their relationship to design, whereby it considers aspects of agency, relationality and scale. Using a design anthropology approach, a theoretical framework is defined for the empirical study of power. The framework is operationalized in a local energy transition project in Amsterdam Southeast. In this empirical study, we describe three power relations that were encountered, the design interventions performed, and their transformative outcomes. Finally, the broader implications for design in societal transitions are discussed.

title: New development: The liberating principle—a systemic foundation for public transformation
Debate: The performance audit paradox—more evidence, more confidence, but not necessarily more insight
abstract: Performance audit operates in an era of unprecedented data availability. Administrative datasets, real-time indicators and analytics offer unparalleled visibility into public activity. Yet performa...

title: Classification Drift: Decisions Passing Quietly but Compounding Inequity
abstract: Public-sector classification systems accumulate classification drift, a widening gap between what employees actually do, how their work is described, and how they are compensated. Because classification shapes pay, role comparison, and internal equity at scale, classification drift quietly compounds into measurable inequity. At a large U.S. urban public school district (the District), this drift manifested as 435 employees sharing the title “Specialist” across 24 pay grades ($47,000–$125,000). This article describes PRISM (Progressive Refinement and Intelligence Synthesis Model), a multi-model AI framework developed with a research-university partner’s Data Science Institute that introduces validation friction at high-stakes decision points. Rather than automating approvals, PRISM surfaces disagreement between independent AI models and routes ambiguous cases to human reviewers with a structured evidence package. Across 992 positions, 173 cases (17%) were flagged for escalated review. This article describes what public HR offices, with or without AI, can do to address classification drift.

title: Stabilizing solutionism: – causal assumptions and the discursive politics of AI in the Swedish parliament
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly framed as a policy priority, with governments and international organizations portraying it as a driver of competitiveness, growth, and social progress. Critical scholarship has cautioned that such narratives of ‘technological solutionism’ carry performative power, shaping governance agendas while obscuring social and political alternatives. This paper contributes to this debate by examining Swedish parliamentary discourse between 2016 and 2022. Drawing on political discourse analysis, the study shows how members of parliament (MPs) construct AI through five recurrent argumentative themes: civilizational promise, strategic competitiveness, practical problem-solving, institutional adaptation, and ethical risk. These themes reinforce AI as inevitable and necessary, rendering investment and adoption a national obligation, while framing risks as governable through regulation. The analysis highlights the constitutive role of parliamentary discourse in stabilizing solutionist imaginaries and points to the need for more critical engagement with how parliaments shape the politics of technological futures.

title: Digital performance accountability and legal governance in China: effectiveness and influencing factors
abstract: While previous studies have documented how the Chinese state deploys law and digital technologies to enhance social control, relatively little is known about whether local officials are more tightly monitored and regulated with the rise of law-based rule and digital governance. By employing a grounded theory approach, this study examines whether digital performance accountability experiments can promote legal compliance, which highlight the application of target management and digital technology. The findings indicate that target content, the task-technology fit in performance information use, and target priority shape the effectiveness of digital performance accountability. Specifically, most legal performance targets are oriented towards procedural formalities rather than substantive legality. While digital technologies effectively meet the demands of routine tasks such as data collection, fulfilling complex tasks like in-depth data analysis still faces some obstacles due to the lack of tacit information, resulting in partial transparency of legal performance. Furthermore, owing to the low target priority, local officials tend to engage in selective legal compliance when confronted with goal conflicts. These findings highlight the role of tacit information in shaping the interplay between digital technology, target management, and accountability and deepen the understanding of legal governance and bureaucratic control in China.

title: Comparative Analysis of Intermediaries in Digital Governance
Skills and far-right support: how education and training systems moderate voting behaviour in the knowledge economy
abstract: Technological change has reshaped labour-market risks for non-tertiary educated workers, but these risks vary across educational tracks and institutional contexts. This article connects comparative political economy research on skill formation with scholarship on far-right voting by asking whether dual vocational education and training systems moderate the relationship between non-tertiary education and far-right vote. Using European Social Survey data on dependent employees covering 42 elections in 18 countries from 2006 to 2019, we compare respondents with general non-tertiary, vocational non-tertiary and tertiary education, linking these profiles to national dual VET prevalence. Multilevel logistic models show that vocational non-tertiary respondents are more likely than general non-tertiary respondents to support far-right parties in low-dual VET contexts, but this premium narrows and reverses as dual VET prevalence rises. We turn to occupational outcomes of vocationally-educated respondents to explain this finding: in higher-dual VET contexts vocational respondents have better occupational outcomes, primarily by means of lower concentration in so-called ‘lousy’ jobs. The findings suggest that skill formation institutions shape exposure to labour market insecurity and far-right appeals, but also point to the limits of supply-side reform alone.

title: Estranged yet engaged: rejection of authority, cognitive engagement, and support for transgressive protest
abstract: Recent episodes of political disruption and intimidation across established European democracies have intensified concerns about citizens’ support for protest that deviates from conventional social and political norms. Political distrust is often invoked to explain endorsement of such transgressive protest, yet empirical findings remain inconsistent. I argue that this ambiguity stems from treating distrust primarily as a scalar attitude, which obscures differential orientations toward political authority. Drawing on original cross-national survey data from eight European democracies, I distinguish authority rejection from cognitive engagement with trust-relevant political information. Distrust intensity is not independently associated with transgressive-protest support once authority rejection and cognitive engagement are taken into account. Instead, endorsement is concentrated among citizens who combine authority rejection with cognitive engagement – a group that resembles engaged authority-accepters in political interest and expressed abstract support for democracy. The findings suggest that support for transgressive protest is structured less by distrust intensity alone than by a specific configuration of authority rejection and cognitive engagement that scalar distrust does not capture.

title: The End of the Observable Infodemic: Privatised Observability and Public Health Monitoring
Coordinating fragmented global AI governance: Control, Rights, and Safety as a regime complex
abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence governance is often discussed as if it were a single global policy domain. In practice, governments confront a coordination problem across partially overlapping agendas pursued through different instruments and actor configurations. This research note conceptualizes global AI governance as a non-exhaustive regime complex organized around three analytically distinct governance logics: Control, Rights, and Safety. The three are selected because each combines a distinct problem definition, recurrent instrument bundle, actor configuration, and set of portable policy objects. Using an Overton-derived corpus of 198,823 AI-related policy documents and a monthly actor-by-regime panel for 1994–2025, I compare metadata-indexed trajectories, cross-regime overlap, leadership shares, temporal alignment, and OECD-relative post-event salience around three named policy moments. A stratified full-text calibration using 73 documents that were substantively readable by both independent coders, drawn from an initial sample of 100, produced high inter-coder reliability but only partial correspondence between metadata and full-text judgments; correspondence was strongest for Control and weakest for Safety. Within that explicitly documentary scope, Control has the highest metadata prevalence (65.8% of regime-bearing documents) but comparatively unsettled leadership and event-linked uptake. Rights is the clearest IGO-centered regime and shows a short-window post-2019 signal that does not survive stronger interpretations of convergence. Safety has the clearest hybrid public-private configuration. Most metadata-coded regime-bearing documents register one regime, while 13.3% combine two or three, locating candidate interfaces for closer examination. The results imply that coordination, coherence, and integration must be designed differently across regimes rather than pursued through a single omnibus strategy.

title: Reconceptualizing power through the theoretical lenses of public management and policy implementation: The disaster recovery of the Siaolin village
abstract: This paper addresses a gap between public management (PM) and policy implementation (PI) in explaining how power operates across policy design and implementation. While PM often begins from questions of institutional design and the management of public authority, PI emphasizes how policies are contested and adapted in practice. Rather than treating these perspectives as irreconcilable, this study develops a processual framework of institutionalized and negotiated power. Institutionalized power refers to power embedded in legal mandates, administrative roles, resources, and recognized participation channels held by both formal authorities and policy recipients, albeit in different forms. Negotiated power emerges when these institutionalized powers interact and contest during implementation. Empirically, this paper traces the post-Morakot housing reconstruction of Siaolin village in Taiwan by showing how an initial government–NGO permanent housing plan produced acceptance among some households but resistance among others. It shows that policy outcomes are neither simply delivered through formal authority nor spontaneously produced through local contestation, instead they emerge through recursive interaction between institutionalized arrangements and negotiated practice. The paper contributes to PM and PI scholarship by offering an integrated account of how formal design, implementation contestation, policy adaptation, and institutional learning are connected in disaster recovery governance.

title: Can artificial intelligence accelerate technological progress? Researchers' perspectives on AI in manufacturing and materials science
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) raises expectations of substantial increases in rates of technological progress, but such anticipations are often not connected to detailed ground-level studies of AI use in innovation processes. Accordingly, it remains unclear how and to what extent AI can accelerate innovation. To help to fill this gap, we explore and assess results from 32 interviews with U.S.-based academic manufacturing and materials sciences researchers experienced with AI and machine learning (ML) techniques. We found that AI was primarily used for modeling of materials and manufacturing processes, facilitating cheaper and more rapid search of design spaces for materials and manufacturing processes alike. Benefits included cost, time, and computation savings in technology development. However, AI/ML tools were unreliable outside design spaces for which dense data were already available; they required skilled and judicious application in tandem with older research techniques; and concerns were raised about the potential to detrimentally circumvent opportunities for disruptive theoretical advancement. Based on these results, we suggest there is reason for optimism about acceleration in sustaining innovations through the use of AI/ML; but that support for conventional empirical, computational, and theoretical research is required to maintain the likelihood of further disruptive advances in manufacturing and materials.

title: Mobilizing ecosystem support for architectural innovation: Broker-mediated expectation formation
Research grant effects across funding modes and industry collaboration
abstract: The impact of public research funding remains debated, with limited evidence on how effects differ across funding modes. In this paper, we provide causal evidence on the impact of a major UK funder and use this setting to explore how its effects vary across institutional features. We implement a regression discontinuity design using novel data on more than 2000 applications evaluated by the Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council (EPSRC). We study the causal effect and examine differences between open, investigator-initiated schemes—characterised by greater researcher autonomy in defining research questions—and directional, funder-initiated schemes—which direct efforts toward predefined priorities. We further explore heterogeneities in how industry collaboration interacts with these funding modes. Our results show that investigator-initiated grants are associated with stronger subsequent performance advantage for funded researchers, but only when projects remain academically embedded. Directional grants, instead, exhibit more positive effects when combined with industry collaboration. While on average research grants have a substantial positive impact in our setting, their effects vary across key features, informing debates on the design of public science funding systems and highlighting the need for further research on the interplay between different funding characteristics.

title: How to craft a mission? A Theory of Action for the strategic public management of mission-oriented innovation policy
abstract: This paper explores the role of strategic public management within mission-oriented innovation policy. While recent scholarship has emphasised multiple aspects of missions, the distinct relevance of strategic public management in their implementation remains under-explored. To address this gap, the paper performs two complementary tasks. First, it uses a qualitative meta-synthesis of the relevant innovation literature to articulate a new Theory of Action for the analysis of missioncraft: namely, the institutional work public managers perform to create or maintain (disrupt) institutional logics supporting (hinder) their effective implementation. Second, it leverages a pre-study of the extant literature to illustrate the Theory of Action with three historical vignettes showing how the ToA can be applied at different scales and under different institutional logics (US' DARPA; China's NEV Plan programme; and EU's RIS3). Overall, the paper argues that the implementation of mission-oriented innovation policy requires public managers to adopt three critical strategic roles: i) enabling strategic learning across the public sector organisations leading the mission; ii) enabling dynamic accountability in the portfolio of projects supported by the mission; and iii) enabling collaborative innovation among the societal actors partaking the mission. By shifting the focus on the micro-foundations of mission implementation from structural underpinnings (i.e., legal, organisational, managerial) to agentic functions (i.e., strategic roles), the paper provides a new diagnostic lens for innovation policy research and practice – reflecting whether and how public managers can support mission-oriented innovation policy in light of the context-specific opportunities and constraints they face in their institutional work.

title: Gender Income Inequality in Ireland and the United Kingdom: Work, Pay and Redistribution
abstract: ABSTRACT We study the evolution and drivers of the gender income gap in the UK and Ireland between 2008 and 2019, a period shaped by the Great Recession and austerity. Using tax‐benefit microsimulation models, we construct individual income measures assuming minimal pooling of resources within couples. We then decompose gender differences in individual market and disposable incomes into contributions from hourly wages, working hours, self‐employment, demographic characteristics, and redistribution through taxes and transfers. Gender income gaps are substantially larger at the top than at the bottom of the income distribution. In both countries, differences in employment, self‐employment, and working hours account for most market income inequality between men and women at the lower end of the distribution. Hourly wage differences between men and women that are unexplained by observable characteristics (or ‘adjusted’ wage gap) become more important in the middle of the distribution, while at the top non‐labour income and demographic factors explain most of the market income gap. We show that the tax‐benefit system reduced gender inequality in market income by around 40% in both countries in 2019, mostly due to progressive taxation. In the UK, redistribution relies more heavily on the transfer system, but has weakened over time, while in Ireland it strengthened following the reversal of austerity measures. Overall, our results point to labour market inequalities as the primary source of gender income gaps and suggest that policies targeting employment and working hours are likely to be most effective, alongside continued efforts to reduce pay disparities.

title: Religious Cross-Pressures and Electoral Decision Making
When AI talks politics: How reliable is ChatGPT?
Bruce Russett Award for Article of the Year in JCR for 2025
Electric imperialism: Europe, state capital and the global political economy of the energy transition
abstract: Foregrounding the growing prominence of European state-owned electric utilities (electricity SOEs) in renewable energy generation, this article sets out to advance a new understanding of the ‘green capitalist state’ and its role in shaping the uneven geographical development of the energy transition. Political economists have emphasized the pivotal role of the state in derisking renewable energy investments, thereby socializing costs while privatizing rewards. This article argues that the role of the green capitalist state extends far beyond merely enabling privatized green accumulation; states are also emerging as major owners and profiteers of the expanding global landscape of renewable energy. It examines the state interventions that have underpinned the growth of major European electricity SOEs, showing how European governments, in response to EU liberalization pressures, have bolstered domestic incumbents both to protect national markets and enhance global competitiveness. The article advances the concept of ‘electric imperialism’ to theorize how European states position themselves at the commanding heights of the green economy by exercising sovereign control over domestic electricity resources and infrastructures while mobilizing corporatized utilities to expand abroad and secure ownership and control of the electricity supply of other nations.

title: Review forum
Populism and impatience
abstract: Abstract We develop a model where highly impatient voters are more likely than others to be subject to institutional frictions in the form of binding borrowing constraints. As impatient, borrowing-constrained voters cannot move long-term policy gains to the present, they turn to short-sighted, typically populist agendas, to politically obtain what the credit market denies them, namely relief from a short-term sacrifice. Empirical analyses based on German and British data show that there is indeed an association between impatience and the likelihood of preferring a populist party which remains substantial even after controlling for life outcomes, as well as across a number of sensitivity analyses. A comparison between populist parties within the German data reveals that impatience is associated with right-wing populism, but not left-wing populism. The results also confirm that the relationship between impatience and the likelihood of preferring a populist party is indeed attributed to voters who are likely borrowing-constrained. We conclude that institutional frictions can lead voters to support short-sighted policy agendas.

title: The effects of changing electoral systems from first-past-the-post to single transferable vote: causal evidence from New Zealand
Elite-led revolutions
Edward Clarke’s struggles
Beyond the myth of suffocating centralization: from legal intent to evidence in early Italy
abstract: Abstract This paper re-examines the widespread claim that the Italian Municipal Law of 1865 effectively suppressed local autonomy. Rather than relying on the statute’s formal design or on later legal commentary, the analysis turns to the actual behaviour of municipalities in the decades after unification. Regional fiscal data from 1866 to 1911 show that local governments retained substantial discretion, adopted markedly different tax and expenditure strategies, and followed trajectories that diverged sharply across the country. These patterns speak directly to the debate between law and economics and public choice. While the legal interpretation stresses the centralising intent of the Law, our evidence suggests that local outcomes were shaped not only by the formal institutional framework but also by differences in local incentives and fiscal preferences. The paper shows that the formal structure of a law does not necessarily determine its practical effects, and that institutional analysis gains much from combining legal and political-economy perspectives.

title: Lobbying by Rebel Groups in the United States: Introducing the Rebel Lobbying Dataset, Version 1, 1945–2012
The cost of job loss in carbon-intensive sectors: Evidence from Germany
abstract: Given global efforts to reduce carbon emissions, the shift of labor away from carbon-intensive activities is likely to increase. To shed light on the implied adjustment costs for workers, we use German administrative data from 1992 to 2020 to estimate the cost of involuntary job displacement for workers in high-carbon-intensity (HCI) sectors. Germany is particularly well-suited for this endeavor, as it has been one of the leading countries in carbon emission reductions since 1990, with considerably declining employment in HCI sectors. Comparing labor market outcomes of displaced and non-displaced workers before and after a mass layoff event, we find that workers displaced from HCI sectors face larger and more lasting earnings losses than those displaced from other sectors. This is mainly due to lower wages after re-employment. We show that a large part of the gap in displacement costs is explained by persistent differences in occupation-, firm- and local labor market-related characteristics across sectors, while differences in worker characteristics play a more limited role. Production processes in HCI sectors are regionally concentrated and involve a specific set of occupations and tasks, while firm wage premia are higher. This reduces outside options for finding jobs with similar skill requirements and pay, increasing adjustment costs for displaced workers. Using an alternative method to identify involuntary job separations, we show that our results also apply to more gradual transitions, signaling that adjustment costs could remain significant in a green transition without mass-layoffs.

title: Settlers and seekers: Immigrant proximity and voter polarisation
abstract: We exploit a natural experiment involving the conditionally random placement of refugee hosting facilities in an urban setting. Using survey data on voting, we estimate the causal effect of proximity to immigrants on political behaviour. By examining both refugee and long-term immigrant presence, we reconcile conflicting findings in the literature and offer a unifying framework highlighting the key role of past experiences in determining polarised responses to refugee shocks. We show that polarisation is driven by voters with limited prior contact and is amplified near migrant services or family-hosting facilities. By contrast, those with high baseline exposure remain unaffected.

title: Editorial Board
Decolonization, legitimacy and fiscal capacity: Event study evidence from Africa
Banks and informality: Two perspectives of microenterprises’ balance sheets
Syrian refugees and the resilience of European economic freedom: Evidence from Austria, Germany, and Sweden
Assessing risk: a toolkit for measuring regional supply-chain exposure to global shocks
Reference-point effects in bargaining
abstract: This paper investigates whether an earned endowment can serve as a salient reference point in unstructured bargaining and thereby reshape focal agreements. In a laboratory experiment with 166 participants, subjects earn endowments in a real-effort task, and subsequent bargaining menus are framed as changes relative to these earned endowments, while disagreement yields zero payoffs. The design distinguishes agreements that equalize total earnings (equal splits in final payoffs) from agreements that equalize the incremental surplus relative to the reference point (equal changes). Under symmetric endowments these notions coincide; under asymmetric endowments they diverge, so equalizing total earnings requires an unequal division of the incremental surplus. Results show that equal splits are not universal even under symmetry, and when endowments are asymmetric they lose focality in favor of equal-change and intermediate compromise agreements. The findings are robust across environments in which the reference point is available, dominated by some feasible agreements, or an infeasible claim. The results highlight how the salience and asymmetry of a reference point affects which notion of equality is focal in bargaining.

title: Local shocks and internal migration: The disparate effects of robots and Chinese imports in the US
abstract: Migration is a key mechanism through which local labor markets adjust to economic shocks. In this paper, we analyze the migration response of American workers to two of the most important shocks that hit US manufacturing since the 1990s: Chinese import competition and the introduction of industrial robots. Exploiting plausibly exogenous variation in exposure across US local labor markets over time, we establish a new fact. Even though both shocks drastically reduced employment in the manufacturing sector, only robots led to a sizable decline in population size. We provide evidence that negative employment spillovers outside manufacturing, caused by robots but not by Chinese imports, can explain the different migration responses. We interpret our findings through the lens of a model that highlights two mechanisms: the cost savings that each shock provides and the degree of complementarity between directly and indirectly exposed industries.

title: Correction: Why moderate voters choose extreme candidates: voter uncertainty as a driver of elite polarization
Mapping Global and Regional Risks: Structural Insights From Systems Thinking and Interpretive Structural Modeling
abstract: This study contributes to global risk analysis by providing a structural and exploratory enhancement to the analytical framework used to interpret the World Economic Forum's Global Risks Report (GRR), particularly the 2024 edition. It explores the complex interactions among critical global and regional risks using interpretive structural modeling (ISM) and systems thinking (ST)-based causal loop diagrams (CLDs). Rather than offering validated intervention guidance or predictive modeling, the study focuses on qualitative and structural mapping of risk interdependencies. Instead of combining the two methodologies, their insights are systematically integrated to provide a deeper understanding of global and regional risk dynamics. Through ISM, the research identifies hierarchical relationships among risks, highlighting key drivers and consequences, while CLDs reveal reinforcing feedback loops and interdependencies that illustrate the cyclical nature of systemic risks. Key findings highlight the critical roles of "extreme weather events," "pollution," and "critical change to Earth systems" in global risk networks, and regional dynamics such as "geoeconomic confrontation" and "technological power concentration" in the Middle East. The complementary use of ISM and CLDs offers exploratory insights beyond existing GRR network metrics by making explicit the hierarchical positioning of risks and their qualitative feedback structures. This study positions its contribution as groundwork for future quantitative modeling and scenario analysis, providing interpretive and structural insights rather than operational decision support.

title: Beyond Good and Bad: Understanding the Contradictory Effects of Positive Leadership Behavior and Negative Leadership Behavior
abstract: Organizational scholarship has long focused on leadership behavior, largely assuming that “good” and “bad” leaders can be distinguished by distinct sets of behaviors that can be organized into constructs with an inherent positive or negative valence (e.g., transformational, ethical, abusive). This assumption has guided extensive construct development and generated a substantial body of evidence consistent with each leadership construct’s expected valence. Yet, emerging research has documented the “dark side” of positive leadership and the “bright side” of negative leadership, revealing effects that contradict these expectations—effects that we call leadership contradictory effects. Despite growing interest in this line of research, the literature remains fragmented, with limited clarity regarding its scope and little theoretical integration explaining why, how, and when such effects occur. This motivates our review, which synthesizes these fragmented findings into a cohesive theoretical account organized around shared themes that cut across leadership constructs. First, we define leadership contradictory effects and review major approaches to operationalize them. Then, we advance an integrative framework that delineates three major theoretical themes, their associated theories, and three categories of boundary conditions to explain why, how, and when leadership contradictory effects arise. Finally, we propose paths forward, including suggestions to guide future research in this emerging domain. Overall, our work reorients scholars and points them beyond valence-based assumptions about leadership effects as a means to explore a broader range of consequences.

title: Voluntary Compliance with COVID-19 Nonpharmaceutical Interventions: Evidence from Mainland China and Hong Kong
Explaining governance with depth: Critical realism and the morphogenetic turn in public administration research
abstract: Public Administration (PA) research remains divided between positivist approaches that privilege regularities and interpretive approaches that prioritize meaning, often at the expense of causal depth. This paper argues that Critical Realism (CR) offers a viable alternative by integrating explanation and interpretation within a stratified ontology. Building on Bhaskar's philosophy and Archer's Morphogenetic Approach (MA), the paper develops a programmatic explanatory framework for PA research that explains how structures, cultures, and agency interact over time in open systems. It shows how retroduction, analytical dualism, and morphogenetic sequencing can be operationalized to analyze reform trajectories, accountability regimes, street-level discretion, informal governance, and public value creation. The paper contributes by consolidating CR–MA across these domains and clarifying how qualitative and mixed-method research can move from empirical observations to generative mechanisms while remaining attentive to context, interpretation, and power. In doing so, it advances an explanatory turn in PA research capable of accounting for variation, change, and legitimacy in complex governance contexts.

title: Small Polity, Hybrid Administration, International Research: Public Administration in Switzerland
abstract: ABSTRACT Switzerland presents a most peculiar political system whose institutional idiosyncrasies shape not only the practice of public administration but also the scientific study thereof. This country study presents the development and state of both public administration as practice and Public Administration as a scholarly discipline. It argues that both are largely determined by three properties of Switzerland as a political context and field of study: Semi‐direct democracy turns the administration into an important political actor. The “Milizsystem” (Switzerland's tradition of non‐professionalized, part‐time public engagement) enables hybrid careers between the public and private sectors and produces a structurally weaker political class that the professional administration regularly outmaneuvers. And the small size of the country has pushed the discipline toward international orientation while simultaneously entangling researchers with their object of study. Taken together, the Swiss case illustrates how political institutions do not merely constrain public administration but fundamentally constitute it.

title: From Symbolic Gender Parity to Substantive Transformation in the Administrative State
abstract: ABSTRACT Mexico has achieved one of the most visible forms of democratic gender inclusion: constitutional parity and women in positions of national authority. Yet parity has not automatically transformed the administrative routines, budgets, and performance systems through which the state responds to gendered inequality. This commentary argues that the next stage of gender reform is administrative rather than only electoral. Using Mexico as an illustrative case, it shows how unpaid care work, the mental load of caregiving, and gender‐based violence reveal limits of symbolic representation when bureaucratic systems remain organized around formally neutral but socially unequal assumptions. The argument is not that substantive representation alone can solve household, market, or cultural inequalities. Rather, it can become transformative only when public organizations translate gender representation into care‐centered budgeting, outcome‐sensitive performance metrics, and administrative training capable of recognizing gendered burdens.

title: Psychological safety, motivations and change-oriented organizational citizenship behaviour in emergency managers
abstract: Fostering change-oriented organizational citizenship behaviour (CO-OCB) is critical for resilience-building in the public sector, yet the psychological mechanisms driving such behaviour among emergency managers remain underexplored. Drawing on a survey of 869 public employees from emergency management agencies in China, this study examines how psychological safety, creative self-efficacy (CSE), and public service motivation (PSM) influence CO-OCB and tests the moderating role of work autonomy. Results reveal that psychological safety and PSM positively predict CO-OCB, whereas CSE unexpectedly suppresses the effect of psychological safety. Notably, work autonomy moderates the impacts of CSE and PSM on CO-OCB. These findings reveal how psychological safety shapes change-oriented behaviour through distinct but interrelated competence-related and motivational mechanisms within bureaucratic contexts. This study advances public-sector innovation theory by uncovering the nuanced role of psychological safety and by emphasizing the importance of public service motivation in enhancing organizational resilience during institutional reforms and crises.

title: Beyond the spectacular event in administrations of memory: the 2004 Republika Srpska Srebrenica Commission
abstract: Studies of memory and transitional justice in post-conflict countries often focus on spectacular events, such as judgments of international tribunals, the adoption of memory laws, the creation of truth commissions and publication of their reports, or the issuing of political apologies. But what happens behind the scenes to produce such events and how can the changes they augur sometimes end up being reversed? The 2004 Srebrenica Commission of the Republika Srpska in Bosnia and Herzegovina provides a seminal case of an administration of memory as the only truth commission in the post-conflict Balkans that produced a report acknowledging a major war crime perpetrated by one’s own side, which led to a cathartic political apology. However, it was then progressively delegitimised and, 14 years later, annulled by parliament. This article examines the work of the commission and the reasons for the ‘frame shift’ it produced, as well as the gradual process of the subsequent ‘frame reversal’ and the commission’s eventual repudiation.

title: The persistence and predictability of policy tool use: Policy styles and the tools of government
abstract: Abstract The relationship between “policy tools” and “policy styles” in literature is often implicit, resting on the assumption that governments’ characteristic ways of doing business shape their tool choices, without clarifying what a “style” is or how it connects to those choices. Resolving this ambiguity requires distinguishing two conceptions of policy style: a process-oriented one, describing how governments make decisions, and an output-oriented one, describing what kinds of instruments they characteristically deploy. Building on this distinction, the article introduces a three-level typology comprising a tool’s “genre,” “variation,” and “calibration” to specify at which level of abstraction a policy style exerts its influence on tool choice. Governance modes generate durable preferences primarily at the genre level – for broad categories such as regulation, public enterprises, or treasury-based instruments – rather than for specific design variations or finer calibrations. Making these linkages explicit advances understanding of policy continuity and improves prediction of future instrument choices.

title: Policy packaging and public acceptance: how size, combinations, and context shape support
abstract: Abstract Policy packages – bundles of multiple policy instruments that pursue a shared policy goal, often by pairing a primary instrument with ancillary instruments – are increasingly recognized as an effective strategy for overcoming opposition to climate policy instruments. We examine how package size (the number of ancillary instruments), policy type, and local context shape public acceptance, addressing key gaps in the literature. Using a randomized survey experiment in five small-to-medium Norwegian cities, we vary four primary instruments (road toll increases, parking charge increases, parking space reductions, and street closures) and bundle them with zero to three ancillary instruments. We find that adding ancillary instruments generally increases acceptance, but effects depend on the primary instrument and the coherence of the package. Price-based instruments, especially road toll increases, show relatively stable acceptance across package configurations, whereas more access-restrictive instruments such as street closures are highly context- and package-sensitive. Certain combinations reduce acceptance, indicating that misaligned bundles can backfire. Overall, the results show that policy packaging can increase public acceptance of restrictive transport policies, but only when ancillary instruments are strategically selected and coherent with the burden imposed by the primary instrument.

title: The architecture of rights: fragmentation and diffusion in EU human rights governance
abstract: This article examines how European Union member states organize governmental oversight for human-rights governance: the institutional machinery that assigns ownership, coordinates across ministries, and routinizes monitoring, follow-up, evaluation, and participation between international review cycles. Drawing on a systematic comparative coding of official state instruments across all EU member states, it maps domestic governance architecture as a carrier of diffusion and develops a typology of four dominant forms: cross-cutting national plans, framework strategies, fragmented thematic regimes, and thin/implicit compliance arrangements (plus a transition category). The analysis shows limited convergence despite shared supranational obligations.
