Only a small minority institutionalize a cross-government policy cycle with explicit accountability and participation devices, while most rely on dispersed sectoral instruments or minimal architectures anchored primarily in baseline legal safeguards and external review processes. The findings show why diffusion can be extensive at the level of commitments yet weakly routinized in domestic administration – clarifying why “having obligations” does not necessarily translate into “having routines.”

title: From Policy Neglect to Research Agenda: Administrative Burdens and Donor‐Conceived Mobilization
abstract: ABSTRACT Donor‐conceived adults are a growing population, mobilizing against the very regulatory arrangements that determined the terms into which they were conceived. In Canada and the United States, where donor conception remains persistently under‐regulated, gamete donation policy has historically prioritized the presumed needs of donors, recipient parents, and fertility clinics, structuring regulation around treatment access and donor supply rather than the long‐term interests of those conceived. The result is a population that bears disproportionate administrative burdens and is now mobilizing through advocacy organizations, legal claims, and the pathways consumer DNA testing has made possible. Yet donor‐conceived adults remain largely outside the scope of policy scholarship. This paper argues that donor conception offers a theoretically distinctive site for the study of administrative burden, policy feedback, and the social construction of target populations. The paper proposes a research agenda organized around the politics of administratively produced populations and the deliberate distribution of administrative burden through policy design.

title: Old and connected versus young and creative: Networks and the diffusion of new scientific ideas
abstract: The adoption of new ideas is essential for progress and involves innovators, potential adopters, and their networks. We apply natural language processing, network analysis, and a novel fixed effects strategy to study how career age affects idea adoption in coauthorship networks in biomedical science. At short network distances (≤3 steps away), young innovators' ideas are adopted the most while, at greater distances, mid-career innovators' ideas have the highest adoption. The main reason for this contrast is that young potential adopters are disproportionately likely to adopt new ideas introduced by nearby young innovators. Simulations show that the aging of innovators and of potential adopters have comparable effects on the adoption of important new ideas.

title: The wisdom of the diverse crowd(funders)
abstract: Crowdfunding platforms aim to democratize entrepreneurial finance by creating ecosystems that elicit the ‘wisdom of crowds’—aggregating the judgments of individual and often amateur funders. However, there is limited evidence on whether crowds can effectively apply their collective wisdom on these platforms. We address this gap by analyzing MyC4, a crowdlending platform that connects Western lenders with borrowers in developing countries. We examine whether lenders effectively screen borrowers, identify platform attributes that influence lenders' screening accuracy, and uncover the underlying mechanisms driving these effects. Empirically, we leverage platform-initiated ‘top-up’ funding by MyC4 administrators, which allows us to observe the counterfactual repayment performance of loans that would otherwise have remained unfunded, enabling us to evaluate lenders' screening ability against an otherwise unobservable benchmark. Our results indicate that crowdlenders can effectively screen creditworthy borrowers, but only when financial information about borrowers is made available. Lenders' screening effectiveness diminishes substantially for prosocial loans, as many funders converge on similar, socially motivated decisions. These findings provide novel evidence on crowdlenders' performance, highlighting key trade-offs for crowdfunding platforms and offering actionable insights for their administrators.

title: Firms' board diversity and radical innovation: mediation mechanism of firms' attention to digital transformation
abstract: This study integrates board information processing theory with the attention-based view to examine how board diversity affects radical innovation through an organizational attention pathway. We argue that board diversity shapes firms' attention to digital transformation (FADT), which in turn promotes radical innovation, and that industry competition conditions this process by heightening the urgency of attending to digital opportunities. Using longitudinal data from 2556 publicly listed Chinese firms from 2008 to 2019, we find that board diversity has an inverted U-shaped relationship with FADT and that FADT positively affects radical innovation. FADT thus mediates the inverted U-shaped relationship between board diversity and radical innovation, producing an inverted U-shaped indirect effect. Industry competition strengthens the relationship between board diversity and FADT, making this indirect effect more pronounced in competitive environments. These findings clarify how board diversity contributes to radical innovation by directing organizational attention toward digital transformation and show why moderate diversity is especially valuable when firms face strong competitive pressure.

title: The Punitive Dimension of Presidential Particularism
abstract: Existing accounts of presidential particularism emphasize the targeted distribution of benefits to electorally valuable constituencies. This research note demonstrates that presidential particularism can also operate punitively, through the selective imposition of costs on constituencies that provided weaker electoral support for the president. I examine this dynamic through the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), a highly centralized and politicized agency created at the start of Donald Trump’s second term. Leveraging data on nearly 700,000 federal contracts linked to DOGE contract cuts and 2024 county-level election returns, I show that these cuts were systematically concentrated in counties that provided weaker electoral support for Trump. These patterns hold across contract- and county-level analyses. Together, these findings broaden theories of presidential particularism by showing that presidents may use administrative authority to impose costs on electorally oppositional constituencies. More broadly, I demonstrate how presidents can wield administrative power as a tool of partisan punishment.

title: Ideas at Work: Educated Colleagues Shape Political Attitudes
Listening to Leaders: Illiberal Speech as a Symptom of Democratic Decline
abstract: Political leaders signal their commitment to democratic or authoritarian values through public speeches. Such signals can constitute a breach of democratic norms and indicate intent to undermine democratic institutions. By listening to what leaders say, we are able to capture a hitherto overlooked sign of a crisis of democracy. We develop indicators for illiberal speech that capture the language by leading representatives of political regimes across the globe. Utilizing a machine learning approach, we fine-tune DeBERTa models to score 27,683 speeches by 452 political leaders representing over 400 administrations in 123 countries between 1989 and 2024, yielding over 400,000 semantically coherent paragraphs. The scores place leaders on an illiberal-liberal scale and have been validated with openai’s gpt-5.2 and human coders. We find that illiberal public discourse is part of the multi-dimensional symptom of democratic decline. Our analysis opens up a new research agenda on the role of public rhetoric in the study of political regimes and their transformation.

title: Leveraging National Party Leaders in Congressional Campaigns: The Case of Nancy Pelosi
abstract: Existing scholarship on negative campaigning has focused on the communication strategies of candidates who are actively contesting specific seats or offices. Yet, political leaders are often featured in ads where they are not a contestant. For example, between 2018 and 2022, the Republican Party spent over 227 million dollars on negative campaign ads featuring Nancy Pelosi, hoping to capitalize on her unpopularity with a wide swath of the voting public. In this paper, we develop a theoretical perspective on this kind of attack by association that emphasizes two processes – ideological signposting and transfer of affect – to explain why campaigns might choose to adopt this strategy. Using Pelosi as a case study, we analyze her depictions in televised U.S. House race ads from 2010 to 2020 and compare them with similarly situated male Congressional leaders. Our approach blends a content analysis of the visual and verbal elements of campaign ads with metadata from the Wesleyan Media Project, providing insights into the conditions under which attacks against Pelosi are likely to emerge. Our findings have implications for understanding not only negative campaigning but also the nationalization of political discourse and the challenges facing women as they advance to leadership positions within Congress.

title: Religiosity and local debt repayment: evidence from Italian mayors
abstract: Abstract Does a politician’s religion influence their policymaking? While existing research has examined how gender, class, and ethnicity shape political decisions, the role of religiosity remains understudied. This paper investigates how religious values influence debt repayment decisions among local politicians. I develop a novel measure of individual religiosity, based on names matching local patron saints, and apply it to 62,908 candidates in Italian municipal elections. Using a regression discontinuity design, I find that narrowly elected religious Catholic mayors are more likely to increase debt repayment. This effect likely reflects two mechanisms: Catholic moral teachings, which stress the obligation to repay debt, and risk aversion rooted in religion. Overall, these findings demonstrate that religion meaningfully shapes the fiscal behavior of elected officials.

title: Two sides of governments: comparing inside and outside executive agendas in Denmark
Citizen participation in the European Union: can it make a difference?
abstract: Citizen participation has repeatedly been put forward as a way to reduce the perceived gap between citizens and the European Union (EU). At the same time, existing citizen participation arrangements have been criticised for not having an impact on actual policy decisions. This article develops a theoretical framework for understanding under what conditions citizen participation in the EU is likely to have an impact on EU policy decisions. Its main argument is that the impact of citizen participation processes can only be understood if it is placed within a broader account of policy-making dynamics. To that end, it draws on insights from the literatures on citizen participation, policy studies, social movements and interest groups to specify how citizen participation processes interact with these broader dynamics. Based on that account, the article identifies six pathways to policy impact and the conditions under which they are likely to occur.

title: Information access and college admission outcomes
abstract: This paper provides quasi-experimental evidence on the effects of information access in centralized college admissions. Using administrative data, we exploit a batched dynamic matching mechanism in the Chinese province of Inner Mongolia to compare students just above and below batch cutoffs. Once higher-scoring students have finalized their choices, those just below the cutoffs gain additional information that helps them identify the set of feasible colleges. As a result, they are more likely to apply to reach options and are admitted to more selective colleges. The effects are strongest near batch cutoffs where information access matters most.

title: Long-term impacts of youth mentoring and therapy: Experimental evidence from Chicago
abstract: We conduct a large-scale, randomized controlled trial of a six-month intervention combining intensive mentoring and group cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) for youth in Chicago, following study participants for up to five years. The program was designed to engage young people at higher risk of involvement with the criminal justice system, and successfully did so with a take-up rate of 62%. Participants averaged 177 hours with mentors and nine hours of group CBT. After 24 months, youth offered the program experienced a 19% reduction in the probability of being arrested. Notably, this impact persists into adulthood, as effects remain stable through five years post-randomization. A reduction in arrests for violent offenses is driving this overall arrest reduction, with a 23% reduction in the probability of a violent-crime arrest after 24 months. The program does not impact school enrollment persistence (graduation or being enrolled), but shows suggestive improvements in school behavior and school mobility. We conclude that programs that combine mentoring and CBT can serve as a model for engaging a harder-to-reach population of youth, and can be effective in reducing criminal justice contact in the longer run.

title: Transporting behavioral insights to low-income households: A field experiment on energy efficiency investments
abstract: Established behavioral insights may not generalize when applied to under-represented target populations. Iterative approaches that identify such external validity failures to guide policy deployment at scale and to inform subsequent design refinements gain importance. We implement this approach in a field experiment involving 1800 low-income households in one of the largest energy efficiency assistance programs. Despite extensive co-designed vetting, most behavioral insights proved ineffective or inefficient. Notably, loss-framed interventions backfired by reducing take-up. We rank insights by their Marginal Value of Public Funds (MVPF), identifying ‘unexpected winners’ that outperform alternatives rated as promising by experts and laypeople. Our analysis suggests that factors specific to low-income households, such as scarcity, fundamentally alter behavioral responses, necessitating guided deployment to optimize future public assistance design.

title: Motivating job seekers. A field experiment
abstract: Reduced motivation over the unemployment spell may contribute to declining job-finding rates. We report findings from a low-cost digital intervention that uses motivational emails to enhance job seekers’ search effort. Using a randomized controlled trial that included 200,720 newly unemployed job seekers in Sweden, we evaluate both supportive messages aimed at encouraging inner motivation, and controlling messages focused on internal and external pressure. The messages increased compliance with mandatory activity reporting, indicating a clear first-stage behavioral response. However, this behavioral change did not translate in more effective job search as both types of emails caused a moderate but significant reduction in search effort and job finding. The supportive messages reduced the number of job applications and showed weakly negative job-finding effects, particularly among men. The controlling messages slightly backfired for job seekers who report strong autonomous motivation at the onset of unemployment. These findings underscore the challenges of motivating job seekers to actively search for jobs and suggest that low-cost digital interventions, in isolation, are inadequate and may even be counterproductive.

title: Machine-Learning to Trust
abstract: Abstract Can society sustain long-run mutual trust when agents’ equilibrium beliefs are shaped by machine-learning predictive methods? I study an infinite-horizon game with state-dependent payoffs, in which each player in his turn decides whether to place trust in his immediate successor. Players best-reply to a probabilistic tit-for-tat belief, which is a coarse fit of the true population strategy with respect to a partition of relevant contingencies. In equilibrium, this partition minimises the sum of the mean squared prediction error and a complexity penalty proportional to its size. Relative to symmetric mixed-strategy Nash equilibrium, this solution concept can significantly narrow the scope for mutual trust.

title: The power to price: pricing regimes and governance of the cobalt global production network
The value of a statistical life year
abstract: Abstract Embedded in the value of a statistical life (VSL) is a stream of valuations of each expected year of life. The value of a statistical life year (VSLY) has a policy-relevant role analogous to the VSL, except that it monetizes risks to short periods of life extension. This article reviews previous studies and reports new labor market estimates of the average VSLY and the variation of these values with age using two methods—inferring the average VSLY based on estimates of the VSL and a new method that provides direct empirical estimates of the valuation of a discounted life year. The direct estimates of the VSLY yield larger values than the constructed estimates. The VSLY based on fatality rates by industry and occupation is $600,000 to $800,000 at a 3% interest rate. Estimates based on age-adjusted fatality rates are somewhat lower. The discount rate used in assessing the VSLY has a pivotal effect on the estimated VSLY. The VSLY is substantially lower in the absence of discounting and more than doubled at a discount rate of 10%. Failure to use a positive discount rate greatly understates the VSLY. The article also reviews previous VSLY studies as well as estimates of the discount rate for years of life expectancy.

title: Work-Related Harassment and Intimidation in Journalism: Testing Identity-, Visibility-, and Influence-Based Explanations
abstract: Prior research shows that exposure to occupation-related harassment and intimidation varies considerably across journalists. This study tests three explanatory frameworks for this variation: identity-based explanations attributing heightened exposure to social hierarchies; visibility- and celebrity-capital-based explanations linking it to journalists’ varying levels of personal visibility and recognizability; and influence-based explanations attributing differences to the nature of journalistic work and its societal influence. Logistic regression analyses of survey data from Finnish journalists ( n = 932), examining verbal, legal, and physical forms of harassment and intimidation, lend strong support to influence-based explanations, partial support to visibility-based explanations, and limited support to identity-based explanations.

title: Steering at China’s Periphery: Tech-Poor Provinces and International Digitalization Ambitions
abstract: China’s Belt and Road Initiative, including its digital dimension, the Digital Silk Road (DSR), is often studied either top-down as ‘grand strategy’ or bottom-up from the perspective of sub-national agency. Applying political steering theory, this article examines tech-poor sub-national governments that operate within, rather than deviate from, central parameters. Through an interpretive policy analysis of Guangxi and Ningxia, this article argues that these regions developed international digitalization initiatives that, using the DSR for legitimization, absorb and evolve in line with successive Five-Year Plan priorities. It proposes the term ‘anchoring steering instrument’ to describe how these regions, as both steering subjects and objects, capture the DSR as a soft steering instrument to build an ‘anchoring’ platform, which expands and accumulates as it aligns with central steering.

title: Creative Belonging: The Qiang and Multiethnic Imagination in Modern China Yanshuo Zhang. Ann Arbor: University of Michigan Press, 2026. 322 322 pp. $39.95 (pbk, also available Open Access). ISBN 9780472057771
