title: Equity, Capacity, and Compliance: A Case Study of Title VI Implementation in Rural Public Transit Systems
abstract: In today’s evolving landscape of public administration, the integration of social equity, diversity, and inclusion (SEDI) is vital in promoting community resilience. The mandate of rural transit agencies to uphold Title VI of the 1964 Civil Rights Act aligns with the principles of SEDI, ensuring that no person is excluded from participation in, denied benefits of, or subject to discrimination based on race, color, or national origin. Yet rural providers often struggle to navigate the complex administrative and procedural demands associated with Title VI compliance. This case study examines how more than 100 transit agencies in Nebraska implement Title VI requirements under federally funded rural and specialized transportation programs. The findings reveal gaps in procedural knowledge, uncertainty regarding Limited English Proficiency populations, and communication challenges that reflect broader administrative capacity constraints. The study highlights how a partnership between the State Department of Transportation (DOT) and a community-engaged research center was beneficial in reducing administrative burden, enhancing procedural equity, and strengthening organizational resilience for transit agencies. Broadly, these partnerships can help rural transit providers more effectively uphold SEDI principles and meet federal civil rights requirements.

title: Decentering Western norms: Reconstructing administrative responsibility from Islamic jurisprudence
abstract: This study examines how Islamic jurisprudence can contribute to reconstructing administrative responsibility beyond dominant Western paradigms in public administration. While modern administrative theory has largely emphasized institutional accountability, procedural rationality, and legal compliance, internal debates within Western administrative thought—particularly the Friedrich/Finer debate, the Simon/Waldo discussion, and contemporary scholarship on administrative evil—have revealed enduring tensions concerning moral responsibility, value neutrality, and bureaucratic obedience. In response, the study argues that Islamic jurisprudence offers a legal–ethical framework that reconnects administrative authority to moral responsibility through the interrelated concepts of amāna (fiduciary trust), maṣlaḥa (public welfare), and ḥisāb (moral accountability). Rather than presenting Islamic jurisprudence as a civilizational alternative to Western public administration, the article reconstructs administrative responsibility as a concept integrating institutional accountability, ethical commitment, and personal responsibility within administrative practice. Through conceptual and interpretive analysis supported by the case study of the Flint water crisis, the study contributes to contemporary debates in administrative theory by introducing non-Western normative frameworks into discussions of public administration, organizational rationality, and moral responsibility. It concludes that reintegrating moral responsibility into institutional structures is necessary to prevent bureaucratic compliance from becoming detached from justice and public welfare.

title: Announcing the 2024 and 2025 best article awards
A Replication of “It is Not Merely About the Content: How Rules Are Communicated Matters to Administrative Burden”
abstract: ABSTRACT This study replicates prior research to examine how rule communication forms shape administrative burden, while also extending their research by investigating how artificial intelligence (AI) services moderate this relationship. AI services are understood to perform two distinct functions: the labeling function, where chatbots output policy rules directly from databases in response to user queries without further processing, and the optimization function, where chatbots collect, analyze, and distill rule information to present users with simplified, prioritized key points. In Study 1, the original research is replicated in the context of natural disaster relief applications in China. The findings demonstrate that bureaucratic language raises learning and compliance costs, stress, and autonomy loss, while complex information structures also increase learning costs, compliance costs, and autonomy loss. These results confirm that rule communication shapes administrative burden across policies, countries, and languages. However, differences emerge compared to the original study, in which bureaucratic language induced stigma and information complexity had no effect on compliance or autonomy loss, potentially due to contextual factors such as the complexity of Chinese logographic writing. Building on this, the extension experiment in Study 2 demonstrates that AI services reduce administrative burden. Notably, and contrary to expectations, the labeling function reduces learning, compliance, and psychological costs, while the optimization function achieves even greater reductions across all dimensions. Collectively, these findings provide empirical evidence supporting the use of AI to improve rule communication and ease administrative burden.

title: Skills, Not Just Will: Experimental Evidence From Uganda on Transparency in Public Procurement
abstract: ABSTRACT Governments are usually the largest purchasers of goods and services, creating significant opportunities for corruption. We study whether offering training and technical assistance to procurement officials in 50 Ugandan districts prompted them to publish procurement actions on an online public portal, as legally required. Among districts that received the training and technical assistance program, we randomized whether procurement officials received information in advance about their eligibility to earn a public award for adherence to these transparency standards. We use national administrative data across multiple financial years and 134 district governments to evaluate impacts. The training and technical assistance program increased the number and value of procurement actions uploaded several‐fold, while award eligibility did not have similarly large effects. These results suggest that motivation problems may be overemphasized in the fight against corruption. Building capacity in accounting and transparency could provide effective guardrails against corruption.

title: What Does Representation Represent? Disaggregating Demographic and Behavioral Components
abstract: ABSTRACT Representative bureaucracy research has often linked demographic representation directly to favorable outcomes, inferring active representation post hoc while rarely separating the behavioral component presumed to accompany such associations from the representation variable itself. This study addresses such gap by drawing on gender differences in leadership literature to operationalize supportive leadership as one behavioral component associated with female supervisory representation and examine the constituent elements of what has been interpreted as a representation effect. Using gender pay inequality across US federal agencies as the empirical context, the findings show that while both female supervisory representation and supportive leadership are each positively associated with nonsupervisory salaries when examined separately, the association attributed to representation loses significance once both are modeled together. These findings do not suggest that representation is unimportant; rather, they indicate that prior representation effects may partially reflect a behavioral component that has not been separately identified.

title: The DOGE Experiment: Algorithmic Governance, Operational Capture, and the Case for Hybrid Intelligence
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) as a case of algorithmic governance whose stated purpose, improving federal efficiency, diverged systematically from its operational effect: enabling unprecedented private‐sector access to federal data systems while dismantling the oversight and civil‐service infrastructure that constrains such access. Drawing on state capacity, bounded rationality, organizational learning, and public value theory, the analysis demonstrates that the conventional efficiency‐failure reading, though correct on its own terms, obscures what made DOGE structurally distinct from the Grace Commission, the National Performance Review, the President's Management Agenda, and Program Assessment Rating Tool, and the Government Performance and Results Modernization Act. The article advances hybrid intelligence, structured human‐AI collaboration with protected institutional capacity, as a paradigm resisting both reform failure and algorithmic capture. International implementations operationalize it. The analysis contributes a stated‐versus‐operational‐goal analytic to the AI governance literature and identifies legislative grounding as a precondition for durable reform.

title: Role strain and job crafting in China’s digitalizing street-level bureaucracy
abstract: This study draws on 87 in-depth interviews with frontline workers specializing in social assistance services in Shanghai, China to examine how digitalization reconfigures street-level bureaucracy. Integrating role theory and job crafting theory, we find that digital platforms could produce multiple forms of role strain: redundant labour and fragmented systems generate role overload; misalignment between algorithmic rules and clients’ lived circumstances triggers role conflict; and emotional exhaustion coupled with the erosion of occupational identity results in role alienation. To ensure effective grassroots operation, frontline workers proactively engage in task, relational, and cognitive crafting, sustaining professional resilience despite constrained autonomy. This study critiques digital systems design for overlooking frontline implicit knowledge and suggests that digitalization in the street-level bureaucracy is an ongoing process of socio-technical alignment. The findings indicate that the design-reality gap in digital welfare reform may be bridged by systematically incorporating frontline knowledge.

title: Debate: Can decision transformation save the NHS juggernaut?
abstract: The UK National Health Service (NHS) is not short of transformation language. What it lacks is an agile, lean and highly professionalized workforce capable of improving decisions, stripping out sys...

title: Contested Coexistence: Transnational Private Governance and Public Regulatory Reform in Global Value Chains
abstract: ABSTRACT This article examines how a transnational coalition of NGOs, unions, and labor rights organizations drove both private and public regulation on gender‐based violence and harassment in Lesotho's garment sector, and how the resulting regulatory systems coexist despite ongoing tension between them. Drawing on 15 months of ethnographic fieldwork, stakeholder interviews, and archival analysis, we show that the coalition leveraged reputational and diplomatic pressures, enabled by Lesotho's structural dependence on the United States as both buyer and donor, to secure the Lesotho Agreement and subsequent public regulatory reforms. The same dependencies that enabled these reforms also generated sustained tensions once the regulatory systems were in place. We term this dynamic contested coexistence —a governance configuration in which a supplying country's structural dependence on a buyer country forecloses rejection of a private regulatory system while constraining open endorsement of it—and identify it as a new form of private‐public interaction within Cashore et al.'s framework.

title: Artificial Intelligence, Regulatory Capacity, and the Adaptive State
abstract: ABSTRACT Artificial intelligence is changing not only what regulators govern but the informational environment through which regulation is conducted. Regulators increasingly use advanced analytics to process evidence and target supervisory attention, while regulated organizations deploy AI across their operations. This paper develops the concept of the adaptive regulatory state to analyze how changing informational capabilities generate behavioral and institutional adaptation. Comparative cases from financial supervision, competition, tax administration, and electronic communications identify three possible trajectories: constructive learning, governed co‐evolution, and adversarial escalation. Effective oversight does not require technological parity with regulated firms, but sufficient informational, organizational, and verification capabilities to respond as the regulatory environment changes. Four institutional principles follow: functional rather than technological capacity; effective inspectability and proportionate assurance; learning with bounded revisability; and coordinated but accountable capacity. The adaptive regulatory state is defined by whether regulatory institutions remain capable, accountable, and legitimate as their informational environment evolves.

title: Making space for research: lessons from a research–practice partnership in adult social care
abstract: Background Research–practice partnerships (RPPs) are increasingly recognised for their potential to build research capacity in adult social care (ASC), yet the mechanisms enabling or constraining their impact remain under-explored. This article reports on the SCRiPT study, a National Institute for Health and Care Research-funded RPP in England that utilised a Communities of Practice (CoP) approach. Aims To operationalise an RPP by establishing Research in Practice Teams (RiPTs) – comprising social care professionals, lived experience contributors and academics – and to evaluate the mobilisation of research learning and identify transferable lessons for embedding collaborative RPPs. Methods Using a convergent multi-method design across four RiPTs, the intervention included bespoke training and support for small-scale projects. Data from interviews, focus groups, observations and questionnaires were analysed using Normalisation Process Theory and informed by CoP principles. Findings RiPTs achieved strong organisational buy-in through senior leadership support and collaborative priority-setting. However, sustained engagement was hindered by systemic infrastructure gaps, operational pressures and complex governance. While lived experience contributions enhanced research relevance, RiPTs functioned more as traditional research teams than CoPs, highlighting tensions between collaborative ideals and organisational realities. Conclusions RPPs can catalyse research engagement in ASC, but sustainability requires structural investment, protected time and context-relevant academic support. SCRiPT highlights that embedding RPPs in complex service environments depends on equitable collaboration, adaptability and multi-level organisational commitment.

title: Tracing policy dynamics through the issue-attention cycle: the case of South Korea’s older driver license surrender policy
abstract: Abstract This study applies Downs’ issue-attention cycle to examine changes in public attention to older driver traffic safety during South Korea’s transition to a super-aged society. Drawing on media coverage, parliamentary records, public opinion data, and interviews with civil society actors, the study analyzes policy responses and public attention across different stages of the issue-attention cycle. The findings show that public attention to older driver traffic safety does not follow the pattern proposed by Downs. Instead, attention is repeatedly reactivated by specific triggering events. This process of issue rekindling is shaped by high-profile traffic accidents with substantial social impact, rapid population aging, and adaptive policy responses. Through this process, policies are continuously adjusted and further responses are developed. This study contributes to the literature by providing a multidimensional analysis of how the issue-attention cycle operates in the context of older drivers’ licensing and related traffic safety policies.

title: Entrapping the Hegemon: How Benjamin Netanyahu's Threat Rhetoric Drives US Military Escalation
abstract: ABSTRACT How do materially weaker junior allies influence a hegemon's military posture? Existing theories rely on unobservable covert diplomacy, leaving alliance entrapment methodologically unresolved. This research note introduces a mixed‐methods framework, integrating computational text analysis, time‐series forecasting, and qualitative process tracing, to test whether allied public rhetoric proactively conditions US military escalation. Comparing the Iraq War buildup (2001–2003) with the contemporary Iran conflict (2023–2026), this article provides evidence of how Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has utilized public threat rhetoric in ways consistent with systematically entrapping the United States into regional wars. The findings challenge unipolar strategic independence, indicating that allied rhetoric systematically precedes and forecasts US military action. While maximalist interventions resolve the allied security dilemma and deactivate rhetorical pressure (the “Off‐Ramp”), proportional restraint paradoxically traps the US in a compounding escalation loop, eroding strategic autonomy and ultimately culminating in the ongoing 2026 joint US–Israeli war against Iran.

title: Types of impact of knowledge brokering organisations: evidence from the UK what works centres
Structural Injustice as Emergent Disorder
abstract: Abstract Structural injustice remains a puzzling concept despite its increasing prominence. I distill recent theoretical challenges into a dilemma: either structural injustice lacks the normative credentials of injustice given that wrongdoing is inessential, or it is redundant given existing theories that trace injustice to culpable state and other institutional failures. I then develop a novel account of structural injustice, the Complexity View, that unravels this dilemma. The emergent properties of human actions in a complex society explain what is “structural” about structural injustice, specifically how it can arise without (culpable) wrongdoing. Structural injustice is unjust because it is wrong to contribute to social processes that cause harm and to passively accept preventable forms of vulnerability and deprivation as tragic misfortunes. But this account of structural injustice has a sobering implication: while complexity explains what distinguishes structural injustice from other wrongs, it also sets significant epistemic limits on social reform.

title: From the center to the fringes: A comparative test of attitudinal explanations for mainstream-to-challenger defection
abstract: The 2025 German Federal Election witnessed unprecedented levels of mainstream-to-challenger defection. Why did former mainstream supporters abandon the political center for the fringes? We contrast four theoretical explanations: general political frustration, positional representation, prioritization of issues “owned” by challengers, and differential performance evaluations. Moving beyond the conventional focus on effects, we assess the relative predictive reach of these explanations using Bayesian finite mixture models. Our analysis of the 2025 GLES Post-Election Cross-Section identifies the so far neglected importance of performance evaluations: beliefs that challengers are more capable political actors than their mainstream competitors consistently emerge as the strongest explanation of mainstream-to-challenger defection. This pattern even holds when accounting for the potential endogeneity of performance evaluations to the rival explanations. Our findings suggest that challengers, despite lacking executive experience, can mobilize support via subjective ascriptions of capability—challenging assumptions that mainstream parties’ accumulated reputational resources necessarily translate into electoral advantage.

title: Terrorist threat decreases citizens’ relative preferences for women candidates: Insights from a Danish conjoint experiment
abstract: Abstract For several decades, democracies across the Globe have faced the persistent threat from terrorist attacks. A possible consequence of terrorist threat is that citizens come to find men candidates relatively more appealing compared to women candidates. However, recent meta-analyses reveal that citizens generally prefer women over men candidates when terrorist threat is absent. Here, we report the results from a pre-registered conjoint experiment testing whether the terrorist risk assessment from the official Danish intelligence authority (Politiets Efterretningstjeneste, PET) affects candidate gender preferences among a sample of 1,034 representative Danes. Results reveal an average marginal component effect of 8.6 percentage points favoring women candidates in the absence of terrorist threat. However, when the risk of terrorism against Denmark is made salient, this effect is significantly reduced to 5.3 percentage points. Follow-up analyses reveal that left-wing respondents change their candidate gender preferences most when terrorist threat becomes salient. Implications for challenges to political representation are discussed.

title: Do voting advice applications have durable causal effects? Evidence from concurrent survey and field experiments
abstract: Abstract Voting advice applications (VAAs) are used by millions of voters, yet their causal effects on political knowledge, preferences, and behavior remain unclear. We present new evidence from two experiments conducted during the 2024 UK General Election: (1) a panel survey experiment that provides access to participants’ VAA advice, achieves high compliance with treatment assignment, and allows us to track outcomes over time; and (2) a concurrent field experiment embedded in a real-world VAA that allows us to assess the ecological validity of our findings. We find that VAA usage leads to durable changes in voters’ perception of how close they are to parties on policy issues, shifts party preferences in line with the advice received, and affects the vote choices of undecided voters. These results suggest that VAAs play an important role in election campaigns. However, we find no evidence that VAAs increase electoral participation.

title: Diaspora diplomacy in the making: The Case of Latvian diaspora professionals working in international organisations
abstract: Abstract Nationals living abroad are increasingly recognised as important, yet often overlooked, actors in international diplomacy. Unlike previous research – which has focused mainly on states and diasporas as singular entities – this study highlights the pivotal contributions of individuals. It introduces a new theoretical framework that emphasises the multifaceted roles of professionals in international organisations as resources for strengthening their home state’s development, influence, and global visibility. The study examines the actors involved in diaspora diplomacy, how diplomatic work is conducted by, for, and through diasporas, and what motivates citizen diplomats. The analysis draws on a survey ( N = 150), six focus groups ( N = 18), and four interviews with highly skilled Latvian professionals in international organisations. Findings reveal the decentralised, networked nature of diaspora diplomacy, challenging the notion of the state or diaspora as a singular actor. Individual diaspora members play vital roles, advancing their home country’s goals and visibility through their professional activities. All core functions of public diplomacy – communication, representation, listening, advocacy, and nation branding – are actively performed at the individual level by citizen diplomats. However, the degree to which states benefit from this resource depends on having a coordinated strategy for diaspora engagement.

title: The political class in citizens’ minds: Mapping public perceptions of politicians
abstract: Abstract Politicians are often portrayed as a socially distinct and internally homogeneous elite – a narrative central to populist rhetoric and scholarly debates on political discontent. Yet we know little about how voters mentally represent politicians. Using survey data from Denmark ( N = 1302), combining free association tasks, open-ended descriptions, and closed-ended items, I demonstrate that most citizens view politicians as both internally homogeneous and socially distinct from the general population. These perceptions correlate with negative characterisations and significantly lower political trust, external efficacy, and democratic satisfaction. Crucially, perceived social distinctiveness matters more than perceived homogeneity: citizens who view politicians as different from ordinary people show substantially diminished political support, regardless of whether they see politicians as similar to one another. By shifting the analytical focus to citizens’ mental representations, this study highlights the importance of not only who politicians are but also how they are imagined by the public.

title: Primaries, caucuses, and momentum: theory and evidence from 48 years of presidential nomination campaigns
Mobile Internet Connectivity and Household Wealth in the Philippines
Propagation of Immigration Shocks through Firm-to-Firm Trade Networks,
abstract: Abstract This paper investigates the extent to which an immigration shock to a region propagates through supply chains. Using the unexpected arrival of Syrian refugees, who are densely concentrated in border regions of Turkey, we estimate how firms across the country are affected in terms of sales, employment, and wages. We also examine the impact of the shock on interprovincial trade, focusing on trade volume and network formation. The results reveal positive spillover effects of immigration for firms with pre-existing links to Syrian refugee-hosting regions through upstream and downstream supply chain connections. Furthermore, we find evidence that the shock expands inter-provincial trade and contributes to the formation of new firm-to-firm linkages between provinces. Finally, we show that traditional spatial approaches that compare regions with differing migration rates may conflate cross-province propagation with the direct effect of migrants; in our setting, this conflation overstates direct effects on sales and employment at both the firm and regional levels of aggregation and masks a negative direct wage effect at the firm level.
journal_name: Journal of the European Economic Association

title: Inattention, Information Provision, and (Failures of) Revealed Preference,
abstract: Abstract Economists often estimate preferences by looking at how demand for an option changes as its attributes change or as beliefs about them change in response to information. I show in a multi-attribute induced-preference experiment that this method can be substantially biased due to differential inattention. Attention is systematically distorted at baseline, with participants reacting much more to some attributes than others. Further, attention is highly malleable: information telling participants about the value of a desirable attribute—even when the information is already known, transparently redundant, and explicitly randomly assigned—greatly increases attention to the attribute it describes and distracts from other attributes. It also boosts average demand for the good, implying that inattention takes the form of neglect rather than shrinkage toward a prior. These results combine to imply that information experiments with passive control groups can be greatly misleading about preferences and can even have the wrong sign: in my experiment, reducing overoptimism about an attribute nonetheless boosts demand for its associated good. I show, both theoretically and experimentally, that active control-group experiments yield preference estimates with the correct sign but biased magnitudes. Finally I show that parallel active control-group experiments (PACEs) can solve this problem: PACEs yield unbiased estimates of preferences under an equal induced-attention assumption, which is testable (and satisfied) in my experiment.
journal_name: Journal of the European Economic Association

title: Green jobs require green skills: Why production subsidies are not enough
Rank Dependent Weighted Average Utility Models for decision-making under Objective Ambiguity
abstract: This paper axiomatically characterizes a family of rank-dependent weighted average utility criteria for comparing finite sets of objective probability distributions over consequences. These sets are interpreted as objectively ambiguous prospects: the relevant probability distributions are part of the description of the alternative, but no likelihood is assigned to their occurrence. The represented criteria evaluate a prospect by applying a utility function to each of its elements and aggregating the resulting utilities through weights that depend on the rank of each element within the prospect. The main theorem characterizes the subclass of such criteria whose rank-dependent weights are generated by a single weighting function on the unit interval. Asecond characterization covers the larger family in which weights mayvary freely with the number of elements in the prospect. The paperalso studies the implications of comparative ambiguity aversion, optimism,and pessimism for the utility function and the rank-dependentweights.

title: Ex Post Strategy-Proofness
Price Information and Cost Uncertainty in Oligopoly
Gendered Effects of the Minimum Wage
abstract: ABSTRACT Women work disproportionately in low‐hours jobs, which pay lower wages and are more exposed to minimum‐wage policies. We estimate an equilibrium search model with worker and firm heterogeneity, jobs differing in wages and hours, and imperfect compliance. Applied to Germany, the 8.50 € minimum wage reallocates women toward higher‐hours jobs and reduces non‐employment, although firm adjustments dampen this effect. Stronger enforcement amplifies the reallocation. Raising the minimum wage up to 14 € reduces gender gaps in wages and hours; at 11 €, changes in hours account for 44.8% of the reduction in the gender income gap.

title: Review of “Island Time: Theory Groups and the Social Production of Scientific Knowledge”
Explaining Science Knowledge Gaps on Social Media: Basic Science Knowledge and Intentional Versus Incidental Exposure
abstract: This study examined whether basic science knowledge helps explain education-based gaps in domain-specific science knowledge and whether intentional and incidental exposure on social media condition those gaps. A national survey of American adults focused on two domains: climate change and algorithms. Results showed that basic science knowledge mediated the relationship between education and domain-specific knowledge across both domains. These indirect relationship were attenuated at higher levels of intentional social media exposure. The findings suggest that strengthening foundational science literacy and encouraging more deliberate engagement with science content on social media may help reduce knowledge disparities.

title: A Legal Theory of State-Owned Enterprises: The China Experience James Si Zeng. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2026. 278 pp. $140.00 (hbk). ISBN 9781009457682
Does Nonviolent Action Still Work?
abstract: Abstract: From Burma to Belarus, one question keeps surfacing: Does nonviolent action still work? The authors argue that the theory hasn’t failed, but rather that the field has fallen behind. Authoritarian regimes have modernized repression while movements have reduced strategic nonviolent struggle to street protest, mistaking visibility for leverage. That gap helps explain why organizers facing lethal repression have turned to arms, even though nonviolent campaigns still outperform violent ones. The authors also challenge how success gets measured: Leader-centric, single-cycle standards obscure real gains. What the field needs now isn’t new doctrine but investment in countering smart repression, rebuilding noncooperation, and sharing lessons across movements.

title: Authoritarian AI’s Last-Mile Problem
abstract: Abstract: Is artificial intelligence the autocrats’ silver bullet? No. AI-empowered autocrats are constrained by the “last-mile problem”: AI can help regimes to see, sort, and predict, but human police officers, soldiers, and local officials remain indispensable for physical coercion. In the long run, human agents will stay relevant: They not only guarantee an effective repressive system but also signal the autocrats’ popularity. For prodemocracy actors, this suggests that the conventional wisdom on combating autocracies, such as encouraging defections among security forces, still holds. The bottom line: Repression in the AI era remains a human affair.

title: Documents on Democracy
Why Welfare States Save Democracy
abstract: Abstract: Rising inequality threatens democratic durability, as societies become increasingly polarized. South Korea and Taiwan have resisted global trends in democratic backsliding by continually expanding their social welfare regimes. Democratic resilience and welfare deepening have been mutually reinforcing in South Korea and Taiwan. Democratization during the 1990s created the political conditions and incentives to deepen the government’s social policy commitments. Over the past three decades, the continued expansion of the social safety nets in South Korea and Taiwan has mitigated the effects of growing inequality and deepened citizens’ trust in democratic institutions and practices.

title: Competitive Authoritarianism In America
abstract: Abstract: The United States crossed the line into competitive authoritarianism during Donald Trump's second presidency: Elections remained real, but incumbents systematically abused state institutions to tilt the playing field against opponents. The administration weaponized the Justice Department, the FBI, and other agencies against critics, universities, law firms, and the press, while national gerrymandering and coerced corporate money skewed competition. Judged by the eleven criteria the authors devised to score 35 regimes in their earlier research, the U.S. case is comparable to Hungary under Viktor Orbán, if far softer than 1990s Russia or Serbia. The new regime is unlikely to consolidate, however: The United States’ vast countervailing power—its wealth, private sector, and civil society—dilutes authoritarian abuse and makes redemocratization by electoral turnover likely. Yet turnover would not mean democracy survived intact. Opposition parties do win unfair elections, and a restored U.S. democracy will remain unconsolidated until both major parties commit to its defense.

title: Polarization Is Not the Problem
abstract: Abstract: Partisan polarization is not the greatest threat to U.S. democracy, but a symptom of a deeper struggle over who belongs and deserves equal rights. Rapid gains by racial minorities, women, and LGBTQ citizens have produced an ethnonationalist backlash whose adherents now wield disproportionate power through the Republican Party. This conflict has intensified partisan animosity and moral disengagement, but a “both sides” diagnosis obscures the asymmetry between a faction seeking to reverse social progress and those resisting it. Polarization is therefore less the disease than democracy’s immune response to an unpopular, antidemocratic movement. Suppressing that response in the name of civility would only strengthen the movement and imperil pluralistic self-government. The United States can still become its most inclusive democracy, but only if leaders defend equal rights and voters hold accountable those who will not.

title: How to Protect the Media in Eroding Democracies
abstract: Abstract: Independent media is not merely one institution among those under attack in eroding democracies; it is the connective tissue linking the electoral, institutional, and popular forms of resistance on which democratic survival depends. Yet the terrain has shifted: A media ecosystem once defined by scarcity and dispersed ownership is now fractured, networked, and funneled through a few platforms that capture most digital-advertising revenue. Comparing democratic decline in Hungary, India, Poland, and Sri Lanka, the author finds that erosion ran deepest where governments dominated digital-media ecosystems—India's ruling party built a propaganda “machine” on WhatsApp, while Hungary's never achieved comparable dominance online, leaving room for Péter Magyar's challenge. Five lessons follow: win the battle for digital distribution, build networked media ecosystems before they are needed, diversify media-financing models, develop legal-defense infrastructures, and connect institutional erosion to citizens' everyday concerns. The question is no longer whether journalism survives, but whether independent media can still help citizens discover common interests and act on them.

title: How to Build the Right Coalition
abstract: Abstract: In competitive authoritarian and autocratic contexts, political parties win elections more frequently by running as public unity coalitions. However, in eroding democracies, voters are often highly polarized. The incumbent often won because the main opposition party was disliked by a plurality or majority of voters. Joining with such a tainted party can harm candidates’ chances. Where elected leaders are eroding once-strong democracies, opposition parties often do better with quiet coalitions in which parties remain fully independent but work together; choosing not to run against one another, or competing electorally to offer voters’ choice, but promising to caucus together post-election.

title: Democratic Resistance in Eroding Democracies
The Age of Authoritarian Abundance
abstract: Abstract: This essay argues that the post-unipolar international order, combined with unprecedented interdependence, has created an “age of authoritarian abundance.” As the relative power of the United States and Europe declines and democratic erosion spreads within the West, Western governments increasingly repurpose their influence toward transactional partnerships with illiberal actors. At the same time, autocrats can draw political, financial, technological, and diplomatic support from a diverse array of great powers, authoritarian middle powers, international institutions, and private firms, reducing dependence on any single patron and exploiting asymmetries in areas such as migration, energy, and digital infrastructure. These mutually reinforcing trends expand the resources available for autocratic survival while leaving prodemocracy forces with little external support. Democracy’s prospects are not foreclosed, but in a fragmented order without a major power committed to promoting democratic norms, they depend on many actors whose interests rarely align with democratic ends.

title: How Courts Survive Democratic Backsliding
abstract: Abstract: When elected leaders attack the courts, why does judicial independence sometimes survive? This essay argues that courts rarely prevent executive power grabs on their own. Rather, judges depend on judicial allies—especially legislators, civil society groups, and international actors—who empower courts to resist executive aggrandizement. By analyzing cross-national evidence as well as case studies of Brazil, Israel, and Poland, the author finds that judicial independence is most resilient when opposition parties retain power in the legislature. Yet even when illiberal governments control the legislature, protests and international actors can still protect the courts. The case studies illustrate that mobilization by judicial allies often generates positive feedback effects, as mobilization empowers judges, whose decisions energize further resistance. At a time when courts are under attack in the United States and globally, judicial allies must not only defend courts but also, in the longer term, reform them.

title: The Real Liberation Technology
abstract: Abstract: Larry Diamond’s “liberation technology”—the internet and social media—has not freed closed regimes: Autocrats own the off switch and weaponize it. The real liberation technology is the democratization of finance. Unlike social media, digital payments are incentive-compatible: They enlarge the economy autocrats live off, so rulers promote them even while blocking the internet. Yet they erode authoritarian rents and create a new digital bourgeoisie whose demand for the rule of law—when it is a challenger, not an incumbent—drives political change. Grounded in evidence from Findex, mobile money, and tax revolts, the argument reframes how outsiders can support democratic evolution.

title: Taiwan’s Deadlocked Democracy
abstract: Abstract: In May 2024, Taiwan's President Lai Ching-te took office while facing off against an opposition party majority in the legislature. Since then, the island has been caught in a slowly escalating constitutional crisis. The Constitutional Court is now paralyzed, key regulatory bodies sit vacant, the annual budget bill is a half-year late, and the premier has refused to countersign legislation. This political dysfunction has been blamed on nationalist polarization, PRC influence, or reckless and irresponsible opposition parties, but these explanations overlook a simpler cause: Taiwan’s institutions are simply not well-designed to handle divided government. The political system lacks adequate safeguards to protect the independence of accountability institutions. Unified government masked this design flaw for many years, but it now threatens Taiwan’s democracy.

title: How to Break an Autocrat’s Coalition
abstract: Abstract: Authoritarian coalitions look unbreakable, but they are not: Allies defect when the costs of loyalty rise and the costs of defection fall, and opposition parties and civil society can engineer both. Moderate institutional strategies—contesting elections, courts, and legislatures—force stealth autocrats to abandon their democratic façade, as in Guatemala, where Bernardo Arévalo's Semilla party stayed on the 2023 ballot and pushed the elite alliance known as the “Corrupt Pact” into overt manipulation that split it. Persistent journalism makes loyalty reputationally costly, as years of corruption reporting in Hungary did before Péter Magyar broke with Viktor Orbán. Depolarization lowers the price of defecting, as when Colombia's opposition refused Alvaro Uribe's provocations, or when Indiana activists sent thank-you notes to Republicans resisting mid-decade redistricting. Such wins are partial—Uribe's chosen successor still won—but defections that build “broad thin coalitions” across ideological lines do shift power, and marginal gains are worth the effort.

title: How Protest Can Halt Backsliding
abstract: Abstract: Mass protest can halt democratic backsliding, but only when it shifts political power away from autocratizing incumbents before they become entrenched. Comparing Brazil, Georgia, Poland, Serbia, and South Korea, this essay identifies three pathways through which protest can make that shift: Empowering institutional actors to curb executive overreach, mobilizing previously disengaged citizens to vote, and eroding support for incumbents among voters and elites. Success depends less on the sheer size of demonstrations than on whether organizers reach beyond the existing opposition, counter polarizing government narratives, and connect street mobilization to effective parties, legislators, and electoral strategies. Where opposition parties are weak, institutions captured, and repression advanced, even sustained mass mobilization may not yield an immediate breakthrough. Protest should therefore be treated as one tool in a broader democracy-defense strategy—one that can slow authoritarian consolidation, build civic capacity, and prepare future electoral or institutional openings.

title: Will AI Surveillance End Bureaucratic Autonomy?
abstract: Abstract: Civil servants are a neglected source of democratic resilience. Their partial autonomy lets them resist abuses of state power. This resistance is possible because politicians cannot perfectly observe bureaucrats’ preferences or behavior. Artificial intelligence is closing this gap. States are collecting more data on their own officials, and AI tools can merge and analyze extensive records that once sat in separate systems. Illiberal leaders can now identify and punish bureaucrats they consider disloyal at scale. Drawing on cases from democracies and authoritarian regimes, this article argues that the legal architecture protecting bureaucratic autonomy must be updated for the data age.

title: Leading Humanistic Transformation of Business, Economy and Society: Lessons From Olivetti’s Blueprint
abstract: Building on the core pillars of Humanistic Management–dignity, ethics, and legitimacy–this study examines how these principles were enacted across organizational, community, and societal levels, and how Humanistic Leadership translated a normative vision of business into concrete managerial, social, and institutional practices. Using an exemplary historical single-case study and an abductive approach, it analyzes Olivetti, the Italian company developed under Adriano Olivetti’s visionary leadership between World War II and 1960. The findings identify Olivetti as a historical example of these principles in practice, showing how dignity, ethics, and legitimacy interacted across multiple levels of leadership to foster both business success and social acceptance. At the same time, the case reveals that the long-term sustainability of this model depended not only on visionary leadership and organizational practices but also on their broader institutional embedding. Olivetti’s legacy serves as an analytical lens for critically reflecting on the transformative potential of Humanistic Management and Humanistic Leadership and the institutional conditions needed to support values-based transformation of business and society and challenge contemporary capitalist logics.

title: Politics everywhere: stigma and political perception in the contemporary United States
abstract: Political ideology has become a pervasive lens through which social and organizational settings are interpreted, a trend intensified through recent political developments. Across everyday interactions, consumer behaviors, and institutional settings, individuals rely on observable cues to infer others’ political beliefs. Though often rapid and inaccurate, these inferences are highly consequential as they function as stigma-based evaluations that attach moral and social meaning to individuals, driving patterns of avoidance, favoritism, or bias. Drawing on stigma theory, this paper examines how ideological cues generate inferred political identities and how those identities subsequently shape social evaluation. Particular attention is given to public administration, where attributed political identities may influence perceptions of competence, impartiality, and legitimacy even when administrators behave neutrally.

title: Shared digital leadership in government: a roles and competencies study
abstract: Digital leadership capabilities and associated clusters of competencies form a foundation for digital transformation in the public sector. This increasingly depends on leadership contributions and strategy-matching competencies shared across organisational levels and professional roles. Drawing on shared leadership theory, we analysed how public sector employees at different organisational levels contribute to digital leadership. The study uses a qualitative research design with independent sources of evidence: document analysis of job descriptions and semi-structured interviews with digital leadership professionals. We mapped the theory-informed competencies to the Skills Framework for the Information Age (SFIA), an industry-recognised competencies framework. We find that digital leadership competencies and contributions should be understood as a shared leadership construct requiring multiple contributions across multiple levels. We offer an illustrative example of our shared digital leadership conceptualisation in practice, using a horizontal and vertical slice of the roles involved in cyber security risk management as the context.

title: Mandating business-to-government data sharing for public interest: Coalitions and their policy beliefs in the shaping of the EU Data Act
abstract: To address complex societal challenges like the climate crisis or pandemics, governments need to make evidence-based decisions based on the best available data. However, data needed to make policy decisions are no longer solely in the domain of the public sector, but increasingly also in the hands of the private sector. As part of its Data Strategy, the European Union (EU) has recently adopted the Data Act, which includes provisions to mandate business-to-government data sharing in situations of exceptional need. Some critics argue that the adopted text of the Data Act has made significant concessions to the interests of the private sector and that the initial text was much more ambitious. In this study, we aim to understand and explain the conflicting narrative framing of the public and private sectors on mandatory B2G data sharing for public interest. To answer our research question, we analyze the public and private narratives found in the public consultation on the Data Act using the method of discourse network analysis (DNA). We established a clear division into two coalitions which partly agreed on the problem, yet widely diverged on the solution. We highlight the difference found in the belief systems of the main coalitions and discuss them through the lens of institutional logics. Our findings showcase that the resulting legislation has aligned more with the policy preferences of the private-sector-dominated coalition favoring a “narrow” data access mandate.

title: Examining the Role of Race and Sector of Employment in Public Participation
abstract: With the racial gap in political-electoral participation well established in the U.S., less is known about racial disparities in other forms of public engagement in governance. This study examines racial differences across nine distinct public participation strategies. It also investigates racial disparities in participation across public, nonprofit, and for-profit sector employees. Regressions conducted using five waves of the Current Population Survey Civic Engagement Supplement suggest that Black and White Americans participate in governance in different ways: Blacks opt for less formal and less costly forms of participation, with ramifications for the diversity of voices included in policy design and implementation. However, contrary to our theoretical expectations, the racial disparities are more pronounced among government employees than among employees in other sectors. Public institutions should create more inclusive opportunities for participation, minimize burdens, and provide incentives for engagement among minorities.

title: Impact of healthy city policy on urban inclusive growth: a multi-stakeholder governance perspective
abstract: This paper examines the impact of China’s healthy city policy on urban inclusive growth through a multi-stakeholder governance framework. Applying several difference-in-differences approaches to panel data covering 278 Chinese cities from 2011 to 2022, we find that the policy significantly promotes urban inclusive growth. Mediation analysis provides suggestive evidence of three stakeholder-related response pathways: (i) government attention, reflected in fiscal investment and institutional responsiveness; (ii) corporate collaboration, reflected in enterprise expansion and participation by small and medium-sized enterprises; and (iii) public awareness, reflected in elevated civic engagement with health and environmental issues. Heterogeneity analysis reveals that while the policy is effective across cities with different healthcare resource endowments, fiscal capacity is a critical enabling condition. These findings offer implications for rapidly urbanizing economies seeking to balance growth and equity.

title: Evolution of South Korea’s welfare state : a growth regime perspective
abstract: This study examines South Korea’s welfare transformation through the lens of growth regimes, analysing how successive growth strategies have interacted with producer group and mass politics. Drawing on Korea’s developmental trajectory, we identify three distinct growth regimes – state-led industrialization, economic liberalization, and the knowledge-based economy – each characterized by different configurations of government strategies, producer group politics, and welfare politics. The analysis shows that while authoritarian developmental legacies constrained welfare expansion, the emergence of labour politics after democratization in 1987 and the rise of electoral competition after 2000 generated new impetus for welfare reform. The transition to the knowledge-based economy, coupled with intensified political competition and growing generational cleavages, drove significant social investment expansion, yet inclusive reform remained limited by insider-oriented labour politics. By tracing how Korea’s successive growth regimes shaped the scope and direction of welfare change, this study advances comparative political economy and offers new insights into how developmental states reconcile growth and welfare under changing political and economic conditions.

title: The enrolment paradox: social insurance, precarity, and digital platform work in China’s productive welfare state
abstract: The rapid expansion of China’s digital platform economy has exposed a critical gap in its contribution-based social insurance system, originally designed for standard employment. Despite recent policy reforms allowing platform workers to voluntarily enrol as ‘flexible employees’, uptake remains low. This qualitative study, based on in-depth interviews with platform workers in four selected cities in China, examines the reasons for this low participation and explores pathways for policy optimization. The findings show that low enrolment is not due to a lack of awareness but to a boundedly rational cost–benefit calculus shaped by an institutional mismatch between current policy and the precarious nature of platform work, compounded in some cases by informational constraints. Key barriers include prohibitive self-contribution costs amid volatile incomes, distrust of the portability and future value of benefits, procedural complexity and the prioritization of immediate financial needs. These factors are exacerbated in less developed regions but persist even in high-innovation hubs. The study concludes that China’s current ‘employer-less’ voluntary model fails to bridge the gap between the insecurity of platform work and the insurance system’s financial demands. It argues for more adaptive and inclusive policies to address this protection gap in China.

title: Food insecurity and political trust amid a public health crisis: government responsiveness and community support
abstract: Maintaining political trust during crises is essential for ensuring public compliance with government policies and for the effective management of the crisis. This study examines the relationship between food insecurity and political trust among residents of Shanghai during the city’s stringent COVID-19 lockdown. The findings reveal a strong negative association between food insecurity and political trust. However, this relationship is observed alongside positive associations between political trust and two key dimensions of crisis governance: government responsiveness and community support. These findings suggest that, in the context of Shanghai’s COVID-19 lockdown, political trust was associated not only with individuals’ experiences of food insecurity but also with their perceptions of government responsiveness and community support. The results provide valuable insights into the complex dynamics between food insecurity and political trust, offering important implications for future crisis governance.

title: From the Margins: Potential Coalitions in Centralized, High‐Capacity States
abstract: ABSTRACT The early stages of coalition formation remain an understudied area, particularly in centralized, high‐capacity political systems. Examining actor dynamics at this formative stage can reveal how coalitions form and how limited pluralism constrains their development. This study examines how potential coalition members emerge, and what shapes their prospects for consolidation in this institutional context. We study sustainability efforts in Singapore‐ a centralized polity with a history of state‐led environmental governance and a recent rise of sustainability nonprofits. Drawing on interviews with 39 nonprofits, we examine evidence of early stages of coalition formation outside of the state‐led coalition within Singapore's sustainability subsystem. Our findings show that both subsystem structure and actor attributes constrain potential coalitions from forming, owing to limited resource support and venues to formally participate in the coalition and coordinate with peers and the dominant state‐led coalition. Uncertainty in positions and learning orientation of other actors foster caution and complacency, entrenching weak horizontal ties. Additionally, crises can open brief windows for coordination, but these can close as routines and hierarchies reassert themselves. This study advances our understanding of coalition formation dynamics in centralized, high‐capacity, and limited pluralism contexts where contestation often remains limited and subtle.

title: Digital Social Administration: A New Paradigm for Understanding the Digital Transformation of Welfare
abstract: ABSTRACT Digital public administration scholarship has expanded on broad trends in government digitalization, yet its generic categories, such as ‘citizen’, ‘user’ and ‘service’, systematically overlook what is distinctive about welfare administration. From automated debt recovery and predictive risk modelling to algorithmic child protection and emerging generative AI applications, the digital transformation of social policy creates profound dilemmas that generic frameworks cannot address. This paper proposes digital social administration (DSA) as a new conceptual paradigm—the ensemble of digitized and automated systems, data infrastructures, algorithmic tools and organizational practices through which welfare states assess eligibility, allocate benefits, govern risk and manage disadvantaged populations. We develop the TOV Three‐Dimensional Analytical Framework to operationalize this paradigm, focusing on the Technical, Organizational and Valuational dimensions of DSA and their relationships. Applying the framework to four signature dilemmas, and considering the emerging challenges posed by advanced AI and AGI demonstrates its ability to reveal dynamics that single‐dimensional approaches overlook. DSA constitutes a qualitatively new administrative form, comparable to the bureau‐professional state or new public management, and demands concepts adequate to its specificity. We conclude by outlining a research agenda organized around the TOV dimensions and identifying implications for social policy, practice, advocacy and legal reform.

title: What's in a name? Name change, memory-work, and symbolic resistance in Rhode Island
abstract: Rhode Islanders voted in 2020 to remove the phrase Providence Plantations from the state's official name despite overwhelmingly rejecting an identical ballot measure in 2010. Drawing on intersecting literatures on critical toponymies, memory-work, and issue framing, we argue that the 2020 ballot measure succeeded where the 2010 measure failed because of three interrelated factors. First, the ongoing memory-work of racial justice advocates in Rhode Island and beyond significantly altered the repertoire of acceptable narratives, images, and symbols available to Rhode Island's political elite between 2010 and 2020. Second, the intense Black Lives Matter protests in May and June 2020 represented a critical juncture that gave supportive Rhode Island politicians the opportunity to reintroduce the name-change ballot measure under the broader banner of reckoning with systemic racism in the United States. Finally, activists and supportive politicians learned from the mistakes of 2010 and in 2020 mounted a more organized public advocacy campaign framed around contemporary racial justice issues designed to persuade Rhode Island voters to adopt the name change.

title: How Does Wage Inequality Affect the Labor Movement?
abstract: Abstract This paper provides evidence on how wage inequality among workers affects the labor movement using three complementary research designs: a vignette experiment with union organizers, a natural policy experiment that increased wage inequality among Wisconsin school teachers, and an information intervention during the 2023 Writers Guild of America strike. Across all studies, we find that inequality undermines union strength through multiple channels. First, workers with high individual bargaining power are more likely to withdraw support in unequal environments, preferring individual over collective bargaining. Second, union organizers facing hypothetical choices strategically respond to inequality in ways that may preserve membership but limit redistribution, such as shifting their campaign away from wages and choosing smaller, more homogeneous bargaining units.

title: Low-Income Families, Maternal Labor Supply, and Welfare Reform,
