title: Recommendation Design: Can Mediators Implement Correlated Equilibria?
abstract: Abstract We report results from a novel experiment studying individuals’ ability to act as mediators by designing incentive-compatible recommendation devices for rational robot agents, that is, to implement correlated equilibria. To test the skills required of a successful mediator, we vary both the games played by the agents and the mediator’s objective. Most participants successfully implement correlated equilibria across games, especially in games where coordination yields benefits. Across objectives, however, many participants initially favour fair and efficient devices, even when these properties are not incentivised, suggesting that fairness and efficiency serve as important heuristics in recommendation design.

title: The role of social connections in the racial segregation of US cities
The spoils of algorithmic collusion: Profit allocation among asymmetric firms
Topology-free Constructions of a Universal Type Space as Coherent Belief Hierarchies
Artificial Intelligence and Climate Risk Shocks
abstract: ABSTRACT Artificial intelligence (AI) has been widely applied across various fields and has demonstrated effectiveness to some extent. However, some scholars have raised concerns about its ethical implications and potential rebound effects, particularly in the context of climate issues. To address these debates, we obtained cross‐national panel data for 51 countries from 1996 to 2023 through the ISETS Energy Finance Network, WIPO, and World Bank databases. A two‐way fixed effects model was used to examine the relationship between AI and physical climate risks. The findings are as follows: (1) AI can effectively govern physical climate risks. (2) The governance effect of AI on physical climate risks comes from risk sensing, risk seizing, and action integration. (3) Compared to AI technologies and application fields, AI functional applications have a greater governance impact. (4) Political and economic integration alliances show a stronger AI governance effect compared to purely economic alliances. (5) The governance effect of AI intensifies as physical climate risks increase. These results provide theoretical support and empirical evidence for government efforts to promote AI applications and achieve climate governance. These findings provide theoretical support and empirical evidence for government initiatives to promote AI applications in climate governance.

title: Bravado and Beguile: When the Beautiful Bet Boldly
abstract: Abstract This paper explores the relationship between facial attractiveness and risk-taking preferences using three standard elicitation methods, each modeled on its own scale. Drawing on incentivized samples of students and professionals recruited directly from LinkedIn (plumbers, lawyers, and MBA-holding business professionals) along with a standard, continuous attractiveness measure, I find that beauty is associated with greater risk tolerance across generalized, financial, and social risk domains, most prominently among lawyers and MBAs. A validated proxy for confidence is consistent with partial mediation in the generalized and financial domains, with strength varying by occupation, while a direct association between attractiveness and risk tolerance persists throughout. Beauty is particularly correlated with cooperation in the socially risky Stag Hunt setting, a link that operates largely outside the confidence channel. These associations have implications for occupational selection, fair talent allocation, digital recruiting, and other managerial settings.

title: Self-reinforcing barriers to municipal digital government: A system dynamics perspective
abstract: Municipal governments have invested substantially in digital government endeavors, yet progress in public sector digital transformation remains surprisingly slow. Although research has repeatedly identified, categorized and reclassified barriers while also proposing numerous strategies to address them, the same obstacles continue to reappear across ongoing digitalization efforts. This persistence suggests that existing knowledge about barriers and their remedies remains insufficient. To address this gap, this study adopts a systemic perspective to explain why the barriers to municipal digital government persist, even after being repeatedly identified and targeted. We conducted 56 semi-structured interviews with 67 municipal employees and employees of GovTech providers in Germany and analyzed them through an inductive multi-stage coding process. Using system dynamics principles, we reconstruct the shared mental model through which actors perceive, explain and interlink barriers into a causal map. The resulting model reveals a dense web of interdependencies among barriers that form extended causal chains and self-reinforcing feedback loops. This perspective provides a dynamic and system-level explanation of persistence that reconceptualizes barriers not as discrete factors, but as generative mechanisms that sustain digital stagnation through their mutual reinforcement.

title: Towards a theory of public-sector organizations with targeted mandates: a case study of New Zealand’s Māori Health Authority
abstract: Public-sector organizations (PSOs) are increasingly created to reduce inequities, yet we know little about how they operationalize ambitious mandates in complex systems. We study Aotearoa New Zealand’s Te Aka Whai Ora / Māori Health Authority (MHA), established in 2022 and disestablished within two years, using an interpretive analysis of 26 interviews with former staff along with available official documents and news reports. This paper conceptualizes operationalization as a dynamic achievement: an operating model must stabilize decision rights, routines, inter-organizational interfaces, and performance controls to translate policy intent into coordinated action. We identify six recurring misalignment patterns that pushed the MHA from visionary intent to operational marginality as system conditions disrupted authority–accountability congruence, interface specification, capacity stability, and performance control. This research introduces recursive system fit, showing how capabilities and system conditions co-shape viability of PSOs. Policymakers should specify operationalization inputs at planning stage rather than retrofit them during implementation.

title: Does level of government and messaging influence public evacuations? Examining public compliance and agency trust
abstract: Extreme weather events are increasing globally, yet research on how public leadership messaging and the level of government delivering crisis communications influence public compliance and institutional trust remains limited. Drawing on public leadership theory and federalism research, we employ a 2 × 3 survey experiment embedded in the 2023 US Cooperative Election Study (N = 409) to examine how messaging style (authoritarian versus democratic) and the level of government agency (federal, state, or local) influence evacuation intent and agency trust. We find that messaging from the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) increases evacuation intent, despite local governments being legally responsible for issuing evacuation orders. Democratic, or collective, messaging is associated with greater trust in agency. However, trust is more strongly associated with pre-existing individual orientations, public service motivation, and political ideology, than with one-time communication cues. Findings have implications for crisis communication strategy, public leadership, and intergovernmental coordination in emergency management.

title: Don't Lead with Climate, Lead with Local Aspirations: Fostering Meaningful Community Engagement in Toronto
abstract: Abstract Achieving the very ambitious climate action goals of cities with net zero GHG emissions targets will require unprecedented levels of political support and behavioural engagement from residents. Climate engagement methods adopted by most cities typically consist of public education about climate change and public input on emissions reductions strategies. However, there is little evidence to suggest that such campaigns will achieve the level of support and engagement required to meet net zero targets. This article outlines an alternative approach that combines the Connected Community Approach and participatory backcasting to articulate a desired neighbourhood future rooted in local activities, and pathways to such a future. Only then does it make connections to the City of Toronto's climate goals and targets. Our hypothesis is that this approach—focusing on local sustainability—will lay the essential groundwork for fostering higher levels of public support and behavioural engagement on urban climate action than conventional engagement methods.

title: From the COVID‐19 Pandemic to Crises: Lessons for Canadian Climate Governance
abstract: Abstract The COVID‐19 pandemic was the most significant governance stress test in recent Canadian history, revealing both the capacities and constraints of Canadian public administration under acute uncertainty. This article examines Canada's pandemic response as a diagnostic case for understanding governance capacity relevant to long‐duration challenges such as climate change. Drawing on interviews with senior public health and climate‐health leaders, and triangulating these insights with federal evaluations, the analysis focuses on coordination, trust, political will, and institutional learning across pandemic phases. Findings show that coordination and political will were episodic rather than durably embedded, trust was a fragile governance resource, and post‐crisis learning was only weakly institutionalized. Rather than treating COVID‐19 as a model for climate governance, the article argues that its value lies in diagnosis: making visible the limits of emergency‐oriented governance and clarifying the capacities required for more anticipatory, durable responses.

title: The Réseau Express Métropolitain as an Evolution of the Public‐Private Partnership
abstract: Abstract This research note explores the Réseau Express Métropolitain (REM) as an exploratory case of partnership for public infrastructure procurement. It seeks to determine whether the REM represents an evolution of the P3 model that has significance for public governance, particularly as it relates to the delivery of public infrastructure. Our study concludes that the REM is more than just an evolution of the P3, as its form and structure differ markedly in several aspects. We propose that the REM challenges how scholars and practitioners view procurement partnerships as these should be viewed as more than merely the sum of their parts. We conclude by calling for more research to develop and assess the evolution of public infrastructure partnerships, both theoretically and in terms of framework development, to advance scholarship and the practice of public administration.

title: Coalitions in EU Environmental Policymaking: A Typology
Making Policy, Making Authority: European Policy Process Research Across Epistemological Divides
Problem Structuring and Policy Design Decoupling: Causes, Consequences, and Pathways to Better Integration
The Micro‐Level Design of Public Subsidies for Private Schools: A Typological Approach
Modeling the Interplay of Policy and Practice in the EUI: Towards a Comprehensive, Multi‐Level Perspective on Europeanization
Does municipal participation in service delivery matter? Service delivery for effective climate policy implementation
abstract: Decarbonising local public services is essential for implementing climate plans. Actors involved, such as utility companies and municipal departments, must balance financial, social and climate goals, often compromising the effectiveness of the ecological transition. While existing literature classifies service delivery arrangements, it offers limited insight into how these arrangements affect climate policy implementation and integration. This paper examines the hypothesis that greater involvement of market-oriented private providers leads to less consistent service delivery with climate mitigation programmes due to increased information asymmetry and coordination costs. It analyses four cities with differing arrangements: Zurich and Lausanne (Switzerland), where public actors are more involved, and Bologna and Padua (Italy), where municipalities rely on private or hybrid providers. Findings draw on 28 semi-structured interviews and relevant policy documents. The analysis suggests that stronger municipal control over service planning and oversight supports more effective climate policy implementation. This contributes to the literature on policy implementation and public management by identifying the institutional contexts that enable collaboration for resolving horizontal collective action dilemmas.

title: Electoral timing and local user charges: evidence from sewerage tariffs in Japan
Busing to Opportunity? The Impacts of the METCO Voluntary School Desegregation Program on Urban Students of Color
abstract: Abstract School assignment policies are a key lever for expanding access to high-performing schools and promoting racial and socioeconomic integration. For over 50 years, the Metropolitan Council for Educational Opportunity (METCO) has bussed students of color from Boston, Massachusetts to relatively wealthier and predominantly White suburbs. I estimate the effects of attending a high-performing suburban school by comparing applicants who receive enrollment offers with applicants who do not. A two-stage least squares approach exploits waitlist assignment priorities and controls for a rich set of characteristics from birth records and application data. Attending a suburban school boosts math and English test scores, reduces dropout, and increases on-time high school graduation. Four-year college aspirations, enrollment, and graduation increase along with earnings in adulthood. Students whose parents did not attend college and boys experience the largest effects. The evidence points to several mechanisms, including access to higher value-added schools, higher achieving peers, and schools with stronger college-going norms. Participants are more likely to be tracked into lower performing classes, implying that effects could be larger with access to more advanced coursework. District value-added estimates suggest that students’ educational trajectories shift at least as much as they would from growing up in the suburban districts.

title: Do Water Audits Work?
abstract: Abstract Water suppliers are showing greater interest in using residential water audits to promote conservation. Yet there is limited causal evidence on their effectiveness, persistence, and welfare implications. We address this gap using a natural field experiment in the United Kingdom that randomly assigns about 45,000 households to receive different behavioural encouragements to complete an online home water audit. Our analysis yields three main findings. First, financial incentives substantially increase audit take-up and lead to large short-run reductions in water use: among compliers, consumption falls by about 17 per cent over a two-month period. The size of the incentive matters for participation but not for the magnitude of conservation. Second, conservation effects attenuate rapidly, becoming undetectable after roughly two months. As a result, the intervention yields small welfare gains, with per capita net benefits typically below £1 under a wide range of assumptions. Third, targeting high-use households roughly doubles short-run conservation effects but remains insufficient to generate sizable welfare gains because conservation does not persist. Overall, while audits and incentives induce meaningful short-run conservation, their policy value depends critically on whether these effects persist.

title: Reconciling Aggregate And Firm-Level Tariff Pass-Through: Evidence From The 2018–2019 Us Tariffs On China
abstract: Abstract Research finds complete tariff pass-through at the product level during the 2018-2019 US-China trade war. Using firm-level customs data, we find a significant decrease in Chinese firms’ ex-tariff prices in response to US tariffs, which indicates incomplete pass-through. A one-percentage-point tariff increase reduces prices by 0.172 percentage points for the highest-priced 25% of exporters while having negligible effects on firms with below-median prices. US tariffs increase Chinese exporters’ probability of exiting the US market, with larger effects for lower-priced firms. The product-level complete pass-through results from two offsetting forces—price reduction by incumbents and market exits by lower-priced firms.

title: Behavioral responses to spatial tax notches in the retail gasoline market
The structure of discrimination against Turkish migrants in Germany
abstract: We study the structure and heterogeneity of discriminatory behavior using an incentivized choice experiment with a representative sample of over 2000 adults in Germany. Decision-makers allocate a fixed endowment between two receivers whose migration background, education, gender, and age are randomly varied. This design allows us to compare discrimination across attributes within an integrative framework, analyze how these dimensions interact, and classify individuals into behavioral types. We show pronounced discrimination against Turkish migrants in allocation choices, comparable in magnitude to gender-based preferential treatment in favor of women. Discrimination against Turkish migrants varies systematically with other receiver attributes and across decision makers, and is particularly strong among non-migrants and individuals with right-wing political preferences.

title: Competitive Search with Repeated Moral Hazard
Perceived valenced news exposure and public acceptance of autonomous vehicles: a Social Amplification of risk perspective
abstract: Drawing on the Social Amplification of Risk Framework (SARF), this study examines who reports greater exposure to positive and negative news about autonomous vehicles and how such perceived exposure relates to adoption intentions. An online survey of Chinese adults (N = 1,000) found that belief in machine heuristics, traditional media use, and generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) use were associated with greater perceived exposure to positive news, whereas individualism was associated with lower perceived exposure to positive news and greater perceived exposure to negative news about autonomous vehicles. Perceived exposure to positive news was associated with stronger perceptions of scientific and social consensus, which in turn were associated with greater perceived benefits, lower perceived risks, and stronger adoption intentions. In contrast, perceived exposure to negative news was associated with greater perceptions of both risk and benefit but showed no significant overall association with adoption intentions. These findings contribute to an individual-level application of SARF by linking perceived valenced news exposure to consensus perceptions and risk–benefit appraisals that underlie public responses to emerging technologies such as autonomous vehicles.

title: Source credibility and responsibility attribution in social media risk communication: evidence from the 2024 cooking oil contamination crisis in China
abstract: This study examines how different types of social media use and perceived source credibility influence responsibility attribution and risk perception during food safety crises. Using a cross-sectional survey of 278 Chinese adults following the 2024 cooking oil contamination crisis, we measured exposure and attention to official, public, and aggregated social media, as well as source credibility, responsibility attribution to individuals, corporations, and government, and food safety risk perception. PROCESS macro analyses revealed that official social media use primarily enhanced responsibility attribution to individuals, while public social media use significantly increased responsibility attribution to corporations and government. Aggregated social media influenced all three attribution types. Responsibility attribution to corporations and government increased risk perception, whereas responsibility attribution to individuals did not. Source credibility moderated the effects of official and aggregated media use on responsibility attribution to corporations, which mediated the pathway from media use to risk perception. These findings extend attribution theory to digital risk communication, highlighting the roles of media type and credibility in shaping responsibility attribution and risk perception among respondents during food safety crises in China.

title: From human touch to aI-based self-service: antecedents of business users’ switching intention in government-to-business services
abstract: Governments are increasingly deploying AI-based self-service technologies (AI-based SSTs) to improve government-to-business (G2B) services, yet little is known about why business users switch from human-assisted G2B services to AI-based SSTs. Drawing on the push–pull–mooring (PPM) framework, this study examines how negative incumbent service experiences, perceived benefits of AI-based SSTs, and status quo biases jointly shape switching intention. Using survey data from 461 business users in Chinese government service agencies and PLS-SEM, we find that perceived intelligence, shaped by responsiveness, personalization, and autonomy, together with physical attractiveness, procedural fairness, and structural assurance, generates pull effects toward AI-based SSTs. Switching costs, habit, and desire for human interaction strengthen inertia, which directly reduces switching intention and weakens the effects of both push and pull factors. The study extends the PPM framework to digital government service delivery and offers guidance for reducing inertia and promoting migration to AI-enabled self-service channels.

title: Merit, autonomy, and corruption: the moderating role of anti-corruption institutions in Africa
abstract: This study examines how merit appointments and bureaucratic autonomy influence corruption in African governments, and whether the independence and capability of anti-corruption institutions condition these relationships. Using two-way fixed effects regression to analyze a panel of 486 African countries from 2013–2021, we find that bureaucratic autonomy is negatively associated with corruption, while the relationship between merit appointments and corruption depends on the capability of anti-corruption institutions: where such institutions lack the capability to hold politicians and bureaucrats accountable, merit appointments are positively associated with corruption; as the capability of anti-corruption institutions increases, this relationship weakens and can eventually reverse. Neither the independence nor the capability of anti-corruption institutions is independently associated with corruption. These findings suggest that professionalizing civil service hiring without corresponding investments to bolster the capability of anti-corruption institutions can backfire and point to the conditions under which anti-corruption reforms are likely to succeed.

title: Building tolerance through experience: administrative engagement and burden tolerance across four countries
abstract: Research on burden tolerance suggests that people who previously faced burdens tend to be less accepting of administrative burdens more generally. However, the empirical focus has been on program-specific burdens and in particular social welfare programs. Thus, it remains an open question whether and how more general, everyday engagement with administrative tasks—and the emotional experiences involved—may influence burden tolerance. To better understand the relationship between administrative engagement, emotions, and burden tolerance, we survey residents in the United States, Mexico, the United Kingdom, and Denmark. We find that frequent engagement with administrative tasks is positively associated with burden tolerance in all countries, except Denmark, and that residents with more positive emotional experiences tend to be more tolerant of burdens. While correlational, we interpret these findings as suggesting that engagement with everyday administrative tasks builds capability for managing administrative burdens, which in turn fosters burden tolerance.

title: Implementation-Oriented design in CARICOM regional policies: A theory informed configurational evaluation
abstract: This study evaluates implementation-oriented design in nine Caribbean Community (CARICOM) regional policy documents, a governance setting marked by fragmented authority and sovereignty constraints. Using fuzzy-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (fsQCA) as a configurational mapping technique, it examines how eleven design dimensions cluster among policies with higher membership in a composite design-readiness set. Goal Clarity and Instrument Suitability recur across the highest-membership cases, while configurations involving Enforcement Mechanisms, Role Definition, and Monitoring and Feedback Systems characterize the strongest design architectures. These set-relational patterns describe higher-order design coherence but are not causal effects and do not indicate observed implementation performance. An OECD Development Assistance Committee (DAC)-aligned crosswalk provides a secondary interpretive summary of the same design scores. The study therefore conceptualizes implementation readiness as a design-based property of policy documents and shows how institutional constraints are reflected in regional policy architecture. The findings offer practical guidance for strengthening procedural clarity, accountability, monitoring, resource specification, and institutional alignment in CARICOM and comparable multilevel governance systems.

title: The 150‐Year‐Old Hybrid Organization: A Historical View on Municipally Owned Corporations ( MOC ) in Sweden
abstract: ABSTRACT This article presents a 150‐year longitudinal analysis of the development of municipally owned corporations (MOCs) in Sweden, tracing their emergence in the mid‐nineteenth century, their expansion during the growth of the welfare state, and their transformation in the era of market‐oriented public sector reform. While MOCs are commonly discussed in relation to New Public Management (NPM) and contemporary forms of hybrid governance, this perspective overlooks their much longer historical trajectory. Drawing on three major Swedish government inquiries (1924, 1965, and 1982), complemented by secondary historical sources, we examine how MOCs have evolved across changing political, economic, and administrative contexts. The article conceptualizes MOCs as constitutional hybrids, organizations that combine elements of public authority and corporate governance by design, and employs insights from institutional theory and historical institutionalism to analyze their long‐term development. The findings identify three historical phases characterized by changing functions, governance rationales, and institutional expectations. Across these periods, MOCs were repeatedly reinterpreted and adapted to new circumstances while maintaining their basic organizational form. The study contributes to the literature on hybridity by demonstrating that hybridity should be understood not merely as a contemporary consequence of public sector reform, but as a historically evolving institutional condition. We argue that the enduring presence of MOCs reflects the adaptive capacity of hybrid organizational forms, whose flexibility allows them to accommodate shifting demands for efficiency, legitimacy, accountability, and public value. By historicizing hybridity, the article offers a new perspective on institutional resilience, and the long‐term evolution of public governance.

title: A Replication of “Your Money, Your Life, or Your Freedom? A Discrete Choice Experiment on Trade‐Offs During a Public Health Crisis”
abstract: ABSTRACT A prior experiment conducted in Italy examined how individuals navigate trade‐offs among money, life, and freedom during government‐mandated lockdowns. This study replicates that experiment across three Confucian societies: Shanghai (China), Singapore, and Taipei (Taiwan). The findings indicate that, in the aggregate sample, the preference pattern of “money > life > freedom” mirrors that reported in the original study. However, when analyzed separately, residents of Taipei show stronger preferences for income and freedom than their counterparts in Singapore and Shanghai. Conversely, Singaporeans demonstrate heightened concern regarding the loss of life. In addition to replicating previous findings, this study contributes to the field of comparative public administration by highlighting the importance of considering contextual nuances in the formulation of crisis‐management practices by public managers.

title: Artificial Intelligence, Bureaucratic Discretion, and Democratic Administration
abstract: ABSTRACT Since the start of the COVID ‐19 pandemic, many countries have been using artificial intelligence ( AI ) to replace civil service personnel. We argue that this practice undermines core democratic values. Using the public values framework, we identify four clusters of values that are threatened when bureaucratic discretion is transferred to algorithms: accountability, fairness and equity, individual consideration, and reason‐giving. Each of these values is incompatible with how algorithms render decisions. Because algorithms produce outputs based on statistical regularities, they diffuse responsibility across multiple parties, fail to make accurate predictions about anomalous cases, and attenuate citizens' claims to individualized consideration. Thus, this article frames AI adoption as a constitutional question about which decisions can be automated, and which should remain under human control because they implicate democratic values. We propose a centaur model in which AI supports rather than replaces human officials, which can preserve efficiency while protecting democratic governance.

title: Unveiling the intangible: a systemic perspective for creativity and innovation in public organizations
abstract: This study examines how systemic creativity manifests empirically in the public sector using Csikszentmihalyi’s systemic model operationalized through 15 empirically grounded categories. By analyzing 60 Brazilian cases from the OECD Observatory of Public Sector Innovation, findings reveal that the most decisive enabling conditions are intangible: trust, psychological safety, shared purpose, and relational dynamics. A consistent pattern of frugal innovation emerges, with resource scarcity activating systemic mechanisms that substitute material resources. Theoretically, the study operationalizes an abstract model of creativity in organizational contexts. Empirically, it expands insights beyond Global North settings. Practically, it offers public managers a lens for rendering visible innovation's invisible infrastructure.

title: Strategic planning for digital technology adoption: drivers and mechanisms in the public sector
abstract: While strategic planning facilitates public sector digital transformation, it remains unclear why public sectors engage in shaping strategic plans for digital adoption. This study employs the 3Ps framework (People–Process–Plan) to construct an adapted explanatory model of these driving factors. Adopting a longitudinal case study (2019–2024), it investigates a Chinese local government’s digital anti-corruption strategizing based on 28 interviews. Findings extend the 3Ps framework by conceptualizing People as multiple stakeholders, differentiating Process into mutually evolving constructive and conflictual processes, revealing the moderating role of resource accessibility, and demonstrating the feedback effect of implementation outcomes on ongoing Strategic Plans, ultimately advancing digital strategizing from static compliance to a purposeful, dynamic closed-loop system.

title: Gender budgeting for adult education: Evidence and indicators
abstract: IMPACTThis article provides a transferable approach for public sector bodies and other organizations with a public interest mandate to strengthen gender budgeting beyond simple women–men comparisons. By utilizing data that municipalities often already collect—provided it is sex-disaggregated and linked to local areas—the study demonstrates the relevance of intersectional gender budgeting for participation and access. To identify spatial disparities and support place-sensitive steering, the article proposes a comprehensive monitoring framework with budget-relevant indicators applicable to other public services such as libraries, sports facilities, and integration services. Ultimately, this framework shifts municipal budgeting from a place-blind, one-size-fits-all distribution to an equity-driven mechanism that channels public resources exactly where socio-demographic barriers impede access. Consequently, these insights are highly relevant for municipal treasurers, budget and management accounting staff, performance controllers, auditors, and service managers alike.

title: The Case for Communities of Prevention: Comparing Responses to Climate and Mass Atrocity at Home
abstract: What action and agency are deployed by communities at the intersection of climate and mass atrocity? This article identifies a new concept of “communities of prevention” that increases focus on group action to prevent direct and structural violence at this intersection. Drawing on political ecology, the article discusses communities of prevention with two comparative cases of community-generated resilience in Nigeria and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). It finds that this new concept shows how such groups are punctuated by agency and lived experience of atrocity and displacement, ecological protection strategies, the dynamics of women’s organizing in sustaining resilience, and adaptability.

title: Labor Market Outcomes Under State Paid Family Leave: A Multistate Analysis
journal_name: Journal of Policy Analysis and Management

title: Interpreting emotions in policy narratives: a pluralist framework
abstract: The influence of emotions on real-world policy processes, particularly in the Global South, remains underemphasized. This article aims to address this gap by arguing that emotional expression can function as a component of policy narratives that contributes to policy processes in such contexts. Using clean air policy in northern Thailand as a case study, the explicit role of emotions in policy narratives is examined. Participatory observation, in-depth interviews, and documentary reviews were conducted as research methods. The epistemologically pluralist narrative policy framework is offered by expanding the boundaries of narratives to encompass factual, contextual, normative, ideological and emotional stories. Through this lens, emotions help confirm feasible policy options, complementing technical feasibility studies. Aside from technical and administrative data, the impacts of the policy depended heavily on public satisfaction with the perceived changes. Accordingly, this study suggests that, instead of ignoring emotions, narrative policy analysis should incorporate them to better understand their actual roles in policy processes.

title: Rethinking public procurement: toward a mission-oriented framework
abstract: Public procurement is a key tool for mission-oriented innovation policies. It has been relevant in industrial policy history, but underused as a tool for shaping markets to tackle social and ecological challenges. This paper argues for a new framework to understand and guide public procurement as a strategic tool to shape markets toward public value: mission-oriented public procurement. Current procurement paradigms—public procurement for innovation and sustainable public procurement—provide frameworks that are limited by their economic underpinnings leading them to consider value as a secondary goal, to lack strategic coherence and to usually rely on static quantitative evaluations. A bold new framework of procurement incorporates value as directional rather than diffuse, assessed dynamically (over time) rather than statically (at a point in time), and co-created rather than individually created, all of which results in a risk-taking public sector rather than the private sector alone taking risks. This change could support policymakers and public buyers renewing their policies and practices to explore the potential of public procurement to catalyze innovation and investment aligned with tackling social and ecological challenges.

title: The relevance of governance quality for enhancing entrepreneurship
abstract: This study examines the impact of institutional quality on entrepreneurial activity, considering the Worldwide Governance Indicators (WGI). Using a panel dataset of 46 countries over the period 2010–2020, the study employs a Two-Step System GMM estimator to address potential endogeneity inherent in cross-country institutional data. Entrepreneurship is measured through Total Early-Stage Entrepreneurial Activity (TEA) and Employee Entrepreneurial Activity (EEA). The empirical results suggest that Voice and Accountability, Government Effectiveness, Regulatory Quality, and Control of Corruption, exert a positive influence on entrepreneurial activity by reducing information asymmetries and transaction costs. However, Political Stability and Rule of Law yield negative or marginally significant coefficients. These findings suggest the presence of institutional sclerosis (Olson Citation1982) in highly stable contexts and a formality trap (De Soto Citation1989), where excessive legal rigidity may increase disproportional compliance costs for nascent firms, thereby displacing informal or marginal entrepreneurship. This research contributes to the literature by challenging the monolithic view of governance. It provides a nuanced understanding of institutional paradoxes, demonstrating that better-quality institutions do not always lead to a higher volume of entrepreneurship. Furthermore, it highlights the systemic nature of governance, which influences independent startups and corporate innovation in a remarkably similar manner.

title: Problem and Solution Framing in Senate Tweets: Scaling Expert Interpretation With Machine Learning
abstract: ABSTRACT Central to theories of agenda setting is the distinction between problems and solutions. Kingdon's multiple streams framework argues these processes are rhetorical and have distinct logics and incentives, yet empirical research struggles to measure them separately in digital, elite communication. Legislators bridge the multiple streams through their representational styles and legislative behavior, yet we lack scalable tools for identifying when elites frame issues as problems and when they promote solutions. This research note introduces a machine learning approach for classifying elite communication according to this core agenda‐setting distinction. We develop and validate a supervised model for 1.68 million tweets from U.S. Senators that categorizes messages into problem and solution frames, demonstrating that the problem/solution distinction can be reliably automated. This methodological research note establishes that the distinction is empirically measurable at scale and offers a validated, dataset‐specific measurement approach and theoretical foundation for classifying senatorial Twitter communication as problems or solutions.

title: Beyond Evidence: How Framing Shapes Public Health Policies During Health Crises
abstract: ABSTRACT Does the level of evidence that accompanies policy action depend on how a problem is framed, and on who frames it? This article examines these questions in the context of health crises. Bridging sociological and equivalence framing theories, it treats frames as preexisting interpretive schemes shared within communities of actors, whose downstream influence depends on the information available. Using a comprehensive textual database of COVID‐19 press conferences held in Quebec, where political decision‐makers held greater authority, and in Sweden, where scientists enjoyed more autonomy, the study combines natural language processing, OLS regressions, and Granger causality tests to analyze how frames and disclosed evidence were articulated with suppression and mitigation policies. Findings show that in Quebec, framing the pandemic as an imminent danger was associated with far‐reaching suppression measures even at low levels of disclosed evidence, while the moderate frame's association with mitigation strengthened as evidence increased. In Sweden, no relationship between framing and suppression policies appeared in public communications; framing instead operated jointly with evidence, the dangerous frame being associated with fewer mitigation references mainly at high levels of disclosed evidence. These results suggest that the relevant question is not how much evidence policy action requires, but by whom that evidence is required, and under what conditions. The evidentiary threshold attached to a frame appears to be a property of the community that carries it, with direct implications for how democratic institutions allocate influence between accountability and expertise.

title: Differentiating Rural Aging Out of Place: A Conceptual Framework and Illustrative Australian Cases
abstract: ABSTRACT Aging in place depends not only on formal care supply or continued residence. Existing research identifies many conditions that support aging in place, including housing, mobility, social connection, and care This article builds on that literature by conceptualizing aging in/out of place as a continuum reflecting whether the supports required for everyday life remain effectively available within or connected to the locality in which older people live, or whether older people become practically excluded from them. The framework distinguishes supported aging in place, borderline aging in/out of place, and de facto aging out of place, and does not treat relocation as the sole marker of aging out of place. It is illustrated through selected rural Australian localities using secondary documentary and statistical sources. The analysis shows how housing disruption, cumulative access pressure, mobility‐limited‐service usability, and provider concentration can strain support viability in different ways within a shared national aged‐care system.

title: How left-wing parties shape the voting gender gap across Western Europe
abstract: Abstract Empirical evidence suggests that the traditional gender gap in voting behaviour has been reversed in many advanced democracies. Cultural and structural factors have led the younger generations of women to shift from voting more conservatively than men to being more likely to support left-wing parties. Although these transformations have affected virtually all advanced democracies, empirical evidence shows that this gap is not uniform across time and space; there is significant variation in both the presence and strength of the association. In this paper, we argue that this variability can be partly explained by the role of left-wing political parties. In particular, we hypothesise that the modern gender gap is stronger when left-wing parties adopt progressive positions on both the socio-cultural and economic dimensions of politics. To test these hypotheses, 19 Western European countries are analysed using a dataset that integrates individual-level data from the European Social Survey (Waves 1–10) with party-level data from the Comparative Manifesto Project, covering 85 elections between 1999 and 2021. The results reveal that the modern gender gap is shaped by party positioning, with left-wing parties’ positions on both the economic and, most relevantly, the socio-cultural dimension playing a key role in reinforcing or mitigating gendered voting patterns.

title: The effects of participating in government-led citizens’ assemblies
abstract: Abstract Contemporary democracies face growing public disaffection and mistrust. Governments have tried to revert these trends by promoting participatory governance. Prior studies established how deliberation can empower citizens. However, whether these effects hold in real-life initiatives initiated by partisan governments remains unclear. We test the ability of citizens’ assemblies to foster democratic attitudes in a natural experiment leveraging the random selection of participants to Lisbon’s citizens’ assemblies Participation led to an increase in issue knowledge and salience, external political efficacy and institutional trust. However, it did not impact internal political efficacy nor helped citizens better recognize the challenges of collective decision-making. The results hold for two assembly editions and reveal the potential of government-led participatory initiatives to reconnect citizens with democracy.

title: Smash the Patriarchy?: Household Ties and Women’s Political Behavior in South Asia
abstract: The household is a difficult setting to study because its operations are, by design, not observable via public behavior. Violence within the household is often concealed; coordination over whom to vote for is not recorded; the bargains struck within marriage are rarely stated in terms that researchers can capture. Soledad Artiz Prillaman and Naila Kabeer take up this problem in India and Bangladesh, respectively. Both authors directly demonstrate the links between household ties and women’s political behavior.

title: Gendered support for the radical right: the role of personal network cues
abstract: Gender shapes support for populist radical right parties (PRRPs), but the role of voters’ immediate social environment remains underexplored. Building on research linking PRRP support to social cues and stigma, this study examines whether the association between cues in personal networks and PRRP support differs for women and men, expecting a stronger association among women in a context of gendered social sanctions and stigma. Flemish (Belgium) data from ‘De Stemming 2023′ (n = 1,921) show that having a PRRP supporter in one’s personal network is indeed strongly associated with support for the radical right party Vlaams Belang, and that this association is significantly stronger among women. Media exposure and neighbourhood-level cues show weaker, non-gendered associations, and gender differences in exposure itself are limited. Personal networks thus matter for PRRP support, and they matter more for women.

title: Here comes the flood: crisis learning and public support for EU disaster solidarity
abstract: This article investigates how satisfaction with the EU’s past crisis management shapes support for EU-level risk-sharing in response to natural disasters, termed ‘disaster solidarity’. Drawing on original cross-country public opinion survey data and a natural experiment conducted during severe flooding, the study distinguishes between inter-crises learning (based on prior experiences) and intra-crisis learning (triggered by an ongoing crisis). Findings reveal that satisfaction with the EU’s performance during the COVID-19 pandemic – a crisis managed with visible supranational coordination – is positively associated with support for disaster solidarity. The refugee and Euro Area crises have no such positive learning effect, suggesting that inter-crises learning depends on the respective policy responses adopted in the past. By contrast, intra-crisis learning reduces support for EU-level risk-sharing and weakens the influence of inter-crises learning. Overall, our results highlight the conditional nature of public support for supranational risk-sharing and the limits of inter-crisis learning under acute threat.

title: JPE Turnaround Times
Recent Referees
Incomplete markets, crop portfolios, and agricultural productivity
abstract: Using the Uganda National Panel Survey, I document that farmers face a trade-off between crop yields and risk, that most grow both high- and low-yield crops, and that poorer farmers concentrate on the low-yield, low-risk ones. I then develop an incomplete-markets model with a crop-portfolio choice, in which households trade off income returns against consumption smoothing. Wealth-poor households optimally under-invest in intermediates and shift toward safer crops. Crop portfolios, intermediate input use, and the wealth distribution are jointly determined in equilibrium. The model also reproduces the low pass-through of both income inequality and income volatility into consumption. Calibrated to rural Uganda, it implies that completing markets raises agricultural productivity by 12.8%, with 15.8% of the gain coming from eliminating the misallocation of inputs across farmers and crops. Consumption rises by 17.6% and welfare by 17.4%, with income inequality rising slightly and consumption inequality unchanged.

title: Together or apart? Migration, education access, and intergenerational mobility in China
Skill certifications and migrant labor market integration: Experimental evidence from Colombia
abstract: This paper studies whether government-issued skill certification improves labor market integration when workers’ skills are hard to verify. We evaluate a randomized offer of access to an occupation-specific certification program in Colombia among locals and migrants, two groups with different ex ante signaling capacity. The program certifies existing skills rather than providing training. Among locals, the offer increases employment by reducing inactivity and raises hours worked. The effects persist unevenly over time and are robust to attrition bounds and alternative outcome measures. Among migrants, estimates are less precise and provide no evidence of effects in employment, hours, or wages. The results show that a common skill certification generates different patterns of labor-market adjustment among locals and migrants.

title: The decay of impact with network distance in linear diffusion processes
abstract: Many processes related to status, power, and influence within social networks have been modeled using forced linear diffusion models; examples include the highly successful Friedkin-Johnsen model of social influence, the status/power scores of Katz and Bonacich, and the widely used network autocorrelation model. While a basic assumption of such models is that the impact of one individual on another through any given path falls exponentially with path length, the total impact of the first individual on the second involves contributions from walks of all lengths; thus, while total impact is expected to decline with network distance, the relationship is not trivial. Here, we provide an approximate solution for the total impact of one node on another as a function of network distance, showing that the total impact is given to first order by a product of eigenvector centrality scores together with an expression in terms of the graph spectrum (eigenvalues of the adjacency matrix) that falls exponentially with distance. We also show how this solution can be refined using higher-order eigenvectors of the adjacency matrix. A numerical study on interpersonal networks drawn from educational settings verifies an average exponential decline in impact strength under the linear diffusion model, and shows that the first-order eigenvector approximation can often be a good proxy for total impact as obtained from the exact solution. This suggests a simple model that can be used to approximate total impact for social influence or status processes in a range of settings.

title: Lexical Utilities, Precautionary Principle, and Continuous Quantities
abstract: Lexical utilities have been proposed as an attempt to model the precautionary principle. However, critics argue that this introduces hypersensitivity and allows for sweeping interventions for the sake of precaution no matter the possible costs. Advocates of lexical precautionary principle (LPP) have advanced a counterargument to this objection by suggesting that in lexicographic structures lower-ranked criteria causally impact on higher-ordered ones and so LPPs are not hypersensitive for they are seeking the precaution that minimizes overall risk. However, lexicographic models preclude, by definition, causal interaction between lower and higher-ordered criteria and, second, they cannot model continuous quantities that are almost always necessary when cost-benefit calculations take place. As a result, lexical utilities constitute a rather impossible modeling strategy of the precautionary principle.

title: The Interactive Dynamic Social Trust Network‐Based Failure Mode and Effect Analysis Method Considering Correlative Cause and Effect Relationships
abstract: Failure mode and effects analysis (FMEA) is a widely utilized tool for risk assessment and reliability analysis. The application of FMEA entails the engagement of members with diverse knowledge and backgrounds, giving rise to numerous issues during the process of determining evaluation information and resulting in deviations in risk management. Thus, an improved FMEA method considering the connection of the interactive dynamic trust relationship in social networks with the interactive mechanism among expert opinions is proposed. First, aiming to derive a comprehensive social trust matrix and expert weights, a multipath and parameter social trust network completion model based on evidence theory is developed. Second, considering the mutual influence between expert evaluation opinions and trust relationships, a dual-interactive-dynamic risk assessment feedback model based on opinion similarity and trust value is established, and the risk levels of each failure mode are quantified through linguistic distribution assessment (LDA). Finally, considering the correlative relationships among risk factors, the improved method considering correlative cause-and-effect relationships is employed for risk priority ranking. By applying the proposed method to the case of high-quality development engineering in the Yellow River Basin, its effectiveness and superiority have been validated through sensitivity and comparative analyses.

title: How Can Multi‐Criteria Portfolio Decision Analysis Help Mitigate Mis/Disinformation?
abstract: In this paper, we examine and illustrate the relevance of multi-criteria portfolio decision analysis as an approach to addressing mis/disinformation risks. After summarizing representative applications of these methods, we draw on the framework for societal resilience developed in the Finnish COVID-19 Science to Panel to elaborate on the range of capabilities that can be leveraged to mitigate mis/disinformation, for example, by maintaining alertness, implementing risk management actions, and interacting with stakeholders to promote awareness. We then present a numerical case study that illustrates how multi-criteria portfolio decision analysis can be combined with probabilistic approaches for modeling voting behavior and the spread of mis/disinformation to identify cost-efficient strategies consisting of combinations of risk management actions. We conclude by discussing some of the challenges posed by mis/disinformation.

title: Shanghai Mundane: Survival and Revival of Bourgeois Sentiments under Chinese Socialism Lei Ping. New York: Bloomsbury Academic, 2025. 336 pp. £95.00 ISBN 9781666951387
Organizational Determinants of Telemedicine Equity Outcomes in Latin American Public Health Systems
abstract: This study examines how organizational factors shaped telemedicine equity outcomes across 623 public hospitals in Chile, Mexico, Colombia, Ecuador, and Uruguay from 2015 to 2025. Using hospital-year data from ministry databases, PAHO registries, waiting-time records, audit reports, training logs, and technology-readiness assessments, the analysis combines descriptive statistics, multilevel regression, difference-in-differences estimation, country-level models, and a limited instrumental-variable sensitivity analysis. Results show that the rural–urban specialist waiting-time gap declined from 5.1 to 1.9 days after telemedicine expansion. Centralized implementation was associated with a 0.187-unit improvement in the Access Equity Index, while each additional 10 hours of staff training was associated with a 0.024-unit improvement. Findings suggest that telemedicine equity depends not only on technology adoption, but also on organizational coordination, workforce preparation, and implementation capacity within public health systems.

title: The Impact of Transparency on Money Laundering Containment: A Qualitative Comparative Analysis of OECD Member Countries
Policy Design under Capacity Constraints: A Comparative Analysis of Capacity-Design Fit
abstract: Why do states with similar policy instruments produce divergent implementation outcomes? This paper proposes the Capacity–Design Fit framework, specifying three mechanisms, namely knowledge-processing pathways, operational routines, and legitimation channels, through which governance capability shapes feasible policy architectures. Comparative analysis of 15 social protection programmes across eight countries in the Middle East and North Africa, combining hierarchical cluster analysis with fuzzy-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis, identifies three cross-nationally recurring design archetypes. Implementation effectiveness varies with capacity–design congruence rather than with design complexity: state capacity, contextual stability, and administrative capacity are each individually necessary for high effectiveness, whereas design complexity is neither necessary nor sufficient. The evidence is exploratory and the framework generates propositions for validation across additional cases and policy domains.

title: Forgive Us Our Sins—Experimental Evidence on Arrears Forgiveness and Bill Payment From Nairobi, Kenya
journal_name: Journal of Policy Analysis and Management

title: When climate policy resonates: the interplay of framing, party preference, and political trust in shaping policy acceptance
abstract: Abstract This article examines whether the effectiveness of three justification framings for a road traffic emission trading system (ETS) in increasing public acceptance depends on political party preference and levels of political trust. The framings emphasized increased energy independence, economic resilience, and efficient climate mitigation. Data were collected via an online survey experiment in Finland, March 2024 ( n = 1,485). Although the justification effects were generally limited, the energy independence framing increased policy acceptance among supporters of the populist radical right Finns Party. Moreover, justification effects were minimal among individuals with high political trust but tended to trigger backlash among those with low trust. Our findings contribute to the literature on climate policy communication by showing that framing effects on policy acceptance depend not only on political preferences but also on political trust.

title: How expert bureaucrats survive illiberal regimes through renegotiating expertise bargains
abstract: This article examines how expert bureaucrats renegotiate their ‘expertise bargains’ under conditions of democratic backsliding and illiberal governance. Focusing on Slovakia following the election of a populist radical right government in 2023, it investigates the individual and collective strategies adopted by expert bureaucrats in response to growing political pressure, challenges to expertise, and attempts to strengthen political control over the bureaucracy. The article builds on the proposition that expert bureaucrats do not merely react to political change, but proactively adapt their strategies in anticipation of shifting political conditions. Conceptually, it distinguishes between a strong form of survival, in which bureaucrats preserve autonomy and influence in policy making, and a weak form of survival, centred on institutional continuity and professional existence rather than policy impact. To analyse these dynamics, the article develops a framework structured around three dimensions of expertise bargaining: anticipatory strategies, collective strategies, and value dilemmas. It argues that anticipatory strategies serve not only to maintain legitimacy and relevance, but also to bridge political polarization within unstable patronage systems. The article further shows how collective strategies moderate more extreme individual responses, reducing both voluntary exits and overt resistance in favour of weaker but more sustainable forms of survival. At the same time, value dilemmas between individual and collective strategies shape how bureaucrats navigate competing identities as political loyalist, expert bureaucrat, and engaged citizen.

title: Family Policy: A Critical Overview of 60 Years of Scholarship
abstract: ABSTRACT This article critically reviews research and scholarship on family policy over the last 60 years focusing on theoretical and methodological developments within the European welfare state context. The first part of the analysis reveals a field that is diverse and vibrant, although it may be more accurately characterised as a set of sub‐fields with distinct patterns of study. The main lines of work—historical, empirical and conceptual—are often quite distanced from each other and there is a strong tendency to study the fine details of policy absent theoretical analysis. In its second part the article identifies developments that merit further scholarship. These include the major demographic changes that are underway, the revisioning of family policy by the new right and the soft left, the need to clarify the socio‐cultural drivers of family policy and better understand the trade‐offs between family policy as addressing socio‐economic factors and socio‐cultural, value‐based tensions and the need for family scholars to engage with the study of care, which has taken much of the feminist and gender focus away from family.

title: What Would It Mean to Democratize Finance? An Evaluation of Divergent Conceptions of Democracy and Finance
abstract: Calls to “democratize finance” abound today. Yet this apparent consensus obscures sharply divergent conceptions of both democracy and finance. This article maps these demands along two axes, distinguishing between access- and power-based conceptions of democracy, and between three dimensions of finance: payment, capital markets, and banking. We then develop three normative claims. First, we argue that conceptions that reduce democratization to expanded market access are not merely insufficient but, when applied to speculative capital markets, amount to predatory inclusion. Second, thicker accounts of democratization as equal inclusion are normatively more promising but internally unstable, as their democratic commitments generate pressures toward power sharing. Third, the most plausible conceptions of democratizing finance are power-centered and involve greater public control over credit creation and allocation. Rather than defending a single institutional solution, the article assesses a range of reform proposals while specifying a normative threshold for evaluating what it would mean to democratize finance.

title: Democratic Accountability with Citizen Coproduction
abstract: Many policies require citizens to actively participate in their implementation in order to be successful, a situation referred to as citizen coproduction. Though citizen coproduction is necessary in many policy areas, it could create difficulties for democratic accountability because citizens and politicians share responsibility for policy failures and attribution of blame may be difficult. We analyze the problem of democratic accountability with citizen coproduction in the context of a model in which politicians, who vary with respect to their competence at selecting policies, choose whether to implement policies whose success depends on citizen coproduction choices. For citizens, the problem is one of attribution: when coproduction is low, it may be hard to select good incumbents because policy failures are frequent even when policy choices are good. Incumbents anticipate these effects, which sometimes implies that they are less likely to choose reforms when they are more likely to be successful.

title: Marriage as Slavery: Oroonoko, the Slave Trade, and the Origins of English Feminism
abstract: Abstract This article investigates Mary Astell’s controversial comparison of marriage to slavery. While existing scholarship situates this analogy within the neo-Roman republican framework, which defined slavery as subjection to absolute rule, I investigate another paradigm: the transatlantic slave trade. To make this case, the article traces the influence of Aphra Behn’s Oroonoko (1688) on early feminist thought. By foregrounding the market logic underpinning chattel slavery, Behn popularized the idea that slavery’s harms were rooted, not in absolute power, but in the commodification of human beings. Astell appropriated this insight, showing that marriage resembled slavery not because husbands wielded power over wives but because the institution had been commodified: women were treated as things to be bought and sold. In uncovering this genealogy of feminist thought, the article highlights the enduring contributions of the “first” English feminists—insights that are entangled with, and shaped by, the development of the slave trade.

title: Pulling for the party: Electoral campaign targeting and local information in Zimbabwe
abstract: How do party activists devise strategies to target different types of voters? We build on a rich body of previous work that seeks to understand how social networks shape party activist strategies to understand which voters are targeted and with what inducements. We argue that past research is largely mixed and inconclusive because it focuses on attributes of the voters rather than the attributes of the voters that are known to party activists . To address this gap, we present a theory that directly considers the role of local information in conditioning inducement targeting, and then test it using original data around Zimbabwe's 2023 elections. We find that information does condition the types of inducements voters receive, especially regarding the dissemination of non-clientelist as well as economic clentelist inducements.

title: From Courtiers to Courtship: Tory Feminism and the Political Dangers of Flattery
abstract: Flattery appears to be a trivial vice, yet it receives a curious amount of attention in contemporary political analysis. Scholars often view flattery as a symptom of autocratic regimes, an association with a much longer history. In seventeenth-century England, republicans likewise understood the courtier’s flattery as a humiliating sign of slavish dependence on the ruler. This article complicates this position by turning to an understudied perspective in the history of political thought: Tory feminism. We show how two Tory feminists, Mary Astell and Judith Drake, challenged the standard republican narrative by drawing on a broader set of experiences—namely, the dynamics of flattery in courtship. We argue that they used the example of courtship to isolate the true wrong of flattery: its employment to subordinate the flattered. Astell and Drake applied this insight to the political realm, contending that the most morally troubling forms of flattery emerge not in monarchical courts, but in republican political spaces. Recovering the perspectives of Astell and Drake is not merely a matter of diversifying the canon; it also shows how gendered assumptions have shaped our conceptual history of flattery. A more complete account of flattery—its value, dangers, and the political environments in which it flourishes—requires attention to the insights of these Tory women.

title: American Public Support for Higher Education in the Trump Era
abstract: Political science researchers have devoted little attention to studying public opinion toward higher education, an oversight we address in this review of recent opinion trends. We demonstrate the complexity of public attitudes toward higher education, which reflect a paradox: declining confidence and negative assessments of the sector have combined with positive ratings for college degrees and for the medical and scientific breakthroughs that occur on college campuses. Partisans are polarized in their broad assessment of higher education and the presence of political bias in the classroom, but they are far less divided on other aspects of higher education, indicating that only some attitudes toward higher education have become politicized in the Trump era. The study of public opinion toward higher education sheds light on a policy area of growing political importance and underscores its potential as a rich topic for political behavior researchers.

title: Toward Solidarity in Democratic Theory and Practice
abstract: I seek to demonstrate that solidarity should be understood as a vital good of democracy, one that is internally, inextricably related to the more familiar democratic values of equality and freedom. Acknowledging solidarity as a vital democratic good, I argue, involves recognizing that democracy entails political agents continually creating for each other the conditions to act as free equals. I build my democratic case for solidarity on Jürgen Habermas’s argument for the co-originality of solidarity with freedom and equality. In particular, I show how a concept crucial to Habermas’s argument, interdependence, can be translated from its original context—discourse ethics and moral agency—to the context of politics and political agency. In doing so, I posit three essential forms of political interdependence: practical, skillful, and ideological interdependence. Drawing on this translation of Habermas’s theory, I explore an immanent movement toward solidarity in three distinct new literatures in political theory that make a place for contentious, extra-institutional practices in democracy. This exploration sets the stage for elaborating a new conception of solidarity highlighting political interdependence.

title: Think Globally, Act Locally: The Determinants of Local Policy Makers’ Support for Climate Policy
Closing the Gap: Gender, Race, and Welfare-State Knowledge
abstract: Abstract Decades of research document persistent gender and racial gaps in political knowledge. However, a growing literature shows that these gaps depend on the content of political knowledge batteries. Building on these insights, I introduce a measure of welfare-state knowledge that captures understanding of what welfare programs do, whom they serve, and how political authority is organized. Using an original survey in the United States, I compare welfare-state knowledge with canonical political knowledge and find pronounced shifts in group-knowledge patterns. Women score lower on canonical items but outperform men on welfare-state knowledge, thereby reversing the gender gap. The racial gap narrows substantially in the welfare domain, with racial minorities scoring indistinguishably from white respondents. These findings challenge prevailing narratives about group-knowledge deficits by revealing domains of political expertise that canonical measures overlook and underscoring how measurement choices shape whose political experiences are represented in the study of public opinion.

title: Divergent Democracy: How Policy Positions Came to Dominate Party Competition. By Katherine Krimmel. Princeton, NJ: Princeton University Press, 2024. 296p.
Postcolonial Global Justice. By Shuk Ying Chan. Princeton: Princeton University Press, 2025. 264p.
Vulnerability Theory and the Trinity Lectures: Institutionalizing the Individual. By Martha Albertson Fineman. Bristol: Bristol University Press, 2025. 140p.
The Disappearance of Political Moderates Online: How the Privacy Function of Social Media Amplifies Observed Political Polarization
abstract: Abstract This article contends that when the privacy function of social media is used for politically relevant audience curation, users may take more partisan stances than they would otherwise, which therefore amplifies the observed political polarization. The privacy function allows users to selectively disclose their content to like-minded people and hide it from out-groups. We argue that, in a safe space created by using the privacy function, people tend to express more partisan stances to impress their in-groups. Through an experiment conducted in Hong Kong, where political polarization between pro-democracy and pro-establishment camps has intensified over the years, we created a social media-like environment for participants and demonstrated that those who were provided with the privacy function were more likely to disclose content to in-groups than to out-groups and, more importantly, exhibited stronger stances on polarizing issues. This article contributes to the understanding of the relationship between social media and political polarization and emphasizes the need to reassess the robustness of the observed polarization level on social media in various societies.

title: Free Gifts: Capitalism and the Politics of Nature. By Alyssa Battistoni. Princeton & Oxford: Princeton University Press, 2025. 328p.
The Noumenal Republic: Critical Constructivism After Kant. By Rainer Forst. Translated by Ciaran Cronin. Cambridge, UK: Polity Press, 2024. 256p.

The Left-Wing Peace & The Right-Wing Peace
