When Losses Matter More: A Dynamic Reference‐Dependent Evaluation of Suicide Risk
abstract: How do individuals transition from distress to suicidal ideation? Existing economic and epidemiological approaches typically model suicide risk as a function of expected outcomes or accumulated stressors, but they offer limited insight into how individuals evaluate worsening life circumstances under uncertainty. In this paper, we develop a dynamic, reference-dependent model of suicidal ideation grounded in cumulative prospect theory. The model captures two behavioral mechanisms: (i) outcomes are evaluated relative to a shifting personal reference point, and (ii) perceived probabilities are transformed into nonlinear decision weights when individuals evaluate uncertain future states. Using longitudinal household-level data from South Korea and a hierarchical Bayesian estimation strategy, we estimate individual-level parameters governing loss aversion, probability weighting, and reference-point adaptation. We find that transitions into suicidal ideation are significantly associated with entry into the loss domain relative to one's own prior well-being, rather than with absolute income or health alone. Loss-side sensitivity, rather than gain-side valuation, shows the strongest association with ideation, especially following recent negative well-being changes. These findings suggest that suicidal ideation is closely linked to how individuals perceive and process deteriorating conditions, rather than to those conditions alone. By integrating behavioral decision theory with longitudinal data, this study provides evidence consistent with a reference-dependent loss-processing pathway under uncertainty and helps explain vulnerability to extreme psychological outcomes.

title: Incorporating Hormesis Into Policy: Opportunities, Risks, and Governance Challenges
abstract: Public policy faces challenges when low and high exposures to the same stressor produce different, and sometimes opposite, biological effects. Hormesis challenges regulatory approaches based on linear assumptions, fixed thresholds, and population-average responses. Here, I develop a policy framework for examining its implications across environmental regulation, public health, medicine, agriculture, and antimicrobial resistance. Dose, timing, duration, recovery, vulnerability, endpoint, and exposure context are essential dimensions of policy evaluation, while controlled interventions differ from involuntary environmental exposures. Hormesis alone does not justify increased exposure or regulatory relaxation, although case-specific changes may be warranted by evidence of net benefit and acceptable risk. Its responsible incorporation can optimize precaution, improve regulatory responsiveness to biological complexity, and prevent low-dose stimulation from being misinterpreted as evidence of safety or benefit.

title: Assessing the Lagged Regional Economic Output Gaps After the 2015 South India Flood
abstract: ABSTRACT Natural hazards can adversely impact society, environment, and human well‐being. The development of mitigation strategies is typically based on estimates of economic losses, but such estimates are difficult when high‐resolution post‐disaster data are scarce. Models such as the input–output model have traditionally served as tools for disaster footprint analysis, although their reliance on equilibrium assumptions and limited treatment of production‐capacity adjustment can constrain their application to short‐run natural‐hazard impacts. This study applies a dynamic sequential interindustry model (DSIM), combining recent developments in dynamic input–output analysis with regression‐based coefficient estimation, to examine conditional temporal output gaps after the 2015 South India Flood. Using monthly industrial production indicators and a two‐region aggregation of the 2015 Indian MRIO table, we investigate aggregate economic propagation between Tamil Nadu and the broader Indian economy. The results should be interpreted as model‐implied, conditional scenario estimates rather than independently validated measurements of the full economic cost of the flood. Under these assumptions, the estimated national output gap is approximately 1.6 times the highest available direct‐damage estimate, suggesting that aggregate interregional spillovers may be policy‐relevant even when only limited post‐disaster data are available.

title: Authoritarian Memory Politics: State Erasure, Manipulation, and Counter-Hegemonic Resistance
abstract: Forgetting and remembering are inherently linked to politics, and this relationship is even more pronounced in authoritarian regimes where autocrats can manipulate and control memory without institutional and societal constraints. This study analyzes the politics of memory within an authoritarian regime by theorizing about the interaction between authoritarian rule and the cultural-political ecosystem. It explores how the state-led erasure of memory and construction of a dominant memory discourse collaboratively produce and sustain cultural hegemony. Simultaneously, counter-hegemonic resistance challenges cultural hegemony. Memories of the COVID-19 pandemic in China are used as a case study to illustrate authoritarian memory politics. The empirical analysis employs rich materials, including interviews, government archives, and social media posts, to illustrate the politics of memory within an authoritarian context.

title: Evangelizing Public Space: Christian Outreach in Republican China
abstract: This article examines how public spaces were shaped by local evangelists in Republican China. It treats public preaching as a dynamic site where Chinese Christians engaged with diverse audiences, integrating evangelistic activities into public life. In this study, the term “public preaching” refers to church outreach ministry in public spaces including streets, parks, and riverbanks. The spatiality of outreach preaching reflects indigenous Christian efforts to ensure the accessibility and visibility of the Christian message across diverse regions. The outreach ministry that expanded throughout Republican China targeted both urban and rural areas, promoting religious revitalization through various forms of public engagement. This article explores a realm of evangelical public space in which Chinese evangelists transcended geographical boundaries and kinship circles. By analyzing various forms of public preaching, I argue that Christian evangelical outreach reconfigured public spaces by introducing religious discourse into local life in both urban and rural areas.

title: Reply to Kettl: Beyond Bureaucracy: Why AI Demands a Fourth Way in Public Administration
abstract: ABSTRACT Kettl argues public administration faces a crisis rooted in widening gaps between scholars and practitioners and between the field's core ideas and current governance issues. We identify a critical example: artificial intelligence (AI) adoption in government. AI fundamentally transforms public organizations, redistributing tasks and discretion between humans and algorithms, embedding instrumental rationality into administrative processes, and reconfiguring authority structures. These developments challenge three longstanding pillars of public administration: bureaucratic neutrality, the politics‐administration dichotomy, and democratic governance. We argue that any proposed “Fourth Way” must center democratic resilience and technological stewardship, incorporating algorithmic transparency requirements and participatory governance structures that preserve public—and especially democratic—values.

title: Public Management of Deregulated Systems: Challenges and Opportunities in the Public Management of Retail Energy Markets
abstract: ABSTRACT Many critical infrastructure services operate within quasi‐regulated (i.e., “deregulated”) markets. Public managers face a unique set of challenges and opportunities in the administration and oversight of these markets. Administrative and regulatory challenges exist because public managers are required to balance an open and competitive marketplace while confronting multiple market failures (e.g., consumer inattention, imperfect competition) alongside organizational, management, and legal and regulatory enforcement challenges. There are real‐world consequences of administrative choices on economic (in)efficiency and consumer equity. This paper provides public managers with a comprehensive review of the public management challenges and opportunities associated with managing deregulated retail electricity markets. It then provides a review of empirical research and an empirical example for one category of these challenges—consumer equity. The paper concludes with a multi‐disciplinary discussion of the role of public managers in deregulated marketplaces and public policy options to address both equity and efficiency challenges.

title: Public Service Motivation Through an Indian Lens: New Theoretical Dimensions
abstract: ABSTRACT Across the globe, contemporary societies face significant challenges, including climate change, inequality, and public health crises. These problems threaten essential public goods and collective well‐being. Addressing them requires individuals with high public service motivation (PSM) who prioritize societal well‐being over their own self‐interest. However, PSM remains underexplored in the global south region. Considering India as a representative of the global south due to its diverse socio‐cultural and religious population, this study aims to understand the nature, structure, and context of PSM in India. Data were collected via an online qualitative survey, yielding 82 valid responses. A multi‐stage thematic analysis identifies dimensions of PSM that both converge with and diverge from Perry's four dimensions. Three new dimensions of PSM—professional execution, relational fortitude, and moral character—emerge in our research. This study found a notable absence of one of Perry's dimensions—attraction to public policymaking.

title: Durable equilibrium: explaining palm oil policy continuity in Indonesia through the lens of punctuated equilibrium theory
abstract: Abstract This paper examines Indonesian palm oil policy across the presidential transition from Joko Widodo to Prabowo Subianto. Contrary to expectations that leadership change would punctuate policy direction, the Prabowo administration reinforces a pro-industry policy equilibrium established under his predecessor. Using Punctuated Equilibrium Theory, we argue that a resilient policy monopoly anchored in the mandatory biodiesel program and the Palm Oil Plantation Fund Management Agency (BPDPKS) has preserved the status quo. Quantitative and qualitative analysis of budget flows, production trends, and consumption patterns (2014–2026) reveal incremental adjustments rather than disruption. Stability is sustained through control of policy image, marginalization of competing problem definitions, and alignment of elite interests. The study contributes by demonstrating how leadership turnover in developing democracies may entrench rather than disrupt monopolies, extending PET to resource-based governance in the Global South, and showing how off-budget funding and narrative control sustain palm oil’s dominance despite environmental and social pressures.

title: Ethnic and gender gaps in private pension participation in the UK
abstract: Abstract Being financially prepared for later life can make the difference between living in poverty and not. Existing research in the UK has evidenced gaps in pension protection between working-age individuals from different minority ethnic communities; however, research that examines how ethnicity interacts, specifically with gender and other demographic, health and socio-economic characteristics to affect pension membership, is lacking. Using data from the UK Household Longitudinal Study between 2009 and 2023, this paper first examines patterns of continuity and change in pension membership among working-age individuals from minority ethnic groups. Focusing on the most recent wave, the analysis then assesses the importance of ethnicity and gender, alongside other demographic, health, socio-economic and subjective wellbeing factors in explaining individuals’ private pension participation and non-pension savings/investments. The findings show persistent ethnic and gender gaps, with Bangladeshi and Pakistani individuals faring worse than other ethnic groups, and women within such groups faring the worst. Factors indicating better socio-economic and subjective financial situation are associated with a greater likelihood of having a personal pension or expecting to use savings/investments in retirement. The paper critically discusses how current policies address the ethnic gaps in pension membership, and how such gaps can be addressed more effectively in the future.

title: Activating relational welfare: insights from Supported Employment
abstract: Abstract In the face of ongoing welfare challenges, a wave of academic and policy thinking has advocated for recentring public policy around the principles and practices of relational welfare. The present paper argues that the potential of relational welfare can be further supported by sharper analytical understanding of its diverse potential forms and their varying key relational characteristics. To explore these priorities, the paper draws on sixty-one semi-structured interviews with thirty-six staff and twenty-five participants from sixteen UK Supported Employment services cast in a relational welfare mould. These grounded lived experiences highlight individuals’ universally positive experiences of these relational interventions, in contrast to past typical activation experiences, and the importance of a subset of Cottam’s relational welfare identifiers to those experiences. Rather than being homogeneous in their qualitative characteristics and requirements, the findings suggest legitimate variation in – and a hierarchical nesting of – relational welfare characteristics across more and less formalised relational interventions. Findings help to further critical understanding of relational welfare interventions and to support scholars and policy makers alike to maximise the reach, purity and potential of relational welfare approaches across diverse policy domains and approaches.

title: Lived experience in deliberative forums: a matter of design
abstract: Deliberative forums, including randomly selected minipublics, are increasingly expected to incorporate lived experience into democratic decision-making. Yet, without careful design, they risk marginalizing, extracting, or essentializing these experiences. This paper argues that scholars and practitioners of deliberative democracy can learn from other democratic practices in which lived experience has been a central concern. Focusing on participatory theatre, protest movements, and digital activism, it shows that, despite their different purposes and institutional designs, these practices have developed valuable ways of engaging with lived experience while reducing the risks of marginalization, extraction, and essentialization. Drawing on three examples from the UK, Brazil, and Finland, all focusing on mental health, the paper identifies design principles for deliberative forums that better support lived experience. It argues that taking lived experience seriously is ultimately a matter of design.

title: Who receives R&D tax incentives? Firm capabilities and stage-dependent access
abstract: This paper examines which firms are able to access and progress through Colombia's R&D tax-benefit scheme. Using firm-level microdata from three waves of the Colombian Manufacturing Innovation Survey, we estimate sequential logit models to assess how firm capabilities are associated with progression from intention to apply, to application, and ultimately to receipt. The results reveal a clear stage-dependent pattern. General innovation capabilities—including R&D effort, internal innovation resources, information-source breadth, export orientation, and university cooperation—are most strongly associated with firms' initial intention to apply. Conditional on intention, progression to application is more closely related to organizational scale and university cooperation. Conditional on application, receipt is less consistently associated with broad innovation effort, while the stage-specific analysis provides only suggestive evidence of associations with more specific organizational and relational characteristics. Additional analyses indicate that exposure to other forms of public innovation support is associated primarily with initial engagement rather than with progression at later stages. These findings suggest that formal eligibility does not translate automatically into effective access to R&D tax incentives. This implies that evaluations of tax incentives should account for the selective processes that precede receipt. For policymakers, the results indicate that broad-based fiscal incentives may need to be complemented by stage-specific information, administrative assistance, and capability-building measures if access is to extend beyond firms already equipped to navigate the scheme.

title: Green Deservingness in the Climate Crisis? Moral Repertoires in Media Debates in Belgium, Germany and Slovenia
abstract: ABSTRACT Both climate change and its political mitigation and adaptation will exacerbate and expand existing social risks, adding extra stress on welfare systems. This could lead to distributional struggles and a public reassessment of social justice and deservingness principles. Drawing on a cultural perspective on welfare legitimacy, this article examines how media debates in Belgium, Germany and Slovenia articulate questions of social justice and deservingness in the context of climate change. Investigating green deservingness, the paper describes how claims to social support and social protection of specific target groups are morally evaluated in relation to climate change‐related risks. Through qualitative content analysis of media coverage, the study traces how principles of need, merit and equality are mobilised to legitimise vulnerability and entitlement. Cross‐country comparisons reveal how deservingness and social justice are intertwined, mediating not only vulnerability but also culpability and legitimacy in climate transitions.

title: The Legacy of Mexico’s Drug War on Youth Political Attitudes
Critical Ties: How NGOs Become Reliable Information Suppliers to International Organizations
When, Where, and Why Might Elected Political Elites Reach for Democratic Innovations?
When attention shapes accountability: Ballot order and information weighting
abstract: Why do voters fail to sanction candidates even when credible information about misconduct is disclosed? We argue that political accountability depends not only on whether information is disclosed, but also on the institutional context in which voters encounter it. Using randomize-and-rotate ballot ordering in nonpartisan superintendent of education elections, we exploit within-candidate variation in ballot position under a common electoral contest. Candidates with ordinary criminal records receive fewer votes when listed first than when they appear in other positions, while candidates with pro-democracy-related convictions receive more votes when listed first. Wealthier candidates likewise receive fewer votes when appearing first. These results show that the electoral consequences of disclosed candidate attributes vary with ballot position and suggest that voter attention matters for how such information translates into electoral outcomes.

title: Out of breath, out of mind: Competing frames and public support for carbon taxation in Spain
abstract: Efforts to implement climate policies often face public resistance. This study, based on a pre-registered survey experiment in Spain, tests how different framings of carbon taxation, emphasizing costs, primary climate benefits, co-benefits, and their combinations, shape public support. Compared to a baseline with no additional information, cost-focused messages reduce support, while benefit frames increase it; co-benefits (cleaner air, better health) produce the largest increase, though in isolation this is not statistically distinguishable from the primary-benefit frame. When paired with cost information, co-benefit framing sustains support more effectively than primary climate benefits, suggesting that immediate, tangible outcomes resonate more strongly with the public than distant climate goals. A dictionary-based analysis of open-ended responses corroborates this interpretation: co-benefit and cost treatments activate frame-aligned language, whereas the primary benefits treatment does not. The study further reveals systematic heterogeneity in responses: cost information reduces support most among left-leaning and lower-income respondents, while co-benefit framing is more persuasive among center- and right-leaning and higher-income respondents. Together, these findings point to a modest but systematic role of framing in shaping attitudes toward carbon taxation, with implications for designing more publicly acceptable climate policies.

title: Online privacy protection: How the varieties of democracy matter
abstract: Abstract Digital technologies have enabled the gathering, storing, and processing of large amounts of data in increasing and unprecedented ways. This has triggered concerns regarding governments’ ability to harvest vast amounts of information on citizens and the consequences of this surveillance on democracy. The reliance of many democracies on digital (surveillance) technologies in response to the 2019 Coronavirus pandemic has amplified these concerns. While most studies focus on how privacy violations affect democracy, this study analyzes how variations in democracy affect the legal protection of citizens’ rights. We rely on data from the varieties of democracy to capture this variation and on data from the Digital Society Project to measure variations in online privacy protection laws. Our results point to a complex and partially unexpected relationship between democracy, its different dimensions, and online privacy protection laws in democratic regimes. The quality of democracy is positively associated with protective online privacy laws in typical times, but changes in democratic quality in the years preceding the pandemic did not affect changes in online privacy laws during the pandemic. However, the relationship between the different dimensions of democracy and privacy laws is more complex, and our results show that egalitarianism and participation are more important than liberalism in protecting online privacy laws. We conclude with a discussion of the relevance of these results to policy.

title: The disciplining effects of European fiscal governance on national pension policymaking
abstract: While pensions are electorally risky to cut back, they are also the largest budget item in most European Union countries, making them central to fiscal stability in the Eurozone. Despite these tensions, member states have since the 1990s implemented convergent cost-containment reforms, showing how supranational pressures force decision-makers to retrench. But what happens when these pressures fade? Using an original dataset linking pension-related country-specific recommendations to reform events, we find that excessive deficit oversight and higher sovereign bond yields encouraged reforms strengthening long-term pension system sustainability. As these twin constraints weakened under the Juncker Commission and vanished during the pandemic-related suspension of the Stability and Growth Pact, policy reversals emerged, undermining the alignment between European Union recommendations and domestic implementation and leading to higher projected pension spending.

title: Full boat, empty boat: The politics of maritime migration and its racial spectres
A Habit-Building View of Democracy: Mary Parker Follett and Motor Activities
abstract: Citizens of democracies should live democratic lives and develop democratic habits. That is one of Mary Parker Follett’s core insights on democracy. A child of the Gilded Age, Follett experienced the erosion of communal relationships, the intensification of socio-economic inequalities, and the alienation of ordinary people from the complex political system that governed their lives. She saw democracy become remote and foreign to citizens who had little control over what happened to them. Her solution was simple: to reinject a dose of democracy into the everyday life of citizens. This paper retrieves Follett’s embodied and habitual vision of democracy for contemporary political theory. Follett claimed that citizens should participate actively in the democratic life of their society; however, she conceived of democratic participation as going beyond decision-making and deliberative activities. She thought that participation in simple forms of embodied joint actions, like recreation and collective chores, could also benefit democracy. Drawing from Follett, I argue that participation in a wide variety of embodied practices of collective action provides benefits to individuals and society by instilling democratic habits in citizens. Those habits incline those who develop them to enter and maintain relationships as free and equal peers with all sorts of people to reach common ends. When faced with collective problems, therefore, these individuals are more likely to choose democratic collective action and to do so more effectively.

title: Why chief executives (dis)obey the law
abstract: Abstract When and why will chief executives obey the law, and when and why will they violate it? This article constructs a general framework for analyzing legal (non)compliance by a rational chief executive. It evaluates benefits and costs that might result from executive lawbreaking by reference to three types of objectives that chief executives may have: policy and governance objectives, electoral and political objectives, and personal objectives. Assessing the benefits and costs of lawbreaking requires examining not only the chief executive but also how other actors respond to lawbreaking, including legislatures, courts, civil servants, and market actors. Additional factors, such as the chief executive’s discount rate and risk tolerance, also bear on benefits and costs. Understanding the determinants of executive obedience or disobedience generates both hypotheses for further research and a potential reform agenda for those worried about executive lawbreaking.

title: Who Runs Interest Groups? A Latent Profile Analysis of Education Interest Group Leaders in Norway
abstract: ABSTRACT Leadership is a key component of how interest groups ensure representation and engage in policymaking within corporatist governance systems. This article examines the profiles of education interest group leaders in Norway and their implications for organizational policy capacity. Building on theoretical expectations that organizations with different types of represented interests in the education system draw on distinct combinations of administrative, representative, and sector‑specific experience, the study anticipates variation in leadership profiles across types of interest represented. Drawing on biographical data for 267 elected and employed leaders across 13 major organizations, the study uses Latent Profile Analysis to identify two distinct experience‑based profiles. Veteran Leaders are established figures with extensive administrative and advocacy experience, while Emerging Leaders are early‑ to mid‑career actors with shorter organizational tenures and closer ties to their constituencies. These profiles are shaped not by age or education but by accumulated functional experience across administrative, representative, and domain‑specific roles. The findings show that leaders bring different combinations of analytical, political, and managerial resources to their organizations, reflecting varied experiential foundations on which policy capacity can develop. By linking leadership composition to multiple dimensions of organizational capacity, the study advances understanding of the micro‑foundations of policy capacity and demonstrates how leaders' functional experiences shape the human resources available to interest groups operating within Scandinavian governance systems.

title: Monetary Policy Invariance, Hysteresis, and Optimal Inflation
abstract: Abstract Standard New Keynesian (NK) models feature an optimal inflation target well below 2%, limited welfare losses from business cycle fluctuations and long-term monetary neutrality. We develop an NK framework with endogenous productivity and downward nominal wage rigidity (DNWR) which challenges these results. The interaction between endogenous growth and DNWR generates asymmetric hysteresis effects on unemployment and R&D. As a consequence, the model features a nonvertical long-run Phillips curve and a trade-off between price distortions and output hysteresis that changes the welfare-maximizing inflation rate to above 2%. Deviations from the optimal target carry welfare costs multiple times those in traditional NK models. Taylor rules that respond to the unemployment rate address more effectively the asymmetric hysteresis in our model. Results are robust to the inclusion of the effective lower bound on interest rates.

title: The long-term effects of teachers’ gender stereotypes on labor outcomes
Income Inequality, Household Consumption and Status Competition in Germany*
Multi-layer network analysis of deliberation in an online discussion platform: The case of Reddit
abstract: This paper proposes a novel multi-layer network model to study deliberation in online discussion platforms. The model comprises two layers: a discussion layer, which represents as a hierarchical tree the comment-to-comment replies within a given post, and an actor layer, which represents the actor-to-actor reply interactions. The interlayer links represent user-comment ownership. We use this network model to extend González-Bailón et al. (2010)’s foundational network analysis of argumentation and representation in discussion, by proposing two network metrics to measure the potential for deliberation in discussion threads. We also propose a new approach for identifying the boundaries that determine whether a given post is identified as deliberative, and for comparing the level of deliberation of collections of posts. We apply our new approach to a large Reddit dataset containing posts from 72 subreddits focused on different topics and demonstrate that our new metrics have construct validity in that observed differences in measured deliberation across categories of subreddits can be explained by the topics and purpose of the subreddits. While we find that some political subreddits exhibit high levels of deliberation thus indicating that online political talk can meet the prerequisites for deliberation, the level of deliberation in regional and sports subreddits was even higher. Analysis of the actor layer shows correlations between the deliberation measured on the discussion layer, and classical network metrics of the actor layer including degree distribution, assortativity, and the global clustering coefficient. These correlations reveal important insights into how the aggregate behaviour of users is related to deliberation.

title: Temporal and Environmental Influences on the Survival of Escherichia coli in Poultry Litter‐Based Soil Amendments in Georgia Sweet Onion Production Systems
abstract: ABSTRACT Previous studies have shown that pathogen survival in the biological soil amendments of animal origin (BSAAO) is mediated by meteorological conditions. Hence, a 2‐year field study was conducted in Georgia with four soil amendment treatments (heat‐treated poultry pellets, HTPPs; composted poultry litter, PL; unamended, UN) inoculated with Escherichia coli TVS 353 (a surrogate for Salmonella enterica ) and negative control plots (unamended, non‐inoculated). Additionally, 14‐day‐old sweet onion bulbs were transplanted into plots managed by HTPP (O‐HTPP), harvested, and left to cure for 14 days in the field. A linear‐mixed‐effect model (LME) was fitted to E. coli population data enumerated from the soil samples collected at specified intervals over 161 days from three replicate plots amended with different soil amendment treatments during both years of the study. Amendment type (UN, PL, HTPP, O‐HTPP) and weather factors (cumulative rainfall (cmrain 2 ), average air temperature (at60 12 ), relative humidity (RH 12 ), soil temperature (ast 12 ) for 2 days before sampling, and wind speed 1 day before sampling (W 1 )) were the predictors for the LME models developed. Significant weather predictors that affected the survival of E. coli across soil amendment treatment plots were RH 12 (+0.35) (Year 1); W 1 (−0.77), at60 12 (−1.66), and ast 12 (+1.57) (Year 2). For plots with and without onions, W 1 (+0.69) (Year 1); at60 12 (−0.92), ast 12 (+1.35), cmrain 2 (+0.37), and W 1 (−0.36) (Year 2) were significant. All coefficient values represent the estimated change in log 10 CFU or Most Probable Number (MPN)/g associated with a one‐unit increase in the respective weather predictor, as estimated by the LME model ( p ≤ 0.05).

title: Risk Characterization for a Multi‐Pathway Quantitative Risk Assessment Model: A Case Study on Extended‐Spectrum Beta‐Lactamas Producing E. coli Spread From Broiler Production
Branding the invisible: Big Tech, naming submarine cables, and the politics of infrastructure (in)visibility
abstract: Submarine cables have historically been invisible: buried, technical and obscured by conventions such as security and language including naming practises that prioritised function over storytelling. However, as Big Tech companies like Google have emerged as major cable investors, increasingly shifting from consortium to sole or private ownership, they have disrupted the cable industry in many ways. This paper demonstrates this disruption through the naming practises adopted by Google for its privately-owned cables. It argues that names are not neutral descriptors but tools that selectively make infrastructure visible and culturally significant which transforms cables from technical objects to cultural products. This allows for cables to be branded and marketed – in the case of Google, as part of a unified brand story. Through storytelling potentials embedded within names (including gender, inclusion, indigenous references), Google signals its progressive credentials and tells a story that connects its different product and services. Thus, nomenclature allows for the company to imbue infrastructure with values while obscuring risks and impact of Google’s cable ownership. Drawing on postcolonial perspectives, infrastructure studies, marketing communication, and political economy of communication, this paper examines how language shapes perception of submarine cables including its ownership, control, risks, power, and public relations.

title: ‘Smart court’ and digital judicialism in China
abstract: How has digital technology been applied to the operation of courts and dispute resolution in authoritarian regimes? Drawing on ethnographic research on the construction of the ‘smart court’ in China, this article explores the impact of digital technology on the judicial system and dispute resolution through the prototypical cases of the ‘shared court’ and the ‘One Network of Courts Nationwide’, which operate, respectively, outside and inside the courts. The article reveals that, unlike in democratic countries, where digital technology is used in a relatively more conservative and limited way, digital technology has been used by the Chinese Communist Party to strengthen state control, monitor society, and maintain political stability, thus giving rise to digital judicialism. The study of digital judicialism shows that while digital technology has certainly improved the efficiency of social dispute resolution to some extent, it has been reduced to a toolkit for the government to recentralize political power and guard against political risks. The findings compel researchers to reassess the role of digital technology in facilitating the resolution of disputes because it can undermine judicial independence and the development of the rule of law under authoritarianism.

title: Women’s Representation Gaps in Korean Municipalities: Workforce Presence, Managerial Authority, and Appointed Committee Participation
abstract: Women’s representation in government is often assessed with a single indicator, obscuring where representational gaps emerge. This article examines women’s representation in Korean municipalities across three institutional sites: workforce presence, managerial authority, and appointed committee participation. Using a balanced 2018 to 2024 panel of 226 municipalities, it compares women’s representation across these locations and evaluates how closely they align within the same local governments. The analysis shows that women’s representation increased across all three sites, but unevenly. The most persistent shortfall appears between workforce presence and managerial authority: municipalities with larger female workforce shares also tend to have larger female managerial shares, but managerial parity remains rare. Appointed committee participation occupies a different position. It is generally more gender-balanced than managerial hierarchy, yet it appears more closely tied to monitored gender-balance benchmarks than to the gender composition of the municipal workforce. Fiscal self-reliance is examined as a contextual municipal characteristic, and it does not account for the main authority gap once basic municipal characteristics are introduced. The findings show that single-indicator accounts can overstate women’s organizational inclusion and that managerial authority remains the main site of representational slippage in local government.

title: The hollowing of knowledge institutions: Why law and science are impeded together in the second Trump administration
abstract: A conversation has begun in these pages about what the second Trump administration is doing to public administration. This contribution turns to the institutions that make accountability possible. An agency is answerable because something outside its own will holds it to a standard it does not set. Law and science supply such standards: law binds what a government may do, science what it may credibly claim. They are knowledge institutions, and accountability is what they produce. Trump 2.0 does not abolish them but hollows them, preserving their form while severing their function. The result is an administrative state that acts while answering to nothing outside executive will.

title: Generative Spaces: Collaboration, Learning and Innovation in a Regulatory Sandbox
journal_name: Journal of Public Administration Research and Theory

title: Citizens' Expectations vs. Recruitment Signals: Are Public Administrations Trying to Attract the Ideal Public Servant?
abstract: ABSTRACT Job advertisements play a crucial role in attracting applicants, yet little is known about how closely they reflect the values citizens expect from public servants. Drawing on signaling theory and prior research on citizens' normative expectations of ideal public servants, this study employs a large language model to analyze 1825 job advertisements from health and transportation departments across seven U.S. states. Compared to the values citizens associate with ideal public servants in previous research, job advertisements predominantly emphasize values, such as expertise and dedication, while undersignaling relational values like serviceability, responsiveness, and honesty. Our findings suggest a misalignment between the values signaled in recruitment practices and those citizens associate with the ideal public servant. By adopting a citizen‐driven perspective, this study prompts scholars and public managers to question recruitment practices that may underemphasize values citizens prioritize in public servants, potentially limiting public administrations' ability to attract qualified candidates.

title: The Right‐Wing Idea Factory: From Traditionalism to Trumpism. By Donald F.Kettl, New York: Oxford University Press, 2026. 248 pp. (hardback). ISBN: 978‐0‐19‐777829‐6
Artificial Intelligence in Policing and Perceived Legitimacy: Does Gender Representation Make a Difference?
abstract: ABSTRACT As artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly transforms public administration, understanding its impact on perceived legitimacy becomes paramount, particularly, in high‐stakes areas such as policing. While existing research offers mixed evidence on whether government AI use enhances or undermines citizens' perceptions of fairness and trust, the conditions moderating these effects remain underexplored. Drawing on representative bureaucracy theory, this study uses a survey experiment to investigate how gender representation moderates the effect of AI use on citizens' perceived fairness and trust in domestic violence units (DVUs). Results show that female representation positively moderates the legitimacy impact of a DVU's AI use; whereas AI use decreases female respondents' perceived fairness and trust in male‐dominated DVUs, these negative effects disappear in female‐dominated DVUs. Our findings identify representation as a key context shaping citizens' responses to government AI use, extending representative bureaucracy theory by demonstrating its indirect symbolic effects.

title: Policymaking in a multilevel setting: perverse effects on regulating gambling
abstract: This article examines how multilevel policymaking influences strategic public management. Multilevel governance arrangements are nowadays a recurrent feature in the public sector; the ability of public authorities to design and implement coherent and effective frameworks is affected by the interaction across multiple levels of government. The research was carried out through a case study focusing on gambling regulation in the Friuli Venezia Giulia Region in Italy. Data have been gathered combining the analysis of documents, interviews and surveys within a few mixed-method research projects (2018–2024). By appreciating gambling policy as a legitimacy-driven and institutionally embedded field, the research allows to see beyond well-known implementation challenges of multilevel policymaking. It shows how incoherent policies and stalemate are not necessarily the result of policy failures but could be due to deliberate decoupling strategic responses. Moreover, the study contributes novel insights on how decoupling operates across governance levels and in multiple directions.

title: Representational lock-in and the depoliticization of seismic risk in Turkish earthquake governance since 1999
abstract: This article examines how seismic risk has been problematized in Turkish earthquake governance since the 1999 Marmara disaster. Drawing on Carol Bacchi’s ‘What’s the Problem Represented to Be?’ framework, it introduces representational lock-in: the self-reinforcing dynamic by which a dominant technical problem representation generates institutional forms that entrench it across governance cycles, foreclosing alternatives through structural rather than discursive means. Attributing seismic risk to structural deficiency and regulatory non-compliance, this representation renders unproblematizable the conditions producing urban vulnerability: construction-sector capital accumulation, the imar affı (construction amnesty) regime, and informal urbanism. Reading Laws 4708, 5902 and 6306 as successive stages of lock-in, and the 2023 Kahramanmaraş earthquakes as a moment of crisis, it shows that the inadequacy of Turkish earthquake governance is not a story of technical failure but of a problem representation whose reproduction is structurally guaranteed at the level of problem constitution.

title: Attributes, abstractions, and combinations: a new taxonomy for studying how parties invoke social groups
abstract: Research increasingly examines which social groups political actors refer to. Yet, existing approaches typically inherit classifications shaped by demand-side perspectives or conflate how groups are defined with how they are framed. We propose a novel, attribute-centered taxonomy of social group references that classifies groups by the attributes political actors invoke, organizes these attributes along nested levels of abstraction, and captures attribute combinations when multiple attributes are invoked within a single reference. To demonstrate the analytical value of our taxonomy, we collect original annotations and develop automated classification methods to quantify the group focus strategies of parties in 36 countries over more than 50 years. Our application underscores that socio-structural, constructivist, and deservingness perspectives on party competition primarily operate at different – though overlapping – analytical levels, and yields substantive insights into how different party families construct and mobilize social groups. Our taxonomy, data, and pre-trained classifiers contribute new resources to facilitate future research on social group references in political discourse.

title: Does perspective-getting reduce bureaucrats’ preferential treatment of mobile EU workers? Experimental evidence from four European countries
abstract: Perspective-getting is a novel anti-discrimination intervention that encourages bureaucrats actively to consider applicants’ viewpoints when performing administrative processing tasks. We evaluate perspective-getting’s effectiveness to reduce bureaucrats’ preferential treatment of certain mobile EU workers which otherwise compromises equal access to social rights under the EU’s Social Europe principles. Using choice-based conjoint survey experiments, we assess the effects of perspective-getting for bureaucrats across four diverse administrative contexts: Denmark, Ireland, Spain, and Switzerland. The results of our Hierarchical Bayes analyses reveal that perspective-getting can decrease some of bureaucrats’ strongest biases in their tendency to preferentially treat individuals’ signalling efforts, for instance via fluent language skills, longer residency, or proven job integration efforts. In addition, the intervention can reduce many country-specific biases regarding clients’ ascriptive traits, such as gender, nationality and age. Overall, results across the four countries suggests that perspective-getting can be a potent tool for promoting more equitable bureaucratic decision-making. At the same time, the mixed strength of the evidence, and some rare cases of increased bias under the treatment, suggest that perspective-getting is most effective when bureaucrats fully engage with the task or when it is combined with other anti-discrimination measures.
