title: The Politics of Policy Change in the European Union's Nature Restoration Regulation: An Integrative Approach
The Problem With Problem Load: Reconceptualizing Load in the Multiple Streams Framework
Who Owns the Landscape? Policy Conflict Over the Proposed Designation of Křivoklátsko as a National Park
abstract: ABSTRACT Nature conservation conflicts increasingly extend beyond ecological objectives to disputes over decision‐making legitimacy, institutional authority, and competing understandings of landscape and expertise. This article examines the conflict over the proposed designation of Křivoklátsko as a national park in the Czech Republic between 2021 and 2025. Drawing on the Policy Conflict Framework (PCF), the study uses a qualitative case‐study design based on 17 interviews, policy documents, legislative materials, and media discourse. Analysis proceeded in two stages: deductive coding organized by the PCF, followed by inductive coding that specified how recurring themes operated in this case. The findings identify four interrelated mechanisms of conflict escalation: epistemic divergence sustained competing standards of credible knowledge; historically rooted distrust conditioned how the proposal was interpreted; early procedural exclusion turned uncertainty into a threat to local control; and venue shifts moved the dispute from expert‐administrative preparation into municipal mobilization and parliamentary politics. Together, these mechanisms reduced willingness to compromise and generated feedback effects, including declining trust in central institutions, consolidation of regional resistance, and increased political salience. The PCF identifies and relates these mechanisms across the policy setting, cognitive and behavioral dynamics, and feedback effects, while the inductive coding specifies their case‐specific operation.

title: The Threshold Effect: Preference Falsification Versus Weak Preferences in Russian War Support
Lobbying together in a crowded, closing space: how democratic backsliding and population densities affect inter-organizational cooperation
abstract: Research on interest group cooperation and coalitions has largely focused on organizational characteristics and issue-specific incentives, leaving underexplored how broader environments shape inter-organizational relationships. This article examines how population dynamics and polity-level change jointly affect cooperation among interest groups. We argue that growing organizational density and democratic backsliding fundamentally alter the costs and benefits of coalition-building, producing both incentives for cooperation and pressures for differentiation. Empirically, we analyze survey data from 428 national-level interest groups operating in Czechia, Hungary, Poland, and Slovenia – four countries that combine dynamic organizational populations with varying degrees of democratic backsliding. Our findings show that perceived increases in organizational density strongly foster inter-organizational cooperation, whereas objective density measures do not. At the same time, closing political opportunity structures and political exclusion suppress policy-oriented cooperation rather than triggering compensatory coalition-building. Oppositional organizations cooperate more frequently overall, but their willingness to cooperate declines as perceived density increases, indicating a tipping point at which identity protection and competition outweigh collective action benefits. The article contributes to interest group and civil society research by linking population ecology and political opportunity structure perspectives and by showing that cooperation under democratic backsliding is contingent, non-linear, and context-dependent.

title: The democratic gap: a staged theory of democratic erosion
abstract: Democratic erosion is often described as a gradual process of institutional decline under a legal façade. Yet we still lack the conceptual and empirical tools to distinguish different forms of erosion itself: democracies that are persistently displaced from consolidation, democracies undergoing systematic institutional dismantling, and democracies beginning to recover. Addressing this gap, this article develops a staged theory of democratic erosion centred on the democratic gap: the distance between a country's observed democratic trajectory and the path of consolidation its prior development had made plausible. The framework distinguishes mild erosion, when shocks, distributive vulnerabilities, and diffusion produce a persistent but reversible gap; severe erosion, when polarization and institutional alignment allow political actors to reproduce and expand that gap through sequenced attacks on constraints; and recovery, when surviving institutional constraints narrow the gap before erosion becomes self-reinforcing. Using country-year data from V-Dem and complementary covariates, the article classifies trajectories through historical and synthetic benchmarks. The results show that mild erosion is associated with systemic diffusion and nonlinear inequality, severe erosion with polarization, and recovery with more benchmark-sensitive institutional configurations. Democratic backsliding is therefore not a single process of decline, but a sequence of interrupted accumulation, internal differentiation, and possible correction.

title: Far right mobilization in hybrid regimes: evidence from Georgia and Ukraine
abstract: How and why does regime type impact far-right mobilization? Most of our knowledge about the far right comes from studies of Western democracies, leaving far-right mobilization in hybrid regimes underexplored and undertheorized. Yet far-right mobilization in hybrid regimes often differs from that in consolidated democracies: First, parties in hybrid regimes are not necessarily vote-seeking, so they prioritize protest over electoral politics. Thus, electoral success may not moderate protest, as it does in democracies. Second, the far right may have more indirect influence in hybrid regimes. Even when far-right parties are electorally weak, their ideas may be absorbed by mainstream parties, giving them agenda-setting power. These arguments have three broad implications. First, the scope conditions of democracy-oriented theories need to be specified before applying them to non-democracies. Second, far-right movements may have less agency in hybrid regimes. And third, the far right may be more detrimental in hybrid regimes than in democracies.

title: The making of strange bedfellows: spatial diffusion in unorthodox coalition building
abstract: Abstract Why do ideologically distant political adversaries sometimes choose to govern together? This article advances research on coalition formation in parliamentary democracies by introducing a diffusion-of-innovation perspective. We argue that cooperation between political archenemies can spread spatially as parties learn from nearby cases. When sister parties in adjacent jurisdictions successfully form such coalitions without electoral punishment or sanction from national leaderships, the normative barriers to similar cooperation are weakened. In this way, unorthodox coalitions become politically imaginable and strategically viable through processes of observation, emulation, and learning. We test this argument in the context of Swedish local government, where an extraordinary transformation has occurred over the past few decades. Historically, cooperation between the Social Democrats and the Moderates – the two dominant rivals for national power – has been virtually unthinkable. Today, however, these former adversaries co-govern in nearly one-fifth of Sweden’s 290 municipalities. This shift in coalition behaviour challenges core expectations in coalition theory, which predict alliances between ideologically proximate parties. Drawing on a unique panel dataset covering eight local election cycles (1994–2022), we employ complementary log-log regression models to test whether exposure to unorthodox coalitions in the surrounding regional environment increases the likelihood of similar coalition formation. The analysis reveals clear evidence of hierarchical regional contagion: Social Democrat–Moderate coalitions are significantly more likely to emerge in administrative regions where similar arrangements existed in the previous term. These findings suggest that coalition formation is a socially embedded process of spatial learning, offering a new account of how political cooperation evolves across space.

title: Pocketbook politics and climate action: How economic strain reduces support for green parties
abstract: Abstract Why do green parties struggle electorally despite overwhelming public support for climate action? While macro-level studies suggest that green party performance is shaped by economic conditions, the micro-level mechanisms driving this relationship remain unclear. This paper investigates whether personal economic strain reduces support for green parties and reshapes climate-related political attitudes. Leveraging rich panel data from Germany (2016–2024), I combine long-term correlational analysis with a difference-in-differences design exploiting the war-related 2022 surge in consumer prices. Voters facing financial hardship consistently evaluate the Greens more negatively and shift their political attention toward inflation and economic growth, while deprioritizing climate protection. However, evidence on vote intentions is mixed. These findings contribute to debates on green party support and the distributive politics of climate action, highlighting the relevance of voters’ pocketbooks and the need for green parties to convincingly address material concerns to ensure electoral success.

title: A complex arc of engagement: Shifting psychological trajectories of international solidarity during sustained geopolitical conflict
Contact as collective action: Positive and negative contact experiences of disadvantaged group members

Reassessing Elitism, Rethinking Democracy Elites and Democracy, by DrochonHugo, Princeton/Oxford: Princeton University Press, 2026, 296 pp.Democratic Elitism: The Founding Myth of American Political Science, by PianoNatascha, Cambridge/London: Harvard University Press, 2025, 256 pp.
The Perils of Improvement: Burke, Slavery, and Colonial Governance in the West Indies
abstract: Edmund Burke’s thoughts on plantation slavery have long been the subject of scholarly attention. Too often, however, discerning Burke’s long-term intention in relation to slavery has taken precedence over examining the specific administrative strategies he proposed for managing enslaved populations in the interim. Seeking to remedy this gap, the article reads Burke’s Sketch for a Negro Code as an exercise in colonial ameliorationism; that is, a reform programme that looked to ameliorate the institution of slavery as a way of strengthening British colonialism in the West Indies and civilising the African coast. Using colonial ameliorationism as an interpretive lens, I argue, allows us to reconstruct a consistent Burkean vision for colonial management in the West Indies, one that survived his vacillations on the question of abolition. It also throws into doubt the common argument that Burke saw imperial governance in negative terms; a matter of taming abuses of power and exercising restraint. In the West Indies, by contrast, Burke’s commitment to ameliorationism led him to embrace a productive form of colonial power aimed at enhancing the physical and mental capacities of the enslaved population through discipline, religious instruction, and the encouragement of biological reproduction. I conclude by showing how Burke’s faith in the improvability of the slave system is vulnerable to his own criticisms of other projects for political reform; namely that a certain guilelessness can blind reformers to the dangers inherent in their projects and reconcile them to what they purport to oppose.

title: Who Marries Whom? The Role of Segregation by Race and Class
abstract: Americans rarely marry outside their race or class group, a pattern with well-documented implications for inequality and intergenerational mobility. Limited exposure may partly explain these low intergroup marriage rates. We instrument for exposure using variation in childhood neighborhoods based on whether other race and class groups had more opposite-sex children of similar age. Exposure increases interclass (high- and low-parent income) marriage but has no detectable effect on interracial (White and Black) marriage. A spatial marriage model predicts that residential segregation—one of many forms of exposure—accounts for more than one-third of marital sorting by class but less than 5 percent by race. (JEL J12, J15, J62, R23)

title: Social Push and the Direction of Innovation
abstract: What are the implications of unequal access to innovation careers for the direction of innovation and inequality? Leveraging novel linked datasets in the United States and Finland, we document that innovators create products more likely to be purchased by consumers like them in terms of gender, socioeconomic status, and age. Homophily exists both within narrow product categories and across industries and has been stable in recent decades. Incorporating this “social push” channel into a growth model, we estimate that unequal access to innovation careers has a large effect on cost of living inequality and long-run growth. (JEL D63, J16, L26, M13, O31, O33, O47)

title: Screening and Segmenting: A Consumer Surplus Perspective
abstract: We analyze consumer surplus when a monopolist can adjust both prices and product qualities across segments, engaging in secondand third-degree price discrimination simultaneously. We characterize the consumer-optimal segmentation and show that it has a striking structure: Consumers with the same value receive the same quality in every segment, though prices differ. Under mild conditions, any segmentation harms consumers if and only if demand is sufficiently more elastic than supply. Hence, potential benefits for consumers depend critically on demand and supply elasticities. These findings have implications for regulatory policy regarding price discrimination and market segmentation. (JEL D42, D83, K21, L12, L15)

title: Fighting for Growth: Labor Scarcity and Technological Progress during the British Industrial Revolution
Taxing Top Wealth: Migration Responses and Their Aggregate Economic Implications
abstract: Using administrative data from Scandinavian countries, we provide evidence on international migration responses to wealth taxes and evaluate their aggregate economic implications. We find significant migration responses among the wealthy: A 1 percentage point increase in the top wealth tax rate decreases the stock of wealthy taxpayers by about 2 percent. A large fraction of the wealthy are business owners, and their businesses are negatively affected by owner out-migration. The aggregate effects are nevertheless modest: The migration responses to a 1 percentage point increase in the top wealth tax rate reduce employment by 0.02 percent, investments by 0.07 percent, and value added by 0.10 percent. (JEL D31, E22, E24, F22, H24, L26, K34)

title: A Model of the Attention Economy: Data, Platforms, and Discovery
abstract: This paper develops a dynamic model of the attention economy featuring two interlinked markets: a product market, where consumers have limited awareness of firms, and an attention market, where platforms attract attention by investing in free services (e.g., social media, streaming, podcasts) and sell targeted ads using data on consumer preferences. The model provides a tractable framework in which platform investment, ad-driven discovery, product demand, and ad revenue are jointly determined. The effects of data and interoperability policies can reverse over time, platform quality may be inefficiently high or low, and the rise of data-rich digital advertising can coincide with a declining ad revenue-to-GDP ratio. (JEL D43, D44, D58, D83, L86, M37)

title: Knowledge Spillovers, Competition, and Individual Careers
abstract: Exposure to better peers in the workplace can influence career trajectories through two opposing channels: positively, via knowledge spillovers, and negatively, through competition for advancement. We disentangle these effects by studying untrained labor market entrants and distinguishing between coworkers in the same occupation with whom they are likely to compete versus those with whom they are unlikely to compete. We find robust evidence of persistent knowledge spillovers but also identify countervailing competition effects of comparable magnitude. Both effects are more pronounced for men than for women. (JEL D83, J16, J24, M53, M54, O33)

title: Truth Elicitation in a Nonstrategic Environment
abstract: A principal decides which party deserves a prize. Only the parties observe the state that determines who is deserving. The principal gives each party a text describing the conditions under which that party deserves the prize and asks each to report the state. The parties are nonstrategic. Each activates a known cheating procedure whose outcome depends on the state and on the text. Implementation is achieved if, whenever the parties disagree, the liar is identified by the “one-way cheating principle”: The truthful party is the unique party who could not have produced his story had the rival's story been true. (JEL D82, D91)

title: Racial Promotion Gaps
abstract: We study racial disparities in promotions in a setting in which promotions are formulaic: the US patent office. Using detailed administrative data that allow us to observe who is eligible for promotion when, we document that Black patent examiners experience delays in promotions they are entitled to, slowing their climb to the top of the career ladder by a year and reducing career earnings by 2.5 percent. Institutional features rule out statistical discrimination with accurate priors. Slow promotions even under Black supervisors argue against taste-based animus. Instead, the patterns fit models of belief-based discrimination. (JEL J15, J41, J71, M12, M51, O34)

title: In sickness and in health: Motivating improved healthcare using holistic patient contracts
Retrieval Failures and Consumption Smoothing: A Field Experiment on Seasonal Poverty
abstract: Abstract People may fail to recall and use information they already know when making decisions. We empirically investigate whether such “retrieval failures” distort consumption-smoothing behavior among Zambian farmers, who derive their income from one annual harvest and spend it over the course of the year. We document that individuals underestimate upcoming spending by 50%, creating scope for undersaving. To improve recall, we randomize an intervention that prompts people to think through their future expenses associatively in categories—without providing any external information or guidance. Treated individuals increase “remembered” expenses by 36%–60%; as predicted by the memory literature, effects are concentrated among small, irregular, and stochastic items. Immediate spending drops and, six weeks after the intervention, treated households hold 15% higher savings. They subsequently enter the hungry season—the final months of the year when consumption typically declines sharply—with one additional month of savings, leading to a flatter spending profile over the year. Households use the increased savings to self-finance additional farm investment, resulting in a 9% increase in the next year’s crop revenue. We replicate the intervention’s effect on beliefs among low-income Americans, suggesting that retrieval failures generalize across settings and populations.

title: The Origin of Risk
abstract: Abstract We propose a tractable model in which risk, at both the micro and macro levels, is endogenous and driven by incentives. In the model, each firm chooses the mean and the variance of its productivity process, as well as how it covaries with the productivity of other firms. Aggregate risk arises when firms select productivity processes that are correlated with one another. The theory predicts that larger firms and those with lower markups are less volatile and less correlated with aggregate productivity. We find support for these predictions in the data. Through their impact on risk-taking decisions, distortions such as taxes and markups can make GDP more volatile in equilibrium. In a calibrated version of the model, removing distortions significantly reduces GDP volatility.

title: Agrarian Origins of Individualism and Collectivism
abstract: Abstract This study examines the influence of agricultural labour intensity on individualism across U.S. counties. We measure historical labour intensity in agriculture by combining data on crop-specific labour requirements with county-level crop mix around 1900. Potential endogeneity in agricultural labour intensity is addressed using climate-induced variation in crop mix. The estimates indicate that a one standard deviation increase in labour intensity is associated with a reduction of 0.2-0.3 standard deviations in individualism (as captured by the share of children with infrequent names). We also document significant changes in individualism over time, in relation to within-county shifts in labour intensity due to mechanisation and the boll weevil shock. Further evidence from contemporary online search queries and social media language suggests that historical labour intensity continues to influence geographic variation in individualism today. Lastly, our decomposition of labour intensity provides insights into the mechanisms underlying this cultural impact.

title: International Migration, Exchange Rate Shocks, and Education Investment
abstract: Abstract International migrants channel resources from abroad, but if they cause the state to reduce public investments back home, they may lead to negative development outcomes. I use Indonesian migrant returnees data and district variations in migration destinations and exchange rate shocks to estimate the effects of foreign income shocks on education investments. Households in higher-shock districts send more children to school, prompting the government to increase public schools. The state also provides other public goods complementing household investments. These responses to shocks are not driven by taxation or elections, but rather by administrative splitting that strengthens accountability channels.

title: Do women comply more than men? Experimental evidence from a general population sample
abstract: Women are typically perceived as more compliant than men; however, the literature provides inconclusive evidence. Using a novel experimental design comprising two complementary experiments, we test this claim in online samples representative of the German adult population. The first experiment (N = 1600) features a probabilistic social dilemma game (PDG) in which participants can increase their individual payoff at the expense of exposing themselves and their group to probabilistic losses. In two treatment conditions, they receive either a recommendation on socially optimal behavior or the same recommendation plus information on weakly non-compliant peer behavior. We find that the recommendation strongly affects behavior, but more so for women than for men. The welfare improvement is substantial. Information on the non-compliant behavior of others erodes compliance with recommendation but does not induce significantly different responses in men and women. In the second experiment (N = 522), we elicit empirical and normative expectations about behavior in the PDG with a behavioral recommendation, in order to study the role of norms in adhering to it. While men and women are expected to hold similar normative beliefs, men are expected to follow the recommendation less often, suggesting that compliance is a (strong) female social norm.

title: Recursive Expected Uncertain Utility
abstract: Gul and Pesendorfer’s expected uncertain utility (EUU) theory describes a decision-maker who assigns probabilities to some events, regards others as unquantifiable, and values a prospect by a probability-weighted average of a utility of the best and worst outcomes it may yield on each quantifiable event. I extend EUU to dynamic settings where information arrives before an act is chosen. Outside subjective expected utility, three natural requirements cannot generally coexist: an act’s value should not depend on how the resolution of uncertainty is described; choices after a signal should depend only on what remains possible; and optimizing at each realization should yield a plan that is optimal in advance. The recursive extension characterized here secures the last two by associating with every signal, ambiguous or not, a unique system of conditional beliefs, while retaining EUU’s treatment of risk and ambiguity. For unambiguous signals it reduces to static EUU; otherwise an act’s value depends on how information is revealed. A tractable subclass accommodates choice patterns, such as Machina’s reflection example, that many ambiguity models cannot.

title: Review of “Privileged Brotherhoods: Becoming Men at Elite All-Boys Schools”
Neighborhood change and Black-White segregation: 2000–2020
abstract: Abstract This study examines the relationship between neighborhood racial change and metropolitan segregation in 2000–2020. The most surprising finding is that the principal source of declining Black-White segregation has not been Black growth in White neighborhoods. Instead, it is a phenomenon that has not been noticed up to now—a substantial Black exodus from Black neighborhoods. The same kinds of neighborhoods where Black newcomers were increasingly concentrated in older, poorer sections of central cities in the 1920–1970 decades are now hollowing out, as residents find new opportunities elsewhere. We show that White exit from predominantly White neighborhoods is also an important source of segregation decline. At the same time, however, many predominantly Black neighborhoods have growing Black populations, pushing segregation upwards. This pattern was described as “succession” in early studies of central cities, but it is now likely to be found in suburban neighborhoods with newer housing, a smaller Black population share, and higher socioeconomic status compared to other Black neighborhoods. These and other findings shed new light on why segregation is declining and also why it is so persistent.

title: From perceived information quality to seeking intent: a PRISM-Informed model for nano-enabled products
abstract: This survey study explores the role of perceived information quality (PIQ) as a key mediating variable in the Planned Risk Information Seeking Model (PRISM), adds benefit perceptions alongside risk perceptions, and tests model relationships in the context of nano-enabled products. Hypotheses were tested using structural equation modeling, and the model showed good fit (χ2 (220) = 423.19, p < 0.001; CFI = 0.95; RMSEA = 0.043). PIQ emerged as a key driver of risk and benefit perceptions. Serial mediation analysis confirmed that PIQ, risk perception, and negative affect jointly accounted for the pathway from perceived seeking control to seeking intent. Notably, risk and benefit perceptions were positively correlated, suggesting that consumers view risks and benefits of nano-enabled products as interconnected. Contrary to PRISM expectations, perceived seeking control was negatively associated with knowledge insufficiency, suggesting that confident seekers may perceive smaller knowledge gaps in this context. The findings highlight the central role of PIQ in linking cognitive control to information-seeking behavior, and underscore the importance of transparent, high-quality communication in fostering informed consumer engagement and responsible adoption of nano-enabled products.

title: To Settle or Not to Settle: Defending Firm Reputation in Litigation Response
abstract: Litigation can pose significant threats to a firm’s competitive advantage, requiring firms to respond strategically, particularly in deciding whether to settle. While prior research on litigation responses has primarily emphasized legal and economic drivers, it has paid limited attention to reputational considerations, offering an incomplete account of settlement decisions. Drawing on the theoretical mechanism of stakeholders’ situational expectations of the firm, we propose and show that a firm’s reputation for innovation is associated with a lower likelihood of settlement in patent litigation. We further find that this relationship is contingent on industry-level innovation intensity and plaintiff type. By examining how reputation shapes litigation responses, we make several important contributions to research on reputation and litigation.

title: Inoculating against fatalistic beliefs: a comparative test of narrative and non-narrative strategies
Managing Hydro-dependence and Risk: Hong Kong’s Water Insurance Policy, 1967–1982
abstract: Abstract Using archival and unofficial sources, this article examines how political calculations, economic considerations, local consumption patterns and international dynamics shaped the colonial administration’s water governance strategies in Hong Kong. It focuses on how the 1967 water emergency prompted the colonial government to recalibrate its approach, from a policy of manageable dependency to one of risk aversion. After 1967, an “insurance policy” ensuring a “basic ration” was pursued. This led to the construction of the Lok On Pai desalination plant. The article then traces developments from 1976 to 1982, when Hong Kong gradually moved to a regionally integrated strategy, driven not only by improved Sino-British relations but also by economic considerations, growing public intolerance of water rationing and the Middle East oil crisis. By 1982, Hong Kong’s water insurance policy had officially ended; Chinese water was classified as “reliable.” By exploring these understudied developments and factors, the article contributes to the histories of water management, colonial Hong Kong and China.

title: Hindered From Making a Difference: How Increasing Organizational Constraints Undermine Public Servants' Perceptions of Prosocial Impact and Why It Matters
abstract: ABSTRACT Public servants often work under organizational constraints that hinder how they experience and carry out their work. Drawing on conservation of resources theory, this research examines how changes in these constraints affect public servants' perceptions that their work benefits others and, in turn, their well‐being and withdrawal behavior. Using data from two longitudinal studies conducted in the United States and France, the findings show that increases in organizational constraints are associated with declines in perceived prosocial impact, which in turn predict lower well‐being and greater withdrawal over time. These results identify perceived prosocial impact as a key psychological resource that links changing work conditions to employee functioning. By emphasizing the dynamic nature of organizational constraints, this study advances the understanding of how evolving administrative conditions can weaken the psychological foundations that sustain meaningful and effective public service.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Punctuated Equilibrium: Shaping Government Attention in the Digital Age
abstract: ABSTRACT How do government attention and policy agendas shift when information constraints are relaxed through technological advancement? Punctuated equilibrium theory links agenda‐setting dynamics to governments' limited information‐processing capabilities, yet we know little about whether and how technology improvement such as artificial intelligence (AI) influences policy agendas. This article proposes a conditional digital punctuation framework to specify the conditions under which technological advancements drive agenda shifts. Using China's implementation of AI initiatives as a quasi‐natural experiment, we find that government attention exhibits a punctuated pattern. AI increases technology‐focused attention, signaling incremental changes, while having minimal impact on general government attention. This selective impact stems from AI's asymmetric effects on information processing. Specifically, AI significantly increases the procurement‐based indicator of information quantity, which is associated with greater attention to technology sectors; however, no significant change is observed in the corresponding indicator of information quality, consistent with its limited impact on general government attention.

title: Reply to Kettl: Great Workplaces, Public Employee Legitimacy and the Fourth Way
abstract: ABSTRACT In Public Administration and the Crisis of American Democracy, Don Kettl asks why some federal agencies are great places to work while others are not, pointing to the persistent gap between NASA and the Department of Homeland Security. This essay argues that the answer may turn on how the legitimate role of public employees in democratic governance is construed. Drawing on three interpretive frames—bureaucracy, democracy, and pragmatism—it examines 2024 employee survey responses at NASA and DHS that map onto these frames. DHS appears dominated by the bureaucracy frame, positioning employees as implementers whose voice is risky and expertise underused. NASA blends all three frames, treating employees as contributors, stewards, and problem solvers. These frames offer a partial explanation for Kettl's puzzle and a conceptual tool for his “fourth way”: great government workplaces are built when public servants are recognized as legitimate contributors to democratic governance, not just cogs in a bureaucratic wheel.

title: Interpretive leadership skill as the meaning-making leadership competency in public service organizations: content, construct, and criterion validity
abstract: This research examines the conceptualization and measurement of interpretive leadership skill (ILS) in public service organizations. ILS is conceptualized as an individual leadership competency for meaning-making whose function is interactive: the leader’s capacity to read the working context, build shared understandings that promote coherent action for the organization, and revise those understandings as conditions change. This research reports three studies using two large-scale samples to validate the psychometric and predictive properties of ILS in the public service logic. Study 1 develops and validates a multidimensional measure of ILS and demonstrates its content validity. Study 2 establishes construct validity by situating ILS within a three-level model of leader development. Study 3 demonstrates criterion validity by showing ILS’s predictive property on organizational public service performance. Together, these studies validate ILS as the meaning-making competency of public service leaders and provide implications for leadership theory and practice across public and non-profit organizations.

title: From reform to reality: governance mechanisms and social capital development in mandated healthcare networks
abstract: Mandated healthcare networks are introduced to achieve reform objectives through collaboration, yet imposed arrangements may not generate the social capital needed for collective action. We examine how governance mechanisms activate key sources of social capital (opportunity, ability, motivation) and shape its subsequent development. Using a longitudinal case study of a mandated hospital network governed by a Network Administrative Organization (NAO), we analyse 55 interviews along with documentary data. We find that while the NAO expanded opportunities for social capital development through network governance mechanisms, these were pseudo-opportunities that failed to enhance the ability and motivation of network members to collaborate. We contribute to theory by explaining how imposed governance can simultaneously appear to provide a key condition for social capital (interaction opportunities) and nevertheless inhibit successful collective action and generate disenchantment. The study highlights the need to distinguish between technical integration and meaningful collaboration in the implementation of governance mechanisms.

title: Partnering with the police: Goal alignment and divergence across three public–private partnerships in policing
abstract: IMPACTMany police services are exploring public–private partnerships (PPPs) to achieve their goals. This research reveals tensions not just between public and private partners, but also between partners with security as a primary or ancillary goal. The involvement of this latter type of partner might also reflect victimhood or facilitation of the phenomenon that the PPP addresses. When divergent interests are not sufficiently managed, value conflict may occur or partnerships may drift away from public aims. Our findings underscore the importance of goal clarity and alignment in PPPs dealing with essentially contested public services such as policing. In addition to the public–private divide, it is useful to focus efforts on potential divergence between organizations with primary and secondary goal orientations towards the public service of policing. In the PPPs under study, a combination of formal steering towards explicit goals through contracts and relational network management helped the PPPs to stay largely on course.

title: Does governance shape local financial condition? Evidence from Brazilian municipalities
abstract: IMPACTUsing a national panel of all 5,570 Brazilian municipalities from 2018 to 2023, this study finds that stronger managerial governance, measured through planning capacity, staffing structure, and transparency, is associated with more favourable fiscal profiles across three dimensions: strongly for indebtedness, and to a lesser degree for current savings and liquidity. Prior research on municipal financial condition has concentrated on mayoral characteristics or structural fiscal variables. The authors show that organizational capacity is a measurable, distinct correlate of local fiscal health. This finding will be of interest to public sector managers, treasury officials, audit bodies, and policy-makers in decentralized systems.
authors: Edzana Roberta Ferreira da Cunha Vieira Lucena

title: Institutionalizing mathematical modelling for public health decision-making: moving from ad hoc collaboration to a sustainable system in Thailand
Universal entitlement, unequal provision: childcare in segregated German cities
abstract: Abstract One mechanism driving persistent inequalities in childcare provision, despite rising investments and a substantial expansion of childcare facilities, may consist in the locational choices of providers, who eschew poorer neighbourhoods. Our analysis is the first to combine georeferenced data on child daycare centres with socio-demographic information from fifty-two German cities and 2,607 neighbourhoods to test this proposition. The study explores the correlation between local access to daycare centres and the proportion of social benefit recipients in the respective neighbourhoods. Our results indicate that neighbourhoods with greater socio-demographic difficulties in German cities have fewer daycare centres. This is exclusively due to the expansion of (publicly subsidised) daycare centres run by non-profit providers in neighbourhoods that are socio-economically better off. While the subsidiary principle in German social law explains the pivotal role of non-profit providers, municipalities should compensate for unequal childcare provision; however, such compensatory provision remains weak. Overall, the unequal spatial provision may contribute to the socially stratified utilisation of childcare in Germany, despite extensive public funding.

title: No constituency for universal basic income? Evidence from seven Latin American countries
abstract: Abstract Despite the expansion of non-contributory cash transfer programmes in Latin America – especially during the COVID-19 pandemic – public support for a universal basic income (UBI) remains remarkably low. Using original survey data from seven countries, we find that fewer than 10 per cent of respondents support both the universality and unconditionality that define UBI. Notably, support for UBI is not significantly shaped by socio-economic status or left-right orientation, and current recipients of targeted transfers are no more likely than others to favour UBI. In contrast, support for targeted programmes – particularly for the extreme poor – is robust and explained by income, education and ideology, consistent with classic self-interest models. These findings challenge the view that targeted programmes may serve as stepping stones toward universalist policies. Rather, they suggest that such programmes may consolidate a political logic of deservingness that constrains broader redistributive ambitions.

title: Unpacking variation in network management: How organizational and implementation context factors shape managerial activity in collaborative policy delivery
abstract: Debates over the effectiveness of policy implementation networks and the role of network management have attracted considerable scholarly attention in recent decades. Research has focused on the tasks network managers perform, proposing that network management improves network performance. This study takes a step back by investigating why some network managers intervene in their networks more intensively than others, addressing an important research gap. Using data from 13 Swiss smoking prevention networks, this article bridges the research on policy implementation and public management by analyzing how organizational features and implementation context-related factors jointly influence managerial action within collaborative policy delivery networks. Rather than assuming that managerial activity is driven by single factors, this paper employs Qualitative Comparative Analysis (QCA) alongside in-depth case study evidence to identify combinations of factors that shape the level of managerial activity. The study suggests that high-intensity network management in mandated networks is shaped by the interplay of network managers’ organizational affiliation (public vs. non-state), the presence or absence of goal conflicts, the level of resources available for network management, and the existence of ties within the network. It finds that NGO-affiliated network managers are more likely to apply high-intensity network management – either proactively under favorable conditions or reactively when facing challenges – while public managers typically engage less due to structural constraints or managerial preferences. By conceptualizing network management as a phenomenon situated at the intersection of organizational structure and implementation context, this study offers a more integrated understanding of how public service delivery is coordinated in complex governance settings.

title: The Representation Trap: How Minority Power Shapes Electoral Politics in India
abstract: Liberal democracy requires that minority groups be represented in politics. This article argues that minority representation can also generate headwinds for political inclusion by dividing the minority group and consolidating the dominant group. I study the combination of these processes, termed the representation trap, through a mixed-methods examination of Muslims in India. Analyses of election results and an original survey of Hindu and Muslim voters show that electing a Muslim representative divides Muslim votes across an increased share of coethnic candidates and consolidates Hindu votes for the majoritarian party in the subsequent election. Qualitative evidence and a vignette experiment trace these patterns to two mechanisms: sub-identity activation among Muslims and super-ordinate identity mobilization among Hindus. By showing how representation restructures elite and voter behavior within both minority and dominant groups, the article highlights the dynamic nature of ethnic politics and complicates the view of minorities as politically unified.

title: The autocratization plateau? The new phase of democratic decline
abstract: Despite broad consensus that autocratization has dominated regime change in recent years, little attention has been paid to this process stabilizes. This article documents a turning point after 2019. Autocratization has stopped spreading to new countries at the same rate, even as global democratic decline persists. Using V-Dem data (2000–2025), this article identifies an autocratization plateau marked by two features: spatial saturation, with the number of affected countries stabilizing at ∼45, and compositional change, with new episodes falling to 15.6% while ongoing ones reach 84.4%. The article theorizes this shift through an extensive-intensive framework borrowed from economic growth theory, and tests two candidate mechanisms: pool saturation and declining authoritarian diffusion. Pool saturation emerges as the dominant driver, while declining authoritarian diffusion operates as an independent complementary mechanism. Regional patterns diverge substantially, with Western democracies and Central Asia now emerging as new epicentres while Latin America, East Asia, and Sub-Saharan Africa have plateaued. These findings challenge the dominant narrative of autocratization as a continuously deepening and spreading phenomenon, and suggest that democracy support strategies should shift from prevention towards proactive reversal of ongoing episodes.

title: Accountability without transformation: ruling-family prosecutions in post-authoritarian African transitions
abstract: Ruling families occupy central positions within authoritarian regimes, yet their treatment after leadership transitions reveals deeper tensions about the purpose of accountability. Why does punitive accountability against ruling families take different institutional forms across post-authoritarian transitions? This article examines six African cases – Angola, Gabon, Senegal, Egypt, Tunisia, and The Gambia – through structured, focused comparison and within-case analysis. Punitive accountability emerges when leadership rupture dissolves protection networks and successor elites perceive legal action as politically advantageous. Three pathways emerge – custodial, criminal in absentia, and financial/administrative – sorted principally by jurisdictional reach, with elite fragmentation and international leverage operating as interacting constraints. Across these cases, accountability is politically initiated but institutionally variable, with its consequences ranging in degree between elite reconfiguration and broader institutional transformation, although the balance falls toward the former. Legal action against ruling families can therefore accompany both democratic consolidation and authoritarian renewal, with its institutional effects shaped by legal opportunity, elite politics, and international constraints.

title: Breaching the firewall: A natural experiment on how unravelling the cordon sanitaire affects voters’ attitudes
Contestation of International Organizations: Patterns, Drivers, and Responses
abstract: Abstract The contestation of international organizations (IOs) over past decades has inspired a rich research program. This essay takes stock of progress by reviewing key findings in existing scholarship and identifying critical areas for future study. We propose a typology that distinguishes between internal contestation, which criticizes the institutions or policies of an IO with the aim of reform, and external contestation, which challenges an IO’s foundational principles and very existence. Building on this conceptual distinction, we review the most important findings of existing research on three key themes: patterns of contestation, drivers of contestation, and responses to contestation. We also argue that this conceptualization helps us better understand the changing nature of contestation: while criticism of how IOs function has long been a staple of world politics, it recently appears to have shifted toward a deeper form involving more fundamental questioning of IOs themselves. We conclude by highlighting the need for dynamic theories and improved measurements to explain when and how IO contestation shifts from internal criticism to external rejection, and by outlining a forward-looking research agenda on organizational robustness, hegemonic contestation, and the relationship between IO contestation and the broader contestation of global governance.

title: Unrest, Shifting Power, and Death-Watch War
abstract: Abstract Domestic unrest often creates problems of both shifting power and shifting preferences. We analyze a model in which a foreign state considers a “death-watch” attack against a domestic state temporarily weakened by unrest in which (1) two polarized factions compete for the power to set policy in the future and (2) the foreign state’s favored faction may support an invasion. Military success allows the foreign state to seize policy control, but defeat may hasten the rise of its disfavored faction when the favored faction links the outcomes of the two conflicts by bandwagoning with the attacker. In equilibrium, decisions to attack and bandwagon depend on the interaction of shifting power and shifting preferences. We show first that temporary weakness causes war, but only when the favored faction is unlikely to survive unrest. Second, increasing factional polarization can encourage or discourage foreign attack and local bandwagoning, conditional on how domestic preferences are shifting. Third, extensions show that (1) death-watch attacks are possible at any distribution of power; (2) the threat of attack may not be sufficient to deter domestic unrest; and (3) attack may be profitable even when alternative options of aiding a favored faction are available. We also use the model to explain why similar episodes of unrest in Ukraine prompted Russian invasion in 2014 but not 2004.

title: Debate and Legislative Productivity in US State Legislatures
Emissions abatement under a rate-based emissions trading system: facility-level evidence from China
abstract: As the world’s largest emissions trading system (ETS) by covered emissions, China’s national ETS uses an unconventional rate-based design to allocate allowances, which inherently creates “winners” (surplus units) and “losers” (deficit units). Utilizing a unique facility-level dataset and a continuous difference-in-differences framework, we show that the national ETS reduces CO 2 emissions from regulated power units by 2.3 %. Crucially, this abatement is mainly driven by reallocating output from deficit to surplus units instead of within-unit efficiency gains or fuel switching. Moreover, such output substitution is more pronounced among units within the same regional grids or parent companies. This policy also delivers substantial co-benefits by reducing air pollution from regulated plants. Our findings contribute ex- post evidence on the effectiveness of rate-based ETSs and offer insights for policymakers seeking to mitigate emissions on a broad scale while maintaining production levels.

title: Place-Based Policies: A Path to Opportunity or a Mark of Stigma for Targeted Neighborhoods?
abstract: Abstract In France, place-based policies channel public subsidies to low-income urban zones labeled ”priority” neighborhoods. Yet, such policies may backfire by stigmatizing the targeted areas. This paper exploits a quasi-experimental discontinuity created by a reform that redrew the subsidy map using a local poverty cutoff to evaluate impacts on school outcomes, population sorting, and urban segregation across labeled and unlabeled neighborhoods. Using a difference-in-differences design, we show that public middle schools in newly designated neighborhoods experienced a persistent decline in enrollment relative to schools in unlabeled areas just above the cutoff. This territorial stigma, driven by school avoidance across all socioeconomic groups, redirected pupils to public schools in unlabeled areas and, among wealthier families, to private schools. Policy designation also depressed housing prices and triggered reverse gentrification, while educational support proved insufficient to offset rising urban segregation. Crucially, the stigma persisted even after neighborhoods lost their subsidized status, leading to sustained declines in academic achievement due to both reputational damage and subsidy withdrawal.
journal_name: Journal of the European Economic Association

title: Premarital migration and marriage payments: Evidence from Indonesian men
abstract: While bride price customs are widespread in many developing countries, little is known about their consequences on men’s decisions. In this paper, we exploit a quasi-natural experiment of a school-building program in Indonesia (INPRES) to investigate the relationship between marriage norms and the internal migrations of young men. Combining anthropological, administrative, and individual-based datasets, we implement a triple-difference approach. We show that the less advantaged young men, who have fewer resources to cope with rising marriage costs, are more likely to migrate out of their district of origin when the women they are expected to marry benefit from the program. These findings suggest that the interaction between marital norms and policies can result in unintended consequences, shaping major economic decisions such as premarital migration.

title: Disparate Treatment of the Irish in 19th Century English Courtrooms
abstract: This paper studies how and why anti-Irish sentiment in 19th century England spills over onto jury decisions at London’s Old Bailey Central Criminal Court. We classify the (perceived) ethnicity of courtroom participants according to whether they have distinctly Irish or English surnames based on place of birth in the 1881 census. Irish-named defendants have significantly worse outcomes: juries are 3% more likely to convict Irish-named defendants and 16% less likely to recommend mercy in sentencing. Sentencing gaps are larger for violent crimes and robust to different classifications of surname Irishness, as well as to the inclusion of case and defendant controls. We argue that these findings are unlikely to be driven by correlated unobservable case or trial characteristics (like defense quality). Rather, we provide two pieces of evidence consistent with the gaps being driven by animus towards those perceived to be Irish. First, taking advantage of exogenous variation in expected punishment driven by the abolition of capital punishment, we show that juries react differentially to shifts in extraneous factors when the defendant is Irish- versus English-named. Second, these gaps are not limited to Irish-named defendants but also seen for other courtroom participants – namely Irish-named victims. Finally, we trace out the longer run evolution of these gaps throughout the 1800s: they first emerge during the capital punishment reform period, widen during the mid-century Irish Potato Famine induced migration to London, and thereafter remain primarily stable.

title: TAIL EXPECTILE ESTIMATION IN THE SEMIPARAMETRIC GENERALIZED PARETO MODEL
abstract: Expectiles have received increasing attention as a market risk measure that is both coherent and elicitable. They are defined as a least squares analog to quantiles. Their estimation from heavy-tailed loss data in an extreme value framework is an important and difficult problem, especially when the target tail expectile is beyond the range of the data. This problem has been studied only fairly recently, using solely the Weissman extrapolation method. The competing generalized Pareto approach, which makes efficient use of tail observations by incorporating the location, scale, and shape extreme value parameters into the estimation procedure, has been left untouched, with a corresponding theory completely lacking. In this article, we challenge the dominance of the Weissman device by presenting and developing the theory of two classes of semiparametric Generalized Pareto estimators: the first class relies on direct asymmetric least squares estimation, while the second is based on extreme quantile estimation. Our estimators are found to outperform the best-known Weissman-type estimators for real-valued profit–loss distributions, while staying competitive for nonnegative loss variables. A forecast comparison exercise is also conducted on various sets of financial returns, showing the superiority of the generalized Pareto approach.

title: ESTIMATION OF HETEROGENEOUS PANEL DATA MODELS WITH AN APPLICATION TO PROGRAM EVALUATION
abstract: This article studies panel data models with two-dimensional unobserved slope heterogeneity and interactive fixed effects. We propose a two-step approach to estimate the parameters in the model. We apply the proposed model to estimate heterogeneous treatment effects at both individual and aggregate levels. Monte Carlo simulations show that the proposed estimators perform remarkably well in finite samples in comparison with some existing methods such as the synthetic control ones. We apply our method to study the effect of economic liberalization on economic growth and find a positive and significant aggregate average treatment effect on the treated.

title: When Populism? Consistent and Opportunistic Populist Communication in the 2022 Brazilian Presidential Elections
abstract: When do presidential candidates use populist communication, and does its prevalence vary across policy domains? We address these questions using an original dataset of 11,885 tweets from nine Brazilian presidential candidates during the 2022 elections. Drawing on the ideational approach, we operationalize populist discourse as the co-occurrence of people-centrism and anti-elitism, measured with fine-tuned BERT-based classifiers, and classify policy domains with the Comparative Agendas Project framework. Our findings reveal substantial heterogeneity across candidates, challenging expectations that populist communication uniformly intensifies during campaigns or systematically varies across policy domains according to ideology. Rather than increasing uniformly during the campaign, populist appeals escalate strategically for some candidates as elections approach, while remaining stable for others throughout the electoral year. We propose a typology distinguishing opportunistic from consistent populists. Across policy domains, government operations serve as a baseline facilitating populist framing. Left-wing candidates increase populist rhetoric in labor/employment, consistent with issue ownership expectations, but right-wing candidates reduce populist appeals in their traditionally owned domains of law and crime and civil rights, contrary to expectations. Overall, we show that populism is neither a universal campaign imperative nor a content-neutral communication style, but a flexible discursive frame shaped by candidate strategy, electoral context, and policy content.

title: A Response to Don Kettl's Debate Article on the Future of Public Administration and Democracy
abstract: ABSTRACT This commentary critically engages with Kettl's analysis of the crisis of public administration (PA) scholarship and its relationship with democratic decline. It argues that both phenomena should be understood within broader global developments rather than primarily as problems specific to the United States. While acknowledging the role of governance failures in facilitating autocratization, it questions the claim that autocratization results predominantly from the failures of PA scholarship and practice. Rather, it emphasizes that broader societal phenomena, such as the erosion of societal trust and the power‐consolidating objectives of authoritarian leaders play a key role. Drawing on Hungary's experience, the commentary illustrates how authoritarian governance may perpetuate administrative instability and institutional transformation long after the (perceived) failures of democratic governance have been addressed in the early phase of illiberal transformation. However, it also argues that poor governance and declining policy performance can eventually undermine authoritarian rule, as illustrated by Hungary's 2026 political transformation. The commentary thus highlights the complex and potentially self‐undermining relationship between authoritarianism and public governance.

title: Explaining user-orientation in public service delivery networks: configurations of network structure, process, and context
abstract: This study explores configurations of structural, process, and contextual conditions associated with high user-orientation in public service delivery networks. Drawing on Public Service Logic, we conceptualize user-orientation and connect it with interorganizational network research. We examine six conditions and apply fuzzy-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis to data from sixty networks. We identify five pathways. Across these pathways, collaboration intensity and organizational simplicity consistently emerge, underscoring the importance of process factors alongside structural conditions. Network size clarifies the distinct roles of centralization and density. One pathway combines high centralization and high density with high user-orientation, nuancing prevailing views about their simultaneous presence.

title: How Healthcare Systems Show Change at the Subnational Level: A Typology Study Based on China's Provincial Data (2012–2019)
abstract: ABSTRACT There is a conspicuous literature classifying healthcare systems into different types, yet evidence on how healthcare systems differ regionally within the same country is still scant and scattered. This article aims to fill the gap by creating a typology of healthcare systems in China in terms of financing, provision and access to healthcare. By using provincial‐level data from 2012 and 2019, we conduct a cluster analysis. We find that: (1) healthcare systems differ considerably across provinces, which we categorise into five clusters; (2) with the new medical reform ongoing, some changes in our chosen indicators of the healthcare system were detected, which might imply that improvements have occurred; (3) although some provinces showed some divergence from their original clusters, the composition and number of the identified clusters have largely remained the same over the observed period. Our suggested typology of Chinese subnational healthcare systems adds value to existing research in that it engages with cross‐country comparative studies while adding more nuance to existing analyses in Chinese‐language literature.

title: Bad news for (young) gamers: Using gaming platforms as news sources is more intimately associated with radical belief dispositions than other online spaces
abstract: Abstract This study explores how digital news use among young Europeans links to radical belief dispositions, particularly within gaming platforms and messengers, where socio‐affective dynamics shape engagement with political information. We argue that online groups are an overlooked locus for biased information processing and the normalization of extremist worldviews. The conflation of an increasingly fragmented online news space with the inherently politicized gaming cosmos can relate to amplified problematic worldviews based on shared activity, identity, and reality. Based on a cross‐country survey ( N = 1489; eight European countries), we compare (the use of) gaming, messenger apps, social media, and traditional media for news in terms of how they afford problematic forms of collectivity, particularly in relation to social, cynical, and radical epistemologies. We find a robust correlation between news use and a set of radical belief dispositions, prominently with messenger apps, but even more so in gaming‐related online environments—less so on social media and none with traditional news use. Notably, a mediation analysis suggests that shared meaning‐making exhibits a negative rather than a positive indirect association with radical belief dispositions. We discuss the complex interplay of how individual factors and platform architectures connect with news engagement utilizing a vulnerability‐affordance framework.

title: From identity to caring: A 44‐country examination of the role of global social identifications in concern for global issues
abstract: Abstract Previous research suggests that people who identify with global communities tend to show greater concern for global challenges. Using student samples from 44 countries across different cultural clusters ( N = 13,055), we examined whether (1) three forms of dispositional global social identification (GSI, with all humanity, citizens of the world, and people all over the world) are related to concern for global issues, (2) situational activation of these identifications increases such concern, (3) country‐level traditional and survival values are negatively associated with global concern, and (4) these values moderate the GSI–concern link. Both dispositional and situational GSIs positively predicted global concern. Situational activation showed inconsistent effects, whereas dispositional GSIs demonstrated moderate and consistent associations with global concern across the full sample and most countries. Overall, dispositional forms of GSI appeared more influential than situational ones. Contrary to expectations, traditional values (and survival values—marginally) were positively related to global concern and showed no evidence of moderating GSI–concern associations. Additional analyses showed the indices of GDP per capita, Human Development, Gini, and poverty as robust predictors of global concern. We discuss how these findings refine claims about the universality of global identification outcomes and highlight the importance of socio‐cultural context in shaping such concern.

title: Educational legacies of christian missions: Evidence from the Democratic Republic of the Congo
Optimal Tax under Dispersed and Distorted Beliefs
When NPM Meets Local Politics: Political Economy of Urban Water Supply Reforms in India
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines whether political alignment—defined as elected representatives at different tiers of government belonging to the same political party or coalition—and political competition shape the implementation and performance of a New Public Management (NPM)‐based urban water supply reform in Nagpur, India. We capture reform implementation using status of capital works and performance is evaluated through indicators of financial sustainability—measured by households' willingness to pay (WTP) water tariffs—and water service delivery outcomes. We capture political alignment and political competition by matching municipal election data with a unique household survey and estimate outcomes using multinomial logit and inverse probability weighted regressions. The findings show that political alignment and higher political competition are associated with faster completion of capital works and improved service delivery. However, these gains coexist with lower WTP water tariffs. Thus, NPM‐oriented reforms remain deeply embedded in local political contexts in developing countries with politics simultaneously enabling implementation and service delivery, and constraining financial sustainability.

title: Digital Governance and the Equity Paradox: Evidence From Indonesia's Local Integrated Planning System
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines the relationship between digital governance and social equity through the equity paradox. Drawing on a qualitative case study of Indonesia's nationally mandated Sistem Informasi Pemerintahan Daerah (SIPD) in Konawe Regency, it examines how procedural improvements occur, how equity enters planning, and why procedural gains do not necessarily translate into equity‐oriented outcomes. Evidence from 39 interviews and documents identifies four administrative mechanisms: standardization, procedural control and auditability, coordination, and transparency. Equity‐related needs enter planning through administrative categories, indicators, evidence, and prioritization processes. Yet fragmented information, uneven organizational capacity, compliance‐oriented practices, and institutional constraints limit the consistent recognition and prioritization of differentiated needs. This gap between procedural gains and equity‐oriented prioritization defines the equity paradox. The study shows why procedural improvement alone does not ensure equity‐oriented planning, contributing to digital governance, social equity, and public administration scholarship.

title: How Do Community Stakeholder Groups Shape Local GHG Inventories? Evidence from U.S. Local Governments
abstract: Community stakeholders play a pivotal role in shaping cities’ decisions about whether to measure local GHG emissions. Using survey data collected at two points in time, this study examines how varying levels of support from different types of stakeholder groups influence cities’ decisions to manage their GHG inventories. Notably, we find higher levels of performance measurement activity in cities where support from the public and environmental groups for climate initiatives is perceived as strong, as well as in cities that perceive opposition from business and neighborhood associations. Drawing on public management theories, we offer insights into stakeholder influence in local GHG emission measurement efforts and identify factors driving the advancement of these practices.

title: A Territorial Approach to Transitioning Oil and Gas Producing Regions: Comparative Practices and Prospects for Canada
abstract: Abstract Oil and gas transitions are relatively new and especially difficult because the sector is large, economically central, and deeply embedded in national energy systems. Territorial approaches—grounded in regional political economies, institutions, and community impacts—offer a politically feasible way to begin meaningful oil and gas transitions in Canada's producing regions. Our article first traces the evolution of Canadian oil and gas governance within federal climate architectures and entrenched fossil regionalisms, then draws on comparative case studies of Esbjerg (Denmark), Taranaki (New Zealand), and Aberdeen (Scotland) to show how territorially grounded policies and just transition institutions can help regions move beyond fossil lock‐in. It concludes by distilling cross‐cutting lessons into a governance framework for regionally differentiated transitions in Canadian oil and gas producing regions.

title: Humanitarian Diplomacy From Below: Muhammadiyah in Indonesia's Response to the Rohingya Crisis
abstract: ABSTRACT The protracted Rohingya crisis has exposed the limits of conventional diplomacy in a regional order constrained by sovereignty and non‐interference. Yet humanitarian engagement has continued through societal actors operating alongside formal diplomatic institutions. This article asks how and under what conditions the humanitarian and societal capacities of Muhammadiyah, one of Indonesia's largest Islamic organizations, acquire diplomatic significance in Indonesia's response to the crisis. Drawing on interviews with Muhammadiyah humanitarian actors and Indonesian government officials, triangulated with organizational documents, official materials, and secondary sources, this study examines medical assistance, humanitarian infrastructure, interfaith engagement, state‐society coordination, and transnational resource mobilization. The findings demonstrate that humanitarian activity does not automatically constitute diplomacy. Rather, it crosses the threshold into diplomatic significance when the capacities it generates become connected to relational or institutional channels through which humanitarian and political engagement is conducted. The case highlights how diplomatic practice and capacity can become pluralised without an equivalent redistribution of sovereign diplomatic authority. Conceptualizing this process as humanitarian diplomacy from below, the article shows how autonomous societal capacities can complement state diplomacy while their effects remain consequential but bounded.
