title: When women lead: local political representation and pro-women institutions
abstract: Whether women in office govern differently from men is well documented; whether they govern differently for women is not. The latter is the crux of active representation theory, which expects representatives to act for those they mirror: does electing women change what governments do for women? We investigate the relationship between electing female mayors and councilors and the existence of Pro-Women Institutions across all 5,565 cities of Brazil during four election cycles (2008, 2012, 2016 and 2020). Our results partially support the active representation relationship. While female mayors’ presence increases the likelihood of pro-women institutions, local councilors either do not or are negatively linked to them. Robustness checks through a regression discontinuity design corroborate these findings, and heterogeneous treatment effects on race paint a wider picture about intersectionality. Our findings highlight how female elected representatives might achieve substantial change for their female constituents in local government.

title: Early formations of European youth policy: the role of the Common Assembly of the European Coal and Steel Community (1952–1958)
abstract: This article examines the early formation of youth as an object of political intervention and policy-making within the process of European integration, focusing on the Common Assembly of the European Coal and Steel Community (ECSC) between 1952 and 1958. Drawing on a Foucauldian dispositif perspective and critical policy discourse analysis, the study analyses 61 documents from the Historical Archives of the European Union, including Assembly’s plenary debates and Social Affairs Committee reports. Three interconnected themes emerged from the analysis: the construction of a ‘young Europe’ associated with renewal and institutional legitimacy; the emphasis on education, vocational training, and mobility; and the incorporation of youth-related concerns into broader discussions of labor conditions, health, housing, and social welfare. The findings show that the discourse of a ‘young Europe’ and emerging youth-related interventions formed part of the same political rationalities through which youth gradually developed as a distinct field of institutional concern within the evolving political order of postwar European integration.

title: Do parties and institutions still matter for healthcare? Multi-dimensional partisanship, veto points, and the legislative politics of healthcare
abstract: Whereas classical welfare state literature viewed party politics and institutional veto points as central to health politics, contemporary literature has cast doubt on this claim. We contribute to this debate by testing whether parties and veto institutions matter for healthcare, drawing on a dataset of health reforms introduced by 719 laws across 33 European countries from 1990 to 2019. Our findings show that political partisanship and veto institutions do remain central for health politics. However, their impact varies by the dimension of partisanship and the health policy sub-issue. While economic left-right partisanship of governments predicts privatisation laws, social left-right partisanship predicts laws that introduce patient rights. Veto points hinder the enactment of privatisation legislation; they do not impede the enactment of patient rights legislation. Based on these findings, we draw three theoretical implications. First, government legislative behaviour reflects partisan priorities in healthcare, constituting a key mechanism of party competition. Second, legislative competition on health is structured along multiple partisan dimensions, positional and valence forms, and is defined through health policy sub-issues. Third, institutional veto points constrain legislative outcomes, but their impact is conditional on the partisan context.

title: Towards mission theory: A systematic literature review of its critiques and avenues for progress (2010–2025)
abstract: During the last 15 years, researchers and practitioners alike showed a newfound interest in the potential of ‘mission-oriented’ innovation policy to tackle current societal challenges. In this period, the approach prompted multiple reflections and critiques from orthodox and heterodox scholars alike. However, a structured appraisal of this debate has been missing. Untangling its analytical complexity, this paper presents a systematic literature review of 224 articles and book chapters published between 2010 and 2025 to appraise the state-of-the-art debate within ‘mission theory’. Using the PRISMA Protocol and abductive thematic analysis, the paper identifies 18 themes mapped across two analytical dimensions: positioning (identifying either ‘external’ challenges or ‘internal’ gaps within mission theory); and layering (identifying challenges and gaps based on a ‘foundational’, ‘theoretical’, or ‘empirical’ ground). Building on the findings, the paper reflects on the sociological conditions preventing the progress of mission theory in contemporary research efforts – ultimately calling for greater epistemological reflexivity in the strategies adopted by researchers and practitioners to develop avenues for its further progress.

title: From impact to legitimacy: Communicative responsibility and the governance of research impact
abstract: Universities face growing pressure to make clearer the public value of research, yet documented impact does not automatically translate into public recognition or legitimacy. This paper develops the concept of Communicative Responsibility, the institutional and ethical obligation to communicate research outcomes in ways that are legible, accessible, and resonant beyond specialist assessment contexts. Drawing on responsible research literatures, including Responsible Research and Innovation (RRI) and Responsible Research in Business and Management (RRBM), we argue that communication should be treated as a core component of research governance and legitimacy. Empirically, we use the UK Research Excellence Framework (REF) 2021 Impact Database to examine the communicative strengths and limitations of existing impact evidence. REF impact case studies are not the only way to understand research impact, nor are they primarily written for public audiences. However, they offer a useful proxy for examining how impact might be perceived and how it could be shared more effectively. Using mixed methods, we combine qualitative content analysis of 119 purposively sampled Business and Management cases with quantitative text analysis of all 504 non-redacted cases in the field. Findings show diverse impacts generated through collaboration, interdisciplinarity, and international partnerships, but also substantial variation in communicability. Cases that identify beneficiaries, pathways to change, and accessible dissemination routes are better positioned to reduce the impact-recognition gap. We contribute to theorizing Communicative Responsibility as a governance-relevant extension of responsible research. Our findings have wider implications for how universities communicate impact beyond assessment systems.

title: Correction to “Comparative Politics and the Synthetic Control Method”
abstract: We thank Joseph Francis for pointing out the mislabeling of the per capita GDP variable in the empirical application of Abadie et al. (2015).The article reported GDP in PPP-adjusted 2002 USD, whereas the analysis used GDP in PPP-adjusted current USD; the mislabeling reflects language carried over from an earlier draft. 1 While the change in units does not affect the validity of the analysis, it does alter the interpretation of the results of the empirical application.Specifically, absolute differences in per capita GDP between title: Gender Bias in Bribe Solicitation: Evidence From Firm–State Interactions
abstract: Previous research has shown that women-led businesses are less likely to bribe officials to bypass administrative burdens, assuming that this is because women are less susceptible to corruption. We uncover an additional mechanism that focuses on the beliefs and practices of corrupt officials: bureaucrats underestimate women as entrepreneurs and hence reduce their demand for bribes from women-led enterprises. We confirm these expectations using the World Bank Enterprise Survey on a sample of 109,929 firms in 149 countries from 2006 to 2022. Split-sample analyses focusing on gender-unequal societies further support our hypothesized mechanism and suggest tentatively that sexual corruption may substitute for bribery as female-led businesses interact with public sector officials. The results have important implications for understanding the drivers of corruption, notably its gendered dimension and the role of women’s leadership as an engine for integrity, though for perhaps unexpected reasons.

title: Why liberal rights define democracy
abstract: Recent scholarly debates highlight conceptual confusion around the term “illiberal democracy” – a term widely used by academics, policymakers, and democracy watchdogs alike. We substantiate the need for greater clarity by evidencing significant ambiguity around the concept “illiberal democracy.” Analysing key definitions of both liberalism and democracy, we show that conceptual confusion underpins central scholarly debates around democratic backsliding and bedevils the labels used by democracy watchdogs. On conceptual terrain, we clarify that contemporary political regimes must have substantial liberal rights to qualify as a democracy. Clearly said, no liberal rights, no democracy.

title: How voters evaluate the proportionality-concentration trade-off: Evidence from a cross-national survey experiment
abstract: Whether electoral systems should foster proportionality or party system concentration is one of the most frequently discussed trade-offs in electoral system design. This question has primarily been addressed through normative theory and empirical research drawing on expert opinions. What remains unknown is how voters evaluate this fundamental trade-off. In this research note, we provide survey-experimental evidence on how voters evaluate proportionality and clear majorities when explicitly confronted with trade-offs between the two. To account for differences in institutional backgrounds, we conducted the experiment across three countries with different electoral systems (Germany, the Netherlands, and the United Kingdom). Across countries and voter groups, support for proportionality declines less strongly than support for clear majorities once trade-offs are made explicit. These findings have important implications for electoral system reform.

title: How perceived economic inequality shapes political efficacy: The mediating role of institutional trust
abstract: Abstract Economic inequality shapes citizens' attitudes and democratic support, yet little is known about how perceived inequality influences political efficacy. This research examines the relationship between perceived economic inequality and political efficacy, testing institutional trust as a psychosocial mechanism underlying this link. Across two correlational and two experimental studies, we present converging evidence for this process. Study 1 ( N = 9985) revealed multilevel evidence of a negative association between perceived economic inequality and institutional trust, beyond the effect of objective inequality, using Latin American survey data. Study 2 ( N = 1536) replicated this finding with a Spanish quota sample, revealing an indirect effect of perceived inequality on political efficacy through institutional trust. Study 3 ( N = 168) involved the experimental manipulation of inequality. Participants in the high‐inequality condition reported lower institutional trust and political efficacy, and the indirect effect was replicated. Study 4 ( N = 638) employed a concurrent double‐randomization design to manipulate perceived inequality and institutional trust. In contexts of high institutional trust, political efficacy differed between highly and less unequal conditions, with lower political efficacy observed in the high‐inequality condition. Similar patterns emerged for collective action. Overall, perceived inequality undermines institutional trust, reducing political efficacy and democratic engagement.

title: External Threats and Support for Military Service under Authoritarian Rule
abstract: As international conflicts escalate, states are increasingly turning to conscription and broader public participation in national defense. This article examines how acute external threats influence public attitudes toward military service. Leveraging original survey data from Iran, fielded before and after the unprecedented April 13, 2024 missile exchange with Israel, I use matching techniques to compare responses across the two periods. Individuals surveyed after the attack were significantly more likely to support mandatory male conscription and to support women’s military service. Importantly, support rose even though conscription is widely unpopular in peacetime and despite Iran’s gender hierarchies. These findings demonstrate that external threats can legitimize coercion in contexts of regime distrust and reconfigure gender boundaries around military participation. The study contributes to research on public perceptions of war, coercion, and militarization by highlighting how geopolitical shocks recalibrate the boundaries of both state authority and gendered citizenship.

title: A supranational alliance: the empowerment of the European Commission (1958–2019)
abstract: Despite severe ruptures, international cooperation remains an integral part of the response to new challenges facing European countries. Nothing better illustrates this than the continued empowerment of the European Commission. A set of legislative games of empowerment is developed to show that this process rests on a supranational alliance between the European Commission and the European Parliament, grounded in both structural and political factors. This novel expectation is tested using nearly the entire corpus of legislative production from 1958 to 2019 (more than 9,000 regulations and directives). The findings show that parliamentary involvement in the legislative process is the strongest driver of Commission empowerment, and its effect increases when the Parliament is ideologically closer to the Commission than the Council. How the European Union resolves this ‘federalism question’ has important implications for its legitimacy.

title: National and socialist: political representation in the left-authoritarian quadrant in Eastern Europe
abstract: The left-authoritarian quadrant of the political space contains forces that are simultaneously ‘national’ and ‘socialist’. Such a combination of positions is rare in Western Europe, but is clearly gaining political traction. Eastern Europe, on the other hand, has been a home to left-authoritarian parties for a long time. This article addresses the characteristics of left-authoritarian parties and their supporters in Eastern Europe, uncovering an interesting paradox – Eastern European left-authoritarians herald from a diversity of ideological families, yet tend to propose similar policies. This article explains this phenomenon by demonstrating the formative role of non-economic divides, particularly ethnicity and religiosity. The article underscores how ethnicity and religiosity determine whether the left-authoritarian space gets populated, and by whom. In doing so, the article provides valuable lessons for Western party systems that will likely see increasing left-authoritarian supply in the near future.

title: Propensity to consume food out of SNAP and its welfare implications
abstract: Using new consumer-panel data across multiple grocery retailers, I estimate that an additional SNAP dollar raises food-at-home spending by 48 cents (s.e. 6 cents). This multi-retailer estimate is broadly in line with the 59-cent estimate in Hastings and Shapiro (2018), reinforcing evidence that SNAP benefits are non-fungible. Linking food-at-home and food-away-from-home purchases to nutritional data, I find that SNAP substantially increases calorie purchases but has little effect on nutritional composition per calorie. A behavioral welfare calibration implies an efficiency cost of in-kind provision of 12–14 cents per SNAP dollar; because this calculation is highly sensitive to the MPC, pinning down the parameter is quantitatively important.

title: Review of “Walmart: Made in China”
Mapping Interactions Within EU Food and Feed Risk Analysis: A Comparative Study of Risk Assessors and Risk Managers
abstract: Considering prominent calls for various forms of cooperation, coordination, and collaboration within risk analysis processes, this empirical research study aims to delineate current forms of interaction between risk assessors and risk managers. Utilizing an online survey, it analyses responses from 95 professionals working in the field of food and feed risk analysis across at least 23 EU countries and determines interaction scores based on the degree of cooperation, coordination, and collaboration. The scores show that current interaction dominantly aligns with cooperation across multiple dimensions. However, multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA) reveals significant perceptual differences between risk assessors and managers regarding their mutual interaction. In particular, risk assessors perceive their interaction with risk management more cooperative and risk managers perceive their interaction with risk assessment more collaborative. A notable difference was also observed in the interaction scores for routine risk analysis versus rapid risk analysis. In addition, clustering analysis and regression analysis was conducted to examine the relation and impact of different interaction dimensions on perceived quality of risk analysis. While the results do not support uniform calls for more collaboration, they show positive effects of open and frequent communication on the perceived quality of risk analysis. These results suggest working towards more individualized and fit-for-purpose interactions as well as to extend practitioner-oriented dialogue on desired modes of interactions, to enhance mutual understanding in their collective risk analysis.

title: Does the TikTok Feed Lean Right? Exposure to Political Content Among Non-Partisan Users in Germany
abstract: We evaluated disparities in exposure to partisan content among new, nonpartisan TikTok users. We performed a sock puppet audit using 118 automated users in Germany ahead of three regional elections in 2024 and the federal election in 2025 (N = 266.161 videos). The design allowed us to account for past individual user behavior, user networks, location, and time. Overall, general political content constitutes 5%–7% of nonpolitical user feeds in our sample. When nonpartisan users encounter unsolicited political content, it is more likely to feature videos mentioning and supporting the far-right populist Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) party relative to all other parties. Further descriptive analysis shows that content by the AfD is associated with a higher volume of accounts and a higher number of viral videos.

Capitalism, Crises, and Constraints in China, 1990s–2000s
abstract: How do states navigate economic crises? How do crises affect state capitalist systems? This article explores how the government of the People’s Republic of China (PRC) understood and responded to the 1997 Asian Financial Crisis and the 2007–2008 Global Financial Crisis. It argues that Chinese policymakers and economic decision makers were often constrained by global political factors and structures, for example, concerns over government legitimacy and domestic political support, World Trade Organization (WTO) membership, and global demand for Chinese exports. We show that the PRC had to adjust its economic policies and, consequently, its state capitalist model in response to these crises to secure its political and economic interests. This research traces the agency behind the rise of the Chinese economy and its intersection with crises, state capitalism, and global economic structural forces.

title: “Task-Based Relations” and the Sustainable Provision of Rural Neighbor-Assisted Eldercare Services in China*
abstract: In the practice of rural neighbor-assisted eldercare, phenomena such as “hot beginnings, cold endings” 热启动、冷收尾 and operational contraction are common, rooted in the nature of services—dispersed providers, embedded processes, contextual needs, and the challenges of effective supervision, all of which make periodic external resource inputs difficult to translate into stable service provision. Taking Village H in North China as a case study, this article analyzes how neighbor-assisted eldercare has achieved long-term, stable operation under resource constraints. Village H established a two-tier network of “centers and neighbor-assisted sites” 驿站—互助点, restructuring rights and responsibilities: The village party branch committee and the village committee adopted a strategy of “providing administrative guarantees without taking full control,” while establishing rules, verifying eligibility, and coordinating procedures. Meanwhile, the “Happiness Eldercare Center” 幸福晚年驿站, as a semi-formal hub, translates external directives and funding into sustainable everyday care through micro-level organization and process coordination. At the level of process governance 过程治理, simplified record-keeping and follow-up visits ensure minimal traceability, while word-of-mouth evaluations and social pressure inherent in rural communities fill supervision gaps. The article further argues that Village H’s success lies not in resource inputs or “capable individuals” but in generating a stable structure of “task-based relations” 事缘关系 centered on eldercare. This structure couples formal bureaucratic rules with local informal networks. By identifying this underlying mechanism, this article contributes to our understanding of the sustainable provision of process-oriented public services in transitional rural China and identifies broader policy implications.

Impact of organizational goals, leadership styles, and organizational culture on employee outcomes in the Korean public sector
abstract: This study examines how organizational goals, leadership styles, and organizational culture influence employee outcomes in the Korean public sector. Using Structural Equation Modelling, data from 6,170 public servants were analysed. Organizational goals positively influenced commitment and performance efforts. Transactional leadership positively affected organizational culture and commitment but negatively affected performance efforts, whereas visionary leadership showed positive effects across all three outcomes. Organizational culture enhanced commitment and performance efforts, while organizational commitment positively influenced performance efforts and perceived organizational performance. Performance efforts also enhanced perceived organizational performance. These findings highlight how goals, leadership, and collaborative culture jointly shape employee and organizational outcomes.

title: Towards Common Ground: Perspectives on Energy Transitions in Canadian Oil and Gas Producing Municipalities
abstract: Abstract Oil and gas producing municipalities host Canada's highest‐emitting industries while facing economic and social risks as the country pursues carbon neutrality. Understanding how these communities envision their economic futures, and the barriers and enablers they encounter in pursuing low‐carbon opportunities, can inform decision‐makers seeking both emissions reductions and more resilient local economies. This study engages ten municipal economic development staff in British Columbia and Alberta to capture their perspectives on transition pathways. Findings demonstrate that staff are exploring diversification but face substantial barriers, including limited staff, technical, and fiscal capacity and the absence of a coherent transition vision. Addressing these challenges requires governance transformation. We argue that transition strategies must move beyond top‐down, universal mandates and embrace more locally grounded approaches. Community‐supported, place‐relevant visions for low‐carbon transitions, co‐created with municipal actors, must be supported by integrated policy packages built on whole‐systems modalities rather than narrow green jobs or sectoral focuses.

title: When the European Council Intervenes: Bargaining Success in EU Legislation
The uses of (mis)information in education policy: introduction to the special issue
abstract: This special issue of Evidence & Policy focuses on growing concerns around misinformation, disinformation and research misuse in education policy. This introduction to the issue shows how education policy is a unique and particularly vulnerable information ecosystem because it is deeply contested, highly politicized, often structurally decentralized and susceptible to intermediaries who frame problems, package evidence and influence policy discourse. Drawing on scholarship across multiple fields – including misinformation studies, policy studies and education research – our introduction highlights how misinformation in education is not only a question of false claims, but also of strategic framing and the selective use of ‘evidence’ in service of ideological agendas. The introduction summarizes the six articles in the issue, which examine topics including civics teachers’ information use, anti-LGBTQIA+ advocacy campaigns, countermeasures to misinformation, authoritarian discourse in Hungary, research misuse in knowledge brokering, and shifting claims about evidence-based education in Australia. Several themes emerge within and across these articles: the centrality of systemic and contextual factors, the importance of intermediaries, the role of language and norms, and the imperative for interdisciplinary, comparative and critically informed approaches to this increasingly critical issue. We conclude by discussing how researchers and practitioners can combine efforts around media literacy, institutional reform, accountability for knowledge brokers, with a more rigorous interrogation of what counts as evidence in education policy.

title: Talking heads: communication and responsiveness at the European Council
abstract: This paper examines how national leaders use public communication during European Council summits to signal responsiveness to their domestic constituencies. Drawing on a novel dataset of over 4500 media engagements during the summits between 2009 and 2025, the study explores how ‘representative claims’ – claims to represent domestic constituencies – in leader's public communication respond to electoral pressures and salience of EU politics. The results show that leaders use more representative claims during their public communication at European Council meetings particularly when facing upcoming domestic elections and when the salience of EU issues is high domestically. However, this pattern emerges predominantly in communication before the start of the negotiations. Hence, whether claim-based rhetoric is driven by strategic or responsiveness motivations remains unclear. These findings highlight that the European Council is both a high-level arena for consensual intergovernmental decision-making and a normalised stage for electorally-oriented public communication in a multilevel polity. The study contributes to the literatures on rhetorical representation and on the role of national elections and public salience in European-level decision-making processes.

title: Algorithmic Literacy and Quotidian Curation Practices: Rethinking User Agency in the Social Media Regulation Era
Crisis as catalyst: regulatory reforms in India’s nuclear safety governance
abstract: This study investigates the role of nuclear crises as catalysts of organizational change within India’s Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB). Using mixed-method approach, the study assesses five drivers of regulatory change: Crisis Learning, International Nuclear Regulatory Regime, Operational Feedback from utilities, Strategic Considerations emanating from India’s nuclear weapons program, and Public Trust Dynamics. The findings indicate that institutional actors accord greater weight to IAEA standards and periodic utility feedback in shaping regulatory change, while post-incident committees restructuring and upgrades attest to the influence of crisis learning. However, organizational culture characterized by institutional values, professional attitudes, and procedural norms, mediates this effect and steers reforms toward targeted, procedure‑focused adjustments rather than comprehensive structural redesign to strengthen independence and transparency. This filtering narrows the limits of crisis learning as a driver of institutional change. These dynamics are particularly salient as India revises its nuclear regulatory framework to facilitate domestic and international private investment. By situating the AERB’s evolution within a multi-causal framework, this study demonstrates how external pressures, such as crises and public perception, subject the establishment to non-routine media and political scrutiny. These episodic forces are absorbed and moderated by deeply embedded, path-dependent organizational norms, resulting in incremental and tactical reforms rather than structural overhaul. An organizational culture premised on trust within constituent units would face increasing strain as participation of “outsider” actors grow. These insights carry implications for policymakers designing nuclear safety governance frameworks and for scholars examining the dynamics of regulation in high‑risk industries.

title: Nordic world class? Region branding and self-benchmarking
abstract: The Nordic Council of Ministers officially strives for a “green”, “competitive” and “socially sustainable” region under what it calls “Our Vision 2030”. To render the aggregate performance of its member states measurable, the Council deploys a total of forty-five indicators for “traffic-light visualizations” of achievements and trends benchmarked against other countries. Connecting scholarship on global benchmarking and place branding, this article examines the production of an idealized world-class region through self-benchmarking, which contrasts with the more common phenomenon of individual states’ performance being assessed by others. I interrogate the assumptions behind the Council’s aspirations by analyzing selected official documents. In line with the special issue theme, the study shows how self-benchmarking transcends the roles of the governors/benchmarkers and governed/benchmarked. Specifically, “Our Vision 2030” subscribes to a mainstream inclusive green growth position, which does little to distinguish the Nordic “brand” from those of other regions but instead rehearses a well-known narrative with a regional twist. The Council’s self-benchmarking apparatus thus risks ignoring evidence of negative ecological impacts and inequitable social outcomes of growth-friendly policies, as well as of the insufficient scope and pace of absolute decoupling of growth from ecological parameters to date.

title: The Global Turn in Policy Process Research: Borderless Problems, Situated Experiments, and the Conditions of Collective Learning
Diagnosing systemic failures in national innovation systems: a coupled functional–structural analysis of Iran’s NIS
More of the Same? Institutional Stability and Change in Contemporary Welfare States
abstract: ABSTRACT While there has been a longstanding debate on welfare state retrenchment and convergence, welfare states have mostly been perceived to continuously diverge along previously established lines. This stability is commonly ascribed to institutional legacies and policy feedback. Yet few studies have explored how established social policy models have evolved over time, and thus how path dependency has shaped such developments. Against this backdrop, this article empirically explores the evolution of social insurance institutions between 1980 and 2020. Using data from the Social Policy Indicator database (SPIN) in combination with secondary literature, we assess the stability of social insurance models and explore to what extent historical legacies matter for the observed patterns of change and stability. Our findings show that while there is substantial heterogeneity between welfare states in terms of levels of social rights and directions of change, boundaries between institutional models have become less distinct over time. We discuss the implications of these findings for common assumptions about path dependence across different institutional models and point towards important avenues for future research.

title: Crime and Participation
abstract: Does exposure to crime mobilize or demobilize political participation? We report findings from a preregistered design, leveraging data from an original survey of 21 major U.S. cities and five waves of the Cooperative Election Study. We assess the relationships between direct victimization, local (ZCTA-level) crime rates, and perceived neighborhood safety and two outcomes: turnout (including validated turnout) and non-electoral participation. We find that direct victimization is significantly associated with more non-electoral engagement but lower turnout. The negative estimated effects of victimization on turnout exceed the magnitude of positive effects associated with common get-out-the-vote efforts. We find only limited evidence that crime rates are associated with participation. Perceived neighborhood safety is associated with higher rates of non-electoral, but not electoral, participation. Our findings offer new, comprehensive evidence on the relationship between crime exposure and political participation and illustrate the importance of distinguishing between types of exposure and forms of participation.

title: Romania’s immigration debate under neoliberal hegemony: Constructing diligent migrants and individualising Transylvanian Hungarians as racist
abstract: Abstract In 2020, a group of residents of the rural Transylvanian Hungarian-majority municipality of Ditró (in Hungarian), or Ditrău (in Romanian), mobilised themselves against two Sri Lankan bakers. Mainstream media portrayed the incident as xenophobic and racist, the locals as right-wing extremists, and the Sri Lankans as merely ‘migrant workers’, turning the ‘Ditrău incident’ into Romania’s first and most important nationwide immigration debate. This article analyses what the media-coverage of these events tells us about the country’s approach to immigration, and how the symbols, signs, languages, meanings, knowledges, and memories articulated around the ‘Ditrău incident’ make this and other relatable events feed into this approach. We employ discourse analysis, including Lotman’s cultural semiotics, and engage with the institutional, political, and historical framing of ‘the incident’, as well as the broader socio-political and historical context of Romania’s immigration debate. In this way, we argue that, first, the ‘Ditrău incident’ was instrumental to Romania’s dominant societal core in portraying itself as closer to ‘the West’, its absolution of any responsibility for xenophobia and racism, the reproduction of the hegemony of neoliberalism and the middle-class ideology, and the construction of ‘diligent migrant workers’. Second, ‘the incident’ was fundamental in the silencing, individualisation, and invisibilisation of working-class voices and particularising Transylvanian Hungarians as racists and extremists. Finally, it allowed Romanian mainstream actors to brand their nation as open, tolerant, and humane, while normalising the commodification and overexploitation of third-country migrant labour.

title: Party and Prejudice: Are Asian American Candidates Better Suited to Win in White Districts?
abstract: ABSTRACT Recent work on Asian American descriptive representation has found that Asian American officeholders are more prevalent in racially diverse districts when compared to Black or Latino representatives, but still face substantial obstacles in very white electoral districts. This work, however, models Asian American representation by observing officeholders only, ignoring both the competitive election environment and Asian American losing candidates, biasing its inferences. We reassess these conclusions using a candidate‐centered approach in thousands of state legislative races in 2018 and 2020. Our results demonstrate that Asian American, Black, and Latino candidates all perform substantially better in white districts than officeholder models predict, and that any differences between minority groups in white districts are due to the partisan match between candidates and their districts. The findings speak to the need for researchers to model vote choice as a candidate‐centered process, paying careful attention to the actual choices on voters' election day ballots.

title: One Message, Multiple Functions: Local Propaganda as Bureaucratic Trace Management
abstract: This article explores how local government propaganda in China can function as a tool for bureaucratic management. I argue that certain propaganda primarily serves as public documentation of government activities and officials’ performance, enhancing bureaucratic transparency and credibility. This documentation is particularly important when leaders lack personal ties with subordinates and thus require independent verification of their work. However, prioritizing record keeping over public persuasion often produces rigid, unengaging media content, which I term “trace-management propaganda.” Analyzing 1.4 million WeChat posts from Chinese local governments, I demonstrate that trace-management propaganda significantly increases during official evaluation periods and is especially prevalent where personal connections between leaders and subordinates are weak. A difference-in-differences analysis further confirms that a lack of personal ties increases reliance on trace-management propaganda. These findings reveal that local government propaganda in China frequently fulfills both administrative and expressive purposes, providing new insights into state media dynamics and bureaucratic oversight.

title: Democratic but Still White: The Impact of Racial Identity Threats on White Democrats’ Support for Racial Justice Protests
abstract: Abstract In recent years, observers have noted an apparent increase in racially progressive attitudes among White Democrats. Among journalists, this “great awokening” of White Democrats is practically taken as a political fact. However, what this consensus about the racial liberalism of White Democrats often overlooks is that while White Democrats have in many ways moved in line with the Democratic Party’s position on race and racial inequality, their White identity makes them vulnerable to racial identity threats. In this study, I test this potential for racial identity-driven backlash among White Democrats in the context of racial justice protest movements. To do this, I conduct a survey experiment in which respondents are exposed to an image from a racial justice protest, and I vary the messaging on the signs in the image as well as the race of the protesters. I find that when protesters use messaging that is critical of Whites and Whiteness, White Democrats’ support for the movement and the protesters declines. Additionally, such messaging causes respondents to distance themselves from the views of the protesters and raises concerns about violence erupting at the protests. These results underscore how racial identity threats can erode White Democrats’ support for political messages and political movements that their increasingly liberal racial attitudes should make them amenable to.

title: O Xenos: Racial Difference, Colorism, and Attitudes Toward Immigrants in Greece
What Works Against Populist Rhetoric? The Effects of Counter-Arguments on Democratic Attitudes
abstract: Abstract Politicians use populist rhetoric – arguments that portray politics as an enduring conflict between “the good people” and “the evil elites” – to generate support for attacks on constitutional safeguards, the media, and minorities. Yet, little is known about how to counteract such rhetoric. We utilize a pre-registered survey experiment in the UK (n $$\cong$$ 4000) to investigate the effects of counter-arguments put forward by fellow citizens. We hypothesize pluralist and democratic elitist counter-arguments to be promising antidotes to populist rhetoric and test to what extent such arguments can strengthen liberal democratic attitudes and weaken populist majoritarian ones. We find that populism can be challenged successfully but not with all types of counter-arguments. Pluralist appeals can decrease support for populist majoritarian democracy, while elitist counter-arguments have no effect on democratic attitudes. Additional analyses suggest that counter-arguments might also affect how voters evaluate candidates. These results contribute by demonstrating the potentials of counter-arguments in strengthening the resilience of liberal democracies vis-à-vis populist challenges.

title: Decoding Corruption Cycles: Extractive versus Collusive Corruption
How Policy Design Affects Perceptions of Beneficiaries and Support for Welfare
abstract: Abstract Most of the public supports welfare policies in the abstract, but many hold deep misgivings about the deservingness of welfare recipients, driving down support for specific policies. Welfare policies are often designed to mitigate these concerns by restricting access to benefits, but it is unclear to what effect. According to an influential strain of research drawing on social construction theory, these restrictions may backfire, instead increasing concerns about a free-riding public. In contrast -- drawing on psychological research on the deservingness heuristic -- I argue that policy features, such as work requirements, signal effort on behalf of recipients and thus deservingness. Using an experiment, I find that several policy features increase perceptions of deservingness and, in turn, increase policy support and generosity. However, some policy features are also perceived as overly burdensome, reducing the effects on policy support. Treatment effects on perceptions of beneficiary deservingness are largest among ambivalent respondents, but largely generalize across partisanship, ideology, and racial resentment. Overall, these findings help clarify the implications of the deservingness heuristic while challenging predictions from social construction theory and informing ongoing debates over public opinion and policy feedback.

title: Questionnaire Democrats? Reconsidering the Relevance of Abstract Democracy Support in the American Public
abstract: Abstract The American public largely favors “democracy,” yet many citizens tolerate undemocratic actions and candidates. This raises doubts about the relevance of abstract democracy support to actual democratic commitment. In contrast, we argue that abstract democracy support is a normatively significant dimension of attitude variation among Americans. Using nineteen surveys fielded between 1995 and 2024, we show that a sizable segment of the public expresses only tepid support for democracy, and that a nontrivial minority expresses opposition. Moreover, commonly used abstract democracy support items converge on a single latent construct which displays high rank-order stability, but also meaningful within-person variation, over a two-year period. Abstract democracy support negatively predicts openness to a wide range of electoral and liberal democratic violations and is associated with greater likelihood of electorally punishing anti-democratic candidates. In panel data, positive within-person deviations in abstract democracy support precede negative within-person deviations in openness to authoritarian governance, suggesting that individual-level shifts in abstract support predict later change in substantive democracy attitudes. Overall our findings suggest that the value of ‘democracy’ is contested among Americans, with potential implications for democratic erosion. We recommend that efforts to understand the American public’s role in democratic backsliding and restoration treat abstract support as a distinct attitude construct, measure it with multi-item scales, and explore whether or not it possesses causal significance.

title: The Marginal Propensity to Hire
abstract: Abstract When financial constraints bind, firms adjust employment in response to cash flow shocks. A 2010 revaluation of business rates, a UK tax levied on business-occupied properties, implied that similar firms, occupying similar properties in narrow geographical locations, experienced different tax changes. I find that, on average, for every ￡1 of additional cash flow triggered by the tax change, 39 pence were spent on employment, with small and leveraged firms responding the most. I use these findings to discipline a general equilibrium model with firm heterogeneity and financial frictions and quantitatively determine the aggregate effects of a fiscal transfer to firms.

title: Macroeconomic Implications of Executive Pay Caps,
abstract: Abstract I study the introduction of statutory caps on executive pay ratios (pay caps) in a span-of-control economy with heterogeneous managerial talent. Managers hire fewer workers than they would in the absence of pay caps, and the marginal product of labour is not equalized among firms. The ability of the marginal manager declines. Inequality between managers and workers, and among managers, declines, but inequality among workers increases. Quantitatively, overall inequality decreases substantially, especially via a reduction in top income shares, but the GDP losses are also significant. In addition, the redistribution favours the “middle” deciles between 50 and 90, rather than the bottom 50% of the income distribution. Future work will build on this “first pass” to analyse the effect of pay caps in economies distorted by monopsony power, non-pecuniary benefits of control, and managerial rent extraction.
journal_name: Journal of the European Economic Association

title: State Legitimation and Its Incorporation of Ideological-Political Education Teachers in China, 1979–2023
abstract: This study explores the Chinese state’s endeavor to reinforce its legitimacy in the domain of education during the reform era, focusing on school ideological-political education as a key vehicle. It examines the incorporation of ideological-political education teachers into the state’s legitimation project. Analysis of data from official documents and teacher interviews reveals that the incorporation process involves both state-driven and teacher-driven activities. The former involves role theorization within curricular and policy discourses and socialization within the framework of teacher professionalization, highlighting the integration of paternalism and professionalism. The latter includes mutual socialization, role adaptation, and instructional customization in professional practice, facilitated by the discourse of professionalism. The study holds implications for research on China’s governance legitimacy, institutional theory, teacher studies, and Chinese citizenship education.

title: International organizations’ role in domestic public sector digitalization: a proposal for a typology examining directions and instruments of influence
abstract: This article examines how international organizations (IOs) contribute to orienting public sector digitalization by analyzing the directions and instruments through which they influence domestic reforms. Building on the literature on policy rationales, it develops a multidimensional typology combining supranational policy instruments with rationales of digitalization. The typology is applied to a dataset of 135 policy initiatives promoted by the United Nations (UN), the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), and the European Union (EU) between 2000 and 2024. The findings show that digitalization strategies are not neutral but reflect politically embedded rationales aligned with institutional mandates. Market-oriented rationales dominate, although human rights-based approaches have gained prominence following the COVID-19 pandemic. Soft instruments prevail, with limited but increasing use of financial and regulatory tools in response to crises. Illustrative national-level evidence further suggests that the degree of influence varies by instrument type and its interaction with domestic implementation capacity and political willingness. The article contributes by extending the analysis of digitalization rationales to the international level and offering a framework applicable across governance contexts.

title: Coping with life-threatening experiences at the street-level: the case of police officers in the October 7 attack in Israel
abstract: How do street-level bureaucrats cope with acute, life-threatening experiences at work, and what are the consequences of such exposure? Based on 30 in-depth interviews with Israeli police officers who operated during the October 7 attack on Israel, we identify two coping mechanisms that enabled them to function under threat: auto-pilot mode, meaning relying on instinct and training, and detachment, meaning suppressing their emotions to complete their task. After the attack, officers reported less trust in state institutions, their organization, and the public. To cope, they relied mainly on peer support from colleagues who had undergone similar experiences. These experiences altered their professional behaviour, leading to cautiousness with citizens. The study contributes to public management by showing how exposure to acute, life-threatening experiences shapes street-level bureaucrats’ coping mechanisms and how these mechanisms may support organizational resilience during and after a crisis. Content warning: This article contains graphic descriptions of a warzone.

title: Insights from co-design for relational policy-making: Farm animal health and welfare policy in the UK
abstract: IMPACTThis article offers practical lessons for policy-makers working in contested, low-trust environments. It shows that co-design can build trust only when participation is supported by relational practices such as shared leadership, peer challenge and clear principles of engagement. It also highlights a common risk in public administration: trust generated during the co-design process can quickly erode if delivery systems, fiscal rules and organizational structures are not aligned with what was agreed. The findings therefore suggest that governments should invest not only in co-design processes, but also in the institutional conditions to enable collaborative innovation needed to carry relational commitments into implementation and throughout the full policy cycle leading to a long-term sector transformation.

title: Sociotechnical and normative support for civil servants’ generative AI use in Finnish municipal technical services
abstract: IMPACTMunicipal leaders and managers should consider technical, social and normative support elements before expanding generative AI use. Respondents rated task benefits, usable and reliable tools, and clear ethical and information-security guidance most highly. In exploratory item-level comparisons, AI users assigned greater importance than non-users to organizational climate, paid tool access, peer support, leadership commitment, and application usability. Many of these support factors can be addressed through managerial attention at relatively low cost. Organizations could use employee assessments to identify local support gaps. National and inter-municipal bodies can provide sector-specific guidance on accountability and data governance, especially for municipalities with limited resources.

title: Democratizing expertise: lived experience as evidence in citizens’ assemblies
abstract: Democratic policymaking is said to require the wisdom of crowds. Yet complex issues require expert input. Citizens’ assemblies, which bring together randomly selected citizens and professional experts, appear to reconcile these demands. However, professional experts often exert strong influence on assembly members, risking the marginalization of lay and local knowledge. This paper evaluates an intervention in the Southampton Citizens’ Climate Assembly that introduced ‘citizen witnesses’ – individuals sharing lived experience relevant to the topic with the assembly members – to foster a more inclusive and democratic knowledge-building process. Analyzing survey data, field notes, and interviews with assembly members, we find that citizen witnesses complemented professional expertise and influenced the assembly not only by providing additional information but also by reshaping how assembly members understood the issue under deliberation. Their testimonies prompted reflection on blind spots, privilege and unequal exposure to policy consequences, broadening assembly members’ understanding of the policy problem. They also encouraged members to draw more confidently on their own experiences during deliberation, reinforcing the legitimacy of lived experience as a source of knowledge in collective decision-making. These findings suggest that citizen witnesses can help democratize expertise within citizens’ assemblies by elevating the standing of lay knowledge alongside professional expertise.

title: Expertise, Interests, and Impact: The Importance of MEP Background on Policy Positions
Policy design under armed attack: instrument calibration and termination under relational uncertainty
abstract: Policy instrument design occurs within complex environments, but the environments studied in the design literature share a common feature: the designer can generate data against which instrument settings are adjusted. Armed attack removes this feature. When a noncombatant state comes under missile and drone strikes, the government must calibrate, adapt, and terminate policy instruments without measurable threat indicators, under extreme time pressure, and with no capacity to influence the threat source. Here a framework is proposed for understanding the design space that governments navigate under such conditions, combining two dimensions that the existing selection-calibration-sequencing model has not needed to distinguish: the type of uncertainty characterizing the design environment and the constraint structure linking design choices across parameters. Drawing on the case of Qatar during the 2026 Iran war, the framework identifies the parameters that must be set when instruments are deployed under armed attack, the constraints that foreclose certain parameter combinations, and the capacity dynamics that result when the design space contracts. The article outlines each of these dimensions and advances three arguments: that armed attack may constitute a distinct design regime operating under relational rather than epistemic uncertainty, that instrument termination under non-controllable threat exposes an unstated assumption in the policy termination literature, and that inter-parameter constraints restructure the relationship between analytical and operational capacity under crisis conditions. The framework is derived from the Qatari case and probed against the other Gulf monarchies that faced the same Iranian and Houthi threat, across which the instrument set and the central constraint recur and the constraint varies with a single factor, the controllability of the threat. The principal contribution to crisis-management scholarship is the measurability-termination constraint, the finding that an emergency regime cannot be terminated on a threat indicator that the threat itself does not generate, and that the severity of this constraint rises as the controllability of the threat falls.

title: The market shaping state: capacities and capabilities for a new generation of mission-oriented policies
abstract: This article sets out a market-shaping theory of the public sector to confront a longstanding tension in public administration: how governments can be stable and agile at the same time, while steering complex socio-technical transformations. Conventional approaches—preoccupied with fixing market failures, chasing efficiency, and reforming management—fall short as guides to transitions across climate, care, digital infrastructure, and industrial renewal. We reconceptualise the state as a proactive shaper of markets and a co-creator of public value, and develop a three-layered framework that distinguishes structural capacities, organizational routines, and dynamic capabilities. Public value emerges through the interaction of these elements, not from any single attribute. The article also introduces and contextualizes the special issue on the new generation of mission-oriented policies, organizations, and capacities, identifying five cross-cutting themes that emerge from the seven contributions.

title: Making Policy Evidence Traceable: A Modular Preregistration Framework for Policy Evaluation
abstract: ABSTRACT Preregistration is increasingly used in policy research, but its value depends on whether preregistered commitments can be clearly linked to reported analyses. Policy studies often involve multiple outcomes, evolving administrative data, consequential design and analytic choices, and adaptive implementation, making it difficult to distinguish prespecified tests from subsequent adjustments. This research note proposes a modular, policy‐oriented companion framework for using existing preregistration infrastructure. The framework combines a shared core that defines the estimand, outcomes, and identification strategy with design‐specific modules for field experiments, administrative‐data quasi‐experiments, and behavioral policy trials. Together, the components serve two purposes: claim traceability, by linking reported results to the original plan, and governed adaptation, by providing a transparent record of changes made during the study. The aim is not to prevent adaptation, but to show which analyses were prespecified, which were revised through documented amendments, and which were developed later. This approach aims to improve the interpretability and transparency of policy research while remaining feasible in applied policy settings.

title: Do MPs Venue Shop? Westminster Hall as a Strategic Policy Choice Venue
abstract: ABSTRACT Research shows that policy actors strategically select different institutional venues to lobby on specific issues to influence policy‐making. But we lack understanding of how Parliament, a key representative and legislative body, may offer itself multiple venue shopping opportunities for internal actors. Our study explores venue shopping at the intra‐parliamentary level in the UK Parliament by MPs themselves, showing how they use Parliament's two debating chambers: the government‐controlled House of Commons chamber and a parallel backbench chamber, Westminster Hall. Drawing on analysis of 60 backbench debates and 17 elite interviews, we find that MPs do engage in intra‐parliamentary venue shopping, utilizing debates differently in each chamber. While the main chamber serves as an agenda‐setting venue, Westminster Hall is used as an accountability venue, creating a policy‐oriented dialogue with government and fostering clearer policy outcomes. Our study makes a key contribution showing that venue shopping can occur intra‐institutionally by internal policy actors. Related Articles Gash, Alison, and Michael H. Murakami. 2015. “Venue Effects: How State Policy Source Influences Policy Support.“ Politics & Policy 43, no. 5: 679–922. https://doi.org/10.1111/polp.12128 . Grossmann, Matt. 2014. “The Varied Effects of Policy Cues on Partisan Opinions.” Politics & Policy 42, no. 6: 881–904. http://doi.org/10.1111/polp.12102/abstract . Rugeley, Cynthia R., and John David Gerlach. 2012. “Understanding Environmental Public Opinion by Dimension: How Heuristic Processing Mitigates High Information Costs on Complex Issues.” Politics & Policy 40, no. 3: 444–470. http://doi.org/10.1111/j.1747‐1346.2012.00352.x/abstract .

title: Does Exposure to Information on Ethnic Minorities' Greater Welfare Dependency Affect Attitudes to Welfare and Welfare Recipients? A Pre‐Registered, Population‐Based Survey Experiment
abstract: ABSTRACT The relationship between ethnic diversity and welfare attitudes has been the subject of much research. However, little is known about how exposure to information on the overrepresentation of ethnic minority individuals among welfare recipients affects attitudes to welfare recipients in general. We scrutinize a potential information exposure effect, and assess two contrasting scenarios, that is, exposure to aforementioned information might strengthen either negative stereotypes of welfare recipients or the notion that welfare dependency is the result of structural conditions. Additionally, we hypothesize that the former (latter) response is more likely among those with more (less) ethnocentric attitudes. We tested this by conducting an original pre‐registered survey experiment among members of a high‐quality probability‐based panel designed to represent the Dutch population ( n = 1527). The treatment group was exposed to information depicting the overrepresentation of Dutch citizens with a Moroccan migration background among welfare recipients in the Netherlands, while the control group was not. It was only among the more ethnocentric respondents that exposure to the treatment increased support for the notions that welfare recipients: (1) are lacking work ethic; and (2) are themselves to blame for their condition. There was (3) no treatment effect on support for welfare schemes in general. We discuss the implications of these findings for a variety of academic debates and make suggestions for further research.

title: Explaining Military Defections in Democracies: The Impact of Executive Self-Coups
Bringing War Back In: Victory, Defeat, and the State in Nineteenth Century Latin America. By Luis L. Schenoni. New York: Cambridge University Press, 2024. 326p.
Russia’s War on Ukraine: The Four Roots of Putin’s Invasion. By Taras Kuzio and Michał Wawrzonek. Cambridge, UK: Cambridge University Press, 2026. 395p.
How Do Voters Reason about Intraparty Democracy? Constraints Rather than Influence
abstract: Widespread intraparty reforms empower party members and create coprincipalship with party voters. This alters the structure of democratic delegation and may lead to policy drift and ineffective accountability. Existing research is vague on how voters see this arrangement, and we therefore ask, What leads voters to accept coprincipalship despite its potential representational costs? We apply exploratory analysis to focus-group data to examine how voters reason about intraparty authority and show that participants accepted their role as coprincipals not for self-empowerment, but for parties’ organizational integrity: they viewed party members as effective constraints on self-serving leaders. Based on these findings, we formulate an intraparty constraint hypothesis stating that voters favor intraparty democracy as a constraint mechanism rather than a participatory venue, which provides a theoretical answer to the unsolved puzzle of why voters want intraparty democracy when they do not intend to use it or reward parties for having it.

title: Un-Priming Politics: A Method to Reduce Overreporting of Political Engagement
abstract: Abstract Survey researchers frequently employ measures of political engagement, yet social desirability pressures can lead to overreporting. Building upon existing literature, we adopt an iterative approach to determine how such overreporting can be reduced. Four preregistered survey experiments were conducted (total N=7,122). We first confirm that social desirability considerations can underlie some types of self-reported political engagement. Second, having tested a variety of interventions that were designed to reduce overreporting, we find that our most effective treatment ( Dampen Politics) was one that aimed to decrease the salience of politics. This treatment significantly reduced (1) the degree to which respondents perceived the survey as political, and (2) some types of self-reported political engagement, particularly political interest and voting. We tested alternative implementations of the Dampen Politics treatment, each time assessing its robustness and validity. Our findings suggest a simple adjustment in survey wording and organization can meaningfully decrease overreporting of political engagement.

title: Permutations of settler colonial rule in Gaza: A generational approach
abstract: This article mobilises generation as a lens for theorising and examining the contingent and permuting character of settler colonial formations, with a specific focus on Gaza. Generation, we argue, calls attention to settler colonial rule as situated and embodied, and temporalities of survival and resistance as layered and heterogenous. We draw on 20 interviews collected just after the 2021 bombings to foreground the reflections of young Palestinians who have grown up in, and never left, a Gaza blockaded and repeatedly bombed by the Israeli settler state. Specifically, we examine how young Palestinians, through reflections on how their generation faces a changed form of settler colonial rule, appraise and “stitch together” the temporalities of past dispossession, their present-day experiences of oppression and resistance, and futures of anti-colonial struggle and liberation. As a whole, we illuminate the importance of studying generational reappraisals and renegotiations of survival and resistance among Palestinians in and beyond Gaza as they struggle against a highly unstable and fragmented settler colonial formation.

title: Conceptualizing and measuring global consciousness
abstract: Abstract To examine the conceptualization and the measurement of global consciousness (GC) in cross‐national contexts, we conducted a secondary analysis on survey data collected from 16,241 individuals across 35 societies. Results demonstrate that GC is best conceptualized as a multidimensional construct by a bifactor ESEM model, in which GC captures an overarching and direct source of common variance across all manifest indicators, whereas domain‐specific residual variance is retained by three existing measures: Identification with All Humanity (IWAH), Cosmopolitan Orientation (COS), and a shortened version of Global Orientations (GOS). Metric invariance was successfully achieved across 30 out of 35 societies. At the individual level, GC was negatively associated with political conservatism, an effect that was amplified in societies with higher HDI, more robust rule of law, and a salient culture of individualism. In an exploratory societal‐level analysis, aggregated GC functioned as an informative ecological indicator, appearing more prominent in the Global South societies across the sample. This preliminary pattern is probably attributable to the open system where GC is measured, reflecting the hopes and aspirations of people in the making.

title: Temporary internal displacement and receiving communities’ voting behavior
Identity politics, partisan sentiment and household spending
abstract: We examine how political shifts affect household economic sentiment and spending in identity-polarized settings. Using panel data on over 178,000 Indian households, we find that sentiment about personal finances—and, to a lesser extent, the national economy—predicts expenditure, even after accounting for income changes. Using close state elections, we show that Muslims become markedly more pessimistic than Hindus about national economic conditions following victories by the Hindu-nationalist party, but exhibit relatively smaller differences in personal financial sentiment and no detectable divergence in overall expenditure. We find some evidence, however, of Hindu-Muslim divergence in potentially deferrable choices—healthcare, luxury spending, and asset purchases—particularly among urban, educated, and white-collar households. A Bayesian learning framework explains the insulation of consumption from politically induced sentiment shocks through the limited and heterogeneous transmission of macro-beliefs to individual behavior in high-volatility environments.

title: Are Markups Too High? Competition, Strategic Innovation, and Industry Dynamics
abstract: Abstract To study competition, innovation, and industry dynamics that arise as a result of their interaction, we develop a new oligopolistic general-equilibrium Schumpeterian growth model. This model ties together the endogenous growth, oligopolistic competition, and dynamic industrial organization literatures in a single unified framework. Within each industry, there are an endogenously determined number of large firms (“superstars”) that compete á la Cournot and a continuum of small firms which collectively constitute a competitive fringe. Firms dynamically choose their innovation strategies, cognizant of other firms' choices, and their entry and exit are endogenous. The model is consistent with the macroeconomic trends observed in the United States since the 1970s, such as the domination of industries by a small number of superstar firms, the rise of markups, market concentration, profits, and R&D spending, and the decline in business dynamism, productivity growth, and the labor share. It replicates the empirical relationship between innovation and competition within and across industries. As an application, we estimate the model to disentangle the effects of separate mechanisms on the structural transition observed in the United States, which yields striking results: (1) While the increase in the average markup causes a significant static welfare loss, this loss is overshadowed by the dynamic welfare gains from increased innovation in response to higher profit opportunities. (2) The increasing costs of innovation are found to be the primary determinant of lackluster productivity growth, i.e., ideas are getting harder to find.

title: Tax distortion on capital and resource misallocation: evidence from China’s VAT reform
Relational Adaptation in Spot Trading
abstract: Abstract Efficient adaptation to fluctuating market conditions is critical to economic agents’ survival and prosperity. Although theory highlights the value of relational contracts in facilitating adaptation, empirical evidence remains limited. Using wholesale transaction data, we show that a buyer initially sourcing on the spot market may repeatedly trade with a seller, offering a price premium in exchange for a relational contract that assures supply. The relational premium adjusts strategically to market-level supply shocks in a manner consistent with maximising the joint payoffs for the pair of traders. This efficient adaptation ensures the sustainability of relationships despite varying market demand and supply.

title: On the empirical relevance of the exchange rate as a shock absorber at the zero lower bound
abstract: The New Keynesian argument is that flexible exchange rate regimes cannot stabilize cyclical developments at the ZLB, as the real exchange rate appreciates in response to adverse demand shocks. We estimate the effects of a negative domestic demand shock on the real exchange rate for the euro area vis-à-vis the United States, Canada, and Japan by state-dependent sign-restricted local projection methods. We find a real depreciation when interest rates are not at the ZLB, but also when they are. The exchange rate can accommodate considerable variations in output, confirming its shock-absorbing capacity away and during ZLB episodes. The stabilizing role of the exchange rate is accompanied by a significant expansion of the ECB’s balance sheet at the ZLB, while it remained unaffected in the non-ZLB period.

title: AVERAGE TREATMENT EFFECT LOCALIZATION: PROJECTION METHODS IN SYNTHETIC CONTROL
abstract: Many real-world policies and business interventions require assessing short-term effects to inform timely decisions, even though most causal inference methods focus on long-term average treatment effects. In this article, we introduce average treatment effect localization (ATEL), which captures localized, short-term policy impacts in panel data settings with a single treated unit and provides early indicators of policy impact. To accommodate both time-varying and nonlinear effects of observed and unobserved covariates, we propose a nonparametric model for untreated outcome, interpreted as a time-varying factor model via sieve approximation. Estimating the time-varying factor model is challenging due to the boundary bias and identification. Our estimation method based on diversified projection can effectively address these issues. We develop an asymptotic distribution theory to facilitate inference for the ATEL estimator. In an empirical application, we apply our proposed methodology to assess the impact of right-to-carry laws on violent crime rate.

title: Discussion of “Sex and the City: Demographics, Spatial Sorting, and the Marriage Market”
abstract: ABSTRACT Discussion of Fang, Huang, Wang, and Yang (2026).

title: AccES: A Framework for Predicting Building‐Level Loss of Accessibility to Essential Services Post‐Disasters Based on Publicly Available Information
Interactions Among Three‐Tier Factors of Community Safety Resilience: A Dual‐Perspective Analysis
abstract: ABSTRACT Enhancing community safety resilience (CSR) is critical for sustainable urban development. Disregarding the complex interactions among CSR factors may cause imbalanced resilience building, limiting a community's capacity to respond to uncertain disasters. This study aims to identify principal CSR factors and examine their interaction mechanisms in the context of Chinese urban communities. We identified 101 factors spanning government, community, and personal tiers. Their interactions were assessed via expert elicitation and analyzed using directed weighted network theory and a modified susceptible‐infectious‐recovered model. The factor interaction network exhibits a sparse, highly modular, core‐periphery structure with small‐world and scale‐free properties. Community‐level governance and infrastructure, together with personal‐level physiological and psychological factors, serve as both hubs and intermediary bridges. Government‐level top‐level design, organizational leadership, and support and investment act as primary drivers, critical in initiating and mitigating risk propagation. Fundamental risk mitigation, especially under dual perturbations, depends on government action, whereas community‐level factors are vital for localized response. These findings provide an analytical foundation for prioritizing interventions and designing system‐sensitive strategies to enhance CSR.

title: The Distinct Roles of Anger and Hope in PFAS Risk Processing: Integrating Mixed Emotional Appeals and Efficacy Information into the EPPM
Socio‐Technical Risk‐Informed AI‐Driven Automation Trustworthiness Evaluation (ST‐RATE): Part 1‐Conceptualization
abstract: ABSTRACT The growing integration of artificial intelligence (AI)‐driven technologies into nuclear power plant (NPP) operations and maintenance holds significant potential to enhance safety, operational efficiency, and reliability. However, deploying such AI‐driven automation technologies in high‐consequence settings requires a rigorous, traceable, and risk‐informed evaluation of their trustworthiness. Although researchers across various domains have proposed definitions and metrics for AI‐driven automation trustworthiness, no agreed‐upon formal or quantitative method exists that is suitable for the highly regulated nuclear sector. To address this gap, this paper, the first in a two‐part series, presents three contributions: (I) a cross‐disciplinary literature review that categorizes existing definitions and evaluation methodologies for AI‐driven automation trustworthiness and identifies their inherent limitations with respect to applicability in the nuclear domain; (II) develops a new definition of AI‐driven automation trustworthiness as “the degree of confidence that the AI‐driven automation system will function as expected across its conditions of use” to address the limitations identified in Contribution I; and (III) building on the new definition, conceptualizes the Socio‐Technical Risk‐informed AI‐driven Automation Trustworthiness Evaluation (ST‐RATE) methodology, grounded in three foundational pillars: (a) risk‐informed performance expectations, (b) socio‐technical context across operational conditions, and (c) uncertainty‐based trustworthiness evaluation. While developed primarily for the nuclear domain, the definition and ST‐RATE methodology has the potential to be adapted for other safety‐critical domains with appropriate modifications. The ST‐RATE methodological framework is operationalized and demonstrated through an AI‐driven automated firewatch case study in a companion paper (Companion paper Part 2, 2025). ST‐RATE is the first‐of‐its‐kind methodology that enables risk‐informed and uncertainty‐based quantification of trustworthiness despite limited empirical data and without over‐reliance on subjective expert judgment, addressing the key limitations of existing approaches identified in the literature review.

title: Aim high or play safe? Commitment, prosocial incentives, and goal setting
abstract: Abstract We examine how behavioral incentives affect goal setting and performance when individuals choose their own goals. Using a model with reference-dependent preferences and effort cost uncertainty, we predict that commitment mechanisms improve performance by inducing more conservative goal selection to increase goal attainability, whereas prosocial incentives enhance performance by increasing motivation. Two experiments confirm these predictions. In an online real-effort task, soft commitment reduced goals relative to controls but significantly increased performance, whereas prosocial incentives, in the form of charitable donations contingent on goal achievement, preserved goal ambition and improved performance without lowering goals. A four-week field experiment in which students set daily exercise goals yields similar results: commitment lowered goals while increasing performance, whereas prosocial incentives maintained ambitious goals and improved outcomes. These effects persisted throughout the experiment. These findings highlight that, under effort cost uncertainty, commitment and prosocial incentives improve performance through distinct mechanisms.

title: Gender Justice Activism and Strategic Abeyance in Post-2020 Hong Kong
abstract: This article examines the post-2020 transformation of Hong Kong’s gender justice movement amid autocratization. Drawing on 20 in-depth interviews and public materials, it develops a profile-shaped framework of abeyance to demonstrate that political risks and adaptive possibilities are distributed unevenly across civil society.
