The study argues that, as a lower-profile sector, gender justice activism faces less direct repression, retains institutional space unavailable to higher-profile pro-democracy movement, and absorbs redirected civic energy. It then demonstrates how activists adapt through self-limitation, arena shifts, and reorganizing structures to exploit this tolerable position. This delicate navigation allows them to remain active without being reclassified as threats in the eyes of authorities. The findings offer broader insights into authoritarian governance, contemporary civil society survival, and movement adaptation in non-democratic contexts.

title: Risk and Resilience: Managing Public Transit Contracting During a Disrupted Market
abstract: This study examines the contracting behavior of U.S. transit agencies during the COVID-19 pandemic to assess two competing predictions: (1) New Public Management expects increased contracting to achieve cost savings and shift risk, and (2) institutional inertia predicts stability due to structural barriers. Our findings demonstrate overwhelming support for institutional inertia. Despite confirming the pandemic was a major disruption, contracting behavior and perceptions remained stable. The mechanism for this inertia is that contracting is not associated with improved operational outcomes, suggesting the absence of economic incentives for change. The stability observed reflects externally insulated resilience of core public management structures.

title: The paradox of experience: Public procurement and delivery timelines across digital solution types
abstract: Lengthy public procurement processes can slow the delivery of essential public services. While most research on procurement duration has focused on infrastructure and public works, digital solutions now play a central role in how public services are delivered. This study uses survival analysis to examine the time required to award contracts, execute them, and report project delivery, drawing on 40,991 digitalization projects carried out by 7838 Italian municipalities under the Next Generation EU program. We proxy experience in procuring digital solutions with historical procurement expenditure and show that its relationship with project duration varies by solution type. Higher prior activity is associated with faster timelines for standardized connections to centrally managed platforms, but with slower timelines for cloud migration and citizen experience projects, where implementation requires more local configuration. Results for interoperability projects are inconclusive. At the median, interquartile increases in prior activity span about 118 days between citizen experience and digital notice projects, or about 22% of median completion duration. These findings challenge the common assumption that procurement experience necessarily speeds up project delivery. Prior activity may reflect both reusable organizational routines and the installed base created by earlier projects, although our data do not directly measure either mechanism. Historical procurement expenditure on digital solutions should therefore not be treated as a general indicator of readiness. Program managers should consider solution category when assessing readiness and setting or monitoring timelines.

title: A Public Philosophy for Public Administration in Times of Democratic Crisis
abstract: ABSTRACT Public administration is at the center of the global democratic crisis. Meeting this challenge requires more than managerial and analytic competence—it requires a public philosophy grounded in the first principles of democratic ethos. We offer such a philosophy, drawing on four seminal thinkers whose concepts reflect the conditions public administrators face in times of democratic crisis. Judith Shklar's liberalism of fear establishes a negative obligation to refuse cruelty and resist its institutionalization. Alasdair MacIntyre's internal goods of practice create a positive obligation to cultivate virtue and protect the integrity of administrative practice. Isaiah Berlin's agony of choice obligates administrators to acknowledge irreducible value conflicts and their consequential impact on democratic life. Hannah Arendt's enlarged mentality provides a framework for thinking across perspectives so that judgment under conflict becomes democratically defensible. Together, these concepts form a public philosophy for public administration with practical significance for administrative judgment, organizational culture, and institutional courage.

title: Is Public Sector a Better Place for Moms to Work? Exploring Sector Difference in Child Penalties on Women
abstract: ABSTRACT With commonly stabler and more flexible working environment, is public sector a better place for moms to work? Theorizing child penalties from sector difference perspective, we argue that childbirth may cause less gender gaps in unemployment and earnings but greater gender disparities in working time commitments in the public sector since job stability and family‐friendliness may form gender norms that depreciate women's work in the public sector. We test our hypotheses by employing event study designs using data from China Family Panel Studies (2010–2022). We found that women public employees experienced smaller child penalties in unemployment and earnings while greater child penalties in working hours than private counterparts, which can be explained by greater family responsibilities and spousal depreciation of women's jobs after childbirth. This paper advances theories of gender equity in public administration by proposing distinct child penalties in the public sector that challenges conventional beliefs.

title: Coproduction Willingness and Citizen Satisfaction: Evidence From an Extended Expectancy‐Disconfirmation Model
abstract: ABSTRACT Citizen satisfaction in coproduction contexts is crucial for public service governance. Drawing on the Expectancy Disconfirmation Model, this study uses survey‐based quadratic response surface analysis to examine how congruence between expectations and performance relates to satisfaction and whether coproduction willingness conditions these associations. The results indicate that (1) satisfaction is higher as both expectations and performance are higher, and is higher when performance exceeds expectations; (2) coproduction willingness weakens the positive association between performance and satisfaction, whereas its moderating role on the expectation‐satisfaction association is not significant; (3) when coproduction willingness is considered, satisfaction shows an inverted U‐shaped nonlinear association with jointly increasing expectations and performance. Viewed through the Expectancy‐Disconfirmation Model, these findings provide bounded empirical evidence regarding the association between coproduction willingness and satisfaction evaluations in public service settings.

title: How to Get Published in a Leading Public Administration Journal
abstract: ABSTRACT Many academic journals are currently experiencing an exponential growth in submissions and consequently the standards required to publish are becoming exceptionally high. As one of the oldest public administration journals, Public Administration and Development has always adapted and changed to reflect the latest developments in practice and in academic publishing. But throughout all of this it remains the only public administration journal that specialises in non‐Western contexts. In maintaining our high academic standards, we must therefore ensure that we do not create unfair or inequitable barriers to publishing for academics based in low‐ and medium‐income countries. In this editorial we aim to shine some light on the publishing process and provide further guidance to authors, particularly early career academics, on how to get published in a leading journal such as PAD . We also take this opportunity to update our authors and readers on the latest changes to our journal in response to the changing publishing landscape.

title: Why Do Public Employees Lose Motivation to Serve? Psychological Contract Breach, Psychological Distance, and Public Service Motivation
abstract: ABSTRACT Why do some people experience a decline in public service motivation (PSM) after entering the public sector? Using construal level theory, we explain this self‐demotivation phenomenon by examining the effect of psychological contract breach on PSM and open the black box of related psychological mechanisms. A mediation model is proposed using a sample of 233 Chinese public sector employees and empirically tested using partial least squares‐structural equation modeling (PLS‐SEM) and necessary condition analysis (NCA). The results show that psychological contract breach is negatively associated with PSM and that temporal and spatial distance partially explain this association. The analysis also indicates a partial mediating effect of temporal and spatial distance. Contrary to expectations, the mediating role of social distance and hypotheticality is insignificant.

title: Citizen‐to‐Citizen Interaction and Information Quality in E‐Government: The Role of Cognitive Social Capital
abstract: ABSTRACT Although citizen‐to‐citizen (C2C) interaction is increasingly embedded in e‐government use, the role of social interaction and its relationship with peer‐driven information flows remain largely underexplored. This study examines how online citizen‐to‐citizen social capital is associated with citizens’ perceived quality of e‐government‐related information shared within informal online peer networks. Drawing on survey data from welfare‐service users in secondary (Tier‐2 and Tier‐3) Indian cities, this study finds that structural and relational social capital are positively interrelated with cognitive social capital, but they are not directly associated with perceived information quality. Only cognitive social capital is significantly associated with a higher perceived quality of peer‐shared e‐government information. These results suggest that network connectedness and interpersonal trust may facilitate information flow without necessarily improving perceived information quality. Instead, shared understanding, communicative clarity, and interpretive alignment are more closely associated with citizens’ evaluations of the reliability, timeliness, and usefulness of government‐related information circulating through peer networks. The study contributes to digital government research by conceptualizing civic interpretive capacity as an explanatory lens for understanding how citizens evaluate peer‐shared e‐government information in contexts of uneven administrative communication.

title: Decentralization as an anticorruption strategy: does revenue autonomy make a difference?
abstract: This study investigates how revenue autonomy is associated with documented municipal corruption risk, distinguishing between own-source tax and non-tax revenues. Drawing on public administration theories of decentralization, it adopts a meso-level analysis of Italian medium-to-large municipalities and relies on an event-based indicator derived from legally mandated anticorruption reports. The empirical strategy combines dynamic correlated random-effects logit, dynamic random-effects probit, and fixed-effects logit models, complemented by sensitivity analyses simulating under-reporting scenarios. Results indicate that higher levels of both tax and non-tax revenue autonomy are negatively associated with documented corruption risk. Tax autonomy shows stronger associations where political competition is higher, whereas the non-tax revenue pattern is more consistent with a service-based responsiveness logic. These findings, observed in the Italian municipal context, suggest that revenue autonomy is not a uniform anticorruption safeguard but an institutional feature whose relevance depends on revenue composition, accountability conditions, municipal capacity, and reporting practices.

title: From Public to Private Governance, and Back—Eco‐Modulation as De‐Privatization in Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR)
abstract: ABSTRACT The European Union is advancing circular economy policies, aimed at reducing the environmental impacts of products across their life‐cycles. Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) exemplifies this strategy. It privatizes the end‐of‐life management of products to their producers, seeking thereby to incentivize the producer to design environmentally more sustainable products. However, EPR has failed to deliver significant improvements in product design. This article examines the EU's attempts to strengthen eco‐design in EPR through ‘eco‐modulation’. Applying the theory of competence‐and‐control, the article argues that the introduction of eco‐modulation will destabilize the public‐private balance in EPR, shifting EPR back from private towards public governance. This de‐privatization is expected to refine EPR's role within the EU's policy mix. Our findings thus offer insights for the development of EPR‐related circular economy policies, while also contributing to theories of privatization.

title: Eradicating or Managing Homelessness? A New Framework for Comparative Policy Framing
abstract: This article develops a six-dimensional framework for comparative policy framing and applies it to homelessness policy in England and Finland. Drawing on interviews with policymakers and practitioners, it shows that England’s approach is organised around a management-oriented frame centred on prevention, legal thresholds, and resource allocation, whereas Finland adopts an eradication-oriented frame grounded in universalism, housing as a right, and state responsibility. The findings demonstrate how interpretative frames structure policy ambition, institutional alignment, and implementation trajectories within contrasting welfare states.

title: The Policy Sciences in Africa: Historical Legacies, Institutional Variation and the Evidence Agenda
abstract: Evidence-informed policymaking (EIP), consistent with the policy sciences’ aim of advancing human dignity, offers a lens for assessing the field’s development in Africa. This paper uses comparative historical and critical policy analysis to examine how divergent national trajectories have shaped capacities for policy-relevant knowledge. It argues that colonialism and structural adjustment programmes unevenly eroded local policy institutions and marginalized indigenous knowledge across West, East and Southern Africa. Consequently, dominant Western policy theories inadequately capture Africa’s complex governance realities. Centring African voices and knowledge, the paper calls for a more inclusive, context-sensitive and globally relevant policy science.

title: Value Sovereignty and the Limits of Democratic Delegation
abstract: ABSTRACT Why do some forms of delegation to non‐majoritarian institutions generate persistent democratic controversy while others, equally insulated from political control, do not? The Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank, for instance, are alike on the standard measures—authorization, accountability, expertise, and performance—yet are judged differently in democratic terms, a difference those measures cannot explain. This paper argues that the missing factor is who retains the authority to revise the criteria by which an institution resolves value conflicts. I call this condition value sovereignty, and treat it not as something a delegation simply has or lacks but as a matter of degree: the further the power to revise an institution's operative criteria has moved from ordinary political reach, the less value sovereignty it retains. This yields a single scale, delegation depth, on which the two banks fall at different points—the Federal Reserve's mandate, revisable by ordinary legislation, near one end, and the European Central Bank's treaty‐entrenched objective further along—and on which systems built to govern open‐ended domains, including advanced artificial intelligence, mark the far limit, where the authority to revise the criteria passes to the delegated system itself. The framework thus supplies a criterion that authorization, accountability, and performance leave unnamed, and orders both established institutions and emerging ones. Related Articles Agoba, Abel Mawuko, Yakubu Awudu Sare, Ebenezer Bugri Anarfo, and Christian Tsekpoe. 2023. “The Push for Financial Inclusion in Africa: Should Central Banks be Wary of Political Institutional Quality and Literacy Rates?” Politics & Policy 51, no. 1: 114–136. https://doi.org/10.1111/polp.12514 . Asongu, Simplice A., Joseph Nnanna, and Vanessa S. Tchamyou. 2021. “Finance, Institutions, and Private Investment in Africa.” Politics & Policy 49, no. 2: 309–351. https://doi.org/10.1111/polp.12395 . Scarlato, Margherita, and Giorgio d'Agostino. 2019. “The Political Dimension of Cash Transfers in Latin America and Sub‐Saharan Africa: A Comparative Perspective.” Politics & Policy 47, no. 6: 1125–1155. https://doi.org/10.1111/polp.12332 .

title: Combining digital and green technologies in regions: How to close the gap with respect to the frontier?
abstract: This paper focuses on the combination of green and digital technologies at the regional level. Using patent data, we put forward an original measurement of the regional speed of green-digital (i.e. twin) combination: the temporal distance between the time at which a combination is realised for the first time in the frontier region and the time at which this same combination is accomplished in the focal region. We proceed by investigating the drivers and the technological impact related to this speed. We find that the speed of combination is enhanced by dealing with broad and diverse twin technologies. The speed at which the gap is closed, also crucially depends on the interdependencies between green and digital domains, captured by the overlap in their knowledge bases. Counterintuitively, the longer the combination paths, the faster the region combines green and digital technologies. This finding is then rationalised further looking at the policy and network characteristics. Finally, we find that the earlier the combination happens, the greater is likely to be the impact on subsequent inventions, but only for granted patents. Overall, these results are discussed in terms of policy recommendations, given the high attention placed by policymakers on the twin transition.

title: Correction to: The university third mission: addressing the refugee crisis caused by war in Ukraine
Teaching the past, informing the present? School history education and attitudes toward foreign countries
abstract: Abstract How does school history education emphasizing past grievances with other countries impact attitudes toward conflict and cooperation with the countries today? We examine this question using original data from 34 classrooms across 17 high schools in Seoul, South Korea. We first test whether exposure to anti‐Japanese content in school history education negatively impacts students' attitudes toward cooperation with Japan. We then compare how the attitudes of students educated with a more pro‐US textbook differ from those using a more anti‐US one. We find that school history education influenced what historical events students believed as “facts” and their evaluation of historical events. However, the effect on students' historical memories did not by itself automatically translate into corresponding attitudes toward present‐day Japan or the United States. Our findings offer various implications for studies on international rivalries and historical memories, as well as for debates on the political effects of school education.

title: The Idea of a Counter-Structure: Rethinking Collective Action against Climate Injustice
abstract: This article argues that addressing the structural injustices of climate change requires rethinking collective action. Disruptive and prefigurative politics are often treated as separate collective action repertoires, but I argue that a just energy transition requires that they work in tandem. To capture this interaction, I propose the idea of “counter-structural” collective action, in which disruptive protest creates windows of opportunity that prefigurative alternatives can then fill. Through analysis of two UK climate movements, Transition Towns (TTs) and Camps for Climate Action (CCA), I show how activists reconfigure structural elements to build new, carbon-free social and political forms. The theory of counter-structural action provides a framework for assessing the empirical cases. The cases, in turn, illustrate a broader conception of collective action that better reflects the social theory grounding structural injustice. Together, the theory and cases support the dual aims of climate justice: challenging fossil-fuel path dependence and advancing egalitarianism.

title: When Can Clientelism Serve Democratic Ends? A Democratic Theory of Distributive Politics
abstract: This article employs normative democratic theory to examine a counterintuitive suggestion raised repeatedly by empirical scholars of clientelism: namely, that practices of particularistic exchange might sometimes serve democratic ends. Certainly, most particularistic practices are widely agreed to undermine democracy, on both intrinsic and instrumental grounds. Yet some observers resist blanket condemnation—and in particular, many highlight the redeeming democratic virtues of certain practices that seem to facilitate collective organization among disempowered groups. Drawing on “realist” approaches to democratic theory, we vindicate this basic insight while clarifying its scope conditions. Countervailing power is a crucial democratic priority, and programmatic methods of promoting it sometimes face serious obstacles: as when clientelist practices are deeply entrenched, or incumbents capture the tools of programmatic competition. Under such conditions, we conclude, democracy-seeking leaders may justifiably employ particularistic practices to promote countervailing power—but only if they respect five constraints tethering them strictly to that goal.

title: How the cultural backlash fails: an investigation into the link between social conservatism and far-right voting in European electorates
Rally around the Liberals or a conservative pushback? Understanding the Trump effect in the 2025 Canadian federal election
abstract: While the influence of Donald Trump's second presidency on the 2025 Canadian federal election is widely acknowledged, the specific mechanisms of this influence remain underexplored. This research note moves beyond asking whether Trump mattered to explain how he mattered, and uses the Canadian case to ask when foreign leaders shape vote choice in other democracies. Using original post-electoral survey data ( N = 508), we test two complementary mechanisms: a “rally-round-the-flag” effect, whereby voters who perceived Trump as a salient threat increased support for the incumbent Liberal Party, and an “anti-Trump conservative pushback,” whereby voters who perceived the opposition Conservative Party as similar to Trump were less likely to support it. We find strong evidence for both mechanisms. The results are robust to region controls and post-stratification weighting, and the pushback holds among left-leaning, centrist, and right-leaning voters alike. We argue that a foreign leader becomes electorally consequential when his actions impose direct costs on another country and when domestic parties can be tied to his political brand.

title: Powered by (discrete) emotions? The consequences of affective polarization for self-censorship and outgroup silencing
abstract: Abstract Amid ongoing debates about political polarization in Western Democracies, this study investigates the role of affective polarization in the context of practices related to political discourse. In doing so, it moves beyond generalized affective polarization and delves into discrete negative emotions (fear, disgust, and anger), examining how they relate to the willingness to engage in self-censorship and the belief in the importance of silencing others, i.e., the respective political outgroup. Findings from a quota-based online survey conducted in autumn 2024 in Germany ( N = 1,918) reveal that the effects of affective polarization vary depending on the underlying emotion: fear of the political outgroup is linked to an increased willingness to self-censor. In contrast, anger is associated with a reduced willingness to self-censor, while all three negative emotions are connected to a higher belief in the importance to silence the political outgroup. These results underscore the critical role of discrete emotions in affective polarization, offering nuanced insights that extend beyond generalized dislike. In addition, they provide valuable insights into how affective polarization may threaten democratic values.

title: Affective geographies of the will to fight: disappointment, hope, and dignity among environmental defenders in the Colombian Llanos
“Russia's border doesn't end anywhere”: Imitation of homeland-making in the nationalist rhetoric of Vladimir Putin
Wait for It: Why Authoritarians Reshuffle Ruling Coalitions After Elections
abstract: This article asks whether elections, even if they are not free and fair, might still have important consequences for authoritarian ruling coalitions, testing the theory that dictators avoid destabilizing their coalition before an election, but can afford to do this once the vote has passed. Disregarding the competitiveness and integrity of elections, the post-electoral period may serve as a face-saving time for resignations and as an opportunity for promotions or other cabinet changes, which autocrats can leverage to manage elites. Examining panel data on authoritarian regimes that held presidential elections in which the incumbent retained office between 1967 and 2023, I find that cabinet turnover is significantly higher in the period following elections. By exploiting the quasi-exogenous timing of scheduled elections and multiple robustness checks, the analysis shows that elections trigger elite reshuffling rather than merely coinciding with it.

title: “We need the right kind of people in this neighborhood”: racial motivation in opposition to new housing construction
abstract: Abstract How we measure racial bias matters. Previous literature demonstrates that direct questioning leads to unreliable responses. Scholars have thus developed a number of techniques to uncover racial bias without cuing a defensive response. I investigate the performance of text- and image-based factorial experiments in the case of racial motivation for opposition to new housing development relative to a more traditional list experiment. My results demonstrate that these often-used methods yield substantially different conclusions about the importance of racial biases in opposition to new housing construction. While the factorial experiments suggest little evidence of racial bias, the more traditional list experiment reveals that the potential for racial change in their neighborhood is a concern for a meaningful share of respondents.

title: PartySOME II: a dataset on parties’ issue agendas on social media
abstract: Understanding how parties compete by shaping agendas and promoting issue priorities is central to the study of party competition. Existing research relies heavily on manifestos, limiting analyses to election periods and offline contexts, while newer datasets lack cross-national breadth, temporal depth, and conceptual harmonisation. This study introduces a comparative dataset of party issue agendas derived from 4,600,000 social media posts for 219 parties across 18 European countries on Twitter, Facebook, and Instagram. Using supervised text classification aligned with the Comparative Agendas Project, monthly measures of salience over more than a decade are generated, providing conceptually standardised, cross-platform, and cross-nationally comparable indicators of issue attention. Our measures are validated through comparisons over time, across party families, major political shocks, and existing databases, and illustrate the dataset’s leverage by showing how mainstream parties’ immigration attention is associated with radical-right support gains. This dataset substantially expands the empirical infrastructure for studying dynamic issue competition.

title: Terrorism and Altruistic Giving: Evidence from Child Sponsorship
abstract: We study how terrorist attacks targeting educational institutions affect private development aid through child sponsorship. Conceptually, terrorist events may increase sponsorship by signaling greater need or reduce it if affected communities are seen as less effective destinations to support. We combine global administrative data from Plan International on child sponsorship across 50 countries over the 2008-2018 period, aggregated at the Primary Sampling Unit (PSU) level, with geocoded terrorism events from the Global Terrorism Database. Our core specification focuses on attacks against educational institutions within 20 km of each PSU. We estimate the causal effect using a heterogeneity-robust difference-in-differences approach suited to staggered, non-absorbing treatments. We find that attacks on educational institutions reduce the share of sponsored children by about 3 percentage points, a 4 percent decline relative to the mean. Back-of-the-envelope calculations suggest this corresponds to funding losses of approximately US$615,000 across affected communities over the study period. Since sponsorship is geographically targeted, these losses fall on the specific communities, underscoring the need to buffer local development funding against security shocks.

title: Heterogeneous patience, population growth, and wealth accumulation
abstract: Abstract We study a neoclassical growth model with population growth and heterogeneous agents. The model can be interpreted as either a Ramsey model with heterogeneous discounting and entry of new agents with zero endowments or an OLG model with infinitely-lived agents with different discount factors. We prove that, in the unique stationary equilibrium, agents other than the most patient may hold capital. Introducing public debt, a labor income tax, or a capital subsidy allows more agent types to save, reducing inequality among agents with different discount factors while increasing inequality among agents with the same discount factor entered in different periods.

title: Massive Open Online Courses and Labor Market Outcomes: Evidence from Colombia
abstract: Abstract This paper studies the impact of MOOC certificates on labor market outcomes using a Coursera initiative that offered free certificates during the COVID-19 pandemic. Although eligibility for free certificates was randomized, course completion rates were low-only 6.2% of eligible participants completed at least one course-so we rely on an event-study design to estimate the effects of receiving a certificate. The results show that MOOC certificates increases formal employment by about 5 percentage points, with larger impacts among participants who were not employed at baseline and those from low-income households, and no clear differences by gender. These gains are concentrated in employment at larger firms and in economic sectors aligned with the course content. Overall, while MOOCs have the potential to improve employment outcomes, additional interventions appear necessary to increase course completion rates.

title: Correction to: You Cannot Force Me Into Caregiving: Paternity Leave and the Child Penalty
Gambling for Re-election
abstract: Abstract We show that gambling-style behaviour is important in politics: politicians ‛gamble for re-election‚ in the context of a political leader selection. We exploit unique access to leaked information on MPs' individual decisions in the 2021 leadership election of Germany's centre-right parties. MPs are more likely to vote for a riskier candidate when facing lower re-election chances. These results match the predictions derived from our model of rational risk-taking. Gambling for re-election shows that MPs trade off leaders' expected quality against their riskiness. It provides a new explanation for intra-party dissent, and rationalises why parties may choose low quality leaders.

title: Remembering Cornelia Staritz: contributions to global production network and crisis research agendas
Income redistribution, preventive care, and longevity
Beliefs undermining protective action against smart speaker privacy risks: perceived benefits, trust in the manufacturer, and nothing to hide beliefs
abstract: The uptake of smart speakers in our homes is steadily increasing. While bringing convenience and access to information, they also bring substantial risks to our privacy. In this study, we investigated which factors undermine taking privacy protective action, drawing on people’s beliefs related to smart speaker privacy identified in earlier qualitative studies. Based on the synthesized analysis of qualitative studies, we hypothesized that perceived benefits of smart speakers, trust in the manufacturer, and nothing to hide beliefs reduce protective action, at least partially mediated by perceived privacy risks. In addition, we examined whether these same beliefs, partially mediated via perceived risks, also affect feeling powerlessness about protecting smart speaker data. To test our hypotheses, we conducted a scenario study, in which participants were asked to imagine receiving a smart speaker as a gift and install it. We recruited a convenience sample (N= 267), consisting of both current smart speaker owners and non-owners. The findings derived from structural equation modelling supported our hypotheses that perceived privacy risks is positively related to protection intention, as well as to feeling powerless. Furthermore, in line with our hypotheses, perceived benefits of the smart speaker, trust in the manufacturer and nothing to hide beliefs were found to undermine protection intention, partially or fully mediated by perceived privacy risks. Finally, trust in the manufacturer also significantly lowered feeling powerless, partially mediated by perceived privacy risks. Overall, these findings offer valuable insights for designing interventions that aim to increase protective action taking against the privacy risks of smart home devices, while attempting not to increase powerlessness.

title: Transaction Hazards Through Ideological Filters: How CEO Political Ideology Influences Vertical Integration Decisions
abstract: Why do firms facing similar transaction environments adopt different boundary structures? Transaction cost theory (TCT) predicts governance choices based on transaction hazards, but persistent heterogeneity in vertical integration suggests that such efficiency-based explanations are incomplete. We examine whether CEO political ideology is associated with systematic variation in firm boundary decisions. Drawing on research on political ideology and strategic leadership, we argue that ideological orientations shape how executives evaluate and prioritize governance trade-offs. Using a panel of 1,198 U.S. public firms from 2001 to 2020 and a firm fixed-effects design exploiting CEO successions, we find that firms led by more conservative CEOs exhibit higher levels of vertical integration. This relationship weakens when asset specificity is high and when industries are more concentrated but is not amplified by demand volatility. Our findings suggest that firm boundaries reflect not only transaction conditions but also systematic differences in executive decision-making.

title: The Politics of the “Non-Political”: A Conceptual Review
abstract: Recent literature has documented a growing entanglement between political processes and many nonpolitical entities. This calls into question the traditional presupposition of politics as a self-contained sphere, highlighting the need to clarify how the conceptual relationship between the political and the nonpolitical has been established. In line with a relational understanding of politics, we provide a boundary analysis by looking at the “non-political” labeling in 140 empirical studies published in political science and communication journals. Two major conceptual treatments are identified: categorical, treating the “non-political” as an inherent, exclusive feature; and contextual, viewing it as a temporary, transformative state. Intellectual traditions, theoretical orientations, methodological standards, and rhetorical norms in academic knowledge production may explain why this boundary has been constructed in such different ways. We call for a more active reconciliation between these treatments, and argue that the nonpolitical, as well as (de)politicization, should be recognized as a meaningful analytical lens. It signifies a relational stance against the explicit, institutionalized politics in political communication studies, offering an indirect yet heuristically productive response to the question of what the political is.

title: Legalising State Capitalism: Reconfiguring SOE Governance in China
abstract: How should China’s contemporary State-owned enterprise (SOE) governance reforms be understood: as the politicisation of corporate governance, or as a deeper transformation in State Capitalism? This article addresses this question by shifting attention from policy discourse to the emerging legislative architecture of SOE governance under Xi Jinping. Drawing on doctrinal analysis and case studies of reform implementation, it shows that recent reforms have restructured external governance through delegated State-owned capital management and ownership-mediated governance centred on State-owned Capital Investment and Operation Companies, while recasting internal governance through a dual legislative track combining Company Law and Party rules. It argues that these developments constitute the legal construction of a hybrid governance order in which Party leadership and corporate governance are institutionally differentiated yet coordinated.

title: Government Capability, Benevolence, and Public Trust in Cyber Risk Governance: Evidence from a Survey Experiment on Telecom Fraud in China
abstract: This study examines how government capability and benevolence shape public trust and whether risk intensity changes the relative salience of these evaluations. A 2 × 2 × 2 between-subjects survey experiment was conducted with 683 participants. Government capability and benevolence were manipulated as high or low, and the risk scenario was varied between low-risk and high-risk conditions. Government trust was measured as the change from pre-test to post-test. Results show that government capability had a stronger effect on trust than government benevolence. The two dimensions also worked in combination: the high-capability/high-benevolence condition showed the only positive mean change in trust, while weakness in either dimension reduced trust. High-risk scenarios attenuated the trust advantage of capability overall, but follow-up analyses showed that this attenuation was concentrated when government benevolence was low. The findings contribute to public administration research by showing how citizens evaluate government trustworthiness in cyber risk governance and by highlighting the importance of administrative capacity, the limits of benevolence without delivery capacity, and the need for expectation management in risk communication.

title: Tax administration beyond enforcement tools: Political settlements, bureaucratic discretion, and fiscal capacity in the Global South
abstract: Tax administration is central to fiscal capacity and public accountability in the Global South, yet enforcement is often treated as a technical problem of compliance, information, and administrative tools. This structured critical review argues that enforcement is shaped jointly by organisational capacity, bureaucratic discretion, informal institutions, and political power. Drawing on Political Settlements Theory and comparative public administration, it develops an enforcement-pipeline framework that locates political exposure across sequential stages from discrepancy detection and audit selection, through audit execution, assessment, sanctioning, appeals, and settlement, to post-audit follow-up. The framework elevates political economy from a background condition to observable administrative mechanisms. Evidence from Africa, Asia, Latin America, and the Middle East shows that audits, third-party reporting, digital data, and algorithmic tools can strengthen compliance, but their effects often depend on who enters the enforcement system, how discretion is exercised, and whether authorities follow through consistently against politically influential taxpayers. The review further shows that digitalisation can reduce some forms of discretion while relocating others into data construction, risk scoring, case selection, overrides, and appeals. Future research should therefore examine enforcement stage by stage, combine causal designs with process tracing and frontline evidence, and test where political exposure alters administrative treatment. For policy, the findings point to the importance of protecting audit-selection integrity, limiting opaque overrides, strengthening appeal and accountability mechanisms, and designing digital reforms around institutional safeguards rather than technological capability alone.

title: Decentralised administrative reform without authority redistribution: Pseudo-collaborative governance and public service innovation in subnational Indonesia
abstract: Decentralised administrative reform is expected to strengthen collaboration and public service innovation, yet less is known about what happens when collaborative arrangements expand without a corresponding redistribution of strategic authority. This study examines this problem through a comparative qualitative analysis of flood governance in three subnational jurisdictions in Southeast Sulawesi, Indonesia, using documentary evidence and 45 semi-structured interviews. Across the three cases, reform expanded cross-sector coordination, participation, and adaptive administrative practices, while authority over priorities, resources, and consequential decisions remained comparatively concentrated. This configuration is conceptualised as pseudo-collaborative governance, in which collaboration becomes operationally consequential without corresponding authority redistribution. One consequence is politically bounded public service innovation: meaningful administrative innovation whose transformative reach remains constrained by comparatively stable strategic authority relations. By separating innovation from governance transformation, the study identifies authority configuration as a political-institutional condition shaping how far decentralised reform can transform underlying governance relations.

title: Reply to Kettl: Public Administration and the Shifting Competing Forces of Accountability
abstract: ABSTRACT The accountability context for how public administrators operate has shifted markedly and has become much more volatile. This shift has placed new and some conflicting demands on public administrators to demonstrate their accountability to various competing governmental actors and has complicated policy and program implementation. The changed context, its causes, and the resultant challenges are analyzed and discussed. Questions are presented for public administration research to help public administrators deal with the challenges.

title: Achievements amidst asymmetries: power dynamics in Swedish civil-military collaboration - an exploratory conceptualization
abstract: This article examines how power dynamics are shaped and managed in day-to-day civil-military collaboration in Swedish total defence. Drawing on semi-structured interviews with key civilian and military actors involved in total defence planning, the article investigates the interplay of power asymmetries, the collaboration’s institutional and relational conditions and how collaborating actors perceive and manage asymmetries in practice. Using thematic analysis, we demonstrate that civil-military collaboration is characterized by imbalances in authority, resources and discursive legitimacy. The paper further sheds light on micro-level practices of power enactment and details how collaborating actors negotiate and manage power asymmetries. The main finding suggests that when the relatively more powerful actors engage in power moderating practices, which we conceptualize as Strategic Power Moderation (SPM), collaborations can perform productively despite asymmetrical relations. The results offer a nuanced understanding of how collaborations fare under conditions of power asymmetry and have implications for both research and practice.

title: Independent Agencies, Regulation‐Compliant Citizens? Evidence From a Survey Experiment on Vaccine Authorization in the EU
abstract: ABSTRACT The effectiveness of regulatory policy in many areas is contingent on citizens adhering to the scientific advice of regulatory bodies. This in turn depends on whether they perceive this advice as credible . One of the biggest threats to regulatory credibility is the concern that regulatory policy can be tainted by short‐term political interests. Consequently, regulation literature points to agency independence as a crucial resource to securing regulatory credibility, which in turn fosters citizen compliance. We test this assumption both observationally and experimentally in the case of the European Medicines Agency's (EMA) risk assessment for the first COVID‐19 vaccine—a prime example of reliance on credibility in regulation under conditions of controversy and concerns over political interference. We conducted a pre‐registered survey experiment with 4000 EU citizens from four countries timed shortly after the vaccine's approval and before its mass distribution. The results provide partial support that independence is beneficial to regulatory credibility and by extension, to regulatory compliance. Citizens who perceive the EMA as more independent found its risk assessment to be more credible and were more willing to take the vaccine. However, our experimental evidence is less conclusive. Thus, while independence might not in and of itself be a “silver bullet” to ensure regulatory credibility and compliance, it does play an important role, and its real‐life substantive significance would scale up considerably at population levels.

title: Executive Aggrandizement: Understanding the Silent Erosion of Democratic Constraints
abstract: ABSTRACT Studies of executive aggrandizement face a double measurement problem. Measures of aggrandizement may include institutions that constitute liberal democracy, while broad composites may treat substantively different executive practices as interchangeable. This article develops a measurement‐oriented classification that reduces direct overlap with the V‐Dem Liberal Democracy Index and compares distinct practices under common analytical rules. Using V‐Dem v15 data and a common sample of 17,404 country‐years across 179 countries from 1901 to 2024, country‐ and year‐fixed‐effects models estimate conditional within‐country associations for five lagged practices. Patronal‐distributive allocation, judicial purges, and personalist/mobilizational legitimation are negatively associated with liberal democracy. Executive corruption is consistently imprecise, whereas politicized administrative appointments are negative only in some specifications. Item‐level, restricted‐period, timing, and first‐difference analyses document practice heterogeneity but also show exceptional persistence; negative future‐lead estimates prevent a causal or sequential reading. The primary contribution is a bounded measurement and modeling strategy that preserves comparability while reducing, rather than claiming to eliminate, outcome overlap. Its linked theoretical contribution is a practice‐family account of executive aggrandizement: politically coordinated practices may coexist and remain interdependent without becoming interchangeable indicators or stages in a common causal sequence.

title: Regulatory Learning or Regulatory Privilege? How Sandbox Design Shapes the Governance Value of Experimental Regulation
abstract: ABSTRACT Regulatory sandboxes are controlled, time‐limited environments in which selected innovations are tested under regulatory supervision. This article asks how sandbox design can make selective experimentation capable of generating public regulatory value rather than regulatory privilege. It develops regulatory learning asymmetry to distinguish private, supervisory, and public regulatory learning and unequal distributions of access, information, learning, and benefits. A structured reading of public documents from five deliberately diverse FinTech and artificial intelligence cases illustrates a six‐element operational framework. The case material is not used to infer private or supervisory learning; it records only publication, generalization mechanisms, and documented uptake. The framework identifies a public‐learning configuration, a supervisory‐learning configuration that public documents cannot verify, and a regulatory‐privilege risk configuration. Market signaling is treated as a cross‐cutting dynamic. The article offers a bounded diagnostic for assessing whether case‐specific experience becomes contestable and institutionally usable knowledge.

title: How do middle-income states select vaccine partners? Projected capacity across sectors in Argentina
abstract: Abstract How do governments select vaccine-production partners when sector-specific capacity is incomplete? The COVID-19 pandemic made this question especially pressing, as vaccine nationalism constrained external supply and pushed middle-income states to expand domestic production despite unproven capacities. Tracing Argentina’s vaccine strategy from 2020 to 2022, this article develops the concept of projected capacity: a mechanism through which states infer potential capacity in one sector from firms’ resources, credibility, and structural position in another. Policymakers rely on proxies for vaccine-production capacity, including industrial legacies, firm–state familiarity, and alignment with health-sovereignty goals. State selection then provides firms with resources, alliances, and legitimacy, transforming projected capacity into sector-specific structural power. The article contributes to debates in political economy and public policy by showing that structural power is not only a pre-existing source of influence over the state; it can also be created through state decisions that select and support firms.

title: Selective universalism in Gulf social protection: a model family analysis of citizenship stratification in Qatar and Saudi Arabia
abstract: Abstract Gulf Cooperation Council welfare states remain absent from comparative welfare regime typologies, although they combine high social expenditure with extreme within-country stratification along citizenship lines. This paper applies the Model Family Approach to Qatar and Saudi Arabia, drawing on original programme-level data collected through the Minimum Income Protection Data Collection Template. Income packages are constructed for citizen and non-citizen households across five family profiles and four earnings levels. The protocol is extended with Monte Carlo simulation ( N = 10,000), Oaxaca–Blinder decomposition of a new Citizenship Welfare Gap indicator, Theil index decomposition and principal component analysis with hierarchical clustering. For families with children, the Citizenship Welfare Gap reaches 174 percentage points of the poverty line in Qatar and 111 in Saudi Arabia. Decomposition attributes 77.2 per cent of the Qatar gap to policy exclusion, whereas 66.0 per cent of the Saudi gap reflects cost-burden differentials. Cluster analysis positions Gulf systems in a separate regime space, distinct from social democratic, conservative-corporatist and productivist groupings. The findings supply programme-level evidence for a candidate regime category, the selective-universalist rentier configuration, offered as a hypothesis for testing across the full Gulf Cooperation Council rather than as a settled classification..

title: Governing knowledge through program architecture: strategic valorization, infrastructural integration, and the autonomy-steering settlement in Horizon Europe after 2027
Two-Faced Janus: Party System Closure and Democracy in Asia
Strategic alienation: The dynamics of group appeals in negative campaigning
abstract: Abstract This paper examines how political parties use social group appeals in negative campaigning. We argue that parties strategically target opponents with group-based attacks to portray them as failing key social groups. Using a novel dataset of Facebook and Twitter posts by parties in the UK (2016–2024), linked to voter perceptions of group representation from the British Election Study, we test whether such attacks are more likely when the sender party enjoys strong group-based credibility, or the target party is seen as a weak representative of the respective group, or both. We find no evidence for the former but strong support for the latter: parties disproportionately target rivals with poor reputations for representing specific groups, and especially so when the sender holds a reputational advantage. These findings advance our understanding of identity-driven party competition, showing that group-based attacks exploit opponents’ representational vulnerabilities rather than reinforce attackers’ own strength.

title: Professionalizing deliberation: a Social Network Analysis of UK climate mini-publics
abstract: Abstract Deliberative mini-publics have become an increasingly prominent feature of climate governance across advanced democracies. In the United Kingdom, their rapid expansion has been accompanied by the emergence of a professional deliberative field composed of facilitators, recruitment agencies, advisory bodies, expert witnesses, and network organizations. While existing scholarship debates whether professionalization enhances deliberative quality or introduces risks of marketization and elite capture, there is limited empirical evidence on how influence, standards, and authority are structured within this field. This article addresses that gap by mapping the actors involved in the design and delivery of UK climate mini-publics using qualitative social network analysis. The analysis examines how professional ties shape the circulation of expertise, standards, and backstage decision-making. The findings identify important and influential actors within the network, and their place within the wider industry. Here, we highlight the unequal concentration and clustering within the network. Rather than finding clear evidence of elite capture, the analysis reveals a form of structural dependency. Responsibility and authority are frequently transferred from commissioning bodies to facilitators, concentrating influence in a small number of actors. While these actors often act as safeguards of deliberative integrity, this reliance also introduces fragility, risks of stagnation, and uneven standards across the field. The article concludes that professionalization is neither inherently corrosive nor unproblematic. By foregrounding the networked architecture of deliberation, the study contributes a new perspective on how democratic innovations are governed, stabilized, and constrained in practice.

title: Geographic representation and information capacity in the European Union
abstract: The European Union prioritizes geographic representation of member states when recruiting staff. Many assume a trade-off between expertise and geographic representation, where the former increases capacity and the latter increases legitimacy. However, this article provides evidence that geographic representation can enhance bureaucratic information capacity. Using the European Commission’s Directorate-General for Economic and Financial Affairs as a case study, I provide evidence that increasing representation of bureaucrats from a member state is associated with higher accuracy in that state’s economic forecasts. This association decreases as member state representation within the Commission increases. These findings suggest that prioritizing geographic balance in the European Union need not come at the cost of information capacity, and may in fact improve it.

title: AI politics and regulation in the European Parliament: Ideological divides and policy convergence amid generative AI’s ascent
abstract: This study examines how European parliamentarians frame artificial intelligence in plenary speech. It also assesses how these frames map onto partisan divisions. Analyzing 666 interventions in the European Parliament (2014–2024), it shows that frames of artificial intelligence follow traditional ideological cleavages, with right-leaning parliamentarians deploying techno-optimistic frames that foreground economic innovation while left-leaning parliamentarians frame the technology through concerns about social risks and employment impacts. Thematic context also shapes framing. When interventions address economic competitiveness, optimistic frames increase significantly across the political spectrum. The findings reveal a cross-partisan consensus in favor of regulating artificial intelligence, regardless of the frames deployed. This suggests that political contestation centers not on the principle of regulatory intervention, but on its modalities and objectives. Emerging technologies are absorbed into existing ideological frameworks while generating zones of strategic convergence when economic and normative considerations align.

title: No vote for recovery? Local electoral effects of NextGeneration European Union funds in Spain
abstract: Do European Union (EU) funds affect voting behavior in local elections? Following the COVID-19 crisis, the EU launched an unprecedented financial effort through the NextGeneration EU program, channeling billions of euros to support reforms and investments across different policy areas in all Member States. Using several empirical designs, including an observational, a Regression Discontinuity Design and a Difference-in-Difference strategy, this article investigates whether these investments influenced electoral outcomes in Spain’s 2023 municipal elections. Despite the scale and policy relevance of the program and the opportunity to claim credit by mayors, we find no evidence that local allocations of recovery funds increased support for incumbent parties. These null results contrast with earlier works from other European funding programs, which have often yielded electoral rewards under favorable conditions, such as high visibility, political alignment, or clear attribution. In Spain, however, the political impact of NextGeneration EU spending appears to be absent, possibly due to the low visibility of projects, the complexity of fund administration, or the lack of clear political ownership. Our findings highlight the limits of top-down economic interventions in generating local political returns and call for a closer examination of the conditions under which supranational spending shapes electoral behavior.

title: The Transmission Problem: A Nationalization-Weighted Forecast for the 2026 Midterm Elections
When Do Prediction Markets Improve Election Forecasts? Evidence from Matched U.S. Races
Changing Maps and Outcomes: Gerrymander Potential and District Dissimilarity in Forecasting the 2026 Midterms
Special Occasions? When Mid-Cycle Contests Predict Congressional Elections, and When They Don’t
Forecasting Gubernatorial Elections in an Era of Polarized and Nationalized Politics
The partisan dilemma: How people evaluate sacrificial dilemma decisions by politicians across the political divide
abstract: Abstract Politicians often face policy decisions where sacrificing some targets benefits others. As motivations behind such decisions can be ambiguous, partisans may ascribe nobler motives to politicians who make decisions they approve of and whose party they identify with. Consequently, evaluations of politicians can be shaped by the politician's decision, party affiliation, the domain of sacrifice, and the evaluator's political orientation. Across three studies, the US and South American participants ( N = 1595) evaluated liberal/left‐wing and conservative/right‐wing politicians who accepted or rejected educational and economic sacrifices. We examined how participants' political orientation influenced judgments of sacrificial decisions. Conservative/Right‐wing political orientation frequently (though not always) predicted higher ratings of conservative/right‐wing politicians and lower ratings of liberal/left‐wing politicians across decision acceptability, vote‐worthiness, warmth, and competence—even when both politicians made the same choice. Study 2 demonstrated that the direction of bias depends on the policy domain, with liberal‐leaning participants less accepting of educational sacrifices and more accepting of economic sacrifices than conservative‐leaning participants. Study 2 further suggested that inferences about politicians' underlying motivations partly drive partisan bias. These findings demonstrate that judgments of realistic sacrificial dilemmas are significantly influenced by the social context—specifically, who is evaluating whom and over which issues.

title: Why do people migrate irregularly? Evidence from a lab-in-the-field experiment in West Africa
abstract: Irregular migration to Europe by sea, though risky, remains one of the most popular migration options for many Sub-Saharan Africans. This study examines the drivers of irregular migration decisions using an incentivized lab-in-the-field experiment in rural Gambia, the African country with the highest per-capita rate of irregular migration to Europe. Potential migrants substantially overestimate the probability of dying en route , reporting an average belief of 51 percent compared with a best available estimate of about 20 percent. In the experiment, reducing the probability of dying en route from 50 to 20 percent raises willingness to migrate irregularly by 3.0 percentage points, while reducing the probability of obtaining legal residence from 50 to 30 percent lowers it by 2.1 points. Our results highlight the importance of potential migrants’ prior beliefs in shaping responses to information and suggest that information policies that fail to account for these beliefs may backfire.

title: Morality and climate policy attitudes
abstract: This paper studies the moral roots of climate policy attitudes. We fielded a survey with a representative sample in the US to study the predictive power of moral universalism in explaining heterogeneity in specific climate policy attitudes. Our results reveal that universalism is significantly related to support for various policy measures that prevail in current policy debates in most countries, including domestic policies such as a carbon tax and a green infrastructure program, as well as international policies such as international burden-sharing. Supporting evidence comes from simple bystander allocation decisions in which respondents are asked to decide “who should pay” to fight climate change or to mitigate the adverse consequences of global warming. Open-text elicitations further corroborate these results and identify moral universalism as a key aspect of how people reason about climate policies.

title: Existence of Bayesian Equilibria in Incomplete Information Games without Common Priors
abstract: This paper focuses on finite-player incomplete information games where players may hold mutually inconsistent beliefs without a common prior. We introduce absolute continuity of beliefs, extending the classical notion of absolute continuity of information in Milgrom and Weber (1985), and prove that Bayesian equilibria exist in a broad class of games, including those with discontinuous payoffs. Examples illustrate the scope and implications of our findings.

title: Communicating risk about autonomous vehicles: uncertainty and source effects in social media risk communication
Hazard or ‘hack’? Exploring risk perceptions of intended and unintended product use among UK regulators and consumers
abstract: Consumers frequently engage in unintended uses of products—referred to as ‘hacks’—such as using an oven to heat a room. While these practices are widely shared within consumers, they may introduce significant risks. This quantitative study (N = 206) examined differences in risk perception between consumers and UK product safety regulators regarding both intended and unintended product uses. Regulators (n = 90) and consumers (n = 116) evaluated ten products on four risk perception dimensions: overall risk judgment, likelihood of harm, severity of harm, and benefits both before and after being presented with hack information. Participants also reported familiarity with the products beforehand and intention to use them after hack exposure. Results indicated that regulators consistently rated products as riskier, with higher likelihood and severity of harm, compared to consumers, both before and after exposure to hack information. Although overall risk judgment increased for both groups after learning about hacks, regulators’ risk perceptions remained significantly higher. This persistent gap indicates that consumers and regulators continued to differ in their evaluations of risks associated with unintended product use, even after exposure to hack information. Perceived benefits were the strongest predictors of intention to adopt hacks. These findings underscore the need for policy frameworks addressing risks from hazardous, unintended product applications.

title: Platformed affective withdrawal: Quiet quitting and the refusal of gendered emotional labour on TikTok
abstract: This article examines #quietquitting on TikTok as a platform-mediated articulation of gendered affective withdrawal. While organisational research interprets quiet quitting as reduced discretionary effort or declining work engagement, this study examines how quiet quitting is articulated as a digitally circulated refusal of feminised emotional labour. Drawing on feminist theories of affective labour and critical platform studies, the analysis explores how workers renegotiate expectations of emotional availability within algorithmically structured visibility regimes. The study is based on a qualitative-dominant mixed-methods analysis of 586 TikTok videos shared under #quietquitting between 2020 and 2026. Combining thematic discourse analysis with descriptive engagement indicators, the findings show that creators frequently frame quiet quitting as a refusal of unpaid relational mediation, emotional management, and workplace care. The article introduces the concept of platformed affective withdrawal to explain how narratives of workplace disengagement circulate through algorithmic visibility systems that amplify and individualise gendered labour inequalities.

title: Praise, rent, and the platform: Substack and the enclosure of blog culture
abstract: This article situates Substack within the platformisation of blogging and the enclosure of cultural production within proprietary infrastructures. Tracing the genealogy of blogging as a decentralised practice that carried within it the seeds of citizen journalism and informal intellectual life, I argue that Substack does not restore an apparently lost cultural practice but renegotiates and interpolates blogging into a platformised logic. Framed as a return to independent, writer-led publishing, Substack instead, as I argue, renders free-labour interaction as a source of rent. I analyse the rhetoric and revolving discourse around Substack’s internal curatorial project, ‘The Substack Post’. Drawing on Jodi Dean’s account of blogs as displaced mediators alongside theories of digital labour and platform capitalism, and approaching Substack as a simultaneously platformised and infrastructuralised formation, I argue that praise operates as a platform-specific form of commodity fetishism, animating the platform while obscuring the labour relations that sustain it.

title: From ephemeral acts to agency pathways: A life-course approach to user agency in platform societies
abstract: I argue in this paper that debates about user agency in platform societies have become stuck between two unsatisfactory positions: the tendency to treat everyday acts of agency as evidence of empowerment, and the tendency to dismiss such acts as inconsequential in the face of platform power. I suggest that both approaches are limited because they focus primarily on the presence of agency rather than on its pathways, trajectories and consequences over time. Drawing on sociological understandings of agency as temporal, I argue that, whilst snapshot approaches can document moments of reflexivity, adaptation and negotiation, they remain poorly equipped to account for how acts of user agency come to matter, if at all, in people’s lives over time. I suggest we think of ordinary users’ agency pathways as a way of tracing how agency unfolds across time and domains, often generating uneven, paradoxical and unintended consequences. I conclude by calling for longitudinal methodologies and approaches that shift analytical attention from whether users have agency to what users’ agency does over time.

title: Self-programmable creative labour: Generative AI and the reorganisation of work in the UK creative industries
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly entering creative work not only as a set of tools, but as a new demand placed on creative practitioners. Existing debates on AI in the creative industries have tended to focus on productivity, creativity or authorship. While important, such framings risk treating AI as a discrete technological intervention rather than as part of a broader reorganisation of creative labour. Drawing on Castells’s concept of self-programmable labour , this article examines how practitioners in the UK film, games and live performance sectors incorporate generative AI into their everyday work. Based on 21 interviews with AI-engaged practitioners, it argues that generative AI is helping to normalise a mode of creative labour in which practitioners are expected to continually retrain, reconfigure their workflows and upgrade their skills in response to technological change. Yet this demand is unevenly distributed, and its rewards remain uncertain. AI may expand what practitioners can produce, but it does not necessarily expand what they can claim in terms of bargaining power, career stability or recognition. The article suggests that in AI-mediated creative economies, self-programmability is becoming less a route to a professional advantage than a condition of survival.

title: Revenge bodies and antisocial media ecologies
abstract: The present article theorises the emergence and persistence of a notable cultural archetype prevalent across 21st century media forms: the revenge body. The promise of personal inviolability offered by this corporeal project is compelling in an era marked by an increasingly insistent discourse of gender polarisation and conflict. Given a contemporary public culture in the global North in which social and political antipathies prevail, we note the emergence of revenge as a public affect that crosses ideological divisions and thrives in a media ecosystem that algorithmically stokes the flames of antisocial feeling. The article tracks this corporeal type across reality television makeover show Revenge Body with Khloe Kardashian (2017–2019) as well as online message boards for the Looksmaxxing community, highlighting the differently gendered manifestations of the revenge body and the wider social conditions that seed such corporeal projects. By couching a self-making project in antisocial rhetoric the revenge body indexes the fraying of bonds of interpersonal intimacy, variously exhibited through the production of heteropessimistic and heteronihilstic cultural texts, and the emergence of post-intimate digital communities.

title: Public construction of evidence: Rethinking scientific evidence in social media environments
abstract: This essay proposes a conceptual framework that reconceptualizes scientific evidence as a process of public construction in contemporary media environments. In social media contexts, scientists, journalists, influencers, NGOs, lay publics and AI agents participate in the circulation and interpretation of evidential claims. The essay’s contribution is to explain how evidential status itself is publicly assembled, circulated, internalized, and fed back into further communication. We distinguish two analytically coupled layers of this process: amalgamated evidence , the publicly visible circulation and recombination of claims across posts, comments and shares, and internalized evidence , the individual representations through which users interpret and evaluate these claims. Their reciprocal “circle of evidence” is driven by three recurring communicative behaviours—consumption, participation and generation—and shaped by platform logics that amplify, recontextualize and remix information. Under these conditions, evidential status emerges from communicative interaction rather than solely from scientific procedures, creating potential divergences between scientific records and what publics perceive as evidence. By conceptualizing evidencing as a socio-technical and communicative process, the framework aims to stimulate debate and outlines a research agenda for examining how public circulation and individual internalization mutually shape the authority of science in digital media environments.

title: Beyond consumer protection in China: Profit-seeking practices of counterfeit hunters
abstract: This article moves beyond debates over motive and legitimacy to examine how profit-seeking among Chinese counterfeit hunters takes shape, operates, and produces social and regulatory consequences. Shaped by punitive damages, complaint and reporting mechanisms, and platform commerce, profit-seeking takes three forms: composite, professionalized, and predatory. Operationally, claiming compensation functions as the foundational practice, while agency services, content marketing, and training schools provide additional revenue paths. These practices burden merchants, generate derivative markets for countering counterfeit hunters, and occupy regulatory resources, prompting the state to turn from enabling consumer-led supervision to managing the supervisors themselves.

title: Public Interest Capacity: The Case of Direct File
abstract: ABSTRACT This article describes the conditions for creating and undermining public interest capacity, that is, the ability of the state to generate public goods with widely distributed benefits. The creation and elimination of Direct File, a free, online public tax reporting system in the United States, offers an instrumental case. The creation of Direct File depended upon political commitment sufficient to overcome private interests: both the traditional dependence on private contractors to produce digital products, and the opposition of the private tax preparation industry which saw Direct File as a competitor. Political will was not enough: creating internal capacity in the form of skilled government tech teams who could build a quality digital product was also necessary. But without this political commitment in the Trump administration, which instead pursued downsizing and was receptive to the tax preparation industry arguments, both Direct File and the team that built it were eliminated.

title: Is parental leave equitable for all? Differences in career continuity by labour market status: evidence from South Korea
abstract: This study aimed to examine the unequal effects of South Korea’s universal parental leave system on women’s career continuity according to labour market status, using the concept of ‘policy refraction’. Using data from the Survey on the Economic Activities of Career-break Women (SEACW) (2016, 2019, 2022), we analysed 2,204 women aged 25–54. We applied generalized structural equation modelling (GSEM) to examine structured patterns of association between labour market status and career continuity, mediated by parental leave utilization. Utilizing parental leave was a key positive mechanism for career continuity. However, policy refraction emerged, with its use concentrated among those in advantageous positions (public institutions, standard workers) while workers in small firms show substantially lower utilization rates. Notably, public institution employees enjoyed a ‘Double Advantage’, whereas small-firm workers showed a negative indirect association through lower parental leave utilization. The parental leave system may function as a mechanism that mediates and deepens existing inequalities within a segmented labour market rather than mitigating them. Tailored policy interventions are required to enhance utilization of the system for vulnerable groups, such as small firm workers, to ensure its substantive universality.

title: How experiential knowledge becomes evidence in lawmaking through consultations with incarcerated people
abstract: Experiential knowledge, grounded in lived experience, is increasingly recognized as an important source of evidence in policy making and legislative drafting. Yet questions remain about how knowledge derived from consultations with affected individuals can legitimately inform broader lawmaking. This article examines how experiential knowledge from targeted consultations with incarcerated individuals is transformed into context-specific legislative knowledge through the interplay of propositional system knowledge, procedural knowledge of navigating the prison system, and implicit analogical reasoning. Drawing on consultation memoranda and a draft Bill produced during the reform of the Finnish Imprisonment Act, we analyse consultations concerning incarcerated individuals’ use of communication technologies to manage essential practical matters beyond prison under conditions of administrative burden. We first construct a narrative from the consultees’ propositional and procedural experiential knowledge and then examine how this knowledge was incorporated into legislative arguments alongside official expert knowledge. Our analysis shows that the draft Bill employed implicit analogical reasoning to transform procedural knowledge of navigating the prison system into propositional claims applicable to broader prison populations sharing similar contexts, institutional routines, and practical needs. By demonstrating how analogical reasoning links propositional and procedural knowledge to generate context-specific generalizations, the article offers a novel conceptual framework for understanding how experiential knowledge can become legitimate evidence in lawmaking. We suggest that this approach is applicable to other institutional settings characterized by standardized living conditions, shared procedures, and common systems of navigation.
