title: Path Dependence and Policy Layering in Australia's Childhood Obesity Response: Explaining the Persistence of Individual Responsibility
abstract: ABSTRACT This article examines how individual responsibility became the dominant narrative shaping Australia's childhood obesity policy response and why this framing has persisted. Using historical institutionalism and the concept of policy layering, the analysis examines how pre‐existing approaches to health and child welfare shaped the policy response when childhood obesity emerged on the policy agenda. A systematic analysis of Hansard parliamentary debates (1970–2022) traces how these inherited ideas became embedded and reinforced across health, education and sport and recreation portfolios. Three phases in the policy trajectory were identified: the origins of the narrative (1970–1989), its embedding through expanding policy activity (1990–2009) and its consolidation through continued layering (2010–2022). Across these phases, policy responses remained centred on individual and family health behaviours, despite increasing recognition of systemic and environmental determinants. The findings demonstrate how successive policy layers can expand government activity while reinforcing an established policy trajectory, constraining the capacity of alternative ideas to reshape the dominant response. This study contributes to understanding policy stability, institutional continuity, and the dynamics of incremental change in public health.

title: The boundaries of global concern: How socioeconomic context shapes the link between global consciousness and environmental attitudes
abstract: Abstract Climate change requires unprecedented international cooperation; yet growing protectionist sentiment poses a significant barrier to collective action. Global Consciousness (GC), a psychological orientation characterized by a connection to humanity and the world as a whole, has been theorized as a key driver of benevolent behaviors, including pro‐environmental attitudes. However, empirical evidence linking GC to environmentalism remains largely confined to specific contexts, leaving the generalizability of this relationship across diverse societies unclear. Leveraging data from the European Values Survey (EVS) and the World Values Survey (WVS), this study examines the link between GC and indicators of environmentalism: confidence, active membership in environmental organizations, and prioritizing environmental protection over economic growth. We further examine whether socioeconomic context moderates this relationship, hypothesizing that the effect of GC on environmental attitudes will be stronger in wealthier nations, as measured by the Human Development Index (HDI). Multilevel models revealed that, across 35 countries in Study 1 ( N = 40,259) and 86 countries in Study 2 ( N = 123,280), GC is consistently and positively associated with environmentalism. Crucially, this relationship is significantly moderated by HDI. These results indicate that the positive effect of GC on environmentalism is stronger in countries with higher socioeconomic progress, suggesting that GC more readily translates into actions when supported by macro‐level structural resources.

title: Too little too late? Nationwide carbon trading in China
abstract: China launched a nationwide, rate-based carbon market in 2021. Covering the world’s top CO₂ emitter, compliance depends on the intensity of carbon emissions rather than an absolute cap. We draw on the theoretical literature of rate-based systems to provide the first empirical evidence on an early adopter. Using plant-level data from satellite imagery and machine learning methods, we find that high-efficiency power plants increased electricity generation and CO₂ emissions by approximately 5% relative to low-efficiency plants. Because its carbon market regulates nearly all coal plants in China, we focus on the differential responses by plant efficiency, finding no evidence of a differential reduction in emission intensity (though these estimates are imprecise). Relative to coal plants in Indonesia and the Philippines, which had no carbon market, China’s high-efficiency plants also increased emissions, while the estimate for its low-efficiency plants is small and insignificant. This pattern of responses suggests that emissions increases of high-efficiency plants exceeded substitution away from low-efficiency plants. Underscoring the production stimulus to more efficient Chinese plants, air quality worsened downwind of high efficiency plants relative to low-efficiency plants, compromising air quality in relatively clean areas of China. To curb the level of China’s carbon emissions and thereby slow climate change, benchmarks need to be tightened within the existing system or an alternative system adopted that does not simultaneously incentivize electricity production.

title: Quality Regulation and Competition: Evidence from Pharmaceutical Markets
abstract: Abstract Quality regulation seeks to ensure quality and foster competition by reducing vertical differentiation, but it may also have adverse effects on market structure. We study this trade-off in the context of pharmaceutical bioequivalence, which is the primary quality standard for generic drugs. By exploiting the introduction of bioequivalence in Chile, we find that stronger regulation reduced the number of drugs in the market by 18% and increased average paid prices by 13%. We estimate a model of drug entry, certification, and demand to study how drug quality, aversion to generics, and certification costs shape the equilibrium effects of quality regulation. We find that quality regulation increased demand for generic drugs by resolving asymmetric information and reducing aversion to unbranded generics, which induced the entry of high-quality drugs in place of low-quality drugs. Consumer welfare increased despite higher prices and a lower number of firms. We compare minimum quality standards with alternative designs of quality regulation, including quality disclosure.

A Dataset on Legislative Decision‐Making in the European Parliament: The DEU‐IV Dataset
Neither isolated nor dependent: Strategic R&D as a pathway to technology sovereignty
Beyond skills: How occupational essentiality and social value relate to attitudes toward immigrant labor – ADDENDUM
Can multi-dimensional descriptive representation increase policy priority alignment? Evidence from South African municipalities
abstract: Abstract Does an increase in the number of shared identity traits between citizens and their public representatives increase the likelihood that they will agree on policy priorities? The identities of citizens and politicians are complex and multi-dimensional, but we know little about how the combination of multiple shared identity traits affects the convergence of attitudes on government policy. In this paper, we analyze two waves of original survey data on local government councillors in conjunction with several surveys of citizens in South Africa. We find that both within and across political parties, greater degrees of trait similarity between citizens and politicians – even beyond the one or two traits considered in most studies of descriptive representation – are associated with modest but consistent increases in alignment on policy priorities, especially when citizens and councillors share traits that reinforce a historically marginalized identity. We also show that trait similarity increases policy priority alignment to a greater degree when politicians have roles that require frequent contact with constituents, suggesting that communication channels may strengthen the substantive impact of descriptive representation.

title: Centripetal narratives under crisis? Media framing and the Europeanization of economic discourse in Portugal, Spain, and Ireland
abstract: Abstract This article examines whether and how national media in Portugal, Spain, and Ireland converged in their interpretation of European economic issues during the Eurozone crisis. Building on research on the European Public Sphere, it analyses how national media located political authority, responsibility, and problem-solving capacity under conditions of intensified EU involvement in domestic economic governance. Conceptually, the article distinguishes between relational convergence, referring to cross-national similarity in media narratives, and directional convergence, capturing within-country shifts in narrative orientation along the national–EU axis. Empirically, the analysis draws on a comparative framing study of 6,070 economic news articles published in six quality newspapers between 2002 and 2015. Narrative interpretation across five framing dimensions—Problem, Cause, Responsibility, Consequences, and Solution—is operationalised through an original Convergence Index capturing the balance between EU-centred and nationally centred narratives. The findings show no generalised relational convergence following the onset of the crisis. Instead, cross-national dispersion in narrative orientation increases in the post-crisis period. Directional convergence towards EU-centred narratives occurs selectively: Spanish and Irish media display modest centripetal shifts, whereas Portuguese coverage follows a contrasting trajectory of systematic re-nationalisation. Overall, these results qualify crisis-driven expectations of communicative integration. While the Eurozone crisis intensified diagnostic and accountability-oriented framing across national media, it did not generate stable or cumulative convergence in narrative interpretation. Media convergence thus emerges as a differentiated and non-linear process, with important implications for how the communicative foundations of a European Public Sphere should be assessed under conditions of systemic stress.

title: Pave the Way to Diversion: Increased Salience of Foreign Policy at the Times of Economic Hardships
abstract: Most research on the diversionary use of force focuses on timing of conflict initiation and target selection, often treating the public as passive observers ready to take the bait. This article challenges this assumption by examining how leaders strategically elevate foreign policy issues in public discourse before resorting to the use of force. We argue that economic downturns lead to anticipatory rhetorical agenda-setting, through which leaders increase the salience of foreign policy in shaping the conditions under which military actions become feasible. Using a large language model, we measure foreign policy salience in 29,286 US presidential addresses and remarks between 1945 and 2019. Combining these data with monthly inflation and US military interventions, we examine whether patterns in presidential rhetoric are consistent with a rhetorical pathway linking economic distress to the use of force. The results are consistent with our theoretical expectation. Higher inflation is associated with increased foreign policy salience in presidential speeches and heightened salience is, in turn, associated with a greater likelihood of military intervention, while inflation itself exhibits no robust direct relationship with the use of force. Our findings align with the expectation that diversionary dynamics may unfold as a mediated process in which leaders place greater rhetorical emphasis on foreign policy issues prior to the use of force. By highlighting the role of anticipatory agenda-setting, this study offers a nuanced perspective on diversionary conflict and highlights the importance of presidential rhetoric as a key component of foreign policy outcome.

title: Big Tech, big risk? How education and ideology shape public attitudes toward Big Tech companies
Spatial Protection Spillovers and the Equilibrium of Crime and Policing
Who Verifies the Verifiers? AI, Local Knowledge Production, and Credibility in Tanzania’s 2025 Election
abstract: This study examines how Factchecking AI tools and community-based credibility practices interacted during Tanzania’s 2025 presidential election. Using data from five regions, we analyzed 342 media materials, 87 interviews, field observations, and 22 distinct contested election events. The findings identify three forms of verification disjuncture. First, AI-assisted translation and transcription sometimes changed the meaning of politically important statements before journalists could verify them. Second, fact-checks and disputed claims often moved through different communication channels, which limited the chances that people would see the correction. Third, some communities trusted personal experience, familiar sources, and collective discussion more than professional fact-checkers. Participants judged credibility through relationships, lived experience, group discussion, humor and satire, and social accountability. These practices sometimes supported the same conclusions as institutional verification and sometimes produced different judgments. We argue that fact-checking becomes politically effective when the meaning of a claim is preserved, the correction reaches the people discussing it, and the source of the correction is recognized as credible. This explains why an accurate fact-check can still have limited public influence.

title: The Citizen’s Seat at the Table: How Private Sector Behavior Fosters Alignment With Citizens in Public-Private Partnerships
abstract: Citizens play a crucial role in public-private partnerships (PPPs). Yet, such citizens often are poorly engaged and excluded from decision-making, leading to situations where their interests do not align with the public and private partners. Recognizing the importance of private sector behaviors in PPPs, we aim to identify how their behaviors play a role in aligning these interests to meet citizen expectations. We use the Economies of Worth framework and a comparative case study to identify behavioral mechanisms to support alignment, such as being available to citizens in person, adaptability, engaging in small goodwill gestures, and sustaining these behaviors over time.

title: Scaling out while staying local: Maintaining inclusive co-production with vulnerable citizens
abstract: Organisations that involve vulnerable people in co-production face a paradox: while increasing the number of participants is seen as necessary to create greater social benefit, scaling risks undermining the locally rooted, relational practices that enable vulnerable people to participate. This paper develops a conceptual model that addresses this tension, by integrating insights from scaling of social innovation, collective action and group size, and scaffolding theory from the learning sciences. The model proposes representative co-producers and peer mentors as contingent, temporary scaffolding functions that support vulnerable people's involvement in co-production. At the same time, it argues that inclusive scaling requires federal group structures that maintain small-group interaction by coordinating multiple affiliated groups rather than enlarging single co-production arenas. The model offers a theoretically grounded framework for understanding how co-production with vulnerable people can scale without sacrificing inclusiveness. Points for practitioners: Scaling co-production with vulnerable people requires both differentiated support for participants and organisational structures that preserve small-group interaction as numbers grow. Representative co-producers and peer mentors can be mobilised as temporary or flexible resources to lower barriers to participation, rather than as permanent substitutes for the involvement of vulnerable people themselves. Expanding participation does not require enlarging co-production forums; scale can instead be achieved by coordinating multiple small groups that enable trust, confidence and meaningful voice to be sustained.

title: Reply to Kettl: The Field of Public Administration in America and an Unpreparedness of Its Own Making?
abstract: ABSTRACT This Reply suggests the sub‐field of U.S.‐specific public administration is under‐prepared to address democratic deconsolidation given its multi‐decade distance from the disciplines of comparative politics and political economy and from the sub‐fields of comparative and development public administration. The narrowness of what is understand as “good” public administration by U.S.‐based scholars has largely excluded cross‐disciplinary and non‐U.S. intellectual histories which, if understood, would have deepened sub‐field intellectual depth and breadth but also, better prepared the sub‐field for America's current administrative state. This Reply suggests the value of drawing upon post‐WWII administration‐linked trends in other disciplines and upon links between administration and prior democratic deconsolidations (the U.S. is not unique). This includes the sub‐field's historical reluctance to research existential insecurity, intolerance (beyond social inequity), the role of democratic restraint, the role of crisis (or lack of) in democratic deconsolidation, and theories of democracy‐to‐autocracy and autocracy‐to‐democracy.

title: Do sovereign ratings capture public pension liabilities in the assessment of public debt? A France–UK comparison
abstract: IMPACTThis article is intended primarily for investors, rating agencies and credit analysts assessing sovereign solvency. Its analysis may also be relevant to finance ministries, audit institutions, parliamentarians, fiscal authorities and public sector accountants. The article’s message is practical: pension liabilities are an important factor affecting sovereign solvency and should be given more weight by credit rating agencies (CRAs). The main difficulty lies in differences in pension systems and accounting methods across countries. The authors propose focusing on states’ income statements presented in financial reports under accrual accounting standards. Official debt must remain the central indicator, but it should not be read alone.

title: Debate: Revoking parliament’s fit-and-proper tests for the appointment of Indonesia’s police chief
abstract: In modern democratic systems, the role of parliamentary oversight is to ensure government accountability through the checks and balances mechanism. In the context of the Indonesian national police ...

title: Doing good well: a dual accountability framework for nonprofits
abstract: IMPACTThis article offers nonprofit practitioners a practical way to distinguish accountability for organizational purpose from accountability for delivery. For boards and executives, the framework separates questions about mission, public benefit, trade-offs and mission drift from those concerning implementation, controls, reporting and performance. For managers, funders, regulators and umbrella bodies, it clarifies how reporting and evaluation systems can strengthen accountability without allowing metrics or compliance requirements to redefine mission. It also broadens accountability to include beneficiaries, affected communities, staff, peer bodies and wider publics. The central lesson for practice is that stronger accountability does not simply mean more reporting. It requires clearer differentiation between governing purpose and governing delivery, together with mechanisms that connect the two without allowing one to displace the other.

title: Imagining the Invisible: Judicial Epistemology, Carceral Regulation, and the Liberal State
abstract: ABSTRACT In many systems judges exercise judicial review over prison officials' decisions. However, judges are often symbolically, institutionally, and practically distant from prison realities. In the current paper, we explore how judges negotiate their limited epistemological awareness of prison through the lens of epistemic injustice. Drawing on interviews with 17 (retired) Israeli Supreme Court justices regarding their prison administrative review decisions, we identify three epistemic gaps: first, the prison's heterotopic nature; second, the tension between commitment to liberty and authorizing the “pains of imprisonment” at sentencing; and third, the division of labor between sentencing and prison phases. The findings suggest that judges bridge these epistemological gaps through three imaginaries: (a) “ epistemic distancing ”; (b) “ epistemic assimilation ”; and (c) “ parallel epistemology ”. These epistemic imaginaries allow judges to compensate for their experiential absence but also structure their judicial oversight, shaping how courts administratively regulate imprisonment without fully confronting its lived realities. The findings show how judicial imaginaries of prison are shaped through top‐down narrative constructions rather than bottom‐up experiential encounters and include self‐produced “epistemic estrangement” from the prison world. We further examine the implications of these epistemic blind spots, demonstrating how they enable the legitimization of carceral power while obscuring and marginalizing the lived experiences of incarcerated individuals.

title: From Judicial Regulation to Judicial Governance: Locating the Courts on the Map of Social Ordering
abstract: ABSTRACT Courts have long been recognized as venues of social control and policymaking. The rise of regulatory capitalism suggests reconsidering the judiciary in regulatory terms, notably through work that casts courts as regulators. This article argues, however, that styling courts as regulators is both analytically and normatively deficient: it obscures the distinctive function of courts and their contribution to social ordering. At the same time, judicial decision‐making plainly exhibits a regulatory dimension. Yet rather than stretching the concept of regulation, this article proposes to capture this dimension through governance theory. On this theoretical foundation, the article outlines a model of judicial governance that elucidates how social ordering emerges from adjudication and how it unfolds over time. In particular, the model highlights the implications of judicial decision‐making for private ordering and draws attention to processes of intermediation through lawyers, media, and advanced digital technologies. It thus opens a set of analytically structured research questions and complements them with a methodological framework to orient future work on judicial governance.

title: Linkage as Leverage: OECD Accession as an Informal and Indirect Graduation Mechanism in the International Climate Regime
abstract: ABSTRACT As global power is shifting, international institutions face a challenge: established powers will often request that rising powers no longer continue to benefit from their status as “developing countries”. Yet only a few institutions have formal rules in place to organize this transition. As a result, tracing the informal pathways through which change occurs becomes relevant. In this article, we study one such mechanism in the international climate regime. In that regime, the so‐called Annex I countries agreed “to take the lead” in reducing greenhouse gas emissions while developing countries remained exempt from a similar obligation. Because Annex I was hard to amend, the regime has frequently been said to lack a graduation mechanism. Yet, once we take the interaction between the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) and its broader institutional environment into account, the process of acceding to the Organization for Economic Co‐operation and Development (OECD) comes into view as an indirect and informal graduation mechanism. We examine the effects and limitations of this mechanism in relation to the accession processes of Mexico (1994), South Korea (1996), and Chile (2010). Our analysis leads to two main results. First, we show that a graduation mechanism based on “linkage as leverage” existed. Second, we sketch three distinct causal pathways that lead to different degrees of graduation in each case. Overall, our study suggests that graduation based on “linkage as leverage” depends on three conditions. First, states needed to activate the mechanism in each case. Second, domestic support was required to sustain graduation. And third, major emitters had to develop an interest in joining a club organization that could exercise leverage.

title: Policy time-spaces: exploring the design and evolution of ‘No Jab’ policies in the Australian federation
abstract: This paper develops the concept of ‘policy time-spaces’ to examine how temporal logics of policy design interact with the spatial architecture of Australia’s federation. Drawing on documentary analysis and interviews with senior policy actors across four states, we analyse the evolution of ‘No Jab’ vaccination policies through three temporal categories: past-present, present-present and present-future. We show how policymakers draw on inherited trajectories, respond to concurrent developments across jurisdictions and project desired futures into present design choices. The framework illuminates how federal and multi-scalar governance structures condition the temporal dynamics through which policies are designed and evolve.

title: Kingdon in non-democracies: a multiple streams analysis of Myitsone dam suspension in Myanmar
abstract: The multiple streams framework (MSF) is widely used to explain agenda-setting. Yet, two gaps persist: the coupling process has received limited attention, and applications of the framework remain concentrated in Western democracies. Little is known about how coupling works in non-democratic and hybrid political contexts. This study addresses that gap by examining the 2011 suspension of the Myitsone Dam project in Myanmar, asking how civil society, acting as a collective policy entrepreneur, brought the issue onto the governmental agenda under severe political constraints. The study is a qualitative single-case study, and documentary materials produced during the dam debate were analysed thematically through an interpretive lens. The findings show that civil society discursively prepared the linkages between the three streams well before a political window opened: it defined the problem through technocratic and emotional frames, legitimized the alternative of suspension within the policy community, and connected both to the reformist political narrative of Myanmar’s 2011 transition, alongside distinct activities of coalition building and mobilization. The study extends the empirical reach of the MSF beyond Western democracies and refines the boundary conditions of framing-based coupling.

title: Time in Education Policy Transfer: The Seven Temporalities of Global School Reform
abstract: The importance of time or temporality as a key component in understanding the drivers, process and outcomes of policies is hardly disputed. Yet what are we talking about precisely when we talk abou...

title: The return of the ‘positive state’? Capacity-building for the protection of critical national infrastructures across Europe
abstract: Critical national infrastructures (CNIs) have come to be viewed as vital security issues across Europe. Yet, European states’ approaches to the protection of CNIs have been far from uniform. When do states engage in state capacity-building to protect CNIs against increasing security challenges? To answer this question, we draw on theories of (European) security policymaking, which highlight different types of security challenges, as well as historical institutionalist approaches, which expect state capacity-building to be contingent on ideational-institutional legacies. A mapping of more than 30 European states’ capacity-building efforts in the telecommunication and energy sectors lends strong support to the former, whereas we find no conclusive evidence for the latter. This underlines the explanatory power of types of security challenges but sheds doubts on expectations that ideational-institutional legacies are a powerful predictor of cross-country patterns of security policymaking reform. Moreover, to show how the type of security challenge matters, we trace, in an in-depth case study of French reforms in energy governance, the political economy mechanism whereby concentrated threats lead to state capacity-building to protect CNIs. Our findings contribute to research on the geopoliticization of CNIs and the instruments of European security policymaking.

title: National, partisan or ideological biases? How EU officials' characteristics can influence infringement proceeding outcomes
abstract: Infringement proceedings serve as a key legal mechanism through which the European Union (EU) enforces compliance with common laws among its member states. This article, for the first time, examines how the nationality and partisanship of EU officials influence outcomes of these proceedings. We argue that Commissioners and Directors-General face a principal–agent dilemma, as they simultaneously act as EU officials and as nationals of their home countries. We expect that infringement proceedings are less likely to escalate when they are overseen by EU officials who share the nationality of the member state under investigation. We further posit that officials' partisan affiliations and ideological leaning may shape the outcomes of such cases. Using a novel dataset combining roughly 19.000 infringement proceedings between 2002 and 2020 with information about the responsible officials, we find evidence of a nationality bias, however, only among Commissioners. By contrast, we find no indication of bias linked to ideology or partisanship.

title: Political trust and inheritance taxation: evidence from four studies
abstract: Inheritance (estate) taxation is a potentially powerful instrument for reducing inequality and raising state revenues, yet it attracts opposition well beyond the small minority who will ever pay it. We argue that political trust helps explain who supports it. Because the tax is levied episodically and reaches few citizens directly, most individuals have little experience of its workings: knowledge is low, beliefs about its incidence are often mistaken, and preferences are unsettled. Citizens are therefore poorly placed to judge whether the tax will be implemented as intended or achieve its purposes, and political trust may consequently shape their willingness to accept that uncertainty. Across four complementary studies – an 11-country panel, an embedded survey experiment, the British Election Study panel, and voting behaviour in a 2015 Swiss referendum – we show that higher political trust is consistently associated with greater support for inheritance taxation across several alternative measures. Our findings thus identify public political trust as a constraint on the political feasibility of wealth taxation and extend research on political trust to support for a specific and contested tax instrument.

title: Elite welfare and the good fortune of just being there
abstract: Abstract This paper examines how senior executives at the UK’s largest publicly listed companies financially benefited from the Coronavirus Job Retention Scheme (CJRS), and seeks to explain this phenomenon with the concept of elite welfare . Using a difference-in-differences research design, we analyse the impact of participation in the CJRS on executive remuneration between 2019 and 2023. Drawing on a sample of Financial Times Stock Exchange (FTSE) 350 firms ( n = 246), we find that receipt of furlough support in 2020 was associated with significant increases in chief executive officer (CEO) performance pay and total remuneration in the immediate post-pandemic year. We interpret these results through a new analytical approach that understands elite income derived from rent-extraction facilitated by public policy or expenditure as a form of welfare. Unlike conventional welfare, which typically comprises relatively modest payments and concessions to broad sections of the population, elite welfare accrues to a small minority in privileged positions, taking the form of extractions of rent arising through opportunities created by government policy. We argue that recognising elite welfare as a parallel welfare system – largely insulated from competitive constraint and market discipline – provides a valuable new perspective on the interdependencies between inequality, public policy and the redistributive logics of the modern state.

title: Explaining the implementation of social impact bonds in Hong Kong through advocacy coalition change
abstract: Abstract This study examined the factors influencing the process underlying the implementation of social impact bonds (SIBs). While early research primarily emphasised the technical challenges, limited recent research has suggested that political and historical factors also influence a region’s SIB development. This paper augments the SIB literature by documenting an empirical case of SIB development in Hong Kong. Using the advocacy coalition framework, we uncovered that SIB’s development involved tension and contestation between two competing coalitions driving the discourse and how discreet coordination among the dominant coalition opposing the SIB agenda helped constrain the development. The findings underscore that a region’s SIB development likely involves power dynamics between opposing actors favouring and resisting the idea. The conceptual fluidity of SIBs enables actors to narrate what SIBs per se represent and to pursue their own coalition’s agendas.

title: Policy Agendas in Coalition Agreements: The Enduring Influence of Policy Inheritance
abstract: ABSTRACT New governments frequently inherit issues from their predecessors, and as a result, various policy problems tend to remain on the agenda for many years. Previous research examining the role of policy inheritance has focused mainly on the agenda during a government's term in office. These studies find that because governments must first contend with the problems they inherit, there is considerably less room for new issues to emerge on the agenda. This study seeks to examine the idea of policy inheritance through the lens of coalition agreements. Coalition agreements, a feature of multiparty governments, are drafted shortly after elections and reflect the outcome of the political struggle. For this reason, one can expect that coalition agreements contain mostly issues that parties regard as important. By implication, changes in the coalition agreements' issue agenda would be a function of the political change produced by the electoral cycle, rather than of inheritance. Analyzing coalition agreements in three countries—Israel, the Netherlands, and Norway—across 42 elections, we find no evidence for this assumption. Agendas in coalition agreements do not vary with changes in the party composition of the coalition, changes in the ideological distance between parties, or changes in the party holding the office of Prime Minister. This indicates that even when new coalition governments are preparing for their term in office, inheritance remains the primary driver of agenda‐setting.

title: Bureaucratic Interests: Does Fiscal Decentralization Impede Efficient Governance?
Beyond ideological polarization: how Serbian students are uniting fragmented opposition voters
abstract: This paper examines how the student movement that emerged in Serbia in late 2024 overcame ideological polarization among opposition voters and generated broad political support in a competitive authoritarian context. Since 2012, Serbia's opposition has been weakened by fragmentation and ideological divisions, primarily between a pro-European civic bloc and a nationalist anti-European bloc. Drawing on theories of opposition coordination in hybrid regimes, civic mobilization, and counter-polarization, the paper argues that the movement's unifying capacity stems from its nonpartisan positioning, participatory organization, and normative framing around justice, accountability, anti-corruption, and democratic integrity. The analysis combines Chapel Hill Expert Survey data, nationally representative surveys from 2019 to 2025, and an original survey of student activists across six public universities. The findings show that, despite persistent polarization on the East–West dimension, the movement displays ideological heterogeneity and strong democratic congruence. Unlike conventional opposition actors, it attracts similar support from pro-EU and anti-EU opposition voters, reduces affective distance across blocs, and mobilizes some former regime supporters. The paper concludes that, in hybrid regimes marked by deep polarization, civic actors can broaden opposition support by downplaying ideological cleavages and reframing conflict around shared democratic norms.

title: The Social Legacies of Repression: Family, Friends, and Political Participation
abstract: Existing scholarship on the legacies of state violence treats families as the primary vehicles through which repression shapes political behavior. Yet individuals are embedded in multiple social groups; a robust literature shows that both kin and non-kin relationships are consequential for political socialization. This paper examines the comparative effects of direct repression and the repression of family members, friends, and community members on subsequent political behavior. We draw on an original nationally representative survey of 1,200 adult Tunisians, supplemented by a targeted sample of 175 sibling pairs. We find that individuals who reported themselves or family members as repressed under the Ben Ali and Bourguiba dictatorships (1956–2011) are significantly more likely to report protest participation. Those who reported repressed friends and community members are more likely to report both recent protest attendance and electoral turnout. Analyses of the sibling pairs show that the relationship between repression of friends and communities and protest participation remains significant when controlling for unobservable family characteristics. Additional analyses indicate that political discussion with friends is a key mechanism through which repression’s behavioral effects are transmitted. These findings suggest that scholars who focus on familial networks risk underestimating the broader reach of repression’s political legacies.

title: Covariate Adjustment in Political Science Experiments: Progress and Recommendations
abstract: Abstract Covariate adjustment can reduce the standard error of experimental treatment effect estimates without increasing the sample size but is vulnerable to abuse unless a specific procedure is preregistered. We assess adjustment practices in ten political science journals in 2013, 2018, and 2023–24. Encouragingly, preregistration and covariate adjustment have each been rapidly adopted. Preregistration is also a good predictor of what practices are used in articles. However, just 12% of articles published in 2023–24 preregister a specific covariate adjustment procedure and use adjustment for the main estimate. Although preregistering an adjusted estimator is not always advisable (when covariates are unavailable or preregistration is not possible), there is substantial room for improvement. We recommend that when feasible, researchers preregister a specific covariate adjustment procedure and use it for their preferred estimate regardless of covariate balance. This may require a shift in preregistration culture away from predicting results and toward constraining analysis.

title: Using Television Drama to Promote Electoral Corruption Reporting: An Evaluation in Northern Nigeria
abstract: Abstract We evaluated an edutainment intervention to encourage electoral corruption reporting in northern Nigeria via a live broadcast of a popular Hausa-language TV show, which aired October–December 2022, shortly before the February 2023 presidential elections. We incorporated behaviorally informed anticorruption messages into the scripts of the TV drama to encourage its tens of millions of viewers to report instances of electoral corruption. We used a randomized encouragement trial design, sampling over 6,000 participants across northern Nigeria through pre-recorded phone surveys. Watching the show caused a statistically significant increase in the perceived helpfulness and frequency of reporting, but we could not detect changes in knowledge of how to report or reporting behaviors.

title: How Do (Mis-)Perceptions of Refugee Gender Composition Shape Attitudes? Evidence from a Survey Experiment
abstract: Abstract People’s perceptions of others, particularly those from other countries, can shape their attitudes and willingness to offer solidarity. We study public beliefs about the gender composition of forcibly displaced populations in a large online survey experiment. Participants ( n = 13,008) representative of the adult population of six EU countries, consistently underestimated the share of women among the people displaced by the Russian war on Ukraine. We show that a belief-correction intervention effectively prompted updates in public beliefs, aligning them more closely with actual numbers. The source of information matters: updates were greater when the intervention cites official statistics rather than other people’s opinions. Although female migrants are typically preferred, the intervention did not change perceptions regarding current refugees’ impact on crime and economy or policy preferences (family reunification). While all these measures correlate with beliefs about gender composition, the intervention did not significantly affect any of them.

title: When Crises Entrench Gendered Power: Male Elite Adaptation in the Ugandan Parliament
abstract: ABSTRACT Recent scholarship argues that crises can create opportunities for women's political leadership. Yet crises also create opportunities for male political elites to adapt strategically to preserve their power. We develop and test a theory of crisis‐induced adaptation, whereby male political elites respond by shifting political attention toward crisis dimensions that reinforce their authority. We examine this theory using the Ugandan Parliament's response to COVID‐19, a health crisis in a policy domain traditionally associated with women. Using the complete corpus of parliamentary debates from 1998 to 2022 and text‐as‐data analyses, we find no evidence that COVID‐19 reduced gender inequalities in legislative speech. Instead, the pandemic widened them. Men's dominance in legislative speech grew as they increasingly framed the pandemic through traditionally masculine policy domains—the economy and national security—rather than public health. Rather than opening space for women, crises can provide men with new opportunities to entrench political dominance.

title: Forecasting a Democratic Resurgence? Partisan Accountability in the 2026 U.S. Midterm Elections
abstract: This article forecasts the 2026 U.S. midterm elections, building on the model developed by Algara et al. (2025) to predict the seats won by the president's party from the generic ballot, net presidential approval, midterm status, and the partisanship of the median seat at stake.First, we update our time series of presidential approval and the generic ballot through 2026, showing that the two evaluations remain distinct and diverge sharply this cycle.We validate the model with 34 rolling-origin forecasts per chamber using only pre-election information.Second, we forecast that Republicans are highly likely to lose the U.S. House, winning 196 seats [95% PI: 160, 221] with a 10% probability of retaining control at their 3-point generic ballot deficit.Third, our model forecasts Republicans narrowly holding the U.S. Senate with 51 seats [95% PI: 42, 61] and a 55% probability of control, reflecting an unusually favorable Senate class, although alternative specifications forecast a Democratic majority.Lastly, we measure how the House lines redrawn for 2026 shift partisan terrain, an effect our historically estimated model only partially absorbs, and show that the new maps could decide a close national contest but would not overturn the current House forecast.

title: Explaining and Predicting the Two-Party Mid-Term House Vote Share: 2026 Prediction
abstract: History of Voting EquationsI first estimated an equation explaining the two-party vote share for president in 1978-Fair (1978)).The general theory behind the equation is that a voter evaluates the past economic performances of the competing parties and votes for the party that provides the highest expected future utility.Within the context of the theory, one can test both how far back voters look in evaluating the economic performances of the parties and what economic variables they use in their evaluations.Many tests were performed in Fair (1978) using data on U.S. presidential elections beginning in 1916.The results supported the view that voters look only at the economic performance of the current party in power, not also, for example, the performance of the opposition party the last time it was in power.The growth rate of per capita real GDP and the inflation rate were the two economic variables.The theory allows some voters to always vote for only one party.It requires only that there are some "swing" voters who are influenced by the economy.

title: Forecasting a President-Centered Midterm: Leader-Centered Personalization in the 2026 US House Elections
abstract: Forecasting models of US midterm elections rely on indicators such as presidential approval, economic conditions, incumbency, district partisanship, and the generic congressional ballot.This paper asks whether these indicators fully capture presidential influence when congressional competition is organized around a highly personalized leader.It distinguishes electoral nationalization, in which local contests respond increasingly to national parties and conditions, from leader-centered personalization, in which those forces are organized around an individual leader.The paper identifies three mechanisms through which personalization may shape district-level electoral choice: candidate alignment, asymmetric mobilization, and electoral translation through campaign framing.It then combines a prespecified district baseline with a structured qualitative assessment of leader centrality and these mechanisms to generate prospective expectations about whether personalization should reinforce, weaken, or leave the baseline unchanged.The diagnostic is applied prospectively to four competitive 2026 US House races.The paper also distinguishes explanatory from predictive value, that is, leader-centered personalization may clarify how congressional accountability operates even when separately measuring personalization does not improve forecast accuracy.

title: Evidentiary Interpretation, Discursive Injustice, and Rap on Trial
abstract: ABSTRACT The submission of rap lyrics as inculpatory evidence (Rap on Trial) is an active prosecution tactic deployed in United States criminal trials. In this paper, I argue that interpretive ambiguity in rap lyrics is exploited in Rap on Trial cases, constituting a novel form of discursive injustice: extractive discursive injustice. Rap, a historically Black American artform, has core oral‐traditional elements such as its usage of Signifyin(g) that render it interpretably ambiguous. Utilizing the concept of hermeneutical impasses, I explain how a pernicious interpretation of rap lyrics nonetheless receives evidentiary uptake, revealing a crucial junction where injustice seeps into the courtroom. I argue that two speech act‐theoretic sites of injustice are present in Rap on Trial cases, detailing how one strain—discursive injustice—occurs. In doing so, I theorize novel forms of constitutive refusal and discursive injustice that occur when an utterance is extracted from one conversational context and deposited into another. I argue these are distinct from traditional forms in the method of arisal, though congruent with their function and display. I conclude by addressing an objection questioning the denial of truth‐telling value within rap lyrics and considering how a valid evidential use of rap lyrics might occur.

title: Democracy and the Politics of Attention in the Digital Age
abstract: In the digital age, attention has become a major issue of public concern. The emergence of various contemporary phenomena – including new digital architectures, new ways of monetizing them, and nefarious actors who have co-opted them – have led many people to argue that our attention is being stolen, fractured, and even traded on the open market. But, while these claims are becoming increasingly prevalent, attention remains an understudied concept in democratic theory. In this paper I work to pull out the relationship between attention and democratic politics in order to help us understand and contend with what is being called the “crisis of attention”. Primarily using the works of William James and Erving Goffman as a roadmap, I argue that it is through attentional fields that participants in democracies establish and negotiate the epistemic terrain from which possible actions are drawn. The upshot of this argument is that attentional fields can be a key resource towards the mobilization of democratic agency, but the erosion or manipulation of attentional fields can also be a vehicle through which democratic agency can be fractured, altered, or distorted.

title: Intersecting Identities: How Gender and Disability Shape Voter Perceptions of Election Candidates
abstract: Voters’ perceptions of election candidates are known to be shaped by stereotypes about candidates’ characteristics and social identities, including gender and disability. More recently, scholars have started paying attention to how the intersection of politicians’ identities shapes citizens’ perceptions of them, recognizing that identities do not simply “add up” but give rise to distinct stereotypes and expectations. This paper explores how candidate gender and disability affect voter perceptions through a survey experiment with a conjoint design in the UK and the US. The findings reveal a complex picture in which candidate gender and disability interact in shaping some, but not the majority, of voters’ perceptions of candidates’ traits, competences, beliefs, as well as voter support. The study underlines that intersectional approaches are fundamental to advancing our understanding of voter attitudes and behavior, candidate competition, and the representation of social groups.

title: An Intersectional Theory of Gendered Political Violence Under Sectarian Systems
abstract: Abstract Political violence against women is often analyzed primarily through gender, leaving underexplored how other systems of domination shape its production and enforcement. This article develops an intersectional feminist institutionalist framework to explain how patriarchal and sectarian formal and informal rules co-produce political violence against women in deeply divided societies. Drawing on Lebanon as a theory-building case study and applying an abductive approach to our empirical data, we argue that such violence is not simply a backlash against women’s political presence, but is core to preserving the sectarian order. We identify three overlapping mechanisms through which political violence against women candidates is enforced by multiple actors, namely family coercion, party- and militia-linked enforcement, and sectarian boundary policing, with all of them mobilizing scripts of honor, purity, loyalty, and communal stability to constrain women’s political agency. Our framework offers broader insights into intersectional political violence across ethnically and religiously divided societies.

title: Government Communication in Denmark: Controlled, Centralized, and More Partisan
abstract: ABSTRACT Governments increasingly coordinate executive communication to manage volatile media environments. In this article, I conceptualize government communication as encompassing greater control over messaging, timing, and media access; greater centralization at the PMO/ministry level; and greater coordination of communication with the public. Using a longitudinal study of Denmark (2010–2024)—a least‐likely case given formal neutrality norms—I document co‐variation between increased control, centralization, and coordination of communication and increased professionalization of staff. The study also indicates growing partisan alignment among staff, measured using a crude indicator derived from career trajectories. While stronger control, centralization, and coordination can improve agenda control, they also coincide with tighter gatekeeping and reduced transparency, echoing Nordic findings and recent Danish diagnoses of accelerated decision‐making and politicization pressures. My contribution is to (1) update Nordic evidence on executive communication centralization, (2) provide a structured mapping of Danish government policy professionals over time, and (3) propose an operational, auditable indicator of increasingly partisan recruitment based on pre‐ and post‐employment.

title: The Globalization of Social Cues: Trump's 2016 Victory Shaped the Salience of Immigration in Europe
abstract: ABSTRACT How did the election of Donald J. Trump in 2016 shape the salience of immigration in Europe? While previous research has documented transatlantic attitudinal spillovers, we know less about how such developments shape the salience of political issues. This study addresses this gap by leveraging individual‐level data from the ESS and the SOM Institute, using the election as an Unexpected Event during Survey Design. Employing regression discontinuity and embedding regression techniques, we analyze attitudinal change as well as open‐ended survey responses to the “most important issue” question to assess the election's effect on immigration salience. Our findings confirm previous work and show subgroup variations in the attitudinal effects of the election by different party groups, where authoritarian voters exhibit the largest liberalizing shift. Turning to salience, the text‐based embedding analyses point to a significant shift in issue engagement, driven primarily by an increase among authoritarian voters, a pattern also evident, though more weakly, in the hand‐coded data. Taken together, authoritarian voters became simultaneously more liberal in their immigration attitudes and more engaged with the issue. The findings underscore the importance of analytically distinguishing between attitudes and salience, illustrate how measurement choice can shape conclusions about salience, and demonstrate how major global political events can reshape the importance of specific political issues.

title: The Direct and Indirect Effects of Online Job Search Advice
abstract: Abstract We study how online job search advice affects job search behavior and labor market outcomes of unemployed workers. In a large-scale field experiment embedded in the online platform of the Danish public employment service, we provide job seekers with vacancy information and occupational recommendations. Using a two-stage randomized design with regionally varying treatment intensities, we examine both direct effects of advice and treatment spillovers. We find that advice significantly increases employment and earnings when provided to a limited share of job seekers. As treatment intensity rises, these effects diminish and eventually disappear. The decline is driven by negative spillovers among treated job seekers, consistent with increased congestion in the occupations toward which job seekers redirect their search. Spillover effects on untreated job seekers are heterogeneous and depend on how advice alters occupation-specific competition in local labor markets.

title: Industrialization and social mobility within a city: evidence from interwar Turin
Information Design in Repeated Interaction
abstract: How does a long-term relationship affect communication among economic entities? In this paper, we study dynamic information design in a simple “agreement game” with repeated interaction, where the state is imperfectly persistent. Disclosing information now influences future belief evolution, which results in a novel distortion relative to the static counterpart. We observe that the interaction of the players’ patience and the state’s persistence parameters is crucial in determining the optimal mechanism. Though an efficient mechanism is optimal with sufficiently small or large patience, with intermediate levels of patience, optimal mechanisms exhibit excessive agreement when states are sufficiently persistent, while they exhibit excessive disagreement with less persistence. How does a long-term relationship affect communication among economic entities? In this paper, we study dynamic information design in a simple “agreement game” with repeated interaction, where the state is imperfectly persistent. Disclosing information now influences future belief evolution, which results in a novel distortion relative to the static counterpart. We observe that the interaction of the players’ patience and the state’s persistence parameters is crucial in determining the optimal mechanism, where both excessive agreement and excessive disagreement can arise. How does a long-term relationship affect communication among economic entities? We study dynamic information design in a repeated “agreement game”, where the state is imperfectly persistent. Information disclosed today influences future beliefs, which results in a novel distortion relative to the static counterpart. We characterize how the optimal mechanism varies with the players’ patience and the state’s persistence. When players are very impatient or very patient, an efficient mechanism is optimal. If their patience is intermediate and the state’s persistence is high, the optimal mechanism may suppress bad news entirely, recommending agreement even when both players would prefer disagreement. If the state’s persistence is also intermediate, the optimal mechanism may do the opposite: recommend disagreement even when both players would prefer agreement, to reduce the informativeness of the bad news conveyed by disagreement.

title: Stories that Make Hawks? Digital News-Based User-Generated Content and Foreign Policy Orientations Among China’s Generation Z
abstract: This study examines the relationships between exposure to news-based user-generated content on Bilibili and Chinese Generation Z’s support for hawkish foreign policies. Guided by the Narrative Policy Framework, a survey ( N = 688) shows that self-reported exposure to villain, hero, and mixed narrative strategies is positively associated with hawkish orientations, both directly and indirectly through national pride and national humiliation. These findings suggest that, within the highly performative and affectively embedded dynamics of social media, nonofficial actors may rely on dramatized storytelling and serve as a nonnegligible component of the broader rise of hawkishness within Chinese youth communities.

title: The False Will Set You Free: How Lower Courts Have Translated the Supreme Court’s Latest Falsity Doctrine into Practice
abstract: This study provides the first descriptive mapping of the impact of the First Amendment’s rationale for advancing truth-seeking being extended counter-intuitively to provide greater protection for intentional falsehoods. Scholarly concerns over the Supreme Court’s Alvarez ruling focused on potentially creating a doctrinal vacuum of limited guidance. The study found lower courts reflected more clarity of guidance when cases involved the sorts of historically unprotected categories of false expression targeting harm beyond falsity—but considerably less so in other types of cases where it was often “not entirely clear what level of scrutiny is appropriate for laws that criminalize lying.”

title: Flattening Without Leveling: Visibility-Driven Flexible Re-Hierarchization in Government Digital Communication
abstract: Effective digital communication is a strategic imperative for government service delivery, yet the emerging information dissemination model emerging remains underexplored. Drawing on Chongqing’s digital-policing reform, this study develops an analytical framework centered on visibility-driven flexible re-hierarchization, based on interviews and observations. The analysis identifies three mechanisms: upward visibility and vertical bypass produce functional flattening without formal delayering; cross-boundary horizontal linkage dissolves departmental silos while preserving centralized coordination; and dual-mode switching shifts the information order between routine networked and mobilizational hierarchical communication. Digital technology does not flatten bureaucracy but endows it with an elastic capacity to switch between the two orders.

title: Neighbor Noise Problem in Multifamily Housing: An Integrative Framework for Resolution
abstract: Multifamily housing is common in urban areas, and neighbor noise is a frequent problem. In this study, a governance-based approach was designed for managing and preventing noise problems, marking an advance from conventional noise-reduction technologies. Using qualitative methods, including interviews with residents and professionals, the proposed framework categorizes five key sectors: individual, community, society, industry, and public. It highlights sector interactions, identifies key actors, and suggests sector-specific activities for resolution. Rather than offering a fixed solution, the proposed governance model is adaptable to various contexts, promoting sustainable and context-sensitive approaches to noise management.

title: Promises, Threats, and Norms: A Mixed Methods Study on Bureaucratic Support for Public Participation
abstract: ABSTRACT Public participation can enhance policy quality and democratic legitimacy but may threaten bureaucratic control. We hypothesize that bureaucratic support for participation is higher when policies are less complex and participants are broadly representative. Using a mixed‐methods design involving Indonesian local public servants, we pursue complementarity by combining a 2 × 2 vignette‐based survey experiment with a Gioia analysis of qualitative reflections to explain the experimental results and further illuminate how bureaucrats evaluate participation. The experiment shows that participant representativeness significantly increases support, whereas policy complexity has no statistically significant effect. Integrating the experimental and qualitative data through joint displays reveals that bureaucrats rejecting participation frequently cite participant‐related risks, whereas supporters emphasize instrumental, procedural, and implementation benefits. Normative values, such as citizens' rights and democratic principles, are acknowledged regardless of bureaucrats' overall support. We conclude that bureaucratic support for public participation reflects how officials balance its promises, threats, and normative foundations.

title: Governing Reserves: Managerial Discretion and Government Creditworthiness
abstract: ABSTRACT A government's ability to generate surpluses and build reserves reflects prudent financial management, with the accumulation of reserves signaling sound budgeting practices. Reserves are essential for sound fiscal governance during economic downturns, and managerial discretion over these resources is crucial to minimizing disruptions in service delivery. While the counter‐cyclical benefits of formal reserves are well documented, less attention has been paid to the discretion managers retain over reserves. Using credit ratings as a proxy for creditworthiness, we find that managerial discretion over accumulated resources enhances fiscal flexibility and strengthens creditworthiness; however, the presence of formal reserves alone does not improve credit ratings. Our study contributes to an emerging literature exploring whether better financial reporting can help us understand the critical balance between management flexibility and accountability mechanisms in public‐sector organizations.

title: Evaluating the validity of performance measurement systems in law enforcement: a pragmatic constructivism approach
abstract: This paper assesses the practical validity of a balanced scorecard-based performance measurement system in a UAE law enforcement agency by examining how well strategic priorities translate into departmental and individual measures. Drawing on pragmatic constructivism, we conduct a single-case qualitative study using manager interviews and archival documents. We find weak translation of strategy into operational indicators and appraisal criteria, uneven awareness of performance indicators, and limited integration of facts, logic, values, and communication, which undermines system validity and strategic alignment. Effective alignment requires clearer cascades from strategy maps to operational indicators and appraisal criteria, role-appropriate access to KPIs, and cross-unit forums connecting planning and appraisal owners. The study’s primary contribution is empirical: it provides evidence of how misalignment emerges between strategy, measures, rewards, and appraisal in a public law enforcement organization. It also elaborates ‘practical validity’ as a criterion for examining how performance measurement systems function in practice.

title: When women lead: women mayors and municipal police effectiveness in reducing homicide in Brazil
abstract: While research highlights women leaders’ influence in traditionally feminine domains such as health, education, and welfare, less is known about their impact in traditionally masculine fields such as policing and crime reduction. Using a Regression Discontinuity design and data from Brazilian municipalities, this study shows that, compared with male mayors, women mayors are more likely to adopt municipal police forces. Municipal policing, in turn, reduces youth homicide rates under women leadership, with this effect amplified by investments in socially oriented infrastructure. These findings demonstrate that women leaders can generate broader community-wide benefits beyond direct representation of women’s interests. The study extends scholarship on gender-responsive governance and women leadership by showing how elected women can shape policy choices and their effectiveness in traditionally male-dominated domains such as policing.

title: Debate: Teaching money is easy; changing behaviour is harder
abstract: This article is of direct relevance to finance and education ministries, school inspection bodies, and the national agencies that fund financial education in the more than 70 countries and economie...

title: Economic Governance and Institutional Design
abstract: ABSTRACT How should institutions be designed to achieve compliance with behavioral rules, including laws, social norms, religious rules, or cultural traditions? This conceptual paper introduces a typology of economic governance institutions and explains how it can be used both by policy makers, administrators, and researchers in all social sciences to improve rule compliance. It explains how effective and efficient institutions can be identified for a given economic governance problem. The framework is built on the microeconomic foundations of economic governance theory, and its applicability extends to any compliance problem that can be formalized as a social dilemma or coordination game. The concepts are applied to two cases: how to create trust in cloud computing technologies, and how to implement data sharing of user‐generated information on data‐driven markets.

title: From bench to Brussels and back: co-producing personalized medicine in the European Union
abstract: Personalized medicine (PM) has emerged as both a major scientific endeavor and a strategic policy priority in the European Union (EU). Drawing on discourse theory and the science and technology studies concept of co-production, we use PM as a case of a co-produced scientific and policy project to examine not only how scientific advances shape policy agendas but also how EU political priorities, funding programs, and governance frameworks shape the scientific field. The study employs a qualitative comparative document analysis of scientific publications and EU policy documents published between 2000 and 2025. Scientific discourse and political narrative were analyzed separately before being compared to identify areas of convergence, divergence, and co-production. The analysis shows that scientific discourse evolved from genomics toward multi-omics, systems medicine, and AI-enabled, data-intensive research, consolidating into platform science organized around shared infrastructures, interoperable data ecosystems, and cross-disciplinary collaboration. In parallel, the EU’s political narrative evolved from promoting genomics-based healthcare innovation to positioning PM as a strategic instrument for digital transformation, competitiveness, and health-system reform. Our findings demonstrate the reciprocal co-production of science and policy in shaping PM as an institutionalized field.

title: Feedback-driven paradigm shifts and event-driven incrementalism: evidence from South Korea through the Multiple Streams Framework
abstract: This study extends the Multiple Streams Framework (MSF) by examining how three subcomponents of the problem stream – focusing events, indicators, and feedback – interact with the timing of decision-window openings to shape modes of policy change. It conducts a comparative analysis of South Korea’s responses to four emerging infectious disease outbreaks – SARS, H1N1, MERS, and COVID-19 – and identifies conditional mechanisms linking problem characteristics to policy outcomes. The findings show that when decision windows open late, both incremental and paradigmatic change remain possible regardless of the problem-stream subcomponent associated with the window. By contrast, when windows open early, the type of problem-stream subcomponent becomes consequential for the mode of policy change. Early-opening decision windows associated with focusing events or indicators tend to produce incremental change, as decision makers under time pressure rely on pre-existing policy alternatives. Early-opening decision windows associated with feedback, however, are more likely to generate paradigmatic change because feedback reveals implementation failures and institutional limitations. By distinguishing event-driven incrementalism from feedback-driven paradigm shifts, this study clarifies how window timing conditions the relationship between problem-stream characteristics and modes of policy change and extends the explanatory scope of the MSF for understanding crisis-induced policy change.

title: Do citizens reward democratic norm enforcement? Experimental evidence on EU backsliding disputes
abstract: Conflicts between international organisations committed to democratic norms and member states experiencing democratic backsliding have become increasingly prominent in contemporary politics. Yet little is known about how citizens evaluate these disputes, and whether democratic norm enforcement is rewarded or penalised. Focussing on the European Union (EU), we field two survey experiments in Germany (n = 2700) and Hungary (n = 1600) that simulate realistic sequences of conflict between the EU and a backsliding government. Across both contexts, we find little evidence that citizens reward the EU for imposing or maintaining sanctions. By contrast, the EU incurs clear reputational costs when it retreats from previously announced enforcement under political pressure. These findings suggest that public opinion creates pressure towards institutions less through demand for democratic enforcement than through punishment of visible inconsistency in disputes over democratic norms.

title: Transcending sports: public demand for gender equity in name, image, and likeness (NIL) policy and its connection to the diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) policy debate in higher education
abstract: Abstract Public demand suggests that salience and opinion shape how individuals interpret policy, creating openings for framing and value branding to influence those views. I apply this framework to assess public demand for gender equity in name, image, and likeness (NIL) policy and examine how it aligns with the broader debate in higher education concerning diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI). Using survey data from 1,510 respondents across five states, I find that attitudes toward DEI significantly structure views of gender equity in NIL. Public demand for equity in NIL follows traditional predictors, including political ideology, age, education, and gender, while support for college sports has an unexpected negative association. I also identify foundational connections between NIL and support for regulating diversity and equity in higher education, suggesting that NIL functions as an emerging equity policy domain shaped by the same political and cultural forces that structure views of DEI.

title: Understanding Early Attitudes Towards Generative AI Regulation in Higher Education: The Role of Academic Scientists’ Experience and Risk Perceptions
abstract: ABSTRACT As generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) technology rapidly permeates higher education, it creates opportunities to transform teaching, research, and workforce preparation while raising ethical, social and environmental concerns. Academic scientists have a unique role in this transition as their early exposure to publicly accessible GenAI tools shapes emerging practices, norms, and institutional responses. Existing research often treats AI‐related risk as a single construct, limiting understanding of how distinct risk dimensions shape regulatory preferences. This study investigates how academic scientists’ experience with GenAI relates to risk perceptions over agency loss and data breach, and how these perceptions are associated with their regulatory attitudes during its formative stage. Using survey data collected between September and November 2023, shortly after ChatGPT became widely accessible, we find that greater GenAI experience is associated with lower perceived risks. Meanwhile, different risk perceptions are linked to distinct regulatory preferences: perceived risk of agency loss is associated with a greater likelihood of supporting federal regulation and a lower likelihood of supporting academic self‐regulation, whereas perceived data breach risk is associated with a greater likelihood of supporting federal regulation but not associated with the likelihood of supporting self‐regulation. These findings provide an early baseline understanding of faculty attitudes toward GenAI regulation in academic contexts.

title: Training and productivity in micro-firms
abstract: This paper examines the effect of training on productivity of micro-firms, defined in official statistics as firms with less than 10 employees. While training may represent a crucial mode of knowledge accumulation in micro-firms, which usually lack resources or structure to devote to formal innovation activities, the specificities of micro-businesses suggest that training may even be detrimental to productivity of this category of firms. Yet, the received wisdom that training should foster their productivity, as it does in larger firms, remains un-tested, mainly due to difficulties in previous literature to analyze micro-firms separately from the wider groups of small or small-medium enterprises. Exploiting a unique administrative panel dataset that records training expenses of a large sample of micro-firms located in three Italian regions, we address whether micro-firms which train enjoy a productivity premium vis-a-vis micro-firms that do not. Our main finding, controlling for endogeneity of training via Inverse Probability Weighted Regression Adjustment methods, combined with firm fixed-effects, is a positive and sizable average treatment effect of training, stable across a series of robustness checks and heterogeneity analysis.

title: The Institutional Sensitivity of Crisis Response: Evidence From Local Government Policy Overreaction in China
abstract: ABSTRACT Effective policy responses are essential to crisis management, yet local governments often adopt measures that exceed what objective conditions require during crises. Such instances of overreaction offer a valuable lens for understanding the institutional dynamics that drive crisis response behavior. This study develops the concept of institutional sensitivity, an adaptive behavioral process through which governments interpret crisis conditions and strategically adjust their response strategies within institutional contexts. Drawing on China's population mobility management policies during the COVID‐19 pandemic, this study applies survival analysis models and spatial analyses to assess how peer effects, administrative accountability, and administrative capacity shape policy overreaction. The findings reveal a pronounced institutional sensitivity in crisis response: peer effects and administrative accountability significantly increase the likelihood of overreaction, whereas administrative capacity has no overall effect. These policy response behaviors also vary systematically across different crisis conditions. During high‐risk conditions, peer effects and accountability pressures increase overreaction, while administrative capacity restrains the likelihood of overreaction; under moderate‐risk conditions, this pattern reverses. This study advances theoretical understanding of the dynamic institutional sensitivity of crisis management and highlights the spatial and temporal effects embedded in governmental policy behavior.

title: The Elderly Sense of Gain in Community Elderly Care Services: A Grounded Theory Analysis
abstract: ABSTRACT High‐quality community elderly care services are widely expected as global aging has become a significant demographic shift. The elderly sense of gain has the potential to reflect the actual needs of the elderly and thus improve service quality. However, it lacks deep theoretical exploration based on emerging cases. Based on grounded‐theory analysis of five communities in City Q, China, the elderly sense of gain unfolds within each service cycle through three temporally linked dimensions: initial, actual and future sense of gain, while future sense of gain may shape service acceptance in the next cycle. Diminishing marginal effects, digital loneliness and negative spillovers may erode actual sense of gain, impede the formation of future sense of gain and reduce subsequent service acceptance. Conceptualizing sense of gain as a dynamic user‐level evaluative process clarifies how publicly enabled benefits are anticipated, experienced and prospectively assessed, and why objective service provision does not automatically become subjectively recognized value. Attention is thereby shifted from service volume to the conditions under which public provision generates and sustains value for older adults.

title: Public Service Decline and Support for the Populist Right: Evidence from England’s National Health Service
abstract: The rise of populist right parties is well-studied, but relatively little attention has been given to how public service performance influences voter support.
