Given that public services are often the primary means through which citizens interact with the state, we argue that declining public services can create grievances that increase the appeal of populist right parties. Focusing on England’s National Health Service (NHS), we combine administrative data on local health facility closures with panel data on public preferences and voting intentions. Using a staggered difference-in-differences design, we find that closures reduce satisfaction with public services and increase support for populist right parties. These effects are moderated by migrant registrations at local health practices, highlighting the interaction between public service performance and immigration concerns in fueling populist right support. Our findings underscore the role of public service decline as a driver of support for populist parties, especially in areas undergoing demographic change.

title: Divergent Legacies: How the Local Instantiation of National Conflict Conditions Postwar Political Engagement
abstract: Under what conditions does violence generate legacies of political [dis]engagement? Victimization is frequently linked to higher rates of political engagement – voting, protesting, attending meetings, etc. Often, however, victims withdraw from politics. These initial responses are evident generations later. I reconcile these disparate trends by analyzing the materialization of national conflict at the local level. When a community experiences violence perpetrated by non-local factions, victimization is more likely to politicize. By contrast, when perpetrated by members of one’s community against other local members, violence is more likely to depoliticize. To test these arguments, I leverage an original survey, archival material, and interviews from the understudied case of Cameroon. From 1956 to 1971, the Union des Populations du Cameroun (UPC) fought against French and Cameroonian state and paramilitary forces. Civilians were heavily targeted by the state, militias, and UPC guerillas. Today, variation in those local experiences is associated with differences in political behavior and socialization practices.

title: Authoritarian orientations and the contestation of liberal self-determination: Cross-national evidence from 30 countries
abstract: Abstract In contrast to expectations of global liberal convergence, liberal values and institutions are increasingly contested. This study investigates whether core liberal conditions for self-determination are likewise subject to contestation and how this varies across societal contexts. Drawing from liberal theory, we identify five enabling conditions for self-determination: physical well-being, basic economic security, learning and personal growth, moral equality, and influence on political decision-making. These conditions differ in their degree of ‘liberal uniqueness’, with the latter two representing distinctly liberal ideals. Using original survey data from over 45,000 respondents across 30 countries, we examine how authoritarian orientations – conceptualised as preferences for authority, conformity, order, and security – relate to support for these conditions. Such orientations are consistently and negatively associated with uniquely liberal conditions, especially moral equality and political influence. In contrast, there is no meaningful relationship with basic economic security and a positive association with physical well-being. Preferences for learning and personal growth fall in between. These associations vary with levels of societal modernisation; in more modernised societies, the gap between respondents with stronger and weaker authoritarian orientations grows wider, with the strongest widening observed for the uniquely liberal conditions. Our findings suggest that authoritarian orientations are linked to different understandings of self-determination. These competing visions of what it means to live freely are more polarised in modern societies. Recognising this divergence helps to better understand the normative foundations of contemporary societal conflicts across diverse countries.

title: Administrative state capacity and the effect of EU democracy assistance on levels of democracy: a time-series cross-sectional analysis, 2007–2021
abstract: Abstract The European Union (EU) is one of the world’s major donors of democracy assistance, which aims to foster democratisation. Its effects, however, depend on various conditional factors. This study explores the nexus between democracy assistance and administrative state capacity. Since democracy assistance seeks to strengthen —not substitute—the state and its institutions, we argue that administrative capacity is a crucial condition for the effectiveness of democracy assistance. To test our argument, we conduct a time-series cross-sectional analysis covering EU democracy assistance allocation from 2007 to 2021 across 23 countries in the EU’s neighbourhood. Our results indicate that assistance allocated to countries with higher state capacity has a more substantial effect on their levels of democracy than assistance allocated to countries with lower state capacity. With that, we address an important research gap and contribute to policy debates on the allocation of democracy assistance.

title: Does politics drive cultural preferences? Voting behavior in the Eurovision Song Contest
abstract: Abstract In the context of growing polarization and culture war conflict, politics is often seen as invading cultural spaces such as sports and popular music. An example is the Eurovision Song Contest (ESC), where political attitudes toward participant countries are thought to influence outcomes. In this study, we administer an online survey in four European countries to examine voting behavior in the ESC. Unlike existing studies, our individual-level data allow us to distinguish political influences on ESC voting behavior from cultural attitudes and song quality. We show that most voting in the contest is idiosyncratic, not political. Political attitudes, cultural attitudes, and song quality all influence ESC voting behavior, but effects and explained variance are small. Moreover, political attitudes only influence voting for those countries—Ukraine and Israel—whose policies generate strong opinions. The results suggest that, even in polarized contexts, cultural preferences are still primarily about aesthetics rather than politics.

title: Privileged Franchise and the Political Representation of Elites: Evidence From Denmark
abstract: ABSTRACT Democratization, via franchise extension, can reduce traditional elite representation and power. We study whether autocratization similarly increases the representation of these elites. We use the case of Denmark from 1849 to 1915. A constitutional change in 1866 created a privileged franchise to the upper chamber of the parliament weighted towards the wealthy and rural areas, while leaving the electoral rules to the lower chamber unchanged. Using MP‐year level data, we apply a difference‐in‐difference approach to study whether this autocratizing reform increased the representation of Danish elites in the upper chamber relative to the lower chamber. We find that this reform indeed increased the share of traditional elites in the upper chamber of the parliament such as the nobility and landed estate owners, including those with political‐dynastic ties, and arguably therefore the nature of democratic representation in 19th century Denmark.

title: Revisiting the Carbon Lock-In: Outlining an Agenda on How Affective Polarization Constrains Climate Policy Making
abstract: Carbon lock-in, the self-reinforcing inertia that perpetuates fossil fuel dependence, emerges from interdependent technological, institutional, economic, and behavioral factors. As climate policy has become increasingly polarized across advanced democracies, the role of affective polarization in reinforcing these barriers remains underexplored. This research agenda asks the following question: How and to what extent does affective polarization sustain the carbon lock-in? Drawing on social identity theory and the carbon lock-in literature, I propose a framework in which affective polarization operates as a cross-cutting process strengthening existing lock-in mechanisms through three pathways: (1) elite framing that activates both institutional distrust and out-group animosity toward pro-climate groups; (2) trust erosion linking vertical (elite–mass) and horizontal (mass–mass) polarization to sustained policy resistance; and (3) self-reinforcing feedback loops between polarizing rhetoric and mass resistance that persist across electoral cycles. Partisan identity sorting can transform climate policies into identity markers, turning otherwise reversible constraints into path-dependent barriers that persist even when policies are economically beneficial or technically effective. The agenda applies specifically to high-polarization contexts and calls for empirical investigation of these mechanisms and of depolarization interventions.

title: Integrated Explanations of Well‐Being
abstract: ABSTRACT According to three plausible assumptions about well‐being, a person's welfare depends on (i) the valence of her experiences, (ii) the degree to which her life resonates with her, and (iii) the extent to which she fulfills her potential. Theories of well‐being have struggled to accommodate all three in a determinate manner. The difficulty can be framed as a dilemma: either jettison considered convictions, or sacrifice the clarity required for measurement and practical guidance. The aim of this article is to show that the three most influential theories are impaled by one of the horns in the dilemma, and diagnose the source of the problem. In doing so, I draw attention to an under‐theorized form of explanation that integrates phenomenological, conative and functional elements in a unified account that might overcome it.

title: Are Citizens Inoculated by Past Democratic Backsliding?
abstract: Across the world, elected governments are dismantling the liberal democracies they inherited. Can these democratic backsliding episodes inoculate citizens into liberal democrats vigilant against future relapses? Because scholars have yet to resolve this puzzle, we lack crucial information to gauge the prospects of democratic resilience. We develop this "democratic inoculation thesis" into a testable theory and assess its validity in the critical case of Slovakia – a backsliding democracy that previously experienced democratic erosion and is often cited as a likely case of democratic inoculation. Through a survey experiment prompting Slovak citizens to reflect on democratic backsliding in the 1990s, we assess whether these reflections heighten their vigilance over their current government and bolster their support for liberal democratic norms. We also evaluate whether factors like affective polarization and education condition democratic inoculation.

“Rights Talk” Can Inhibit Persuasion and Compromise

Buying Data from Consumers: The Impact of Monitoring in U.S. Auto Insurance

TESTING FOR ENDOGENEITY: A MOMENT-BASED BAYESIAN APPROACH
abstract: A standard assumption in the Bayesian estimation of linear regression models is that the regressors are exogenous in the sense that they are uncorrelated with the model error term. In practice, however, this assumption can be invalid. In this article, using the exponentially tilted empirical likelihood (ETEL) framework, we develop a Bayes factor test for endogeneity that compares a base model that is correctly specified under exogeneity but misspecified under endogeneity against an extended model that is correctly specified in either case. We provide a comprehensive study of the log-marginal ETEL. We demonstrate that our testing procedure is consistent from a frequentist point of view: as the sample grows, it almost surely selects the base model if and only if the regressors are exogenous, and the extended model if and only if the regressors are endogenous. The methods are illustrated with simulated data and problems concerning the causal effect of automobile prices on automobile demand and the causal effect of potentially endogenous airplane ticket prices on passenger volume.

title: From catastrophe to efficacy: a longitudinal analysis of The New York Times ’ visual and narrative climate framing on Facebook (2013–2023)
abstract: This study examines how The New York Times packaged climate-related journalism on Facebook from 2013 to 2023. Using a stratified random sample of 650 posts, the present study applies O’Neill et al.’s climate-frame typology and codes dominant frame, emotional valence, visual-asset format, and central human depiction. Chi-square tests and logistic regressions show significant temporal changes within this single outlet-platform case. Disaster and Moral/Ethics frames declined, whereas Opportunity frames increased; Political/Ideological Struggle remained stable. Standard press photography became less prevalent, while data graphics, text-overlay graphics, and other non-photographic assets became more common. Images centered on political elites declined, while those centered on affected citizens increased. These findings document a production-side shift toward more response-oriented and visually self-contained climate-post packaging, although they do not demonstrate that Facebook caused the changes, that the formats or frames improved performance, or that audiences experienced greater engagement or efficacy. This study contributes a bounded longitudinal baseline for comparative, platform-sensitive, and audience-centered climate-communication research.

title: Enterprise Architecture Threat Modeling for Cybersecurity Risk Management
abstract: Organizations invest heavily in cybersecurity capabilities, yet the relationship between deployed defensive portfolios, practitioner judgments of coverage, and empirically observed adversary behavior remains difficult to assess. This study examines that relationship by integrating practitioner elicitation with threat-informed cybersecurity architecture analysis. A model-derived analytical baseline was constructed using the Cybersecurity Architecture Review (CAR) methodology aligned with MITRE ATT&CK version 17, quantifying protect, detect, and respond coverage for 12 commonly deployed cybersecurity capability categories. Survey data from 65 cybersecurity practitioners were used to characterize capability portfolios, perceived coverage, and factors influencing capability-selection decisions. Results show uneven modeled coverage across the ATT&CK lifecycle and substantial functional overlap among capability categories. Across 910 respondent-tactic observations, practitioner-estimated coverage exceeded corresponding respondent-specific modeled coverage by approximately 27 percentage points on average, although the magnitude and direction of perception-model divergence varied by tactic. Most subgroup comparisons by professional role, responsibility, and experience did not identify statistically significant differences, while government respondents exhibited slightly higher mean divergence than nongovernment respondents in one pairwise comparison. Capability-selection decisions reflected multiple organizational and external influences, with formal internal threat modeling reported less frequently than peer practices, regulatory or compliance requirements, independent research, and analyst or consultant reports. The findings demonstrate how threat-informed architecture analysis can complement practitioner judgment by making modeled coverage, gaps, overlap, and divergence explicit within organizational cybersecurity risk governance.

title: Between the Lines: Decoding Signaling Differences in Public and Private Sector Job Advertisements
abstract: ABSTRACT To compete in the “war for talent,” public sector employers must demonstrate advantages over private employers. While public service motivation (PSM) predicts sector preference, scholars disagree on whether public employers (can) effectively signal PSM in job advertisements. Consequently, this article examines how public and private job advertisements differ in language. We collected 5000 advertisements from both sectors and performed natural language processing (NLP) and qualitative content analysis. Both sectors use specialized language that can narrow the applicant pool. PSM signals appear more often in the public sector, but affective motives are rarely communicated; instead, self‐sacrifice is framed as a legal obligation. Public sector advertisements adopt a rational tone instead of explaining purpose and societal value. Legally mandated, saturated signals may be perceived as low‐cost and ineffective. The findings explain the mixed results concerning PSM signaling and underscore the gap between theory and practice in PSM‐related recruitment efforts.

title: How collaborative platforms shape power dynamics and outcomes in local collaboration: evidence from disaster mitigation planning
Mission Without Merit? Public Service Career Satisfaction, Patronage Promotions, and Public Service Motivation
abstract: While merit-based personnel systems are widely linked to improved performance and reduced corruption, less attention has been given to how an erosion of merit affects civil servants. Drawing on psychological contract and distributive justice theories, this study links perceptions of patronage in promotion processes, where personalistic, relational, or political criteria are perceived to displace formal advancement mechanisms, to diminished public service career satisfaction. It further argues that those with high levels of public service motivation (PSM) may interpret patronage-based promotion as both a threat to their own careers and a violation of the public values that make government service meaningful. As such, the negative association between perceived patronage and career satisfaction may be particularly severe for employees with higher levels of PSM. Using a large-scale survey of South Korean central and local government officials, the study develops a patronage perceptions index using forced-choice responses about perceived promotion factors and presents empirical evidence for the theoretical model. This research provides novel insight into how personalistic practices in the public sector may weaken civil servants’ satisfaction with public service as a career and discusses future research questions relevant to safeguarding the integrity of human resource management in the public sector.

title: Institutional setting and vaccine sector capabilities. The cases of Japan, Indonesia, and Vietnam
abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic exposed the urgent need for stable vaccine provision worldwide. This paper examines how three Asian countries developed technological, regulatory, market-enabling, and coordination capabilities for vaccine provision during the COVID-19 crisis, with particular attention to the catalytic role of institutional capacity in reshaping vaccine-sector incentive mechanisms. Using a comparative institutional analysis, the study compares Japan, Indonesia, and Vietnam before, during, and after the COVID-19 pandemic. Drawing on semi-structured interviews and secondary sources, the analysis shows that while COVID-19 acted as a catalyst, outcomes varied significantly across the selected countries because of differences in pre-existing capabilities. The study argues that even during a crisis, institutional transformation remains strongly path-dependent and incremental: crisis arrangements reverted once pressure receded, while those bound by contract or market instruments remained.

title: Means‐Tested Public Transportation Subsidies: Causal Evidence and Implications
journal_name: Journal of Policy Analysis and Management

title: Returns to Caring? Health and Well‐Being Effects of Subsidized Long‐Term Care
abstract: ABSTRACT We estimate the health and well‐being effects of subsidized access to long‐term care (LTC). Our analysis exploits the staggered implementation of Spain's 2007 System of Autonomy and Care for Dependent People (SAAD), which expanded publicly funded and universal LTC subsidies and supports, as well as its subsequent reform. Using two decades of administrative and survey data and leveraging exogenous regional and individual‐level variation in program exposure, we find that access to SAAD benefits reduces the care receiver's depressive symptoms by approximately 10 percentage points, increases its survival probability by 2.6–3 percentage points, and raises its life satisfaction by 0.24–0.50 scale points. Cost‐effectiveness estimates indicate that the implied cost per quality‐adjusted life year (QALY) gained lies below commonly accepted efficiency thresholds for public health spending in Europe. These findings document sizeable health returns and efficiency gains from publicly subsidized LTC provision.
journal_name: Journal of Policy Analysis and Management

title: Spatiality of preemptive coercion: How autocrats demolish informal settlements for political control
abstract: Abstract Why do authorities demolish informal settlements in metropolises? The social sciences have a long tradition of addressing this issue through the lens of economic development or welfare provision. I instead propose a theory of political control. Autocrats adopt demolition as a preemptive and coercive tool to remove communities substantively and symbolically less legible to them, thereby ensuring societal compliance and restoring visual order. Empirically, I compile a unique dataset of 320 demolished and undemolished informal settlements in Beijing between 2017 and 2018, based on satellite imagery, digital street views, and fieldwork. The results indicate that the low legibility of informal settlements to authorities correlates with a greater likelihood of demolition. This paper contributes to the social science literature by connecting legibility politics with urban governance. It also introduces a spatial perspective and leverages novel data sources to deepen our understanding of preemptive coercion under authoritarianism.

title: Killing #MahsaAmini on Persian Twitter: the repertoire of false information in authoritarian regimes
abstract: Despite the growth of research on false information (FI), most work, which is largely based on Western democracies, still relies on coarse dis/misinformation binaries and prioritizes automation and coordination (e.g. bot activity). This emphasis is limiting for authoritarian contexts, where verification is structurally constrained, and FI often operates through more nuanced, context-dependent practices. Focusing on Iran's Women, Life, Freedom (WLF) movement, this study examines the repertoire and user ecology of FI on Persian Twitter during contentious politics. Drawing on critical discourse analysis, we manually analyzed 36,255 popular tweets from 4,807 users posted during the first two months of movement (September 15, 2022–March 30, 2023). Findings show a significant shift from blatant fabrications toward FI accusations and unverified information (UI), generating credibility warfare and weaponized unverifiability. We argue that authoritarian FI is structured by unverifiability as much as falsity, which cannot be captured through text-only computational detection. The user ecology of FI is camp-specific, while inauthentic coordinated behaviour is limited. We theorize authoritarian FI as a repertoire shaped by verification constraints and credibility struggles, with implications for comparative research.

title: Perceiving Politics: Considering the Political Categorization of Faces
abstract: Abstract Categorizing people into groups is a fundamentally human trait, but we know very little about how people assign political identities to strangers. Across two innovative survey experiments, we consider how people politically categorize others according to a single source of information: faces. We find that displays of emotions, particularly negative emotions, predict the political sorting of strangers. Faces featuring negative emotions are categorized as out-partisans, whereas faces exhibiting happiness are categorized as co-partisans.

title: The Synthetic Imputation Approach: Using LLMs to Generate Synthetic Texts for Underrepresented Categories in Supervised Classification Tasks
abstract: Abstract Annotated text data are central to many empirical applications in political science, yet many annotation tasks involve categories that are sparsely populated. These low- N categories pose problems for both encoder-only and decoder-only (generative) Transformer large language models (LLMs), leading to low performance, biased evaluation and measurement error in downstream analyses. This article introduces the synthetic imputation approach, a targeted method for expanding sparse categories while remaining consistent with the category-defining content of the human-coded examples. The approach uses a generative LLM to produce additional texts for underrepresented categories by conditioning on small, rotating subsets of human-coded examples. Rather than paraphrasing or replacing the original data, synthetic imputation adds informative variation only where data are thin. I evaluate the approach using both encoder-only and decoder-only LLM classifiers across multiple political science applications. The results show that synthetic imputation substantially improves performance and evaluation stability in sparse settings, recovering full-sample performance once a modest number of true observations is available, with limited and predictable overfitting at very low levels of N .

title: Partisan Wishful Thinking in Polarized Times
Banal assimilation and minority politics in northern Sweden
Alternative energy nationalisms: Energy futures on display at Expo mega-events
Leaking energy externalities: exploring Mozambique-EU relations within the global energy market
From misogyny to mobilization: Hostile sexism and conflictual online discussions indirectly predict men's rights activism via heightened identification as a men's rights supporter
abstract: Abstract Although sexism may serve as a gateway into the men's rights movement, few studies have examined group processes in online environments that fuel this reactionary movement. We address this gap by examining whether interacting with like‐minded others fosters an emergent social identity as a “men's rights supporter” among sexist men; and whether identification predicts willingness to engage in reactionary actions undermining gender equality. Across two studies ( N s = 443, 755), men completed a hostile sexism measure and read about the perceived impacts of feminism on men. Participants then either discussed whether feminism negatively impacts men in an online chatroom (group deliberation) or reflected individually (individual deliberation). Hostile sexism predicted identification as a men's rights supporter, and this link was stronger in the group deliberation condition. In turn, identification predicted greater reactionary action intentions. Unexpectedly, these effects emerged only among men who indicated that their group was unsure about the impact of feminism after the discussion. A post‐hoc content analysis of the pooled chat logs revealed that these men engaged in discussions marked by conflict and disagreement, suggesting that identification with the movement emerged through dissent rather than consensus. These findings highlight complex social dynamics underpinning engagement with the men's rights movement.

title: King’s Equality
abstract: In a 1962 speech, Martin Luther King Jr. distinguished between a “stagnant equality of sameness” and a “constructive equality of oneness.” Scholars have rarely paused over this distinction, presuming King’s equality to be a mere extension of liberal or Christian moral equality. This article argues instead that King advances a distinctive idea of equality, one that refigures his understanding of politics. His equality begins not with future-focused reforms that seek to equalize various forms of power but instead with acknowledging specific realities that already equally bind us: our dependence on others to make sense of who we are, our inescapable historical indebtedness, and the tragic and limited nature of human understanding and action. To acknowledge these facts is not resignation; it is political work. King’s equality reorients politics away from power understood as mastery and control, and toward a practice of humility and awareness, constructively making different forms of political relation and action possible. Recovering this neglected strand of King’s thought offers a new way to understand equality—as an ongoing relation to reality—as well as a new image of King as a political realist.

title: Love of variety? An experimental study of heterogeneous responses to foreign brands in the marketplace
abstract: Abstract Do everyday encounters with foreign brands shape political attitudes? We argue that brand origin cues activate national identities, producing different responses among nationalists and cosmopolitans. In an online shopping experiment, U.S. participants were randomly assigned to compare American (control), European, or Asian (treatment) sport utility vehicles without explicit mention of brand origin. Exposure to foreign brands increased opposition to trade and immigration and support for Donald Trump among nationalists. Cosmopolitans generally showed little change. These effects are not reducible to partisanship, revealing within-coalition divides among Republicans and among Democrats and Independents. Our findings show that subtle consumer experiences spill over into politics, creating a bottom-up channel of polarization that links nationalism and populism to support for neomercantilist and nativist policies.

title: Trade, Human Capital, and Income Risk,
abstract: Abstract In this paper, we study the causal relationship between trade exposure and individual income risk, with emphasis on the role of human capital. We use a rich worker-level longitudinal dataset from Germany spanning the period 1976-2012, and find industry trade exposure to be causally related to income risk: Imports increase risk and exports decrease risk in an economically significant manner. Importantly, there is a complex interplay between human capital and the linkage between trade and risk: On average, individuals with higher levels of industry- or occupation-specific human capital experience lower risk. However, an increase in industry net imports increases risk more for workers with higher levels of industry tenure. Although net imports are also associated with declines in the mean income of these workers, the estimated effect on income levels is economically small. Our welfare framework, which jointly considers both mean income and income risk, shows that the welfare consequences of trade exposure are quantitatively dominated by the risk channel.
journal_name: Journal of the European Economic Association

title: PROXIMAL ESTIMATION AND INFERENCE
abstract: Abstract We develop a convex-analytic framework for constructing and analyzing a broad class of penalized estimators. Our method defines penalized estimators by applying proximal operators to benchmark estimators, rather than by penalizing the benchmark criterion itself. We establish general finite-sample properties, derive unified asymptotic distribution results, and provide tractable conditions for oracle selection and oracle asymptotic efficiency. We then apply the framework to linear regression with irregular designs, including singular and nearly-singular cases. In this setting, where the coefficient vector need not be point identified, we motivate the Ridgeless estimand as the inferential target, construct a n $\sqrt {n}$ StartRoot n EndRoot -consistent modified Ridgeless benchmark estimator, and combine it with adaptive proximal penalization to obtain, to the best of our knowledge, the first penalized estimator achieving the oracle property under both regular and irregular designs.

title: The Dynamics of the Racial Wealth Gap
abstract: ABSTRACT We study the dynamics of the racial wealth gap (the wealth of Black households relative to white ones) using a dynamic equilibrium model of overlapping generations. We match the model to the cross‐sectional distributions of wealth and earnings by race. We find that equalizing earnings is critical for permanent reductions in racial wealth inequality, and that one‐time transfers will have only transitory effects unless earnings are also equalized. Our results are robust to the introduction of racial differences in returns to saving, which only matter after earnings inequality is reduced.

title: Network members can hide from group centrality measures
abstract: Group centrality measures are a generalization of standard centrality, designed to quantify the importance of not just a single node (as is the case with standard measures) but rather that of a group of nodes. Some nodes may have an incentive to evade such measures, i.e., to hide their actual importance, in order to conceal their true role in the network. A number of studies have been proposed in the literature to understand how nodes can rewire the network in order to evade standard centrality, but no study has focused on group centrality to date. We close this gap by analyzing four group centrality measures: degree, closeness, betweenness, and GED-walk. We show that an optimal way to rewire the network can be computed efficiently given the former measure, but the problem is NP-complete given closeness and betweenness. Moreover, we empirically evaluate a number of hiding strategies, and show that an optimal way to hide from degree group centrality is also effective in practice against the other measures. Altogether, our results suggest that it is possible to hide from group centrality measures based solely on the local information available to the group members about the network topology.

title: When perceived risk spreads: cross-category spillover effects from a food safety crisis
abstract: Risk perception during food safety crises can extend beyond the directly affected product, yet the mechanisms shaping cross-category spillover remain insufficiently understood. This study examines whether perceived risk associated with a pox outbreak affecting goats spills over from goat meat to related meat and dairy categories and whether trust in regulatory authorities mediates these relationships. Survey data were analyzed using structural equation modeling across five categories: beef, pork, goat milk, goat yogurt, and goat cheese. The findings reveal significant direct relationships between goat meat perceived risk and perceived risk for beef, pork, and goat milk. For goat yogurt, the total association was significant, although neither the direct effect nor the indirect effect through trust reached statistical significance, while no significant relationship was found for goat cheese. Trust in regulatory authorities mediated the spillover relationships for beef, pork, and goat milk, but not for goat yogurt or goat cheese. These findings show that cross-category risk spillover is product-specific and that institutional trust constitutes an important, but non-uniform, mechanism through which perceived risk may extend across food categories. The study contributes to understanding the boundaries of risk spillover during food safety crises and offers practical implications for policymakers, regulatory authorities, and industry stakeholders regarding product-specific crisis communication and the management of consumer risk perceptions.

title: Ambient Air Pollution Health Impacts in High‐Income Countries, Part II: A Case Study in the United Arab Emirates
abstract: ABSTRACT Ambient air pollution poses major global public health risks, particularly in rapidly developing regions, including the Arabian Gulf. This study estimates the disease burden attributable to anthropogenic air pollution (particulate matter [PM] and ozone) in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, for 2019–2022 and compares findings to previous estimates for 2008. Burdens were calculated using updated air quality, population, and health incidence data for 2019–2022 along with concentration–response functions from recent epidemiologic evidence. Results show that Abu Dhabi's investments in air quality management have paid off in preventing air quality from deteriorating as much as would be expected given the doubling of the population between 2008 and 2022. However, epidemiologic evidence gathered during this period indicates that PM exposure has stronger negative effects on mortality risks than previously thought. As a result, estimated deaths attributable to anthropogenic ambient air pollution increased between 2008 and 2022, from 231 (90% uncertainty interval [UI]: 59–427) to 1249 (90% UI: 507–2169). Total hospital visits attributable to PM and ozone exposure also increased. These increases reflect combined effects of population growth, higher pollutant exposures, improved medical record‐keeping, and updated evidence on health risks. Urban centers, with higher pollutant concentrations and population densities, experience the highest risks, highlighting the need for targeted interventions to address air pollution hotspots. This work provides policymakers with up‐to‐date insights on the health impacts of ambient air pollution and underscores the importance of continued investments in air quality management in Abu Dhabi.

title: Steering and Setting Free: Insights From a 20‐Year Retrospective Case Study of a Security and Justice Organization's Digital Transformation
abstract: ABSTRACT Advances in digital technologies are expected to fundamentally change how organizations operate and create value. Empirical studies show that public organizations face difficulties organizing and sustaining this digital transformation. To better understand these challenges, this study examines the organizational mechanisms underlying digital transformation in a public organization over the past 20 years. Our findings show that this transformation was primarily enabled by an emergent change approach, with influential planned changes occurring only occasionally. We identify the organizational mechanisms underlying both types of change and analyze their interdependence. Our findings suggest that both emergent and planned change approaches may be needed to enable digital transformation in public organizations effectively, but that combining them is complex in practice.

title: Staging the invisible: tracing public value co-creation through sub-micro infrastructures configured by information coordination organizations in China’s disaster information services
abstract: In disaster information services, citizen- and volunteer-generated information arrives as dispersed, uncertain reports rather than usable response information. This qualitative case study examines how Organization Z, a Chinese NGO functioning as an Information Coordination Organization (ICO), makes such information usable for response through sub-micro infrastructures. Data comprise 43 volunteer and 11 coordinator interviews, longitudinal participant observation, and multi-source materials. Four mechanisms emerged: emotional activation makes participation visible; epistemic calibration supports report credibility through traceability and comparability; cross-sector translation makes verified information interpretable and acceptable as a basis for response action; and reflexive learning makes response experience partially reusable. We conceptualize staging as a conditional account of public value formation organized around the four thresholds of visibility, credibility, legitimate actionability, and partial reusability. The study contributes to public value co-creation research by explaining how ICO information work conditions whether information-related participation contributes to disaster response and public value formation.

title: New development: Accountability without capability? Civil society organizations as infrastructure for ‘accountee-ability’
abstract: IMPACTAmid democratic backsliding and declining public trust, public accountability systems fail not because of insufficient reporting, but because society has limited capability to interrogate complex financial data. Civil society organizations (CSOs) serve as vital democratic infrastructure to bridge this gap, acting as direct accountees, enablers and co-producers of oversight. Public managers and oversight bodies should view CSOs as capability builders, not merely consultees, embedding financial literacy and participatory infrastructure into public finance reforms. Concurrently, CSO leaders should invest in technical and analytical skills to sustain independent, long-term democratic scrutiny.
