title: New development: Can existing frameworks protect the social mission when purpose meets profit?
abstract: IMPACTThis article is addressed to nonprofit managers, foundation trustees, charity regulators and policy-makers responsible for co-production frameworks. As third sector organizations increasingly enter partnerships under public funding contracts with private actors to deliver essential social services, the risk of mission drift and social-washing is growing. This article identifies the accountability gap at the heart of these arrangements and draws on evidence from Italian social co-operatives, university–industry research partnerships and cultural institutions to argue that existing governance frameworks lack mechanisms to detect or prevent mission drift before it becomes embedded in organizational practice. The findings are relevant to any practitioner or regulator seeking to strengthen accountability mechanisms before partnership agreements are signed, not after the damage is done.

title: Proactive, open, platform-based and data-driven: Assessing the institutional foundations for AI in EU public administration
abstract: IMPACTThis article speaks to senior civil servants, digital government strategists and EU policy-makers who allocate AI and digital transformation funding, particularly those managing recovery and resilience facility investments and national digital government strategies. It offers a practical diagnostic tool, the AI Foundations Index (AFI), which identifies which specific institutional foundation—anticipatory capacity, open data practices, platform infrastructure, or data-driven decision-making—is weakest in a given country, rather than relying on aggregate digital rankings that can mask critical gaps. The findings show that even digitally advanced states, such as the Netherlands, may lack the institutional scaffolding needed to deploy AI responsibly. Moreover, the nearly 15-to-1 disparity in anticipatory capacity across the EU suggests that funding AI pilots before strengthening these foundations risks reproducing the institutional failures exemplified by the Dutch childcare benefits scandal. Practitioners can use the index to sequence investment so that foundation building precedes, rather than follows, AI-specific initiatives.

title: Motivation in third sector co-production settings: A Self-Determination Theory perspective on sequential co-production
abstract: IMPACTThe article shows how third sector organizations can move beyond the repeated recruitment of volunteers and instead develop a renewable pipeline of co-producers. The concept of ‘sequential co-production’ explains how beneficiaries can be motivated to become future co-producers of services when programs deliberately foster competence, autonomy, relatedness and beneficence. For practitioners—namely trustees, commissioners, service designers, volunteer managers, and youth, community and sport-development professionals—this article offers a practical lens for redesigning participant journeys, volunteer development and performance measures around sustained engagement rather than short-term outputs. It also shows why relational and motivational infrastructure can strengthen legitimacy, community capacity and resilience when funding pressures or external shocks disrupt conventional delivery. The article helps leaders in charities, social enterprises and public-service partnerships ask a crucial question which goes beyond delivering services: how are we designing communities capable of sustaining services they benefit from?

title: When Geography Dilutes Accountability: Managerial Discretion and Fiscal Expansion in Local Government
abstract: Democratic accountability assumes that the citizens who bear the costs of government decisions can sanction the officials who make them. We identify a structural break in this assumption. When a city funds itself through taxes that fall partly on nonresidents (highway travelers, commuters, and regional shoppers who cannot vote in local elections) the electoral link between bearing costs and imposing sanctions weakens. Analyzing two decades of Texas municipal data (2000–2019) with two-way fixed effects and generalized synthetic control methods, we find that cities better positioned to shift costs onto nonvoters raise resident fiscal exposure more, after they adopt dedicated local sales taxes. This pattern is strongest for cities on or near major metropolitan areas and highways, whereas geographically isolated cities, where residents bear nearly all costs, show little change. It reverses the relief that classical tax-exportation theory predicts and reveals an accountability gap that funds discretionary fiscal expansion. The gap proves temporary: fiscal outcomes across contexts converge within six to thirteen years. Geography, we conclude, shapes democratic accountability as powerfully as electoral rules.
journal_name: The American Review of Public Administration

title: Not just mirror images: how political trust and distrust relate to public service experiences
abstract: Political trust and distrust are increasingly recognized as distinct judgements of political institutions, rather than opposite ends of a single continuum. While poor performance of and unfair processes in public services are assumed to fuel distrust, most research infers distrust from low trust. We address this gap by using measures designed to capture both political trust and distrust. Specifically, we examine whether outcome and procedural dissatisfaction relate to political distrust in the same way they relate to trust. Using a two-stage design, we analyze a cross-sectional survey of service users across eight European countries and a pre-registered vignette experiment that manipulates information about public service experiences. Cross-sectional evidence shows that positive outcome and process experiences are linked to higher political trust, and that their combined absence marks the lowest trust. In contrast, only process experiences are associated with political distrust. Experimentally, evidence indicates primarily that exposure to both negative outcome and process experience information decreases trust and increases distrust, though distrust does differ more across process than outcome manipulations. Overall, we conclude that satisfactory service outcomes primarily align with political trust, while fair and respectful processes are more tied to political distrust, though experimental evidence is more mixed.

title: Gambling Advertising and Problem Gambling in the United States: Multi‐Level Evidence Beyond Sports‐Betting Legal Status
abstract: ABSTRACT US gambling debates often center on the legal status of sports‐betting, but advertising can also be used as a distinct policy lever. This paper presents the findings of two related studies. Study 1 links quarterly state‐level gambling advertising outlays across paid media (2014–2023) to Google Trends indices for 116 problem‐gambling help‐seeking queries across 41 states (1640 state‐quarters). Study 2 combines surveys with passive digital traces from 419 exposure‐eligible mobile‐platform users. Higher state‐level ad spend, but not sports‐betting legal status, was associated with greater help‐seeking search interest, and this association strengthened over time. Platform‐specific gambling‐ad exposure on Facebook, TikTok, and X was associated with gambler status, gambling frequency, and the probability of any observed gambling‐site visit. Clean gambling ads were also associated with higher 24‐h odds of subsequent gambling touchpoints, especially web visits; among gamblers, ad‐triggered touchpoints were associated with problem‐gambling scores more consistently than raw clean ad volume. Convergent state‐level and individual‐level evidence links gambling advertising with engagement and harm‐related indicators, while the observational designs do not identify causal effects. The findings support stronger restrictions on advertising volume, placement, inducements, and targeting.

title: Governing parties’ regulatory responses to informal miners
abstract: How do governing parties regulate informal miners and what explains regulatory response variations? Drawing on Ghana and leveraging original and secondary data, this paper shows that National Democratic Congress (NDC) incumbents tolerated most local miners even when President Mahama raided the informal mining sector. By contrast, while the New Patriotic Party’s (NPP’s) Kufour and Akufo-Addo attacked local miners, Akufo-Addo largely let off Chinese miners and their local collaborators. These dissimilar regulatory responses arise because most local miners appear electorally more salient to the NDC. By contrast, NPP political entrepreneurs cultivated economic ties with Chinese miners while this governing party got hugely indebted to China and was accordingly constrained from sanctioning Chinese miners and their local collaborators. Taken together, I argue that the differential electoral relevancies of local miners to Ghana’s dominant and rival parties, economic ties between domestic political entrepreneurs and Chinese miners, and indebtedness to Beijing can make mining groups more or less salient to parties, producing targeted responses of repression and forbearance. Such instrumental responses undermine ASM formalization, beckoning international financial institutions to tie credit and loan facilities to concrete formalization indicators, which could compel governing elites to adopt non-partisan, holistic, practical, and long-term formalization approaches.

title: The Effect of Population Health on Corruption
External collaboration and local knowledge divergence in regional knowledge spaces
abstract: This study investigates the association between regional collaboration structures and the semantic position of locally produced scientific knowledge. Drawing on the Regional Innovation Systems framework, it distinguishes between intra-regional and inter-regional collaboration as complementary dimensions of scientific knowledge production. Using over nine million Web of Science publications from European regions between 1998 and 2021, this study employs semantic text embeddings to measure local knowledge divergence, defined as the semantic distance between each publication and the established regional knowledge base. Within the same region–field–period, externally collaborated publication groups exhibit slightly higher average local knowledge divergence than internally collaborated groups. However, the estimated difference is substantively negligible and varies across periods. The principal pooled-sample finding is an inverted U-shaped association between external collaboration share and regional local knowledge divergence, with the fitted curve reaching its maximum at an external collaboration share of approximately 45%. The realised magnitude of this association is modest, and heterogeneity analyses show that it is most pronounced in life sciences and biomedicine and after 2010. These findings identify a context-dependent association rather than a causal or universally optimal collaboration structure, demonstrating how regional scientific collaboration portfolios relate to the evolution of publicly disclosed knowledge trajectories.

title: Innovation adoption across regions: psychological openness and the early diffusion of digital platforms
abstract: Early regional adoption is crucial for platform-enabled innovations because their viability depends on enough people within a region adopting them to generate network effects. Existing research on regional innovation diffusion explains early adoption largely through demographic, economic, infrastructural, or institutional conditions, paying limited attention to regional population psychology. We conceptualize regional psychological openness as an invisible social infrastructure that is relevant for understanding early platform adoption. To test this idea, we introduce a newly curated dataset that allows us to trace the initial development of three major platform innovations (i.e., accommodation sharing platforms, ride-sharing platforms, social media platforms) across hundreds of U.S. metropolitan regions. Across all three platform types, regions differ markedly in early adoption. We link these adoption data to large-scale geo-referenced personality information from millions of U.S. residents ( N = 3,234,899). Results show that regional psychological openness consistently predicts earlier uptake even after accounting for demographic, socio-economic, social, infrastructural, geographical, and other psychological characteristics. In sum, the study advances a behavioral perspective on regional innovation adoption by integrating population psychology into explanations of platform diffusion.

title: Contested credibility: Public perceptions of scientists as experts
abstract: Science is widely embraced as an important prerequisite for innovation, and there is widespread support for public investment in science on that basis. However, it remains more contested whether and when science is recognized as a relevant source of expertise in contemporary debates beyond the academic sphere. Drawing on nationally representative survey panels from two European countries (the United Kingdom and Sweden), we investigate whether scientists are perceived as more credible senders of messages regarding societal challenges compared with attribution to other types of expert groups (government, businesspersons, and issue advocates). Evidence from a conjoint analysis paints a rather bleak picture: scientists’ credibility is only superior to that of government officials, but not businesspersons or issue advocates. We furthermore find that scientists are more credible when communicating technological issues than non-technological ones. This pattern can be traced back to three types of perceived sources of distrust (vested interest, partisanship and irrelevance) that are activated more strongly for non-technological issues. The same three sources of distrust also underpin the general credibility disadvantage of scientists as experts. Implications for our understanding of the social contract of science are discussed.

title: Domestic collaboration network and City research productivity: the moderating role of international structural holes
Democracy’s challengers: need for chaos and desire for greatness in German political culture
abstract: Liberal democracy has been under pressure from the success of populist radical right parties, high levels of affective polarization, and an increasing number of citizens who feel left behind by established political elites. In this novel survey study from Germany in 2023, we examine psychological profiles that we hypothesize are more or less detached from democratic values: we combine the constructs Need for Chaos, recently developed, and Desire for Greatness, a synthesis of “dark personality” traits such as Machiavellianism and narcissism. Thus, we conceptualize and empirically test the claim that status-seeking is a core motivation for overcoming the current political order. Specifically, we argue that extreme political discontent should be particularly strongly expressed by people high in both Need for Chaos and Desire for Greatness as they are motivated to deconstruct societal institutions and personally gain in the process of reconstruction. We identify latent profiles varying in the degree of Need for Chaos and Desire for Greatness. Subsequently, we demonstrate which socio-demographic factors relate to the profile high in both Need for Chaos and Desire for Greatness, and show its political relevance. Our study has implications for public and scientific discourse about polarization and developments that potentially erode liberal democracy.

title: Digital turnout mobilization: Enhancing voter turnout with digital messaging
abstract: Abstract Voter turnout is declining across Europe, raising concerns about democratic legitimacy and prompting a search for effective mobilization strategies. The new digital era has transformed the landscape for political communication, making it possible to mobilize voters through direct digital messages. These messages have proven to be a low-cost and easily scalable tool, capable of reaching millions of voters efficiently and with broad coverage. We synthesize existing evidence through a comprehensive meta-analysis of voter mobilization experiments from the past decade that apply digital messages as a Get-Out-The-Vote (GOTV) tool. The analysis assesses the overall effectiveness of digital messaging in increasing turnout, with particular attention to its potential for engaging marginalized groups and promoting participatory equality. Second, we present results from a new population-wide GOTV experiment conducted during the 2024 European Parliament election in Denmark – the first to apply digital messages to the entire electorate. The intervention increased turnout by 0.5 percentage points. By using year-of-birth bins to estimate effects across all age cohorts and disaggregating the immigrant category into Western and non-Western subpopulations, we can examine previously unexplored in-depth heterogeneous effects. We find that digital messages consistently have positive effects on turnout, including among marginalized voters.

title: Updating the Fundamentals: Forecasting the 2026 Midterm Election Post-Gallup
abstract: Statistical forecasts of congressional and presidential elections have become a regular feature of our discipline, and most rely on presidential approval, which has historically been provided by the polling firm Gallup.In 2025, Gallup discontinued its monthly presidential approval series, ending 88 years of continuous approval data collection.We introduce a proxy measure derived from RealClearPolitics approval estimates (Adj.R 2 = 0.97).Updating the Lewis-Beck and Rice political economy model of seat change, and applying it to the 2026 midterm elections, the model anticipates a Republican loss of roughly 42 House seats and 9 Senate seats.Finally, we present a quarterly forecast series for the House and Senate from 1948 to the present and show how early in the cycle these forecasts acquire predictive value.

title: Polling Without People: Can Silicon Samples of CASM-Inspired LLM Personae Mimic Human Respondents in Pre-Election Polling?
abstract: We introduce a framework for simulating pre-election survey responses with large language model (LLM) synthetic personae.Drawing on the Cognitive Aspects of Survey Methodology (CASM) literature, our approach combines synthetic biographies, salient-event memories and conditional news exposure with a staged cognitive process for answering turnout and candidate-choice questions.We apply the framework to a single weekly wave for the 2026 US House elections and produce national and district estimates using multilevel regression and post-stratification.Relative to a demographicsonly synthetic personae baseline, CASM-inspired enrichment shifts estimates towards Democrats, consistent with the direction suggested by contemporary polling.However, the estimated Democratic margin is 18.7 percentage points, compared with 8.7 points in the polling average.Personae randomly assigned to news-based judgement construction produce a larger Democratic margin than retrievers, who are not exposed to news, although uncertainty is substantial.These comparisons show that our enrichment strategy changes synthetic responses in the correct direction, but do not isolate the effects of all components or establish predictive accuracy conclusively.The framework offers a structured approach to studying synthetic survey responses whilst highlighting persistent challenges of leftward bias, uncertainty calibration and benchmarking novel methodologies during an election campaign.

title: A District-Level Forecast of the 2026 U.S. House of Representatives Midterm Elections
abstract: We develop a district-level forecast for the 2026 U.S. House of Representatives midterm elections.The model includes four district-level variables (past district vote, whether the race is competitive or unopposed, expert assessments of the likely winner, and the ratio of campaign donations to the Democratic and Republican candidates), two variables that capture national political conditions (national congressional vote intentions and incumbent presidential party if the election is a midterm), and state-level congressional vote intentions to capture state-level conditions.Before-the-fact tests based on data from 100 days (or more) prior to past elections show impressive historical accuracy, with an overall accuracy rate of 96% since 1996.An analysis of races that experts classified as tossups shows that statistical chance does not account for our model's accuracy.100 days before the election, our 2026 forecast gives Democrats a 9-in-10 chance of winning a majority of House seats.We also present a map of the expected outcome for each district.The conclusion highlights how the historical accuracy of the model can be used to understand any potential unexpected outcomes in the upcoming midterm elections.

title: Demslide or republican resilience? A political history forecast of the 2026 us congressional elections
abstract: The history book on the shelf is always repeating itself," an oft-cited line from ABBA's song Waterloo, captures the intuition that politics often shows persistence and is governed by identifiable patterns or "laws."Building on this, we take a structural approach to election prediction, moving away from the customary focus on short-term rational choice explanations, and instead incorporate a perspective rooted partly in Historical Institutionalism, emphasizing long-term party performance and governance trends, to see if Political History (PH) offers reliable guidance on the Democratic Party's prospects in U.S. congressional races.We demonstrate that ex-post models that rely on PH provide credible, accurate forecasts of both party control of Congress and Democratic seat counts in each chamber from 1946 to 2024.We extend the PH model to forecast the 2026 elections.It forecasts that the Democratic Party is likely to win Control of Congress, with a 78% likelihood of winning the House and a 66% chance of winning the Senate.While the PH model forecasts the Democratic Party is on course for victory, it looks set to fall short of a DEMSlide and instead predicts a consequential but bounded gain for the party.

title: Forecasting 2026 Congressional Control: A Comparison of IEM and Kalshi Prediction Markets
abstract: We report Iowa Electronic Markets (IEM) and Kalshi prediction market forecasts for the congressional control configuration resulting from the 2026 U.S. midterm elections.Both exchanges run separate markets on House and Senate control.Both indicate the most likely outcome is Democratic House control, but split on Senate control.Each exchange also runs a joint control market across the two chambers.In both markets, the most likely outcome has shifted from a Democratic House and Republican Senate to Democratic control of both chambers.Vector autoregressions show that neither market consistently leads the other in dayto-day price changes.IEM prices exhibit no significant momentum or reversal, consistent with efficient pricing.Kalshi prices sometimes display momentum, consistent with the presence of large-scale hedgers, speculators, and/or momentum traders attracted by Kalshi's scale and liquidity, but seemingly absent from the investment-capped IEM.

title: Political Economy Forecasts: The 2026 Midterms
abstract: We employ a political economy model to forecast the outcome of the 2026 midterm elections in the House and Senate.Earlier versions of our model have been utilized, to good effect, since 2010.The model draws on sound theory, which posits the importance of political and economic fundamentals.Midterm election contests are considered referenda on the president's party.If the White House party appears to be delivering a good performance, it is rewarded with more votes; otherwise, it is punished at the ballot box.We begin with a baseline political economy model containing three independent variables: presidential approval, income growth, and the term sequence.We adjust that model, by incorporating local conditions, and then by revising the specification to include variables that tap candidate quality and time in office.These revisions allow for a range of possible incumbent seat outcomes for the House in 2026, ranging from a lesser loss of 17 seats to a greater loss of 33 seats.We follow the same strategy for the Senate, where the forecast numerical range is quite narrow, -6 to -7.This suggests that the pickup by Democrats needed for Senate control (i.e., 4 seats) is more likely than not.

title: How Model Choice Obscures Forecast Uncertainty: The Rashomon Effect and the 2026 Senate
abstract: Election forecasts report ostensibly precise predictions that depend on modeling choices.These include the size of the incumbency advantage, the weight on state partisan lean, and how strongly national conditions move individual races.We show that the record of Senate elections between 2010 and 2024 is insufficient to adjudicate such choices.While hundreds of Senate races provide information about racelevel relationships, the role of shared national conditions must be learned primarily from comparisons across only eight election cycles.Indeed, of 120 plausible models varying these weights, 117 predict past elections similarly well.This "Rashomon set" illustrates how different assumptions can produce comparable predictive performance but distinct substantive findings.Our reference model predicts a 50.6% chance of Democratic control of the 120th Senate with 50.5 expected seats (90% interval 45-56).The 117-model Rashomon set, however, puts the chances of Democratic control anywhere between 43.2% and 57.6%.We recommend reporting this range alongside conventional predictive intervals from a single model.

title: Culture Holds us Together: Confucian Clan Culture and Collective Actions in China’s Land Expropriation
Daughters and Political Preferences of Politicians: A Preregistered Prospective Study on Swedish Politicians
abstract: Abstract Important studies have suggested that politicians become more liberal by having daughters, but more recent work has been unable to replicate this result. It is therefore essential to further clarify how politicians’ family situations affect their policy making in different contexts, and in particular when it comes to gender-related policies. We provide a unique test based on prospective data collection on Swedish politicians based on a pre-analysis plan strictly followed in all analyses and tests. Data is collected in two surveys implemented after the 2022 general parliamentary election in Sweden on members of parliament and candidates in the parliamentary election (n=1,147 complete responders are included in our analyses). In our primary hypotheses, we test whether having daughters is associated with more left-leaning political preferences, a stronger preference for female-favoring policies, and a weaker preference for male-favoring policies. We find no evidence of an effect on left-leaning political preferences or female-favoring policies. These results do not support the original work on this topic but are in line with the more recent null results. We also find suggestive evidence (p<0.05) that having daughters is associated with a weaker preference for male-favoring policies. As the effects of having daughters on male-favoring policies have not been explored earlier, this opens up an interesting avenue to investigate in future studies.

title: Conversation Without Conversion: Evidence from Cross-Partisan Interactions on a Mobile Chat Platform
Relational Clientelism, Information Processing, and Accountability
abstract: Abstract Research shows that providing information on incumbent programmatic performance often has limited impact on citizen attitudes towards incumbents, even if citizens tend to care strongly about corruption and service delivery. We use a survey experiment in South Africa and Tunisia to study if relational clientelism, a type of clientelism often valued by clients, plays a role in this puzzle. We present respondents with a radiocast that varies the profile of the politician (clientelistic vs. neutral) and his performance in service delivery and corruption (good vs. bad). We find that, when clientelistic politicians are valued, performance information on them matters less than for neutral politicians. The effect appears to operate via motivated reasoning: Respondents are less likely to process negative performance information when exposed to the clientelistic profile. Our findings suggest that, in certain contexts, relational clientelism is a valued candidate characteristic that can offset bad programmatic performance akin to co-partisanship or co-ethnicity.

title: Misperceptions of Male Bias Against Female Candidates: An Obstacle to Women’s Political Representation?
abstract: Do people believe that others in their community prefer male to female political candidates? To what extent is that perceived bias actually misperceived , and who do people view as the most biased? Perceived gender norms often diverge from actual levels of support for gender equality globally, particularly among men. These (mis)perceptions, often stemming from pluralistic ignorance, may undermine women’s political ambition and access to political power. In a nationally representative survey of Moroccans, we embed a conjoint experiment that asks respondents to identify not only the candidates they personally prefer but also the candidates they perceive male and female voters as preferring. We find no evidence of pro-male bias in respondents’ own preferences. We do find that respondents perceive that men are biased in favor of men and that women are biased in favor of women. We also find that men express greater personal bias against female candidates when they are primed to think first about others’ preferences.

title: Voice After Exit: the Prioritization of Homeland-Facing Foreign Policy Among the Hong Kong Diaspora
abstract: Abstract Citizens around the world have migrated under the shadow of authoritarianism, and many are increasingly acquiring political and voting rights in their host countries. Yet we know little about the content of their foreign-policy preferences or the salience with which they prioritize homeland-facing issues relative to domestic concerns. We argue that experiences of authoritarian rule prior to migration generate anti-regime sentiments among diasporas, inclining them toward hawkish foreign-policy positions toward the homeland regime. These preferences heighten the salience of homeland-facing foreign policy, even relative to highly consequential domestic issues. We test this argument with harmonized candidate-choice experiments administered to an original sample of Hong Kong diasporas in four host countries (Australia, Canada, the United Kingdom, and the United States). We find that respondents strongly preferred candidates advocating hawkish economic and geopolitical policies against China. These foreign-policy positions were consistently prioritized over salient domestic issues such as healthcare and the economy, and this structure of preferences held across subgroups with varying degrees of host-country integration and homeland ties. Our findings provide novel experimental evidence that diasporas continue to care intensely about and voice on behalf of their homeland even after exit.

title: Piecing the ‘Land puzzle’: The invisible labours of India's national land digitalisation initiative
Egotropic and sociotropic negativity bias in social policy reform preferences
abstract: Abstract Although negativity bias is widely documented in political psychology, evidence is far more mixed when it comes to voters' preferences for social policy reform, particularly when they are confronted with trade‐offs between personal and societal outcomes. Building on existing theories of political communication, this article examines how voters evaluate policy reforms when considering realistic information about potential losses and gains. Empirically, we analyze a simu‐survey experiment examining how voters update their reform preferences in response to information derived from microsimulation modeling about the predicted effects of policy reform on their pocketbook and on the poverty level. The results show that negative information weighs more heavily than positive information in shaping reform preferences at both the egotropic and sociotropic levels. In the case of competing information, the effects are asymmetric: Positive pocketbook information tends to be neutralized by negative poverty information, whereas negative pocketbook information outweighs positive poverty information. However, egotropic negativity bias is most pronounced for smaller pocketbook losses, which are more likely to violate voters' prior expectations than larger losses. Consistent with this pattern, expectation violations—rather than differences in recall of, or trust in, information—seems the primary mechanism underlying negativity bias in policy preferences.

title: A Theory of Economic Coercion and Fragmentation
Closing Ranks: Organized Labor and Immigration
Gas Flaring, Agricultural Productivity and Labor Reallocation: Evidence from Nigeria
abstract: of the Paper This paper investigates the impact of natural gas flaring—a byproduct of oil production—on agricultural productivity in Nigeria. Using a panel dataset of Nigerian households from the Living Standards Measurement Study (LSMS) spanning 2012–2018, combined with geocoded data on monthly gas flaring volumes from oil fields, the study employs variation in the timing of interview surveys to assess effects of gas flaring during harvest and planting seasons. The analysis focuses on southern Nigeria, where oil production is concentrated, and leverages a 2010 policy reform (Local Content Act) that increased local onshore oil activities and thus gas flaring. The empirical strategy includes fixed effects (household, and region-by-month-by-year) to control for unobserved heterogeneity, weather variables (precipitation and temperature), and an instrumental variable approach using global oil price changes interacted with pre-sample flaring intensity to address endogeneity. Key outcomes measured are real crop yield per hectare and labor productivity (real agricultural output divided by worker-days). The findings reveal significant negative effects during the harvest season, particularly in rainy periods, but minimal impacts during planting. Mechanisms are explored through satellite data on air pollutants, showing elevated levels of black carbon, sulfur dioxide, and nitrogen dioxide in flaring areas. Robustness checks confirm the results against various confounders like conflicts, oil spills, and placebo tests. The paper contributes to literature on the impact of air pollution on worker productivity and crop yields and climate change impacts on agriculture, highlighting policy needs to mitigate environmental costs from extractive industries in developing countries.

title: Balancing the Burden: Shared Responsibility in Intergenerational Financial Support in Rural Ghana
Conflict or Compromise? Theory and Evidence from Africa and Asia
abstract: Abstract Civil wars are a recurring phenomenon undermining development in weak states. Faced with the possibility of costly conflict, why don’t leaders share power? I investigate the role of an unexplored commitment problem, both theoretically and empirically. The model features a leader who can appease challengers by sharing power, but doing so increases their effectiveness at launching a rebellion. I show that commitment worsens as the opposition becomes stronger, and derive testable non-monotonic implications of group strength on power-sharing and conflict. As challengers become stronger, the likelihood of inclusion (positive transfers) increases up to a threshold, beyond which the leader prefers to exclude an opposing group and face conflict. I test the model using data on politically relevant ethnic groups in Africa and Asia, their access to executive power, and on armed organizations that claim to represent them. I use within-country variation in population share to proxy for group strength. The empirical findings strongly accord with the predictions of the theory. I then structurally estimate the model parameters and explore policy-relevant counterfactuals, including the effects of democratization, changes in military capacity, financial aid, sanctions, and quotas.
journal_name: Journal of the European Economic Association

title: Immigration and the Slope of the Labour Demand Curve: The Role of Firm Heterogeneity in a Model of Regional Labour Markets
abstract: Abstract In this paper, we provide new explanations for the puzzling findings that migrants do not decrease natives’ wages and that skilled immigration can increase them. We develop a model with regional labour markets and heterogeneous firms in which workers of different skill levels are imperfect substitutes, but for a given skill level, natives and migrants are perfect substitutes within a firm. In this setting, a skilled labour supply shock due to immigration induces skill-intensive firms to expand. These across-firm reallocations reduce the within-firm substitution between skilled and unskilled workers, thus limiting relative wage adjustments. When this mechanism is coupled with human capital externalities that are skill-neutral at the firm level but skill-biased on aggregate, the same skilled immigration shock can increase absolute and relative skilled wages. These two mechanisms are quantitatively important: the negative impact of immigration on natives’ wages is reduced by at least one-third when the across-firm reallocation mechanism is at work, and human-capital externalities can revert the sign of this relation.

title: ESTIMATION AND INFERENCE OF NONLINEAR AUTOREGRESSIVE DISTRIBUTED LAG MODELS WITH TIME TREND BY ORDINARY LEAST SQUARES
abstract: This study examines the large-sample behavior of an ordinary least squares (OLS) estimator within a correctly specified nonlinear autoregressive distributed lag (NARDL) model for nonstationary data. Although the OLS estimator suffers from an asymptotically singular matrix problem, it remains consistent for unknown model parameters and asymptotically follows a mixed normal distribution. Additionally, we examine the large-sample behavior of the standard Wald test, as defined by the OLS estimator, for asymmetries in long- and short-run NARDL parameters, and enhance this analysis with a super-consistent long-run parameter estimator. We then confirm the theory on the Wald test using Monte Carlo simulations. Finally, using U.S. GDP and exogenous fiscal shock data, we demonstrate the use of the OLS estimator and show statistical evidence of long- and short-run symmetries between the effects of tax increases and decreases on U.S. GDP.

title: ON THE RELATION BETWEEN DISCRETE- AND CONTINUOUS-TIME AFFINE OPTION PRICING MODELS
abstract: This article studies the weak convergence of discrete-time generalized autoregressive conditional heteroskedasticity (GARCH) and stochastic volatility (SV) option pricing models that allow for fat tails, multi-component volatilities, and non-monotonic pricing kernels. We introduce a general affine framework that enables the simultaneous derivation of new diffusion limits for Gaussian and inverse Gaussian GARCH models based on distributional invariant parametric convergence rates. When restricted to one-component specifications, our limits yield non-degenerate bivariate diffusions, generalizing the existing results in the affine GARCH literature. By using alternative parametric convergence rates, we further provide a comprehensive classification of all possible limits for two classes of affine and non-affine discrete-time SV models. Specifically, we show that the canonical affine classes of models popularized in discrete and continuous time are not analogous to one another. Our theoretical results are supported by a series of numerical experiments that investigate the impact of parametric scaling assumptions and model features on the convergence of European option prices. Overall, we find that the new limiting diffusions produce option prices that are closest to their discrete-time counterparts sampled at daily frequency.

title: Debt Aversion: Theory and Measurement
abstract: ABSTRACT We propose a model of debt aversion and conduct an experiment with real debt and saving contracts to jointly elicit debt aversion and preferences over time, risk, and intertemporal losses. We find that 89% of participants are debt averse, which strongly influences their choices. The estimated “borrowing premium,” the compensation an average person requires to accept debt, is around 16% of the principal. Applying a validated survey module to a representative sample of German households, we find that debt aversion is both statistically and economically significantly associated with actual debt‐taking and financial health.

title: Modeling Logical Interdependencies: Quantifying Systemic Risk From Rule‐Governed Actions
abstract: Systemic risk in critical infrastructure is often analyzed through physical, geographic, and cyber interdependencies. Yet infrastructures are also interdependent through the governing rules that organize human action. These rule-mediated connections are a form of logical interdependency, and breakdowns in rule-governed action can create pathways through which disruption spreads. This paper develops a framework for diagnosing and quantifying this underrecognized source of systemic risk. It does so by modeling logical interdependencies as rule-mediated control relations that shape whether interconnected infrastructures remain within safe operating bounds or drift toward failure. Integrating Institutional Grammar, STAMP, and Bayesian inference, the framework translates governing rules into structured control relations, represents them within a socio-technical control architecture, and quantifies how failures in those relations propagate across interconnected infrastructures. We demonstrate the framework through a reservoir system case study centered on Lake Mendocino, California, where safety depends not only on reservoir infrastructure and hydrologic conditions, but also on distributed authority, communication requirements, and operational protocols. The results show that logical interdependencies make non-trivial contributions to modeled systemic risk, with baseline probabilities of 7% for Coyote Valley Dam failure and 3% for downstream community impacts under the modeled conditions. More importantly, the analysis reveals hidden logical risk: rules and control relations that appear routine in normal operation yet become disproportionately important when the Bayesian model traces which factors most strongly contribute to a failure scenario. The paper moves logical interdependencies from a residual conceptual category to a systematically identifiable and quantitatively analyzable pathway of systemic risk.

title: Inseparability in Disaster Risk Science: Accounting for Coupled, Co‐Evolving Systems
abstract: Contemporary risk landscapes are shaped by systemic phenomena-compound disasters, cascading failures, non-stationarity, and cross-domain crises-that challenge conventional frameworks. While the classical risk equation (Risk = Hazard × Vulnerability × Exposure) remains a useful heuristic, it relies on a separability assumption that breaks down in feedback-rich, co-evolving systems. This failure reflects a familiar diagnosis: risk can be mistaken for a complicated problem, decomposable and optimizable, when it is a complex one, characterized by emergence and adaptation. Our contribution herein is not this distinction but its analytical consequence. Drawing on an interdisciplinary workshop on systemic risk and resilience, we propose inseparability as a foundational premise for disaster risk science. Hazard, exposure, and vulnerability might be better understood as dynamically coupled processes rather than separable variables. We derive implications across four axes: reframing vulnerability as a non-ergodic system property; addressing cross-scale dynamics; shifting from risk control to adaptive management; and treating knowledge co-production as a scientific necessity.

title: Stress and self-efficacy under artificial intelligence disruption: A mixed-methods study on the usage of artificial intelligence among Finnish workers
abstract: Rapid workplace integration of artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping work practices and challenging employees’ self-efficacy and well-being. This mixed-methods study examines these experiences using national survey data ( N = 2109) and qualitative interviews ( N = 54) with Finnish workers. Frequent AI use, AI-induced identity threat, and organizational AI deployment are associated with higher AI strain, whereas AI self-efficacy relates to frequent use, positive AI attitudes, and subjective well-being. Identity threat moderated several of these associations, highlighting the role of professional identity in AI-related experiences. Analysis drawing on Greimas’ semiotic modalities (must, can, know, and want) explains how these patterns are interpreted and negotiated in practice, revealing tensions between perceived self-efficacy and pressures to integrate AI. AI use was often described as voluntary. However, participants anticipated increasing competence demands and responsibility. The findings emphasize the need for organizational strategies that address identity-related challenges and support employee well-being in AI-driven work transformations.

title: The coercion of care: Compulsory connectivity in assistive communication
abstract: Assistive communication expands autonomy, participation and social life. Under particular conditions, the capacity to communicate becomes a duty to remain available. I describe this configuration as compulsory connectivity. It arises when mediated output functions as evidence of presence, nonresponse attracts an adverse default and refusal threatens care, support or recognition. Advanced amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and locked-in syndrome provide the central case because augmentative and alternative communication may enable speech, environmental control, relationships and access to care. Bringing disability media studies into conversation with deep mediatisation and digital disconnection, the essay identifies three mechanisms: the labour of legibility, recursive interpretation in care and divergence between technical and relational states. Together they make output perform presence and render silence legible as loss. The normative alternative is protected ambient presence: social recognition without continuous communicative production. A two-layer protocol gives that principle operational form: communication status distinguishes engagement from recognised withdrawal, while an independently governed safety channel preserves agreed clinical safeguards. Smartphone messaging isolates availability pressures under weaker dependence; brain–computer interfaces provide a prospective test of the boundary between detectable neural activity, communicative intent and consent. Accessibility becomes emancipatory when control extends beyond how a person communicates to whether communication is owed.

title: What Makes Child Harm Newsworthy? Event Characteristics, Victim Characteristics, and Media Attention
abstract: Media coverage shapes public understanding of social problems, yet harmful events receive uneven attention even when they involve children. This study examines factors shaping media visibility of child harm in Kazakhstan. Using a corpus of more than 230,000 Telegram news posts (2020–2025), we identify 1,571 incidents involving harm to children and estimate negative binomial regression models to test explanations derived from news values and ideal victim theory. Results show that event characteristics predict media attention more strongly than victim characteristics. Fatal interpersonal violence receives more coverage, while systemic failures receive less. Victim age and gender are not significant predictors.

title: Rethinking Multilevel Governance. By ArthurBenz. Cheltenham, UK: Edward Elgar Publishing, 2024. 208 pp. ISBN: 978‐1‐03‐530628‐2
Governance innovation for crisis-stricken smart cities: A roadmap to recovery and sustainability
abstract: Over the past decade, cities have emerged as centres of economic, social and environmental development. Challenges such as an ageing population, issues of inclusion, evolving poverty, migration patterns and environmental preservation are among the issues urban areas faced. In such a complex environment, municipalities are expected to play a pivotal role in territorial governance. The increasing responsibilities and the reduction of financial resources often generate financial crises for municipalities. In this scenery, a smart city framework, based on innovative collaborative governance and the use of technology, offers a potential roadmap to guide public administrations in overcoming urban crises. Focusing on the case study of Parma and its transformation into a smart city, the paper witnesses a potential blueprint for administrations seeking to implement virtuous processes capable of establishing an efficient and effective model for smart services. Parma, which represents the second largest city in the Emilia-Romagna region, in northern Italy, and a key hub for food production in Europe, offers a fascinating example. In fact, Parma has not only managed to overcome the crisis but, since 2017, has also become one of the top smart cities in the annual “ICity Rank index”. Furthermore, the smart city framework has provided Parma with an urban ecosystem that has strengthened its resilience. This paper examines how a near-default financial crisis triggered the implementation of a smart city model, and how a collaborative governance model, operationalised through a smart city strategy used as a window of opportunity, supported both financial recovery and cross-domain administrative reform.

title: Routinized Deference: Predictive Screening and Bureaucratic Capacity in Child Protective Services
abstract: Abstract Predictive algorithms are increasingly used to support frontline decision-making in public administration, but evidence remains limited on how they affect bureaucratic capacity. This study examines county-level adoption of predictive screening tools in U.S. Child Protective Services using NCANDS data (2010–2023) and a stacked difference-in-differences design. Leveraging staggered adoption, I find no change in the total number of investigations opened and a sizable decline (about 15%) in the share of investigations that are substantiated. These results are inconsistent with operational capacity gains and more consistent with misclassification that erodes analytical capacity. These findings are consistent with a mechanism of routinized deference: under workload and accountability pressures, algorithmic recommendations can become procedurally defensible defaults. Overall, this study argues that predictive screening is not capacity-enhancing by default, as routinized deference can undermine the professional judgment central to bureaucratic work.
journal_name: Journal of Public Administration Research and Theory

title: Co‐Production as State‐Building: Relational Capacity and the Prevention of Violent Extremism in the Global South
abstract: ABSTRACT This article advances a theory of co‐production as a relational state‐building strategy for countering youth radicalisation in fragile states. Grounded in fieldwork in northern Togo, affected by jihadist incursions from the Sahel and home to a predominantly young population, we argue that co‐production extends state presence into ‘brown areas’ and re‐legitimises authority by expanding the state's relational capacity to hear and respond to citizens. The framework specifies three interconnected mechanisms, face‐to‐face contact through service provision, civic inclusion via institutional channels, and the building of durable relational bonds, that jointly disrupt the recruitment pathways of extremist groups. Empirically, we show these mechanisms cultivate trust, dialogue and critical thinking among youth, while their structural reach is moderated by limited training and decision‐making authority. The findings reframe co‐production as a constitutive political force in state‐citizen relations, offering transferable insights for security policies across the Global South.

title: Unpacking the causal complexity of collaborative effectiveness in urban marginalized community regeneration: a fuzzy-set configurational analysis
abstract: This study examines the causal conditions shaping collaborative effectiveness in the regeneration of marginalized urban communities. Using fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis of 22 Chinese cases, it identifies facilitative leadership as a necessary condition for achieving high collaborative effectiveness and weak institutionalization as a necessary condition for low effectiveness. The sufficiency analysis reveals three distinct pathways to effective collaboration and three to ineffective collaboration. The findings show that collaborative effectiveness depends on context-specific configurations of resource support, institutionalization, governance structure, and facilitative leadership. No single condition is sufficient in isolation; rather, effectiveness emerges through complementarity, functional equivalence, and asymmetric substitutability among conditions. The study contributes to a more context-sensitive and configurational understanding of collaborative governance.

title: Mapping empathy in policy work: how public servants understand and use it
One size does not fit all: management strategies to reduce turnover intention among public sector employees
abstract: Public sector organizations face persistent challenges in retaining a diverse workforce, as systemic barriers continue to shape the experiences of female and minority employees. This study examines how workplace practices – specifically, organizational justice, management support, and leadership representation – are associated with turnover intention in public sector agencies. Using survey data from 1,572 procurement professionals in the United States, we assess both overall effects and subgroup differences. Results show that management support is associated with turnover intention across all groups, and organizational justice is associated with lower turnover intention among female and minority employees. In contrast, diversity and representation alone do not reduce turnover intention and, in some cases, are associated with higher turnover intention among minority employees. These findings suggest that representation without fair and supportive organizational systems is insufficient for retention. The study offers practical recommendations for public managers and contributes to ongoing theoretical discourse in public administration and human resource management.

title: Unlocking collaboration among nonprofit organizations: The case of health and social services for marginalized people
abstract: Collaboration among nonprofit organizations (NPOs) is essential for delivering services to users with complex needs. The dynamics underlying informal collaborations among NPOs, which can represent a distinct mode of collaboration or a precursor to formal collaboration, remain underexplored. This study examines informal collaborations among NPOs, exploring their characteristics and perceptions of barriers and opportunities for collaboration. The research adopts a multiple case study of 10 Italian NPOs delivering health and social care services to marginalized people, using qualitative and quantitative analysis. Results show that NPOs perceive barriers concerning, among others, capacity saturation, lack of reciprocal knowledge, and structured collaboration methods. Reported opportunities relate to acquiring competences and improved motivation. These mostly confirm that dynamics known from broader collaboration literature also hold for informal collaborations, while lack of reciprocal knowledge, learning and improved motivation extend it further. Finally, sharing cultural aspects among NPOs increases the probability of declaring a collaboration.

title: Representative Bureaucracy in Private Philanthropy: Testing Discretion and Racial Representation in Community Foundation Grantmaking
abstract: As public service delivery increasingly involves non-governmental actors, public administration theory needs to examine how its core frameworks operate beyond traditional bureaucracies. This study extends representative bureaucracy theory to private philanthropy, an increasingly crucial actor in local public service delivery, by testing whether racial representation in leadership corresponds with equitable grantmaking outcomes. Analyzing longitudinal data from 912 U.S. community foundations between 2012 and 2016, this study finds that racial representation in foundation leadership corresponds with increased grantmaking to organizations serving communities of color when leadership retains sufficient discretion, but that this relationship weakens as donor control rises, particularly through donor advised funds. These patterns are consistent with representative bureaucracy theory's emphasis on discretion as a key mechanism linking passive and active representation. These findings advance theoretical understanding by illuminating the interplay between representation and discretion within private philanthropy, while carrying implications for equitable resource distribution as public services increasingly involve non-governmental actors.
journal_name: The American Review of Public Administration

title: Who is more deserving of welfare rights? Evidence from a survey experiment on the perceived welfare deservingness of rural-to-urban migrants in Shanghai, China
abstract: Abstract How society views the welfare deservingness of migrants significantly impacts their welfare rights. However, little attention has been paid to the welfare deservingness of domestic migrants in developing countries. Drawing on the theory of deservingness criteria, this study constructs an analytical framework for the welfare deservingness of rural-to-urban migrants in China based on five key factors: hukou status, length of urban residence, employment status, migration patterns, and homeownership. This study constructed thirty-two vignettes based on the above five factors, collected a set of experimental data through an online survey and used multilevel modelling to analyse factors affecting the perceived welfare deservingness of rural-to-urban migrants. The results show that hukou status is the most significant factor affecting the perceived welfare deservingness of rural-to-urban migrants. In addition, there are significant differences between locals and non-locals in the views on welfare deservingness of rural-to-urban migrants in terms of identity, need and attitude, but not in reciprocity and control. Moreover, the five deservingness criteria have no significant differences in their impact on the different dimensions of welfare deservingness. This study contributes to the understanding of the social underpinnings of the welfare system in China.

title: Who Gains from creative destruction? Evidence from high-quality entrepreneurship in the United States
abstract: The question of who gains from high-quality entrepreneurship is crucial to understanding whether investments in innovative startup firms produce socially beneficial outcomes. Although entrepreneurship is widely viewed as a central driver of economic growth, recent research has raised concerns that it may also exacerbate inequality and other undesirable social outcomes. We bring new evidence to this debate by analyzing the impact of entrepreneurship on a variety of local economic outcomes, including income inequality, average incomes, and income mobility, using IRS and U.S. Census Bureau microdata. We find that entrepreneurship indeed increases income inequality, although this effect fades in the years after firm founding. While entrepreneurship produces statistically significant income gains across the distribution, the economic magnitude of these effects varies dramatically, with benefits concentrated among top earners. We also find that entrepreneurship can serve as a mobility tool for less well-off individuals, increasing their probability of rising to the top of the income distribution. These income and mobility gains, however, are uneven across demographic groups.

title: Climate Change in the State Executive Agenda
abstract: ABSTRACT State of the state (SOTS) speeches represent an annual opportunity for governors to identify issues they intend to prioritize in the coming year. The speeches represent a finite agenda space directed at lawmakers as well as the general public. In this paper, we use SOTS speeches to assess the attention American governors directed toward climate change from 2020 to 2024. Climate change is a particularly useful topic to explore substantively because of the outsized role states play in climate policy in the United States. We address three research questions. (1) What role does gubernatorial party have in determining the agenda presence of climate change? (2) What is the influence of legislative control versus divided government on climate agenda presence? (3) To what extent is climate change associated with other issues in SOTS speeches? Our dataset contains 60,801 manually coded quasi‐sentences from 235 speeches. We find that Democrats mention climate change more than Republicans, that this difference is greatest between government trifectas, but that Democratic and Republican governors speaking to divided legislatures shape their message to meet the partisan split. We also find that climate change is associated with a host of other issues, but that Democratic governors associate climate change with a broader range of issues than Republicans. Our work contributes to gubernatorial politics, climate politics, and agenda‐setting scholarship.

title: Perspective: is AI about to erode science’s legitimacy?
Perpetrator Identity and Post-Conflict Ethnic Attitudes: The Legacies of Intragroup and Intergroup Violence
abstract: Researchers have extensively examined how political violence shapes social and political behavior, yet most studies focus on interethnic violence and assume a binary conflict structure. This study challenges that assumption by examining how perpetrator identity, ingroup versus outgroup, shapes postwar intergroup relations. Using original survey data from Tamil civilians in Northern Sri Lanka, we analyze exposure to intragroup and intergroup violence during Sri Lanka’s 26-year civil war, which involved substantial violence both across and within ethnic groups. We find that exposure to intragroup violence is associated with lower trust toward coethnics, reduced ingroup favoritism in attitudes and behavior, and weaker reliance on ethnic cues in political choice. In contrast, exposure to intergroup violence increases interethnic prejudice and social distance, heightens discrimination in behavioral interactions, and strengthens ethnically motivated political behavior. These findings indicate that perpetrator identity shapes the social legacies of wartime violence and can generate opposing postwar dynamics.

title: Autocratization in Post-Communist Democracies. The Architecture of Strategic Authoritarian Rule in Hungary and North Macedonia

title: Trivializing religion: the nominal-religious populism approach
abstract: This study aims to explain how traditionalism and civilizationism may not be able to capture and account for the totality of Europe’s PRR. Focusing on six parties across Europe (FdI/Italy, VOX/Spain, AfD/Germany, SNS/Slovakia, Fidesz/Hungary, and SD/Sweden) in the period between 2019 and 2024, we analyze how these actors mobilize religion within their discourse and political performance. Utilizing Ostiguy’s socio-cultural approach, we suggest that references to religion operate as mere symbolic gestures with ostensibly political implications. Mainly drawing on data from official party platforms, this study advances two core findings. First, it demonstrates that religion is not mobilized in isolation but is strategically intersecting with anti-immigration rhetoric, Islamophobia, traditionalism, and Euroscepticism to forge salient boundaries. Second, the analysis challenges the prevailing tendency to label these PRR actors as “religious populist” either framed as “civilizational” or “devout-conservative”. We argue that religion, when viewed through a socio-cultural lens, is increasingly subject to banalization and we propose the notion of “nominal-religious” populism, i.e. a type characterized by the strategic and symbolic invocation of religious references, devoid of theological depth, institutional affiliation, or even performative religiosity, and distinct from the civilizationist paradigm that explicitly advocates in favour of the social liberal agenda.

title: Polarization, crises, and accountability: The role of conditional partisan bias in economic perceptions
abstract: Does partisanship undermine economic accountability? Although research shows that partisan bias in economic perceptions varies across economic conditions, the explanation for this variation remains contested. An ambiguity account expects the partisan gap to narrow whenever economic signals are clear, in booms as in busts; a threat account expects it to narrow only when conditions deteriorate severely. Because both accounts predict compression during downturns, separating them means observing strong, sustained growth as well, ideally among the same citizens who lived through the crisis. Using twelve waves of Spanish panel data covering a full economic cycle (2010–2020), I find the asymmetric pattern the threat account predicts: the gap between government and opposition partisans compresses sharply during crises but persists, and widens, during strong expansion. Strong identifiers display roughly twice the gap of weak identifiers at every point in the cycle, yet both groups compress at similar rates as conditions deteriorate. Finally, economic evaluations continue to shape government approval and incumbent support in a pattern consistent with the theorized accountability chain. Even in one of its more politically and economically turbulent decades, Spain shows that accountability is still solid when it is most needed.

title: Spillover effects of a far-left populist's victory: Revisiting the 1998 Venezuela election
abstract: Can far-left populists' electoral success change public opinion in other countries? If so, what attitudes are affected? While previous research shows that far-right populist's victories abroad can influence citizens' immigration and democratic attitudes, little is known about the spillover effects of far-left populist's victory. My research addresses this ideological imbalance by examining this topic. I argue that this foreign election outcome raises salience and reveals mass support for the political attributes of far-left populists. In turn, this can prompt citizens to update their economic and democratic attitudes through genuine preference updating and/or perceived norm change. Moreover, the direction of such attitudinal changes can be moderated by citizens' ideology. To test these expectations, I study the impacts of Chávez's 1998 presidential victory in Spain and Guatemala, where the Latinobarómetro survey was fielded amid this election. My analysis demonstrates that citizens become more pro-state intervention and more supportive of democracy after this far-left populist's victory. Additionally, I explore which ideological subgroups are more likely to experience these attitudinal changes. The heterogeneity analysis suggests the changes in economic attitudes and preference for democracy are concentrated among right-wing citizens in Guatemala. I discuss how these findings enrich the literature on autocratization, far-left politics, and transnational learning.

title: Introducing the Peace Observatory: Peace Negotiations and Mediation in Armed Conflicts
abstract: This article introduces the Peace Observatory, a new global dataset that captures over 10,000 rounds of peace negotiations in interstate, intrastate, and non-state conflicts between 1989 and 2023 with regular updates planned for additional years. The Peace Observatory disaggregates peacemaking into distinct negotiation rounds. To demonstrate the value of the dataset, the article examines how the involvement of autocratic states as mediators is associated with negotiation outcomes across different phases of the peace process. Unlike many existing datasets that operate at the conflict-year level and do not systematically distinguish between stages of peacemaking, the Peace Observatory records the specific phase of each negotiation round – prenegotiation, negotiation, or implementation. This enables analysis of whether mediator characteristics matter differently at distinct stages of the process. The analysis shows that autocratic involvement is positively associated with the conclusion of peace agreements during the negotiation phase, but not in the prenegotiation or implementation phase.

title: The Role of Identity-Related Issues in Partisan Shifts Among White Americans, 2016–2020
abstract: ABSTRACT During the 2020 US presidential election, identity-related issues—immigration, racial justice, and white identity—were central to public discourse. This study examines how these issues shaped shifts in partisanship among white Americans who changed their affiliation from 2016 to 2020. Using American National Election Study panel data, we analyze how attitudes toward immigration, the Black Lives Matter (BLM) movement, and white identity relate to Democratic Party, Republican Party, and Independent affiliations. We find that stronger white identity and restrictive immigration views increased the likelihood of switching to the Republican Party, whereas support for BLM increased the likelihood of identifying as a Democrat. These findings suggest identity-related issues played a key role in reshaping partisan alignments, especially in strengthening the Republican Party’s identity-based appeal.

title: Agenda over Authority: Why Right-Wing Populists Contest the Liberal International Order
abstract: Right-wing populist (RWP) governments are widely regarded as major challengers of the liberal international order (LIO), yet existing scholarship has not systematically established why they contest some international organizations more strongly than others. Is such contestation driven by populist opposition to supranational authority, or by substantive conflicts between right-wing ideology and particular international organizations’ agendas? We distinguish these mechanisms and derive expectations across the domains of human rights and the rule of law, trade, and security. To test them, we draw on an original cross-national expert survey measuring RWP governments’ approval of individual international organizations in 13 countries. The results show that an organization’s agenda matters more consistently than its authority. RWP governments are least supportive of organizations promoting human rights and the rule of law, display mixed attitudes toward trade-related bodies, and are more approving of security organizations. In the security domain, greater international organization authority is associated with higher rather than lower approval. These findings challenge explanations that attribute RWP contestation primarily to populist anti-elitism or generalized resistance to supranational authority. Instead, such contestation is selective and reflects a deeper conflict between right-wing ideological commitments and the egalitarian norms advanced by parts of the LIO.

title: Do Appeals to the Diaspora Affect their Attachment to the Homeland? Findings from Jewish-Americans before and during the Israel-Hamas War
abstract: Abstract Due to the growing importance of diasporas in contemporary geopolitics, many states seek to cultivate diasporic attachment and encourage diaspora mobilization using strategic narratives. Are such appeals effective? We report results from a pre-registered two-wave survey experiment conducted among Jewish Americans before and during the Israel-Hamas war. Our intervention assesses the impact of three common appeals identified by prior work: threats to the homeland, shared historical memory, and discrimination in the diaspora’s country of residence. We find that none of these appeals influenced Jewish-Americans’ attachment to, support for, or intent to mobilize for Israel, even during a war in the “homeland.” Instead, baseline differences in these outcomes reflect deep-seated generational, denominational, and partisan cleavages within the Jewish American community. These findings suggest that intra-diaspora fragmentation and long-standing views of the “homeland” might dominate short-term rhetorical interventions. Consequently, strategic frames deployed by kin states and political animators may be less effective on diaspora audiences than intended.

title: Between reconciliation and peace making and brutalization: The Israeli case
abstract: Abstract This article examines the relationship between peacemaking, reconciliation, and brutalization in violent conflicts. It argues that these processes are deeply interconnected: effective peacemaking and reconciliation can interrupt or reverse brutalization, whereas unsuccessful or incomplete peacemaking may allow brutalization to persist, deepen, and become normalized, even alongside formal reconciliation initiatives. This article is organized into two parts. The first one reviews the scholarly literature on peacemaking, reconciliation, and brutalization. It examines each process separately. Then proposes an analytical model that explains the emergence, escalation, and persistence of brutalization. Finally, it conceptualizes its relationship with peacemaking and reconciliation. The second part applies this model to the Israeli–Palestinian conflict, focusing on Israeli Jewish society in its confrontation with Palestinians in the Gaza Strip. This case study serves to illustrate the model and assess its explanatory value. Beyond examining peacemaking and reconciliation, the article's primary objective is to develop a comprehensive conceptualization of brutalization by defining its nature, identifying its underlying psychological and social mechanisms, and analyzing its antecedents and consequences for collective cognition, emotions, behavior, and norms.

title: Supporting Violence in a Violent Land: Condonation of Political Violence in South Africa
abstract: Research on public support for political violence has focused on three types of support: violence in the abstract, in the context of specific, contextualized events, and behavioral support. Most research uses abstract measures to indicate support, more limited research focuses on attitudes toward actual violent events, and little research addresses behavioral support. In this analysis, we examine the interrelationships of these three types of measures, based on a 2024 survey in a South African province with a long and recent history of widespread political violence. We draw three specific conclusions from our analyses: abstract attitudes are not entirely irrelevant, but some indicators are more useful than others. Abstract attitudes have some value for predicting how people judge realistic acts of political violence, just as these attitudes are to some degree connected to actual violent behavior. Our most important overall conclusion is that much more attention must be paid to measurement issues if scholars want valid and reliable evidence of popular support for political violence.

title: Private-sector support for programmatic candidates: evidence from a Senegalese election
abstract: Abstract Demand for clientelism in low-income countries distorts political incentives and constrains growth. Informal workers are seen as a strong clientelist constituency because they rely on forbearance and targeted benefits, yet they also constitute an electoral bloc that could coordinate in support of beneficial programmatic policies. We examine whether—and how—such demand for clientelism can be attenuated. We implement an information experiment with firm owners ahead of Senegal’s 2022 local elections, during which an upstart political faction campaigned on programmatic reform. Reminding informal workers of their coordination capacity reduced engagement with dominant clientelistic networks. This shift did not translate into support for programmatic alternatives but into political disengagement. Demand for clientelism can be mitigated, but programmatic mobilization remains a challenge.

JACKKNIFE EMPIRICAL LIKELIHOOD FOR INFINITE-ORDER U -STATISTICS
abstract: Infinite-order U -statistics play a vital role in modern statistics. However, given their degree k n $k_n$ k Subscript n depends on the sample size n , quantifying their variability is quite challenging, as fixed-degree theories cannot be directly adopted. In this article, we propose a jackknife empirical likelihood (EL) framework that can be used to construct confidence intervals for an infinite-order U -statistic. We establish sufficient conditions for the limiting chi-squared distribution of the JEL ratio statistic and introduce an efficient partition-sampling realization for practical implementation. To evaluate the performance of the proposed methodology, we conduct simulation studies in the context of subsampling-based ensemble methods and the maximum test, respectively, comparing its performance with four competing methods. The simulation studies yield satisfactory results across the board. Finally, we demonstrate the practical application of our method using a United States Forest Service timber auctions dataset to predict the highest bid at an auction.
