Locating bureaucracy in disaster risk reduction scholarship: differentiated administrative vocabularies and temporal reconfiguration
abstract: Disaster risk reduction (DRR) scholarship addresses administration through overlapping terms such as bureaucracy, public administration, governance, coordination, and crisis management, but it is unclear whether these vocabularies form a consolidated knowledge structure. This study examines their relational, temporal, and social organization in Scopus-indexed scholarship published between 2000 and 2024. A documented substantive re-adjudication produced a final inferential corpus of 81 articles, including 73 with Author Keywords. Co-word analysis used conservative lexical normalization, full counting, a two-document occurrence threshold, and association-strength normalization, with prespecified sensitivity checks. Results show connected differentiation rather than conceptual consolidation. Public administration was much more strongly associated with disaster management than explicit bureaucracy, while bureaucracy and public administration never directly co-occurred as Author Keywords. Bureaucracy occupied a smaller resilience/recovery-oriented community, whereas public administration was more strongly connected to disaster-management and policy vocabulary. Temporally, resilience peaked in 2015–2019 rather than rising monotonically, while governance and policy-implementation terminology became recurrent only in 2020–2024. The literature represented 38 identifiable countries but remained unevenly produced and predominantly single-country; 19.23% of geographically classifiable publications involved international co-authorship. Administrative DRR scholarship is therefore connected but not consolidated, and bibliometric salience should not be interpreted as evidence of institutional effectiveness.

title: Privileged precarity: Working freelance in the TV industry
abstract: Despite growing interest in the television industry’s freelance labour market, little is yet known about how workers interpret and manage the instability, intermittent employment and organisational ambivalence that characterise these skilled contingent careers. This article investigates the lived experience of freelance television work through qualitative interviews with practitioners in the UK and Australia. It maps the recurrent cycle of employment, unemployment and job seeking that defines working life in the sector and analyses the strategies and resources required to navigate it. The analysis critically revisits two widely used but imprecisely applied concepts: precarity and privilege. By tracing their intellectual lineages and examining their empirical manifestations in television work, the article demonstrates how persistent insecurity coexists with structural advantage. Privilege does not negate precarity; rather, it enables freelancers to endure it – at least for a time. The article advances the concept of ‘privileged precarity’ to articulate this distinctive feature of skilled contingent labour in television production, with implications for understanding similar dynamics in other areas of cultural work.

title: Manufacturing controversies: Media, politics and censoring contemporary art in Australia
abstract: Censorship campaigns targeting contemporary art are increasingly visible in liberal democracies, yet their operation is frequently treated as episodic controversy rather than as a structured social and media process. This obscures how such campaigns are assembled, amplified, and translated into institutional pressures, reshaping the arts sector in disquieting ways. From artists Juan Davila to Bill Henson, this study examines how censorship is produced through the interaction of political intervention, media framing, and social media circulation. While contextualizing gallery-museums as discursive spaces within democracies struggling to negotiate conflicting ideas, I argue that censorship operates less through formal prohibition than through iterative escalation, in which reputational, professional, and organizational pressures accumulate regardless of whether artworks are successfully prohibited. These dynamics produce forms of mediated governance that exceed individual controversies, reconfiguring the conditions through which contemporary art is produced, circulated, sustained, and constrained.

title: Institutional Logics, Empowerment Structures, and the Service Space Production of the Communist Youth League—A Case Study of the “Youth Homeland” Project in City G
abstract: This study aims to address a core theoretical and practical question: Under the dual constraints of institutional limitations and resource scarcity, how does the Communist Youth League, as a mass organization, actively produce service spaces to fulfill its service functions? To explore this question, our analysis integrates Lefebvre’s theory of space production with the institutional logics perspective to construct an analytical framework of “institutional logics–empowerment structure–organizational space production.” Through a case analysis of the “Youth Homeland” project in City G, this study finds that the Communist Youth League is not passively constrained by institutional environments and resource limitations. Instead, it proactively leverages its “structural hole” advantage at the intersection of multiple institutional logics—political, social, and professional—by employing a combined strategy of administrative empowerment, social empowerment, and technological empowerment to secure critical resources for the production of service spaces. Among these, administrative empowerment defines the core boundaries and legitimacy of service spaces, social empowerment expands their peripheral boundaries and resource networks, and technological empowerment reshapes the processes and effectiveness of service delivery. The investigation further reveals that institutional logics determine the empowerment structure, the integration of institutional factors opens windows of opportunity for space production, and institutional changes drive the transformation and restructuring of service spaces. The article’s theoretical contribution lies in expanding the study of organizational space production from an internal material analysis to an external social field perspective. It introduces “institution,” “agency,” and “co-production” into organizational space research, uncovering the micro-mechanisms through which mass organizations strategically employ empowerment to expand their action spaces by leveraging institutional logics in an authoritarian context. This offers a new analytical perspective for understanding the service functions and transformation of mass organizations and similar institutions in contemporary China.

title: Regulatory Agencies Under Mutating Populism in Office: Insights From Italy (1990–2025)
abstract: ABSTRACT Our paper builds a bridge between the emerging strand of research on public administration under populist rule and the established literature on delegation to independent regulatory authorities (IRAs). We focus on Italy, a critical case in Western Europe, which between 2001 and 2025 experienced six coalition governments dominated or strongly influenced by populist parties of different ideological orientations. Findings highlight that delegation to IRAs is remarkably resilient once institutionalized, even under sustained political contestation. Despite repeated populist participation in government since the early 2000s, Italian IRAs have not been subject to systematic de‐delegation or statutory retrenchment. However, the preservation of formal independence has not implied the absence of means for political control. Our analysis shows that populist governments have systematically relied on political appointments. Interestingly, political appointments have not been driven by partisan loyalty or overt politicization. Instead, the intervention of populist parties has operated along a different dimension of political control that has received less attention in delegation theory: the specialization of appointees. Populist governments have displayed a preference for appointing IRAs' board members with lower levels of domain‐specific specialization, privileging generalist profiles over specialists.

title: Institutional Amnesia and the Loss of “The Why Rationale” in Central Government Agencies
abstract: ABSTRACT Data from 115 interviews conducted with officials in the Westminster systems of Australia, New Zealand, and the United Kingdom is used to substantiate a corrosive relationship between institutional amnesia and the ability of public servants to make sense of their organizational context. A process in which public servants question why the policies, procedures, and organizational frameworks that surround them is proposed as one medium through which this relationship operates. Four problematic effects produced by this relationship and process are subsequently analyzed: (1) public servants following but not understanding procedures, (2) inexplicable organizational aspects getting abandoned, (3) the layering of new organizational features on top of old ones, creating complexity, and (4) public service inefficiencies and associated public servant frustration. The article concludes with the implications of this important relationship for public administration scholars and practitioners.

title: Green trade governance and vulnerable groups in Vietnam: free trade agreements, state capacity and non state participation
abstract: New-generation free trade agreements shape environmental governance in Vietnam through implementation pressures extending beyond formal treaty commitments. This article examines how the European Union–Viet Nam Free Trade Agreement (EVFTA) and the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP) connect market access, environmental standards, supply-chain data, domestic legal reform, distributive capacity and participatory accountability. Using Vietnam as a structured policy case, it combines treaty and domestic environmental-law analysis, policy-document review, a structured synthesis of scholarship and secondary empirical indicators from official and international sources. It develops the concept of just green trade governance, arguing that implementation requires regulatory capacity, distributive protection and politically realistic non-state participation alongside formal legal compliance. The evidence shows substantial legal progress, particularly through the Law on Environmental Protection 2020 and related climate, fisheries and environmental reforms. However, persistent constraints in coordination, firm-level capacity, local implementation, data infrastructure and participatory accountability limit implementation. The article contributes to Asian public policy by operationalizing just green trade governance through measurable indicators and showing how export-oriented developing economies can evaluate green trade commitments through effectiveness, equity and accountability.

title: Perpetrator Programmes in Penal‐Welfare Governance: Variation in Programme Intake Across Italy
abstract: ABSTRACT Perpetrator programmes are an established component of institutional responses to violence against women. Drawing on the Italian case, this article examines how organisational and institutional configurations are associated with variation in programme intake. Using a national dataset of 94 identified programmes, we estimate two regression tree models, distinguishing between overall and criminal‐justice‐mediated intake. The fitted trees identify conditional in‐sample patterns but show negligible cross‐validated predictive performance. Overall intake is differentiated mainly by the number of access points and, among programmes with fewer access points, by financial resources. Criminal‐justice‐mediated intake is differentiated first by provincial population size and subsequently, depending on context, by funding, formal network representation, bilateral institutional ties and motivation‐based admission rules. Programme intake is conceptualised as an institutional outcome associated with context‐specific combinations of organisational resources and local integration. These exploratory patterns suggest that efforts to expand programme access should consider both available resources and reported institutional relationships within local violence response systems.

The Power of Identity Pause: Perimenopause and the Embodiment Process
abstract: A growing volume of identity scholarship has started to challenge the Cartesian separation of body and mind, highlighting the importance of embodiment. While such research is enlightening, studies do not provide in-depth understanding of how some workers, but not others, are able to develop embodied identities (i.e., identities that are bonded with and bounded by their physical body). In particular, little is known about how this embodiment process occurs—or fails to do so—when changes within a worker’s body threaten their idealized identities (who they want and believe they should be). We examine this puzzle through an inductive study of perimenopause, which is a naturally occurring physiological transition experienced by most women. Unlike studies that have emphasized the importance of remedial identity or body work, our findings point to the criticality of an identity pause, which involves taking respite from striving to enact idealized identities. We illuminate how an identity pause gives workers the space to develop somatic attunement: the capacity to connect with, listen to, and respect their changing bodies. In so doing, our study calls attention to distinctive mechanisms that help develop embodied identities, advancing research on the body–identity nexus, embodiment, and women and work.

title: Event System Theory: A Decade of Progress and a Future of Potential
abstract: Published 10 years ago, event system theory (EST; Morgeson, Mitchell & Liu, 2015) has become a highly influential organizational theory. EST consists of a complex of three interacting event components: event strength, event space, and event time. It has been used by scholars across domains in a variety of different ways and serves as a key catalyst for event-oriented research and theory. In this article, we reflect upon the development of EST and discuss the impact it has had on the field. We then identify the different ways EST has been used, offer suggestions for studying events, and discuss all the work that still needs to be done.

Helping Oneself by Helping a Rival: Social-Media Platforms’ Policies on Enabling Features for Influencers
abstract: Social-media platforms and influencers are often seen as collaborators. However, both rely primarily on advertising services, introducing a competitive dimension to their relationship. As the dominant players in this relationship, platforms have used design features, which they control, to manage this dynamic. Some platforms have adopted an antagonistic approach by disabling certain features (e.g., clickable shopping-related hyperlinks) for influencers, while others take a more cooperative stance, allowing influencers to use these features for free or for a fee. We develop a game-theoretic model to explore the competition between the two parties and study the platform’s decision to enable or disable a feature that enhances the effectiveness and efficiency of an influencer’s service. We show that even when the platform cannot charge the influencers for using the feature, it can still benefit if the advertisers' valuation of the platform's service is not significantly lower than that of the influencer's service. While enabling the feature may result in a loss of market share, the platform can potentially offset this loss by raising its prices. Enhancing the influencer’s effectiveness can benefit the platform, but efficiency improvements alone never do, highlighting that the platform's benefit from helping the influencer depends on the nature and extent of the support. A win–win situation for the platform and the influencer may come at the expense of some advertisers, suggesting the platform’s helping the influencer can lead to a “collusive” outcome, despite the competition for advertisers. If the platform can charge a fee for using the feature, it should always enable the feature at an appropriate fee, as this will benefit the platform. The additional fee revenue may come with no change in the platform’s advertising revenue, with an increase in the advertising revenue, or at the expense of some advertising revenue. The platform strategically uses the fee to influence the influencer’s service offering, which affects the platform’s revenue mix under the new business model.

title: Facade of Trust: The Impact of Adopting AI-Enhanced Profile Pictures on Trust
abstract: Virtual profiles are critical elements of online social interactions, often featuring portraits enhanced by AI-driven tools such as beauty filters and virtual makeup. While the increasing use of these technologies reshapes how individuals present and perceive themselves, little is known about their implications for trust-related behavior. Drawing on self-presentation theory, this study examines how adopting an enhanced profile photo influences behavioral trust and trustworthiness toward others. We conducted a randomized experiment based on the trust game and adapted it by embedding a novel profile photo enhancement module. Participants were assigned to either a treatment group, in which they adopted an AI-enhanced profile photo, or a control group, in which they used their original photo. Our findings reveal an intriguing asymmetry. Senders with an enhanced photo demonstrated less trust by sending smaller amounts. Conversely, receivers with an enhanced photo displayed greater trustworthiness, returning higher percentages. These effects were offset when participants were interacting with an opponent using an enhanced photo. Further analysis indicates that enhanced self-presentation increases perceived risk, which explains the observed reduction in trust. We also document gender differences: female senders show a larger decline in trust, while male receivers exhibit a greater increase in trustworthiness. Overall, this research highlights the asymmetric behavioral consequences of AI-powered self-presentation and underscores the role of risk perception in linking profile photo enhancement to trust behavior in online interactions.

title: Navigating the Sea of Reviews: Unveiling the Effects of Introducing AI-Generated Summaries in E-Commerce
abstract: Amidst the burgeoning incorporation of generative AI into commercial realms, numerous companies are exploring ways to leverage generative AI tools in practice. However, there is still a lack of empirical evidence to examine their effectiveness. In this research, we explore how AI-generated summaries (AIGS), a relatively new generative AI tool, influence consumer review behavior. While one may assume that AI-generated content diminishes users’ incentive to contribute by replacing user-generated content, we find the opposite: the introduction of AIGS actually leads to an increase in the volume of consumer reviews. We propose that this effect is driven by enhanced perceptions of collective efficacy. By highlighting the value of consumer reviews as a collective force, AIGS reinforces contributors’ belief that their individual input meaningfully contributes to a shared body of product knowledge, thus motivating participation. This mechanism is supported by an additional controlled laboratory experiment where we directly measure perceived collective efficacy and find that it mediates the effect of AIGS on the likelihood of leaving a review. Our moderation analysis results reveal that the positive effect of AIGS on review contributions is more pronounced among products that are well-reviewed (vs. under-reviewed) and polarizing (vs. non-polarizing). Moreover, a fine-grained review content analysis shows that reviews after the AIGS introduction exhibit enhanced content richness and provide complementary information beyond the AIGS content. Specifically, contributors discuss fewer product attributes already covered by AIGS, discuss more product attributes not covered by AIGS, and elaborate on AIGS product attributes rather than restating the summary. Taken together, these findings advance our understanding of how AI integration influences consumer review behaviors in e-commerce and offer valuable practical guidance for business strategies on employing generative AI.

title: Honesty in Causal Forests: When It Helps and When It Hurts
Fixed, Proportional, or Menu-Based? A Study of Managed Security Service Provider Contracts
Revenue Maximization for Seaport Terminal Operations Considering Multimodal Cargo Flows
abstract: We study the optimal pricing problem for operations at a seaport terminal within a multimodal transport network, where the terminal operator sets differentiated prices for processing cargoes arriving via and transferred to various modes of transport. The problem incorporates two critical features: (i) the influence of port congestion on cargo suppliers’ terminal selection and (ii) the hierarchical choice structure that predicts how cargo suppliers select transport modes and routes for their cargoes. To capture these features, we formulate the problem as a nonconvex, nonlinear program involving a nested logit choice model and an equilibrium constraint reflecting the congestion effect, which is challenging to solve or analyze. To address this difficulty, we apply a change of variables to reformulate the price-based model as a flow-based model, where cargo flows, rather than prices, are the decision variables, thereby making the model more amenable to analysis. By exploiting the structure of the flow-based model, we derive an optimality equation whose dimension scales only with the number of origin-destination (O/D) pairs, which effectively reduces the computational complexity by avoiding directly handling the numerous variables associated with transport routes. This approach not only applies to seaport revenue management problems that often involve multiple transport modes and a substantial number of routes, but also contributes a structure-exploiting method for addressing a broader class of nonlinear programs involving equilibrium constraints and customer choice models. We show that, for each O/D pair, the optimal mode-dependent prices decompose into a component common across modes plus a mode-specific adjustment. We also establish analytical bounds on the revenue loss induced by misspecifying cargo suppliers’ choice structure. We evaluate the performance of the algorithm by comparing it with several widely used benchmark methods through numerical analysis. Our findings indicate that our algorithm outperforms the benchmark methods in both revenue maximization and runtime. Moreover, we find that accurately modeling the choice structure has a larger impact on revenue than explicitly modeling congestion. title: A Preconditioned Augmented Lagrangian Method for Solving Semidefinite Programming Problems
abstract: In this work, we propose a preconditioned augmented Lagrangian method (ALM) for solving semidefinite programming (SDP) problems. The preconditioner is implemented via a weighted penalty function in the ALM subproblem, with the weight matrix derived from the projection operator onto the tangent space of the feasible region. This simple yet effective modification significantly accelerates ALM, particularly for ill-conditioned SDPs. By combining the preconditioned ALM with our previously developed feasible method, SDPF, we develop SDPF+, an SDP solver capable of handling convex problems with possibly nonlinear objective functions. Extensive numerical experiments demonstrate the efficiency and robustness of SDPF+, showing that it can generally outperform other solvers on large-scale SDPs whose optimal solutions exhibit low-rank structure. title: A Novel and Efficient Formulation and Solution Approach for the Region Coverage Problem with Identical Circles
abstract: The problem of covering a two-dimensional region with identical circles of minimal radius (CRICMR) is a classic optimization problem with many relevant real-world applications. However, due to the nonconvexity and the multiply-connected nature of the region to be covered, designing an efficient formulation and solution approach for the problem is very challenging. In this study, we first propose a unified optimization model for two classic variants of the problem (i.e., the CRICMR problems with and without center placement constraints), and then present an effective heuristic algorithm for solving both variants. The proposed model is based on the clipped Voronoi diagram and converts the intractable region coverage problem into the much easier vertex covering problem with respect to the clipped Voronoi polygons. The proposed algorithm incorporates several key components: a two-phase monotonic basin-hopping method; a subregion-based local optimization method; two perturbation operators, and a radius adjustment method for the covering circles. Computational experiments on popular benchmark instances demonstrate the efficiency of our approach, which significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods by improving the current best-known solutions for nearly all benchmark instances. title: Editorial Board
Note from the Editor
Branch-and-Price for the Team Orienteering Problem with Time Windows and Bivariate Time-Varying Profit
abstract: Motivated by multiple real-world applications, this study investigates the team orienteering problem with time windows and bivariate time-varying profit (TOPTW-BTP), where the profit collected at each node is modeled as a nonlinear function of both the arrival time and the service duration. We model the problem on a time-expanded network and introduce the concept of the bivariate-time (BT) arc, proving that dominated BT arcs can be systematically eliminated to reduce the solution space. To capture diverse real-world temporal profit patterns, we consider three types of arrival-time profit functions, monotonic (typically decreasing), concave, and others (e.g., bimodal), and discuss tailored modeling approaches for each case to avoid unnecessary arrival-time discretization. Especially for the concave case, we propose a novel route extension method that exploits the structural properties of concavity to mathematically formalize the extension as direct functional additions, thereby achieving a compact representation. This method is also applicable to related problems such as vehicle routing with time windows and convex node costs. A branch-and-price framework is developed to solve the TOPTW-BTP. Computational experiments show that the proposed algorithm efficiently solves instances with up to 100 nodes across all three types of arrival-time profit function, with the theoretical simplification in the concave case naturally leading to a more streamlined implementation than the state-of-the-art approach. title: Stationary Coupled-Flow Approximation for Time-Varying Retrial Queues
abstract: Although stationary queueing models, such as Erlang-C and Erlang-A, are widely used for performance evaluation in service systems, they do not account for time dependence and retrials, which limits their applicability. Building on stationary [Formula: see text] formulas and point-wise stationary approximations (PSAs), this paper proposes the stationary coupled-flow (SCF) approximation. The method partitions the time horizon into intervals, models each as an [Formula: see text] in steady state, and iteratively determines the arrival rate, accounting for new customers and retrials. This yields an approximation of long-run performance metrics of retrial queues with stationary or time-varying arrivals. We prove that the SCF approximation converges to a finite limit for constant and cyclic arrival rates. Extensive numerical experiments demonstrate the high accuracy of the SCF approximation. Furthermore, SCF outperforms PSA, particularly during peak periods. Therefore, SCF provides a fast, transparent tool for planning and staffing in services with retrials. It remains reliable when the exact distribution of retrials is uncertain, enabling day-to-day scheduling and scenario testing under time-varying demand. We find that the retrial probability plays a stronger role than the retrial-time distribution. The impact of retrials in time-varying queues is driven by two effects: the state at the abandonment epoch and the cycle length-retrial time interaction. We posit that as retrial times increase, the first effect dampens congestion feedback, whereas the second effect can amplify or smooth fluctuations. Under sufficiently high variability in retrial times, the cycle length-retrial time interaction becomes negligible, leaving the system governed by the abandonment-epoch state. title: Learning to Simulate: Generative Metamodeling via Quantile Regression
abstract: Stochastic simulation models effectively capture complex system dynamics but are often too slow for real-time decision making. Traditional metamodeling techniques learn relationships between simulator inputs and a single output summary statistic, such as the mean or median. These techniques enable real-time predictions without additional simulations. However, they require prior selection of one appropriate output summary statistic, limiting their flexibility in practical applications. We propose a new concept: generative metamodeling. It aims to construct a “fast simulator of the simulator,” generating random outputs significantly faster than the original simulator while preserving approximately equal conditional distributions. Generative metamodels enable rapid generation of numerous random outputs upon input specification, facilitating immediate computation of any summary statistic for real-time decision making. We introduce a new algorithm, quantile-regression-based generative metamodeling (QRGMM), and establish its distributional convergence. Extensive numerical experiments demonstrate QRGMM’s efficacy compared with other state-of-the-art generative algorithms in practical real-time decision-making scenarios. Unintended Regulatory Spillovers: The Impact of Bank Regulatory Oversight on Environmental Enforcement
abstract: ABSTRACT We explore whether bank regulatory oversight affects the ability of environmental enforcement to reduce industrial emissions. A major objective of environmental enforcement is to reduce industrial emissions by encouraging firms to employ greener production processes and technologies. However, such changes often require external financing obtained from banks, and prior research shows that regulatory oversight of banks can affect bank lending. We find that, on average, the reduction in air pollution in response to county‐level environmental enforcement is attenuated in counties exposed to increased bank regulatory oversight, as measured by severe enforcement actions. Furthermore, we show that the negative impact of bank regulatory oversight on small business lending to affected counties is the likely mechanism behind this on‐average effect. However, when bank regulatory oversight targets banks with stronger capitalization, we find that the negative effect of bank regulatory oversight on environmental enforcement is mitigated. Collectively, our findings suggest that bank regulation has a nuanced effect on the extent to which environmental enforcement reduces emissions, indicating that one regulator's mission can impact the objectives of another.

title: The effect of the mandatory disclosure of corporate tax returns on reporting bias
abstract: ABSTRACT How do investor reactions to the mandatory disclosure of firm tax information influence managers' reporting choices? To answer this question, we build a structural model of reporting bias, which we test with a unique data set of Turkish firms that have been mandated to publicly disclose their tax returns since 2009. We find that both book and tax income numbers are informative to investors. Structural estimates are consistent with disclosure of the tax report reducing both market incentives to manage book earnings and investor uncertainty about underlying firm value. Tax disclosure is associated with higher reported tax income, though the increase is not statistically significant. Counterfactual estimates suggest that book‐tax‐conformity could change financial and tax reporting biases, but lead to a lower quality information environment relative to the separate disclosure of book and tax reports.

title: Externalities of Responsible Investments
abstract: ABSTRACT We develop a model to study the efficiency of socially responsible investing (SRI) as a mechanism to control firms' externalities. When SRI is not too popular, responsible investors favor strategies that lead to a concentration of SRI in a subset of firms in the economy. This concentration can mitigate coordination issues in adopting green technologies, but it can also crowd out the green investments of excluded firms and increase the price of green products. In equilibrium, responsible investors continue to favor concentration even as SRI becomes more popular, and concentrate the most when concentration is least desirable.

title: Risk, Specialization, and Covered‐Interest Parity
abstract: ABSTRACT Prevailing theories of financial intermediation assume an integrated financial sector with frictionless risk‐sharing. However, we identify substantial risk‐sharing frictions linked to intermediary specialization using currency derivatives markets as a laboratory. Using confidential supervisory data covering $25 trillion in daily bank exposures, we document imperfect hedging in banks' FX‐swap intermediation: banks rarely hedge their synthetic dollar lending with maturity‐matched foreign safe assets. Intermediaries specialize in markets in which they have expertise in managing the associated exposures, giving rise to cross‐market variation in deviations from covered‐interest parity. Our results highlight the importance of intermediary specialization and its impact on risk premia.

title: Generative AI and Firm Values
abstract: ABSTRACT How do recent advances in Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) affect firm value? We construct the first measure of firms' workforce exposures to Generative AI and show that an “Artificial‐Minus‐Human” portfolio earned 5% in the two weeks following the release of ChatGPT. The labor‐exposure effect is more pronounced for firms with greater data assets and is distinct from the effect of firms' product exposures to AI. We assess whether exposed workforces are substituted or complemented by Generative AI based on whether their exposed tasks are core or supplemental. Examining firms' labor demand and profitability following the release of ChatGPT supports a labor‐technology substitution channel.

title: Feedback and Contagion through Distressed Competition
abstract: ABSTRACT Firms tend to compete more aggressively when facing financial distress. This intensified competition reduces profit margins, pushing them further into distress and adversely affecting their industry peers. To study such feedback and contagion effects, we incorporate strategic competition in a dynamic model with long‐term defaultable debt, exploring various peer interactions such as predation and price wars. The feedback effect represents a novel source of financial distress costs associated with leverage, which helps explain the negative profitability‐leverage relation across industries. Owing to the contagion effect, firms' optimal leverage is often excessively high from an industry perspective, undermining the industry's financial stability.

title: The Financial Premium
Flow‐Driven ESG Returns
abstract: ABSTRACT I show that the recent returns to environmental, social, and governance (ESG) investing are strongly driven by price impact from flows toward ESG portfolios. Using data on trades, I estimate the market's ability to accommodate ESG flows, which is given by the elasticity of substitution between ESG and other stocks. I show that every dollar flowing toward a representative ESG portfolio increases the market value of ESG stocks by $0.8. The growing institutional flows into the ESG portfolio are the main driver of ESG returns and have caused an annual flow‐driven return of 1.9%. In the absence of flows, ESG stocks would not have outperformed the market from 2012 to 2023.

title: When Do Treasuries Earn the Convenience Yield?—A Hedging Perspective
abstract: ABSTRACT We document that the convenience yield of U.S. Treasuries exhibits properties consistent with a hedging perspective of safe assets, that is, Treasuries are valued highly if they appreciate with poor aggregate shocks. In particular, the convenience yield tends to be low when the covariance of Treasury returns with the aggregate stock market returns is high. A decomposition of the aggregate stock‐bond covariance into terms corresponding to the convenience yield, the frictionless risk‐free rate, and default risk reveals that the covariance between stock returns and the convenience yield itself drives the effect in a substantive capacity.

title: Targeted Philanthropy: Evidence from M&As
abstract: ABSTRACT I show how firms optimize the allocation of charitable funds around investments that require external stakeholder support, such as mergers and acquisitions. Acquirers increase donations to target‐related charities before making a takeover offer, but scale funds back after withdrawing from a deal. Firms redistribute funds from nontakeover‐related areas to target insider–affiliated charities, employee communities, and counties with a regulatory presence. Targeted donations that encourage blockholder reciprocity and employee commitment are associated with better deal performance through decreased merger premiums and lower integration costs. Overall, the results highlight firms’ use of philanthropy to manage stakeholder relations in takeover decisions.

title: Disagreement of disagreement
abstract: We show that leading investor disagreement proxies have near-zero cross-correlation – making disagreement pricing inferences challenging. We develop a frictionless model that generates overpricing from latent disagreement, jointly rationalizes major proxies, and generates new testable predictions. Equilibrium interrelationships motivate a new disagreement measure, DIS, which is more predictive of returns cross-sectionally than major proxies and more consistently predictive across macroeconomic regimes. We provide evidence that the friction-based channel of Miller (1977) and a frictionless mechanism coexist and are empirically separable. DIS also provides a micro-founded, disagreement-based account of the IVOL puzzle, absorbing IVOL’s predictability while revealing its regime and friction dependence.

title: Charitable capital allocation: Evidence from private foundations
Heterogeneous beliefs, asset prices, and business cycles
abstract: We develop a complete-market production economy in which heterogeneous beliefs about productivity growth affect both asset prices and real activity. Firms must hire workers before productivity is realized, so operating leverage increases the exposure of profits to productivity risk. Because the firm’s discount factor depends on a wealth-weighted aggregation of investor beliefs, shifts in optimism compress risk premia and raise employment, while reversals trigger contractions. This mechanism generates an equilibrium feedback between asset prices, hiring, and risk exposure. A taxonomy of belief systems shows that only extrapolative beliefs produce amplification and endogenous risk build-up. Disciplined by survey expectations, the model jointly matches key asset-pricing, trading-volume, and business-cycle moments.

title: Chronologically consistent large language models
abstract: Large language models are increasingly used in social sciences, but their training data can introduce lookahead bias and training leakage. A good chronologically consistent language model requires efficient use of training data to maintain accuracy despite time-restricted data. Here, we overcome this challenge by training a suite of chronologically consistent large language models, ChronoBERT and ChronoGPT, which incorporate only the text data that would have been available at each point in time. Despite this strict temporal constraint, our models achieve strong performance on natural language processing benchmarks, outperforming or matching widely used models (e.g., BERT), and remain competitive with larger open-weight models. Lookahead bias is model and application-specific because even if a chronologically consistent language model has poorer language comprehension, a regression or prediction model applied on top of the language model can compensate. In an asset pricing application predicting next-day stock returns from financial news embeddings, we find that ChronoBERT and ChronoGPT’s real-time outputs achieve Sharpe ratios comparable to a much larger and potentially biased Llama model. Our results demonstrate a scalable, practical framework to mitigate training leakage, ensuring more credible backtests and predictions across finance and other social science domains.

title: The decline of branch banking
abstract: We study branch openings and closures in U.S. banking. Both are concentrated where depositors are rate-sensitive and place less value on physical access, patterns driven by financially sophisticated households with greater digital adoption. The effects are strongest for large banks, with lending playing a lesser role. Incumbents retain branches where depositors are less sensitive and more reliant on proximity; entrants avoid such markets because sticky customers are difficult to attract. The Pandemic accelerated closures while allowing banks to retain deposits through online channels. Overall, depositor sophistication — through rate sensitivity and reduced branch reliance — drives modern branch restructuring.
