Simulating competitive collocation strategies with deep reinforcement learning
abstract: Abstract This paper introduces a simulation model based on deep reinforcement learning to study competitive collocation strategies of two internationalizing firms. Drawing on the strategic interaction and competitive collocation literature in IB, we explore the factors determining the performance-optimizing degree of collocation in market-seeking internationalization for a duopoly in product markets. Our simulation suggests that a high degree of collocation between the two firms is optimal in many circumstances. Whereas mid-to-high levels of collocation are driven by low competitive intensity, low entry barriers, low home-market size, and high market-size variation, complete collocation emerges under high competitive intensity, low first-mover advantage, and smaller home-market size. High entry barriers, combined with low variation in market size and strong liabilities of foreignness, drive the opposite case of complete mutual avoidance. A key takeaway from the simulation is a focus on the competing firm in global expansion: in many cases, it becomes key to limit the rival’s growth options and to enter key markets before access becomes more restricted. We discuss the possibilities of using computer-simulation-based approaches to theorizing on internationalization.

title: Repricing the green transition: market reactions to COP26 among MNCs diversified in pollution havens
From trade-off to paradox: a configurational theorizing and “quantum” approach to the resilience–sustainability tension in global sourcing
abstract: Abstract Global sourcing is increasingly caught between two persistent pressures: to be sustainable and resilient. While this relationship is often framed as a trade-off, we draw on paradox theory to conceptualize it as a persistent paradox, especially for MNEs coordinating complex supplier networks. Most paradox research addresses either how tensions are embedded in organizational systems or how they are socially constructed by managers, but rarely both. Drawing on the "quantum" approach to paradox, we bridge these ontological and epistemological perspectives, arguing that the resilience–sustainability tension is rooted in the structure of global sourcing systems and made salient through how managers interpret and combine sourcing decisions. Following a configurational roadmap of three stages—scoping, linking, and naming—we theorize five systemic sourcing factors (location choice, supplier redundancy, inventory buffer, green certification, and the sustainability premium) and examine how they are evaluated by 72 Italian procurement managers through a factorial survey, a fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis, and interviews. Managers favor coherent bundles over standalone levers, combining certification-based sustainability assurance alongside resilience-oriented levers such as proximity, redundancy, and buffers. We conceptualize three archetypal sourcing logics— integrator , resilience-first , and cost-only —offering managers a practical vocabulary for framing and legitimating sourcing choices when both pressures collide.

title: EXPRESS: The Collecting Mindset: Viewing Purchasing as Collecting Enhances Acquisition Experience and Product Desirability
abstract: Abstract Managers often struggle to make acquisition processes engaging. While the dominant approach to reducing search costs has been to streamline the acquisition process, seven preregistered studies plus one supplemental study (N = 3,306) reveal an alternative pathway: Prompting consumers to view purchasing as “collecting” by positioning products as additions to their own collections, rather than as ad hoc purchases, improves consumers’ acquisition experience and increases product desirability. The authors demonstrate that activating such a collecting mindset shifts consumers’ psychological focus of the shopping process from securing a standalone product to instead investing in advancing their collection, thereby making them derive positive experience utility from the process, and in turn, elevating the desirability of the sought products. This research also offers practical guidance on how marketers can maximize the effectiveness of activating a collecting mindset: (i) encouraging active engagement in search, (ii) ensuring that search yields products that meaningfully advance the collection, and (iii) aligning the collection with an identity consumers value, as the effect may otherwise attenuate or reverse. These findings advance theory on everyday collecting and consumer search, and show how retailers and brands can strategically turn purchasing into a more positive acquisition experience that enhances product desirability.

title: EXPRESS: The Role of Digital Ad Clutter in Ad Viewership and Memory
abstract: Advertisers face an increasingly cluttered digital ecosystem where customer attention matters. Despite this, the extent to which digital advertising clutter influences ad viewership remains unclear. This paper presents three separate eye-tracking experiments (subjects: N = 99, N = 250, and N = 575) using over a dozen custom-built web pages to better understand how digital ad clutter affects consumers’ viewing of digital ads. Across experiments, we show that increased clutter led consumers to allocate more attention to the overall advertising space and adjust how they distribute viewership across ad positions. A complementary survey revealed that clutter also reduced ad memory and recall for individual ads. We discuss the implications for advertisers and publishers regarding ad pricing and placement in crowded digital environments.

title: EXPRESS: Correcting omitted-variable bias without instruments: An ICA-based alternative to Gaussian copula methods
abstract: This paper proposes an instrument-free correction for omitted-variable bias and overcomes a key limitation of Gaussian copula control function (GCCF) approaches. Omitted-variable bias is the most common source of endogeneity in marketing, and many articles apply GCCF to address it. Yet GCCF require a nonlinear regressor-error relation, whereas textbooks assume linear, additive relationships between regressors and omitted variables. The authors prove that GCCF is biased in classical omitted-variable settings. Extant articles that address omitted-variables with GCCF also show language cues implicitly assuming linear relationships, which invalidate the use of GCCF. The proposed endogeneity correction is tailored to this prominent case, utilizing independent component analysis (ICA). It assumes a latent normally distributed component that additively influences both the endogenous regressor and the error. This can be interpreted as the sum of omitted variables, which, according to the Central Limit Theorem, add up to a normal distribution. Through ICA, this component is identified and extracted from the endogenous regressor, rendering the regression model free of endogeneity and enabling causal inference. The paper proves that the model is point-identified despite endogeneity due to omitted variables, that the proposed estimator is consistent and asymptotically normal, and that Jackknife resampling yields valid standard errors.

title: EXPRESS: Why are products so similar despite diverse consumer needs? The interplay between advertising and horizontal product differentiation
abstract: Firms are often less differentiated than standard price-competition models predict. We explain this gap by showing how firms can use informative or reminder advertising to soften competition. When firms choose locations, advertising, and prices endogenously, they may choose to soften price competition through limited advertising rather than greater product differentiation, allowing them to locate closer together while limiting price competition. This outcome of low advertising and central collocation is especially likely when advertising costs are high. We also observe that partially-differentiated equilibria, with one firm locating centrally and the other at an edge, and full differentiation, can each emerge under certain conditions. Thus, firms endogenously choose a mix of advertising and product differentiation to moderate price competition. Further, the shape of travel costs influences the equilibrium outcome. If the disutility from distance is highly convex, such as occurs when consumer preferences exhibit satisficing, central collocation becomes the unique equilibrium when more consumers are concentrated at the edge locations. However, when the disutility from distance is linear, having more customers located towards the edge locations makes collocation less likely. Overall, the interaction of advertising costs, consumer preferences, and location choices help explain why firms often forgo product differentiation.

title: Collaborating on Research Transparency
EXPRESS: Lifestage Bias: How the Visual Representation of Product Lifespan Shapes Replacement Timing
abstract: To guide consumers’ decisions regarding when to replace products such as water filters, printer ink cartridges, and engine oil, companies often provide visualizations of the product’s lifespan. We document a lifestage bias in which representing a product’s lifespan with more (vs. fewer) visually distinct stages increases replacement intentions even when the product’s actual usage is the same. The effect emerges because a greater number of visually distinct stages leads consumers to mentally simulate previous use, thus enhancing the perception that a product has progressed through its lifespan and encouraging product replacement. Ten studies document lifestage bias and provide support (via mediation and moderation) for the underlying usage simulation mechanism. Notably, lifestage bias is eliminated when stages are represented non-visually or when stages are not visually distinct. Furthermore, lifestage bias is attenuated when product deterioration can be observed directly. These findings provide important insights into how consumers make product replacement timing decisions. Adjusting the number of distinct stages in product replacement guides offers firms and policymakers a practical tool to influence replacement timing—accelerating it when timely replacement is necessary for health, safety, or regulatory reasons (thus improving consumer welfare), or delaying it when items can be safely used for longer (thus reducing waste).

title: Competition and Diversity in Generative AI
abstract: Recent evidence, both in the laboratory and in the wild, suggests that the use of generative artificial intelligence reduces the diversity of content produced. As generative AI penetrates more markets and reaches widespread adoption, should we still expect to see content homogenization? Our work begins with a simple observation: content producers do not act in isolation. Instead, they compete with one another (e.g., for customers or attention). We explore the impact competition has on both content diversity and overall social welfare when producers use generative AI. Through a formal game-theoretic model, we show that competitive markets select for diverse AI models, mitigating monoculture. We further show that a generative AI model that performs well in isolation (i.e., according to a benchmark) may fail to provide value in a competitive market. Our results highlight the importance of evaluating generative AI models across the breadth of their output distributions, particularly when they will be deployed in competitive environments. We validate our theoretical results with a series of experiments involving generative text and image models. Overall, our results suggest that homogenization due to generative AI is unlikely to persist under strong competition. This paper was accepted by Itai Ashlagi, market design, platform, and demand analytics. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.02761 .

title: The Buy-in Effect: When Increasing Initial Effort Encourages Follow-Through
abstract: Behavioral interventions often focus on reducing friction to encourage behavior change. In contrast, we provide evidence that adding initial friction to a sign-up process can increase follow-through behavior. In a field experiment with a state department of transportation ([Formula: see text]), we test whether adding modest friction during sign-up for a carpool platform increases usage. Although a more effortful sign-up process leads to 25% fewer sign-ups, overall usage increases. Importantly, these results were only partly explained by selection: Using an intent-to-treat analysis, participants with a more effortful sign-up process took 1.6 times more carpool trips per week over four months, leading to more overall trips despite fewer users. In a second experiment with online task work, participants with more effortful sign-up were 37% more likely to return the next day and completed more work overall. These results suggest that adding friction may be an overlooked strategy when follow-through, rather than initial uptake, is the primary goal. This paper was accepted by George Wu, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Funding: The authors acknowledge funding from the University of Konstanz for Study 2, Harvard University Pershing Square Foundation for Human Research, and Harvard Business School. The funders had no role in data collection and analysis, the decision to publish, or preparation of this manuscript. Supplemental Material: The online appendices and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.03600 .

title: Shipment Monitoring, Allocation, and the Impact on Food Waste
abstract: Often advocated for the potential to reduce waste in fresh produce supply chains, sensor technologies enable firms to monitor the condition of each product unit and allocate them to markets at different transportation distances, thereby matching units with shorter shelf lives with closer markets. In this paper, we consider a firm purchasing and transporting a fresh produce product for sale in two destination markets. Postharvest processes cause a proportion of the product to be in risky condition, potentially becoming unsalable (“spoiled”) due to shelf-life deterioration during transportation. With monitoring technology, the firm first determines a purchase quantity and then decides how to allocate each unit (in either good or risky condition) between markets. We characterize the optimal allocation policies, which can be used to efficiently determine the optimal purchase quantity. Our analysis shows that such technology may inadvertently increase total waste by inducing larger purchase quantities; this increase is often, but not always, accompanied by a lower waste rate and improved distribution efficiency. As firms increasingly adopt monitoring technology for shipment allocation, additional policy and managerial attention may be required. Improvements in postharvest processes can strengthen the waste-reduction benefits of monitoring technology. Firms seeking to maintain their sustainability goals can capture most of the profit gains from monitoring by carefully moderating increases in purchase quantities. This paper was accepted by Jeannette Song, operations management. Supplemental Material: The online appendices and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.07382 .

title: Retail on Wheels: A Time-Sensitive Traveling Salesman Problem
abstract: Rapid advancement in self-driving technology has brought mobile retail into the spotlight. Motivated by its potential, we present a model, theory, and insights into the operations of mobile retail, where a fleet of wheeled stores traverses a service region, selectively seeks locations in which to perch, and fulfills local customer demand. The goal of retailers is to strike a balance between perching and migrating to maximize total revenue. To dispatch such stores, retailers need to consider the following time-sensitive factors: (i) how busy the service is, (ii) how soon customers will arrive, and (iii) how quickly freshness decays. We propose and analyze a model that incorporates these factors into the classical traveling salesman problem (TSP), which we call the “time-sensitive TSP.” Using the continuous approximation approach, we derive the optimal revenue as well as the upper and lower bounds in the asymptotic regime as candidate locations increase to infinity. The tightness of the bounds is validated. Our analysis demonstrates that store mobility creates value by bringing proximity to customers. We further uncover the effects of these time-sensitive features on decision making. Specifically, the scaling relationship between revenue and fleet size is affected by customer tardiness and busyness. Busyness determines stores’ ability to expand their service, whereas tardiness affects how effectively stores can utilize the initial high-freshness period. These findings deepen our understanding of mobile retail operations. This paper was accepted by Karan Girotra, operations management. Funding: J. Cao acknowledges the support from McCombs Research Excellence Grant. W. Qi acknowledges the support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grants 72242106, 72188101, and 72521001]. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.04259 .

title: AI-Driven Human Task Substitution: Evidence from Google Translate and ChatGPT
abstract: We examine how different generations of artificial intelligence (AI) substitute for human knowledge worker tasks, leveraging two sequential natural experiments in the translation industry. We study the introduction of Google Neural Machine Translation (GNMT), a predictive, task-specific AI, as well as ChatGPT, a broad, general-purpose generative AI, in a major online labor market. Distinguishing between analytical tasks (regular translations) and intuitive tasks (transcreations, which require creative and cultural adaptation), we estimate difference-in-differences models on transaction-level data from 2016 to 2017 and 2022 to 2023. We find that GNMT reduced the demand for analytical tasks by economically meaningful magnitudes, while having no detectable effect on intuitive tasks. By contrast, ChatGPT produced substantially larger and more uniform reductions for both analytical and intuitive tasks, indicating a marked expansion in the scope and magnitude of AI substitution. By comparing these two technological shocks within the same labor market, we show that conclusions about which types of human work are resilient to automation do not straightforwardly generalize from predictive to generative AI. This paper was accepted by Joshua Gans, business strategy. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.06740 .

title: Systemically Important Banks and Loan Performance: Evidence from India
abstract: We examine whether designating banks as systemically important affects loan performance in an emerging-market setting where such banks are large domestic institutions and market imperfections make monitoring crucial for loan performance. Using loan-level data and the staggered designation of banks as Domestic Systemically Important Banks (DSIBs) in India, we find that loan performance deteriorates following DSIB designation. The evidence points to bank-level moral hazard as the underlying mechanism: DSIBs reduce postorigination monitoring and weaken loan recovery efforts. Borrowers respond accordingly, exhibiting poorer financial health and loan repayment, particularly on loans extended by DSIBs. This paper was accepted by Jan Bouwens, accounting. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.03238 .

title: Why Do We Discriminate? Directional Beliefs and Biased Information Processing
abstract: Identifying the cause of discrimination is crucial to designing effective policies and to understanding discrimination dynamics. This paper provides a potential link between existing models of taste-based and statistical discrimination by studying directional belief formation through biased information search and processing. By selectively acquiring and processing information, individuals form directional beliefs and consequently discriminate based on these beliefs. Through a series of experiments in which individuals endogenously acquire and process various signals, I document discrimination stemming from directional beliefs and demonstrate important differences in how it manifests compared with taste-based and statistical discrimination. Finally, I show that limiting individuals’ scope to interpret information reduces such discrimination. This paper was accepted by Marie Claire Villeval, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Funding: Financial support from the Sustainable Architecture for Finance in Europe Experiment Center Frankfurt [Grant 232406], the Interdisciplinary Public Policy Mainz [Grant A2021011], and the Mainzer Wissenschaftsstiftung is gratefully acknowledged. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.01818 .

title: Comment Letters, Connected Investors, and Corporate Bond Issuance
abstract: Using a proprietary data set that documents corporate bond issuances in China, we find that bond regulators’ comment letters (CLs) on issuers’ public disclosures generally target opaque firms and reduce bond issuance success. We also find, however, that connected investors—financial institutions with prior business relationships with the issuers—purchase a relatively larger share of bond issuances from CL recipients than from non-CL recipients, and this greater participation contributes to overpricing. Further analysis shows that connected investors support CL recipients because they possess superior private information and obtain private benefits from their connections. This paper was accepted by Ranjani Krishnan, accounting. Funding: R. Zhang acknowledges financial support from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada [Grant 31-R833984]. Supplemental Material: The internet appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.07607 .

title: The Effect of Small Quasi-Cash Rewards on Prosocial Behavior: The Case of Voluntary Plasma Donations
abstract: To better understand how prosocial behavior can be effectively encouraged, we study four unresolved issues: whether small rewards also motivate prosocial behavior, how short-term effects differ from longer-run behavioral adjustments, whether incentives induce substitution away from other prosocial activities, and whether reminders about existing rewards meaningfully influence behavior. We examine these issues in a long-run randomized field experiment across 12 donation centers of the Belgian Red Cross-Flanders. Donors normally receive one thank-you-coupon (worth €1.5) for a blood donation and two coupons for a plasma donation. Informing donors about the existing rewards increases plasma donations by 4.6% during the nine-month information period, although this effect fades with repeated reminders. Rewarding plasma donors with an extra coupon raises plasma donations by an additional 7.1% during the six-month reward period; this effect grows during the reward period but disappears immediately afterward. We also document a substitution effect; the plasma reward reduces blood donations by 3.3%. Survey evidence suggests that small rewards act as signals of increased need or as gifts eliciting reciprocity and that our findings may extend to volunteering decisions more broadly. This paper was accepted by Marie Claire Villeval, Behavioral Economics and Decision Analysis. Funding: This paper is based on research funded by the Belgian Red Cross-Flanders; the content reflects solely the views of the authors and not those of the Red Cross. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.08081 .

title: Collective Activism
abstract: Can investor stewardship codes that call for coordinated activism be satisfied by an Investor Collective Action Organization (ICAO)? In an ICAO, investors work collectively, like a large shareholder, to monitor management and increase value. We analyze the endogenous formation of an ICAO and its equilibrium size, considering free-rider problems and coordination costs. While the ICAO overcomes free-rider problems among its members, it exacerbates them between the ICAO and solo activists. The benefit of joining an ICAO is hump-shaped in size. With moderate coordination costs, ICAO formation features multiple equilibria. Small changes in coordination costs significantly influence ICAO formation and activism. This paper was accepted by Will Cong, finance. Funding: L. Yang thanks the support from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada [Grants 435-2021-0040, 435-2026-0060] and the Bank of Canada [Fellowship]. Supplemental Material: The online appendix is available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.02975 .

title: Predicted Incrementality by Experimentation for Ad Measurement
abstract: Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) provide the most credible estimates of advertising incrementality but are difficult to scale. We propose Predicted Incrementality by Experimentation (PIE), which reframes ad measurement as a campaign-level prediction problem. PIE uses a sample of RCTs to learn a mapping from campaign features to causal effects, then applies it to campaigns not run as RCTs. Because the RCTs identify the causal effects, PIE can incorporate post-determined features—campaign-level aggregates such as test-group outcomes, exposure rates, and last-click conversions, computed after campaign completion. These metrics reflect the consumer behaviors that generate treatment effects, so they carry predictive information about incrementality, even though they would be invalid controls in a causal model. Using 2,226 Meta ad experiments, PIE achieves an out-of-sample [Formula: see text] for incremental conversions per dollar, compared with [Formula: see text] for industry-standard seven-day last-click attribution. In a decision-making framework, PIE disagrees with RCT-based decisions in only 8%–12% of campaigns, compared with 12%–20% for last-click attribution. We conclude that PIE can help scale causal measurement from a limited number of RCTs to a large set of nonexperimental campaigns. This paper was accepted by Raphael Thomadsen, marketing. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.01108 .

title: Personalization, Engagement, and Content Quality on Social Media: An Evaluation of Reddit’s News Feed
abstract: Digital platforms increasingly curate their content through personalized algorithmic feeds. Platforms have an incentive to promote content that increases the predicted engagement of each user to lift advertising revenues. This paper studies how ranking content to maximize engagement affects the credibility of news content with which users engage. In addition, I evaluate how the ranking algorithm itself can be designed to promote engagement with high-credibility content. Using data from the Reddit politics community, I exploit a novel discontinuity in the ranking algorithm to identify the causal effect of a post’s rank on the number of comments it receives. I use this discontinuity to identify a model of user comment decisions and estimate the credibility of news content that users engage with under a personalized engagement-maximizing algorithm. The personalized engagement-maximizing algorithm exacerbates differences in the credibility of news content with which users engage. I then evaluate a credibility-aware algorithm that explicitly promotes credible news publishers and find the platform can substantially increase the share of engagement with high-credibility publishers for a small reduction in total engagement. These findings suggest algorithmic interventions can be a useful tool for managers to balance engagement quantity and content quality. This paper was accepted by Hemant Bhargava, information systems. Supplemental Material: The online appendices and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.06298 .

title: Using Representation Learning and Website Text to Identify Competitor Networks
abstract: This paper introduces a new approach to identify competitors using company websites to map competitive relationships among public and private firms. We apply representation learning techniques to create embeddings of companies based on website content, emphasizing information about industry-specific products and services. By placing all firms, public and private, within the same embedding space, we construct a peer competitor network that supports analysis of company interactions and market evolution. We label this new approach and set of network competitors as the website text-based network industry classification (WTNIC). We evaluate the quality of the network using multiple ground truth datasets and benchmarks and show that it offers a robust alternative for understanding competition at scale. Despite using noisy website data, WTNIC matches or outperforms prior approaches that rely on curated data. We demonstrate the value of WTNIC through a case study examining how competition from China affects the public and private peers of a focal firm, highlighting the importance of placing both public and private companies within the same embedding space. Funding: This work was supported by the National Science Foundation [Grants 1561068 and 1937153], the Tuck School of Business at Dartmouth College, the USC Marshall Institute for Outlier Research in Business (iORB), and the Smith School of Business at the University of Maryland. Supplemental Material: The data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.06516 .

title: Money Creation for Crypto Space: Stablecoins or Central Bank Digital Currencies?
abstract: Stablecoins are the current go-to digital money to settle transactions on the blockchain. We explore the implications of introducing competing tokenized public digital monies (i.e., tokenized central bank digital currencies (CBDCs)). When they pay a moderate interest rate and guarantee users’ anonymity, tokenized CBDCs crowd out stablecoins. However, when they pay a high interest rate and have low anonymity features, stablecoin issuers could use tokenized CBDCs as collateral, promoting the creation of stablecoins. We identify conditions under which introducing a CBDC to compete with stablecoins in the crypto sector would be socially optimal. This paper was accepted by Will Cong for the Virtual Special Issue on Digital Finance. Funding: Support from Swiss National Science Foundation (SNSF) [Grant 100018 219835].

title: Trading Off Business and Family Investments: Evidence from U.S. Entrepreneurial Households
abstract: Investing in children’s human capital reduces business investments for U.S. entrepreneurial households. Using financial account data of 90,000 small businesses linked to their owners and a regression discontinuity design that compares the business performance of households with college-aged dependents (18–22) to those with near-college-aged dependents (14–17), I show that business revenues and expenses decline sharply when owners’ children reach age 18. Despite the declines, profitability and productivity remain largely unaffected, suggesting a general downsizing rather than a loss in efficiency. Heterogeneity analysis shows that downsizing is concentrated among highly indebted owner households and businesses with volatile cash flows. For each dollar increase in household spending associated with a child turning 18, business expenses decline by $2.26. These findings are consistent with entrepreneurial parents reallocating capital from business investments toward their children’s human capital, as both compete for the same pool of internal family financial resources. This paper was accepted by Camelia Kuhnen, finance. Supplemental Material: The data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.04789 .

title: The Welfare Effects of Selling Leads in a Two-Sided Marketplace
abstract: Digital platforms that connect customers with service providers often monetize by selling customer leads to interested providers. Examples include Bark, Google Local Services, HomeAdvisor, Modernize, Porch, and Thumbtack. This paper develops a game-theoretic model to analyze how lead pricing affects customer and provider welfare. When the platform raises the fee-per-lead for a customer-type, those customers—conditional on receiving the same number of provider quotes—are quoted lower prices. However, if the fee is sufficiently high, providers purchase fewer of these leads, which can reduce the number of quotes and diminish customer surplus. To maximize social welfare, a simple policy that sets a market-clearing fee-per-lead for each customer-type guarantees at least [Formula: see text] of the first-best welfare and at least [Formula: see text] of the welfare under the welfare-optimal fees. The first-best outcome can be achieved by subsidizing providers for each job well done, so that experienced providers with cheaper sources of leads do not exit the platform. Understanding these welfare trade-offs can help platforms design policies that support balanced marketplace growth and preserve a sustainable revenue stream. This paper was accepted by Srikanth Jagabathula, market design, platform, and demand analytics. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.07399 .

title: Editorial Board
Enhancing Safety Signaling: Integrating Clinical Trials and Post-Marketing Adverse Event Reports
abstract: Problem definition: Adverse drug reactions (ADRs) cause numerous emergency room visits and thousands of deaths annually in the U.S. Although regulators like the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) aim to detect safety issues during clinical trials, these trials are often too small, short, or restrictive to capture rare or delayed ADRs. Consequently, regulators rely on spontaneous adverse event reporting systems (eg, FAERS) to identify potential safety issues—termed safety signals—by detecting side effects that occur disproportionately among patients taking a particular drug. However, these observational data are subject to selection and reporting biases, which can lead to false signals or missed risks. Methodology/results: We propose a Bayesian framework to enhance the hypothesis generation step in safety signaling, offering two methodological advances over standard approaches that rely solely on observational data. First, it integrates pre-approval clinical trial and post-approval observational data. Second, it uses information from common ADRs to estimate and correct bias in rare ADRs. We assess the approach using an analytical model and a large-scale numerical study with real clinical trial and FAERS data. Incorporating clinical trial data substantially reduces signaling costs, and using a common ADR for debiasing yields further gains. This refinement improves decisions for about 1% of ADRs, translating to expected cost savings of 1.5–2.3% (approx. $32–159 million), with performance robust to moderate parameter misspecification. Managerial implications: By using existing regulatory data, our approach supports a more efficient and timely hypothesis generation process in post-approval surveillance.

title: Dialysis Clinic Patient Flow and Work Design
abstract: Problem Definition: For 433,000 patients in the United States with advanced kidney failure, hemodialysis is a life-sustaining treatment. Approximately 7,600 outpatient dialysis clinics serve these patients, whose treatments cost over $25 billion annually. Each treatment involves a pre-treatment “put-on” task and a post-treatment “take-off” task performed by patient care technicians (PCTs). These frontline workers face intense, overlapping demands that can compromise patient safety and contribute to PCT burnout. We study how to jointly schedule PCTs and patients to reduce makespan and increase labor efficiency in dialysis clinic operations through better patient flow. Methodology/Results: We first analyze the prevailing “push” approach, which starts put-ons as soon as a technician and station are free. We then propose two alternatives: an “interlaced” scheme that staggers put-ons and take-offs to reduce idle time, and a “tandem” scheme that pairs two PCTs — one specializing in put-ons and the other in take-offs — across twice as many stations. We derive closed-form expressions for each approach’s makespan under constant treatment durations and show that interlaced schedules achieve the shortest completion time, whereas tandem configurations can reduce labor per patient. We also incorporate heterogeneous treatment durations and stochastic task times and arrivals to show numerically that our insights are robust. Managerial Implications: In contrast to the push-focused approach, these insights direct facility administrators’ attention to the primary driver of labor efficiency: minimizing the time that stations sit unoccupied between successive patients. Due to the inefficiencies of the push approach for a single pod, transitioning to an interlaced or tandem system while increasing the standard time allotted for tasks can alleviate workplace stress and promote patient safety without increasing labor costs. Specifically, dialysis clinic managers could move from the common 15/15-minute put-on/take-off scheduling standard to a 25/20-minute standard, thereby allotting PCTs 50% more time to complete tasks. Methodology/Results: We first analyze the prevailing “push” approach, which starts put-on tasks for treatment as soon as a station is free. We then propose two alternatives: an “interlaced” scheme that staggers put-ons and take-offs to reduce idle time, and a “tandem” scheme that pairs two PCTs — one specializing in put-ons, the other in take-offs — across twice as many stations. Under standard conditions, we derive closed-form expressions for each approach’s completion time and show that interlacing finishes earliest with homogeneous treatment durations, while tandem configurations can lower labor per patient. We also incorporate heterogeneous treatment durations to show numerically that our insights are robust. Managerial Implications: In contrast to the push-focused approach, these insights direct facility administrators’ attention to what is most important for labor efficiency: minimizing the time that a station is unoccupied between successive patients. Due to the inefficiencies associated with the push approach, transitioning to an interlaced or tandem system with increased standard task times can alleviate workplace stress and promote patient safety without increasing labor costs. Specifically, dialysis clinic managers could move from the common 15/15-minute put-on/take-off scheduling standard to a 25/20-minute standard, thereby allotting PCTs 50% more time to complete tasks.

title: Operations Management in the Sharing Economy: Advances, Challenges, and Opportunities
abstract: The rapid growth of the sharing economy over the past decade has changed many industries in profound ways. The innovative business models that have emerged in the sharing economy present unique opportunities as well as challenges, which have attracted a significant amount of attention from researchers in the operations management field. In this paper, we discuss the advances, challenges, and opportunities for research on operations management in the sharing economy. We divide sharing economy into eight categories: Ride Sharing, Space Sharing, Bike Sharing, Vehicle Sharing, Group Buying, Crowdfunding, Freelancing, and Last-Mile Delivery. For each business category, we identify the gaps and current challenges in the existing literature, discuss emerging industry trends and research topics, and suggest several future research directions. Our goal is to stimulate discussion and ideas about future studies in this area.

title: A Continuous-Time Model of Subscription and Repeat Purchase
abstract: Problem definition: We present a continuous-time model of consumers’ joint decisions of membership subscription and repeat purchase. A consumer pays a flow membership fee; her valuation follows a Brownian motion, purchase needs arrive via a Poisson process, and she chooses whether to buy and when to unsubscribe. The model is analytically tractable thanks to the connection between consumer lifetime and hitting time of Brownian motions. Methodology/results: Consumers’ unsubscription decision solves an optimal-stopping problem with a closed-form valuation cutoff; purchase occurs when valuation exceeds the transaction price. These thresholds generate three fluid consumer modes—buyer, tracker, and churner. We find that consumers who are about to terminate subscription tend to purchase less frequently, and who are currently subscribing are more likely to continue subscription. This endogenous customer loyalty is captured by a one-parameter retention formula [Formula: see text], which can accommodate rapid early attrition and an asymptotic slow decay. Managerial implications: For empirical estimation, we cast latent-valuation filtering as a heat-diffusion problem and develop a kernel-iteration likelihood approximation with vanishing discretization errors. Three empirical studies that feature two distinct firm-customer relationships demonstrate that our model performs on par with or better than existing models. Based on the model estimates, firms can infer consumers’ latent engagement and churn risk from purchase histories and devise the optimal package of membership fee and transaction price.

title: Designing Surprise Bags for Surplus Foods
abstract: Problem definition: Surplus-food marketplaces, such as Too Good To Go, enable retailers to monetize leftover inventory and reduce food waste by selling discounted “surprise bags.” Participating stores, however, face complex operational challenges. They must jointly set a reservation price and the number of bags made available before daily demand and end-of-day surplus are realized, while customers’ ex-post experiences affect future demand through the platform’s rating system. Moreover, although evenly distributing surplus across bags is intuitive and operationally convenient, it remains unclear whether bag-value differentiation can improve consumer experience and profitability. Methodology/results: We study these questions through an infinite-horizon two-stage stochastic dynamic program. In each period, the store first sets a reservation price per bag and the number of bags available and then, after observing accepted reservations and surplus, allocates surplus food across surprise bags, potentially supplementing from regular inventory. We show that this infinite-dimensional allocation problem can be reduced to a scalar choice of average bag value. Specifically, the optimal allocation is characterized by the upper concave envelope of the consumer utility function and requires at most two bag types. Building on this structural reduction, we develop linear value-function and deterministic fluid approximations that provide explicit performance guarantees and transparent implementation rules. The linear value-function approximation captures most of the dynamic-program profit improvement and produces the lowest average modeled total waste across the main grid, while the deterministic fluid approximation yields transparent steady-state comparative statics. Managerial implications: Price and the reservation cap are not interchangeable: price shifts latent requests and customer net utility, whereas the cap truncates high-request realizations before surplus is known. This division of control provides a basis for platform decision-support tools that balance retailer profit with food recovery.

title: Managing Consumer Bracketing Behaviors for E-Tailing Operations
AI on Time? Evidence from Curb-to-Gate Facial Recognition
Music Marketing with Generative AI
abstract: The multibillion-dollar music industry faces severe content creation bottlenecks, making multimedia marketing assets prohibitively costly for smaller artists. This practice paper introduces a Marketing Asset Generation Engine (MAGE) that can produce over 700 million video ad variations reflecting each artist’s visual identity using only a music track’s audio and album cover as inputs. Collaborating with one of the world’s largest music labels, we conduct four preregistered field studies with over 11 million impressions across 75 campaigns for 33 music tracks on TikTok and Meta to validate MAGE. First, pooled across studies, MAGE-generated ads significantly outperform human-designed ads on TikTok with on average 26% higher click-through rates and 10% higher engagement, while we do not detect statistically significant performance differences on Meta, all at 98% lower production cost. Second, neither marketing professionals nor laypeople can reliably identify winning ads such that random sampling of MAGE’s outputs performs as well as human-curated selections. In contrast, an AI-in-the-loop system trained on past performance data can predict pre-launch which MAGE-generated ads will perform best for specific audience segments. These findings demonstrate that generative AI democratizes music marketing by making effective, on-brand video ads accessible at scale.

title: Can Facebook Ads Prevent Malaria? Two Field Experiments in India
abstract: Two field experiments evaluate a nationwide Facebook malaria prevention campaign in India, finding effects concentrated in urban, more advantaged populations.

title: From Data to Decisions: Marketing Analytics, Mental Performance, and Firm Growth in an Emerging Market
abstract: Using a field experiment with 550 Rwandan firms, we show marketing analytics causally enhances entrepreneurs’ cognition and raises firm sales and profits.

title: The Identification of the Dynamic Discrete-Choice Model with Stockpiling
abstract: We study the identification of the discount factor for dynamic discrete-choice (DDC) models of demand with stockpiling of a storable good. We show that the DDC has built-in exclusion restrictions that set-identify the discount factor without requiring any auxiliary assumptions. We compare this approach to previous work that assumes auxiliary structure on the storage cost function, clarifying how such structure generates exclusion restrictions and the corresponding data moments used for identification. Our key results show that these auxiliary restrictions are not necessary for identification; but that they are testable and can be included to achieve point identification and improve statistical efficiency. Using a case study of laundry detergent from earlier published work, we find a mean discount factor estimate of $0.957$, rejecting myopic models of choice in favor of the dynamic model. In counterfactual simulations, we show that some of the promotional lift during a discount period is indeed due to forward-buying. However, we predict considerably higher incremental sales compared to a standard discrete-choice model, which predicts that promotional discounts mainly cause substitution between brands. These results contribute to the long-standing discussion about the effectiveness of price promotions.

title: From Live to Recording: Consumer Demand and Response to Price Across the Livestreaming Lifecycle
abstract: Using data from a knowledge-sharing platform that sells recorded versions of paid livestreams, this paper finds that demand is surprisingly more price sensitive before the event than after, which is explained partly by consumer self-selection and the lower quality uncertainty once the livestream ends.

title: Visual Plant Imagery and Property Valuation: A Descriptive Analysis
abstract: Online home profiles with more plant imagery are associated with higher property valuations, even after accounting for extensive property, neighborhood, listing, and market factors.

title: Online Decisions with (Biased) Offline Data
abstract: Making Better Decisions with Imperfect Historical Data Historical data can provide valuable information for online decision making, but its usefulness may be limited when the environment has changed. In “Online Decisions with (Biased) Offline Data,” Ahn, Zhang, and Zhang study how firms can combine potentially biased offline data with newly collected online observations in two canonical operations management problems: dynamic inventory decisions and dynamic pricing. The authors develop two online learning policies that balance the benefits of historical information against the risk of relying on data from a different distribution. The soft-switch policy automatically adjusts the reliance on offline and online data without requiring prior knowledge of the degree of bias. The hard-switch policy instead uses information about the magnitude of the distributional shift to determine when to rely primarily on online data. Both policies achieve optimal regret up to a logarithmic factor, whereas the analysis quantifies how the value of offline data depends on its size and bias.

title: Stochastic Dual Dynamic Programming for Log-linear Autoregressive Uncertainty in the Right-hand Side
abstract: We consider the generation of cuts in stochastic dual dynamic programming (SDDP) for multistage stochastic linear programming problems with stagewise dependent uncertainty in the right-hand side described by a nonlinear autoregressive process. We first derive cut formulas for the general nonlinear autoregressive process. For these general cuts, the computational tractability becomes a major challenge for SDDP-type algorithms. We are, however, able to develop tractable closed-form cut formulas for the special case of log-linear autoregressive processes. The obtained cuts are in general non-convex in the history of the stochastic process, but still linear in all decision variables, and thus can be directly incorporated into the subproblems in SDDP without compromising their linearity. If solvers do not allow for this, our formulas can be used to adapt the intercept of a given cut to a scenario at hand in a computationally tractable way. In this sense, cuts generated for one specific scenario are shared with other scenarios. Our findings are supported by a computational study of a hydrothermal scheduling problem, which demonstrates a favorable performance of our proposed version of SDDP compared to approaches from the literature.

title: Learning Optimal Classification Trees Robust to Distribution Shifts
abstract: We consider the problem of learning classification trees that are robust to distribution shifts between training and testing/deployment data. This problem arises frequently in high stakes settings such as public health and social work where data is often collected using self-reported surveys which are highly sensitive to e.g., the framing of the questions, the time when and place where the survey is conducted, and the level of comfort the interviewee has in sharing information with the interviewer. We propose a method for learning optimal robust classification trees based on mixed-integer robust optimization technology. In particular, we demonstrate that the problem of learning an optimal robust tree can be cast as a single-stage mixed-integer robust optimization problem with a highly nonlinear and discontinuous objective. We reformulate this problem equivalently as a two-stage linear robust optimization problem for which we devise a tailored solution procedure based on constraint generation. We evaluate the performance of our approach on numerous publicly available datasets, and compare the performance to a regularized, non-robust optimal tree. We show an increase of up to 12.48 percentage points in worst-case accuracy and of up to 4.85 percentage points in average-case accuracy across several datasets and distribution shifts from using our robust solution in comparison to the non-robust one.

title: Competition for Customer Attention is Creating Oversupply Pockets in US Micromobility
abstract: We present analytical and empirical arguments that competition over a nearly homogeneous service forces operators to oversupply scooters in urban centers. First, using deployment and ride data from operator APIs and city transportation departments, as well as telemetry data from one of the top three U.S. operators, we estimate average daily scooter utilization across nine major U.S. cities at 3.9%—half the 7.7% minimum utilization target set by transportation departments. Second, using a parsimonious game-theoretic model, we argue that if riders choose among available scooters roughly at random (e.g., the closest one), then in equilibrium all operators need to inflate their fleet sizes to preserve their market shares. Third, using granular data on riders’ choice sets and choices from Kansas City, MO, we provide evidence that these choices are indeed roughly random. Fourth, using our structurally estimated game-theoretic model, we find that in Kansas City, MO: (i) there is a 406% oversupply of scooters, (ii) the interaction between rider choice and competition accounts for 81% of this oversupply, and (iii) if the transportation department issued one more operator permit, oversupply would increase by an additional 82 pp. We conclude that transportation departments should be frugal with the number of permits they issue, and should welcome the consolidation of the scooter market.

title: Optimality of Public Persuasion for Single-Good Allocation
abstract: When Sharing the Same Information Is Optimal Should a school advisor tailor recommendation letters to different employers or share the same information with everyone? Similar questions arise in start-up fundraising and biotech partnerships. In “Optimality of Public Persuasion for Single-Good Allocation,” Chen and Qi study how a sender can strategically disclose information when allocating an indivisible good to at most one self-interested receiver. The sender may send tailored private messages to individual receivers or publicly broadcast the same information to everyone. Surprisingly, the authors show that, when the sender has a known preference ordering over receivers, public persuasion is optimal even if receivers can subsequently communicate and share information. The optimal public mechanism can be derived from a simpler first-best allocation problem subject only to receivers’ participation constraints. The authors also develop a dual approach to characterize the structure of optimal mechanisms when the good’s characteristics are captured by a one-dimensional variable and all receivers’ utility functions are linear in this variable and reveal an intriguing decoupling structure.

title: Community-Oriented Market Design for Nonprofit Resource Exchange
abstract: Unlocking Value Through Nonprofit Resource Sharing Nonprofit organizations often operate under tight budgets while idle equipment, unused space, and shareable skills and expertise are frequently underutilized, with existing resource exchanges in the nonprofit sector limited to bilateral barter or relatively homogeneous resources. In “Community-Oriented Market Design for Nonprofit Resource Exchange,” Huang et al. propose Sharing With a Purpose (SWAP), a resource-sharing system that enables nonprofits to exchange heterogeneous resources without monetary payments. SWAP combines an auction-based process, SWAPcredit valuation, and integer optimization to facilitate multilateral exchanges, allowing nonprofits to obtain needed resources by contributing resources of their own. The authors implement this market design through the SWAP Hub, a digital platform deployed with nonprofit communities in multiple regions. Through repeated exchange episodes, participating organizations have shared not only physical assets but also a wide range of skills, services, and expertise, including marketing, management, event planning, and organizational development. The study demonstrates how innovative market design can unlock latent value in community resources, alleviate resource constraints, and encourage new connections and collaboration among nonprofit organizations.

title: Convexity of Inverse Blocking Curves in Loss Systems
abstract: Why Larger Service Systems Benefit More from Scale How much extra demand can a service system handle when capacity is increased while keeping the same target level of customer blocking? In the paper “Convexity of Inverse Blocking Curves in Loss Systems,” Benjamin Legros establishes an exact economies-of-scale result for loss systems. The paper proves that the maximum supportable demand is an increasing and globally convex function of the number of servers. In practical terms, as a system becomes larger, each additional server can support progressively more additional demand while maintaining the same blocking target. Equivalently, the extra capacity required to accommodate additional demand decreases as the system grows. The result provides a rigorous mathematical foundation for resource pooling in capacity-constrained services. It applies to the classical Erlang-B loss model and extends to systems with a finite waiting room, with potential relevance for telecommunications, healthcare, emergency response, and other service operations.

title: Optimizing Input Data Collection for Ranking and Selection
abstract: We study a ranking and selection (R&S) problem when all solutions share common parametric Bayesian input models updated with the data collected from multiple independent data-generating sources. Our objective is to identify the best system by designing a sequential sampling algorithm that collects input and simulation data given a budget. We adopt the most probable best (MPB) as the estimator of the optimum and show that its posterior probability of optimality converges to one at an exponential rate as the sampling budget increases. Assuming that the input parameters belong to a finite set, we characterize the optimal static sampling ratios for input and simulation data that maximize the convergence rate. Using these ratios as guidance, we propose the optimal sampling algorithm for R&S (OSAR) that achieves the optimal ratios almost surely in the limit. We further extend OSAR by adopting the kernel ridge regression to improve the simulation output mean prediction. This not only improves OSAR’s finite-sample performance, but also lets us tackle the case where the input parameters lie in a continuous space with a strong consistency guarantee for finding the optimum. We numerically demonstrate that OSAR outperforms a state-of-the-art competitor.

title: Planning Stormwater Retention for Resilience Against Extreme Rainfalls
abstract: Rethinking How Cities Prepare for Extreme Rainfall Cities often prepare for extreme rainfall using a single “design storm,” such as a 100-year storm of a predetermined duration. But storms with the same return period can produce very different flooding losses. In “Planning Stormwater Retention for Resilience Against Extreme Rainfalls,” Liu, Qi, and Zhang develop a robust optimization framework that identifies the most damaging rainfall scenario for a city based on its existing drainage and retention infrastructure. Case studies of Toronto, Manhattan, and New Orleans show that the storm a city should prepare for changes with local infrastructure and climate conditions. The analysis also challenges the idea that greener is always more resilient; although green infrastructure offers important environmental benefits, concentrated gray infrastructure can become more valuable when rainfall is severe or budgets are tight. In Toronto, robust planning could save an estimated $6 million annually today and as much as $1.5 billion annually by 2050.

title: Colleagues that work together move together: How co-moving among newcomers affects individual and team performance.
abstract: As teams and team membership become more dynamic, colleagues from the same prior team increasingly transition together to a new team as a cohort: a phenomenon known as co-moving. Drawing on theories of shared team experience and team receptivity, we develop a multilevel, multi-theory, and multi-period model to examine how co-moving affects individual and team performance. We theorize that co-movers carry forward proximal shared team experience which they can leverage immediately to support their own performance relative to solo movers, who must build new working relationships. However, we also theorize that co-movers’ proximal shared team experience hinders team performance, though these detrimental effects attenuate over time. We test our theory using archival data from the National Basketball Association, supplemented by qualitative interviews with individuals involved in professional basketball. Our findings reveal that co-movers exhibit better individual performance than solo movers on their new teams and in our robustness checks we find that greater shared tenure on the prior team further enhances this advantage. At the team level, teams with co-movers perform worse than teams with solo movers, and we find partial support that this disadvantage attenuates over time. Additional analyses show that co-movers’ individual performance advantage persists over time in the new team. The findings from our interviews illuminate how these processes unfold both on and off the court. Our research contributes to the literature on shared team experience and newcomer integration by highlighting a multilevel tradeoff: while co-moving benefits individuals, it can initially undermine collective performance.

title: Reconceptualizing Network Change: Robustness and Resilience of Interorganizational Networks
abstract: Existing research on interorganizational network dynamics has largely treated network change as gradual, local, and primarily oriented toward private organizational advantage. Yet contemporary cooperative interorganizational systems are highly interconnected across industrial sectors and geographies and are routinely exposed to shocks that simultaneously disable multiple organizations or relationships among them. These shocks stem from pandemics, natural disasters, wars, sanctions, and cascading partner failures, and can rapidly reconfigure whole‑network architectures and undermine collective outcomes. In light of this new reality, we reconceptualize interorganizational networks as loci of frequent, punctuated change at the whole network level, with primary implications for collective outcomes. We develop this reconceptualization through a robustness–resilience lens, defining network robustness as an interorganizational network’s capacity to maintain its collective outcomes in the immediate aftermath of a shock, and network resilience as its capacity to recover and potentially surpass pre‑shock collective outcomes over the longer term. We then outline the theoretical and methodological opportunities that this robustness–resilience perspective opens for the study of network change.

title: Legal Chameleons: Political Ideology, Institutional Histories, and Firms’ Management of Identity Cues
abstract: This study examines how foreign firms strategically manage the salience of foreignness when facing unfavorable domestic evaluators. Foreign firms do so by altering the ethnic composition of the agents representing them before the evaluators. We examine this question in the context of Asian firms’ selection of legal counsel in U.S. federal courts. Prior research suggests that foreign firms may anticipate less favorable evaluations in courts that have historically favored domestic over foreign firms and in those with conservative judges. We argue that, in such evaluative settings, Asian firms adjust the ethnic composition of their external legal teams to manage the salience of foreignness, and that such adjustments are especially likely in courts that combine judge conservatism with pro-domestic ruling histories. We test these arguments using data on U.S. patent litigation from 2000 to 2016 and validated measures of courts’ political ideology and pro-domestic ruling histories. We find that Asian firms reduce the proportion of Asian-origin lawyers and increase the proportion of White lawyers when litigating in conservative courts, particularly when these courts also have pro-domestic ruling histories. By contrast, the ethnic composition of lawyers representing domestic firms remains stable across courts. Evidence of implicit bias against Asians among legal professionals provides additional support consistent with the theorized mechanism. Post-hoc analyses reveal that adjusting the ethnic composition of external legal teams attenuates the likelihood of unfavorable outcomes in conservative courts. These findings contribute to research on liability of foreignness by identifying agent selection as a specific mitigation mechanism in evaluative arenas.

title: When Data Scientists Meet Domain Experts: Artificial Intelligence, Epistemic Conflict, and Knowledge Transformation
abstract: Predictive AI models developed by data scientists promise to transform organizational knowledge, yet in practice the predictions remain inscrutable to domain experts. Existing explanations situate the problems in the opacity of the AI tools, failed adoption, or jurisdictional conflict, but offer limited insight into how to make the knowledge accessible. Here we show how the problem emerges from the competing epistemic stances of data scientists and domain experts, which create conflict over how to produce and evaluate knowledge. We then ask how data scientists and domain experts address that conflict so that their work with AI satisfies each group’s standards for producing and evaluating knowledge. Drawing on an 18-month inductive study of three large Indian banks, we show that the data scientists produce new knowledge, but domain experts hold the power to decide whether it is deployed. Our findings distinguish between epistemic and jurisdictional conflict. We show that data scientists first try to address the epistemic conflict directly through assimilative practices that follow one epistemic stance or the other. When these practices fail to transform knowledge, data scientists learn to address the conflict indirectly through four bridging practices. These practices help the domain experts transform knowledge by embedding the data scientists’ predictions in the boundary objects and practices that the domain experts already use. Our findings reveal how power based on expertise rather than jurisdictional control can make possible the coproduction of knowledge.

title: Early Environmental Shocks and Organizational Reconfiguration in High-Growth Ventures
abstract: We study whether shocks from local natural disasters can leave durable organizational traces in young high-growth ventures. In principle, such firms may be relatively resilient to localized disruption because they are designed to scale beyond local markets and rely heavily on knowledge-based assets. We examine this possibility using a panel of 19,984 U.S. startups founded between 1985 and 2010 that subsequently received venture financing. We identify ventures whose founding counties experience natural disasters within 12 months of founding using FEMA Major Disaster Declarations. Ventures exposed to disasters at an early stage exhibit higher subsequent failure hazards and no general advantage in follow-on financing, yet show higher IPO hazards in favorable market windows, a pattern consistent with greater responsiveness to opportunities requiring substantial organizational reconfiguration. Descriptive employee-level evidence further documents differences in organizational structure and composition consistent with greater retained fluidity among exposed ventures. Drawing on organization design and imprinting theory, we interpret these patterns as consistent with the possibility that disasters function as forcing environments that entrench early-stage coordination features such as flatness, role fluidity, and broader expertise that would otherwise attenuate as ventures mature. These durable organizational traces may, in turn, shape ventures’ subsequent capacity for reconfiguration. We discuss implications for organizational adaptation, imprinting, entrepreneurial geography, and organizational responses to crises.
