EXPRESS: From Institutional Expansion to Exposure-Driven Co-Evolution: Reinterpreting “Operations and Supply Chain Management in China”
abstract: This paper builds on and reinterprets Wu (2026a,b), which offers a comprehensive account of the rapid institutional, educational, and research development of Operations and Supply Chain Management (OSCM) in China. While the Institutional–Dynamic–Organizational (IDO) framework effectively captures domestic structural transformation, it under-theorizes a critical external driver of this evolution: international knowledge exposure and collaboration. To address this gap, we complement Wu’s analysis with a bibliometric study of published articles in Production and Operations Management from 1992 to 2026. The evidence shows that China’s growing presence in OSCM research is overwhelmingly collaboration-mediated, with China–U.S. co-authorship constituting the dominant channel of integration. The rise of China in top-tier OSCM journals is therefore not primarily an autonomous national trajectory, but a structurally embedded phenomenon within global co-authorship networks. Our findings suggest that China’s OSCM evolution cannot be fully explained by domestic institutional expansion, policy support, or educational scaling alone. Instead, it reflects a broader process of exposure-driven co-evolution within a globally integrated knowledge system. In this system, international collaboration is not merely a byproduct of scientific development but a central mechanism shaping the structure and trajectory of global OSCM knowledge production.

title: EXPRESS: Mind the Cost of Disturbance: Firm-Level Supply Chain Risk and the Bank Loan Cost
abstract: This study investigates whether and how supply chain risk, a core operational vulnerability, is priced in financial credit markets. Using a novel text-based firm-level measure, we show that elevated supply chain risk leads to higher loan interest spreads. Exploiting natural disasters as exogenous shocks to production networks, we provide causal evidence that shocks increase perceived supply chain fragility and, in turn, raise borrowing costs. These effects are amplified when lenders face greater private-information deficiency, and are further strengthened when external information production is more intensive — the former heightening lenders’ concern over supply chain exposure, the latter enhancing their capacity to recognize and price it. Critically, lenders treat supply chain fragility as a form of credit risk: firms with higher supply chain risk face increased default risk, and firms whose production networks are struck by supplier disasters face a higher probability of covenant violation and tighter covenant restrictions, signaling lenders’ anticipation of repayment difficulties. Our findings highlight a new financial consequence of operational risk, showing that supply chain disruption directly affects corporate financing outcomes.

title: Multi-self presentation and knowledge contribution in platform operations: Evidence from a natural experiment
abstract: Operations of online user-generated content (UGC) platforms often involve tackling under-provision , wherein users lack motivation to contribute sufficient content. We study a novel design deployed to address this issue: the integration of a proprietary social feature that allows users to post casual free-form content (e.g., casual social content) alongside standard formal content on the platform. Leveraging a quasi-experiment on a large Chinese online knowledge-sharing platform, we assess the effects of integrating such a social feature on users' formal knowledge contribution (i.e., writing answers to others' questions ). Using difference-in-differences (DiD) analyses paired with various matching strategies, such as propensity score matching and look-ahead propensity score matching, we find that users who adopt and frequently use the feature (i.e., high adopters) show a stronger incentive to contribute answers without compromising quality. These results are further validated by a set of robustness checks. Further mediation analysis suggests that such a complementary effect might be because of two mechanisms related to the integrated social feature's multi-self presentation function: First, the new feature increases high adopters' engagement on the platform and leads them to consume more knowledge content, which in turn facilitates knowledge contribution; Second, high adopters receive more social recognition benefits by building a more complete self through the integrated social feature, and such increased social recognition benefits further motivate more subsequent content contribution. Moreover, employing a text-mining approach to assess the semantic similarity between users' casual social content and their formal knowledge contributions, we find that the complementary effect is amplified for high adopters whose casual posts remain more closely connected to their formal knowledge domain (i.e., are more semantically aligned with their formal knowledge). Our results have novel implications for platform design and operations to motivate users to contribute valuable content.

title: EXPRESS: Pricing and Information Provision in Service Platforms with Heterogeneous Customers
abstract: Service platforms frequently employ virtual queues where customers have differing sensitivities to wait times and cannot see their precise positions in line. In these settings, providers often disclose waiting-time information to influence customers' decisions on whether to join or balk. A natural benchmark is to report the long-term average waiting time, yet whether this deterministic disclosure policy is optimal remains unclear when both pricing and customer participation are endogenous. This study develops a stylized theoretical framework to explore the joint structure of pricing and waiting-time information disclosure for service providers managing diverse customers in a virtual queue. The provider decides on both the service price and the waiting-time disclosure policy within a rational-expectations framework. Our findings reveal that the optimal disclosure strategy is captured by scaled Rademacher distributions, meaning at most two distinct announcement values are required. This reduces a complex infinite-dimensional problem to a more manageable finite-dimensional optimization task. Leveraging this framework, we derive the optimal strategies for pricing and disclosure, identifying scenarios where variability in announced waiting times is beneficial. Our analysis shows that noise is advantageous when customers can handle uncertain wait-time signals or initially perceive the service as quick. The optimal level of noise correlates with system congestion, offering the greatest benefits when there is a notable disparity between perceived and actual congestion levels. This provides significant advantages when disclosing waiting times with noise. These findings offer actionable insights for service platforms, guiding them in creating cohesive strategies that encompass pricing, information disclosure, and service configuration, ultimately enhancing customer experience and operational efficiency.

title: EXPRESS: Valuation Bottlenecks: Why Isn’t a Better Business Enough for a Higher Market Capitalization?
abstract: Firms often improve operations, disclosure, governance, or financing capacity without an immediate and proportional market-capitalization response. Could a single unresolved concern limit the market's response to improvements elsewhere in the firm? Classical multifactor and machine-learning models ask which risks or characteristics explain or predict returns. We ask whether the relatively weakest among several coexisting firm conditions receives disproportionate valuation weight. We model equity value as the lower envelope of lens-specific valuations. A hard minimum makes one lens locally binding; a soft minimum assigns continuous, state-dependent weights. We use exploratory factor analysis on 268 accounting characteristics to construct five firm-state lenses, with membership and weights determined by the loading structure rather than by an economic taxonomy, and rank each lens within industry, size, and quarter peers. We document a weakest lens effect : beyond the additive effects of all five lens ranks, a firm's weakest lens carries an incremental association with next-quarter returns, and it survives saturated joint rank-quintile controls. Gating the test at the bottom decile and then the bottom quintile of the peer distribution, the association is concentrated among firms whose weakest lens is weak against peers and not merely lowest within the firm. In baseline soft-min specifications, it fades steadily as the gate is widened. We then investigate whether analyst attention may help explain this pattern. We use large language models on 1.7 million earnings-call questions and find that, in baseline specifications, the weakest lens attracts a larger share of questions, especially when it is also weak among peers; this cross-sectional alignment is consistent with an attention channel as one possible explanation for the observed return pattern. The framework offers managers seeking to maximize market capitalization a new perspective on prioritizing scarce managerial attention.

title: Response efficiency versus response customization: An examination of firms’ responses to platform-empowered group complaints
abstract: The rise of group complaints on digital platforms, where consumers can publicly voice collective concerns, presents significant challenges for firms’ service recovery operations. Prior research assessing service operations on digital platforms has focused primarily on individual complaints, and less is known about how firms respond to platform-empowered (PE) group complaints. We examine this question through the lens of a trade-off between response efficiency and response customization and argue that this trade-off evolves as group complaints develop over time. Based on a large-scale dataset from Tousu, a leading complaint platform in China, we find that group complaints paradoxically increase response time and decrease empathy and explanation in firms’ responses. Further analyses indicate that these effects depend on dynamic group size and dynamic need diversity. When dynamic need diversity is low, larger groups are associated with more standardized, efficiency-oriented responses, whereas when dynamic need diversity is high, larger groups are associated with slower but more customized responses. These findings extend research on service operations by showing how PE group complaints reshape firms’ complaint handling. Our study also provides operational guidance for managing group complaints more effectively.

title: Operations management for sustainable development and public policy making
abstract: Public policy making often faces challenges in implementation due to a lack of attention to operational realities. Operations management (OM) research, with its strong empirical component and focus on detailed model-based mechanisms, offers unique insights for successful policy execution. This paper explores the synergies between economics, development economics, and OM in addressing public policy implementation, arguing that OM’s process-level understanding, empirical rigor, and focus on operational feasibility can enhance policy design and evaluation. We illustrate this potential through examples from sustainability and social development, demonstrating how OM can bridge the gap between economic policy insights and operational execution.

title: Modeling collective action in POM: The Strategy–Operations–People framework
abstract: While many business situations relevant to Production and Operations Management (POM), e.g., supply chain coordination or sustainable operations, involve some form of collective action, managerial frameworks for collective action appear to be rarely applied to POM contexts. Valuable insights for effectively solving POM problems may thus be missed, reducing the implementation and effectiveness of proposed POM solutions. Conversely, these managerial frameworks typically lack the mathematical formalism that is characteristic of POM models, creating ambiguity around the defining scope of their elements. To bridge this gap, this paper develops a mathematical formalization of a framework for collective action proposed in the organizational behavior literature. It then illustrates its relevance to POM by mapping it to case studies in supply chain coordination and sustainable operations. The framework under consideration, which we call the Strategy-Operations-People (SOP) framework, is structured in three levels, each consisting, respectively, of three, two and one elements. First, the Strategy level induces and enforces solidarity among all team members by specifying common goals, shared values, and well-defined rules. Second, the Operations level organizes the decentralized execution of collective action in autonomous subgroups through the detailed specification of roles and processes. Third, the People level requires the individual commitment of all team members to the proposed collective action program, since a team’s performance rests on the individual contributions of its members. The framework thus addresses the common, subgroup, and individual dimensions of collective action. The SOP framework provides POM with a systemic approach to studying collective action. Mapping the framework to two problems in supply chain management and sustainable operations also illustrates the broad applicability of the framework, originally designed for teams within organizations, to guide collective action taking place across organizations. Its mathematical formalization brings operational clarity on the defining scope of its elements, and provides a check list for detecting potential blind spots affecting the effective implementation of proposed POM models.

title: Central Bank Economic Transparency and Managerial Learning
abstract: Abstract Central banks increasingly disclose their private information regarding the economy’s current and future state (CBET). Consistent with CBET shifting investors’ collection and pricing of aggregate-level (where managers do not have an information advantage) toward firm-level (where managers do have an information advantage) information, we find that CBET reduces managers’ learning from stock price. The results are (1) pronounced when firms do not provide guidance and when noise trading in firms’ stock is low, and (2) robust to using the 2013–2014 amendments to the Bank of England’s Inflation Report as an exogenous shock. Additional evidence suggests that CBET lowers investment efficiency. (JEL E22, E52, M41)

title: Directing the Labor Market: Shared Directors and Employee Flows
abstract: Abstract Using résumé data on over 20 million U.S. workers, we find that the flow of employees between a pair of firms sharply drops by about 20% during periods in which the firms share a board director. This relationship is stronger in settings where firms have greater potential gains from limiting worker mobility and is most pronounced for higher-skilled employees. Moreover, we find more connected firms have lower rates of internal promotion and no improvements in employee satisfaction. The evidence is consistent with shared directors serving as a mechanism for labor market coordination.

title: A platform for change? Core component innovations, complementor adaptation, and multihoming in platform‐based ecosystems
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Digital platforms coordinate complementor innovations through interfaces into their core components. However, when interfaces themselves evolve alongside core component innovations, complementors may exhibit behaviors that are not entirely predictable. Using granular data from Apple's five major iOS releases, we abductively examine App developers’ responses following Apple's core component innovations. We document that, in post‐release periods, complementors simultaneously increase co‐innovation on iOS while being more likely to multihome by diversifying to the competing platform. These choices are further explained by whether architectural changes reflect cross‐platform standardization or platform‐specific differentiation. Standardization spurs both complementor co‐innovation and multihoming, while differentiation reduces diversification tendencies. The patterns that we document reveal an important tension: governing through interfaces enables platforms’ scalability but constrains their ability to control complementors as platforms evolve. Managerial Summary Digital platforms like Apple coordinate large scale innovation through standardized interfaces, but those interfaces must evolve as platforms compete, and the direction of that evolution has consequences managers should attend to. Analyzing Apple's five major iOS releases, we find that architectural changes are associated with increased co‐innovation but also a higher likelihood that developers diversify to a competing platform. This pattern is particularly pronounced when updates bring iOS closer to Android, suggesting that architectural convergence may lower the barriers to cross‐platform expansion for developers. Importantly, this behavior is strongest among highest‐value developers. Platform managers should therefore treat architectural evolution not merely as a technical decision, but as a strategic one with direct implications for ecosystem loyalty, competitive differentiation, and the retention of valuable ecosystem partners.

title: Organizational Zemblanity: How Organizational Learning Can Reinforce Rigidity, Error, and Misalignment
abstract: Organizational learning can help organizations improve and adapt, but it can also reinforce error and misalignment. These negative outcomes are often interpreted as implementation problems or as signs of incomplete learning. We instead examine the possibility that dysfunction can arise from learning processes themselves, even when those processes operate as intended. We review 290 articles to identify recurring assumptions in the literature and the conditions under which they do not hold. We then identify three mechanisms that can turn learning systems into sources of rigidity and misalignment, and conceptualize the self-reinforcing trajectory produced by their interaction as learning-based organizational zemblanity. Our review shows how organizational learning can generate both adaptive and dysfunctional trajectories and outlines a research agenda on identifying and interrupting negative learning trajectories.

title: Combining management control practices for organizational learning: A situational strength perspective
abstract: Organizational learning (OL) is a critical organizational capability. Yet designing management control (MC) that effectively supports OL is challenging, as learning outcomes are often intangible and unfold over extended time horizons. Employing situational strength theory, we examine combinations of MC practices that affect OL contingent on environmental uncertainty. Drawing on a survey of 210 senior business unit controllers, we use fuzzy-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (fsQCA) to identify multiple combinations of MC practices that achieve high OL in different uncertainty contexts. In a subsequent step, we examine whether the situational strength of certain combinations of MC practices is associated with OL. Results show that in a low-uncertainty environment, the combined use of diverse performance measures and social controls, as well as performance pay and a mechanistic administrative structure, have a synergetic effect on OL. In a high-uncertainty context, the combined use of measure diversity and deliberate formal strategic planning is beneficial for achieving OL. Our results suggest that the effectiveness of MC practices for OL depends on aligning MC practices with the internal as well as the external context.

title: How do audit committee members' and audit partners' communication styles jointly influence client managers’ negotiation behavior?
abstract: Auditor-client negotiations over contentious accounting issues can shape reported financial outcomes, yet little is known about how communication dynamics between audit committee (AC) members and auditors influence client negotiation behavior. We conduct an experiment in which experienced financial executives, assuming the role of chief financial officer, negotiate a disputed inventory obsolescence allowance with a simulated audit partner in the presence of an AC member; the AC member's distributive communication style (offensive vs. defensive) and the audit partner's reflective empathy (high vs. low) are manipulated between participants. Drawing on relational framing theory in interpersonal communication, we predict and find that a distributive-offensive AC communication style leads clients to establish their reporting positions and concede less to the auditor's proposed adjustment, unless it is accompanied by high reflective empathy from the audit partner, which neutralizes this resistance. This pattern emerges in the client's initial negotiation position and persists through the final negotiated allowance. Our findings suggest that auditors can use empathetic communication as a strategic tool to defuse the competitive posture that an assertive governance signal may provoke. Overall, our results provide insights into how AC members' and auditors' communication styles jointly shape client negotiation behavior, highlighting the importance of communication strategies in achieving effective audit negotiation outcomes.

Could That Happen to Me? Auditor Response When Colleagues Are Named in Lawsuits
abstract: ABSTRACT Litigation risk is an important source of motivation for auditors to conduct high‐quality audits, but theory suggests that certain lawsuits will have a more salient disciplining effect on auditor behavior. To this end, we identify lawsuits naming an individual partner as a co‐defendant along with the audit firm. We then examine how these lawsuits affect subsequent behavior of other auditors in the office of the sued partner. Relative to lawsuits naming only the firm, our results indicate that lawsuits naming individual partners as co‐defendants are significant office‐level events that motivate a meaningful response from non‐sued audit partners in the form of higher quality and fees on existing clients and more careful client portfolio management. These results have practical implications about how auditor litigation incentivizes individual auditors to fulfill their professional duties. For regulators and audit firms seeking to promote audit quality, these findings highlight the disciplining effect of auditors' concern for their personal reputation and litigation exposure. Furthermore, audit committees, clients, and investors may observe elevated audit quality, effort, and fees following partner‐level litigation in the local office.

title: Would a Balanced PCAOB Inspection Approach Increase Auditors' Use of Innovative Audit Procedures?
abstract: ABSTRACT Prior research criticizes PCAOB inspection reports for focusing solely on audit deficiencies, arguing that this encourages auditors to pursue traditional procedures to demonstrate compliance with standards rather than procedures that maximize audit quality. We contribute to this debate by examining whether the PCAOB's approach discourages auditors from considering innovative audit procedures (that are potentially more effective), since they are, by definition, less standard. We compare the PCAOB's current inspection approach (which focuses on reporting audit deficiencies) to a balanced inspection approach that discloses examples of audit strengths as well as deficiencies discovered during inspections. We predict and find that when the risk of material misstatement (RMM) is moderate, a balanced inspection approach leads auditors to consider the potential effectiveness of innovative audit procedures to a greater extent, ultimately prioritizing more of them in audit plans. Our findings contribute to both research and practice by enhancing our understanding of ways to encourage audit innovation and ultimately improve overall audit quality.

title: Choosing the Stage: The Strategic Role of Disclosure Venues in Guidance Revisions
abstract: ABSTRACT When managers revise earnings guidance between earnings announcements, they choose not only what to disclose but also where to disclose—in a standalone release, a guidance call, an investor conference, or an analyst/investor (A/I) day. These venues differ in audience, format, and visibility, raising the question of whether venue choice is a strategic communication decision. In a large sample of unbundled revisions, we find that managers use calls for relatively large negative revisions and when litigation risk is higher and that they use conferences and A/I days for smaller revisions and when analyst disagreement is greater. Textual analysis reveals that calls feature cautious, litigious language for both upward and downward revisions, whereas conference and A/I day communications remain optimistic. In line with these framing differences, calls are associated with amplified reaction to negative news and are followed by more favorable earnings surprises, suggestive of effective expectation management, whereas conferences and A/I days are associated with muted reactions and reduced analyst dispersion and are followed by less favorable surprises. Our findings suggest that venue choice is a dimension of disclosure strategy for managers and an informative signal for investors.

title: Specialists' Evidence Evaluation and Judgments in Audits
abstract: ABSTRACT Audits of complex fair value estimates involve evaluating and challenging key client assumptions. Auditors generally lack the necessary expertise to perform this work, and thus, they often engage valuation specialists to perform this audit work. However, valuation specialists primarily perform advisory work and may not put enough care into their audit work. We examine whether valuation specialists' psychological ownership of audit work and auditors' infringement on that work affect specialists' judgment quality. Using a survey and an experiment with practicing valuation specialists, we find that higher psychological ownership improves specialists' evidence evaluation and judgments, but only when auditors do not behave intrusively by infringing on their work. When auditors behave intrusively, the benefits of specialists' higher psychological ownership disappear. Our findings show that audit quality depends not only on specialist behavior but also on auditor interactions with specialists. Our study offers practical guidance to audit firms on how to organize audit work and manage internal working relationships between auditors and valuation specialists.

title: Industrial-organizational science that matters: Social impact and policy implications in the Journal of Applied Psychology.
A meta-analysis of the dynamism of emergent states and team processes.
abstract: Prevailing theories of teamwork propose that a team's cognitive, affective, and motivational states (i.e., emergent states) and its members' interdependent actions (i.e., team processes) are inherently dynamic. Nevertheless, much of the existing literature overlooks critical components of theories on system dynamics (e.g., inertia, coevolution, feedback) and has largely failed to consider how time operates, ultimately leading to a predominantly static view of teams. To extend our understanding of team dynamism, we synthesized over 3,000 correlation coefficients from longitudinal studies, representing more than 11,000 teams on average. Using cross-lagged, meta-analytic structural equation models, we found that (a) emergent states and team processes exhibit inertia over time, although this varies by construct (affect exhibits the least inertia, while conflict exhibits the most); (b) some constructs (team affect and team cognition) tend to coevolve with team processes over time, whereas others (team motivation and team conflict) are consistently predicted by earlier team processes; (c) team performance exhibits consistent feedback loops, predicting subsequent emergent states and processes, which, in turn, predict later performance; and (d) the length of time between observations moderates these dynamics. Drawing on these results, we outline several key theoretical considerations for understanding team dynamics, highlight important methodological considerations for conducting longitudinal causally identified teams research, and offer recommendations for advancing beyond the current static perspective to a more dynamic understanding of teams. title: The judgment-based approach to entrepreneurship: The uncertainty–heterogeneity nexus
abstract: The judgment-based approach (JBA) has emerged as an important contemporary perspective in management and entrepreneurship research. The JBA offers a distinctive theoretical account of entrepreneurship, centered on the formation and implementation of subjective theories of value creation under conditions of Knightian uncertainty, which highlights resource ownership, heterogeneous capital structure, organization and the firm, institutions, uncertainty, and the overarching need to appraise and coordinate all these factors using judgment. We present and develop the JBA by articulating the uncertainty–heterogeneity nexus, in which the joint presence of fundamental uncertainty and heterogeneous resources gives rise to the need for entrepreneurial judgment and makes its exercise economically consequential. Because judgment is subjective, tacit, and difficult to communicate or contract upon, entrepreneurs must rely on ownership and residual control rights to create value, linking judgment to the combination and deployment of resources, profit and loss, and organizational structure. The purpose of this article is threefold. First, we provide a systematic statement of the JBA as a theoretical framework, clarifying its core constructs, causal mechanisms, and domain of application. Second, we engage with key critiques and distinguish the JBA from related approaches, including opportunity-based, effectuation, and bricolage perspectives. Third, we outline directions for future research that build on the JBA's emphasis on judgment, ownership, and the organization and deployment of heterogeneous resources under uncertainty. By integrating these elements, we position the JBA as a coherent and distinctive theory of entrepreneurship with broad implications for research in management, organization, and strategy.

title: Co-founder selection from a marriage market perspective: How the dark triad shapes judgments of interpersonal attraction, resources, and equity demand
abstract: Co-founder selection is a pivotal decision in new venture formation, yet how lead founders evaluate potential partners remains underexplored. Drawing on insights from marriage market theory, we conceptualize co-founder selection as an act of individuated judgment guided by cooperative logic and associated joint utility projection, wherein lead founders assess co-founder candidates based on social-emotional, instrumental, and distributive considerations reflected in interpersonal attraction, resource contributions, and equity demand. We further propose that lead founders' dark triad shifts this judgmental process from joint utility logic to personal utility maximization. Using a conjoint experiment with 206 entrepreneurs making 3296 co-founder selection decisions, we find that interpersonal attraction and resource contributions positively influence willingness to select a co-founder candidate, whereas higher equity demand reduces candidate attractiveness. Critically, lead founders higher in the dark triad display distinct patterns: they discount interpersonal attraction and display heightened sensitivity to equity dilution—assessments that indicate their prioritization of personal over joint value creation. Taken together, these findings reveal how dispositional tendencies influence the judgments underlying co-founder selection, indicating a shift away from the cooperative logic assumed in marriage market theory and co-founder selection toward greater emphasis on personal utility considerations. We discuss theoretical implications of these findings and offer practical guidance for navigating the complexities of co-founder selection.

Marketing misinformation in the age of AI
abstract: Abstract We shine a spotlight on marketing misinformation—claims about products and brands that contradict or distort verifiable facts. Misinformation may be created unintentionally or intentionally by companies, competitors, customers, or third parties seeking to harm companies or consumers. We focus on the role of AI in creating, obfuscating, and disseminating misinformation in the form of text, audio, images, and videos generated using large language models. This type of information can pose a substantial risk for brand safety. Consumers may be aware that AI can generate misinformation but may lack the ability to guard against it. We discuss how different stakeholders in the information ecosystem can help in the prevention and correction of misinformation and propose a future research agenda in this critical and fast‐growing area.

title: Exploitation in the marketplace: A consumer behavior perspective
abstract: Abstract This paper examines exploitation in the marketplace from a consumer behavior perspective. We define marketplace exploitation as occurring when one party leverages structural and/or situational resource asymmetries to extract disproportionate value in ways that undermine fairness or autonomy, even when exchanges appear voluntary and mutually beneficial. We distinguish marketplace exploitation from related concepts including fairness, deception, and discrimination, arguing that it centers on the morally problematic use of contextual advantage. Adopting a dual lens, we develop conceptual frameworks for both firm‐to‐consumer exploitation (e.g., price gouging, dark patterns) and consumer‐to‐firm exploitation (e.g., free trial abuse, exploiting firm mistakes). These frameworks delineate how structural and situational asymmetries give rise to objective exploitative acts, when such acts are perceived as exploitative, and how they shape emotional, cognitive, and behavioral responses. We synthesize a research agenda and outline methodological approaches for studying the antecedents, perceptions, and consequences of exploitation. This work contributes to consumer psychology by conceptualizing marketplace exploitation as both a subjective psychological experience and a strategic marketplace behavior, with implications for theory, policy, and ethical firm practices.

title: Signaling uniqueness: The psycholinguistic effect of language precision on product perceptions
abstract: Abstract This research reveals a psycholinguistic effect whereby more precise words in product communications increase consumer perceptions of product uniqueness. Drawing on Categorization Theory, the authors propose that more precise words in product descriptions are situated deeper within their semantic categories and denote narrower subsets of referents, thereby eliciting perceptions of product uniqueness. [Correction added on 15 October 2026, after first online publication: The reference in the preceding sentence has been removed.] Four experiments provide robust evidence supporting the “precise‐unique effect” and its underlying psycholinguistic mechanism driven by categorical depth. The findings further suggest that consumers' need for product uniqueness moderates the downstream effects of language precision on perceived attractiveness and behavioral intention via perceived uniqueness. This research contributes to the growing literature on language effects in consumer psychology and provides practical implications for making strategic lexical choices that enhance product positioning and differentiation.

title: CEO Ideologically (In)Congruent Activism and Investor Reactions: An Attribution of CEO Intentions Perspective
abstract: Abstract The phenomenon of chief executive officers (CEOs) taking activism stances on contested sociopolitical issues is increasing, yet it remains unclear how observing investors discern CEO intentions behind activism engagements, thereby shaping their judgments and subsequent reactions. By relaxing the assumption that CEO activism is an unabashed expression of personal beliefs, we propose the concept of CEO ideologically (in)congruent activism and develop a framework wherein investors may attribute CEO intentions underlying incongruent (versus congruent) activism engagements as more organization‐driven (versus self‐driven) interest pursuits, thereby leading to more positive investor evaluations and reactions. Furthermore, we argue that the positive effect of CEO ideologically incongruent activism on investor reactions will be amplified when the CEO owns a higher level of stock ownership but weakened when the firm receives a greater corporate social responsibility (CSR) rating. We corroborate our propositions using a sample of CEO activism events for S&P 500 firms from 2012 to 2021. Our findings demonstrate the heterogeneity and critical influence of CEO intentions behind activism engagements and shed light on how investors integrate multi‐informational cues when evaluating and reacting to managerial incongruent behaviours.

title: How Strategic Leaders Drive Firms in Ecosystems: Envisioning Value, Orchestrating Knowledge, and Shifting Roles
abstract: Abstract Research on business ecosystems has illuminated how ecosystems emerge, evolve, and transform, revealing ecosystem‐level dynamics and the central actors that orchestrate them. Yet, it is individual firms that continuously attempt to establish and shift the roles they play within ecosystems through the vision and choices of their strategic leaders. How do strategic leaders drive these shifts? Through a longitudinal case study of Dallara Automobili (1972–2025), we trace how the CEO's prior professional experience shaped an evolving theory of value – a set of conjectures about how value should be created that guided the development of organizational routines enabling progressively more expansive knowledge orchestration. This process shifted Dallara from a peripheral component supplier to a boundary‐spanning knowledge orchestrator. Our recursive process model theorizes how the leader's conjectures drive firm role shifts within an ecosystem: experience shapes the leader's theory of value, which drives organizational routines and knowledge orchestration; knowledge orchestration, in turn, redefines the firm's ecosystem role. Ecosystem responses then feed back, augmenting prior experience and, in turn, refining the theory of value so that each round operates at a broader scope. We contribute to ecosystem research by identifying knowledge orchestration as the mechanism through which a leader's theory of value translates into shifts in the firm's role and by showing how this process unfolds recursively as ecosystem responses reshape the leader's conjectures.

title: Pet-owner synchrony: Operationalization, application, and implications
abstract: Abstract Despite the pet industry’s significant economic and social importance, academic attention to this sector of the economy has been limited. Rather than focusing solely on the household demographics of pet ownership or the attitudinal components of the pet-owner relationship, we explore actual purchase decisions of pet owners. In this study, we examine pet-owner synchrony, a behavioral operationalization of pet-owner relationships that is grounded in attachment theory, anthropomorphism, and the extended self. Utilizing scanner data from 875,853 market baskets including 23 million transactions collected from a regional supermarket chain, we analyze cross-category co-occurrence patterns within shopping baskets. Our analysis reveals affinities, or parallels, in pet owners’ purchases of health and wellness products and hedonic products for both themselves and their pets, which we attribute to pet-owner synchrony. We identify two moderators that influence the strength of pet-owner synchrony: pet type (cat versus dog) and the presence of young children in the household. In addition, we evaluate how basket size, holidays, and price elasticities impact pet-owner synchrony. Our findings deliver useful insights into pet-owner relationships, have direct implications for retail and manufacturing managers, and yield recommendations for public policy.

title: Can green innovations enhance competitive advantage?
abstract: Abstract Sustainable New Product Introductions (SNPIs) enable firms to meet consumers’ increasing demand for sustainable options while addressing rising expectations for corporate environmental responsibility. This study demonstrates that SNPIs can also strengthen brands by enhancing brand equity. Drawing on signaling theory, we propose that SNPIs serve as product-based sustainability signals that enhance brand equity by generating social goodwill. A staggered event study of the initial launch of a sustainable product line by a major laundry detergent brand shows that SNPIs can increase parent-brand equity. A complementary analysis of subsequent SNPIs across 15 leading brands in 12 retail chains reveals that this effect is moderated by parent firms' ethical reputation and retail chains' sustainable assortment share. These findings advance our understanding of whether and under what conditions sustainable products serve as credible signals of environmental responsibility and enhance brand equity.
journal_name: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science

title: Populism and sustainable marketing practices: Insights from consumer-packaged goods manufacturers’ new product launches
abstract: Abstract While sustainable marketing practices have traditionally been grounded in stakeholder capitalism, the rise of anti-climate-action populism presents new challenges to firms’ sustainable strategies. Drawing on resource dependence theory, this study argues that anti-climate-action populism prompts firms to reduce sustainable marketing practices, specifically the use of environmentally friendly packaging in new product launches. However, we propose that subnational formal and informal institutions, such as economic freedom and cultural tightness, attenuate this effect. To test these hypotheses, we employ a quasi-natural experimental design, using the announcement of the United States’ exit from the Paris Agreement to analyze its impact on sustainable marketing practices, based on a global sample of product launches by consumer-packaged goods manufacturers. Our difference-in-differences analysis supports these hypotheses. This study advances the understanding of the dynamic relationship between populism and subnational institutions, highlighting how different institutional pillars shape firms’ sustainable marketing strategies.

title: Does Global Slowing Explain Age Effects in Inhibitory Control?
abstract: A long-standing debate in the study of cognitive aging centers around the issue of whether aging results in a selective deficit in inhibitory control beyond general slowing of cognitive processing. Previous studies have obtained mixed findings, in part because the typical free-response-time paradigm lacks the specificity required to disentangle component processes underlying inhibitory control. Here, we apply a forced-response paradigm and computational model to test whether aging results in overall speed differences or a selective deficit in inhibitory control. Across two experiments, over 200 older adults and younger adults completed a forced-response arrow-flanker task. We found strong evidence that older adults demonstrate a global slowing of processing without any selective deficit in inhibitory control in this task. Furthermore, we demonstrate that global slowing is sufficient to explain the mixed findings in previous free-response-time studies. Overall, these results argue against a selective inhibitory-control deficit in older adults.

title: Artists Can Design Memory, and AI Can Predict It
abstract: Can artists deliberately design artworks to be remembered-or forgotten? Across three experiments, we tested whether visual-memory outcomes can be shaped through artistic design and how they are predicted by artists, laypeople, and artificial intelligence. We launched a nationwide art contest in which artists submitted works intended to be memorable or forgettable. Using recognition tasks with adults based in the United States (119 from Amazon Mechanical Turk, 892 from Prolific, and 62 visitors from a Chicago gallery), we found that artists achieved their intended memory outcomes. However, their success was asymmetric: Memorability was more readily increased than reduced. A neural network, ResMem, consistently outperformed human observers and artists in predicting which artworks would be remembered. Data-driven analyses identified psychologically interpretable features that explained nearly half the variance in memory and aligned with ResMem's predictions, but not with human judgments. Together, findings suggest that visual memorability can be engineered by humans, though asymmetrically, and is better captured by computational models.

title: Commentary on Alister et al. (2025): Individual Differences or Unsystematic Noise?
abstract: Alister et al. (2025) reported individual differences in the extent to which people find source-dependent and source-independent claims persuasive, but an exploratory analysis showed no discernible relationship between these individual differences and demographic variables such as age, education, politics, and social-media use. Here I show through simulations that the individual-difference patterns Alister et al. identified are largely consistent with random across-trial variation in the absence of underlying differences between individuals. This casts doubt on the strength of their evidence for individual differences and provides one plausible account of why their exploratory analyses did not yield systematic relationships.

title: Do Children Who Develop Faster Go on to Age Faster in Midlife?
abstract: We quantified the association between rate of child development and pace of midlife aging in the Dunedin Study and the Add Health Study. Physical development was quantified in Dunedin participants ( N = 1,037; age 45) using a composite comprised of (1) birth weight for gestational age, (2) toddler weight gain, (3) timing of behavioral milestones, (4) adiposity-rebound age, (5) timing of adolescent growth spurt, and (6) tempo of adolescent growth spurt. Social development was quantified using the Vineland Social Maturity Scale. Multi-organ-system (cardiovascular, metabolic, renal, immune, dental, pulmonary) longitudinal biological aging was used as the adult outcome. Fast physical development in childhood was associated with faster midlife aging. This was replicated in Add Health ( N = 1,537; age range = 33–44 years), where girls who menstruated earlier had faster midlife aging. By contrast, faster social development in childhood was associated with slower midlife aging. Findings contribute initial empirical evidence characterizing the link between child-development rate and adult aging in humans.

title: Face-Matching Lineups: A Method to Control Mistaken Identifications in Video Evidence
abstract: When crime is caught on video, suspects can be identified by matching their faces to the perpetrator in the footage. However, errors in face-matching decisions have led to wrongful arrests. We tested face-matching in a nonprofessional student sample from a Canadian university ( N = 905) with one-to-one comparisons and lineups. On the basis of findings in the eyewitness identification literature, we hypothesized that if face-matching lineups were fair and included known-innocent fillers (i.e., nonsuspects), they would control the error rate on trials with innocent suspects and increase the accuracy of suspect “match” responses. This hypothesis was supported. However, the accuracy of suspect-nonmatch responses was greater for one-to-one comparisons than for lineups. Additionally, we found that applying wisdom-of-crowd approaches to multiple independent decisions could eliminate errors in both match and nonmatch responses. Whether to control face-matching errors with lineups, with the wisdom-of-crowds, or with both depends on practical considerations.

title: So similar, yet so different: comparing the US GAAP and IFRS experience at eliciting greater transparency on pension asset disclosures
abstract: Abstract We exploit two regulatory changes, one under US GAAP and the other under IFRS, that mandate improved disclosure of pension asset allocation. While the changes are otherwise similar, US GAAP retains the expected rate of return (“ERR”) on pension assets, which preparers can more easily manipulate if asset allocation remains opaque, while IFRS eliminates the ERR. We find that the IFRS standard improves pension asset transparency more than the US standard, which only mandates higher-quality disclosure without changing recognition or measurement and hence leaves unchanged preparers’ incentives to obfuscate. The US standard elicits a mixed response that reduces transparency in some respects. We isolate the relative deterioration in US firms’ transparency to firms with stronger incentives to inflate ERRs. Overall, our study highlights the potential for standard setters to learn from each other by comparing their regulatory experience on a specific accounting topic with clearly identifiable managerial incentives.

title: Measuring Measurement Error
abstract: Abstract We collect 2,848 instrumental variable (IV) regressions from 391 papers published in top economics and finance journals and show that estimated IV coefficients are often much larger than their OLS counterparts, even when theory suggests they should be smaller. We derive meta-regression estimators that distinguish measurement error bias from omitted variable bias and simultaneity bias; applying our estimators to a set of 1,040 comparable regressions from 139 papers, we find that measurement error shrinks reported coefficients by about two to four times. Measurement error remains quantitatively important even after accounting for weak instruments, publication bias, instrument invalidity, and heterogeneous treatment effects. Our results suggest that measurement error is a severe, pervasive, and understated source of bias in economics and finance.

title: Competing Digital Money
abstract: Abstract We study competition between two payment instruments: bank deposits and digital platform tokens. Using a Hotelling model that integrates the theory of two-sided markets and payment economics, we assess how this competition is affected by a public payment infrastructure that makes private payment instruments interoperable. We show that interoperability, whether implemented as a fast payment system (FPS) or a central bank digital currency (CBDC), may eliminate payment access exclusion and increase trade volumes and social welfare, but at the cost of some disintermediation. When new payment service providers (PSPs) enter and compete for consumers, they soften competition for merchants: incumbent intermediaries then charge merchants higher fees and earn higher profits. This contrasts with entry of PSPs on the merchant side, which disciplines incumbent fees instead.

title: The Depositary of Last Resort
abstract: Abstract What are the consequences of making central bank deposits accessible to actors beyond the banking sector? We collect novel micro data on deposit accounts historically held with the Bank of England by individuals and firms other than banks to study their role in the financial panic of 1866. We document that the use of deposit accounts at the central bank soared during the crisis, while commercial banks permanently lost funding. The expansion in the number of active accounts was fueled by individuals, but the intensive margin increase in balances came almost entirely from firms. Recourse to central bank deposits was heterogeneous and persisted well beyond the panic, reflecting easy access, low opportunity costs, and positive network externalities. At the same time, retail borrowers seeking liquidity support from the Bank during the crisis preferred receiving loan proceeds in the form of cash rather than deposits. JEL Classification: E58, G01, G11, G20, N13, N23

title: Creation After Destruction? Financial Intermediation and Firm Entry After Bank Cleanups
Artificial intelligence and venture capital: Revisiting sourcing, selection, and nurturing activities
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Venture capital (VC) is an information‐intensive form of entrepreneurial finance conducted under extreme uncertainty. Investors must originate promising opportunities, select ventures with sparse and strategically disclosed information, and monitor and support firms after investment. Prior research documents both formal mechanisms (e.g., staged financing, syndication) and informal mechanisms built on referrals, reputation, and constant interaction. Geographic and social proximity enable these mechanisms by lowering the cost of obtaining contextual information and coordinating action. We develop a mechanism‐based account of how data and Artificial Intelligence (AI) reconfigure this established model. Our framework yields propositions on geographic dispersion in sourcing, portfolio selection, and the distinct effects of AI on monitoring versus value‐added support. It also identifies boundary conditions associated with institutional setting and heterogeneous AI adoption. Managerial Summary For venture capital firms, AI is not a single tool and adoption is not a binary choice. A fund may use data systems to identify founders, machine‐learning models to organize deal flow, generative AI to summarize diligence materials, or analytics to monitor portfolio companies. Each application changes a different part of the VC process. In sourcing, AI can widen the funnel beyond warm introductions and local ecosystems, especially in sectors such as software and e‐commerce where hiring, product, and customer signals are visible. In selection, AI can make diligence faster and more consistent, but models trained on past investments may favor ventures that resemble previously funded companies and may miss novel opportunities for which historical analogues are weak. In post‐investment activity, continuous operational data can partly replace physical presence for monitoring, while value‐add support such as customer introductions, recruiting, strategy advice, and founder coaching remain relationship‐intensive. The practical implication is a task‐level approach: automate codifiable search and processing, retain independent human judgment where uncertainty is fundamental, and use AI to strengthen rather than erode trusted investor–founder relationships. Funds also face organizational choices about building proprietary infrastructure, buying external tools, or combining the two. The appropriate configuration depends on data access, strategy, scale, and the activity in which the fund seeks advantage.

title: Entrepreneurial theorizing with generative artificial intelligence
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Whether large language model (LLM) assistance changes how entrepreneurs construct theories remains unclear. On the one hand, LLMs may help entrepreneurs build more developed causal structures and surface diverse information that supports the formulation of distinctive theories. On the other hand, LLMs may steer causal structures toward conventional forms and discourage the counterintuitive reasoning needed to develop distinctive theories. In a within‐subject experiment with 199 participants theorizing both with and without LLM assistance, we find no significant average treatment effect on either structural or content properties. However, this null average effect masks a redistribution effect, where LLM assistance supplemented theorizing when unaided theories were less developed or distinctive but displaced participants' own theorizing when their theories were already more developed or distinctive. Managerial Summary Large language models (LLMs) can help entrepreneurs develop business ideas by surfacing knowledge across domains and sharpening causal logic. At the same time, LLMs may also push reasoning toward conventional patterns and away from the counterintuitive ideas that are a source of breakthrough opportunities. In a study of 199 participants theorizing with and without LLM assistance, we find that LLMs supported the development of causal structure and content distinctiveness when unaided theories were less developed or distinctive, whereas they had the opposite effect when those theories were already more developed or distinctive. This suggests that while LLMs can scaffold entrepreneurs still developing their theories, greater caution is warranted for those whose theories are already more developed or distinctive, as assistance may diminish those properties.

title: Theorizing future phenomena: Metaverse, wearables, and humanoids
abstract: Abstract Research Summary We propose that entrepreneurship and strategy research can develop theory about phenomena of the future rather than only explain those of the past. Research has potential for practical relevance when researchers make claims towards applications to decisions practitioners have yet to make. Theory grounded in a world that may differ from the observed world can be built through a process of extrapolation from technological trends, a practice utilized by entrepreneurs and science fiction authors alike. Assuming advances in artificial intelligence, we apply this process to three emerging phenomena: governing scarcity in metaverse virtual worlds, redesigning organizations around pervasive monitoring via wearable devices, and allocating the intellectual property rights of humanoid robots. We argue that embracing theory that speaks to the future can enhance the practical and educational relevance of management research. Managerial Summary Assuming artificial intelligence continues to improve, we highlight three impending phenomena poised to transform conventional approaches to entrepreneurship and strategy. First, in metaverse virtual worlds, managers must manage resources governed by artificial scarcity. Second, with wearable devices allowing continuous monitoring, managers must consider alternative structures for vertical hierarchy and horizontal collaboration. Third, deployment of humanoid robots will complicate intellectual property rights and asset ownership. We propose that scholarship towards developing theoretical frameworks addressing these and other phenomena of the future will be relevant to both managers and students.

title: Value creation and capture in artificial intelligence‐enabled ecosystems
abstract: Abstract Research Summary We develop an ecosystem perspective on AI‐enabled value creation, grounded in AI's characteristics as a general‐purpose technology. We consider that AI can support multiple value propositions realized through distinct but interconnected ecosystems. Within this structure, AI innovators face choices concerning which value propositions to support, whether to pursue them through general‐purpose or specialized offers, and whether to make those offers open or closed. Users, in turn, are strategic actors facing choices among alternative ecosystem configurations of focal offers and complements through which the same value proposition might be realized. These choices by innovators and users may alter ecosystem roles and competitive relationships over time. We conclude by outlining research opportunities for strategy and innovation scholars examining how firms create and capture value in AI‐enabled ecosystems. Managerial Summary Value creation with AI depends not only on the technology's capability but on the actors whose combined contributions deliver a value proposition. AI supports many value propositions, each through its own ecosystem, with some elements shared across them. AI innovators choose which value propositions to serve, whether to do so through general‐purpose or specialized offers, and whether to make their offers open or proprietary. User firms choose among alternative configurations of offers and complements through which the same value proposition can be realized. These choices may shift the competitive relationships between actors within an ecosystem over time. This perspective surfaces questions of relevance for scholars and practitioners regarding value creation and capture with AI.

title: Whither business model innovation strategy in the age of AI ?
abstract: Abstract Research Summary We argue that business models are transformed into auto‐adaptive systems through embedded AI inference and learning activities. The competitive advantage of focal firms may increasingly depend on how effectively their activity systems learn relative to competing business models, with learning serving as a meta value driver. Such learning‐based advantages may be difficult to replicate when they are costly to create, path dependent, anchored in distinctive accumulated data, and rely on tightly coupled recursive feedback loops among business model activities. Entrepreneurs and corporate leaders thus become architects and curators of evolving learning systems and innovators of novel business models that are critical to their firm's value creation and sustainable performance. Managerial Summary The competitive advantage of focal firms increasingly depends on new AI learning and inference activities, which serve as meta‐value drivers in business models that learn faster, more broadly, and more reliably than competing business models. These dynamic learning‐based advantages are difficult to replicate because they are costly, path dependent, anchored in specific accumulated data, and rely on tightly coupled recursive feedback loops among business model activities. In this paper we argue that entrepreneurs and corporate leaders need to become architects and curators of evolving, auto‐adaptive learning systems and innovators of novel business models that are critical to their firm's value creation and sustainable performance.

title: New wine, old bottles? Effective strategies of new GenAI firms
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Blending insights from GenAI, strategic reasoning, and empirical grounding in five illustrative ventures, we contribute a theoretical framework for effective strategies of new GenAI firms. They face bifurcated uncertainty (i.e., high uncertainty of a nascent market, moderate uncertainty of a somewhat predictable technology trajectory) such that two complementary strategic logics —Process Perspective (PP) and Resource‐based View (RBV)—are relevant. Second, we identify process‐based (i.e., well‐designed business model and product innovation process) and resource‐based (i.e., superior data, efficient orchestration, complementary resources) advantages. Some relate to GenAI, some generalize. Third, we address what is unique about GenAI entrepreneurship, including strategic implications of GenAI, technology strategy when there is upstream technical dominance and many downstream firms, and a cross‐technology comparison with technologies like software and predictive AI. Managerial Summary The rapid trajectory of GenAI is stunning. Yet many new GenAI firms are simply thin wrappers around well‐known LLMs. Drawing on five illustrative ventures, we contribute a framework for effective strategies for new GenAI firms. These firms face bifurcated uncertainty (i.e., high uncertainty of a nascent market, moderate uncertainty of a somewhat predictable technology trajectory). This calls for creating advantage by navigating high uncertainty markets to accomplish key strategic tasks and relying on foresight to build strategically valuable resources. Specifically, we identify process‐based (well‐designed business model and product innovation process) and resource‐based (i.e., superior data, efficient orchestration, complementary resources) advantages. We also address what is unique about GenAI entrepreneurship, including strategic implications of GenAI and a cross‐technology comparison with technologies like software, predictive AI, and quantum.

title: How ventures maintain stakeholder support amidst operational legitimacy threats
abstract: Abstract Research Summary We explore how ventures mitigate operational legitimacy threats— threats that originate within the venture and challenge claims relating to the venture's ability to deliver on its promised value proposition . Through an inductive study of four ventures working to deliver their promised products following successful crowdfunding campaigns, we reveal a process of three rhetorical practices that ventures can use to maintain stakeholder support: humanizing the venture , normalizing setbacks and resolutions , and revising pragmatic claims . The first two practices contribute to the formation of dispositional legitimacy buffers that allow the third practice to be effective in mitigating fallout from exposed operational legitimacy threats. We conclude by offering contributions to the cultural entrepreneurship literature and to research on venture–stakeholder communication. Managerial Summary Entrepreneurs must often determine whether to disclose operational issues to stakeholders. On one hand, entrepreneurs may resolve these operational issues without stakeholders ever knowing of their occurrence. On the other hand, such issues could balloon to negatively impact whether a venture can deliver its promised offering. We identify three rhetorical practices, two of which entrepreneurs can utilize before an operational issue even occurs, to generate favorable judgments with stakeholders and increase the likelihood that their ventures will be able to maintain support if an operational issue becomes exposed.

title: Re‐thinking academic entrepreneurship: Micro, meso, and macro perspectives
Paid‐free differentiation in freemium: Understanding the balance between discovery and cannibalization and its implications for paid product sales
Code and Data Repository for Efficient and Flexible LLMs-Generated Content Detection
abstract: The software and data documentation in this repository are a snapshot of the materials used in the research reported in “Efficient and Flexible LLM-Generated Content Detection” by Wan Tian, Zhongfeng Qin, and Yijie Peng, accepted for publication in INFORMS Journal on Computing.

title: The New Rules of Brand Visibility in AI Search
abstract: As LLM-driven search grows, brands are facing two distinct challenges: visibility and accuracy. For AI search, SEO is now entwined with GEO, generative engine optimization. As zero-click LLM responses replace direct links on search result pages, new metrics are replacing traditional traffic analytics. New research suggests ways leaders can ensure that their brands become more visible, more accurately represented, and more competitively positioned over time.

title: When Compliance Workarounds Backfire
abstract: Companies facing new regulations often reach for minimal compliance — narrow fixes that preserve the business model. But in algorithmic businesses, such fixes leave auditable traces and can spread beyond leaders’ control, inviting the very redesign they tried to avoid. Drawing on cases involving Glovo, Deliveroo, Airbnb, Uber, and Meta, the authors identify four signals that tell leaders when a workaround will hold — and when to prepare for a costly redesign.

title: The Real Reasons Why Digital Projects Fail
abstract: Digital tools meant to improve business processes don’t always deliver value when implemented on the front lines, but efforts to identify what’s behind such failures often don’t get at the real cause. One reason is that leaders simply blame poor adoption on user resistance to change, for example. A new framework can help them take a closer look at data quality issues and system usability issues, both of which can cause problems for users.

title: EXPRESS: Evaluating the Impacts of Bundling on a Firm’s Product Demand and Operational Decisions
abstract: Firms use bundles to influence customer demand, but supplying those bundles often requires operational capacity that is shared across the portfolio. Changing the price, composition, or availability of one bundle can therefore trigger two reallocations: customers reallocate expenditure across bundles, and the firm reallocates operational capacity across the demand those bundles generate. We develop a data-driven framework that links these two decisions. Heterogeneous consumers choose discrete bundle quantities subject to a common budget, while the firm jointly chooses bundle prices and quantities subject to bundle-specific and shared-resource requirements. We estimate the demand and supply models from observed discrete decisions using Bayesian Markov Chain Monte Carlo, retaining the integer structure in estimation and counterfactual analysis. We apply the framework to three empirical settings: public bike sharing, online retail, and theme-park services. The empirical analyses reveal several consequences of evaluating bundles as part of a portfolio. Customer value and profit contribution need not be aligned: a bundle that creates substantial customer value can make little or no incremental contribution to optimized profit, and removing some bundles can increase profit after the remaining portfolio is re-optimized. Price responses differ across bundles because discrete purchases adjust at different thresholds. A bundle's response to tighter shared-resource requirements depends on how its resource use changes the allocation of operational capacity elsewhere in the portfolio, rather than on its characteristics alone. Finally, deeper discounts need not generate larger incremental profit contributions; in the theme-park application, an intermediate discount can outperform both deeper and shallower discounts after the portfolio is re-optimized. Bundle design is a portfolio problem: a bundle's contribution depends not only on the demand it generates, but also on the customer and operational adjustments it induces elsewhere in the portfolio.

title: Indirect Variational Inference: Applications to Earnings Dynamics
abstract: Latent-variable models are central to economics but often entail intractable integration. Variational inference (VI), widely used in machine learning, turns this integration into tractable, differentiable optimization by replacing the likelihood with a variational objective. However, guarantees of recovering the true parameters remain limited when the variational family is insufficiently flexible -- a key obstacle to the adoption of VI in economics. We first evaluate VI in models of earnings dynamics and show that the choice of variational posterior is crucial. We then introduce indirect variational inference (IVI), which treats VI as an auxiliary model and corrects the bias induced by the variational approximation. IVI retains much of VI's tractability because it does not require computing the likelihood. We apply these methods to models allowing for nonlinear persistence, non-Gaussian and serially correlated transitory shocks, and latent heterogeneity. Across simulated and empirical applications, flexible variational families combined with IVI deliver reliable estimates.

title: Measurement Error in Self-Reported Data on Stigmatized Behavior: Experimental Evidence on Intimate Partner Violence
abstract: Error in the measurement of key development outcomes affects our understanding of socioeconomic phenomena and their policy implications.This paper focuses on measuring intimate partner violence (IPV), a public health issue affecting women globally.We introduce a novel, privacy-enhancing data collection method using a ballot, comparing it to standard survey techniques in which responses are not kept private from enumerators, and list experiments, an approach ensuring complete anonymity.Our findings show that improved privacy yields higher and more accurate IPV reports than both, especially among women with low education.By linking our data with two natural experiments, we demonstrate that the non-random nature of underreporting with standard methods can lead to biased estimates of IPV determinants.

title: Explaining Realized Returns: Roll’s R2 40 Years Later
The Relationship between Income and Health: Evidence from Nationwide Health Exams in Korea
