title: Taxing Entrepreneurial Wealth: Evidence from Norway, 2021–2025
abstract: Whether imposing higher taxes on business owners adversely affects business activity by constraining investment and inducing capitalist flight is a central question in the ongoing debate on how to tax the ultra wealthy.To shed new light, I exploit a series of related Norwegian reforms during 2021-2024 that increased dividend tax rates, removed migration-related capital gains tax loopholes, and nearly doubled the effective marginal tax rate on business wealth.These reforms spurred international debate and, allegedly, an "exodus" of Norwegian billionaires (Financial Times, 2023).While I document clear effects on migration, these responses are concentrated among the top 0.1% of the wealth distribution and mostly confined to 2022 and 2023.My results indicate that at most 100 individuals left due to the reforms.I find no evidence of significant outmigration or reduced inflows of startup founders or inventors.I estimate that absent any outmigration, wealth tax revenues would have increased by 75%from 2021 to 2024.Reform-driven outmigration lowers the revenue gain to 71.5%.My findings further show that outmigrating owners' firms remain economically active and do not reduce investment.In a broader set of analyses, I examine whether business outcomes are affected, regardless of whether owners outmigrate, since firms may reduce investment both due to liquidity constraints or distortions to owners' savings decisions.I compare firms owned by Norwegian individuals subject to the wealth tax with firms owned by foreigners and other tax-exempt entities.By merging historical ownership data from Orbis with the Norwegian shareholder register, I perform these analyses on both Norwegian and foreign-domiciled firms.Across settings, I find no evidence that Norwegianowned firms pay out more dividends or invest less after the reforms, nor is there any evidence that the reform induced more bankruptcies.These findings indicate that the short-run economic costs of wealth taxation, in terms of migration and firm investment, are more limited than the public debate implies.

title: Randomized to Opportunity: Measuring Place Effects for Refugee Children
abstract: Area-level measures of economic opportunity are increasingly used to guide place-based policies.We study whether these measures predict long-run outcomes for a vulnerable population: over 12,000 refugee children quasi-randomly assigned to municipalities under Denmark's 1986-1998 dispersal policy.We focus on predetermined measures of opportunity available when children arrive and validate them using a mover-exposure design among permanent residents.Moving from a low-to a high-opportunity area (a two-standard-deviation increase) raises adult income rank by 3 percentile points (7.5 percent) and employment by 4 percentage points.It also reduces criminal convictions by 14 percent and teen parenthood by 19 percent, with more modest effects on educational attainment.Economic opportunity predicts crime and teen parenthood more strongly than other area characteristics, including local crime rates.For adult income, area-level inequality is a particularly strong predictor.These findings suggest that social mobility in the areas where refugee children grow up meaningfully shapes their long-term wellbeing.

title: Approximating the Equilibrium Effects of Informed School Choice
abstract: This paper studies the potential small and large scale effects of a policy designed to produce more in-formed consumers in the market for primary education. We develop and test a personalized information provision intervention that targets families of public Pre-K students entering elementary schools in Chile. Using a randomized control trial, we find that the intervention shifts parentsâ€™ choices toward schools with higher average test scores, higher value added, higher prices, and schools that tend to be further from their homes. Tracking students with administrative data, we find that student academic achievement on test scores was approximately 0.2 standard deviations higher among treated families five years after the intervention. To quantitatively gauge how average treatment effects might vary in a scaled up version of this policy, we embed the randomized control trial within a structural model of school choice and competition where price and quality are chosen endogenously and schools face capacity constraints. We use the estimated model of demand and supply to simulate policy effects under different assumptions about equilibrium constraints. In counterfactual simulations, we find that capacity constraints play an important role mitigating the policy effect but in several scenarios, the supply-side response increases quality, which contributes to an overall positive average treatment effect. Finally, we show how the estimated model can inform the design of a large scale experiment such that reduced form estimates can capture equilibrium effects and spillovers.

title: Voluntary Corporate Climate Targets in a Patchwork Policy Landscape
abstract: Many large, publicly-traded companies adopt voluntary greenhouse gas emission reduction commitments in the presence of a fragmented public policy landscape.To explore the potential emission implications of such commitments, we develop a framework for understanding how firms' voluntary emission targets interact with carbon pricing, regulatory mandates, subsidies, and heterogeneous policies across political jurisdictions.This analysis highlights the difficulty of distinguishing incremental voluntary emission abatement from policy-induced emission reductions.We introduce the Salata Institute Corporate Climate Targets Database, which we produced from public domain reports published by Russell 3000 firms over 2000-2024.The database documents the growth, form, scope, and sectoral distribution of voluntary greenhouse gas emission targets, including net-zero, carbon-neutral, carbon-reduction, energy-related, and qualitative commitments.Comparing this database with CDP, a non-profit organization formerly known as the Carbon Disclosure Project and the most common source of corporate emission targets used in the research literature, reveals substantial omissions in their survey-based data, especially in recent years.We show that voluntary corporate targets often mirror government-established goals and public policies, and some firms benchmark their internal carbon prices to existing carbon taxes and emission trading systems.The paper concludes by outlining empirical challenges and future research needs for evaluating the emission impacts of voluntary commitments.

title: Citizens' perceptions of accountability in AI-based public sector decision making
abstract: Research has increasingly focused on identifying and analyzing the key components of accountability in the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in the public sector. However, much of the existing literature takes a government-centric approach, emphasizing how public organizations implement accountability measures while paying limited attention to citizens' perspectives. This study addresses this gap by empirically examining whom citizens believe should be held accountable and what information about AI-based decisions should be communicated to the public. Using data from a nationally representative sample of U.S. citizens, our analysis reveals several overall trends in public perceptions of accountability for AI-based systems, as well as demographic differences. These findings provide valuable empirical insights to advance research and practice on the use of AI in government.

title: Balancing risk communication and accountability concerns in risk management: A study of major public project investments
abstract: Abstract Effective administration of public organizations requires timely responses to emerging risks, yet communicating those risks up the hierarchy can expose operational managers to blame in politicized accountability environments. This study examines how public managers navigated that tension in an analysis of 130 risk reports filed over a seven-year period associated with two major procurement and maintenance projects in the Danish Defence. Using an abductive qualitative approach, we develop a dynamic model of risk management with four phases: (1) risk as an operational concern, (2) turning risk into an organizational problem, (3) assigning blame and accountability, and (4) initiating mitigation and response. We find that risk and accountability communication are interdependent processes rather than independent sequential processes. Operational managers attempt to raise awareness of emerging risks while simultaneously deflecting potential blame and catering to higher-level concerns about public scrutiny. This tension generates pressure to only report when it is absolutely necessary, while higher-level managers often postpone action to avoid political exposure. These practices contribute to delays, projects not meeting specifications, and significant budget overruns. The study advances a dynamic theory of public sector risk management and explains how hierarchical communication practices influence whether, when, and how emerging risks are addressed.
journal_name: Journal of Public Administration Research and Theory

title: Beyond Paychecks: HRM Strategies for Commitment and Turnover Intentions of Public Healthcare Workers During Crises in Saudi Arabia
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines the effectiveness of human resource management (HRM) practices in reducing turnover intentions and strengthening organizational commitment among public healthcare workers in Saudi Arabia during crises. Using survey data from public healthcare employees across three regions, the findings reveal that comprehensive training and organizational support for work‐life balance significantly reduce turnover intentions, while financial incentives have limited effects. The influence of HRM practices varies by occupation groups, with healthcare professionals responding more strongly to training than administrative staff. These results challenge the assumption that financial rewards are the primary retention tool in Saudi Arabia's public sector and highlight the importance of supportive and developmental HRM practices in centralized healthcare systems. This study provides valuable insights for policymakers and public health managers for strengthening workforce stability in Saudi Arabia and other developing or transitional state contexts during crisis conditions.

title: Lack of public service motivation as a value-constraining mechanism in entrepreneurial ecosystems
abstract: This paper examines how public service motivation (PSM) shapes public value creation (PVC) within publicly funded entrepreneurial support organizations (ESOs). As public service ecosystems, ESOs play a pivotal role in entrepreneurial ecosystems (EEs), yet how they create public value remains underexplored. While existing research emphasizes PSM at the individual level, less is known about how PSM translates into intentional PVC in boundary-spanning ecosystem contexts. Drawing on an empirical qualitative multi-case study, we show that although ESO staff exhibit a strong commitment to enhancing the public interest, regional-level PVC is constrained by unclear and narrow organizational goals, inconsistent practices, and limited leadership support. Our findings highlight the need for leadership grounded in transformative, supportive, and human-centred practices, as well as leadership collaboration spanning organizational boundaries. This paper clarifies the organizational conditions under which PSM contributes to PVC in hybrid governance settings.

title: Public Participation as Administrative Practice: Evidence from Federal Entitlement Communities
abstract: Public participation is widely recognized as an important component of democratic governance, yet empirical studies often evaluate participation by the methods employed rather than the institutional structures through which participation is organized within administrative processes. Drawing on an analysis of 289 local jurisdictions receiving federal block grants, this study examines participation as structured administrative practice rather than simply a collection of engagement methods. Using inductive analysis of Consolidated Plans, the study develops a typology of four participation structures: Minimal Compliance, Structured Consultation, Institutionalized Consultation, and Embedded Participation.
journal_name: The American Review of Public Administration

title: 'We are no longer Allowed to be Human': Officers’ Experiences Policing the Compounding Crises of the COVID-19 Pandemic and Civil Unrest in the United States
abstract: Local police officers are among the most prominent frontline public servants, interacting daily with people, communities, and other agencies and stakeholders. They are, in the most literal sense, street-level bureaucrats. These interactions were greatly tested in the summer of 2020. Police managed – or in some cases refused to manage – enforcement orders for a global pandemic while at the same time policing in the aftermath of the murder of George Floyd. This article explores how officers in three local jurisdictions navigated these dual, compounding crises – which we can certainly expect many more of in the future – and the implications for police interactions, discretion (including de-policing) and job satisfaction. The article concludes with a discussion of how police leaders, local officials and community advocates can better support law enforcement professionals during times of crises.
journal_name: The American Review of Public Administration

title: Does Citizen Political Ideology Shape Bureaucratic Responsiveness? Evidence From an Audit Experiment
abstract: Government workers often take shortcuts when making decisions about delivering public services. When these shortcuts are influenced by stereotypes or bias, citizens may receive unequal treatment. This research examines whether bureaucrats in U.S. housing authorities and parks departments discriminate based on citizen political ideology. Using a pre-registered 2 × 3 email audit experiment ( n = 974), we test whether responsiveness varies when citizens signal conservative views, liberal views, or no political views. The results show that street-level bureaucrats are more likely to respond to citizens signaling conservative views than to citizens with no stated political views. Responsiveness does not differ between citizens signaling liberal views and citizens with no stated political views. However, when a reply is provided, citizens signaling liberal views receive more helpful responses. Interaction models suggest that responsiveness to citizens signaling liberal views differs across public housing authorities and parks departments. These findings suggest that political ideology may shape bureaucratic responsiveness in ways that have implications for fairness in public service delivery.
journal_name: The American Review of Public Administration

title: Understanding UK behavioural research capability in 2024: a cross-sector survey
abstract: Abstract Behavioural research can inform effective responses to global challenges, but its application across sectors remains uneven and poorly coordinated. This survey study aimed to map the current ecosystem of behavioural research across UK sectors to identify priorities for its application, capability needs and opportunities for strategic integration to address these challenges. Invitations were distributed via mailing list, website, social media and snowball sampling. We received 657 responses from people who conduct or use behavioural research in public, private and voluntary sectors. Respondents reported conducting applied (93 per cent) and/or pure (27 per cent) research across the UK. Current priorities for the application of behavioural research centred on climate action, health, methodological advances and artificial intelligence. Perceived capability gaps differed across sectors and include technological abilities and knowledge relating to intervention design, implementation and evaluation. Broader barriers to conducting behavioural research include lack of confidence, limited funding and training, access to expert support and limited acceptance of behavioural research. Findings highlight a need to increase capability through addressing skills and knowledge gaps, leadership engagement and increasing resources for collaborative translation of behavioural research into practice. Approaches to addressing findings are being explored through sector-specific workshops to inform future survey waves.

title: Populist opposition to climate policy: the role of policy design
abstract: Populist actors increasingly pressure policymakers to navigate a trade-off between effective climate policy and its public feasibility. However, one may ask whether a populist worldview is inherently more opposed to some types of climate policies than to others, and if so, why? An emerging literature has found populist citizens oppose climate policies writ large. Building on this literature, we argue that populist citizens do not oppose all climate policies to the same extent. Differentiating climate change policies based on their policy design, we hypothesise that populist citizens substantially reject climate policies more if they are ‘push’ measures, leverage market-based instruments or target ‘the people’. We test these arguments by utilising high-quality Austrian panel data. We find that populist citizens are indeed less supportive of climate policy, however, this relationship is moderated by policy design and independent from thick-ideological leanings. Populist backlash is particularly pronounced for policies that target individuals and leverage ‘push’ measures. Vice versa, policies targeting companies or employing incentivising measures face significantly less backlash. These findings suggest that policy design indeed can mitigate the populist backlash against climate policy and policymakers can utilise this evidence to create more robust climate policy packages.

title: Inclusivity, equity, and empowerment in ‘citizen science’ research: persistent issues for science, policy, and participation
abstract: Abstract ‘Citizen science,’ an umbrella term for researchers and public participants collaborating to produce scientific knowledge, has both produced data informing public policies and been included in policies guiding future scientific inquiries. Yet, its use and influence remain challenging. Research has found incorporating inclusivity, equity, and/or empowerment principles into citizen science can bolster its value to science and society. This scoping review of 127 citizen science publications, identified via the Web of Science and other sources, explores how these publications describe the application of these principles in citizen science, and their linkages to data quality and ethics. The results describe linkages between these three principles, data quality, ethics, and the achievement of citizen science aims. Incorporating these principles requires significant design choices, influencing the distribution of costs, risks, and responsibilities. The findings also highlight multiple gaps in knowledge and related policies regarding applying these principles in citizen science.

title: Coordinating energy and innovation policies: UK R&D Policy for emerging renewables under Blair, 1997-2003
abstract: Abstract The design of novel green industrial policies presents a coordinative challenge for national governments, crossing many policy domains. This paper focuses on the coordination of Science, Technology and Innovation (STI) policies and energy policies, asking: How do elected political leaders coordinate STI and energy policies on emerging energy innovations? We answer this question by considering the case of STI and energy policy coordination in the UK between 1997 and 2003, describing the political leadership of key members of the Blair government. The case illustrates that strong political leadership guided by a party-specific cross-cutting political-economic agenda (e.g. New Labour) can play a critical role in coordinating policy reforms across multiple domains. In the European context, the case provides a precedent for how STI and energy policies may be aligned to support European competitiveness, in that it points to the importance of both formal institutional reforms and informal political leadership.

title: The Ambiguities of Ownership and Class: A Reply to Nicholas Vrousalis
abstract: The article replies to Nicholas Vrousalis’s attempt to rescue radical republicanism from my critique that it fails on three counts: its non-contingency, domination, and structural injustice theses. Central to my response are the claims that (i) capitalist power cannot be reduced to legal ownership of the means of production, as the process of capitalization is constitutive of capital; (ii) neither neo-republican nor Kantian notions of domination adequately capture what is inherently wrong with capitalism, and (iii) the concept of “class domination” remains theoretically puzzling. I then defend an alienation-centered critique: capitalism’s mode of investment subjects citizens to an impersonal and anarchical form of governance, which, by being necessarily alienating, contradicts democratic self-determination. Overall, this critique forms the core of a “political, political theory of capitalism” and grounds the case for a specific kind of democratic socialism—socialism as reconciliation—which is more demanding than both republican and liberal socialisms.

title: On Liberalism’s Global Career: Dadabhai Naoroji and Representative Government
abstract: This article reconsiders the relationship between the globalization of political liberalism and the globalization of political equality. Departing from interpretations of liberal theories of rights and representation as egalitarian or democratic, the article reconstructs an elitist paradigm of liberal representative government from the colonial world. It does so by offering a new reading of the thought of Indian political leader Dadabhai Naoroji. It recovers Naoroji’s overlooked commentary on political representation and imperial reform. I show that Naoroji drew upon analyses made by the first generation of Indian liberal thinkers about imperial political economy and mass-elite relations and used these arguments to formulate a distinctive model of electoral politics as a form of hierarchical tutelage. The recovery of Naoroji’s theory illustrates the deep tensions between representation and mass politics that marked liberalism’s global circulation.

title: Citizen forecasts and the 2026 us congressional midterm elections: Do americans still expect the iron law to hold?
abstract: In American midterm congressional elections, the president's party usually experiences a net loss of seats.This generalization holds so often it has taken on the mantle of an "iron law" (Abramowitz, Cover, and Norpoth 1986).However, the 2026 election paints a complicated portrait of American elections, with fundamentals such as the economy and mid-decade redistricting creating challenges for straightforward fundamental models.Citizen forecasts, relying on asking citizens who they think will win the election rather than whom they intend to vote for, can be used in complex electoral contexts to help forecast electoral outcomes.Using four waves of citizen forecasts from September 2025 to May 2026, our citizen forecast predicts that the Democrats have a strong probability of taking control of the House in November, but that Senate is very much up for grabs.

title: Opinionrot: Toward a Theory of Collective Reasoning Decay in the Age of Synthetic Consensus
abstract: This article introduces the concept of opinionrot to describe the structural erosion of collective reasoning within contemporary information systems. Rather than treating post-truth politics as a failure of individual rationality or as a decline in information quality alone, the article argues that public reasoning is increasingly shaped by infrastructures that capture attention, monetize cognitive bias, and automate the conditions under which claims become visible and credible. Methodologically, the article proceeds through a conceptual-historical reconstruction, tracing how persuasion became institutionalized, platformized, and increasingly predictive. It identifies three mechanisms through which opinionrot intensifies today: cognitive capture, infrastructural decay, and discursive saturation. The framework is illustrated through debates over equality and affirmative action, showing how communicative infrastructures can transform contested political concepts into predictable and polarized semantic routines. By shifting the analysis from discrete falsehoods to the conditions under which public judgment is formed, contested, and revised, the article offers a diagnostic vocabulary for studying how information infrastructures increasingly convert deliberation into statistical efficiency within contemporary economies of attention.

title: Downward Competition: How Perceived Economic Proximity Reduces Support for Redistribution to the Poor
abstract: ABSTRACT How does inducing comparisons to both the poor and the rich shape support for redistribution toward the poor? I argue that when individuals who identify as middle-income perceive economic proximity to the poor alongside distance from the rich, one of two opposing mechanisms is activated: a social affinity mechanism, which increases support for redistribution, or a status and economic competition mechanism, which reduces it. Drawing on two survey experiments in the United Kingdom ( n = 3,470) that induce bidirectional comparisons, as well as observational data from 14 democracies, I find that support for redistribution to the poor is lowest when perceived downward proximity coincides with upward distance. Suggestive evidence shows that economic and status-based competition drive this relationship. Together, these findings advance our understanding of how social comparison processes shape attitudes toward redistribution and offer insights for policy makers when designing redistributive policies.

title: The Politics of Black Classification: Sociopolitical Cues and Racial Perception
abstract: What makes someone Black in American society today? From Donald Trump questioning Kamala Harris’s racial identity to Joe Biden’s claim that hesitant Black voters “ain’t Black,” American politics frequently brings questions of racial authenticity and belonging to the surface. Yet political science often approaches race as a fixed attribute, rather than a social construction. Here, we seek to understand how Americans define blackness in social and political life. Using a conjoint experiment with a racially diverse sample that includes Black, White, and mixed-race Black-White respondents, we evaluate how ascribed and acquired traits influence perceptions of blackness. The results show that inherited characteristics—particularly parentage and skin tone, which are the strongest determinants of racial classification—play a central role, yet sociopolitical cues such as partisanship, neighborhood context, and spousal race also influence racial classification. Using a continuous measure, we also show that respondents make graded assessments of blackness rather than purely binary classifications, with some individuals perceived as more Black than others. Black respondents are more likely than White respondents to classify a broader set of profiles as Black, consistent with a more inclusive understanding of racial membership; however, they also place greater emphasis on shared political identity. These findings clarify how racial categories are socially constructed and why that construction carries real political and social consequences.

title: A secondary bond: Why economic threats boost compensatory preference for government control in China
abstract: Abstract Compensatory control theory suggests that threats to personal control increase the desire for external control. Yet, despite the growing salience of global economic instability—amplified by trade conflicts, protectionist policies, and heightened geopolitical tensions—empirical research has rarely examined this dynamic in the context of economic threats. Moreover, the direct psychological consequences of endorsing external control—whether it ultimately enhances or diminishes personal control—remain largely unexplored. Addressing both gaps, the present research focuses on the socio‐political context of China to investigate whether individuals facing economic threats and diminished personal control show increased preference for government control, a particularly powerful and salient external source of control in Chinese society. Across studies, the results showed a positive relationship between perceived economic threats and preference for government control, mediated by a reduction in personal control (Studies 1–3). Furthermore, we found that endorsement of government control helped enhance, rather than undermine, personal control (Studies 4 and 5). These findings suggest that government control serves as a compensatory source of control in response to economic threats.

title: Solidarity between U.S. people of color: Synthesizing evidence, highlighting challenges, and proposing actionable solutions
Friends of the far right? Interest group behaviour in the European Parliament
abstract: The past decade has witnessed a notable surge of far-right parties in European legislatures. Yet, little is known about their interactions with interest groups. Traditionally, far-right parties tend to engage less frequently with interest groups than mainstream parties, in part due to a form of normative resistance grounded in prevailing social norms. However, as the far right becomes increasingly normalised, the dynamics of party-group relations may be shifting. This study explores under what conditions interest groups engage with the far right, and whether they have normalised far-right engagement or reflect continued resistance. An analysis of an original dataset of meetings between 686 interest groups and far-right Members of the European Parliament (MEPs) shows that interest groups generally avoid engagement with far-right MEPs. However, this resistance is conditional: far-right MEPs who hold rapporteur positions are significantly more likely to be engaged, and national ties further increase the likelihood of interaction.

title: Polycrisis and global production networks: a framework for understanding industry dynamics in times of accumulated uncertainty
abstract: Abstract Global production networks (GPNs) are currently impacted by multiple crises. Yet, crises have received little attention in GPN scholarship. This article shows how the entangled drivers of polycrisis affect the economic geographies of suppliers and their integration into GPNs. It develops an analytical framework for exploration of accumulated uncertainties in conjunctural moments of polycrisis. The management of unknown ‘uncertainties’ other than ‘risk’ for lead firms is a key element. Focusing on Bangladesh’s apparel industry, this article explores the industry’s responses and struggles, and provides insights into the wider processes of inclusion and exclusion in the global economy during polycrisis.

title: The hold-up problem and communication: Experimental evidence
PHILLIPS–SOLO ASYMPTOTICS FOR CONTINUOUS-TIME ARMA PROCESSES SAMPLED IN DISCRETE TIME
abstract: Phillips and Solo (1992, Annals of Statistics 20, 971–2001) provided sets of conditions concerning the summability of coefficients and the properties of innovations in discrete-time linear processes such that normalized sums satisfy certain asymptotic properties, such as laws of large numbers, central limit theorems, and invariance principles. In this article, we consider ARMA processes in continuous time that are sampled at discrete-time intervals and provide conditions on the continuous-time process such that the results of Phillips and Solo can be utilized for normalized sums of the discrete-time observations. We utilize a state-space representation in the case of stock and flow variables, both of which are a linear combination of the state vector, and derive the relevant asymptotics based on multivariate extensions of the Phillips–Solo results. An illustrative application of the results to unit (zero) root testing is provided.

title: TRUE AND PSEUDO-TRUE PARAMETERS
abstract: Parameter estimates in misspecified models converge to pseudo-true parameter values, which minimize a population objective function. Pseudo-true values often differ from quantities of economic interest, raising questions of how, if at all, they are relevant for decision-making. To study this question, we consider Bayesian decision-makers facing a linear population minimum distance problem. Within a class of priors motivated by the minimum distance objective, we characterize prior sequences under which posteriors concentrate on the pseudo-true value. This convergence is fragile to small changes in priors, implying that pseudo-true values are relevant for decision-making only in special cases. Constructive results are nevertheless possible in this setting, and we derive simple confidence intervals that guarantee correct average coverage for the true parameter under every prior in the class we study, with no bound on the magnitude of misspecification.

title: Growing Pains: Inefficient Resource Allocation in Emerging Economies
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper investigates how economic catch‐up shapes resource allocation in emerging economies. I develop a model that features firm‐specific technology adoption and costly adjustment of production factors. Rapid technological progress during catch‐up creates strong demand for reallocating resources from slow to fast adopters, amplifying the consequences of adjustment costs. The amplification fades as technological change gradually slows during convergence to a more advanced and efficient steady state. I evaluate the model using Chinese and German enterprise data and find that differences in development stage account for at least 40% of their labour allocative efficiency gap.

title: Internal Control over Financial Reporting and Mortgage Fraud
How Black Accounting Faculty Exercise Agency to Navigate Career Advancement within Institutional Structures
Productivity versus Efficiency: The Effect of Incentive Focus on Target Setting in Participative Budgets
Does Private Equity Hurt or Improve Healthcare Value? New Evidence and Mechanisms
abstract: What is the impact of private equity (PE) ownership on healthcare value? Does PE ownership reduce healthcare value, and if so, can its effect be mitigated using health information technologies (IT)? Given the significant investments by PE firms in the healthcare sector in recent years, it is increasingly important for stakeholders, including policy makers, care providers, and patients, to understand their likely impact and whether PE ownership is aligned with their interests. Because PE firms seek to improve efficiency and generate short-term financial returns, the cost-cutting strategies used to achieve these goals may come at the expense of care quality, leading to competing hypotheses on the impact of PE ownership on healthcare value. We argue that IT-enabled health information sharing capabilities can help PE-owned hospitals to better manage this cost-quality tension and achieve higher healthcare value. Using a staggered difference-in-differences approach and data from US hospitals from 2008 to 2020, we estimate changes in healthcare value following PE acquisition and ownership. Overall, we find that PE ownership of hospitals reduces healthcare value. This decline is partially driven by reduction in clinical staffing following PE ownership. We further find that pre-existing, hospital health information sharing capabilities mitigate the negative impact of PE ownership on healthcare value. Specifically, such capabilities can strengthen the effect of PE ownership on cost reduction and, at the same time, mitigate PE-induced, care quality deterioration. Our results highlight the critical role of common data standards needed to promote IT-enabled information sharing between healthcare providers, which, in turn, can align the incentives of PE firms with the goals of value-based care.

title: Technology-Mediated Services in Health Care: Evaluating Telehealth Delivery Models for Underserved Populations
abstract: This study examines how telehealth delivery models are associated with access to care and protocol adherence in underserved populations. While prior research reports mixed evidence on telehealth’s effectiveness, we argue that these inconsistencies arise because telehealth is not a single intervention but is implemented through distinct service configurations that address different barriers. Drawing on the theoretical framework of digital economics, we conceptualize telehealth as a technology-mediated service that can alter key economic frictions, including search and verification, transportation, tracking, and setup costs. We focus on two widely adopted models—specialist-facilitated telehealth and remote telehealth—and theorize that each addresses different subsets of these frictions, leading to distinct effects on care access and protocol adherence across settings. Using panel data from U.S. Community Health Centers on mental health services, we document three findings. First, adoption of the specialist-facilitated model is associated with increased access to mental health care, particularly in areas with greater clinical need. Second, remote telehealth is not associated with increased access on average but is associated with higher adherence to standardized depression screening and follow-up protocols. These effects are consistent with improvements in screening and documentation processes rather than increases in utilization. Third, the estimated effects of both models vary across local cost environments. The access effects of specialist-facilitated telehealth are larger in areas where search and verification frictions are greater. In contrast, the effects of remote telehealth are attenuated where patient-side setup costs are high but are larger where transportation barriers and documentation frictions are greater. These findings advance a model-specific perspective on telehealth’s effects, extend the digital economics framework to technology-mediated services, and provide evidence that the estimated effects of digital health interventions vary with how delivery models interact with underlying cost environments.

title: A Mere Presence Effect of Asymmetric Information
Political Voice and (Mortgage) Market Participation: Evidence from the dilution of Voting Rights Act
abstract: Using US Supreme Court’s narrow-decision on Shelby v. Holder as a shock that diluted voting rights of Black Americans in covered counties, we document the relationship between political voice and economic decision-making. We show fewer Black Americans buy homes after their de-facto disenfranchisement, reflected through lower mortgage applications. Among those who apply for mortgages, there is a flight to Black lenders. Leveraging individual-level survey data, we show confidence in government and financial institutions plays a significant role in driving these effects. Our findings demonstrate that the effects of disenfranchisement extend beyond the ballot box to fundamental economic decisions like homeownership.

title: EXPRESS: Expanding Markets or Capturing Share? The Competitive Effects of Subscriptions on Spending in Restaurant Delivery
abstract: Subscription programs are increasingly central to platform strategy, but their effects on competitors and category demand remain unclear. The authors study restaurant delivery subscriptions using individual-level transaction data on Postmates Unlimited, the first widely available U.S. subscription program in the category, and DoorDash's later DashPass program. Using a matched, staggered difference-in-differences design, they find that signing up for Postmates Unlimited is associated with a 90.4% increase in spending at the focal firm, with no significant average change in competing-firm spending and no offsetting decline in adjacent food categories, consistent with category expansion. Competitive effects depend on customers' prior platform usage. For “singlehomers” (who only used Postmates prior to subscribing), subscribing is associated with increased spending at both the focal firm and competing platforms, even after cancellation. For “multihomers” (who had also previously used competing platforms), the focal-firm effect is larger, and competing-firm spending falls while customers remain subscribed; after cancellation, the focal-firm lift persists, but the decrease in competitor spending does not. DashPass results are broadly similar, but customers with prior Postmates subscription experience show little increase in category spending. Together, these findings suggest subscriptions can both expand markets and capture share, depending on prior platform usage and subscription experience.

title: Conditional and Lenient Drug Approvals
abstract: Firms are often allowed to sell new drugs based on preliminary efficacy evidence, with final approval contingent on confirmatory testing. We characterize optimal approval policies for a government agency that maximizes consumer welfare while considering the firm’s incentives. We assume that firms have private information about testing costs and the government’s payoff depends on the drug’s expected efficacy. The optimal policy may include partial conditional approval for drugs with low expected efficacy, and leniency in granting final approval below conventional standards. Our calibration suggests these tools can generate hundreds of millions of dollars in annual social value. This paper was accepted by Martin Bichler, market design, platform, and demand analytics. Funding: The authors received no external funding for this research. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.03836 .

title: Disagreement and Bond PEAD
abstract: This paper documents post-earnings announcement drift (PEAD) in corporate bond prices using transaction data. We find a counterintuitive relationship between the drift and trading volume: PEAD is more pronounced for more heavily traded bonds than for less frequently traded bonds. Across markets, PEAD is observed for credit default swaps but not for stocks. We explain these findings using a unified model that incorporates both debt and equity trading, where investors possess private information about the underlying firm’s cash flows and may hold differing opinions. Our empirical evidence supports the model’s prediction that payoff structures and investor disagreement account for the distinct price dynamics across asset classes. This paper was accepted by Lukas Schmid, finance. Funding: The authors acknowledge research support from the Center for Investing at HKUST. Y. Xiong thanks the support by National Natural Science Foundation of China [NSFC 72422007] and the Research Grants Council of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region, China [Project 16501523]. Supplemental Material: The online appendices and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.07966 .

title: Operational Implications of Diagnostic Discrepancies: The Weigh-In of Focal and Related Physician Experience
abstract: Problem Definition: Diagnostic discrepancies, defined as mismatches between patients’ admitting and principal diagnoses, are common but heterogeneous claims-based markers. These discrepancies represent a misalignment in the diagnostic process, reflecting diagnostic updating, reprioritization, residual clinical complexity, documentation practices, or error, without establishing clinical preventability, and may signal latent operational burden in subsequent physician decision-making. We examine whether this retrospective operational flag identifies inpatient stays with larger adjusted resource-use differentials and whether those differentials vary with physician experience. Methodology/Results: Leveraging a patient-level dataset of 5.7 million emergency-department-origin inpatient stays from Florida hospitals, we examine the operational burden associated with diagnostic discrepancies, measured by total costs per hospitalization. Our results show that discrepancy-flagged inpatient stays have a 6.62% higher adjusted total cost after rich patient risk adjustment and high-dimensional fixed effects. The adjusted differential is smaller at higher focal experience (treating similar diagnoses) and larger at higher related experience (treating diverse diagnoses). The pattern remains qualitatively similar across alternative discrepancy definitions, richer diagnosis and service-line controls, risk-adjusted benchmarking, physician matching, alternative experience measures, and alternative samples. Exploratory analyses further show that flagged inpatient stays exhibit higher costs across multiple resource-use domains with varying intensity, higher diagnostic and procedural intensity, and longer adjusted time to first procedure. Managerial Implications: The discrepancy flag is most appropriately used for retrospective monitoring, benchmarking, and case-review triage, not as a direct measure of preventable error or as an automatic performance score. The physician experience patterns motivate prospective evaluation of assignment, consultation, training, and decision-support practices.

title: Gendered Effects of a Crisis-induced Work-from-Home Shock: A Time-Motion Study Using Digital Footprints
abstract: Problem definition: While organizations are adopting hybrid and even remote-first work schedules, the potentially gendered impact of work-from-home (WFH) on operational outcomes remains poorly understood. Methodology/results: To examine this question, we combine a crisis-induced shock (i.e., the Covid-19 lockdown) that forced a shift to WFH due to stay-at-home orders, with a novel methodology to gather contextualized digital trace data. We examine the online time allocation — akin to a time-motion study for white collars — of 1,094 individuals across various activities and industries, when in-person work related and leisure activities were abruptly curtailed by the pandemic, inducing a shift to home-based work and online activities. Analysis of over 30 million website visits reveals that overall, this crisis-induced WFH increased the time devoted to both work-related and leisure pursuits online. However, these gains are significantly larger for men, giving rise to new gender gaps. We observe notable disparities in online work and leisure activities, including on smartphones, suggesting that crisis-induced WFH reshapes workers’ daily activities differently across genders. These gender differences are amplified among parents — a pattern consistent with increased household obligations placing greater constraints on women’s ability to fully benefit from the flexibility offered by WFH. Furthermore, we observe a substantial relative decline in women’s job search activities after the WFH shock, also corroborated using a large, external dataset from a major online recruitment platform. Managerial implications: These results underscore how sudden WFH mandates as response to a major crisis can differentially affect women’s work, employment prospects and long-term career trajectories. Our findings call attention to the importance of factors outside of the office in determining the success of WFH arrangements. Even though WFH could lower facilities cost and carbon footprint and increase workers’ flexibility, gender-specific constraints — especially those related to household responsibilities — can produce uneven outcomes. These results highlight the need for organizations and policymakers to design WFH policies that effectively address gender disparities, particularly in environments where childcare and other domestic duties fall disproportionately on women.

title: The Motivational Paradox: How Aspirational-Goal Communications Influence Sales Performance and Information Acquisition
abstract: This study examines how aspirational-goal communications influence sales agents’ performance and information-seeking behavior. In a field experiment across 100 stores in Sweden, agents in the treatment group received daily personalized text messages with aspirational sales goals tailored to their prior performance. Results show that these communications increase sales performance, particularly among low-performing agents, primarily through higher unit sales. At the same time, they reduce agents’ willingness to monitor within-day sales progress—reflecting the ostrich effect—which can adversely affect performance. Information acquisition, in the form of sales-progress monitoring, typically aids effort provision, but aspirational-goal communications suppress such behavior, complicating performance management. These findings highlight the dual effects of aspirational-goal communications: while they enhance motivation, they may also prompt information avoidance. The study contributes to research on goal setting and sales management by clarifying the trade-offs in designing effective motivational and communication strategies.

title: AI in Disguise—Quasi-Experimental Analysis of a Large-Scale Deployment of AI-Generated Ads
abstract: As Taboola prepared to launch its GenAI Ad Maker, a tool that lets advertisers create ad images within the platform, it faced a consequential question about whether AI-generated ad images would perform well with real consumers, and under what conditions. Working with Taboola, we construct a quasi-experimental comparison of 4,633 ‘sibling ads,’ meaning AI-generated and human-made images launched by the same advertisers, in identical campaign settings, at the same time. These ads span more than 369 million impressions and 2.5 million clicks. We do not find a detectable average click-through-rate disadvantage for AI-generated images relative to their human-made siblings. However, this average masks an important boundary condition: ads with AI-generated images outperform human-made ads when the AI images do not ‘look like AI.’ We identify key visual features influencing consumers’ perceptions of whether an ad looks AI-generated. While AI generates sharper, clearer, and less blurry images with larger faces, consumers associate these features with human-made ads. On the other hand, in line with consumers’ expectations, aesthetics, lower warmth, and intense color saturation in ads signal AI generation. These findings support Taboola’s roll-out communication, advertiser guidance, and continued refinement of the GenAI Ad Maker.

Semibandit Learning for Monotone Stochastic Optimization
abstract: Learning When Demand Is Unknown Airlines launching new routes cannot wait for years of historical data before deciding how many seats to offer at each fare or what prices to charge. They must learn when operating, often from incomplete feedback: selling 30 economy plus seats does not reveal whether demand was 30, 40, or more. In the accepted Operations Research paper “Semibandit Learning for Monotone Stochastic Optimization,” Rohan Ghuge, Zhengjia Zhuo, Arpit Agarwal, and Viswanath Nagarajan develop a general framework for such decisions. They identify a basic property, monotonicity, that allows an optimization method built for known demand distributions to become a learning algorithm for unknown distributions. The framework applies to airline and hotel revenue management, sequential posted pricing, and optimal-stopping problems. Even with partial, censored, or yes-or-no feedback, its cumulative performance gap grows essentially at the square root rate, best possible up to logarithmic factors. Firms can, therefore, improve decisions as data arrive without pausing operations for a separate data-gathering phase.

title: Action-oriented Narratives. How Innovation Emerges from Crowd Discussions
abstract: Crowds are increasingly invited to tackle complex innovation problems. However, our understanding of how crowds solve these problems has limited our ability to utilize them effectively. In this article, we examine how a crowd tasked with finding ways to preserve New Zealand’s native flora and fauna achieves solutions to this complex innovation problem through discussion. Our analysis reveals that discussions leading to innovative solutions differ from those leading to non-innovative solutions: innovation-yielding discussions (1) mobilize more Resources than Constraints, (2) converge on a single Goal, and (3) specify few (often one) responsible Subject(s); vis-à-vis, discussions leading to non-innovative solutions often surfaced multiple goals—thereby sustaining multiple problem framings—while subjects remained vague, implicit, or multiplied, and constraints frequently outnumbered resources. Moreover, we show how the specific weavings of these discursive elements support the crowd’s navigation of the complex innovation problem. Three discursive maneuvers – subject-goal anchoring, repurposing distant knowledge, and layering resources – are fundamental navigational tools used by the crowd to form what we call ‘action-oriented narratives:’ simple, dynamic, and evolving linguistic structures that enable collective problem exploration while giving room for localized improvisation. We contribute to the literature on problem solving by showing how specific linguistic activities alter individuals’ capacity to contribute to and solve complex problems. We also contribute to the literature on linguistic structures supporting innovation by showing that the types of discussions that support innovation depend on the openness of the setting.

title: EXPRESS: Improving Operational Performance through Boarding Time Slack: Evidence from the U.S. Airline Industry
abstract: Flight delays have a significant impact on airlines, passengers, and the U.S. economy. Airlines also use flight on-time performance (OTP) – a metric based on the proportion of delayed flights – to attract travelers by demonstrating service reliability. It is well established that adding buffers to flight time and ground time improves on-time arrivals. However, such buffers can impose significant costs. The flight and ground times comprise multiple activities, and prior research has primarily focused on studying the impact of aggregate buffers. In this paper, we study the impact of increasing the buffer of a critical ground time activity, namely boarding time, potentially without increasing the aggregate ground time buffer, on flight delays. To do so, we use the context of Delta Air Lines' recent policy changes wherein the airline increased the boarding time for domestic narrow-body flights by 5 minutes and started compensating flight attendants for pre-flight boarding. Using a Difference-in-Difference-in-Differences framework, we analyze and quantify the impact of these policies on Delta’s flight delays. Our findings indicate a significant reduction in departure delays following the policy changes, with increased boarding time playing a critical role in improving on-time departures. Our analysis finds no evidence that boarding compensation contributed to the improvement in on-time departures. We show that the increase in boarding time can improve the likelihood of on-time departures, potentially without requiring additional total ground time or incurring additional scheduling costs. We observe that the benefit is more pronounced for longer flights, busier routes, and later departures in the day. Airlines are often criticized for relying on costly, ad hoc schedule buffering to improve OTP. However, our results demonstrate that carefully planning buffer time for critical activities can significantly improve operational performance.

title: EXPRESS: Assortment Optimization Given Basket Shopping Behavior Using the Ising Model
abstract: In markets where customers tend to purchase baskets of products rather than single products, assortment optimization is a major challenge for retailers. Removing a product from a retailer's assortment can result in a severe drop in aggregate demand if this product is a complement to other products. Therefore, accounting for the complementarity effect is essential when making assortment decisions. In this paper, we develop an analytical framework designed to address this problem. We model customers' choices using the binary Ising model, which is a special case of a Markov random field. This model captures pairwise demand dependencies as well as the individual attractiveness of each product, with binary variables indicating whether products are included in the purchased basket. For estimation, we utilize existing methods developed for the spin formulation of the Ising model and then apply a parameter transformation to express the fitted model in the binary form used for assortment optimization. We show that the assortment optimization problem under the Ising model is NP-hard. We also provide multiple theoretical insights into the structure of the optimal assortments based on the graphical representation of the Ising model, and propose several heuristic algorithms that can be used to obtain high-quality solutions to the assortment optimization problem. Our numerical analysis demonstrates that the developed simulated annealing procedure leads to an expected profit gain of 15% compared to offering an unoptimized assortment (where all products are included) and around 5% compared to using a revenue-ordered heuristic algorithm.

title: Optimal Information and Security Design
abstract: Abstract An asset owner designs an asset-backed security and a signal about its value. After experiencing a liquidity shock and privately observing the signal, he sells the security to imperfectly competitive buyers. With flexible information design, the security’s informational sensitivity is a blessing, not a curse. Among double-monotone securities, the issuer prefers to sell the asset in combination with an appropriate signal rather than design more complex securities. Within the class of monotone securities, live-or-die securities are optimal and strictly dominate asset sales. When signals are restricted to be sufficiently informative about the upside, debt and additional-tier-1 debt become optimal. (JEL D82, D86, G32)

title: Ethnographic Theorizing in Human Resource Management: From Theory‐as‐Design to Theory‐in‐Use
abstract: ABSTRACT Research on human resource management (HRM) has generated influential frameworks for explaining the relationships between HR practices and organizational outcomes. Existing accounts offer less insight into how the frameworks informing those practices acquire meaning, authority, and practical traction in organizational settings. We conceptualize this as a gap between theory‐as‐design and theory‐in‐use and develop ethnographic theorizing as a mode of examining the use‐life of selected design‐oriented HRM frameworks. Our contribution is twofold. First, we specify how sustained immersion, temporal depth, embodied co‐presence, and relational obligation enable researchers to follow frameworks as they are enacted and negotiated. Second, we develop three recursively related analytic moves for theory development— Complement, Complicate, and Reframe —through which ethnographic evidence can elaborate, qualify, or revise existing theoretical accounts. We demonstrate this approach through two ethnographic studies of HR analytics in different organizations. The comparison shows how legitimacy work, identity negotiation, and meaning‐making shaped the enactment of data‐driven HRM in these settings. The paper thus offers a structured approach for studying how established HRM frameworks operate in use and for assessing when situated evidence warrants changes to their constructs, relationships, or boundary conditions. In addition, we discuss implications for HRM theory, research design, and practice.
