Who benefits from board quotas? Intersectional disparities and the moderating role of experience for women directors in India.
Competing against whom? Competitor identification and opportunity belief revision
abstract: Entrepreneurship theories acknowledge that competitive conditions matter for opportunity beliefs, yet how entrepreneurs identify competitors and how this identification shapes venture concept development have received little theoretical or empirical attention. We develop a process account of how entrepreneurs identify competitors and revise opportunity beliefs and venture concepts in response. Unlike market demand or technological feasibility, competitors are strategic agents who can adapt in response to entry, and as the venture concept evolves, so does the set of competitors it faces. We theorize an adaptive cycle in which encountering a competitor prompts threat assessment, which raises perceived competitive pressure and lowers confidence in venture success while motivating venture concept adaptation that can partly restore perceived viability. A controlled experiment isolates the cycle's components and shows that identical competitive information produces widely divergent threat assessments. A behavioral simulation in which participants develop their own ventures and search for competitors shows that entrepreneurs starting from similar concepts identify largely non-overlapping competitor sets. Some reposition their ventures spontaneously in response to what they find, and adaptation attenuates the link between threat and perceived competitive pressure.

title: Who Governs the Ungovernable? Policy Orphans and Public Service Innovation in the Voids of Indonesia’s Migration Governance
abstract: What happens when the very populations whose sacrifice drives policy success are erased from the governance systems that profit from them? We theorize “policy orphan status” as a condition where populations are (a) essential to a celebrated policy outcome, (b) structurally excluded from related governance frameworks, and (c) locked into invisibility by the logic that produces that success. Unlike underserved groups, policy orphans do not fall through cracks in existing institutions—they exist outside the architecture of governance altogether. Through qualitative comparative fieldwork across three East Javanese districts, drawing on 12 in-depth interviews and three focus group discussions with 45 participants, we examine how street-level bureaucrats invent governance from nothing when Indonesia’s labor migration system creates millions of children no framework can see. We find officials building institutions without blueprints, extending theory beyond street-level bureaucracy and policy entrepreneurship into institutional genesis within cross-jurisdictional, post-territorial governance voids.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Public Administration
abstract: Scholars in public administration are beginning to see the inevitability of “intelligent management.” Emphasizing the effective and efficient use of AI in public administration, Dr. Skotnicka-Zasad...

title: Building Integrity in the Global South: Lessons from Pakistan’s Struggle Against Public Sector Corruption
abstract: Why do formally mandated anti-corruption institutions fail in contexts of entrenched political patronage? This study addresses that question through an embedded case study of the Anti-Corruption Establishment of Sindh, Pakistan, combining the document analysis, case-file examination, enforcement statistics from 2015 to 2023, and interviews with twelve retired officials. Three contributions emerge: process-level evidence of how subnational institutions are operationally hollowed out rather than merely underperforming on aggregate indices; demonstration of how political interference, capacity deficits, legal loopholes, and neglect of preventive functions interact as a compounding failure ecosystem; and extension of institutional theory to subnational governance in federal developing states, offering transferable lessons where elite capture constraints accountability reform. The findings confirm that patronage networks convert formally mandated anti-corruption institutions into ritualistic procedure rather than substantive restraint, with accountability outcomes systematically conditioned by political affiliation rather than evidentiary merit.

title: Extending the Structure-In-Evolution Approach: Mechanisms and Patterns of Institutional Evolution
abstract: Traditional research on policy change offers valuable but fragmented accounts of policy evolution. Gradualist approaches identify types and mechanisms of incremental change, while other strands of scholarship propose processes associated with abrupt or punctuated shifts. These perspectives, however, tend to privilege one mode of change and do not address well how lower level mechanisms scale into system level patterns. The structure-in-evolution model overcomes the fragmentation by bringing together structure and different dynamics of change into an integrated, patterns-based approach to policy and institutional change. Despite its unifying potential, the model currently lacks a specification of the mechanisms that correspond to its patterned forms of change. This paper extends the model by identifying and systematically mapping such mechanisms. The resulting integration links causal processes across levels of analysis and enhances the model’s capacity to explain long term policy system evolution.

title: Debate: Material for whom? The missing public in the IPSASB’s climate disclosure standard
abstract: In January 2026, the International Public Sector Accounting Standards Board (IPSASB) published IPSASB SRS 1, Climate-related Disclosures (IPSASB, 2026a), the first international sustainability repo...

title: Rethinking public resource allocation: Basic service provision and economic performance in South Africa
abstract: IMPACTThis article speaks to senior and middle-level public finance practitioners: budget analysts and program managers in national and provincial treasuries; officials who design intergovernmental grants and equitable share formulae; municipal chief financial officers and integrated development planning managers; and public sector auditors and performance evaluators. Using South African data, it shows that the number of households relying on municipal basic and free basic services is more closely associated with economic performance than poverty, unemployment or infrastructure investment: years in which more households depended on this support were years of weaker economic performance. The practical message is that how budgets are prioritized matters as much as how much is spent. Practitioners can use the findings to argue for treating basic services as economic rather than purely social expenditure, for protecting these programs during fiscal consolidation, for sequencing infrastructure and service grants ahead of transfers that are likely to be less effective where services are absent, and for adding economic outcome indicators to service delivery and audit reporting.

title: Social Safety Nets and Corporate Tax Avoidance: Evidence From Paid Family Leave Programs
abstract: ABSTRACT Social safety nets are essential to a resilient and adaptive economic system. This study examines their influence on corporate tax avoidance using the staggered implementation of U.S. state‐level paid family leave (PFL) programs, social safety net policies designed to enhance employees' work‐life balance, as a quasi‐natural experiment. We find a statistically and economically significant decline in corporate tax avoidance following PFL adoption. The results hold across various robustness tests. A structural equation model shows that the effect is mediated by decreases in employee turnover and improvements in employee productivity. The effect is stronger among firms facing greater financing frictions and among labor‐intensive firms. Overall, this study identifies a reduction in corporate tax avoidance as an unintended consequence of social safety nets.

title: Attitudes of health economists to policy engagement activities: a Q methodology study
abstract: Background Health economists are key actors in analysing and advising on healthcare policy decisions. Policy engagement is increasingly emphasised in health research, yet little is known about how health economists perceive their role in this process. This study explored the attitudes of health economists in the UK and the Netherlands to policy engagement activities and identified the factors shaping their approaches. Methods Q methodology was used to capture and compare attitudes on policy engagement strategies. As part of this, a set of 28 statements mapped from nine categories of policy engagement activities was developed. Thirty-one health economists, from the UK and the Netherlands, ranked the statements onto a quasi-normal shaped grid and provided qualitative comments. Factor analysis was used to identify patterns in the ranking data, which – together with the qualitative data – were interpreted as attitudes to policy engagement activities. Results Four distinct attitudes were revealed: investing in relationships; intrinsic motivation; incentive driven; and effective communication. These attitudes captured differing perspectives about how to approach engagement and what drives impact, including trust-based collaboration, personal ethics, institutional incentives and strategic communication tailored to policy needs. Conclusion The attitudes to policy engagement differs among health economists. Therefore, flexible strategies acknowledging that their motivations, perceived barriers and facilitators, and institutional and policy contexts differ, are likely to facilitate and stimulate more effective translation of health economics research into policy.

title: From knowledge uncertainty to adaptive policy implementation: knowledge governance and integration in policy responses
abstract: Policy implementation under knowledge uncertainty requires governments to respond to evolving scientific evidence, professional knowledge, and implementation conditions. Yet, how institutional arrangements shape the use of diverse knowledge and its relationship with adaptive implementation remains insufficiently understood. This article examines these relationships in Indonesia’s COVID-19 response through a predominantly qualitative study combining a survey of 505 health workers in Depok, Surakarta, and Medan, six semi-structured interviews, document analysis, and policy process tracing. The analysis focuses on adjustments to diagnostic testing policies and workforce and healthcare service capacity. The survey identified multiple channels through which health workers contributed suggestions to policy discussions, including direct submissions to government (88 respondents), professional associations (87), and academic forums or conferences (61), with some respondents using more than one channel. Among the 138 respondents reporting contributions through these channels, 126 provided substantive follow-up responses, while 12 provided no substantive follow-up response. Of these 126 respondents, 42 (33.3%) reported no follow-up, 35 (27.8%) reported that their proposals remained under discussion, 22 (17.5%) reported incorporation into regulations, and 27 (21.4%) reported implementation. These self-reported findings indicate variation in follow-up but do not establish whose contributions shaped particular decisions. The findings indicate that, at the national level, professional organizations were formally involved in developing collaborative clinical guidance, providing an institutional basis for responding to evolving knowledge. However, local implementation depended on institutional capacity, resources, and socioeconomic and contextual conditions. Thus, knowledge integration may support adaptive implementation but does not automatically produce it.

title: Designing implementable digital government under institutional constraint: recruitment rules, administrative burden and contestability in Kazakhstan
abstract: Digital recruitment is often evaluated by deployment, competition and speed, yet these indicators say little about whether an applicant can understand, correct or challenge an adverse decision. This article investigates the design of contestability in Kazakhstan’s digital civil-service recruitment, with particular attention to the E-qyzmet selection environment. The documentary base combines the Agency’s annual civil-service reporting series for reform years 2018–2024 and its 2024 administrative competition reporting, compiled as of 1 January 2025, with the recruitment rules applicable to digital competitions in 2024–2025 and a separately dated comparison with the rules effective in 2026. The analytical framework distinguishes four interfaces: entry requirements, assessment and explanation, activation of review, and corrective feedback. Formal legal provisions establish complaint, inspection and documentary-access routes that are much less prominent in the achievement-oriented reporting series. This contrast is treated as a genre-conditioned visibility asymmetry, not as evidence that safeguards are absent or ineffective. Connecting policy-instrument calibration to administrative-burden theory clarifies how state-imposed rules may generate learning, compliance and psychological costs even in a voluntary, competitive selection process. The contribution is an evidence-sensitive model of contestability that separates legal specification, public intelligibility and demonstrated operation, and identifies what a credible audit of digital recruitment would need to measure. A limited open-data check is also used to identify which aggregate recruitment, testing and oversight variables are publicly recorded, without treating those series as candidate-level evidence of review.

title: Democracy in the crossfire: The electoral fallout of extremist political violence
abstract: What are the effects of political violence on election outcomes in established democracies? We argue that exposure to political violence raises citizens’ demands for security. Existing accounts disagree on whether this demand rewards incumbents, conservative parties, or the radical right, but they agree that it should cost extremist parties perceived as contributing to instability. Using a novel police dataset of 148 incidents of political violence, almost all from the far left or the far right, during Greece’s snap parliamentary elections of May and June 2012, we employ a difference-in-differences design at the voting center level in Athens and Thessaloniki. We find no evidence that political violence affects voter turnout. Further, we find only tenuous evidence of an electoral boost from violent incidents for populist radical right parties. Political violence does, however, reduce the combined vote share of extremist parties in exposed areas. Separating far-left from far-right incidents suggests that each extremist party loses support after violence from its own ideological side, though the evidence is stronger for the far right and we treat the pattern as descriptive. We argue that the backlash against extremist parties as a whole speaks to research on how voters punish parties associated with violence, as well as to wider debates about democratic resilience in times of crisis.

title: Forecasting the US Midterm Congressional Elections Without Poll Data
abstract: This article develops a long-term forecasting model for the US midterm elections which does not require polling data.It uses Congressional House and Senate seats captured by the Democrats in every presidential and midterm election since the end of the Civil War to develop the model.A general to specific econometric modelling strategy is utilised to derive the best Data Generating Process for the forecast.In addition, it uses a split sample estimation strategy to detect structural changes in Congressional voting over time.The results suggest that economic voting has been a feature of Congressional elections since the Civil War and it can be effectively modelled without poll data.The model predicts that the Democrats will win control of the House with 237 seats but not the Senate with 47 seats in the Mid-Term elections.

title: Introduction to Forecasting the 2026 US Midterm Elections Special Issue at PS: Political Science & Politics
abstract: Who will win the 2026 US midterm elections?Featuring a collection of 17 new forecasting articles, the special issue provides new perspectives on how we predict American midterm elections.From new methods using Artificial Intelligence or betting markets to classic politicaleconomy or state level models applied to the complex political landscape of 2026, from predicting individual Senate races to who will control the governors' mansions, this collection not only helps us to predict the outcome of these critical elections, but shines new light on our understanding of American politics in 2026.This introduction sets out the context of these elections, and discusses the particular challenges that forecasters had to contend with, including partisan polarization and substantial mid-decade redistricting, and introduces each of the 17 articles.The contributions to this special issue include forecasts for the House, the Senate and for gubernatorial contests with a variety of classic and novel methodologies and approaches, along with commentary and conceptual notes on forecasting.While all included forecasts for the House of Representatives predict a victory for the Democratic Party, forecasts are split when it comes to the fortune of the Senate, leading us to expect a close and contentious electoral contest.

title: A blind spot for dominance? Why liberals underestimate dominant leaders more than conservatives
abstract: Abstract The success of dominance‐oriented leaders often evokes surprise and dismay. We offer a psychological explanation beyond partisan reasoning, positing a systematic tendency among liberals to underestimate the appeal and efficacy of such leaders compared with conservatives. Drawing on moral foundations theory, we propose that liberals' heightened emphasis on harm avoidance and fairness explains their reduced liking for dominance‐oriented leaders, and that this reduced likability helps explain why they underestimate these leaders' prospects of success more than conservatives do. We test our predictions across multiple studies, including both political and organizational contexts, demonstrating that political liberals consistently perceive dominance‐oriented leaders as less likely to succeed than conservatives do—even when the leader's political affiliation is irrelevant, unknown, or aligned with their own. We conclude our investigation by suggesting that these diminished expectations from liberals might paradoxically enhance the success trajectories of dominant leaders.

title: The Climate Tribunate. Using conflict-focused democratic innovation to address the climate crisis
The Distinctive Nature of Non-Partisanship: How Independents Pursue and Prioritize Political Information
The Left Misunderstood: How Voters’ Perceptions of What Matters to the Left Benefit the Right
Steering or building? How crisis type shapes organisational change in the EU
abstract: How do crises reshape the internal organisation of EU institutions? Existing research treats crises as catalysts for change but offers limited guidance on what kinds of organisational reforms different crises generate. Building on an attack/failure typology of crises, the article argues that attack crises spur steering-oriented changes, whereas failure crises spur operationally-oriented changes. To test this, the article relies on an original data set of 101 organisational changes in the European Commission and the Council in five crises, including the rule of law crisis and Brexit, COVID-19 and the migration crisis, and the Russia–Ukraine war as a mixed case. The findings strongly support the theoretical expectations that attack crises produce steering-oriented organisational changes concentrated on enforcement, compliance monitoring, negotiation management, and political coordination, while failure crises produce operationally-oriented changes. The pattern is robust to recoding contested cases and to alternative decisions about the universe of cases. This article contributes to institutionalist theories of crisis-driven change by specifying how crisis origins shape not only policy outputs but also the administrative architecture that produces them.

title: Changing the terms of conflict: electoral revolution in the 2026 Hungarian parliamentary election
abstract: The 2026 Hungarian parliamentary election ended sixteen years of uninterrupted Fidesz rule under Prime Minister Viktor Orbán. The Respect and Freedom Party (TISZA), led by Péter Magyar, won 53.18 per cent of the party-list vote and 141 of 199 seats at record post-1990 turnout. This outcome is interpreted as an electoral revolution produced through asymmetric agenda competition. TISZA did not primarily challenge Fidesz by taking opposing positions on the incumbent’s preferred issues. It shifted attention from war, sovereignty, and Brussels towards government performance, corruption, public services, transport, territorial inequalities, and democratic renewal. Our analysis of party Facebook communication and press coverage documents this divergence, while survey evidence shows how the strategy united most of the former opposition, mobilised some previous non-voters, and attracted a smaller but consequential share of former Fidesz voters. This produced a socially and territorially broad coalition despite persistent age, education, occupation, and settlement gradients. The election transformed the government and party system, although it did not complete democratisation. TISZA’s constitutional majority now places rapid institutional repair in tension with legal continuity and pluralist restraint.

title: Implementing an Optimal Tax Plan with Short Term Debt
Welfare and the Act of Choosing
National Wage Contracts, Monopsony, and Welfare in a North-South Economy,
abstract: Abstract In countries characterized by significant geographical disparities in productivity, nationwide labour contracts may cause local unemployment by preventing the adjustments that would occur in a competitive labour market. Here we argue, however, that when there are mobility frictions and monopsony power, nationwide contracts may still be preferable to local contracts. Using a spatial general equilibrium model calibrated on the Italian North-South divide, we suggest that nationwide wage contracts may still lead to narrower regional welfare gaps if monopsony power is sufficiently strong in low-productivity areas.
journal_name: Journal of the European Economic Association

title: Networks of Dissent: Social Leaders and Protest in an Autocracy
The Immigration Surplus Revisited
abstract: Abstract We extend the immigration surplus results of Borjas (1995). In a closed competitive constant-returns economy, we show that an influx of migrants (holding their skill mix fixed) must increase the total real income of natives, for any number of factor inputs, any pattern of substitutability or complementarity between them, and any number of intermediate or final goods – with larger gains if natives and migrants differ more in skill mix. If natives supply labour elastically across skill types, their welfare gains are diminished, even if they respond by moving to higher-paying jobs. We illustrate our results using a US calibration.

title: Export Controls and the Economics of National Security
abstract: Export controls restrict trade to limit adversaries' access to goods that contribute to military capability, but their effectiveness depends on how trade and production adjust across countries.We combine new data on U.S. export control classifications and licensing outcomes with a quantitative general equilibrium model featuring dual-use production, input-output linkages, and separate civilian and military final expenditure.We estimate large export and entry frictions from these controls.These effects are substantially smaller for U.S. exports to members of multilateral export control regimes (MECRs): the differential is equivalent to an export cost of 15 to 29 log points.Relative to a counterfactual without differential controls on adversaries, multilateral controls reduce their imports of controlled products far more than unilateral U.S. controls.Only 7% of the reduction in controlled exports under the multilateral regime is replaced by other countries, compared with 28% under unilateral U.S. policy.Multilateral controls reduce adversaries' real military expenditure by increasing their military price index.The security impact, measured as U.S. real military expenditure relative to adversaries, rises by about 1 log point under multilateral controls but only 0.14 log points under unilateral controls, with both imposing a similar civilian real cost.Even a U.S. embargo fails to reproduce the multilateral security outcome.

title: The Impact of the Great Recession on Mortality: A Dynamic Factor Analysis
abstract: We use a dynamic factor time series model to estimate the national mortality impact of the Great Recession.In aggregate, the Great Recession reduced the average annual, age-adjusted mortality rate by about 2 percent, with effects persisting for at least a decade.In a calibrated model of the welfare effects of the estimated impacts of the Great Recession on consumption and mortality, we find that the welfare gain from the estimated mortality decline is quantitatively significant relative to the welfare loss from the estimated consumption decline.The estimated mortality decline is also quantitatively close to prior mortality estimates using cross-sectional variation in the severity of the Great Recession, implying limited general equilibrium effects of the Great Recession on mortality.More broadly, our findings suggest that prior evidence from local labor markets that recessions are good for health can be extrapolated to the likely mortality consequences of nationwide recessions.

title: The Robust Properties of Economies with Endogenous Production Networks
abstract: We characterize equilibria in a canonical class of economies with endogenous production networks, showing that log-prices equal a min-max over networks of a primitive affine function of logproductivities.This formula captures how resilience and fragility interact: the "min" reflects resilience from substituting suppliers, while the "max" reflects fragility from complementarityinduced rigidity.Applying these results, we generalize Hulten's theorem, finding that local Domar weights are generally insufficient to describe propagation of even small shocks.Moreover, we characterize how microeconomic volatility affects GDP, finding that smooth changes in Domar weights overstate its adverse effects by omitting option value from switching suppliers.

title: Infinite Factor Structure in Conditional Asset Pricing

title: Green Subsidies with Demand Distortions
abstract: Credit constraints and other demand distortions are pervasive in lower-income contexts.A model of clean technology adoption shows that demand distortions can increase the welfare gains from green subsidies.This arises through two channels: shifting the marginal adopter toward higher private and social benefits, and increasing demand elasticity.We test this by cross-randomizing purchase price subsidies, usage subsidies, and access to an interest-free loan for a US$84 induction stove among 2,134 charcoal users in Kenya.Usage subsidies of 75% have a precise zero effect on adoption and usage.Purchase price subsidies, however, generate large welfare gains.Credit constraints raise the subsidy's efficacy by 35%-73%, up to US$10-US$12 in observable welfare gain per subsidy dollar.This demand distortion also lowers the subsidy cost of abatement by 41%, to US$12 per tCO 2 e.This operates through the two channels identified in the theory: credit constraints raise the marginal adopter's positive externality by 19% and fuel savings by 30%, and lower the subsidy cost per marginal adoption by 29%.In a counterfactual without demand distortions, the abatement cost rises to US$137 per tCO 2 e. Contexts with large demand distortions could offer many cost-effective opportunities for climate change mitigation financing.

title: Credit Markets with New Screening Technologies
abstract: We study equilibrium market structure in a model of credit-market competition with correlated or uncorrelated screening errors and endogenous screening technologies.A pool externality arises because rejected borrowers reapply elsewhere, so lenders' screening and pricing choices affect competitors' applicant pools.With independent errors, a single market segment emerges, with rates rising smoothly as lenders who choose better technologies lend to more adversely selected borrowers.With correlated screening errors, potentially stemming from similar AI systems and overlapping financial-sector data, ex-ante identical lenders instead specialize across qualitatively distinct segments, generating a hockey-stick interest-rate schedule: segments with uniform rates but heterogeneous borrower quality coexist with segments featuring uniform quality but dispersed rates, echoing traditional banking, fintech, and high-rate indiscriminate lending.We show how technological and regulatory changes affecting screening costs, including frontier AI innovation and various forms of open banking, unevenly affect financial access and can either benefit or harm financially excluded borrowers.

title: From Politics to Process: Evidence from Progressive Era Naturalizations
abstract: States that delegate governance to local officials face a trade-off between the benefits of local knowledge and the costs of biased administrators.Can imposing federal standards discipline bias and improve uniformity?We study this question by examining the introduction of federal standards to apply for citizenship under the 1906 Naturalization Act.Using newly-digitized census records covering over five million immigrants and a 30-year period, we show that standardizing adjudication of citizenship applications resulted in rapid convergence of naturalization practices across cities.While naturalizations were around 30% higher in election years pre-reform, this electoral cycle disappeared after the introduction of federal standards.Exploiting the staggered adoption of municipal civil service reforms aimed at removing patronage during the Progressive Era, we find that the reduction in political cycles was strongest in unreformed cities.Finally, the contraction in election year naturalizations changed the composition of new citizens.Affected cohorts earned 7% more, were more likely to enter citizenship-restricted occupations, and gave children more Americanized names.Our results thus show that standardizing administrative procedures can discipline politically-biased policy implementation.

title: The Long March to Innovation: R&D and Competitive Evolution in the Indian Pharmaceutical Industry

title: The Impact of Social Insurance on Household Debt
abstract: This paper investigates how the expansion of social insurance affects households' accumulation of debt.Insurance can reduce reliance on debt by lessening the financial impact of adverse events such as illness and job loss.But it can also weaken the motive to self-insure through savings, and households' improved financial resilience can increase access to credit.Using data on 10 million people and a quasi-experimental research design, we estimate the causal effect of expanded insurance on household debt, exploiting ZIP-level heterogeneity in exposure to the staggered expansions of one of the largest US social insurance programs: Medicaid.We find that a 1 percentage point increase in a ZIP code's Medicaid-eligible population increases credit card borrowing by 0.38%.Decomposing this effect in a model of household borrowing, we show that increased credit supply in response to households' improved financial resilience drives the rise in borrowing and contributes 30% of the net welfare gains of expanding Medicaid.

title: Correcting for Heterogeneity in the Use of Subjective Scales
abstract: Analyses of survey data may be confounded if people use response scales differently.We formalize and generalize the theory behind using "calibration questions," such as vignettes, to correct for scale-use heterogeneity.Finding, in our (N 10,000) and existing data, that the mapping between respondents' scales is approximately linear, we develop a simple estimator for scale-use-corrected regressions.We validate it using subjective-scale ratings of height and weight and illustrate it with life satisfaction regressions, where correction leaves the main qualitative findings intact but can substantially change coefficient ratios, for example tripling the estimated cost of unemployment relative to income.

title: Foreign Giants' Broad Shoulders: The Causal Effect of Foreign Ideas on U.S. Innovation
abstract: We study the role of foreign ideas in U.S. innovation by constructing a directed "genealogy" of technologies from the full text of 13 million patents filed between 1887 and 2024.By tracing which earlier technologies appear in the founding patents of new ones, we recover a large-scale inputoutput network of technological recombination that identifies the foreign technologies that serve as inputs into innovation in the United States.We report four main findings.First, foreign ideas are pervasive: 54% of U.S. technologies build on at least one foreign input, and the most fertile U.S. technologies rely on foreign inputs most heavily.Second, foreign ideas have large causal effects on U.S. innovation.Using the historical settlement of migrants as a source of exogenous variation in local ancestry, we show that U.S. counties more exposed to knowledge from a given foreign country absorb substantially more technologies from that country and, in turn, invent significantly more U.S. technologies building on them.Third, foreign ideas shape not only the level but also the direction of technical change: U.S. counties are far more likely to pioneer the specific technologies whose foreign inputs are already in their local idea stock, and the changing origins of foreign ideas accompany the shift of American innovation from its historical heartland toward the coasts.Fourth, these effects leave a lasting imprint on local labor markets: decades later, counties that absorbed more of an origin's ideas host more jobs working with those ideas, and even more work with the U.S. technologies descended from them.

title: Understanding Migration Responses to Local Shocks
abstract: We examine how to interpret estimates from a commonly used migration regression relating changes in local population or employment to exogenous local labor demand shocks. Using a simple model of local labor markets with mobility costs, we find that common conclusions drawn from migration regression estimates are likely to be substantially misleading. Intuitively, the conventional migration regression is misspecified due to the bilateral nature of location choices. Workers choose where to live based not only on the shock to their current location, but also on the shocks to potential alternative locations, which are omitted from the regression. Analytical results and simulations based on Brazilian data show that conventional migration regression estimates are inaccurate for the within-sample effects of observed shocks on local populations and uninformative on the effects of counterfactual shocks to local labor demand. These problems are particularly acute when workers face industry switching costs in addition to geographic mobility costs. ∗All errors are our own. †Department of Economics, University College London (k.borusyak@ucl.ac.uk) ‡Department of Economics, Duke University (rafael.dix.carneiro@duke.edu) §Heinz College, Carnegie Mellon University (bkovak@cmu.edu)

title: Upgrading Financial Markets
abstract: Expanding access to financial services may not be enough to develop markets in low-income settings: providers also need to be held accountable to consumers.We test this in a field experiment across 195 rural Sierra Leonean communities, upgrading Village Savings and Loan Associations (VSLAs) into mobile money and bank agents, cross-randomized with a monthly consumer feedback mechanism.Upgrading expands access, but feedback drives large operational improvements (+20.5 pp, 85%), particularly in privacy and consumer protection, raising usage and revenues.Upgraded VSLAs also show higher savings digitization and higher incomes, evidence that disciplining agent actions benefits not only consumers but also the principal that finances and stands behind its agent.Interpreted through a framework of delegated intermediation, we show accountability, not infrastructure alone, aligns provider incentives with consumer welfare and is central to designing scalable financial intermediaries.

title: Firms' Investment and the Real Transmission of the Global Financial Cycle
abstract: We study how global financial conditions transmit to firms' investment.We document that increases in risk premia are followed by large investment contractions, particularly among firms with higher default risk.We develop a quantitative heterogeneous-firm open-economy model where firms finance investment with defaultable debt priced by risk-averse global investors.We identify a strong risk channel linking changes in the global price of risk to financing costs through firms' quantity of risk-the sensitivity of debt repayment to global shocks.This introduces a risk dimension to stabilization policy: smoothing cash flows reduces firms' quantity of risk and dampens international financial transmission.

title: Venture Capital and Customer Capital
abstract: Venture capital specializes in the financing of customer capital intensive firms-firms with higher sales and marketing expense to revenue ratios, a higher wage bill for sales and marketing employees, and a higher tendency to apply for trademarks-and they do so more than other financial intermediaries.Venture capitalists target high customer capital industries with low knowledge capital but avoid high knowledge capital industries that lack customer capital.Firms tilt investment toward customer capital leading up to the initial venture capital investment, after which their scale accelerates rapidly.Venture capitalists focus on financing customer capital because such investments require tolerance for substantial risks of failure in pursuit of extreme upside potential, as characterized by power law returns.This return profile fits customer capital investments more closely than investments in knowledge capital.Venture capitalists that sprinkle small investments across a large number of firms, colloquially referred to as the "spray and pray" strategy, target customer capital industries for investment, whereas venture capitalists that commit larger amounts to a small number of firms target knowledge capital industries.The venture capital focus on customer capital reflects a shift away from its traditional focus on knowledge capital intensive firms over the past 30 years.

title: The Net Present Value of the California Billionaire Tax Act
abstract: This paper examines the revenue and migration impact of the 2026 California Billionaire Tax Act, a one-time 5 percent tax on the worldwide net worth of individuals exceeding $1 billion.Using data from the Forbes Billionaire List, news reports detailing the residential real estate holdings of California billionaires, and public announcements of billionaire departures from the state, we estimate the behavioral response and associated revenue loss to this new tax using several different methodologies.Even before accounting for reductions in other tax bases such as the income tax, we estimate that the Act will collect approximately $30 billion (range $28 to 36 billion), less than a third of the $100 billion projected by Galle et al. (2025).This range accounts for the publicly confirmed taxpayer migration that has already eliminated nearly 30 percent of the Act's wealth tax base, applies a litigation-survival discount to the remaining base, and is validated by the wealth tax base elasticity literature.We estimate that California's billionaires contribute $3.3-5.8 billion annually in state income taxes.The present value of permanently lost income tax collections from departures more than offsets the one-time wealth tax revenue, yielding a net present value of negative $38.9 billion.Across 100,000 simulated revenue and discount rate combinations, 85 percent of plausible outcomes produce a negative net present value of state revenues.

title: The Effects of a Shorter Workweek on Employment, Output, and Productivity
abstract: Do shorter workweeks generate work-sharing and productivity gains, as intended by policymakers?We study France's pay-preserving reduction in the workweek from 39 to 35 hours, bundled with employer payroll tax cuts.We first exploit the staggered implementation by firm size to identify the impact of the reform package.We then use differential exposure to the hours cut and tax cut to separate their effects.We combine matched employer-employee, balance-sheet, and survey data to study worker, firm, and local labor market effects.The reform package left employment unchanged.This zero masks large offsetting effects: absent the tax cuts, the shorter workweek would have reduced employment by 3.8%.The effects are skill-biased, raising employment among managers and professionals while reducing it among other employees.Finally, shorter hours raised total factor productivity by 2%, limiting the output decline to 1% despite a 6% fall in total hours.Surveys point to work intensification and organizational changes as potential drivers of productivity gains.

title: The Why and How of Foreign Aid
abstract: Foreign aid has become a melting pot of motivations and policies, where differently-motivated actors often converge on recommended policies while the similarly-motivated diverge.Breaking down the "why" and the "how" can illuminate real tensions and reveal false ones.The "why" asks which problems to tackle and who benefits: the recipient, the donor through economic, political, or soft-power returns, or everyone through global public goods.The "how" asks which strategy most cost-effectively addresses a chosen problem.Evidence is central to the "how": use it where it exists, produce it where it does not.In particular, approaches which improve state capacity to use and generate evidence can satisfy multiple objectives: strengthen recipient countries, benefit donors, and provide a global public good of knowledge.Ultimately, the "how" is not a linear process, but rather an iterative one of learning, adopting, adapting, repeating, and then sharing so others can learn as well.

title: Will Medical Care Strangle or Save the Federal Budget?
abstract: Forecasts of the federal budget depend greatly on trends in medical spending.Since 1970, medical spending has nearly tripled as a share of gross domestic product (GDP).However, spending growth has barely exceeded GDP growth since 2010.This difference in growth rates makes forecasting spending difficult.I present scenarios for future spending derived from considering the sources of spending increase, ranging from rapid increases in new, expensive treatments to a reduction in spending due to cost-reducing technology.Even modest increases in spending relative to GDP are likely to overwhelm the federal government's ability to pay for medical care using current tax instruments.

title: Inside Central Bankers’ Calendars: How Do Fed Chairs Allocate Their Time?
Home-Foreign Elasticity Functions and the Gains from Trade
abstract: Gains from trade are typically calculated using a constant trade elasticity estimated from substitution across foreign countries.For general homothetic preferences, we show how to calculate these gains from the initial domestic expenditure share and the home-foreign elasticity function along a price path to autarky.While this function generally depends on the specific price path, under weak separability it does not.We provide conditions for its nonparametric identification and estimate sector-level elasticity functions using tariff changes implied by trade agreements.Across WIOD and OECD ICIO data, estimated home-foreign elasticities generally rise with domestic expenditure shares.Using estimated elasticity functions in a multi-sector model with intermediate inputs, the median gain across the WIOD countries is 19.37 log points, compared with 24.43 when each country-sector elasticity is held fixed at its initial value.

title: Pricing Power in the Mortgage Market: Evidence from GSE Fee Waivers
abstract: Market power may arise not only from firms, but also from individual salespeople who can exploit informational advantages over consumers.We explore this phenomenon in the mortgage market by examining a Fannie Mae/Freddie Mac fee waiver targeted at lower-income first-time homebuyers.We estimate that mortgage intermediaries capture over 60% of $1.5 billion in total fee waivers during 2023-2024, rather than fully passing these savings through to borrowers.Pass-through varies substantially across loan officers: those with a track record of originating expensive mortgages (independent of lender pricing) pass through less than 20% of the waiver.Our evidence suggests that loan officers retain incentives to steer borrowers into higher-rate mortgages, despite post-crisis regulations designed to limit such practices.

title: Staying Connected: Experimental Effects of Coach-Delivered Text Messages in an Adult High School
A Model of U.S. Monetary Policy and the Global Financial Cycle
abstract: We propose a general equilibrium model in which U.S. monetary policy affects global risk premia by revaluing the wealth of currency-mismatched arbitrageurs.Assuming their portfolios are meanvariance efficient, arbitrageurs must be short the dollar.A U.S. tightening thus erodes arbitrageurs' net worth and raises the global price of risk.We discipline this mechanism to rationalize the effects of U.S. monetary policy on international asset prices, and we quantify the associated macroeconomic spillovers and role of policy responses abroad.In a potential future with higher dollar interest rates, arbitrageurs' dollar funding and U.S. monetary policy spillovers are dampened.

title: Transportation as a Barrier to Education Access: Evidence from Chicago Public Schools
abstract: School choice can weaken the link between residential neighborhood and educational opportunity only if students can reach the schools available to them.We study school choice in Chicago, where high schoolers can choose among schools throughout the city but generally rely on public transit, making the structure of the transit network a key determinant of opportunity.Using student-level rankings and public transit travel times, we document two systematic patterns: Black students are less likely to rank top-rated schools first and face longer public transit times to such schools.We estimate a discrete choice model to separate the value placed on schools from the costs of reaching them.We find that high schools vary substantially in how they are valued and that there is a high degree of agreement across racial groups in their relative ranking.However, transit times vary significantly across neighborhoods, generating racial differences in demand for top-rated schools.Counterfactually, giving Black students the travel times of white students increases demand for top-rated schools by 23 percentage points.Finally, we identify underserved neighborhoods where public transit access constrains demand and quantify how targeted bus service would increase demand for high-quality schools.Our counterfactuals quantify how transportation expands school access.

title: Modeling and Evaluating the Labor Market and Fiscal Effects of Immigration
abstract: Immigration affects natives through both labor markets and public budgets, yet these channels are usually studied separately.We combine them in a general-equilibrium model with search-andmatching frictions, skill-specific progressive labor taxes, capital taxation and public goods, calibrated to 17 OECD countries over 2015-2019.The welfare effect on natives of a onepercentage-point increase in immigrant inflows varies in sign and size across countries, hinging on immigrants' skill mix, immigrant-native wage gaps, resident unemployment, and tax progressivity.For inflows matching the skill composition of 2019-2024 arrivals, native welfare rises in 14 of 17 economies, and in most cases both skill groups gain, through different channels.Lower-skilled natives gain mainly from higher pre-tax earnings, driven by job creation and complementarity with skilled immigrants; higher-skilled natives gain mainly from lower labor-tax burdens.Evaluating immigration policy thus requires modeling labor-market and fiscal channels jointly: either channel alone gives an incomplete picture of who gains and why.

title: Are We Consuming Too Much Groundwater?
abstract: We study the optimality of human groundwater extraction from many of the world's 3,400 aquifers, where institutional or market failures may produce non-optimal extraction decisions.We use remote sensing and economic data to estimate a dynamic model of water extraction for each aquifer, recover the discount factor that rationalizes observed groundwater extraction, and compare it against Ramsey and market benchmarks.Three-to four-fifths of aquifers are extracted more rapidly than is optimal, decreasing aquifer present value by several percent, and creating trillions of dollars in present value welfare losses.Policies that guarantee users constant water quantities indefinitely, through subsidies or prior appropriation, or policy rules that fully discount future extraction, generate larger welfare costs.A sustainable extraction path that maintains current fill forever generates meaningfully lower welfare than the optimal extraction path, because most aquifer stocks are already inefficiently low.

title: The Role of Organization in Firm-Sponsored Training
abstract: Some firms are more likely than others to invest in workers' skills.We document this phenomenon and discuss its implications in light of models of firm-sponsored skills training.The data show that better managed firms, even in the same industries and labor markets, are more likely to train, while training clusters around either managerial or frontline worker development.We argue that organizational differences provide incentives for firms to train beyond traditional explanations that focus on labor market frictions.We illustrate how organizational heterogeneity can generate training investments through a knowledge hierarchy framework where top managers with different skills build bespoke organizations tailored to their unique needs.This in turn makes general skill firm-specific, allowing firms to capture returns on training investment.

title: Leaving together: social influence and church decline
abstract: Abstract Church membership has declined across much of the Western world in recent decades. Existing research has identified individual characteristics that affect individuals’ likelihood of leaving their churches, but far less is known about how social interactions influence church decline. We examine (1) how exposure to others leaving the Church of Sweden affects individuals’ likelihood of leaving and (2) the aggregate membership dynamics generated by these micro-level processes. Using full-population register data from 2002 to 2023 and a dynamic matched-sample design, we estimate social-influence effects and assess how susceptibility varies with religious embeddedness, defined as the extent to which individuals are socially connected to other church members. We use these estimates to calibrate an agent-based simulation model linking individual behavior to aggregate membership decline. The results show that exposure to leavers increases individuals’ likelihood of leaving the Church, particularly among those with weak religious embeddedness. The simulations indicate that social influence contributed appreciably to the numerical decline of the Church of Sweden, while religious embeddedness moderated this effect. Social influence can thus amplify ongoing religious decline, while religious embeddedness attenuates this amplification.

title: Structuralizing the stress process: states as contextual determinants of stress and mental health
abstract: Abstract Despite growing evidence that policy environments influence mental health, we have limited knowledge of how policy environments influence the stress processes that shape mental health. This study develops and tests a theoretical framework that structuralizes the stress process model by explicating how the state policy context (1) directly influences mental health, (2) indirectly influences mental health via stress exposure, and (3) mitigates the impact of stressors on mental health. This study uses nationally representative data from the Household Pulse Survey (2020–2023; n = 3,043,961) and the Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (BRFSS; 2015–2019; n = 1,989,932) merged with state policy liberalism data to consider how state policy liberalism—the ideological orientation of state policies—shapes mental health. Results show that more liberal state policies were associated with lower odds of probable depression, probable anxiety, and frequent mental distress and weakened associations between three focal economic stressors—income loss, financial hardship, employment status—and mental health outcomes. Moreover, the association between state policy liberalism and mental health was partially mediated by financial hardship. Findings differed slightly by age: mediation via financial hardship was more evident among older adults (65+), whereas the buffering of economic-related stressors was mostly among adults under sixty-five. Overall, this study demonstrates the importance of a structuralized stress process model for mental health research.

title: Social distancing under strategic uncertainty: The role of strategic sophistication in the COVID-19 pandemic
abstract: Abstract This study examines how individuals’ strategic sophistication shapes social distancing during the early stages of the COVID-19 pandemic, when distancing was a costly protective decision under two sources of risk: the private risk of infection and strategic uncertainty about whether others would comply. We develop a weakest-link public goods game with private costs of social distancing, in which agents differ in their level- k depth of reasoning about others. The model predicts that the probability of distancing rises with the level- k type when baseline compliance is low. We test this prediction using large-scale, nationally representative survey data that include incentivized experiments to measure participants’ level- k types. We find that a one-level increase in level- k lowers the probability of leaving home daily by 1.6 percentage points in Singapore and is associated with a 3.4 percentage-point lower probability of maintaining or increasing outdoor activity in South Korea.

title: Sacrificial merit: Working time, commitment and inequality in UK television production
abstract: Research on media and creative labour has long shown that television work combines creative fulfilment with insecurity, long hours and unequal access. This article argues that excessive working time matters not only because it damages wellbeing, but because it becomes an evaluative mechanism through which professional worth is judged. In doing so, it helps explain why overwork remains difficult to challenge. Drawing on 40 semi-structured interviews and ethnographic observations from a UK returning drama production, alongside participants’ accounts of wider television work, the article introduces the concept of sacrificial merit to describe a labour culture in which the willingness and capacity to absorb unreasonable working demands is interpreted as evidence of professionalism, commitment and suitability. Participants described working days of up to 24 hours, unpaid preparatory labour, missed breaks and schedules that undermined care, health and career sustainability, while workers were expected to demonstrate commitment through availability and endurance. In project-based labour markets structured by freelance insecurity, informal reputation and discretionary hiring, sacrifice becomes an indicator of employability, converting organisational demands into apparently individual evidence of professional worth. The article extends debates on good work, creative labour and television production by identifying a mechanism through which workplace evaluation reproduces inequality.

title: Balancing Act: How Unaffiliated Analysts Navigate Private Information Disadvantages
IPOs and Foreign Tax Structures
Seeing Less, Engaging More: Rethinking Early User Experience on Generative AI Cocreation Platforms—Findings from a Field Experiment
Machine Learning Measure-Supported Empirical Studies: A Survey
abstract: Machine learning and data science techniques have been widely used in practice and have received significant attention. In research settings, business scholars have begun to adopt machine learning as methodological tools. This paper reviews the literature that leverages machine learning-generated measurements to support empirical analysis and yield business insights, where machine learning can reduce reliance on human coding or enable new theoretical perspectives. We summarize the workflow, constructs, and measure structures in these machine learning measure-supported empirical studies. We believe machine learning holds substantial potential to advance business research. History: Accepted by Ram Ramesh, Area Editor for Data Science & Machine Learning. Funding: This work was supported by the Shanghai Pujiang Program, Shanghai Municipal Human Resources and Social Security Bureau [Grant 23PJC097]; Research Grants Council, University Grants Committee [Grants 11500625 and 11501722]; and National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grants 72301067 and 72502212]. Supplemental Material: The online appendix is available at https://doi.org/10.1287/ijoc.2024.0918 .

title: Scalable Multistage Stochastic Optimization for Freight Procurement in Transportation-Inventory Systems
abstract: The procurement of freight services is an important element for the supply chain management of a shipper (i.e., a manufacturer or retailer) that sources transportation services from the third-party logistics market. Motivated by a practical freight procurement problem faced by shippers, we provide a holistic approach to designing freight procurement strategies for transportation-inventory systems that captures the interconnections among freight procurement, transportation, and inventory management. In view of supply and demand uncertainties, we consider the problem on the basis of a multistage decision process with uncertain data. To handle instances of realistic size, we propose an enhanced stochastic dual dynamic programming solution approach. We conduct extensive numerical experiments to test the performance of the approach. The results demonstrate that our approach scales to very large instances with up to [Formula: see text] scenarios and that the proposed enhancement strategies significantly improve its performance. Compared with methods commonly adopted to solve similar problems, our approach achieves significant cost improvements based on generated instances calibrated from established benchmark instances and stochastic simulations. History: Accepted by Andrea Lodi, Area Editor for Design & Analysis of Algorithms–Discrete. Funding: This work was supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grants 72301230, 72288101, and 72322022]; the Research Grants Council of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region, China [Grant 25223223]; and the Fundamental and Interdisciplinary Disciplines Breakthrough Plan of the Ministry of Education of China [Grant JYB2025XDXM211]. Supplemental Material: The software that supports the findings of this study is available within the paper and its Supplemental Information ( https://pubsonline.informs.org/doi/suppl/10.1287/ijoc.2025.1141 ) as well as from the IJOC GitHub software repository ( https://github.com/INFORMSJoC/2025.1141 ). The complete IJOC Software and Data Repository is available at https://informsjoc.github.io/ .

title: The Dedicated Docket in U.S. Immigration Courts: An Analysis of Fairness and Efficiency Properties
How Private Equity Fuels Nonbank Lending
abstract: Abstract We demonstrate how private equity (PE) promotes nonbank lending by substituting for bank monitoring. Relative to non-PE-backed loans, PE-backed loans exhibit lower bank monitoring, smaller loan shares retained by lead banks, and larger shares held by nonbanks. The substitution is strongest when sponsors have greater incentives to engage with portfolio firms, is not associated with weaker loan performance, and persists during borrower distress. Our findings suggest that PE sponsors’ active engagement—through monitoring and support in distress—reduces banks’ need for monitoring and information production, enabling them to retain less skin in the game and sell loans to nonbanks.

title: Investors' ideology and corporate symbolic and substantive climate actions
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Prior research suggests that institutional investors' liberalism is associated with firms' engagement in environmental sustainability, yet whether this association manifests in symbolic or substantive actions remains unclear. Taking a question‐driven approach, our analyses of Russell 3000 firms (2010–2020) reveal that investor liberalism, measured as the proportion of donations made to the Democratic Party, is positively associated with symbolic climate actions only from 2016 onward (a period when political polarization intensified), reversing a negative association during 2010–2015. Its positive association with substantive actions from 2016 onward, however, appears only among consistent Democratic donors (stronger liberal values), among dedicated investors, or in firms without CEO duality (greater investor influence). These findings indicate that liberal investor ownership may encourage, rather than deter, firms' environmental decoupling. Managerial Summary Liberal institutional investors tend to favor greater corporate environmental sustainability efforts, but are they associated with firms' symbolic or substantive climate actions? Our findings based on U.S. firms reveal that across the full 2010–2020 period, firms with more liberal investors, as indicated by their Democratic‐leaning political donations, do not exhibit more symbolic or substantive climate actions. From 2016 onward, as political polarization intensified, firms with more liberal investors exhibited more symbolic climate actions but not substantive ones. During this period, only investors with stronger liberal commitment (i.e., consistent Democratic donors) are associated with more substantive actions. Democratic‐donating investors are also associated with more substantive actions when they are dedicated investors or when firm CEOs do not chair their boards.

title: Synthetic diversity: Racial depictions influence consumer responses to AI ‐generated models in advertising
abstract: Abstract As brands seek to increase racial representation in their advertising, many are turning to AI‐generated images of humans (i.e., synthetic models) as a scalable solution. This research demonstrates that consumer reactions to synthetic models are asymmetric, depending on the racial identity being depicted. Across five studies, we demonstrate that disclosing the AI‐generated nature of models lowers firm evaluations when the featured models are from racially underrepresented groups (e.g., Black, Hispanic, and Asian models), but not when they are White. This effect is driven by reduced perceptions of the authenticity of the firm's inclusion efforts, which in turn elevate inferences of manipulative intent. Importantly, these negative effects can be mitigated when consumers are informed that the firm is owned by members of the depicted racial community, suggesting that credible signals of authentic community ties can neutralize the evaluative penalty of AI disclosure. Our findings extend research on racialized depictions in advertising by identifying synthetic depiction as a novel threat to the evaluative benefits of minority representation, and by theorizing why this threat operates asymmetrically by race. More broadly, our results highlight that technological innovations in advertising cannot be divorced from the social and historical contexts that shape their meaning.

title: Insurance and Assurance: Government Interventions and Depositor Behavior in Crisis
abstract: Abstract We examine how different forms of government intervention - explicit deposit insurance, implicit guarantees from nationalization, and assurance effects from re-privatization - shape depositor behavior during a banking crisis. Using proprietary monthly account-level data, we show that depositors respond to formal insurance limits even in an environment of broad state support, but adjust only partially. Stabilization is markedly stronger after the takeover by a financially strong private bank than during state ownership, despite unchanged statutory coverage. These patterns are inconsistent with a strong bailout-expectations view in which explicit insurance is largely irrelevant and instead point to credibility as a key determinant of depositor behavior. We further show that political trust amplifies the effectiveness of government guarantees. Overall, our findings highlight that the form and credibility of government backstops, rather than coverage levels alone, are central to retail deposit funding stability during crises.

title: Local Economic Dependence, Official Rank, and Accountability in China: Evidence From Coal Mine Accidents
abstract: This article examines accountability after coal mine accidents in China using an original dataset of 968 accidents involving 3,503 government officials. It analyzes how accident severity, official rank, local economic dependence on coal, and the strengthening of coal mine safety supervision shape both the probability and the severity of accountability. The results show that more severe accidents are more likely to trigger sanction and result in harsher punishment. Higher-ranking officials are less likely to receive severe sanctions, and the effect of accident severity on their accountability probability is comparatively weaker. The findings also show that the impact of local coal dependence on accountability conditions on strengthening of coal mine safety supervision. Before 2003, greater local coal dependence weakened the responsiveness of accountability to accident severity and widened rank-based disparities in sanction severity, largely through harsher punishment of lower-ranking officials. After 2002, these coal-related hierarchical distortions were substantially reduced, although the general disparity sanction severity across administrative ranks persisted. These findings contribute to the study of official accountability in China by showing how bureaucratic rank, local economy, and regulatory environment jointly shape accountability outcomes.

title: When Public Employment Spills Over into Civic Action: Environmental Co-Production in China
abstract: Do public sector jobs foster civic engagement beyond the workplace? Using national survey data from the 2021 CGSS, this study examines whether Chinese public sector employees are more willing to engage in environmental co-production. The study disaggregates co-production into production, capturing routine pro-environmental behaviors, and cooperation, capturing multi-actor deliberation. The results show that public sector employment is significantly correlated with environmental cooperation but not production. Specifically, employees in public institutions and state-owned enterprises are more inclined toward neighborhood cooperation, whereas government agency employment is marginally positively correlated with stakeholder cooperation. Exploratory mediation analyses suggest that these associations are consistent with a pathway through institutionally embedded self-efficacy, rather than altruism or informational advantages. Managerial positions weaken the association between public sector employment and neighborhood cooperation. The findings suggest that promoting environmental sustainability requires not only moral mobilization and information provision, but also the cultivation of citizens’ civic efficacy and procedural confidence.

title: Bureaucratic Capacity and Autonomy as Drivers of Innovation Climate
abstract: Governments face growing pressure to innovate in response to complex societal demands, yet little is known about how bureaucratic features shape public employees’ perceptions about innovation. This study examines how bureaucratic capacity and autonomy influence public employees’ perceptions of innovation climate. We argue that capacity, understood as organizational resources and capabilities, and autonomy, or insulation from political influence, foster conditions conducive to innovation. We analyze over 30,000 survey responses from public employees across the 32 Colombian intermediate governments between 2015 and 2023, combined with administrative data. Findings show that autonomy is consistently and positively associated with a stronger innovation climate. Capacity also matters, but only when measured through employees’ perceptions of sufficient resources, not through fiscal performance indicators. These results contribute to understanding organizational drivers of individual innovation antecedents. Specifically, the study underscores the role of bureaucratic features in fostering innovation climates in politically complex subnational contexts.

title: Windows of adversity: how crises entrench carbon lock-in in corporatist democracies
abstract: Do economic crises open windows of opportunity for green transformation? A prominent strand of recent literature argues they can. We show that, in corporatist democracies, the opposite can occur: Crises entrench fossil fuel dependence and deepen carbon lock-in. Extending Mildenberger’s theory of double representation, we argue that political urgency and acute economic threats consolidate the power of carbon-intensive interests, as governments rely on them for information, legitimacy, and rapid implementation. This dynamic intensifies when key political actors are weak – under minority governments, or when left parties, electorally weakened, lean on unions tied to fossil fuel industries. Under these conditions, the institutional channels that normally constrain ambitious climate policy shift from veto to appropriation: Carbon-intensive actors no longer simply block reform but capture state resources on exceptionally generous and weakly conditional terms. We probe this argument using Norway’s COVID-19 response, drawing on interviews with key stakeholders. The case traces how an initially moderate government proposal for oil-industry support was expanded into an exceptionally generous tax package. Our findings challenge the assumption of crises as ‘windows of opportunity’ for green transformation, showing instead how corporatist institutions can produce ‘windows of adversity’ – with implications for climate politics and crisis policymaking across corporatist democracies.

title: Deterrence and retribution as motives for supporting punitive public policies
abstract: Abstract Punitive policies such as migrant detention and benefits sanctions are growing in popularity. Politicians claim that the threat of harsher punishment deters undesired behavior, yet much evidence suggests that this is incorrect. Why, then, is it popular with voters? Building on literature from crime and punishment, I use vignette experiments in the UK to test whether this is because they believe that punishment acts as a deterrent, or because they view it as retribution for immoral behavior. Respondents rated the likelihood of desired behavior from hypothetical migrants and benefits claimants, and from themselves, in response to punishments of varying severity. They believed that some punishment had a deterrent effect but harsher penalties had little further payoff. Punishment was supported because migrants and benefits claimants fail to live up to people’s behavioral standards, particularly amongst authoritarians. Thus punitive measures enact retribution against outgroups, reinforcing moral boundaries and a rule-bound, orderly society.

title: Policy reinvention and policy performance within vertical authority structures—evidence from China’s rural revitalization policy
abstract: Policy reinvention has received substantial scholarly attention. However, little is known about how reinvention at different government levels influences policy implementation outcomes. This study examines the dynamics of multilevel policy reinvention within vertical authority structures. The findings demonstrate that while municipal policy reinvention positively contributes to policy outcomes, excessive policy reinvention at the provincial level can impede municipal policy performance. Contrary to our expectation, faster provincial adoption weakens the positive relationship between municipal reinvention and policy performance. An exploratory typological analysis further shows that conservative reinvention is associated with significantly better outcomes than prudent reinvention. Robustness analyses confirm the stability of these theoretical claims. These findings contribute to a more nuanced understanding of intergovernmental policy processes and offer practical insights into achieving better alignment between policy reinvention efforts across government tiers and policy implementation performance.

title: The effect of mass–elite congruence in representational style on citizens’ democratic satisfaction
abstract: Abstract Satisfaction with democracy and confidence in political institutions are often linked to policy or ideological alignment between voters and elected officials. While policy congruence has been widely studied, less attention has been paid to process congruence—the gap between citizens’ preferences for representation and politicians’ perceptions of their duties. This paper uses data from three Portuguese election cycles (2005, 2011, and 2015) to examine how process congruence affects satisfaction with democracy. It also assesses whether political interest and educational attainment moderate this relationship, shaping the extent to which citizens respond to congruence between their own representational preferences and those of political elites. The results indicate that policy congruence is by far the strongest correlate of satisfaction with democracy. By comparison, the independent association of process congruence is small and not statistically robust: once policy and ideological congruence are accounted for, moving across the observed range of process congruence is not reliably related to satisfaction, and the estimates are inconsistent in direction across representative targets (i.e., whether congruence is measured in relation to all MPs, government MPs, or one’s preferred-party MPs). Citizens’ underlying representational preferences are nonetheless related to their satisfaction—those who favour a delegate style tend to be less satisfied than those who favour a trustee style. Contrary to expectations, this relationship is not stronger among the politically interested or the more educated; the limited moderation we detect—by education—runs opposite to expectations. Taken together, these findings caution against treating process congruence as a determinant of democratic satisfaction comparable to policy congruence, while suggesting that how citizens think representation should work is not irrelevant to how they evaluate democracy.

title: Social Capital, Platform Power, and the Private Authority of Big Tech Firms: Theorizing The Micro-Foundations of Platform Power Among Social Networking Sites
Digitally Networked Territorial Control: Digital Communication and Hybrid Order in the Urban Periphery
abstract: How do armed actors leverage digital communication for territorial control? In violently contested urban environments (often known as “hybrid orders”), territorial control involves regulating who belongs in a specific geographical area. Enforcing these rules, in turn, requires gathering fine-grained information to evaluate threats and selectively project violence. This study illustrates how the affordances of digital communication platforms help armed actors to do so. Using a comparative ethnographic approach and open-source research methods, the article analyzes three digital intelligence-gathering practices used by criminal groups and militarized police in Fortaleza’s urban periphery (Brazil): smartphone inspections, digital information-sharing networks, and social media monitoring. The findings reveal how the structural features of digital communication platforms facilitate accessing and disseminating strategic information, which in turn introduces effectiveness, flexibility, and efficiency gains in territorial control. This suggests that digital media affordances play an important role in contemporary forms of territorial competition by armed groups.

title: From the Authoritarian Playbook: Academic Freedom and the Politics of Self-Censorship in Florida
abstract: Between 2021 and 2023, the State of Florida enacted numerous bills and took administrative actions interfering with university autonomy and academic freedom amid a combative political discourse vilifying universities as too “woke.” Defenders of these interventions have argued that academic teaching and research content have not been censored. However, research on self-censorship under authoritarianism suggests that the effects of forceful state intervention may be more complex and long-lasting than they appear. This article addresses this issue by expanding theories on “chilling effects” in democracies, conceptualizing them as a potential instrument of soft repression that illiberal political actors may use to suppress content while circumventing judicial scrutiny. Based on 60 qualitative interviews conducted in early 2024 at six higher education institutions in Florida, the study shows how pervasive uncertainty and informal intimidation led scholars to self-censor in their teaching and research in ways not prescribed by law. Although these behaviors vary across individuals and are partly mediated by institutional responses, they are not isolated cases and are likely to have a significant impact on Florida higher education.

title: Beyond Sovereignty or Exile: The Limits of Exilic and Diasporic Jewish Politics and the Egalitarian Potential of Jewish Nationality
