abstract: This article argues that Jewish accounts of exile or diaspora predicated on disaggregating Jewishness from Zionism cannot sustain the nonsovereign Jewish politics they endorse. Although these accounts provide new grounding for Jewish critiques of Zionism and the State of Israel, they prioritize a Jewishness that is not implicated in Jewish political responsibility for Palestinian subordination. As a result, they have a more contingent relationship to binational political equality between Jews and Palestinians. To overcome these issues, I offer a normative alternative: a creolized reading of Jewish nationality. I argue that such an account, which accepts the Zionization of Jewishness, can better support a Jewish communal turn toward binational political equality. This is a reading of Jewish nationality defined as the enactment of a localized, binational coalition with Palestinians based on a recognition of present inequality and shared opposition to Palestinian subordination. Such a politics could frame the State of Israel as a threat to Jewish politics not because it abrogates an idealized notion of Jewish identity or ethics but because it is hostile to the egalitarian, binational partnership on which any such politics must rest.

title: The Labour Market Link: An explanation of Brexit support
abstract: Abstract Where can we expect support for populist parties and initiatives to be weakest, and why? We argue support will be weakest in places that have experienced strong growth of employment in high-quality jobs, because such growth has positive spillover effects that shape wider perceptions of the economic status quo and the prevailing ideological climate. We test this proposition in relation to Brexit support at the time of the 2016 EU referendum and in the present day, using Census data to proxy the rate at which highly paid jobs replaced low- and mid-paid jobs in English and Welsh Local Authority Districts 1991–2016, and substantiate it at both the area and the individual-level. High-quality employment growth is a more powerful predictor of Brexit support than alternative local economic indicators and individual-level effects are sizeable. All else being equal, analysis of Understanding Society data shows the probability of Brexit support is only 30% among respondents in places that experienced very strong high-quality employment growth, compared to 55% among those in places with negative growth. These findings have important implications for how left behind places should be defined and for strategies that seek to address political discontent.

title: Immigration and Nationalistic Attitudes: Panel Evidence from Chile
abstract: Abstract Does rapid and large-scale migration fuel nationalism? Using administrative and panel survey data from Chile, we show that sudden, large-scale migration inflows increase identity-based nationalistic attitudes, such as national pride, among native-born citizens. These “immigration shocks” appear to activate perceptions of identity threat, leading to stronger expressions of national pride and belonging. Supplementary evidence from surveys, media reports, social media, and crime records suggests that this nationalism is predominantly exclusionary: areas most affected by migration also experienced spikes in anti-migrant rhetoric, hate crimes, and support for a newly formed far-right party. These findings underscore how rapid demographic changes can reshape political attitudes and contribute to the rise of exclusionary forms of national identity.

title: Political psychology in an era of personalization: Misinformation research, generative AI, and the promise of tailored experiments
abstract: Abstract Voters increasingly inhabit personalized information environments, where content, algorithms, and social cues vary across people. Yet popular approaches to studying and addressing features of information environments such as misinformation exposure often flatten this heterogeneity: Measures and interventions are developed for populations rather than individuals. Using misinformation as an illustrative case, I argue that population‐based methods for measuring and intervening on beliefs can obscure why some beliefs matter politically while others do not. I advocate for tailored approaches that adapt research designs to groups and individuals. Tailoring can increase relevance, facilitate persuasion, and create fruitful conditions for testing influential theories of opinion formation and change. I conclude by discussing the promise of a personalized political psychology that aligns measures and interventions with the idiosyncratic ways voters form and express opinions.

title: Climate change and conflict: The vicious cycles undermining climate action, and what can be done to break them
abstract: Abstract In this review, we synthesize evidence to argue that climate change and conflict are mutually reinforcing. We first examine conflict as a barrier to mitigation, focusing on four faultlines that slow climate action: (a) ideological polarization, (b) “elite versus ordinary people” narratives, (c) intranational, place‐based conflicts, and (d) international disputes. The consequence of these conflicts is worsening climate change, which in turn increases the prevalence of factors known to be conflict amplifiers: heat stress, economic stress, widening inequality, and forced displacement. Our analysis points to the potential for recursive “climate–conflict loops”, fuelled in part by erosion of institutional trust, shrinking moral circles, political polarization, and de‐prioritization of long‐term climate goals. In a spirit of optimism, however, we identify three buffers capable of breaking these vicious cycles: maintenance of procedural and distributive justice, enhancing information integrity, and scaffolding institutional cooperation. We conclude by proposing a research agenda that integrates psychological mechanisms into dynamic, multi‐level accounts of how climate impacts and political conflict coevolve.

title: A BOOTSTRAP SPECIFICATION TEST FOR SEMIPARAMETRIC MODELS WITH GENERATED REGRESSORS
abstract: This article provides a specification test for semiparametric models with nonparametrically generated regressors. Such regressors are not observed by the researcher but are nonparametrically identified and estimable. Applications of the test include models with endogenous regressors identified by control functions, semiparametric sample selection models, or binary games with incomplete information. The statistic is built from the residuals of the semiparametric model. A novel wild bootstrap procedure is shown to provide valid critical values. We consider nonparametric estimators with an automatic bias correction that makes the test implementable without undersmoothing. In simulations, the test exhibits good small sample performance, and an application to women’s labor force participation decisions shows its implementation in a real data context.

title: Poverty-Reducing Income Taxation with Endogenous Income
Modeling Exposure–Mortality Relationships for Indoor Heat
abstract: ABSTRACT Most individuals spend the majority of their time indoors. However, epidemiological evidence of the association between heat and mortality is dominated by studies using outdoor temperature as a proxy for personal exposure. To demonstrate how an exposure–response relationship between indoor heat and mortality may relate to that between outdoor heat and mortality, we develop a novel mathematical modeling approach. This approachuses the relationship between regional daily average indoor and outdoor temperature to map the exposure–response relationship for outdoor heat, estimated by epidemiological studies, to indoor heat. Due to the modifying effect of buildings on heat exposure, we show that a change in indoor temperature may be associated with a greater change in mortality than an equal change in outdoor temperature. This has implications for researchers seeking to assess the health impact of changes in indoor heat exposure. Furthermore, it provides a new theoretical framework for interpreting potential differences in the temperature‐mortality relationship of indoor and outdoor heat exposure in epidemiological studies.

title: Seasonal Multivariate and Spatial Assessment of Heavy Metal Contamination and Associated Ecotoxicological and Human Health Risks in Urban Park Soils: A Case Study From Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam
abstract: ABSTRACT Urban parks in rapidly developing cities face increasing heavy metal contamination, yet seasonal dynamics remain poorly understood. This study evaluated seasonal variations in heavy metal contamination and associated human health risks in two major parks in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam. We analyzed 48 surface soil samples (24 locations × 2 seasons) for eight metals using ICP‐OES. Pollution levels were evaluated using indices (EF, I geo , CF, PER, mHQ, TU, and TRI) and GIS‐geostatistics. Sources were apportioned via multivariate analysis and positive matrix factorization (PMF), and health risks to children and adults were simulated using Monte Carlo methods. Al (Go Vap 12,475 ppm; Gia Dinh 13,998 ppm) and Fe (Go Vap 12,324.1 ppm; Gia Dinh 7620.7 ppm) dominated soil composition. In Go Vap, there was an increase in Al, Mn enrichment and Pb spikes (EF = 91.69) in the dry season; Gia Dinh had Cr (EF = 4.43) enrichment in the dry season and higher Mn (EF = 4.19) in the rainy season. PMF identified four sources: traffic solid waste (31.4%), traffic emissions and construction dust (15.8%), natural weathering (20.1%), and redox processes (32.7%). Spatial analysis revealed dry‐season high‐risk hotspots expanding to 39.41% of Gia Dinh and 36.02% of Go Vap park areas. Cr posed the highest health risk (HQ = 0.53 for children, 0.057 for adults), primarily via ingestion. All risk indices intensified during the dry season ( p < 0.05). Dry seasons increase the risk of contamination in tropical urban parks, especially Cr. This study supports seasonal monitoring and enhanced protection for children in monsoon‐affected green spaces.

title: Less is more: Decision-making under increasingly complex ambiguity
Guardians of the cyberverse: Dispositional, attitudinal, and autobiographical correlates of user engagement against misogynist digital hate
abstract: As digital misogyny remains widespread, user intervention is an essential complement to lenient platform governance. Yet, willingness to intervene varies considerably across individuals and cultural contexts. In a cross-national survey conducted in Austria ( n = 791), France ( n = 800), Hungary ( n = 775), and Sweden ( n = 785), we examine how dispositional, attitudinal, and autobiographical characteristics relate to users’ direct and indirect intervention and support for moderation. Empathic anger consistently emerged as the strongest positive predictor of all three outcomes across countries. Perspective-taking, online self-presentation, and victimization experiences showed meaningful positive associations with intervention, while misogynist attitudes were inconsistently related. Toxic disinhibition showed a dual pattern, negatively associated with moderation support but positively associated with direct intervention across all countries, suggesting its potential to be cleverly repurposed toward counterspeech. These findings underscore the importance of emotionally activating literacy programs and highlight the need for culturally sensitive intervention models.

title: Invisible Women in Economics: Almost Two Centuries of Gender Representation in the Financial Times and The Economist (1843–2021)
abstract: This study examines gender representation in the Financial Times and The Economist between 1843 and 2021. Using millions of articles and name-frequency analysis, it traces the long-term evolution of women’s visibility in economic news. Results reveal a U -shaped pattern: relatively high representation in the nineteenth century, a decline through much of the 20th century, and a gradual recovery since the 1980s. Comparisons with benchmarks of women’s participation in high-status occupations and economic sectors show a persistent gap between media visibility and real-world presence. The findings point to a lasting paper ceiling in economic journalism. JEL codes: J16, N34, L82

title: Taking a Note from Music: Conceptual Sampling and the Creative Logic of Theory Development
abstract: How do scholars develop new theoretical explanations from existing ideas? Although management research has established clear criteria for evaluating theoretical contributions, it has devoted comparatively less attention to the creative processes through which those contributions are generated. In cumulative knowledge systems, theorists rarely develop ideas from entirely new conceptual materials. Instead, they build on existing concepts, mechanisms, and explanations to generate new theoretical insights. This review essay introduces conceptual sampling as a process framework for understanding creative theorizing in management. Drawing on scholarship on music sampling in jazz, electronic music, and hip-hop, we argue that theorizing often proceeds through three distinct processes of conceptual transformation: (1) rearticulation, (2) recombination, and (3) recontextualization. These processes respectively deepen existing theoretical frameworks, build new explanations by integrating ideas across literatures, and extend concepts into new contexts. By integrating scholarship on music sampling with work on theory development, this essay illuminates how scholars transform established conceptual resources into new theoretical explanations, thereby advancing insights on theory development in management.

title: Unaffiliated Component Auditors and Audit Fee Models: The Case of Lowballing
A Decision-Support Framework for Food Bank Operations: Overcoming Waste and Uncertainty in Food Distribution
abstract: Problem definition: Food banks face the complex operational challenge of allocating uncertain and per- ishable food donations to maximize community benefit. This requires navigating difficult trade-offs between effectiveness (delivering nutritious and fresh food relative to need), efficiency (maximizing food distributed and minimizing waste), and equity (ensuring fair distribution), a task for which traditional myopic poli- cies are often ill-equipped. Our research addresses how food banks can design practical, forward-looking allocation strategies in this dynamic and challenging environment. Methodology/results: We develop a comprehensive dynamic programming framework to model the food bank allocation problem. From this, we derive two practical and implementable policies: a simple, static Scaled Fluid (SF) policy and an adaptive Re-Optimized (ReOPT) policy. We provide rigorous theoretical proofs that both policies are asymptotically optimal. Furthermore, extensive simulations using both synthetic and real data show that our proposed strategies yield significant utility gains. Managerial implications: This research provides food bank man- agers and decision-makers with theoretically sound and empirically validated tools to improve their opera- tions. Our framework offers a clear path to enhance the impact and sustainability of food distribution efforts, enabling organizations to better serve their communities by making more efficient, effective, and equitable decisions with the resources they have.

title: Cross-Cluster Referrals and Subsidy Schemes in Multi-Cluster Healthcare Systems
abstract: Problem definition: Excessive and highly variable waiting times for specialty services are a long-standing problem for public healthcare systems. Healthcare authorities in some jurisdictions have begun to experiment with schemes to improve system performance, including cross-cluster referrals which allow patients to switch from their home cluster to other clusters with shorter waiting times, and opt-out subsidies which help patients seeking services from private providers outside the public system. However, few studies in the literature have examined the structure of the problem or offered analytical insights to the design of such schemes. Methodology/results: We construct a multi-cluster service network model to study optimal routing policies under both individual and system optimization. We define externalities in a network setting and establish their properties, and further identify conditions under which referrals are effective or counterproductive in reducing system costs. We also show that lowering the switching cost could inadvertently degrade overall system performance. In contrast to the classic result for single-cluster systems (e.g. Naor 1969), our analysis of opt-out and switching incentives reveals that fixed subsidies generally cannot fully coordinate a multi-cluster system due to the cross-cluster effect of externalities. However, they can effectively reduce system costs in wide ranges of system parameter values. We further show that dynamic (state-dependent) subsidies can achieve perfect alignment between individual and system optimization. Managerial implications: Our study suggests that cross-cluster referrals are effective when there is a substantial workload imbalance but without excessive system congestion. They should be implemented with proper operational control: referrals should be promoted when the workload imbalance is high, but discouraged when the overall system workload is very high while the imbalance is insubstantial. Furthermore, fixed opt-out and switching subsidies can effectively improve system performance under different demand conditions and should be applied strategically: focusing on switching subsidies when the system workload is moderate and the imbalance is substantial, but shifting the focus to opt-out subsidies when the overall system workload is high.

title: Humanitarian Aid Management under Corruptible Distribution and Oversight Agents
abstract: Problem Definition: In many crisis contexts, such as armed conflicts, natural disasters, or refugee emergencies, one of the most pressing challenges is to regulate the delivery of humanitarian aid to the final beneficiaries in the presence of both corruptible agents (those responsible for delivering aid) and corruptible inspectors (who may be bribed not to report uncovered misappropriations). Strengthening anti-corruption efforts by hiring more inspectors and/or rewarding inspectors’ truthful reporting can reduce corruption but draws on the finite humanitarian aid financing, reducing the aid delivered to the beneficiaries. Methodology/Results: We develop a three-stage game-theoretic model in which a government agency chooses inspection intensity and the reward rate for inspectors’ truthful reporting, managers decide how much aid to misappropriate, and inspectors decide whether to report detected misconduct or accept a bribe to conceal misappropriation. The government agency aims to maximize the amount of humanitarian aid reaching the beneficiaries. We find that the role of inspectors depends on the financing available. When the financing is low, inspectors serve to detect misconduct; when the financing is sufficiently high, inspectors also affect managers' behavior and deter misappropriation. The reward can also serve two purposes. It can either induce truthful reporting and eliminate bribery, or increase the bribe that managers must pay, thereby reducing their incentive to misappropriate. We characterize the impact of key parameters on the optimal anti-corruption levers. Managerial Implications: Our results provide guidance for agencies and donors on how to balance aid provision with anti-corruption measures, and how to adjust inspection intensity and incentive for truthful reporting to maximize the amount of aid reaching its intended recipients. As financing changes, resources should be allocated toward adjusting inspection intensity. In contrast, the reward rate for truthful reporting should be calibrated to the enforcement environment, and not be mechanically increased with the amount of financing.

title: The Effects of Search Interface on Consumer Preferences: Evidence from a Randomized Experiment
abstract: While structured search interfaces—such as filters and sorting tools—help consumers reduce search frictions on digital platforms, they also shape how consumers encounter product information during search. This paper studies how search interface design influences revealed preferences and market outcomes. We develop a theoretical framework linking interface design to attribute preferences through salience reallocation and information-based preference updating. The framework generates two predictions that can be formally derived: restricting faceted filters reduces the concentration of attribute importance weights (i.e., preference dispersion) and increases the diversity of products chosen (i.e., choice diversity). We test these predictions using a randomized, incentive-aligned online experiment in which 1,200 participants searched for wireless headphones on a custom-built e-commerce platform. Restricting filters led consumers to explore more broadly and resulted in more evenly distributed attribute importance weights and more diverse, higher-priced product choices. Mediation analysis further suggests that increased exploration was associated with shifts in attribute preferences. Our findings demonstrate that search interface design can construct, rather than merely reveal, consumer preferences.

title: Belief Traps Hinder Small Business Climate Action
abstract: Climate (in)action by small business owners is not driven only by policy or economic considerations but also by sociological and psychological factors, as leaders mimic the behaviors they perceive among their peers. We find that these social inferences about what others believe are often incorrect. In this registered report of 4,432 small-to-medium business owners and leaders across seven countries, we observe a persistent gap between perceived and actual beliefs. And this gap matters: small-to-medium enterprise owners exhibiting a larger gap have fewer sustainability policies in place. These results highlight how peer effects can spur climate action among business leaders.

title: The Paternity Leave Ripple Effect in the Finance Industry: Shaping Norms and Social Cohesion
abstract: ABSTRACT Paternity leave shifts work‐life policy from accommodating women's caregiving to legitimizing men's involvement in care. We examine how this is experienced in male‐dominated workplaces and interpreted by those around leave‐takers through interviews with fathers who took extended paternity leave in French finance organizations, and other stakeholders at work (colleagues, HR representatives, top managers) and at home (life partners). Following an interpretivist, context‐dependent approach, we find that participants associated paternity leave with changes in social relations, connectedness, and concern for collective well‐being. We theorize that, under certain conditions, these changes may coalesce into relational and collective experiences aligned with social cohesion beyond the workplace. We further theorize two pathways. In a transformative cycle, paternity leave may disrupt descriptive and injunctive gender norms, and experiences aligned with social cohesion occur. In a maintenance cycle, established norms persist, and such experiences largely do not arise. These divergent pathways depend on the favorability of nested contextual conditions: meso‐ (policy design, top management engagement, organizational climate) and micro‐ (manager, peer support), within the macro‐context of a male‐dominated industry. The study extends work‐life policy research beyond individual and organizational outcomes and identifies conditions under which paternity leave may challenge gendered divisions of labor within and beyond organizations.

title: Framing the unknowable: The role of language and frame multiplicity in early‐stage startup pitches
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Early‐stage startup pitches must make largely unknowable futures plausible. As such, they bear a rhetorical burden. This study theorizes how multiple frames jointly shape this burden and, consequently, affect investor evaluations. Specifically, it considers how future growth frames interact with concreteness and novelty frames. Evidence from 618 startup pitches and ad‐hoc investor evaluations reveals that growth frames relying more on entrepreneurs' own assertions than on established grounds tend to receive lower investor evaluations. This evaluative discount is alleviated when growth is expressed concretely but becomes more pronounced when the pitch emphasizes novelty. These findings extend framing theory by explaining the relevance and possible implications of frame multiplicity in pitches and entrepreneurial communication more broadly. Managerial Summary Mobilizing support for a new venture is difficult because founders must often describe a future that does not yet exist. This study of 618 startup pitches shows that growth‐related messages can shape investor evaluations even at the earliest stage, but only if configured well. Because growth frames must appear plausible amid the uncertainty surrounding new startups, framing early‐stage startups around growth is rhetorically burdensome. Findings show that pitches are evaluated less favorably when they rely more on founders' own projections and reasoning than on established grounds such as market analyses. Concrete language can alleviate this burden, while novelty framing intensifies it. As such, this study reveals intricate and potentially unintended interactions among multiple frames within a single pitch.

title: When machines learn with organizations: AI ‐enabled knowledge creation and entrepreneurship
abstract: Abstract Research Summary To promote entrepreneurship and new business development, firms will increasingly rely on new forms of knowledge creation to manage environments marked by technological change and radical uncertainty. We argue that as generative artificial intelligence (Gen‐AI) becomes embedded in organizational processes, knowledge creation will no longer remain solely a human activity. Instead, it will increasingly emerge from hybrid interactions between human actors and firm‐specific, closed Gen‐AI systems. These systems begin to participate directly in how knowledge is generated, recombined, internalized, shared, and converted into entrepreneurial initiatives such as corporate entrepreneurship, spin‐offs, and new business models. We also reconceptualize organizational knowledge creation as a hybrid human–AI process and propose a reordered knowledge creation cycle that induces multiple knowledge spirals, captures the emergence of new agents, and the generation of diverse types of knowledge, with faster temporal dynamics. Building on this perspective, we offer a research agenda for future scholarship. Managerial Summary We discuss how firm‐specific generative AI systems are likely to fundamentally alter the ways firms generate knowledge, respond to change, and sustain long‐term renewal. We propose that rather than replacing human judgment, closed Gen‐AI changes where knowledge originates as well as how quickly it evolves, and how broadly it circulates across organizational boundaries. This means that the managerial challenge is less about adopting AI and more about designing knowledge systems and structuring knowledge flows. Executives and entrepreneurs alike need to decide how to structure human–AI collaborations, how much autonomy to grant closed Gen‐AI systems, and how to prevent speed from overwhelming sensemaking. Our work underscores that although hybrid knowledge creation promises faster and more diverse learning, it also introduces risks related to opacity, trust, and cognitive lock‐in. Firms that deliberately orchestrate the role of closed Gen‐AI in their learning systems will be better positioned to shape future advantage by promoting innovation and entrepreneurial activities of different types.

title: Fostering Innovative Work Behavior to Improve Organizational Performance: The Roles of Public Service Motivation and Innovative Organizational Culture
abstract: This study examines how innovative work behavior is associated with organizational performance, focusing on the mediating role of public service motivation and the moderating role of innovative organizational culture in public organizations. Based on responses of 4,133 Korean central and local government employees, the findings indicated that innovative work behavior is positively associated with organizational performance. The results also show that public service motivation partially mediates this relationship and that innovative organizational culture moderates the association between innovative work behavior and organizational performance. These findings advance understanding of the relationship between innovative work behavior and organizational performance by highlighting the motivational role of public service motivation and the contextual role of innovative organizational culture in public organizations.

title: Data Science Integration as Practice: Micro-Level Dynamics from Intelligence Agencies
abstract: Public organizations face growing pressure to integrate data science and AI into their work, yet empirical insight into how such integration unfolds in practice remains limited. This article examines data science integration through a multiple embedded case study of intelligence agencies in the Netherlands and the United States, drawing on 28 semi-structured interviews with personnel in managerial, analytic, and data science roles. Using a strategy-as-practice perspective and a micro-level Ability-Motivation-Opportunity (AMO) lens, the study analyzes how public servants encounter and respond to organizational, technical, and legal challenges in everyday work. Interviewees linked integration to leadership literacy, data culture and expertise, opportunities for experimentation, technical and acquisition conditions, and legal and accountability requirements. The analysis identifies different patterns of integration, including fragmented and ad hoc use, incorporation into specific workflows, and more routinized use. The article contributes to public management research on digital governance by conceptualizing integration as a practice-based organizational process in which data-driven tools have to become useful and justifiable within everyday work. It also shows how the AMO framework can help explain the micro-level conditions under which personnel engage with such tools and identifies implications for strategic prioritization, validation, cross-role collaboration, and sustained integration.

title: Perspectives: artificial intelligence and scientific autonomy: a policy agenda for emerging research systems
abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence is becoming part of the infrastructure through which scientific knowledge is produced, yet access to computing, data, advanced models and expertise remains highly uneven. This Perspective argues that, for emerging research systems, the central science-policy challenge is not simply AI adoption but scientific autonomy: the capacity to choose, understand, adapt, evaluate and govern the technologies on which research increasingly depends. Scientific autonomy is not technological self-sufficiency; it is strategic interdependence supported by domestic capabilities. Drawing on Brazil as an illustrative case, we propose four dimensions of autonomy—epistemic, infrastructural, human-capability and governance autonomy—and a six-part policy agenda based on shared computing, research-data infrastructure, AI literacy, interdisciplinary networks, adaptive governance and capability-building international cooperation. Without deliberate capacity-building, AI may accelerate discovery while deepening structural asymmetries between research systems.

title: JPE Turnaround Times
Recent Referees
Will markets provide humane jobs?
abstract: Legislation regulates the key amenities of our jobs—paid sick leave and holidays, working hours, safe working conditions, and workers’ compensation—and social movements have been essential to their adoption. Why do laws, rather than markets, secure these amenities? This paper studies one answer: adverse selection on productivity. When workers who value an amenity more are, on average, less productive, employers offering it attract a lower-productivity workforce. The resulting compensating wage differential exceeds the direct cost, leading to underprovision—even when the amenity is costless. I formalize this mechanism using a new notion of stochastic dependence, the correlation in expectation , which captures the severity of adverse selection. In a competitive screening equilibrium with heterogeneous jobs, underprovision intensifies with the strength of this correlation and, in extreme cases, the market unravels entirely. A universal mandate is optimal when the correlation is strong; when it is moderate, policies leveraging observable heterogeneity—such as flexibility rights for parents—outperform both the mandate and laissez-faire. The paper contrasts this productivity-based selection with the traditional cost-based selection studied in prior work and discusses the distinct empirical tests each implies.

title: Robust Aggregation of Correlated Information
abstract: Abstract Decisions are typically made by drawing on multiple sources of information, yet the correlation among these sources is often hard to assess. We study robustly optimal strategies—those that maximize the worst-case payoff guarantee across all correlation structures. With two states and two actions, the robustly optimal strategy is strikingly simple: use only the best information source and ignore the rest. With more actions, a robustly optimal strategy decomposes the problem into local comparisons and assigns each comparison to the source that is best at that comparison. With more states, the same specialization logic survives through a concavification characterization: the decision problem is decomposed into payoff-relevant components, and each component is assigned to its best source. These results offer a new rationale for why ignoring information can be optimal and highlight the benefit of using specialized information sources when correlations are ambiguous.

title: When Should We (Not) Interpret Linear IV Estimands as LATE?
abstract: Abstract In this paper I revisit the interpretation of the linear instrumental variables (IV) estimand as a weighted average of conditional local average treatment effects (LATEs). I focus on a situation in which additional covariates are required for identification while the reduced-form and first-stage regressions may be misspecified due to an implicit homogeneity restriction on the effects of the instrument. I show that the weights on some conditional LATEs are negative and the IV estimand is no longer interpretable as a causal effect under a weaker version of monotonicity, i.e. when there are compliers but no defiers at some covariate values and defiers but no compliers elsewhere. The problem of negative weights disappears in the interacted specification of Angrist and Imbens (I1995), which avoids misspecification and seems to be underused in applied work. I illustrate my findings in an application to the causal effects of pretrial detention on case outcomes. In this setting, I reject the stronger version of monotonicity, demonstrate that the interacted instruments are sufficiently strong for consistent estimation using the jackknife methodology, and present several estimates that are economically and statistically different, depending on whether the interacted instruments are used.

title: Positioning enjoyment and appreciation as key components of news use
abstract: Abstract In response to the continued convergence and hybridization of news and entertainment media content, this research explores the roles of enjoyment and appreciation in contemporary news use. Three studies (two surveys and one experiment) show a clear link between enjoyment, appreciation, and news use. Both enjoyment and appreciation are positively related to agreement, value alignment, attitude change, and attitude reinforcement in the context of news use. News enjoyment is related to increased positive and decreased negative emotions, while news appreciation is connected to an increase in and tolerance of mixed emotions. Importantly, news enjoyment decreases actual knowledge while facilitating greater affective polarization. News appreciation increases more positive feelings toward other people. These results illustrate the value of merging research on entertainment and news media, and they also suggest that news enjoyment is a driving factor in the growth of less democratic news use outcomes.

title: Buffering institutional erosion: organizational ties and SME exports under populism
abstract: Abstract We argue that pre-existing organizational ties can partially buffer against the adverse effects of populist deinstitutionalization. In contrast with the chronic institutional weakness emphasized in prior literature, populist deinstitutionalization reflects a politically driven weakening of institutions that firms had previously relied on. This disrupts established routines and increases the transaction costs of cross-border exchange. For SMEs, which are highly dependent on external institutional support for internationalization, pre-existing ties to government actors, international suppliers, and foreign owners can provide partial buffering by replacing some of the coordination, information, and enforcement functions lost through institutional erosion. We test these arguments using data on 10,399 SMEs across 29 economies in Central and Eastern Europe and Central Asia. The results support our theoretical expectations: while populism is negatively associated with SME exporting, pre-existing organizational ties attenuate this adverse association, with foreign ownership providing the strongest buffering effect. Our findings extend institution-based research by identifying politically driven institutional erosion as a distinct challenge for international business and by showing that organizational ties can function as selective, imperfect buffers rather than substitutes for formal institutions.

title: Share Issues vs. Share Repurchases
abstract: Almost all firms repurchase shares through open-market repurchase programs. In contrast, issue methods are more diverse; at-the-market offerings, analogous to open-market repurchases, and seasoned equity offerings, analogous to rarely used tender-offer repurchases, are both used by significant fractions of firms. Furthermore, average seasoned equity offerings are larger than at-the-market offerings. We show that this asymmetry in the diversity of transaction methods in issuances and repurchases and the size-method relation in issuances are natural consequences of the single informational friction of a firm having superior information to investors. Moreover, although this friction always leads firms to issue inefficiently little, it leads firms to repurchase too little if they maximize long-term shareholder value but too much if the primary goal is to boost short-term share prices. This paper was accepted by Bo Becker, finance. Funding: Y. Yuan acknowledges support from the Paul Woolley Centre, the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Projects 72342020 and 72495152], and University College London. H. Zhong acknowledges support from the Economic and Social Research Council [New Investigator Grant ES/T003758/1]. Supplemental Material: The online appendix is available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.03301 .

title: Inpatient Overflow Management with Proximal Policy Optimization
Filtering the Labor Pool: How Digitalization Redistributes Hiring Costs
Return on AI (RoAI): A framework for assessing AI investments in the marketing organization
abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping marketing as firms increasingly delegate activities and decisions previously performed by marketers to AI systems. As AI assumes a greater role in market-facing decisions, understanding the value firms realize from these investments becomes increasingly important. Building on marketing accountability and resource-based theory, we develop a Return on AI (RoAI) framework that conceptualizes AI investment through the people, processes, and capabilities that enable its deployment and governance. RoAI evaluates incremental benefit while accounting for value retention, evidence durability, and the full costs of deployment over time. The framework identifies a distinctive consequence of delegated judgment, wherein AI can improve current performance while reducing the experiential practice through which marketers develop and maintain the judgment required to evaluate and redirect the AI solution. This mechanism helps explain heterogeneity in AI returns across firms and over time. We develop seven testable predictions and an agenda for research on creating, appropriating, and sustaining value from AI.
journal_name: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science

title: Identifying and managing milestones in consumers’ goal journeys
abstract: Abstract Understanding consumers’ holistic journeys as unfolding events is paramount for managing service design and delivery. Touchpoints, “moments of truth” and critical incident research primarily focus on firm-facing events and consumers’ evaluations of firm encounters, rather than critical events in consumers’ own goal pursuit. This article introduces and uncovers the significance of milestone events in consumers’ journeys. Milestones are significant events that mark a major step or turning point in a consumer’s journey. Multi-stage, multi-context qualitative consumer journey research is used to inductively identify the key features and implications of milestones. They are distinct from other service events and consequential for consumers’ lives. This research fills a significant research gap in understanding consumer goal journeys. Identifying and understanding consumers’ milestone events enables service firms to support and improve goal progression; increase confidence in success; help consumers prepare for and interpret milestone outcomes; and manage risk by adjusting or pivoting from the goal.
journal_name: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science

title: Governance Convergence in the EU—A Matter for Interpretation
abstract: European Union (EU) enlargement represents an ambitious institutional transformation. Our analysis explores whether recent EU accessions have resulted in governance quality convergence. Using the World Bank Worldwide Governance Indicators, we examine the progression of governance quality across both EU and non-EU countries and assess whether it has converged toward EU Core member states’ performance level. We apply panel regression and dispersion trend analysis to measure beta and sigma convergence, within and in-between pre-specified country groups. Results are of strong beta and mixed sigma convergence. We find that NonEU_East former communist countries and recently EU‑integrated, predominantly former communist countries, experience convergence regardless of EU membership, with consistently stronger convergence among the latter, suggesting EU accession may play an important role in governance convergence. Importantly, our findings support an interpretation of governance performance deterioration within EU Core member states as a possible contributing factor to the observed convergence outcomes.

title: Public Administration and the Crisis of American Democracy
abstract: ABSTRACT The field of public administration stands amid genuine crisis. Americans don't trust government or its administrators. Elected officials have attacked the career service as agents of the “deep state” and, though it might be hard to admit, many of public administration's critics have a point. Government's performance too often falls short of what people expect, practitioners too often seem too unresponsive to elected officials, and researchers too often seem to have only fuzzy guidance for practitioners. However, public administration undoubtedly is more important now than ever in translating public goals into effective action, and in bringing to life the democratic aspirations Madison and his colleagues wished for the country at its founding. The field urgently needs new strategies and tactics for solving the new generation of puzzles the country faces. In coming together, practitioners and researchers build on these puzzles to chart an exciting road forward.

title: Differentiation from mentors and the gender productivity gap in research: Evidence from electrical engineering
The Symbolic Politics of Housing
abstract: Voter opposition to development contributes to America’s housing shortage. Prevailing explanations emphasize NIMBYism (opposition to housing nearby) and homeowners’ self-interest. However, homeownership often fails to predict housing policy views, while NIMBYism offers little insight into support for policies that do not concern specific proposed housing projects—the focus of much recent policymaking. Drawing on symbolic politics theory, we argue that voters’ affect toward groups that housing policies make salient powerfully shapes their judgments about housing policies. We present evidence supporting this theory. Experiments show that affect toward developers and investors who build housing, government actors who approve it, and residents who move into it explain anti-development preferences when policies make these groups salient. Providing further causal evidence, short-form videos that manipulate affect toward developers have meaningful downstream effects on support for new development and permitting reforms. Ironically, voter dislike of the very actors who could ameliorate the housing shortage further exacerbates it.

title: Queenpins: Women Leaders and Violence in Organized Crime
abstract: How does women’s leadership affect the behavior of criminal organizations? Organized criminal groups are male-dominated patriarchal organizations that use violence to govern, compete, and control territory. Qualitative research suggests that women leaders—though rare—reduce their organization’s violent behavior. We examine this expectation through Mexico’s Tijuana Cartel, leveraging the sudden 2008 ascension of a woman to leadership. Although violence increased under her tenure, synthetic control results show greater reliance on hidden violence and less on visible violence and territorial expansion. Original data on male cartel leaders reveals that systematic gender differences in trajectories help explain these patterns. Our results indicate that women leaders are not necessarily less violent than men but instead strategically employ different violent repertoires. Case studies of 44 women leaders across 18 countries since 1850 assess the broader applicability of these findings and identify important scope conditions. Our findings underscore the importance of incorporating gender into organized crime research.

title: Powers of ecological horror
Attitudes Toward LGB and TGD Rights in Latin America
abstract: Abstract Research on attitudes toward transgender and gender-diverse (TGD) individuals lags behind research on opinion on the lesbian, gay, and bisexual (LGB) population, leaving open questions about public opinion on these two LGBTQ+ subgroups, in general and in particular in the Global South. While a sizeable gap exists in US public opinion toward TGD and LGB rights, we do not know whether that finding is generalizable to other contexts. With a focus on Latin America, we draw on a range of scholarship to identify factors that could result in a similar divergence of attitudes toward these subgroups or, instead, relative convergence. Our analyses focus primarily on novel survey data from representative surveys across thirteen Latin American countries. Our results demonstrate a fair amount of convergence in mean levels, item nonresponse rates, and predictors of views on LGB versus TGD rights. We present some notable differences across countries and issues, with results for the former (countries) varying by socio-political context and the latter (issues) varying across political and nonpolitical domains. We identify these patterns as constituting a future agenda for researchers of opinion on LGBTQ+ topics. We conclude that, in the contemporary period, the Latin American public holds fairly similar mental schemas toward LGB and TGD groups.

title: How the Public Makes Sense of Gender Politics: Textual, Emotional, and Symbolic Dimensions
abstract: Abstract How do ordinary citizens make sense of gender politics? While research has examined public support for feminism and gender equality either separately or as interchangeable concepts, far less is known about the meanings citizens attach to these labels and whether they evoke distinct political meanings. This article compares the textual, emotional, and symbolic associations of three related but distinct framings of gender politics: feminism, gender equality, and equality between men and women. Drawing on an original pre-registered survey experiment in Spain, respondents were randomly assigned to define and evaluate one of the three labels, allowing us to analyze their meanings across textual, emotional, and visual dimensions. We find that while most respondents express sympathy toward all three labels, feminism stands as the most contested. Feminism also has the sharpest sociopolitical profile, eliciting greater support from young, highly educated, progressive women. Text analyses reveal that the public frames feminism in terms of collective action, conflict, and women’s identity, drawing heavily on political language, while the other two labels emphasize policy and material concerns. Emotionally, gender politics elicits more positive than negative responses across all three labels, though men report slightly higher negative emotions toward feminism. Feminism is also the only label consistently associated with images of women’s mobilization and protest, reinforcing its distinctively political resonance. These findings show that feminism and gender equality tap related but meaningfully distinct constructs in the public mind, with implications for how scholars measure attitudes toward gender politics and interpret public support for equality-related policies.

title: Compulsory schooling mitigates health inequality: Anthropometric evidence from two centuries of height data
Building without income mixing: public housing quotas in France
abstract: Abstract We study the effects of the SRU law introduced in France in December 2000 to support scattered development of public housing in cities and favor social mixity. This law imposes 20 per cent of public dwellings to all medium and large municipalities of large-enough cities, with fees for those not abiding by the law. Using exhaustive fiscal data, we evaluate the effects of the law over the 1996–2008 period using a difference-in-differences approach at the municipality and neighborhood levels. We find that the law stimulated public housing construction in treated municipalities, but only slightly increased the presence of low-income households. Indeed, new public dwellings enter categories to which medium-income are eligible and most additional occupants are not poor. Within municipalities, the policy decreased public housing segregation but it barely decreased low-income segregation. This comes from local authorities increasing over time the presence of public dwellings in neighborhoods away from existing public housing but in places concentrating low-income households.

title: Multi‐Agent Contracting With Network Externalities
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper analyzes how the structure of externalities‐encompassing both pure spillovers and interactive components‐reshapes the classic trade‐off between incentives and risk in multi‐agent contracts. The interplay of network effects and moral hazard generates congestion effects among agents with a common neighbor, which we decompose into a sum of weighted Katz‐Bonacich centralities. This tractable characterization enables clear comparative statics on the externality structure. We further apply the framework to examine how organization structures shape firm boundaries, and the design of Pigovian taxes to generate social security.

title: Editorial Board
From lifestyle to citizenship: Social influence and political consumerism in egocentric networks
abstract: Political consumerism has become a widespread form of civic engagement, yet the social mechanisms driving boycotting and buycotting remain insufficiently understood. This study investigates how perceived citizenship norms within individuals’ egocentric networks are associated with their own civic orientations and subsequent participation in consumer activism. Using a national survey of 543 U.S. adults reporting on 1822 social ties, we integrate social learning and social influence theories to examine how network environments cultivate engaged and dutiful citizenship norms. Results show a strong correlation between perceived network norms and individuals’ internalized norms, with engaged citizenship norms significantly predicting both boycott and buycott behaviors. Dutiful norms show no significant association. Structural equation modeling reveals that network influence operates indirectly through internalized engaged norms rather than direct social pressure. The study concludes with practical implications for advocacy groups and public relations practitioners, emphasizing how value-aligned messaging and network-based mobilization strategies can more effectively activate consumer activism.

title: Excess Movement in Option‐Implied Beliefs
abstract: ABSTRACT We derive bounds on the rational variation in option‐implied beliefs about market returns. While risk preferences distort option‐implied (or risk‐neutral ) beliefs away from subjective beliefs, one can nonetheless bound risk‐neutral belief movement under a general assumption on the stochastic discount factor. The resulting test requires no knowledge of the objective distribution and allows significantly more flexibility in discount rates than standard volatility tests. Implementing our test empirically using index options, we find that there is so much movement in risk‐neutral beliefs that the bounds are routinely violated. Our results imply significant excess index‐price volatility.

title: Editorial Board
Pay‐for‐prominence: The (un)intended consequences of monetary incentives on employees' networks and attrition
abstract: Abstract Research Summary We introduce the concept of pay‐for‐prominence , a system where employees are monetarily incentivized to become knowledge hubs in the intrafirm network and examine its effects on employees' networks and attrition. Integrating social network theory with relational incentives theory, we argue that pay‐for‐prominence motivates strategic networking behaviors that lead to the emergence of prominent connectors. However, these changes are associated with higher attrition as employees are preoccupied with networking, thus suggesting a trade‐off between enhanced connectivity in the short term and the risk of network fragmentation in the long term. Using a field quasi‐experiment in a multinational firm, we show that organizations can successfully incentivize employees' network prominence, but doing so may produce unintended consequences. Managerial Summary We examine the impact of using monetary incentives to encourage employees to become knowledge hubs in the workplace informal network—a term we label pay‐for‐prominence. We find that offering monetary rewards based on network metrics encourages employees to broaden their connections, enhancing knowledge flows within the firm. However, employees who become more socially prominent experience higher attrition than those who do not, as they become preoccupied with networking. Therefore, while incentivizing networking can improve knowledge sharing, it also requires careful management to avoid unintended consequences, such as the exit of key players that could cause fragmentation of the social network. Managers should weigh the benefits of increased connectivity against the risks of fragmentation when designing incentive programs aimed at fostering informal networks.

title: Auditors' Response to Clients' Cyber Breaches: A Human‐Capital Perspective
abstract: ABSTRACT Using online job postings data, we explore whether auditors adjust their human capital in response to clients' cyber breach incidents. We find that audit offices increase their demand for cybersecurity specialists after their clients' cyber breaches, implying that cyber breaches change not only client risk but also their auditor's production function. Consistent with expectations, we document that this impact is larger when breaches involve their own clients (rather than those of peer offices within the same audit firm) and when breaches directly involve financial information. Our evidence holds for both cyber‐focused and non‐cyber‐focused offices, highlighting the broad impact of cybersecurity risks on audit practices. Additionally, we find that audit offices with relatively high investment in cybersecurity human capital are better able to preserve their market share among clients in high‐cyber‐risk industries after a client's cyber breach.

title: Do entrepreneurs live longer? A Cox survival analysis of entrepreneurship and lifespan
It's in the Small Steps: Navigating Knotted Change‐Stability Tensions in Complex Collaborations
abstract: Abstract Addressing societal challenges requires collaborative arrangements that can adapt to changing environments while maintaining coherence. Existing research highlights collaborative responses to change, yet the processes through which such responses emerge remain poorly understood. Notably, collaborative change involves not only balancing change and stability but also navigating knotted collective‐individual tensions that arise in realigning interests, coordination structures, and operations. To advance understanding of these dynamics, we conduct an in‐depth longitudinal study of collaborative change in a cross‐sector disaster relief partnership. Across successive change stages, we identify stability drivers emerging from collective‐individual tensions that prompted the partners to adopt specific balancing practices. These practices enabled a change process that was incremental and fragile in progression, yet resilient in its cumulative pattern. We develop a process model that explains the dynamics of collaborative change and shows how balancing change and stability enables partners to progressively broaden and occasionally transcend collective‐individual alignment as trust and mutual understanding deepen. This study advances collaboration and paradox theory by exposing balancing practices tailored to collaborative settings that enable adaptation in dynamic environments and by proposing a gradual approach to navigating knotted paradoxes.

title: Closer to the leader, above the coworkers? How leader gratitude expression shapes employee responses across relational targets
journal_name: Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes

title: Generative AI and the ability of entrepreneurial opportunities to generate sustained competitive advantages
abstract: Abstract Research Summary This paper examines how generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) affects the ability of entrepreneurial opportunities to generate sustained competitive advantage. We argue that GenAI's impact is conditional on how those opportunities are formed. Discovery opportunities originate from exogenous industry shocks. However, widely available GenAI tools are likely to commoditize opportunity recognition in these settings and thus reduce advantages that might have been generated by exploiting these opportunities. Creation opportunities emerge endogenously, under conditions of Knightian uncertainty, through entrepreneurial action and interaction with the environment. However, GenAI cannot fully resolve the Knightian uncertainty inherent in creation settings, so sustained advantage here depends on whether resources and capabilities developed through creating an opportunity are inimitable. Unawareness opportunities rely on competitive neglect. GenAI may reduce the advantages of firms in these settings when it makes rents legible to potential competitors and when search is directed toward these invisible markets. Managerial Summary Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools like ChatGPT and Claude help entrepreneurs spot opportunities, but every competitor can potentially access the same tools. Whether GenAI can create sustained competitive advantages, this paper argues, depends on how an opportunity is formed. When opportunities arise from entrepreneurs noticing an external market shift, GenAI levels the playing field by commoditizing recognition and pushes entrepreneurs to win through execution and hard‐to‐copy complements. When opportunities are created through actions and interactions of entrepreneurs with their environments, GenAI does not fully remove the uncertainty that makes these efforts entrepreneurial but can speed up experimentation. When opportunities emerge from entrepreneurs operating in markets neglected by competitors, GenAI may have a limited effect on advantage unless it makes invisible markets publicly known.

title: Threat perception, issue knowledge, and citizen coproduction preferences: evidence from a national public survey on environmental health
abstract: Building on the literature on citizen coproduction, this study examines how threat perception and issue knowledge influence individual citizens’ coproduction preferences in the issue domain of environmental health. Drawing on prior research, we propose a conceptual framework and derive theoretical expectations about the relationships between threat perception, issue knowledge, and citizens’ willingness to engage in coproduction. Empirically, we use data from a nationally representative public survey (N = 1,207) to test our hypotheses. Across multiple model specifications and robustness checks, the regression results consistently support our expectations: holding other factors constant, individuals who perceive greater threats and those who possess more issue knowledge tend to express stronger willingness to participate in co-planning and co-investment activities with public entities. In conclusion, we discuss the study’s key contributions, directions for future research, and practical implications for environmental health policy and management.

title: The blurred line between ends and means: how frontline workers factor production attributes into results in performance evaluations
abstract: Results-based performance management assumes that organizational performance can be evaluated by defining and measuring desired results. Yet frontline workers, who translate performance goals into service delivery, may interpret results through their knowledge of how services are produced. We examine whether production attributes enter frontline evaluations of formal results. Drawing on theories of sensemaking and cognitive judgment, we argue that task difficulty and effort provide salient cues through which frontline workers contextualize performance information. We test these expectations using a conjoint survey experiment with 1,371 Danish high school teachers, randomly varying production attributes alongside formal results. Teachers rate schools serving more disadvantaged students more favorably and increase ratings when schools demonstrate greater effort. Both effects exhibit clear dose-response patterns, with effort effects comparable to those of formal results. The findings show that frontline evaluations systematically incorporate production information, revealing how performance management can generate divergent understandings of organizational performance.

title: Assessing performance in collaborative governance networks: testing the Productivity Performance Matrix
abstract: Performance measurement for collaborative governance presents significant challenges both practically and theoretically. With the goal of refining theory grounded in empirical application, we use Emerson and Nabatchi’s Productivity Performance Matrix and their Integrative Framework for Collaborative Governance, to examine data from a five-year longitudinal comparative case study of collaborative governance regimes (CGRs) in three European cities.Our research showed that the indicators of the Productivity Performance Matrix (PPM) had significant relevance to actual performance outcomes observed in the CGRs studied, albeit with some modifications. Proposed modifications include removing the ‘participant organization’ as a distinct level of analysis in network-centred evaluations, reconceptualization of equity as ‘perceived equity’, distinguishing between internal and external legitimacy, and shifting from ‘sustainability’ to ‘systemic change’ as a performance indicator for adaptation. The refinement of performance indicators and the improved conceptual coherence between the PPM and the Integrative Framework are the primary contributions of this work.

title: Impact of Anti‐Money Laundering Enforcement on Suspicious Activity Reporting—Empirical Evidence From Real Estate Agencies in Norway
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper examines the impact of anti‐money laundering (AML) oversight on suspicious activity reports (SARs) filed by real estate agencies in Norway. Using unique data on inspections, sanctions, and confidential SARs, the study estimates the effects of inspections on reporting through a difference‐in‐differences approach. The results show an increase in reporting post‐inspection driven by entities with a low, positive number of prior filings, while report quality remains unchanged. There is no evidence of spillover effects; inspections do not influence the reporting of uninspected entities either geographically close to or affiliated with inspected ones. The findings suggest that AML oversight may create a learning effect for inspected entities but does not lead to sector‐wide improvements beyond local effects. This paper contributes to the modest empirical literature on AML oversight effects and the general literature on regulatory enforcement and provides recommendations for improvements to the AML system.

title: Exceptional Circumstances: Electoral Boundary Conflict in Canada's Territories
abstract: Abstract This article investigates why electoral districting, which across most of Canada was reformed by the “electoral boundary revolution,” is instead increasingly fraught in two northern jurisdictions, the Northwest Territories and Yukon. While independent electoral‐boundary commissions and judicial rulings have depoliticized and professionalized districting elsewhere, the same developments in the territories have sparked lawsuits, legislative rejections, and political crises. Conducting a narrative analysis of a half‐century of legal, legislative, and archival documents, this article identifies three broader sources of territorial districting conflict. First, demographic concentration produces unusually acute urban‐rural tensions. Second, remoteness and small population size create distinctive representational challenges involving community‐of‐interest protection and constituency service. Third and most fundamentally, electoral boundaries have become entangled with unresolved questions of Indigenous self‐determination, constitutional development, and the political character of northern territories themselves. Together, these factors help explain why districting disputes in the North are more frequent, intense, and politically consequential than elsewhere in Canada. The article concludes that territorial districting may require distinctive legal and institutional frameworks capable of accommodating demographic realities, Indigenous rights claims, and the constitutional fluidity of Canada's North.

title: Transforming Canadian Federal Governance in a Polycrisis
abstract: Abstract Since 1995, scientific consensus has linked human activity to climate change, yet the political and financial power of the carbon economy remains entrenched. Under conditions of polycrisis, many states continue to miss emissions targets and, in some cases, retreat from climate commitments. Transformative political will is therefore urgently needed to achieve carbon neutrality. To examine constraints on federal climate action, we conducted interviews with 35 senior governance actors, including former public servants, environmental leaders, quasi‐institutional intermediaries (See footnote at the bottom of the page), and private sector advisors. Their experiences point to persistent governance barriers. Findings suggest the political process remains the primary constraint, shaped by short electoral cycles, policy reversals, limited public engagement, and entrenched financial power. We conceptualize these dynamics as limits to the governability of climate change, highlighting the need for stronger coordination, institutional capacity, and durable governance arrangements to sustain climate action under polycrisis conditions.

title: Structure and agency in emancipatory reform: A blueprint from a Black union
abstract: Abstract The National Labor Convention of 1869, the first of its kind for African American workers, yielded a grand strategy for achieving full emancipation, in which those long subjected to domination might attain durable independence. Drawing upon decades of Black republican thought, this agenda combined macro‐level reforms targeting agrarian and industrial monopolies with micro‐level interventions into the habits of the working class. While the project fell short, its multivalent approach nevertheless offers republican theorists today a framework for better understanding the structural dynamics of domination and how to overcome them.

title: Rejecting authoritarianism: When threats to democracy shape values
abstract: Abstract As politicians with authoritarian tendencies win elections globally, it becomes urgent to understand the social psychological mechanisms underlying support for such candidates. Prior research identifies authoritarianism as a likely predictor of vote choice. Contrary to views of authoritarian parenting as a stable, exogenous disposition, however, we argue that such attitudes can also evolve during campaigns, as voters take cues from elites. Analyzing AmericasBarometer data and a five‐wave panel study, this paper assesses authoritarian parenting values over Brazil's 2018 presidential campaign. Consistent with prior literature, authoritarian parenting attitudes early in the campaign predict who supported and opposed the authoritarian candidate Bolsonaro. However, these attitudes change over the campaign. This polarization is asymmetric, limited to Bolsonaro's opponents, who become increasingly anti‐authoritarian. The results illuminate how polities can resist authoritarian leaders and call for a reconsideration of authoritarianism in the public.

title: Relative affluence and mental health: Evidence from quasi-random class assignments
Review of “Family Legal Vulnerability: How Immigration Policy Shapes the Lives of Latino College Students”
abstract: Family Legal Vulnerability: How Immigration Policy Shapes the Lives of Latino College Students is an important contribution to immigration studies. To date, most research in this area has focused separately on young people in college who are undocumented or US citizens of undocumented immigrant parents. One of the key contributions of the book is to examine the lives of these young people together to understand how US immigration policy impacts their trajectory to and through college in similar and different ways. While the college students they follow in the book may have different legal statuses, their own and their families’ lives are profoundly shaped by the increasingly anti-immigrant sociopolitical landscape in the United States. The authors argue that while in college, immigration-impacted students, a concept used to capture both those who are the children of undocumented parents and those who are themselves undocumented, must navigate the collective constraints and cascading consequences of immigration policy.

title: Asymmetric behavioural responses to updating caloric information
abstract: Abstract Calorie labels are widely used as an information disclosure policy, yet their behavioural effects remain debated. Across four studies ( N = 2,067), including one nationally representative online sample of the U.S., we examine how individuals adjust portion-size choices after updating misperceptions about meal calorie content. Using more than 45,000 incentivised calorie estimates and 6,000 food choices, we find that food characteristics, not individual traits, better predict misperceptions, and that larger misestimations are associated with extreme portion choices. Portion-size adjustments after a label reveals the caloric content are substantially smaller than the initial estimation errors. Responses are asymmetric: correcting underestimation is associated with larger reductions in portion size than the increases observed after correcting overestimation. Individuals who estimate calories accurately show little to no adjustment. Increases after correcting overestimation are concentrated among healthier foods and lower-conflict eaters. These results highlight asymmetric behavioural responses to disclosed information and suggest that average calorie changes may obscure important heterogeneity.

title: The managed sisterhood: Gendered labor and intimacy in Chinese fashion influencer industry
abstract: As China’s leading multi-channel network (MCN) institutions become increasingly industrialized and bureaucratic, their operations are paradoxically characterized by intensified emotional dynamics. Drawing on ethnographic research within a women-dominated fashion influencer team, this study identifies a sisterhood-based production model that embeds sisterly ties within hierarchical organizational structures. It traces the formation and collapse of this managed sisterhood. By cultivating an illusion of unity and belonging, intimacy makes labor more governable, obscuring coercion while facilitating the mobilization of emotional, aesthetic, and physical capacities. In this way, sisterhood becomes integral to production, intensifying labor and rendering precarity routine. Under platform capitalism, traditional Chinese sisterhood, once grounded in kinship and flexible resistance, is reconfigured into an occupational form of informal labor control, producing “disposable kinship” in which affective bonds become temporary and replaceable. This study challenges dominant political readings of sisterhood and demonstrates how intimacy itself becomes a mechanism of governance within platform capitalism.

title: ‘Dirty work’ in UK television: Ancillary work and the grey zones of creative labour
abstract: UK television ancillary workers, the cleaners, drivers, caterers and security staff who service television productions, occupy a paradoxical position: essential, yet routinely excluded from conceptions of the creative workforce and subjected to inferior working conditions, status and recognition. Drawing on an in-depth mixed-methods study, we argue that specialised ancillary workers should be recognised as part of the television production workforce and given scholarly and industry attention. We apply the sociological concept of ‘dirty work’ to creative labour, adapting it into our understanding of the ‘grey zones’ of creative work: marginalised, peripheral forms of work overlooked by academic and policy frameworks. We engage with media and cultural industries approaches to show how a narrow focus on those designated ‘creative’ workers reproduces existing class hierarchies. The article calls for a broader, more inclusive research agenda as a matter of social justice and scholarly responsibility. The findings highlight pervasive issues faced by ancillary workers, including long hours, low pay, lack of basic amenities and lack of respect, alongside their own perspectives and identity work. Excluding ancillary work from the creative labour paradigm is analytically and ethically flawed, and we propose an expanded framework that values all labour in the production process.

title: Dependence or Interdependence? A Folk-Theories Perspective on Journalists’ and Activists’ Mutual Perceptions
abstract: Drawing on folk theories , this study explores how mutual perceptions and experiences shape the journalist–activist relationship. We analyze data from two German interview studies: activists from diverse protest movements ( N = 33) and journalists covering them ( N = 38). Both groups tend to hold simplified views of each other’s work yet apply similar criteria when evaluating “good” journalism/activism and affirm the importance of their roles for democracy. Conflicts often arise from unmet expectations. The study offers insights into how journalism is understood in movement contexts and vice versa. It also clarifies the recently debated boundaries between journalism and activism.

title: Algorithmic Control, Technostress, and Gaming Behavior in China’s Public Sector
“We’re Not Handling Cases, We’re Shaping Lives”: How Lawyers Preserve Professional Authority and Advance Social Responsibility via Moral Identity-Based Client Persuasion
abstract: Professionals are increasingly expected to deliver socially responsible services that protect vulnerable third parties, yet their authority may be threatened when such recommendations appear to conflict with clients’ perceived self-interests and desired end goals. Drawing on a qualitative study of 91 legal cases in China, we examine how lawyers navigate this tension when persuading initially resistant clients to accept socially responsible counsel. We develop a process model of “moral identity-based client persuasion,” a form of relational expertise that enables lawyers to preserve professional authority by reconstructing clients’ desired end goals to incorporate third-party welfare. The process begins with client moral identity discernment, through which lawyers determine whether a client’s moral identity is situationally salient. It unfolds through three linked practices: (1) articulating moral identity threats, (2) providing moral identity affirmations, and (3) legitimizing moral identity enactments. Together, these practices render socially responsible counsel both self-relevant and technically defensible to clients. We further identify three client-level inhibitors of success: insufficient moral identity salience, entangled decision locus, and limited emotional resilience. These findings augment research on professional work by identifying a novel form of relational expertise that mobilizes clients’ personal identities to secure compliance, and extend moral persuasion research into professional service contexts.

title: Breaking the Silence: Developing an Organizational Mental Health Capability
abstract: Organizations invest heavily in mental health resources, yet employee utilization remains strikingly low.
