This disconnect may signal low need but often masks latent demand: the unobserved gap between employees’ mental health needs and their expressed demand for support. Latent demand persists when organizational and individual barriers suppress recognition, access, and permission to seek help, confronting organizations with a capability-building challenge: the conditions sustaining latent demand also suppress the information needed to address it. Because this problem requires organizational adaptation, dynamic capabilities theory offers a starting point. Under latent demand, however, sensing can misread silence as sufficiency, seizing can leave resources unused, and transforming can learn from biased feedback. Integrating dynamic capabilities with positive organizational scholarship, we theorize how organizations develop an organizational mental health capability to recognize, act on, and adapt to employees’ observable and latent needs. We identify positive social capital as the bridging mechanism that scales relational micro-practices into organizational infrastructure through stage-contingent structural, relational, and cognitive pathways, each addressing a binding constraint. Our theory extends dynamic capabilities to contexts where information is suppressed rather than merely noisy, shows how positive organizational scholarship enables capability building under latent demand, and advances a macro-level perspective on workplace mental health.

title: Capital Market Pressure and Racial Inequality in Labor Violations
Enabling Employee Adaptability to Change: The Joint Effect of Compensation Contract and Process Accountability
Do long-term yields help to estimate short-term risk premia?
abstract: We identify a new and important property of affine term structure models: at long maturities, the slope of the term structure of risk premia becomes “almost observable”. Exploiting this property by fitting models to long-maturity data dramatically improves the precision of estimates of risk premia and expected short rates across the term structure. In a Monte Carlo experiment we show that using rates with maturities up to 25 years, rather than 10 years as is standard in the literature, reduces the standard deviation of estimation errors in risk premia, expected short rates and term premia by over 70%. Applying this approach to US Treasury data, we find that variation in expected short rates accounts for a much larger share of variation in yields (and variation in term premia a correspondingly smaller fraction) than in the widely used estimates reported by the Federal Reserve. Accounting for time-variation in yield volatility is key to successful extraction of the risk premium information in long rates. Our approach therefore departs from much of the empirical literature in two important respects: it incorporates long-maturity yields and allows for time-varying yield volatility, whereas most existing studies ignore long-term yields and rely on constant volatility models.

title: Information Transparency, Choice Confidence, and Customer Retention: Field and Laboratory Evidence from Markets for Credence Goods
abstract: How does information transparency affect customer retention in markets where quality is difficult to verify? Conventional wisdom suggests that transparency intensifies price competition and increases customer churn. We challenge this view by showing that acquisition-stage transparency can strengthen retention in markets for credence goods characterized by delayed feedback and persistent uncertainty, where customers revisit their decisions without clear quality signals. We develop a transparency-confidence-retention framework, in which transparency at acquisition builds choice confidence, a psychological switching cost that anchors customers to their initial decisions. Using 83,835 auto insurance contracts from a European insurer and multiple identification strategies, we find that customers acquired through transparent channels are 4.6%–11.8% less likely to churn than those acquired through less transparent channels. A randomized, controlled experiment with 1,515 participants shows that transparency reduces customer churn primarily by strengthening choice confidence rather than increasing conventional switching costs, such as brand trust or product fit. Decomposing transparency into attribute, comparative, and evaluative dimensions reveals that evaluative transparency exerts the strongest influence. Analyses of boundary conditions indicate that the retention effect of transparency is amplified when public and private signals remain congruent with earlier informational cues. These findings reconceptualize transparency as a relational mechanism that fosters decisional assurance and stabilizes retention under quality uncertainty. This paper was accepted by Anindya Ghose, information systems. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2020.02865 .

title: From Bytes to Bites: Examining the Online and Offline Spillover Impacts of Online Food Delivery Platform Subscriptions
abstract: With the rapid expansion of online food delivery (OFD) platforms, subscription models have emerged as a strategic tool to retain users and shape consumption behavior. Despite their growing prevalence, the broader impacts of these subscriptions—both within the OFD sector and across downstream consumer activities—remain underexplored. Leveraging a difference-in-differences approach and a large-scale individual-level transaction data set, we identify a significant shift in consumption from a competing platform to the focal platform following the introduction of a subscription service. This shift did not result in cannibalization; instead, overall food consumption within the OFD market increased. Geospatial analysis shows that subscribers were more likely to engage in offline spillovers, including increased local dining and activity in nearby noncompeting economic sectors. These patterns suggest that subscriptions in physical services, like OFD, not only reshape digital engagement, but also, they influence consumer mobility and stimulate localized economic ecosystems. Mechanistic testing supports the interpretation that these effects are driven by increased variety-seeking behavior for offline restaurants that predominantly serve non-OFD cuisines within a proximal location, suggesting that such behavior is constrained by transportation costs. Overall, this study offers novel insights into how subscription models in physical service platforms can expand market demand, foster crosschannel engagement, and generate positive spillovers in adjacent sectors. The findings offer actionable guidance for platform designers and policymakers to enhance consumer welfare and support local economic vitality. They also provide new evidence for restaurants that additional platform usage costs may be offset by latent economic benefits from heightened consumer engagement. This paper was accepted by D. J. Wu, information systems. Funding: F. J. Costello acknowledges funding by Fundação para a Ciência e a Tecnologia (UID/00124/2025, UID/ PRR/00124/2025, Nova School of Business and Economics DOI: https://doi.org/10.54499/UID/00124/2025 ), UID/PRR2/00124/2025: DOI: https://doi.org/10.54499/UID/PRR2/00124/2025 and LISBOA2030 (DataLab2030 - LISBOA2030-FEDER-01314200). Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.00954 .

title: From Winning to Giving: The Effect of Gold Medals in Crowdsourcing Contests
abstract: We examine how users respond to winning symbolic awards in online crowdsourcing contests. Our setting is a machine learning competition platform that grants symbolic medals to recognize participants’ contest achievements. Employing a regression discontinuity design, we find that gold medal winners participate less in subsequent contests but engage more in prosocial activities, evidenced by a greater volume and length of posts, as well as more substantial and frequent code contributions. In contrast, bronze and silver medals do not seem to exert a significant influence on recipients’ subsequent behaviors. Drawing on self-determination theory and the needs-as-motives hypothesis, we provide evidence that need-driven goal shifting plays an important role in driving the dual effects of gold medals—diminished contest participation but enhanced prosocial contributions. Further analyses reveal that winners with previous competition medals are more likely to favor contributing content over competing again, whereas winners with more prior contribution medals are less inclined to further increase contributions. Moreover, team winners exhibit a lower tendency than solo winners to shift their efforts from competition to contribution. We add to the symbolic awards literature by uncovering a novel goal-shifting effect induced by contest medals, where award receipt redirects user effort from the focal rewarded domain to other forms of platform engagement. This paper was accepted by D. J. Wu, information systems. Funding: Financial support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grants 72032006, W2611101, and 72371192] and the “Digital-Intelligent Operations Risk Management” Innovation and Entrepreneurship Team Project of the Sanqin Talent Special Support Program in Shaanxi Province [2025STD03] is gratefully acknowledged. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.07419 .

title: Why Zoning Is Too Restrictive
abstract: Economists estimate that zoning regulations raise house prices, lower productivity, and reduce aggregate welfare, yet regulations remain widespread. We develop and solve a model in which fragmented zoning authority leads to overly strict regulations: Homeowners impose stricter regulations to mitigate local congestion but fail to internalize the broader impact on metro-wide affordability. Empirically, the Herfindahl-Hirschman index of local governments explains 12% of the variation in zoning restrictiveness. Using an instrument based on 19th-century municipal fragmentation, we show that greater fragmentation leads to stricter zoning and higher housing costs. These findings suggest that centralizing zoning decisions could alleviate housing affordability challenges. This paper was accepted by Lukas Schmid, finance. Funding: This work was supported by the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada [Grant AWD-027881 SSHRC 2023]. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.02844 .

title: Women’s Approachability Premium in Sales: A Field Experiment Among Microentrepreneurs
Serial or Parallel? Sublexical Scanpath Analysis of Eye-movement Sequences in Single Word Reading
abstract: Are the letters of a written word processed sequentially or in parallel? Despite an abundance of research on visual word recognition, the evidence in this longstanding debate rests almost entirely on indirect inferences from word-length effects and conventional whole-word eye-movement measures. We sought direct evidence on the serial-parallel question by investigating sublexical gaze-fixation sequences—so-called scanpaths . This study is the first to apply scanpath analysis to fixation sequences within single words. Thirty-four Hebrew-speaking adult university students read aloud three-letter and five-letter real words and pseudowords while their eye movements were tracked. As expected, real words showed more parallel processing, whereas pseudowords displayed more sequential, letter-by-letter scanpaths. Surprisingly, longer words tended to elicit serial processing regardless of word familiarity. Our findings support the applicability of scanpath analysis in visual word recognition and its potential to open up new perspectives on word-recognition processes.

title: Everything everywhere all‐at‐once? AI , expertise–output decoupling, and new entrepreneurial strategy trade‐offs in the age of abundance
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Generative AI democratizes entrepreneurship by lowering barriers to ideation, creating an environment of abundance. Yet while AI produces speed, scale, and local autonomy, these benefits may come at hidden costs to output quality. Using illustrative vignettes to ground and elaborate, we particularly identify explainability, traceability, and generalizability as costs of abundance. As AI separates observable output from the expertise traditionally required to produce it, the entrepreneur's attention to evaluation becomes the scarce resource. We identify three trade‐offs and their interdependencies for entrepreneurs: speed‐to‐understanding, scale‐to‐oversight, and local autonomy‐to‐system‐wide relevance. Implications for human accountability of AI systems and governance (organizational design) challenges for entrepreneurs are discussed. Managerial Summary AI allows entrepreneurial firms to produce ideas and other outputs faster and at greater scale than ever before. As AI separates output from the expertise traditionally gained while creating it, the scarce resource shifts from generation to evaluation. This creates new managerial tensions: speed versus understanding, scale versus oversight, and local autonomy versus system‐wide relevance. These tensions help explain concerns about AI “going rogue”: simply keeping a human in the loop is not enough if the human expertise no longer includes the ability to understand, trace, question, and override the system. Entrepreneurs are challenged to design organizations that preserve meaningful human expertise and accountability.

title: Balancing Workplace Demands Against Employee Wellbeing for Street Level Bureaucrats: The Intricate Interrelationships Between Psychological Capital, Burnout, Discretionary Power, Work Harassment and Wellbeing
abstract: This study integrates Behavioural Public Administration (BPA) and Conservation of Resources (COR) theories to undertake a deep dive into understanding the personal, contextual and organisational complexities correlated by the discretionary power of Street Level Bureaucrats (SLBs). Survey panel data at two time points, with a 4-week time lag, were obtained and included 259 healthcare SLBs in Australia. SEM was used to analysis the data. The results show that burnout and institutional work harassment fully mediate the relationship between PsyCap and employee wellbeing, with the variance explaining more than half of SLBs’ wellbeing. The implication for SLBs research is that combining BPA and COR theories provide a useful platform for examining the previously hidden psychological impacts on SLBs outcomes. The implications for those who manage SLBs is that training and performance managing implemented to achieve increased wellbeing will require a change towards reducing employee burnout , and a fundamental redeveloped of the resourcing models that assume institutional work harassment is ethically, legally or prosocially appropriate.

title: The Hidden Upside of Tech Challenges
abstract: The stresses of technological roadblocks and challenges can result in employee ambivalence and easily lead to disengagement. But tech stress isn’t always bad. New research shows that increasing constructive technology challenges offers employees engaging growth opportunities — if annoying tech hindrances have already been mitigated. The researchers share a three-part approach for creating a stimulating work environment while minimizing tech hurdles and employee ambivalence.

title: Constitutionally Bounded Sequential Incrementalism: Criminal Justice Reform and Prosecutorial Governance in Comparative Perspective
abstract: This study explains why criminal justice and prosecutorial reform often proceeds through gradual institutional adjustment rather than radical replacement despite severe politicization and legitimacy crises. Drawing on historical institutionalism, comparative judicial politics, legitimacy research, and prosecutorial-governance scholarship, it develops the concept of “constitutionally bounded sequential incrementalism,” in which constitutional constraints, bureaucratic embeddedness, and professional authority channel reform pressure into sequential layering and conversion. South Korea is the primary case, examined through comparative historical analysis and process tracing, with the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Japan, the United States, and Italy as structured reference cases. A brief Latin American comparison clarifies the concept’s scope conditions. The analysis shows that politicization increases reform pressure, but institutional constraints and implementation capacity shape reform outcomes. The study contributes by explaining when and why criminal justice reform follows recurring patterns of constrained institutional adaptation.

title: Social and Behavioral Effects of Decentralization on Health Services Delivery: Evidence from the Honduran Health Sector
abstract: Decentralization is widely promoted to improve local service delivery, yet evidence on frontline officials’ behavioral role remains limited. We study Honduras’ health-sector reform using lab-in-the-field experiments with 240 officials across 31 matched municipalities and administrative data on maternal health services, examining four behavioral mechanisms—motivation, cooperation, coordination, and trust—via linear regression and fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis. Decentralized settings show higher motivation and cooperation, and greater provision of prenatal, follow-up, and postpartum services. Decentralization acts as a necessary enabling condition across maternal-care stages, though mechanisms vary by outcome: early uptake aligns with motivation, later stages with multiple configurations, demonstrating equifinality. Decentralization thus operates less as a single causal lever than as a modifier of the institutional environment enabling behavioral pathways. Motivational gains stem primarily from new-hire selection, while cooperation benefits both new and existing staff. Institutional trust appears unaffected, suggesting it responds to longer time horizons than other mechanisms.

title: Environmental Policy Capacities in Local Governments. The Case of Chilean Municipalities
abstract: This article examines the uneven development of environmental policy capacities among Chilean municipalities. Drawing on the policy capacities framework, we distinguish operative, analytical, and political capacities and measure them through the first nationwide survey exclusively focused on municipal environmental management (84.6% response rate). We construct composite indicators for each capacity and an integrated index to map territorial patterns and internal imbalances. Regression models combining survey and administrative data assess variation in municipal policy capacity. Results reveal substantial subnational inequality: the size of the municipal administration is the most robust predictor, whereas general fiscal resources show no consistent effect. Civic density is positively associated with capacity, particularly its political dimension, while extractive industry presence is negatively associated with operative capacity. Environmental and economic pressures do not automatically generate capacity; their effects are conditional on municipal resources and context. Environmental policy capacity thus depends on organizational endowments and state–society relations across territories.

title: Policy as Punchline: Algorithmic Attention and the Public Communication of Policy
abstract: In the run-up to the 2025 New York City mayoral election, a candidate waded into the winter Atlantic at Coney Island in an inexpensive suit and, on emerging, delivered a single line: he was there t...

title: Which costs loom largest? How public employees view the relationship between administrative burdens and performance
abstract: Although research on administrative burdens has mainly focused on clients’ experiences, burdens also matter to employees in public bureaucracies. In this study, we examine how burdens shape public workers’ experiences, focusing on how they perceive the relationship between administrative burdens and performance. Using a choice experiment with 21,301 public healthcare professionals, this study estimates the relative causal impact of different costs embedded in job procedures on the perceived performance of a given work situation. Psychological costs exert the strongest causal impact on perceived performance, with stressful procedures having the largest negative effect, followed by procedures that diminish autonomy. Learning costs (stemming from complex or confusing procedures) and compliance costs (arising from time-consuming or effortful tasks) also lead to lower perceived performance, though to a lesser extent. Heterogeneous effects show that the negative impact of administrative burdens on performance is larger for medical doctors and less so for nurses, for those under-fifty, and for male professionals.

title: How governance configurations shape subjective well-being: Evidence from cross-national data
abstract: Subjective well-being (SWB) has become an important indicator of societal progress in cross-national research, yet substantial variation persists even among countries with similar levels of economic development. Existing studies increasingly recognize the role of governance quality in shaping well-being outcomes but often rely on linear models and average effects that overlook institutional heterogeneity across countries. This study uses cross-national panel data covering 163 countries from 2011 to 2024 to examine how governance indicators relate to SWB. Drawing on complexity-oriented and configurational perspectives, we conceptualize governance as a multidimensional system and classify countries into four institutional configurations based on government effectiveness and voice and accountability. Using ensemble models with SHapley Additive exPlanations-based attribution, we find that SWB can be predicted with high accuracy. While economic conditions remain fundamental predictors, the relative salience of governance indicators differs across institutional contexts. In governance-deficit settings, government effectiveness serves as the primary governance predictor, suggesting that output-based performance is particularly relevant where institutional capacity is weak. In capacity-dominant regimes, economic conditions dominate. In balanced regimes, voice and accountability and rule of law gain prominence, reflecting a shift toward input-based legitimacy. During the COVID-19 pandemic, this pattern intensifies: Rights-based and procedural indicators become the leading predictors, suggesting that procedural safeguards gain salience under crisis conditions. These results suggest that the governance–well-being relationship is not universal or additive; rather, it varies across institutional contexts and shows non-linear patterns. This supports a configurational perspective and highlights the need to align policy priorities with countries’ institutional configurations. Points to practitioners This study highlights that governance reforms should be tailored to institutional context rather than following a uniform template. In settings with weak administrative capacity, prioritizing basic service delivery and government effectiveness is essential for well-being. Where administrative capacity exists but accountability mechanisms are limited, strengthening economic security and labor market resilience may yield greater returns. In contexts with open participation but limited capacity, anti-corruption efforts and procedural transparency become central. Where both capacity and accountability are relatively strong, reforms should emphasize participatory and legal-procedural dimensions. These findings underscore that aligning policy priorities with a country's institutional configuration is critical for improving societal well-being.

title: Expectations, Reputation, and Accountability in Scandals: A Configurational Analysis of 15 Cases in China
abstract: ABSTRACT Social media has emerged as a powerful instrument enabling citizens to reveal misconduct and improper actions of government officials, with such scandals frequently attracting significant public scrutiny. Nonetheless, the extant scholarly literature offers limited insight into the account‐holding decisions made by local governments to manage and respond to these scandals. By integrating principal‐agent theory and reputation management theory, this research employs the Qualitative Comparative Analysis method to investigate 15 scandals involving government officials that were publicized on Chinese social media platforms. Our study has identified two mechanisms, namely the political signaling mechanism and the reputation‐restoration mechanism, in explaining the high strength of accountability of Chinese local governments in governing scandals involving government officials. Moreover, our findings highlight one primary factor, performance‐reputation threats, as an essential determinant of local governments' adoption of stringent account‐holding measures in response to these incidents. This study advances accountability theory and deepens understanding of how local governments in China strategically deploy sanctions to manage scandals and preserve legitimacy through accountability.

title: Nudging citizens to use chatbots: an information and default option approach
abstract: Governments are increasingly adopting chatbots to reduce administrative burdens and improve service quality, yet citizens’ willingness to use them remains limited. Drawing on nudge theory, this study examines how information framing and default options influence citizens’ willingness to use chatbots in public services. Using a survey experiment in China, the results show that participants exposed to a loss frame were more willing to use chatbots than those exposed to a gain frame. The default option alone did not significantly affect willingness. However, the interaction between information framing and default settings was significant. Specifically, the positive effect of loss-framed information on citizens’ willingness to use chatbots was stronger when a default option was presented, suggesting that defaults amplify the effect of loss framing. Overall, the study offers practical insights into designing strategies to promote chatbot adoption in public services.

title: “A bridge over troubled water?”: conceptualizing third parties’ involvement in administrative burden
abstract: Abstract While the mediating role of third-party actors in shaping administrative burdens has gained growing recognition, their theoretical conceptualization remains underdeveloped. Through a two-stage deductive-inductive process combining conceptual synthesis from the administrative burden literature with an illustrative case study of the Israeli disability benefits system, this article proposes a multidimensional analytical framework for understanding third-party actors in administrative burden contexts. The article identifies three core dimensions characterizing third-party actors: their functional role (agents, service providers, verifiers, and reformers); their level of formality (formal, semi-formal, and informal); and their institutional position (state, non-state, and hybrid). Together, these dimensions provide a systematic understanding of the varied mechanisms through which third parties shape burdensome citizens’ encounters, extending administrative burden beyond the citizen-state dyad and widening the definition of who counts as a third party.
journal_name: Perspectives on Public Management and Governance

title: To protect or empower? A critical exploration of legislators’ views on social media user agency
abstract: Empowering citizens by enhancing their agency is a cornerstone of human rights theory, yet it is unclear whether today’s governments afford human agency the same primacy online (i.e. user agency) as offline. Laws combating social media harms are especially consequential for user agency. Such regulations aim to make the online sphere safer, but how policymakers weigh empowering users against protecting them is often unclear. This project analyzes the formation of Ireland’s Online Safety and Media Regulation Act (OSMR) of 2022. Through a critical frame analysis of 15 legislative debates, it finds that Irish legislators predominantly framed social media users as needing protection and, for the most part, did not seek to empower them. Instead, legislators often presented themselves as victims of harm and made ambiguous statements about whom OSMR served. Such findings reveal a lack of consideration for users’ agency and underscore the need for meaningful user engagement in policymaking.

title: Correction to “Forgive Us Our Sins—Experimental Evidence on Arrears Forgiveness and Bill Payment From Nairobi, Kenya”
abstract: Fuente, D., R. Mulwa, M. Mwaura, J. Gitu, and J. Cook. 2026. “Forgive Us Our Sins—Experimental Evidence on Arrears Forgiveness and Bill Payment From Nairobi, Kenya.” Journal of Policy Analysis and Management 45, no. 4: e70132. https://doi.org/10.1002/pam.70132. We apologize for this error.
journal_name: Journal of Policy Analysis and Management

title: The Promise of Multistakeholderism: Transnational Influence and Legitimacy at the Internet Governance Forum
abstract: ABSTRACT Multistakeholderism is widely regarded as a means to ensure equal representation for stakeholders, promote democratic processes, and enable effective governance. Given the interconnected nature of the internet, much of global internet governance is influenced by multistakeholder approaches with a prominent role of transnational actors. This raises questions about the effects of transnational influence on the legitimacy of multistakeholder internet governance. Therefore, this article explores how transnational influence affects the input, throughput, and output legitimacy of the Internet Governance Forum (IGF), a key node within the internet governance ecosystem. The analysis combines qualitative content analysis of 600 statements made during cybersecurity governance debates at the IGF from 2016 to 2023 with 18 expert interviews. The findings reveal that transnational actors affect the IGF's legitimacy unevenly, producing both legitimacy gains and legitimacy deficits. Broad stakeholder participation contributes to high levels of input legitimacy, yet the prominence of specific transnational actors in panel discussions and policy contributions raises concerns regarding throughput legitimacy, reflecting persistent inequalities in access, resources, and visibility. While transnational actors' contributions significantly shape IGF policy outcomes, their influence is disproportionately concentrated among Global North actors. This article contributes to scholarship on transnational influence, the legitimacy of international organizations, and multistakeholderism.

title: Concern vs control: a public servant’s guide to impact
abstract: Public servants operate in a complex working environment, navigating 40 distinct factors while striving to create public value through their policy practices. This paper applies Covey’s Circles of Concern framework, a longstanding and widely regarded management approach, to explain how public servants can better control these influences upon their policy practice. In doing so it provides a guide for how public servant can enhance their ability to drive desirable public outcomes. Building on Covey’s argument that focussing on what you can control will lead to greater impact, the article argues public servants will enhance their capability to deliver public objectives if they first master the factors within their reach. This mastery will enable them to influence the expression of those factors as opportunities rather than barriers to public value creation. The paper finds individuals who recognize the constellation of factors and actively work on those within their control, will likely be more effective public servants and policy entrepreneurs.

title: Authorization environments for climate policy: a public value–based typology across countries
Understanding the influence of education and training on policy analytical capacity development
Industrial policy in times of market power
abstract: We explore the effects of different industrial policies in a macroeconomic agent-based model calibrated to reproduce the decline in US business dynamism over the last half-century. R&D subsidies to innovators raise GDP growth but exacerbate the trend toward rising market power, while financial subsidies to adopters and standard capital-replacement schemes have negligible aggregate effects. A meaningful reversal of market power emerges only when innovation support is paired with adoption-oriented measures that relax the knowledge constraints of small adopters, e.g. the establishment of a National Competence Center providing technology transfer and knowledge upgrading. The effectiveness of each policy is dependent on the underlying technological regime: the growth–dynamism trade-off is sharpest in science-based regimes and attenuated in scale-intensive and supplier-dominated ones.

title: Editorial Board
Learning traps
abstract: Abstract When constituents are uncertain about whether leaders' policy preferences align with their interests, policy choices generate a trade‐off between payoffs and information. Leaders can experiment with their preferred policy, but if the outcome is bad, constituents learn this and threaten office removal. I use a repeated model of political agency to analyze how this trade‐off shapes long‐lived, term‐unlimited leaders' policy choices. When there is uncertainty about the optimal policy for constituents, leaders implement “learning traps”: spatially intermediate policies that halt learning about what the best policy is. They experiment only when their preferences are very likely to be aligned with constituents, a contrast to the “gambling for resurrection” logic ubiquitous in the literature. I provide a case study that examines how the 1861 reforms ending Serfdom in Imperial Russia represented the logic of a “learning trap” and illustrate additional applications of the model to political contagion and economic policymaking.

title: National Narratives in Comparative Politics: Theories, Methods, and Insights From Asia
abstract: In this introduction to the special issue, we define and explore the concept of national narratives in East and Southeast Asia. First, we define national narratives as collectively shared stories about a nation’s origins, boundaries and purposes. Second, we discuss three undertheorized elements of the narrative: the identity of the storyteller, the content of the stories, and contestation over the dominant narrative. Finally, we assess some methodological and measurement challenges in the literature before introducing the papers in this special issue. Drawing on cases from China, Vietnam, Indonesia, South Korea, Taiwan, Myanmar and the Philippines, we address questions related to the construction of personality cults and colonial memory. We also discuss how democratization impacts the identity of the storytellers, and how this impacts views on national boundaries and political violence.

title: National identity in Africa: peace, democracy, and everyday national narratives
abstract: For decades, the literature on sub-Saharan African democratization has been haunted by a structuralist dilemma: how can stable democratic systems take root in states characterized by deep ethnic fr...

title: The Medieval Peace Dividend: Post-Alfredian Anglo-Saxon State Formation, Political Networks, and Peace
Breaking the Conflict Trap: Nonviolent Mobilization and the Recurrence of Civil War
Economic Statecraft Trumps Ideology: Experimental Evidence on US Sanctions against Chinese Investment
Making Sense of Disrupted International Order
The Weight of the Law: How International Law Affects Foreign Policy Preferences
Putting your money where your mouth is: Expressions of Chinese nationalist sentiments are not just cheap talk
abstract: Abstract Do nationalist expressions reflect a willingness to pay costs or are they cheap talk? This is important because theories expect nationalism affects a wide range of outcomes that pose costs to participants, including international conflict and participation in boycotts. However, past research has either relied on self‐reports that cannot rule out cheap talk or outcome measures at higher levels of analysis, such as international trade flows, that do not directly link individual‐level nationalist sentiment to behavior. In contrast, we measure both nationalist sentiments and costly behavior on an individual level using the content of millions of Chinese social media posts and the nationality of the brand of users' devices, for example type of cellphone, as a costly behavioral measure. We find that nationalist sentiment makes citizens less likely to use US and Japanese brands with an instrumental variable analysis.

title: Announcements
Same Race, Different Paths: Socialization, Orientation, and the Black Partisan Gender Gap
abstract: Abstract Black women have long anchored Black political cohesion, yet little explains why a gender gap persists within a group marked by strong Democratic loyalty. Drawing on historical and sociological work, we argue that Black women’s collective-first orientation—shaped by gendered social roles across enslavement, Jim Crow, and modern civic life—heightens the political significance of the antecedents of Black Democratic partisanship: racial identity salience, perceived discrimination, and racially homogenous social networks. Using an original national survey of 4,200 Black Americans, we find that the partisan gender gap widens because the composition of their social networks more strongly shapes Black women’s political preferences. Accounting for racial identity salience and perceived discrimination substantially reduces the gender gap. These findings illuminate how racialized gender roles structure the pathways through which group-based norms translate into partisan behavior, providing a mechanism for intragroup variation and guiding more nuanced strategies for political engagement and mobilization.

title: Rising inequality, declining mobility: The evolution of intergenerational mobility in Germany
Crime and Prices:Thefts of expensive precious metals from cars
abstract: Whether economic incentives matter for crime is studied in a novel way, from expensive precious metal thefts by thieves stealing catalytic converters from cars. Sharp and sizable variations in the prices of precious metals embedded in converters are combined with newly assembled U.S. crime data. Precipitously fast increases in precious metal prices generated a sizeable rise in auto-part thefts, while subsequent price declines and policy responses quickly reversed this pattern. The resulting boom-and-bust dynamics provide clean evidence that prices affect crime, and for these crimes that local resale infrastructure and target availability shape both the magnitude of this effect and the effectiveness of policy response.

title: Optimal Flood Insurance in a Second-Best World: Fiscal Spillovers, Reclassification Risk, and Moral Hazard
abstract: Abstract Intensifying climate change makes protection against natural disaster risk – either through ex ante insurance or ex post aid – a first-order public policy issue. Flood risk protection in the U.S. traditionally featured ex post aid through FEMA and heavily subsidized insurance through the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP). In an effort to correct subsidy-induced overbuilding and under-mitigation in flood-prone areas, the NFIP recently moved to actuarially fair insurance premiums. But this change has two unintended consequences: a fiscal spillover onto FEMA disaster aid as insurance coverage declines in flood-prone areas, and household exposure to uninsurable reclassification risk from uncertain climate projections. We develop a model of optimal flood insurance that incorporates the static and dynamic tradeoffs of subsidizing premiums. We then use a variety of identification strategies and data to estimate the five key parameters needed to implement this model. We find that the fiscal spillover and reclassification risk protection benefits significantly outweigh the moral hazard costs, and that the optimal subsidy to flood insurance is 51%, comparable to the level of subsidization before the recent reform.

title: How New Products Enter Markets: Social Networks, Consumer Imports, and Retailer Learning
abstract: Abstract This paper studies how new varieties enter markets and become locally available. We provide causal evidence of demand externalities that operate in two steps. First, information about new varieties diffuses directly through real-world social ties among consumers. Second, early purchases generate an indirect spillover to firms: local retailers learn from “pioneer” consumers which new varieties are most likely to succeed and adjust their product offerings accordingly. We study this process in the context of direct-to-consumer imports. Using customs records on individuals’ purchases matched to population-wide social networks, international migrant links, and retailer catchment areas, we document economically meaningful demand externalities. Product-specific expenditure shocks abroad transmit through migrant networks and shift which varieties consumers purchase. Leveraging these shocks as a plausibly exogenous source of local demand variation, we show strong peer effects: prior purchases by close neighbors, coworkers, or friends increase an individual’s likelihood of purchasing the same variety, especially for premium and visible goods. We leverage this result to identify an indirect spillover from consumers to firms: retailers are more likely to add a variety to their assortment when it becomes popular among consumers in their catchment area. Combining the instrument with linked consumer–retailer data and a self-conducted retailer survey, we show that this response reflects learning about latent demand for varieties not yet stocked locally. Together, social diffusion and retailer learning generate demand multipliers that reshape local product availability and expand access to global variety.

title: Is American Soft Power a Casualty of the Trade War? Evidence from U.S. Movie Viewership in China
abstract: Abstract The US trade war against China can either enhance or diminish American soft power in China, depending on whether Chinese citizens view it as legitimate. We study how US movie viewership, a measure of American soft power, responds to the trade war. We find a significantly greater reduction in US movie viewership in regions more exposed to the Trump tariffs, but no corresponding decline in non-US movies. The decline is stronger for action and drama movies, which tend to embody greater perceived “Americanness.” Survey data also show a sharper decline in trust in Americans in more tariff-exposed regions.

title: Contracting Structures in Public Procurement: Evidence from Donor-Funded Electrification in Kenya
abstract: Abstract We study how contracting and monitoring structures in public procurement affect large-scale infrastructure construction. Starting in 2016, Kenya’s public electric utility ran competitive auctions and then awarded and administered dozens of procurement contracts to connect millions to electricity. The causal analyses leverage natural and experimental variation and granular, independentlycollected construction quality data. Kenya Power contracts funded by the World Bank featured unbundled contract components known as ‘design-bid-build’ and enhanced monitoring compared to African Development Bank-funded contracts. Unbundling contracts delayed construction progress but improved quality. Randomized inspections improved quality without large delays. Bundled contracting with additional independent monitoring could improve outcomes.

title: Tax Incentives and Return Migration
abstract: Abstract We study how tax incentives affect the return migration of high-skilled expatriates to their home country, exploiting a generous income tax break for returnees in Italy. Using administrative data and a Triple-Difference design, we estimate a migration elasticity to the average net-of-tax rate just below one. Responses are sizable across the upper half of the earnings distribution, indicating that tax-induced migration is not limited to top earners. A cost-benefit analysis reveals that, while costly in the short term, the scheme pays for itself in present value if a sufficiently large fraction of returnees remains after the scheme elapses.

title: How Credible Are the Findings from Online Experiments?
abstract: Abstract Online experiments have surged in popularity, but how credible are their published results? We examine the universe of hypotheses tested on Amazon Mechanical Turk and reported in leading journals between 2010 and 2021. We find evidence of widespread p-hacking, publication bias, and under-powered studies. The extent of the problems varies substantially across fields, with marketing particularly badly afflicted and little evidence of distortion in economics. We explore correlates of increased credibility and compare the online results to laboratory results from the same outlets, finding similar distortions in both, with bunching just above the significance threshold more pronounced on MTurk.

title: Blended Finance and Female Entrepreneurship
abstract: Abstract We study the real and allocative consequences of relaxing gender-specific credit constraints by analyzing a blended finance program designed to expand bank lending to female entrepreneurs in Turkey. Merging credit registry, tax, and matched employer-employee data, we find participating banks raised their credit share to women by over 18%, spanning repeat, poached, and first-time borrowers. Beneficiary firms invest more, grow employment, sales, and profits, diversify their networks, and exit less. Treated banks also expand lending to male entrepreneurs, though the increase is smaller and disproportionately directed toward higher-productivity firms, suggesting reallocation rather than crowding out. District-level effects are absent, reecting the program’s modest scale.

title: Hostility, Population Sorting, and Backwardness: Quasi-Experimental Evidence from the Red Army after WWII
abstract: Abstract How can short episodes of localized hostility shape regional economic trajectories that even amplify over time? I exploit economic differences across the idiosyncratic and short-lived line of contact between the Red Army and the Western Allies in South Austria at the end of WWII. The 74-day hostile presence of the Red Army shaped the age- and occupation-structure via refugee flows, causing amplifying demographic effects over time and backwardness in sector development and tax revenues. My findings also point to the isolated role of the Red Army’s hostile actions after WWII in understanding the European economic East-West divide.

title: Structuring Cash Transfers: Cash Flow Preferences, Seasonality, and Financial Decisions in Rural Kenya
abstract: Abstract We examine the preferences of low-income households in Kenya over the structure of unconditional cash transfers. Most preferred lumpy transfers, and some preferred deferred receipt—in contrast to the typical structures of safety-net programs, but consistent with evidence on the financial challenges of poverty. Turning to consequences, receiving transfers later in the year raised income 1.5 years later—but willingness to defer receipt was sensitive to small changes in cash flow around the time of decision-making. Taken together, these results illustrate how adapting cash transfer design to the decision-making environment of those in poverty could improve financial choices and outcomes.

title: The Equilibrium Effect of Information in Consumer Credit Markets: Public Records and Credit Redistribution
abstract: Abstract Information is central to consumer credit, but little is known about its equilibrium effects. We study a 2017 natural experiment in which non-bankruptcy public records were purged from U.S. credit reports. The large information-removal differences across states allow us to identify equilibrium impacts. Available credit increased for consumers who lost negative information directly. Consistent with our model, available credit declined indirectly for consumers who did not lose the negative information because they could no longer distinguish themselves. The direct and indirect effects nearly canceled, so the net equilibrium effect after a year was nearly zero but with substantial redistribution.

title: Parental Response to Fetal Shocks and Macroeconomic Volatility
abstract: Abstract We examine parental response to a fetal shock using data from 150 Demographic and Health Surveys in 50 developing countries. Focusing on the impact of Ramadan fasting, a common shock experienced by more than a billion Muslims worldwide, we find that children exposed to Ramadan fasting during pregnancy have lower rates of full vaccination for DPT and polio compared to their non-exposed siblings. Further, parents tend to compensate for the fetal shock during booms and reinforce during economic downturns. Our estimations suggest that this has resulted in approximately half a million excess infant deaths over the past three decades.

title: The Female Sensitivity Hypothesis: Evidence From Experimental Economics
abstract: Abstract We assess the empirical evidence for the hypothesis that women more than men respond to changes in treatment. First, we examine whether the results of over two hundred experimental economics papers support the female sensitivity hypothesis. Second, using data from two studies (DellaVigna and Pope, 2022; Exley et al., 2025), we conduct over two hundred pairwise tests of the hypothesis. Both analyses show that gender is not predictive of responsiveness to treatment. We further examine how the hypothesis has been disseminated in the literature and find that it is referenced predominantly by papers that support it.

title: Professional Networks and the Labour Market Assimilation of Immigrants
Cognitive ability, risk preferences and errors
abstract: Abstract In this paper we examine the link between cognitive ability, risk preferences and the errors that people make. We build a unique dataset that contains almost 260,000 decisions made under risk in a variety of tasks by approximately 13,000 individuals, with each person having completed a test designed explicitly to measure their cognitive ability. Our analysis suggests that intelligence has (1) no impact on risk preferences and (2) a robust link to errors. Our results have implications for the development of theories that seek to explain the impact of cognitive ability on decision making.

title: Risk Assessment of an Illegal Laboratory in Reedley, California, Using Geospatial Analysis of Open‐Source Epidemic Intelligence Data
abstract: ABSTRACT An illegal laboratory discovered in Reedley, California, in December 2022 was in a warehouse, operating without a license, handling about a thousand transgenic mice, chemicals, and possibly over 20 pathogens, including vials labeled Ebola, which were never tested but destroyed. This study aimed to estimate epidemic signals around the Reedley illegal laboratory using open‐source epidemic intelligence data. We utilized data from EPIWATCH, from October 2021 to October 2023, a year prior to and a year after the establishment of the illegal laboratory. The spatial pattern of outbreak signals was analyzed using hotspot analysis, and the distances of outbreak signals from the laboratory were measured. In California, an upward trend in outbreak signals of pathogens associated with the laboratory was noted in December 2022, April 2023, and August 2023. In the hotspot analysis, California and eight other states in the United States (US) were identified as hotspots. Narrative evidence revealed the presence of a sick employee working in the laboratory, whose child also became ill. Changes in disease patterns reported in California or the US in the year following the establishment of the illegal laboratory may or may not be linked to the illegal laboratory. A subsequent illegal lab linked to Reedley was identified in Las Vegas in 2026, highlighting the ongoing threat to biosecurity. EPIWATCH geospatial and temporal analysis can enhance the public health risk assessment of threats associated with illegal laboratories, especially when there is no available testing or reporting.

title: Enhancing Democratic Listening in Online Discussions: The Role of Reaction Buttons, Discussion Moderation, and Large Language Models
abstract: Political communication research in general – and research on political online discussions in particular – has previously focused on the exercise of democratic voice and thus largely neglected the complementary practice of democratic listening. Against the backdrop of a wide-spread perception that democratic listening is lacking in online discussions, we investigate whether listening can be strengthened through novel platform affordances. We developed an experimental online written discussion platform with listening-oriented reaction buttons and both human and AI moderation (based on GPT-4). We then conducted an experiment involving n = 740 respondents in 40 discussion groups (N = 4,355 comments), each lasting 30 minutes, covering three experimental conditions and a control condition. We compare the effect of (1) listening-oriented reaction buttons versus (2) a combination of these buttons and listening-oriented human discussion moderation versus (3) a combination of buttons and AI moderation on the level of democratic listening demonstrated in discussants’ textual contributions. We find that listening-oriented buttons alone do not enhance democratic listening. However, when combined with listening-oriented AI moderation, they are associated with a democratic listening rate of 27% within discussions, compared to 21% in the condition without either feature. Our findings lay the basis for the implementation of a combination of listening-oriented buttons and discussion moderation on news media websites, social media apps or dedicated discussion spaces using LLM-based chatbots.

title: Campaigns That Click: Unleashing the Power of Push Notifications on Mobile Apps
abstract: As mobile apps increasingly mediate digital engagement, push notifications have emerged as a key tool for directing user attention, yet systematic evidence on their behavioral and ecosystem-level effects remains limited. Using data from over 200 push campaigns and 60 million user-campaign observations on a leading U.S. mobile-offer marketplace, we combine large-scale observational analyses with controlled experiments to study how push notifications shape user engagement. We find that push notifications significantly increase same-day click-throughs to advertised merchants, with substantial heterogeneity across merchant characteristics, user characteristics, message design, and delivery timing. Beyond focal-merchant responses, notifications are associated with increased engagement with non-advertised merchants both within and across categories, suggesting that push notifications reshape attention across the marketplace ecosystem. Both the large-scale empirical analysis and controlled experiments yield evidence consistent with two complementary mechanisms—content-driven processing of notification information and reminder-based attention activation. The results also identify attentional saturation as a key boundary condition—repeated exposure produces diminishing responsiveness and may even reduce engagement at high notification frequencies. These findings position push notifications as a mobile-native attention-allocation lever that platforms can strategically deploy, while underscoring the need to balance engagement gains against user fatigue and attention costs.

title: Mobile Location-based Recommendation Systems and Local Businesses: Evidence from the Restaurant Industry
abstract: We investigate the impact of mobile location-based recommendation systems (MLBRS) on the performance of local businesses. Leveraging a comprehensive dataset of 16,720 restaurants and quasi-experimental variation generated by the official launch of a leading MLBRS, we employ a 2-Stage Least Squares instrumental-variable framework to estimate the effect of algorithmic exposure on consumer engagement. Our analysis reveals that a 1% increase in exposure is associated with a 0.078% increase in clicks; separately, a 1% increase in clicks is associated with a 0.053% increase in visit intentions. Importantly, the estimated exposure effect is larger for geographically disadvantaged restaurants, but primarily at the discovery stage (clicks). This pattern highlights a boundary condition of MLBRS: algorithmic visibility can aid, but it does not by itself resolve the uncertainty involved in acting on a recommendation. Downstream conversion is stronger when restaurants provide richer digital information and reputation signals, including consumer reviews and owner-curated information such as photos and menus. Auxiliary credit-card sales data from a restricted Seoul subsample provide consistent evidence of a positive association between algorithmic exposure and revenue, suggesting that MLBRS can shape the connection of online recommendations to offline economic outcomes.

title: “Generate” the Future of Work through AI: Empirical Evidence from Online Labor Markets
abstract: Large Language Model (LLM)-based generative AI systems are general-purpose tools capable of augmenting or even automating a wide range of job functions, positioning them to reshape labor market dynamics. However, predicting their precise impact a priori is challenging, given AI’s simultaneous effects on both demand and supply, as well as the strategic responses of market participants. Leveraging an extensive dataset from a leading online labor platform, we document a pronounced displacement effect and an overall contraction in submarkets where required skills closely align with core LLM functionalities. Although demand and supply both decline, the reduction in supply is comparatively smaller, thereby intensifying competition among freelancers. Notably, further analysis shows that this heightened competition is especially pronounced in programming-intensive submarkets. This pattern is attributed to skill-transition effects: by lowering the human-capital barrier to programming, ChatGPT enables incumbent freelancers to enter programming tasks. Moreover, these transitions are not homogeneous, with high-skilled freelancers contributing disproportionately to the shift. Our findings illuminate the multifaceted impacts of general-purpose AI on labor markets, highlighting not only the displacement of certain occupations but also the inducement of skill transitions within the labor supply. These insights offer practical implications for policymakers, platform operators, and workers.

title: Exact Algorithms for Two-Dimensional Knapsack Problems: A Unified Framework with New Benchmark Results
abstract: This paper investigates two-dimensional knapsack problems modeled as the Generalized Two-Dimensional Knapsack Problem (G2KP), a variant not previously studied in the literature. The importance of the G2KP lies in its crucial role in designing Branch-Price-and-Cut (BPC) algorithms for the classical Two-Dimensional Bin-Packing Problem. We propose a novel and effective exact solution framework that incorporates both nonnumerically exact and numerically exact algorithms tailored to G2KP. The framework also achieves state-of-the-art performance on the well-known Two-Dimensional Knapsack Problem (with and without item conflicts) and the Two-Dimensional Orthogonal Packing Problem, solving several previously unsolved instances and establishing new benchmark results. These findings highlight the framework’s potential to inspire algorithmic developments for pricing problems in related BPC methods and higher-dimensional packing problems. To support future research, we make the algorithm code, instance data, and detailed results publicly available. History: Accepted by Andrea Lodi, Area Editor for Design & Analysis of Algorithms–Discrete. Funding: This study was supported by the Natural Science Foundation of China [Grants 72271062, 72671084, and 52575565], Science and Technology Projects in Guangzhou [Grant 2024A04J01019], and the Province Natural Science Fund of Guangdong [Grants 2025A1515011297 and 2024A1515010246]. Supplemental Material: The software that supports the findings of this study is available within the paper and its Supplemental Information ( https://pubsonline.informs.org/doi/suppl/10.1287/ijoc.2025.1423 ) as well as from the IJOC GitHub software repository ( https://github.com/INFORMSJoC/2025.1423 ). The complete IJOC Software and Data Repository is available at https://informsjoc.github.io/ .

title: EXPRESS: The Dark Side of Competition for Market Share: Competitive Pressure May Trigger Corporate Misconduct
abstract: There is an ongoing debate about the role of market share and market share–based competition in shaping corporate behavior and performance. This study advances the discussion by analyzing how a firm’s specific competitive situation drives corporate misconduct and how such misconduct affects future market share. Based on a theory-in-use approach, the authors propose the Theory of Market Share–Based Competitive Pressure (TMCP) and introduce four new market share–based constructs that reflect different dimensions of competitive pressure. Using a global sample of 2,145 firms across 254 industries over 11 years, they find that firms that are closer to market leadership and more closely followed by competitors are more prone to misconduct. The results demonstrate that misconduct systematically weakens the very market positions that created the pressure in the first place, with particularly strong penalties for environmental and governance–related misconduct incidents. Importantly, organizational characteristics such as compensation design, board composition, and marketing capabilities condition the extent to which competition translates into corporate misconduct. Together, these findings demonstrate that while misconduct may appear as a shortcut to defend competitive positions, it ultimately undermines them, and there are ways to reduce incentives for misconduct in the first place.

title: Bargaining and Contract Forms in Distribution Channels: Why Do Slotting Fees Arise and Linear Contracts Persist?
abstract: Two empirical patterns emerge in business-to-business settings, particularly in retail distribution channels such as grocery markets. First, linear contracts are widely observed alongside nonlinear contracts with fixed payments, despite the claimed efficiency advantages of the latter. Second, when fixed payments arise, they often flow from suppliers to retailers (slotting fees) rather than the reverse. We develop and analyze a model of multilateral bargaining in which a supplier negotiates separately with competing retailers to explain these patterns. The key mechanism is a trade-off between two distortions: under linear contracts, wholesale prices reflect bargaining power and can be either above or below the channel-profit-maximizing level, whereas under two-part tariffs, wholesale prices are set to maximize bilateral surplus independently of bargaining power but are systematically too low from an overall channel perspective because of rent shifting across relationships. As a result, neither contractual form uniformly dominates; instead, relative performance depends on how bargaining shapes gains from trade across firms. When bargaining leads to slotting fees, two-part tariffs yield higher channel profits than linear contracts, whereas when it would imply payments from retailers to suppliers, linear contracts may perform better. These findings offer a unified explanation for the persistence of linear contracts alongside two-part tariffs, the direction of fixed payments, and the conditions under which each contractual form is likely to arise. This paper was accepted by Miguel Villas-Boas, marketing. Supplemental Material: The online appendix is available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.03426 .

title: Looking Under the Hood of Commodity Currency Predictability
abstract: This paper revisits the exchange rate predictability of commodity currencies through the lens of market efficiency. Focusing on currencies with strong contemporaneous exposure to commodity prices, we show that changes in country-specific commodity export or import prices predict exchange rate fluctuations both in sample and out of sample. We establish four empirical facts: (i) the sign of the predictive relationship runs counter to standard risk-based explanations; (ii) predictability is concentrated at short horizons; (iii) predictability is driven by a small set of thinly traded currencies; and (iv) even sophisticated speculative traders adjust positions sluggishly in response to commodity price shocks in these currencies. Together, these findings suggest that predictability arises from the slow incorporation of information in less actively traded currencies, which is likely due to liquidity and position-building constraints, rather than from compensation for risk. The results also clarify the sources of commodity-based predictability in carry trade returns. This paper was accepted by Lukas Schmid, finance. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.07249 .

title: Thank You, Now What? How Donors Respond to Calls to Action
Online Allocation with Heterogeneous Supply and Minimum Workload Guarantees
abstract: Keeping Gig Workers Working How should platforms allocate jobs when workers need a minimum amount of work to stay engaged? In their accepted paper, “Online Allocation with Heterogeneous Supply and Minimum Workload Guarantees,” Garud Iyengar and Raghav Singal study this question in online labor marketplaces, where workers differ in quality, capacity, and desired workload. The authors show that intuitive allocation rules can perform poorly. A first-come-first-served policy can favor lower-quality workers, whereas a quality-based greedy policy can cause high-capacity workers to leave when their workload requirements are not met. They develop Tracker, an online policy that combines admission control with a simple target-tracking rule: Each worker is assigned a target workload, and arriving jobs are directed toward workers who are most under their targets. Despite the stochastic nature of demand, the authors establish that Tracker is optimal. Computational experiments calibrated to a real labor marketplace show substantial improvements in allocation quality relative to standard policies, while maintaining workers’ minimum workload guarantees.

title: On the Maximization of Long-Run Conditional Value-at-Risk for Markov Decision Processes
abstract: Optimizing Risk-Seeking Sequential Decisions via Conditional Value-at-Risk Decision makers may exhibit risk-seeking preferences in finance, energy operations, and stochastic resource management, yet corresponding Markov decision process (MDP) theories remain underdeveloped. In this paper, “On the Maximization of Long-Run CVaR for Markov Decision Processes,” Xia, Yu, and Wu investigate infinite-horizon MDPs maximizing long-run conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) for instantaneous rewards. They prove optimality for stationary randomized policies and show deterministic policies may fail; an optimal policy randomizes over at most two actions. By converting the original problem into a minimax saddle point formulation, the authors develop solvable linear programming and globally convergent gradient descent algorithms. Results are further extended to joint mean-CVaR optimization and validated on real-world microgrid scheduling data. This work fills gaps for risk-seeking MDPs and delivers practical computation tools for tail-oriented sequential decision making.

title: Optimize-via-Estimate: How to Make Finite-Sample Corrections for Sampling Uncertainty in Data-Driven Optimization
abstract: We propose a novel procedure for correcting for the effects of sampling and parameter uncertainty in data-driven convex optimization. We consider the data-driven setting wherein the distribution lies in a parametric family with unknown parameter. The decision-maker possesses a historical data set, from which solves a prescriptive solution as a function mapping such a data set to decisions, and measures its out-of-sample performance as an average over data sets of the same size under the sampling distribution. As the parameter is unknown to the decision-maker, we argue that this problem is ill-defined and further prove that there cannot exist solutions generalizably optimal over all parameters. As such, we formulate the problem as a weighted multi-criteria optimization with weights defined by a density (termed ‘prior’) over the uncertain parameter, and call its optimal solution prior optimal. We prove that sufficient conditions for prior optimality reduces to functions of the sufficient statistic of the parametric family, and this function can be solved as a point-wise optima of a corrected function of the original objective, with terms accounting for parameter uncertainty and sampling uncertainty respectively. The correction for sampling interpretation is verified by a close to (but not) zero ex-ante regret against a perfect information oracle in numerical illustrations on the newsvendor and portfolio optimization problems.

title: Real-Time Solution of Quadratic Optimization Problems with Banded Matrices and Indicator Variables
abstract: We consider mixed-integer quadratic optimization problems with banded matrices and indicator variables. These problems arise pervasively in statistical inference problems with time-series data, where the banded matrix captures the temporal relationship of the underlying process. In particular, the problem studied arises in monitoring problems, where the decision-maker wants to detect changes or anomalies. We propose to solve these problems using decision diagrams. In particular we show how to exploit the temporal dependencies to construct exact and approximate decision diagrams. For problems over matrices with bandwidth equal to one, the proposed method runs in polynomial time. Moreover, if the bandwidth and condition number of the matrix is fixed, then we show that the proposed method can be modified to run into an additive approximation scheme. We also describe how to construct the convex hull of the set under study from the decision diagrams, and how to deploy the method online to solve the problems via a shortest path algorithm. Computational experiments show that, for problems with bandwidths less or equal than three, our proposed algorithm compares favorably to a state-of-the-art off-the-shelf solver in the offline setting, and that we are able to solve problems in milliseconds for the online setting.

title: EXPRESS: What Drives Physician Efficiency? Evidence from Emergency Department Operations
abstract: Emergency department (ED) physicians play a critical role in healthcare, serving on the frontline of acute care delivery. Yet increasing demand, resource constraints, and growing patient complexity pose significant challenges to physician efficiency. In this study, we investigate the determinants of ED physician efficiency using a multi-stage framework. First, we apply Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA) to measure individual physician efficiency based on data from 110,325 patient visits at a leading U.S. hospital. Second, we use a Tobit regression model to analyze how physician experience, shift familiarity, and patient severity influence physician efficiency. Third, we conduct comprehensive robustness checks, including omitted variable bias sensitivity analyses, permutation tests, and machine learning-based classification analyses, to address concerns regarding endogeneity and potential model misspecification. Our results show that physician efficiency increases with experience at a diminishing rate. Efficiency also varies with shift familiarity, with the estimated association weakening as physician experience increases. In addition, higher patient severity is associated with lower physician efficiency, consistent with the greater resource demands of caring for more clinically complex patients. This negative association is attenuated for more experienced physicians, suggesting that experienced physicians are better able to maintain efficiency when managing more demanding clinical conditions. Our findings offer actionable recommendations for improving ED operations. Staffing strategies that assign relatively more experienced physicians to higher-severity patients may help maintain physician efficiency, while shift familiarity may inform a scheduling strategy that emphasizes greater scheduling consistency for relatively less experienced physicians and greater flexibility for relatively more experienced physicians. Simulation results further illustrate the potential reductions in physician resource use associated with these strategies. Together, these findings highlight the value of evidence-based physician staffing and scheduling to improve physician efficiency in EDs.

title: EXPRESS: Harnessing Renewable Portfolio Standards for Sustainable Futures: An Empirical Examination of Spillover Effects
abstract: Given the importance of managing industrial energy consumption, setting standards and implementing policies that encourage renewable energy use is crucial for incentivizing sustainable firm practices. Public policy designs must align closely with firms’ environmental policies to help mitigate greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and support a sustainable future. While research on policy impacts on firm environmental performance and the supply chain's role in sustainability is growing, a critical, understudied effect is the spillover of government rules to supply chain partners and peer firms, especially those outside the direct purview of environmental regulations. This paper presents a novel approach that integrates data from the Carbon Disclosure Project (CDP) and the Renewable Portfolio Standards (RPS). The latter refers to state-driven initiatives that incentivize electricity consumption from eligible renewable resources. We examine the causal effects of state-level policies on firm-level GHG emission intensity, with particular emphasis on the spillover effects of policies on unregulated firms across markets. We break down emission intensity into Scope 1 and Scope 2 and capture facility-level data to analyze spillover effects in granular detail. Using a staggered difference-in-differences methodology, our analysis finds a promising negative association between RPS introduction and GHG emission intensity among unregulated firms across industries. Interestingly, firms headquartered in states with more conservative initial targets during RPS adoption and progressive, milestone-based implementation strategies have significantly lower GHG emission intensity than those headquartered in states with more aggressive initial targets or long-term absolute targets. Our findings have significant implications for developing environmental regulations and public policies aimed at reducing GHG emission intensity.

title: EXPRESS: Participation Governance in Consumer and AI Co-creation: Whether to Intervene and How to Design It
abstract: Artificial intelligence reshapes digital mass customization by altering the structure of consumer co-creation. When consumers start from a draft generated by artificial intelligence rather than a blank canvas, outcomes are jointly determined by two stages: whether consumers initiate co-creation and, conditional on participation, how much refinement effort they exert. This separation makes participation a governable design margin—an issue that is largely muted in traditional blank-canvas customization, where participation and effort are tightly bundled. Partnering with a leading United States online retailer of personalized photo products, we study whether and how firm interventions at the participation stage shape downstream purchase outcomes. We develop a two-stage model in which, relative to a baseline with organic participation, a nudge lowers start-up frictions and expands voluntary entry, whereas a mandate serves as a strong boundary-case intervention that guarantees entry but can weaken how participation translates into purchase, generating a reach–efficiency trade-off. We examine these predictions in two randomized experiments. In Study 1, a light-touch nudge increases participation by 5.98 percentage points and raises revenue and order frequency. The evidence is consistent with gains arising primarily through expanded entry into consumer co-creation with artificial intelligence. In Study 2, mandates increase participation relative to nudges, but we find no clear evidence of additional gains in purchase or revisit intentions. Instead, mandates increase low-value participation, in which consumers exert minimal effort and report low purchase intention. Together, these findings show that in mass customization enabled by artificial intelligence, participation governance is a consequential design choice: firms must consider not only how many consumers initiate co-creation, but also whether the participation they induce creates downstream value.

title: EXPRESS: When Good Practices Go Too Far: Overshooting in Organizational Culture
abstract: Business research has examined how useful practices can be made to spread and develop in organizations. However, practices have been observed “overshooting”: either over-diffusing—too many employees adopt them, including some whose usage is unproductive; or becoming over-sophisticated—the practice becomes too elaborate, reducing organizational performance. Independent models of over-diffusion and over-sophistication have been proposed; this paper integrates both aspects in a simple, unified model of overshooting. We offer a cultural evolution model that studies how interaction dynamics among employees are able to diffuse and stabilize an equilibrium of underperforming cultural practices, at the same time over-developing the practice so its sophistication goes beyond productive levels. People adopt practices from others based on information about the practice’s productive value, but also influenced by social dynamics with other employees, such as status. Our model clarifies the circumstances in which over-diffusion and over-sophistication can arise, and how these two elements of overshooting relate to each other. We map our model in detail to two cases---process management practices (e.g., six sigma) and Uber's aggressive culture---and discuss the managerial implications.

title: EXPRESS: From Chit-Chat to Conversion: Cost-Efficient Conversational Recommendation via Retrospective Learning and Isolated Reflection
