abstract: Conversational recommendation systems help digital platforms elicit user preferences through multi-turn interaction, but they often face a practical tension between recommendation accuracy and interaction cost when users provide vague or low-information inputs. This study follows a design science approach to develop a cost-conscious conversational recommendation artifact for such ambiguous service encounters. The artifact is guided by two design principles. First, retrospective outcome-guided supervision uses successful historical conversion trajectories as downstream anchors for improving responses at earlier low-information states. Second, isolated reflection separates recommendation generation from consistency checking, enabling diagnostic regeneration when candidate responses conflict with previously stated user constraints. In implementation, the artifact instantiates these principles through parameter-efficient adaptation of open-source large language models and prompt-isolated role switching over a shared backbone model. We validate the artifact on three conversational recommendation datasets covering movie and e-commerce settings, using outcome efficacy, interaction efficiency, process analysis, ablation analysis, robustness checks, and human evaluation. Here, interaction efficiency refers to user-visible dialogue turns, while computational burden is reported separately through training, memory, and latency measurements. The empirical results show that the artifact improves recommendation effectiveness while maintaining a favorable balance between interaction burden and conversion outcomes under the tested conditions. Process-level analysis further characterizes how recommendation behavior evolves over the course of dialogue. This study contributes transferable design principles for embedding retrospective preference optimization and isolated reflection into conversational recommendation systems, offering operational guidance for platforms seeking to improve personalization under constraints on interaction cost.

title: EXPRESS: Interoperability Meets Accountability: How Data Interoperability and Experiential Quality Influence Malpractice Lawsuits
abstract: A persistent challenge that many patients continue to face is substandard care including errors in their medical records (Sharma et al., 2019). To address this situation, health information exchanges (HIE) have been established to seamlessly share patient data across organizations. In this study, we examine whether policy-driven support for data interoperability—operationalized through health information exchange (HIE) systems—is associated with increased malpractice liability. Drawing on the empowerment literature, we argue that greater operational transparency enabled by data sharing may empower patients to scrutinize care quality, thereby elevating the risk of litigation. Using an eight-year panel data set covering 952 U.S. hospitals from 2010 to 2017 and over 24,000 malpractice case filings, we find that HIE adoption is associated with a statistically significant 10.5% increase in malpractice lawsuits. However, this effect is moderated by hospitals’ experiential quality, as measured by patient-reported experiences of communication, empathy, and responsiveness. In hospitals with high experiential quality, the effect of HIE adoption on malpractice lawsuits is reduced by 20.4%, suggesting that positive patient interactions can reduce the legal risks associated with HIE adoption. Our findings highlight a critical trade-off. While data interoperability improves operational coordination and patient engagement, it can also elevate legal exposure. This research contributes to the operations management and public policy literature by reframing interoperability not just as a backend coordination tool but also as a patient-facing technological development with reputational and legal implications.

title: EXPRESS: Do You Lose When You Sell Loose? Impact of Unpackaged Sales on Profit and Waste
abstract: Loose sales — the sale of unpackaged products by unit or weight — are frequently promoted as a way to reduce waste because they allow consumers to purchase exactly the quantity they want, rather than being constrained by the fixed quantities dictated by the pre-packaged format. We study a retailer selling a highly perishable product under two possible formats: fixed-size packages and/or loose. The retailer chooses prices and package size to maximize profit. Consumers perceive loose products as fresher, but they also incur an inconvenience cost arising from the additional time and effort required. For the retailer, loose sales carry a higher unit variable cost due to increased labor requirements. In a homogeneous market, we show that, if consumers place substantially higher value on the loose option and its cost is not significantly greater than that of packaged sale, the retailer can make more profit selling only loose at a high price to consumers who buy the quantity they desire. Otherwise, the retailer is better off selling packages of large size, forcing consumers to buy more than they desire to purchase. Interestingly, consumer waste can actually be greater when the product is sold exclusively in loose format. In a heterogeneous market with two consumer segments which differ in the magnitude of their consumption needs, three possible optimal strategies emerge: selling only loose to both segments, selling only (relatively small) packages to both segments, or selling (relatively large) packages to high-consumption needs consumers and selling loose to the low-consumption needs consumers. Our results also demonstrate that selling loose instead of or alongside packages can often be a win-win strategy, simultaneously boosting retailer profits and reducing consumer waste compared to selling only packages. However, in some cases, introducing loose sales may increase waste. These findings indicate that retailers may derive financial gains from offering products in loose form; however, they should ensure that the associated sustainability benefits are genuine before positioning it as a green strategy. Likewise, policymakers seeking to reduce food waste should carefully consider product- and market-specific conditions rather than promoting loose sales as a universally effective waste-reduction measure.

title: The Rise of Alternatives
abstract: Abstract Since the 2000s, U.S. public pension funds have actively shifted their risky investments away from public equities and toward alternative assets like private equity and hedge funds—some much more than others. We explore a range of possible explanations for these trends and argue that beliefs about the risk-adjusted return of alternatives have played a central role. Pension beliefs are shaped by investment consultants, peers, and experience in the 1990s. Other demand-side channels related to risk-seeking motives, spending needs, and fund governance have weaker empirical support. We also consider supply-side factors and agency interpretations of the data. (JEL G11, G23, G41, H75)

title: Managing the dual nature of customer engagement in product innovation: A sensegiving and sensemaking perspective
journal_name: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science

title: The Economics of Data Unions: Optimal Data Sharing and Coordination
abstract: Abstract We develop a model of data-driven competition in which product quality depends on users’ data contributions and firms’ investments in data infrastructure. Users’ inability to internalize the value generated by their data, together with firms’ strategic investment incentives, can lead to data underinvestment—limiting quality—or overinvestment—concentrating market power. We introduce a data union that coordinates users’ contributions and can be implemented through a data trust or intermediary that aggregates user data. By shaping data compensation, the union enables users to capture and internalize more of their data’s value, enhancing user welfare, especially when combined with data sharing among firms. We apply these insights to financial data, digital payments, and Open Finance. Our analysis shows that data portability can strengthen competition but, without coordination, may leave data investment too low or excessive.

title: “Borrowing intelligence to build a business”: The promise of open‐source AI for entrepreneurship
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Open‐source artificial intelligence (OSAI) is an increasingly important yet poorly understood frontier for entrepreneurial activity. We identify four defining features that shape new ventures' engagement with OSAI communities: dependence on sponsoring firms, layered licensing regimes, regulatory risks, and nation‐state influence. We develop the OSAI Framework for Market Entry to explain how open‐weight models relocate, rather than merely lower, entry barriers across six domains in AI‐enabled product and service markets. They may reduce resource barriers but create dependence on the governance of borrowed components, shifting the binding constraint from technical to commercial entry and value capture through complementary assets. We discuss contributions to research on entrepreneurial entry and strategy, private‐collective innovation, the openness paradox, and the new venture life cycle, and outline directions for future research. Managerial Summary Open‐source artificial intelligence (OSAI) offers new ventures access to powerful resources for developing AI‐enabled products and services without building AI capabilities from scratch. Yet new ventures must often contend with four key governance dependencies that shape how they engage with OSAI communities: reliance on large technology firms that contribute and steer critical layers of the AI stack, licensing terms that vary by layer, emerging regulatory requirements, and growing nation‐state influence over OSAI. Our OSAI Framework for Market Entry identifies where OSAI can lower entry barriers, where constraints shift instead, and how new ventures can manage the trade‐offs resulting from governance dependencies. It helps new ventures and investors evaluate when, where, and how to build on OSAI components, and which complementary assets can protect their returns.

title: Population Aging and Citizen Preferences for Automation and Immigration: A Cautionary Tale for Advanced Aging Economies?
abstract: ABSTRACT Extensive research highlights public apprehension toward immigrants and robots, but few studies examine how demographic challenges, particularly population aging, influence these perceptions. The public may not naturally consider population aging when evaluating immigration or automation policies, as these issues are often discussed in silos. We thus hypothesize that priming the public to consider population aging will lead them to view automation and immigration more favorably. Using pre‐registered survey experiments in three countries—Japan, South Korea, and France—we investigate whether providing factual information about population aging alters attitudes toward immigration and automation. We find that in Japan, the world's most aged country, such information generates more favorable attitudes toward both immigration and automation. In Korea, the fastest‐aging country, it improves only immigration attitudes. In France, where the elderly population is average for the EU, we find no significant effect. We find, however, that these positive effects in Japan and Korea do not persist when respondents consider automation and immigration policies alongside other options like adjusting the retirement age. These findings suggest that the public's policy preferences in response to population aging are subject to country‐specific contexts, as well as to different issue linkages activated in policy discussions.

title: Peer benchmarking and digital upgrading: Field experiments on business websites
abstract: Can low-cost comparative information trigger firms to improve the performance of a digital asset they already own? Using two large-scale randomised controlled trials with approximately 7000 UK firms in the distilling and retail sectors, we study whether peer benchmarking of website performance prompts measurable improvement. Firms receiving benchmarked website metrics and targeted recommendations exhibit modest average improvements, with more favourable effects among initially underperforming firms, consistent with partial convergence towards the industry frontier. The catch-up dynamic is strongest on mobile metrics, including as a spillover in the first experiment, in which reports contained desktop metrics only, a pattern consistent with firms focusing improvement efforts where performance gaps are greatest. Treated firms also show suggestive report-aligned increases in the adoption of mobile-optimisation and content-delivery technologies. These patterns are consistent with comparative performance information helping firms identify and respond to performance shortfalls. The findings position peer benchmarking as a scalable, low-cost instrument for narrowing the digital divide among SMEs: informational aspiration cues generate more favourable responses among firms furthest behind than among firms nearer the frontier.

title: Motivation or ability? Explaining the effect of party polarisation on proximity voting
abstract: Previous work finds that party polarisation increases proximity voting. However, there is surprisingly little evidence about how. This article compares the importance of two possible mediators. First, party polarisation reduces the indifference voters have towards parties' policy platforms. As a result, party polarisation should increase voters' motivation to evaluate parties based on policy agreement. Second, party polarisation makes it easier for voters to know the relative positions of the parties, improving their ability to choose the closest party. Drawing on cross-national data from the most recent European parliamentary elections, the voter's motivation is operationalised as the ‘policy differential’ – the spread of party distances relative to the closest party. Similarly, the voter's ability is measured in terms of ‘party position knowledge’, the fraction of parties the voter places in the same order as country experts. A causal mediation analysis shows that both the voter's indifference and their party position knowledge have comparably sized, substantial mediation effects, accounting for the vast majority of the total effect of ideological party polarisation on left-right proximity voting. Therefore, this article contributes rare evidence about the mechanism by which party polarisation leads to proximity voting.

title: What Do Mini‐Publics Prove?
abstract: ABSTRACT Lottocracy is a novel political arrangement that replaces elected politicians with ordinary citizens selected at random. It is unlike any political system that currently exists, so it is natural to have anxiety about how it would work in practice. To mollify these concerns, many lottocrats point to the successful performance of mini‐publics as evidence that lottocracy would work well, if tried. This inference resembles a claim about external validity, I argue, and develop a framework for evaluating it by relying on work from the social sciences and philosophy of science about when such claims are warranted. With this framework in hand, I show that mini‐publics teach us little about how lottocracy would work in practice, although the strength of this conclusion depends on which specific version of lottocracy is under consideration. Mini‐publics, however, do provide evidence about the abilities of ordinary citizens more generally, undermining some of the strongest claims about their lack of political competence. The framework developed here applies to a broader class of arguments in political philosophy: arguments that use the performance of existing institutions to predict how similar but untried institutions would perform.

title: What Drives Voter Bias Against Muslim Politicians? An Experimental Examination
abstract: Abstract Religious and ethnic minorities remain underrepresented in political office, but its reasons are debated. Using administrative data from Norwegian local elections, we show that candidates with Muslim names receive fewer personal votes, and propose that this is (partly) due to political beliefs about Muslims as politicians.To examine this claim, we identify salient political beliefs and implement a conjoint experiment that estimates anti-Muslim bias with and without information on these beliefs.In a low-information setting, respondents exhibit a substantial anti-Muslim bias, but providing belief-relevant information reduces this anti-Muslim bias by 2–5 percentage points. The largest reduction occurs when respondents learn candidates’ positions on minority-rights issues. This reduction is driven by right-wing voters and is large enough to eliminate the left-right gap in anti-Muslim bias. These findings show a strong political component in the anti-Muslim bias.

title: Beliefs About Public Opinion and the Perceived Legitimacy of Policy Decisions
abstract: Abstract Democratic legitimacy is typically thought to depend on whether political decisions reflect public opinion, or majority preferences. Do citizens share this standard? And what if citizens are wrong about public opinion? We study how beliefs about public support for controversial policy proposals are associated with the perceived legitimacy of adopting them, and whether accurate polling information changes these judgments. In a representative survey experiment in Germany, respondents reported their own position on four such proposals, estimated public support, and rated the legitimacy of adopting each one. For a random subset of proposals, respondents received accurate polling information showing that the proposal lacked majority support. We find that perceived public support predicts legitimacy judgments even after accounting for respondents’ own policy preferences. Yet these perceptions are often inaccurate and shaped by respondents’ own views. Corrective polling information modestly lowers perceived legitimacy, especially among those who initially overestimated public support. The findings suggest that misperceptions of public opinion can distort, but accurate information can also partly correct, citizens’ assessments of democratic legitimacy.

title: Forest governance as carceral formation: Policing and punishment in the ordinary governance of British Columbia's forests
Worth a try? The electoral consequences of symbolic legislation
“Manifestly unlawful”: How US troops think about the duty to disobey illegal orders
Childbirth and Welfare Inequality: The Role of Bargaining Power and Intrahousehold Allocation
Matching Function Equilibria with Partial Assignment: Existence, Uniqueness and Estimation
abstract: We argue that models coming from a variety of fields, such as matching models and discrete choice models among others, share a common structure that we call matching function equilibria with partial assignment. This structure includes an aggregate matching function and a system of nonlinear equations. We provide a proof of existence and uniqueness of an equilibrium and propose an efficient algorithm to compute it. For a subclass of matching models, we also develop a new parameter-free approach for constructing the counterfactual matching equilibrium. It has the advantage of not requiring parametric estimation when computing counterfactuals. We use our procedure to analyze the impact of the elimination of the Social Security Student Benefit Program in 1982 on the marriage market in the United States. We estimate several candidate models from our general class of matching functions and select the best fitting model using information based criterion.

title: Spillover Effects of Old-Age Pension across Generations: Family Labor Supply and Child Outcomes
Labor Market Signals: The Role of Large Language Models
Effect of State and Local Sexual Orientation Anti-Discrimination Laws on Labor Market Differentials
Specific Skills, Peer Effects, and Academic Outcomes: Evidence from Quasi-Randomly Assigned Roommates
Earnings Dynamics and Firm-Level Shocks
Uncovering economic policy uncertainty during conflict
Exponential-family random graph models in resident-healthcare provider networks: An application using data from long-term healthcare facilities in the United States
Religion and early fertility in the United States: changes during the second demographic transition
abstract: Abstract We assess how changes in early fertility varied among US women with different religious characteristics, and how the associations between religion and early fertility changed across birth cohorts from 1950 to 1993. Using data from the National Survey of Family Growth, we examine the timing of nonmarital, marital, and overall first births through age 24. Results from life tables and discrete-time event history models reveal that increases in early nonmarital first births were smaller among women who attended religious services more frequently in childhood, whereas early marital births declined at similar rates irrespective of childhood religious service attendance. Because early births became increasingly nonmarital across birth cohorts, women who attended religious services more frequently in childhood became less likely to have an early birth overall. Early fertility differences by religious tradition generally converged across cohorts, although women raised conservative Protestant continued to have higher likelihoods of early birth relative to women raised in other religious traditions net of controls. Women who were raised nonreligious remained similar to conservative Protestants in their likelihood of nonmarital childbearing across cohorts and became statistically similar to them in their overall early births in the latest cohort. Changes in early fertility during the second demographic transition therefore varied by religious background and reshaped the relationship between religion and early fertility.

title: An Integrated Risk‐Informed Optimization Framework for Disinformation Interdiction in Coupled Information‐Physical Networks
abstract: ABSTRACT The manner in which society consumes and responds to information has significantly evolved in recent years, increasing the potential risk of interacting with, reacting to, and spreading misinformation and disinformation. In this paper, we introduce a novel integrated optimization framework that simultaneously models the dynamics of an information layer (where correct information or false information spreads) and a physical layer (where users interact with a physical infrastructure system). We consider an over‐the‐horizon problem in which an adversary seeks to disrupt physical infrastructure by spreading false information about its operation and performance, prompting users to behave in ways that degrade system performance. Focusing on public transit, we study how disinformation about station closures alters user behavior and system efficiency, and develop an optimization model to identify effective interdiction strategies that mitigate these impacts. The information layer incorporates personality‐driven susceptibility and simulates dis/information diffusion, while the physical layer uses a multicommodity network flow model to capture user movements and expose the effects of disinformation on travel time. Our integrated approach enables the joint analysis of both layers, revealing complex interdependencies that are overlooked when studied separately. A case study of the New York City subway system shows that even limited protective interventions can significantly reduce travel delays. In contrast, unmitigated disinformation can substantially degrade system performance. This research highlights the importance of integrated optimization‐based strategies for enhancing the resilience of transportation systems to information‐based threats and provides a foundation for future studies on dynamic disinformation influence on physical infrastructure systems.

title: Promoting Support for Anti-Racism Movements and Intentions to Intervene: Effects of Common-Identity Narratives and the Moderating Role of Prior Prejudice
abstract: Two experiments examined whether emphasizing a common ingroup identity with racially different characters, operationalized as university affiliation with an African American character (Study 1) and parent identity with an Asian American character (Study 2), enhanced the impact of victim narratives. Findings indicate that emphasizing a common ingroup identity increased perceived similarity and identification with the character and reduced perceived social distance, which then fostered greater support toward anti-racism movements and stronger intentions to intervene. Common-identity narratives were particularly effective among participants with higher prior prejudice, and the moderation effect was mediated by reduced social distance.

title: When it’s your own child: effects of media narratives on U.S. parents’ support for their LGBTQ+ teen
abstract: Abstract Parents’ responses to their LGBTQ+ child are varied, often intense, and have important consequences for the child. To examine how media depictions may shape responses, a pre-registered online experiment of 494 parents tested effects of viewing two TV narratives, depicting either control (non-LGBTQ+) family interactions, parental rejection, gradual growth toward acceptance, or unalloyed acceptance, of a lesbian or transgender teen, on parents’ support and behavioral intentions regarding their own LGBTQ+ teen. Guided by theories of vicarious contact and inspiring media, we assessed mediation via identification with characters, and via feelings of inspiration and manipulation, testing baseline support as a moderator. Effects of condition were indirect-only, and contingent on baseline support. Among highly supportive parents, growth and acceptance narratives (vs. control) increased feelings of inspiration, which predicted positive behavioral intentions. Among less supportive parents, rejection and (unexpectedly) growth narratives reduced identification with depicted LGBTQ+ teens, indirectly decreasing support and behavioral intentions.

title: Measurement Error, Manipulation, and the Value of Short‐Term Performance in Job Retention
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper studies how the accuracy of a short‐term performance measure affects its value when a principal decides whether to retain or fire an agent, who can manipulate that measure. Compared with ignoring performance and never firing the agent, the performance measure is valuable when the savings in the expected cost of the retention error is more than the expected cost of the firing error. A more accurate performance measure can have a non‐monotonic effect on its value: Greater accuracy improves the principal's ability to correctly identify the agent, which increases efficient firing, but it causes the incompetent agent to increase manipulation to avoid being fired, which increases inefficient retention. With a less accurate performance measure, the incompetent agent has weaker incentives for manipulation, and an increase in accuracy increases its value due to the identification effect. With a more accurate performance measure, the manipulation effect dominates, and an increase in accuracy decreases its value. The results imply that the principal prefers an imperfect performance measure when the agent can choose the level of manipulation.

title: Trust in Crisis: Unraveling the Affective and Cognitive Mechanisms of Government Response in Shaping Public Trust
abstract: ABSTRACT Severe digital service failures with crisis‐like characteristics often arise from routine technical problems and coordination failures. When such failures escalate into events that threaten public trust in government, rebuilding trust becomes especially challenging. Unlike isolated external shocks, such failures signal potential systemic competence deficiencies, making restoration efforts more complex. However, empirical evidence on how government responses contribute to trust recovery through underlying psychological mechanisms remains limited. Drawing on uncertainty management theory, this study develops and empirically tests a dual‐pathway model for trust recovery. Results from a vignette experiment with 270 Chinese citizens reveal that government responses combining timeliness and transparency are particularly effective in restoring public trust. Specifically, such combined responses restore affect‐based trust by reducing anger and strengthen cognition‐based trust by reducing risk perceptions. By illuminating how the combination of response dimensions functions through distinct psychological pathways, these findings advance understanding of how governments can rebuild public trust following digital service failures with crisis‐like characteristics. This study also provides guidance for policymakers in designing response strategies that address both emotional and cognitive concerns, thereby sustaining public trust amid digital transformation.

title: Learning from Coalition Politics: How Episodes of Increased Complexity Can Enhance Citizens’ Political Efficacy
Newsworthy workplace deaths
abstract: Using high-frequency administrative data from Italy, this study examines how workplace fatalities and related media and public attention affect safety outcomes. Our empirical strategy combines event-study and difference-in-differences designs with variation in newspaper circulation, article-level reporting, and exogenous shifts in public attention from unexpected football results. We find that “newsworthy” deaths—those involving young, female, or foreign-born workers—reduce non-fatal injuries, especially where media exposure and coverage are higher, but the effect weakens when attention is diverted by competing football events. These results highlight media salience, shaped by public attention, as an informal mechanism for improving workplace safety.

title: What Do “Most People” Believe? Race, Gender, and the Generalized Other
abstract: When people form beliefs in social life, they often calibrate their own thinking against what they anticipate “most people” think. Although prior research demonstrates the importance of these inferences, scholars have yet to examine who is best proxied by “most people.” Given persistent inequalities in U.S. society that advantage White men, as well as theories of cultural hegemony, we hypothesize that “most people’s” imagined beliefs are closely proxied by those of White men. We test these ideas using an original survey experiment conducted with a nationally representative sample of U.S. adults ( N = 2,089) in which we adapt 64 core items from the General Social Survey. Respondents were randomly assigned to answer these questions either from the perspective of most people, or from the perspective of designated race-gender groups. Contrary to our hypothesis, we find strong and consistent evidence that White men are not seen as standard-bearers for most social issues. Instead, perceptions of what most people believe are highly aligned with the imagined beliefs of White women. Importantly, this pattern emerges not because White women are seen as influential, but because White women are perceived as less extreme than other groups. We also observe variation across respondents, such that respondents tend to center their own race-gender group in conceptualizing most people’s beliefs (with White women typically close behind).

title: Do Political Elites Evaluate Election Outcomes More Favourably than Citizens? Evidence from Parallel Surveys
Does policy advocacy generate good PR? Evidence from labor unions and minimum wages
Picture book of apportionment and voting difficulties
abstract: Abstract The geometry associated with apportionment and voting methods enables us to “see" what difficulties will arise, why certain complexities are inevitable, how to create supporting examples, and identify similarities of the problems afflicting both areas. Although several new results become apparent, such as the harsh consequences for a method satisfying IIA and a replacement for the modified divisors that are used with monotone apportionment approaches, the emphasis is to use this picture book approach to explain why certain behaviors must happen.

title: Does Compassion Shape How Much Citizens See Others in Charge During Societal Crises?
abstract: ABSTRACT Recent evidence shows that compassion prompts personal action in response to societal crises. We argue that compassion—the awareness of suffering and the desire to alleviate it—is also associated with assigning greater responsibility to multiple societal actors, thus possibly facilitating more wide‐ranging crisis responses. As citizens in democracies elect politicians to address the issues they care most about, the recognition of suffering and the desire to alleviate it should prompt citizens to also demand institutional responses (i.e., from politicians, authorities, and organizations). Analyses of nationally representative panel data from Sweden demonstrate that compassion is associated with personal actions and the assignment of responsibility to other societal actors. While an experiment in the US provides no causal evidence that inducing compassion shifts these outcomes, it corroborates our correlational findings: people reporting more compassion also report greater personal action, demands for institutional responsibility, and monitoring of various actors' crisis responses. Together, while further evidence on the causal effects of compassion is needed, our results suggest that compassion's effects may go beyond personal action, facilitating the multi‐layered responses that complex societal crises require.
