Implementation Fragility in State-Owned Enterprises: Governance, Capability and Regulatory Transition at Namibia’s National Reinsurer
abstract: State-owned enterprises can remain formally strategic while losing the ability to execute. This article conceptualizes that condition as implementation fragility: delayed, partial and vulnerable execution that emerges before organizational failure becomes visible. Using an interpretivist qualitative case study of Namibia National Reinsurance Corporation Limited, the study examines preparedness for the phased withdrawal of per-policy cessions by 28 March 2028. Evidence from 12 semi-structured interviews and six categories of organizational documents is analyzed through agency theory, dynamic capabilities theory and the McKinsey 7S alignment lens. Findings show that regulatory transition exposed pre-existing weaknesses in accountability, technical oversight, actuarial and analytical capability, digital systems, procurement routines, performance contracts and strategic alignment. The article explains dynamic capabilities in a state-owned enterprise as governance-conditioned and advances a sequencing argument: accountability repair should precede capability investment, which should precede major transformation where protected revenue is being withdrawn. Transformation plans become performative when announced before credible decision rights, implementation indicators, budgets, systems and strategic skills are in place. The findings provide boards, regulators and policymakers with an early-warning lens for diagnosing execution risk before regulatory shocks turn latent fragility into financial and strategic failure.

title: Experiencing Remote, Hybrid and In‐Office Work in the Canadian Public Sector: Evidence from a 90‐Day Workplace Study
abstract: Abstract Governments across Canada are actively reasserting control over where and how public servants work through return‐to‐office mandates, often in the absence of fine‐grained evidence about how different work arrangements shape employee experience. This article examines how in‐office, remote, and hybrid work arrangements relate to public servants' self‐reported well‐being and perceived productivity. Using high‐frequency, longitudinal data collected over 90 days from 38 Canadian government employees, the study combines traditional survey instruments with repeated app‐based “check‐ins” capturing mood, energy, motivation, and productivity. The findings suggest that hybrid work arrangements are associated with lower reported work stress and higher perceived productivity, though work location alone does not fully explain variation in employee experience. By introducing a diagnostic, real‐time approach to measuring public servant well‐being, this study contributes to ongoing debates about hybrid work and provides evidence relevant to public sector managers implementing work‐location policies.

title: Canada's Path to a Just Carbon‐Neutral Economy
abstract: Abstract Canada's climate governance is entering a critical inflection point amid accelerating ecological impacts, shifting geopolitical dynamics, and growing domestic policy uncertainty. This special issue examines how Canadian public administration can better respond to the climate polycrisis by addressing the institutional, political, and governance barriers that impede effective climate action. Despite decades of policy development, Canada's progress remains uneven, constrained by federal‐provincial tensions, fragmented policy instruments, and persistent support for fossil‐fuel development. The contributions in this issue argue that the core challenge is less a lack of policy tools than a misalignment between governance systems and the long‐term demands of decarbonization. Through analyses spanning federal institutions, industrial strategy, regional transition, market instruments, and municipal experimentation, the articles collectively highlight the need for more coherent, collaborative, and adaptive governance architectures capable of coordinating climate action across sectors and scales in a federated state.

title: When does artificial intelligence strengthen the case for markets? Revisiting the socialist calculation debate
The cultural roots of state-owned enterprises: evidence from Europe
abstract: Abstract This paper examines the cultural roots of state ownership of enterprises. Drawing on data for European countries, we show that the scale of state ownership of enterprises is smaller in individualist societies than in collectivist ones. This relationship is robust to a broad set of cultural, economic, and historical controls. We address endogeneity concerns by using genetic, epidemiological, and linguistic data as instruments for individualism. We propose several political economy mechanisms underlying this relationship. First, in collectivist societies, voter preferences are tilted toward more extensive state ownership of enterprises. Second, in collectivist societies, interest groups may be stronger and democracy may be weaker, both of which can result in a larger share of state-owned enterprises in the economy. We provide empirical evidence supporting these channels. Finally, we show that the negative relationship between individualism and the scale of state ownership also holds in non-European countries.

title: Nonviolent protest and ideological change in education: a public choice approach
abstract: Abstract This paper applies a public choice framework to examine how successful nonviolent protest campaigns are associated with changes in the ideological orientation of state education systems. We conceptualize education as a site of political bargaining in which organized interests shape educational governance and classroom political socialization. Using cross-national data on political mobilization and educational ideology, we estimate the effects of successful nonviolent campaigns on nationalist, socialist-communist, and democratic ideological emphasis within classroom instruction. We find that successful nonviolent campaigns are associated with declines in nationalist and socialist-communist ideological emphasis alongside increased emphasis on democratic norms and democratic institutions. We do not interpret these shifts as movement from indoctrination to ideological neutrality. Rather, following recent work on political socialization and educational ideology, we treat all educational systems as engaged in ideological transmission and interpret the findings as shifts in the ideological orientation emphasized within educational practice. The results suggest that successful nonviolent mobilization is associated with broader political and institutional realignment that reshapes educational political socialization. Parallel estimates for successful violent campaigns do not display the same consistent pattern, although this contrast is descriptive rather than a direct test of the difference between campaign types.

title: Judicial performance and public procurement choice
abstract: Abstract This paper investigates whether judicial performance influences the choice of procurement procedures adopted by public authorities. Using data on Italian municipal public works contracts between 2009 and 2012, it examines the choice between negotiated procedures and formal tendering mechanisms in a range where both options were legally available. Identification relies on a spatial discontinuity design that exploits exogenous variation in judicial delay across court jurisdictions, further refined through intra-regional border comparisons and coarsened exact matching. The results show that longer judicial delays significantly reduce the likelihood of using negotiated procedures and increase the use of formal auctions. Consistent with a growing body of literature showing that inefficient courts increase contractual uncertainty, we argue that poor judicial performance shifts procurement choices toward highly formalized procurement mechanisms rather than more discretionary and market-oriented forms of contracting. In this sense, formal procurement procedures may partially compensate for weak judicial enforcement by shifting transaction governance toward greater ex-ante specification, procedural control, and verifiability. More broadly, the paper suggests that judicial ineffectiveness may contribute to the expansion of bureaucratic controls, shifting governance away from market-based arrangements and toward increasingly proceduralized administrative structures.

title: Conceptual search: A generative view of entrepreneurial imagination
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Entrepreneurs cannot pursue ventures they never imagine. This article develops a generative view of entrepreneurial imagination as the construction of an evolving candidate set through generation, provisional evaluation, and revision. Conceptual search represents venture concepts as text, transforms them through interpretable operations, and compares their promise. A large language model prototype demonstrates complementary modes: local refinement lifts a concept from sixteenth to third among 30 ventures under a validated evaluator, while global recombination reaches distant possibilities that refinement makes competitive. The framework shows how search architecture determines what enters, survives, and develops, and how AI may broaden imagination within firms while producing correlated imagination across firms. By making imagination programmable, auditable, and experimentally tractable, conceptual search opens a research program on how entrepreneurial possibilities are constructed. Managerial Summary Entrepreneurs can pursue only the ventures they imagine, and valuable ideas routinely go unbuilt because nobody thinks of them. AI makes imagining cheap: it can draft, critique, and rewrite venture concepts in seconds, so developing ideas becomes a process that can be designed, run, and audited. I demonstrate a system that evolves real venture concepts: step‐by‐step refinement lifted a middling concept to third place among 30 real ventures, as ranked by an AI judge shown to predict fundraising, while recombining distant ideas created novel concepts that refinement made competitive. The entrepreneur's job shifts from generating a few ideas to governing many: choosing what to search, keep, and test in the market. One caution: rivals using the same AI will imagine similar ventures; advantage comes from proprietary problems, data, and evidence.

title: Colonial logics in contemporary governance: The role of outsourcing in Indigenous affairs
abstract: Abstract This paper explores the ways in which Indigenous Peoples’ right to self‐determination is undermined through government outsourcing processes in Indigenous affairs in Australia. These processes, which are themselves based on settler colonial interpretations of ‘independence’ and ‘efficiency’ that are naturalised within the state, work to deny First Peoples’ governance of their own futures. This paper explores the ways in which outsourcing is used to inhibit Indigenous Peoples’ collective self‐determination, both as land‐based political entities and as service delivery organisations with policy expertise. The rise of New Public Management (NPM) in Australia through the 1980s and 1990s transformed the relationship between service delivery organisations and government more broadly. Subsequently, championed by a conservative Howard government, the early 2000s saw a particular intensification of NPM in Indigenous affairs. As a result, Indigenous community organisations have experienced a deeply politicised and racialised version of these changes. The privatisation of public infrastructure has been a central pillar of NPM, but with that has travelled the privatisation of policy expertise. We argue that outsourcing policy expertise evokes a narrative of impartiality and cost‐efficiency that helps government cut through the political noise of failure and crisis in Indigenous affairs. Enlisting entities like large management consulting companies to conduct policy research and develop policy advice creates both a sense that the work is done at arm's length from governments and that it is delivered in a more cost‐effective way than government can deliver it. Outsourcing policy research and advice can be understood as part of the larger project of privatisation, which enables not only asset stripping of the public sector but also ‘expertise stripping’ that moves governance of Indigenous affairs even further away from Indigenous Peoples. We argue that the privatisation of policy research on Indigenous issues functions to normalise market values that are then used to further alienate Indigenous People from their ancestral lands and invalidate Indigenous policy expertise. Points for practitioners Privatisation and outsourcing in Indigenous affairs is often understood by public servants as a neutral and efficient process, but it is not and has had negative political, social, and policy effects. Outsourcing as currently operating has maintained government control of policy and programmes, while putting the burden of compliance and outcomes on Indigenous community organisations. It has also resulted in funding insecurity and the defunding of this crucial sector. Given the loss of policy expertise in government agencies, block grant funding or other mechanisms should be used to allow policy decision‐making within, and funding control by, Indigenous community organisations. Indigenous community organisations juggle competing accountabilities to governments and to their communities. Government should shift its approach to support these organisations to meet community accountabilities, instead of burdening them with excessive administrative and financial requirements.

title: Climate, Nature, and the Uneven Expansion of Financial Governance
abstract: ABSTRACT Financial authorities have developed extensive climate‐related policies, but nature‐related financial policy remains less widespread. Using data on individual policy instruments across 116 jurisdictions from 2000 to 2025, this paper compares the adoption, policy areas, binding status, and source of climate‐ and nature‐related policies. Nature‐related policies appear in 27 jurisdictions, compared with 60 for climate‐only policies. National nature adoption is positively associated with a larger existing body of climate and environmental financial policies, mainly through the broader environmental component rather than climate‐specific policy. Climate‐only policies are used more frequently in prudential supervision and credit allocation than policies that combine nature with climate or broader environmental concerns. Nature‐related policies have a higher mandatory share over the full period but a lower share than climate‐only policies in 2023–2025. In the European Union, broad EU‐level coverage coexists with limited national issuance. The paper contributes a common framework for comparing climate and nature policies and distinguishes EU‐level coverage from national policy development. The results show that the climate‐nature gap concerns not only adoption, but also where policies are used, how binding they are, and which level of authority issues them.

title: Translation in State Governance. By DongshengRen, LinJiao, and SanjunSun, Cambridge, UK: Cambridge University Press, 2026. 72 pp. US $68.33(hbk). ISBN: 978‐1‐00‐965981‐9; US $23.75 (ebk), ISBN: 2633‐6480
Turning the Tide. Studying the Impact of People Management on Teacher Turnover Intentions: The Mediating Roles of Role Ambiguity and Emotional Exhaustion
abstract: Teacher turnover poses a significant challenge to educational quality worldwide, with turnover intention serving as a critical precursor to actual turnover. This study explores how people management—defined as the integration of the implementation of human resource management practices and leadership behavior—affects teachers’ intentions to leave their positions. Grounded in conservation of resources theory, we examine how people management can serve as a crucial resource in reducing turnover intentions by alleviating role ambiguity and emotional exhaustion, two key issues in the teaching profession. Role ambiguity arises from the increasing demands placed on teachers, while emotional exhaustion exacerbates intentions to leave. Our results show support for the (serial) mediating role of role ambiguity and emotional exhaustion, providing new insights into how people management impacts teacher retention. The findings contribute to the understanding of how people management activities can effectively support teachers, reducing turnover intentions and ultimately enhancing overall education quality.

title: From Policy to Sustainability: The Evolution of Sustainability in Public HRM in Aotearoa/New Zealand in the SDG Era
abstract: This study examines how sustainable human resource management (SHRM) has been incorporated into public sector HRM policy in Aotearoa/New Zealand before and after the introduction of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Drawing on a longitudinal qualitative analysis of HRM policies from 10 local councils between 2010 and 2021, it explores how sustainability concerns across social, economic, and environmental domains were integrated into public HRM. The findings show that sustainability entered public HRM primarily through incremental layering onto existing HRM frameworks rather than transformational change. Following the SDGs, policy attention to equity, diversity, and wellbeing increased; however, broader social justice commitments remained uneven, while environmental sustainability received limited attention. By examining HRM policies as organizational signals, the study contributes to public HRM and SHRM scholarship by showing how sustainability priorities are communicated before implementation and may remain constrained by institutional logics of compliance, efficiency, risk management, and organizational performance.

title: Advocacy Coalitions and Policy Change in Africa
abstract: Public policy scholarship in Africa has expanded considerably over the last six decades. Yet African experiences remain less integrated into mainstream policy-process theory. Much of the field’s es...

title: Lobbying Priorities in Agenda‐Setting: Agenda Breadth, Direction, and Responsiveness Across Economic and Citizen Groups
abstract: ABSTRACT Interest groups are key actors in shaping political agendas. Yet, we know surprisingly little about how they determine their lobbying priorities at the earliest stage of the policy process. This study advances a novel conceptual framework for studying interest groups' issue prioritization in the agenda setting stage along three complementary dimensions: agenda breadth, agenda direction, and agenda responsiveness. Drawing on original survey data from 630 EU level interest groups, our results show that issue prioritization is driven primarily by the type of constituents a group represents. Economic interest groups tend to pursue broader lobbying agendas, focus on defending the policy status quo, and are more responsive to internal member pressures when prioritizing undesired issues. Citizen groups, by contrast, typically adopt narrower agendas, prioritize challenging the status quo, and respond more strongly to external issue salience when determining their lobbying priorities. Overall, the study advances our understanding of how interest groups navigate competition for political attention and contributes to broader debates on agenda‐setting in contemporary democracies.

title: The threat‐enhancing effect of authoritarian power sharing
abstract: Abstract Power‐sharing deals can potentially solve the autocrat's commitment problem, yet often fail to prevent conflict. This article develops a dynamic model to examine a largely overlooked friction: Sharing power within an authoritarian regime bolsters the opposition's coercive capabilities. The resultant threat‐enhancing effect creates two distinct commitment problems for the opposition, which determine if and when power sharing occurs. First, the opposition cannot commit to refrain from leveraging its enhanced threat. The ruler prefers to incur a revolt than peacefully share power if the threat‐enhancing effect is large. Second, the threat‐enhancing effect tempts the opposition to wait for a future power‐sharing deal, which undercuts the opposition's commitment to revolt today. New dynamic implications arise: delayed power sharing, conflict, or an increased willingness for the ruler to share power are all possible. Scrutinizing the opposition's limited commitment ability contrasts with the predominant existing focus on the autocrat's commitment problem.

title: When Politics Enters the Waiting Room: Far-Right Electoral Victories Exacerbate Discrimination in Access to Healthcare
abstract: Abstract Far-right political shifts have been linked to increased racism, raising concerns about their impact on minority access to public services. This study investigates whether far-right electoral victories encourage discrimination by street-level bureaucrats, who are expected to act impartially. We conducted a nested research design in Italy, combining a field-experimental audit with a regression discontinuity design focused on municipalities near the electoral threshold for far-right mayors. Research assistants with native-Italian and West-African accents contacted municipal healthcare offices to request registration with a general medical practitioner. Compared to native-Italian callers, those with West-African accents faced significantly higher rates of scrutiny and dismissive responses. Leveraging close elections, we find that this disparity was exacerbated in municipalities where far-right candidates narrowly won. These findings demonstrate that far-right electoral success can undermine impartiality and equal access to essential services.

title: Geoengineering, Moral Hazard, and Disrespect
Gender inclusivity and perceptions of party ideology: Observational and experimental evidence
abstract: Abstract Do citizens use gender-based heuristics to infer political parties’ ideological positions? We posit that citizens view more ‘gender inclusive’ parties as more left-leaning than comparable male-dominated organizations. Cues about gender inclusivity, moreover, come not only from women’s presence in parties’ legislative delegations but also from other visible signals of women’s incorporation into parties – including as leaders and supporters – and through organizational rules promoting women’s inclusion. We present analyses of election survey data from 21 Western publics over time, which show that, controlling for the left–right tones of parties’ manifestos, citizens perceive more gender-inclusive parties as more left-wing and that the cumulative impact of the various dimensions of gender inclusivity is substantial. We next report experimental evidence from four countries, which provides further support for gender-based heuristics. Our findings highlight the importance of not just the message but also the messenger in shaping citizens’ assessments of parties’ ideological perceptions.

title: Contested terrain: How attitudes toward gender issues relate to voting behavior
abstract: Abstract While research increasingly links sexist attitudes to far-right support, public debates have moved well beyond women’s equality to encompass LGBTIQ+ rights. Yet studies have been slow to follow, leaving a significant gap in our understanding of attitudes toward trans, intersex, and non-binary people and how they associate with party choice, especially beyond far-right support. Drawing on original data from the German Social Cohesion Panel (2022/23), we are, to our knowledge, among the first to investigate a broader range of gender-related attitudes and find, first, that these constitute two empirically distinct dimensions, binary and non-heteronormative gender issues , that while conceptually intertwined, warrant separate examination. Second, while support for binary gender issues is widespread, non-heteronormative issues remain highly contested. Third, these dimensions relate differently to vote choice: attitudes toward binary gender issues show partisan sorting across the left-right spectrum, while attitudes toward non-heteronormative gender issues reveal a specific antagonism between the Greens and (center-)right parties. Finally, considering both dimensions together uncovers an asymmetry: voters of (center-)right parties form a cohesive conservative bloc, while supportive voters with different attitudinal profiles disperse across (center-)left parties.

title: Haste makes waste: How public pressure increases legislative duration in the European Union
abstract: While increased decision-making complexity and membership predispose the European Union to protracted negotiations and legislative gridlock, still some legislative proposals are adopted faster than others. What explains this variation? Drawing on models of democratic responsiveness, we argue that politicisation potential – captured by public salience, opinion division, and planned European Union authority expansion – increases legislative duration. To test our expectations, we measure public opinion using Eurobarometer surveys and classify the integration potential of legislative proposals between 2009 and 2019 using semi-supervised machine learning. Our findings indicate that European Union policymakers legislate longer on policies of higher public salience and proposals broadening the European Union authority. These results contribute to research on policymaking responsiveness and efficiency in supranational settings, demonstrating how politicisation affects legislative processes in the European Union.

title: Beyond the Battlefield: Localized Civilian Clashes and Political Attitudes in Violent Conflict
abstract: Abstract In protracted conflicts, civilians frequently encounter low-level, hostile actions from adversary civilians in nearby communities, yet the political consequences of these events remain understudied. We investigate this question in the Israeli–Palestinian context, examining how community-level exposure to hostile actions by Israeli settlers shapes Palestinian political attitudes in the West Bank. Leveraging a novel data set containing thousands of geo-coded conflict events from 2010 to 2020 paired with forty-six Palestinian public opinion polls in the West Bank, we find that district-level increases in settler hostilities are significantly associated with heightened political militancy among local Palestinians, associations that are larger and more robust than those from local Israeli military actions. A second empirical strategy examining changes in Palestinian attitudes before and after the establishment of nearby settler outposts reveals that this form of civilian land expropriation likewise leads to modest increases in political militancy among Palestinians in proximate towns. These findings highlight the distinct political impact of localized, low-level civilian actions and territorial expropriation—central but often overlooked features of sectarian territorial conflicts—offering insights for territorial and ethnic disputes globally.

title: Human Development and the Architecture of Everyday Worry: Latent Worry Profiles in the World Risk Poll
abstract: ABSTRACT Whether public concern about risk rises or falls with national development has been debated for three decades, but the debate has compared countries hazard by hazard, asking how much people worry rather than how worry is organized. We provide a person‐centered analysis of everyday worry at global scale, applying latent class analysis to the six‐hazard worry battery of the Lloyd's Register Foundation World Risk Poll and linking profiles to the Human Development Index (HDI) in 140 countries (; 2023 wave), with the 2021 wave (; 119 countries) as an independent replication. Four worry profiles replicate almost exactly across waves, including a configurationally distinct secure‐basics profile (15% of respondents) combining low worry about food and water with high worry about crime, severe weather, and traffic. Profile prevalence is consistent with the ordered sequence predicted by a need‐priority account of worry allocation: pervasive worry falls from 33% to 13% between low‐ and very‐high‐HDI countries, low worry nearly doubles, and the secure‐basics profile holds steady across low‐ and medium‐HDI countries before declining at higher development. Traffic accidents are the most intense worry in every tier below very high HDI. These gradients persist after adjustment for self‐reported recent harm and demographic composition and are only partly accounted for by the objective hazard environment, though the cross‐sectional design cannot separate development from macroregional clustering. Development is associated with the composition of worry, not only its overall level; risk communication may be better matched to a country's worry architecture than to a single global template.

title: Comparing Like With Like in Biological Invasion Risk Analysis
abstract: Biological invasion decision-support methods are often compared under broad labels such as "risk assessment," even when they perform different functions. This Perspective argues that functional commensurability must be established before methods are compared. In biological invasion risk analysis, screening serves an initial risk identification function, flagging extant or horizon non-native species within a defined risk assessment area for prevention, surveillance, or more detailed evaluation. Comprehensive risk assessment examines entry or introduction, establishment, spread, and their ecological, economic, and socio-cultural consequences in greater detail. Risk management integrates risk with feasibility, cost, effectiveness, legal constraints, and stakeholder values. Impact classification and post-establishment population prioritization may contribute to these functions without being equivalent to them. Published comparisons show how conflating such functions can create false equivalence. The emerging Dispersal-Origin-Status-Impact (DOSI) literature provides an illustrative example through its comparisons with applications of the globally implemented Invasiveness Screening Kit (ISK) decision-support tools: population status and management priority are not the same quantities as prospective invasion risk screening, and species-based screening does not imply coarse spatial resolution. Forty-five peer-reviewed ISK-family studies report local or subnational screenings, including spatial resolutions comparable with or finer than DOSI applications. Valid comparisons require a shared decision objective, explicit spatial and temporal boundaries, independent evaluation evidence, and assessment of uncertainty and the consequences of error. These requirements permit methods to be evaluated for a common use, or combined within adaptive management, without treating disagreement between unlike outputs as evidence of superior performance.

title: “The Minimum Wage Is the Maximum Wage”: How Goal Replacement Perpetuates Means–Ends Decoupling
abstract: This research examines how organizations contribute to the perpetuation of means–ends decoupling (MED) within issue-based fields organized around societal problems, under conditions of heightened field scrutiny. In such settings, organizations often profess commitment to field goals and visibly comply with institutionally prescribed practices to satisfy monitoring, reporting, and public evaluation requirements. However, many adopted goals remain underachieved, raising questions about how compliance without progress endures and how claims of commitment remain credible under transparency regimes intended to spur substantive goal pursuit. Our data came from 75 interviews with 68 brands, suppliers, and third-party organizations pursuing worker well-being in global fashion supply chains. We unveil auditability-based goal replacement as an organizational-level mechanism through which actors rhetorically foreground compliance as public evidence of commitment while narrowing internal goal pursuit to auditable thresholds that serve their core goals, thereby allowing shortfalls to persist. Self-silencing about this substitution and the instrumentalizing of shortfalls close the configuration into a self-reinforcing loop. The study advances MED scholarship by (i) showing how organizations leverage field conditions and appropriate the existing scrutiny infrastructures to advance their core goals while reproducing the means–ends gap, (ii) problematizing the authenticity of commitment claims, and (iii) explaining how goal-ineffective compliance prevails as a credible substitute for adopted goals. It also extends research on organizational responses to institutional complexity and calls for greater attention to institutional impact—that is, the realized advancement of the societal aim an institution emerged to address.

title: Contesting the infrastructures of attention: Climate activism and asymmetric visibility in France
abstract: Drawing on two years of ethnographic fieldwork with Extinction Rebellion Paris and allied movements, semi-structured interviews with activists, and analysis of media coverage and investigative reporting on police surveillance technology, this article examines how French climate movements have reoriented their political practice from seeking visibility within an existing media system toward contesting the infrastructures of attention through which public visibility is produced and governed. It argues that this reorientation reflects a shift in the politics of climate communication: from a logic of media access to one of infrastructural contestation, targeting media ownership and security apparatuses. The analysis examines how activists experience narratives of disorder and eco-terrorism as challenges to their political legitimacy, alongside the expansion of biometric surveillance documented by investigative reporting. It develops the concept of asymmetric visibility regimes to capture the resulting double bind, in which activists struggle for recognition in the media sphere while becoming increasingly identifiable in the security sphere. The article contributes to debates on media power, hybrid media systems, and the communicative conditions of democratic dissent.

title: Hybrid Kidney Allocation: Improving Equity by Fair Integration of Deceased Donor-Initiated Chains in Kidney Exchange
abstract: Problem definition: Living donor kidney exchange programs (KEPs) expand access to transplants by enabling exchanges among patient-donor pairs. However, highly sensitized patients are disproportionately hard to match and face long waits. Deceased donor–initiated chains (DDICs) have been proposed to enable more transplants by diverting an occasional deceased donor kidney from the waitlist to start a KEP chain, which ends by returning a kidney to the waitlist. Yet, DDICs have seen virtually no implementation. In the U.S., this is largely due to concerns that the kidneys returned may differ in blood-type distribution from those diverted, disadvantaging waitlist patients of certain blood types. We study how DDICs can be integrated into KEPs while explicitly protecting blood-type-specific waitlist access. Methodology/results: We develop two forward-looking optimization approaches: one that solves a stochastic model using Sample Average Approximation (SAA) and one that solves a static model with forward-looking constraints. Through simulation, we show that forward-looking models are needed to preserve the blood-type distribution of donations to the waitlist. Under both models, even limited use of DDICs significantly increases transplant rates for highly sensitized patients. While the static approach requires only modest extensions to models as currently used in practice, the more complex and time consuming SAA-based approach yields larger equity gains. Managerial implications: DDICs can improve access to life-saving transplants for the most disadvantaged KEP patients without reducing access for any blood type on the waitlist. By explicitly controlling the blood-type distribution of waitlist donations, matching policies can address objections that have hindered DDIC adoption, calling for renewed policy evaluation.

title: Synthesizing Information-Driven Insider Trade Signals
abstract: Abstract We propose a novel approach to synthesize presumably information-driven insider trading signals for the cross section of stocks. We find that the resulting straightforward composite strategy can often forecast returns in a global sample. This predictability is strongest in equal-weighted portfolios, short holding periods, and insider-buying signals, and it improves further with global diversification. Cross-country analysis reveals that varying insider trading restrictions between countries have limited explanatory power for the performance of the composite strategy. Overall, the results are consistent with a short-term informational advantage of insiders, which might be due to the skillful interpretation of non-private news.
journal_name: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis

title: Craft and Industrialization: Uncovering the Plasticity and Frontier of Craft
abstract: Abstract Craft as an approach to work has been proposed as an alternative to industrial mass production. While industrialization has led to the replacement of craft logic with industrial logic to create uniformity and scale operations, the role of craft in industrialization remains ambiguous. Building on the analysis of engineering work performed at an R&D laboratory in the pulp and paper industry, we explore how and why craft enables industrialization. Our findings reveal how elements of craft manifest in engineering work by helping to transform ideas into useful objects, balancing scientific accuracy with practical usefulness, and fostering a sense of community and identity within the engineering field. These findings point to the plasticity of craft logic , suggesting that elements of craft can be transferred into new contexts and reinterpreted to address new objectives. Considering that these activities took place in an R&D laboratory that drove industrialization, they also reveal the existence of a craft frontier that escapes standardization by providing a context for crafting candidates for future standards. Craft frontier enables the coexistence of craft and industrial logics, where craft can contribute to industrialization by establishing foundations for managerial control without being absorbed into it.

title: Transparency and toxics: policy tool interactions in environmental regulation
abstract: Abstract Toxics information disclosure programs have been hailed by some as being among the most successful environmental programs in history. Yet critics have argued that these policies may invite abuse by reducing traditional regulatory monitoring and enforcement, leading to poorer policy outcomes. Leveraging variation in U.S. state toxics transparency programs, we assess these conflicting claims. We find that information disclosure policies are associated with differences in agency monitoring and enforcement actions as well as with emission levels, but that these relationships are conditioned by the severity of the pollution problem. Overall, our evidence suggests that public information policies and traditional forms of regulation are imperfect substitutes, and successfully reducing toxic emissions requires both policy tools working in concert.

title: A memory policy review: exploring perspectives on memory policies
abstract: Abstract This paper examines the field of memory policy research within the broader study of memory politics. It asks how memory policies are conceptualized in existing scholarship and whether they are approached from a policy studies perspective. Previous research has addressed diverse memory-related practices but has failed to provide a consistent and policy-oriented conceptualization of memory policies. To address this gap, we integrate a scoping review with a systematic literature review structured through the PRISMA approach. We analyze peer-reviewed articles to map trends, assess conceptual uses, and reconstruct the notion of memory policies by examining how scholars define and evaluate them across different empirical contexts. Our findings demonstrate the need for a clearer, policy-focused framework to better understand the dynamics and implications of memory policies.

title: The Geography of Local Politics: How Jurisdiction Size Shapes Local Policy Agendas
abstract: Abstract One of the enduring questions in political science is whether large communities behave differently from small ones. While prior research has examined the political, democratic, and economic implications of community size, a key dimension remains underexplored: how political agendas differ across jurisdictions of varying sizes. This study addresses this gap by examining how the size and geography of local jurisdictions shape the size, issue diversity, complexity, and issue content of local policy agendas. Drawing on a systematic collection and coding of thousands of local council meeting agendas from Danish and Norwegian municipalities, the analysis reveals significant differences in agenda characteristics between large and small communities. The findings contribute to a deeper understanding of how jurisdiction size shapes democratic processes and local governance.

title: Generalizing Causal Effects with Noncompliance: Application to Deep Canvassing Experiments
abstract: Abstract Standard approaches in generalizability often focus on generalizing the intent-to-treat effect. However, in practice, a more policy-relevant quantity is the generalized impact of an intervention across compliers. While instrumental variable methods are commonly used to estimate the complier average causal effect (CACE) within samples, standard approaches cannot be applied to a target population with a different distribution from the study sample. This article makes several key contributions. First, we introduce a new set of identifying assumptions in the form of a population-level exclusion restriction that allows for identification of the target CACE (T-CACE) in both randomized experiments and observational studies. This allows researchers to identify the T-CACE without relying on standard principal ignorability assumptions. Second, we propose a class of inverse-weighted estimators for the T-CACE and derive their asymptotic properties. We provide extensions for settings in which researchers have access to auxiliary compliance information across the target population. Finally, we introduce a sensitivity analysis for researchers to evaluate the robustness of the estimators in the presence of unmeasured confounding and extend existing tests to evaluate instrument validity in this context. We illustrate our proposed method through extensive simulations and a study evaluating the impact of deep canvassing on reducing exclusionary attitudes.

title: Polity size and women’s representation: evidence from two large-scale boundary reforms
abstract: Abstract Do larger polities hinder gender parity in elected office? We theorize that when populations grow faster than elected assemblies, a “seat congestion” effect intensifies competition for nominations, enabling men candidates to crowd out women. We test this argument using two nationwide natural experiments: Swedish municipal amalgamations in 1952 and 1973 that abruptly increased electorates. We track the effects in newly digitized historical panel data. Where electorate-per-seat ratios rose, growth in women’s representation slowed. Decomposition analyses show that expanding councils only partially offsets congestion. By identifying polity size as a systematic brake on descriptive representation, the study adds a demographic dimension to debates on institutional design and points to an overlooked cost of increasing jurisdictional size.

title: Do felon voting rules affect criminal prosecutions?
abstract: Abstract Felon disenfranchisement laws can alter the composition of the electorate. Accordingly, we argue that in states with such laws, elected prosecutors may be tempted to assign felon status strategically. We test our argument using criminal case data from Virginia and leveraging a sudden policy change—unexpectedly announced by the Governor on April 22, 2016—enfranchising all felons upon completion of their prison or probation sentence. Using well-known racial differences in partisanship as a measure of likely political alignment, we show that the announcement corresponded to an increase in criminal charge severity and sentence length for defendants who were politically unaligned with their prosecutors, and a decrease for aligned defendants. Evidence suggests that these changes may have been partially motivated by partisan concerns in the lead-up to the 2016 federal elections.

title: Price Gouging and the Monopoly Option
abstract: Abstract We investigate a dynamic oligopoly model with two phases: a normal phase where an essential input is available, and a disruption phase where firms must rely on inventories. Disruptions create an overcutting pricing incentive arising from the option to forgo sales and monopolize the market once rivals stock out. This monopoly option causes the price to jump to a supracompetitive level at the advent of the disruption and to remain above the competitive price path throughout. Price caps raise welfare, but reduce inventory investment. Government reserves reduce prices and raise buffer stocks, as do reserve mandates when financially feasible.

title: Do black politicians matter? Political leadership and racial composition in top public sector positions
Reassessing the benefits of European integration and the European Union’s ability to achieve strategic autonomy
The effect of prime brokers’ balance sheet constraints on hedge fund performance: Evidence from the GSIB surcharge
The Equity Market Implications of the Retail Investment Boom
abstract: We quantify the equilibrium impact of retail traders on the U.S. equity market within a structural model of asset demand. Estimating investor-specific demand curves, we find that Robinhood traders are fundamentally distinct from all other investors, including other households: their demand is the most elastic and tilts most strongly toward volatile and microcap stocks. Each dollar invested through Robinhood generates more than five dollars in aggregate equity repricing, exceeding hedge funds, other households, and all other investor types. We decompose the cross-sectional variation in stock returns during Robinhood’s growth surge in 2020 into investor-specific components and find that shifts in Robinhood traders’ latent demand drove 11% of small-cap return volatility despite their negligible aggregate wealth share. To explain these demand shifts, we show that Robinhood traders are the only investor group whose latent demand is well explained by attention proxies: their demand exhibits a V-shaped response to past returns and rises sharply with trading volume. Our findings suggest that the growth of retail trading platforms represents a fundamental shift in the composition of equity demand with equilibrium consequences disproportionate to retail investors’ share of aggregate wealth. This paper was accepted by Lukas Schmid, finance. Funding: P. van der Beck acknowledges financial support from the Swiss National Science Foundation. Supplemental Material: The data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.04854 .

title: Corporate Pension Risk-Taking in a Low Interest Rate Environment
abstract: We examine how funding deficit pressures shape the risk-taking of U.S. corporate defined-benefit pension plans and how targeted regulatory relief can mitigate these incentives. Using the 2012 Moving Ahead for Progress in the 21st Century Act reform, which temporarily eased funding pressure by revising discount rate calculations, we show that plans receiving greater relief significantly reduced their equity allocations and shifted toward safer assets. This derisking was most pronounced among active plans and those sponsored by more financially constrained firms. Our findings demonstrate that targeted regulatory relief can curb risk-taking incentives even without altering underlying economic conditions or financial reporting standards and shed light on the likely (and unlikely) frictions driving such behavior. This paper was accepted by Bo Becker, finance. Funding: R. Pinto acknowledges financial support from the Lancaster University Management School Pump Prime Program. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.02928 .

title: Structural Estimation of Intertemporal Externalities with Application in ICU Admissions
Managing Newsvendors via Demand Shifting
abstract: How Demand Allocation Shapes Inventory Decisions Online platforms that fulfill orders for independent sellers often bear inventory costs without choosing how much sellers stock. In the paper “Managing Newsvendors via Demand Shifting,” Yilun Chen and Jiaqi Lu study how reallocating customer demand among substitutable products can influence sellers’ inventory decisions. The platform commits to a demand-shifting rule that effectively alters the demand distribution perceived by the sellers. Its optimal rule reduces demand fluctuations around a target inventory level, making that level attractive to sellers and pooling demand risk across them. The authors characterize this rule in closed form. When shifting demand is inexpensive, the platform can achieve the profit available under centralized inventory control, whereas sellers and customers also benefit. However, when shifting is costly and inventory is expensive for the platform, its optimal intervention can reduce customer service levels. The findings show why platforms should assess how demand allocation changes stocking incentives and customer outcomes.

title: Two-Sided Assortment Optimization: Adaptivity Gaps and Approximation Algorithms
abstract: On the Power of Adaptivity in Choice-Based Matching Platforms Online labor, lodging, and carpooling platforms decide not only whom users can choose but also when those options are shown. Simultaneity can crowd attention around a few popular users and leave many good matches unrealized. In the forthcoming Operations Research paper, “Two-Sided Assortment Optimization: Adaptivity Gaps and Approximation Algorithms,” the authors study how much platforms gain by updating assortments after observing earlier choices. They compare four policy classes, ranging from showing all assortments at once to fully adaptive policies that process users one by one. They prove that adaptivity within one side improves performance by at most a factor of [Formula: see text], whereas fully adaptive policies improve on one-sided adaptive policies by at most a factor of two; both bounds are tight. They also develop efficient approximation algorithms, extend their results to constrained settings, and empirically show that their methods perform far better than their worst-case guarantees.

title: Designing fulfilling and productive workdays: Effects of task meaningfulness sequences on daily engagement and performance.
abstract: Given the importance of experiencing fulfilling and productive workdays, scholars have focused on ways to boost employees' daily engagement and performance, suggesting this may be accomplished by increasing meaningfulness of their work tasks. However, an alternative approach may be needed in multifaceted work contexts where employees need to complete sets of varied tasks each day, including tasks that lack meaningfulness. To address this issue, we integrate the workday design perspective with research on residual engagement to examine implications of strategically sequencing tasks in terms of their meaningfulness. We theorize that because of a process we refer to as engagement cascade, performing the day's most highly meaningful tasks earlier and in a concentrated manner will tend to produce higher levels of daily engagement relative to sequences in which the most highly meaningful tasks occur later or are disbursed. We use agent-based modeling to formalize the engagement cascade process and generate specific predictions regarding how daily engagement is impacted by different task meaningfulness sequences. Findings from an intensive longitudinal design study with National Aeronautics and Space Administration and Russian Space Agency crew members (Study 1), an experience sampling field experiment with full-time employees (Study 2), and two controlled laboratory experiments with undergraduates (Study 3 and Supplement to Study 3) provide support for our hypotheses. Specifically, the decreasing task meaningfulness sequence engendered higher levels of daily engagement and, in turn, daily performance, relative to the increasing, inverted U-shaped, and U-shaped sequences. title: Common ownership and consumer welfare
abstract: Abstract Rival firms with shared institutional investors (i.e., common owners) may compete less aggressively, potentially harming consumer welfare. Yet, research on common ownership has primarily focused on firm performance, often overlooking welfare outcomes or revealing contradictory results. This paper adopts a strategic network perspective to examine how common ownership affects firms’ service quality and pricing levels, which directly impact consumer welfare, and how customer and competitor factors that alter the focus of competitive strategy moderate these effects. To test the hypotheses, the authors analyze a rich, multi-market dataset of U.S. airline firms from 1995 to 2025. Findings reveal that competing firms with higher common ownership tend to have lower service quality and set higher prices. However, this effect is attenuated for firms with high customer-asset value and amplified among rivals competing across multiple markets. The findings demonstrate common ownership’s influence on firms’ marketing mix strategies and offer actionable insights for managers, policymakers, and investors.
journal_name: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science

title: Integrity Ministry: Watchdog, lapdog, or dead dog?
abstract: Abstract Integrity is central to public trust and good governance. Drawing on Queensland's recently established Minister for Integrity as a rare contemporary example, this article examines the concept, function, and practicalities of an integrity minister within a modern accountability framework. Using data synthesised from publicly available sources and assessed through an evaluative model adapted from Bramstedt, the article assesses the extent to which the portfolio possesses the authority, autonomy, and capacity necessary to exert meaningful oversight. It argues that, at best, the Minister for Integrity is a symbolic construct that lacks the authority and autonomy required for substantive impact. We conclude by suggesting that comparative application of this evaluative framework across jurisdictions may assist in determining whether integrity minister models are capable of delivering substantive governance reform as distinct from signalling political commitment to integrity. Points for practitioners In November 2024, the Queensland Government introduced a new ‘Minister for Integrity’ to strengthen Queensland's integrity framework. In this article, we reviewed the capacity of the Minster for Integrity to deliver on that promise by analysing both the formal scope of the role and its place in a Westminster governance system, and the actions of the inaugural Minister in the first 12 months in the role. In terms of the formal scope of the role, we noted significant limitations. The performance indicators set for the Minister were not ambitious, but more concerningly, the structural and political pressures place the Minister in an impossible situation where they are expected to perform a watchdog function, but do not enjoy any of the features necessary for an effective watchdog such as independence and a clear mandate. In terms of the Minister's performance in the first 12 months, we find limited effectiveness in the role. While the Minister did meet the unambitiously low‐performance targets, we note that the structural and political limitations have meant that the Minister did not, and cannot, take an active approach to the role.

title: The global spread of lean management in the public sector: A systematic mapping review of practices, patterns, and regional variations
abstract: Abstract This article presents a systematic mapping review examining the global diffusion of lean management practices in the public sector. While previous systematic reviews have generally treated lean as a unitary managerial approach, this study unpacks lean management into four analytically distinct pillars: pull logic, muda elimination, kaizen, and employee empowerment. Drawing on 85 articles published between 2003 and 2023, it analyses how these pillars have been selectively adopted across different geographical regions and policy sectors. The findings reveal growing scholarly interest in lean public management across multiple countries, with healthcare emerging as the dominant application sector (60%). While muda elimination appears in 92% of the analysed articles, the remaining pillars show substantially lower levels of adoption, suggesting that lean is typically implemented through selective combinations of individual principles rather than as a comprehensive managerial philosophy. Distinct patterns of adoption also emerge across geographical regions and policy sectors. By analysing lean management through the four‐pillar framework, this article offers a more nuanced understanding of how lean public management has been interpreted in the literature and provides a framework for analysing its heterogeneous diffusion across public sector contexts. Points for practitioners Lean management is not implemented as a single, standardised model across the public sector. Public organisations adopt different combinations of lean principles depending on their organisational priorities and policy context. Managers should therefore avoid assuming that all lean initiatives pursue the same objectives or require the same implementation strategy. The four‐pillar framework developed in this article (pull logic, waste elimination, continuous improvement, and employee empowerment) can be used as a practical diagnostic tool for planning, evaluating, or reviewing lean initiatives. Identifying which pillars are emphasised—and which receive less attention—can help practitioners better understand the strategic orientation of organisational reforms. Lean initiatives place different emphasis on efficiency, user orientation, organisational learning, and employee involvement. Recognising these different configurations can help public managers align lean practices with the specific challenges and objectives of their organisations, rather than treating lean as a fixed set of managerial tools.

title: Designing long‐term policies accepted by the public: Evidence from a vignette experiment
abstract: Abstract Democratic governments routinely struggle to build public support for policies whose benefits materialise only after electoral cycles have ended, yet systematic evidence on what drives citizen support for such policies remains scarce. This article reports findings from a vignette experiment conducted with 1738 Australia‐based respondents, who evaluated hypothetical long‐term policy proposals varying across four dimensions: policy domain, financing mechanism, time horizon, and expert assessment. Respondents discounted delayed benefits: support declined as time horizons extended from 5 to 40 years. This penalty, however, was concentrated between the 5‐ and 20‐year horizons and flattened thereafter, a pattern consistent with hyperbolic discounting. Relative to receiving no expert assessment, an expert endorsement raised support, whereas an expert statement of uncertainty depressed it. Respondents also favoured corporate taxation over consumption‐based financing and expansionary over restrictive policy domains. Exploratory interaction analyses qualify this additive picture: the expert endorsement premium was largest for short‐horizon policies rather than offsetting the temporal penalty, while debt financing became relatively more acceptable as horizons lengthened, a pattern consistent with intergenerational cost‐sharing. These findings suggest that democratic myopia is real but bounded and patterned: citizens do not reflexively reject long‐term policies, yet no single design feature neutralises temporal discounting. The political viability of long‐term policies depends on the joint configuration of their design features, including how, and by whom, their prospective effectiveness is communicated. Points for practitioners Public support for long‐term policies declines as benefits recede over time, but the penalty is concentrated in the first two decades: policies promising benefits in 40 years fared little worse than those promising benefits in 20 years. Most of the political cost of long‐termism is incurred as soon as benefits move beyond the immediate political cycle. Independent expert endorsement raises support relative to providing no assessment, while communicated expert uncertainty reduces it. Endorsement should not, however, be treated as an antidote to short‐termism: in our data, its premium was largest for policies with near‐term benefits. Corporate taxation is the most consistently popular mechanism for financing long‐term policies. Public debt becomes relatively more acceptable as time horizons lengthen, suggesting that citizens may regard borrowing as more legitimate when costs and benefits are both shared across generations. Expansionary policy domains, such as renewable energy, rail infrastructure, pensions, and lifelong learning, attract substantially more support for long‐term investment than restrictive domains such as border management and military technology. No single design feature guarantees support. Practitioners should consider financing, expert validation, and time horizon jointly from the outset of policy development, rather than treating communication as an afterthought.

Containment, social protection, and confidence in public institutions and government: Global evidence from 144 countries during the COVID-19 pandemic
abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic required governments to balance restrictive containment policies with measures to mitigate their socioeconomic consequences, raising questions about the relationship between these policy responses and public confidence and trust. Existing research has largely examined containment and economic support separately, often within individual countries or during the pandemic's initial months. We constructed a global country-level panel by integrating administrative policy data with survey measures of public confidence from the Gallup World Poll, covering 144 countries from 2006 to 2023. Using regression models with country and pre-pandemic year fixed effects, this study examined how changes in institutional and government confidence were associated with lockdown trajectories (sustained low-level, rapidly easing, and sustained high-level) and the scale, breadth, and composition of social protection responses. We found that countries following sustained high-level lockdown trajectories generally experienced less favorable changes in confidence than those following rapidly easing trajectories. Under sustained high-level lockdowns, greater social protection spending and a larger number of social protection measures were generally associated with more favorable changes in confidence. Income protection spending was more positively associated with institutional confidence than job protection spending under sustained high-level lockdowns, but this distinction was not supported for government confidence or trust. These findings highlight the importance of considering containment and social protection jointly and suggest that income protection may be particularly relevant to institutional confidence during prolonged restrictions, with broader implications for governing large-scale crises. Points to Practitioners Restrictive crisis measures may be less likely to erode citizens' confidence in public institutions and government when accompanied by broad social protection. Income protection may be particularly relevant for sustaining confidence in public institutions during prolonged restrictions. Crisis strategies should consider containment and social protection together rather than treating them as separate policy domains.

title: Debate: An army of founders—Is Ukraine’s entrepreneurial military the future of defence governance?

title: How the European Union Fell Out of Love With Open‐Source Software
abstract: ABSTRACT This article explains why the European Commission diluted the 2004 European Interoperability Framework's provisions favoring open‐source software and open standards when it revised the framework in 2010. Using an extended Multiple Streams Framework with a technology stream, the study shows how pro‐openness policy entrepreneurs secured the 2004 provisions and why incumbent advocacy became more effective during revision. Drawing on annotated drafts and expert interviews, the study traces actors' lobbying strategies across the problem, politics, and policy streams and examines how technology‐stream developments altered the feasibility and political salience of competing solutions. The analysis shows how changing standards and licensing dynamics, incumbent advocacy, and declining political support for the earlier pro‐openness package enabled a new coupling around business‐model neutrality and licensing flexibility, diluting the 2004 provisions. Beyond the European case, the study informs debates on open‐source artificial intelligence and advances theory on institutional dynamics in regulatory governance.

title: Recruiting for SDGs-Oriented Profiles: Unpacking Drivers of Employer Attractiveness in Hybrid Organizations
abstract: Recruitment is critical for equipping public service organizations with the competencies required to advance the sustainable development goals (SDGs). This is particularly salient for public utilities, hybrid organizations mandated to contribute to the SDGs through essential services in water, waste, and energy management. This study examines employer attractiveness for profiles considered critical to SDG implementation in Italian utilities. Drawing on self-determination theory, we combine semi-structured interviews with HR and Employer Branding managers from 16 utilities with two discrete-choice experiments involving STEM and vocational-technical students and professionals. Salary and competence-related opportunities are consistently important across both groups. Remote work does not significantly affect STEM respondents’ choices, whereas workplace proximity is the strongest driver for vocational-technical respondents. Relatedness, operationalized as environmental and community impact, is not a significant differentiating attribute, suggesting that in organizations whose public value mission is already highly visible, social and environmental impact may function as a baseline expectation.

title: Don’t say it’s green! How green framing can depress support for renewable energy
abstract: Abstract The green transition implies a shift towards renewable energies. However, their deployment has faced some backlash. This article assesses whether (a) the type of renewables and (b) framing can affect support for deployment. Through a survey experiment, three types of renewables (hydropower, onshore wind, offshore wind) and three types of frames (energy sovereignty, economic competitiveness, green transition) are evaluated, in general and for two typically skeptical groups (the least climate-worried and the less-educated ruralites). Using the case of Norway, we find strong effects for the type of renewables but little evidence for general framing effects. There are two exceptions: green framing has a negative effect on support for renewables where citizens have more fluid preferences (offshore wind) and depresses support among the least climate-worried and the less-educated ruralites. For these citizens, remaining silent about the climate benefits of renewable energy will actually boost support for its deployment.

title: From policy experimentation to policy absorption: how regulatory sandbox outputs enter standing policy decisions

One, two, many postdoctoral careers? Subjective and objective career perspectives in academia and beyond
abstract: Abstract Using a convergent mixed-methods design, this study examines how labor-market conditions and subjective career experiences shape postdoctoral trajectories in Germany. We integrate employment biographies for 5,927 PhD holders with 60 interviews conducted with postdocs in experimental particle physics and modern history to trace transitions within and beyond academia. Quantitative analyses reveal strong disciplinary disparities five years after the PhD: physicists more often secure full-time, better-paid, permanent jobs outside academia, while historians face fragmented, lower-paid, and insecure paths. Qualitative findings complement these patterns: physicists anticipate and prepare for non-academic transitions, whereas historians experience ongoing uncertainty, hidden unemployment, and limited orientation toward alternatives. Across fields, fixed-term contracts compress time horizons and foster a gradual, drawn-out exit process, although strong commitment to research often delays departure. We conceptualize transitions as continuous, discipline-sensitive processes that begin early in the postdoc phase and highlight the need for employer recognition and institutional reforms to reduce precarity.

title: Is There a Subjective Well-Being Crisis among Young Canadians?
