Beyond Legislation: Monetary Policy Governance in Canada
Is There Something in the Water? A Case Study of Community Water Fluoridation Readoption in Calgary, Alberta, Canada, 2011–2021
Consociation without reconciliation: two logics of post-conflict order in Lebanon
abstract: Societies that implement power-sharing arrangements after conflict often succeed at preventing renewed violence while at the same time experiencing poor governance, low civic trust, and corruption. In this article, I argue that this outcome reflects a fundamental tension between two logics of post-conflict political order: consociationalism and political reconciliation. Consociationalism theorizes peace as a problem of managing relations among communal elites, and defines success as the prevention of renewed violence. Political reconciliation theory theorizes peace as a transformation in relations between citizens and the state, and among citizens themselves, one that demands credible institutions, inclusive citizenship, and ongoing civic contestation. Drawing on Lebanon's post-Ta’if order as a paradigmatic case of corporate consociationalism, I specify three mechanisms through which the consociational logic constrains legitimate post-conflict order: institutional capture erodes state credibility, exclusionary boundaries fix political membership in rigid communal categories, and static equilibrium inhibits the civic contestation that reconciliation requires. This analysis reframes consociational outcomes as peace without reconciliation and proposes a framework for evaluating post-conflict power-sharing beyond the prevention of violence.

title: How dictators leave peacefully: understanding non-resistant exits and their consequences
abstract: Autocracy research has comprehensively examined irregular, or coercive, removals of dictators, largely overlooking the logic and consequences of their regular exits. Here, we hone in on a particular type of regular exits, namely non-resistant departures. First, we develop a typology of four distinct forms of non-resistant regular dictator step-downs – downshifters, liberalizers, acquiescers, and good losers – and derive expectations about their post-tenure fates. Second, we introduce new data that distinguish genuinely non-resistant exits from those involving a degree of resistance by the incumbents. Among regular exits from 1960 to the present, roughly one quarter involve some form of resistance. The remaining three-quarters – 107 autocrats, or nearly one-third of all autocrats – exit without resistance. Drawing from our newly collected data combined with illustrative case studies, we show that non-resistant exits indeed encompass four distinct scenarios, from weakened leaders leaving after electoral defeat or through an elite consensus to strong rulers managing controlled successions or initiating liberalization. Third, we show that, compared to those who resist, dictators who leave office in a non-resistant manner are twice as likely to avoid negative post-tenure consequences. Overall, our findings highlight that how autocrats leave power matters: non-resistance constitutes a distinct and relatively safe mode of exit.

title: Competitive autocracy goes online: analysis of the Turkish case
abstract: Research On digital repression has primarily focused on closed authoritarian regimes characterized by centralized censorship and comprehensive surveillance. Less is known about how repression operates in competitive authoritarian regimes where global social media platforms remain accessible, but enforcement is selective. This study argues that, rather than suppressing digital speech uniformly, such regimes exploit legal ambiguity and discretionary enforcement to generate asymmetrical political risk for users. This process skews political expression across user groups and reshapes the visible digital public sphere according to users’ proximity to political power. We examine Turkey’s 2022 act against disinformation, which sharply increased perceived risks surrounding online political expression. Using an original user-day panel of more than 16,000 Twitter users who follow verified local branches of political parties, we estimate user fixed-effects Poisson models for two outcomes: daily retweet volume and political tweeting. The results demonstrate a pattern in which opposition-aligned, left-wing, and high-visibility users significantly reduced online expression, while regime-aligned, right-wing, and low-visibility users do not exhibit comparable restraint and, in some cases, increase online activity. These findings suggest that, much as competitive authoritarian regimes preserve formal democratic institutions while bending them towards incumbent advantage, they preserve formally open digital spaces while tilting visibility towards regime-aligned users

title: ‘The winners take it all, the losers standing small’: Party centralization and Duverger's law
abstract: Do electoral rules shape party centralization? Duverger posed the question seven decades ago; confounding factors have kept it open ever since. We argue that centralization also responds strategically to institutional and ecological incentives, not only to inheritance, imitation, or top-down imposition. Brazil's bifurcated mayoral rules offer a quasi-experimental test: municipalities under 200,000 registered voters elect mayors by single-member plurality (SMP); larger ones use a two-round system (TRS). A regression discontinuity design at this threshold identifies the causal effect of electoral rules on party organization, using elected (decentralized) versus appointed (centralized) local branches as the outcome. TRS municipalities sustain about two to three more elected branches than comparable SMP municipalities, and under SMP the probability of gaining a new branch drops sharply once about two parties hold one — consistent with Cox's M+1 rule. A cross-national analysis of 365 parties in 56 democracies with directly elected presidents is consistent with the pattern. Restrictive rules centralize parties from the bottom up.

title: Populism and conspiracy theories: A cross-national analysis
abstract: How prominent are conspiracy theory beliefs among supporters of populist and radical right movements? Are they characteristic of the populist ‘thin-ideology’ rather than the ‘thick’ ideologies that accompany it and are they associated with supporting candidates in elections? While the literature notes a convergence between the populist worldview and conspiratorial beliefs, most studies analyze single countries, and miss out on broader cross-national patterns. In two studies, I examine whether conspiracy theory beliefs are associated with support for populist and radical right parties across Europe, distinguishing populism’ s effect from accompanying ideologies, using two large cross-national European datasets, the Voices of Central Europe dataset (9 countries) and European Social Survey (24 countries). Study 1 shows nuanced results with conspiracy theory beliefs strongly associated with support for both populist and radical right parties in Central Europe when controlling for party family, with radical right ideology being the strongest predictor, while Study 2 demonstrates similar associations with latent populist attitudes and authoritarianism, as well as feeling close to a populist or radical right party and having voted for them in the previous election. While conspiracy theory believers are shown to be more likely to support populist candidates, this relationship leans heavily rightward. These results further our understanding of the consequences of conspiracy theory beliefs on voter behavior by providing cross-national evidence for the conspiracy theory-populist connection.

title: Presenting the Updated Non-State Actor Dataset
abstract: This data feature presents an update (Version 4.0) to the Non-State Actor (NSA) data, which provide information on the characteristics of rebel groups in all state-rebel group dyads in the Uppsala Conflict Data Program/Peace Research Institute Oslo Armed Conflict Dataset (ACD). The previous version of the NSA data ended in 2011, and Version 4.0 extends coverage through 2024, adding more than 250 new dyad spells and aligning pre-2011 data with Version 25.1 of the ACD. The added period is a consequential one for the study of conflict: the number of conflicts and conflict fatalities have risen substantially, while international conflict management efforts have declined. We describe the coding process and present descriptive analyses showing marked increases in rebel strength relative to the government and in rebel territorial control over the post-2011 period. We also discuss applications of the data to research on rebel governance and violence against civilians, two areas where scholarship has grown substantially since the data were last updated. The update further allows the range of data projects built on the NSA to be extended, supporting research on how the changing character of contemporary conflict shapes its dynamics and outcomes.

title: Optimal avoidability in cross-border minimum taxation
abstract: Many tax regimes collect revenue to the extent that other governments do not. This paper develops a theory of how such cross-border minimum taxes should be designed, focusing on choices that affect avoidance of the regime. Making a minimum tax more difficult to avoid retains more firms within the regime but weakens competition among tax havens. Havens then raise their rates toward the minimum, reducing the top-up tax rate on shifted profit. As a result, an avoidable minimum tax can raise more revenue for the governments that impose it than an unavoidable one.

title: Pricing climate risks: Evidence from wildfires and municipal bonds
abstract: How are public finances affected by climate-driven changes in wildfire risk? Using high-resolution meteorological forecasts, land use data, and US municipal bond spreads, we find that municipalities facing greater future wildfire exposure already incur higher borrowing costs: A one standard deviation increase in future wildfire risk is associated with a 7 (8) basis point rise in primary (secondary) market spreads—over 15% of the sample mean. Impacts appear larger in areas with higher minority populations and greater reliance on local revenue. Our study contributes to the broader literature by introducing a new approach to evaluating the capitalization of evolving physical climate risks.

title: The impact of preference programs in public procurement: Evidence from veteran set-asides
Conversations at Scale: Robust AI-led Interviews
Salinization and Development,
abstract: Abstract Climate change-intensified seawater intrusion creates a dual shock of transitory freshwater shortages and lasting soil degradation. We study its impacts on agricultural production in the Vietnamese Mekong Delta, a major rice exporter. Combining river salinity observations and detailed canal network data to map localized hydrological shocks, we find that salinity reduces rice yields but generates disproportionately larger declines in output and revenue. These losses are driven by a contraction in land under cultivation and limited substitution toward salt-resistant crops, pointing to constrained short-run adaptation. Using household and firm data, we further document reductions in own-farm employment alongside minimal transition to non-agricultural sectors, suggesting frictions in labor adjustment. Beyond income effects predicted by Engel curves, households reallocate expenditures toward healthcare and children’s schooling. The increase in schooling spending is driven by higher participation and may reflect shifts in opportunity costs, though we cannot rule out forward-looking responses.
journal_name: Journal of the European Economic Association

title: Optimal Taxation of Indistinguishable Activities
abstract: Optimal tax policy frequently prescribes different tax treatments for activities that are difficult in practice for tax administrators to distinguish, such as expenditures undertaken for business versus personal purposes.We study the optimal design of income tax deductions for such expenditures under the assumption that a common deduction rate must be applied to both forms of the expenditure.The Pareto optimal common deduction turns on the relative compensated spending response for each margin, weighted by the income tax wedge.We also characterize the welfare gain from distinguishing between the two expenditure forms as a harmonic mean of the compensated responses.We illustrate both results with an application to air travel expenses.

title: Tax Productivity and Economic Development: A Quantitative Macroeconomic Analysis
abstract: This paper examines the role of government capacity to collect taxes in driving economic development.We first draw on a new macro-historical database to document that tax collections relative to tax administration expenditures rise sharply with GDP per capita.We then interpret this finding in a neoclassical growth model with a tax administration sector in which labor inputs are required to raise tax revenues.Countries differ in their levels of tax productivity, capturing how effectively labor is used to raise taxes, as well as their levels of productivity in creating consumption and investment goods.Governments use tax revenues to provide public capital that complements private factors in production and to make transfers.Quantitatively, our model predicts that increases in tax productivity in low-income economies can raise GDP per capita substantially more than suggested by Hulten's theorem.

title: Regional Variations and Productivity Puzzles in Health Care
abstract: Health care utilization per capita varies widely across the United States, yet higher utilization areas have no better patient health.In the late 2000s, this pattern was widely interpreted as evidence that health care costs could be cut substantially without harming patients, which in turn shaped the 2010 Affordable Care Act.We describe how our understanding has since evolved, emphasizing three points.First, new evidence indicates quantitatively meaningful roles for both supply-side and demand-side factors in driving regional variation in health care and in health outcomes.Second, health care productivity varies substantially across providers; improving it requires better understanding of why productivity differs.Third, we know even less about the sources of area-level productivity differences.We suggest several ways in which greater engagement with the productivity literature outside of health care could yield valuable insights.

title: Generative AI, Managerial Expectations, and Economic Activity
abstract: We use generative AI to extract managerial expectations about their economic outlook from 120,000+ corporate conference call transcripts. The resulting AI Economy Score predicts GDP growth, production, and employment up to 10 quarters ahead, beyond existing measures like survey forecasts. Moreover, industry and firm-level measures provide valuable information about sector-specific and individual firm activities. A composite measure that integrates managerial expectations about firm, industry, and macroeconomic conditions further significantly improves the forecasting power and predictive horizon of national and sectoral growth. Our findings show managerial expectations offer unique insights into economic activity, with implications for both macroeconomic and microeconomic decision-making.

title: Comparative Advantage and Economies of Scale under Uncertainty
abstract: We study how regional specialization patterns and welfare are affected by uncertainty and economies of scale in an open economy.We use a spatial equilibrium model with sectoral economies of scale, aggregate uncertainty, and irreversible mobility decisions made by heterogenous workers.We analytically characterize how the interactions between comparative advantage, both of workers and firms, economies of scale, and uncertainty shape specialization patterns and, hence, the gains from trade.We find empirical support for the model predictions by documenting the impact of aggregate changes in volatility of sectoral productivity on U.S. regional economies.We calibrate the model using detailed data on U.S. commuting zones and international trade, and extending hat-algebra methods to accommodate uncertainty.Quantitatively, we find that uncertainty shifts employment away from riskier sectors and locations, relative to a deterministic benchmark, lowering the U.S. aggregate gains from trade by around 20 percent.The interaction between uncertainty and scale economies brings down the benefits of specialization.For regions that would otherwise lose from trade, the presence of agglomeration forces and a more elastic labor supply mitigates those losses.

title: Losing Their Religion
abstract: Afrim Krasniqi and Juliana Rexha for very helpful insights on Albania.This paper investigates the economic consequences of the banning of religion and does not take a stand on the ethics or morality

title: The Returns to Temporary Migration: Experimental Evidence from the H-2A Program
abstract: In 2024, 315,000 H-2A temporary seasonal work visas were issued to agricultural workers in the US.The H-2A program is controversial: earnings are high, but critics argue that workers face poor working and living conditions and that families bear the costs of separation.We randomize H-2A seasonal visas for Mexican workers.During a single US season, migrants earn more than USD 16,000 and send 70% of these earnings to origin households.Living standards in Mexico rise: food security increases, the probability of living in poverty falls by 10 percentage points, and families invest in home improvements, durable assets, and debt reduction, with little investment in businesses or productive assets.Migration has spillovers onto the household: the mental health of household respondents worsens and they avoid higher-risk situations such as walking at night, and intra-household dynamics change.Migrants generally report satisfaction with H-2A jobs and contracts, all report that they would migrate again, and 85% do so the following season.

title: Ratings, Debt, and Deficits: An Exploration
abstract: We look at the effects of debt and primary fiscal balances on sovereign credit ratings through the lens of a simple model.We find that the ratings differ from the implications of the model in three important ways.They give much more weight to debt relative to forecast primary balances.They understate the effects of the difference between the interest rate and the growth rate.They give a very large role to country effects.For the same level of debt and forecast primary balances, they imply extremely different ratings across countries, and imply extremely different levels of debt needed to reach a given rating.

title: Training Your Replacement: Worker Incentives and the Pace of Automation
abstract: Firms ask workers to train AI systems that will replace them.We model this with a worker who can shirk, cooperate with training, or obstruct training while maintaining productivity.Because training ends the job but only cooperation completes training, dismissal becomes a weaker penalty for shirking.The firm must raise the worker's rent, and the worker gains from their replacement.AI can create jobs paying more than they produce and eliminate jobs it never automates.Firms paying only wages may slow training.A credible completion bonus equal to the worker's rent without AI removes both the gain and the slowdown.

title: fevc: Leave-Out Bias-Corrected Variance Decompositions in Stata
abstract: Variance decompositions from worker and firm fixed-effect regressions measure heterogeneity and sorting in linked data, but estimation noise can substantially bias their components.This article introduces fevc, a Stata command implementing the leave-out bias correction of Kline, Saggio, and Sølvsten (2020).It reports corrected variances of worker and firm effects, their covariance, and the variance of their sum.Researchers choose the deletion unit, treatment of controls, and weights defining the target population.The command also reports standard errors for projections of fixed effects on observed characteristics.A source-only Mata implementation runs wherever Stata runs, while a parallel Rust plugin handles large datasets.Random-projection calculations report Monte Carlo standard errors measuring numerical precision.In a public extract of Italian social-security records, the correction halves the estimated variance of firm effects and reverses the worker-firm covariance's sign.In synthetic benchmarks with 6.4 million observations and 28 threads, the Rust backend is 1.3 to 3.5 times as fast as the KSS Matlab package.Under match deletion, measured peak memory is about 30 percent of the Matlab package's.

title: College Success: Understanding the Roles of Financial Aid, Loans, Preparation, and Incentives
abstract: Over the past four decades, the earnings gap between college graduates and non-graduates has widened substantially, prompting interest in policies aimed at promoting higher education among low-income students.A key challenge for these policies is the high college dropout rate.This paper develops a dynamic model of college enrollment and completion with rich individual heterogeneity to assess how various factors influence college attendance, dropout, and graduation.We estimate the model using data from longitudinal surveys, results of quasi-experimental studies on grant aid, and large-scale randomized controlled trials.We use the model to simulate the effects of tuition subsidies, college loans, financial incentives, and increased pre-college skills on attendance and completion.We find moderate effects of most unconditional financial policies on attendance, with small effects on completion conditional on attendance.By contrast, some meritbased incentives, such as forgiving student loans upon receipt of a bachelor's degree, have substantial effects.However, this type of policy and other financial subsidies accrue even more than the others to students from relatively wealthy backgrounds.Overall, it appears infeasible to design a financial aid policy that is simultaneously effective in raising attainment and fiscally progressive.By comparison, we find that the greatest potential for increasing attainment could come from better preparing students for college.

title: An LLM Workflow for Functional Form Sensitivity Analysis
abstract: We introduce an LLM workflow for functional form sensitivity analysis.A researcher estimates the value of an object of interest by maximizing the fit of a working model to some data.The working model assumes an arbitrary form for some function.We define sensitivity by how much it is possible to change the estimate of the object of interest, without compromising fit, by selecting a different functional form.The workflow first looks for an analytic solution.If it fails to find one, it approximates the solution via numerical methods that respect the fit constraint at each step of a solver path.The workflow yields a verifiable lower bound on the in-sample sensitivity of the researcher's estimate, and is fast in many practical situations.We illustrate with an application to the welfare cost of adverse selection in health insurance.

title: Sex and Subsistence: Income Effects on Risky Sexual Behavior and Partner Selection
abstract: Whether to engage in sex and with whom are extremely consequential decisions for young women worldwide, and particularly in sub-Saharan Africa, where HIV rates are high and adolescent pregnancies are common.Yet little is known about the extent to which these decisions are financially motivated.We combine a randomized controlled trial of monthly cash assistance to female students at the University of Zambia with detailed, high-frequency data on sexual behavior and partner characteristics.We find that this temporary increase in income significantly changes women's sexual behavior.Treated participants are 5.1 percentage points less likely to have sex during the treatment period, and the rate of condomless sex falls by 30%.Among women who were not sexually active at baseline, the likelihood of having sex falls by 43%, and partner quality conditional on sex greatly improves.Financial assistance also reduces financial precarity, increasing food security, mental health, and cognitive capacity.These results can be rationalized with a dynamic model of partner search in which women can choose to search for boyfriends or high-income partners who provide financial support and bargain over both transfers and condom use.We conclude that a substantial share of sexual activity is financially motivated in this setting, even in a population not typically regarded as vulnerable.Increasing young women's income may be a useful tool for reducing the negative externalities of risky sex and improving match quality.

title: A Network Approach to Geopolitics
abstract: We develop a tractable framework for analyzing geopolitics as a network of coordination and strategic influence.Countries choose geopolitical actions that trade off domestic interests against incentives to align with connected countries.They can exert costly bilateral influence to affect one another's actions.We characterize equilibrium actions and bilateral influence in closed form.Cross-country differences in domestic interests decompose into latent geopolitical cleavages, each of which the network transmits into geopolitical actions independently of the others.The crosscountry covariance matrices of domestic interests and of geopolitical actions identify the cleavages and their importance, from which we recover the network.We implement the framework using data on United Nations voting and democratic orientation.The inferred network is well approximated by a few dimensions, aligns with external measures of geopolitical ties, and recovers well-known historical cleavages.We undertake counterfactuals for domestic interests and network connections and quantify three notions of geopolitical power

title: Who Can Control Our Firms? National Security and Foreign Ownership Regulation
abstract: Governments invoke national security to regulate foreign acquisitions of domestic firms.Why is ownership regulation a distinct policy margin beyond standard tools, like production subsidies and trade taxes?We show that contractual frictions make multinational firm boundaries central to geoeconomic policy.Within firms, ownership allocates residual control that affects outcomes through non-contractible decisions.Between governments, the absence of enforceable agreements makes the economic costs of conflict shape geopolitical bargaining.Foreign ownership depends on private returns to foreign control, but also determines national exposure to geopolitical conflict.It can increase foreign dependence, technology transfer, or sabotage scope.If such margins were contractible, the government could regulate them directly.When they are not, ownership regulation is the second-best tool that changes control rights and, thus, geopolitical outcomes.Consistent with our mechanism, U.S. regulation emphasizes the nationalsecurity risks of foreign control over firm decisions, has tightened with rising geopolitical tensions, and is tighter in sectors with higher exposure to defense demand and contractual frictions.

title: We Just Created More Than 1,000 Synthetic Controls To Study California's $20 Fast Food Minimum Wage

title: Homework in Climate Economics: Household Production, Environmental Preferences, and Climate Policy
abstract: All potential errors are our own.This paper relies on data from a survey administered by the Understanding America Study, which is maintained by the University of Southern California.The views expressed in this paper are our own and do not reflect the views of USC, UAS, the National Bureau of Economic Research, the Federal Reserve System or its staff.At least one co-author has disclosed additional relationships of potential relevance for this research.

title: Tariff Staggering
abstract: Using a panel of U.S. imports and customs duties at the HS 6-digit level, we document that in a typical quarter about 20 percent of tariffs rise, 20 percent fall, and 60 percent remain unchanged.Motivated by these facts, we develop a model of staggered tariff setting and embed it in a dynamic open-economy framework.Staggering changes the dynamics of the cross-sectional mean tariff, generating hump-shaped macroeconomic responses to tariff shocks.Staggering also overturns the Razin-Svensson trade-balance neutrality result for permanent tariff increases, because the gradual adjustment of the mean tariff creates an anticipation effect that induces agents to front-load net imports.Inherited tariff dispersion has first-order macroeconomic effects, allowing tariff harmonization to be studied with linear approximation methods.We find that eliminating tariff dispersion while holding the mean tariff unchanged has effects akin to a transitory tariff cut in an economy without staggering.

title: Competition in Generative AI: Evidence from Consumer Demand
abstract: How competitive will the market for generative AI be as it matures?Using novel transaction level credit and debit card data covering 174 million consumers and 114 billion transactions, we study the adoption of paid services and the demand-side foundations of competition in this market.As of April 2026, approximately 2.9% of U.S. consumers pay for at least one major generative AI service, with adoption highest among younger and higher-income consumers.Nearly all of these paid users subscribe to basic plans that cost $30 or less per month.Three patterns suggest limited differentiation and low switching costs.First, although multihoming is common, it has declined as providers' capabilities have expanded.Second, annual customer retention rates range from 20% to 45% across major AI providers, lower than those for many other subscription products.Third, switching rises around major model releases.Motivated by these findings, we develop and estimate a structural model of AI service demand and supply that reveals strong competitive pressure.Consumers are highly price sensitive, have much weaker preferences for particular providers than for AI overall, and view AI services as increasingly close substitutes.Our results suggest that, absent a substantial increase in AI model quality differentiation, growing substitutability among services will constrain providers' pricing power and allow consumers to capture a large share of the surplus generated by these services.

title: Insuring Landlords
abstract: This paper shows that insuring landlords against non-payment risk can improve housing access and upward geographic mobility for fragile tenants.We study Visale, a large-scale publicly funded rent guarantee insurance policy in France, free for eligible tenants and landlords.Using administrative household and claim payout data and quasi-experimental eligibility variation by exact age, we show the guarantee increased access to private-sector rental housing, especially for immigrants, newly formed households, and low-income renters.The scheme eased long-distance mobility toward expensive, high-wage neighborhoods at a moderate fiscal cost per marginal move, though potentially displacing comparable ineligible tenants through higher rents.

title: Selective Admissions in Nursing Homes: Evidence from a Randomized Audit Study
abstract: It has been widely documented that patients in the US who are associated with disadvantaged demographics receive care at lower quality nursing homes.To understand the role that selective admissions may play in contributing to this pattern, we conducted a nationwide audit study of the impact of patient race, payer, and medical condition on responses to about 5,500 availability inquiries sent to about 3,000 nursing homes.We find 10-15% lower availability for Medicaid patients compared to private-pay patients and for patients with Alzheimer's disease compared to those without; these availability gaps generally increase with nursing home quality.We find no statistically significant evidence of differential availability by race.To quantify the implications of these selective admissions practices, we embed the audit study results in a model of constrained nursing home choice.We estimate that if, counterfactually, Medicaid patients had the same choice sets as their private-pay counterparts, they would attend higher quality nursing homes on average, but the private-Medicaid gap in quality would be reduced by only 5-10%.Our results suggest that supply-side availability differences by payer are widespread, but that they are unlikely to be the primary factor behind the observed gap in quality of nursing homes attended.

title: Implications of Policy Interventions on Eliminating Gender Gaps
abstract: This paper studies policy interventions intended to eliminate gender differences in labor market outcomes, principally wages.Because gender is an individual attribute rather than a manipulable treatment, the ideal experiment of randomly assigning gender to evaluate its effects is infeasible.Policies that remove gender labels from the employment process are the closest feasible counterpart.We quantify both the intended and unintended consequences of the policies through simulated interventions of an estimated equilibrium model of statistical discrimination with dynamic choices of education and labor market participation.In the short run the policy that requires gender free applications in the market for skilled labor eliminates wage gaps but once education choices respond the effects are attenuated.A more comprehensive policy that enforces gender free compensation reverses the wage gap in skilled markets and eliminates it in unskilled labor markets, even once education adjusts.These interventions impact college rates, the college premium gap and participation rates as well.The final section studies these interventions using a difference-in-differences (DID) approach to analyze the simulated data.With education fixed, the DID method recovers the policy effects but this is not the case once education adjusts, reflecting the effects of the intervention on both treated and control groups through equilibrium adjustments in beliefs.

title: Strategic Monetary Policy in Open Economies
abstract: We examine optimal non-cooperative monetary policy in a two-country New Keynesian setting with complete financial markets and pricing to market for goods.In contrast to the case in which the law of one price holds for goods, currency misalignments are an important consideration even for selforiented policymakers.Financial markets are critical in the analysis.Under "full" commitment, the optimal policy considers the effects on asset values and hence wealth distribution across countries.Optimal policy under full commitment differs from the "partial" commitment case in which the policy commitment is not made until after asset markets clear.Surprisingly, the optimal targeting rule under strategic policy with full commitment is the same as under cooperative policy.In this setting, changes in state-contingent claim prices offset the wealth a self-oriented policymaker might seek through terms-of-trade manipulation, and we show that there are no gains from cooperation.Although a policy chosen under partial commitment may be desirable from a country's perspective, the resulting Nash equilibrium yields lower welfare.

title: The Impact of Silver Loading in ACA Health Insurance Marketplaces

title: HouseholdBench: Evaluating Large Language Models as Predictors of Household Economic Behavior
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have the potential to meet a key goal in economics: a quantitative model of household decision making, across a variety of settings. Yet existing evaluations cover few surveys and outcomes, and do not study how households adjust to changing economic conditions. We introduce a new evaluation, HouseholdBench, which unites 6 U.S. household surveys and 32 prediction tasks spanning numeric, categorical and probabilistic outcomes, related to consumption, income, labor, expectations, and housing. Using past behavior, demographics and macroeconomic conditions, the tasks test whether LLMs predict behavior, including how households adjust to changes in various policies. We evaluate 13 proprietary and open-weight LLMs against a no-change baseline and a gradient-boosted tree model. Most LLMs outperform the no-change baseline, including for policy response tasks -- with the best model lowering error for numeric outcomes by 12.2%. Across most tasks, gradient-boosted trees rank first; leading proprietary LLMs approach their performance, but open-weight models lag. LLMs exhibit systematic over- and underprediction across different tasks. We identify methods that enable a 4 billion parameter open-weight model to match proprietary models'performance: fine-tuning and aggregating 16 predictions per observation. Improvements generalize to policy-response tasks, which are excluded from fine-tuning. We release our datasets, code, and leaderboard on our website: https://jn-huang.github.io/householdbench

title: Behavioral Finance at 40
abstract: Behavioral finance seeks to improve our understanding of markets, investors, and firms by adopting a psychologically realistic description of how people think.While behavioral finance ideas have been part of human discourse for decades if not centuries, the modern research effort in the field began in the 1980s.Forty years later, behavioral finance is a vibrant area of financial economics.In this article, I explain why by reviewing some of its recent progress.I focus on three topics -beliefs about future earnings, beliefs about future returns, and prospect theory -and on their applications to understanding asset prices and investor behavior.I close by commenting on some new directions in the field -cognitive foundations, non-traditional decision processes, and artificial intelligence.

title: The Great Game: A Model of Geoeconomic Competition
abstract: We build a model of two hegemons that have valuable trading relationships with each other and at the same time compete in exerting geoeconomic power over countries in the rest of the world.When the hegemons trade with each other, their optimal policy is shaped both by classic economic considerations -the profitability of that specific trade -and by geoeconomic competition -how the trade affects the power of each hegemon vis-a-vis the rest of the world.We show that containment, a policy mix in which a hegemon limits sales of its inputs to the rival hegemon and uses its power to demand that the rest of the world shift away from sourcing from the rival, arises when the two hegemons offer relatively substitutable exports, are less interdependent with each other, and have more direct geopolitical rivalry.Countries in the rest of the world benefit, all else equal, from hegemons containing each other since they partially squander their power with offsetting demands.However, containment policy can also worsen the efficiency of global production, leaving the rest of the world worse off.

title: Coasian Stakeholder Theory
abstract: Stakeholder theory asks who is in, who is out, and who gets what.Existing work illuminates important dimensions of firm-stakeholder relationships but does not supply a common, transaction-level rule connecting these questions.We use the Coase theorem to develop such a rule.A Coasian stakeholder is an actor with shutdown power, defined as the de facto capacity, within the relevant time horizon, to prevent, materially delay, or substantially reduce the expected joint value of a focal value-creating transaction.If all such actors are identified and bargaining and enforcement are costless, value-maximizing transactions proceed, although rights and bargaining positions may affect who captures value.When transaction costs are positive, however, identification, bargaining, coalition formation, and enforcement can delay, distort, or suppress those transactions.Across six propositions, we explain how shutdown power is identified and acquired, how complementarity and bargaining conditions shape value capture, how firms reshape stakeholder sets through coalition costs and governance design, and why consolidated opposition can sometimes preserve transactions that fragmented claims would suppress.

title: The Occupational Ladder: Implications for Life-Cycle Wage Dynamics
abstract: Some occupations pay higher wages than others, even conditional on worker characteristics, implying that occupations can be ranked on a ladder.We develop a simple decomposition to study the role this occupational ladder plays in average wage growth and in the fanning out of wages over the life cycle.We present three main findings.First, the distribution of employment shifts towards higher-paying occupations as workers gain experience.This contributes modestly to average lifecycle wage growth, with greatest impact in early career.Second, this upward movement in the occupational employment distribution is not accompanied by increasing dispersion; thus, the occupational ladder does not directly contribute to the fanning out of wages.Third, early-career workers who are well-positioned on the occupational ladder tend to earn wages far below the occupational average.However, by mid-career, workers' relative wages within occupations (their positions on the job ladder) no longer depend on their occupation.This change in the covariance between individuals' positions on the job and occupational ladders is a major contributor to the fanning out of wages over workers' careers.

title: Gender Gaps: International Evidence on the Role of Family Policy
abstract: We use Luxembourg Income Study and International Social Survey Programme microdata on 27 countries over the 1986-2019 period, augmented by policy and labor market information, to estimate the impact of family-friendly policies on gender gaps in employment, wages, earnings, and part-time work, as well as child penalties in employment and earnings.We find that longer duration of parental leave generally lowers gender gaps in wages, employment, earnings, and child penalties in employment and earnings, except for high levels of this entitlement, where further increases in leave raise gender gaps.We also find that the right to request a part-time work schedule raises relative female part-time employment but lowers employment and earnings gender gaps.Higher government expenditures for childcare lower employment, earnings, and part-time employment gender gaps as well as child employment and earnings penalties.These results are generally stronger for the less educated than for the highly educated, possibly reflecting higher costs of taking time off for highly educated women.Finally, expansion of family-friendly policies over this period can account for 24-33% of our sample's reduction in gender gaps in employment and earnings and 46-76% of the reduction in child penalties in these outcomes.The slower expansion of such policies in the United States than elsewhere accounts for 6-15% of the slower reduction in US gender employment and earnings gaps and 20% of the slower fall in the US child employment penalty.

title: When Cash Wakes Up: Inertia in Institutional Money Market Funds and the Potential Effects of AI Disruption
abstract: We study institutional cash management by constructing a novel dataset that records the specific money market funds (MMFs) held by each mutual fund in each month from 2010 to 2024.We document remarkably high inertia: more than half of mutual funds never switched their MMF choice throughout the sample period, despite non-negligible yield dispersion.To decompose the sources of this inertia, we develop a two-stage structural model that separately identifies the determinants of portfolio managers' attentiveness ("waking up") and their conditional preferences once attentive.We estimate the model using a methodology that combines BLP-style contraction mapping with maximum likelihood.We establish three main findings.First, MMFs with less attentive investor bases engage in greater liquidity transformation while offering lower yields.As a result, they earn higher profits and exhibit significantly higher survival rates, especially during periods of low interest rates.Second, we find that aggregate flows appear more yield-sensitive during low interest rate periods (the well-documented "reaching for yield" phenomenon) not because individual investors become more yield-seeking, but because a larger fraction of investors becomes attentive-a composition effect rather than a preference shift.Third, counterfactual analysis reveals a potential tension between market efficiency and financial stability if AI-driven automation reduces investor inattention.In the absence of inattention, fees fall by approximately half, yield dispersion collapses to near zero, and market concentration declines by roughly 20%, but monthly fund flows increase by about three times and the incidence of fund-months in which redemptions exceed a fund's weekly liquid assets rises by about six times, raising the risk of fire sales and MMF runs.

title: The Value of (Sub) Specialization: Evidence from Oncology
abstract: We estimate the returns to specialization in medical oncology, in which subspecialists focus on specific cancer types.Using 2.2 million Medicare chemotherapy episodes from 2008-2020, we instrument for subspecialist access with differential distance to cancer-type-specific subspecialists versus general oncologists.Access to a relevant subspecialist reduces three-year mortality by 4.5 percentage points (10 percent), without increasing Medicare spending or measured provider fragmentation.Subspecialists also increase the use of newer therapies and diagnosis-specific clinical trials.These findings show that specialization raises productivity when expertise is closely matched to the task.

title: Global Entrepreneurial Talent Flows: Widely Funded, Selectively Successful?
abstract: Immigrant founders of US venture-backed startups exit successfully more often than native founders.Does this hold worldwide?Using career histories for 913,226 founder-firm pairs in 213 countries , we compare founders who build abroad (expats) or return home after foreign experience (returnees) with comparable local founders in the same country.Both expats and returnees raise early funding more often globally.Expats' success premium, however, concentrates in the US (18 percent) and UK (26 percent), especially among those entering the US through graduate school, work, or direct founding.Returnees rarely show such a premium.Capital follows mobile founders across borders, but success follows them selectively.

title: Representation, Innovation, and Product Adoption
abstract: During research and development, firms must decide which types of individuals to engage in developing and testing their products.We investigate how lowering the cost of including one group shapes its representation, subsequent innovation, and product adoption.In 2000, Medicare expanded coverage of clinical trial costs for elderly trial participants, a historically underrepresented group in drug development.This policy increases representation: trial sponsors expand trial eligibility to include elderly participants and increase the share of elderly participants.We find an immediate and large increase in the number of clinical trials for diseases common among the elderly, with the largest increase in drugs not yet approved and in approved drugs tested in new diseases.We document an increase in drug utilization of newly tested drugs among elderly individuals and analyze trial results, adverse events, and drug approvals.Our findings show how financial incentives can increase representation in product development and shift the rate, direction, and adoption of innovation to potentially benefit underserved groups.

title: Mechanisms reinforcing and countering segregation: How existing friendship and dislike ties impact friendship homophily and dislike heterophily among Muslim and non-Muslim students in German schools
abstract: Homophily is an important social force in many social networks. While homophilous tendencies among positive relations (such as friendship) and heterophilous tendencies in negative tie networks (such as dislike) have been extensively studied, less is known about how such tendencies might become stronger or weaker as a result of past experiences. Focusing on homophilous and heterophilous tendencies between non-Muslim and Muslim students in schools, this paper explores whether, in line with Intergroup Contact Theory , existing friendship connections with outgroup members will reduce their inclination to dislike outgroup peers compared to ingroup peers (i.e., reduce dislike heterophily), and reduce their preferences for ingroup friendships over outgroup friends (i.e., reduce friendship homophily). On the other hand, in line with Attribution Theory and Social Identity Theory , we propose that existing dislike connections with outgroup members are likely to strengthen dislike heterophilous tendencies and friendship homophilous tendencies, thus further reinforcing religious segregation in schools. To test these hypotheses, we apply Stochastic Actor-Oriented Models (SAOMs) to the friendship and dislike networks of 1678 Muslim and non-Muslim students (FIS data) across 17 German school settings where this religious divide is particularly salient. Contrary to what we expected based on Intergroup Contact Theory , our study shows that prior interreligious friendships do not weaken a person’s tendency for friendship homophily. However, it does seem to reduce heterophily in dislike, but only because it makes students more likely to dislike ingroup peers. On the other hand, prior interreligious dislike ties are found to amplify dislike to outgroups, while not affecting friendship homophily. Surprisingly, our study also shows that ingroup friendships reduce dislike for outgroup members. We explore the implications of the findings that friendship homophily appears unaffected by prior interreligious contacts, while dislike heterophily is strengthened by existing negative outgroup ties, but reduced by both outgroup and ingroup friendships.

title: Review of “Major Trade-Offs: The Surprising Truths About College Majors and Entry-Level Jobs”
abstract: We are constantly told that the humanities (and, to some extent, the social sciences) are dying; sometimes these pronouncements are met with celebration. Who needs those woke navel-gazing disciplines anyway? Students should move over to more “practical” majors such as engineering and computer science. Even amidst an accumulating mass of stories reporting how AI has eviscerated many good jobs in these “hard/real” sciences, the media continues to report on, and public officials continue to decry “useless” majors such as English and sociology. Well, Corey Moss-Pech has news for them. Turns out, there is little connection between what skills students learn in school and what they do at work, at least in their first jobs. More than that, though, the practical skills students learn in the liberal arts turn out to be more useful than any of those skills learned in their more “practical” courses. Liberal arts students may find it more difficult to find jobs when they graduate, and those jobs may pay less, but it is not because they have less valuable skills. Something else is going on.

title: Review of “Defending Democracy in the European Parliament: An Institutional Drama”
Toward Understanding Implications of AI‐Powered Intelligent Transportation Systems on Risk Research and Practice
abstract: The rapidly evolving use of artificial intelligence (AI)-powered intelligent transportation systems (ITS) and other emerging technologies in the transportation sector has the potential to deliver unprecedented improvements in safety and efficiency. However, recent research has also raised concerns about the implications of using AI and automation, as these technologies can introduce new, understudied risks to such systems. This perspective article evaluates AI-powered ITS through three lenses: risk assessment, concerning whether current conceptual and methodological tools remain sufficient for these systems; the human element, relating to how analysts and operators interact with AI outputs, including explainable AI (XAI) and human-in-the-loop oversight; and governance, concerning frameworks needed to manage these systems. Across these lenses, the article uses risk characterization as a diagnostic tool for locating where established risk practice must adapt and translates the resulting gaps into specific research directions. Although the practical interpretation and application of fundamental risk concepts may change when viewed through the lens of AI-powered ITS, the work of this article provides a basis for research directions and requirements needed for risk practice to adapt to new and emerging technologies and to support future research and training within the risk analysis community. This perspective will be of interest to risk researchers, practitioners, and policymakers.

title: The Signaling Role of Seemingly Myopic Investment Behavior
Diversification versus Consumption Motives for Early Exercise of Employee Stock Options
Innovation booms, easy financing, and human capital accumulation
Are direct lenders more like banks or arm’s-length investors?
Unpacking the micro–macro transmission mechanism: how home-country culture selectively shapes cognitive orientations in entrepreneurial internationalization
abstract: Abstract International business accounts treat national culture as a country-level antecedent that shifts average export propensity uniformly, leaving the individual-level mechanisms producing within-country heterogeneity in internationalization intensity unspecified. We address this micro–macro transmission gap using social cognitive theory, examining how individualism versus collectivism and risk avoidance versus tolerance selectively recalibrate three cognitive orientations in entrepreneurial export decisions: perceived self-efficacy, perceived opportunity availability, and fear of failure. Our multilevel analysis of 40,529 observations across 41 countries spanning 2010–2019 reveals divergent rather than uniform moderation: individualism amplifies self-efficacy and opportunity availability beliefs through the social validation pathway, while risk avoidance constrains opportunity availability beliefs and fear of failure through the anticipatory self-regulation and outcome expectancy pathways. Fear of failure’s directional relationship with internationalization is contingent on the expectations of failure costs that the home-country cultural environment establishes through the outcome expectancy pathway, rather than being uniformly inhibitory as prior frameworks assume. These findings advance international business microfoundations theory by specifying the observable transmission pathways through which national cultural dimensions produce heterogeneous export intensity outcomes within the same national context. For policymakers, the findings imply that interventions to strengthen self-efficacy or opportunity awareness work best when calibrated to a country’s cultural profile.

title: Correction: National identity rhetoric under bilateral geopolitical tensions: evidence from Taiwanese MNEs
EXPRESS: Incentive Design for Sales Managers: Impact on Resource Allocation and Performance
abstract: Many firms struggle to design effective incentives for sales managers . Yet despite a vast literature on salespeople’s incentives, little theoretical or empirical research has examined managers’ incentive structures. The authors address a common dilemma that firms face: Should managers’ incentives be based on achieving an aggregate target ( Aggregate Target Scheme , ATS) or instead be linked to the target achievement of each individual territory or salesperson ( Individual Target Scheme , ITS)? A quasi-experiment reveals that, despite ATS’s flexibility and apparent alignment with firm objectives, an ATS-to-ITS transition improved performance , with larger gains among lower-performing and higher-span territories. A scenario-based experiment with sales managers suggests that these effects may stem from the reallocation of resources from high to low performers but provides no evidence of an increase in managers’ overall resource investment. A survey of sales leaders indicates that a sales star bias —a managerial tendency to overallocate resources toward high performers relative to their marginal returns—likely drives suboptimal resource allocation under the flexible ATS. Finally, a supplementary field study documents that, following an ATS-to-ITS transition, managers increased joint fieldwork , especially with the lowest performers, and performance again improved. These results provide insights into managerial incentive design and offer guidance for firms.

title: Navigating the Rugged Data Landscape: The Impact of Data-Extrapolation Technologies on Knowledge Production
abstract: Data-extrapolation technologies enable progress by importing and applying empirical patterns from one domain to another. Their reliance on empirical patterns, however, is also their limitation: these tools can only be applied where data are abundant. Using the setting of structural biology, I investigate the impact of a data-extrapolation technology on innovation. I exploit the variation in prior data availability to compare areas in which the tool was usable to those in which it was not. I find that the tool increased the quantity of research in data-rich areas: the resulting output yielded limited biological insights but was methodologically rigorous and contributed to downstream research. This paper was accepted by Toby Stuart, entrepreneurship and innovation. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.04115 .

title: Selection into Financial Education and Effects on Portfolio Choice
abstract: We study the impact of a financial education program on portfolio choices in a setting that allows us to examine both participation decisions and differences in program benefits across individuals. We directly elicit willingness to pay for financial education and show that individuals with higher financial literacy, greater confidence in applying new knowledge, and higher expected returns are willing to pay more. Using incentivized portfolio allocation tasks, we develop outcome measures tailored to individual risk preferences and show that financial education improves decision quality along these dimensions. The program increases the share of participants who experience an improvement by 20 percentage points, corresponding to average gains of 3.2 percentage points of initial wealth. Individuals with the highest willingness to participate benefit disproportionately from the program, with important implications for the design and evaluation of financial education initiatives. By isolating a specific investment skill in a setting with voluntary participation, our design sheds light on how selection into financial education shapes measured program effects and informs the assessment of broader workplace and public training programs. This paper was accepted by Marie Claire Villeval, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Funding: The authors thank the Pension Research Council of Wharton School at the University of Pennsylvania, as well as the Retirement and Savings Institute at HEC Montréal, for generous research funding. Supplemental Material: The online appendices and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.08268 .

title: Experience and Pivoting in Entrepreneurial Product Development
Machine Learning Instrument Variables for Causal Inference
abstract: A machine learning framework for constructing strong instrumental variables from weak exogenous data achieves semiparametric efficiency with applications to advertising and demand estimation.

title: Fulfillment by Platform: Competition and Upstream Market Power
abstract: Fulfillment by Platform: Competition and Upstream Market Power E-commerce platforms increasingly offer fulfillment services that promise faster delivery and easier access to customers. This study shows that these services create a trade-off. Using transaction-level data from a major online marketplace, the authors find that platform fulfillment improves the customer experience and raises consumer welfare, but it also changes competition among sellers. Because fulfillment through the platform adds costs for merchants, smaller sellers with thinner margins must raise prices more than larger sellers. As a result, large merchants gain share while smaller merchants lose ground, increasing upstream market concentration. The findings matter for regulators, platforms, and merchants because they show that a service that benefits consumers can still weaken competition on the seller side. The paper provides rare empirical evidence from both sides of an e-commerce marketplace and highlights why platform policies should be evaluated not only by customer benefits, but also by their effects on market structure.

title: Location-Allocation of Emergency Service Systems in Light Traffic
abstract: Light-Traffic Asymptotics for Emergency Service Planning Timely emergency response depends on where rescue teams are stationed and which areas they serve—decisions that shape response times and uncertainty in each team’s service durations and availability. In “Location-Allocation of Emergency Service Systems in Light Traffic,” Xin Wang, Weiliang Liu, Loon Ching Tang, and Zhisheng Ye use light-traffic asymptotics to explicitly capture these decision-dependent effects in tractable queueing-based location-allocation optimization models. The key innovation is to turn limiting queueing behavior as call arrival rates approach zero into explicit approximations for performance losses associated with calls that have to wait. These approximations connect queueing performance to planning decisions, enabling mixed-integer linear programming formulations with theoretical guarantees on solution quality in the light-traffic regime. In simulations using Singapore lift-trap rescue data, the optimized plans reduced projected annual late rescues by about 70% relative to the existing arrangement.

title: EXPRESS: Tactical Workforce Planning and Deployment with Timing Coordination Requirements
abstract: We address a tactical planning problem facing organizations that must perform geographically dispersed jobs with timing dependencies using appropriate teams of workers and equipment. This Tactical Workforce Planning and Deployment (TWPD) problem, which is motivated by the annual planning and budgeting activity for rail infrastructure maintenance and upgrades, requires making simultaneous decisions on resource sizing and selection, resource-to-job assignment, and resource repositioning to complete all jobs while minimizing resource and transportation costs. Key challenges include timing coordination among jobs, varying resource capabilities, and sequence-dependent changeover costs. Prior scheduling and routing models often focus on short-term decisions, assuming a given set of resources, and do not incorporate complex timing coordination requirements. We propose a large-scale optimization model, with strong timing coordination constraints, that integrates all the features of the TWPD problem. To solve this difficult problem, we propose three new families of valid inequalities to further strengthen the model and develop problem reduction procedures as well as an optimization-based multi-stage algorithm to identify good initial feasible solutions. Our Composite method applies these acceleration strategies before initiating an exact branch-and-bound solution procedure. To test the effectiveness of this method, we first apply it to real data sets for track maintenance from a leading railroad company and compare its performance with a method that uses a standard solver without our enhancements. We find that our method dramatically outperforms the standard method. We also test our method on many randomly generated problems to validate its superior performance and identify problem features that make this problem difficult to solve. When compared to a manual tactical plan, our method quickly generates a near-optimal solution that saves over 15% in annual total cost, demonstrating the practical value and viability of our model and method. We conclude by discussing some managerial implications and insights from our results.

title: EXPRESS: Optimal Return Policies with Heterogeneous Search Rewards
abstract: This paper studies return policy design for an online seller serving consumers who can resolve product-fit uncertainty through costly pre-purchase search, with search rewards varying across consumers. Return policies shape not only post-purchase return behavior but also ex-ante search and purchase decisions, thereby generating endogenous consumer segmentation. One might expect that inexpensive search would reduce the seller's incentive to offer a generous refund. In our baseline model, however, we show that full refund outperforms no refund when search costs are sufficiently low. We trace this result to a fundamental trade-off in implementing a full-refund policy: the search-relief effect versus the return-inducing effect. Full refund substitutes for search by allowing consumers who would otherwise search to purchase directly and evaluate fit after purchase, thereby removing their search-based information advantage and restoring the seller's pricing power. However, it also induces returns from consumers who would otherwise purchase without search and keep the product, sacrificing the revenue generated by their tolerance for misfit. When search costs are sufficiently low, most consumers would otherwise search, and the search-relief effect therefore dominates the return-inducing effect. As search costs fall further, full refund can also achieve a win-win outcome, indicating that pre-purchase search may be socially inefficient. These findings explain when and why sellers may optimally discourage ex-ante search in favor of ex-post product evaluation.

title: EXPRESS: Design and Pricing of Online Dating Subscriptions
abstract: Online dating is now the most common way for new couples in the U.S. to meet, with more than 30% of U.S. adults having used a dating app and with global industry revenues exceeding three billion dollars annually. Most dating apps monetize primarily through subscription pricing, offering users fixed periods of access to paid features for recurring fees. However, applying subscription pricing to online dating apps presents some unique challenges. Unlike other digital services, users' valuations of dating app services typically decline with use, as continued participation can be costly in terms of both time and emotional effort, and repeated renewals signal unsuccessful app-mediated searches. Moreover, users who achieve their goal of finding a partner subsequently exit the platform, creating an apparent tension between providing value by successfully matching users and a dating app’s goal of generating profit and sustaining a large userbase of paying subscribers. Given these unique challenges and the transient nature of user engagement with dating apps, it is interesting to note that leading U.S. dating apps, such as Hinge and Bumble, have begun offering increasingly long subscription options, including lifetime subscriptions. In this paper, we analyze the performance of subscription pricing strategies with varying period lengths for online dating platforms. We propose a natural model of dating app monetization and use it to evaluate how subscription length affects both profit and steady-state userbase size. We find that suitably priced lifetime subscriptions can Pareto-dominate all finite-period subscriptions over both objectives, providing a compelling explanation for their emerging use. We then extend our analysis to subscription menus with two options and show that offering one short-term subscription option and one lifetime option guarantees approximately 59.4% of the optimal two-option menu performance.

title: Incentivizing Equality? How Work-Family Policies Affect Parenthood Penalties in 27 Countries
abstract: Work-family policies are theorized to shape the division of paid labor after parenthood, but recent studies have cast doubt on their importance. Leveraging harmonized longitudinal data spanning 27 countries and an analytic focus on couples and couple dynamics, our study shows that work-family policies do shape how divisions of paid labor change with parenthood, and that they also moderate the importance of couples’ relative resources as a determinant of the division of labor. We find that moderate-length paid maternal leave and greater childcare availability reduce parenthood penalties in couples’ division of paid work time, while prolonged leave exacerbates penalties. Furthermore, by focusing on couples, we provide novel evidence that partners’ relative resources do not operate uniformly across work-family policy contexts, showing that policies can incentivize couples to divide paid work in ways their relative resource profiles would not otherwise predict. We find that moderate-length paid leave and greater childcare availability encourage egalitarianism among male-breadwinner couples, although extended leave encourages greater gender traditionalism among female-breadwinner couples. These findings reveal that classic theories of household specialization and bargaining are not universal, and highlight the need for greater theoretical attention to how country- and couple-level forces interact to shape gender inequality.

title: Simply a Sign of the Season? Christmas Trees as Cultural Ciphers in Local Government Management of Diversity
abstract: How do local governments symbolically manage the diversity of their residents? Drawing from an original representative sample of local government officials, we use a novel survey experiment with open-ended survey responses to examine preferences for cultural objects that symbolically manage religious diversity, an axis of difference that is increasingly salient to social conflict. Our experiment randomly varies the content of holiday displays on government property to measure diversity management strategies. Results show that government officials prefer the assimilationist strategy of a Christmas tree—by itself—over multiculturalist and exclusivist strategies, which both include sectarian religious content. Officials also evaluate Christmas trees as the content least likely to signal government endorsement of religion, compared to other holiday displays. We argue that these patterns can be explained by conceiving of a Christmas tree as a cultural cipher, a well-known cultural object that affords a range of meanings and resonates across social identities as innocuous. We argue that cultural ciphers are useful for an assimilationist approach to managing diversity because their ambiguity allows them to act as a vehicle of symbolic inclusion while also sustaining the meanings of majority groups. We also consider how cultural ciphers may lose their power for civic solidarity.

title: Do PCAOB Inspection Deficiencies Related to Management Review Controls Affect Financial Reporting Decisions? Evidence From Goodwill Impairments
abstract: ABSTRACT We examine whether PCAOB inspection deficiencies related to management review controls (MRCs) affect financial reporting decisions. Using the goodwill impairment setting, we find that firms are more likely to record goodwill impairments when their auditors have received more PCAOB inspection deficiencies related to goodwill MRCs. The association is stronger when inspection deficiencies are more likely to lead to changes to the design or implementation of an internal control (repeat deficiencies and deficiencies related to MRC precision). We observe some evidence that MRC inspection deficiencies increase the likelihood of goodwill impairment even when unrelated to goodwill, indicating that improving the audit of MRCs can broadly affect financial reporting. Our findings provide evidence that PCAOB inspections affect not only auditor behavior but also the financial reporting behavior of audit clients. Specifically, inspection feedback appears to influence reporting outcomes through changes in the audit and evaluation of MRCs, identifying a channel through which regulatory oversight affects issuers. The results have implications for audit firms seeking to remediate inspection deficiencies, for management and audit committees responsible for overseeing significant estimates and impairment analyses, and for regulators evaluating the broader effectiveness of the PCAOB inspection process.

title: The Efficiency Trap of Agentic AI in Human Resource Management
abstract: ABSTRACT Agentic AI transforms HRM from data‐driven support to autonomous execution. Organizations deploy these recursive workflows to eliminate human implementation variance, yet we challenge the assumption that such alignment remains optimal. Drawing on Weick's theory of loose coupling, we argue that delegating HR execution to agentic AI creates algorithmic tight coupling. While this generates immediate hyper‐fit, the removal of strategic slack leads to structural calcification, compromising organizational resilience during polycrises. Human line managers provide a critical buffer, enabling the sensemaking necessary to absorb systemic shocks. In contrast, agentic AI workflows governed by instrumental rationality lack the value rationality required for complex organizing. We propose a governance framework to reconcile machine‐driven consistency with the human stewardship required to preserve long‐term organizational adaptability.

title: The Weight of Compliance: Anti-Money Laundering Enforcement, Banking Sector Composition, and Lending
abstract: Abstract We examine how strengthened anti-money laundering (AML) enforcement affects the U.S. banking sector. Heightened enforcement disproportionately raises compliance costs for small banks, especially in counties more exposed to money laundering. In these areas, small banks contract while large banks expand, increasing standardized, government-supported, and secured lending. While aggregate county-level credit does not decline differentially, local outcomes improve. Small establishments grow, non-tradable employment and wages rise, and real estate prices increase. The evidence is consistent with a reallocation mechanism in which AML enforcement shifts activity toward large banks, potentially improving intermediation quality through changes in the composition of local financial intermediation.
journal_name: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis

title: Numerical gap effect in multigenerational brand names: The role of perceived innovation momentum
journal_name: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science

title: Color me aroused while keeping the cool
abstract: Abstract Drawing on visual complexity theory and the arousal properties of color, this paper challenges the prevailing assumption that only warm (longer wavelength) or highly saturated colors can induce arousal in consumers. Instead, we propose a novel pathway: multicolor logos with cool hues can elicit arousal through triggering curiosity. Across a total of eight experiments (seven preregistered with a total of 1,724 participants recruited), of which six experiments are reported in the main text, including a behavioral lab study employing biometric measures (eye tracking, galvanic skin response, pupil dilation), and three studies utilizing real product choices, we consistently find that multicolor cool logos are more arousing than single cool color designs. This heightened, curiosity-driven arousal subsequently impacts marketing outcomes, including willingness to pay and choice. These findings offer marketers alternative strategies for inducing arousal in brand communications and provide actionable guidelines for effectively designing logos.

title: Spoiler alert! Watch movies before they are spoiled
