title: Generative AI use in entrepreneurship: An integrative review and the Empowerment–Entrapment Framework
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Despite the growing use of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in entrepreneurship, research on its impact remains fragmented. To address this limitation, we provide an integrative, entrepreneur‐centered review of how GenAI influences entrepreneurs at each stage of the entrepreneurial process: (1) opportunity recognition and ideation, (2) opportunity evaluation and commitment, (3) resource assembly and mobilization, and (4) venture launch and growth. Based on our review, we propose the Empowerment–Entrapment Framework, which not only catalogs GenAI's benefits and costs throughout the entrepreneurial process but also identifies potential trade‐offs underlying GenAI's double‐edged role. For example, GenAI may improve venture idea quality yet produce hallucinations and biases; boost entrepreneurial self‐efficacy yet heighten overconfidence; increase functional breadth and self‐sufficiency yet reduce prosociality; and enhance productivity yet diminish cognitive engagement, learning, and memory. We also identify features of GenAI that underlie these empowering and entrapping effects. Moreover, we explore boundary conditions that moderate GenAI's effects, including entrepreneurs' expertise, approaches to GenAI use, and personal traits and values. Beyond these theoretical contributions, our review and framework offer practical guidance for entrepreneurs seeking to use GenAI strategically while managing its risks. Managerial Summary We review how GenAI influences entrepreneurs at each stage of the entrepreneurial process: opportunity recognition and ideation, opportunity evaluation and commitment, resource assembly and mobilization, and venture launch and growth. Based on this review, we propose the Empowerment–Entrapment Framework to help entrepreneurs understand GenAI's trade‐offs at each stage. The future of entrepreneurship will depend less on whether entrepreneurs use GenAI than on how they use it. Used thoughtfully, GenAI may empower entrepreneurs by expanding their capabilities to engage in entrepreneurial activities. Used uncritically, GenAI may entrap entrepreneurs by restricting or eroding those capabilities. Entrepreneurs should therefore verify what GenAI produces, calibrate GenAI use to their expertise and task demands, and decide which tasks to delegate to GenAI while retaining human judgment for consequential decisions.

title: Policing and Relationships: Examining the Impact of Community and Organizational Relationships on Job-Related Attitudes in Law Enforcement
abstract: In many front-line professions, especially those in law enforcement, the people-centered nature of the job and work relationships are essential considerations for understanding organizational effectiveness. The relationships among citizens, constituents, or other service recipients and the state are particularly critical to shaping the outcomes of important public policies. This article explores the impact of the relational nature of work in policing on job-related attitudes of satisfaction and organizational commitment, both of which are related to individual performance and organizational outcomes. This study uses data from a web-based survey of sworn law enforcement officials across the United States on perspectives of roles and work. Findings here indicate that community relationships, transformational leadership, coworker trust, and public service motivation are positively related to both job satisfaction and organizational commitment. Implications for theory, practice, and future research are discussed, followed by concluding comments on the future of policing.

title: “Nobody Wants a Trailer That Had Dead Bodies in It”: A Descriptive Study of the Ethics of Public Sector Deathcare
abstract: Death is all around, yet more research is needed to understand it is a critical public management function especially at the local level of government. Medical examiners and coroners are public servants guided by science and jurisdictional rules, yet get caught in a swirl of empathy, politics, and resource constraints when acting as citizen-state agents. Using interview data with 18 medical examiners, coroners, and deathcare leaders throughout the US, this article finds that: ethical leadership guides decision making; neutral competence and professional standards are used yet sometimes challenged; and personal conduct in the face of internal and external pressure remains key to accountability. Findings are not meant to generalize but rather give insight into public servants dealing with socially and politically challenging topics and how they exercise decision-making abilities within these situations.

title: Equity and Development in Transportation Planning: The FHWA’s Reconnecting Communities Pilot Program
abstract: On President Biden’s first day in office, he issued Executive Order 13985 directing federal agencies to revise their policies to address historical inequities. One such effort is the Reconnecting Communities Pilot (RCP) program. The program’s goal was to reconnect communities separated by transportation infrastructure by removing, retrofitting, or mitigating divisive transportation facilities. This was part of an equity agenda for the US Department of Transportation which is currently inactive. This article examines the program’s 17 construction grants which attempted to achieve equity goals in local transportation development. This multiple case study approach identifies how RCP construction grants operationalized equity through local development, access, community participation, and procedural and workforce strategies. One of the program’s most significant innovations is the attempt to merge equity goals with local development plans. This study finds that the program’s most significant innovation was its effort to weave equity into local development plans, although several cases show tensions over community participation, environmental review, and the distribution of benefits.

title: Toxic Managerialism in Public Organizations: A Thematic Network Analysis
abstract: This study explores how managerialist arrangements interact with organizational contexts to enable, legitimize, and reproduce toxic managerial behavior in public organizations. While research on toxic leadership has largely focused on individual traits and interpersonal dynamics, less attention has been paid to the structural and ideological conditions through which harmful managerial practices become accepted and sustained. Using an expert-informed qualitative interpretivist design, this study analyzes semi-structured interviews with 22 management experts through thematic network analysis. The findings identify four overarching themes: managerialism as a public-sector governing logic, manifestations of toxic managerial behavior, legitimation and reproduction of toxic managerial behavior, and erosion of human capital, service quality, and public trust. The findings suggest that managerialist arrangements may redefine competence through numerical achievement, prioritize upward accountability, legitimize harmful practices, and normalize authoritarian control and psychological pressure. The study advances toxic leadership research by highlighting organizational conditions beyond leader pathology.

title: Sick of change? Sickness absence following ownership conversions in Norwegian kindergartens
abstract: Abstract The expansion of mixed-provider welfare systems has intensified debates about the consequences of public, nonprofit, and for-profit provision. Existing research focuses primarily on efficiency, service quality, and citizens' outcomes, while less is known about ownership conversions’ consequences for employees. We depart from research suggesting that ownership conversions can disrupt employee-organization value congruence as well as change the incentive structures. Leveraging population-wide administrative data from Norwegian childcare services (2015-2019), we examine whether ownership conversions are associated with changes in employee sickness absence. Using a staggered difference-in-differences design, we find that sickness absence increases following nonprofit-to-for-profit conversions. At the same time, public-to-for-profit transitions show little consistent relationship with sickness absence. These findings suggest that employee responses to ownership change are shaped less by the public-private divide than by differences in organizational missions and values. More broadly, the study highlights organizational value congruence as a potential mechanism linking ownership arrangements to employee well-being, and suggests that the nonprofit-for-profit boundary may be more consequential for employees than the conventional public-private divide.
journal_name: Journal of Public Administration Research and Theory

title: Feedback Control for Sustainability: Integrated Planning, Capabilities and Performance Management in Constrained Local Governments
abstract: Local governments worldwide are increasingly experiencing the impacts of extreme climate events such as flooding, drought and wildfires. This has created a growing impetus on the part of public administrators to better assess and address the sustainability of the infrastructures which support public goods or services. This study investigates efforts to integrate local government sustainability-related planning, capabilities and performance information use as a means of regulatory feedback control. Our primary research objective is to better understand how and why constrained, smaller governments enhance the types of feedback they process in the Anthropocene. Drawing from a unique dataset of text, environmental and survey data from municipalities in the U.S. state of Indiana, we find greater exploratory information-gathering in comprehensive land-use and capital planning, and greater financial investment in sustainability efforts, are positively associated with sustainability-related performance information use. We find no linkage between sustainability-focused economic development planning, dedicated administrative capacity and performance use, indicative of the resource-constraints and challenges in adapting existing processes and capacities for ambiguous threats.

title: Work Interruptions and Family Life: Time Pressure and Prolonging Working Hours as Pathways
abstract: A harmonious work-life interface is critical for promoting both employee well-being and organizational effectiveness. The existing literature provides valuable insights into how various employee-friendly policies and practices influence employees’ work-life balance and their work outcomes. However, how workplace dynamics influence the family domain of public employees remains largely underexplored within the field of public administration. This study contributes to filling the gap by examining the association between work interruptions and employees’ family lives and by exploring the pathways connecting work interruptions to family outcomes. Serial mediation analysis results indicate that interruptions at work are associated with work interference with family, directly and indirectly through time pressure and longer working hours across independent and sequential pathways. The article concludes with a discussion of its theoretical contributions and practical implications, as well as study limitations and suggestions for future research.

title: Governing for Digital Resilience: Rethinking Inclusion for WSIS+20 and Beyond
abstract: ABSTRACT At the WSIS+20 juncture, this article asks what conditions enable individuals to participate meaningfully in digital life, and how governance arrangements should be assessed accordingly. Multistakeholder governance has distributed authority across actors, but not necessarily the capacity to shape or respond to digital conditions. We argue that assessing this gap today requires attention to the different forms of power through which these conditions are produced, and to individuals' experiences as evidence of how those governance conditions operate in practice. Building on socio‐ecological resilience theory and the capabilities approach, we reconceptualise digital resilience not as an individual trait but as a process shaped by governance conditions and by the substantive freedom people have to adapt, recover, and participate over time. We then introduce the DRIVE (Digital Resilience Indicators for Veritable Empowerment) framework, an indicator‐based diagnostic architecture spanning six drivers and five levels—individual, familial, communal, platform, and state—that shifts assessment from individual preparedness towards enabling conditions. Using fraudulent advertising on Meta's platforms as an illustration, we show how DRIVE can identify evidenced constraints, evidence gaps, and appropriate sites of remedy. Rather than offering a universal score, DRIVE provides a flexible architecture for context‐specific assessment of the conditions under which digital resilience develops.

Economic Self-Interest and Support for Redistribution: New Evidence Using Election Results Data
abstract: A formidable corpus of scholarship explores the role of economic self-interest in shaping public support for redistribution. One striking feature of this literature is its near-exclusive reliance on reported preferences in surveys, with little-to-no research analyzing revealed preferences in the form of actual voting on redistribution. Leveraging eight redistributive ballot initiatives across six American states and a total of 73,053 observations of revealed support for redistribution, we uncover consistent evidence that the economic standing of precinct voters is systematically related to their support for redistribution. We find that lower- to upper-middle-income precincts are each significantly more supportive of redistribution than upper-income precincts, with pronounced decreases in support associated with the increasing prevalence of high-income households subject to proposed tax increases. Finally, we observe the largest class differential in support for redistribution in more heavily Republican precincts.

title: Bulwarks or Enablers? Political Elites’ Attitudes to Political Candidates with Armed Group Linkages
abstract: Many elections feature candidates with ties to violent groups, yet little is known about the nomination stage. To understand whether political elites serve as gatekeepers against such candidates or whether other desirable traits lead selectors to overlook violent linkages, we study selectors’ preferences in candidate selection. Using an experiment with 11,392 Colombian local political elites, we examine how alleged armed group collusion is weighed against experience, track-records, popular support, and endorsements. We find that candidates with rumored armed group ties face a significant penalty in selectors’ evaluations. Some attributes, particularly experience, reduce this penalty, but none fully offset it. Candidates with ties to armed groups are also less rewarded for strong performance, suggesting that violent linkages diminish returns to otherwise desirable qualities. These findings indicate that the prevalence of violence-linked candidates is not primarily driven by selectors’ willingness to accommodate them, redirecting attention toward concealed linkages and constrained candidate pools.

title: State-Building at What Cost? The Consequences of Military Control in Medieval China
abstract: A key challenge to state-building in conflict-prone societies is the proliferation of autonomous armed actors. As governments seek to enhance their monopoly over violence, consequences of military centralization deserve scholarly attention. We argue that centralization undermines state’s coercive capacity: by weakening the leaders of armed groups, it simultaneously erodes the military efficiency and discipline of these groups, which also serve as agents of coercion for the state. We leverage a centralization reform in China’s Tang Dynasty (618-907 CE) after a civil war, using unique data on soldier mutinies, rebellions by local generals, civilian uprisings, and battle outcomes. Difference-in-differences estimates reveal that centralization successfully reduced local generals’ rebellions, but led to increased soldier mutinies against the generals and more civilian uprisings. It also worsened battlefield performance. While research on state capacity has focused on its extractive and administrative dimensions, these findings deepen our understanding about another important aspect: the coercive dimension.

title: Estimating effective electoral thresholds
abstract: Electoral thresholds determine which parties win seats. Yet existing models of the effective threshold—the vote share at which a party has a 50% chance of winning its first seat in a district—rest on strong simplifying assumptions. I develop a new logical model that derives the effective threshold from two electoral quantities: the district magnitude and the effective number of vote-winning parties. A non-linear Bayesian model fitted to historical electoral data corroborates my theoretical logic and outperforms three existing alternatives in both explanatory power and out-of-sample prediction. The results show that effective thresholds decline with both district magnitude and electoral fragmentation. The model extends the Taageperian programme of parsimonious, interlocking electoral models and provides theoretically grounded propensity scores for studying the causal effects of representation.

title: When Firms Lead States: Financial Intermediaries and the Politics of Sovereign Green Bond Issuance
abstract: Abstract Sovereign green bonds typically appear only after corporate green bond issuance has accumulated—a sequence at odds with the policy consensus that sovereign borrowing anchors debt market development. I argue that the inversion reflects market building by global investment banks. The four banks that authored the Green Bond Principles in 2014 used early private corporate transactions to build the verification practices, pricing conventions, and investor networks needed for a functioning market, then served as lead managers when sovereigns entered, transferring accumulated expertise across the public–private divide. States entered a market whose institutional infrastructure they did not design. The Cox proportional hazards model shows that accumulated corporate issuance significantly accelerates sovereign entry, while government agency issuance delays it by substituting for direct sovereign participation. A bank-level triangulation shows that founding-bank presence at sovereign entry reflects green-bond-specific expertise transfer rather than general dominance in sovereign debt underwriting. The findings identify financial intermediaries as a distinct channel through which sustainable finance reaches sovereign borrowers and show how privately constructed market conditions shape the terms on which states engage with global climate finance.

title: Historical Border Changes and Contemporary Public Health Outcomes
Feeling the body politic: Interoception as a mechanism of political stress resilience
abstract: Abstract Politics can substantially harm physical and mental health, especially in polarized contexts, making political polarization a major non‐medical cause of disease and suffering. We examined whether citizens can protect their health without undermining civic engagement. Across three studies with over 2000 participants during the 2022 U.S. midterms and 2024 presidential election, we show that interoceptive sensibility, that is, the ability to perceive and trust one's internal bodily signals, protects against politics' adverse health effects. Higher interoceptive sensibility consistently predicted lower emotional, physical, behavioral, and social health costs, controlling for political identity, demographics, and emotion regulation. During the charged 2024 election, it further predicted fewer negative emotions, more hope for the future, and less fear, particularly when their candidate lost. Interoceptive sensibility also correlated with political engagement and efficacy, suggesting it enhances rather than inhibits participation. Our findings highlight it as a promising trait for mitigating political stress without reducing civic involvement.

title: Do “warm glow” feelings affect climate mitigation behaviors? A field experiment on consumer electric energy choices
abstract: Abstract Addressing the climate crisis is going to require behavioral change in many aspects of daily life. A growing literature suggests the promise of “warm glow” messaging that features the pleasure and satisfaction one experiences from acting sustainably. Yet previous research has relied almost exclusively on self‐reported behavioral intentions, leaving open whether such appeals meaningfully affect real‐world, costly choices. We partnered with a local organization to conduct a field experiment on energy choices in Hanover, New Hampshire. Using a randomized roll‐out design in early 2025, we systematically varied the timing of postcard mailers that contain a warm glow message encouraging customers to increase the renewable content of their energy option. Analyses of administrative data on consumer energy choices reveal that warm glow messages delivered in a field setting have a null effect on adoption of higher‐renewable power choices, with a small number of customers changing to the greener but more costly option. Our study provides novel behavioral evidence on the real‐world impact of intrinsic motivation appeals in the climate domain.

title: Why Activist Stories Matter and How They Lead to Change: The Reproductive Privacy Act in Rhode Island
abstract: “ Roe v. Wade is not going to be overturned. I think that’s a concern that’s not founded in reality,” said Rhode Island House Speaker Nicholas Mattiello in 2018 (Donnis 2022). As much as his words stung activists working to protect the right to abortion, they also signaled that he was out of touch with concerns about access to abortion in the nation as well as the state. National polling generally shows that 7 in 10 people support the right to abortion, and the same was true in Rhode Island (Bender 2018). So how did the smallest, most Catholic state in the United States manage to legislatively protect the right to abortion in 2019 without his support or the support of Rhode Island Senate Leadership?

title: Tragic but Rare: Abortion Storytelling in Local News Coverage One Year Past-Dobbs
abstract: This essay examines local news coverage of abortion stories during the year following the United States Supreme Court decision, Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization (2022), in states with trigger bans and states considering legislation to severely restrict abortion. Framing theory stipulates that news narratives are never neutral. The way stories are structured inevitably foregrounds certain themes while pushing others to the margins (Chong and Druckman 2007; Pope, Pelletier, and Guertin 2018). We analyzed 1600 local news articles 1 for the presence of thematic frames, which focus on the big-picture context of a political event, and episodic frames, which more closely resemble a case study (Feezell, Glazier, and Boydstun 2021; Iyengar 1994). Our initial framing analysis found that only a small handful of articles, 66 out of 1,600, used episodic frames to tell the abortion stories of individuals. 2

title: Testifying in Texas: Reflecting on We Testify Texas , a State-based Abortion Storyteller Retreat
abstract: “I want to talk about my complicated feelings and how I was treated during my abortion procedure,” a Texas 20-something declared as they 1 hoisted themself out of the pool’s deep end. Three others considered the proposed topic and quickly tiptoed across the surrounding hot deck toward the shaded chairs to join the conversation. The 22 Texans lounging around the pool deck were part of We Testify ’s first state-based abortion storytelling cohort, We Testify Texas , held at a small retreat center in Mineola, a rural town east of Dallas in 2019. The We Testify Texas program sought to strengthen the state’s robust reproductive justice organizational advocacy infrastructure by training Texans who have had abortions 2 to share their stories and engage with advocacy efforts to preserve and expand abortion access and challenge hostile criminalization efforts in Texas. Although storytelling has been a tactic integral to feminist and social justice organizing (Fernandes 2017; Ganz 2024; Polletta 2022; Ross 2008), nonprofit organizational efforts primarily focused on the production of stories for public consumption, rather than engagement with the storytellers as local experts and organizers. This creates a transactional relationship between advocacy organizations and the people most impacted by the issue, separating storytellers from their stories and leaving storytellers as an untapped resource of testimonial expertise in communities. How can social justice movements and advocacy organizations center people who have had abortion experiences to lead cultural and state-based policy change work? This Notes from the Field reflects on the We Testify storytelling model as implemented through the We Testify Texas program, including the national-local partnership, programmatic activities, impact of the cohort, and how such a program could be replicated in similar political climates and distinct communities.

title: Do Gender-of-Interviewer Effects Differ Across Immigrant Generations? Survey Evidence from Italy
abstract: Abstract Interviewer gender has been shown to affect responses to survey questions on gender attitudes and norms, but does its influence vary across groups with different migration backgrounds? I study this question using the Between Origin and Destination (BOnD) survey, conducted in Lombardy, Italy, between 2024 and 2025. Consistent with gender-of-interviewer effects, a type of social desirability bias, female interviewers elicit more progressive responses on a summary index of gender norms and on an index of the acceptability of homosexuality, abortion, divorce, casual sex, and premarital sex. The effect is concentrated among natives and second-generation individuals; first-generation immigrants show little response to interviewer gender. One possible explanation is that social desirability pressure from a female interviewer operates through host-country social norms: Individuals more embedded in the Italian normative context are more responsive to cues from a female interviewer. These findings have implications for the design of surveys administered to mixed native-immigrant populations.

title: Absorbing technocracy: party competition and ideological polarisation in times of crisis
abstract: Do crises polarise technocratic attitudes along ideological and partisan lines? Does technocracy serve as an anti-incumbency weapon for the opposition? This article addresses these questions with a unique eight-wave individual-level panel survey of Spanish voters, covering January 2020 to January 2024, and a difference-in-differences empirical design. Although technocratic attitudes initially rose across the board, they soon diverged along political lines: right-wing respondents, opposed to the incumbent left-wing coalition, became markedly more technocratic, while left-wing respondents reverted closer to pre-pandemic levels. The ideological gap widened by roughly 70% and remained at that level four years later. Polarisation was strongest where the opposition was best placed to shape opinion: among politically informed citizens, in opposition-led regions and close to regional elections. The shift appears driven by disapproval of the prime minister’s handling of the pandemic rather than by ideological radicalisation. Technocracy was thus absorbed into existing dynamics of party competition.

title: Fiscal accountability: Institutional discipline and behavioral frictions
Motherhood and Constraints during Job Search
abstract: Abstract Why do women’s labour earnings drop upon motherhood? We shed new light on this question by analysing the changes in job search behaviour associated with motherhood. We exploit data on the job applications sent on a popular online platform linked with administrative registers for 350,000 involuntarily unemployed workers in France. After losing their job, mothers have a 11.7% lower probability to find a job than similar women without children and send 12.2% fewer job applications. To explore the underlying mechanisms, we analyse the timing of job applications. Unlike other women, mothers’ rate of applications decreases by about 20.5% in the hours when there is no school. Moreover, the French reform that introduced school on Wednesday in 2014 led mothers to send more applications on Wednesdays. Our results highlight that childcare creates constraints on the timing of job search activities for mothers. We finally provide suggestive evidence that these constraints decrease their return-to-search, and thereby contribute to their lower application and job finding rates.

title: Credit, Privacy, and Data Monetization by Digital Platforms
Real Activity and Uncertainty Shocks: The Long and the Short of It
abstract: ABSTRACT We propose a nonrecursive VAR identification strategy that separately identifies short‐term and long‐term uncertainty shocks by exploiting sign restrictions implied by a stylized framework and a DSGE model featuring both types of shocks. We find that long‐term uncertainty shocks exert strong and persistent effects on real activity, whereas short‐term shocks have limited real effects. We use the DSGE model to study their differential propagation and show that time‐to‐build is an important ingredient allowing the model to account for the stark empirical asymmetry in investment and, in turn, output—both contract sharply after long‐term shocks but only modestly after short‐term shocks.

title: “Demographic Change and Migration: Facts, Models and Policy Implications” – An Introduction to the Special Issue
abstract: Demographic change, driven by lower fertility rates and declining mortality, is a central long-run phenomenon impacting all major economies around the world.The papers in this special issue study the interactions between demographic change, internal and external migration, technological progress, and economic development, with a particular focus on Asian economies.Scientific collaboration represents one form of cross-border interaction through which knowledge and human capital contribute to economic development.When the international migration of researchers is subject to frictions, international cooperation in the production of scientific output becomes crucial.In Scientific Isolation?The Consequences of Trump's China Initiative on Chinese Research , by Philippe

title: Asset Market Participation, Redistribution, and Asset Pricing
abstract: ABSTRACT We study how redistribution between asset holders and non‐asset holders links macroeconomic fluctuations to expected stock returns. Aggregate and relative consumption growth forecast excess returns with opposite signs and at different horizons. We interpret these patterns using a production‐based asset‐pricing model with limited participation and external habits. Aggregate (relative) consumption captures variation in the price (quantity) of risk. Technology shocks drive macroeconomic fluctuations, whereas redistributive shocks generate large short‐run movements in inequality and are the main source of priced risk. This points to a macro‐finance disconnect between the drivers of business cycles and those governing risk premia.

title: Beyond economic bargaining power? Work-related internal migration and subjective well-being in couples
abstract: Abstract Bargaining theory posits that both partners’ utility shapes couples’ migration decisions. Yet, most empirical tests focus on individual incomes, thus overlooking non-economic factors in couples’ deliberations about spatial mobility. We argue that considering holistic indicators of utility, such as subjective well-being, can advance our understanding of couples’ decision-making. Using data from the German Socio-Economic Panel (SOEP, 1991–2021) and fixed effects panel regressions, we analyze changes in life satisfaction following work-related internal migration on both individual and dyadic levels. Moreover, we examine whether these changes depend on shifts in partners’ economic bargaining power (EBP, defined as female partners’ share of total household labor income), thereby evaluating the common assumption that couples’ bargaining centers around income. Our results show that, on average, both partners experience increases in their life satisfaction following migration. Distinguishing whether women’s EBP remains unchanged, decreases, or increases with migration, we find that women’s life satisfaction gains are only weakly related to changes in their EBP. In contrast, men’s life satisfaction only increases if their partner’s EBP decreases or remains unchanged, but not if it increases—a pattern consistent with the notion of gendered expectations about the within-couple income distribution hampering men’s well-being gains. Overall, our findings suggest that well-being is an important factor in couples’ migration decision-making and that income-based measures of bargaining power provide only an incomplete account of partners’ bargaining positions.

title: Review of “Disposable Workers: The Transformation of Employment”
abstract: t is generally accepted that the post-World War II norm (at least for white men) of the “standard” employment relationship (whereby work is done at the employer's place of business, under the employer's control, with the mutual expectation of continued employment, and eligibility for legally mandated benefits and protections) was transformed during the past half-century into various nonstandard forms, such as contract and temporary work, involuntary part-time work, and independent contractors. Research on the incidence of such nonstandard workers, the reasons for their use, and their consequences for individuals, organizations, and society have long been of considerable interest to sociologists and economists, among others. In this book, Paul Osterman, an institutional labor economist and veteran observer of labor and organizations, contributes to this topic by describing and explaining the adoption by employers of a human resource strategy that emphasizes “disposable workers, not employees,” whereby employers seek to get work done while minimizing the economic and process costs associated with standard employment. The book builds on the work of numerous scholars who have also studied these issues (many of whom are acknowledged in his preface) and seeks to provide a unified theory of different forms of disposable workers that serves as a useful guide to policies to improve their situations.

title: Information Spillovers Across Media Markets: Risk Perceptions and Cyclospora Outbreaks in U.S. Bagged Salads
abstract: From 2018 to 2022, contamination of fresh produce by Cyclospora cayetanensis, primarily affecting bagged salads, caused more than 3,300 outbreak-associated illnesses across the United States. Yet the economic consequences of these outbreaks, and the role of information exposure in shaping consumer responses, remain poorly understood. This study quantifies changes in bagged salad purchases and associated retail losses during six selected large multistate outbreaks occurring from 2018 to 2022 and examines how risk perceptions evolve across outbreak-affected and neighboring regions. Guided by a risk perception framework emphasizing risk proximity and information-driven belief updating, we integrate epidemiologic outbreak data, designated market area (DMA)-level Google Trends search intensity as a geographically granular proxy for information exposure, and NielsenIQ household purchase data. Because DMAs often cross state lines, this design identifies information spillovers to non-outbreak states sharing a media market. A Heckman selection framework accounts for purchase participation and unobserved heterogeneity, while complementary retail scanner data assess whether retailer stocking adjustments contributed to the observed purchase declines. Across the outbreak periods examined in this study, weekly bagged salad purchases declined by an average of 3.89%, implying cumulative retail losses of approximately $373.67 million. Outbreak-specific searches (e.g., "Cyclospora") were associated with greater perceived risk and larger purchase reductions, while general salad-related searches were associated with smaller reductions. Spillovers across shared media markets further reduced purchases in non-outbreak states by 3.33% per week. Retailer analysis found no statistically significant store-level stocking reductions during outbreak or recall periods, supporting the interpretation that the observed purchase declines were primarily demand-driven. These findings highlight the economic significance of information-driven consumer responses and the importance of timely, accurate, and geographically targeted risk communication during foodborne outbreaks.

title: Winning at Defense by Playing Offense: Discrediting by Target Firms in Activist Hedge Fund Campaigns
abstract: Prior research highlights the far-reaching strategic and governance consequences for firms targeted in activist hedge fund (AHF) campaigns. Yet, how target firm executives and directors can effectively defend against these campaigns remains underexplored. Drawing on impression management (IM) theory, we reason that executives and directors use discrediting in their public rebuttal letters to negatively influence shareholders’ evaluations of AHFs’ reputation. To nuance this prediction, we develop a taxonomy distinguishing between source-focused discrediting, which directly attacks AHFs’ reputation, and message-focused discrediting, which challenges the validity of AHFs’ claims to indirectly tarnish their reputation. We theorize that both discrediting subtypes enhance target firms’ defense success, particularly when deployed in combination. Adopting a temporal perspective on IM theory, we further argue that the effectiveness of discrediting diminishes as more time elapses between an AHF’s public attack and executives and directors’ rebuttal. A manual content analysis of 841 rebuttal letters issued during U.S. AHF campaigns (2000–2023) provides robust support for these predictions. Beyond contributing to shareholder activism research by offering new insights into the determinants of campaign outcomes, our study advances IM theory by conceptualizing discrediting as a multidimensional influence tactic and exploring its effectiveness and temporal dynamics in adversarial contexts.

title: Practicing love with algorithms: How online communities narrate and make sense of human–AI intimacy
abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes embedded in everyday life, emotionally intimate interactions with AI companions are becoming increasingly visible. Yet prior research has focused mainly on individual experiences, leaving limited understanding of how human–AI intimacy is collectively interpreted and negotiated in online communities. This study examines community discourse on RedNote, a major Chinese social and lifestyle platform, using 13,059 comments from 58 relevant posts. Combining BERTopic modeling with a human–large language model (LLM) hybrid emotion classification procedure, the analysis identifies three thematic clusters: intimacy as co-construction, intimacy as infrastructure, and intimacy as boundary negotiation. Co-construction centers on persona design, roleplay, and narrative world-building and is marked mainly by joy and curiosity. Infrastructure-related discourse is associated with frustration and sadness, while boundary negotiation reflects ambivalence toward intimacy with AI.

title: Affect-Infused Reflective Process in Responding to Burdensome Role Expectations: An Affect-Cognition Theory Extension of Yagil’s “I Don’t Want To”
Analysts’ Perspectives on Climate Change: An Examination of Analyst Reports
Audit Quality and Audit Partner Ownership of Non-Audit Businesses: Evidence from China
Sales-Based CEO Incentives and Their Effect Across the Supply Chain

Robust Auction Design with Support Information
abstract: A seller wants to sell an item to n buyers. Buyer valuations are independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) according to a distribution unknown to the seller; the seller only knows that the support is included in [a, b]. To be robust, the seller chooses a dominant strategy incentive compatible mechanism that optimizes the worst-case performance relative to the ideal expected revenue the seller could have collected with knowledge of buyers’ valuations. Our analysis unifies the regret and the ratio objectives. For these objectives, we derive an optimal mechanism and the corresponding performance in quasi-closed form, as a function of the support information [a, b] and the number of buyers n. Our analysis reveals three regimes of support information and a new class of robust mechanisms. (i) When a/b is below a threshold, the optimal mechanism is a second-price auction (SPA) with random reserve, a focal class in earlier literature. (ii) When a/b is above another threshold, SPAs are strictly suboptimal, and an optimal mechanism belongs to a class of mechanisms we introduce, which we call pooling auctions (POOL); whenever the highest value is above a threshold, the mechanism still allocates to the highest bidder, but otherwise the mechanism allocates to a uniformly random buyer, that is, pools low types. (iii) When a/b is between two thresholds, a randomization between SPA and POOL is optimal. We also characterize optimal mechanisms within nested central subclasses of mechanisms: standard mechanisms that only allocate to the highest bidder, SPA with random reserve, and SPA with no reserve. We show strict separations in terms of performance across classes, implying that deviating from standard mechanisms is necessary for robustness. Lastly, we show that the same results hold under other distribution classes that capture “positive dependence,” namely i.i.d., mixture of i.i.d., and exchangeable and affiliated distributions, as well as i.i.d. regular distributions. This paper was accepted by David Simchi-Levi, revenue management and market analytics. Supplemental Material: The online appendices are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.02703 .

title: From Employer Responsibility to Environmental Irresponsibility: Unintended Impacts of Social Insurance Law on Pollution Emissions
abstract: This study investigates the unintended effect of the introduction of the 2011 Social Insurance Law on corporate pollution emissions. Using a difference-in-differences framework, our analysis reveals that enhanced social insurance contributions lead to higher industrial pollution emissions, as measured by chemical oxygen demand and wastewater emissions. The mechanism analysis indicates that the enforcement of the law increases firms’ labor costs and financial distress, motivating them to reduce efforts on end-of-pipe treatment activities and measures taken during the production process, which results in higher pollution emission intensity. Our study highlights the potential conflict between employee protection and corporate environmental goals. Further analysis suggests that stronger environmental monitoring and environmental, social, and governance disclosure requirements can partially mitigate this tradeoff, providing valuable insights for policymakers. This paper was accepted by Caroline Flammer, sustainability. Funding: Y. Li acknowledges research support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grant 72403026]. Y. Qin acknowledges research support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grant 72342031]. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.00714 .

title: Estimating the Pricing Kernel: A Simple Regression-Based Dimension-Reduction Approach
abstract: We propose a simple framework for estimating the pricing kernel in factor space by constructing the mean–variance efficient factor portfolio via an ordinary least squares formulation with least absolute shrinkage and selection operator regularization. The method accommodates high-dimensional settings in which the number of candidate factors exceeds the sample size and automatically shrinks redundant factor weights toward zero. We show theoretically that the out-of-sample Sharpe ratio of the estimated portfolio converges to the theoretical maximum at the fastest rate among existing regression-based approaches. Applying the method to 174 characteristic-based factors together with the market factor, we obtain an out-of-sample Sharpe ratio of 3.59, substantially outperforming competing strategies and delivering the smallest aggregate pricing errors. The selected factors vary over time in both composition and number, averaging about 50. We further develop a model comparison test and reject the hypothesis that eight widely used sparse factor models are sufficient to span the pricing kernel. This paper was accepted by Kay Giesecke, finance. Correlated Demand Shocks and Asset Pricing
abstract: Abstract I propose a mechanism through which institutional investors’ correlated demand shocks provide a source of market risk in asset pricing. Institutional investors have mandates to beat a similar market index. During periods of strong stock market performance, their incentive to outperform intensifies as more of them fall short of the market index. This incentive induces procyclical risk-taking behavior, generating correlated demand that elevates the market betas and risk premia of exposed stocks. Quasi-experiments using exogenous changes in index membership support a causal interpretation of the mechanism. Elevated betas are associated with a higher perceived cost of capital and reduced firm investment. (JEL G1, G2)

title: What Interruptions Say About Your Organizational Culture
abstract: Recent research suggests that interruptions when meeting attendees are speaking are significant moments that affect how employees experience workplace culture and can lead to self-censoring. Taking a different approach to meeting facilitation can help leaders become more aware of when this is occurring so that they can improve participant dynamics, encourage meeting attendees to contribute, and more effectively respond to interruptions.

title: A louder bark for Australia's fiscal watch dog
abstract: Abstract This research note analyses the arrangements both in Australia and overseas in relation to fiscal rules and parliamentary budget offices/independent fiscal institutions. When first introduced in Australia, fiscal rules were expressed in numerical terms (such as target debt to GDP) but have more recently been expressed in more general terms (such as ensuring there are ‘fiscal buffers’). The note recommends that fiscal rules be required to be specified in quantitative terms and to cover a specific time frame. Compliance with the fiscal rules can then be assessed numerically. Australia's national independent fiscal institution, the Parliamentary Budget Office (PBO), shares many similarities with like organisations overseas, but it has a much more limited remit. The role of the Australian PBO should be expanded to include assessment of compliance with fiscal rules, a much higher public profile, and, unlike most overseas counterparts, preparation of fiscal policy recommendations. This research note is intended to contribute to informed public policy debate and so improve fiscal policy decisions and fiscal policy implementation. Points for practitioners Fiscal rules and independent fiscal institutions—in Australia, the Parliamentary Budget Office (PBO)—play an important countervailing force against biases in fiscal decision‐making. Changes to the Charter of Budget Honesty should be made to require that fiscal rules in Australia be expressed more clearly by specifying the time frame over which they need to be met and as numerical targets (such as a numerical target debt as a percentage of GDP in, say, 3 years). The role of the PBO should be expanded to include assessment of compliance with fiscal rules, as occurs in many overseas economies, adopting a much higher public profile, and preparation of fiscal policy recommendations. Other recommendations include the PBO providing assessments of the total fiscal impact of election commitments before, rather than after, elections. Some expansion in the PBO's role, such as adopting a much higher public profile, can be undertaken without legislative change.

title: Through the eyes of Turkish public employees: How organisational citizenship behaviour, job satisfaction, and public service motivation shape perceived job performance
abstract: Abstract The purpose of this study is to explore the impact of organisational citizenship behaviour (OCB), job satisfaction (JS), and public service motivation (PSM) on public employees’ evaluations of their peers’ job performance. Studies in the literature have addressed these factors separately; therefore, it has not been discussed which of these factors most significantly influences performance perception or how they collectively affect performance perception. This study fills this gap by discussing these factors together and comparatively within the framework of experimental vignette design. The study found that high OCB and high job satisfaction produce the largest increases in perceived performance, while high PSM has a weaker (but still positive) cue effect; additionally, the results indicated that elevated levels of each cue, both independently and collectively, were correlated with considerably higher performance ratings. Survey respondents’ own PSM levels also shaped evaluations, with higher‐PSM respondents assigning slightly stricter performance ratings overall. These results advance public administration research on performance appraisal by clarifying which motivational/attitudinal signals raters weigh most and by highlighting rater PSM as a potential source of systematic appraisal bias. Points for practitioners Behavioural cues strongly shape performance evaluations in public organisations. Practitioners should recognise that employees who display helping behaviour or express pride in their work are likely to be viewed as higher performers, even when formal performance metrics are ambiguous. Evaluators with high PSM may unintentionally apply stricter standards. For practitioners, this highlights a potential source of appraisal bias. OCB, JS, and PSM operate independently, so improvements in one area do not substitute for improvements in the others. The absence of interaction effects indicates that each behavioural cue contributes uniquely to perceived performance. Performance evaluation systems should account for both employee behaviours and evaluator dispositions. Since perceptions of performance depend on both employee behaviours and who evaluates them, organisations should design appraisal systems that minimise subjective bias.

title: Innovation diffusion of local governments in digital governance: event history analysis based on the Government Chief Data Officer System
Policy adaptation frequency: central interventions and local policy outcomes in China’s governance system
abstract: Policy adaptations by central governments are often viewed as essential for institutional agility. However, little is known about how often such adaptations should be implemented to improve policy outcomes at the local level, particularly in hierarchical governance settings. To address this gap, we considered policy adaptation frequency as a structural driver of local outcomes, using China’s Business Environment Optimization reform as a case study. Specifically, we constructed an original policy document database and gathered city-level panel data for 253 cities across 31 provinces. Our analysis revealed an inverted U-shaped relationship: moderately frequent adaptation enhanced local policy outcomes, whereas excessively frequent adaptation diminished them. Mechanism analysis indicated that overly frequent adaptation undermines effectiveness by weakening policy goal clarity, overloading policy instruments, and increasing interdepartmental coordination costs. Conceptually, we shifted the focus of policy adaptation research from the traditional questions of ‘why’ and ‘how’ to the often-overlooked dimension of ‘how often.’ Per our findings, we underscore the need to manage the frequency of central interventions to enhance local policy outcomes. Thus, we offer new insights into the dynamic tension between central flexibility and local stability in China’s governance system.

title: Dueling Political Fictions and Public Administration and Democracy in an Era of Populism and Authoritarian Impulses
abstract: ABSTRACT The political fictions used in political discourse, during the English Civil War period, remain relevant to contemporary public policy and administration. Mainstream public administration discourse has too often employed the fiction of a singular and unbounded popular sovereignty that emerged during this period, leaving public administration ill‐equipped to deal with the authoritarian impulses of contemporary populist governments. What is needed in public administration discourse, in dealing with these authoritarian impulses, is not an ethic of administrative neutrality, such as has traditionally dominated much of our field, but an ethic of constitutionalism that draws on the fiction of the individual that was also articulated during the English Civil War period by the English Levellers and subsequently by the founders of the American Constitution.

title: Assessing Villagers’ Preferences of Gender-Stereotypic Leaders in Village Development Programs: The Case of Rural Sri Lanka
abstract: This study examines how villagers evaluate leadership candidates in community-based programs by distinguishing between category-based evaluation (preferences based on a candidate’s gender) and attribute-based evaluation (preferences based on gender-associated leadership characteristics). Although recent studies suggest that leadership qualities commonly associated with femininity are increasingly viewed positively, women remain underrepresented in leadership roles in many rural communities. This discrepancy raises the question of whether gender itself or gender-associated leadership characteristics play a stronger role in leader selection. To investigate this issue, we conducted a choice-based conjoint experiment with 1,147 villagers in rural Sri Lanka, in which respondents evaluated hypothetical candidates for the chairperson position of Village Development Programs. Candidate profiles randomly varied across five dimensions: gender, leadership trait (agentic or communal), leadership style (autocratic or democratic), policy priority area (finance, infrastructure, education, or healthcare), and gender ideology (conservative or liberal). The results reveal an important pattern in villagers’ leadership evaluations. Although respondents prefer candidates with democratic leadership styles and liberal gender ideologies, they consistently favor male candidates over female candidates. In contrast, leadership traits and policy priorities do not significantly influence candidate choice. These findings indicate that category-based gender bias persists even when leadership attributes associated with femininity are valued.

title: Form Before Capability? AI Governance Adoption, Functional Capability, and the Limits of Index‐Based Evidence in the Global South
abstract: ABSTRACT Governments across the developing world have adopted artificial intelligence governance instruments at high speed, though the relationship between formal adoption and the capability to operate those instruments remains poorly understood. This article asks whether the expansion of AI governance architecture across the Global South has been matched by the functional capabilities on which regulatory effectiveness depends, and what explains the answer. Drawing on panel data for 82 countries across five Global South regions and six waves of the Government AI Readiness Index, it reports that within the period of stable index architecture (2020–2024) measures of regulatory form rose by 20.3 points on a 0–100 scale while measures of functional capability rose by 0.4 points, a within‐country differential present in 90% of sample countries and surviving removal of the single step‐scored indicator of national strategy adoption. The pattern of the differential discriminates among explanations: formal adoption rose four times faster in states in the top quartile of administrative capacity than in the bottom quartile, where capability fell; the most aid‐dependent states adopted least; and the differential is unrelated to regime type. This is inconsistent with the view that legislation is simply quicker to produce than infrastructure and with the view that adoption is decoupled from performance for external audiences, and consistent with adoption conditioned on administrative capacity, in which capability in the weakest states erodes while capability in stronger states grows more slowly than the instruments that depend on it. Vietnam and India are developed as confirming and deviant cases. Cross‐national dispersion widened on both dimensions, and patterns that appear only when the 2025 wave is included cannot be separated from the redesign of the index in that year.

title: Understanding the many faces of climate denial
Cumulating precarity in a hybrid platform economy: gender, class, and the social exclusion of single mothers in Taiwan
abstract: The growing reliance on precarious and platform-mediated work raises fundamental questions about how labour markets, care arrangements, and welfare institutions allocate risk, particularly for single mothers. This article examines why single mothers in Taiwan are disproportionately concentrated in insecure and gig-based employment, challenging accounts that frame flexibility as individual choice. Based on a theory-informed qualitative re-analysis of 31 in-depth interviews, the study shows that such employment trajectories result from the interaction of long-hours working-time regimes, privatized care responsibilities, and heterogeneous forms of gig governance under solo caregiving. The analysis demonstrates that the gig economy is internally differentiated, generating distinct flexibility regimes and risk distributions, and that non-standard and platform-mediated work, flexible in promise but insecure in practice, produces cumulating precarity over the life course by constraining work hours and weakening social insurance accumulation. Theoretically, the study integrates social reproduction, work–family, and life-course perspectives to highlight time and cumulative risk as central mechanisms of labour-market inequality. Policy implications emphasize the need for reforms in working-time governance, care infrastructure, and the expansion of publicly funded childcare, and a shift towards citizenship-based social protection that decouples entitlements from employment status.

title: Fix the broken mirror: using compensation and punishment to repair political trust after local government failures in responding to natural disasters
abstract: When a natural disaster strikes and the local government fails to respond effectively, shortcomings in emergency management can lead to a decline in political trust, threatening social cohesion and governance stability. Repairing political trust after emergency response failure is essential for effective disaster management. Drawing on the theory of the social-equilibrium mechanism, we conducted three experiments, demonstrating how governments can restore political trust by employing compensation and punishment behavioural strategies. Our findings reveal that both strategies are effective in repairing trust following local government failures, whether the failure stems from competence-based trust violation or integrity-based trust violation. However, when the failure is a competence-based trust violation, compensation shows a stronger effect than punishment. This research contributes new insights into the trust repair during natural disasters. It further suggests that relevant government departments should closely monitor changes in political trust after local governmental failures in natural disasters and implement diverse, context-sensitive strategies to rebuild and maintain it.

title: When Disclosure Is Not Enough: A Comparative Policy Analysis of Institutional Design in EU Whistleblowing Regimes
abstract: Directive (EU) 2019/1937 has expanded formal whistleblower protection across the European Union, yet stronger legal architectures do not consistently translate disclosure into public-integrity outcomes. Combining fuzzy-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (fsQCA) of the 27 EU Member States with structured comparison of Denmark, Ireland, and Slovakia, this article examines how institutional design shapes that relationship. By examining how different state resources are mobilised, it shows that public-integrity activation depends on whether disclosure remains connected to protection, investigation, and enforcement across the governance system. Administrative capacity, coordination, sectoral and organisational conditions, and rule-of-law safeguards shape whether formal protection enables authoritative action on reported wrongdoing.

title: Capacity building in EU boundary governance: from rules to resources?
abstract: The European Union (EU) has traditionally been described as a regulatory state – strong in legislative and judicial authority for making binding rules but weak on executive powers and resources. Recent developments, however, suggest a gradual shift toward a polity that combines rule-making with capacity building. We examine the EU’s resource equipment for boundary governance through a framework emphasizing functional pressures. Using a dataset covering internal and external boundaries since the 1980s, we employ fractional logit regression to test our hypotheses. While member states remain generally cautious about pooling resources for boundary governance, we show that resources are more likely to be centralised when boundaries exhibit higher EU legislative and executive authority, and in response to crises. Moreover, at the external boundaries of the EU, capacity building through resource centralization is higher when boundaries are more closed and regulate human mobility.

title: Discrimination in Bureaucratic Recruitment Under Civil Service Exams
abstract: ABSTRACT Meritocratic recruitment is a central tenet in Weber's theory of bureaucracy, which states that employees should be hired based on merit. However, extensive research has shown evidence of hiring discrimination against minorities, breaking with basic principles in bureaucratic selection. This paper examines whether ethnic and racial minorities are discriminated against when bureaucratic organizations use civil service exams to assess candidates' merit and fitness for positions. Drawing on data from the local government of New York City and a candidate list fixed effects approach, we find that Black and Hispanic candidates are slightly more likely to be hired than White candidates with similar exam scores, suggesting that these ethnic minorities hold a small advantage in bureaucratic selection. However, examining the starting compensation levels of new hires, we show that minorities are hired at lower salaries and are compensated less for high exam scores than comparable White hires. Our findings suggest that civil service exams might be an important lever for securing fair and unbiased bureaucratic selection but also that they do not prevent discrimination in later steps of the recruitment process.
journal_name: Journal of Policy Analysis and Management

title: Childhood obesity and government action – experimental evidence on public demand for childhood obesity intervention across 40 OECD countries
abstract: Abstract Childhood obesity rates are rising sharply worldwide, creating urgent questions: does the public support government involvement? And do people see obesity as a structural or individual problem? These questions matter for the legitimacy and effectiveness of public policy. Research on comparative public attitudes remains limited. This study addresses that gap. We analyse representative survey data from forty Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) countries, including 39,746 respondents. Childhood obesity carries serious consequences for health, education, employment and life expectancy. Parental choices shape children’s diets and activity levels, yet government involvement remains contested, balancing policy goals against personal freedom. At the structural level, a powerful food industry drives rising obesity rates. An experimental vignette design tests the causal effect of the level of risk to a child on public support for government involvement. We also examine links between support, trust and political values and how childhood obesity is framed. A clear majority supports government involvement, consistent with child rights regulations. The level of risk to a child causally increases support. Trust and preferences for values of care and order correlate positively with support. Most respondents frame obesity as a health issue. Few identify it as a structural issue; a finding with significant implications for policy effectiveness.
