The effects of national security assessments in public procurement on competition, sustainability, innovation, and critical technology procurement
abstract: By strategically leveraging public procurement, governments can harness market competition to drive business innovation and sustainable development. It remains unclear, however, how this premise is affected by heightened security awareness due to increasing geopolitical tensions. Focusing on European Union (EU) member states, we examine how security-oriented practices in public procurement affect tender outcomes. Using data from a recent pan-European survey of 1613 procurement projects, coupled with data from the EU's tender platform Tender Electronic Daily, we test the effect of using national security assessments (NSAs) during tender preparation on competition, innovation, sustainability, and critical technology procurement. We find that conducting such assessments has positive effects on innovation and on critical technology procurement, but only for tenders won by domestic suppliers. NSAs can thus create urgency and mobilize resources to innovate through public procurement, but possibly in a way that reinforces national rather than EU-wide technological development. We identify a tension between the need for research and coordination of NSA development at the EU level to avoid market distortions arising from uncontrolled NSA proliferation versus a heightened bureaucratic burden for suppliers. We also argue that stimulating joint cross-border innovation procurement, particularly of critical technologies, is key to fully leveraging the benefits of the EU internal market when pursuing strategic policy goals.

title: Understanding mission management: a multi-focal approach for mission-oriented innovation policy
Regional Poverty Within a National Welfare State: Evidence From Seoul and Busan
abstract: ABSTRACT Regional poverty can vary substantially even within a common national welfare state, yet the mechanisms underlying such variation remain underexplored. Using Seoul and Busan Welfare Condition Surveys, this study compares poverty in Seoul and Busan in 2018–2022. Poverty is assessed using national and city‐specific thresholds and both contemporaneous relative and CPI‐anchored thresholds. The analysis examines the prevalence and poverty risks of vulnerable groups and uses Shapley decomposition to estimate the poverty‐reducing contributions of earned income, property income, private transfers, and public transfers. Poverty was generally higher in Busan, particularly among older adults, female householders, and single‐person households, although the magnitude of regional differences varied with the poverty threshold used. Differences in vulnerable‐group prevalence were relatively modest, whereas their poverty risks were substantially higher in Busan. Earned income made the largest contribution to poverty reduction in both cities, but its contribution weakened significantly in Seoul between 2018 and 2022, while the poverty‐reducing contribution of public transfers weakened in Busan. These findings demonstrate that regional poverty differences within a common national welfare state reflect not only population composition but also regional variation in poverty risks and income‐based poverty‐reducing mechanisms.

title: Subsistence Citizenship: Welfare Informalisation and the Politics of Survival in Southeast Asian Prisons
abstract: ABSTRACT Welfare state theory is rarely applied to the carceral domain, yet prisons are among the most resource‐intensive coercive institutions of the modern state. This article examines how survival is organised within Southeast Asian prisons, drawing on 154 policy documents and 37 elite interviews across Malaysia, Thailand and the Philippines. Synthesising welfare pluralism, feminist political economy and theories of informal governance, we show that prisons operate through a carceral welfare mix. Specifically, the state provides custodial infrastructure, while everyday subsistence (i.e., food, medicine, hygiene and care) is displaced onto families—primarily through women's unpaid labour—and civil society organisations. The COVID‐19 pandemic exposed this dependence. When visitation bans severed family supply chains, prisons experienced immediate crises of hunger and health with no compensatory state provision, revealing a governance arrangement that had long been obscured by routinisation. We conceptualise this condition as subsistence citizenship : in particular, a regime in which prisoners remain fully subject to state authority, while welfare protection is privatised, conditional and stratified. By repositioning prisons as sites of welfare analysis, the article disrupts established assumptions about informal provision, citizenship under punishment and boundaries of state responsibility. Its implications hence apply to any context where incarceration expands while welfare retreats.

title: Globalization and the Hinterland: International Trade and the Rural–Urban Divide
abstract: The growing political divide between rural and urban regions is often attributed to rural deindustrialization and import competition in manufacturing. Yet this cleavage emerged in many countries well before rural industrialization, pointing to underlying economic forces that existing accounts have overlooked. We argue that comparative advantage in agriculture is one such force: rural voters are more likely to support protectionist parties and policies when local agriculture is uncompetitive, since this sector is often central to their communities’ economic and social life. Using a new harmonized dataset of surveys from 123 countries and extensive data on voting behavior in the European Union, we find strong support for our argument. An additional analysis exploiting exogenous subnational variation in agricultural competitiveness in the United States post-NAFTA further corroborates our findings: the political divide between rural and urban voters is pronounced in uncompetitive regions but negligible in those possessing a comparative advantage in agriculture.

title: Incubating Revolution: How Social Networks and the Built Environment Sustain Mobilization
abstract: How do challengers sustain mobilization under conditions of extreme repression? Social networks and the built environment are critical, interacting at two time scales. Settlement, chain migration, and everyday cooperation produce dense relational environments that shape motivations and constitute latent resources. When contention erupts, those dense social networks can be repurposed to sustain high-risk collective action, providing shelter, escape routes, information, and support. But their efficacy is limited without the organic built environment in which they form; its proximity, limited visibility, and constrained access amplify the effect of dense social ties in facilitating challenge under threat. We substantiate these claims using disaggregated data on protest in Damascus during the 2011 Syrian uprising, finding that neighbourhoods with both dense networks and organic built form exhibit significantly more frequent and confrontational mobilization. By analytically separating the social from the spatial, this article illuminates the mechanisms through which urban neighbourhoods become incubators of rebellion.

title: Policy Interpretation and Implementation: Expanding Abortion Access in Latin America
Exit, voice, loyalty, and neglect in an electoral autocracy: Hungarian university students’ political engagement and perceptions of system legitimacy
abstract: This study examines political participation and perceptions of system legitimacy among university students in Hungary’s electoral autocracy through an adapted Exit–Voice–Loyalty–Neglect (EVLN) framework. Drawing on the 2024 Active Youth survey, it investigates how patterns of political engagement and disengagement relate to subjective regime evaluations while testing the EVLN framework beyond democratic contexts. The findings reveal that students’ political behaviour is more fluid and ambivalent than the original framework anticipates. The EVLN strategies do not form a single, coherent continuum. Instead, a sharp polarisation emerges along the loyalty–voice axis, while exit and neglect occupy a more ambivalent and overlapping position. The findings suggest that the relationship between political participation and system legitimacy is reconfigured under electoral autocracy, implying that assumptions developed in democratic settings require reinterpretation. More broadly, the study shows how participation and withdrawal may coexist in ways compatible with regime stability despite widespread political discontent.

title: Social media use and generational support for democracy in Australia
abstract: There is a persistent narrative that the younger generations are less supportive of democracy than the older and that this is explained by their use of social media. Using nationally representative data from both the 2025 Australian Election Study and previous waves to critically examine this proposition, we ask three questions. First, do the generations show different levels of ‘diffuse’ and ‘specific’ support for democracy? Second, are different patterns of media consumption across generations associated with positive or negative views of democracy? Third, does social media use in particular account for any observed variations? Our results confirm observable generational differences in media exposure and support for democracy, while suggesting caution should be exercised in making generalisations. We find that as expected the young are less supportive of democracy than the old, especially since the early 2000s. However, we also find few effects on trust in politicians and significant variations in how media use affects attitudes toward democracy in 2025, with Millennials and Boomers negatively impacted by social media while Gen X and Gen Z are not. Our research contributes to a better understanding of the generational impacts of the ongoing process of mediated political engagement on attitudes toward liberal democracy, especially as an emergent Gen Z takes on a distinct political identity.

title: Possessive Familialism and the Crisis of Democracy in the United States
abstract: Amid rising concern over a crisis of democracy in the United States, one point of political alignment across the political spectrum stands out: valorization of the family. This is especially striking because it would seem to conflict with the core ethos of the dominant neoliberal political rationality. We propose that both convergence and crisis are fueled by a logic of possessive familialism. Taking up recent feminist, Marxist, and critical analyses of neoliberalism to situate our claim and tracing the genealogy of this thinking to John Locke, we argue that possessive familialism more aptly describes foundational commitments and assumptions of liberal, and now neoliberal, politics. At the core of the governing rationality of our time, the solo, self-sufficient family obscures the realities of human interdependence and fuels capitalist extraction and accumulation. Feeding the fantasy that individuals, families, and polities survive—and even thrive—absent cross-cutting, overlapping nests of social supports, possessive familialism is the linchpin of neoliberal political rationality that starves democratic imagination, culture, and structures, and fuels the current crisis. We identify five elements of possessive familialism; illustrate its operations through several contemporary examples, including the case for marriage equality and the COVID-19 pandemic; and show how it threatens the very conditions of democratic politics in the US.

title: Rebuilding Trust in Higher Education: Strategies for Addressing the “Diploma Divide”
abstract: The Trump administration is using all the levers of executive power to intervene in universities, including multimillion-dollar cuts, investigations into federal regulation violations, visa withdrawals for international students, and ideological pressures. The outcome of this fight over the purpose of higher education could shape the sector for decades. This reflection essay argues that these attacks have been facilitated by a decade-long loss of public trust in higher education. It addresses two main questions: Why have colleges and universities lost the support of society, and what should they do to restore public trust? The essay argues that this loss of support is driven primarily by rising costs, perceived ideological bias, and questions about degree value. By situating these discussions within scholarship on polarization, populist backlash, and the “diploma divide,” this essay moves beyond causes to explore sector-specific solutions. These include improving educational access, redefining political messaging, demonstrating nonpartisanship, supporting their communities, redefining diversity to include social class, and bridging the cultural divide to protect the university as a democratic institution.

title: Causal Attribution and Trust Evaluations in the Multilevel Structure of Civil-Military Relations
abstract: Public trust in the military and the civilian leaders who control it is central to democratic governance and national security. However, we know relatively little about how such trust is formed. This study examines how citizens update their trust in each actor following military-related events and whether information about the multilevel structure fundamental to democratic civil-military relations influences this process. Existing research has largely relied on performance theories, which assume a straightforward causal link between event outcomes and trust, and on observational data that complicate causal identification. Building on attribution theory, this study refines performance-based accounts by highlighting the multilevel structure. It conducted three survey experiments and a supplementary survey in Japan, a consolidated democracy with a considerable armed force and a population with a relatively strict view on civilian control. The results indicate that event outcomes influence evaluations of civilian and military actors to a similar degree, although underlying mechanisms are asymmetrical depending on the outcome’s direction. Moreover, differing from theoretical expectations, information about the multilevel structure does not substantially alter the effect of outcome information on trust in most cases, although it shapes attributional reasoning. These findings challenge conventional understandings of trust and accountability in democratic civil-military relations.

title: Investigating the Utility of LLM-Based “Silicon Samples” in Political Science Conjoint Experiments
abstract: Abstract This research note is the first study to explore the viability of using LLM-generated respondents in forced-choice conjoint experiments. I generate naive “silicon samples” using three models, GPT 4o-Mini, Llama 3.2, and Magistral-small-2506, benchmarked to a large sample of live conjoint respondents, allowing for direct comparisons between human and silicon choices. The resulting analyses suggest that naively generated silicon samples are insufficient to simulate human decision-making in conjoint tasks; these results also suggest that there are systemic differences in the way demographic covariates shape LLM and human choices in experimental contexts. In total, this analysis makes two important contributions: it establishes a descriptive baseline understanding of LLM-generated respondent performance in conjoint experiments and suggests that naive silicon samples cannot accurately infer human choices using demographic traits in experimental decision making contexts. Finally, the implications of these results imply that LLMs consider covariates differently than live respondents do in micro-level decision making contexts.

title: State capacity and wildfire mitigation: Evidence from state-led forest conservation in China
Matching on Gender and Sexual Orientation,
abstract: Abstract We study the mating patterns of non-heterosexual individuals, who represent a significant and increasing portion of the population, particularly among the youth. We estimate a multidimensional matching model of the marriage market where partner’s gender is endogenously chosen conditional on the agent’s sexual orientation, and is subject to trade-offs that depend on both the agents’ preferences and the pool of potential partners. We show that same-sex couples experience lower gains from live-in relationships, a “same-sex penalty”. Absent this penalty, the share of same-sex couples in the U.S. would increase by about 50% (from 1.36% to 2.04% of all couples).
journal_name: Journal of the European Economic Association

title: Union Membership and Native-Immigrant Labour Market Gaps
abstract: Abstract We estimate the causal effects of union membership on labour market outcomes for natives and immigrants, exploiting quasi-experimental variation from large increases in Norway’s tax deduction for union dues. Union membership raises earnings and improves employment protection for native workers, while the private returns for non-Western immigrants are substantially smaller and often close to zero. Complementary survey evidence suggests that this gap is not explained by differences in information, preferences, or engagement with unions: immigrants receive similar information when joining, report similar preferences over job amenities, and are more likely than natives to seek union assistance. Instead, the combined administrative and survey evidence is consistent with differences in union-side behaviour. Immigrants report lower satisfaction after contacting unions for support and are more likely to believe that native workers and those with strong local networks receive greater benefits from membership. The impact is most pronounced in concentrated labour markets, indicating that relying on unions to address monopsony-based market failures may unintentionally amplify group inequalities.

title: People, places, and firms: improving our understanding of wage and productivity disparities
abstract: Abstract In many countries spatial disparities in wages and productivity are large and persistent. This raises questions about the causes and consequences of such disparities. Two inter-related issues—the sorting of high skilled workers and the productivity benefits of urban density—are central to the way in which urban economists have approached these questions. In this commentary, we argue that despite the emerging consensus that sorting matters for wage disparities, the literature has made less progress on other dimensions of these disparities and a number of methodological issues remain unresolved.

title: When immigrants meet exporters: A reassessment of the migrant-native wage gap

Behind the organizational chart: The emergence of “gurus” in advice networks
abstract: Explaining the endogenous emergence of “gurus” – high-status professionals who are referred to for advice but are unlikely to seek it themselves – in organizations requires an integrated approach. This approach must consider the interplay of individual attributes (e.g., skills and status), structural factors (e.g., informal networks), and organizational contexts (e.g., knowledge-sharing infrastructure and internal competitiveness) from a dynamic perspective. In this study, we develop an agent-based model of advice network formation calibrated on an empirically observed network to identify the factors and processes driving “guru” emergence. Our results show that the emergence of “gurus” depends primarily on status differentials, homophily, and organizational context. In low-competitive settings, a relatively stable proportion of “gurus” emerges once the advice network reaches equilibrium. However, as competitiveness increases, network equilibrium is associated with fewer “gurus”, whose emergence is decoupled from formal hierarchical roles. Contrary to common sense, differences in skills among professionals contribute only marginally to network dynamics and “guru” formation. Overall, our findings suggest a fundamental misalignment between formal hierarchies and informal status dynamics within organizations, which could lead to tension.

title: Mistrust, uncertainty, fear, and vaccine acceptability: quasi-experimental data from the United Kingdom and Portugal during the COVID-19 pandemic
abstract: Using a quasi-experimental design, this study tests a cognitive-affective model of vaccine acceptability focusing on the effects of relationships between trust, certainty, attitudes, and fear in a sample of 1132 adults in the UK (N = 648 [51.7%]) and Portugal (N = 486 [48.3%]) during the COVID-19 pandemic. A path model of the relationships between the variables was assessed using structural equation modeling. Participants in the experimental condition were asked to list what they thought were the major societal uncertainties concerning the COVID-19 vaccines (N = 566 [49.9%]). When subsequently asked, those in the experimental condition reported lower vaccine certainty than those in the control condition (N = 568 [50.1%]). Across the entire sample, lower vaccine certainty was associated with lower vaccine acceptability. Higher vaccine uncertainty was associated with less negativity toward vaccine refusers (which in turn was associated with lower vaccine acceptability). In addition to the direct positive effect of trust in science and scientists upon vaccine acceptability, there were mediated effects: higher trust in science and scientists was associated with higher fear. Fear was positively associated with vaccine certainty. Fear was also positively associated with negativity toward vaccine refusers. The results suggest that, in health crises, people may be more susceptible to identify with other vaccine refusers (and potentially ‘anti-vaxxer’ groups) if levels of uncertainty and mistrust are higher, thereby undermining vaccine uptake. The study makes an original contribution to the literature on vaccine acceptability by showing that vaccine certainty (and changes in vaccine acceptability) can be modified by a single intervention that asks people to describe what they think are important vaccine uncertainties. Furthermore, by examining the relationship of attitudes to ‘anti-vaxxers’ with the cognitive-affective model of vaccine acceptability, the research indicates the potential significance of uncertainty and fear upon social attitudes.

title: Forecasting LLM‐Enabled Biorisk and the Efficacy of Safeguards
abstract: ABSTRACT Capabilities of large language models (LLMs) on several biological benchmarks have prompted not only excitement about their usefulness for research but also concern about biosecurity risks. We recruited 46 subject‐matter experts in biology and biosecurity, and 22 generalist forecasters to estimate the risks of growing LLM capabilities. Most respondents expected some hypothetical LLM capabilities to increase their estimates of risk and dramatically underestimated the rate of LLM progress in those capabilities. When these capabilities arose, the median forecast did update as anticipated. The median expert initially predicted a 0.3% annual risk of a human‐caused epidemic that causes 100,000 deaths. This estimate then rose to 1.5% conditional on several hypothetical LLM capabilities, including matching the performance of a top‐performing team of virologists on a virology troubleshooting test, which the median expert did not expect to occur until 2030. Given this finding, we conducted a baselining study and found that LLMs already crossed this performance threshold in April 2025. A follow‐up survey conducted after these results were available found that forecasters significantly updated their median unconditional risk estimates upward, with the new median expert forecast of annual risk rising to 1.5% (as anticipated by the earlier conditional forecasts). More encouragingly, most experts thought that the adoption of LLM safeguards and mandatory nucleic acid screening would negate the risk associated with some hypothetical LLM capabilities.

title: Assessment of Risks, Efficiency, Costs, and Gain of Natural Hazard (Catastrophe) Consequences Prevention Based on Geophysical Monitoring
abstract: ABSTRACT The purpose of this paper is to quantitatively estimate the efficiency of forecasting hazards and catastrophic processes induced by high‐energy terrestrial sources, based on an integrated monitoring of the state of geophysical processes. Using methods of mathematical statistics and detection theory, relations have been obtained that can be used to calculate the coefficients of the efficiency of warning of catastrophes and the costs associated with a predicted event. The hazard (catastrophe) prevention efficiency coefficient has been shown to be dependent only on the conditional probability of missing a hazard. The relative cost parameter is a function of five parameters: a priori probability of the unwanted event, a conditional false alarm probability, a conditional missed detect probability, relative costs in the case of false alarm probability, and costs to minimize consequences of the hazardous event in case it has been accurately forecast. The gain from organizing geophysical monitoring has been estimated for a few dangers and catastrophes of terrestrial nature. The gain has been shown to be significant in many cases. An energy‐based classification of the most important natural sources of hazards and catastrophes, as well as their consequences, is proposed or improved.

title: An Agent‐Based Model for Post‐Disaster Resource Allocation Considering Dynamic Demand
abstract: ABSTRACT In the response phase of a disaster, effective and equitable resource allocation is critical for meeting the needs of affected populations and maintaining the social order in disaster‐stricken areas. However, dynamic demand driven by the mobility of disaster‐affected populations can substantially impact resource allocation outcomes. To consider this mobility in the resource allocation problem, in this paper, we employ an agent‐based model to simulate cross‐shelter movements and assess the performance of resource allocation strategies considering a gradual increase of total available resources over time. A novel resource allocation strategy is proposed, which leverages demand estimation through a machine learning (ML) method‐XGBoost. We then compare this approach against two conventional strategies: uniform distribution and historical data averaging. Through case studies using real‐world data of Typhoon Ragasa from Shenzhen in China and Lal‐lo in the Philippines, we demonstrate that our proposed strategy comprehensively outperforms the other two in terms of effectiveness, equity and stability. In conclusion, this ML‐based prediction approach offers valuable insights to support decision‐makers in the formulation of resource allocation plans.

title: Systemic Risk Revisited: A Working Definition and Diagnostic Framework for Risk Analysis
abstract: ABSTRACT Systemic risk has gained increasing attention across disaster risk reduction, climate governance, finance, infrastructure, and other domains, yet its meaning and application remain inconsistent. Existing definitions emphasize interdependence, contagion, complexity, uncertainty, cascading effects, and system‐wide disruption, but differ in analytical focus and operational use. This paper reviews major definitional traditions and argues that a working definition and diagnostic framework can clarify the analytical basis of systemic risk. We define systemic risk as potential damage, loss, and impact that propagate through interdependencies, feedbacks, and nonlinear processes within or across interconnected systems. Building on this definition, the paper develops a diagnostic framework based on system structure, propagation pathways, dynamic mechanisms, and cascading consequences. These dimensions help distinguish systemic risks from risks that are severe, complex, or large scale but remain relatively contained, and provide a structured basis for examining how adverse consequences propagate within and across interconnected systems in different domains.

title: Extending the Deservingness Framework to Communication Sciences
abstract: While communication research has documented how media frame social groups as victims or threats, little is known about the evaluative criteria through which mediated discourse constructs minority representations. This study introduces deservingness as a framework for analyzing such evaluative logics, drawing on the Control, Attitude, Reciprocity, Identity, Need (CARIN) criteria. We illustrate this through an analysis of 7,561 Belgian newspaper articles across three migration contexts (2015, 2021, 2022), combining automated dictionary-based content analysis with a theory-driven qualitative content analysis of 284 articles. Results reveal a stable but context-sensitive deservingness communication. We position deservingness as a transferable tool for research on moral evaluation and conditional solidarity.

title: Perceived Sources Matter: Implications of Misinformation on Media Trust and News Avoidance Under Different Levels of Press Freedom
abstract: Extant research on the impact of misinformation on media trust and news avoidance behavior has produced competing arguments and findings. The present study argues that the relationships among misinformation, media trust, and news avoidance can be better specified by considering whether people perceive misinformation as coming primarily from established institutions or non-institutional sources. Given the close linkage between the mainstream news media and established social and political institutions, people are likely to exhibit lower levels of news trust and higher levels of news avoidance if they perceive misinformation as coming from institutional sources. In contrast, when people perceive misinformation as coming from non-institutional sources, they may rely on the news media as authoritative fact-checkers and hence trust the news more and avoid it less. Societal-level press freedom is likely to moderate such relationships. The arguments and hypotheses are tested by an analysis of Digital News Report 2025 data.

title: Improving Competitiveness: A Freelancer-Centric Approach for Recommending Reskilling Strategies
Do Experimental Asset Market Results Replicate? High‐Powered Preregistered Replications of 17 Key Results
abstract: ABSTRACT Experimental asset markets provide a controlled approach to studying financial markets. We attempt to replicate 17 key results from four prominent studies, collecting new data from 166 markets with 1,544 participants. Only three of the 14 original results reported as statistically significant were successfully replicated. We fail to replicate findings on emotions, self‐control, and gender differences in bubble formation but confirm that experience reduces bubbles and cognitive skills explain trading success. Our study demonstrates the importance of replications in enhancing the credibility of scientific results in this field.

title: Decoupling voting and cash flow rights
Inflexibility and Leverage
abstract: Firms’ inflexibility to adjust their scale persistently explains capital structure variations in a comprehensive sample and randomly selected subsamples. Higher inflexibility leads to lower financial leverage, potentially due to higher default risk and lower value of tax shields. Contraction inflexibility determines leverage more than expansion inflexibility. Moreover, our inflexibility measure explains financial leverage significantly better than other variables that potentially capture certain aspects of adjustment costs for capital or labor. In addition, inflexible firms increase leverage more following a positive credit supply shock. Analyses employing instrumental variables estimation confirm our main finding. Our results suggest inflexibility shapes corporate financial policies. This paper was accepted by Bo Becker, finance. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.08672 .

title: Multitype Information Acquisition in a Strategic Trading Model
abstract: We analyze information acquisition in a strategic trading model with multidimensional uncertainties. Our main result is that the equilibrium can exhibit multiplicity because of the integer nature of the number of informed traders and the strategic interactions across different types of informed traders. We show that the number of equilibria can be arbitrarily large. Moreover, asymmetric equilibria can arise even in symmetric settings. As information costs rise, fewer traders acquire information, yet prices can become more informative. These results shed light on the instability of financial markets and yield testable empirical predictions. This paper was accepted by Lukas Schmid, finance. Funding: This work was supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grants 72472171 and 72372011]. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.08463 .

title: Contest or Contract: Assessing the Effectiveness of Contests in Online Labor Markets
abstract: Online labor markets have become increasingly popular among companies seeking global access to workers. Some platforms have adopted a contest-based scheme, allowing employers to review multiple submissions before selecting the best one. This practice raises a crucial question: Given a predefined budget, should employers choose a contest or contract scheme for tasks? This study examines the comparative effectiveness of contests versus contracts in achieving better job outcomes, focusing on design tasks characterized by high uncertainty. Using a comprehensive data set from a leading online labor market, we employ multiple empirical strategies, combined with machine learning and text mining techniques, to examine the impact of compensation schemes on job quality. Our results suggest that contract-based jobs yield better performance than contests in the context of ideation tasks. Further analysis, such as examining image similarity among pairwise solutions within a task, identifies “copying” behaviors as a key mechanism undermining the effectiveness of contests. In the public setting of contests, workers can observe others’ submissions and revise their own, leading to imitation rather than innovation. As competition intensity increases, workers have weaker incentives to exert effort, reducing solution quality. Consequently, the negative incentive effects in contests outweigh both the potential positive incentive and parallel effects. Moreover, although information availability can enhance work quality, contests inherently offer limited informational advantages compared with contracts. Taken together, our findings suggest that contract-based schemes are more effective than contests for design tasks, offering important implications for both employers and platform designers in online labor markets. This paper was accepted by Karan Girotra, operations management. Funding: N. Zhang acknowledges the support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grant 72302053]. Supplemental Material: The online appendices and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.07082 .

title: Willingness to Compete in Dirty Competitions
abstract: Competitive environments often leave room for “dirty” practices such as sabotage, retaliation, or dishonesty. We use an online experiment to document aggregate levels and individual differences in the willingness to engage in dirty competition and in the willingness to enter competitions where the opponent may play dirty. We then use the experimental data to validate a set of survey questions that capture willingness to engage in dirty competition above general willingness to compete. We elicit these questions in a representative survey panel and show that willingness to engage in dirty competition is a strong predictor of holding a management or supervisory position and of working in the private—versus the public—sector, but also of worse self-esteem, worse social relationships, and increased feelings of guilt and shame. Men, younger people, and lower-educated people are on average more willing to engage in dirty competition. This paper was accepted by Dorothea Kübler, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.01218 .

title: A Forest Approach for Analyzing the Heterogeneous and Nonlinear Effects of Sellers’ Response Time
The Problem of Ignoring the Ignorability Assumption in Advertising Measurement: A Matrix Completion Solution
abstract: This paper frames the overlap violation problem in online advertising auctions as a missing-data problem and proposes a matrix completion approach to correct the resulting bias in observational studies with algorithmic ad allocation.

title: EXPRESS: A Learning and Searching Method for Integrated Process Planning and Scheduling
abstract: The integrated process planning and scheduling problem combines process route planning and shop scheduling to achieve high efficiency in manufacturing and maximize resource utilization, which is crucial for modern manufacturing systems. Traditional approaches, such as mixed-integer linear programming and heuristic algorithms, often struggle to balance solution quality and computational efficiency, particularly in large-scale scenarios. To address this, we propose learning-then-searching, an efficient framework combining deep reinforcement learning with heuristic search to solve integrated process planning and scheduling problems. We formulate the problem as a Markov decision process and develop a deep reinforcement learning method tailored to capture the complex relationships among operations, machines, and jobs. With the learned policy distributions, Monte Carlo tree search employs learned priors and problem-specific rollouts to further refine scheduling strategies, effectively balancing exploration and exploitation to achieve better solutions. Experimental results show that the proposed framework improves solution efficiency and quality over traditional methods across benchmark and large-scale instances, with pronounced advantages when route ambiguity is high. It also offers practitioners a flexible tradeoff between rapid policy-based decisions and further refinement through tree search when additional computation time is available.

title: The Future of Entrepreneurship Research Includes Online Panel Data—If Used Correctly
abstract: As online panel data (OPD) become more widely used across the behavioral sciences, editors, reviewers, and researchers in entrepreneurship are asking whether it has a legitimate place in our field. We believe the answer is yes—provided three conditions are met. First, the online panel’s participants and definition of entrepreneur must match the research question. Second, studies must incorporate best practices for sample verification. Third, generalizability must be explicitly addressed as part of the study (or set of studies). If researchers do these things, OPD can meaningfully advance both theory and practice in entrepreneurship research. That said, real questions remain. What kinds of studies are suitable for OPD? Who are these respondents, and are they who they say they are? Are they human, and are they entrepreneurs as commonly defined in the literature? Our recommendations and checklist aim to enable entrepreneurship researchers to answer these questions and make informed choices when collecting data and publishing results using OPD.

title: When People Management Backfires: A Qualitative Study of Unintended Consequences of Line Managers' Support for Employees
abstract: ABSTRACT This article examines how and why well‐intended people management can backfire, resulting in unintended consequences such as reduced well‐being and performance. Although people management—the combination of line managers' implementation of HR practices and their leadership behavior in supporting employees—is generally assumed to result in positive outcomes, emerging evidence suggests that benevolent line manager behavior may have adverse effects. However, insight into the underlying mechanisms through which such backfire occurs remains limited. To address this gap, we utilized a multi‐actor qualitative approach by conducting 55 interviews among line managers and employees in the Dutch hospital sector using the Critical Incident Technique. We identify three mechanisms through which backfire unfolds: (1) constrained communication in the context of policies and regulations, (2) overcompensation in the context of performance pressure, and (3) accountability in the context of conflicting fairness perceptions. Across these mechanisms, we show that backfire emerges not from poor managerial intent but from the interaction between line managers' intentions and behaviors, employees' interpretations, and structural constraints. By conceptualizing backfire as a structurally constrained and interactional process, this study advances people management research beyond dominant explanations focused on implementation quality or outcome trade‐offs, and highlights the importance of context in shaping employee responses.

title: Supplemental Material for What Do We Know About Job Knowledge Tests? A 30-Year Update of Validity Evidence
Context Matters, Doesn’t It? The Role of Context in Everyday Emotion Regulation Strategy Use
abstract: A common maxim holds that “context is everything.” This perspective transformed the field of emotion regulation, which evolved from understanding which regulation strategies people use, to understanding how strategy use varies by context (i.e., strategy–situation fit). Theoretical accounts suggest contextual features are crucial in guiding strategy use. However, empirical evidence is isolated in piecemeal studies with inconclusive results. To comprehensively explore context-dependent emotion regulation, we need data on emotion regulation across many contexts, at scale. Combining up to 11 experience-sampling data sets collected from Belgian and Australian samples in an integrative analysis ( N ID = 500–1,696, N observations = 27,023–101,114, M age = 25.38 years, 71% women), we examined how regulation-strategy use varies as a function of three theory-derived contextual features— intensity , controllability , and social features (i.e., the presence and closeness of others). We found limited support that context matters for daily emotion-regulation strategy use. Our study provides a well-powered foundational step to test a theory central to emotion-regulation research and highlights the complexity of capturing strategy–situation fit in daily life.

title: Production-Based Option Pricing
abstract: We show that a structural model incorporating firms’ real options and financial leverage decisions can generate forward-looking equity distributions of various shapes, resulting in highly flexible implied volatility surfaces. In contrast, exogenously specified models with stochastic volatility and jumps can only generate smiles and downward-sloping curves. We explain the observed negative relationship between downward sloping implied volatility surfaces and the value of real options: real options contribute positively to equity skewness, and more so the more convex their payoff, which is the case when the real option is “at-the-money” and has the lowest value.

Trade-Offs in Authoritarian Participatory Digital Surveillance: Evidence From China’s Sharp Eyes Project
abstract: How do authoritarian regimes overcome the limits of digital surveillance? They complement camera systems with citizen monitoring and reporting, creating participatory surveillance in which residents interpret what cameras capture and supply local knowledge technology alone cannot provide. I study this hybrid form of control in China’s Sharp Eyes Project, which gives selected residents access to camera feeds and encourages reports of suspected misconduct. I use a staggered difference-in-differences analysis of administrative and survey data from Chinese cities. The program increases citizen reporting by 11%, reduces crimes susceptible to community monitoring, and lowers trust in neighbors. Reports expand the state’s informational reach, but the system makes residents uncertain about how neighbors may interpret and report their behavior. The study places political participation at the center of digital surveillance and shows how authoritarian regimes turn relations among citizens into a source of state power while weakening the foundations of collective action.

An Analysis of Position-Taking and Position-Avoidance in the U.S. House of Representatives
abstract: Scholars of legislative politics have extensively explored the political factors that incentivize members of Congress to engage in position-taking. This has led to a well-developed body of work focusing on why legislators skip congressional roll-call votes. Current scholarship offers mixed conclusions on whether electoral considerations influence a representative’s likelihood of abstaining from a roll-call vote. To help clarify these mixed findings, we analyze a broader range of electoral forces. In this study, we examine all roll-call abstentions among members serving in the U.S. House of Representatives from the 85th to the 117th Congress. We find that electoral considerations can indeed impact abstention behavior; however, the effect depends on the type of election. Specifically, lawmakers vulnerable in their primary race are more likely to avoid taking a position on a roll-call vote, whereas electoral vulnerability in the general election appears to have little effect. These findings deepen our understanding of how elections influence representation.

title: Beyond Incivility: Bellicose Politics, Violence, and the Dangers of Illiberal Encroachment in the United States
abstract: The United States seems to be experiencing a volatile period where its core values and institutions have come under threat, accompanied by what many observers identify as a rise in uncivil speech and behavior. Yet, much of this contentious rhetoric and behavior seemingly goes beyond instances of incivility and into something more serious, including threats, intimidation, physical assaults, insurrectionary riots, and assassination. This raises two important questions: is the concept of incivility adequate for describing and analyzing such speech and behavior in contemporary politics, and how should threats and violent actions be understood within a broader civility framework? In this article, I argue that many of the illiberal pathologies afflicting contemporary democracies—including political violence—fall outside the scope of incivility. Drawing on recent work in normative political theory, I unpack the concept of civility and examine how violent speech and actions fit within its various dimensions. I then introduce the concept of “bellicose politics” and provide examples from the United States in which contentious rhetoric and behavior exceed the bounds of incivility. I conclude by considering how this concept may improve the way we analyze and respond to violent rhetoric and actions in political life.

abstract: Abstract This paper examines paternalistic preferences in two large-scale experiments with participants from the US general population. Participants decide whether to intervene when a stakeholder is about to make a choice misaligned with the stakeholder’s own preferences. Willingness to intervene depends on which intervention is available: only a minority implements a hard intervention, which restricts the stakeholder’s choice set, while a majority implements a soft intervention that provides information without restricting choice. A substantial share of participants does not defer to the stakeholder’s stated preferences when evaluating welfare. Our framework estimates that about half are welfarists and a third libertarian paternalists.

The integrative theory of supportive network (re)structuring: a case study in the context of LGBTQ+ hate speech
abstract: Abstract Social support is a fundamental human need and communication process. Yet, scholars theorizing about social support have been limited by several pervasive assumptions: (a) people are able to recruit support when needed, (b) others are willing and able to provide support, (c) what counts as “good” support is mutually understood and desirable, and (d) support seeking is binary and static. Researchers must productively move beyond these assumptions to enhance the depth and breadth of theorizing about the process of support seeking. By addressing these assumptions and consolidating the literature concerning support seeking and marshaling, we set forth the novel, field-general integrative theory of supportive network (re)structuring (ITSNS) grounded in the interpretive paradigm. To accomplish this, we introduce process theorizing, forward three propositions forming the ITSNS’ heuristic framework, and offer criteria for evaluating the ITSNS. Finally, to illustrate the utility of the ITSNS in research practice, we offer a case study in the context of LGBTQ+ people seeking support following an experience of hate speech.

Too Little too Late? Nationwide Carbon Trading in China
abstract: China launched a nationwide, rate-based carbon market in 2021.Covering the world's top CO2 emitter, compliance depends on the intensity of carbon emissions rather than an absolute cap.We draw on the theoretical literature of rate-based systems to provide the first empirical evidence on an early adopter.Using plant-level data from satellite imagery and machine learning methods, we find that high-efficiency power plants increased electricity generation and CO2 emissions by approximately 5% relative to low-efficiency plants.Because its carbon market regulates nearly all coal plants in China, we focus on the differential responses by plant efficiency, finding no evidence of a differential reduction in emission intensity (though these estimates are imprecise).Relative to coal plants in Indonesia and the Philippines, which had no carbon market, China's high-efficiency plants also increased emissions, while the estimate for its low-efficiency plants is small and insignificant.This pattern of responses suggests that emissions increases of highefficiency plants exceeded substitution away from low-efficiency plants.Underscoring the production stimulus to more efficient Chinese plants, air quality worsened downwind of highefficiency plants relative to low-efficiency plants, compromising air quality in relatively clean areas of China.If China's goal is to reduce its carbon emissions, then benchmarks will need to be tightened within the existing system or an alternative system that does not simultaneously incentivize electricity production will need to be adopted.

title: Inference for Regression with Clustered or Spatially Correlated Data I: Framework and Clustering
abstract: Many regression analyses use observations that are correlated within uncorrelated clusters and/or are correlated in distance or other spatial measure.Such data are often positively correlated.This reduces the information content of an additional observation compared to the default of independent observations.Consequently, failure to adjust standard errors for such correlation leads to confidence intervals that are too narrow, and to hypothesis tests that over reject.In this paper we first provide a general framework.We then focus on inference when observations are correlated within cluster and uncorrelated across clusters.We detail cluster-robust inference methods, particularly methods that provide improved finite-sample performance when there is not a large number of clusters.Such adjustments are often necessary.A companion paper, Cameron and Miller (2026), presents inference when correlation is spatially dampening in the distance between observations.The two papers are intended to provide a guide to empirical researchers.

title: A Framework for Integrating Climate Goals into Trade Agreements
abstract: A critical tension in global governance is that trade agreements have evolved largely in isolation from climate policy.This paper shows that the two domains generate systematic cross-externalities: larger gains from trade are associated with greater climate externalities imposed on partners, while linking carbon taxes to trade agreements produces distributive externalities that undermine the balance of trade concessions.To address this tension, we present a framework to integrate harmonized carbon pricing into the WTO subject to institutional and political-feasibility constraints.We explore two linkage designs.The first is a centralized Climate Fund, where all members apply a common demand-side carbon tax and contribute a portion of the revenues to the fund, capped by fiscal constraints.The Fund then reallocates these contributions to balance the tax burden across countries, subject to informational constraints.Quantitative analysis shows that even a simple fund allocation rule can sustain a carbon price of $138 per ton of CO2, reducing global emissions by 54%.The main binding constraint is informational: knowing the precise incidence of the carbon tax across countries ex ante would raise the feasible price to $265.The second is a decentralized design without transfers.Each member meets a carbon tax revenue floor but retains full discretion over its mix of demand-side and supply-side taxes.Energy exporters choose supply-side taxes while energy importers opt for demand-side taxes.These choices organically balance the tax burden and yield a 47% reduction in global emissions, almost rivaling the centralized Climate Fund.

title: Welfare Analysis with Complementarities: When Direct and Total Responses Are Sufficient
abstract: Complementarities can have important welfare consequences, but quantifying these effects would seem to require identifying and valuing the underlying mechanisms separately.This paper shows that this need not be the case.I provide necessary and sufficient conditions under which baseline subsidized activity and the direct and total responses to a subsidy determine aggregate willingness to pay.A sufficient condition for valuing the equilibrium adjustment is that it has the same effect on utility as an additional subsidy common to all agents and relevant actions.The formula is easy to apply to existing estimates and guides the design of new experiments.

title: Limits to Arbitrage and Prediction Market Efficiency: the Case of PredictIt
abstract: PredictIt is a CFTC-regulated US prediction market focused on political outcomes. It was very successful in attracting participants in the 2016-22 period, running liquid markets on topics predecessors had tried unsuccesfully. During this period, investors were limited to $850 positions in each contract, which limited arbitrage trading. PredictIt exhibited much larger pricing biases than previously studied prediction markets. Bid prices often persistently added to more than 110, implying an immediate arbitrage profit even after fees. Prices exhibited an overpricing of longshots that was larger than in other prediction markets. The experience of PredictIt suggests that limiting stakes may undermine the ability of prediction markets to accurately price event probabilities.

title: Are Prediction Markets Politically Biased?
abstract: This version of the paper is preliminary; it will be revised following the 2026 midterms to include those elections and data from Polymarket.The author would like to thank the prediction markets included in the sample for making their data available for academic research.The pre-2007 data included in the sample was collected jointly with Andrew Leigh and Justin Wolfers for a project that never led to a paper.I have traded on prediction markets, but have no financial relationship with any of the markets mentioned in this work.The views expressed herein are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the views of the National Bureau of Economic Research.

title: Targeted Acceleration in Middle School Math: Impacts on College Entry, Degree Completion, and STEM
abstract: We study an accelerated 3-year math curriculum offered in the middle schools of a large urban district that enables students to finish Algebra I and Geometry before high school.Entry to the program is based on 5th-grade math test scores, with a cutoff at the 80th percentile.Continuing eligibility requires at least a B grade in the previous year; successful completion of all three years is highly correlated with an index of non-cognitive skills.Following students for 6 years after high school graduation, we find that the impacts of admission vary widely by non-cognitive skill and gender.Marginally eligible boys with high non-cognitive skills have a 33 percentage point (ppt.)increase in the probability of completing calculus by 11th grade and a 12 ppt.increase in the probability of completing a major in STEM or business within 6 years; boys with lower noncognitive skills take more advanced math classes in high school but have no significant effects on their college outcomes.Like their male peers, marginally eligible girls with high non-cognitive skills are more likely to complete calculus by 11th grade (+17 ppt.).Their rate of graduating with a STEM or business major is unaffected, but they switch from social sciences to the core STEM majors (science, engineering and math).Girls in the two lower terciles of non-cognitive skill are also strongly affected by entry to the program, with higher participation in advanced math classes in high school, higher rates of entry to selective 4-year colleges, and higher rates of completing a STEM or business major (+12 ppt).

title: Living in a Ghost Town: The Geography of Depopulation and Aging
abstract: How do depopulation and population aging evolve differently across regions within a country, and what are their implications for aggregate economic activity and regional inequality?Using spatially disaggregated data from Japan over the past several decades, we show that rural areas have experienced significantly faster depopulation and aging than urban areas, driven by low fertility and sustained out-migration of young cohorts.Regions undergoing these trends face declining local amenities and rising per-capita public service costs.To study the future evolution and economic consequences of these dynamics, we develop and calibrate a dynamic life-cycle spatial general equilibrium model.The model predicts widening geographic disparities in depopulation, aging, and economic activity in the coming centuries.While subsidies to declining regions can lower regional inequality, they come at the cost of lower aggregate efficiency and higher public service expenditures.

title: Communicating Performance: Textual and Financial Disclosures in Private Equity
abstract: Private capital fund managers appear to possess significant information about the relative quality of their portfolio firms even within the first three years after the investment.But the way this information is disclosed to investors changes dynamically: Textual discussions of portfolio companies have substantial information about the firms' ultimate performance in the early stages of investment, while interim valuations are less important.Over time, this pattern reverses, with interim valuations becoming more important in explaining future returns, especially after portfolio companies have a financing event.The results vary not only with the tone but also with the content of fund manager disclosures.In an opaque market with substantial information asymmetries, textual discussions seem to serve as a signal about general partner quality.

title: The Geopolitical Trap: How Great Power Rivalry Protects Rising Powers
abstract: The authors used OpenAI's ChatGPT (various GPT-5-series models available through the ChatGPT service during 2026) to assist with drafting and editing portions of the manuscript, checking and refining formal arguments, identifying potentially relevant literature and historical sources, and improving the organization and presentation of the analysis.All sources suggested through ChatGPT were independently checked against the cited materials.The authors reviewed and revised all AI-assisted output and take full responsibility for the accuracy, originality, arguments, citations, and final content of the manuscript.The views expressed herein are those of the authors and do not necessarily reflect the views of the National Bureau of Economic Research.

title: Reassessing the 2000s Housing Cycle After Two Decades of Research
abstract: What caused the 2000s housing cycle?This article synthesizes two decades of research, including reduced-form empirics and structural models.Although often contentious, the literature coheres once one accounts for each study's timing, place, methodology, and measurement.The cycle was a perfect storm that occurred in distinct stages.Starting in the late 1990s, fundamentals improved, and credit supply increased across the income distribution due to automated underwriting and financial deregulation.In the early 2000s, a decline in interest rates was followed by a further expansion in securitized and subprime credit, the origin of which remains controversial.This sequence of shocks produced a persistent boom that triggered two shifts in beliefs: average expectations became overly optimistic, pushing prices higher, and expectations diverged, fueling speculation.In the bust, prices overshot primarily due to mortgage defaults, which removed buyers and contracted credit supply.How these forces interact and how expectations form require further research.

title: An LLM Workflow That Reproduces, Improves, and Extends Published Economics Research
abstract: We introduce an open-source workflow that enables an LLM to reproduce, improve, and extend an economics article using the article's published replication package.First, the workflow attempts to reproduce the original calculations, checks for discrepancies with published findings, and performs automated sensitivity analysis.Across 4,452 published replication packages for five economics journals, the workflow flags discrepancies in 3,460 articles or their appendices.Second, the workflow improves the original calculations by using a different implementation or algorithm.In 496 articles, the workflow is able to reduce a calculation's computation time, at similar or greater accuracy, by more than a factor of 10.Third, the workflow extends the original analysis.In 923 articles, the workflow develops an extension that does not appear in the original article and that is aligned with the original article's goals and assumptions.

title: (How) Do We Teach Emotions?
abstract: Emotional intelligence constitutes a key component of human capital, shaped partially by educational materials.Using machine learning and generative AI tools, we examine emotional content in public-school textbooks and children's literature.A stark mismatch emerges: text exposes children to a broad emotional range, but images overwhelmingly depict happiness and calm, regardless of emotions described in text on the same page.Nearly half of pages show zero overlap between the emotions described in text and those shown in images.This pattern persists across time, contexts, and identities.Household purchases and library inventories suggest content may be endogenously shaped by consumer demand favoring "positive" cover imagery, implying market forces narrow the emotional landscape children encounter.

title: Price Setting During a Currency Changeover
abstract: We use the euro cash changeover, a large-scale and purely nominal reform that requires all firms to redenominate posted prices, to distinguish among theories of price rigidity. We develop a nonstationary menu-cost model in which firms anticipate the changeover date and may combine currency adoption with real price adjustment. The announcement makes the firm’s inaction region time-varying, a singular control problem with a moving boundary for which closed-form characterizations are rarely available. We solve this problem analytically by perturbation, recovering the whole path of the boundary, the date at which firms begin adopting the new currency, and the implied pricing moments. The model predicts that, as the changeover approaches, firms adjust more frequently but by smaller amounts, compressing the distribution of price changes. We test these predictions using historical CPI micro data from Austria, Finland, Greece, and Slovakia, a UK benchmark, and daily price data from the recent changeovers in Croatia and Bulgaria. Across changeovers, adjustment frequency rises while the size and dispersion of price changes fall. The model adds a single parameter to the standard menu-cost setup, the cost of pricing in the wrong currency. Calibrating it to the observed rise in adjustment frequency, the model reproduces the decline in the size of price changes and its subsequent recovery, neither of which is targeted. The evidence supports state-dependent price-setting models over models in which nominal redenomination leaves real pricing behavior unchanged. Institutional subscribers to the NBER working paper series, and residents of developing countries may download this paper without additional charge at www.nber.org.

title: Here, There, and Everywhere: Remote Work’s Impact on Employment in the UK
abstract: Remote work is often touted as a way for disabled and older workers to remain in the labour market.Post-Covid, the incidence of remote work has increased in the UK.Following Bloom et al. (2026), we test the effects of remote work on employment for these two groups using the pandemic's increase in work from home rates as a quasi-experiment.We compare occupations with high growth in work from home (WFH) to those with lower growth in work from home, with growth rates measured among the non-disabled or younger.We then instrument using pre-pandemic remote work scores from Dingle and Neiman (2020).We find significant evidence that rising WFH increases employment of disabled and older workers in the UK.We additionally find decreases in commute time and wages for both groups, but no effect on hours worked.

title: Impact of Adults’ College Completion on their Parents’ Mortality: Evidence from the 1993 Korean Higher Education Reform
abstract: A large literature examines the economic and health returns to college education.We extend this literature by studying the upward intergenerational effects of children's education on parental mortality.We exploit Korea's 1993 Higher Education Reform, which we estimate raised college completion by 13 percentage points among eldest children in the 1974-1983 birth cohorts relative to the prior 10-year cohort.Using data from the Korean Longitudinal Study of Aging, reducedform estimates indicate a 27% (s.e.=10%) reduction in mortality among parents whose oldest child was in the reform-affected cohort.Because the reform affected college completion but not other education levels or quality, we use it as an instrumental variable (IV) for child college completion.IV estimates indicate a 20% (s.e.=7%) reduction in parental mortality for children induced to complete college by the reform.These parents received greater financial support and contact from their children and had lower smoking and higher physical activity, although these mechanisms explain only a small share of the mortality benefit.Effects were larger for parents of daughters in reduced-form analyses, although IV estimates did not differ significantly by child gender.Future research should further investigate the mechanisms through which children's college education affects parental mortality.

title: The Macroeconomic Effect of AI: Sizing the Software Engineering Channel
abstract: We measure how artificial intelligence (AI) affects the economy through its impact on software engineering productivity. We use information from financial markets to develop a forward-looking measure that is available in real time. We estimate the sensitivity of each firm’s stock return to an AI stock market index, and how this sensitivity depends on the share of firm payroll in software engineering. We use a model to map this cross-sectional relationship into software engineering productivity gains. From November 2022 to December 2025, AI increased the market’s expected present value of software engineering productivity by the equivalent of a permanent 32.6% productivity increase. The corresponding effect on the level of GDP is 3.6% in the baseline and 6.5% when higher software engineering productivity also raises R&D productivity. By mid-2026, amid rapid progress in coding agents, the effect of AI on productivity and GDP had more than doubled relative to the end of 2025. Institutional subscribers to the NBER working paper series, and residents of developing countries may download this paper without additional charge at www.nber.org.

title: Permits as Real Options: Anticipation and Regulatory Leakage
abstract: We identify a new channel for regulatory leakage: the “permitting channel”. In many settings, permits lock in the regulatory regime at approval, allowing firms to acquire the option to invest under current rules. Unlike the conventional Green Paradox response, this channel operates without accelerating physical investment and pollution. We develop a framework in which firms can use real options to avoid anticipated regulation. We estimate the framework using Colorado’s oil and gas reforms, where permits surged before regulation but drilling did not. Policy-relevant designs that remove the permitting channel substantially reduce the health risks from pollution despite amplifying anticipatory investment. Institutional subscribers to the NBER working paper series, and residents of developing countries may download this paper without additional charge at www.nber.org.

title: Innovation, Business Cycles, and the Climate Transition
abstract: We study how business cycle fluctuations shape the pace and direction of innovation. Non-green innovation is procyclical, while green innovation is countercyclical, both over the cycle and in response to economic shocks. We explain this divergence in a dynamic general equilibrium model with endogenous green and non-green innovation. Green patents derive more value from distant profits, making green innovation less sensitive to short-run fluctuations. Endogenous innovation costs reinforce this mechanism, making green and non-green innovation effective substitutes. Evidence from market-implied patent valuations and scientist earnings supports the mechanism. The model implies larger and greener effects of innovation subsidies during downturns. Institutional subscribers to the NBER working paper series, and residents of developing countries may download this paper without additional charge at www.nber.org.

title: The Early Impacts of AI on Employment among Recent College Graduates
abstract: The impact of AI on the employment prospects of recent college graduates is hotly debated with no consensus on the magnitude of impacts nor even the timing of those potential impacts.Using CPS microdata, we provide the first estimates of the effects of AI on the unemployment of recent college graduates in June, July and August 2026.We provide evidence suggesting that unemployment rates are especially high for summer months and that 2026 might be the first year of widespread enough AI use in the workplace to detect impacts of AI on recent college graduates, the group argued to be most vulnerable to AI replacement.Taking an agnostic approach to defining treatment timing, we find that unemployment rates did not spike in summer 2026 relative to summer months in previous years and did not rise in a significant way relative to older college graduates or young workers without a college degree.We also provide the first analysis of an expanded definition of unemployment that includes those who report "wanting a job" which adds nearly two percentage points to the unemployment rate of recent college graduates but we find no evidence of a statistically significant increase in summer 2026 even after adding these "sidelined unemployed."We estimate difference-in-differences and event-study interaction models using both older college graduates and young non-college graduates as comparison groups and do not find evidence of an increase in relative unemployment rates.Finally, we estimate models in which we interact 2026 unemployment with AI exposure and remote work availability by occupation and find some evidence of a positive relationship with remote work availability.

title: Property Rights Uncertainty, Prices, and Speculation: Evidence from China's Housing Market
abstract: We examine the causal effect of uncertainty in property rights on housing prices and speculative behavior. We take advantage of a distinctive setting in Shenzhen, China, where neighboring residential units that are otherwise similar differ in the strength of their property rights protections. Some units have full property rights (FPR) with a 70-year leasehold, whereas others have only limited property rights (LPR) protections. Using detailed listing data, we find that the sales market prices these protections, while the rental market does not. Our estimates imply that the perceived probability that FPR rights could be questioned at the end of the 70-year term is between 7% and 21%, and that the probability the LPR receives no legal protection in any future year exceeds 50%. We further show that LPR units are more susceptible to speculation, as reflected in higher turnover and greater price volatility. Lastly, we show that the public release of new urban planning codes raises listing prices and lowers turnover and price volatility for LPR properties relative to matched FPR units. Institutional subscribers to the NBER working paper series, and residents of developing countries may download this paper without additional charge at www.nber.org.

title: Are Guidelines Worth Following? Decision-Making Under Incomplete Evidence
abstract: Medical guidelines translate clinical evidence into treatment rules, but the evidence may identify treatment benefits more clearly than harms.We study anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation, combining randomized trials with Veterans Health Administration data.Trial evidence reveals substantial heterogeneity in stroke-prevention benefits but does not reliably identify how treatmentinduced bleeding harms vary across patients.In the target population, patients with larger predicted stroke benefits also have higher untreated bleeding risk, making this ambiguity consequential.We evaluate existing guidelines and develop maximin and minimax-regret treatment rules robust to alternative harm structures.At a benchmark preventing 50% of preventable strokes, robust rules induce 33-41% fewer bleeds than random treatment and outperform existing guidelines.Finitesample uncertainty generates noticeable instability in fine patient rankings but little instability in treatment assignments or welfare.Physician performance and the relationship between guideline adherence and skill also depend substantially on assumptions about how treatment-induced bleeding harms vary across patients.

title: The Wealth of Nations: Origins of Prosperity and Seeds of Inequality
abstract: What ignited humanity's momentous ascent from millennia of stagnation to an era of sustained economic growth?And what are the roots of the vast disparities in the wealth of nations?These enduring mysteries, which have preoccupied scholars across generations, lie at the core of Unified Growth Theory.This encompassing framework captures the evolution of societies over the entire course of human history and identifies the universal wheels of change that governed humanity's long journey, propelled the growth process, and shaped inequality across the globe.The theory uncovers the forces underlying the dramatic transformation in living standards over the past two centuries, emerging from an economic ice age of near stagnation, while highlighting the enduring historical roots of the immense divergence in the prosperity of nations.It suggests that forces set in motion in the distant past played a pivotal role in shaping development across the globe and remain essential for the design of effective policies that foster economic progress and mitigate inequality in the wealth of nations.

title: The Political Foundations of Industrial Policy: Emergence, Endurance, and Exhaustion
abstract: We study how politics shapes industrial policy through two paradigmatic twentieth-century cases: the Cassa per il Mezzogiorno in Italy (1950–1984) and Kennedy's Moonshot in the United States (1961–1972). Drawing on historical and primary political sources, we show that each policy originated in a broader political project rather than in an economic diagnosis: the Christian Democrats' pursuit of national integration and democratic consolidation, and Kennedy's New Frontier. We introduce the concept of industrial policy vision - a publicly articulated, transformational objective that political leaders attach to a set of ideals and pursue through state-led intervention in the economy - and develop a five-component definition that makes it empirically tractable. We then trace each vision through decades of newspaper coverage, combining topic modeling and sentiment analysis with systematic close reading. In both cases, public debate proceeded largely within the frame the vision set, granting the policies tolerance for setbacks and expense. The cases diverge in their fates: the Moonshot's bounded vision was redeemed on schedule, while the Cassa's open-ended vision was exhausted by accumulated failure and the policy outlived it only briefly. This divergence points to our central conclusion: while a vision holds, it sets the terms on which an industrial policy's performance is judged, including what counts as failure and how much time the policy is given to deliver. Institutional subscribers to the NBER working paper series, and residents of developing countries may download this paper without additional charge at www.nber.org.

title: Injury, Workload, and the Strategic Response of Coaches in the NBA
abstract: Worker effort increases contemporaneous output but may result in injury or burnout.Directing effort away from the workers most exposed to injury would reduce this risk, but information on the exposure is often hidden.We ask whether managers act on such private information, studying the NBA as a data-rich workplace.Instrumenting workload with teammate absence, we find that work causally raises injury risk, which contrasts with the spurious negative correlation commonly found in sports medicine studies.We also show that coaches rest players in response to injury risk shocks.By acting on this private information, coaches can raise player productivity.

title: Beveridgean Phillips Curve
abstract: This paper develops a Beveridgean model of the Phillips curve.
